title: ARMORED
synopsis: Negligible heist flick about six guards employed by a Los Angeles armored car company who attempt to pull an inside job, during which only an Iraq War hero (Columbus Short) exhibits scruples and smarts; his greedy colleagues, led by his godfather (Matt Dillon), instead demonstrating the old adage about the paucity of honor among thieves. Working from a flimsy script, director Nimrod Antal keeps the nondescript action moving along without undue complications. Considerable, though not excessive, action violence, including gunplay and knife use, some profanity, much crude language
full_review:
Guards employed by a Los Angeles armored car company demonstrate the old adage about the paucity of honor among thieves in the negligible “Armored” (Screen Gems). The pleasures of a good heist flick are well concealed, in this addition to the genre, behind a flimsy script, mediocre acting, and dull action sequences.

The newest employee to join the security outfit Eagle Shield is Iraq War hero Ty Hackett (Columbus Short) whose parents have recently died, leaving him with considerable debts and a teenage brother with a talent for graffiti art to mentor.

Ty’s colleague and godfather Mike Cochrone (Matt Dillon) urges him to participate in an inside job along with four fellow guards – Mike’ s trigger-happy brother-in-law Baines (Laurence Fishburne), Quinn (Jean Reno), Dobbs (Skeet Ulrich), and a Born-again Christian named Palmer (Amaury Nolasco).

Ty reluctantly agrees because he’s desperate for money to pay the two mortgages on his house – the bank is threatening to foreclose – and wants to keep his little brother out of the clutches of Child Services.

Mike’s plan, such as it is, entails stealing $42 million by staging the fake hijacking of two cars transporting funds from the local Federal Reserve branch. Sure enough, things quickly go awry in the abandoned steel plant where the crew endeavors to stash the dough. When blood is spilt, Ty is the only character to exhibit scruples or a modicum of smarts. Arguably, the behavior of his ostensibly salvation-seeking cohort Palmer is the most damnable.

At least director Nimrod Antal keeps this nondescript effort moving along without undue complications. Set in an empty industrial sector of the city, the gray ghost of a production lacks atmosphere and flare. James V. Simpson’s thin screenplay only gestures at a theme concerning working stiffs or regular Joes – ex-servicemen like Ty – getting their shot at a slice of society’s financial pie.

One thing’s for sure, the system owes them more than “Armored” can deliver.

The film contains considerable, though not excessive, action violence, including gunplay and knife use, some profanity and much crude language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III – adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 – parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Aliens vs. Predator: Requiem
synopsis: Limp sequel to 2004's "Alien vs. Predator," set in a remote Colorado town having the misfortune to be near where a Predator spacecraft full of the slimy, fast-breeding, insectlike aliens (seen in five previous films) crash-lands. Directing brothers Colin and Greg Strause and screenwriter Shane Salerno opt for stale, predictable chaos rather than originality, and the Predator, a rogue warrior whose powers include invisibility, is reduced to plodding through a sewer. Brief partial nudity; rough, crude and profane language, nearly all of it by fighting teenagers; a very brief attempted seduction by a teenage girl; and aliens who, as expected, pop out of a couple of rubbery human midsections; but most of the gore consists of special-effects blood splashing on windows
full_review:
Toward the end of "Aliens vs. Predator: Requiem" (20th Century Fox), the residents of a small town, having been menaced for nearly 90 minutes by rapidly breeding, human-impaling aliens, find a nuclear missile coming their way to liven things up. An atomic explosion as plot relief indicates how stale the "Predator/Alien" franchise (two of this combo so far, with another on the way) has become.
Directing brothers Colin and Greg Strause and screenwriter Shane Salerno opt for predictable chaos without irony or a shred of wit, and the Predator, a rogue warrior whose powers include invisibility, is reduced to plodding through a sewer and down hospital hallways. Even the aliens -- those slimy, insectlike creatures who scamper about, use humans as breeding hosts, then pop out of rubbery midsections -- look bored in their sixth outing.
They wouldn't have made it to earth this time around, anyway, except that the critters get loose on a Predator ship that falls from outer space into a Colorado forest. A lone Predator armed with high-powered weapons and lots of bright-blue acid to erase his tracks soon arrives as well; he's sort of an intergalactic Dirty Harry looking for vengeance. He doesn't see his mission as saving people, though, and anytime he encounters earthlings he tends to skin 'em alive.
The only actor of note is Reiko Aylesworth as Kelly, a muscle-shirted homage to Sigourney Weaver's character, Ellen Ripley, in the original "Aliens." She fights the creatures while protecting her daughter, Molly (Ariel Gade), but there's no big smackdown with a toothy queen. Instead, the Predator and a rather large alien face off like a couple of tired professional wrestlers.
The film contains brief partial nudity; rough, crude and profane language, nearly all of it by fighting teenage boys; a very brief attempted seduction by a teenage girl; and aliens, as they always do, popping out of a couple of people and the Predator leaving behind a skinned corpse; but most of the gore consists of syrupy special-effects blood splashing on windows. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Aaron Loves Angela
synopsis: The story of a teenage romance between a black youth (Kevin Hooks) and a Puerto Rican girl (Irene Cara) is told in a lifeless movie that tries to get too much mileage out of the charm of its two young principals. Director Gordon Parks Jr.'s absurdly melodramatic conclusion involves violence between a brutal but soft-hearted heroin pusher (Robert Hooks) and some syndicate types

title: Aaron Slick from Punkin Crick
synopsis: Lackluster musical comedy set in the 1890s with a country lass (Dinah Shore) off to Chicago after selling her farm to a slick operator (Robert Merrill) who expects to strike oil but doesn't, then schemes to get his money back until her rural beau (Alan Young) comes to town. Director Claude Binyon's broad, tongue-in-cheek tale of rural folk outsmarting city slickers lacks charm and has little appeal beyond cornball humor and forgettable songs. Romantic complications and confidence schemes

title: Aaron's Magic Village
synopsis: Animated version of Isaac Bashevis Singer's stories about a Jewish village in Poland which becomes threatened by a wicked sorcerer's Golem until an orphaned lad helps save the hamlet and its foolish residents. Directed by Albert Hanan Kaminski and narrated by Fyvush Finkel, the humorous tale conveys the distinctive flavor of Jewish culture and tradition, though the story tends to drag in between lively musical numbers

title: Abandon
synopsis: Gloomy, plodding, campus thriller about a student (Katie Holmes), her missing boyfriend and an investigating detective (Benjamin Bratt) that occasionally strikes an intelligent chord and real suspense before falling off into a draggy lull. As directed by Stephen Gaghan, the film walks a fine line between a stylized slasher-style movie and a moody detective story, ultimately offering little resolution as a hollow psychodrama and failing to develop richer themes about bright young students. Some violence, a few sexual encounters, brief substance abuse and minimal profanity
full_review:
"Abandon" is a gloomy, plodding college campus thriller that occasionally strikes an intelligent chord and rivets into real suspense before falling off into a draggy lull. The film walks a fine line between a stylized teen slasher-style movie and a moody detective story. It ultimately offers little resolution as a hollow psychodrama and fails at developing richer themes about bright young students.

Writer-director Stephen Gaghan, who won an Academy Award for his screenplay for "Traffic," mindfully captures an atmosphere of the anxious, uncertain tension of a young woman (Katie Holmes). She is days away from her final exam, does not yet have the conclusion to her thesis, and has just applied to one of the top investment firms in the country. To make her life even more nerve-wracking, she is the central figure in the investigation of her missing boyfriend (Charlie Hunnam) by a persistent and handsome detective (Benjamin Bratt).

"Abandon" attempts to portray interesting college students. Embry Larkin (Hunnam), the missing boyfriend, is a mercurial young man with innovative artistic tendencies. He produced his own opera and experimental theater. Harrison Hobart (Gabriel Mann) organizes demonstrations against "globalization." And Katie Burke (Holmes) is a very attractive, driven, self-assured young woman who came from a working-class background and knows how to dazzle a group of corporate recruiters with a steely confidence and self-understanding that is a rarity among most people.

Police detective Wade Handler (Bratt) carries a certain intrigue. His father was a teacher, and he seems to be very well read, as his bookshelves are filled with classic literature. But these details, as well as the fact that he is a semi-recovered alcoholic who has sabotaged his relationship with a woman with whom he once built a log cabin, seem to be window dressing. "Abandon" floats between the mystery and the not-so-mysterious about the missing Embry Larkin and poses the questions: Who is terrorizing Katie Burke, who will snap under academic and peer pressure, and who will turn up missing next?

It is ironic "Abandon" never probes very deeply into who Katie Burke, its central character, is. She even attends therapy sessions where her doctor ultimately tries to seduce her. The only thing that seems to be revealed about Katie is that most men are extremely attracted to her. There is reference and vague flashback sequences that show how Katie was abandoned by her father when she was a little girl. This is the film's key theme, but does not properly come to a dramatic conclusion.

Because of sexual encounters between college students and others, mild language, violence, use of marijuana, and one instance of heavy drinking, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13. (2002)

title: Abandon Ship!
synopsis: Taut moral exercise in life and death decisions face an officer (Tyrone Power) of a sunken ocean liner who must choose which of 27 survivors should have a place in a lifeboat designed to hold 14 people. Writer-director Richard Sale develops the hazards of the open sea realistically while providing a human dimension for each survivor with harrowing consequences for all. Much menace and stylized violence

title: Abbott and Costello Go to Mars
Abbott and Costello in Hollywood
synopsis: Bud Abbott and Lou Costello play Los Angeles barbers who turn talent agents when they try to help a young singer (Robert Stanton) get a job. Director S. Sylvan Simon sets up a comic situation that goes nowhere as the boys clown their way through Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer's shooting stages and backlot with largely unamusing results. Slapstick humor. A-I (br) 1945

title: Abbott and Costello in the Foreign Legion
Abbott and Costello Lost in Alaska
Abbott and Costello Meet Captain Kidd
Abbott and Costello Meet Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
Abbott and Costello Meet the Ghosts
Abbott and Costello eet the Invisible Man
synopsis: Abbott and Costello Meet the Invisible Man -- This time around the boys play private detectives hired by a prizefighter (Arthur Franz) who's used an invisibility serum to escape the police after being framed for murder by a gangster (Sheldon Leonard). Directed by Charles Lamont, the formula comedy's highlight is a boxing match in which the inept Costello gets some help in the ring from his unseen client. Comic violence

title: Abbott and Costello eet the Killer
synopsis: Abbott and Costello Meet the Killer -- Comic murder mystery with the boys finding, then trying to lose a couple of corpses in a hotel whose guests include the usual likely suspects, including a sinister swami (Boris Karloff). Directed by Charles Barton, it's mildly amusing fare for the comedy team's fans. Comic violence

title: Abbott and Costello eet the Mummy
synopsis: Abbott and Costello Meet the Mummy -- Tired formula comedy directed by Charles Lamont has the boys helping an adventuress (Marie Windsor) search for a lost Egyptian tomb whose treasures are guarded by an unfriendly mummy. Comic menace

title: Abby
synopsis: Low-budget, black version of "The Exorcist" in which God and the Devil clash, this time in the form of a young woman (Carol Speed) possessed by a demon unleashed by her archaeologist father-in-law (William Marshall) who, fortunately, also happens to be a clergyman. Directed by William Girdler, it has all the defects and excesses of the original plus a few of its own. Exploitative sex and violence

title: Abe Lincoln in Illinois
synopsis: Raymond Massey stars as the future president with Ruth Gordon playing Mary Todd in this well-acted drama based on Robert Sherwood's Pulitzer Prize-winning play. Directed by John Cromwell, the movie's emphasis is upon the development of Lincoln's character as a backwoodsman-turned-lawyer and his compassionate confrontation with adversity

title: Abilene Town
synopsis: Sturdy Western with Randolph Scott as marshal of 1870 Abilene trying to stop a war between cattlemen and sodbusters, while the fearful townspeople stand on the sidelines. Director Edwin L. Marin paces the action with some comic relief (Edgar Buchanan's reluctant lawman) as well as Scott's romantic interest in a shopkeeper's daughter (Rhonda Fleming) and a dancehall beauty (Ann Dvorak). Frontier violence and menacing situations

title: About a Boy
synopsis: Offbeat comedy-drama about a shallow, feckless thirtysomething Londoner (Hugh Grant) who scams his way into dates with single moms by pretending to have a son, but through his liaisons he meets an odd 12-year-old boy who helps him find true meaning in his life. Based on the book by Nick Hornby, directors Chris and Paul Weitz deftly combine humor and pathos in a film that pulls on the heartstrings without pouring on the syrup. An attempted suicide, a few sexual references, much profanity and fleeting rough language
full_review:
An odd 12-year-old boy helps a shallow, immature man learn about the important things in life in the offbeat comedy-drama "About A Boy" (Universal).

Based on the 1998 best-selling novel by British author Nick Hornby, "About A Boy" was directed by an unlikely choice, Paul and Chris Weitz, better known for their 1999 gross-out comedy "American Pie." But the Weitz brothers combine humor and pathos in a film that pulls on the heartstrings without pouring on the syrup. "About A Boy" never gets too deeply involved in the characters, keeping things mostly light and frothy. But it has enough of a bite to maintain interest in what will happen next with this eclectic, endearing crew. And between fans of Hugh Grant, who plays the lead, and those of author Hornby (whose other best-selling novel, "High Fidelity," was turned into a film starring John Cusack in 2000), the film is likely to attract an audience willing to overlook some of its faults.

The film does have drawbacks, mainly due to its split personality. It can't settle on whether it wants to be a romantic movie or one about a man's journey into self-discovery. But the directors Weitz manage to blend these styles well enough to make the film a diverting time-passer. The jokes aren't the laugh-out-loud type, but they are amusing enough to keep a smile on your face. And when Grant finds his groove as the bumbling romantic lead, his charm shines forth in a nearly irresistible form.

Grant stars as Will, a Peter-Pan type who fears commitment and thoroughly enjoys his child-free, slacker lifestyle. Living off the royalties from his father's corny Christmas song, "Santa Super Sled," Will loafs about free of the responsibilities of a job or career, with only women on his mind. His quest for no-strings-attached relationships leads him to date single moms, whom he views as willing partners too wrapped up in themselves to want more than some carefree dating.

This leads him to join a meeting of SPAT -- Single Parents, Alone Together -- where he's surprised to find that the women are either ugly, men-bashers or a little off-kilter. But he does salvage something by scamming a date with the sole beauty of the group, Suzie (Victoria Smurfit), after inventing a 2-year-old son named Ned to drum up some sympathy and legitimize why he's there in the first place.

Paralleling Will's story is that of grammar-school geek Marcus (Nicholas Hoult), whose mother, Fiona (Toni Collette), still walks him to school, saying "I love you," as they part, much to Marcus' embarrassment and fueling the already mean-spirited bullying he takes at school. An ex-hippie vegetarian who refuses to allow Marcus to go to McDonald's, Fiona doesn't seem to be aware of the tough time her son is going through. The fact that she weeps uncontrollably also points to her emotional imbalance.

Suzie is her supportive best friend, who, on a date with Will, takes Marcus along for the day to give Fiona a break. Here the film's two plots connect, setting the stage for the main story: a rather mature but lonely 12-year-old and an immature but lonely 38-year-old discovering together that everybody needs somebody.

With his Mr. Spock eyebrows and page-boy haircut, Hoult is convincing as a bullied boy yearning for a manly role model or even just a friend to help him forget about his problems at home and at school. Will is appropriately cool to the young boy, unable to figure out just what Marcus may want from a self-absorbed cad such as himself. The warming up to each other, though inevitable, grows naturally. Some of the best scenes are of the two of them just sitting around in Will's fab bachelor pad, watching the British quiz show "Countdown" without really saying as much as a word to each other.

"About A Boy" is really about two boys, one thrust into the adult world of handling an unstable mother and the pressures of pre-teendom, and the other trying to stave off the responsibilities of adulthood despite already being an adult. The film doesn't tap the emotional depths it could have, considering the source material, but it is nonetheless entertaining fare for the adult moviegoer.

Due to an attempted suicide, a few sexual references, much profanity and fleeting rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: About Adam
synopsis: Off-putting romantic comedy set in Dublin in which a charming young man (Stuart Townsend) seduces a sweet nightclub chanteuse (Kate Hudson), and then unbeknownst to her, proceeds to also bewitch her two sisters (Frances O'Connor and Charlotte Bradley). Told in flashbacks from varying points of view, director Gerard Stembridge's selfish characters and meandering narrative show little respect for marriage or family ties while conveying that sex is a cure-all. Several sexual encounters with fleeting nudity and recurring rough language and profanity. The U.S. Catholic Conference

title: About Face
synopsis: Flat musical version of the military school comedy, "Brother Rat" (1938), is unimaginatively directed by Roy Del Ruth with Gordon MacRae as the leader of the pack and Eddie Bracken as the secretly married cadet who is about to become a father. Silly romantic situations

title: About Last Night
synopsis: Romance set against the vulgar background of the singles scene where the immaturity and insecurities of two young professionals (Demi Moore and Rob Lowe) doom to failure their struggle to form a lasting bond. Played for comedy by director Edward Zwick, the movie is socially, emotionally and morally uninformed about the nature of a truly loving relationship. Rough language and nudity in a sexual context

title: About Mrs. Leslie
synopsis: Sentimental tearjerker about a good-hearted nightclub singer (Shirley Booth) who takes an annual decompression holiday with an overly intense business man (Robert Ryan), then cuts him dead when she discovers he's married. Directed by Daniel Mann, the bittersweet romance is told in maudlin flashbacks, though Booth's sunny performance is likeable, if not credible. Muddled romantic complications

title: About Schmidt
synopsis: Poignant tale of a newly retired and newly widowed 66-year-old (Jack Nicholson) who tries to reconnect with his daughter (Hope Davis) while hoping to abort her upcoming wedding. Nicholson shines in director Alexander Payne's bittersweet comedy about a man coming to terms with his unexceptional life and finding peace in tolerance, forgiveness and generosity of spirit. Implied affairs, fleeting nudity, occasional rough language and recurring profanity
full_review:
Newly retired and suddenly widowed, an Omaha, Neb., actuary heads out in his Winnebago for what becomes a journey of self-discovery in the wonderfully moving "About Schmidt" (New Line).

After a lifetime of working at an insurance company, Warren Schmidt (Jack Nicholson, likely to earn another Oscar nomination) finds himself at loose ends. His wife (June Squibb) is looking forward to traveling the country in their new RV, but in Warren's letters to the little Tanzanian boy he sponsors for $22 a month, the retired husband describes how annoying his wife can be now that he's home all the time.

But when he finds her dead on the kitchen floor from a blood clot, Warren is distraught and anchorless. After making a wrenching discovery about his wife, he decides to hit the road, destination Denver. There he hopes to persuade his semi-estranged daughter, Jeannie (Hope Davis), that her imminent wedding to waterbed salesman Randall (Dermot Mulroney) is a big mistake.

Along the way he makes nostalgic stops that lead him to reflect on his life and become eager to mend fences with his only child.

In Denver, not only is Warren turned off by underachiever Randall, he's appalled by the groom's divorced mom (Kathy Bates), who brags about her sexual capacity and looks ready to pounce on Warren, going as far as joining him in a hot tub, uninvited and au naturel! This is the last family Warren would want for his daughter, but as her wedding day dawns Warren sees little hope of dissuading her and keeping her affection.

Directed by Alexander Payne from his script with co-writer Jim Taylor, the film locates genuine human emotion and the cast delivers the goods in sharply drawn portrayals. But it is overwhelmingly Nicholson's artistry that drives the film from a simple story of an Everyman at a crossroads to an affecting portrait of grief and self-discovery.

Adding real comedy to the bittersweet story is the device whereby Warren in voiceover reads his candid letters to little 6-year-old Ndugu, which, while often hilarious, allows Warren to evaluate his 66-year-old life and where it is going.

In the film's most touching scene, Warren, having worked through his rage over his wife's transgressions, forgives her and regrets his own shortcomings as a husband. As he eyes the nighttime sky thinking of her, he is rewarded by a shooting star that moves him to make a grateful sign of the cross.

Warren also learns about the serenity in St. Francis' prayer and has occasion to forgive another traitorous friend (Len Cariou) in his life. These scenes of anger, resignation and acceptance ring true and all of the characters are treated with generosity and dignity despite their failings.

The movie's doleful tone is shot through with comical situations that are credible and never mean-spirited. And, just when the narrative is about to end on a melancholy, almost despairing note, something unexpected buoys Warren's spirits and gives him the impetus to continue life's journey toward the eternal.

"About Schmidt" is entertaining, but it is also profound in its gentle dissection of the human condition, which is what makes it so memorable.

Due to implied affairs, fleeting nudity, occasional rough language and recurring profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Above the Law
synopsis: Silly convoluted detective yarn featuring a Chicago cop (Steven Seagal) whose martial arts expertise and former involvement with the CIA make him a target for every macho crook and dirty dealing CIA agent in town. Directed by Andrew Davis, it's a disappointing, politically confused story focusing mainly on the martial arts for which Seagal is noted. Excessive violence, much grisly gore and a liberal dose of profanity

title: Absence of Malice
synopsis: Ambitious Miami reporter (Sally Field) is duped into reporting false information on the son of an organized crime figure (Paul Newman). Though director Sydney Pollack slickly stacks the deck against the news media, the movie does succeed in raising serious issues about media responsibility and public opinion. Incidental details include suicide, abortion and an illicit sexual relationship

title: Absolute Beginners
synopsis: Youth-oriented musical drama starring David Bowie as an ad man selling materialism to adolescents, represented by a teenage song-and-dance team (Eddie O'Connell and Patsy Kensit). British production directed by Julien Temple links the euphoria of young people in the late l960s with the birth of a youth sub-culture and consumer market. Mainly, however, it celebrates lack of conscience and good judgment as the substance of adolescence. An intense scene of violence and a confused perspective on adoloscent sexuality

title: Absolution
synopsis: A priest (Richard Burton) at a British Catholic boys school is driven to commit a grisly murder after his teenage protege (Dominic Guard) torments the priest in confession with lies about sexual trysts and murder. Director Anthony Page invests the scenario with a promise of menace never fulfilled by screenwriter Anthony Shaffer. Remorseless, gruesome murders and some profanity

title: Accepted
synopsis: Comedy about a savvy slacker (Justin Long) who, rejected by every college to which he applied, comes up with a face-saving scheme to create a fake school out of an abandoned hospital, which snowballs out of control when a motley mob of other misfits show up on the school's doorstep with acceptance letters. Displaying only occasional wit amid a "coarse" load of mindless humor, director Steve Pink's farce stealthily wraps its subversive nonconformity message in lighthearted, if lowbrow, satire that would seem to extol benign themes of acceptance and self-expression. Recurring crude sexual language and humor, including vulgar sight gags and innuendo, drug content, skimpy bikinis, some profanity and a use of the f-word
full_review:
If a movie could earn a college degree, the campus comedy "Accepted" (Universal) would graduate summa cum lousy.

Justin Long plays high school senior Bartleby "B" Gaines, a savvy slacker who, rejected by every school to which he applied, saves face by creating a fake college, forging an acceptance letter, a Web site and -- with the help of some friends (Jonah Hill, Columbus Short, Maria Thayer and Adam Herschman) -- transforming an abandoned hospital into a college campus.

His gullible parents (Mark Derwin and Ann Cusack) don't ask too many questions. They just write him a check for tuition and drop him off at his new "dorm." When they request a meeting with the school's dean, Bartleby recruits his buddy's iconoclast Uncle Ben (Lewis Black) to play the part.

The scheme snowballs out of control and a mob of self-described rejects and misfits shows up on the school's doorstep, testing even Bartleby's talent for thinking fast.

The semester plays out like one big poolside keg party. (Tuition is $10,000 a head, which Bartleby uses to buy booze and video games.)

title: Accident
synopsis: Cryptic Harold Pinter script begins with an auto crash killing the young man engaged to an Oxford coed, after which the events and forces contributing to the "accident" are presented in flashback, including the rivalry of two dons for the woman student's affection. Director Joseph Losey and an excellent cast use the sparse dialogue and strained situations to give clues to the violence developing beneath the tranquil surface of academic life. Adult situation and treatment

title: Accused of Murder
synopsis: Routine crime story directed by Joe Kane in which a police detective (David Brian) falls for a blonde singer (Vera Ralston) whom his partner (Lee Van Cleef) suspects murdered a shady lawyer (Sidney Blackmer). Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Ace Eli and Rodger of the Skies
synopsis: Cliff Robertson and Eric Shea play a father-son team of Kansas barnstormers in the early 1920s who are flying away from the tragic death of the woman in their life. For Eli, his wife's death triggers a streak of womanizing while for his 11-year-old son, the loss of a mother brings out a raunchy maturity and wisdom far surpassing that of his father but also the search for a new mother-figure. Director Bill Sampson's failed drama is a confusing and confused, large1y unmotivated, concoction of scenes alternately nostalgic, crude, cruel, near-perverse and sappy

title: Ace High
synopsis: Revenge with a humorous twist is the theme of this low-budget Italian Western starring Eli Wallach as a bug-ridden, baby-sitting Greek bandit. Director Giuseppe Colizzi's action is slapdash but unflagging enough to compensate for rough dubbing, poor color and ragged editing. Stylized violence

title: Ace in the Hole
synopsis: Cynical reporter (Kirk Douglas) parlays the local story of a man trapped in a New Mexico cave into a national news event by getting a corrupt sheriff to delay the weakening victim's rescue for a week. Director Billy Wilder's dark study of media manipulation and the public's appetite for sensationalism has few characters with any integrity, save the reporter's editor (Porter Hall), the tragic victim and his devoted parents. Continuing menace and unsavory characters

title: Aces High
synopsis: World War I tale of the Royal Flying Corps as an idealistic English youth (Peter Firth) arrives in 1917 France at an airbase whose hardened commander (Malcolm McDowell) is sick of sending young pilots to their death. Directed by Jack Gold, the British production pays close attention to period details and stages numerous dogfights between vintage biplanes, but the picture's anti-war perspective and stereotyped characters are too familiar to make any fresh impression of their own. Wartime violence, sexual situations and innuendo, fleeting nude photos and occasional profanity

title: Aces: Iron Eagle III
synopsis: Action-packed sequel follows former World War II fighter pilots (Louis Gossett, Jr., Horst Buchholz, Sonny Chiba and Christopher Cazenove) to Peru where they intend to blow up a cocaine factory with souped-up vintage aircraft. John Glen directs a predictable shoot-'em-up whose comic overtones make the violent outbursts and characters seem cartoonish. Recurring violence

title: Ace Ventura: Pet Detective
synopsis: Deadening comedy in which a nerdy gumshoe (Jim Carrey) gets involved sexually with two women (Courtney Cox and Sean Young) while attempting to rescue kidnapped Miami Dolphins quarterback Dan Marino and the team mascot on the eve of the Super Bowl. Tom Shadyac directs what is little more than an obnoxious parade of scatological jokes, demeaning sexist remarks and mindless violence. Realistic brutality played for laughs, some bedroom scenes, brief nudity and occasional profanity

title: Ace Ventura: When Nature Calls
synopsis: The further adventures of the manic pet detective (Jim Carrey) land him in the African jungle where he overcomes assorted dangers in rescuing a kidnapped white bat. Writer-director Steve Oedekerk gives rubber-faced Carrey free rein to mug his way through a series of inane physical skits whose humor ranges from the outrageous to the tasteless. Slapstick violence, occasional sexual innuendo and fleeting nudity

title: Across 110th Street
synopsis: Anthony Quinn plays a tough old-time cop compelled for politica1 reasons to work with a black new-breed policeman (Yaphet Kotto) in tracking down the three blacks who ripped off a syndicate-controlled, black-managed Harlem numbers bank. Unfortunately, director Barry Shear develops neither the broader implications of the story's social conflicts nor the potentially interesting personality clash of his principals, apparently too involved with the mechanics of all the violence that is so grossly in evidence

title: Across the Great Divide
synopsis: Two orphans on the pioneer trail to Oregon in 1876 are guided through the perils of frontier America by a charming gambler (Robert Logan). Directed by Robert Raffill, it provides a familiar mixture of attractive characters, photogenic animals and gorgeous scenery. The slick use of these wholesome elements at the expense of any realism may strike some viewers as rather calculated but that does not lessen its value as fantasy entertainment for family audiences

title: Across the Universe
synopsis: At once spectacular and schizophrenic, this musical tribute to the Beatles chronicles the adventures of a Liverpool dockworker (Jim Sturgess) as he travels to America, befriends a rebellious preppy (Joe Anderson), falls in love with the preppy's sister (Evan Rachel Wood), pals around with his Janis Joplin-like singer-landlady (Dana Fuchs), her Jimi Hendrix-like bandmate (Martin Luther McCoy), and a former cheerleader turned bohemian (T.V. Carpio). As conceived and directed by Julie Taymor, the film is a highly imaginative, visually stunning fantasia, employing the music of the Fab Four to elucidate the 1960s, though its contrived story line too often leaves both cast and audience bogged down in a mire of cliches. Partial, rear and upper female nudity, cohabitation, a sexual embrace, a disrespectful sequence with a priest, drug use, occasional rough and much crude and crass language
full_review:
As conceived and directed by Julie Taymor, "Across the Universe" (Revolution) is a bold undertaking. An attempt to portray and explain the entire decade of the 1960s through the music of the Beatles, the film is highly imaginative and, at times, visually stunning. But its weaknesses are also difficult to overlook.

Essentially, this is a lavish music video impeded by a contrived attempt at storytelling. While the musical and visual elements are often original and striking, the plot is a series of period cliches, resulting in a film at once both spectacular and schizophrenic.

Jude (Jim Sturgess) is a Liverpool dockworker who journeys to the United States to seek his fortune and also his father (Robert Clohessy), a former G.I. unaware of Jude's existence. At Princeton, where he learns his father works as a handyman, Jude meets a rebellious frat brother named Max (Joe Anderson), who has decided to drop out and move to Greenwich Village in New York.

Jude and Max become friends and roommates, renting a ramshackle apartment from Sadie (Dana Fuchs), a singer in the mold of Janis Joplin. Her main musical collaborator is JoJo (Martin Luther McCoy), a guitarist who bears more than a little resemblance to Jimi Hendrix. Also on the scene is former cheerleader turned bohemian, Prudence (T.V. Carpio).

Along with these newfound friends, Jude also discovers Max's sister, Lucy (Evan Rachel Wood), and the two promptly fall in love. The times are tempestuous, however, and it's not long before Max is drafted, Sadie and JoJo have artistic differences and Lucy's political involvement puts a strain on her relationship with Jude.

As the characters' names suggest, there are plenty of inside references for Beatles fans to relish. There are also some enjoyable cameo appearances -- by Bono, Joe Cocker and British comedian Eddie Izzard -- and some remarkably effective set pieces matching imagery with music.

For all their appeal, however, the cast members, many of them newcomers, are enmeshed in a plot that is simply a rehash of familiar rhetoric about the era: The Fifties were repressively conventional; we should all do our own thing; the Vietnam War was a big mistake.

"Across the Universe" also celebrates some aspects of hippie culture that remain morally problematic. These include the use of drugs, cohabitation without marriage and a mocking attitude toward organized religion.

The film contains partial, rear and upper female nudity, cohabitation, a sexual embrace, a disrespectful sequence with a priest, drug use, occasional rough and much crude and crass language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Across the Wide Missouri
synopsis: Colorful Western adventure about a mountain man (Clark Gable) taking a polyglot company of hunters into 1829 Montana country where he weds a Blackfoot woman (Maria Elena Marques), then stays with her people to raise their son after she's killed by an Indian renegade (Ricardo Montalban). Director William A. Wellman does well with the rugged setting of the early West and its clash of cultures but the narrative turns flat with subsequent domestic contrivances. Stylized violence and romantic situations

title: Action in the North Atlantic
synopsis: The captain (Raymond Massey), first mate (Humphrey Bogart) and crew (Alan Hale, Sam Levene, Dane Clark, etc.) of a torpedoed oil tanker sign on to another tanker in a convoy bound for Murmansk, heroically fighting off U-boats and air attacks along the way. Director Lloyd Bacon's lengthy tribute to the merchant marine may have stirred World War II audiences, but the action seems artificial now and the patriotic sentiments heavy-handed. Wartime violence

title: Action Jackson
synopsis: The ultraviolent exploits of a Detroit police detective (Carl Weathers) are detailed in a contrived series of bloody killings, car chases, crashes and explosions perpetrated by an exotic collection of villains in the hire of a power-mad businessman (Craig T. Nelson). Director Craig R. Baxley laces the special-effects pyrotechnics with some sexual titillation and drug scenes. Excessive violence, some nudity and much rough language

title: Action of the Tiger
synopsis: Potboiler in which a Frenchwoman (Martine Carol) gets an American adventurer (Van Johnson) to help smuggle her blind brother out of Communist Albania, picking up a band of refugee children along the way. Directed by Terence Young, it has an exotic setting and some colorful action but the story is plodding and predictable, including the silly twist ending. Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Act of Agression
synopsis: French vigilante movie about a man (Jean-Louis Trintignant) whose wife and daughter have been brutally raped and murdered, apparently by vicious bikers, and his lust both for revenge and for his wife's sister (Catherine Deneuve). Director Gerard Pires never grapples serious1y with the vendetta theme but concentrates instead on the romance, employing some nudity and kinky sexuality

title: Act of Vengeance
synopsis: Exploitation melodrama about rape and the efforts of five victims, led by Joann Harris, to entrap their assailant, a sadist with a penchant for singing "Jingle Bells." Director Robert Kelljan seems less concerned about showing the degradation and humiliation of rape as an act of violence against women than as using an anti-rape theme as an excuse for displaying naked bodies as sex objects

title: Adalen '31
synopsis: Swedish production re-creates a 1931 labor strike by focusing on the lives of individual workers involved in the struggle for subsistance. The political conflict and social commentary are crystal clear, but remarkably unobtrusive amid the vignettes of daily life in a small town during hard times. When scab workers arrive, a peaceful demonstration ends in violence and death. Using a mixture of romantic fiction and economic realities, director Bo Widerburg successfully combines social awareness with lyric beauty. Brief nudity and casual acceptance of abortion

title: Adam at 6 A.M.
synopsis: West Coast college professor (Michael Douglas), searching for the values of heartland America, spends a summer doing construction work in Missouri, decides to settle down and marry a local belle (Lee Purcell) but then realizes that life in the Midwest will be no less conformist than that of the world from which he has fled. Director Robert Scheerer employs a number of easy stereotypes to characterize America's geographic and cultural polarities, but beneath the movie'slick surface is a profoundly cynical commentary upon the country's heritage and the values of its people

title: Adam had Four Sons
synopsis: Artificial tearjerker about the travails of a French governess (Ingrid Bergman) in caring for the boys of a New York stockbroker (Warner Baxter) from 1907 until the youths enlist in World War I. Directed by Gregory Ratoff, the nub of the story turns on the devoted governess' determination to shield her preoccupied employer from learning that his son's wartime bride (Susan Hayward) is a greedy conniver. Sudsy picture of a virtuous woman contrasted with a selfish one

title: Adam Sandler's Eight Crazy Nights
synopsis: Cartoon comedy, with songs, in which a 33-year-old Jewish wastrel (voiced by Adam Sandler) redeems himself during Hanukkah by coaching basketball, befriending a fatherless boy and helping an elderly man win a prize. As directed by Seth Kearsley, positive values flood the final scenes but only after a considerable quantity of gross behavior and rudeness that is designed to delight an irreverent, impressionable young audience. Recurring vulgarity that takes many forms, a lot of it involving bodily functions and off-putting images, and brief alcohol abuse
full_review:
The cartoon feature "Adam Sandler's Eight Crazy Nights" (Columbia) cloaks itself as a tale of redemption that unfolds during Hanukkah and the days leading up to Christmas.

Despite multiple references to the parallel holy seasons and to the good that can be achieved through selfless behavior, the feature-length cartoon dwells on abundant rudeness and gross behavior that are designed to delight an irreverent, impressionable young audience.

The depiction of Hanukkah and the anticipation of Christmas are entirely secular, although the central character does finally perform good deeds, which coincide with, more than they're directly linked to, the season at hand.

Adam Sandler, who is credited with creating the derivative story, gives voice to all three of the principal characters -- Davey Stone, Whitey Duvall and Eleanore Duvall -- as well as to a deer.

Davey Stone is a 33-year-old Jewish wastrel and Sandler look-alike, a once-promising boy who began acting miserably toward everyone else when his parents were killed in an auto accident.

Whitey, a fireplug-sized elderly referee of boys' basketball with an annoyingly high voice, takes Davey under wing and even provides him with shelter.

Whitey's twin sister Eleanore, whose wigs and thick glasses are nearly as large as she, is less trusting about the arrangement. But because the film unfolds from the vantage of a young person, Eleanore is depicted as being exceptionally out of it.

Directed by Seth Kearsley, the picture gives Davey and others about an hour to heap ridicule onto people less hip and cynical than themselves including the Duvalls and a boy mortified by his enlarged breasts.

Davey's inevitable redemption, ever so loosely linked to the passing of the Jewish holidays, isn't just unpersuasive. It becomes a license to let him behave as outrageously as he can beforehand.

"Eight Crazy Nights" is packed with behavior ranging from the rude (long burps, public drunkenness, cruel remarks, flipping the bird) to bad taste involving epilepsy and features many instances of gross-out behavior involving assorted bodily functions and degrading physical abuse.

Not the least of its cliches is Davey's renewed interest in a single mother (Jackie Titone voicing the part of Jennifer) and in her son Benjamin (Austin Stout).

Some moderately appealing songs are saddled with crude lyrics.

Perhaps more offensive is the abundance of shopping mall product placement, sometimes accompanied by dialogue laced with advertising.

Audiences in search of seasonal sentiments won't want to wade through the movie's first hour. Sandler's core audience is just as likely to find the concluding scenes too sappy for what leads up to them.

Because of recurring vulgarity that takes many forms, a lot of it involving body functions and off-putting images, and brief alcohol abuse, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Adam's Rib
synopsis: Sly romantic comedy about married attorneys (Spencer Tracy and Katharine Hepburn) battling over the issue of women's rights when she defends a wife (Judy Holliday) on trial for shooting her philandering husband (Tom Ewell) while he represents the wounded man. Director George Cukor injects the witty dialogue and visual comedy with screwball overtones and the Tracy-Hepburn exhanges are prime, though the feminist views seem tame today. Comic view of the battle of the sexes

title: Adam's Rib
synopsis: Living in a cramped Soviet apartment, a twice-divorced working mother (Inna Churikova) tries to juggle taking care of her own aged mother, two troubled unmarried daughters and a new man in her life. Ukrainian director Vyacheslav Krishtofovich has nothing particularly new to say about mother-daughter relations or the travails of single women, though the cultural context may make them seem a little more interesting than our own domestic melodramas. Subtitles. Some discussion of sexual matters, a comically interrupted bedroom tryst and minimal rough language

title: Adaptation
synopsis: Oddball tale of a self-loathing screenwriter (Nicolas Cage) whose frustrations adapting a book about an orchid smuggler and a reporter (Chris Cooper and Meryl Streep) increase when his shallow twin brother (also Cage) easily sells his cheesy first screenplay. Written by Charlie Kaufman and directed by Spike Jonze, it's a wackily creative mix of serious ponderings and quirky satirical humor offset by Cage's whiny character, but the final half-hour goes into lethal overdrive. Brief but intense violence, recreational drug use, a sexual encounter, implied masturbation, fleeting nudity and glimpses of a pornographic Web site, much rough language and some profanity
full_review:
"Adaptation" (Columbia) is the oddball movie of the year, about a blocked screenwriter who out of desperation writes himself and his frustrations into his film adaptation.

It's the kind of out-there movie that some will find brilliant while others will scratch their heads or look longingly toward the exit door.

The movie is about real-life screenwriter Charlie Kaufman ("Being John Malkovich"), who is played by Nicolas Cage. Cage also plays Charlie's fictional twin brother, Donald, who is writing a first screenplay whose cheesy plot has already attracted studio interest, much to his serious brother's chagrin.

Charlie can't get a handle on adapting the nonfiction book "The Orchid Thief" by Susan Orlean (Meryl Streep), a reporter who tracked down fanatical orchid breeder John Laroche (Chris Cooper) in the Florida Everglades and wrote about his colorful past and how his passion inspired her to find some passion in her own life.

We see how she pursued her story about Laroche -- and Cooper is terrific as the seedy yet occasionally profound eccentric, while Streep's journalist is less believable when she undergoes a bizarre personality transformation in the contrived finale.

After feeling he must write about the beauty of the orchid -- a theme he knows won't sell with the studio suits -- Charlie decides instead to write himself and his quest into the film.

His scornful advice to his brother to not stoop to hack-level writing about a serial killer with a multiple personality falls on sweetly deaf ears and soon easygoing Donald sells his script and is considered Hollywood's new hot writer. This sibling relationship is what makes the movie touching; Charlie is jealous and acid-tongued, but Donald just keeps on loving and trying to help his brother no matter how mean-spirited Charlie becomes.

Although Charlie keeps assuring his agent his writing is going well, he is consumed with self-loathing, seeing himself as fat, bald and ugly and unable to get at all physical with the woman (Cara Seymour) who likes him.

Neurotically shy, he flies to New York to meet the book's author, then can't get up the courage to say hello even when she happens to share an elevator with him. When his brother meets Susan it sets off a chain of violent events that plunge the film toward a crazed conclusion that goes quite over the top. This is where the script's basis in fact meets fiction, and the transition is a jarring one.

Written by Charlie Kaufman and directed by Spike Jonze, the film is highly original and engrossing in its depiction of Charlie as a creative person striving to excel in an industry that only cares about the box-office take, as evidenced by Donald's instant success with a cliched script. But Charlie's whiny character gradually grates on the nerves, his constant insecurities and pathetic self-lacerations making him less sympathetic even as we feel for his desire to do a good job.

Taken in its comic-satiric context, the movie's deadly conclusion springs from a fevered imagination to give some kind of an ending to an impossible-to-adapt film. It certainly shouldn't be taken as an endorsement of Susan and John's behavior. The wildly melodramatic ending may be deliberate but it's so at odds with the rest of the film's dogged but nutty earnestness it simply doesn't work.

Due to brief but intense violence, recreational drug use, a sexual encounter, implied masturbation, fleeting nudity and glimpses of a pornographic Web site, much rough language and some profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Addams Family Values
synopsis: Macabre comedy sequel has the Addams children (Christina Ricci and Jimmy Workman) attempting to eliminate their mustachioed baby brother while their lovestruck uncle (Christopher Lloyd) marries a murderous fortune hunter (Joan Cusack). Director Barry Sonnenfeld injects some outrageous black humor into a broad, predictable slapstick comedy that is more concerned about style than content. Frequent comic menace to a baby, violence played for laughs and occasional sexual innuendo

title: Adelaide
synopsis: Director Jean-Daniel Simon has been unable to elevate this pulp story of a widow whose new husband continues to carry on an affair with her teenage daughter. Static and introverted atmosphere, incomprehensible plot development and determined underplaying by Ingrid Thulin and Jean Sorel supply no motivation for the senseless actions of the story's characters

title: Adieu Philippine
synopsis: French production about a young man awaiting his army call-up who begins a flirtation with two girls who are intimate friends, a situation left unresolved by the boy's departure but with the sense of embarking on a new, more mature phase of life. Directed by Jacques Rozier, this 1961 movie is a mosaic of scenes, beautifully photographed and evocative of the carefree romanticism of youth, carefully knit together by the juke-box music of the period. Without a traditional narrative, however, its appeal is mainly to those who enjoy watching a well-crafted film

title: Adios, Sabata
synopsis: Routine Italian Western with bounty hunter Yul Brynner polishing off great gobs of humanity in his relentless pursuit of a Mexican revolutionary and a share of Maximillian's gold. Taken seriously, all this violence would be alarming, but played tongue-in-cheek under Frank Kramer's direction, it's a comic fantasy for those who enjoy such action programmers

title: The Adjustment Bureau
synopsis: Curious adaptation of Philip K. Dick's 1954 short story "Adjustment Team" in which the agents of a supernatural bureaucracy (principally Anthony Mackie, John Slattery and Terence Stamp) intervene to break up the budding relationship between a New York politician (Matt Damon) and a gifted dancer (Emily Blunt) because it runs contrary to the predetermined plan of an unnamed higher power. Writer-director George Nolfi's feature debut pitting love against fate -- or perhaps against divine providence -- will intrigue some and strike others as an uneasy attempt to blend science fiction, romance and philosophical speculation. Though this is not a film for young people, the metaphysical elements of the plot can be interpreted by mature viewers in a way that squares with Judeo-Christian faith. Complex themes, brief nongraphic premarital sexual activity, a couple of uses of profanity and rough terms, and considerable crude and crass language
full_review:
With its unusual blend of the ordinary and the supernatural, not to mention its "Mad Men"-era costuming, "The Adjustment Bureau" (Universal) might suitably be subtitled "The Angel in the Gray Flannel Suit."

Of course, writer-director George Nolfi's script for this curious drama -- adapted from Philip K. Dick's 1954 short story "Adjustment Team" -- plays predictably coy when it comes to pinning down the exact identity of these dapper characters and the precise origins of their superhuman powers. Asked directly about the A-word, for instance, one of them replies, "We've been called that."

But, presuming they do hail from the choirs celestial, as opposed to being mere aliens or something else entirely, we may at last have the answer to a question no scholastic philosopher of the Middle Ages ever thought to ask: "Do angels look good in fedoras?"

And just what, you wonder, are these retro-chic denizens of a hidden world (played, principally, by Anthony Mackie, John Slattery -- best known for his role on the aforementioned "Mad Men" -- and Terence Stamp) doing in contemporary Manhattan?

As the officials of an invisible bureaucracy to end all bureaucracies, they're intent on breaking up the budding relationship between promising youthful politician David Norris (Matt Damon) and gifted dancer Elise Sellas (Emily Blunt). The success of the couple's courtship -- which was never supposed to get started in the first place -- would, it seems, run contrary to the predetermined plans of an unnamed higher power.

Having been informed of all this -- as well as of the dire consequences of trying to thwart the workings of destiny -- David reluctantly but abruptly walks out on Elise. But fortune, which can't seem to make up its mind, eventually brings the pair back together again.

With its ambitious pitting of love against fate -- or perhaps against divine providence -- Nolfi's feature debut will intrigue some viewers, even as it strikes others as an uneasy attempt to blend science fiction, romance and philosophical speculation.

Though this is certainly not a film for young people -- in addition to the quasi-theological issues underlying the story, David and Elise's liaison becomes physical prematurely -- the metaphysical elements of the plot can be interpreted by mature viewers in a way that squares with Judeo-Christian faith.

The film contains complex themes, brief nongraphic premarital sexual activity, a couple of uses of profanity and rough terms and considerable crude and crass language. The Catholic News Service classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Adrift
synopsis: Czechoslovakian production about a fisherman who rescues a beautiful woman from drowning and his gradual disintegration (told in flashbacks mixing reality with fantasy) driven by desire for the girl (Paula Pritchett) who has become a member of his household. Although not entirely successful in its fancy time sequences, director Jan Kadar's leisurely pace builds steadily towards his powerful conclusion concerning man's vulnerability to temptation. The erotic element of the film is a neccssary one counterbalanced by the very human portrayals of the fisherman and his wife (Rade Markovic and Milena Dravic)

title: Adventure
synopsis: Flat-footed seriocomic romance between a footloose sailor (Clark Gable) and an independent-minded librarian (Greer Garson) who clash, marry and divorce until reunited in a maudlin finish. Directed by Victor Fleming, the two leads are hopelessly miscast in a clunker that even wastes performances by Joan Blondell as the other woman and Thomas Mitchell as a sailor who's lost his soul. Stylized violence, sexual innuendo and bogus virile posturing

title: Adventure for Two
synopsis: (see: " The Demi-Paradise ")

title: Adventure in Baltimore
synopsis: Vacuous romantic comedy set in 1905 concerns an earnest young suffragette (Shirley Temple) whose unchaperoned meetings with a young man (John Agar) stir up considerable gossip just when her minister father (Robert Young) is being considered for bishop. Director Richard Wallace treats the contrived proceedings in heavy-handed fashion but especially tiresome is Temple's role as an idealistic meddler

title: Adventureland
synopsis: Sensitive but downbeat coming-of-age tale, set in 1987 Pittsburgh, about an awkward college graduate (Jesse Eisenberg) who takes a summer job at a third-rate amusement park and falls for one of his co-workers (Kristen Stewart), not realizing she is having an adulterous affair with an older employee (Ryan Reynolds). Though generally restrained in its presentation of sexuality, director Greg Mottola's wryly nostalgic romance takes a benign view of its characters' frequent indulgence in marijuana and reaches a morally unacceptable conclusion. Nongraphic adulterous and premarital sexual activity, brief partial nudity, repeated drug use, some sexual and fleeting scatological humor, pervasive rough and crude language, a few uses of profanity

title: Adventures in Babysitting
synopsis: Teenage babysitter (Elizabeth Shue) and her wards suffer through an evening of harrowing escapades while trying to rescue their runaway friend stranded in a downtown Chicago bus station. Flawed seriocomic tale deals with real urban dangers in a treatment made irresponsibly light and mundane by writer-director Chris Columbus. Some violence, sexual innuendo and profanity mar this trite diversion aimed at youngsters

title: Adventures of Captain Sebastian
synopsis: Romantic potboiler set in pre-Civil War New Orleans where an ambitious maid (Micheline Presle) on trial for murder is saved by a sea captain (Errol Flynn) whom she spurns to marry a devious merchant (Vincent Price), with dire consequences for all three. Directed by William Marshall, the result is a clumsy melodrama which sputters lifelessly along until its hokey climax. Stylized violence and sexual situations

title: Adventures of Chico
synopsis: Simple tale produced by Stacy and Horace Woodard follows the ordinary activities of a Mexican goat herder and his young son and their encounters with the rural area's wildlife, including a quail hunt and the father's tracking down a maurading cougar. Ineffective narration but fine nature photography. no ratings

title: Adventures of Don Juan
synopsis: Lumpy tale of the lusty 17th-century cavalier (Errol Flynn) who's caught in a London boudoir and deported home to Spain where he saves the throne from a nasty usurper (Robert Douglas) and wins the heart of the queen (Viveca Lindfors) before resuming his amorous pursuits, Directed by Vincent Sherman, the swashbuckling action is as unconvincing as the romantic melodramatics are dull, with tiresome results. Period violence, implied affairs and sexual innuendo

title: Adventures of Gallant Bess
synopsis: After training a wild mare to be a trick horse, a rodeo rider (Cameron Mitchell) is injured and his prize horse taken away by a crooked rodeo owner (James Millican). Directed by Lew Lander, the story of the bond between a cowboy and his horse is routine fare, though the location footage is colorful and questions are raised about training animals to perform in show business. Some tense situations

title: Advise and Consent
synopsis: Sprawling potboiler about Washington politics revolves around the nomination of a liberal academic (Henry Fonda) as Secretary of State, with a vengeful Southern senator (Charles Laughton) getting a troubled clerk (Burgess Meredith) to charge the nominee with communism while a wildeyed junior senator (George Grizzard) tries to influence the hearings by blackmailing the committee chairman (Don Murray) over his homosexual past. Directed by Otto Preminger from Allen Drury's novel, the performances in this rogues gallery of bickering politicians are enjoyably broad, though the melodramatic proceedings end abruptly with the death of the ailing President (Franchot Tone) and his ignored Vice President (Lew Ayres) firmly taking charge. An off-screen suicide, sexual situations and unethical political conduct

title: Aeon Flux
synopsis: Stylish but nonsensical sci-fi action adventure set in a distant future where the last remnant of a plague-thinned humanity lives in a walled, socially engineered "perfect" society, and centers on a female assassin (a cat-suit-clad Charlize Theron) conflicted about her assigned target: the utopia's totalitarian ruler (Marton Csokas), whom she senses holds the secret to the unexplained disappearance of citizens as well as to her own shrouded past. Directed by Karyn Kusama and based on the popular series of MTV animated shorts, the film's "Matrix"-style acrobatics and visual panache can't disguise emotional flatness and a barely coherent script littered with video-game carnage. Much stylized violence, brief gore and a sexual encounter
full_review:
It's safe to say that if Charlize Theron wins a second Academy Award this year, it will be for her powerful performance in "North Country" and not "Aeon Flux" (Paramount), a stylish but nonsensical sci-fi action-adventure based on the popular series of MTV animated shorts.

Set in a distant future where the last remnant of a plague-thinned humanity lives in a walled, socially engineered "perfect" society, Theron (clad in a cat suit) stars as Aeon Flux, an assassin with an underground resistance group committed to overthrowing the totalitarian government, who is conflicted about her assigned target: the ruler of this utopia, Trevor Goodchild (Marton Csokas). She senses he holds the secret to the mysterious disappearance of citizens as well as to her own shrouded past.

Directed by Karyn Kusama, the film's "Matrix"-style acrobatics and visual panache can't disguise emotional flatness and a barely coherent script littered with video-game carnage.

The film contains much stylized violence, brief gore and a sexual encounter. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Affair in Havana
synopsis: Turgid melodrama directed by Laslo Benedek and filmed in Cuba where a visiting American pianist (John Cassavetes) falls for the greedy wife (Sara Shane) of a wheelchair-bound industrialist (Raymond Burr) who winds up murdered. Stylized violence and an adulterous relationship

title: Affair with a Stranger
synopsis: Formula sudser starts with gossip about a Broadway playwright (Victor Mature) seeking to divorce his wife (Jean Simmons), then uses a series of flashbacks to trace the couple's courtship, marriage, growing fame and adoption of a son before returning to the present and the predictable outcome. Directed by Roy Rowland, the sentimental story is well-intended but has little charm and no surprises. Mild sexual innuendo

title: Affliction
synopsis: Compelling drama charts the inevitable fall from grace of a small-town, part-time cop (Nick Nolte) after an acrimonious divorce, continued verbal abuse by his alcoholic father (James Coburn) and fears that his best friend may have murdered a union official. Director Paul Schrader's adaptation of Russell Bank's bleak novel uses spare dialogue and chilling imagery to show how a lifetime of emotional and physical violence has left a tortured soul unable to cope with his demons. Scattered violence, alcohol abuse, an implied affair, recurring rough language and frequent profanity

title: Afraid of the Dark
synopsis: Bizarre, disjointed thriller about a disturbed child (Ben Keyworth), his endangered baby sister, his mother (Fanny Ardant) who may or may not be blind and a neighborhood slasher (Paul McGann). Director Mark Peploe's twisted tale of deadly menace and mayhem is badly structured and largely unintelligible. Exploitative violence, especially that involving two children, a lingering nude shot and frequent nasty menace

title: Africa Addio
synopsis: Cruelty, violence, blood, gore and human indignity are highlighted in director Gualtiero Jacopetti's Italian documentary which claims that its aim is to enlighten viewers concerning the :2O birth pangs'' of emerging African nations. Exploitation of serious subject

title: Africa Blood and Guts
synopsis: (see: " Africa Addio ")

title: African Cats
synopsis: Actor Samuel L. Jackson narrates this impressive nature documentary charting the varied fortunes of a pride of lions and a clan of cheetahs living on the savannah in Kenya's Masai Mara National Reserve. Splendid landscape footage and remarkably detailed animal close-ups provide the whole family with a top-quality cinematic safari. Directors Keith Scholey and Alastair Fothergill discreetly spare younger viewers the nitty-gritty of predatory behavior, though not the harsh Darwinian dynamic that ruthlessly eliminates the weak -- however sympathetic
full_review:
An impressive safari is as close as the nearest cineplex thanks to the arrival of the nature documentary "African Cats" (Disneynature). Better yet, the titular felines -- though, on occasion, they're ferocious to one another -- prove "purrfectly" friendly to family audiences.

As actor Samuel L. Jackson narrates the story of a pride of lions and a clan of cheetahs -- both of them living on the savannah in Kenya's Masai Mara National Reserve -- their varied fortunes take on the interest of a savage soap opera.

The lions are threatened by the rivalry between their veteran but aging alpha male, Fang, and Kali, the relatively youthful, thoroughly aggressive leader of a neighboring group of unmated males. Should Kali succeed in his conquest, he will drive off Fang's existing offspring and replace them with new young of his own.

For no-nonsense single cheetah mom Sita and the pack of playful cubs over which she watches, meanwhile, potential perils -- ranging from roaming bands of hyenas to the aforementioned kings of the jungle -- seem to lurk everywhere.

Splendid landscape footage of verdant hills and meandering waterways lends a sense of exotic adventure to this screen outing. And remarkably detailed animal close-ups -- in which each strand of fur seems, at times, distinctly visible -- create an unusual bond of intimacy with its personality-rich subjects.

Directors Keith Scholey and Alastair Fothergill considerately spare youngsters the nitty-gritty of predatory behavior by discreetly cutting away at the climax of each combat.

But the harsh Darwinian dynamic that ruthlessly eliminates the weak -- however familiar and sympathetic they may have become to viewers -- is not disguised. As a result, sensitive tykes may not be the only ones who feel their heartstrings being yanked as nature takes its necessary, but sometimes uncongenial, course.

The Catholic News Service classification is A-I -- general patronage. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is G -- general audiences. All ages admitted

title: African Fury
synopsis: (see: 1952's " Cry, the Beloved Country ")

title: African Safari
synopsis: Interesting and exciting documentary excursion into Central and East Africa with beautiful photography of the area's wild life and native customs. Directed and photographed by Ron E. Shanin, it is a rewarding experience both for young people and sophisticated moviegoers. A few graphically violent animal sequences

title: Africa Screams
synopsis: The usual comedy of errors begins with Manhattan book clerks (Bud Abbott and Lou Costello) joining a crook (Hillary Brooke) on an African safari through cannibal-infested jungles in quest of diamonds. Director Charles Barton garners few laughs from the boys' tired routines while encountering domestic thugs, wild animals, puzzled natives and real jungle veterans Clyde Beatty and Frank Buck. Slapstick violence and African stereotypes

title: Africa - Texas Style
synopsis: Texas cowboys are hired to herd wild animals on the plains of Kenya because domestic cattle are turning the land into a dust bowl. The idea of switching from cattle ranching to game ranching is an intriguing one that director Andrew Marton keeps moving with old-fashioned Western action in exotic African settings. Good family entertainment

title: After Dark, My Sweet
synopsis: Manipulative ex-cop (Bruce Dern) involves a lonely widow (Rachel Ward) and an escaped mental patient (Jason Patric) in a deadly kidnapping plot. Intense performances prop up director James Foley's unsavory tale of three losers mired in mutual mistrust until an unexpectedly moral ending provides a positive note. Brief violence and menace to a child, an extended sexual encounter and minimal rough language

title: Afterglow
synopsis: The shaky marriages of two couples (Julie Christie and Nick Nolte; Lara Flynn Boyle and Jonny Lee Miller) are further complicated by an affair between the older husband (Nolte) and the younger man's wife (Boyle), forcing each spouse to re-evaluate their relationships. Writer-director Alan Rudolph begins with a serious treatment of infidelity and its consequences, only to reduce the story to the level of bedroom farce leading to a bogus sunny conclusion. Sexual situations with nudity, brief violence, some rough language and considerable profanity

title: After Hours
synopsis: A bored yuppie (Griffin Dunne) from Manhattan's fashionable East Side ventures into a dangerous part of town to meet an eccentric date (Rosanna Arquette) only to encounter a series of life-threatening misadventures before escaping back to the safety of his own turf in the dawn's early light. Director Martin Scorsese's black comedy lacks satiric bite, preferring instead to wring laughs out of mental instability and bizarre sexual practices. Sophomoric nihilism and some brief nudity

title: After Office Hours
synopsis: Dated but breezy newspaper yarn in which a crusading editor (Clark Gable) falls for a bright debutante (Constance Bennett) after using her to gain access to a philandering lawyer (Harvey Stephens) he suspects is a murderer. Scripted by Herman J. Mankiewicz and directed by Robert Z. Leonard, the far-fetched plot is of less interest than the witty dialogue and colorful characters. Stylized violence, sexual innuendo and implied adultery

title: After the Fox
synopsis: Scriptwriter Neil Simon and director Vittorio de Sica col1aborated on this surprisingly flat and frequently overdone comedy revolving around a bungling ex-convict (Peter Sellers) who hatches a preposterous scheme to steal the fortune in gold that he has been hired to smuggle into Italy. There are some mildly vulgar jokes but they offend only one's sense of humor

title: After the Sunset
synopsis: Lackluster caper directed by Brett Ratner about a master thief (Pierce Brosnan) who, after calling it quits and retiring to a tropical island with his sexy accomplice (Salma Hayek), is tempted to steal a priceless gem aboard a cruise ship docked in port, while being watched by an FBI agent (Woody Harrelson) gunning to nail him. Despite good cat-and-mouse chemistry between Brosnan and Harrelson, the film's warmed-over premise doesn't really contribute anything new to the heist genre and in making light of the felonies committed suggests that crime pays handsomely. A glamorized portrayal of larceny, crime without consequence, brief violence, several implied sexual encounters and some racy images, as well as an instance of rough language and intermittent crude language
full_review:
In director Brett Ratner's new caper comedy, "After the Sunset" (New Line), Woody Harrelson's beleaguered FBI agent divides the world's population into two distinct groups: "Those who like watching sunsets and those who don't."

Moviegoers may find themselves equally split between those who view films like this as diversionary popcorn fun and those who see them as derivative drivel, or worse, as glamorizing crime.

Sporting beach-bum scruff, Pierce Brosnan plays Max Burdett, a master thief with a sweet tooth for the Napoleon diamonds (three golf-ball-sized jewels which adorned the hilt of the legendary Corsican's sword). Having already pilfered two of the gaudy gems, Max and sexy accomplice Lola (Salma Hayek) call it quits and retire to a life of luxury on a tropical island where the only rock Lola wants to think about is the one that comes attached to an engagement ring.

But all play and no work makes Max a restless boy. Unable to kick the habit, he gets quick fixes by picking the pockets of unsuspecting couples over dinner at the beachfront resort.

Harrelson plays Stan, an inept G-man who's made a career out of trying to nab Max, with all the success of Wile E. Coyote trying to catch the Road Runner. Tracking Max down to his Bahamian hideaway, Stan drops the bait that one of the cruise ships in port is housing a rare jewel exhibit headlined by the third -- and sole remaining -- Napoleon diamond, betting the farm that Max will be unable to resist the itch of one last score. Helping Stan is Sophie (Naomie Harris), a beautiful local cop with whom he becomes romantically involved.

While the likable knave has long been a staple in the canon of caper cinema, it is understandable if some viewers find it difficult to root for a character who is, by all accounts, a common thief. And though some moral inroads are made late in the game, he remains, by and large, unreformed and unrepentant, taking particular glee in stealing and leaving the law holding the bag.
Whether or not Max will end up on the beach with Lola and an umbrella drink is never much in doubt; still, the film's ending seems to make light of the felonies committed and suggests that crime pays quite handsomely. As for the diamond, no spoilers here.

Even without his Aston Martin and 007 tux, Brosnan oozes roguish charm, an asset when trying to make a scoundrel like Max appealing. However, much of his performance seems retread from burglar roles in past movies such as 1999's remake of "The Thomas Crown Affair" and "The Tailor of Panama." Hayek has proved in films like "Frida" that she is more than just eye candy, but here she is reduced to curvy set-dressing, prancing around in increasingly revealing bikinis (pushing the envelope of the picture's PG-13 rating).

Unlike the purloined diamonds, the script is anything but flawless, detouring into subplots that go nowhere, including one involving an island kingpin (Don Cheadle). Also, the final jewel heist lacks any real tension. Still the film has its strengths, including good cat-and-mouse chemistry between Brosnan and Harrelson and some clever references to movies like "Jaws" and "Raiders of the Lost Ark."

In the final analysis, however, "After the Sunset" filches freely from past heist flicks (double-dealings, deftly choreographed capers, etc.) without ever really contributing anything new or innovative to the genre.

Due to a glamorized portrayal of larceny, crime without consequence, brief violence, several implied sexual encounters and some racy images, as well as an instance of rough language and intermittent crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: After the Thin Man
synopsis: The first of five sequels to 1934's "The Thin Man" brings private eye Nick Charles (William Powell) and wife Nora (Myrna Loy) on a visit to her rich family in San Francisco where Nick helps a local flatfoot (Sam Levene) solve a murder case. Though the mystery is not as perplexing as the original, director W.S. Van Dyke II makes it seem almost as much fun, thanks to the breezy byplay between the sleuthing couple and an odd gallery of suspects (notably James Stewart, Joseph Calleia and George Zucco). Murder mystery menace

title: After Tonight
synopsis: World War I romantic melodrama in which an Austrian officer (Gilbert Roland) falls in love with a nurse (Constance Bennett) while investigating reports of espionage at a military base, then discovers she's a Russian spy. Directed by George Archainbaud, the hokey mix of wartime romance and secret agents limps along without much conviction until collapsing in a tacked-on happy ending. Menacing situations and romantic complications

title: Against All Flags
synopsis: Colorful swashbuckler in which an English sea captain (Errol Flynn) joins a pirate crew in order to enter their impregnable island fortress, then destroy it. Directed by George Sherman, the formula plot focuses on the hero's problems with a suspicious buccaneer (Anthony Quinn), a lovely pirate captain (Maureen O'Hara) and the Grand Mogul's captured daughter. Stylized violence and romantic situations

title: Against All Odds
synopsis: Los Angeles bookie and entrepreneur (James Wood) sends his buddy, an aging pro football star (Jeff Bridges), to find his runaway mistress (Rachel Ward).
