synopsis: Al Pacino stars as an honest but abrasive anti-establishment lawyer who is blackmailed into defending a "law and order" judge (John Forsythe) accused of rape. A heavyhanded and muddled potboiler directed by Norman Jewison. Foul language and sexual promiscuity

title: And Now for Something Completely Different
synopsis: This random sampling of skits from "Monty Python's Flying Circus," the BBC zany comedy series, offers some distinctly British humor ranging from social satire and black comedy to broad slapstick and sexual jokes, most notably at the expense of homosexuals. Under director Ian MacNaughton, the young cast come over as a quite likeable group of performers, which helps when jokes fall flat. Best of all, however, are Terry Gilliam's animated pieces linking the skits but also standing on their own as contemporary graphic humor. However, it is comedy not for all tastes

title: And Now Ladies and Gentlement
synopsis: Curious story about an English jewel thief (Jeremy Irons) trying to start a new life and a nightclub singer (Patricia Kaas) nursing a broken heart whose paths intersect when they wind up in the same hospital suffering from severe memory lapses and discover that love just may save their lives. Hopping from London to Paris to Fez, director Claude Lelouch's film is visually alluring as it plays with the sequence of events, in an imitation of the characters' blackouts; however, the script becomes increasingly muddled and loses momentum. Subtitles. Affairs and romantic complications with a smattering of crass words and an instance of rough language
full_review:
A jewel thief and a nightclub singer meet under curious circumstances in the unusual drama "And Now Ladies and Gentlemen" (Paramount Classics).

Jeremy Irons never seems to take on a straightforward, ordinary character. His characters always seem to reside in the gray area of life. It is no different with his latest protagonist, Valentin Valentin (so named because of his birth on St. Valentine's Day). Englishman Valentin is a jewel thief and master of disguise who has managed to pull off heists from Bulgari and other haute-bauble shops using humorous bluff and charming deceit. But now he is being nagged by a secret wish: to start anew, and possibly even to reimburse those from whom he has stolen. He begins by setting sail on a luxury yacht, seeking solace in the deep blue sea.

Meanwhile, jazz chanteuse Jane Lester (recording artist Patricia Kaas) is nursing a broken heart, thanks to a philandering trumpet player. Her heartbreak leads her to Morocco, where she takes a gig singing in a grand Fez hotel, and where Valentin's boat has crashed. But what draws them together are these strange symptoms they both have been experiencing. At various times, Jane and Valentin suffer from blackouts and severe memory lapses. She has been forgetting the lyrics to the song she's singing and he can't remember where he has stashed the stolen merchandise, or whether he has stolen at all. They "meet cute" awaiting their individual CAT-scans.

Within the story is another layer, where director Claude Lelouch plays with the sequence of events and punctuates reality with the characters' dreams. As Jane is experiencing one of her "moments," she is seen fading from full color to sepia then to black and white, until the moment passes and she returns to full color. Lelouch has also rolled light-hearted moments into this downbeat love story, mostly associated with Valentin's disguises and trickery when he robs. Yet, Lelouch has difficulty maintaining an even tone throughout the film. It seems he wants to imitate the various ups and downs of life, but the result is not as good as the intent. And as the film moves leisurely on, the script becomes increasingly muddled and loses momentum.

Although Valentin's desire to make amends for his wayward ways is commendable, the film's tenor can make his thievery seem "cool." In a twisted way, the film seems to indicate that his brain tumor is his punishment. But even this seems tenuous.

Strange, visually intense and with some parts better than others, "And Now Ladies and Gentlemen" is a mixed bag, leaving the viewer reflecting yet vaguely dissatisfied.

Subtitles.

Due to affairs and romantic complications with a smattering of crass words and an instance of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops' classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: And Now Miguel
synopsis: An engaging portrayal of a year in the life of a small boy (Pat Cardi) in New Mexico whose only wish is to become a shepherd like his father (Michael Ansara). Produced by Robert B. Radnitz and based on Joseph Krumgold's prize-winning novel, the film emphasizes the strength of Hispanic family life rooted in mutual love and respect, with the natural beauty of the land and a credible cast contributing to its realistic picture of pastoral life

title: And Now My Love
synopsis: French production using the history of Europe from World War I to the present as the backdrop to a love story tracing, in almost surrealistic fashion, the heritages and key events in the lives of a young Jewish heiress (Marthe Keller) and an ex-convict turned film director (Char1es Denner). Beautifully produced and directed by Claude Lelouch, history is interestingly put at the service of love and there is no denying that the optimism of his romantic fable makes one feel good even though aware that its selective view of the past is being used only to make a romantic trifle seem more consequential than it really is

title: And Now the Screaming Starts
synopsis: British horror movie directed by Roy Ward Baker offers no more than average example in this 18th-century tale of inherited guilt from a diabolically-inspired family curse. Good production values and special effects and the cast includes horror veterans Peter Cushing, Patrick Magee and Herbert Lom. A number of the plot elements involve rape and other forms of brutality but their treatment is restrained

title: And Now Tomorrow
synopsis: Creaky sudser directed by Irving Pichel in which a poor but earnest doctor (Alan Ladd) seeks to restore the hearing of a wealthy deaf woman (Loretta Young) while opening her eyes to the needs of the less fortunate and unlocking her heart to the throbs of true love. Romantic complications

title: Andre
synopsis: Pleasant fact-based story of a family living on the Maine coast where in the 1960s father (Keith Carradine) and daughter (Tina (Majorino) rescue an orphaned seal pup who becomes so attached to its adopted human family that for 24 years the seal made its way back to them after every winter thaw. Director George Miller embroiders the playful antics of the personable seal with several subplots about prickly individuals and community misuunderstandings in a sentimental story stressing positive parent-child relationships

title: Andrei Rublev
synopsis: Russian production about a 15th-century monk (Anatoli Solonitzine) who perseveres in painting icons and other religious art despite the civil disruptions and cruel turmoil of his times. Director Andrei Tarkovsky visualizes brilliantly the story of a devout man seeking through his art to find the transcendent in the savagery of the Tartar invasions and the unfeeling brutality of Russian nobles. Subtitles. Stylized historical violence

title: Androcles and the Lion
synopsis: Satiric misfire from George Bernard Shaw's play about a group of Christians (headed by patrician Jean Simmons) who are saved from martyrdom in Rome's Colisseum by a lion from whose paw one of them (Alan Young) had once extracted a thorn. Directed by Chester Erskine, the sluggish narrative is bouyed by some droll exchanges on secular power vs. religious faith and many eccentric performances (aggressive pacifist Robert Newton, dim emperor Maurice Evans, shrewish wife Elsa Lanchester, etc.). Romantic situations and humorous probes into religious matters

title: And Soon the Darkness
synopsis: Two pretty English lasses (Pamela Franklin and Michele Dotrice) on a bicycle tour of France have a row and Dotrice disappears on the site of an unsolved grisly sex-murder leaving Franklin to search for her friend while eluding the crazed killer. British thriller directed by Robert Fuest takes her up and down any number of verdant but blind alleys, establishing everyone she meets as a prime suspect, but even the pretty French countryside cannot compensate for the overall disappointment in the climax

title: And the Band Played On
synopsis: Ambitious but uneven docudrama from Randy Shilts' book about the first years of the AIDS epidemic begins in 1981 with the efforts of medical researchers (notably Matthew Modine) to identify a mystery disease seemingly limited to homosexuals, then details the indecisive action of government and medical officials in the battle against what was becoming a worldwide crisis. Directed by Roger Spottiswoode, the scenario's attempt to provide a comprehensive account of complex events results in an unwieldy narrative which gathers dramatic impact from its diverse picture of individuals confronting the reality of this deadly disease. Sympathetic treatment of homosexual relationships and a realistic depiction of the human tragedy of AIDS and the indifference of some to it

title: And Then There Were None
synopsis: Mystery classic from the Agatha Christie novel in which 10 strangers invited for a weekend on a remote island are each charged by their unseen host with an unpunished capital crime for which he begins to kill them one by one. Director Rene Clair and scriptwriter Dudley Nichols embroider the cunning plot with elaborate chills and deepening suspense, laced with gallows humor and carried off in style by an accomplished cast (led by Barry Fitzgerald, Walter Huston, Louis Hayward and June Duprez). More menace than violence

title: And There Came a Man
synopsis: Part documentary and part re-enactment, this screen biography of Pope John XXIII features Rod Steiger as narrator and stand-in for the person of the title. The Italian production is best in its unpretentious re-created scenes of Pope John's early boyhood but director Ermanno Olmi is less successful in depicting his clerical career

title: Andy
synopsis: The aging parents of a grown man (Norman Alden) with the mind of a small child are forced to make the decision to commit him to an institution. Writer-director Richard Sarafian captures the less-than-understanding attitudes of society toward the mentally handicapped but tinges the realism of the New York City locale with poetic images affirming the joys of simple existence. Challenging but worthwhile fare

title: Andy Hardy Comes Home
synopsis: Clunker directed by Howard Koch tries to revive the Hardy series with the original cast except family patriarch Lewis Stone. Best forgotten

title: Andy Hardy Gets Spring Fever
synopsis: Judge Hardy (Lewis Stone) falls for an aluminum scam while son Andy (Mickey Rooney) develops a crush on the new high school drama teacher. Directed by W.S. Van Dyke II, it offers the usual family sitcom fare, though Andy's involvement with the school play has its moments

title: Andy Hardy Meets a Debutante
synopsis: In order to rescue the town orphanage trust fund, Judge Hardy (Lewis Stone) journeys to New York City, taking the family along on a trip that threatens to disgrace Andy (Mickey Rooney) back home until he's saved by a wealthy friend (Judy Garland). Directed by George B. Seitz, this edition of the Hardy series provides some period amusement as well as an incidental lesson in democracy

title: Andy Hardy's Blonde Trouble
synopsis: As a college freshman, Andy (Mickey Rooney) gets off on the wrong foot with the dean (Herbert Marshall), a lovely co-ed (Bonita Granville) and a contrary blonde who turns out to be identical twins (Lee and Lyn Wilde). Directed by George B. Seitz, it's one of the feebler efforts of the series, sorely lacking the interplay of the Hardy family circle

title: Andy Hardy's Double Life
synopsis: While Judge Hardy (Lewis Stone) is preoccupied with an accident case, flirtatious Andy is perplexed by girlfriend Polly (Ann Rutherford) and her visiting pal (Esther Williams). Directed by George B. Seitz, the usual domestic misunderstandings culminate in a big finish at the train station seeing Andy off to college

title: Andy Hardy's Private Secretary
synopsis: Disorganized Andy (Mickey Rooney) gets a secretary (Kathryn Grayson) to help him keep up with his busy activities as a Carvel High senior in a typical episode of the Hardy series under George B. Seitz's direction

title: Andy Warhol's Dracula
synopsis: In this variation on the Dracula theme, the ever-thirsty Count must live on "wirgin's blood," as it is rendered in one of the dreadfu1 accents abounding here. Besides the accents, there's no lack of other offensive elements in director Paul Morrissey's campy efforts in trying to make perversion seem hilarious

title: Andy Warhol's Frankenstein
synopsis: Written and directed by Warhol's alter ego, Pau1 Morrissey, this version emphasizes the fatal and the perverse aspects of the Mary Shelley original, ever escalating the campy hijinks for shock value. If one isn't offended by the gross nudity and kinky sex combinations, perhaps the gory charnel scraps flying all over the place will

title: An Everlasting Piece
synopsis: Mildly amusing Irish comedy set in 1980's Belfast about two barbers, one Catholic (Barry McEvoy) and the other Protestant (Brian F. O'Bryne), who set out to corner the toupee market in Northern Ireland, unintentionally getting mixed up with the IRA. Director Barry Levinson's film entertains with a few chuckles, but plot inconsistencies and an a clashing serious and sentimental turn undermines the film's comic momentum. Frequent rough language and profanity and fleeting rear nudity. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Angel
synopsis: Advertised as "High school honor student by day, Hollywood hooker by night" is all one needs to know about this dismal effort by director Robert Vincent O'Neil to tell the story of a young prostitute (Donna Wilkes) who helps a detective catch a psychopathic killer. Nudity, graphic sex and violence

title: Angel and the Badman
synopsis: Enjoyable low-key Western in which a wounded outlaw (John Wayne) is nursed back to health by a Quaker family whose daughter (Gail Russell) tries to get him to hang up his guns rather than square accounts with a bushwacker (Bruce Cabot). Directed by James Edward Grant, the unpretentious yet thoughtful story features a very likeable cast, including Harry Carey as the sage sheriff. Solid social values with some meaningful stylized violence

title: Angel, Angel Down We Go
synopsis: An 18-year-old virgin (Holly Near), desperate to lose that state, is helped out by a rock singer (Jordon Christopher) who also gives sexual aid to her wealthy mother and father and then destroys them all. Blaming a corrupt society for the depicted immoral activity, director Robert Thom's presentation tries to smooth over the guilt feelings of viewers slightly ashamed at their own voyeurism. Promiscuity and several insulting references to religion

title: Angela's Ashes
synopsis: Faithful though emotionally bleak dramatization of Frank McCourt=s Pulitzer Prize-winning account of growing up in 1930s-40s Limerick where he lives in desperate poverty with his long-suffering mother (Emily Watson), alcoholic father (Robert Carlyle) and younger siblings until stealing his fare to America at age 19. British writer-director Alan Parker presents a realistic depiction of an impoverished youth=s struggles through puberty and growing alienation from his family and Catholic upbringing but the sober, disciplined result lacks both the poetic flair and humorous punctuation of the book. Intense depiction of domestic crises, numerous sexual situations and references, alcoholic excess, recurring rough language and some profanity

title: Angel Eyes
synopsis: Tiresome drama in which a tough Chicago cop (Jennifer Lopez) dealing with an abusive childhood and a mysterious stranger (Jim Caviezel) recovering from a traumatic event fall in love, but must reconcile with their respective pasts to make things work. Director Luis Mandoki unsuccessfully blends thriller and romance genres as perfunctory performances, artificial sentiments and a mechanical script culminate in a forced ending. A sexual encounter, sporadic sexual references, brief violence and intermittent rough language with fleeting profanity. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Angel Face
synopsis: Dark crime melodrama in which an unhinged heiress (Jean Simmons) embroils an unwitting car mechanic (Robert Mitchum) in the murder of her wealthy stepmother (Barbara O'Neill), with dire consequences for both. Directed by Otto Preminger, the story is a mess of contrived situations and unconvincing characters. Stylized violence including suicide in the plot resolution

title: Angel Heart
synopsis: Director Alan Parker's bloody, often disgusting depiction of one man's grappling with the devil and the consequences of his refusal to face the evil within him forms the core of this parable about a private eye (Mickey Rourke) hired to find a missing person only to discover it is a missing soul. Graphic mix of sex and violence in a demonic setting, nudity and vivid results of dismemberment

title: Angel in My Pocket
synopsis: A newly ordained minister (Andy Griffith) comes to serve his first congregation in a small Kansas town where he immediately becomes involved in the feud between two families that has wrecked the ministry of all his predecessors. Directed by Alan Rafkin, the comedy is broad and mindless, the characters stereotypes and the sugary situations enough to give some viewers diabetes

title: Angel on My Shoulder
synopsis: Seriocomic fantasy about a murdered gangster (Paul Muni) whom the Devil (Claude Rains) puts in the body of a lookalike judge to destroy the man's virtuous career but things don't go according to plan. Though it doesn't make a whole lot of sense, director Archie Mayo has some fun creating the sulfuric pits of hell down below as well as with the tough-talking mug's reformation by the judge's fiancee (Anne Baxter). Some stylized violence and devilish goings-on

title: Angels' Alley
synopsis: Formula slapstick comedy with the Bowery Boys (notably Leo Gorcey and Huntz Hall) battling a gang of car thieves whose sneering boss (Nestor Paiva) gets decked by a priest running the local youth center

title: Angels & Demons
synopsis: Highly improbable but mindlessly entertaining sequel to “The Da Vinci Code” - adapted from Dan Brown’s prequel written in 2000 -- in which religious symbologist Robert Langdon (Tom Hanks) and a scientist (Ayelet Zurer) join forces with a church official (Ewan McGregor) to try to prevent the destruction of the Vatican and the murder of a quartet of kidnapped cardinals by following a trail of clues left across Rome by the secretive Illuminati cult of anti-Catholic intellectuals. Though director Ron Howard has toned down some of the book’s most egregious elements, the historical church is still portrayed as a relentless and at times violent foe of science, but the film ends on a positive note from a faith perspective and the final image of the Church is relatively positive

title: Angels and the Pirates
synopsis: (see: 1951's " Angels in the Outfield ")

title: Angels Die Hard
synopsis: Unenlightened motorcycle movie about a gang of bikers who invade a small town, brutally torment the locals and linger nearby to do it again. Underdeveloped conflicts center around the sheriff's blustering threats to shoot them down, especially since his teenage daughter is keen on joining them. Director Richard Compton leans to admiring shots of the gang riding the road but the coarse customs and cruelty of these outlaw heroes far outweigh any suggestions of their benevolent humanity

title: Angels in America
synopsis: An ambitious, compelling and stirring television adaptation of Tony Kushner�s award winning theatrical production, originally on Broadway in 1993 and 1994. Well-written, timely and poignant, the play hit upon many controversial themes as the new millennium approached: the gay lifestyle and the advent of AIDS in America, the Reagan era, apocalyptic fears, religion, and a time-worn human quest to define heaven while grappling with mortality. Directed by Mike Nichols, the television film is true to the play, with excellent production values and a superb cast.: Patrick Wilson, Mary-Louise Parker, Justin Kirk, Al Pacino, Emma Thompson, Meryl Streep and Jeffrey Wright. One cannot write off a play that presents such affecting physical and spiritual anguish yet �Angels in America� has flaws and numerous troubling aspects that would make many Catholic viewers unable to endure it. An unqualified recommendation is therefore difficult, but there is value in such a spectacularly mounted production that presents much thought-provoking fodder. (HBO) 2003

title: Angels in the Outfield
synopsis: Remake of the 1951 syrupy fantasy in which the surly baseball manager (Danny Glover) of the last-place California Angels starts relying on the advice of a young boy (Joseph Gordon-Levitt) who claims to see heavenly angels assisting various players during the games. William Dear directs a slow-paced, old-fashioned crowd-pleaser in which a foster child's prayer for a family is answered and cynical adults begin believing that, with a little faith, miracles can happen. Fleeting violence and a few instances of profanity. A-II (PG) (1994)

title: Angels in the Outfield
synopsis: Sentimental baseball fantasy in which the lowly Pittsburgh Pirates begin winning games after the team's ill-tempered manager (Paul Douglas) starts listening to an orphan who sees angels on the playing field. Directed by Clarence Brown, the proceedings are mostly good-natured hokum, though some may find them overly sweetened

title: Angels with Dirty Faces
synopsis: Depression melodrama in which a gang of New York toughs (Billy Hallop, Leo Gorcey and other Dead End Kids) regard a local gangster (James Cagney) as a hero until a priest (Pat O'Brien) who was his boyhood pal persuades him to help the boys by feigning cowardice on the way to the electric chair. Directed by Michael Curtiz, the simplistic plot is buttressed by convincing performances, especially the counterpoint between Cagney's cocky crook and O'Brien's sincere cleric. Stylized violence and justice questions

title: Angel Unchained
synopsis: Routine motorcycle melodrama about a biker (Don Stroud) who leaves his cycling buddies to join a commune but when its peacefu1 members are harassed by the local cowboys he calls on his old friends to help even out the odds in the big showdown. Director Lee Madden's contrived plot provides the opportunity for some hard-hitting brawls, a touch of sex, an abundance of beer and pot and, of course, plenty of daredevil bike riding

title: Angel with the Trumpet
synopsis: Sprawling saga of an Austrian family from 1888 through World War II, focusing on the Jewish wife (Eileen Herlie) of the family's head (Basil Sydney) as they struggle to survive the disasters of war, financial ruin and the aged woman's suicide under Nazi rule. Directed by Anthony Bushell, the British production interweaves the drama of the family's changing fortunes with the history of the Austrian nation from monarchy to republic to occupation by the Germans, then the Allies. Wartime violence, suicide and implied sexual affairs

title: Anger Management
synopsis: Displeasing comedy in which a meek businessman (Adam Sandler) is ordered to take intensive anger management behavior modification from a volatile therapist (Jack Nicholson) who proceeds to steal his girlfriend (Marisa Tomei). As directed by Peter Segal and targeted to teen boys, the emphasis on sex and that size matters is disturbing while the plot contrivances are unconvincing. Some comically intended violence, continuous sexual references, brief same-sex kissing, an implied affair and an instance of rough language
full_review:
Adam Sandler and Jack Nicholson make the latest odd-couple pairing in the displeasing comedy, "Anger Management" (Columbia).

A misunderstanding on an airline flight forces unassertive businessman Sandler to endure the attentions of volatile psychotherapist Nicholson.

Meek and underappreciated ad exec David finds himself sentenced to anger management behavior modification after a flight attendant and sky marshal misinterpret his actions. And, as luck would have it, his court-ordered therapist, Dr. Buddy Rydell, turns out to be the very guy who was the real troublemaker on the plane.

Group therapy with some rather scary individuals (including a bug-eyed John Turturro) is awful but then abrasive Buddy boldly moves right in with David to impose even more intensive therapy on his appalled subject. What could be worse? Well, Buddy's hitting on David's girlfriend, Linda (Marisa Tomei), might be the final straw that compels David to become the madman he's been assumed to be all along.

Director Peter Segal takes a reasonably funny premise -- a gentle soul tethered to a hot-tempered therapist -- but goes for cheap laughs involving transvestite hookers, making Buddhist monks turn to violence and jealous lesbians. The constant sexual references are at gutter level, and for a movie aimed at Sandler's target audience of impressionable pre-teen and teen males, the emphasis on how male anatomical size really matters is not a good -- or even funny -- message to send.

Sandler fills his role well compared to Nicholson, who looks uncomfortable in the sillier scenes, although a scene in which he smashes someone's car window clearly refers to Nicholson's own famously reported fit of anger against a motorist. As David's girlfriend, Tomei is a spunky, upbeat presence throughout the film, giving it some heart to balance out the frequent crude moments.

The story shows how David must learn to recognize his own inner rage and properly channel it, but some scenes, as when the Buddhist monks are deliberately provoked, can be interpreted as suggesting that violence is a good way to settle problems.

With its powerhouse male stars, "Anger Management" is likely headed for a big bite of the box office, but it's not a good choice for its target audience.

Due to some comically intended violence, continuous sexual references, brief same-sex kissing, an implied affair and an instance of rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Angie
synopsis: Soggy tearjerker about a working-class Brooklyn girl (Geena Davis) who becomes pregnant by her plumber boyfriend (James Gandolfini), then dumps him for an eccentric high-class lawyer (Stephen Rea) who walks out after the baby is born, leaving her to face single parenthood with the support of loving family and friends. Directed by Martha Coolidge, the melodrama never gets to the heart of its feminist heroine whose struggle for independence is complicated by yearnings for the mother she never knew, though along the way there are some positive discoveries about the responsibilites of parenthood and the importance of family. Premarital relationships, a flash of nudity, some raunchy humor and occasional rough language

title: Angi Vera
synopsis: Marvelously subtle Hungarian production set in 1948 during the early days of the Communist regime when a young woman with a talent for survival (flawless performance by Veronica Papp in the title role) is sent by the Party to a political training center where she has an affair that cou1d threaten her future. Looking back at the tragic and confused mix of idealism and opportunism that marked the era, director Pal Gabor shows that human nature has a way of infiltrating the most resistant of ideologies. Adult situations and politically complex themes

title: Angry Harvest
synopsis: Set in a Polish village during World War II, a simple but devout farmer abuses the trust of a Jewish refugee he is sheltering by his lust for her. In the Polish production, director Agnieszka Holland offers a compelling portrait of a man whose loneliness undermines his basic moral character resulting in betrayal and death. In this context, several brief scenes of partial nudity and simulated sex are anything but titillating

title: Angus
synopsis: Formula comedy in which a tubby teen (Charlie Talbert) must overcome low self-esteem and taunting classmates before finding courage to talk to the girl of his dreams (Ariana Richards). Cardboard characters and Patrick Read Johnson's dull direction result in a preachy, predictable tale about beauty being only skin deep. Some sexual innuendo, comic roughhousing, crude slang and a needless instance of rough language

title: Animal Behavior
synopsis: Muddled romance between a sincere music teacher (Armande Assante) and a spacy psychology professor (Karen Allen) who's too caught up in her communication research with a chimp to relate in a man-woman context. Directed by H. Anne Riley, the movie's dopey, implausible script and miscast, overwrought characters fail in a humorless attempt at screwball comedy. Minimal rough language and some sexual innuendo

title: Animal Factory
synopsis: Drab prison drama about a newly sentenced young drug dealer (Edward Furlong) who begins to change into a hardened criminal under the influence of a tough, older inmate (William Dafoe) in the state penitentiary. Director Steve Buscemi's sophomore effort lacks the necessary tension to make it compelling as the sometimes ambiguous narrative only minimally develops the characters. Recurring drug abuse, homosexual innuendo, intermittent violence and constant rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Animal House
synopsis: (see: " National Lampoon's Animal House ")

title: Animals Are Beautiful People
synopsis: Wildlife documentary filmed in a vast tract of desert, swamp and mountains in Southwest Africa with an exotic variety of animal species. Director Jamie Uys provides some humorous as well as fascinating moments, marred slightly by a Disney-style anthropomorphic slant and what some might detect as a paternalistic attitude toward blacks

title: Anna and the King
synopsis: Lavish historical drama set in 1862 Siam where the absolute monarch (Chow Yun-Fat) and the widowed English schoolteacher (Jodie Foster) he hired to teach his 58 children about the West learn much from each other even as a duplicitous general plots to kill the king and all his heirs. After a sluggish start director Andy Tennant goes beyond sumptuous visuals in exploring contrasting East-West cultures and beliefs while maintaining suspense about the assassination plot. Sporadic violence and references to polygamy and concubines

title: Anna and the King of Siam
synopsis: Intriguing story of a widowed English governess (Irene Dunne) who arrives in 1862 Siam to instruct the royal household's 67 children, then clashes with the king (Rex Harrison) over a suitable house but ultimately wins his respect and trust by proving as strong-willed as he. Directed by John Cromwell, the exotic palace setting is pure Hollywood but the two central characters are quite credible in their efforts to work together despite cultural differences and personal misunderstandings. Children may need support in coping with the tragic death of the widow's young son and a palace execution on charges of infidelity

title: Annabel Takes a Tour
synopsis: Thin Hollywood spoof in which a movie star (Lucille Ball) kicks off a studio publicity tour in Chicago where her dizzy press agent (Jack Oakie) cooks up a romance with a viscount (Ralph Forbes), but she thinks it's on the level and quits show business. Directed by Lew Landers, the laughs come mainly from the wacky antics of Ball and Oakie, abetted by their dim studio head (Bradley Page) and his wise-cracking secretary (Ruth Donnelly). Romantic complications

title: Anna Christie
synopsis: Cast includes Greta Garbo, Nita Naldi, Vilma Banky, and John Gilbert. Directed by Clarence Brown. A-III (nr) 1930

title: Anna Karenina
synopsis: Opulent adaptation of Leo Tolstoy's 19th-century novel of Czarist Russia contrasts the hard-won love story of an eventually happy couple (Alfred Molina and Mia Kirshner) with the doomed romance of a married woman (Sophie Morceau) who forsakes husband and child to run off with a wealthy officer (Sean Bean). Screenwriter-director Bernard Rose's elaborate period piece is visually lush in portraying the hypocrisy of class distinctions and exploring characters who question the morality of their actions. Brief violence, fleeting bedroom scene and a suicidal character's drug dependency

title: Anna Karenina
synopsis: Cast includes Greta Garbo, Fredric March, Basil Rathbone, Maureen O�Sullivan and Freddie Bartholomew. Directed by Clarence Brown. L (nr) 1935

title: Anna Lucasta
synopsis: Lurid melodrama about a guilt-ridden old man (Rex Ingram) and his daughter (Eartha Kitt) who turned to prostitution after being driven from home as a teenager, but whom the family now insists return to wed a man whose money will benefit them. Directed by Arnold Laven from Philip Yordan's play, the contrived proceedings grow increasingly muddled though convincing performances by an all-black cast hold interest, especially those of Kitt in the title role and Sammy Davis, Jr., as her ex-sailor lover. Sexual situations and innuendo

title: Ann and Eve
synopsis: Swedish story of a jaded journalist (Gio Petre) who takes a young innocent (Marie Liljedahl) on a vacation to a Yugoslav resort where she is initiated into a predictable series of sexual adventures around town. Arne Mattsson directs the lurid melodrama with clinical coldness toward the characters who meander through arbitrary situations. Excessive nudity

title: Annapolis
synopsis: Diverting but derivative drama about a scrappy shipyard worker (an appealing James Franco), who, after being accepted to the U.S. Naval Academy, must prove his mettle while training for the school's boxing tournament against his no-nonsense drill instructor (Tyrese Gibson). Though director Justin Lin's adrenalized climax achieves its desired rousing effect, this retread of "An Officer and a Gentleman" is hollow and formulaic. Brutal boxing sequences, an attempted suicide, some sexually crude language and humor, as well as profanity
full_review:
The plot of director Justin Lin's diverting but derivative "Annapolis" (Touchstone) -- young man tries to prove his mettle while pursuing dream of becoming a Navy officer -- sounds like a good idea for a movie. Just as it did for "An Officer and a Gentleman"!

Bearing some resemblance to young Richard Gere, an appealing James Franco stars as Jake Huard, a scrappy shipyard worker and amateur boxer who, for vague and improbable reasons, is accepted into the prestigious U.S. Naval Academy.

There he is pushed to the limit, as he and his fellow "plebes" (Naval Academy speak for freshman cadets) are put through a rigorous gauntlet of mental and physical tests.

As with these "be all you can be" military melodramas, there is no shortage of instructors who try to break them. It is during these sequences that the echoes of "Officer" are clearest, with Jake at several points declaring defiantly, "I ain't quittin'!" There is a further ripped-off subplot in which Jake helps a struggling classmate make it through a grueling obstacle course.

Though played with more steel-jawed understatement (and fewer expletives) than Louis Gossett Jr.'s tough gunnery sergeant, Tyrese Gibson co-stars as ex-Marine company commander and Jake's chief antagonist, Midshipman Lt. Cole. (Eyes locked in dagger-shooting mode abound!)

The film switches midway from boot camp to boxing ring, as Jake, eager for some payback, prepares to face off against Cole at the academy's annual tournament.

Jordana Brewster also co-stars as Ali, an instructor at the school who becomes Jake's love interest. The inter-rank romance is only one of the implausible story elements. How is it that Jake isn't expelled for blatant bad sportsmanship and attacking a senior officer when another cadet is tossed for merely lying about taking a shower?

Chi McBride and Donnie Wahlberg serve limited duty as a boxing coach and member of the school's brass, respectively.

Apart from some barracks banter, there is relatively little objectionable content, though many viewers may find the intense ring violence off-putting.

Though Lin's adrenalized climax achieves its desired rousing effect, the film is hollow and formulaic. At best, you may want to wait until this adequately entertaining film drops anchor in your video store.

The film contains brutal boxing sequences, an attempted suicide, some sexually crude language and humor, as well as profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Anne Frank Remembered
synopsis: Compelling documentary portrait of the Jewish teenager known to millions through the diary she kept while hiding with her family in Amsterdam until they were betrayed and sent to the Nazi death camps. Written, produced and directed by British filmmaker Jon Blair, the film puts Anne's life in historical perspective by interviews with those who knew her as a child or met her in the camps as well as the dramatic use of visuals provided by family photographs, period artifacts and archival footage, including scenes of a 1941 wedding at which Anne is briefly glimpsed. A work poignant with its sense of loss and painful visuals of the Holocaust

title: Anne of Green Gables
synopsis: Charming dramatization of the Lucy Maud Montgomery novel about a spunky teenaged orphan (Anne Shirley) who overcomes assorted obstacles to win the hearts of a taciturn farmer (O.P. Heggie) and his domineering sister (Helen Westley) on Canada's Prince Edward Island at the turn of the century. Directed by George Nicholls, the story of a lonely waif finding the loving home of her dreams has special appeal for young viewers while reminding older ones of youth's yearning for unconditional love. Fine family fare

title: Anne of the Thousand Days
synopsis: Screen version of Maxwell Anderson's play about the romance between Henry VIII (Richard Burton) and Anne Boleyn (Genevieve Bujold). Directed by Charles Jarrott, the story centers on all the dynastic complications that motivated Henry's break with Rome and his six-year pursuit of Anne. Though the action is limited, the acting is impressive, especially that of Anthony Quayle as Cardinal Wolsey. For those who are not history buffs, there is plenty of royal pageantry, colorful costumes and well-preserved castles. In dealing with the period and its characters, there is some blood-letting and sexual candor

title: Anne of Windy Poplars
synopsis: Pedestrian sequel directed by Jack Hively follows the now-grown orphan (Anne Shirley) on her first teaching position in a small town whose nasty matriarch (Ethel Griffies) schemes to have her fired until the woman's nephew (James Ellison) steps in to save the school's Christmas play and Anne's fiance (Patric Knowles) cures a local child's pneumonia. Though warmly played, the characters and situations are as predictable as the wholesome ending is saccharine

title: Annie
synopsis: Although John Huston's direction of the screen version of the popular stage musical is somewhat cynical and largely disappointing, it does preserve much of the exotic ambiance of the comic strip about the little orphan (Aileen Quinn) and Daddy Warbucks (Albert Finney). With awkward dance numbers, some coarse dialogue and Carol Burnett's mean-spirited characterization, the movie's appeal is somewhat limited beyond uncritical viewers

title: Annie Get Your Gun
synopsis: Big and brassy version of the Irving Berlin musical in which rustic Annie Oakley (Betty Hutton) gets some polish working with Frank Butler (Howard Keel) in a sharpshooting act, then finds fame and finally gets her man (Butler) after Buffalo Bill (Louis Calhoun) makes her a star in his Wild West Show. Directed by George Sidney, this show has lots of stunt riding, staged Indian attacks and shoot-outs which make a suitable backdrop for Hutton's overcharged performance, with the result memorable chiefly for its songs ranging from the romantic "The Girl That I Marry" to the comedic "Doing What Comes Naturally" and "Anything You Can Do" and the signature tune, "There's No Business Like Show Business." Romantic complications

title: Annie Hall
synopsis: Director Woody Allen's romantic comedy about an on-again, off-again relationship between a Jewish comedian from New York (Allen) and a WASP from the Midwest (Diane Keaton). Although the movie is frequently very funny and has a touch of humanity lacking in Allen's earlier work, it falls far short of its more ambitious intention of making a serious statement about human relationships. Some rough language and much humor derived from sexual matters

title: Annie Oakley
synopsis: Robust story of an Ohio country girl (Barbara Stanwyck) whose prowess with a hunting rifle starts her on the way to fame as the star sharpshooter of Buffalo Bill's Wild West Show. Director George Stevens provides a lively picture of late 19th-century America as well as a gentle story of Annie's love for a boastful trick shooter (Preston Foster). Enjoyable both for its colorful Western action and appealing success story

title: Another 48 Hrs.
synopsis: Eddie Murphy and Nick Nolte reteam as the convict and the cop in this savage sequel centering around their efforts to nail a drug kingpin before his gang ices them. Director Walter Hill revs up the violence to the max, with brutal shoot-ups at close range taking precedence over storyline, characterizations and comic relief. Excessive violence, continuous raw language and brief nudity

title: Another Day in Paradise
synopsis: Abhorrent violence marks the tale of a callous thief (James Woods) and his junkie lover (Melanie Griffith) who take a similar younger couple (Vincent Kartheiser and Natasha Gregson Wagner) on the road for a big heist that goes murderously awry. Director Larry Clark's raw picture of not-so-innocent-youth-further-corrupted is less a cautionary tale than a glamorization of daily doses of drugs, alcohol and deadly violence as an exciting lifestyle. Intermittent gory violence, sexual encounters with nudity, recurring substance abuse as well as incessant profanity and rough language

title: Another Man, Another Chance
synopsis: French director Claude Lelouch's romantic sagebrush drama about a widowed veterinarian (James Caan) who falls in love with a charming widowed photographer (Genevieve Bujold). Despite the movie's striking photography and excellent acting, Lelouch's calculatedly relaxed style of characterization and glossy romanticism do not lend themselves well to the more austere mood of a Western. Brief violence in a scene of rape

title: Another Man's Poison
synopsis: Clumsily contrived doings on the English moors where a wealthy mystery writer (Bette Davis) poisons her estranged husband, then tries to pass off a stranger (Gary Merrill) as the missing spouse -- until a neighbor (Emlyn Williams) grows suspicious. Directed by Irving Rapper, the plot's melodramatic claptrap triggers a scenery-chewing performance by Davis as the deadly, willful schemer who cares more for her chestnut stallion than any human. Murder, menace and some romantic trifling

title: Another Part of the Forest
synopsis: Convoluted family saga set in an 1880 Southern town whose wealthiest citizen (Fredric March) is despised by his neighbors as a Civil War profiteer, but his years of lording it over the townspeople and his own conniving offspring (Edmond O'Brien, Dan Duryea and Ann Blyth) come to an end when his downtrodden wife (Florence Eldridge) reveals a dark secret from his past. Directed by Michael Douglas from Lillian Hellman's prequel to "The Little Foxes," the melodramatic proceedings feature a fine cast but the plotting is ragged and the ending is mawkishly contrived. Domestic tensions and justice questions

title: Another Stakeout
synopsis: Uneven sequel to 1987's "Stakeout" reteams Seattle detectives Richard Dreyfuss and Emilio Estevez with assistant D.A. Rosie O'Donnell posing as a make-believe family who rent a home next door to a couple (Dennis Farina and Marcia Strassman) who are the friends of a government witness (Cathy Moriarty) running for her life. Director John Badham opens and closes with murderous violence totally at odds with the hilarious meat of the movie in which the innocent neighbors are constantly confused by mixed-up versions of the fake family's cover story. A live-in relationship, some intense violence and a few off-color remarks

title: Another Thin Man
synopsis: Enjoyable sequel with Nick and Nora Charles (William Powell and Myrna Loy) in New York trying to solve the murder of a wealthy family friend (C. Aubrey Smith) while keeping his daughter (Virginia Grey), their one-year-old son, Nicky, Jr., and canine cut-up, Asta, out of harm's way. Directed by W.S. Van Dyke II, the twisty plot has more red herrings than clues, with plenty of sinister suspects (Sheldon Leonard, Abner Biberman and Don Costello) and comic relief from flustered cops (Otto Kruger and Nat Pendleton) as well as a children's party thrown by ex-cons. Stylized violence and muted sexual innuendo

title: Another Time, Another Place
synopsis: Weepy sudser directed by Lewis Allen in which an American reporter (Lana Turner) in World War II London falls for a married BBC radio correspondent (Sean Connery), suffers a breakdown when he dies in an air crash, recovers after journeying to Cornwall to commiserate with his widow (Glynis Johns), then goes off with the man (Barry Sullivan) who has loved her all along. Unconvincing portrayals of cardboard characters and their hokey romantic affairs

title: Another Woman
synopsis: On her 50th birthday, a philosophy professor (Gena Rowlands) is forced to face the fact that she is not as loved and respected as she previously assumed, nor is her life the success that it had seemed. In this serious examination of mid-life regrets, writer-director Woody Allen continues to be sensitive to female protagonists. Brief, explicit talk of marital infidelity and a past abortion

title: Another You
synopsis: When a pathological liar (Gene Wilder) is released from a mental hospital, he is persuaded to pass himself off as a missing millionaire by a con man (Richard Pryor). A needlessly convoluted script makes director Maurice Phillips' garbled comedy misfire badly with hardly a laugh to be had. Recurring rough language and mild sexual innuendo

title: Antarctica
synopsis: When a 1957 Japanese expedition leaves its sled dogs behind at the South Pole, two of its members (Ken Takakura and Tsunehido Watase) return the next year to rescue any canine survivors. Director Koreyoshi Kurahara restages the fact-based story amdist spectacular polar landscapes, but the result succeeds better as a nature documentary than as a drama of polar scientists searching for their lost huskies. Dubbed. Life-threatening situations in a frozen wasteland make heavy sledding for children

title: Antonia's Line
synopsis: Multigenerational tale of a fiercely independent Dutch woman (Willeke van Ammelrooy) whose lesbian daughter and eventually her granddaughter and great-granddaughter live on the matriarch's farm where all confront emotional crises over the decades, drawing strength from their female solidarity. Writer-director Marleen Gorris celebrates non-traditional families and the resilience of women in a whimsical story overpopulated with village eccentrics, misfit clerics and disposable men. Subtitles. Several bedroom scenes with nudity, occasional violence including rape, an off-screen suicide and an instance of rough language

title: Antonio Das Mortes
synopsis: Brazilian folk epic about a gunman hired by a feudal landlord to eliminate the leaders of a peasant rebellion in the hills and how the hired assassin eventually joins the rebels himself. Using a gaudy co1or photography that suits his strange story and setting, director Glauber Rocha intermingles black and Indian rituals and ceremonies with Christian saints and symbols to create a world of bizarre superstitions and revolutionary fervor. It is an episodic movie of unusal power and beauty that some tastes may find too exotic

title: Antwone Fisher
synopsis: Inspirational true-life story of a troubled naval recruit (Derek Luke) who with the help of a Navy psychiatrist (Denzel Washington) learns to cope with the emotional devastation wreaked by childhood rejection and physical abuse. Despite a sometimes predictable narrative, Washington's directorial debut is a moving account of strength and survival, as well as a testament to the nobility of spirit inherent in every person. Some violence including depictions of child abuse, an implied sexual encounter and minimal rough language and profanity
full_review:
"Antwone Fisher" (Fox Searchlight) is the inspirational true-life story of a troubled young naval recruit's triumph over the emotional devastation wreaked by a lifetime of abuse and rejection.

Based on Fisher's autobiography, "Finding Fish," and his own screenplay, this moving account of survival and strength marks an impressive directorial debut of Academy Award-winner Denzel Washington. Although the narrative is at times predictable, the film features a commanding lead performance by newcomer Derek Luke.

The story opens at a naval base in southern California. Fisher (Luke) is a seaman with a hair-trigger temper whose volatility has drawn the ire of his commanding officer (a brief, uncredited cameo by James Brolin). Faced with the brig and the looming threat of a dishonorable discharge, Fisher is forced to attend counseling sessions with a navy psychiatrist, Jerome Davenport (Denzel Washington).

At first evasive and silent, Fisher gradually warms to Davenport's willing ear, seeing in the older officer the first father figure he has ever known. A bond of trust quickly evolves, coaxing out painful secrets from the young man's past. Through flashbacks, the cruel hand dealt to Fisher is slowly revealed.

His mother, incarcerated at the time, abandoned him at birth, just two months after his father was gunned down by an angry lover. He was raised in a Cleveland foster home, where the sadistic matriarch, Mrs. Tate (Novella Nelson), had two abiding passions: giving witness at an evangelical, storefront church and beating Antwone senseless. Soon after being released from reform school, finding himself homeless, he enlisted.

Encouraged by Davenport and his supportive girlfriend, Cheryl (Joy Bryant), Fisher begins to let go of his anger. Welcomed into Davenport's home, Fisher seems to exert a restorative influence on the psychiatrist's own strained marriage. However, when Fisher learns of the naval mandate limiting counseling to three sessions, the serenity of his fragile psyche is threatened by yet another perceived desertion. To fully exorcise Fisher's demons, Davenport recommends that he take the final step toward healing by searching out his real family.

Surprisingly, while novice Luke brings a refreshing vulnerability and tenacity to the role of Fisher, the more accomplished Washington turns in a less inspired performance as the paternal Navy psychiatrist. Despite moments of genuine emotion, a few scenes come across as heavy-handed in eliciting the desired audience response. Yet, overall, the story and Fisher's rocky journey to wholeness ring resoundingly true.

Adapting Fisher's memoir for the screen called for considerable streamlining with inevitable narrative gaps such as how the young Fisher was able to avoid the pitfalls which led his friends to crime. Viewers also may be curious about what fueled his voracious appetite for reading, writing poetry and foreign languages. Washington, an actor known for his measured subtlety, fleshes out a subplot about Davenport's previously unspecified marital problem with a closing scene that ties its resolution to his relationship with Fisher.

However, the film's cavalier attitude towards sex is unsettling. Other sailors persistently question Fisher's sexuality, scornful of how a "normal," attractive young man of 24 could still be a virgin. They are unaware of the childhood sexual abuse that fuels his anger. His girlfriend is more understanding and, although they do eventually begin a love affair (off-screen), she represents sexual healing and genuine caring rather than carnal lust to Fisher.

The film centers on a powerful message of hope, courage and nobility of spirit in the face of the most challenging of circumstances. Despite some blemishes, "Antwone Fisher" is a compelling testament to the sacred value and potential inherent in each and every person.

Due to some violence including depictions of child abuse, an implied sexual encounter, minimal rough language and profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Any Given Sunday
synopsis: Frenetically jumbled look at a professional football team trying to make the playoffs under a veteran coach (Al Pacino) who puts his career on the line by starting an ailing but reliable old-timer (Dennis Quaid) as quarterback rather than the hotshot young maverick (Jamie Foxx) favored by the club's devious owner (Cameron Diaz). Directed by Oliver Stone, the strictly formula sports story follows the underdogs to the big game in a jazzed-up narrative with jarring scenes of physical and verbal violence on and off the field, in locker rooms, bedrooms and corporate suites, while the coach philosophizes, cajoles, screams and whispers about team unity and the game's dignity. Much stylized violence, brutality, sexual situations, locker-room frontal nudity, drug abuse, recurring rough language and occasional profanity

title: Any Number Can Play
synopsis: Dreary melodrama of a day in the life of a gambling-house owner (Clark Gable) with a bad heart, a loving wife (Alexis Smith), an estranged son (Darryl Hickman), a weak brother-in-law (Wendell Corey) and an exotic clientele, one of whom (Frank Morgan) is on a winning streak. Mervyn Le Roy directs a fine cast in a plodding scenario crowded with contrived incidents, including an attempted robbery and a hokey finish. Lots of anxiety and a bit of stylized violence

title: Anyone Can Play
synopsis: Failed Italian sex farce with Ursula Andress, Virna Lisi and Jean-Pierre Cassel tends to condone adultery. Clumsily directed by Luigi Zampa, its emphasis is on sexual titillation

title: Anything But Love
synopsis: Modestly charming tale of a struggling cabaret singer (co-writer Isabel Rose) torn between her corporate lawyer fiance (Cameron Bancroft) and a destitute musician (Andrew McCarthy) who shares her love of a bygone musical era. Co-written and directed by Robert Cary, the film's romantic predictability is balanced by its low-budget plucky spirit, colorful production design and appealing follow-your-dream theme. Occasional profanity and fleeting homosexual innuendo
full_review:
A young woman clings to her hopes of becoming a classy cabaret singer while torn between two love interests in the nostalgia-laden "Anything But Love" (Goldwyn).

Billie Golden (Isabel Rose, who also co-wrote the script) may be singing her beloved standards to a pathetic handful in a dumpy lounge near JFK airport, but she carries on imagining the venue as a swell nightclub from the 1940s filled with glamorous couples. She lives for and dresses as if she's in the bygone era between the Hepburns -- Kate and Audrey.

At home, her widowed, hard-drinking mom (Alix Korey) wants her to give up waitressing by day so she can warble at night, and just get married. And Mom might get her wish when old high school classmate and now prosperous corporate lawyer Greg (Cameron Bancroft) bumps into Billie and is drawn to her unique personality. Romance blossoms despite Greg's lack of enthusiasm for her fragile cabaret career.

Meanwhile, Billie hires pianist Elliot (Andrew McCarthy) to hone her own piano-playing skills. Once he helps her find her true voice as opposed to imitating chanteuses, he finds her irresistible. Newly engaged, she wants to resist. On hand to purr romantic advice between husky torch songs is Eartha Kitt playing herself.

The outcome is fully predictable, although Billie doesn't make up her mind until just after the wedding (by a minister -- not a priest, one presumes, as he is later seen wearing his collar while on a very public date with Billie's best friend).

But the movie's modest charms lie not in the familiar love triangle but in the creative way director Robert Cary has stretched his low-budget film to include fantasy musical sequences and period detail from 50 years ago that make Billie's love of that era so convincing. A dozen standards are performed, although her repeated renditions of "I Can't Give You Anything But Love" don't bear close scrutiny. Indeed, at times the movie flirts with becoming a vanity production for Rose.

On a positive note, heavy metal, rap songs, bedroom scenes and violence play no part in this sweet tale of a young woman following her dream, albeit not without making any mistakes. The colorful production design, costumes and coiffures are seeped in nostalgia that is celebratory, not in the least satirical or cynical.

While the ending is too pat and cuddly, it's hard not to enjoy the plucky spirit of this feel-good movie.

Due to occasional profanity and fleeting homosexual innuendo, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Anything Can Happen
synopsis: Sudsy romantic comedy in which an emigrant (Jose Ferrer) from Georgia, USSR, works hard at becoming a U.S. citizen while falling along the way for one of the natives (Kim Hunter). Director George Seaton gives superficial treatment to the cultural differences facing a group of immigrants in New York City, preferring to portray them as quaint eccentrics with predictable problems in contrived circumstances. Well-intentioned but sugar-coated view of America's ethnic melting pot

title: Anything Else
synopsis: Romantic comedy about an aspiring New York writer's (Jason Biggs) rocky love affair with a sexually free-spirited ingenue (Christina Ricci). Though frequently funny, the film, written and directed by Woody Allen (who also appears in a supporting role), retreads material from many of Allen's earlier movies, and its observations about interpersonal relationships are undermined by the filmmaker's angry, fatalistic cynicism. A nihilistic view of morality, several sexual encounters, recurring sexually crude and religiously irreverent humor, an instance of drug abuse, as well as a few instances of profanity
full_review:
At the close of Woody Allen's latest foray into emotional dysfunction, the nebbish New York nihilist counsels his young protege that if he cannot be original in his writing, then steal from the best. Apparently Mr. Allen has done just that, pirating material from his own earlier movies for his new romantic comedy "Anything Else" (Dreamworks).

Told with his patented brand of Borscht Belt wit, "Anything Else" is not so much a new film as a rehashing of several previous works upgraded with a sexy cast of fresh, hip faces -- neurotics for the next generation. In it, Allen returns to familiar thematic territory -- namely, interpersonal relationships in flux.

Taking Allen's place on the psychoanalyst's couch is Jason Biggs as Jerry Falk, an aspiring writer and jokesmith, hacking one-liners for stand-up acts in order to pay his rent and shrink bills. Like most tightly wound denizens of Woody's world, he is a study in existential angst and postmodern promiscuity. Falk's taut psyche becomes the rope in a tug-of-war between his literary ambitions and his sexual cravings, represented by the two characters who, along with Falk, make up the triumvirate around which the narrative revolves.

On one side of the equation is Amanda (Christina Ricci), Falk's libidinous live-in girlfriend, an ingenue whose free-spirited sexuality he finds addictive. Countering her carnality is David Dobel (Woody Allen), a paranoid iconoclast working for the New York City Board of Education who, in between highbrow-referenced rants, helps stoke the young lothario's creative embers.

Despite much of the film's pretentious, literary-laced banter seeming forced and foreign when spoken by its two Gen-X leads, Biggs and Ricci are well cast. Unfortunately, the derivative roles were better suited for Diane Keaton and Allen himself when they performed them in their original manifestations. And while Biggs proves that his acting range need not limit him to comic shtick with baked goods, he at times reverts to mimicking the Manhattan mensch's stuttering shtick. The young actor in effect serves as a protagonist by proxy, since age (and good taste) prevented Allen from playing the part.

To his credit, no one can consistently tell the same joke over and over again and still make it sound as funny as Woody Allen. In a similar vein of praise, no one has yet proved more adroit at painting such romantic images of New York when limited to Gotham's palette of muted grays and faded brick reds, imbuing even innocuous side streets with a sense of asphalt poetry.

Regrettably, the philosophy fueling Allens film's is not as picture perfect. "Anything Else," like much of his oeuvre, is not so much driven by plot but by Allen's particular world view, especially his ideas concerning love, sex and death. "Anything Else" takes its place on Allen's resume as yet another polemic on despair and alienation, a bleak dirge railing against the hostility and meaningless absurdity of life.

While his philosophy -- atheistic nihilism -- saturates every frame, undermining what is arguably one of the most original voices in cinema, his films routinely raise profound theological questions. In fact, the case could be made that no contemporary filmmaker grapples more consistently with the issue of faith for modern man. Yet, according to Allen's own assessment, he is ultimately wrestling alone in a cold barren universe, a fatalistic sentiment given voice in "Anything Else" when one of the characters echoes Nietzsche's grim pronouncement that "God is dead."

This inability to come to grips with a loving, personal Creator opens the door for much of vitriolic -- almost systemic -- cynicism vented by Allen through his characters. Lacking the bittersweet humanity of "Annie Hall," "Anything Else" is pervaded by angry, misogynistic undertones. Middle-class morality is mocked and personal autonomy is extolled as the highest and only good, all in the name of hedonistic libertinism. Sexual intimacy, divorced from morality and stripped of its beauty and sacred dignity, becomes a recreational sport, a purely biological function rating no higher on the cosmic scale than defecation. Valium and cocaine offer the only respites from this postmodern purgatory.

While "Anything Else" continues to explore the dynamics of human relations, it does not have anything profound, or even novel, to say about the subject matter, begging the question of Allen, Is there anything else?

Due to a nihilistic view of morality, several sexual encounters, recurring sexually crude and religiously irreverent humor, an instance of drug abuse, as well as a few instances of profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Anything Goes
synopsis: So-so musical in which a veteran performer (Bing Crosby) agrees to team with a rising newcomer (Donald O'Connor), then each signs a different leading lady (Mitzi Gaynor and Jeanmaire, respectively) while vacationing in Europe, but they resolve the mix-up on the voyage home. Directed by Robert Lewis from Sidney Sheldon's leaden adaptation of the Broadway classic, the result lumbers along with stilted production numbers, surprisingly few laughs and even the few Cole Porter songs from the original seem flat. Romantic complications and some sexual innuendo

title: Any Wednesday
synopsis: Jaded wealthy businessman (Jason Robards) is a good husband six days of the week but Wednesday is reserved for a young lady (Jane Fonda) until his wife (Rosemary Murphy) forces a showdown and his lady friend finds the man of her dreams (Dean Jones). Under Robert Ellis Miller's direction, it's a lively, sappy, broad comedy with some serious overtones about the pain of infidelity

title: Any Which Way You Can
synopsis: An auto repairman and free-lance streetfighter (Clint Eastwood) finds happiness with a skittish prostitute (Sondra Locke). Director Buddy Van Horn's salute to machismo presents an abundance of violence and an atmosphere of sleazy immorality

title: Anzio
synopsis: Huge, sprawling World War II epic about the Allied invasion at Anzio in southern Italy with Robert Mitchum, Peter Falk and Robert Ryan in the thick of combat. Directed by Edward Dmytryk, the movie is graphic in its depiction of the grim images of battle, with appropriately harsh action and language

title: Apache
synopsis: When Geronimo and his band are sent to Florida in chains, one Apache warrior (Burt Lancaster) manages to escape and find his way back to New Mexico where he makes his last stand with wife (Jean Peters) and infant son. Director Robert Aldrich treats the Indians with sympathy while showing the injustices against them, though the movie's clash-of-cultures theme is on the simplistic side, most notably in its corn-grows-in-the-badlands ending. Stylized violence

title: Apache Ambush
synopsis: Lame Western about a Union officer (Bill Williams) at the end of the Civil War trying to get a herd of Texas cattle to Kansas, despite battles with ex-rebels, Mexican bandits and Apache hostiles. Some nasty frontier violence and mild sexual innuendo

Springsteen, it is noteworthy only for the remarkably bad acting of DeForest Kelley as a crazed gunman. Stylized violence

title: Apartment for Peggy
synopsis: Heavy-handed comedy about the post-war housing shortage causing a veteran on the G.I. Bill (William Holden) and his pregnant wife (Jeanne Crain) to move into the unused attic of an aging college professor (Edmund Gwenn) who's decided to commit suicide. title: Apartment Zero
synopsis: Unsettling hothouse thriller set in 1968 Buenos Aires delves into the uneasy relationship between a wealthy, repressed movie theater owner (Colin Firth) and his mysterious tenant (Hart Bochner), a professional assassin.
