title: Apocalypse Now
synopsis: Director Francis Ford Coppola's uneven attempt to transpose Joseph Conrad's "Heart of Darkness" to a Vietnam setting follows an intelligence officer (Martin Sheen) on a mission to kill a renegade Special Forces officer (Marlon Brando) who has set up a private domain deep in the Cambodian interior. Much ambiguous and unresolved soul-searching in between several brilliant battle sequences but stealing the show is Robert Duvall's turn as a gung-ho helicopter commander. Much graphic violence and some rough language

title: Apocalypto
synopsis: Visually bold but extremely bloody action-adventure set in 15th-century Central America about the desperate odyssey of a jungle tribesman (Rudy Youngblood) to get back to his pregnant wife (Dalia Hernandez) and child after he and other members of his tribe are taken captive by the ruling Mayans following the massacre of his village. In what is essentially a chase movie, director Mel Gibson impressively re-creates the world of the Mayans -- the sights, sounds and savagery -- using an indigenous cast speaking entirely in Mayan dialects, but the intoxicating imagery and human drama are undermined by so much gore that, even if historically accurate, the cumulative result registers as gratuitous. Intense and graphic violence, including scenes of slaughter, human sacrifice, beheadings and a man being mauled by a jaguar, disturbing images, some sexual humor and innuendo, a suggested marital encounter, partial nudity, an instance of rough language and a few crude expressions
full_review:
For all its merits, "The Passion of the Christ" was an extremely brutal film. But director Mel Gibson's "Apocalypto" (Touchstone) actually surpasses that movie's violence. Yet despite the troubling amount of blood that pervades almost every scene, the ambitious cinematic work demonstrates Gibson's talent as a filmmaker to tell a story through strong visuals.

Set in 15th-century Central America -- at the twilight of the Mayan civilization -- and using a cast of indigenous actors speaking entirely in Mayan dialects, the tale chronicles the desperate odyssey of a jungle tribesman, Jaguar Paw (Rudy Youngblood), to get back to his family after he and other members of his tribe are taken captive by their ruling neighbors, following the massacre of his village.

Before being captured, he hides his very pregnant wife (Dalia Hernandez) and young son in a pit, where they are threatened by starvation, drowning and vicious monkeys.

The prisoners are marched to a thriving metropolis by the raiding party's leader, Zero Wolf (Raoul Trujillo), and his sadistic second-in-command, Snake Ink (Rodolfo Palacios). There, Jaguar Paw and the others are herded up a pyramid temple to be killed as sacrificial offerings to the local sun god.

Jaguar Paw escapes and takes flight with Zero Wolf and his warriors in pursuit, as the plot kicks into typical jungle chase mode.

While Jaguar Paw's character is fully developed -- his relationships with his wife and father, Flint Sky (Morris Bird), give the action elements emotional traction -- we learn little about the Mayan people beyond their penchant for practical jokes and delight in decapitations.

What Gibson does do impressively is re-create the physical world of the Mayans with its exotic sights and sounds, spectacle and savagery. The intoxicating imagery and human drama, however, are undermined by so much gore that, even if historically accurate, the cumulative result registers as gratuitous.

Gibson has said his film is about "the spark of life that exists even in a culture of death." If he is trying to say something about the self-destructiveness of societies and the role of hope in the cyclical march of civilizations -- and that's not at all clear -- what comes across on-screen is more sanguinary than sanguine.

Despite Gibson's undeniable artistry and serious intent, the relentless barbarity will severely limit the film's appeal.

Subtitles.

The film contains intense and graphic violence, including scenes of slaughter, human sacrifice, beheadings and a man being mauled by a jaguar, disturbing images, some sexual humor and innuendo, a suggested marital encounter, partial nudity, an instance of rough language and a few crude expressions. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Apollo 13
synopsis: Fact-based story of the April 1970 moon launch aborted on its third day in space after an incapacitating problem diminished the oxygen, power and computer systems, making the safe return of the three astronauts (Tom Hanks, Bill Paxton, Kevin Bacon) an almost insurmountable problem for Houston Mission Control. Director Ron Howard keeps emotional tensions taut and suspense levels high throughout this salute to the courage and perseverance of all involved in the dicey rescue mission. Fleeting sexual innuendo and minor profanity

title: Apollo 13 Imax Format
synopsis: The rerelease of the 1995 Academy Award-winning movie is changed only in that the screen image is up to eight stories high, allowing for some startling vistas and close-ups, although panning shots look momentarily blurry. The original capsule review follows: Fact-based story of the April 1970 moon launch aborted on its third day in space after an incapacitating problem diminished the oxygen, power and computer systems, making the safe return of the three astronauts (Tom Hanks, Bill Paxton, Kevin Bacon) an almost insurmountable problem for Houston Mission Control. Director Ron Howard keeps emotional tensions taut and suspense levels high throughout this salute to the courage and perseverance of all involved in the dicey rescue mission. Fleeting sexual innuendo and minor profanity
full_review:
The Academy Award-winning "Apollo 13" (Universal) hit the big screen in 1995, but now it's coming back on a really big screen.

This rerelease marks the first time a live-action motion picture has been converted from standard 35 mm format to the digitally remastered 70 mm Imax format. Imax screens in over 100 theaters across the country project visuals up to eight stories high for exceptional detail and clarity of image.

But since Imax projectors can only accommodate movies no longer than two hours, director Ron Howard had to trim about 20 minutes from his original film. Happily, the cuts included a few mild cuss words, a slightly risque shot of a woman in the shower and an off-duty astronaut getting tipsy. Otherwise, it's the same movie, only a lot larger.

"Apollo 13" was a good choice for the first Hollywood movie to go Imax as the space vistas are even more impressive in the magnified format and some of the close-ups are startling. The panning shots, however, exaggerate the momentary blurriness on screen while the camera is moving.

"Apollo 13" is a wonderful movie and after a few minutes you actually forget about the size and scope of the images as the story takes hold. And that is the challenge for the Imax people : If they remaster a fine film it's all to the good, but a poorly written, acted or directed movie won't play any better simply by virtue of its improved technology.

The original review of the 1995 film follows:

The prognosis looked grim back in April 1970 when three American astronauts in space were ordered to abort a moon landing and instead attempt to return to Earth on diminishing supplies of oxygen and electrical power. Such is the dramatic true story of "Apollo 13" from director Ron Howard and Universal Pictures.

Veteran astronaut Jim Lovell (Tom Hanks) is delighted when his moon mission comes up ahead of schedule and practice sessions with fellow co-pilots Ken Mattingly (Gary Sinise) and Fred Haise (Bill Paxton) demonstrate solid teamwork.

However, when measles-exposed Mattingly is scrubbed at the 11th hour, less experienced Jack Swigert (Kevin Bacon) steps in. Dismissing superstitious warnings that the Apollo mission was number 13, taking off at 13:13 hours and set to land on the moon on April 13, the trio blasts off. Watching takeoff at Cape Canaveral are Mrs. Lovell (Kathleen Quinlan) and Mrs. Haise (Tracy Reiner), who hide their fears behind fake smiles for the press.

Nearing the moon a smooth 55 hours into the flight a routine procedure backfired, followed by an explosion that crippled the spacecraft. With oxygen leaking out and power and guidance systems compromised, Houston Mission Control flight director Gene Kranz (Ed Harris) canceled the moon landing and directed the engineers, mathematicians and scientists assembled to focus exclusively on getting the three men home alive.

Left back on earth when Apollo13 took off, Mattingly's experience in the simulator suddenly becomes crucial in desperately trying to devise new methods of return and re-entry using the minimal power available.

With temperatures plummeting to freezing, the three are forced to abandon the command module and cram into the lunar module, designed for two people with a two-day supply of oxygen. They are four days from the earth's atmosphere. It is doubtful their power will last that long. Dangerous levels of carbon dioxide are building and there is no precedent on how to safely return the damaged spacecraft under such alarming conditions.

With the focus squarely on the human element, Howard quickly builds on the emotional tensions and keeps the suspense level simmering. This is no mean feat when so much of the action -- or waiting really -- takes place within the tight confines of the tiny module. Cutting from space to the intense search for solutions at mission control to Walter Cronkite updating a tense America, the pacing never lags as even more problems present an ominous picture of insurmountable odds.

Only one aspect of the story is thoroughly predictable and staged flatly: the relationship between the two married astronauts and their worried wives, teary-eyed children in tow.

However, the blastoff and re-entry sequences are spectacularly filmed, heart-stopping, and not only give one a sense of the majesty of space but of the mind-boggling preparations necessary to ensure a successful space mission.

Hanks turns in his accustomed fine performance, keeping his imperiled shipmates on an even keel when the finger-pointing begins and refusing to let either believe that Houston knows they are doomed but won't say so. Harris is also especially good as the barely contained flight director for whom "failure is not an option."

If anything, the movie errs on the side of flag-waving, with all the big and little guys at mission control portrayed as both ingenious and heroic in their round-the-clock efforts to save the astronauts. And the closing narration implies the space program should be a higher priority, unnecessarily politicizing the story, which is based on Lovell and Jeffrey Kluger's book, "Lost Moon."

Lay people may find some of the technical jargon a bit daunting but it never gets in the way of the riveting rescue mission at hand.

With Americans starved for heroes in this cynical age, "Apollo 13" offers a slew of them and its box office is likely to reach and stay at celestial heights for many moons.

Because of fleeting sexual innuendo and minor profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

title: Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery
synopsis: Lame James Bond spoof in which a British secret agent and his evil nemesis (Mike Myers in a dual role) are revived after both were cryogenically frozen during the swinging �60s and once again face off with the agent trying to foil the villain�s plot to destroy the planet. Also written by Myers with Jay Roach directing, it�s merely a vanity vehicle for Myers� tasteless asides and leadenly drawn-out skits. Fleeting sexual encounter, some comically intended violence, much crude humor and an instance of profanity
full_review:
Playing a dual role as hero and villain, comic actor Mike Myers portrays a leftover Swinging Sixties single, ``Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery'' (Gramercy).

As written by Myers and directed by Jay Roach, this is a fairly lame spoof of the James Bond 007 movies, opening in 1967 when gaudy, big-toothed secret agent Austin Powers is inexplicably a magnet to all the young women in swinging London. The opening musical number is actually quite zippy and a colorful send-up of the mod look of the era as plastic-booted, miniskirted women pursue their idol.

However, when Powers' nemesis, the villainous Dr. Evil (Myers), chooses to be cryogenically frozen to continue his misdeeds in the future, Powers does likewise.

Presto -- it's 1997 -- Dr. Evil reanimates with Powers in his wake and once again they must face off lest the dastardly doctor activate all the earth's volcanoes simultaneously.

 

That's about it as far as plotting goes with most of the time lavished on -- some would argue wasted on -- Myers' boorish, leering Powers, who is assigned a female partner (Elizabeth Hurley) he expects to bed as easily as in the good old days.

The movie is simply a vanity piece for Myers' brand of tasteless toilet humor and sexual innuendo, in a series of drawn-out skits better suited to late-night TV shows.

But for movie addicts there are the inside joke references to previous films that add a little much-needed fun to the mix because the one-joke premise of both characters being behind the times wears thin pretty darn quickly.

In fact, Powers' ubiquitous crushed velvet suits have more life in them than some of the worn-out sight gags that are trotted out and stretched to death.

 

Clearly in the flick just for the paycheck are Robert Wagner, Michael York, Carrie Fisher and Mimi Rogers in roles you would miss if you blinked.

Myers' fans may enjoy his mocking of all things British, but the movie is hard-pressed to sustain a comic sensibility even for its modest 87 minutes.

Due to a fleeting sexual encounter, some comically intended violence, much crude humor and an instance of profanity, the U.S. Catholic Conference classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned that some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me
synopsis: Mindless sequel to the ‘97 spoof in which the swinging British secret agent (Mike Myers) time travels back to the ‘60s to recover his libido and joins forces with a comely CIA agent (Heather Graham) to again save the world from the wacky machinations of Dr. Evil (Myers in a dual role). As directed by Jay Roach, the silly shenanigans alternate with gross toilet humor and puerile sexual innuendo for a mixed bag of goofy but tasteless entertainment. Comically intended violence, frequent sexual innuendo, crude references, rude gestures and a few instances of profanity
full_review:
Continuing his puerile on-screen antics, Mike Myers plays a trio of parts, including the title role, in the more-of-the-same sequel, ``Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me'' (New Line).

Once again, cocky British secret agent Powers is up against his wacky nemesis, the megalomaniacal Dr. Evil (Myers). And, after Powers' honeymoon goes bust (don't ask; it involves bride Elizabeth Hurley's surefire bust), his new sidekick is the bodacious CIA operative Felicity Shagwell (Heather Graham). The negligible story line is the flip side of the original in which cryogenically frozen Powers and Evil defrosted from the '60s into 1997; now they time-travel back to the Swinging Sixties so the spy can recover his stolen mojo (again, don't ask -- think liquid libido).

Of less importance to Austin is that the world, or at least Washington, must also be saved from Dr. Evil and his creepy cronies. Which brings us to two new villains: Mini-Me (Verne J. Troyer), a knee-high, condensed clone of the evil doctor, and a grotesquely obese Scot (Myers once more) whose character name is too crude to print and whose bodily functions are detailed with repelling regularity.

 

There are sprinklings of goofy comedy and moan-out- loud puns to be endured or enjoyed, but these alternate with gross humor and leering sexual innuendo usually appreciated by underage boys at best. The visual high point in director Jay Roach's unoriginal sequel is a vibrant musical production number with Burt Bacharach playing ``I'll Never Fall in Love Again'' on piano while Elvis Costello serenades Austin and Felicity amid a riot of color and wild prints on the mod and miniskirted passers-by.

On the downside, those viewers previously spared the sight of TV talk-show host Jerry Springer orchestrating chaos among his guests will be subject to just that when Dr. Evil appears in a scene as Springer's verbally and physically combative guest to express his ire that his only son, Scott Evil (Seth Green), isn't living up to his name. A meant-to-be-clever opening-credit scene has Austin gallivanting in the buff through a crowded hotel with precisely positioned credits, foliage, bananas or sausages barely saving the movie from a more restrictive rating.

Visually stretched to the limit, the lame sight gag soon goes limp, although another racy section also dealing with male private parts features some amusing sound editing from scene to scene.

 All in all, the silly sequel breaks no new ground, confident of its continuing appeal after theatrical success and astounding video sales. If anything, it's a triumph of tastelessness in a pop culture enamored of all things dumb and dumber.

� Due to comically intended violence, frequent sexual innuendo, crude references, rude gestures and a few instances of profanity, the U.S. Catholic Conference classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned that some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Appointment in Honduras

title: Apprentice to Murder
synopsis: In rural 1927 Pennsylvania, an itinerant preacher-faith healer (Donald Sutherland) takes a 16-year-old youth (Chad Lowe) under his wing, but their friendship ends when an attempted exorcism causes the death of a local hermit (Knut Husebo), seemingly possessed by the devil. title: Apres Vous
synopsis: Affecting and funny French comedy about a do-gooder (Daniel Auteuil) who rescues a suicidal sad sack (Jose Garcia) who's been dumped by his girlfriend (Sandrine Kiberlain), and attempts to secretly bring the couple back together, but finds himself falling in love with her instead. Director Pierre Salvadori's film, with perfectly judged performances, gets off to a leisurely start, but as the story builds so do the plot complications and the laughs, buttressed by good Samaritan messages about caring, generosity, friendship and kindness. Subtitles. Sporadic rough and crude words, mild profanity, some sexual banter, casual premarital relationships
full_review:
"Apres Vous" ("After You") (Paramount Classics) is an affecting and funny French comedy about a do-gooder, Antoine (Daniel Auteuil), who rescues neurotic sad-sack
Louis (Jose Garcia) from hanging himself in a park.

It turns out Louis has been dumped by his girlfriend, Blanche (Sandrine Kiberlain), now working in a florist shop.

Antoine, who works as a maitre d' at a local restaurant, takes in the lumpish Louis, over the objections of his own girlfriend, Christine (Marilyn Canto), and eventually gets him a job at his restaurant as a sommelier. His audition for the job is quite hilarious, as Antoine attempts to throw him clues behind the back of the brasserie's owner (Michele Moretti).

When he lands the job as wine steward, he follows Antoine around like a puppy dog, and continues to be utterly inept. "There's more wine on the tablecloths than in the glasses," the owner notes wryly. Louis seems to barely respond to or appreciate all of Antoine's efforts, which even include paying his medical bills, but Antoine is determined to be a good Samaritan.

Furthermore, Antoine surreptitiously attempts to interest Blanche in her old flame, but Blanche now has a new fiance, whom Antoine discovers to be a ne'er-do-well. Antoine contrives to have Blanche witness his infidelity, but the fianc� still pursues her.

Before long, Antoine finds himself falling in love with Blanche, plunging him into a morass of confusion, and setting up a role reversal with the depressed Louis.

After a bouncy credit sequence suggesting a brisk French farce, director Pierre Salvadori's film takes a little time to get going, but as the story builds so do the plot complications and the laughs, and the film lives up to its farcical promise and is full of felicitous and telling touches.

The plot imparts worthy messages about caring, generosity, friendship and kindness.

Against all odds, Antoine refuses to give up on Louis. Essentially, it's a buddy movie, on a higher level than the kind turned out by Hollywood. There's greater complexity here, including the betrayal that can often underlie friendship.

The acting is superb, with the peerless Auteuil giving a brilliantly nuanced performance, his expressions conveying each passing emotion. He's well-matched every step of the way by Garcia whose depressed phobic personality morphs into growing confidence under Auteuil's unwavering support.

If you stick with "Apres Vous" after its leisurely start, you'll be rewarded with a touching and wise comedy of human relationships, and a lesson that helping your fellow man can bring surprising rewards.

Subtitles.

The film contains sporadic rough and crude words, mild profanity, some sexual banter and casual premarital relationships. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: April Fool's Day

title: April in Paris

Romantic complications and sexual innuendo keyed to a bogus wedding

title: April Love

title: Aqua Teen Hunger Force Colon Movie Film for Theaters
synopsis: The cult TV cartoon about pointlessness becomes a highly uneven 86-minute feature film with series regulars Frylock, Master Shake and Meatwad involved in a surreal plot about an exercise machine that threatens civilization. Some of the gags are funny, but writer-directors Matt Maiellaro and Dave Willis repeat them to death, and use far raunchier material than even the highly flexible standards of basic cable allow. A great deal of rough and crude language and profanity, pervasive sexual and scatological humor and an implied sexual encounter, cartoon violence and drug references
full_review:
Clearly skewed to the 18- to 34-year-old male who likes his comedy surreal and peppered with raunchy non sequiturs, "Aqua Teen Hunger Force Colon Movie Film for Theaters" (First Look) is the feature-length version of the Cartoon Network's late-night cult hit, here untrammeled by not even the not-so-stringent standards of basic cable.

Writer-directors Matt Maiellaro and Dave Willis, who also provide some of the voices, revel in images and language that are meant to shock, albeit in a humorous way. Although it wears its sophomoric elements as a badge of honor, the inhabitants of "Aqua Teen," unlike those of "South Park," neither riff on pop culture nor offer ponderously shallow moral lessons. This is a self-contained world, based in a shabby New Jersey tract house, where the point usually is that there is no point.

With all that, there is still a coherent and conventional plot for Frylock (a floating, brainy box of fries), Master Shake (a milkshake who's mostly id) and Meatwad (a dimwitted and oddly flexible meatball) involving an exercise machine that spawns destructive alien robots, and an intentionally aimless subplot about their origins, lampooning the style of superhero epics.

Some of the gags are funny if repeated to death, and needless to say, there are the inevitable lifeless stretches that occur when a TV cartoon designed to be shown in 11-minute segments is stretched to 86 minutes. Even were it not for the flagged elements below, this highly uneven film would be strictly for die-hard fans.

The film contains a great deal of rough and crude language and profanity, pervasive sexual and scatological humor and an implied sexual encounter, cartoon violence and drug references. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. title: Arabella

title: Ararat
synopsis: Powerful tale of a contemporary Armenian family's journey from dysfunction to healing by facing the ghosts of their collective cultural past -- the genocidal extermination of Armenians by Ottoman Turkish forces in 1915. Acclaimed Canadian writer-director Atom Egoyan masterfully weaves past and present in this provocative exploration of the nature of truth and the repercussions of denial, although his humanistic perspective does not explore any transcendent or redemptive value in suffering. Explicit violence, depictions of torture and a rape, a sexual encounter with nudity, sporadic profanity and some rough language
full_review:
"Ararat" (Miramax) is a powerful tale of a contemporary Armenian family's journey from dysfunction to healing, as family members come to grips with the ghosts of their collective cultural past -- the genocidal extermination of Armenians by Ottoman Turkish forces in 1915.

Acclaimed Canadian writer-director Atom Egoyan masterfully weaves past and present, subtly fashioning a tapestry of the human condition, as well as a provocative indictment of man's capacity for cruelty. Divergent storylines blend seamlessly in this compelling exploration of the nature of truth, and the repercussions of denial on both a grand and an intimate scale.

Raffi (newcomer David Alpay), an idealistic young Armenian living in Toronto with his estranged mother, Ani (Arsinee Khanjian), cannot escape the shadow of the death of his Armenian nationalist father, killed while attempting to assassinate a Turkish official. Raffi's romantic involvement with his disaffected stepsister, Cecilia (Marie-Josee Croze), has created an emotional rift between him and Ani. Ani, an art historian at the university, finds solace in her near-religious obsession with a painting, "The Artist and His Mother," by Arshile Gorky (1904-1948), an Armenian considered by many as one of the pioneers of abstract expressionism.

Before emigrating to America, Gorky survived the Armenian genocide, which resulted in the extermination of two-thirds of the Armenian population, a crime still denied by the Turkish government (Hitler himself quelled his officers' hesitancy to proceed with their 'final solution' by asking, "Does anyone even remember the Armenian genocide?"). Ani's knowledge of Gorky's life and work lands her a position as a consultant on a film about the tragic events of 1915 by legendary (but fictitious) director Edward Saroyan (Charles Aznavour), who lost his own mother in the massacre.

This "film-within-a-film," based on the historical eyewitness account written by an American missionary, is the nexus used by Egoyan to link past and present. Forced to confront the painful legacy of these atrocities, Ani and Raffi find the resolve to exorcise the personal demons that have tormented their relationship.

While capturing the barbarity inflicted on the Armenian people with disturbingly graphic effectiveness, the film fails to plumb the profundity of the enigma of evil. Egoyan seems content to hold a mirror up to man's darker nature rather than offer any illumination of the mystery of suffering, though in the face of such unspeakable horror any exegesis admittedly would be woefully inadequate.

Religious references and iconography permeate much of the film, yet the divine element of the mystery of suffering is noticeably absent. Several characters pose the eternal existential question "why?" but the filmmaker embraces a somewhat humanistic view, lowering their gaze from the heavens to each other. Egoyan's choices suggest that we must find or make our own answers by sheer acts of will or creativity when confronted with such senseless evil, and not search for any transcendent or redemptive value in suffering.

Though several sequences are difficult to watch, Egoyan, who is himself of Armenian descent, deserves credit for bringing attention to a dark -- and, unfortunately, neglected -- chapter of 20th-century history and for reminding us that "what is destroyed in genocide are not only human lives, but the very imprint of humanity in us."

Due to explicit violence, depictions of torture and a rape, a sexual encounter, nudity, sporadic profanity and some rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Arch of Triumph
synopsis: Muddled melodrama in which an Austrian doctor (Charles Boyer) hiding from the Nazis in 1938 Paris falls in love with a troubled woman (Ingrid Bergman), but loses her to a former lover while undertaking the murder of a visiting Gestapo officer (Charles Laughton), then is interned as an illegal alien at the start of World War II. Directed by Lewis Milestone from Erich Maria Remarque's novel, the tangled romance is too contrived to earn sympathy, though the movie's depiction of the uncertainties of refugee life still holds interest. Stylized violence, implied sexual relationships and a veiled reference to a quack abortion

title: Arctic Tale
synopsis: Queen Latifah delightfully narrates an absorbing story charting the parallel journeys of a polar bear cub and a walrus pup in the Arctic Circle from birth to maturity, and showing how they manage to survive a changing environment with ever-decreasing ice seriously impeding both their natural habitat and their ability to obtain food. Co-directors and cinematographers Adam Ravetch and Sarah Robertson have fashioned an impressively photographed "fable" out of the challenges facing these creatures in light of global warming, rendering the film a vivid animal counterpart to Al Gore's "An Inconvenient Truth." Though restrained in its presentation, the film includes some images of animal violence and death, perhaps precluding viewing by the very young
full_review:
"Arctic Tale" (Paramount Classics) is an absorbing story charting the parallel journeys of Nanu, a polar bear cub, and Seela, a walrus pup, in the Arctic Circle, from birth to maturity. It shows how they manage to survive a changing environment with ever-decreasing ice seriously impeding both their natural habitat and their ability to obtain food.

These are new challenges never before encountered by these species, we are informed in the film's eco-friendly narration, thanks to Linda Woolverton, Mose Richards and Kristin Gore's whimsical script.

The scenes of young Nanu and Seela being nurtured by their mothers -- and in the case of Seela, by another walrus referred to as Auntie, who takes Seela under her wing -- are extraordinary. (Auntie will eventually make the ultimate sacrifice when the walrus herd is attacked by a big bear.)

Other highlights include Nanu's mother teaching Nanu how to hunt walruses, and later, permanently driving Nanu away from her when she cannot care for both of them. This scene, like all the others, is given a highly anthropomorphized spin, but on the whole, you willingly succumb to the storytelling.

The close-ups of the walruses are a particular revelation, as we see what a close-knit community they are, and how they care for their young, memorizing each other's faces with their whiskers.

How much of this so-called "fable" can be chalked up to dramatic license is difficult to determine, but events play out plausibly.

An inspired choice as narrator, Queen Latifah strikes just the right tone: both knowledgeable and accessible.

Co-directors and cinematographers Adam Ravetch and Sarah Robertson (husband and wife) have fashioned an impressively photographed National Geographic production (with Visionbox Films). The challenges facing these creatures in light of global warming render the film a vivid animal counterpart to "An Inconvenient Truth," written by Kristin Gore's dad, Al.

The admirable environmental message -- by 2040, the film asserts, the summer sea ice could be almost completely gone -- is clear enough without a somewhat cloying credit sequence at the end, with children telling us such factoids that if we turn off a light bulb we'll be saving the planet. But the film itself is a winner.

Though restrained in its presentation, the film includes some images of animal violence and death, perhaps precluding viewing by the very young. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-I -- general patronage. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is G -- general audiences. All ages admitted.

title: Are We Done Yet?
synopsis: Only fairly amusing sequel to 2005's "Are We There Yet?" as a couple (Ice Cube and Nia Long), along with her two kids, relocate to the great outdoors and a huge house desperately in need of refurbishing. Director Steve Carr trots out every cliche imaginable and relies too heavily on slapstick humor, but the film does carry a strong affirmation of family and friendship and virtually no objectionable material. Brief innuendo, a comedic physical scuffle and other slapstick violence, scenes of drinking, marital discord and a tense nongraphic birth scene
full_review:
"Are We Done Yet?" (Columbia/Revolution) is an only fairly amusing sequel to 2005's "Are We There Yet?" The script is a reworking of the Cary Grant-Myrna Loy screwball classic "Mr. Blandings Builds His Dream House," which also inspired the 1986 Tom Hanks-Shelley Long hit ''The Money Pit."

The film begins with clever animated credits that reintroduce us to the main characters. Now married, Nick Parsons (Ice Cube) and Suzanne (Nia Long) and her two kids from a previous marriage are living in cramped harmony in his old bachelor pad.

When Suzanne announces she's pregnant with twins, Nick decides to relocate his family to the great outdoors and a huge house desperately in need of refurbishing. The new addition to the cast is Chuck (John C. McGinley), a real estate agent who turns out to wear many more hats, including that of "baby whisperer," who wins over everyone in the family but Nick.

Predictable shenanigans ensue but there's way too much slapstick, even though done in cartoon style. (No matter how many times Nick falls through the roof, he is never really hurt.)

The film veers into buddy-movie territory, with overbearing Chuck challenging frustrated Nick into fixing up the house himself. Of course, Chuck and Nick bond, Suzanne goes into labor while in the house, and by the film's conclusion everyone has learned his or her share of life lessons.

Director Steve Carr ("Next Friday") trots out every cliche imaginable, but the film does have a strong affirmation of family and friendship, and virtually no objectionable material. Another plus are several montage sequences, accompanied by some good R&B music.

The film contains brief innuendo, a comedic physical scuffle and other slapstick violence, scenes of drinking, marital discord and a tense nongraphic birth scene. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested. Some material may not be suitable for children.

title: Are We There Yet??
synopsis: Leaden road comedy about a smooth-talking skirt-chaser (Ice Cube) with no patience for kids who gets more than he bargained for when he falls for a pretty divorcee (Nia Long) and volunteers to taxi her two mischievous children (Philip Daniel Bolden and Aleisha Allen) from Portland, Ore., to Vancouver, British Columbia, where she is staying on business, so they can all be together on New Year's Eve. Directed by Brain Levant, this film runs out of gas early, leaving viewers to endure a bumpy ride of scatological sight gags and mean-spirited mishaps (making it unsuitable for younger adolescents) which, unfortunately, dampens its sincere, albeit sentimental, message about the importance of family and parenthood. Recurring crude humor and comic violence, and some mildly crass language
full_review:
A smooth-talking skirt-chaser gets more than he bargained for when he volunteers to taxi his girlfriend's two children from Portland, Ore., to Vancouver, British Columbia, in the leaden road comedy "Are We There Yet?" (Columbia).

Ice Cube stars as Nick Persons, a former minor-league ballplayer and major-league ladies' man who runs a sports memorabilia shop in the Pacific Northwest.

As an avowed bachelor, Nick possesses a deep-seated dislike of kids -- "they're like cockroaches, except you can't squish 'em" -- which supplies the story's conflict when he falls for pretty divorcee Suzanne (Nia Long) with two rug rats (Philip Daniel Bolden and Aleisha Allen) at home.

For their part, the kids are under the delusion that their deadbeat dad will come back and that they'll again be a happy family. To ensure that their mom stays off the dating market, they scare away prospective suitors; one unlucky gentleman caller gets pelted with paint balls.

When Suzanne is called out of town for business (she is a party planner and is catering a New Year's Eve shindig in Vancouver), Nick -- hoping to score some points -- offers to baby-sit and ferry the mischievous youngsters to Canada in time for a reuniting round of "Auld Lang Syne."

Of course, all this goes against Nick's better judgment, not to mention the advice of his computer-animated conscience, a Satchel Paige bobblehead doll (voiced by Tracy Morgan) he keeps on his dashboard.

After attempts by plane and train prove disastrous, Nick bites the bullet and piles the tykes into his prize possession, a shiny, souped-up SUV, which you just know will be scrap metal by the end credits.

Anything that could go wrong does, as the terror twins use everything in their repertoire to make the trip a living hell for Nick.

While Ice Cube has undeniable charisma, the film runs out of gas early, leaving viewers to endure 94 minutes of scatological sight gags and unfunny -- and often mean-spirited -- mishaps (making it unsuitable for younger adolescents). You know you're in for a bumpy ride when the film's idea of a punch line involves carsickness and kicks to the groin. The picture's sadistic slapstick echoes that of "Home Alone," but at least in that movie the bungling burglars were getting their just rewards. Here, Nick is victimized for no apparent reason other than to wring a few cheap laughs out of the movie's flat-tire script.

Director Brian Levant tries to elicit some sympathy for the kids with some late sentimentality and by making one of them asthmatic, but for much of the film they come across as selfish, ill-mannered brats.

Buried somewhere beneath the potty jokes is a sincere message about the importance of family and parenthood, but by the time it surfaces the question being asked is not "Are we there yet?" but "Is it over yet?"

The film contains recurring crude humor and comic violence, as well as some mildly crass language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

title: Arguing the World
synopsis: Feature documentary on the life and times of writers Irving Kristol, Nathan Glazer, Daniel Bell and the late Irving Howe, all of whom attended New York's City College during the 1930s, then went their different ways in the political ferment of post-war America. Writer-director Joseph Dorman uses vintage newsreel footage as well as interviews with the writers and others in providing a nostalgic look at the urban culture from which they came as well as a lively chronicle of how their views grew increasingly conservative over the years. Deals with matters beyond the experience of youngsters

title: Arise, My Love
synopsis: Uneven romantic comedy in which an eager reporter (Claudette Colbert) creates her own scoop by rescuing an American flier (Ray Milland) from a Spanish firing squad, then is fired for being with him instead of on the job when Hitler invades Poland, but gets rehired when the liner taking both of them back to the States is torpedoed. Director Mitchell Leisen has lots of fun with the romantic fluff but the laughs are chilled by the heavy period atmosphere and warnings about the Nazi menace. Veiled sexual situations and innunedo

title: Arizona
synopsis: When a Tucson frontierswoman (Jean Arthur) faces loss of her booming freight business to a cheating competitor (Porter Hall) and his Confederate partner (Warren William), she gets some needed help from a smitten cowboy (William Holden). Directed by Wesley Ruggles, the plot is weak but sturdy enough to anchor the action, including Apache raids, North-South rivalries, well-staged shootouts and a fitful courtship that ultimately proves quite charming. Stylized violence and assorted villainies

title: Arizona Bound
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Spencer Bennett offers another adventure of the Rough Riders (Buck Jones, Tim McCoy and Raymond Hatton), retired lawmen who join forces this time to save a desert stagecoach line from a gang of robbers. Tame action fare

title: Arizona Bushwackers
synopsis: Routine Western directed by Lesley Selander in which a Confederate agent (Howard Keel) stops a renegade (Scott Brady) from selling a cache of rebel guns to the Indians and the movie concludes happily with the end of the Civil War. Stylized violence

title: Arizona Raiders
synopsis: Formula Western in which one of Quantrill's Raiders (Audie Murphy) is let out of prison after the Civil War to help the Arizona Rangers stamp out the last of the now-outlawed band. Directed by William Witney, the flimsy plot is held together by the usual action scenes but only the concluding segment involving a small Indian mission holds any interest. Stylized violence

title: Arizona Whirlwind
synopsis: Grade-B Western starring Ken Maynard, Hoot Gibson and Bob Steele as a team of lawmen who find a gang of jewel thieves (!) operating out of a frontier town. Director Robert Tansey's formula shoot-em-up ends with a race against time to free a boy locked in a bank safe. Stylized violence

title: Armed and Dangerous
synopsis: Posing as social spoof, this failed slapstick movie concerns security guards (John Candy and Eugene Levy) who fight organized crime by being more aggressive and anti-social than the criminals. Violent and destructive imagery sprinkled with profanity and sexual sight gags that fail as burlesque

title: Armored Attack
synopsis: (see: " The North Star ")

title: Army of Darkness
synopsis: Mindless sword-and-sorcery movie about a present-day macho guy (Bruce Campbell) zapped back to the Dark Ages where he must rescue a damsel in distress (Embeth Davidtz) and do battle with legions of undead skeletons before he can return to his own time. Director Sam Raimi's inept attempt at comic horror fails miserable, save for a few briefly interesting special effects. Frequent comic violence and mild sexual innuendo

title: Arnold
synopsis: At least half of this creaky horror-comedy takes place in a fog-bound graveyard, and all of it centers around a well-heeled, well-preserved cadaver (in the title role). The gimmick derives from a condition in the deceased's will that his wife (Stella Stevens), who married him hastily just after his demise, has to keep him near her for the rest of her life, a condition that leads to a number of murders and other preposterous goings-on. All director George Fenady can do with this bizarre material is to play it for laughs and these do come at reasonably close intervals

title: Around the Bend
synopsis: Offbeat but appealing story of intergenerational bonding as ex-con grandfather (Christopher Walken), single dad (Josh Lucas), and young son (Jonah Bobo) travel to Albuquerque spreading the ashes of great-grandfather Henry (Michael Caine). Though writer-director Jordan Roberts's film -- which, at its core, is all about reconciliation and forgiveness -- is not without its flaws, he has fashioned a winning film with excellent performances, touching sentiment, considerable humor, an eclectic soundtrack, and pretty scenery to counterbalance what could otherwise have been a downbeat story. Some rough and crude language, brief bloody images, and an irreligious dispersal of ashes
full_review:
You might think a story about two men and a child traveling around the Southwest to scatter the ashes of the family patriarch would be a total turnoff. Yet, in spite of this seemingly downbeat theme, "Around the Bend" (Warner Independent) is an affecting, albeit offbeat, tale of the loving bond among four generations of males, and a touching story of healing and forgiveness.

Eccentric family patriarch Henry Lair (Michael Caine) lives with his recently separated grandson, Jason (Josh Lucas), who works in a bank, and 6-year-old great-grandson, Zack (Jonah Bobo), as well as a daffy Danish nanny (Glenne Headly) who is unaccountably enamored of horror films.

One day, a scruffy man shows up on their doorstep, and it turns out to be Jason's father, Turner (Christopher Walken), an ex-heroin addict who abandoned the family when Jason was 2. Henry is overjoyed that his long-lost son has returned at last, and insists the four go out and celebrate at his idea of the paragon of elegant dining: Kentucky Fried Chicken.

Turner's plan to leave town after this emotionally tumultuous homecoming is thwarted by Henry's death in the KFC restaurant, after which Turner and Jason discover Henry had left detailed instructions on how he'd like his remains handled. Having predicted his beloved dog would die shortly after he did, Henry asks that their ashes be commingled and scattered in an elaborate ritual that involves traveling through the desert to Albuquerque, N.M., and eating at specific KFCs until they reach the final destination.

Along the way, Jason finally vents his long-pent-up frustration at his early abandonment by Turner, while the latter comes to value the son -- and now grandson -- he had never known. Zack observes the dynamic between the adults with a wisdom well beyond his years.

The film climaxes with the highly charged revelation of circumstances of why Turner walked out on the family years before, but ends on a sweet and poignant note.

On the whole, this is a lovely, small-scale film that holds your interest throughout its 85 minutes. The performances are predictably fine, and even though Caine's character dies very near the beginning, his presence lingers memorably throughout. Young Bobo is particularly endearing, and gives one of those astonishingly good kid performances.

Jordan Roberts -- who was inspired by his own relationship with an absentee father to explore themes of grief and estrangement -- has written a script that doesn't always avoid cliche, and though for the most part the film successfully avoids cheap sentiment, there are some occasional lapses.

Some cheerfully eclectic songs on the soundtrack are astutely used to undercut the downbeat aspects of the story, though Leon Russell's "A Song for You" is oddly jarring when it comes up during a pivotal plot development.

There is some salty language, some of which is said in the presence of Zack -- and the spreading of the ashes would be considered disrespectful from a Catholic viewpoint -- but the themes of forgiveness and reconciliation are what really matter here.

Because of some rough and crude language, brief bloody images and an irreligious dispersal of ashes, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Around the World in 72 Days
synopsis: An "American Experience" biography of crusading 19th century journalist, Nellie Bly, who posed as a mental patient, chorus girl and domestic for her exposes then became the most famous woman on Earth in 1889 by duplicating the fictional voyage described in Jules Verne's "Around the World in 80 Days." Documentarian Christine Lesiak entertainingly chronicles a pioneering feminist whose "stunt reporting" sometimes led to social reform and paved the way for future female journalists

title: Around the World in 80 Days
synopsis: In Mike Todd's lavish production of the Jules Verne classic, an English armchair adventurer (David Niven) makes a bet that he can encircle the globe within 80 days and sets off with his valet (Cantinflas) to prove it. Michael Anderson's direction makes the most of the cultural splendor of the late Victorian period, visits just about every scenic locale worth a postcard and offers an all-star marathon of cameo appearances. The result is a wonderful romp that is great fun for all

title: Around the World in 80 Days
synopsis: Entertaining extravaganza set in Victorian times about an eccentric English inventor (Steve Coogan) who, along with his trusty, chop-socky valet (Jackie Chan), embarks on a globetrotting steam-age adventure in order to win an outrageous wager that they can do what the title says. Based on the classic yarn by Jules Verne, the film, directed by Frank Coraci, combines lavish action sequences, romance and madcap comedy in serving up a family-friendly spectacle that is both campy and clever -- and, as an added attraction, quite fun for all but the youngest viewers. Recurring action violence, some mildly crude language and humor, and brief drunkenness
full_review:
An eccentric inventor and his chop-socky sidekick embark on a globetrotting adventure in order to win an outrageous wager in the lavish, family-friendly romp, "Around the World in 80 Days" (Disney).

Based on the classic yarn by Jules Verne and directed by Frank Coraci, the film combines action, romance and heaping dollops of madcap comedy to serve up an entertaining, continent-hopping spectacle that is both campy and clever -- and, as an added attraction -- quite fun.

Opening in Victorian-era London, the film stars Steve Coogan as the visionary techno-tinkerer Phileas Fogg, an armchair adventurer who, desperate to gain the respect of his crusty critics at the stuffy Royal Academy of Science, makes an outlandish gentleman's bet to circumnavigate the globe in no more than 80 days.

Action-star Jackie Chan co-stars as Passepartout (pronounced "passport to"), his lightning-limbed traveling companion whom viewers first meet fleeing a phalanx of bumbling Bobbies after robbing the Bank of London. As it turns out, Passepartout, whose real name is Lao Xing, was sent from China to recover from the bank's vault a sacred jade statue of Buddha which was stolen from his village by a female Asian assassin named General Fang (Karen Joy Morris). Also along for the riotous ride is Monique (Cecile de France), a French tart with an eye for art and a nose for adventure.

Their journey by land, air and sea takes the trio on a whirlwind tour of the world's most exotic locales, including pit stops for centerpiece action sequences in Paris, Istanbul, India, China and the American West. But their path is fraught with obstacles, set by Lord Kelvin (Jim Broadbent), the stuffed-shirt head of the Royal Academy who, working in cahoots with Fang, wants to discredit Phileas.

Along the way they learn gushy lessons about friendship and loyalty, encountering a host of celebrity cameos including Luke and Owen Wilson as the Wright brothers, Kathy Bates as Queen Victoria and a shock-wigged Arnold Schwarzenegger as a vain Turkish vizier.

Taken for what it is -- eye-candy -- "Around the World in 80 Days" is surprisingly satisfying. Like the helium that lifts Phileas' balloon high above the Champs d'Elysee, the film's refreshingly lighthearted levity elevates it above the smash-and-crash action clones glutting summer screens. Much of this is owed to the appealing pairing of Coogan and Chan (roles played by David Niven and the inimitable Cantinflas in the Oscar-winning 1956 film version), whose onscreen chemistry makes up for many of the flick's shortcomings. And while Jules Verne probably didn't envision kung-fu fights along the Rive Gauche, Chan never ceases to amaze with his high-flying feats, and feet.

Though it runs a bit too long, "Around the World in 80 Days" is that rare kind of film that can be appreciated by the entire family, though some parents may feel the action is too intense for very young children. Older kids will have a ball with Fogg's goofy gizmos and will get a kick -- literally -- out of the martial-arts choreography, including one scene where a brawl turns into an impromptu lesson in impressionistic painting.

Like Phileas Fogg, you may just want to bet on this one!

Due to recurring action violence, some mildly crude language and humor, and brief drunkenness, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-- parental guidance suggested.

title: Around the World Under the Sea
synopsis: Producer-director Andrew Marton's underseas adventure with scientists (Lloyd Bridges, David McCallum, Brian Kelly, Shirley Eaton) setting earthquake warning devices on the ocean floor and meeting monsters of the deep should appeal to most youngsters

title: Arrivederci, Baby!
synopsis: Dull, tasteless and vulgar vehicle for Tony Curtis clownishly playing a con man who marries and murders a series of wealthy women. Written, produced and directed by Ken Hughes, the attempts at humor fall flat making the proceedings all the more vulgar and pointless

title: Arrowhead
synopsis: Dark Western in which an Indian-hating Army scout (Charlton Heston) helps the post's new commander (Brian Keith) put down an Apache uprising led by a messianic warrior (Jack Palance). Directed by Charles Marquis Warren, there's plenty of action but most of it is as unconvincing as the vicious hostiles. Nasty Indian stereotypes and stylized violence

title: Arrow in the Dust
synopsis: Wooden Western directed by Lesley Selander in which an Army deserter (Sterling Hayden) masquerading as an officer winds up saving a wagon train from maurauding Apaches. Frontier violence

title: Arruza
synopsis: Documentary by Budd Boetticher on the final years of the legendary Mexican bullfighter, Carlos Arruza. Narrated by Anthony Quinn, it fails to explore the make-up of the man, presenting instead a cold, distant portrait of the torero seen totally from the outside. What will impress most viewers, however, is only the foolish, cruel and debasing side of this contest between man and beast

title: Arsenic and Old Lace
synopsis: Droll adaptation of Joseph Kesselring's madcap stage hit about an irascible theater critic (Cary Grant) whose dotty maiden aunts (Josephine Hull and Jean Adair) serve lonely old men elderberry wine laced with poison. Director Frank Capra's black comedy features a great cast, including Boris Karloff and Peter Lorre as criminal interlopers, but the wacky proceedings are not for all tastes

title: Artemisia
synopsis: Melodramatic French production based on the life of 17th-century Italian artist Artemisia Gentileschi (Valentina Cervi) who at age 17 falls in love with her drawing instructor (Miki Manojlovic), but after her father discovers them in bed, the lover is sentenced to prison for rape and she goes off to start her own painting career. Writer-director Agnes Merlet changes the historical record of the 1612 rape trial into an upbeat feminist romance which turns Artemisia into a modern woman breaking with the artistic and moral conventions of her time. Subtitles. Several fairly graphic sex scenes, some nudity and occasional rough language

title: Arthur
synopsis: A rich and spoiled young man named Arthur (Dudley Moore), who spends his days and nights drinking to excess and pursuing all sorts of women, falls in love with a waitress (Liza Minnelli). Director Steve Gordon tries to distill humor from the playboy's sexual weaknesses and from his indecision about meaningful commitment but most of the humor comes from John Gielgud's performance as the snobbish, harsh-tongued valet. Adult situations

title: Arthur
synopsis: The utterly frivolous, merrily alcoholic heir (Russell Brand) to a billion-dollar corporate fortune is threatened with disinheritance unless he marries a domineering executive (Jennifer Garner) who plans to curb his wayward lifestyle. A chance encounter with a working-class New York City tour guide (Greta Gerwig), however, leaves the previously heedless playboy smitten and forced to choose between luxury and love. Though director Jason Winer's remake of Steve Gordon's popular 1981 comedy intermittently touches on the limits of materialism, it gives a pass to its main character's promiscuity and tends to trivialize his problem drinking. The fitful laughs on offer mostly derive from the tart observations of Helen Mirren as the man-boy's affectionate but not uncritical British nanny -- the distaff counterpart to John Gielgud's butler in the original. A fleeting nongraphic bedroom scene, an obscured nude image, brief irreverent humor, frequent sexual references, a couple of uses of profanity and a few crude terms
full_review:
Though hardly a cinematic landmark, writer-director Steve Gordon's 1981 comedy "Arthur" was one of that year's most popular films and garnered two Academy Awards: one for John Gielgud as best supporting actor, the other for the pleasant -- if somewhat bland -- "Arthur's Theme (Best That You Can Do)," as best original song.

Flash-forward 30 years and director Jason Winer's eponymous remake (Warner Bros.) just about matches that modest legacy, presenting -- as did the original -- a mixed bag of both moral and aesthetic qualities.

Russell Brand takes Dudley Moore's place in the title role. As the utterly frivolous, merrily alcoholic heir to a billion-dollar corporate fortune, Arthur Bach lurches from one headline-worthy mishap to another, aided and abetted by his chauffer Bitterman (Luis Guzman).

Exasperated by such antics, his mother Vivienne (Geraldine James) threatens to disinherit Arthur unless he agrees to marry Susan (Jennifer Garner), a domineering executive in the higher reaches of the family's conglomerate who plans to curb his wayward lifestyle.

A chance encounter with Naomi (Greta Gerwig), a working-class New York City tour guide, however, leaves Arthur -- heretofore a heedless playboy -- smitten and forced to choose between luxury and love.

Observing her charge's adventures, through it all, is Helen Mirren as Hobson, the man-boy's affectionate but not uncritical British nanny -- the distaff counterpart to Gielgud's tart-tongued butler in the original.

As Gielgud did before her, Mirren provides most of the fitful laughs on offer by delivering a sophisticated running commentary on Arthur's inexhaustible childishness. (In some ways, both versions of this relationship recall the dynamic between comic novelist P.G. Wodehouse's delightfully dim man-about-town Bertie Wooster and Bertie's supremely urbane "gentleman's gentleman," Jeeves.)

Peter Baynham's script intermittently touches on the limits of materialism, especially as plot developments leave Arthur feeling increasingly isolated and no longer distracted by the partying and toys (e.g., a magnetic bed that seemingly floats in mid-air) that once cheered him.

At one point, in fact, Arthur re-enacts -- albeit comically -- a pivotal incident in the life of St. Francis of Assisi by divesting himself of the formal, upper-class clothing that symbolizes both his ultimately unsatisfying wealth and his exalted but restrictive social status.

Yet the movie gives a pass to Arthur's promiscuity, and tends to trivialize his problem drinking -- early scenes of which, indeed, serve as unabashed product placement for Maker's Mark, a pricy brand of Kentucky bourbon.

The film contains a fleeting nongraphic bedroom scene, an obscured nude image, brief irreverent humor, frequent sexual references, a couple of uses of profanity and a few crude terms. The Catholic News Service classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Arthur 2: On the Rocks
synopsis: Comedy sequel about the perpetually drunk millionaire wastrel (Dudley Moore) whose marriage to a perky waitress-shoplifter (Liza Minnelli) is threatened by a tycoon (Stephen Elliott) and his daughter (Cynthia Sikes). Though director Bud Yorkin adds some weight with a subplot about the couple's adoption of a baby, alcoholism is no laughing matter. Some vulgar language

title: Arthur Rubenstein -- Love of Life
synopsis: Extraordinary documentary about one of the world's greatest piano virtuosos is concerned not only with music but also with humanity. Directed by Francois Reichenbach, it captures the artist and the man at age 82 and is equally important as a commentary on classical music as it is a testament to a rare human being. Of far greater appeal than the specialized art audience

title: Article 99
synopsis: Fast-paced drama set in a veterans' hospital where a dedicated doctor (Ray Liotta) and his new intern (Kiefer Sutherland) continually run afoul of the hospital's budget-conscious director (John Mahoney). Directed by Howard Deutch, the choppy mix of comedy and dramatic exaggeration focuses attention on the plight of sick and disabled veterans at the mercy of government bureaucracy. Brief violence, including several graphic shots of open-heart surgery, an instance of sexual innuendo and recurring rough language

title: Artists and Models
synopsis: Frenetic, fitfully amusing comedy about an artist (Dean Martin) who uses the vivid dreams of his nutty pal (Jerry Lewis) as the basis for a comic strip that attracts the attention of foreign agents. Director Frank Tashlin's outlandish brand of comedy is unusually flat-footed here, wasting Shirley MacLaine and Dorothy Malone as the romantic interests. Comic violence and sexual innuendo

title: Art School Confidential
synopsis: Oddball story that can't decide if it's a touching coming-of-age story, gross-out frat movie, murder mystery or mordant black comedy, though it does make some sharply satiric points about the art world. Director Terry Zwigoff's sporadically amusing film adapted by Daniel Clowes from his comic strip concerns a sensitive art school student (Max Minghella), smitten with an attractive artist's model (Sophia Myles) and struggling to find his artistic voice amid loutish roommates, colorful teachers (John Malkovich and Angelica Huston), and an embittered and alcoholic failed artist (Jim Broadbent), against the backdrop of a mysterious strangler killing off the students. Pervasive profanity, rough language and vulgarity, full-frontal male and partial female art-model nudity, much sexual banter and innuendo, a couple of minor gay characters, and a stylized strangling
full_review:
"Art School Confidential" (United Artists/Sony Classics) has an identity crisis.

The film can't decide if it's a touching coming-of-age story, gross-out frat movie, murder mystery or mordant black comedy.

Director Terry Zwigoff's only fiftully amusing film was adapted by Daniel Clowes from his comic strip, as with the pair's previous "Ghost World."

This one concerns a sensitive art school student Jerome Platz (Max Minghella), who enrolls at the smallish Strathmore Institute.

He chooses the school as much for the attractive artist's model, Audrey (Sophia Myles), on the cover of the brochure as the curriculum, and as he begins his freshman year struggles to find his artistic voice amid loutish classmates, colorful teachers like Professor Sandiford (John Malkovich) and Sophie (Angelica Huston), and an embittered and alcoholic failed artist, Jimmy (Jim Broadbent). All of this plays out against the backdrop of a mysterious rash of strangulation murders on campus.

He indeed meets Audrey, herself the daughter of a famous artist, fairly early in the game, and she treats him kindly, but keeps him at a friendly distance.

Jerome has the perception (and probably the true talent) that most of the others lack, but time and again his paintings are overlooked in favor of the inferior output of his classmates, including blond jock Jonah (Matt Keeslar), whose simplistic work is unaccountably lauded.

"Art School Confidential" does make some sharply satiric points about the art world. (Jerome, in desperation, must resort to imitation, then plagiarism, to make his mark, though there are dire consequences.) The politics of artistic success are well illustrated, as in the jockeying for position with restaurateur Broadway Bob, played by an unbilled Steve Buscemi, who allows promising students wall space in his establishment.

But the overall tone of the film is fairly raunchy, courtesy of Jerome's roommate Vince (Ethan Suplee), a foul-mouthed would-be filmmaker, and his dopey friend Bardo (Joel David Moore), who try to jump-start their friend's love life, resulting in an uneasy mixture of adolescent angst and "40-Year-Old Virgin" crudeness.

The coarse language (and the two extended scenes of art-class nudity) almost push this into the "O" classification, but there's just enough substance here -- the main themes of a talented artist trying to find himself, and the fraudulence of many elements of the art world -- to justify the still restrictive "L" rating.

The film contains pervasive profanity, rough language and vulgarity, full-frontal male and partial female art-model nudity, much sexual banter and innuendo, a couple of minor gay characters, and a stylized strangling. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: As Good As It Gets
synopsis: Acerbic comedy in which a misanthropic author (Jack Nicholson) tries to rejoin the human race after falling in love with a tolerant waitress (Helen Hunt) and befriending a broke homosexual artist (Greg Kinnear). Directed by James L. Brooks, the thin plot begins with the mean-spirited humor of Nicholsons nasty, self-centered sociopath, then turns mushy as he attempts to reform but the proceedings are overlong and only sporadically amusing. Stylized violence, sexual situations, recurring rough language and occasional profanity

title: Ash Wednesday
synopsis: Dowdy middle-aged matron (Elizabeth Taylor), on the verge of losing her successfull lawyer husband (Henry Fonda) to a younger woman, undergoes body sculpture in a posh European clinic but it will take Liz a good deal longer than the audience to figure out that no amount of face-lifting will change Henry's mind. Director Larry Peerce elicits solid performances from a good cast and the plot moves along smoothly through a series of plush settings but it is no more than a well-made but uninvolving melodrama without any perspective upon the actions and motivations of its characters and their lifestyle

title: Aspen Extreme
synopsis: Two Detroit buddies (Paul Gross and Peter Berg) become Aspen ski instructors and end up paying a price for succumbing to the seductive dangers of life among the rich and glamorous. Writer-director Patrick Hasburgh fails to mount much of a story around his main focus -- daredevil ski footage and impressive mountain scenery. Implied affair, brief nudity, a shot of drug abuse and minimal rough language

title: Assassination
synopsis: Through his experience and cunning, a Secret Service agent (Charles Bronson) protects the wife (Jill Ireland) of the President of the United States from assassination. Directed by Peter Hunt, the movie is relatively restrained in its violence and sexual treatment

title: The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford
synopsis: Unusual and compelling Western dramatizing the circumstances that lead up to the shooting of notorious outlaw Jesse James (Brad Pitt) by Robert Ford (Casey Affleck), a member of his own gang, and the publicity generated afterward. Writer-director Andrew Dominik tells the story intelligently at a leisurely but controlled pace with penetrating close-ups of the excellent cast -- Affleck is particularly outstanding -- to probe psychological motivations, while the relatively restrained violence is presented with an admirable realism devoid of glamorization. Some crude language and profanity, innuendo, a nongraphic sexual encounter, several shooting deaths with blood and scenes of physical violence, suicide and brief rear male nudity,
full_review:
Those with memories of an idealized Jesse James as played by Tyrone Power in the 1939 film are in for a vastly different -- but satisfying -- experience with this latest cinematic incarnation of the famous Western outlaw.

"The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford" (Warner Bros.), based on the novel by Catholic author Ron Hansen, is an unusual and compelling dramatization of the circumstances that led up to the 1882 shooting of the notorious bandit, played here with impressively mercurial mood shifts by Brad Pitt, who also produced the film. Calm and charming one moment, he's laughing maniacally the next.

His killer would be Robert Ford (Casey Affleck), a junior member of Jesse's own gang, who at the film's start longs to be part of the group, like his older brother, Charley (Sam Rockwell). He had grown up idolizing Jesse, with treasured dime novels of his exploits kept under his bed.

The 19-year-old Robert, or Bob as he's mostly called, is brushed off as little more than a pest by the other gang members, including Jesse's brother, Frank (Sam Shepard), who's about to retire from a life of crime. But Bob's persistence eventually wins over Jesse, who takes him in and allows him to be part of the Blue Cut train robbery, and afterward to help him change houses.

Jesse's glory days are pretty much behind him, and the robbing of that train -- on which he shows great brutality in handling the sympathetic official guarding the safe in the luggage compartment, is his last robbery. Thereafter he lives in anonymity under the name Thomas Howard, a churchgoing man with a wife (Mary Louise-Parker) and two small children.

But his presence is still formidable, and the gang members, including Jesse's cousin, Wood Hite (Jeremy Renner), womanizer Dick Liddil (Paul Schneider), and Ed Miller (Garret Dillahunt), still live in fear that Jesse might get wise to any treachery. (Jesse's interrogation of a quivering Miller at one point is superbly played.)

Always aware that his life might be in danger, Jesse seemed to have a sixth sense about when to change houses and move on. But as fate would have it, he was gunned down while dusting a picture on his wall, unarmed at that fateful moment.

Writer-director Andrew Dominik tells the story intelligently and at a controlled pace with penetrating close-ups of his excellent cast -- Affleck is particularly outstanding -- to probe psychological motivations. Did Bob envy Jesse? Did he wish to become Jesse? Had his admiration turned to anger? Was he afraid of him? Was he just after the reward money?

The film, though speculative, lets you contemplate every angle, as well as exploring the nature of celebrity and hero worship, and far from ending with Jesse's fatal shooting, the film goes on to chronicle the vaudeville re-enactments of the crime performed by Bob afterward.

The violence is relatively restrained by today's standards, and presented with an admirable realism devoid of glamorization. The lingering death of one shooting victim is strikingly different from the "bang, bang, you're dead" mode of so many films.

There's a moral gravity to everyone's actions here, and even some spiritual reflections, as when Jesse ruminates on life "on the other side."

The film unfolds at a leisurely 160 minutes, but should reward those not expecting a standard Western shoot-'em-up.

The film contains some crude language and profanity, innuendo, a nongraphic sexual encounter, several shooting deaths with blood and scenes of physical violence, suicide, and brief rear male nudity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Assassination Tango
synopsis: Disappointingly shallow tale of a Brooklyn hit man (Robert Duvall) on assignment in Buenos Aires where he becomes involved with an expert tango dancer (Luciana Pedraza). Also written and directed by Duvall, the tango dancing is entrancing in an otherwise bland and morally bankrupt exercise in which cold-blooded murders are treated with casual indifference. Sporadic violence, a shadowy sexual encounter, crude expressions and recurring rough language
full_review:
Robert Duvall wrote, directed and starred in "The Apostle" in 1997, an insightful story of faith and failings, so it comes as quite a disappointment that his similar commitment to "Assassination Tango" results in such a morally bankrupt film.

Duvall plays aging Brooklyn hit man John J. Anderson, who owns several beauty salons and keeps his true profession hidden from his live-in beautician girlfriend, Maggie (Kathy Baker). John loves her 10-year-old daughter Jenny (Katherine Micheaux Miller) much more, and only accepts his latest assignment in Buenos Aires when he is assured he will be back in time for Jenny's birthday.

However, once in Argentina, the fastidious hit man does not trust his local contacts (Ruben Blades and Julio Oscar Mechoso) and becomes infuriated when they tell him his target, a murderous retired general, won't be in the area for a few weeks and he must stay.

To fill his time he wanders into a dance club and becomes fixated on sleek tango dancer Manuela (Luciana Pedraza). Already a fan of the tango, John becomes immersed in the tango culture and flirting with Manuela when not making exacting preparations for murder.

He tells her about Maggie and how her daughter may be the reason for their relationship and laughingly admits to cheating on her as well. Single mom Manuela suggests she's sexually available but he seems more interested in embracing her vertically than horizontally.

On the appointed day of the assassination, John does not follow the schedule and doesn't hesitate to kill a few more individuals to accomplish his goal and escape capture. Surprisingly, he does spare one cop's life before resuming his pleasant existence -- apparently without the slightest pang of conscience, only pride in his killing skills.

As its co-producer, writer, director and star, Duvall's movie sadly smacks of a vanity production to indulge his real-life love of the tango, and of his girlfriend, Pedraza, who makes her film debut here. While he gives a reliably credible performance, the script is quite bland, populated by underdeveloped characters, such as Manuela, Maggie and the four men involved in the assassination planning. They are all colorless ciphers the audience has no emotional investment in and what should then at least be a character study of hit man John is utterly shallow. The film has almost no pulse except for the sensual dancing sequences, which are alluring to behold but can't carry the entire movie.

Neither the romantic elements nor what should build to the suspenseful aspect of the crime ever comes to life. With its flat dialogue and lack of any moral sensibility, "Assassination Tango" ends up a wallflower.

Because of sporadic violence, a shadowy sexual encounter, crude expressions and recurring rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Assassin of Youth
synopsis: Dated exploitation picture in which a cub reporter (Arthur Gardner) poses as a soda jerk while working on a story about marijuana-crazed youth, then saves a friendly customer (Luana Walters) from losing her inheritance by exposing those who framed her as a drug addict. Directed by Elmer Clifton, the ludicrous proceedings make the anti-drug message difficult to take seriously. Substance abuse, sexual situations and brief partial nudity

title: Assassins
synopsis: Ultraviolent tale of rival hit men (Sylvester Stallone and Antonio Banderas), each assigned to kill the same thief (Julianne Moore) who has possession of a computer disk containing compromising information. Director Richard Donner focuses on suspenseless bloodshed since there is little story and no character development among this trio of hardened criminals. Numerous casual murders and much rough language

title: Assault on a Queen
synopsis: Navy veterans (Frank Sinatra and Richard Conte) raise a sunken U-boat and use it to hi-jack and rob the Queen Mary in mid-ocean. Directed by Jack Donahue, it's routine escapist entertainment with the bad guys getting their just desserts and the good guys escaping, but without the loot

title: Assault on Precinct 13
synopsis: Brutal and violent -- though reasonably gripping -- story of a desolate Detroit police precinct under siege by crooked police who are out to silence a criminal (Laurence Fishburne) incarcerated there, to cover up what he knows about corruption within their ranks, effecting an unusual alliance between the police and criminals within the station house who must unite to defend themselves. Jean-Francois Richet's remake of the 1976 film features good performances by Fishburne, Ethan Hawke and Brian Dennehy, but the bloodshed and violence seem unnecessarily explicit, and the improbable story calls for major suspension of disbelief. Graphic and bloody violence and related gore, much rough, crude and profane language, and some sexual innuendo
full_review:
John Carpenter's 1976 film -- a cult classic -- is back with a twist. In this updated adaptation, the bad guys are cops.
"Assault on Precinct 13" (Rogue) is a brutal and violent -- though reasonably gripping -- story of a desolate Detroit police precinct under siege by crooked police who are out to silence a criminal (Laurence Fishburne) incarcerated there, to cover up what he knows about corruption within their ranks, effecting an unusual alliance between the police and criminals within the precinct who must unite to defend themselves.
The film opens on a horrific sequence showing an undercover drug bust going awry. Sgt. Jake Roenick (Ethan Hawke) is wracked by guilt when his colleagues are killed after he instructs them to run in the wrong direction.

Flash ahead: Roenick is now under the care of a police psychiatrist, Alex Sabian (Maria Bello), who pays him visits at the station house to get to the root of a psychological scarring which has left him largely dysfunctional. Banter between them indicates that there's a mutual attraction despite her protestations to the contrary.

It's a snowy New Year's Eve, and the staff of Precinct 13 is getting ready to celebrate the holiday. That includes Officer Jasper O'Shea (Brian Dennehy), sexy secretary Iris Ferry (Drea de Matteo), and Lt. Holloway (Peter Bryant).
