His Hollywood career continues with "Scarface" and the then-notorious "The Outlaw," in which actress Jane Russell's well-publicized decolletage -- showcased in a bra which he specially designed -- brought him into conflict with the Motion Picture Association censors. He wins the battle by proving that the association approved other films with equal cleavage on display.

His great love -- aviation -- drives him to invent various aircraft (the H-1 Racer, the XF-11 spy plane, and the giant seaplane, the Hercules), set speed records, circle the world in four days and take over TWA.

At the same time, he copes with partial deafness, battles psychological demons stemming from his childhood, and develops germ phobias and peculiar proclivities about various foods and milk. His behavior turns more and more strange, and he becomes a hermit, living in reclusive squalor without clothes (a little rear nudity here), collecting his urine in milk bottles. Other unpleasant aspects of Hughes' personality are touched on unflinchingly: his obsessive-compulsive disorders, his bouts of intense paranoia and his underhanded wiretapping of the women in his life.

The production design is splendid, and the aerial sequences are among the most thrilling ever filmed. One of the most exciting sequences involves his plane stalling when testing the XF-11 and having to make a terrifying crash landing, ripping off the roofs of Beverly Hills homes, and leaving him with burns over much of his body.

After learning that Hughes is going to start trans-Atlantic flights, PanAm's president, Juan Trippe (Alec Baldwin), Hughes' chief rival and adversary, contrives through his buddy, Maine Sen. Owen Brewster (Alan Alda in a superb portrayal), to have him brought up in front of Congress in 1947 to testify about wartime contracts and "defrauding the American public."

In reality, Trippe wants to sustain PanAm's monopoly on those flights, the revelation of which allows Hughes to leave the Senate chambers in triumph.

Some of the period details -- re-creations of the Coconut Grove, for instance -- seem more cliched than truly authentic, but this is minor carping for such a visually rich cavalcade.

The film ends rather abruptly on a career highpoint, but with troublesome harbingers of future psychological trouble, and not even a postscript about what happens to Hughes later in life. After nearly three hours, it's remarkable that you can still be left wanting more.

This is one of the most commercial films of Scorsese's career. The film maintains a terrific momentum, and the Scorsese stamp is unmistakable, several of the scenes leaving an indelible impression: Hughes manically washing his hands in a public lavatory and then being afraid to open the germ-laden door; Hepburn coming to Hughes in his most reclusive state and compassionately talking to him through the locked door, and many more.

Re-enactments of famous people are always difficult to carry off. Blanchett, though not a dead ringer for Hepburn, captures her voice and mannerisms impressively, and Jude Law's a passable Errol Flynn, though Gwen Stefani and Kate Beckinsale are a far cry from the real Jean Harlow and Gardner. Ace film buff Scorsese should have known better and risen above the sort of inaccurate casting usually found in made-for-TV films. Ian Holm, John C. Reilly, Danny Huston, Adam Scott, Willem Dafoe and Edward Herrmann all shine in supporting roles.

But above all, it is DiCaprio's film. He etches a totally convincing portrait of a great if tortured visionary.

Because of reoccuring profanity and intermittent crude expressions, and an instance of rough language, as well as implied sexual situations and innuendo, a violent plane crash and brief rear nudity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: The Awakening
synopsis: The mummy of a dead Egyptian queen tries to fulfill an ancient prophecy with devastating consequences for the family of the archeologist (Charlton Heston) who opened her tomb. The best asset of director Mike Newell's plodding horror story is the location photography of the Valley of the Kings. Implications of incest and some gore

title: The Awful Truth
synopsis: > After suspicion of infidelity, a New York couple (Cary Grant and Irene Dunne) are granted an interlocutory divorce, and while waiting for the final decree the wife reluctantly takes up with an Oklahoma oil man (Ralph Bellamy) and the huband witha n heiress, though each tries to sabotage the other's relationships because, at heart, they still love each other. Leo McCarey's classic comedy showcaes the two stars at their peak, working with a witty script with the kind of serious subtext that anchors the best comedies, and overall provides a ringing affirmation of marriage. Implied infidelity, sophisticated banter, mildly suggestive nightclub number. The DVD includes a featurette, "In Love With Cary Grant," with Grant biographer Marc Eliot and others. A-II (nr) 1937

title: A Beautiful Mind
synopsis: Absorbing biography of mathematical genius John Forbes Nash, Jr. (Russell Crowe) who was afflicted with schizophrenia, but eventually triumphed over the disease with the help of his devoted wife (Jennifer Connelly), going on to win the Nobel Prize. Elegantly weaving scenes from a fine script, director Ron Howard presents a very human story of brilliance, insanity and marital love, despite the familiar trappings of an inspirational story. Intense, mature theme dealing with mental illness, a few sexual references, a scene of violence and minimal crass language and profanity

title: A Bell for Adano
synopsis: Bell for Adano, A -- Sturdy adaptation of John Hersey's World War II novel in which a U.S. Army officer (John Hodiak) in charge of a liberated Italian town promises to find a replacement for a bell prized by the local community. Directed by Henry King, the story demonstrates the virtues of democracy as well as the common bond of humanity, put over by a good supporting cast, including Gene Tierney as an Italian girl pining for the safe return of her soldier boyfriend. Menacing situations and sexual innuendo

title: A Big Hand for the Little Lady
synopsis: Big Hand for the Little Lady, A -- Henry Fonda, Joanne Woodward, Jason Robards, Burgess Meredith, Paul Ford and Kevin McCarthy are among the ensemble playing cards in the Old West's most comical and colorful poker game. Director Fielder Cook places emphasis on the personalities and the plot's ingenious bluffing makes for fascinating entertainment, even without the clever surprise ending

title: A Bill of Divorcement
synopsis: Bill of Divorcement, A -- Stilted melodrama from Clemence Dane's play about a young woman (Katharine Hepburn) whose marriage prospects dim after her father (John Barrymore) returns from an asylum to find his wife (Billie Burke) has divorced him and is about to remarry. Directed by George Cukor, the maudlin proceedings gain interest mainly from Barrymore's cheerful delusions and Hepburn's acceptance of the situation. Questions of divorce and hereditary insanity

title: A Bill of Divorcement
synopsis: Bill of Divorcement, A -- Remake of the 1932 original, with Maureen O'Hara as the young Englishwoman who learns insanity runs in her family when her father (Adolphe Menjou) returns from an asylum on Christmas Eve. Directed by John Farrow, the cast is fine but the situations seem even more dated than in the original. Sympathetic treatment of divorce and dated view of hereditary insanity

title: A Boy, a Girl and a Dog
synopsis: Boy, a Girl and a Dog, A -- Sentimental World War II tale in which a city lad (Jerry Hunter) finds a mutt to the delight of a young neighbor (Sharyn Moffett) but when neither is allowed to keep the dog, they enlist him to the Army canine corps and his trainer (Lionel Stander) takes him to the Pacific where the dog becomes a war hero. Battlefield violence

title: A Boy and His Dog
synopsis: Boy and His Dog, A -- A not very bright boy (Don Johnson) and his extremely intelligent dog try to survive in a nuclear-ravaged world. The two, moreover, can communicate telepathically with one another until the inevitable love triangle is introduced (Susan Benton). The acting, including that of the dog, is very good but the violence and sex are questionable elements in this black comedy from director L.Q. Jones based upon the Harlan Ellison novella

title: A Boy Called Hate
synopsis: Boy Called Hate, A -- An alienated youth (Scott Caan) resuces a cynical teenager (Missy Crider) from being raped by shooting the attacker, then both become fugitives from the law after killing a highway patrolman they mistakenly assumed was going to arrest them. Writer-director Mitch Marcus' shrill road movie is of minimal interest save for a redemptive ending which underscores the grave consequences of violent behavior. Sporadic violence, a discreet sexual encounter and much rough language

title: A Boy Named Charlie Brown
synopsis: Boy Named Charlie Brown, A -- First animated movie version of the Peanuts comic strip characters created by George Schulz centers on Charlie Brown's obsession with failure as he enters a national spelling bee contest. The animation team under director Bill Melendez has been completely faithful to the stylized world of the comic strip in giving movement and voice to the small fry characters. Refreshing but meaningful amusement for both youngsters and grown-ups

title: A Boy Ten Feet Tall
synopsis: Boy Ten Feet Tall, A -- Orphaned boy journeys alone across the length of Africa to find an aunt and matures considerably during the course of his adventures. Directed by Alexander Mackendrick, the story is slight but very appealing, especially for youngsters

title: A Breath of Scandal
synopsis: Breath of Scandal, A -- Leaden romantic comedy from Ferenc Molnar's play about a spirited Hapsburg princess (Sophia Loren) who gets involved with an American engineer (wooden John Gavin) seeking a mining concession in 1907 Austria. Director Michael Curtiz finds nothing amusing in a creaky period piece featuring listless court intrigues and bogus romantic misunderstandings. Sexual situations and innuendo. A-III 1960

title: A Bridge Too Far
synopsis: Bridge Too Far, A -- Director Richard Attenborough's epic re-creation of the tragic Allied offensive code-named Market Garden details the fate of the massive paratroop force dropped behind German lines in Holland during World War II. The excellent all-star cast includes Dirk Bogarde, Anthony Hopkins, Laurence Olivier, Robert Redford, Ryan O'Neal, Gene Hackman and Elliot Gould. Although the violence is unusually graphic, the movie has value as an historical dramatization that has tried to be faithful to the facts

title: A Brief History of Time
synopsis: Brief History of Time, A -- Documentary on British physicist Stephen Hawking whose speculations on the origins of the universe and related matters have been achieved despite his progressive disablement since 1963 from the muscular disease ALS. Directed by Errol Morris, the result is a challenging introduction to Hawking's cosmological theories and ambivalence over the question of its Creator, but what's most impressive here is the human portrait of a determined indvidual overcoming the confinements of a wheelchair and inability to speak except through a voice synthesizer. Big concepts may confuse small children

title: A Brief Vacation
synopsis: Brief Vacation, A -- Italian portrait of a woman (Florinda Bolkan), her health broken from overworking to support three children and several relatives, who is sent to a sanitarium to regain her strength. There she has a brief affair with a younger man, but he comes from another class and her life remains unchanged. Director Vittorio de Sica contents himself with a realistic portrayal of a complex human being, letting viewers draw their own conclusions about the larger social implications in his story of the plight of the poor. Mature themes

title: A Bright Shining Lie
synopsis: Bright Shining Lie, A -- Fact-based account of the unfulfilled life of career Army officer John Paul Vann (Bill Paxton) who clashes with his superiors in 1964 Vietnam, then returns as civilian obsessed with showing the military how to win the war until his death in a 1972 helicopter crash. Directed by Terry George from Neil Sheehan's 1988 Pulitzer Prize-winner, the dramatization portrays Vann as a flawed, contradictory figure whose actions in Vietnam raise questions about the war that divided Americans then and are still troubling today. Wartime violence, sexual situations, rough language and profanity

title: A Bronx Tale
synopsis: Bronx Tale, A -- Growing up in the 1960s, an Italian-American youth (Lillo Brancato) is torn between the decent values his bus-driver father (Robert De Niro) and the easy-money life of the neighborhood crime boss (Chazz Palminteri) who treats him like his own son. Also directed by De Niro, the well-realized drama makes a convincing moral statement in its picture of a youth who comes to recognize the emptiness of dirty money and the deadly violence it spawns. Some violence, racial slurs, sexual references and much rough language

title: A Bullet for Pretty Boy
synopsis: Bullet for Pretty Boy, A -- Bloody account of the life of 1930's gangster Pretty Boy Floyd (Fabian Forte) who commits some daring crimes and is eventually gunned down in a violent shoot-out. Directed by Larry Buchanan, it is of minimal interest

title: A Bullet for the General
synopsis: Bullet for the General, A -- Italian Western directed by Damiano Damiani consists of a series of wanton killings and excessive brutality. O 1968

title: Babar: The Movie
synopsis: In a delightful, animated version of the children's books by Jean and Laurent de Brunhoff, King Babar recalls for his own kids how as a boy he saved Elephantland from the rhinos and became an unlikely hero. Director Alan Bunce's Canadian production underscores the value of commitment to friends and family, while Babar's fears in an alien jungle will be identifiable to young children just beginning to explore unfamiliar turf. The movie will enjoy a long life as a family video

title: Babe
synopsis: Live-action barnyard charmer in which a kindly Australian farmer (James Cromwell) enters his unusual piglet (voice of Christine Cavanaugh) in a sheepdog competition, unaware that his farm animals can talk to one another as they pull together to make the little pig's dream of herding sheep come true. Director Chris Noonan's enchanting comic fable is filmed entirely from the animals' point-of-view, with delightful visuals and an endearing message of learning to live and work in harmony

title: Babel
synopsis: Quietly powerful film charting three interconnected stories: an American couple (Brad Pitt and Cate Blanchett) stranded in Morocco when the wife is seriously wounded by a stray bullet on their tour bus; the deaf-mute teenage daughter (Rinko Kikuchi) of a widower father (Koji Yakusho) in Tokyo who achingly longs for love; and a Mexican governess (Adriana Barraza) and her nephew (Gael Garcia Bernal) who take her two young charges across the border to attend a wedding with tragic results. Director Alejandro Gonzalez Inarritu's somber and lengthy film imparts an admirable message about a shared global humanity and the senselessness of violence, even as it blames U.S. foreign policy and bureaucracy as an obstacle, has superbly empathetic performances by an international cast, and ultimately packs an emotional wallop. Partially subtitled. Some rough language and profanity, crude expressions, some violence including a killing, full female nudity, some discreet sexual elements, and alcohol and drug use
full_review:
What, if anything, do the three disparate stories -- set, respectively, in Morocco, the United States (and then Mexico), and Tokyo -- have to do with each other, you may find yourself wondering at the start of the quietly powerful "Babel" (Paramount Vantage).

The plot strands are very much interconnected as the narrative skillfully develops, but part of the film's pleasure is the way it all unfolds, so we won't spoil it.

Suffice it to say, there's an American couple, Richard (Brad Pitt) and Susan (Cate Blanchett), who find themselves stranded in Morocco when the wife is seriously wounded by a stray bullet on their tour bus. The shot was innocently fired by one of two young Moroccan boys testing a new rifle (bought by their goatherd father merely to ward off jackals). Before long, the wounding of an American tourist becomes an international incident as the U.S. government assumes terrorism.

In truth, the native people are treating Richard and Susan with the utmost kindness. We also get to know the herder and his family, and react with horror when they are caught up in the tragic incidents that follow.

Then there's Tokyo widower father Yasujiro's (Koji Yakusho) deaf-mute teenage daughter, Chieko (Rinko Kikuchi), who achingly longs for love. She misses her mother terribly, and fails to see that her businessman father wants to connect with her. Chieko acts out her desperate loneliness with sophomoric pranks (exposing herself to some teenage boys who recoiled from her when they realized her handicap), and, most poignantly, offers herself sexually to an empathetic detective who comes looking for her father.

And, finally, there's Amelia (Adriana Barraza), a Mexican governess who needs to attend a family wedding back home, and when she can't find a sitter for her two American charges (whose parents are away), decides to bring them to the wedding, driven by her hotheaded nephew, Santiago (Gael Garcia Bernal) -- a bad move, as it will transpire.

Director Alejandro Gonzalez Inarritu's somber and lengthy film -- from a script by Guillermo Arriaga -- imparts an admirable message about our shared global humanity and the senselessness of violence. Government bureaucracy, especially on the U.S. side, comes in for some bad knocks. Along the way, the film makes a powerful case for a more compassionate view of undocumented workers.

The film's international cast gives extraordinary performances across the board. Pitt is outstanding as the husband frantic to get aid for his injured wife, and he and Blanchett share one of the screen's most tenderly romantic moments in the most unromantic of circumstances. Kikuchi and Barraza will break your heart.

The film is leisurely paced and resolutely noncommercial, but if you stick with it and can look past some provocative elements, you may find yourself both devastated and uplifted.
Partially subtitled.

The film contains some rough language and profanity, crude expressions, some violence including a killing, full female nudity, some discreet sexual elements, and alcohol and drug use. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Babes in Arms
synopsis: With the talkies having put their vaudeville parents out of work, their adolescent offspring (led by Mickey Rooney and Judy Garland) get together to earn some money by putting on a variety show. Director Busby Berkeley's period piece showcases Rooney's talents as a juvenile hoofer and madcap comic but shortchanges the Rodgers and Hart musical upon which the zestful proceedings are based. Youthful optimism wins the day, despite the creaky plot cliches

title: Babes in Toyland
synopsis: Disappointing Disney adaptation of the Victor Herbert operetta in which Mary Quite Contrary (Annette Funicello) is saved from the clutches of the villainous Barnaby (Ray Bolger) by a silly pair of apprentice toymakers (Gene Sheldon and Henry Calvin). Directed by Jack Donohue, the live-action musical works hard to create the fantasy of a fairy tale world but the result lacks the fun and charm of the 1934 Laurel and Hardy version (aka "March of the Wooden Soldiers"). The nursery rhyme characters and special effects will keep the children entertained but hold only sporadic interest for their elders

title: Babette's Feast
synopsis: Screen version of a story by Isak Dinesen, set in a rugged Danish fishing village in 1871, shows the impact of a French housekeeper (Stephane Audran) on two pious sisters who carry on their late father's work as pastor of a dwindling religious flock. The conclusion follows the preparation and consumption of an exquisite French meal, with focus on its sensual and religious implications and its healing effect on the austere sect and the Frenchwoman who prepares it. Danish director Gabriel Axel's low-key and understated work is rich with detail and fine, controlled performances. Subtitles. Cerebral treatment

title: Baby Mama
synopsis: Frequently funny but morally problematic romantic comedy about a hard-driving grocery chain executive (Tina Fey) who, incapable of bearing a child, hires an unpolished woman (Amy Poehler) to be a surrogate mother, subsequently becoming her roommate when the latter splits from her deadbeat common-law husband (Dax Shepard) while herself becoming attached to an ex-lawyer turned juice-bar owner (Greg Kinnear). Writer-director Michael McCullers' partially improvised feature debut, with a cast that also includes Sigourney Weaver and Steve Martin, abounds in comic energy but implicitly accepts current mores regarding fertility that are contrary to Catholic values. Acceptability of surrogate parenting and artificial insemination, implied premarital sex, some crude and crass language, sexual and scatological humor, and a drug reference
full_review:
"Baby Mama" (Universal/Relativity) is a frequently funny but morally problematic romantic comedy about one woman's obsession with having a child.

Thirty-seven and single, hard-driving grocery chain executive Kate (Tina Fey), who has long put career ahead of family, has begun to hear her biological clock tolling. Discovering that adoption could take as long as five years, she tries artificial insemination. When this fails, she consults an obstetrician who tells her that her chances of conceiving are one in a million.

Not to be deterred, she turns to Chaffee (Sigourney Weaver), the imposing head of a surrogate mother agency, and is soon visited by the, shall we say, unpolished Angie (Amy Poehler), who, at the urging of deadbeat common-law husband Carl (Dax Shepard), eventually agrees to bear the child.

When she and Carl temporarily split, Kate takes in Angie as a roommate, with predictable "Odd Couple" consequences. Love, meanwhile, finds its way into Kate's life in the person of ex-lawyer -- now juice-bar owner -- Rob (Greg Kinnear).

Writer-director Michael McCullers' partially improvised feature debut, with a cast that also includes Steve Martin as Kate's dippy boss, abounds in comic energy. But for most of its running time, the film implicitly accepts current mores regarding fertility that are contrary to Catholic values.

Procedures such as artificial insemination and surrogate motherhood inevitably separate the unitive and procreative aspects of human sexuality and may remove procreation from its God-given context of committed marital love. Here, they are accorded the status of acceptable alternatives to natural conception, even if -- forgive the partial spoiler -- the ending manages to skirt most of these issues.

The film contains acceptability of surrogate parenting and artificial insemination, implied premarital sex, some crude and crass language, sexual and scatological humor, and a drug reference. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Baby Blue Marine
synopsis: World War II bootcamp washout (Jan-Michael Vincent) pretends to be a Marine Ranger and is received as a hero in a small Colorado town. When a waitress (Glynnis O'Connor) falls for him, he has to prove his courage. Although the story is abundantly sentimental, director John Hancock warmly evokes the people and the period, the acting is good and the result is a fairly entertaining movie

title: Baby Boom
synopsis: High-powered businesswoman (Diane Keaton) chooses the transforming love of motherhood and the ego boost of self-employment when she inherits a baby whose parents have died tragically. Director Charles Shyer's wry and insightful situation comedy has the good sense to affirm that new life is more important than new clients

title: Baby Boy
synopsis: Disjointed drama about the life of an unemployed young African-American man (Tyrese Gibson), living with his mother (A.J. Johnson), who is learning what it means to be a man while sorting out his relationship with his girlfriend (Taraji P. Henson). Writer-director John Singleton's theme that society infantilizes black men is lessened by incoherent storytelling, haphazard editing and an ending condoning immoral behavior. Several explicit sexual situations with nudity, an abortion, brief brutal violence and constant rough language and profanity. (

title: Baby Doll
synopsis: Meandering social satire set in rural Mississippi where an Italian-American newcomer (Eli Wallach) takes revenge on the redneck (Karl Malden) who torches his cotton gin by seducing the man's bird-brained wife (Carroll Baker). Directed by Elia Kazan from Tennessee Williams' Script, the halted narrative and eccentric characters never quite jell into coherent story, though Boris Kaufman's photography provides haunting images of racial animosites, crumbling facades and deep-seated rural poverty. Stylized violence, implied marital infidelity and leering sexual situations

title: Baby Face
synopsis: Tawdry tale of a young hustler (Barbara Stanwyck) who skips out of her dad's speakeasy in Eire, Pa., takes a secretarial job in a Manhattan banking corporation, then sleeps her way up the ranks of management until a scandal exiles her to the bank's Paris branch where she finds true love with the firm's new head (George Brent). Directed by Alfred E. Green, the woman's seduction of ever higher executives is implied rather than depicted, though her smug satisfaction in exchanging sex for wealth makes her an unlikely candidate for redemption in the tacked-on moral ending. Some off-screen violence, implicit sexual affairs and much sexual innuendo

title: Baby, It's You
synopsis: Bright daughter of a Jewish doctor (Rosanna Arquette) and the son of working-class Catholic parents (Vincent Spano) fall in love when they're high school seniors in Camden, N.J., in the late 1960s. Director John Sayles's perceptive, compassionate, if uneven, movie is made memorable by an absolutely pitch-perfect performance by Arquette and very good acting by Spano. Some needlessly graphic sex scenes and nudity

title: Babylon A.D.
synopsis: Pointless futuristic action outing in which a mobster (Gerard Depardieu) hires a mercenary (Vin Diesel) to escort a mysteriously gifted young woman (M�lanie Thierry) and her guardian (Michelle Yeoh) from Mongolia to New York and deliver her to the minions of her cult�s high priestess (Charlotte Rampling). Though not excessively violent, director Mathieu Kassovitz� leaden adaptation of French author Maurice G. Dantec�s novel �Babylon Babies� is driven by a muddled mythology that includes the repetition of a Gospel miracle, a plot turn requiring, though hardly meriting, mature interpretation. Moderate action violence, one use of the F-word, some crude language, a couple of profanities, brief background view of a stripper
full_review:
When a director describes his own film as “pure violence and stupidity,” expectations ebb to Dead Sea level. As it turns out, Mathieu Kassovitz’ characterization of “Babylon A. D.” (Fox) in an interview with AMCtv.com is a shade pessimistic. The violence quotient of this pointless futuristic action outing is not that high, but then its I.Q. is even lower.

Mobster Gorky (Gerard Depardieu) hires Toorop (Vin Diesel), a mercenary, to escort Aurora (Melanie Thierry), a mysteriously gifted young woman and her guardian, Sister Rebeka (Michelle Yeoh), from Mongolia to New York and deliver her to the minions of her cult’s high priestess (Charlotte Rampling).

These gun-toting foot soldiers wear a variation on a clerical collar and have tin lapel pins with black crosses on them, indicating that the phony, power-hungry sect is a sort of anti-church. But the endurance of orthodox Christianity is implied by a market scene where crucifixes and statues of the Blessed Mother are on sale. And, surprisingly for this type of character, Toorop is seen early on pausing for a silent grace.

 

Though not excessively violent, director Mathieu Kassovitz’ leaden adaptation of French author Maurice G. Dantec’s novel “Babylon Babies” is driven by a muddled mythology and includes the repetition of a Gospel miracle (the virginal Aurora gives birth to twins), a plot turn requiring, though hardly meriting, mature interpretation.

The film contains moderate action violence, one use of the F-word, some crude language, a couple of profanities and a brief background view of a stripper. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Baby Love
synopsis: Psychotic teenager (Linda Hayden) is taken into a wealthy London home where she proceeds to destroy each member of the family out of resentment against the father who had had an affair with her own mother (Diana Dors). Alistair Reid directs the British production as if it were a manual on sexual pathology ranging from attempted rape to lesbianism, with plenty of nudity and little concern for characterization, consistent motivation or common sense

title: Babymother
synopsis: Incoherent, convoluted musical drama set in London about a young, sassy, single mother (Anjela Lauren Smith) struggling to become a reggae rap star whose biggest competition is the children's father (Wil Johnson), a local reggae star with his own ambitions. Writer-director Julian Henriques' feature debut is full of funky music and colorful, outrageous costumes, but a scant story line and amateurish acting make the film seem more like an extended music video than a serious depiction of a musician's rise to stardom. Shadowy sexual encounter, brief, mild violence, an instance of profanity and some rough language

title: Baby's Day Out
synopsis: Crawling away from three dopey kidnappers (Joe Mantegna, Joe Pantoliano and Brian Haley), a 9-month-old infant blissfully enjoys a visit to the zoo, a department store and a construction site all on his own as the klutzy trio scrambles to recapture him. Director Patrick Read Johnson's mildly entertaining formula comedy gets its mileage out of the juxtaposition of the adoreable baby (twins Adam and Jacob Worton) amidst incredible situations. Frequent slapstick violence and fantasy treatment of an infant in jeopardy

title: Baby: Secret of a Lost Legend
synopsis: Baby: Secret of the Lost Legend -- American couple (William Katt and Sean Young) exploring in Africa discover a cute baby brontosaurus which they later reunite with mama from whom it had been separated by some villains. Directed by B.W.L. Norton, it's a pleasant enough adventure tale for most age groups. A violent battle scene and some mild vulgarity

title: Baby, Take a Bow
synopsis: Little Shirley Temple gets her first starring role as a pre-schooler who recovers the jewels her father (James Dunn) is accused of stealing, then helps nab the real thief. Directed by Harry Lachman, the formula melodrama has little interest other than its Depression-era family setting and, of course, the bubbly presence of its precocious star. Brief violence endangering a child

title: Baby the Rain Must Fall
synopsis: Paroled convict (Steve McQueen) returns to his wife (Lee Remick) but her love and encouragement are not enough to reform his violent ways. Directed by Richard Mulligan, the narrative never quite jells into an understandable situation, though the backcountry locales and characters provide some interest

title: Bachelor Flat
synopsis: Failed farce in which a hapless British archaeologist (Terry-Thomas) on the faculty of a California college has trouble fending off amorous American women, including the pretended advances of the adolescent daughter (Tuesday Weld) of his fiancee (Celeste Holm). Director Frank Tashlin gets few laughs from the tiresome misunderstandings and tasteless situations that pad out the proceedings. Much sexual innuendo

title: Bachelor in Paradise
synopsis: Weak romantic comedy in which a playboy author (Bob Hope) moves into an exclusive California housing development to research the mating game among the affluent, then falls for its pert business manager (Lana Turner). Directed by Jack Arnold, the script's satiric pretensions fall flat and the sexist humor wasn't funny even then. Much sexual innuendo and marital strife

title: Bachelor Knight
synopsis: (see: "The Bachelor and the Bobby-Soxer" )

title: Bachelor Mother
synopsis: Flimsy romantic comedy revolves around a shopgirl (Ginger Rogers) who finds an abandoned infant, then tries to convince her boss (David Niven) that she's not the baby's mother. Directed by Garson Kanin, the complications arising from this comic premise are broadly farcical yet always related to the inevitable sentimental ending. Veiled references to unwed motherhood

title: Bachelor Party
synopsis: Prospective bridegroom Tom Hanks has a tasteless time with crude friends in director Neil Israel's sex farce full of gross, unfunny jokes, exploitive nudity and demeaning raps about women

title: The Back-Up Plan
synopsis: In this dull and predictable romantic comedy single pet store owner Zoe (Jennifer Lopez) conceives twins through artificial insemination, and seems blissfully happy until Mr. Right appears in the form of cheese maker Stan (Alex O'Loughlin). Zoe falls hard, but when she confesses her condition to Stan, he freaks. Despite a "happy" ending, director Alan Poul's film presents a thoroughly warped view of love, marriage and parenthood, and contradicts Catholic moral teachings on the necessity of maintaining the connection between the unitive and procreative aspects of marital love. Morally skewed treatment of human sexuality, graphic premarital sexual activity, rear and partial nudity, scenes of defecation, much crude language, graphic gynecological exams, and a gruesome water birth scene

title: Back at the Front
synopsis: Slack sequel to "Up Front" has veteran goldbricks Willie (Tom Ewell) and Joe (Harvey Lembeck) recalled to active duty in post-war Tokyo where they are duped by smugglers (Mari Blanchard and Richard Long) and chased by MPs. Directed by George Sherman, the comic scrapes into which these retread GIs get themselves are overly familiar, the Japanese locations don't make them any fresher and there's not a peep about the Korean War

title: Backbeat
synopsis: Tragic, fact-based story of Stu Sutcliffe (Stephen Dorff), one of the original Beatles and close friend of John Lennon (Ian Hart), who left the band in order to remain in Hamburg with his fiancee (Sheryl Lee) and hopes of a painting career, but died months later of a brain hemorrhage. Director Iain Softley's downbeat movie is little more than a routine buddy story which fails to capture the quirky energy of the Beatles as they first burst onto the international scene. Restrained bedroom scenes, intermittent nudity, brief violence and drug use and much rough language

title: Back Door to Hell
synopsis: Plodding low-budget picture directed by Monte Hellman in which a U.S. reconnaissance team (led by Jimmie Rodgers) lands on 1944 Luzon, links up with suspicious Filipino guerrillas (led by Conrad Maga), then join in taking some Japanese prisoners but before transmitting what they've learned back to base, their radio operator (Jack Nicholson) is killed. Wartime violence, menacing situations and the off-screen torture and killing of prisoners

title: Backdraft
synopsis: Deep-rooted conflicts boil over when a rookie Chicago firefighter (William Baldwin) is placed under the command of his estranged brother (Kurt Russell) during the investigation of a string of arson-related murders. With the terrifying nature of fire emerging as the real star of the movie, director Ron Howard ambitiously tackles a relationship story, a murder mystery and a special effects action movie with modest success. Some grisly shots of charred bodies, very brief nudity, fleeting sexual innuendo, occasional fisticuffs and intermittent rough language

title: Backfire
synopsis: Convoluted mystery in which an ex-G.I. (Gordon MacRae) tries to clear his missing buddy (Edmond O'Brien) of a murder rap with the help of a nurse (Virginia Mayo), another ex-G.I. (Dane Clark) and a mystery woman (Viveca Lindfors) with mob connections. Directed by Vincent Sherman, the muddled plot relies on murky flashbacks which never quite add up, even after the twist ending. Stylized violence, menacing situations and romantic complications

title: Back in the USSR
synopsis: Muddled thriller about a U.S. tourist (Frank Whaley) in post-Soviet Russia on the run from rival gangsters (Brian Blessed and Roman Polanski) after a priceless icon they think he's hidden. Directed by Deran Sarafian, the helter-skelter plot generates more confusion than suspense, though the Moscow locales add some interest. Stylized violence, a brief sexual encounter and minimal rough language

title: Backlash
synopsis: Murky Western in which a gunfighter (Richard Widmark) tracks down the lone survivor of an Apache massacre of Arizona gold miners to learn if his long-lost father (John McIntire) was among them. Directed by John Sturges, the quest is complicated by a woman traveler (Donna Reed) who keeps getting in the gunman's way, an Apache attack on a trading post and an all-out range war pitting father against son. Assorted frontier violence and romantic complications

title: Back Roads
synopsis: A prostitute (Sally Field) and a cheerful down-and-outer (Tommy Lee Jones) hit the road for California, and in the course of their misadventure, fall in 1ove. Under Martin Ritt's direction the performances are appealing but the basic narrative has an air of sentimental romanticism. Its soapy mix of sexuality and occasional violence is disappointingly emphasized

title: Back to Bataan
synopsis: World War II melodrama of an American officer (John Wayne) organizing an underground movement against the Japanese occupation of the Philippines, it pays tribute to the contribution of these guerrillas in the liberation of their homeland. Directed by Edward Dmytryk, the patriotic derring-do of the Filipino resistance fighters begins and ends with the freeing of Allied prisoner-of-war camps. Wartime violence and national stereotypes

title: Back to God's Country
synopsis: Dim adventure directed by Joseph Pevney is set in the 1890's Yukon where an American sea captain (Rock Hudson) struggles to protect his wife (Marcia Henderson) and cargo of furs from a vicious villain (Steve Cochran) whose nemesis is a murderous Great Dane. Stylized violence, including an attempted sexual assault

title: Back to School
synopsis: Rodney Dangerfield provides a special brand of uncouth humor in this story of a self-made millionaire who returns to college to help his son but finds that there are some things that money can't buy. Alan Metter's direction keeps things moving in a somewhat tame sophmoric comedy about higher education. Brief instance of nudity and a bit of foul language

title: Back to the Beach
synopsis: Frankie Avalon and Annette Funicello return to the seashore and discover that the chaste relationships of the 1950s have evolved into the sexual alliances of the 1980s. Fanciful nostalgic trip from director Lyndall Hobbs is inconsistent in winking at the plot's implied premarital sex while offhandedly affirming the virtues of enduring marriage and fidelity

title: Back to the Future
synopsis: Above-average entertainment about a teenager (Michael J. Fox) who is transported back through time and obliged to serve as matchmaker for his parents or face retroactive non-existence. A major problem is that his mother-to-be finds him far more attractive than she does his father-to-be. Directed by Robert Zemeckis, it is funny and clever with a bit of genuine sentiment, that unfortunate1y is marred by casual profanity, the depiction of violence as manly and, though there is no depiction of it, an implicit acceptance of sexua1 promiscuity as standard teenage behavior

title: Back to the Future II
synopsis: Back to the Future Part II -- Mediocre sequel with the time-traveling doctor (Christopher Lloyd) taking Marty McFly (Michael J. Fox) and his girlfriend (Elizabeth Shue) to the year 2015 to save Marty's son (also Fox) from the ravages of destiny and then back to 1955 to stop the growing power of arch-villain Biff (Thomas F. Wilson). Director Robert Zemeckis makes an empty show of technical wizardry out of a nonsensical script that features a succession of product endorsements, including a trailer for Part III. Minimal rough language laced with incidental sexual innuendoes

title: Back to the Future III
synopsis: Back to the Future Part III -- Tame, tired sequel finds Marty (Michael J. Fox) transported to the Old West of 1885 where his professor pal (Christopher Lloyd) has fallen in love but is about to take a bullet in the back. With little more to go on than cardboard characters, cartoon situations and special effects that have by now grown stale, the team of writer Bob Gale and director Robert Zemeckis can't quite triplicate the sense of fun and ingenuity that made the original so appealing. Minimal street language and mild, cartoon-like violence

title: Bad Behaviour
synopsis: Low-key comedy-drama set in London where a long-married Irish couple (Stephen Rea and Sinead Cusack), tired with the daily grind of work and parenting, go through a restless phase in their marriage with good-humored impatience. Working without a script, director Les Blair gets convincing, down-to-earth performances from the actors meandering through droll slice-of-life situations that ring true to the discontents of mid-life malaise and the comforts of marital commitment. An implied sexual encounter, some heavy drinking and occasional rough language

title: Bad Boys
synopsis: Sean Penn stars as a vicious young criminal sent to a reformatory in this brutal exploitation movie trying to pass itself off as socially significant. The uninspired direction of Richard Rosenthal of a cliche-littered script owes little to real life and everything to some five decades of Hollywood prison movies. Bereft of moral or social perspective, it places a heavy emphasis on violence and vengeance within the gruesome context of prison life

title: Bad Boys
synopsis: Thin buddy movie of Miami detectives (Martin Lawrence and Will Smith) saddled with protecting a murder witness (Tea Leoni) while trying to recover a huge stash of heroin stolen from the police evidence room. Director Michael Bay's explosive action story is stuffed with wall-to-wall violence made to look like little more than manly fun and all part of a day's work for macho cops. Excessive violence, much sexual innuendo, fleeting nudity and incessant rough language

title: Bad Boys II
synopsis: Mindlessly violent action flick in which Miami narcotics cops (Will Smith and Martin Lawrence) must bring down a Cuban drug lord (Jordi Molla) smuggling millions of dollars worth of ecstasy pills into the United States while protecting an undercover DEA agent (Gabrielle Union) in over her head. Director Michael Bay's protracted sequel visually assaults with its senseless, slow-motion gunplay and explosions while the strained plot is a pastiche of extraneous scenes. Relentlessly stylized graphic violence, a sexual encounter, recreational drug abuse and constant rough language with some profanity
full_review:
Original bad boys Martin Lawrence and Will Smith reunite eight years after their first buddy-cop movie in the mindlessly violent action flick "Bad Boys II" (Columbia).
The protracted sequel, brought to the screen by producer Jerry Bruckheimer and director Michael Bay, visually assaults the audience with its senseless, slow-motion gunplay and explosions. With careening shots and whiplash cuts, Bay throws out one action sequence after another until they are a blur on screen. The film stretches on and on as the body count rises and the strained plot resembles a patchwork of incoherent scenes stapled together. And painted in broad strokes, the underdeveloped villains are silly caricatures.

Smith and Lawrence once again play Miami narcotics cops Mike and Marcus, this time after a Cuban drug lord (Jordi Molla with a perpetual three-day beard) smuggling millions of dollars worth of ecstasy pills into the United States. Gabrielle Union joins the duo as Marcus' sister, an undercover DEA agent going after the same target.

Missing is a zippy rapport that could have made Smith and Lawrence's comic scenes zing instead of fizzle. The sequel feels tired, and after so many long car chases and shootouts, so does the audience. The swaggering cops emerge from crushed cars and fiery explosions with nary a scratch, making the gruesome violence seem like just a game.

Loud, long and leaden, "Bad Boys II" may work at the box office, but let's hope most audiences will have had enough with the equally mind-numbing first one.

Because of relentless stylized graphic violence, a sexual encounter and some sexual innuendo, drug content and constant rough language with some profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Bad Company
synopsis: Inconsistent comedy-drama in which a streetwise bookie (Chris Rock) is convinced by a top CIA agent (Anthony Hopkins) to take the place of his twin brother, an agent killed during a secret operation, in order to seize a suitcase-sized nuclear weapon before it falls into the hands of fanatical terrorists. Despite a few exciting action sequences and some humorous moments, director Joel Schumacher(s film stumbles along until its protracted ending, using nuclear terrorism as a plot device to create suspense. Intermittent violence with a few intense action sequences, brief sexual suggestiveness and sporadic crass words with an instance of rough language
full_review:
Coming on the heels of “The Sum of All Fears” which also dealt with nuclear terrorism, the comedy-drama “Bad Company” (Touchstone) may suffer from bad timing. Although it is popcorn entertainment with some thrilling action sequences, the uneven film hits a little too close to home for comfort with its plot about fanatical terrorists gaining possession of a suitcase-sized nuclear weapon. And even despite its star billing of Anthony Hopkins and Chris Rock, “Bad Company” may not be able to transcend audience feeling about not wanting to be exposed to a story about nuclear weapons in the wrong hands in their entertainment choices when there is enough real news about such horrific possibilities.

Hopkins portrays steely CIA agent Oakes, a man who genuinely believes in “duty to country.” Somber opening scene places Oakes in Prague with his Harvard-educated, highly trained partner Kevin Pope (Rock) haggling with a Russian black-marketer Vas (Peter Stormare) over the price of a compact nuclear weapon. The rapid-fire action that follows has a rival bidder make his presence known, fatally wounding Pope as he saves Oakes life.

The film then cuts to the laughs that Rock fans maybe expecting. Rock reappears as Jake Hayes, a fast-talking, streetwise hustler separating folks from their cash by winning chess games and scalping tickets. Jake has no idea that he had a twin brother separated from him at birth. Oakes and his team appear and persuade Jake to pose as his brother for the good of the country and a boat load of money.

Director Joel Schumacher procures some funny moments out of the nine training days the CIA operatives have to prepare Jake before returning to Prague to seal the deal. But what is missing in these scenes, and throughout the rest of the film, is any connection between Rock and Hopkins. As if to counter Rock’s high-spirited acting, Hopkins offers a very restrained performance. But the result is a rather bland, remote character who clearly has a conscience but little else to make him a compelling character. As Pope, the secret agent, Rock mistakes stiffness for formality. Yet even in his cardboard portrayal of the agent, it seems like he might break out at any moment into his characteristic wide-eyed, toothy grin.� Playing Jake, a role more in keeping with his comedic talents, Rock fares better. Surprisingly, he is better when Jake stands up for himself, angrily telling off Oakes’ snide, condescending boss in a memorable scene, than when he plays the wise-cracking fool shouting out silly quips as he avoids being shot or stabbed.

The action sequences can be exciting, particularly a car chase through the countryside outside of Prague, but they can also be quite intense. When one of the rival bidder’s henchmen unsuccessfully tries to kill Jake (thinking he is still Pope) and is cornered, his chooses to leap off a tall building, reinforcing the now all-too-familiar persona of the suicide terrorist. And Schumacher doesn’t just show you his hurtle downward, but in quick flashes, his landing and a closeup of his face, which is probably more than most viewers want to see.

Skimpy characterization detracts from the film as well. Oakes’ team is strictly one-dimensional, although the actors try hard to make their presence felt. The identity of the rival bidder (Matthew Marsh) is revealed to be a ruthless terrorist from Yugoslavia intent on blaming the United States for the status of things around the world. But he’s just an ugly mug without much more to his character other than a taste for American bloodshed. The film’s protracted ending wears the viewer down, with it’smany twists and turns, and especially because it is these scenes that vividly show the real potential for nuclear terrorism.

“Bad Company” was initially to be in theaters last fall but the release was postponed to give it some distance from the Sept. 11 attack. A scene toward the end of film offers a nod to patriotism, but seems to have been inserted at the last moment for effect. However, neither time nor this scene might be able to warm the chill some viewers may feel as a result of the slick story’s close resemblance to real world events.

Due to intermittent violence with a few intense action sequences, brief sexual suggestiveness and sporadic crass words with an instance of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Bad Company
synopsis: French production composed of two dramatic variations on a single theme: loneliness is only masked by the companionship of equally lonely pals. Director Jean Eustache skillfully communicates the desperate bravado which hides the gnawing uncertainties of the immature youths in these two stories. Viewers may be put off by the movie's drab documentary style and some gross sexual language but none will be unmoved by the pathetic nature of these young lives

title: Bad Company
synopsis: Clean-cut Pennsylvanian youth (Barry Brown), fleeing conscription during the Civil War, joins up with a youthful band of Missouri toughs (led by Jeff Bridges) and as they make their way West, he becomes as adept as any of them at robbing banks and killing hombres. Directed by Robert Benton, its morality tale is not very profound but the period piece is beautifully mounted and painstakingly detailed. One wonders, however, if all the cursing and updated sex talk is really credible for teenagers in 1862

title: Bad Company
synopsis: Double crosses abound in Ross Thomas' cynical story about a disgraced ex-CIA agent (Laurence Fishburne) who gets a job with a shady industrial espionage firm, then plots with his partner (Ellen Barkin) to kill their boss (Frank Langella) and take over the company. Director Damian Harris supplies an edgy atmosphere and sleek visual style to an unsavory story about greedy cardboard characters. Several brief bedroom scenes, fleeting nudity, brief violence and some rough language

title: Bad Day at Black Rock
synopsis: Morality tale in the form of a tense thriller set in a small Western town whose residents are forced to face their guilty past when a one-armed stranger (Spencer Tracy) arrives in 1945 asking for the whereabouts of a Japanese-American farmer. Director John Sturges gets much suspense from the uneven odds against the lone, handicapped outsider confronted by increasingly hostile locals (Robert Ryan, Lee Marvin and Ernest Borgnine). Growing menace and brief but painfully effective violence

title: Bad Education
synopsis: Triangular drama set in Spain about a young, gay filmmaker (Fele Martinez) who, after encountering a former classmate (Gael Garcia Bernal) -- now a struggling actor -- whom he had once been enamored with, decides to make a movie about their youthful experiences as students at a strict, all-boys Catholic boarding school, in particular the pederast predations by their headmaster, a priest (Daniel Gimenez-Cacho). Stylishly directed by Pedro Almodovar, the movie's plot takes classic film-noir conventions and gives them a homoerotic twist. In touching on the hot-button issue of sexual abuse by the clergy, Almodovar paints an unflattering -- and unbalanced -- picture of Catholic priests; however, his primary motive seems to have been to use the crimes as a catalyst for the story rather than as a weapon to target the church in general for condemnation. Subtitles. Several intense homosexual encounters, implied pedophilia, murder without consequence, recurring drug content, transvestism, a scene of two boys masturbating, brief nudity, fleeting violence, instances of irreverent humor and frequent rough and crude language
full_review:
A young film director looking for his next project. A struggling actor with sultry good looks and a shrouded past. A predatory priest. These are the spicy ingredients in "Bad Education" (Sony Classics), the newest decadent dish served up by Spanish filmmaker Pedro Almodovar.

For Almodovar, the controversial film -- chosen as the opening-night selection of the 2004 Cannes Film Festival and the centerpiece of the 2004 New York Film Festival -- continues his trend toward more serious-toned material (including 1999's "All About My Mother" and 2001's "Talk to Her") and away from the ribald comedies which won him international acclaim, like "Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown" (1988) and "Tie Me Up, Tie Me Down!" (1989).

Still, while the movie deals with the hot-button issues of priest pedophilia and homosexuality, the Iberian auteur manages to sprinkle in some of his trademark humor in exploring his
touchstone themes of sin, seduction and cinema.

Heavily influenced by film-noir classics and tenuously inspired by personal recollections, the picture's story-within-a-story framework covers three time periods in Spain: 1964, 1977 and 1980, where most of the action takes place.

Revisiting themes explored in his "Law of Desire" (1986), Almodovar opens his new film in Madrid in 1980, where Enrique Goded (Fele Martinez), a successful movie director, is combing through newspaper stories searching for script ideas. An attractive young man (Gael Garcia Bernal) serendipitously shows up at the production office and introduces himself as Ignacio, an old classmate with whom Enrique had been enamored while they were students at a strict Catholic boarding school.

Ignacio gives Enrique a semiautobiographical short story he wrote about their youthful experiences, in particular, the pederast predations of Father Manolo (Daniel Gimenez-Cacho), the school's headmaster, whose lustful fixation for Ignacio cut short the budding boyhood romance. In the fictional version, Enrique grows up to be a frustrated family man, while Ignacio headlines a flamboyant drag-queen cabaret act.

Enrique agrees to turn it into a film and casts Ignacio in the lead role.

The plot shuttles back and forth, not only between past and present, but between the "real" world and the multilayered memories of the short story, weaving a triangular tapestry of deception, blackmail and murder created by the intersection of the three men's lives.

The concentric story lines are fuzzy at times, making it difficult to sort out reality from fiction within the world of the film. Keeping track of who's who also requires some heavy mental lifting -- or at least a scorecard -- for some actors perform multiple roles, or, as in the case of Father Manolo, the same character is played by two different actors (Gimenez-Cacho and, later, Lluis Homar). However, Almodovar, at the top of his cinematic game, manages to keep all the balls in the air without dropping any.

"Bad Education" contains several homoerotic scenes which are extremely suggestive without being necessarily explicit. In fact, the only nudity is a fleeting shot of Enrique's rump after he emerges from a skinny-dipping game of cat-and-mouse with Ignacio in his pool.

Despite charges to the contrary, Almodovar -- an agnostic who was raised Catholic -- has publicly stated that it was not his intention to make an anti-clerical film. Still, such denials must be weighed against what actually appears on screen. On this count, the verdict could go either way. The very choice of setting the story in a Catholic school is telling, as are the sinister shades with which he paints the two main priests, Father Manolo and Father Jose (Francisco Maestre) -- a sexual predator and a bullying brute, respectively.

However, while such unflattering portraits of ecclesiastical authority are hardly accidental, Almodovar's primary motive seems to have been to use Father Manolo's abuse of power as a catalyst for the story rather than as a weapon to target the church in general for condemnation. The film does take some shots at Catholicism and includes an irreverent scene where two characters
steal sacred vessels from a chapel.

On the positive side, by dramatizing the devastating effects sexual abuse has on victims' lives, the film can hopefully -- at least according to Sacred Heart Father Peter Malone, an Australian priest who is president of the World Catholic Association for Cinema -- "contribute to the church's continuing examination of conscience." In that sense, even a "Bad Education" can offer an opportunity for learning.

Subtitles.

Due to several intense homosexual encounters, implied pedophilia, murder without consequence, recurring drug content, transvestism, a scene of two boys masturbating, brief nudity, fleeting violence, instances of irreverent humor and frequent rough and crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.

title: Badge 373
synopsis: New York City detective (Robert Duvall), suspended from the force pending an investigation into the death of a Puerto Rican drug pusher, becomes a one-man crime-stopper. Director Howard Koch places his violent action in the slums and dives of the big city, showing in gritty detail racism, graft, greed and venality on every human level. Add constant coarse language and seamy situations, and the result is a cynical view of humanity

title: Bad Girls
synopsis: Superficial feminist Western in which disenchanted prostitutes (Madeleine Stowe, Mary Stuart Masterson, Andie MacDowell and Drew Barrymore) flee a murder charge in Texas only to run into a gang of sadistic outlaws (led by run by James Russo and Robert Loggia). Director Jonathan Kaplan's empty oater is coated with a slick Hollywood veneer but its feeble story is nothing more than a string of tired Western cliches substituting female for male leads. Some gunfights, revenge murders and frequent sexual references

title: Bad Influence
synopsis: Stylish, menacing and perverse thriller about a cunning drifter (Rob Lowe) who lures a wimpish yuppie (James Spader) into a decadent life of sex, lies and murder. Director Curtis Hanson chillingly develops the cat-and-mouse relationship between his two doomed protagonists in a story updating the Faust legend to modern-day Los Angeles. Rough language, recreational drug use, some grisly violence and several explicit sexual scenes with nudity

title: Badlands
synopsis: Fact-based story of a drifter (Martin Sheen) who takes his teenage sweetheart (Sissy Spacek) on a bizarre shooting spree across South Dakota and Montana in the 1950s. Director Terrence Malik presents a panoramic view of American life and myths, looking at the reality and the fiction behind the American Dream from the perspective of two archetypal characters. It is a dark and troubling vision with senseless violence at its core

title: Bad Lieutenant
synopsis: Rancid melodrama about the crackup of a New Nork City police detective (Harvey Keitel) who's over his head in gambling debts, drugs and sex, all of which is compounded by self-pity and a warped sense of moral guilt. Director Abel Ferrara's disjointed exercise in the emotional turbulence of going over the edge lacks credibility and leads nowhere. Excessive violence, graphic sex, substance abuse and rough language

title: Bad Man of Deadwood
synopsis: Roy Rogers and Gabby Hayes bring their medicine show to a crook-infested town and help its good citizens run them out in a low-budget but good-natured Western directed by Joseph Kane. Simple, clean-cut action with some mild violence

title: Badman's Country
synopsis: Low-budget Western teams ex-sheriff Pat Garrett (George Montgomery) with Wyatt Earp (Buster Crabbe), Bat Masterson (Gregory Wolcott) and Buffalo Bill Cody (Malcolm Atterbury) in saving Abilene from Butch Cassidy (Neville Brand) and his Wild Bunch. While director Fred F. Sears provides matinee thrills for the small fry, older viewers may find the outlandish collection of characters something of a hoot. Stylized violence

title: Bad Man's River
synopsis: Tame Italian Western with Gina Lollobrigida as a shady lady whose hobby is bilking amorous males (among them, Lee Van Cleef and James Mason) of whatever they're worth. Director Gene Martin stages a lot of forgettable action involving a sheriff's posse, a horde of revolutionary banditos and the Mexican Army. Waste of time

title: Badman's Territory
synopsis: Wild West yarn in which a Texas sheriff (Randolph Scott) on the run from trumped-up charges winds up in the Oklahoma panhandle which serves as a sanctuary for outlaws such as the James Brothers and the Dalton gang. Directed by Tim Whelan, it's a good guy-bad guy muddlement with comic relief from Gabby Hayes. Stylized shoot-outs and fisticuffs

title: Bad Medicine
synopsis: Misfit American students (led by Steve Guttenberg and Julie Hagerty) attend a bogus medical school in Central America. Director Harvey Miller's movie fails both as social satire and as broad comedy, offering litt1e more than some insulting humor pointed at Hispanic stereotypes along with bad jokes about incest and drug abuse

title: Bad Men of Missouri
synopsis: Standard shoot-'em-up turns the Younger Brothers (Dennis Morgan, Wayne Morris and Arthur Kennedy) into Western Robin Hoods robbing a villainous carpetbagger (Victor Jory) to save their neighbors' farms. Director Ray Enright provides some vigorous action, with occasional comic relief (Walter Catlett) and mild romance (Jane Wyman). Muddled justice theme and stylized violence

title: Bad Moon
synopsis: Inept monster movie in which a man (Michael Pare) visiting his sister (Mariel Hemingway) and young nephew manages to keep them in the dark about spending his nights as a demon werewolf, but he can't fool the family's pet dog. Director Eric Red fails to build any interest in the characters as they plod through an inane story with some gruesome chills and cheesy special-effects gore. Mindless sex, violence and rough language

title: Bad News Bears
synopsis: Bawdy, albeit entertaining, remake of the 1976 kiddie sports comedy about a boozing ex-big leaguer (Billy Bob Thornton in the Walter Matthau role) hired to coach a bungling team of Little League misfits and ends up turning their season and his own life around. Directed by Richard Linklater, the new version follows the original's coarsely sardonic lead, and, though ultimately redemptive, strikes out as recommendable family fare. Pervasive crude language and humor, as well as profanity by adults and children, drunkenness, some ethnic insensitivity, delinquent behavior, an implied sexual encounter and some risque situations
full_review:
In a summer that has already recycled one 1970s sports comedy ("The Longest Yard") comes a remake of the bawdy youth baseball laugher "Bad News Bears" (Paramount).

Billy Bob Thornton (still in "Bad Santa" mode) stars as Morris Buttermaker -- played by Walter Matthau in the original 1976 movie -- a boozing former big leaguer who briefly pitched in the majors (two-thirds of an inning) and now works as an exterminator.

As before, Buttermaker is hired to coach a team of hopelessly inept Little Leaguers whose sewer-mouthed lexicon gives new meaning to the term "foul ball." The runts are reasonable facsimiles of the '76 lineup, including Timmy Deters as the pugnacious Tanner Boyle and Brandon Craggs as pudgy catcher Mike Engelberg.

After being embarrassed in their first game, Buttermaker recruits flame-throwing ex-tomboy Amanda Whurlitzer (Sammi Kane Kraft), with whose mother he had once been romantically involved, and slugging biker boy Kelly Leak (Jeffrey Davies).

The underdogs start coming together as a team and winning, clawing their way to the championship game against their archrivals, the Yankees, a bullying squad of adolescent all-stars aggressively coached by Greg Kinnear.

Original screenwriter Bill Lancaster -- son of Burt -- gets a screen credit, and rightfully so since the faithful (almost to a fault) film follows the 1976 version practically scene by scene, in some cases, shot by shot. (Yes, the bungling Bears still kick the ball around to Bizet's "Carmen.")

"Bad Santa" writers Glenn Ficarra and John Requa have made some cosmetic changes.
Unfortunately, they have also added an unnecessary sexual subplot involving Buttermaker and one of the Bears' single moms (Marcia Gay Harden) that ends with them sleeping together (implied). Also troubling is a scene where Buttermaker treats the team to a postgame celebration at an adult eatery whose buxom barmaids later serve as the Bears' cheering section.

Director Richard Linklater ("School of Rock") also makes some concessions to political correctness: a physically challenged teammate has been added to the roster; Buttermaker doles out "nonalcoholic" beer to his players, underage smoking is out, as are racial slurs and the F-word (alternative expletives abound).

Despite giving his curmudgeon a sleazy (and slightly less sympathetic) edge, Thornton is nevertheless appealing. But it's hard to top Matthau's hangdog performance. Kinnear and Kraft are no Vic Morrow and Tatum O'Neal.

Back in 1976, this office wrote that the original conveyed "a cynical ... critique of middle-class values." Same holds true here.

But "Bears" is not all bad news. Both versions ultimately impart a positive message that promotes self-esteem and criticizes winning-at-all-costs competitiveness, while exploring themes of redemption (Buttermaker's) and reconciliation (Buttermaker and Amanda).

It is still distressing to watch young kids, cute though they are, swear like sailors.
While entertaining and admittedly funny at times, "Bad News Bears" strikes out as recommendable family fare.

The film contains pervasive crude language and humor, as well as profanity by adults and children, drunkenness, some ethnic insensitivity, delinquent behavior, an implied sexual encounter and some risque situations. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Bad Santa
synopsis: Abrasive black comedy about a self-loathing safecracker (Billy Bob Thornton) who, along with his dwarf accomplice (Tony Cox), poses as a department store Santa to rob shopping malls of their holiday loot -- that is, until a friendless overweight boy (Brett Kelly) stirs his booze-soaked conscience. Director Terry Zwigoff should expect coal in his stocking for assaulting viewers with a nonstop barrage of obscenities and vulgar raunchiness which leave Santa's red suit soiled -- in more ways than one. By taking the "merry" out of Christmas and portraying its sleazy St. Nick stand-in as a foul-mouthed, drunken, chain-smoking, suicidal sexual predator, the film undermines its tacked-on redemptive message. Excessive rough and crude language and profanity, recurring lewd sexual encounters, much crass humor, pervasive alcohol abuse, an attempted suicide and some violence
full_review:
You better watch out. You better not cry. You better not pout, I'm telling you why: A chain-smoking, skirt-chasing, foul-mouthed Santa is coming to town -- or at least to a theater near you.
Billy Bob Thornton stars in "Bad Santa" (Dimension), director Terry Zwigoff's bilious black comedy about a burned-out burglar who steals the "merry" out of Christmas.

Thornton plays Willie T. Stokes, a self-loathing, perpetually pickled safecracker who dons the red suit each holiday season and poses as a department store Santa in order to gain after-hours access to the store's loot.

Viewers first meet the lecherous lout sitting alone in a bar wearing a stained Santa outfit wallowing in misanthropic misery. After an astringent, Chopin-scored voice-over, a well-lubricated Willie stumbles out into the back alley and vomits just as the title card appears. Nothing puts an audience in the holiday spirit quite like a Currier & Ives upchucking.

The film then flashes forward a year. Willie is roused from his annual 11-month stupor when Marcus (Tony Cox), his dwarf accomplice -- the brains of the operation -- summons him to Phoenix where he has staked out a shopping mall ripe for the taking.

Right off the bat, Willie's rancid attitude and potty-mouthed rants raise red flags with the store's strait-laced manager (John Ritter, in his final role), who alerts the mall's chief of security (Bernie Mac) to the new hangdog hires.

After coming home to find the square-shield sniffing around his motel room, Willie hides out in the tony digs of Thurman (Brett Kelly), a friendless overweight 8-year-old whose white-collar criminal father is serving jail time, leaving the sad-sack kid alone in the house with only his senile grandmother (Cloris Leachman).

The two misfits strike up a co-dependent relationship, the youngster proving a most unlikely antidote to the yegg-nog's poisoned soul. After beating up a bunch of skate-boarding neighborhood bullies who had been terrorizing Thurman, Willie begins to feel the first stirrings of his booze-soaked conscience.

Willie also finds love -- or at least lust -- with a libidinous barmaid (Lauren Graham), who has a fetish for men in Santa suits. Being raised Jewish, she never got a chance to sit on Santa's lap and is now apparently making up for lost time.

In fairness, it is somewhat of a misnomer that the film presents Santa in a sleazy light, since Thornton's character is not Kris Kringle but only a store stand-in. Still, Zwigoff deserves coal in his stocking for soiling Santa's red suit (in more ways than one) by dragging a beloved symbol of Christmas into the proverbial gutter -- and barely avoiding an NC-17 rating in the process.

Given the crass commercialization of Christmas which has systematically stripped it of its religious significance, it should not be surprising that such a caustic bashing of one of the holiday's most beloved symbols isn't met with public indignation.

Far from raising eyebrows, the film has earned praise from many critics as a welcome relief to the sugarplum sentimentality of more traditional yuletide yarns. Such positive reviews seem to underline the toxic bah-humbug cynicism that has infected modern secular society.

In addition to assaulting viewers with a nonstop barrage of obscenities, the film's "naughty" list includes several raunchy sexual encounters (though nudity is surprisingly absent) and repeated use of the "f word" in scenes involving young children. Much of the film's ribald one-note humor is fueled by the prevailing belief that if it is offensive it's funny, and if it is heartless it's hip. Though perfectly cast as the soused scrooge, Thornton scowls through the film sounding like a foul-mouthed Grinch.

And while the twisted tale does offer a whisper of repentance and redemption, the film's criticism of consumer culture is a clear case of too little, too late and is hardly commensurate with the steady stream of smut leading up to it.

Rather than applauding Zwigoff for such a determinedly mean-spirited attack on Christmas, perhaps he deserves, in the words of Charles Dickens, to be "boiled with his own pudding and buried with a stake of holly in his heart."

Due to excessive rough and crude language and profanity, recurring lewd sexual encounters, much crass humor, pervasive alcohol abuse, an attempted suicide and some violence, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Bad Timing: A Sensual Obsession
synopsis: Director Nicolas Roeg's coldly somber account of obsessive love in modern Vienna stars Art Garfunkel as a smug, domineering psychiatrist and Theresa Russell (whose performance gives the movie the only life it has) as an unstable American woman. Some very explicit sex scenes

title: Bagdad
synopsis: Clunky tale of desert intrigue directed by Charles Lamont pits an English-educated Bedouin princess (Maureen O'Hara) against the man (Paul Christian) accused of murdering her father as well as the Turkish governor (Vincent Price) in cahoots with the real culprit (John Sutton) whose maurauding Black Robes are terrorizing the desert tribes. Revenge tale with stylized violence and romantic bosh

title: Bagdad Cafe
synopsis: Lovely little fable about the restorative powers of love and friendship set at the Bagdad Cafe, a rundown truckstop, luncheonette and motel in the desert outside Las Vegas. German director Percy Adlon tracks the unlikely friendship between a German tourist (Marianne Sagebrecht) and the Bagdad's proprietor (CCH Pounder), a black single mother. Also in focus are the Cafe's oddball regulars, including an old Hollywood set painter (Jack Palance) who falls for the tourist. Much profanity and some nudity in several brief scenes involving an artist's model

title: Bait
synopsis: Insubstantial seriocomic actioner in which a bumbling petty thief (Jamie Foxx) is used by the government to trap a computer mastermind (Doug Hutchison) who stole gold bullion worth millions from the Federal Reserve. It's style over substance in director Antoine Fuqua's slick flick which starts off promisingly then fizzles with a scrambled script, one-note characters and a too-neat Hollywood ending. A sexual encounter, intermittent violence and recurring rough language with fleeting profanity. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Ballad of a Soldier
synopsis: A 19-year-old soldier, on a six-day furlough, makes his way home through the war-torn Russian countryside, encountering a variety of people, each with his or her own unique experience of World War II. Director Grigori Chukhrai avoids the blatant Soviet propaganda of previous Russian exports while fashioning a warm and humanistic tribute to the integrity and goodness of ordinary people

title: Ballet Russes
synopsis: Superb dance film about the trendsetting troupe that began with the legendary choreographer Serge Diaghilev (and the participation of great artists like Picasso, Nijinsky and Stravinksy), and after his death came under the leadership of autocratic Russian Col. Wasily de Basil with the name Ballet Russes de Monte Carlo, and how, after some internecine struggle, splintered into two troupes, one keeping that name, the other calling itself the Original Ballet Russes. Having interviewed many of the great dancers at a Ballets Russes reunion in 2000, filmmakers Dan Geller and Dayna Goldfine have juxtaposed priceless footage and still photographs of the great dancers in their youthful primes, making an incredibly poignant contrast. The various rivalries between the companies, and individual choreographers like Leonide Massine and George Balanchine give the narrative heightened dramatic interest. Pitch-perfect narration by actress Marion Seldes. The anamorphic DVD features numerous extras, including additional footage, stills galleries and a 12-page booklet by New York Times dance writer Jack Anderson

title: Ballistic: Ecks vs. Sever
synopsis: Trashy, ultraviolent tale in which a former FBI agent (Antonio Banderas) pursues a deadly kidnapper (Lucy Liu) only to discover they have a common enemy (Gregg Henry). As directed by Kaos, car bombings, shootouts and mayhem are almost nonstop in an absurdly contrived narrative of bogus emotions and glamorized violence. Excessive violence and brief rough language
full_review:
So explosively violent is "Ballistic: Ecks vs. Sever" (Warner Bros.) that stars Antonio Banderas and Lucy Liu are almost beside the point. They are mere instruments of destruction in this trashy tale of vengeance-motivated kidnapping and killing.

The narrative, in fact, is murky and confusing, especially concerning Liu's murderous character, agent-turned-kidnapper Sever, who repeatedly goes up against a slew of armed men surrounding her, and, with flying fists and lethal limbs, comes out unscathed. Such is the nonsensical level of this movie.

Another character believes his wife was murdered, just as she conveniently believes he was murdered, so now she is married to the villain of the piece, and harboring a far-too-easy-to-guess secret about her child.

The director, who uses the single name Kaos, an abbreviated form of his Thai surname, orchestrates a nearly nonstop barrage of shootouts, car bombings and utter mayhem which suggest that violence is simply exciting entertainment. And then we are to believe that the murderous Sever is actually good, her kidnapping of a child and multiple shootings all justified by her need to avenge her own son's death, which she accomplishes with icy determination.

Ex-FBI agent Ecks (Banderas) is on her tail but eventually they learn they have a common enemy (Gregg Henry).
