Punchy, overloud music underscores the brutality of the hand-to-hand fighting and extended shootouts -- which are the true focus of the story, not the bogus emotions that are ridiculous to watch. With stick-figure characters and its rationalization of homicidal violence, the misleadingly titled "Ballistic: Ecks vs. Sever" is a total time-waster.

Because of excessive violence and brief rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Ball of Fire
synopsis: Uneven romantic comedy about 8 erudite professors (led by Gary Cooper) whose work writing an encyclopedia is disrupted by a burlesque queen (Barbara Stanwyck) hiding from the D.A. seeking an indictment of her gangster boyfriend (Dana Andrews). Directed by Howard Hawks, the fish-out-of-water plot generates some smiles but never quite measures up to the comic potential of the situation which increasingly falters into sentimental melodrama. Romantic complications and comic menace

title: Balls of Fury
synopsis: Exhausting comedy about a washed-up pingpong prodigy (Dan Fogler) who is asked by an FBI agent (George Lopez) to help catch a mysterious crime lord (Christopher Walken). Along the way the former champ turns to a blind pingpong master (James Hong) to regain his skills, falls in love with the master's daughter (Maggie Q) and eventually must play in a tournament with life-or-death stakes. Frequently crude and always preposterous, director and co-writer Ben Garant's film has some flashes of originality and gets in a few good satiric swipes, even as it revels in its own silliness. Much crude language, one instance of profanity, suggestive gestures, gross and scatological jokes, and mild gay-themed humor
full_review:
"Balls of Fury" (Rogue) follows the comic fortunes of a washed-up pingpong prodigy named Randy Daytona (Dan Fogler). Having disgraced himself as a teenager at the 1988 Olympic Games, Daytona ekes out a living as a stunt pingpong performer in Reno, Nev., until he is approached by FBI agent Rodriguez (George Lopez).

Rodriguez asks Daytona to help the FBI catch a mysterious and powerful crime lord named Feng (Christopher Walken), who also happens to be a rabid fan of Daytona's sport. Since Feng was responsible for killing Daytona's father (Robert Patrick) over a gambling debt incurred when Daytona lost at the Olympics, the former champ quickly overcomes his initial doubts and agrees to do what he can.

Feng, Rodriguez explains, now holds secret pingpong tournaments to which he invites only the best players. The plan to catch him thus depends on Daytona's ability to receive such an invitation, which eventually comes in the form of a golden paddle.

Daytona has become rusty since his days of early prowess, so Rodriguez places him under the tutelage of Wong (James Hong), a blind master of the sport. Wong's daughter, Maggie (Maggie Q) -- also a prodigiously gifted player -- soon becomes Daytona's practice partner, with predictable romantic results.

Frequently crude and always preposterous, "Balls of Fury," directed and co-written by Ben Garant, has some flashes of comic originality. Walken's Feng, for instance, is a bizarre amalgam of early Dracula, late Elvis and a 6-year-old. And how can one fail to feel at least some affection for a film in which the archvillain's first line of dialogue is: "Okey-dokey, artichokey"?

The script by Garant and Thomas Lennon, who also get in some good satiric swipes at everything from kung fu movies to 1980s heavy metal music along the way, never takes itself seriously, reveling in its own silliness, though too often straying from the path of good taste. As for the slapstick, it's strictly anything for a laugh, including such questionable conceits as the sight gag of Siamese twins with a paddle in each hand playing a solitary opponent.

"Balls of Fury" is thus a little too furious and a little too frantic for its own good. By the time it's over, viewers are apt to feel more exhausted than amused.

The film, though acceptable for older adolescents, contains much crude language, one instance of profanity, suggestive gestures, gross and scatological jokes, and mild gay-themed humor. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Baltimore Bullet
synopsis: Moderately funny comedy about a master pool hustler (James Coburn) who takes on a young protege (Bruce Boxleitner) in order to fulfill the veteran's dream of getting revenge on the greatest pool sharpster of them all (Omar Sharif). Sexual scenes played in a leering and demeaning manner make this Robert Ellis Miller directed road show with Ronee Blakley unsuitably vulgar

title: Balto
synopsis: Uneven animated adventure about an outcast dog (voice of Kevin Bacon) who gets through an Alaskan blizzard in the winter of 1925 with the antitoxin needed to save snowbound Nome from a diptheria epidemic. Directed by Simon Wells, the animation is more imaginative than the formula characters in a story which starts slowly, then becomes a series of thrills as Balto overcomes the perils of the frozen wilderness and a nasty canine rival

title: Bambi
synopsis: Walt Disney's classic animated feature conveys the simplicity, charm and excitement of Felix Salten's novel, especially in its appealing characterization of Thumper, Flower and all the others who inhabit the young deer's forest world. The story has some intense moments, notably the forest fire sequence and the death of Bambi's mother, though in a context not beyond the resources of most young viewers. The DVD premiere of "Bambi" is all you could wish for: a pristine print with a more accurate color palette than even on the film's ballyhooed laserdisc incarnation, restored soundtrack (as well as alternate French and Spanish tracks), and multitudinous features spread over two discs. There are aural re-enactments of Walt Disney's story meetings -- lasting more than an hour -- wherein you can hear how the final film so closely mirrored the original concept. This, like the "Restoring Disney" feature on the second disc, is hosted by Patrick Stewart, who will play Bambi's father in the upcoming sequel, which gets its own plug in "The Legacy Continues" feature. There's a 53-minute "Making of Bambi" documentary; Walt Disney explaining on his television show how some of the film's effects were achieved; a look at the vast Disney archives where seemingly every scrap of Disney material is lovingly kept; a look at the actors who voiced the characters, including Thumper; and a couple of deleted scenes, though those are storyboard reconstructions rather than fully animated scenes. Add to all these a 1937 "Silly Symphony" that presaged some of Bambi's animation techniques, a 1942 time capsule, and a plethora of games and activities for the kids, and you have first-rate family entertainment. But even if there were no extra features, this is one of the true Disney masterpieces, and a must-have for the family library. A-I (G) 1942

title: Bambi II
synopsis: > Touching, surprisingly good follow-up to the highly revered Disney classic "Bambi," with the story focusing on the period following the death of Bambi's mother. Here Bambi's father, The Great Prince (voice of Patrick Stewart), reluctantly agrees to nurture his offspring after no surrogate mother can be found, taking a "tough love" approach at first. Bambi (voice of Alexander Gould) is unsure of his father's love, but the inevitable bonding that ensues has echoes of "The Lion King." The plot is sound, and though the artwork is far less detailed than the richly designed original, it's still eye-filling, and the main characters -- including Bambi's friends Thumper (now with sisters), Flower and Faline -- are well-drawn. Strains of the original score and a couple of the songs hearken back to the beloved original, only slightly marred by some bland contemporary ballads. This coming-of-age story is almost good enough to have been released in theaters rather than direct to video. The DVD includes a making-of featurette with the animators paying due homage to the original, and the usual games and activities. Apart from the reference to the mother's death, and some scenes of peril from human hunters and their voracious dogs, which might frighten toddlers, this is fine entertainment for the kids and Disney buffs in general. A-I (G) 2005

title: Bambina
synopsis: Insensitive Italian comedy about a con artist who tries to exploit a retarded teenage girl but who winds up marrying her instead. Vestiges of humanism and serious intent are overridden by distasteful treatment of mental retardation

title: Bamboo Gods and Iron Men
synopsis: Honeymooning in the Orient, an African-American couple (James Iglehart and Shirley Washington) gets mixed up with a ruthless gang. The inept Philippine production, clumsily directed by Cesar Gallardo, spices up its dreary martial arts violence with a massage parlor sequence

title: Bamboozled
synopsis: Ambitious satire in which an African-American television writer (Damon Wayans) creates a comedy featuring black-faced minstrels to make a statement about the stereotypical imagery of blacks in mass media, but his plan backfires when the show meets with overwhelming success. Taking on racism in network television, writer-director Spike Lee's indulgent film begins promisingly, but loses potency with an overly elaborate and melodramatic narrative. Briefly intense violence, theme of racism, sexual references and recurring rough language with some profanity. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Bamse
synopsis: Swedish import about a young man who falls in love with his dead father's mistress (Grynet Molvig) but she does not reciprocate his affections. The situation is far from being morally or psychologically healthy, but it is handled with restraint and artistic sensitivity

title: Banana Peel
synopsis: Enjoyable French crime spoof about a gang of con artists (notably Jeanne Moreau and Jean-Paul Belmondo) trying their best to outswindle each other. Directed by Marcel Ophuls, the plot doesn't add up to much but it's fast-paced and good-natured. Subtitles. Comic violence and sexual references

title: Bananas
synopsis: Woody Allen's patchwork comedy is loosely tied to a Latin American revolution which serves as the excuse for the standard fare of tasteless insult and irreverence, chock full of gratuitous nonsense dragged in seemingly because there was still a little film in the camera. As those familiar with Allen's approach might expect, religious orthodoxy comes in for its share of ecumenical jibes that many will find needlessly offensive

title: Bandit Queen
synopsis: Beaten and raped as a youngster, a low-caste Indian woman (Seema Biswas) joins a gang of thieves, eventually leading them on a murderous rampage against unarmed upper-caste men after the 1981 murder of her lover. In a fact-based story with no tolerance for love or forgiveness, director Shekhar Kapur presents the title character as a furious feminist heroine, lionized by the lower castes for her insistence on political and social equality. Subtitles. Excessive violence, including multiple rapes, a massacre and savage beatings, prolonged full nudity and much rough language

title: Bandits
synopsis: Sentimental but stylish French mystery-romance about an aging criminal (Jean Yanne), his daughter (Marie-Sophie L.) and a handsome, daring young crook (Patrick Bruel). Though Claude LeLouch's direction tends to be slick and glossy, there is some substance to the characters and their feelings. Several scenes of violence, brief nudity and implied sexual situations

title: Bandits
synopsis: German production romanticizes four women convicts who form a rock band in prison, manage to escape and go on the run as their recordings become hits and their ability to evade the police dragnet turn them into counterculture heroes. Directed by Katja von Garnier, the film is a wildly implausible hodgepodge of music videos and glamorized fugitives. Subtitles. Sympathetic depiction of criminal behavior, some violence including suicide, an extended sexual encounter with nudity, recreational drug abuse and recurring rough language

title: Bandits
synopsis: Ill-conceived crime comedy in which two bank robbers (Billy Bob Thornton and Bruce Willis) both fall for the disillusioned housewife (Cate Blanchett) they kidnap, who joins them in their lawless exploits. In director Barry Levinson's inconsistent, meandering narrative, not only does crime pay, the selfish trio carry on a three-way relationship that disregards morality. Flippant treatment of fidelity, some violence, implied sexual encounters and brief crass language and profanity

title: Band of Angels
synopsis: Crowded Civil War sudser from the Robert Penn Warren novel in which the mulatto daughter (Yvonne De Carlo) of a bankrupt Kentucky aristocrat is sold at auction to a New Orleans cotton millionaire (Clark Gable) with a shady past who treats her with respect and ultimately wins her love. Directed by Raoul Walsh, the script raises period issues of racial oppression and human rights but they get lost in the stew of melodramatic action and tawdry characters. Stylized violence, sexual situations, injustices of slavery and racial epithets

title: Band of Brothers
synopsis: Ambitious, well-crafted World War II 10-part series about a paratrooper division in the U.S. Army named Easy Company which landed in France on D-Day, fought the Battle of the Bulge and captured Hitler�s Eagle�s Nest at Berchtesgaden. Based on Steven E. Ambrose�s nonfiction best seller, the film�s executive producers Tom Hanks and Steven Spielberg have meticulously recreated the dark, anxious atmosphere of the battle and the rigid hierarchical command of the Army, but the long sequences of the fighting, while not gratuitous, are nonetheless harrowing and sometimes explicit. Many scenes of war violence

title: Bandolero
synopsis: Uneven Western starring Jimmy Stewart and Dean Martin as brothers who redeem their shady past but who finally redeem themselves in a battle against Mexican bandits. Directed by Andrew V. McLaglen, the characterizations are interesting, women are treated in a positive fashion and the humor is sly and refreshing. Some vulgar language and violent climax

title: Bandslam
synopsis: Genial comedy with music in which a newcomer (Gaelan Connell) at a New Jersey high school overcomes his socially disastrous past when befriended by a popular fellow student (Alyson Michalka) who makes him the manager of her rock group as they prepare for the titular battle-of-the-bands competition, his confidence getting a further boost from his blossoming romance with a bookish goth (Vanessa Hudgens). Though it deals with a few mature topics, and is unlikely to interest very young viewers, director and co-writer Todd Graff's exuberant salute to clique-defying friendship is free of anything unsuitable for the tween-and-up audience at whom it's aimed

title: Bandwagon
synopsis: Comic road movie in which four disparate youths (led by Lee Holmes) set out to make a name for their rock 'n roll band by playing gigs all over the South until a record contract with strings attached threatens to break them up. Writer-director John Schultz uses some low-key, good-natured humor to make the proceedings mildly entertaining despite a thin storyline and halting pace. Benign attitude towards theft, implied substance abuse, occasional profanity and a few uses of rough language

title: Bang, Bang, You're Dead
synopsis: Standard espionage story directed by Don Sharp in which an American (Tony Randall) gets swept away by romance and intrigue in Morocco. Stylized violence and a bedroom scene

title: Bangkok Dangerous
synopsis: Grim shoot-�em-up about a solitary hit man (Nicholas Cage) who travels to the titular city to carry out four contract killings for a local crime boss (Nirattisai Kaljareuk), but finds his emotional isolation thawed by his friendship for the petty thief (Shahkrit Yamnarm) he hires as an assistant and his feelings for a pretty pharmacy clerk (Charlie Young) who can neither hear nor speak. As directed by the Pang Brothers, this remake of their 1999 Thai film features considerable violence and muddled moral values, with its hero instructing his protege in the art of killing even while ostensibly reassessing his own viciousness. Brief graphic sexual activity, upper female nudity, intense action violence with gore, suicide, occasional rough and crude language
full_review:
In the grim shoot-‘em-up “Bangkok Dangerous” (Lionsgate), Joe (Nicholas Cage), a solitary hit man, travels to the titular city to carry out four contract killings for a local crime boss (Nirattisai Kaljareuk). This, he hopes, will be the lucrative climax of his career.

Once there, however, he falls under the exotic city’s spell and finds the emotional isolation necessary to his work thawed by his friendship for Kong (Shahkrit Yamnarm), the petty thief he hires as an assistant, and by his feelings for the pretty Fon (Charlie Young), a pharmacy clerk who can neither hear nor speak.

As directed by the Pang Brothers, this remake of their 1999 Thai film features considerable violence and muddled moral values, with its hero instructing his protege in the art of killing even while ostensibly reassessing his own viciousness.

The film contains brief graphic sexual activity, upper female nudity, intense action violence with gore, suicide and occasional rough and crude language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Bang the Drum Slowly
synopsis: Director John Hancock's humorous and touching portrait of a young baseball player who wants to play one last season before he dies made Robert De Niro a name to remember. Michael Moriarity co-starred as the best friend who shares his hopes and pains. Realistic but sensitive treatment of terminal illness

title: Bank Robber
synopsis: Vapid surrealistic tale written and directed by Nick Mead features a moronic bank robber (Patrick Dempsey) hiding out in a seedy hotel room where he is troubled by real and imaginary visitors. Explicit sex scenes, violence, drug abuse and rough language

title: Bank Shot
synopsis: George C. Scott plays a safecracker sprung from jail in order to use his unique skills to direct a bank robbery. Director Gower Champion's fast-paced comedy is a satire on the criminal mind but its theme may give youngsters the wrong impression that crime pays

title: Banning
synopsis: Director Don Winston's story of corruption among the operators and affluent members of a California golf club overdoes the plot elements of vice and greed. O 1967

title: Bar 20 Rides Again
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Howard Bretherton with Hopalong Cassidy (William Boyd) getting some help from a young cowhand (Jimmy Ellison) and an old prospector (George Hayes) in stopping a gang of rustlers led by an admirer (Harry Worth) of Napoleon's tactics. Frontier violence

title: Barabbas
synopsis: Uneven costume epic follows the tormented path of the criminal (Anthony Quinn) who, after being freed by Pilate instead of Christ, is sentenced to the sulphur mines in Sicily, brought to Rome to be a gladiator (with Jack Palance as grimacing tutor-adversary) and finally crucified as a Christian under Nero. Directed by Richard Fleischer, the movie begins promisingly with a sequence counterpointing Christ and Barabbas but the religious level gets lost in Quinn's one-note performance as the surly, ever questioning survivor until reemerging in the ironic conclusion. Stylized violence

title: Baran
synopsis: Moving drama about a teen-age boy (Hossein Abedini) working on a construction site who loses his cushy job to an illegal Afghani worker (Zahra Bahrami), but his bitterness unexpectedly gives way to compassion when he discovers the worker's secret. , Despite slow pacing, director Majid Majidi probes the difficulties of Afghani workers in Iran by setting his lyrical film against a romantic backdrop with beautiful visuals. Fleeting violence and crass language

title: Barberella
synopsis: Barbarella -- French production about the misadventures of a vulnerable earth woman (Jane Fonda) facing various perils in a science-fiction world where evil has the upper hand. In a movie which is part comic strip and part Marquis de Sade, director Roger Vadim concentrates on the kinky and the unwholesome in this French production. Sexist theme and brief nudity

title: Barbarosa
synopsis: Country-western singer Willie Nelson plays the title role of a grizzled outlaw who is an unwilling participant in a 30-year old feud with the aristocratic Mexican family into which he married. Gilbert Roland is the patriarch who keeps sending out young men to kill him and Gary Busey is the young farmer with whom he teams and who ultimately receives Barbarosa's mantle. Offbeat concept, mediocre script, but Nelson's performance is fine. Australian director Frank Schepsi's American debut contains restrained violence

title: Barbershop
synopsis: Set in Chicago's South Side, the enjoyable ensemble comedy has the owner (Ice Cube) of a local barbershop selling it to a sinister loan shark (Keith David), but then trying to buy it back once he realizes the shop's worth as a gathering place for the community. As directed by Tim Story, the film is flawed by silly stereotypes and predictability, but manages to be endearing as it touches on racism, the black man's place in society and the importance of fellowship. Some sexual innuendo, fleeting drug content and sporadic crass expressions and profanity with an instance of rough language
full_review:
"The cornerstone of the community" is how one character describes the local haircutting establishment in the enjoyable ensemble comedy "Barbershop" (MGM).

Set over the course of a day in Chicago's South Side, director Tim Story's film focuses on the importance of a local tonsorial parlor in an African-American neighborhood as a gathering place where more than just haircuts are given. The movie is flawed by silly stereotypes and predictability, yet manages to be endearing as it touches on racism, fellowship and the black man's place in society.

A hub of conversation and gossip as well as a safe haven for free speech, the barbershop hosts spontaneous discussions on everything from reparation, the guilt or innocence of O.J. Simpson and the beauty of a certain female body part. Inheriting the barbershop from his father, Calvin (Ice Cube) is more interested in get-rich schemes (from herbal franchises to a do-it-yourself recording studio in his basement) than running the shop.

Already deep in debt, he decides to sell the store to sinister loan shark and local gangster Lester (Keith David), who is only missing a twirling mustache to go with his powder-blue suit and derby to more clearly indicate him as the dastardly villain. But when Calvin learns that Lester plans to turn the shop into a strip joint, turning the haircutters out into the street, he realizes his mistake and must somehow convince Lester to call off the deal.

The barbershop's motley crew includes old-timer Eddie (Cedric the Entertainer in a graying, Al Sharpton-like wig), the group's loud-mouthed historian with strong opinions and no customers. Pretentious latte-sipping Jimmy (Sean Patrick Thomas), who wears his superiority complex like a merit badge, is constantly sparring with Isaac (Troy Garity), a white barber who just wants a chance to prove he can cut hair with the best of them in the 'hood. Ricky (Michael Ealy) is an ex-con with two strikes against him who's trying to stay straight and out of the way of Terri (rap star Eve), the only female hair clipper, who can't get over her addiction to her two-timing boyfriend or get people to leave her apple juice alone.

A sideline story that eventually ties into the main narrative involves the theft of an automated-teller machine by a pair of bungling burglars (Anthony Anderson and Lahmard Tate) that plays like a poor man's Abbott and Costello slapstick scene. Although the humor sometimes dips into the arena of sexual suggestiveness, it stays above puerile toilet humor, succeeding in garnering a few laughs. The script allows for plenty of ad-libbing from the actors, who bounce off one another in the convincing, natural manner of people who have long been in each other's faces.

"Barbershop" is a pleasant surprise that, while mainly superficial in its treatment of heavy subjects, entertains with an underlying tenderness for the local community hangouts that have been replaced by more impersonal places like Starbuck's.

Due to some sexual innuendo, fleeting drug content and sporadic crass expressions and profanity with an instance of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Barbershop 2: Back In Business
synopsis: Raucous sequel which finds the owner (Ice Cube) of the titular storefront being squeezed by a slick businessman (Harry Lennix) bent on putting him out of business by opening a trendy super-salon directly across the street. Director Kevin Rodney Sullivan maintains the politically incorrect tone of the original, but if you listen carefully, you can hear a positive message about the importance of community, beneath the shouts and coarse comments of the colorful, though endearing, neighborhood characters (including Cedric the Entertainer). An implied sexual encounter, fleeting drug content, brief violence, and recurring crude language and humor, as well as profanity
full_review:
A mom-and-pop haircutting establishment gets shaved by some big-name competition in "Barbershop 2: Back in Business" (MGM).

Tim Story, who directed the sleeper hit "Barbershop" in 2002, hands over the director's, as well as the barber's, chair to Kevin Rodney Sullivan. The sequel, continues its predecessor's irreverent, politically incorrect brand of humor, finding farce in follicles and laughter in lather.

Ice Cube returns as Calvin Palmer, the pensive proprietor of the titular tonsorial parlor he inherited from his father. A cornerstone of Chicago's South Side community, the storefront hangout is a place where a motley crew of old-timers, young homies and hangers-on gather to chat, chill, play dominoes and even get haircuts. Having steered the shop safely through the financial straights of the earlier film, Calvin has settled comfortably into fatherhood, trying, as best he can, to live up to his own dad's pillar-of-society legacy.

But when "Nappy Cutz," a national chain equipped with state-of-the-art grooming equipment, wide-screen TVs and an indoor basketball court waiting area, sets up shop across the street, threatening to put them out of business, Calvin and his barbershop sextet find themselves singing the blues.

Further complicating matters is Nappy Cutz's oily business rep, Quentin Leroux (Harry Lennix), who entices several other local shopkeepers to sell their properties to large real estate interests -- all in the seductive name of "progress."

Helping Leroux in his efforts is Alderman Brown (Robert Wisdom), a slick-talking political parody whose graft-greased palm gives new meaning to the barbershop phrase "take a little off the top."

Of course, all this plot stuff takes a back seat to the boisterous banter and raucous rhetoric that is the film's raison d'etre. The story line, though weightier than that of the first movie, serves the similar purpose of supplying the film's comic spark.

Familiar faces include token white boy Isaac (Troy Garity), uptight Jimmy (Sean Patrick Thomas), gentle-souled Dinka (Leonard Earl Jones) and sassy Terri (rapper Eve). But the sharpest scissors (and tongue) still belong to Eddie (Cedric the Entertainer), the shock-wigged storefront philosopher who holds court cutting what's on your head while he speaks what's on his mind.

Sound-off topics range from the daffy (biracial celebrities) to the disagreeable (including calling the D.C. Sniper the "Jackie Robinson" of crime because he broke the color barrier of serial killers), to the downright distasteful (Michael Jackson's child molestation allegations). And while some might find the raw repartee off-putting, it is refreshing to see a depiction of an ethnically diverse group not only co-existing peacefully but thoroughly enjoying each other's company.

And though some viewers may wish to split hairs, the film presents a positive image of inner-city life. There are none of the usual ghetto cliches (drug dealers, pimps or gang members), just honest, hard-working people concerned about their families and neighborhood. In doing so, it imparts a strong message about the importance of community in maintaining the fabric of a healthy society.

This point is driven home during a Capraesque speech which Calvin delivers before a city review board, which, apart from some unnecessary coarse expressions, is commendable for its incorporation of Gospel values into its discussion of social justice issues. It also reminds us that in our materialistic world of ubiquitous Starbucks, it is people who make communities, and when family-run businesses are elbowed out by superstore conglomerates, neighborhoods lose not only shops but part of their soul.

"Barbershop 2" is a film with heart as well as hair.

Due to an implied sexual encounter, fleeting drug content, brief violence, and recurring crude language and humor, as well as profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Barb Wire
synopsis: Cheesy exploitation tale set in 2017 when the U.S.A. is wracked by a civil war of no particular consequence for a busy nightclub owner (Pamela Anderson Lee) until the murder of her brother causes her to side with the rebels. Directed by David Hogan, the murky proceedings are transparently ridiculous, especially those in which the dour heroine teases men with her body before blowing them apart with assorted weaponry. Mindless violence, sexual situations, fleeting nudity, profanity and coarse language

title: Barcelona
synopsis: An American (Taylor Nichols) based in Barcelona is visited by an obnoxious cousin (Chris Eigeman), but after becoming involved with two unpredictable local women (Mira Sorvino and Tushka Bergen), the cousins' old antagonisms resurface until resolved when one is nearly killed in a burst of anti-American violence. Writer-director Whit Stillman invests the somewhat bland story with an abundance of droll dialogue, gently mocking the political pretentions and sexual mores of young Americans and Spaniards whose facade of sophistication masks their insecurities. Implied promiscuity, fleeting bedroom scenes, brief violence and minimal profanity

title: Barefoot in the Park
synopsis: Young married couple (Jane Fonda and Robert Redford) live in a five-flight walk-up which leads to a number of amorous mix-ups. Directed by Gene Saks, Neil Simon's adaptation of his own Broadway hit, offers surefire broad comedy with strong supporting cast (Mildred NatWick and Charles Boyer)

title: Barnyard
synopsis: Clumsy if colorful computer-animated tale set on a farm where, unbeknownst to the farmer, the animals can walk and talk like people, and centers on a callow young cow (voiced by Kevin James), who must grow up quickly, reluctantly assuming leadership to stand up to a marauding gang of coyotes after his father (Sam Elliott) is killed defending the barnyard from the predatory pack. Directed by Steve Oedekerk, the film's admirable, if heavy-handed, message about embracing responsibility and putting the common good ahead of one's own self-interest is undermined by a mediocre script padded with raucous, redundant mayhem and silly sight gags at the expense of story and character. Mildly crude humor, some menace and peril that may be upsetting to very young children, heedless theft and several mature story elements
full_review:
So far, summer 2006 has been a good one for pixilated pleasures, like "Cars," "Monster House" and "The Ant Bully." That winning streak hits a hiccup, however, with the colorful but clumsy computer-animated "Barnyard" (Paramount).

Set on a farm where, unbeknownst to the owner, the animals can not only walk and talk like humans, but hold nightly hoedowns after lights out. Party animal Otis (voiced by Kevin James) is a callow young cow, who spends his days carousing with his barnyard buddies -- a rooster, pig, ferret and wisecracking mouse who gets the film's best lines.

But when his upright dad, Ben (Sam Elliott), the barnyard's vigilant guardian, is killed defending the henhouse from marauding coyotes, Otis must take his father's place in standing up to the predatory pack whose chicken coop raids become increasingly brazen.

Other voice talent includes Courteney Cox as Daisy, a widowed pregnant cow; Wanda Sykes as Bessy, her sassy best friend; and Danny Glover as wise mule Miles.

In more skillful hands, the film could have been a fine fable about coming of age in the animal world: in other words, "The Lion King." (Just substitute coyotes for hyenas.)

As it is, the writing -- apart from a few moments between Otis and Ben -- is mediocre and much of the humor is of the im-moo-ture barnyard variety, including a scene where Otis and company steal the farmer's car to teach some pranksters a lesson and later "borrow" motorcycles from outside a bikers bar -- not the best message for children.

Director Steve Oedekerk is quoted as saying he wanted the film to echo the raucous mayhem of the old Warner Bros. cartoons. Forget it. The tediously boisterous musical numbers are more likely to induce weary sighs than laughter, especially one involving a manic hairball creature called "Crazy Mike."

Saving the film from being udder-ly disappointing is its admirable, if heavy-handed, message about embracing responsibility and putting the common good ahead of one's own self-interest. "A strong man stands up for himself. A stronger man stands up for others," Ben counsels Otis repeatedly.

The preachy and obvious manner in which it is conveyed works against the noble sentiment. Still, given our arrested-development age which celebrates extended adolescence and bemoans growing up, perhaps a little preaching is in order.

The film contains mildly crude humor, some menace and peril that may be upsetting to very young children, heedless theft and several mature story elements. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested. Some material may not be suitable for children.

title: Baron Blood
synopsis: Italian horror movie about an evil medieval baron whose American descendent (Elke Sommer) rejuvenates him to continue his evil doings in the form of an invalid millionaire (Joseph Cotten). Director Mario Bava stresses a fine assortment of torture machines but the story is a perfectly forgettable bit of nonsense

title: Barquero
synopsis: Uneven Western directed by Gordon Douglas about a ferryman (Lee Van Cleef) who takes on a horde of bandits who want to use and then destroy his barge to delay their persuers. It proceeds as a battle of wits with some caustic dialogue, amusing characterizations and occasional violence and sexual references

title: Barren Lives
synopsis: Brazilian production set in an arid area of the interior where in 1940 a poor family looks for a place to settle and live like human beings instead of like migrant laborers the wor1d over. Stark and unrelieved, filled with the accusing silence of the destitute, this work by director Nelson Pereira dos Santos visualizes a powerful sermon on social justice and the dignity of the human person

title: Barricade
synopsis: Western clunker in which fugitives (including Ruth Roman and Dane Clark) seek refuge from the law by slaving in a desert gold mine for a sadist (Raymond Massey) who enjoys tormenting his workers while awaiting a showdown with its rightful owner. Directed by Peter Godfrey, the mangled story doesn't make much sense despite using a plot lifted from "The Sea Wolf." Much stylized violence and brutality, some of it quite nasty

title: Barry Lyndon
synopsis: Delicate screen adaptation of William Makepeace Thackeray's novel about the manners and morals of 18th-century Europe is pictorially exquisite and has an appropriately elaborate musical score. Director Stanley Kubrick pays more attention to setting and mood than to the human dimensions that are part of its story of an ambitious young man (Ryan O'Neal) trying to rise to social prominence. Mature themes

title: Bartleby
synopsis: Adaptation of Herman Melville's short novel about a perplexed accountant (Paul Scofield) who can neither get his pallid clerk (John McEnery) to do the work desired, nor can he bring himself to fire him. Director Anthony Friedmann's austere movie is faithful to the spirit, if not the flavor, of the original and the acting is superb. However, the decision to update the period the present can only be labeled an interesting failure

title: Barton Fink
synopsis: Lured to Hollywood by a fast-talking studio boss (Michael Lerner), a promising playwright (John Turturro) suffers writer's block until his beefy next-door neighbor (John Goodman) provides unexpected inspiration. The writing-directing team of Joel and Ethan Cohn have produced a dark satire and stylish evocation of Tinseltown in the 1940s that eventually falters with its morbid imagery. Some gory violence, discreet sexual innuendo and minimal rough language

title: Basic
synopsis: Unsatisfying military thriller in which an ex-Army Ranger (John Travolta) and a prickly Army captain (Connie Nielsen) must try to unravel the truth behind the Panama jungle deaths of a hated Special Forces sergeant (Samuel L. Jackson) and four trainees under him while two survivors spin an elaborate series of stories about what happened. Director John McTiernan's macho action flick takes a "Rashomon"-like approach to the narrative, but the dozen characters, murky visuals and constant plot twists eventually become tedious. Recurring violence, much rough language and intermittent profanity
full_review:
When a Special Forces training operation in Panama goes bad, a ex-Army Ranger is called in to unravel where the bodies are and what happened in the macho action flick, "Basic" (Columbia).

A muscular and cocky John Travolta dominates most of the scenes as an investigator pressed into service by a former colleague, Col. Styles (Tim Daly). Capt. Osborne (Connie Nielsen) is getting nowhere questioning surviving trainee Dunbar (Brian Van Holt), but resents the presence of Tom Hardy (Travolta), now a DEA agent under suspicion of being dirty.

Dunbar reluctantly spins an ugly tale of how the hated Sgt. West (Samuel L. Jackson) pushed his six trainees to the limit and beyond, dropping them from a chopper in the Panama jungle at night during a hurricane -- and ended up being shot by one of them.

In the angry recriminations that followed among the six, more shots are fired and only Dunbar and a wounded Kendall (Giovanni Ribisi) were rescued, the other bodies having washed away in the storm. The hospitalized Kendall tells a slightly different story, however, incriminating Dunbar. Col. Styles wants it to end there with Dunbar as the culprit, especially since Kendall is the gay son of a general who could ruin Styles' career if his son is ensnared in the scandal.

Osborne however has her doubts, and with Hardy alongside, digs deeper.

In the style of the 1950 film classic, "Rashomon," the different versions of what happened to the sergeant and those under him are seen in fast-paced, nighttime visuals which are replayed with alterations when the survivors' stories change. With nearly a dozen characters to keep track of, and all the murky visuals dished out to numbing effect, the serpentine plot twists, at first interesting and involving, gradually become tedious.

Taye Diggs plays a black trainee first accused of shooting West, and Harry Connick Jr. has a role as a military doctor with questionable ethics, but Travolta carries the brawny movie on his confident shoulders.

Director John McTiernan delivers the action goods proficiently, but the film is so densely plotted that characterizations suffer. Ultimately the plot twists prove unsatisfying and one feels mostly relief when it is all over. Nielsen is unremarkable as the female investigator and her occasional Southern accent only calls attention to itself.

The movie seems more impressed with its own cleverness than with distinguishing among the trainees and beckoning the audience to care about their fates.

While it may find a receptive young male audience, its repetitive shootings and preponderance of assaultive language and profanity make it of much less interest to the Catholic audience.

Because of recurring violence, much rough language and intermittent profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Basic Instinct
synopsis: Violent and sordid potboiler has a troubled homicide detective (Michael Douglas) willingly ensnared in an affair with a bisexual murder suspect (Sharon Stone) who throws suspicion on his police psychiatrist girlfriend (Jeanne Tripplehorn). As directed by Paul Verhoeven, this cat-and-mouse thriller is an empty exercise in audience shock value stressing graphic scenes of rough sex and bloody carnage. Exploitative mix of sex and violence, much nudity, grisly killings and frequent rough language

title: Basic Instinct 2
synopsis: Sequel to the 1992 erotic thriller which finds that film's manipulative vamp character (Sharon Stone) relocated to London, where, implicated in the murder of a soccer star, she matches wits with a criminal psychiatrist (David Morrissey), leading him down a path of seduction, deception and murder. With its femme-fatale protagonist and murky style, director Michael Caton-Jones' potboiler aspires to film noir, but its shadowy sordidness can't hide a cartoonish lead performance and an insipid, tangled script which distracts with salaciousness to make up for its lack of suspense and intelligence
full_review:
The poster for "Basic Instinct 2" (Columbia) opines that "everything interesting begins in the mind." Unfortunately nothing interesting happens in this film, which, despite its cerebral tagline, is anything but.

The sequel to the 1992 erotic thriller, "Basic Instinct 2" finds its predecessor's vamp character -- icy and manipulative crime novelist Catherine Tramell (a perpetually smug Sharon Stone) -- relocated to London, where, implicated in the murder of a soccer star, she matches wits with a criminal psychiatrist (David Morrissey, looking and sounding like Liam Neeson), and leads him down a path of seduction, deception and murder.

With its femme-fatale protagonist and murky style, director Michael Caton-Jones' potboiler aspires to film noir, but its shadowy sordidness can't disguise a cartoonish lead performance and an empty, tangled script which distracts with salaciousness to make up for its lack of suspense and intelligence. "The Big Sleep" would have been a better title, if Raymond Chandler hadn't already used it.

The film contains several graphic sexual encounters with partial frontal and rear nudity, a flash of full-frontal nudity, a shadowy orgy scene, violence, several lurid images, rough and sexually explicit language and several drug references. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Basic Training
synopsis: Director Andrew Sugerman's totally offensive sex farce poses as political satire but has the look and sense of a badly re-edited, X-rated home videocassette

title: Basquiat
synopsis: Hollow dramatization of the short career of Jean-Michel Basquiat (Jeffrey Wright), a black graffiti artist in New York City who achieved international fame as a self-taught painter before dying from a drug over-dose in 1988 at the age of 27. Written and directed by Julian Schnabel, the episodic script develops little emotional involvement in the character and lacks insight into his work or the bohemian art group which brought him fame. Frequent scenes of drug abuse, implied sexual encounters, profanity and rough language

title: Bastard Out of Carolina
synopsis: Harrowing tale of domestic violence set in 1950's South Carolina where a little girl is mercilessly beaten and eventually raped by her unstable stepfather (Ron Eldard), despite the efforts of her mom (Jennifer Jason Leigh) to protect her. Directed by actress Anjelica Huston, the disjointed narrative is relentlessly realistic in depicting the recurring violence to the child as well as the squalid working-class poverty of her relatives, but the result adds nothing new to the tragic topic of child abuse. Graphic violence, including a rape scene, and sexual references

title: Bat 21
synopsis: Suspenseful, fact-based story of a high-level intelligence officer (Gene Hackman) who is shot down in the jungles of Vietnam and, lacking firsthand experience with combat survival skills, has to rely upon radio contact with a spotter pilot (Danny Glover) who keeps him going until rescued. Compassionate interracial characterizations by Hackman and Glover and crisp direction by Peter Markle make it one of the better films about Vietnam heroics. Intense but non-gratuitous fire-bombings and individual killings. Some locker room language

title: Bataan
synopsis: World War II melodrama about the battle for the Bataan peninsula where a small group of American soldiers (including Robert Taylor, George Murphy, Thomas Mitchell and Lloyd Nolan) die one by one holding a position against overwhelming enemy forces. Directed by Tay Garnett, the doomed squad is a composite of melting-pot America whose patriotic fervor turns defeat into a moral victory badly needed on the homefront then and of some historical interest today. Much wartime violence and anti-Japanese stereotyping

title: Bathing Beauty
synopsis: Slapdash musical comedy directed by George Sidney with Harry James, Xavier Cugat and their orchestras trying to pick up the slack in the silly story of a songwriter (Red Skelton) enrolling in a woman's college in order to win back his estranged wife (Esther Williams) who's a teacher there. Romantic complications

title: Batman
synopsis: Movie version of the TV series based on the comic book characters of the Masked Marvel (Adam West) and the Boy Wonder (Burt Ward) has them battling a plot against the United Nations. Directed by Leslie H. Martinson, the very young will find the action exciting and those over 12 may be amused by the movie's consciously heavy-handed tongue-in-cheek treatment of events

title: Batman
synopsis: Dark, haunting vision of the caped crusader (Michael Keaton) who must battle not only the evil Joker (Jack Nicholson) but the demons left over from his own tragic childhood. Director Tim Burton does not make the eternal fight between good and evil an easy one but virtuoso performances by the leads and Anton Furst's production design of a Gotham City full of shadowy gothic and modernistic spires make the movie noteworthy. Some grisly comic-book violence and a suggested sexual encounter are too intense for young vieweers

title: Batman Begins
synopsis: Dark and brooding prequel that explains how Bruce Wayne (Christian Bale) became the costumed crimefighter and reveals the "hidden years," detailing his training as a member of a clandestine order of ninja-like vigilantes, leading up to his donning the cape and cowl to become Gotham City's self-appointed guardian. Director Christopher Nolan goes for a more gritty "reality-based" approach, focusing on the psychological dimension of Bruce/Batman's inner conflict rather than comic-book heroics. Intense action violence, some frightening images and mature thematic elements, as well as a few crude expressions and an instance of profanity
full_review:
Gotham's grim guardian is back in what is the darkest and arguably the best of the Batman movies, and the first to take its title character seriously.

Forget about the "Biff! Pow!" campiness of the 1960s' television series. This movie finally gives us a Dark Knight deserving of the name and revitalizes a film franchise that reached its nadir with Joel Shumacher's 1997 "Batman & Robin."

As its title implies, "Batman Begins" (Warner Bros.) explains how billionaire playboy Bruce Wayne first comes to don the iconic cape and cowl.

Most viewers already know the essentials: As a child, Bruce (Gus Lewis), heir to the Wayne empire, watched helplessly as his parents (Linus Roache and Sara Stewart) were gunned down in an alley by a mugger, and how the traumatic incident inspired him to later take on the mantle of avenging angel.

What director Christopher Nolan's character-driven film does is fill in the gaps between that fateful night and his emergence as the costumed crimefighter.

The movie opens with a memory-haunted Bruce (played as an adult by Christian Bale) languishing in a gulag, in what appears to be Tibet, after years of wandering the globe in an attempt to escape his past.

Seesawing between past and present, flashbacks recount his parents' murder and how, as an Ivy League dropout, Bruce came close to avenging their death before fate intervened.

During his absence, he is declared dead and control of Wayne Enterprises passes to Richard Earle (Rutger Hauer), the company's slimy CEO.

Bruce's ferocious -- if undisciplined -- fighting spirit catches the eye of a mystery man named Ducard (Liam Neeson) during a prison-yard brawl. He recruits Bruce to join a clandestine vigilante order -- the League of Shadows -- headquartered in a Himalayan fortress, overseen by the enigmatic Ra's Al Ghul (Ken Watanabe). Bruce ultimately rejects their methods, which include punishing the innocent for the sins of society.

Several grueling training sequences later, Bruce returns home to Gotham. Inspired by an incident from his childhood, Bruce bases his costume on a bat and renovates the catacombs beneath Wayne manor into the "Bat Cave."

With his secret identity known only to his trusty butler, Alfred (Michael Caine), Bruce/Batman declares war on Gotham's underworld, starting with reigning kingpin Carmine Falcone (Tom Wilkinson) and the menacing Dr. Jonathan Crane (Cillian Murphy), aka "The Scarecrow," a criminal psychologist who has found a way to harness fear as a weapon.

Morgan Freeman plays Lucius Fox, a techno-whiz who, like James Bond's "Q," provides Bruce with an arsenal of high-tech bat gadgets, including the Batmobile (here a tricked-out armored Humvee).

To deflect suspicion, Bruce keeps up his front of spoiled socialite, compromising his relationship with a love interest, Assistant District Attorney Rachel Dawes (a bland Katie Holmes).

With its moody atmospherics heavily influenced by Frank Miller's edgy Batman graphic novels, the film takes a grittier approach to the myth, emphasizing the complex psychological dimension of Bruce's inner conflict rather than comic-book heroics. One could say it deals with the "dark night" of the Dark Knight's soul.

And while the impulse for vengeance comes into play, what makes this caped crusader more sympathetic is that he is fueled less by rage than by guilt over not being able to save his parents.

Bale is equally at ease in tuxedos and body armor, walking a fine line between idealism
and psychosis, and even injects some humor into Bruce's bipolar broodiness.

Though going for a more realistic style, the violence is more suggestive than graphic.

The film is not without flaws. Some dialogue is pretentious, a few characters are underdeveloped, there is no one central villain, and, near the end, the script tends toward smash-and-crash action mode.

Some viewers may feel that the movie's overall tenor is too bleak. But portraying Batman as a tormented and tragic figure is true to the tone of creator Bob Kane's original vision.

Bruce's defining moment comes early, when, as an act of fealty to Ra's Al Ghul, he is ordered to execute a criminal. He refuses, defiantly stating that compassion is all that separates true justice from revenge and vigilantism. (Batman never kills anyone, though he does allow one baddie to die.)

What separates Batman from other superheroes -- and what the movie conveys -- is that his mystique taps into our fears and sense of helplessness. And while he is after all just a comic-book character, the film's archetypal image of Batman standing solitary vigil on a rooftop turret speaks to our deep desire for protection against life's uncertainties.

Batman is a superhero without superpowers. He is one of us. Human. Flawed. But as the movie suggests his enduring appeal is that of a noble idea: that one man can make a difference and be a force for good in the world.

The movie contains intense action violence, some frightening images and mature thematic elements, as well as a few crude expressions and an instance of profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Batman Forever
synopsis: Frenetic sequel with Batman (Val Kilmer) distracted by a sultry psychologist (Nicole Kidman) and a vengeance-crazed Robin (Chris O'Donnell) while battling two lunatics (Tommy Lee Jones and Jim Carrey) out to destroy the Caped Crusader. Director Joel Schumacher's dark comic fantasy has little narrative interest, relying instead on violent special effects, sleek visuals and exaggereated performances by the two villains. Recurring stylized violence and brief sexual innuendo

title: Batman: Mask of the Phantasm
synopsis: Murky animated adventures of the comic-book superhero as he tries to revive a failed romance while chasing after whoever is murdering Gotham gangsters dressed in a Batman-like outfit. Directors Eric Radomski and Bruce W. Timm give the picture a sleek visual style, but the cluttered, confusing storyline is too menacing for children while not sophisticated enough for their elders. Frequent stylized violence

title: Batman Returns
synopsis: Bigger isn't better in this overproduced sequel in which Batman (Michael Keaton) must save crumbling Gotham City and himself from the fiendish Penguin (Danny DeVito), a schizophrenic Catwoman (Michelle Pfeiffer) and a power-crazed industrialist (Christopher Walken). Director Tim Burton leaves out the human element of the story in his zeal for mind-boggling mayhem that offers much sound and fury but only signifies the shallowness of Hollywood's interpretation of pop culture. Much stylized violence, some of it quite nasty, and occasionally blatant sexual innuendoes

title: Batteries Not Included
synopsis: Failed fantasy about a group of tenement dwellers, headed by an old couple (Jessica Tandy and Hume Cronyn), who are being terrorized by thugs in the pay of a greedy real estate developer until two miniature spaceships come to their rescue. Directed by Matthew Robbins, the alien reproducing metalworks are cute and there are some whimiscal special effects, but the fantasy level of this urban melodrama never gets very far off the ground. Some scenes of intense menance and realistic violence

title: Battle Beneath the Earth
synopsis: Low-budget adventure fantasy directed by Montgomery Tully in which maverick Chinese Reds, underming the United States with a network of tunnels containing atomic bombs, are stopped by a unit of Marines led by Kerwin Mathews. Stylized violence

title: Battle Beyond the Stars
synopsis: Young volunteer Richard Thomas goes on a hunt to hire mercenaries to defend a planet threatened with conquest by an intergalactic tyrant. Scripted by John Sayles and directed by Jimmy T. Murakami with some style and humor, it is a moderately entertaining science fiction action fantasy. Many sexually oriented jokes

title: Battle Command
synopsis: Old-fashioned war movie of uncertain origin -- all the soldiers seem to be Italian no matter what their uniforms -- done on a limited budget and with an appalling lack of skill

title: Battle Cry
synopsis: Hokey World War II sudser from the Leon Uris novel follows a Marine battalion from boot camp to combat, though most of the plot concerns a recruit (Tab Hunter) in a hopeless affair with an officer's wife (Dorothy Malone) and the reformation of his womanizing buddy (Aldo Ray) by a New Zealand war widow (Nancy Olson). Director Raoul Walsh sets the wartime scene convincingly enough, but its contrived romances and cardboard characters never rise beyond bad melodrama. Wartime violence, sexual situations and an unwed pregnancy

title: Battlefield Earth
synopsis: because of much stylized violence, explosive mayhem and brief sexual innuendo,

title: Battle for the Planet of the Apes
synopsis: Final sequel to the series with Roddy McDowell heading up the ape cast and John Huston as a campy sort of simian Moses. Directed by J.Lee Thompson, the most entertaining sequences are excerpts from the previous movies used as the background of the story

title: Battleground
synopsis: Centering on the dogged resistance of an American infantry unit cut off in the Battle of the Bulge -- Hitler's last desperate offensive in the West -- the movie makes the most of its cross-section of G.I.s (Van Johnson, John Hodiak, Ricardo Montalban, James Whitmore, George Murphy, et. al.) as representative of the nation's ethnic, regional and social diversity. Veteran director William Wellman keeps the action taut and credible, uses the battlefield's snow-filled terrain to add further misery to the unit's plight and tries to keep his grab-bag collection of civilian-soldiers from turning into superheroes. Wartime violence and mild sexual references

title: Battle Hymn
synopsis: Fact-based story of Col. Dean Hess, the "flying parson" who returns to service during the Korean War, takes command of a squadron of inexperienced fighter pilots and starts an orphanage for the area's displaced children. Directed by Douglas Sirk, the dramatization will strike some as overly idealistic though Rock Hudson gives a credible performance as the dedicated minister willing to fight for a just cause, yet troubled in conscience by the need for killing. Wartime violence

title: Battle in Outer Space
synopsis: Aliens use the moon for an attack on Earth in this Japanese sci-fi clunker directed by Inoshiro Honda. The stoic heroics of the dubbed characters, cheesy model work and cardboard special effects offer little excitement or interest

title: Battle: Los Angeles
synopsis: Aliens are on the attack again, mounting an invasion of our planet. And, for no very apparent reason, Los Angeles is the last hope for humanity, the only city left that can mount a counterattack. So it's time to call in the Marines, led by a decorated combat veteran (Aaron Eckhart) who is also fighting demons of his own. Haunted by soldiers who died under his watch in the past, the present crisis offers him a chance for redemption, as well as the opportunity to expend a whole lot of ammunition. What ensues, under Jonathan Liebesman's direction, is a pastiche of films like "Independence Day" and "War of the Worlds," but with a major increase in the body count and noise level. Relentless action violence, gory images of carnage, at least one use of the F-word, some crude language
full_review:
There's a delicious irony in a major Hollywood studio making a film that effectively lays waste its host city. But that's what happens in the aptly titled "Battle: Los Angeles" (Columbia) in which seemingly no neighborhood of the City of Angels escapes destruction, either from invading aliens or our own military might.

"One thing is clear: The world is at war," intones a radio announcer as the film opens. And how: Chaos has encircled the globe. Though originally thought to be benign, meteorites falling off the coast of every country actually contain an alien army, mounting an invasion of the planet.

We're never told why the aliens are here, nor do we really get a good look at them. But their presence provides an excuse for endless violence and carnage, not to mention a great deal of noise.

We're also never told why Los Angeles is the last hope for humanity, the only city able to mount a counterattack. "We cannot lose L.A.!" barks a general. So it's time to call in the Marines, led by Sgt. Michael Nantz (Aaron Eckhart).

A decorated combat veteran, Nantz is also fighting his own demons. Haunted by soldiers who died under his watch in the past, the present crisis offers him a chance for redemption, as well as the opportunity to expend a whole lot of ammunition.

As Nantz leads a platoon into the heart of the battle -- there goes Santa Monica! -- we learn a bit about the back stories of the other Marines. All the stock characters are present: the newly-married father-to-be; the rookie who longs to lose his virginity (he doesn't); the daredevil.

Michelle Rodriguez, memorable as a sassy fighter pilot in "Avatar," plays sassy Air Force pilot Elena Santos, who exclaims, memorably, "Kill anything that isn't human!"

Of course our brave soldiers stumble upon civilian survivors, including three adorable moppets, a turn of events that allows for a ratcheting up of emotion.

Directed by Jonathan Liebesman ("The Texas Chainsaw Massacre: The Beginning"), "Battle: Los Angeles" is a pastiche, borrowing heavily in visual style and plot from several sci-fi films, including "War of the Worlds," "District 9," and, of course, "Independence Day." The story is neither unique nor compelling; it's just one tedious slog along what was formerly the beautiful California coast.

By the end of this film, viewers may share the sentiment of the platoon medic, who exclaims, "I'd rather be in Afghanistan!"

The film contains relentless action violence, gory images of carnage, at least one use of the F-word and some crude language. The Catholic News Service classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Battle of Britain
synopsis: With the fall of France in 1940, Great Britain stood alone against the might of the German air force. The movie pays tribute to the smaller number of British fighter pilots who, in the months that followed, downed so many planes that the Luftwaffe was unable to mount its massive raids. Laurence Olivier, Michael Redgrave and Trevor Howard star in this huge and impressive British production directed by Guy Hamilton. Wartime violence

title: Battle of Neretva
synopsis: Yugoslavian production about the 1943 victory of Tito's Partisans over the German Army re-creates the horror of a ferocious battle and is a tribute to their sacrifices enacted by a large international cast. Directed by Veljko Bulajic, the work is developed with little dramatic punctuation and evokes only mild sympathy and audience identification with the events it portrays

title: Battle of Okinawa
synopsis: Japanese re-creation of the ferocious, last-ditch defense of the island of Okinawa by its undermanned garrison. Directed by Kihachi Okamoto, it has a semi-documentary objectivity that distances viewers from the considerable amount of special-effects battle gore and mass suicide by part of the civilian population

title: Battle of Rogue River
synopsis: Western clunker directed by William Castle is set in 1850's Oregon where an Army officer (George Montgomery) averts an Indian war by nabbing the frontiersman (Richard Denning) who's been stirring up all the trouble. Stylized violence

title: Battle of the Amazons
synopsis: Extremely low-budget sexploiter, directed by Alfonso Brescia, features scantily attired, man-hating Amazons in an endless round of battles, sadistic rituals, stylized orgies and gruesome torture scenes

title: Battle of the Bulge
synopsis: Henry Fonda, Robert Shaw and Robert Ryan star in a big-budget re-creation of the last, desperate German offensive against American forces in December 1944. In an ambitious, wide-ranging epic, director Ken Annakin tries to turn one of the most brutal battles of World War II into star-studded entertainment. Wartime violence

title: Battle of the Coral Sea
synopsis: Captured while gathering intelligence on the Japanese fleet, a U.S. submarine captain (Cliff Robertson) escapes with his crew in time to help win the decisive 1942 naval battle of the title. Directed by Paul Wendkos, the main part of the narrative takes place in a P.O.W. camp where the heroics are standard-issue and the acting perfunctory. Some stylized violence and Japanese stereotyping

title: Battle of the Worlds
synopsis: Dubbed Italian production directed by Anthony Dawson provides limp sci-fi thrills as Earth is threatened by an alien planet which the military seek to vaporize before a cantankerous scientist (Claude Rains) can learn its secrets. Unconvincing models in space battles, mild tension and weak romance

title: Battlestar Galactica
synopsis: A fleet of survivors of an alien attack travel through deep space in search of a refuge they call Earth. Lorne Greene is at the helm of the flagship avoiding the dreaded Cylons in this compiliation of episodes from the television series. As directed by Richard A. Colla, the only peril is its worshipful portrayal of the military in contrast to a foolish civil government

title: Battle Zone
synopsis: Formula service picture directed by Lesley Selander in which two Marine Corps combat cameramen (John Hodiak and Stephen McNally) vie for the affections of an Italian Red Cross worker (Linda Christian) during the Korean War, with plenty of newsreel battle footage and a hokey back-lot sequence in which the two go behind enemy lines to photograph hidden military targets. Wartime violence and romantic complications

title: Be Kind Rewind
synopsis: Zany, warmhearted comedy about a New Jersey video store worker (Mos Def) who comes up with a scheme to create amateur video versions of classic films when his bungling friend (Jack Black) accidentally erases all the tapes after the manager (Danny Glover) leaves town to investigate saving the building from demolition. Despite its intentionally rough-hewn, indie ambience, a wildly improbable plotline, and too much low-comedy schtick, writer-director Michel Gondry's valentine to filmmaking ultimately delivers a touching story of friendship, with a strong affirmation of community and good fellowship, as the townspeople rally to the aid of the threatened business. Some vulgar humor, brief sexual references and mild comic violence
full_review:
This modest little film is just endearing enough to earn some sort of cult status before long.

The frenetic but warmhearted "Be Kind Rewind" (New Line/Partizan) centers on a small video store slated for demolition in a shabby neighborhood of Passaic, N.J.

Elderly store manager Mr. Fletcher (Danny Glover) can save it from the wrecking ball, provided he's able to come up with money for necessary repairs to the small building that houses the store.

When he goes on a trip to commemorate the death of Fats Waller, the African-American jazz great he idolizes who was allegedly born in that building, he leaves his loyal assistant Mike (Mos Def) in charge with a strong admonition to keep out Jerry (Jack Black), Mike's bungling mechanic pal, since the hapless Jerry causes mayhem at every turn.

When Jerry tries to sabotage the power plant near his trailer home, claiming its microwaves are zapping him, he nearly electrocutes himself. The next day, despite Mike's efforts to keep him out, Jerry stumbles into the store and wanders dazed among the shelves.

As dissatisfied customers start returning blank tapes soon after, Mike figures out that Jerry inadvertently erased them all because of the magnetic field he absorbed at the power plant, and comes up with a scheme to create short, amateur video versions of classic films, "Ghostbusters," "The Lion King" and "Driving Miss Daisy" among them. He and Jerry will enact the major roles, along with game newcomer Alma (Melonie Diaz) from the neighboring dry cleaners, and they'll rent them out in the original commercial boxes.

Surprisingly, the tapes are a hit -- even with sweet but critical Miss Falewicz (Mia Farrow) -- who periodically surveys the store on behalf of her friend, Fletcher.

Complications ensue when their supply of the "Sweded" videos -- the boys claim they get them from Sweden -- can barely keep up with demand, Fletcher returns with his own ideas for saving the store, and Hollywood lawyers (Sigourney Weaver among them) claim copyright infringement.

Despite its intentionally rough-hewn, indie ambience, wildly improbable plotline and too much low-comedy shtick, writer-director Michel Gondry's movie can be viewed as a loving valentine both to filmmaking in a YouTube-nurtured generation and to Waller, whose "life story" is interspersed via a faux-antique black-and-white video bio that has an affecting payoff in the film's final reels.

Above all, this is a touching story of friendship, with a strong affirmation of community and good fellowship, as the townspeople rally to the threatened store's aid. Apart from some very fleeting sexual banter near the start of the film, there are scarcely any objectionable elements at all.

The film contains some vulgar humor, brief sexual references and mild comic violence. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Beach Ball
synopsis: Fun-in-the-sun clunker directed by Lennie Weinrib in which a quartet of college drop-outs (led by Edd Byrnes) form a rock band, then try various ruses to get the money needed to pay for their instruments until saved by a quartet of co-eds from becoming beach bums. Sexual situations and innuendo, substance abuse and tawdry scams

title: Beach Blanket Bingo
synopsis: Dated youth comedy in which California beach pals (Frankie Avalon and Annette Funicello) get involved with a smirky agent (Paul Lynde) whose publicity stunts for a new singer (Linda Evans) end in her being kidnapped by a wacky biker (Harvey Lembeck). Directed by William Asher, the nonsensical story treads water with occasional songs, surfing and skydiving sequences, a shy mermaid (Marta Kristen) and a hapless comic foil (Buster Keaton). Slick but empty merriment

title: Beaches
synopsis: The ups and downs of the 30-year friendship between a California blueblood (Barbara Hershey) and a Jewish singer-dancer from the Bronx (Bette Midler) are tracked through rites of passage, life crises, petty jealousies and ultimate tragedy. Director Garry Marshall's positive portrait of a committed friendship overcomes the story's weepy moments with many comedic and rousing musical sequences but gets a tad too sudsy during the poignant climax. Some off-color language and vulgar humor, brief fisticuffs and a risque musical number

title: Beachhead
synopsis: Routine World War II adventure as Marines (Tony Curtis, Frank Lovejoy and Skip Homeier) search a Pacific island for a French planter (Eduard Franz) and his daughter (Mary Murphy) to get information on Japanese forces in the area. Director Stuart Heisler stages the jungle action adequately but the characters are cardboard and Curtis' heroics less than convincing. Stylized violence and mild sexual innunedo

title: Beach Party
synopsis: Sun-baked youth comedy in which an ogling anthropologist (Bob Cummings) rents a California beach house to study the mating rituals of a pack of youthful surfers, then gets involved with one of them (Annette Funicello) to the dismay of her boyfriend (Frankie Avalon) and the researcher's faithful assistant (Dorothy Malone). Directed by William Asher, the banal proceedings are paced by surfing interludes, forgettable songs, bikini-clad dancers and occasional brawls. Slapstick violence, sexual situations and much sexual innuendo

title: Beach Red
synopsis: Directed by and starring Cornel Wilde, the movie attempts to explore the inhumanity of war in the story of a World War II assault on a Pacific island, but it fails by its repetitious emphasis on the realistic details of carnage and its degrading treatment of women in flashbacks. O 1967

title: Bear Tooth
synopsis: Settling into a backwoods cabin, a garrulous old codger (Dub Taylor) and a stray dog spend the winter in director Zack Belcher's low-budget production which has little of interest except the Montana scenery. The result is often pretty to look at but lacks any human depth

title: Beastly
synopsis: Director Daniel Barnz's adaptation of Alex Flinn's novel retells the classic fairy tale "Beauty and the Beast" for the Facebook generation, offering good lessons in humility, kindness and old-fashioned romance along the way. Handsome and wealthy, but also self-absorbed and shallow, a popular teen (Alex Pettyfer) ridicules the ugly and less fortunate, including his high school's resident witch (Mary-Kate Olsen). In revenge, she casts a spell turning Kyle into a hideous monster, and gives him a year to find the true meaning of love and inner beauty or remain in his repulsive new guise forever. So he sets out to win the pure heart of a classmate (Vanessa Hudgens) who prefers substance to style. Probably acceptable for mature adolescents. Brief action violence and a few crass terms
full_review:
"Love is never ugly." That's the central message of "Beastly" (CBS Films), a modern take on "Beauty and the Beast" set in the fairy-tale land of high school.

Chronicling the fall and redemption of the biggest man on campus, this good-natured film offers its Facebook-generation target audience some rarely told lessons in humility, kindness and old-fashioned romance.

We first meet Kyle (Alex Pettyfer) as he's campaigning to be president of the student body. He has it all: looks, admiring ladies and lots of money. "Beautiful people get it better. That's just the way it is," Kyle tells his constituents.

His proud and equally shallow father (Peter Krause), a handsome TV anchor, backs up his son, saying, "People like people who look good. Anyone who says otherwise is dumb -- or ugly."

Enter two ladies who disagree.

The lovely Lindy (Vanessa Hudgens) may secretly pine for her new president but says, smartly, "I prefer substance over style." The eccentric Kendra (Mary-Kate Olsen), the school's resident witch, sees through Kyle's facade. After he publicly humiliates her, she sets out to teach this spoiled brat a lesson.

It's not nice to fool with Mother Nature, let alone an Olsen twin, and Kendra casts a spell, turning Kyle into a gruesome creature, giving him just one year to learn the meaning of true love and inner beauty or risk being hideous forever.

As the beast, Kyle is not the furry animal of Disney lore, but more a grunge artist covered with exotic tattoos, deep scars and metallic appliques.

Repulsed by his newly ugly son, Dad exiles him to his own luxury townhouse, where Kyle becomes a recluse. Leave it to two wise souls -- Zola (Lisa Gay Hamilton), a housekeeper with a heart of gold, and Will (Neil Patrick Harris), a blind tutor -- to teach Kyle about love, healing and helping others.

"Find someone who can see you better than you can," Zola advises.

Kyle, who hides in the shadows and now goes by the name Hunter, recalls Lindy's warmth and kindness. He rescues her from her criminal father, depositing her in his apartment in a kind of witness-protection program. Thus begins a very long (and refreshingly charming) courtship of beauty by the beast using roses and poetry.

"When I am around you, I don't feel ugly at all," Hunter/Kyle tells Lindy. She, in turn, is learning to love as she peels away his layers: "That something underneath is pure catnip for me," she says.

Based on the novel by Alex Flinn and directed by Daniel Barnz ("Phoebe in Wonderland"), "Beastly" is a warm-hearted film that sets a good example for today's teens. Thus, despite the elements listed below, it's probably acceptable for mature adolescents.

The film contains brief action violence and a few crass terms. The Catholic News Service classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Beast of Blood
synopsis: Philippine horror movie in which a scientist (John Ashley), searching Blood Island for the crazed creature that shipwrecked him, discovers a mad surgeon (Eddie Garcia) experimenting on human head transplants. Directed by Eddie Romero, the spurting blood, slicing blades and a rape scene will upset the squeamish

title: Beast of the Yellow Night
synopsis: Stonefaced John Ashley and toothy Mary Wilcox team up for some terrible acting and a spot of torrid lovemaking in a preposterous tale of a vicious army deserter who sells his soul to the devil in a Southeast Asian jungle. Director Eddie Romero packages his low-budget Philippine production of soap-opera sex and disgusting gore with plenty of static dialogue

title: Beat Street
synopsis: Skimpy plot, involving the aspirations of young blacks and Hispanics in the Bronx, loosely holds together a series of production numbers, many of which involve break dancing. Director Stan Lathan's lavish production fails because of its pretension and high gloss. Some rough language now and again but the movie is innocuous for the most part

title: Beau Geste
synopsis: Silent adventure classic from Percival Christopher Wren's novel in which the title Englishman (Ronald Colman) enlists in the French Foreign Legion after a fabulous family gem disappears, then is joined by his brothers (Neil Hamilton and Ralph Forbes) in battling rebellious Arabs as well as a villainous sergeant (Noah Beery), until two brothers return home for the truth about the missing gem. Directed by Herbert Brenon, the story revolves around deeds of loyalty, comradeship and honor, with visually striking action scenes, the most memorable being the Viking's funeral in a Saharan fort manned by Legionnaire corpses. Stylized violence

title: Beau Geste
synopsis: Dandy adventure classic from the P.C. Wren story about three brothers, two of whom (Ray Milland and Robert Preston) follow the eldest (Gary Cooper) into the French Foreign Legion where they wind up in a Saharan outpost besieged by rebel Arabs and commanded by a sadistic sergeant (Brian Donlevy).
