Evading the unwelcome attentions of the police while they drill the tunnel, however, turns out to be just the first of the team's challenges. After their heist, they draw the ire of two powerful opposing forces.

The first is crime lord Lew Vogel (David Suchet), who's allied -- for the moment at least -- with militant black-power leader Michael X (Peter de Jersey). The other is the British counter-intelligence service, represented by agent Tim Everett (Richard Lintern).

While Vogel has massive corruption to conceal, Everett and his superiors are out to protect the jewel-in-the-crown of royal secrets. Terry and his friends have unwittingly threatened both with exposure.

Director Roger Donaldson's film is primarily an intelligent and engaging piece of intrigue. But be warned: "The Bank Job" delves, along the way, into the seamy details of some of its characters' private lives; it also pulls no punches in portraying the underworld brutality. While these elements may be dramatically justified, they limit the movie's appeal for many Catholics.

The film contains nongraphic sexual activity, some of it aberrant, upper female and rear nudity, torture, much rough, crude and crass language, adultery, pornography, drugs, prostitution, and a passing anti-Catholic reference. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: The Barbarian and the Geisha
synopsis: Arriving in 1856 as the first American consul to Japan, Townsend Harris (a bemused John Wayne) is officially ignored until his efforts to stem a cholera epidemic bring an invitation to the Shogun's court where he's marked for death by a patriotic nobleman. Directed by John Huston, the beautifully framed but largely static proceedings are a visual treat but lack character interest, especially the flimsy role of the geisha (Eiko Ando) as spy in the consul's household. Pedestrain clash of cultures in a picturesque setting

title: The Barbarian Invasions
synopsis: Morally hollow drama about an estranged son (Stephane Rousseau) who returns home to Quebec in order to visit his ailing father (Remy Gerard), an unrepentant womanizer dying of cancer, and, in trying to brighten up his final days, organizes a reunion of his father's highbrow hedonistic friends and former mistresses. In this sequel to his 1987 film "Decline of the American Empire," director Denis Arcand revisits familiar themes of sex, love and politics among aging baby boomers, which, while purporting to celebrate la dolce vita, actually presents a depressing nihilistic view of life and interpersonal relationships. Subtitles. A cavalier attitude toward promiscuity and adultery, a condoning depiction of assisted suicide, much sexually explicit language and humor, some rough language and profanity, as well as recurring drug abuse
full_review:
Seventeen years ago French-Canadian filmmaker Denys Arcand explored love, sex and politics among a group of highbrow, hedonistic baby boomers in "The Decline of the American Empire." In "The Barbarian Invasions" (Miramax), Arcand revisits the same circle of friends, reuniting the original cast, who have grayed and grown paunchy in the intervening years.

Set in Quebec, the film focuses on the group's truculent torchbearer, Remy (Remy Girard), an erudite history professor and unrepentant philanderer who is diagnosed with inoperable cancer. At Remy's hospital bedside is his ex-wife, Louise (Dorothee Berryman), who, despite a divorce, has maintained an amiable relationship with him.

Unable to reach their seafaring daughter, Louise calls their son, Sebastien (Stephane Rousseau), a wealthy London investment banker, imploring him to return to Canada. Sebastien, whose rocky relationship with his father has kept him away for years, is hesitant to rekindle old antagonisms, but begrudgingly agrees to come home. No sooner is Sebastien off the plane than the two are fighting.

Still harboring resentment over his father's womanizing, Sebastien sees Remy as intolerably contentious. To the self-professed "sensual socialist," Sebastien is a self-righteous "puritanical capitalist," a portent of the coming "barbarian" invasions. Needled by Louise, Sebastien sets about making Remy's remaining time more comfortable by using his financial resources to upgrade Remy to a private room (a feat that involves greasing the palm of the hospital's Mafia-like union boss), paying off Remy's students to visit him, and even employing an addict (Marie-Josee Croze) to illegally purchase and administer heroin to Remy as a painkiller.

More importantly, he organizes a reunion of Remy's bed-hopping buddies. His hospital room is soon abuzz with lusty laughter as the sex-obsessed assembly reminisces about old times, their bacchanalian banality masking shared fears and tears. As Remy's condition worsens, the party shifts to the setting of the first film, a lakeside cottage, lending symmetry to the sequel and bringing the narrative full circle. Serving as a visual metaphor for lost vitality and the approach of death, the autumnal backdrop sets the emotional stage for cathartic mea culpas between father and son. The film ends on a morally bleak note with Remy electing euthanasia.

Reviving their roles from "Decline" are Louise Portal and Dominique Michel as Diane and Dominique, Remy's disillusioned ex-mistresses. Pierre Curzi returns as Pierre, whose former virulently anti-marriage views have given way to bourgeois domesticity. Also returning is Yves Jacques as Claude, an aging homosexual. Johanne Marie Tremblay plays Sister Constance, a Catholic nurse who tackles Remy's skepticism with humor and invites him to "embrace the mystery" of suffering.

Though the film draws comparisons between the sack of Rome and the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, Arcand uses the term "barbarians" to encompass a broad range of toxic influences which he sees as having an erosive effect on society, among them drugs, the health care bureaucracy and unrestrained capitalism. However, flying in the face of Arcand's assertion that the story is ultimately life-affirming are the film's pervasive nihilism and cynical view of traditional morality in favor of sexual autonomy, compounded by its reprehensible solution to suffering -- murder, the most "barbaric" act of all.

In one scene, the concupiscent comrades sit on the cabin's porch listing the ideologies to which they have subscribed over the years. As the camera pans across their abject faces it becomes apparent that it is a litany of despair, a roll call of the 20th century's attempts to replace divine truth with shoddy human substitutes -- all of which have left them existentially unsatisfied.

Despite its la dolce vita overtones, the barren terrain explored is devoid of any genuine hope. The music has stopped; the party is over. The sullen swingers are left reaping the bitter harvest of their chosen life trajectories -- ruined relationships, loneliness, alienation and finally despair. The compassion displayed is a pagan compassion that confuses murder for mercy. In the words of the Catholic novelist Flannery O'Connor, such modern notions of compassion, divorced from moral truth, "lead to the gas chamber" or as the case may be, to a picturesque lakeside cabin in Quebec. The barbarians have conquered from within.

Subtitles.

Due to a cavalier attitude toward promiscuity and adultery, a condoning depiction of assisted suicide, much sexually explicit language and humor, some rough language and profanity, as well as recurring drug abuse, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: The Barclays of Broadway
synopsis: When illness forced Judy Garland out of this MGM Charles Walters-directed film, Fred Astaire teamed with old partner Ginger Rogers after 10 years. It was the last one they'd make together (and the only one in color), playing a married musical comedy team, with the wife having aspirations to break up the act and be a "tragic" dramatic actress. Entertaining musical numbers, though not the equal of their earlier work at RKO. No commentary

title: The Barefoot Executive
synopsis: The title character in this Disney spoof is a chimpanzee with an uncanny taste for quality TV programs. An ambitious office boy (Kurt Russell) uses the talents of his monkey friend to become the boy wonder of network programming. The movie is really stolen by dead-panning Wally Cox and a building-ledge sequence as well-timed and suspenseful as Harold Lloyd's silent comedies

title: The Baron's African War
synopsis: Feature version of a serial directed by Spencer Bennet in which an American secret agent (Rod Cameron) is sent to Casablanca to stop a Nazi spy ring from fomenting an Arab holy war against the Allies. Hokey violence and menace

title: The Basketball Diaries
synopsis: When a basketball star (Leonardo DiCaprio) in a Manhattan Catholic high school turns to crime with two buddies (Mark Wahlberg and James Madio) after getting hooked on heroin, he winds up in prison to mull going straight. Directed by Scott Kalvert from Jim Carroll's autobiographical novel, the raw anti-drug tale graphically illustrates how drugs bankrupt body and soul, but the last-minute redemptive ending is weakly delivered and the Catholic background is depicted mainly in negative stereotypes. Brief violence, graphic scenes of drug abuse and criminal activity, several sexual encounters, fleeting nudity and continuous rough language

title: The Bat
synopsis: Modest thriller from the Mary Roberts Rinehart story of a mystery writer (Agnes Moorehead) vacationing in a spooky old mansion while the police hunt a missing fortune and a killer dressed as a bat. Directed by Crane Wilbur, the melodramatic proceedings creak along with the usual red herrings and obvious suspects (including Vincent Price) but it adds up to considerable fun for those in the mood. Mild menace and stylized violence

title: The Battle of Algiers
synopsis: The 1954-58 Algerian struggle for independence from French rule is re-created in this French production directed by Gillo Pontecorvo. Sympathetic to the rebels, yet compromising neither the facts nor the personalities involved, the film's documentary-like authenticity is achieved without resort to actual newsreel footage. It is a remarkable look at the process of revolutionary terror and counter-terror that victimizes ordinary citizens on both sides. Subtitles. Stylized violence

title: The Battle of Chile
synopsis: Documentary on the 1973 overthrow of the Allende government, it shows in painstaking detail the growing agony of a society on the verge of civil war and the inevitable brutal usurpation of power by the military. Assembled from footage smuggled out of Chile and edited in Cuba under the direction of Patricio Guzman, it is a partisan account but one does not have to accept its Marxist politics in examining for oneself the visual record of events showing how the elected government of a constitutional democracy was subverted and overthrown. Some violent actualities

title: The Battle of El Alamein
synopsis: B> -- Italian-French shoot-em-up World War II movie seen from the Axis point-of-view in which Rommel (Robert Hossein) loses to the superior British forces of Field Marshall Montgomery (Michael Rennie). Directed by Calvin Jackson, it's not strong on characterization but it does have a sturdy string of exciting battle sequences

title: The Battle of the Sexes
synopsis: Battle of the Sexes, The -- Droll British comedy set in Edinburgh where an American business consultant (Constance Cummings) convinces the bumbling owner (Robert Morley) of a centuries-old clothing firm to switch from hand-woven tweed to synthetic fibers, until a senior company official (Peter Sellers) finds a way to get rid of her. Directed by Charles Crichton, the picture spoofs old-fashioned as well as new-fangled business methods, but the comic highpoint is how Sellers turns from killing the consultant to discrediting her. Murderous menace and some misogynistic humor

title: The Bawdy Adventures of Tom Jones
synopsis: Bawdy Adventures of Tom Jones, The -- Dull and unimaginative adaptation of a stage musical based on the Henry Fielding novel. More boring than bawdy, director Cliff Owens has made a sexual burlesque of the original with much sexual innuendo and some partial nudity

title: The Beach
synopsis: Beach, The -- A dissatisfying thrill-seeking drama about a restless American traveler (Leonardo Di Caprio) who convinces a French couple (Guillaume Canet and Virginie Ledoyen) to journey with him to an idyllic, remote island off Thailand, but once there, they must pay a deadly price to keep the perfect beach a secret. Director Danny Boyle's visually beautiful but chaotic film becomes muddled as the beach's bohemian residents realize that evil exists even in paradise. Some gory violence including a suicide, a few shadowy sexual encounters with frontal nudity, some recreational drug abuse, and recurring rough language

title: The Beachcomber
synopsis: Beachcomber, The -- Droll romantic comedy from the Somerset Maugham tale of an English reprobate (Charles Laughton) carousing in the Dutch East Indies until reformed by the shrewish sister (Elsa Lanchester) of a missionary (Tyrone Guthrie), who herself is changed in the process. Producer-director Erich Pommer mixes narrative, character and locale in wry fashion, abetted by the whimsical observations of the colonial governor (Robert Newton), but the real fun is the battle royal between the two principals. Comic treatment of human weaknesses and puritanical compunctions

title: The Bear
synopsis: Bear, The -- Glorious nature drama set in turn-of-the-century British Columbia tracks the unlikely companionship of a wounded male Kodiak bear and an orphaned cub, as they explore their natural habitat and fend off two relentless human predators. Director Jean-Jacques Annaud dramatizes the story from the bears' point of view, using impressive wildlife photography to connect these majestic animals to humans in astonishing and unforgettable ways. Some bloodied dogs and horses, ongoing menace to the bears and a realistically audible mating sequence may be too intense for very young children

title: The Bear and I
synopsis: Bears and I, The -- A Vietnam veteran (Patrick Wayne) trying to find peace on a remote Indian reservation, unknowingly breaks a tribal taboo when he starts raising three bear cubs whose mother has been killed by a poacher. Disney outdoor adventure directed by Vincent McEveety should please the younger set with its wilderness background and the cute antics of the baby cubs

title: The Bear and the Doll
synopsis: Bear and the Doll, The -- Rather flat French farce about radio cellist (Jean-Pierre Cassel) preoccupied with providing for a young son and four nieces and apparently the only man in France not willing to fall instantly at Brigitte Bardot's adorable feet. Directed by Michele Deville, there are some amusing moments in this adult comedy but the two principals seem impossibly mismatched

title: The Beast
synopsis: Beast, The -- Set in 1981 Afghanistan, the story begins with the brutal destruction of a village by a squadron of Soviet tanks and then follows its aftermath in which a lone, lost tank is stalked by Afghan rebels. Directed by Kevin Reynolds, the gruesome opening massacre is eventually counterpointed with philosophical and psychological conflicts, mainly between the heartless tank commander (George Dzundza) and a young tank driver (Jason Patric) who emphathizes with the brutalized Afghans. Extremely graphic violence

title: The Beast
synopsis: Beast, The -- Formula marine thriller in which a hungry giant squid threatens an island resort's inhabitants and property values until a local fisherman (William Petersen) takes on the monster from the deep while romancing a feminist Coast Guard officer (Karen Sillas). Directed by Jeff Bleckner from the Peter Benchley novel, the television production offers a cast of underdeveloped characters and an overdeveloped sea beast whose tentacles and beady eyes fail to arouse the same kind of fright as do the jaws of a shark. Stylized violence, menacing situations and sexual innunedo

title: The Beast from 20,000 Fathoms
synopsis: Beast from 20,000 Fathoms, The -- Slack monster movie in a prehistoric Arctic dinosaur is thawed by an atomic blast, then makes its way down the Atlantic coast to attack New York City until cornered in Coney Island and killed by a radioactive isotope. Directed by Eugene Lourie, the script does little with the human element (scientists Paul Christian and Cecil Kellaway) and Ray Harryhausen's special effects are seldom more than perfunctory. Menacing situations

title: The Beast in the Cellar
synopsis: Beast in the Cellar, The -- Pair of dotty spinsters (Beryl Reid and Flora Robson) brick up their draft-age brother in the cellar rather than see him sent off to the Western Front. Director James Kelly's horror movie has its scary moments, but far too much is given over to the doting sisters trying to rationalize their past errors in rearing their now-mad sibling. Sordid seduction-murder scene

title: The Beast Must Die
synopsis: Beast Must Die, The -- British thriller in which a millionaire (Calvin Lockhart) invites some guests (Peter Cushing, Tom Chadbon, Michael Bambon) to spend a weekend at his remote country estate where everything is wired for sight and sound because the host knows that one of them will turn into a beast when the moon is full. Directed by Paul Annett, the updated werewolf tale offers some novelty and a fair amount of trumped up horror and gore for fans of this kind thing

title: The Beast of Hollow Mountain
synopsis: Beast of Hollow Mountain, The -- An American (Guy Madison) ranching in Mexico faces dastardly rustlers and a special-effects dinosaur. Directed by Edward Nassour and Ismael Rodriguez, the routine Western story is of little interest until the proceedings perk up with a prehistoric monster in a fantasy ending. Mild thrills for pre-schoolers

title: The Beast with Five Fingers
synopsis: Beast with Five Fingers, The -- Minor horror movie set in the Italian villa of a famous pianist (Victor Francen) whose sudden death brings terror after his sinister secretary (Peter Lorre) reports seeing the dead man's severed hand scuttling about, though the local police chief (J. Carrol Naish) is unconvinced. Directed by Robert Florey, the story's eerie atmosphere is sustained by Lorre's maniacal performance and fearsome visuals of the antic hand. Scenes of menace and suggestions of the occult but rational explanations are never far away

title: The Beat
synopsis: Beat, The -- Grim, inner-city drama about some drugged-up, aimless teens who take a turn for the better when they befriend a weird new boy (David Jacobson) who slinks around reciting poetry. They all become poets and are drawn into the boy's mystical fantasy world. Writer-director Paul Mones provides no background on these derelict kids, and no explanation for the boy's spacey behavior. Wall-to-wall profantity, much violence and a clear suggestion of teen sexual promiscuity

title: The Beautiful Blonde from Bashful Bend
synopsis: Beautiful Blonde from Bashful Bend, The -- Western farce in which a saloon singer (Betty Grable) skips town after shooting a judge (Porter Hall) instead of her two-timing lover (Cesar Romero), then is mistaken for the new schoolmarm in a mining town whose leading citizen (Rudy Vallee) woos her until learning of her past. Writer-director Preston Sturges turns the plot into a shambles of eccentric characters and slapstick action, some of it very funny but most of the gags are overdone and rather witless. Comic violence, romantic complications and sexual innuendo

title: The Beautiful Swindlers
synopsis: Beautiful Swindlers, The -- Cheap European production consists of three stories on the theme of foolish older men being taken advantage of by young seductive women. Sexually exploitative. O 1967

title: The Bed-Sitting Room
synopsis: Bed-Sitting Room, The -- Three years after World War III, which took place in less then two-and-a-half minutes, 20-odd survivors wander around the bizarre remains of London, including such grotesques as Sir Ralph Richardson turning, quite literally, into a bed-sitting room. Director Richard Lester's screen version of playwright Spike Milligan's surrealistic farce is meant to be a commentary on the horrors of war and middle-class morality but the result is merely a disappointing jumble of British wit and rude humor

title: The Bedford Incident
synopsis: Bedford Incident, The -- An American destroyer and a nuclear-armed Soviet submarine are on a collison course that, unless one of them yields, will cause an international incident. Director James Hill builds the psychological tension on board the destroyer as its cold-warrior captain (Richard Widmark) comes into conflict with an inquisitve journalist (Sidney Poitier) and others on deck (Martin Balsam, Eric Portman and Wally Cox). Heavy seas for youngsters

title: The Bedroom Window
synopsis: Bedroom Window, The -- Steve Guttenberg plays a young, carefree executive whose affair with his boss's wife (Isabelle Huppert) ends in her death when a killer-rapist they tried to bring to justice is freed. Directed by Curtis Hanson, the engaging, though convoluted plot deals with themes of dishonesty and betrayal and the treatment includes brief instances of violence, nudity and profanity

title: The Beguiled
synopsis: Beguiled, The -- Civil War story in which a wounded Union soldier (Clint Eastwood) takes refuge in a Southern school for ladies whom he must keep beguiled or risk being turned over to the Confederates. Directed by Don Siegel, this murky gothic horror story ends with the captive paying dearly for his ingratitude towards his captors' sick brand of Southern hospitality. In addition to the implied sexual situation, there is an explicit seduction followed by a gruesome amputation scene

title: The Believer
synopsis: Interesting drama about the tumultuous journey of a self-loathing young Jewish New Yorker (Ryan Gosling) who joins a neo-Nazi organization and becomes a powerful figure in the white supremacy movement, but his carefully constructed persona is jeopardized when a news reporter threatens to reveal his origins. The off-putting subject matter in writer-director Henry Bean's film prompts thought on faith versus intellect yet its stilted narrative doesn't deliver the expected punch despite Gosling's commanding performance. Some hateful violence, a suicide, a sexual encounter with nudity and recurring rough language
full_review:
Though the tough subject matter is likely to put off many viewers, "The Believer" (IDP) prompts thought on faith versus intellect. However, despite a salient performance by Ryan Gosling as a Jew turned neo-Nazi who rises through the ranks of the white supremacist movement, the stilted film never delivers the forceful punch of which it initially seems capable.

Writer-director Henry Bean's film made its debut at the 2001 Sundance Film Festival, where it was awarded the festival's top prize. But despite critical acclaim and audience enthusiasm, the film didn't immediately find a distribution home. Distributors weren't willing to gamble on a controversial and possibly alienating film. Showtime finally bought it for a cable premiere last fall, and it is now getting its release with Fireworks Pictures and its theatrical distribution joint venture, Independent Distribution Partnership.

The incomprehensible contradictions of Danny Balint (Gosling) are what propel the film forward. Inspired by the 1965 true story of Daniel Burros, a Nazi Party member who killed himself when The New York Times revealed he was Jewish, "The Believer" is a searing depiction of a man in conflict with himself. Flashbacks reveal Danny, even as a 12-year-old Yeshiva student, to be bright, quick and thoughtful. At Yeshiva, he gamely sparred with his teacher over the implications of the story of Abraham, which seems to be at the heart of what turned him into an anti-Semite. According to Danny, the Jews are willing to ignore what seems to like common sense in favor of an illusive thing called faith. His view is that they are weak doormats who instead of fighting back, allowed themselves to be victims in the Holocaust. His loathing of Jews defines him.

Charismatic and physically fearless, shaven-head Danny is attracted to an underground fascist movement lead by Curtis Zampf (Billy Zane) and Lina Moebius (Theresa Russell). Although they recognize Danny to be a diamond in the rough, Curtis and Lina disagree with Danny's fervent hatred of the Jews and his desire to kill them, fearing that such virulent hostility could be detrimental to their cause. Nonetheless, they invite Danny to be one of their main players, leading "educational" sessions designed to "enlighten" folks about the Jews.

As a young man bursting with hatred, it is Danny's intellect that is more dangerous than his explosive temperament. He continues to study Hebrew and revere the Torah, which he justifies to his new admirer and lover, Carla (Summer Phoenix) as a means by which one knows and conquers the enemy. When Danny speaks to a reporter about his views on the Jewish people, he is articulate and definite in expressing how the Jews have forced "communism, infantile sexuality and the atom bomb" upon the world. Normally cool and collected, Danny is thrown when the reporter asks how he reconciles his hatred with the fact that he, himself, is a Jew. His carefully constructed persona and his position in the neo-Nazi circles are jeopardized and the threat pushes Danny to the extreme.

Throughout the film, Danny remains conflicted, at once attracted and repulsed by Judaism. And while the narrative falters in various areas with its inconsistencies, Gosling is never less than commanding. It is disturbing to watch scenes of a synagogue being desecrated, including the vandalizing of a sacred Torah scroll. Or to see Danny beat a young Jewish man without cause or provocation. But the film is not exploitative in its use of scenes such as these. Through Danny, the film aims to explore the challenging theological questions of faith and asks how intellect and reason fit in with belief and surrender to God.

"The Believer" is not a film for the casual moviegoer who wants escapist fare. It is a challenging, difficult film, which despite its flaws, is thought provoking in its complex presentation of one man's struggle with faith.

Due to some hateful violence, a suicide, a sexual encounter with nudity and recurring rough language., the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: The Believers
synopsis: Believers, The -- Desperate crime caper in which a New York City detective (Martin Sheen) tries to saves his son from a ritual death at the hands of a cultist group who derive power from human sacrifices. Director John Schlesinger's flawed, superficial treatment of a serious subject is marred by graphic shots of naked corpses, bloody animal entrails, gruesome murders and a violent suicide

title: The Belle of New York
synopsis: Belle of New York, The -- Thin musical romance features a turn-of-the-century playboy (Fred Astaire) transformed by his love for a crusading social reformer (Vera-Ellen). Director Charles Walters concentrates on the colorful decor and costumes of the period as well as the staging of several flashy dance numbers but the flat, predictable storyline is uninvolving and the songs are pleasant but unmemorable. Mild romantic misunderstandings

title: The Belles of St. Trinians
synopsis: Belles of St. Trinians, The -- Zany British comedy based on Ronald Searle's cartoons about a bizarre girl's school whose eccentric headmistress (Alastair Sim) vies with her shady brother (also Sim) over a racehorse stolen by students and hidden in the dorms. Directed by Frank Launder, the result is a series of farcical vignettes involving the teachers, one of whom is an undercover police agent (Joyce Grenfell), and the students' extracurricular activities, including distilling gin in the chemistry lab and using a mallet to win a hockey tournament. Comic violence and veiled sexual innuendo

title: The Bell Jar
synopsis: Bell Jar, The -- Dreary, painful adaptation of the Sylvia Plath autobiography detailing a seemingly well-adjusted college girl's mental breakdown after the death of her father and her rude encounters with the realities of the New York publishing world. Director Larry Peerce resorts to extensive use of nudity groping for the muddled sexual basis for the tragic heroine's problems

title: The Benchwarmers
synopsis: Lame comedy about three grown nerds (Rob Schneider, David Spade and Jon Heder) who are recruited by a former geek turned billionaire (Jon Lovitz) into playing against various Little League teams of bullying jocks in a tournament he's sponsoring. By beating them, the trio will win respect for every picked-on kid. Despite a commendable underdog message and some occasional funny moments, director Dennis Dugan's film strikes out, its "Bad News Bears" script straining under forced laughs and sophomoric slapstick. Recurring crass humor and sight gags, some sex jokes including running gay innuendo and a crude gesture, as well as a smattering of crude language
full_review:
Even if you were picked last in gym class, you'll find little amusement in "Benchwarmers" (Columbia), a lame comedy about inclusion, sportsmanship and embracing your inner nerd. And while it's a marked improvement over star Rob Schneider's last outing as "Deuce Bigalow: European Gigolo," the bar was set mighty low.

Schneider plays undersized landscaper Gus, who, together with his dorky buddies -- video clerk Richie (David Spade) and newspaper delivery boy Clark (Jon Heder of "Napoleon Dynamite") -- is recruited by geek-turned-billionaire Mel (Jon Lovitz) to play against various Little League teams of bullying jocks in a tournament he's sponsoring. By beating them, the trio will win respect for every picked-on kid.

Despite a commendable underdog message and some occasional funny moments, director Dennis Dugan's film strikes out, its "Bad News Bears" script straining under forced laughs and sophomoric slapstick.

The film contains recurring crass humor and sight gags, some sex jokes including running gay innuendo and a crude gesture, as well as a smattering of crude language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: The Benny Goodman Story
synopsis: Benny Goodman Story, The -- Standard Hollywood biography of the popular bandleader (Steve Allen) from his youth in Chicago to his heyday in the 1940s, with Donna Reed as the romantic interest. Directed by Valentine Davies, the treatment is strictly superficial but the nostalgic period music is good and plentiful. Not for fidgety youngsters

title: The Best Intentions
synopsis: Best Intentions, The -- Episodic Swedish family saga set in the early 1900s focuses on the troubled courtship and stormy marriage of a dour, strong-willed Lutheran minister (Samuel Froler) who had grown up in poverty and his bright, willful bride (Pernilla August) whose wealthy family had opposed their wedding. As directed by Bille August, Ingmar Bergman's autobiographical script offers a moody meditation on the emotional affinity of two completely opposite temperaments whose bond of love withstands the resulting clashes of personality and inevitable misunderstandings only because they are willing to forgive one another and go on together. Subtitles. Restrained scene of premarital relations with brief nudity, some domestic violence, a suicide and a life-threatening scene involving a small child

title: The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas
synopsis: Best Little Whorehouse in Texas, The -- Broadway musical about a Texas brothel threatened by a clean-up campaign has been made into a vehicle for Burt Reynolds and Dolly Parton. The characterizations and country music are so lackluster that the virtues of the original must remain a mystery to anyone who has not seen it. Director Colin Higgins resorts to quite a bit of nudity and several fairly graphic bedroom scenes

title: The Best Man
synopsis: Best Man, The -- To win presidential nomination at the national convention, an idealistic liberal candidate (Henry Fonda) seeks support from his party's leader (Lee Tracy) but is threatened by the unscrupulous tactics of a conservative rival (Cliff Robertson). Directed by Franklin Schaffner and adapted by Gore Vidal from his own stage play, the political back-room maneuverings seem depressingly familiar, though brightened by some sharply satiric humor. Ambiguous treatment of a candidate's religion

title: The Best of Everything
synopsis: Best of Everything, The -- Glossy soap opera about the romantic travails of three secretaries in a Manhattan publishing firm where Hope Lange settles for sad Stephen Boyd; Diane Baker is betrayed by wealthy Robert Evans; and Suzy Parker goes off the deep end because of arty Louis Jourdan. Directed by Jean Negulesco, the lugubrious proceedings alternate between heartthrobs and heartaches, furtive liaisons and gushy weddings, young employees and senior executives (bitter Joan Crawford and womanizing Brian Aherne). Sexual situations and veiled references to abortion

title: The Best of Times
synopsis: Best of Times, The -- Slack comedy about middle-aged out-of-shape losers (Robin Williams and Kurt Russell) who get a second chance to replay the big football game they lost as high school seniors. Starting with some wry, tongue-in-cheek humor, director Roger Spottiswoode lets the comic situation go downhill and the quest of grown men for their lost youth grows ever more tiresome. Much rough language, some sexual innuendo and a passing reference to locker room drugs

title: The Best Way
synopsis: Best Way, The -- From France comes a drab and pale little film devoted to the theme of sexual ambivalence. Director Charles Miller loosely sets the drama in a boys camp in 1960, but provides undeveloped characters in a story about a sexual confrontation between two counselors (Patrick Dewaere and Patrick Bouchitey). Occasional nudity

title: The Best Years of Our Lives
synopsis: Best Years of Our Lives, The -- Three World War II veterans (sergeant Fredric March, bombardier Dana Andrews and sailor Harold Russell with hooks in place of hands) meet on their way home to resume civilian lives in the same small town where they try to help each other readjust to peacetime. Director William Wyler gives sympathetic treatment to the post-war rehabilitation of returning G.I.s, portraying in fairly realistic detail their career difficulties as well as personal problems with wives and girlfriends (Myrna Loy, Teresa Wright, Virginia Mayo and Cathy O'Donnell). Mature themes, including a broken marriage

title: The Betsy
synopsis: Betsy, The -- Supremely trashy novel by Harold Robbins, adapted into a supremely trashy movie about the obsession for power, sex and wealth among the upper echelon of the automobile industry (Laurence Olivier, Robert Duvall and Katherine Ross). Director Daniel Petrie's potboiler contains nudity and is lacking completely in moral perspective

title: The Bible: In The Beginning
synopsis: Bible: In The Beginning, The -- Six episodes from Genesis (Creation, Adam and Eve, Cain and Abel, Noah, the Tower of Babel and Abraham) are pictured as literally as they were written, largely leaving their interpretation to the viewer. John Huston directs, narrates and plays the part of Noah in this reverent but entertaining spectacular. George C. Scott as Abraham takes acting honors among a cast including Ava Gardner, Richard Harris, Ulla Bergryd and Michael Parks

title: The Bicycle Thief
synopsis: Bicycle Thief, The -- Simple yet compelling study in desperation as a worker (Lamberto Maggiorani) must find his stolen bicycle or lose his new job. Ignored by the police and others, the man and his young son (Enzo Staiola) search the streets for it until, in despair, he himself tries to steal a bicycle. Scripted by Cesare Zavattini and directed by Vittorio De Sica, the result is an engrossing picture of the human realities of life on the edge of poverty, shot on the streets of Rome with a cast of non-professionals that brought a new realism to the postwar screen and a new emotional honesty to the stories it told. Subtitles. Some earthy references

title: The Bigamist
synopsis: Bigamist, The -- Contrived melodrama in which a married sales executive (Edmond O'Brien) falls for a Los Angeles waitress (Ida Lupino), gets her pregnant, then weds her before seeking a divorce from his wife (Joan Fontaine) in San Francisco. Also directed by Lupino, the scenario treats the husband sympathetically as a gentleman motivated by a reluctance to hurt either woman, though viewers are likely to render a harsher judgment. Adult themes

title: The Big Bang
synopsis: Big Bang, The -- An astronomer, a gangster, a painter, a model and a nun-philosopher are among the diverse mix of 19 individuals who tell what they think about love, life, death, the origins of the universe and what lies beyond the grave. Director James Toback's documentary interweaves the interviews into a relatively painless talk show, offering an uneven grab-bag of ideas ranging from the provocative to the pretentious and, at times, preposterous. Some rough language and an explicit description of a sexual encounter

title: The Big Bird Cage
synopsis: Big Bird Cage, The -- Poorly-made Philippine movie directed by Jack Hill in which a woman (Pam Grier) smuggles her boy friend into a women's prison camp in order to foment a rebellion. Much nudity, savagery and raw language

title: The Big Blue
synopsis: Big Blue, The -- Mysterious young Frenchman (Jean-Marc Barr), who was taught to dive long and deep by his fisherman father, sets the world diving record but his affinity for dolphins ultimately ruins his chances for a normal life on land. Exquisite seascapes and beautiful underwater cinematography can't make up for a poorly realized script directed by Luc Besson. Two intense drowning sequences and fleeting nudity in a brief but explicit sexual encounter

title: The Big Bonanza
synopsis: Big Bonanza, The -- Western programmer directed by George Archainbaud in which an Army officer (Richard Arlen) on the run from false charges finds his young brother (Bobby Driscoll) in the care of an old pal (Robert Livingston) whom he learns is now a crook, set on separating the rich title mine from its owner (Russell Simpson). Stylized violence and menacing situations involving women and children

title: The Big Bounce
synopsis: Big Bounce, The -- Young drifter (Ryan O'Neal) becomes deeply involved with a supposedly lovable psychotic (Leigh Taylor-Young) whose desire for thrills eventually drives him away, but only after she has committed murder. Directed by Alex March, the heavy-handed melodrama is totally unconvincing. Several ludicrous nude scenes and much coarse language used so self-consciously as to emphasize its offensiveness

title: The Big Bounce
synopsis: Insipid caper comedy about a petty thief (Owen Wilson) who is lured by a well-connected judge (Morgan Freeman) and a sultry island seductress (Sara Foster) into robbing a wealthy Hawaiian real estate developer, but his payday turns sour when the scam leads to double-crossings and murder. The film is based on a pulp crime novel by Elmore Leonard and directed by George Armitage; pretty scenery is about all this black comedy has going for it, thanks to a script shakier than a hula-dancer's hips, flat-line performances that not even Leonard's sharp dialogue can resuscitate and a disconcerting assertion that crime not only pays, but pays quite well. A few sexual encounters with partial nudity, a casual attitude toward murder and larceny, an implied homosexual situation, recurring violence, some crude humor and language, as well as racial slurs
full_review:
A two-bit thief is recruited by a well-connected judge and a thrill-seeking temptress to double-cross a shady real estate developer in the cringe-worthy caper comedy, "The Big Bounce" (Warner Bros.).

Situated strategically between the year-end rush of Oscar contenders and summer slew of blockbusters, January and February have traditionally been the months during which studios try to unload their duds onto moviegoers willing to fork over cash for just about anything to get out of the cold. After Tinseltown cleaned out its fridge, providing a holiday season feast of epics and nuanced character pieces, director George Armitage serves up what can only be described as cinematic leftovers.

Based on a novel by dime-store crime icon Elmore Leonard, the film stars Owen Wilson as Jack Ryan, a slacker, surfer, charmer and all-around trouble magnet who, after drifting about as far west as one can go without a pocket full of yen, finds himself working construction in Hawaii for Ray Ritchie (Gary Sinise), a slimy resort magnate. After a run-in with Ray's pit-bull foreman (Vinnie Jones) and his flunky (Charlie Sheen) lands him in jail, a local magistrate (Morgan Freeman), intrigued by the petty pilferer, offers Jack a handyman job at the Oceanside condo complex he owns.

The paradisiacal playground offers more than enough temptations for a man of Jack's predispositions, including Nancy Hayes (Sara Foster), a sultry island seductress who just happens to be Ray's mistress. It doesn't take long for Jack to get the itch, and Nancy is just the girl to scratch it. She quickly lures Jack out of his clothes and into a scam which will score them $200,000 of Ray's money, setting the stage for the elaborate shell game of double and triple dealings one has come to expect from Leonard adaptations.

Despite the picturesque Hawaiian backdrop provided by Oahu's North Shore, the silly story is shakier than a hula dancer's hips, full of awkward reversals and plot twists. Unlike the wickedly funny "Get Shorty" (1995), which was also based on a novel by Leonard, "Bounce" lacks, well, bounce, resulting in a flat-line black comedy, more pallid than it is pulp, which not even Leonard's whip-smart dialogue can resuscitate.

During the movie's opening voiceover, Jack blames his albatross karma on his two constant traveling companions: "bad luck" and "bad choices"; the latter companion must be two-timing it with the actor playing him, as evident in Wilson's poor choice of scripts.

However, while Wilson is competent as the likable loser, the same cannot be said for Foster, a former model with the acting range that profession usually implies, who prances through most of her scenes scantily clad in string bikinis or less -- justifying the film's buoyant title.

The remaining cast, made up of such impressive players as Sinise, Freeman, Sheen and Bebe Neuwirth, who plays Ray's conniving wife, seem to be just going through the motions as they tag along for the paycheck and excuse to be in Hawaii. You know you're in trouble when the best performance is by the saxophonist punctuating each scene with a jazzy "Harlem Nocturne" riff.

More disconcerting than the insipid script is the film's wink-wink assertion that crime not only pays, but on occasion pays quite well. Though Armitage keeps the tone lighthearted -- the characters are more rogues than hardened criminals -- by the movie's end, Jack and Nancy not only literally get away with murder, but cut a very sweet profit in the process. Also troubling is the atheistic mantra, "God is just an imaginary friend for adults," which is repeated throughout by various characters for supposed comic effect.

Early on, the judge warns Jack, "Things aren't always what they seem." "The Big Bounce" is exactly what it seems -- a big waste of time.

Due to a few sexual encounters with partial nudity, a casual attitude toward murder and larceny, an implied homosexual situation, recurring violence, some crude humor and language, as well as racial slurs, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: The Big Bus
synopsis: Big Bus, The -- A parody of disaster movies, it follows the misadventures of a nuclear-powered bus on its maiden run non-stop from New York to Denver. The gags work about 30 percent of the time, not too bad an average for this type of film, and director James Frawley keeps a light touch on the often heavy-handed proceedings. Innocent, mostly sophomoric humor except for several sexual references

title: The Big Cat
synopsis: Big Cat, The -- Soured relations between rural neighbors in 1933 Utah worsen when the city nephew (Lon McCallister) of one (Forrest Tucker) arrives to take a job with the other (Preston Foster), but the feud is ended by a rampaging mountain lion. Director Phil Karlson delivers a credible period piece about simple country folk trying to survive hard times, but the melodramatic rivalry between the two men escalates from nastiness to brutality. Some fairly intense violence

title: The Big Chill
synopsis: Big Chill, The -- Seven old friends (William Hurt, Kevin Kline, Glenn Close among them) from college days in the 1960s are reunited by the suicide of the most brilliant of their number. After the funeral they spend the weekend together soul-searching and, to some degree, mourning their lost innocence. Director Lawrence Kasdan indicates no political awareness on the part of his characters despite their supposed sophistication and the result is an entertaining but shallow and contrived work. Brief nudity, rough language and a benign attitude toward adultery

title: The Big Circus
synopsis: Big Circus, The -- Big-top owner (Victor Mature) faces financial ruin, thanks to devious activities of a traitor working for a rival circus. Director Joseph M. Newman's hackneyed storyline is buttressed by some good circus acts, a few thrills (notably aerialist Gilbert Roland walking a tightrope across Niagara Falls) and a cast including Vincent Price as the ringmaster and Peter Lorre as a clown. Some stylized violence and mild romance. A-I 1959

title: The Big City
synopsis: Big City, The -- From India comes this unassuming but dignified story of the problems that occur when a young mother must work in the city to help support her family. Director Satyajit Ray generates considerable human warmth out of a simple situation of ordinary Bengali family life that, despite the cultural differences, many will find universal. Subtitles. Domestic tensions

title: The Big Clock
synopsis: Big Clock, The -- Intriguing suspense thriller embroils a crime magazine editor (Ray Milland) as the chief suspect in a murder committed by his megalomaniacal publisher (Charles Laughton). Directed by John Farrow, the tense narrative is nicely keyed to a collection of quirky characters (including Elsa Lanchester, George Macready and Henry Morgan). Mounting menace and some stylized violence

title: The Big Combo
synopsis: Big Combo, The -- Overheated crime story in which a weary but determined cop (Cornel Wilde) tries to bring down a ruthless syndicate boss (Richard Conte) by getting the criminal's unhappy mistress (Jean Wallace) to tell what she knows. Directed by Joseph Lewis, the plot plods along with the cop stymied at every turn until a sudden break brings the downfall of the feared crime boss and his sadistic thugs. Brutal crime scenes and sexual innuendo

title: The Big Cube
synopsis: Big Cube, The -- Lana Turner is sent over the psychic edge by George Chakiris who has been spiking her medicine with LSD in order to control her fortune when she is declared incompetent. Director Tito Davison's low-budget melodrama shot in Mexico splices in some scenes of over-age hippies cutting up at drug parties

title: The Big Doll House
synopsis: Big Doll House, The -- Low-budget Philippine sex melodrama directed by Jack Hill about a bunch of desperate women prison inmates (Judy Brown, Roberta Collins, Pam Grier) is full of innuendo as heavy as the passionate breathing on the sound track

title: The Big Easy
synopsis: Big Easy, The -- Quirky romance about a Cajun detective (Dennis Quaid) and an assistant district attorney (Ellen Barkin) who weather a conflict of interests and the low moral atmosphere of New Orleans to solve a drug-related crime. Director Jim McBride's nervously stylistic movie stays light and often dopey despite some gruesome flashes of murder victims, a shot of topless dancers and an explicit, albeit fumbling, lovemaking scene

title: The Big Fisherman
synopsis: Big Fisherman, The -- Muddled Gospel-era tale from the Lloyd C. Douglas novel in which an Arabian princess (Susan Kohner) blames her wicked father, King Herod (Herbert Lom), for her mother's death and vows to kill him until befriended by Simon Peter (Howard Keel), a disciple of the heard but unseen Nazarene. Directed by Frank Borzage, the result is a tediously overlong melodrama, more ponderous than uplifting, with the title character of Peter reduced to a supporting player. Stylized violence and muted sexual innuendo

title: The Big Fix
synopsis: Big Fix, The -- A Los Angeles private eye (Richard Dreyfuss), a former 1960's campus radical, is now cynical, disenchanted and divorced, scraping a living out of minor gumshoe jobs. When an old college friend (Susan Anspach) asks him to investiagate a smear campaign aganist a political reformer, he is drawn back into the idealism of his youth. Director Jeremy Paul Kagan has made an entertaining though convoluted detective thriller that benefits greatly from the vitality of Dreyfuss' performance. Some of its humor and its less than adequate treatment of the political and moral issues it deals with make it mature fare

title: The Biggest Bundle of Them All
synopsis: Biggest Bundle of Them All, The -- Comic crime melodrama directed by Ken Annakin about the kidnapping of an American gangster relies excessively on sexual innuendo. O 1967

title: The Big Green
synopsis: Big Green, The -- The economically depressed residents of a tiny Texas town get back their fighting spirit after a perky new teacher (Olivia d'Abo) from England, assisted by the local sheriff (Steve Guttenberg), shape the listless junior high schoolers into a winning soccer team. Writer-director Holly Goldberg Sloan's bland story of underdogs beating the odds is an innocuous, slightly amusing family film which never ventures beyond the thoroughly predictable

title: The Big Gundown
synopsis: Big Gundown, The -- In this Italian-made Western, snickering ex-lawman (Lee Van Cleef) aids in tracking down a shifty Mexican (Tomas Millian) accused of rape and murder but, discovering his quarry's innocence, he then joins with him to punish the real culprits. Director Sergio Sollima's formula plot is simply an excuse to string together chases and places for the hero to exhibit his brutal brand of six-gun justice. Particularly objectionable in this film is sadistic violence and perversion perpetrated by and upon women

title: The Big Heat
synopsis: Big Heat, The -- Gritty crime thriller in which a homicide detective (Glenn Ford) whose wife is murdered by a bomb intended for him turns in his badge and goes it alone to bring down a powerful crime syndicate, its unsavory boss (Alexander Scourby) and his corrupt City Hall cronies. Directed by Fritz Lang, the melodrama's harsh action, sordid atmosphere and seedy characters are relieved by the idealistic cop and a gangster's abused girlfriend (Gloria Grahame) who dies helping to crack the case. Much menace and stylized violence, some of it quite nasty

title: The Big Knife
synopsis: Big Knife, The -- Muddled Hollywood version of the conflict between art and commerce from the Clifford Odets play about a movie star (Jack Palance) blackmailed by an unscrupulous producer (Rod Steiger) into signing a contract for a movie he's dead set against doing. Director Robert Aldrich's melodrama has little action, much high-minded dialogue and good character bits by Ida Lupino, Jean Hagen, Shelley Winters and Wendall Corey. Sexual references and suicide in plot resolution

title: The Big Land
synopsis: Big Land, The -- Routine oater in which a Texas cattleman (Alan Ladd) persuades Kansas farmers (led by John Qualen) to join him in getting a railroad spur to the area in order to end their mutual dependency on a crooked Missouri trader (Anthony Caruso). Director Gordon Douglas seems more comfortable with cattle drives and shootouts than frontier links to Eastern markets and a sappy subplot involving a reformed alcoholic (Edmond O'Brien) and his marriageable sister (Virginia Mayo). Stylized violence

title: The Big Lift
synopsis: Big Lift, The -- During the Russian blockade of Berlin, an American (Montgomery Clift) in the massive airlift of supplies to the beleaguered city falls in love with a German resident, despite the advice of his anti-German buddy (Paul Douglas). Filmed on location in semi-documentary style by director George Seaton, this tribute to the airmen who braved the dangers of the Berlin route is convincingly authentic, though marred by the contrived love story and great gobs of patriotic rhetoric. An outburst of vengeful violence and a romance based on deceit

title: The Big Mouth
synopsis: Big Mouth, The -- Working from what seems an almost totally improvised script, director Jerry Lewis takes a bank clerk (Jerry Lewis) who happens to look exactly like a gangster (Jerry Lewis) through a tediously meandering story line. The look-alike gimmick sets up encounters with a hotel manager, a lunatic who thinks he's an FBI agent, a group of smugglers, amusement parlor police, cruel Orienta1s and so on until its frantic conclusion. For Jerry Lewis fans

title: The Big One
synopsis: Big One, The -- Thin video record of the mischieveous adventures of corporate critic Michael Moore as he crosses the country promoting his book, "Downsize This!," while giving talks to college students, visiting laid-off workers and trying to see corporation heads, though he gets nowhere with the only one (Nike's Phil Knight) willing to meet with him. Also written, produced and directed by Moore, it's the picture of a one-man band beating the drum for social justice, though his impish tactics of provocation grow tiresome along the way. Some mean-spirited humor about nuns and sporadic rough language

title: The Big Parade
synopsis: Big Parade, The -- Silent World War I epic centers on a small-town Army recruit (John Gilbert) who goes to France, falls in love with a village girl (Renee Adoree), joins in the Big Push at the front and returns minus a leg. Director King Vidor mounts the large-scale sequences of troop movements and the chaos of battle with realistic vigor that, combined with small scenes of human tenderness and comic byplay, add up to a convincing picture of men in war and its inhuman cost. Wartime violence and romantic situations

title: The Big Picture
synopsis: Big Picture, The -- Rambling satire of Hollywood focusing on an aspiring young filmmaker (Kevin Bacon) determined not to compromise his values on the way up the ladder of success -- but, of course, he does. Director Christopher Guest beats his rags-to-riches-to-rags message into the ground with cornball fantasy sequences and show biz in-jokes that make the result similar to the self-indulgent, high-gloss student films it seeks to lampoon. Sexual innuendoes and vulgar references

title: The Big Question
synopsis: > Curious documentary in which filmmakers Francesco Cabras and Alberto Molinari pose several direct questions to fellow cast and crew members on the set of "The Passion of the Christ" -- Mel Gibson among them -- about their personal religious beliefs, eliciting responses both poignant and pretentious from a diversity of creeds as well as from agnostics and atheists. Cleverly shot using the ancient Southern Italian town where Gibson's movie was shot as a backdrop, and with many of the respondents in full biblical costume, the film works for the most part, despite consisting of little more than people candidly discussing their ideas of the divine, interspersed with artsy images of a dog wandering the landscape. Subtitles. A brief drug reference
full_review:
What do you do in between takes on the set of "The Passion of the Christ"? If you're Francesco Cabras and Alberto Molinari, both of whom were extras in the movie, you shoot "The Big Question" (THINKfilm), a curious documentary that ponders the query: Who is God to you?

Fashioned after "Comizi d'amore" ("The Debates of Love," 1965), in which Pier Paolo Pasolini took to the streets to survey ordinary Italians about sex, Cabras and Molinari ask cast and crew members, as well as locals, what -- if anything -- they personally believe about God and religion, with the ancient Southern Italian town of Matera (where parts of "The Passion" were filmed) serving as an appropriate mood-setting backdrop.

Ranging from poignant to pretentious, the responses represent a kaleidoscope of creeds -- Christians, Muslims, Jews, Buddhists -- in addition to New Agers, agnostics and atheists. The filmmakers' unbiased approach allows equal voice to believers and skeptics alike.

Each of the film's 12 cleverly titled segments poses a different question, linked by artsy images of a stray dog roving through Matera's deserted streets and surrounding countryside.

Adding to the overall biblical effect, many of the respondents -- none of whom is identified -- appear in costume. Roman centurions speculate and members of the Sanhedrin squabble. Even Satan (actress Rosalinda Celentano) is shown chewing over life's inscrutable mystery.

One morose gentleman enlists Shakespeare's "Macbeth" to give his nihilism a theatrical accent, but the hopelessness in his eyes speaks volumes.

There are three recognizable faces: Italian actress Monica Bellucci (who played Mary Magdalene), a bloodied Jim Caviezel (who played Christ) and the film's producer-director, Mel Gibson, who talks candidly -- if in generalities -- about returning to his Catholic faith after years of self-destructiveness, explaining how his religious convictions are underscored by a bedrock belief that man is hardwired for eternal happiness.

Many of the respondents were raised believing in God, but, for varied reasons, have come to reject (in part or outright) what they were taught, choosing in a number of cases to subscribe to materialistic interpretations of reality. (The existence of evil and suffering ranks high as a stumbling block to accepting God.) Some also make the in-vogue distinction between "spirituality" and "religion," the latter carrying a hint of condescension.

A Jesuit priest -- and recovering alcoholic -- provides thoughtful comments, though some may question his implied contention that it is arrogant for Christians to think they have all the answers. In contrast, several other Catholic priests are unapologetic in their apologia, one stating, "We have to tell the pagans ... we have something much better."

The most effective moments, however, are filled with silence, shots of furrowed brows and wringing hands, as those interviewed formulate their responses, struggling to articulate the inexpressible.

Ultimately, the film says nothing new: Some people believe; some don't. But in conveying the sincerity of the varied seekers, "The Big Question" does at least suggest that searching for God is, perhaps, the first step toward finding him.

The film, with subtitles, contains a brief drug reference. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: The Big Red One
synopsis: Big Red One, The -- Director Samuel Fuller's attempt to honor the bravery of the U.S. Army in World War II has sadly resulted in an episodic and tedious work. Lee Marvin seems to be sleepwalking through his pivotal role as the sergeant in charge of a special infantry unit. Instead of conveying the sacrifice and futility of war, it doesn't get much beyond obnoxious characterizations of some of the G.I.s who fought it. Wartime violence and incidental vulgarities

title: The Big Sky
synopsis: Big Sky, The -- Kentucky frontiersmen Kirk Douglas and Dewey Martin join veteran mountain man Arthur Hunnicutt on a fur-trapping expedition up the Missouri River into hostile Indian territory. Long, sprawling Western adventure directed by Howard Hawks, the period details of the journey are more interesting than the slow pace of the narrative and its occasional bursts of action. Frontier violence and some veiled sexual references

title: The Big Sleep
synopsis: Big Sleep, The -- Classic hard-boiled crime caper with Raymond Chandler's private eye, Philip Marlowe (Humphrey Bogart), taking a routine blackmail case that turns into a convoluted murder mystery involving a millionaire's bewildering daughters (Lauren Bacall and Martha Vickers). Director Howard Hawks keeps the plot complications simmering with plenty of rugged action, colorful tough guys, much sardonic humor, snappy dialogue and the promise of romance. Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: The Big Sleep
synopsis: Big Sleep, The -- In a remake of the 1946 Howard Hawks-Raymond Chandler private eye classic, writer-director Michael Winner makes a disasterous mistake by taking the hard-boiled yet soft-edged detective Philip Marlowe out of his era and environment and plunking him down in contemporary London. This cultural dislocation only adds further confusion to the story's flurry of killings, eccentric cast of characters, and incredibly complex plot. Under the circumstances, Robert Mitchum has no chance of competing with Humphrey Bogart's performance as Marlowe in the original. Violence, brutality and some nudity

title: The Big Sombrero
synopsis: Big Sombrero, The -- Western programmer in which singing cowboy Gene Autry saves a Mexican se�orita (Elena Verdugo) from losing her ranch to a gang of stateside swindlers. Directed by Frank McDonald, the simple storyline is padded out with genial comedy and pleasant country music but there is little action until the big showdown in the final reel. Mild violence

title: The Big Stampede
synopsis: Big Stampede, The -- Amiable low-budget Western directed by Tenny Wright is set in New Mexico where a plucky sheriff (John Wayne) out to nab a slick gang of rustlers (headed by Noah Berry) evens the odds by deputizing a Mexican bandit leader (Luis Alberni) who proves his worth in a climax justifying the title. Mild frontier action

title: The Big Steal
synopsis: Big Steal, The -- Nifty chase thriller on Mexican backroads with a U.S. Army officer (Robert Mitchum) fleeing arrest by a fellow officer (William Bendix) for the theft of an Army payroll while he pursues the real culprit (Patric Knowles) with the help of a Spanish-speaking American (Jane Greer). Director Don Siegel's cat-and-mouse tale has plenty of eccentric curves, some deftly paced comic relief and appropriately tough characterizations. Stylized violence, mild romance and mostly positive Mexican stereotypes

title: The Big Store
synopsis: Big Store, The -- Weak Marx Brothers vehicle in which the veteran comics play department store detectives who turn the place into a shambles before unmasking the gang of thieves (headed by Douglas Dumbrille) out to bankrupt the store. Directed by Charles Reisner, the story's a bust and the Brothers' slapstick routines and zany wordplay are only intermittently amusing. Comic violence and double entendres

title: The Big Tease
synopsis: Big Tease, The -- Entertaining light comedy about a gay hairdresser (Craig Ferguson) from Glasgow who arrives at a Los Angeles international hairstyling competition intent on winning -- only to discover he is just an observer which sets in motion a series of humorous situations until the hair-raising finale. Director Kevin Allen cleverly satirizes the superficiality of a hairdressers' competition by elevating it to the status of a black-tie affair. An implied sexual encounter, homosexual references, brief rear nudity and recreational drug abuse, and occasional rough language

title: The Big T.N.T. Show
synopsis: Big T.N.T. Show, The -- Concert film directed by Larry Peerce and featuring such performers as Roger Miller, Ray Charles, Joan Baez, Donavan, The Byrds, Petula Clark, Ike & Tina Turner and Bo Diddley. Mixed bag of positive, wholesome songs and tribal chants whose lyrics are understandable only by rock cultists

title: The Big Town
synopsis: Big Town, The -- Small-time hustler (Matt Dillon) tries his luck shooting dice for big-time operators (Lee Grant and Bruce Dern) while taking his time deciding between a nice girl (Suzy Amis) and a strip-teaser (Diane Lane). He learns some lame lessons in director Ben Bolt's dingy melodrama which offers sex, violence and nudity instead of anything remotely uplifting

title: The Big Trail
synopsis: Big Trail, The -- Colorful Western adventure in which a seasoned mountain man (John Wayne) tracks those who killed his friend to a wagon train, then serves as scout guiding the settlers across the wilderness while getting the goods on the killers. Directed by Raoul Walsh, the melodramatic plot fairly creaks today, though the picture still holds interest for its visual spectacle of a pioneer wagon train overcoming swollen rivers, rugged mountains, desert wastes and wild Indians on the journey from Missouri to Oregon. Frontier violence

title: The Big Trees
synopsis: Big Trees, The -- Wooden turn-of-the-century melodrama about a claim-jumping logger (Kirk Douglas) who tries to wheedle a California religious sect into letting him cut down the giant redwoods they revere as symbols of the eternal. Director Felix Feist's contrived plot lumbers along from one complication to another until the logger's unsurprising reformation. Beautiful forest scenery, stylized violence and mild romantic allusions

title: The Big Wheel
synopsis: Big Wheel, The -- Formula tale directed by Edward Ludwig in which the son (Mickey Rooney) of famous race-car driver lands in a heap of trouble trying to emulate his dead dad, then straightens out in time to race in the Indianapolis 500. Racetrack accidents and sexual situations

title: The Bingo Long Traveling All-Stars and Motor Kings
synopsis: Bingo Long Traveling All-Stars and Motor Kings, The -- Warmly nostalgic comedy about a black baseball team barnstorming through the Midwest during the Depression summer of 1939, an era when black players were barred from the major leagues. Starring Billy Dee Williams, James Earl Jones, and Richard Pryor as top players who start hamming it up in the style of the Harlem Globe Trotters to make their victories against white teams go down easier. Director John Badham's movie looks back at the way it was, good and bad, without finding villians or making excuses. Good entertainment but coarse language and a brothel vignette unfortunately limit its appeal

title: The Birdcage
synopsis: Birdcage, The -- Comic complications ensue when the son of a gay Miami nightclub owner (Robin Williams) invites his fiancee and her ultra-conservative parents (Gene Hackman and Dianne Wiest) home for dinner and the gay man's lover (Nathan Lane) shows up in drag, pretending to be the son's mother. Producer-director Mike Nichols' remake of "La Cage aux Folles" (1979) pokes fun at flamboyant homosexuals and those who shun them while stressing the vulnerable humanity of both groups. Sympathetic depiction of the gay lifestyle, many sexual references and intermittent rough language

title: The Birds
synopsis: Birds, The -- Classy adaptation of Daphne du Maurier's story of nature in revolt begins leisurely as a romantic comedy that gradually shifts into high gear as a suspense thriller when seagulls, crows and other usually harmless birds suddenly turn malignant and band together in murderous attacks on a seaside community. Director Alfred Hitchcock is up to his old tricks in transforming the ordinary into the menacing as he puts his vulnerable principals (Rod Taylor, Tippi Hedren, Jessica Tandy and Suzanne Pleshette) through an emotional wringer trying to fend off nightmare attacks by the winged avengers. Mounting menace and special effects violence, with a key sequence involving schoolchildren that youngsters may find especially frightening

title: The Birds, the Bees and the Italians
synopsis: Birds, the Bees and the Italians, The -- Director Pietro Germi's biting satire on Italian hypocrisy may prove offensive to some viewers because its story concerns adultery and because of coarse language

title: The Bird with the Crystal Plumage
synopsis: Bird with the Crystal Plumage, The -- Failed Italian thriller in which a passer-by (Tony Musante) saves a woman (Eva Renzi) from the black-cloaked knifer and then finds himself and his sleep-in girlfriend (Suzy Kendall) the target of the ripper. Directed by Dario Argento, the loose ends and false clues are so apparent that the state of terrifying suspense so necessary to such a film is never fully realized

title: The Birthday Party
synopsis: Birthday Party, The -- Good adaptation of Harold Pinter's play about two overnight guests (Patrick Magee and Sydney Tafler) who entertain the permanent lodger (Robert Shaw) with disastrous consequences. Director William Friedkin succeeds in conveying the play's never explained mood of fear that pervades the menacing rooms of the house and the acting is superb. Mature themes

title: The Birth of a Nation
synopsis: Birth of a Nation, The -- D.W. Griffith's still controversial, still powerful picture of the Civil War and Reconstruction links the lives of two families, North and South, each sacrificing sons in the fratricidal conflict, then focuses on the Southern family's plight under greedy carpetbaggers and black opportunists until the Ku Klux Klan rides to the rescue in a swirl of racist propaganda. Griffith's mastery of the silent medium succeeds in combining the sweep of historical spectacle with the intimacy of individual lives in a fashion that still engages viewers' emotions. Though it has a place in film history as the first feature to demonstrate fully the dramatic potential of the medium, the work presents an uncritical view of 19th-century myths justifying white supremacy. Not for casual entertainment but has a place in film study programs where its racist perspective can be properly addressed

title: The Biscuit Eater
synopsis: Biscuit Eater, The -- Sentimental but unpretentious melodrama from James Street's story of a little white boy (Billy Lee) and his black chum who, despite numerous mishaps, train the seemingly worthless runt of the title into a champion bird dog, then face a tragic loss that will leave few viewers dry-eyed. Director Stuart Heisler makes effective use of the rural Georgia locales, including a fearsome swamp, but the heart of the movie is in the interaction between the boys and their beloved dog. Rewarding family fare

title: The Biscuit Eater
synopsis: Biscuit Eater, The -- A couple of kids (Johnny Whitaker and George Spell) train a rejected bird dog for the regional championships which, if it wins, will make Johnny's dad (Earl Holliman) look bad in the eyes of his boss (Lew Ayres). Director Vincent McEveety's version of the James Street classic will appeal mainly to the elementary school set since it follows the Disney formula of animals exceeding humans in intelligence

title: The Bishop's Wife
synopsis: Bishop's Wife, The -- A debonair, smartly tailored angel (Cary Grant) uses his heavenly powers to help the neglected wife (Loretta Young) of a busy Episcopalian bishop (David Niven) renew her husband's ministry to those in need rather than in raising the money for a new cathedral. Director Henry Koster's sentimental Christmas fable has the virtue of a good script, sincere performances and some amusing moments with Grant's angelic powers and Monty Wooley as a softhearted old cynic. Most of the family will find it charming entertainment

title: The Bitter Tea of General Yen
synopsis: Bitter Tea of General Yen, The -- Exotic tale set in war-torn China where an American refugee (Barbara Stanwyck) is rescued from the fighting by a cruel but cultured warlord (Nils Asther) whom she finds strangely appealing, then unwittingly causes his downfall. Directed by Frank R. Capra, the romantic melodrama succeeds in creating the unsettled, menacing atmosphere of a war zone as the bandit patiently woos the rescued woman, then contemplates a double suicide upon learning she was responsible for his defeat. Stylized violence and sexual situations

title: The Black Belly of the Tarantula
synopsis: Black Belly of the Tarantula, The -- Confusing Italian murder mystery directed by Paolo Cavara in which a sultry female voice sighs on the sound-track while a hooded psychotic stalks inadequately clad women and commits a series of excessively graphic crimes

title: The Black Bird
synopsis: Black Bird, The -- Unfunny spoof of "The Maltese Falcon" private eye classic with George Segal playing Sam Spade Jr. and Stephane Audran as the femme fatale who has not quite mastered the American idiom. Director David Giler strains hard for laughs, even trying for some religious parody, but nothing works. The language is frequently blasphemous

title: The Blackboard Jungle
synopsis: Blackboard Jungle, The -- Screen version of Evan Hunter's novel about an idealistic English teacher (Glenn Ford) confronting juvenile delinquents in an inner city high school to win over a potential drop-out (Sidney Poitier) and the rest of his class. Directed by Richard Brooks, the movie called attention to the growing problems of public education after World War II and, though dated by its melodramatic treatment, its tribute to the teaching profession is as valid today as then. Some nasty violence and much menace, especially that directed at the teacher's pregnant wife

title: The Black Cauldron
synopsis: Black Cauldron, The -- Disney's animated adventure about the brave attempts of a peasant boy to prevent the evil Horned King from gaining possession of a black cauldron capable of producing an army of supernatural warriors. The result is a delightful fantasy saga during which the boy learns about love, loyalty, courage and the importance of friendship over power. Some creepy moments

title: The Black Dahlia
synopsis: Adaptation of James Ellroy's novel built around the never-solved, true-life case of a young Hollywood hopeful (Mia Kirshner) -- whose mutilated body was found in a vacant lot in 1947 -- focusing on two L.A. cops (Josh Hartnett and Aaron Eckhart) who are involved in the case. The Hartnett character finds himself in a platonic menage with his partner and the latter's longtime girlfriend (Scarlett Johansson), then falls under the sway of a seductive rich girl (Hilary Swank) who resembles the murder victim. Brian DePalma's film-noir homage is uneven as drama (with its overly complex script), despite his customary stylish flourishes and good, if occasionally over-the-top, performances, but the pileup of sordid revelations, though expected in the noir genre, and sundry other lurid plot elements preclude recommendation. Rough and crude language, general decadence, sexual situations and innuendo, much violence, a couple of brutal boxing matches, some grisly imagery, a re-creation of the lesbian underworld, pornography, adultery, incest, rear nudity, murder, suicide and drug use
full_review:
When the horribly mutilated body of aspiring actress Elizabeth "Betty" Short was found in a vacant lot in Los Angeles in 1947, the crime caught the public's imagination like few others, and the never-solved crime continues to be the stuff of legend.

"The Black Dahlia" (Universal) is Brian DePalma's adaptation of writer James Ellroy's novel -- which was penned as a catharsis for the author, who saw parallels between Short's story and the murder of his own mother when he was 10.

In Ellroy's version, though, Short herself is secondary to the saga of two Los Angeles cops, Dwight "Bucky" Bleichert (Josh Hartnett) -- whose exposition-heavy narration runs throughout -- and Lee Blanchard (Aaron Eckhart), who become friends after facing off in the boxing ring to promote the LAPD and later are chosen to investigate the case of the young woman with the trademark black wardrobe and flower in her hair.

Bucky soon finds himself in a platonic menage with Lee and the latter's longtime girlfriend, Kay (Scarlett Johansson). Bucky and Kay become attracted to each other, but rather than betray his friend, Bucky instead lets himself fall under the sway of a seductive rich girl, Madeleine (Hilary Swank), who, as it happens, resembles murder victim Betty (Mia Kirshner), and whose powerful father, Emmet (John Kavanagh), and loony mother, Ramona (Fiona Shaw), seem like bad news from the get-go.

DePalma's film-noir homage looks terrific in terms of production design, but is uneven as drama (with an overly complex script). So, too, there are many stylish flourishes and generally good performances, particularly by Hartnett and Eckhart. Though Johansson and Swank look great in their 1940s' attire, they don't quite live up to actual screen ladies of that period.

Unfortunately, the pileup of sordid revelations, though part and parcel of the noir genre, in addition to sundry other lurid plot elements, pushes what might have been an "L" film into the "O" category.

The film contains rough and crude language, general decadence, sexual situations and innuendo, much violence, a couple of brutal boxing matches, some grisly imagery, a re-creation of the lesbian underworld, pornography, adultery, incest, rear nudity, murder, suicide and drug use. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: The Black Godfather
synopsis: Black Godfather, The -- Low-budget black exploitation movie with heavy doses of unrelieved brutality and shrill racism. Written, produced and directed by John Evans, it offers a low view of humanity in general and of black life in particular

title: The Black Hole
synopsis: Black Hole, The -- Disney science fiction movie with some fine special effects and a mediocre plot about a maverick scientist (Maximilian Schell) and his mysterious space laboratory. Unfortunately, director Gary Nelson has made the experience no more intriguing than a ride at Disneyland. Incidental violence

title: The Black Knight
synopsis: Black Knight, The -- A blacksmith (Alan Ladd) wins knighthood and his lady fair (Patricia Medina) by saving King Arthur (Anthony Bushell), Camelot and Christianity from the treachery of Cornwall's pagan king (Andre Morell) and his Saracen allies (led by Peter Cushing).
