Bruce Humberstone with Honolulu detective Chan (Warner Oland) getting some unwanted help from Number One Son (Keye Luke) in solving the murder of a racehorse owner aboard an ocean liner with suspects including gamblers, crooked jockeys and racetrack rivals. Off-screen murder and comic racial stereotyping

title: Charlie Chan at the Wax Museum
synopsis: Eerie mystery directed by Lynn Shores in which the title Honolulu detective (Sidney Toler) and his Number Two Son (Sen Yung) spend an evening in a New York crime museum owned by a plastic surgeon (C. Henry Gordon) whose criminal clientele includes an escaped murderer (Marc Lawrence) and his former partner (Ted Osborn). Menacing situations and shadowy frights

title: Charlie Chan at Treasure Island
synopsis: Engrossing mystery in which Chan (Sidney Toler) seeks to link the murder of a friend (Louis Jean Heydt) to a blackmailing psychic, with some help from a magician (Cesar Romero) performing at the San Francisco World's Fair. Directed by Norman Foster, the proceedings have some eerie moments involving illusions created by the phony psychic as well as the unsettling powers of the magician's mental telepathist, but the focus is on the twisty case and its surprise solution. Menacing situations

title: Charlie Chan in City in Darkness
synopsis: (see: " City in Darkness ")

title: Charlie Chan in Honolulu
synopsis: Despite the comic-relief antics of Number Two Son (Sen Yung), Chan (Sidney Toler) manages to solve two murders and the theft of $300,000 aboard a freighter carrying a menagerie of wild animals as well as the usual suspects (Phyllis Brooks, George Zucco, Eddie Collins, Marc Lawrence and Robert Barrat). Directed by H. Bruce Humberstone, this was Toler's first appearance as Chan who nabs the killer just before the birth of his first grandchild. Menacing situations

title: Charlie Chan in London
synopsis: Intricate mystery set in England where Chan (Warner Oland) has only three days in which to save an innocent man (Douglas Walton) from the gallows by finding the real killer among his circle of country gentry friends (Alan Mowbray, Ray Milland and others). Directed by Eugene Forde, Chan perseveres despite snooty servants, uncooperative witnesses, another murder, an attempt on his own life and a puzzling military connection before laying an ingenious trap for the killer. Stylized violence and some intense menace

title: Charlie Chan in Panama
synopsis: Formula mystery with Chan (Sidney Toler) trying to save the U.S. Fleet from being blown up while moving through the Canal, but the saboteur's trail leads to a Czech refugee (Jean Rogers), a Chicago schoolteacher (Mary Nash), an Egyptian tobacconist (Frank Puglia), a nightclub owner (Jack La Rue) and an Austrian scientist (Lionel Royce). Directed by Norman Foster, much of the plot is lifted from the 1934 espionage thriller, "Marie Galante," and the bumbling antics of Number Two Son (Sen Yung) are mostly tiresome. Menacing situations

title: Charlie Chan in Paris
synopsis: Intriguing mystery as Chan (Warner Oland) gets some unneeded help from Number One Son (Keye Luke) as well as the head of the Paris police (Minor Watson) while solving the murder of an apache dancer (Dorothy Appleby) who had information about counterfeit bank bonds. Directed by Lewis Seiler, the case turns on a recurring mysterious figure, a double disguise and a secret room in the Paris sewers. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Charlie Chan in Reno
synopsis: Convoluted mystery with Chan (Sidney Toler) coming to Nevada's divorce mill to save a friend's wife (Pauline Moore) accused of murdering the woman (Louise Henry) who stole her husband's affections. Directed by Norman Foster, the plot is loaded with suspects (notably Ricardo Cortez, Phyllis Brooks and Kay Linaker) and much comic relief from Number Two Son (Sen Yung), the local sheriff (Slim Summerville) and a daffy cab driver (Eddie Collins). Stylized violence and messy divorce proceedings

title: Charlie Chan in Rio
synopsis: Formula mystery with Chan (Sidney Toler) helping Rio de Janeiro's police chief (Harold Huber) solve the murders of a nightclub singer (Jacqueline Dalya) and her butler (Leslie Denison), with suspects including the dead woman's secretary (Kay Linaker), fiance (Ted North), ex-husband (Truman Bradley), jealous girlfriend (Mary Beth Hughes) and a Hindu mystic (Victor Jory). Directed by Harry Lachman, the heavy-handed plot hinges on the woman's unsavory past, with rather dour results despite the comic diversions of Number Two Son (Sen Yung) and Toler's silly mugging while smoking a supposedly drugged cigarette. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Charlie Chan in Shanghai
synopsis: Formula mystery in which Chan (Warner Oland) visits Shanghai on a holiday with Number One Son (Keye Luke) but his real objective is nabbing a ring of opium smugglers. Directed by James Tinling, Chan and the city's police commissioner (Halliwell Hobbes) have matters well in hand until an American G-man (Russell Hicks) gets in their way. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Charlie Chan on Broadway
synopsis: Twisty mystery in which Chan (Warner Oland) helps a New York homicide detective (Harold Huber) solve the murder of a blackmailer (Louise Henry) whose diary was sought by gangster Leon Ames, nightclub owner Douglas Fowley, newspaper editor J. Edward Bromberg and ace reporter Donald Woods. Directed by Eugene Forde, the story is tightly plotted, paced with comic relief from Chan's Number One Son (Keye Luke) and matters are wrapped up in satisfactory fashion. Menacing situations

title: Charlie Chan's Murder Cruise
synopsis: Formula mystery with Chan (Sidney Toler) joining an ocean cruise because among the ship's passengers (notably Lionel Atwill, Leo G. Carroll, Don Beddoe, Charles Middleton and Cora Witherspoon) is a killer whose strangled victims include a Scotland Yard colleague (Montague Shaw). Directed by Eugene Forde, the plot involves a recurring mysterious figure, a double disguise and a bitter divorce, with the usual comic relief from Number Two Son (Sen Yung). Some gruesome murders and much menace

title: Charlie Chan's Secret
synopsis: Convoluted mystery in which Chan (Warner Oland) comes to San Francisco in search of a missing heir who turns up dead in a spooky house during a seance held by his aunt (Henrietta Grossman). Directed by Gordon Wiles, Chan easily unmasks the trickery of the seance's phony psychics (Gloria Roy and Arthur Edmund Carew), but finding the killer proves less simple and a lot more dangerous. Sinister situations

title: Charlie's Angels
synopsis: High-energy blend of comedy and action fuels this TV-series based tale of three brainy, brawny and beautiful investigators (Cameron Diaz, Drew Barymore and Lucy Liu) whose cagey clients (Sam Rockwell and Kelly Lynch) pose a threat to their elusive boss Charlie (voice of John Forsyth). Video director McG's glossy feature-length debut is a fast-paced escapist fantasy about girls who just want to have fun while kickboxing their way out of assorted outlandish dangers. Frequent stylized violence, an implied sexual encounter, a few coarse expressions and minimal profanity. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Charlie's Angels: Full Throttle
synopsis: Lively action flick in which three gorgeous gumshoes (Cameron Diaz, Drew Barrymore and Lucy Liu) investigate the theft of a witness protection program database after several people on the list turn up dead. A campy script and slick, big.budget action scenes make director McG's sequel entertaining, effervescent escapism with empowered women in heels drop.kicking the bad guys; yet the film is almost a carbon copy of the original, with several flirty scenes meant to show off the stars' tight bodies in slightly risque outfits. Intermittent stylized violence, fleeting crass language and profanity, a live.in relationship and some mild sexual innuendo
full_review:
Like uncorking a bottle of champagne and letting the bubbles tickle one's nose, "Charlie's Angels: Full Throttle" (Columbia) is an effervescent, giddy ride that duplicates the first, which isn't necessarily a bad thing.

Inspired by the popular 1970s' TV show and again directed by McG, the sequel is more of the same slick action scenes with empowered women in heels drop.kicking the bad guys. The campy script has the three private eye Angels (Cameron Diaz, Drew Barrymore and Lucy Liu) investigating the theft of two titanium finger rings on which are encrypted the list of people in the federal witness protection program now that several of the witnesses have turned up dead.

But the shallow premise is really just a perfunctory measure on which to drape the exciting action scenes that have Natalie (Diaz), Dylan (Barrymore) and Alex (Liu) scantily clad in haute couture doing flips and kicks (shown in slow motion, of course) to outwit the villains. It's a B.movie with a big budget and name stars that ludicrously equates female empowerment solely with brawn and a bodacious body.

Watching the film, one could understand how young girls could be attracted to the Angels. They are strong, smart, and tough, and they can outkick, outpunch and out.thump their male counterparts while still being feminine and fun. Yet "feminine" has a slightly risque interpretation here, as the women in their skintight (and baring) outfits use not only their flowing hair and bright.white smiles, but their abundant cleavage and tight abs and butts to distract and then clobber the enemy.

However, the film's tone is light.hearted and frivolous, never taking itself, or its actors, too seriously. And the leading ladies join in on the fun, almost winking at the camera as they shake their booties, seeming not to mind the gratuitous shots of the derrieres.

In a tongue.in.cheek homage to "The Matrix," "Mission: Impossible" and the James Bond films, among other well.known (and male.dominated) actioners, "Charlie's Angels: Full Throttle" has the cherub trio performing death.defying feats all in the line of duty. In fact, much like the original "Angels" film, the sequel opens with a 007.like sequence where the Angels make their escape by leaping out of a military truck that has plunged over a bridge and jumping inside an airplane to land safely with their rescued victim. And the action skyrockets from there to include a
dangerous dirt bike race, an over.the.top car chase and many leaps from tall buildings, which of course leave the gorgeous gumshoes relatively unscathed.

Replacing Bill Murray as the new Bosley is Bernie Mac, who adds a bit of zing and his unique comedic flair to the film and acts as a foil to the girls' flirty spy games. John Forsyth returns as the voice of Charlie (still communicating through speaker box), which anchors the film and recalls its TV roots. And in a much.hyped role, Demi Moore stars as Madison Lee, a fallen Angel who just may pose the biggest threat to the good.hearted, crime.fighting threesome. And, as if to justify the apparent millions of dollars supposedly spent on "touching up" her body, the film boasts a few gratuitous shots of Moore running on the beach, "Baywatch".style, or lounging in lacy lingerie and spiked heels as she plots world domination.

The cast seems up for the silly melodramatic style of the film, which has a toe.tapping, finger.snapping score that dares anyone not to bounce along with the beat. Diaz shines as the flighty Natalie, mixing an irrepressible smile and giggle with a deadly "hi.yah!" martial arts chop to thwart the baddies. Liu is still the aloof acrobat, stretching her folded body out of a crate and flipping her hair as if to say, "no big deal." Barrymore keeps up with her buddies, as the former bad.girl.turned.Angel who still has a soft spot for the bad guys.

Goofy, exciting and completely forgettable, "Charlie's Angels: Full Throttle" perfectly fits the definition of popcorn summer fare.

Because of intermittent stylized violence, fleeting crass language and profanity, a live.in relationship and some mild sexual innuendo, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A.III .. adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG.13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Charlie, the Lonesome Cougar
synopsis: Disney wildlife documentary featuring an agile cougar named Charlie who has outgrown the northwoods lumber camp where he was raised and finds happiness with a female cougar in a nearby game preserve. Charlie is a very photogenic animal but his "adventures" are on the cute side and begin to wear thin

title: Charlie Wilson's War
synopsis: Adept, sophisticated political drama, based on real events, recounting how an obscure, high-living Texas congressman (Tom Hanks) united with a wealthy, ostensibly pious political supporter (Julia Roberts) and a gifted but volatile CIA agent (Philip Seymour Hoffman) to defeat the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. Director Mike Nichols' rollicking film revels in the comic divide between its central character's disreputable lifestyle, which is portrayed at times quite graphically, and his historic achievement, with perhaps an invitation to excuse or even celebrate the one in light of the other. Sustained upper female and rear nudity, implied nonmarital sex, drug use, sexual humor, irreverent dialogue, pervasive rough and some crude and crass language, and scenes of wounded children
full_review:
A rollicking, hard-driving comedy, "Charlie Wilson's War" (Universal) is also a sophisticated political drama based on real events. The story it tells is, like its protagonist, at once breezy and serious, likable but morally muddled.

In the early 1980s, Charlie Wilson (Tom Hanks) was an obscure yet quietly powerful Texas congressman with a taste for single-malt whiskey, casino hot tubs and questionable companions. Well ahead of most of his colleagues, however, he took an interest in the plight of the Afghan people following the ruthless Soviet invasion of their homeland that had begun in 1979.

Sharing his concern, and his insight into the potential advantages of a Russian defeat, was wealthy, ostensibly pious socialite Joanne Herring (Julia Roberts). Together they made a potent duo, with Wilson able to appropriate ever-increasing sums through Congress and Herring making sure all the "right" people were on board. In between, they were also casual lovers.

Out in the cold over at CIA headquarters, meanwhile, was gifted but volatile agent Gust Avrakotos (Philip Seymour Hoffman). Thanks to his uncouth manner and his confrontational approach toward his superiors, he had been languishing for years without a real assignment.

Discovering a kindred spirit in Wilson, Avrakotos soon sets to work patching together an unlikely alliance of Israeli and Arab leaders willing to work together behind the scenes to funnel money and arms to the then-little-known mujahedin fighters. Once those supplies began to reach the guerrillas, the toll on the Russian forces in terms of tanks, helicopters and planes quickly escalated.

Veteran director Mike Nichols' film recounts these events adeptly. The cast is uniformly convincing, with Ned Beatty putting in a brief but fine-tuned appearance as Wilson's indispensable committee chairman, "Doc" Long.

The script revels in the comic divide between its main character's disreputable lifestyle, which is portrayed at times quite graphically, and his historic achievement. Yet the implication that we are being invited to excuse, or even celebrate, the one in light of the other is certainly problematic. As a vivid cinematic treatment of a crucial chapter in recent American history, however, "Charlie Wilson's War" achieves its objectives.

The film contains sustained upper female and rear nudity, implied nonmarital sex, drug use, sexual humor, irreverent dialogue, pervasive rough and some crude and crass language, and scenes of wounded children. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Charlotte Gray
synopsis: Weak drama set during World War II about a young Scottish woman (Cate Blanchett) living in London who joins the French Resistance hoping to save her pilot boyfriend (Rupert Penry-Jones) who has been shot down. Based on the novel by Sebastian Faulks, director Gillian Armstrong somehow turns spying into banal work, while stripping the film of any sense of urgency, suspense or passion and ending on a pointlessly melodramatic note. An implied sexual encounter, some war-related violence and fleeting rough language

title: Charlotte's Web
synopsis: Charming animated musical version of E.B. White's classic fable about a piglet named Wilbur who develops from runt of the litter into the county fair champ with the help of his friends, most notably the spider of the title. Directed by Charles A. Nichols, the Hanna-Barbera production is a gentle introduction to the natural cycle of life that will entertain youngsters and most others in the family

title: Charlotte's Web
synopsis: Charming live-action adaptation of E.B. White's beloved children's classic about a runt pig (voiced by Dominic Scott Kay) who is saved from slaughter by the love of a young girl (Dakota Fanning), a barnyard of computer-enhanced talking animals (voiced by Oprah Winfrey, Steve Buscemi, John Cleese and Robert Redford, among others), and the fancy web work of a sage spider, Charlotte (voiced by Julia Roberts). Hewing closely to the book, director Gary Winick makes sure that the techno-wizardry never overshadows the story and its simple, timeless themes of friendship and the bittersweet cycle of life. Some mildly crude humor
full_review:
Director Gary Winick spins magic with "Charlotte's Web" (Paramount), a live-action adaptation of E.B. White's beloved children's classic and one of the best family films of the year.

Hewing fairly closely to the book, the tale centers on Wilbur (voiced by Dominic Scott Kay), a runt pig who is saved from slaughter by the love of a young girl, Fern (Dakota Fanning), a barnyard of talking animals, and the fancy web work of a sage spider, Charlotte (voiced by Julia Roberts).

While the 1973 animated version is hard to beat, Winick's use of live action -- enhanced by computer effects as in "Babe" -- is charming, and the all-star voice talent, including Oprah Winfrey, Steve Buscemi, John Cleese, Robert Redford, Reba McEntire, Cedric the Entertainer, Kathy Bates and Sam Shepard as the narrator, is obviously impressive.

Capturing the innocence of White's fable, Winick takes care that the techno-wizardry never overshadows the story with its timeless themes of friendship and the bittersweet cycle of life.

To deter the farm's owner from serving Wilbur as Christmas dinner, Charlotte weaves adulatory adjectives over the pig's stall, which the farmer then interprets as a miraculous sign. "Terrific" is one of them. And the same word most emphatically applies to this delightful film.

The film contains some mildly crude humor. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-I -- general patronage. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is G -- general audiences. All ages admitted.

title: Charly
synopsis: Mentally retarded adult (Cliff Robertson) becomes a genius during a medical experiment that has only one drawback, and it's a heartbreaker. A somewhat sentimental adaptation of Daniel Keyes' short story, "Flowers for Algernon," the intriguing plot is delicately handled by director Ralph Nelson and given dramatic impact by the range of Robertson's performance in the title role. Mature treatment of romantic subplot

title: Charro!
synopsis: Elvis Presley sings only one song, and that off-camera, in a silly Western vehicle about a gang of outlaws and a golden cannon in Old Mexico. Directed by Charles Marquis Warren, it contains stylized violence, a bit of sadism and some double entendres

title: Charulata
synopsis: Director Satyajit Ray's story is of a wife neglected by her husband's total commitment to his work. As the film ends with a freeze-frame of the couple reaching for each other, the picture reaches far beyond the boundaries of Ray's native Bengal

title: Chase a Crooked Shadow
synopsis: Limp British thriller directed by Michael Anderson is set in Barcelona where a South African diamond heiress (Anne Baxter) comes to fear for her life after a stranger (Richard Todd) shows up claiming to be her brother, with a preposterous twist ending. Some fairly intense menace makes it unlikey fare for children

title: Chasing Amy
synopsis: When a lesbian (Joey Lauren Adams) falls for a lovestruck male (Ben Affleck), their affair is shattered by his friend (Jason Lee) revealing details of her kinky bisexual past. Writer-director Kevin Smith mines the topic of sexual identity for some weak laughs in a raunchy, long-winded tale that views promiscuity as harmless fun. Sexual situations, blue humor, drug abuse and constant rough language with occasional profanity

title: Chasing Liberty
synopsis: Conventional teenage romantic comedy about the president's daughter (Mandy Moore), who, frustrated that her every move is monitored, ditches her Secret Service handlers while traveling abroad with her father (Mark Harmon) and embarks on an impromptu European adventure, aided and abetted by a dashing Brit (Matthew Goode) with a secret of his own. While giving parent-teen angst a presidential twist, there is little to hail about director Andy Cadiff's touching on issues of independence and parental trust while seemingly equating personal freedom with irresponsible behavior. An implied sexual encounter, some sexual humor, brief rear nudity, and minimal mildly crude language
full_review:
Teenage dating has never been easy. But when your father happens to be the leader of the free world the normally awkward enterprise can be downright impossible. This dating dilemma forms the framework of Andy Cadiff's "Chasing Liberty" (Warner Bros.), a flavorless romantic comedy about a president's daughter who goes AWOL while accompanying her parents on a state visit to Europe.

Pop singer Mandy Moore stars as 18-year-old Anna Foster (Secret Service designation "Liberty"), a frustrated first daughter fed up with her every move being monitored by a vanload of bodyguards -- men-in-black government chaperones have a way of cramping one's social life. Despite having lived her whole life in the public eye, she is just a normal angst-ridden adolescent -- a fragile melange of defiance and insecurity.

Mark Harmon plays her two-term presidential father, who, while holding a 63 percent approval rating, is in the dark about, er, domestic policies. Like most overprotective dads he is reluctant to admit his little girl has grown up -- yet unlike most he must juggle paternal panic with the economic fate of developing Third World nations.

While attending a G8 conference in Prague with the first folks, Anna shows off some diplomacy of her own by striking a bargain with her father which will allow her one night out on the town as a "normal" teenager, unencumbered by a phalanx of Secret Service agents. But when he reneges and actually beefs up her pared-down security detail, Anna gives her handlers the slip at a local club, and, aided and abetted by a dashing young Brit named Ben Calder (Matthew Goode), embarks on an impromptu barnstorming tour of Europe.

However, unbeknownst to Anna, Ben is actually a CIA field agent planted by her dad to keep an eye on her while she enjoys the illusion of independence. Needless to say, his undercover assignment ends up under the covers, making his inevitable coming clean about the deception all the more devastating to Anna.
Having grown up in the spotlight, Moore is well-groomed for the role, though the subplot involving her romantically gun-shy handlers (played by Jeremy Piven and Annabella Sciorra) proves far more entertaining than her pouting and pining. Apart from a mildly amusing opening sequence at 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. which puts a cute spin on pre-date jitters, much of the humor is flat and caters to ethnic stereotyping.

On its surface the film is a breezy story about a girl at a crossroads in her life. Stripped of the commander-in-chief complications, Anna's dilemma is no different than that of any teen struggling with independence and identity issues. Likewise, while few if any parents have access to stealth helicopters to track their son or daughter's whereabouts, her father's sheltering instinct resonates with any parent who finds it difficult to cut the proverbial apron strings.

However, if the filmmaker's intent is to argue for parents trusting their children, he presents a rather self-incriminating case. From the outset, Anna proves that she is anything but responsible, getting drunk, stripping for a quick skinny-dip in the Danube and, after one magical kiss on a romantic gondola ride in Venice, deciding that she is ready to sleep with Ben, a guy she barely knows.

Underneath its fresh-scrubbed facade, the film seems more concerned with the pursuit of happiness than life or liberty. And the "happiness" sought is not what St. Thomas Aquinas would call the "summa bonum" (the final good) but a cheap hedonism, exemplified by "The Love Parade," an orgiastic Mardi Gras-like rave at which Anna and Ben wind up in Berlin. During the bacchanalia a song proclaims, "You've got to live your life free to do what you want to do," exposing the film's underlying message of false emancipation. What is being chased is not liberty, but libertinism. Moore's 1999 debut album, "So Real," struck gold with the hit single "Candy," which is exactly what this movie is -- sugary sweet, but ultimately corrosive.

Due to an implied sexual encounter, some sexual humor, brief rear nudity, and minimal mildly crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Chasing Papi
synopsis: Fatuous comedy about three women who collide over the affections of a suave, hunky advertising executive, who has deceived each into thinking that she is the only love of his life. This debut film by Linda Mendoza, though sporting an easy-to-look-at, up-and-coming Hispanic cast, is doomed by an inane script and flat, forced humor which ultimately proves to be about as appetizing as a three-day-old burrito. Some mild sexual humor
full_review:
Three women collide over the affections of a suave, hunky advertising executive who has deceived each into thinking that she is the only love of his life in the fatuous comedy "Chasing Papi" (Fox). This debut film by Linda Mendoza, though sporting an easy-to-look-at, up-and-coming Hispanic cast, is doomed by an inane script and flat, forced humor which ultimately proves to be about as appetizing as a three-day-old burrito.

Tomas Fuentes (Eduardo Verastegui) is handsome, intelligent and charming -- he is also on the verge of a nervous breakdown. The problem is, he is in love with three women, each safely separated by frequent-flyer miles, and blissfully ignorant of the amorous competition for their "Papi Chulo" -- a term of endearment in Latin culture meaning "my beautiful man."

First there is Lorena (Roselyn Sanchez), a Chicago lawyer whose blend of brains and beauty appeals to Tomas' sensitive, intellectual side. Behind door No. 2 is the Latin bombshell Cici (Sofia Vergara), a Charo-like Miami cocktail waitress whose curvaceous salsa physique satisfies his less cerebral needs. Then there's the New York heiress, Patricia (Jaci Velasquez), sophisticated and spoiled, who sees in Tomas an escape from her stifling Iberian blueblood mother.

Prompted by insecurity and the exhortations of famed television astrologer Walter Mercado -- whose televised horoscope readings seem tailor-made for each woman -- the three Latin lovelies chart courses for Los Angeles, each hoping to surprise Tomas. Yet not even his Don Juan good looks can help him charm his way out of trouble when, after showing up on his doorstep simultaneously and discovering they have been triple-timed, they descend on him like harpies. Ah, what tango-ed webs we weave!

Faced with the unenviable task of choosing one, Tomas passes out -- due in part to shock, and to the tranquilizers his doctor prescribed to treat his anxiety -- triggering a sequence of events which quickly cha-chas from the silly to the absurd. Along the way the filmmaker wedges a subplot into the story revolving around Cici's car and a bag of stolen money which serves no purpose beyond supplying pursuers from whom the women can flee in high heels.

Predictably, the competitors join forces to save their comatose Adonis, who -- mercifully for him -- remains unconscious through much of the film. However, in the end Tomas is left hung out to dry, as the women discover that the bond of friendship that has developed among them is more fulfilling than anything one man could offer them.

Very little of the narrative holds together and the film's strained dialogue and contrived plot devices amount to the worst Latin endeavor since the Bay of Pigs.

Due to some mild sexual humor, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

title: Chastity
synopsis: Produced by Sonny and starring Cher, the movie intends to be a personal statement about dropping out and searching for identity and true relationships, here depicted in time-honored trial-and-error fashion. Directed by Alessio De Paola, it unfortunately suffers from a lack of sophistication and insight as well as the severe technical limitations that are common in small budget films

title: Chato's Land
synopsis: Failed Western about a half-breed Indian (Charles Bronson) who is goaded into killing a brutish sheriff and becomes the object of an intense manhunt led by an ex-Confederate officer (Jack Palance) which ends in the parched Indian country of the title. Directed by Michael Winner, the problem is that once the movie gets into the groove of steady killing, it becomes both tedious and glaring in its cumulative brutality

title: Chattahoochee
synopsis: Dark, tedious account of an emotionally disturbed Korean War hero (Gary Oldman) who in the mid-1950s is sent to a degrading mental institution from which he, with the aid of his sister, alerts officials to the brutal mistreatment of the inmates, resulting in legislation that improved treatment of the mentally ill across the country. Mick Jackson's unimaginative direction dilutes the power of the young man's gradual transformation into a mature person committed to social justice. Graphic scenes of brutality, shower room nudity, implicit masturbation and locker-room language

title: Che!
synopsis: Dramatization of different points of view on the life and career of Ernesto (Che) Guevara (Qmar Sharif), the Argentinian who was the theoretician and moving spirit behind Cuban revolutionary Fidel Castro (Jack Palance). Directed by Richard Fleischer, it's a boring and lifeless illustrated lecture, devoid of the passion, politics, urgency and conflict that might have involved viewers in potentially interesting and significant political realities

title: Cheaper by the Dozen
synopsis: Warm family comedy about the unusual domestic arrangements in the New Jersey household of a no-nonsense efficiency expert (Clifton Webb), his equally proficient wife (Myrna Loy) and their 12 children (Jeanne Crain is the eldest). Set in the early part of the century, director Walter Lang's episodic, fact-based story has a strong nostalgic appeal along with a genial sense of humor about family life, some of which proves more than funny (e.g., Mildred Natwick as a bemused planned parenthood representative). Still pleases

title: Cheaper by the Dozen
synopsis: Fitfully amusing comedy about a family with 12 children veering out of control when Mom (Bonnie Hunt) must go a national book tour leaving Dad (Steve Martin) to hold down the very rebellious fort while the demands of his university football coaching job allow scant time for his unhappy youngsters. The family-first message follows director Shawn Levy's predictable parade of pranks, pratfalls and parenting problems, including dismay over their 22-year-old daughter moving in with her boyfriend. A discreetly implied affair, occasional toilet humor and brief slapstick violence
full_review:
A better job for Dad and a book deal for Mom undo a big happy family in "Cheaper by the Dozen" (20th Century Fox).

A distinctly different (as in less witty) remake of the 1950 same-titled comedy starring the persnickety Clifton Webb and the unflappable Myrna Loy, this updated version has its laughs as well. Steve Martin and Bonnie Hunt will also click with easy-to-please audiences as the harried parents who always wanted a big brood but got more than they asked for -- as in 12 tax deductions. However, predictable pranks and pratfalls predominate where originality and freshness might have lifted it above routine remake status.

The set-up agreeably chronicles how Mom and Dad met, married and started a family as Dad settled for a small-college football coaching job while Mom gave up journalism to be a full-time homemaker.

Twenty-three years later, grown-up Nora (Piper Perabo) has moved in with her airhead model-boyfriend (a very funny Ashton Kutcher), to her parents' dismay, but otherwise the family is thriving. That is, until Dad accepts a job offer at his alma mater, requiring the family to relocate -- under protest from the kids.

No sooner do they move in than Mom's first book gets published and she finds herself off on a national book tour lasting not the anticipated three days but two mighty long weeks, enough time for the Baker family to go into full meltdown.

As directed by Shawn Levy with its positive but hammered-home message about family life requiring sacrifice, Martin and Hunt are well-paired, he in manic mode, she a constant calming influence on all.

The fun for most viewers will be in the predictable chaos usually abetted by a marauding animal -- a frog wrecking family breakfast time, a dog getting up close and very personal with boyfriend Hank, and a snake creating havoc at a birthday party.

For supposed siblings, the child actors look nothing alike (except identical twin brothers Brent and Shane Kinsman). Yet Forrest Landis as lonely little Mark is touching while teen star Hilary Duff makes little impression as a self-aware clothes horse, though "Smallville" star Tom Welling gets a bit more to work with as the oldest son beginning to stand up to Dad.
As is clear from frame one, Mom and Dad will recognize that family comes first just as Nora will end her relationship with vacuous Hank.

But, as moral lessons learned are not enough for a flagrantly feel-good movie, the ending assures the audience that, after putting their careers on the back burner, Mom and Dad get success anyway, icing on the cake of this supersweet, family-friendly confection.

Due to a discreetly implied affair, occasional toilet humor and brief slapstick violence, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

title: Cheaper By the Dozen 2
synopsis: Agreeably entertaining sequel to the 2003 comedy which finds the Baker brood -- mom (Bonnie Hunt), dad (Steve Martin) and their 12 children -- vacationing at a lakefront cabin where their summer holiday unravels into a battle for bragging rights against a rival clan headed by a hypercompetitive blowhard (Eugene Levy). Director Adam Shankman serves up a similar helping of mildly amusing slapstick and heart-tugging sentiment, slightly more satisfying this time around, while again affirming a strong family-values message. Much comic mayhem, and some mildly crude humor, language and innuendo
full_review:
Following on the disappointing heels of "Yours, Mine & Ours" comes "Cheaper by the Dozen 2" (Fox), another big-brood comedy, which, while boasting not as many tax deductions, delivers considerably more charm and family-friendly fun.

A sequel to the 2003 remake of the 1950 Myrna Loy-Clifton Webb domestic farce, the agreeably entertaining film revisits the Chicago-based Bakers: mom Kate (Bonnie Hunt), dad Tom (Steve Martin) and their 12 children.

With pregnant eldest daughter Nora (Piper Perabo) moving to Houston with hubby Bud (Jonathan Bennett), grown son Charlie (Tom Welling) mulling a change of address, and newly graduated Lorraine (Hillary Duff) heading off to New York, Tom and Kate start feeling empty-nest angst.

Hoping for one last hurrah before the kids go their separate ways, they pitch an idea to the troops tailor-made for comic disaster: an outdoorsy vacation together at Lake Winnetka, Wis., the Bakers' summer getaway.

Their holiday soon unravels, when Tom becomes involved in a game of obsessive one-upmanship with longtime nemesis Jimmy Murtaugh (Eugene Levy), a hypercompetitive blowhard who heads a rival clan and owns most of the lakefront properties.

Jimmy suggests that Tom pit his Bakers' dozen against his own Murtaugh litter to compete in a series of contests for the lake community's prized Winnetka Cup.

Much pint-sized pandemonium ensues -- the Bakers' pooch, Gunner, once again causes havoc -- but by time the dust settles all involved gain a deeper appreciation of the bonds they share.

Taking over the reins from Shawn Levy, director Adam Shankman serves up a similar helping of mildly amusing slapstick and heart-tugging sentiment, slightly more satisfying despite an uninspired script.

Martin is in top farceur form, occasionally ratcheting down his mugging to allow for some tender daddy's-little-girl moments with daughter Sarah (Alyson Stoner), whose awkward affections for one of Murtaugh's boys is complicated by their fathers. The puppy-love angle adds a sweet touch to the madcap mix.

As before, Hunt brings a calming, maternal warmth, while Levy injects his low-key brand of drollery. Even former "Baywatch" beauty Carmen Electra gets a nice upgrade from her usual airhead roles.

The laughs are still lightweight and many of the silly sight gags seem rehashed, but the movie's absence of objectionable content and strong affirmation of family makes it easy to smile past its shortcomings.

The film contains much comic mayhem and some mildly crude humor, language and innuendo. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

title: Cheaper to Keep Her
synopsis: A divorce lawyer (Tovah Feldshuh), concerned about late alimony payments, hires a private investigator (Mac Davis) who is newly divorced himself in a dreadfully acted, determinedly vulgar attempt by director Ken Annakin at romantic comedy. The humor, when not lewd, comes at the expense of homosexuals and Hispanics

title: Checkered Flag or Crash
synopsis: Joe Don Baker plays a driver in a 1000-mile road race in the Philippines, with Susan Sarandon as an intrepid photographer-journalist. Directed by Alan Gibson, it is mindless even by the modest standards of racing movies and exhibits a disregard for human life

title: Checking Out
synopsis: Failed, badly written comedy about one man's fear of mortality when an airline executive (Jeff Daniels) flips out after the sudden death of his best friend (Allen Havey). Director David Leland offers little beyond tasteless ethnic jokes, tired coronary gags, numbingly selfish characters and a particularly gross sex scene

title: Check Your Guns
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Ray Taylor in which a singing cowboy (Eddie Dean) is made sheriff of a lawless Colorado town and uses his six-shooter to tame it. Frontier violence

title: Cheech and Chong's Next Movie
synopsis: Second movie with the comedy team of Cheech and Chong (Cheech Marin and Thomas Chong) assaults thc audience with drugs, foul language, crude sexual references and a plot that goes nowhere. Directed by Chong

title: Cheech and Chong's Nice Dreams
synopsis: The dopey duo this time out are entrepreneurs dealing marijuana from an ice cream truck which leads to the usual ramb1ing misadventures with drugs and sex

title: Cheech and Chong's "The Corsican Brothers"
synopsis: Cheech and Chong take the plot of the venerable o1d swashbuckler and bedeck it with their usual slapstick gags, though this time they avoid drugs and nudity. Directed by Thomas Chong, however, it's all very unfunny, especially its gross sexual humor

title: Cheers for Miss Bishop
synopsis: Sentimental drama of an unmarried teacher (Martha Scott) at a midwestern college from her student days in the 1870s to her retirement in the 1930s. Directed by Tay Garnett, the result has plenty of heart in its depiction of the teacher's failed romances (William Gargan and Sidney Blackmer) and her dedication to niece, grandniece and students, as well as a patriotic theme equating knowledge with democracy. Romantic complications

title: Cheetah
synopsis: Disney live-action adventure of two teenagers who adopt an orphaned Cheetah cub while spending the summer with their parents in Kenya. Directed by Jeff Blyth, the movie may bore parents familiar with the similar, better movie, "Born Free," but children will be content with the movie's nature photography and the warm friendship that develops between the American youngsters and a local Masai lad who shows them the wonders of his world

title: Cherry
synopsis: Inept romantic comedy in which a 29-year-old virgin (Shalom Harlow) spurns marriage yet wants to have a baby, then can find no likely candidate until suddenly pursued by a professional clown (Donovan Leitch) and her gynecologist (Jake Weber), with cloyingly predictable results. Co-directed by Jon Glascoe and Joseph Pierson, the attempt to make the bogus situation and phony characters seem whimsical is painfully unamusing. Considerable sexual innuendo and occasional rough language

title: Cherry, Harry and Raquel
synopsis: Marijuana operation in the Arizona desert is interfered with by a pesky Indian. Sex exploitation job directed by Russ Meyer with extensive nudity and perverse acts

title: Cher Victor
synopsis: French black comedy to which director Robin Davis brings a hard-edged sensibility in a story of two old men for whom petty quarrels turn into a vendetta that ends in tragedy. Bernard Blier and Jacques Dufilho, two great character actors, give a performance worth seeing as the geriatric odd couple who are locked in a symbiotic relationship neither can break. The movie is amusing yet underneath lurks the truth that the frailities of old age await each viewer

title: Cheyenne
synopsis: Thin Western directed by Raoul Walsh is set in the Wyoming Territory of 1867 where a gambler (Dennis Morgan) working for Wells Fargo nabs a stagecoach robber known as the Poet (Bruce Bennett), chiefly by playing footsy with the outlaw's wronged wife (Jane Wyman). Stylized violence and implied marital infidelity

title: Cheyenne Autumn
synopsis: Western epic of Indian courage in the face of the white man's neglect and broken promises in the story of a Cheyenne tribe who leave a squalid reservation for their homeland and an officer (Richard Widmark) who sympathizes with their plight but whose orders are to bring them back. Director John Ford's rugged locales match the grandeur of the trek even though the melodramatic narrative falters at times

title: Chicago
synopsis: Zesty musical set in Prohibition-era Chicago finds two rival song-and-dance gals (Renee Zellweger and Catherine Zeta-Jones) each jailed for murder using the same unscrupulous attorney (Richard Gere) to exploit their celebrity and get them off the hook. Adapted from Bob Fosse's 1975 Broadway show, director Rob Marshall's spirited black comedy weaves fantasy and reality together for a naughty, razzle-dazzle take on the corrupting power of greed and fame. Brief violence, a fleeting sexual encounter, double entendres, intermittent profanity and an instance of rough language
full_review:
Scaling the heights of razzle-dazzle theatricality is the movie musical "Chicago" (Miramax), starring a threesome not previously known for singing and dancing talents.

Catherine Zeta-Jones as vaudeville star Velma Kelly is terrific. She outshines the musical's lead star, Renee Zellweger. And, well, the less said about Richard Gere's singing and dancing the better. Nonetheless, this zesty adaptation of Bob Fosse's Broadway show is a spirited, toe-tapping melange of familiar show tunes and voluptuous visuals.

Theater purists, especially those who have been to the 1975 production and/or the successful 1997 revival of "Chicago," may find fault with the screen version. Choppy editing lends the impression that the film is fast-paced, but such quick cuts can undermine the musical's fluidity. And one may have preferred to get the whole picture of a dance number rather than crosscuts to close-ups of feet, hands and the performers' facial expressions. One hit song from the show, "Class," is dropped while another is added. All that said, the movie is a rousing crowd-pleaser that boldly jumps from stage to screen and doesn't look back.

It's set in Prohibition-era Chicago, where, early on, Velma takes center stage alone for a number usually performed with her singing sibling. Watching her enviously from the audience is chorus girl Roxie Hart (Zellweger). Suddenly, the cops burst in and arrest Velma, who's just rubbed out both her traitorous sister and her cheating husband.

Soon after Velma lands in the pokey she's followed by sweet-faced Roxie, who's knocked off her lying lover after he promised to further her career, then laughed in her face. Roxie's chump of a husband (John C. Reilly) was ready to take the fall for Roxie but the cops tricked her into admitting the dirty deed.

Enter money-lusting lawyer Billy Flynn (Gere), who's representing Velma, and now takes on Roxie, fabricating a poor, convent-bred-girl-fallen-low fiction about Roxie to win her notoriety and public sympathy before the trial. And Roxie's happy to use murder as the means to win fame; the musical numbers in the movie often spring from Roxie's imagining herself at the center of the spotlight.

Though Roxie and Velma spurn each other in jail out of jealousy, the public's short attention span for scandal requires them to team up to keep the spotlight.

Fosse's Broadway musical was originally based on Maurine Dallas Watkins' 1926 dramatic play, but director Rob Marshall's energetic adaptation brings out the black comedy elements of the piece. The movie takes on a naughty tone with Velma and Roxie seen as anti-heroines and everyone winking at the rampant corruption in a city where murder is regarded as entertainment.

Queen Latifah is introduced in a dynamite production number as the opportunistic but sympathetic prison matron who shows a deft hand for comedy as well.

Zellweger is game to sing and dance, but her puffy face atop a very skinny body appear at odds, especially when seen alongside robust-looking Zeta-Jones. Yet in her fantasy sequences Zellweger is photographed so glamorously with the platinum hairdo and ruby red lips that she looks like the "preincarnation" of Marilyn Monroe. Where she excels is in conveying her character's surface innocence, which hides her cold and calculating ambition.

Movie musicals being few and far between these days, "Chicago," with its enduring melodies and lyrics, is a vibrant if cynical take on the corrupting power of greed and fame.

Due to brief violence, fleeting sexual situations, double entendres, intermittent profanity and an instance of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Chicago 70
synopsis: Witty anti-establishment satire intertwines the Chicago conspiracy trial of Bobby Seale and Abbie Hoffman with Lewis Carroll's "Alice in Wonderland." Director Kerry Feltham photographed the stage play as performed by the Toronto Workshop, with its bizarre, colorful costumes and a minimum of props in a black limbo setting. Mature themes

title: Chicago Cab
synopsis: Sour slice-of-life treatment of a day the life of a harried taxi driver (Paul Dillon) as seen in his interaction with a strange assortment of fares ranging from the rich and boorish to drunks, junkies and wierdos. Directed by Mary Cybulski and John Tintori, the colorful Chicago backgrounds provide more visual interest than the cab's depressing interior, though the largely failed attempt to deal with the potential human drama in all this is not without interest. Some nasty menace, sexual situations and references, much rough language and occasional profanity

title: Chicago Joe and the Showgirl
synopsis: Stationed in World War II London, a G.I. (Kiefer Sutherland) and an exotic dancer (Emily Lloyd) take their Hollywood-inspired crime fantasies to deadly lengths within days of meeting each other. Directed by Bernard Rose, the fact-based movie restages the pair's murderous rampage without offering any insight into such cold-blooded behavior. Brutal depictions of violent crimes, brief shots of sexual activity and partial nudity

title: Chicken Little
synopsis: Disappointing computer-animated comedy adventure based on the classic nursery rhyme about a little chick (voiced by Zach Braff) who, after humiliating himself by sounding the alarm that the sky is falling, gets a chance to save face -- and his hometown -- when his apocalyptic announcement later proves true. Directed by Mark Dindal, the movie's vibrant, through unremarkable, animation goes for a more 3-D look, but the flat story and characterizations lack much emotion, charm or wit, undercutting the film's warm themes of family bonds and believing in oneself
full_review:
The poster of Disney's "Chicken Little" jokingly announces, "The end is near." If the movie is any indication of things to come, that just might be true for Disney's storied reign as the gold standard of animated entertainment.

The studio recently abandoned its traditional hand-drawn operations to compete with the digital dominance of Pixar ("Toy Story," "Monsters Inc.," "Finding Nemo" and "The Incredibles") and DreamWorks ("Shrek"), so "Chicken Little" marks its first fully computer-animated feature film.

Sadly for the mouse house, this "Chicken" is a bit of a turkey.

Based on the classic children's story, the movie centers on a confidence-challenged chick (voiced by Zach Braff) who sounds the apocalyptic alarm by reporting that the sky is falling, sending his panicked neighbors into a tizzy. It all turns out to be a humiliating mistake, but not before half the town is ruined, along with his reputation.

To salvage some dignity and win the approval of his disappointed dad, Buck Cluck (voiced by Garry Marshall), Chicken Little joins his school's baseball team and lifts his squad to an upset victory over their archrivals, exorcising the bad taste of his recent embarrassment.

But no sooner has he redeemed himself than a piece of sky really does conk him on the head, heralding what appears to be an alien invasion. But will anyone believe him this time?

Much zaniness ensues, as Chicken Little -- aided by buddies Runt of the Litter (Steve Zahn), Abby Mallard, aka Ugly Duckling (Joan Cusack), and Fish Out of Water (Dan
Molina) -- races to save face and his hometown.

Rounding out the cast are Patrick Stewart as Mr. Woolensworth, Don Knotts as Mayor Turkey Lurkey and Amy Sedaris as Foxy Loxy.

Disney is new to the computer-generated image game and the film shows it, falling short of the bar set by Pixar. Vibrant through unremarkable, the animation displays "Little" of the warmth and charm of Disney films of old.

And while the 'toons may be more 3-D than in Walt's day, the story and characterizations are disappointingly two-dimensional and lack much personality.

Stringing together a series of mildly amusing sequences and zippy sight gags, the film drags on for most of its first hour with the "War of the Worlds"-flavored plot elements arriving much too late.

Following current trends, director Mark Dindal wrenches in numerous pop-culture references, further diluting any hoped-for timeless appeal.

The movie's unmemorable songs, including "One Little Slip" and "Shake a Tail Feather," will hardly leave you shaking yours.

Still, with its father-son story line, "Chicken Little"-- like many Disney films before it -- celebrates the love shared between a parent and child, while imparting a family-friendly message about believing in oneself.

The film is dedicated to the late Joe Grant, a longtime Disney animator and story man who worked on classics old and new, like "Dumbo," "Pinocchio," "Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs" and "The Lion King."

And while recommendable as wholesome entertainment, compared to those masterpieces "Chicken Little" pales, providing strong indication that, while the sky might not be falling at Disney, the quality of its storytelling has.

The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-I -- general patronage. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is G -- general audiences.

title: Chicken Run
synopsis: The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Chief Crazy Horse
synopsis: Impelled by a boyhood vision, the Lakota Sioux warrior of the title (Victor Mature) unites rival tribes against the invading whites but, after Custer's defeat, his allies disperse and he finally surrenders, only to be murdered by a Lakota outcast (Ray Danton). Director George Sherman gives sympathetic treatment to the Indian struggle for their homelands, though handicapped by the weak device of the chief's story being told by an unlikely white friend (John Lund). Frontier violence

title: Childhood II
synopsis: Group encounter sessions held in the nude because, we are told, without clothes people can be more honest and open with one another. Martin J. Spinelli's documentary indicates that this technique is as inadequate as most other shortcuts to mental health

title: Children of a Lesser God
synopsis: A deaf girl (Marlee Matlin) who has resigned herself to a life of solitude and mediocrity painfully comes to accept the love and admiration of a professor (William Hurt) at the school for the deaf where she works as a janitor. A well-acted sentimental love story, its potential insights into the problems of interpersonal comnunication are undercut by director Randa Haines' concentration on the sexual aspects of the lovers' relationship. Nudity and harsh language

title: Chidren of Fate
synopsis: Children of Fate -- Compelling documentary focuses on an abused wife and mother in a Sicilian slum plagued by childhood mortality and pervasive unemployment, where boys aspire to join the Mafia. As Directed and edited by Andrew Young, and Susan Todd, the documentary combines 30-year-old footage of the mother's sorry situation then with her family's current conditions, resulting in a moving family portrait of poverty's lasting effects upon generations of the disadvantaged. Subtitles. Several references to wifebeating, drugs, sexual situations and criminal lifestyles

title: Children of Heaven
synopsis: Charming story set in Tehran where a 9-year-old Iranian boy loses his little sister's only shoes, forcing the two to share wearing his sneakers to school until he hears of a footrace in which the third prize is a pair of new shoes. Director Majid Majidi spins a slender but sweetly evocative tale of genuine childhood stress made bareable by bonds of love and their generosity to an even less fortunate child. Subtitles. Depictions of poverty and brief menace

title: Children of Light
synopsis: In relating the Nativity to the contemporary world, the program combines classical paintings with children's drawings of the Lord's birth, the Magi's gifts and Herod's cruelty, together with documentary footage and the children's commentary on today's youthful victims of poverty and oppression throughout the world. Produced by Father George Torok, the 15-minute video looks at Christmas through the innocent eyes of young people who see its meaning today in sharing with children less fortunate than themselves. A rewarding family experience

title: Children of Men
synopsis: Bleak futuristic political thriller in which a mysterious infertility has stopped the birth of babies, and a disillusioned London bureaucrat (an excellent Clive Owen) races to carry the world's only pregnant woman (Clare-Hope Ashitey) to safety, while dodging refugee terrorists, the authorities, explosions and bullets at every turn. Director Alfonso Cuaron's adaptation of a P.D. James novel is intentionally dark and disturbing, if exciting in its chase sequences, and though the first-rate cast includes Michael Caine, Julianne Moore, Chiwetel Ejiofor and more, some appearances are virtual cameos. The somber palette and relentlessly downbeat milieu may not be for every taste, though some may discern biblical parallels in the "miraculous" birth of the child. Pervasive rough and crude language and some mild profanity, crude expressions, heavy but not graphic violence including explosions and shootings, a childbirth sequence, brief partial nudity and drug use
full_review:
"Children of Men" (Universal) is a bleak futuristic political thriller with pointed parallels to the present day.

A mysterious infertility has halted the birth of babies, and a disillusioned London bureaucrat, Theo (an excellent Clive Owen), races to carry the world's only pregnant woman, Kee (Clare-Hope Ashitey), to safety, while dodging refugee terrorists, the authorities, explosions and bullets at every turn.

Director Alfonso Cuaron's adaptation of P.D. James' novel is intentionally dark and disturbing. But the chase sequences are undeniably exciting and quite brilliantly done, and it is in those sequences that the film is most compelling.

Though the first-rate cast includes Julianne Moore as Julian, the head of the dissident group known as the Fish (and who years before had a child with Theo in his activist days); Chiwetel Ejiofor as Luke, one of her henchmen; and Michael Caine as Jasper, a sort of aging hippie old friend of Theo, some of these roles can best be described as cameos. (Moore, for instance, gets bumped off quicker than Janet Leigh in "Psycho.")

The somber palette and relentlessly downbeat dystopian milieu may not be for every taste, though some may discern biblical parallels in Kee's giving birth to "the miracle the whole world's waiting for," as Jasper describes it.

The film contains pervasive rough and crude language and some mild profanity, crude expressions, heavy but not graphic violence including explosions and shootings, a childbirth sequence, brief partial nudity and drug use. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Children of Rage
synopsis: Set in 1968, after the disastrous Arab losses in the Six Day War, this movie tries to explain why the Palestinians adopted the desperate policy of terrorism in their fight against the state of Israel. An embarrassingly amateurish production directed by Arthur Allan Seidelman, its failure to do so in any coherent fashion can only serve to exacerbate the feelings of both sides. Violence

title: Children of the Corn
synopsis: Some nasty kids, in the sway of a demonic power, slaughter all the adults in a Midwestern town where a doctor and his wife (Peter Horton and Linda Hamilton) chance to stop on an auto trip. Fritz Kiersch directs this dull, predictable horror movie adapted from a story by Stephen King. Violence

title: Children of the Revolution
synopsis: Australian cold-war spoof starts with a dedicated party member (Judy Davis) being wooed by Stalin (F. Murray Abraham) at a 1952 Moscow congress, returning home pregnant and raising her son, Joe (Richard Roxburgh), to be like her but he grows up more like the father he never knew. Writer-director Peter Duncan's lighthearted political comedy grows increasingly heavy-handed as communism self-destructs and Joe seeks political power in 1990 at the head of a police union. A restrained sex scene, sexual situations, brief nudity, some rough language and occasional profanity

title: Child's Play
synopsis: Failed screen version of Robert Marasco's play about the tragedy of evil that grows from the school rivalry between a paranoic Latin teacher (James Mason) and a jovial paternalistic English teacher (Robert Preston) who has come to hate him. The only mystery is why director Sidney Lumet weakened what was originally a straight chiller by throwing in all kinds of side-long glances, creaky doors, murky corridors and unsubtle theatrical effects

title: Child's Play 2
synopsis: Chucky, the doll possessed by the spirit of a psychopath, is reassembled and goes on another murderous rampage as he tries to get his hands on the little boy (Alex Vincent) he's determined to inhabit. Director John Lafia's schlocky sequel is as predictable as it is trite and repulsive. Intermittent gory violence and recurring rough language and gestures

title: Chicago Joe and the Showgirl
synopsis: Child's Play 3 -- Formula horror sequel has killer doll Chucky (voice of Brad Dourif) at a military academy intent on transferring his soul into an 8-year-old (Jeremy Silvers) unless a previously intended victim (Justin Whalin) can prevent it. Director Jack Bender sets the foulmouthed doll on another killing rampage in a contrived plot centering on murder and mayhem. Excessive violence, continual menace to a child and much rough language

title: Child's Play
synopsis: A widow (Catherine Hicks) buys a talking doll for her son's sixth birthday, but the doll is possessed by the soul of a psychopath (Brad Dourif). Although the boy (Alex Vincent) knows the doll is deadly, no one believes him, including the Chicago cop (Chris Sarandon) investigating the doll's murder victims. Director Tom Holland overdoes the doll's brutal rampages in a tasteless horror movie exploiting a child as ghoul bait

title: Child Star: The Shirley Temple Story
synopsis: Lackluster biopic covers the juvenile years of Twentieth Century Fox's biggest star in the 1930's, beloved by Depression audiences for her natural talent and unrestrained zest for life. Blandly upbeat and flatly directed by Nadia Tass, young Ashley Rose Orr is reduced to slavishly imitating the unique child star in a formulaic restaging of scenes from her films that fails to capture the era or the ups and downs of Shirley's young life. A-I general patronage. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America. 2001

title: Chimes at Midnight
synopsis: Robust but poignant dramatization drawn from Shakespeare's plays about Prince Hal (Keith Baxter) and his youthful carousing with such scalawags as Sir John Falstaff (Orson Welles) before succeeding his father, Henry IV (John Giegud), to the English throne. Also directed by Welles, the tangled historical period of Henry V is re-created with flair and conviction, but at the heart of the narrative is the well-rounded figure of the aged Falstaff, a good-natured but irresponsible rascal whose excesses bring him to a pathetic, but well-mourned end. Battlefield violence, sexual references, a flash of rear nudity and alcoholic excess

title: China
synopsis: World War II morale-booster in which a American neutral (Alan Ladd) selling fuel to the Japanese invaders reluctantly gives a lift to a stranded American teacher (Loretta Young) and her Chinese women students, but when his truck is strafed and a baby killed by Japanese planes, he joins the Chinese guerrillas just before Pearl Harbor. Directed by John Farrow, the story is simplistic and emotionally manipulative but is still watchable today as one of the better examples of the patriotic melodramas that flourished in the war years. Stylized violence, much menace and some sexual innuendo

title: China Gate
synopsis: Creaky melodrama set in 1954 Indochina where an American explosives expert (Gene Barry) joins a French commando team to blow up the key munitions dump supplying the Vietnamese Reds, then learns their guide through enemy lines is his Eurasian wife (Angie Dickinson) whom he deserted five years before. Writer-director Samuel Fuller handles the raid with much unconvincing derring-do and the characters are as shallow as the themes, though it has interest as Hollywood's first look at the Vietnam conflict. Wartime violence, marital rancor and racial prejudice

title: China Girl
synopsis: Interracical teen romance blooms amid a climate of gang warfare in New York's Chinatown and Little Italy. Director Abel Ferrara emphasizes action and setting over characterization and an understanding of ethnic loyalties and traditions of prejudice that rule the lives of two generations of Chinese and Italians. Bloody violence, a love-making scene and profanity abound

title: China Is Near
synopsis: Italian satire on the country's politics and morals centers on a man's campaign for office in a small town where everything revolves around sex, politics and religion. Marco Bellocchio's confusing direction lacks a clear enough viewpoint to support its heavy-handed and at times offensive treatment

title: China Moon
synopsis: Grim crime thriller in which a Florida homicide detective (Ed Harris) falls for a troubled woman (Madeleine Stowe) and, after she kills her abusive, wealthy husband (Charles Dance), helps her cover up the crime only to wind up accused of having committed it. Director John Bailey's elaborately twisted tale of sexual obsession, murder and betrayed loyalties has a game cast of hard-working actors and plenty of arty photography but the pulp story, bogus plot contrivances and empty ending aren't worth the bother. Some graphic violence and sex scenes, extramarital relationships, nudity and occasional rough language

title: China Sky
synopsis: World War II melodrama from the Pearl S. Buck story of American doctors (Randolph Scott and Ruth Warrick) providing care for Chinese guerrillas (led by Anthony Quinn) in a mountain base betrayed to Japanese paratroopers by a treacherous prisoner (Richard Loo). Directed by Ray Enright, the routine action story falters in a clunky romantic subplot involving Scott's cowardly wife (Ellen Drew). Wartime violence and romantic complications

title: Chinatown
synopsis: Jack Nicholson plays a private eye trying to unravel a murder bound up with a civic scandal in the Los Angeles of the 1930s. Faye Dunaway is the mysterious, frightened woman at the center of the plot along with wealthy tycoon John Huston. Director Roman Polanski plays a sinister heavy. A superior entertainment altogether adult in its theme of social and personal corruption, especially its implication of incest

title: Chinatown at Midnight
synopsis: Low-budget crime thriller directed by Seymour Friedman is set in San Francisco where a cunning crook (Hurd Hatfield) commits a murder, then tries to throw the police off his trail by planting evidence pointing to a Chinese perpetrator. Stylized violence

title: Chinese Box
synopsis: Disjointed pastiche of scenes from the unhappy life of a dying British reporter (Jeremy Irons) in Hong Kong on the eve of the Crown Colony's return to Chinese sovereignty. Directed by Wayne Wang, the use of the dying reporter as a metaphor for the end of British rule only gets in the way of what is essentially an impressionistic picture of Hong Kong as a cultural crossroads of East and West which its new rulers will likely find as puzzling as American viewers. Sexual situations and some rough language

title: Chisum
synopsis: Boisterous, good old-fashioned Western stars John Wayne as cattle baron John Chisum, who figured prominently in the bloody Lincoln County cattle wars involving the likes of Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid. Directed by Andrew V. McLaglen with the usual oversimplification of moral issues in the taming of the West, the movie will appeal to those who like action at the expense of historical accuracy

title: Chocolat
synopsis: Set in the French Cameroons on the eve of independence in the late 1950s, this picture of life in colonial Africa is seen through the eyes of the young daughter (Cecile Ducasse) of a colonial official (Francois Cluzet). Director Claire Denis takes an unsettling look at the inhumanity of master-servant relationships, especially the anger and sexual frustration arising between the lady of the house (Giulia Boschi) and the devoted family manservant (Isaach de Bankole). Subtitles. Fleeting nudity

title: Chocolat
synopsis: Unpalatable fable set during the late 1950s in which a single mother (Juliette Binoche) arrives at a provincial French village to open an enticing chocolate shop during Lent, causing bitterness and opposition from the townsfolk tempted by her rich confections during a season of penance. Director Lasse Hallstrom's film insults with its disingenuous rallying cry for tolerance while it mocks faith traditions, religious tenets and Catholic sacraments. Brief violence, a sexual encounter with shadowy nudity, an instance of profanity and fleeting crass language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Choke Canyon
synopsis: Cowboy-scientist (Stephen Collins) fights for his rights against big business, foils the flying hit man (Bo Swenson) sent to silence him, exposes the effort to turn his canyon lab into a toxic waste site, saves his horse, gets the girl and manages to complete his experiment turning sound waves into energy. Supposedly about integrity and personal initiative, the story gets derailed by juvenile action scenes, pyrotechnics, romance and a small bit of rough language

title: C.H.O.M.P.S.
synopsis: Young engineer (Wesley Eure) invents the perfect home protection device -- a robot watchdog -- and wins the hand of the boss' cute daughter despite the machinations of some inept industrial spies. This weak little comedy from Hanna-Barbera might be of passing interest to very young children if its producers had not seen fit to add a sizable amount of vulgar language

title: Choose Me
synopsis: Smug, irritating little comedy-drama about a man (Keith Carradine) who gets involved with three very talkative women who are supported by their lovers in Los Angeles. He suffers, but viewers suffer more. Directed by Alan Rudolph, it has a benign view of sexual amorality

title: Chopper
synopsis: Pointless biography of Australian criminal Mark ``Chopper'' Read who became a cult figure after committing several violent acts while in jail for a bungled kidnapping attempt. Writer-director Andrew Dominik's meandering film about an unrepentant man who achieves notoriety for his savagery lacks depth and is painful to watch both because of its brutality and tedious story-telling manner. Much gory violence, some drug abuse, fleeting nudity and constant rough language with some profanity. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Chopper Chicks in Zombietown
synopsis: The inhabitants of a sleepy desert town are threatened by the arrival of 8 tough motorcycle babes and a host of flesh-eating zombies. Writer-director Dan Hoskins' cheap horror spoof lumbers along, mired in hackneyed characterizations and dripping with gory dismemberments and witless, vulgar humor. Excessive violence played for laughs, intermittent rough language, some sexual innuendo and a flash of nudity

title: Chosen Survivors
synopsis: Group of people (Bradford Dillman, Jackie Cooper, Diana Muldaur, Barbara Babcock, Alex Cord and a handful of others) are thrown together in a self-contained underground environment and told that they are the only survivors of a nuclear holocaust. Their problems begin, however, when vampire bats start invading the ventilating system. Directed by Sutton Rolley, it is a scary movie psychologically, especially if bats are not quite your dish

title: Christa
synopsis: Swedish story about a woman (Birte Tove) looking for someone with whom she'd be sexually compatible and who would make a nice father for her illegitimate son. Producer-director Jack O'Connell seems interested only in putting as much of his actress on display as the law allows

title: Christian the Lion
synopsis: George Adamson, whose story was dramatized in "Born Free," again becomes involved with the task of rehabilitating a tame lion cub to survive in the perils of its natura1 African habitat. Assisting in this real-life adventure are the stars of "Born Free," Virginia McKenna and Bill Travers who co-directed the film with James Hill. Beautifully photographed in Kenyan game preserve, it is an engrossing picture of wildlife and worthwhile family fare

title: Christine
synopsis: Adaptation of Stephen King's novel about a 1959 car that kills people either for the sheer fun of it or because they're rude to its teenage owner (Keith Gordon) who rescued it from a junkyard and restored it to pristine splendor. Director John Carpenter's plodding, mediocre movie has foul language, sex, violence and an unwholesome view of family life

title: Christmas at Maxwell's
synopsis: Ohio-based wine merchant (Andrew May) copes with the cancer-related illness of his wife (Jack Hourigan), while raising their two children (Charlie and Julia May), and struggling with profound guilt about the past, until an elderly nursing home resident (Angus May) changes their lives at Christmas time in this Ohio-set tale. Inspired by personal experience, director-writer William C. Laufer (who also plays a priest) has made a heartfelt film with admirable messages about God's forgiveness, the strength of family and being a Good Samaritan, and features a touching conclusion, but the picturesque film is handicapped by languid pacing, an episodic script and mostly colorless performances, except for a reasonably convincing Hourigan. Mild profanity, crass expressions, mild sexual innuendo and mature thematic material
full_review:
Here's the latest entry in that most popular of cinematic genres: the Christmas movie.

"Christmas at Maxwell's" (LauferFilm) concerns wine merchant Andrew Austin (Andrew May), who is coping with the cancer-related illness of his wife, Suzie (Jack Hourigan), while trying to raise their two children, Chris and Mary (Charlie and Julia May). With the holidays approaching, Andrew can't understand why he doesn't "feel anything anymore." (Of course, a gravely ill wife might have something to do with it.)

He starts drinking, but manages to resist the temptations of a former flame (Lauren Dowden) to "relieve his frustration" and go home with her.

There are several flashbacks that outline his courtship of Suzie: They knew each other in college, grew apart, she became a singer in New York (several musical sequences with a now-robust Hourigan demonstrating her vocal chops), and though they both had romantic involvements they came together again. But there was a catch: She was pregnant with another man's child. Therein lies part of the secret that so torments Andrew. Still, until Suzie was stricken with cancer, they had a good life, with Suzie giving singing lessons as an outlet for her talent, and sometimes magnanimously refusing payment.

Profoundly unhappy and struggling with heavy guilt about that mysterious past event, Andrew takes the family to their summer home -- Maxwell's Hospitality House (thus, the title) -- on Lake Erie in a desperate attempt to rekindle the Christmas spirit.

Matters are at their bleakest -- as is the medical prognosis -- when a lovable old nursing home resident (Angus May), whom they (improbably) take in for the holidays, effects a miraculous change in their lives.

Inspired by personal experience, director-writer William C. Laufer (who also plays a priest to whom Andrew goes for counseling) has made a heartfelt film -- clearly, a labor of love -- with admirable messages about God's forgiveness, the strength of family and being a good Samaritan, with a touching conclusion. But the film is handicapped by languid pacing, an episodic script and mostly colorless performances -- except perhaps for Hourigan, who conveys some variety.

The picturesque film was shot in various Cleveland locales.

The film contains mild profanity, crass expressions and mature thematic material. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

title: Christmas Eve
synopsis: Sentimental melodrama directed by Edwin L. Marin in which a greedy nephew (Reginald Denny) tries to have his wealthy aunt (Ann Harding) declared incompetent but the old lady's three adopted sons (playboy George Brent, gangster George Raft and rodeo cowboy Randolph Scott) show up on Christmas Eve to save her. Mixed in with the sticky proceedings is a violent confrontation with a Nazi war criminal, a baby adoption racket and assorted romantic complications

title: Christmas in Connecticut
synopsis: Breezy romantic comedy in which the unmarried writer (Barbara Stanwyck) of a popular homemaker column has to invent a husband, baby and country home after her unsuspecting publisher (Sydney Greenstreet) invites a war hero (Dennis Morgan) to celebrate Christmas with her "family." Directed by Peter Godfrey, the slickly contrived proceedings benefit from a capable cast but the slapdash humor is uneven and the romance less than convincing. Romantic situations, sexual innuendo and much comic duplicity

title: Christmas in the Clouds
synopsis: Romantic comedy about a young widow (Mariana Tosca) who travels from New York to Michigan to surprise her pen pal-suitor (Sam Vlahos), an elderly man whom she's never met, only to fall in love with his good-looking son (Tim Vahle), a ski resort owner. She mistakes the son for her correspondent, while the son, in turn, confuses her with a hotel critic. Producer-writer-director Kate Montgomery's Sundance, Utah-shot film has assembled an appealing largely Native American cast, offering an agreeable, refreshingly offbeat story of love and forgiveness during the holiday season. Smattering of crude language, mild sexual humor and innuendo, a nongraphic bedroom scene, and a permissive view of premarital sex
full_review:
No teepees and tomahawks, thank you. A largely Native American cast notwithstanding, this is basically an old-fashioned romantic comedy which, in its modest way, should help dispel misguided notions of that often stereotyped ethnic group.

"Christmas in the Clouds" (Slowhand Cinema/Majestic Films), which has been playing the festival circuit, concerns young widow Tina (Mariana Tosca), who, on a whim, travels from New York to Michigan to surprise her pen pal-suitor Joe (Sam Vlahos), whose sardonic narration amusingly opens and closes the film.

They've never met, and she doesn't know he's an elderly man, just as he assumes that, as a widow, she must be a mature matron.
