title: Deuces Wild
synopsis: Generic drama set in 1958 Brooklyn about a gang (led by Stephen Dorff) trying to protect their turf from a violent rival group whose leader (Norman Reedus) wants to bring drugs to the neighborhood. As directed by Scott Kalvert, the film is artificial and forced in its recreation of the era and melodramatic in its depiction of gang warfare. Much bloody violence, a sexual encounter, brief drug content and recurring rough language
full_review:
"Deuces Wild" (MGM) deals moviegoers a bad hand. In its artificial recreation of 1950s street gang wars, it is melodramatic and overdone, telling the most generic of stories without mustering up enough energy to sustain interest.

Stripping away any of the ethnic complexities found in the far superior "West Side Story" (a film "Deuces" attempts to imitate without the benefit of a great score or interesting story), director Scott Kalvert goes for a gritty, realistic feel that is never accomplished. If it weren't for the violence, the film could almost be considered campy as the director throws in one dramatic flair after another.

Deuces gang leader Leon (Stephen Dorff) has sworn to protect his Italian neighborhood from drugs after his brother Al died from a heroin overdose fed to him by Marco (Norman Reedus), the leader of the rival Viper gang. Three years later, the Dodgers have moved to Los Angeles and Marco is out of jail. The truce between the Deuces and Vipers ends, as Marco plans to set up a lucrative drug trade in the 'hood with the help of local gangster Fritzy (Matt Dillon).

In clumsy fashion, the film spells out that for the Deuces, loyalty is everything. So when Leon's brother Bobby (Brad Renfro) falls for the Annie (Fairuza Balk), the sister of Viper member Jimmy Pockets (Balthazar Getty), bonds are tested. But this romantic angle is strained, as if writers Paul Kimatian and Christopher Gambale knew this needed to be an ingredient in the script, but didn't know exactly what to do with it. The script itself seems stalled, as if scenes were poorly copied from other similar films as they went along.

Director Kalvert has staged the bloody fisticuffs -- powered by frenetic music -- in such a manner that it's hard to distinguish who's beating whom. Any realistic tone he tried to set is cancelled by the slow-motion camera work that draws way too much attention to itself. And despite the meticulous period costumes, cars, etc., the atmosphere feels phony, never transcending the trappings of a backstage lot. The age discrepancies of the actors and the characters they play are obvious. Leon is supposed to be a near manhood 18-year-old, but Dorff seems far older. On the other hand, Dillon seems too young to be a respected mafia man running the block.

The supporting cast is thrown away, with Deborah Harry hidden behind a ridiculous wig as Annie's loopy mother and Vincent Pastore as an ineffectual priest who advocates peace over violence.

An unimaginative display of silly macho posturing, "Deuces Wild" presents an overly familiar story without any fresh angles.

Due to much bloody violence, a sexual encounter, brief drug content and recurring rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. 2002

title: Diary of a Mad Black Woman
synopsis: Uplifting if at times heavy-handed melodrama set in Atlanta about a grievously wronged woman (Kimberly Elise) who tries to pick up the pieces of her life after her successful but coldhearted husband of 18 years (Steve Harris) demands a divorce, and who struggles to start anew with the support of a colorful extended family, including a plus-size, pistol packing grandmother figure (played in drag by screenwriter Tyler Perry) and a chivalrous new love interest (Shemar Moore). Based on the stage play by Perry and directed by Darren Grant, this woman-overcoming-adversity movie mixes emotional drama, zany dark-edged comedy, and rousing gospel music resulting in a moving, fitfully funny and occasionally spiritually soaring affirmation of faith and family that celebrates the healing power of forgiveness. Some violence, including domestic abuse, mature thematic elements, an implied sexual encounter, brief drug content, and crude sexual language and humor
full_review:
In "Diary of a Mad Black Woman" (Lions Gate), Kimberly Elise plays a grievously wronged wife struggling to piece together her shattered life and start anew.

Directed by Darren Grant, this woman-overcoming-adversity saga mixes emotional drama with dollops of dark-edged comedy, resulting in a moving -- if at times melodramatic -- and fitfully humorous affirmation of faith, family and forgiveness, the tone of which alternates between raucously zany and spiritually soaring.

Based on Tyler Perry's stage play of the same name, the story centers on long-suffering Helen McCarter (Elise), a woman married to a successful and wealthy but abusive and unfaithful Atlanta lawyer, Charles (played to coldhearted perfection by Steve Harris).

On the outside, of course, the McCarters are the picture of upper-class bliss. Charles feigns affection for Helen at an award ceremony in his honor, blowing her a kiss from the podium. But as Helen observes in her first of many "diary" voice-overs, "Looks can be deceiving."

The charade comes to an abrupt end on the night of their 18th wedding anniversary, when Charles shows up at their palatial home with a gold digger (Lisa Marcos) -- with whom he has sired two children -- and demands a divorce, literally dragging Helen out the front door when she refuses.

However, to prove that he is not completely heartless, Charles hires a U-Haul truck to take Helen and her possessions -- which he conveniently packed beforehand -- wherever she wants to go. The truck's sympathetic, cornrowed driver, Orlando (Shemar Moore), tries to comfort the understandably distraught Helen, and though their first encounter ends badly their paths keep crossing, with pity blossoming into friendship and eventually love.

With nowhere to go and no career skills, Helen ends up on the doorstep of Madea, a plus-size, pistol-packing neighborhood grandmother figure, and her crotchety, pot-smoking brother, Joe, both played by playwright Perry, appropriately aged and padded a la Eddie Murphy in "Nutty Professor II: The Klumps."

Slowly Helen begins to move past the pain and get her life back on track, taking a waitressing job and enjoying strolls through romantic montage sequences with Orlando (many of which resemble cheesy music videos -- not surprising since that is the medium in which Grant cut his directorial teeth).

But not until a role-reversing twist of fate reunites Helen and Charles does she realize that the road to inner healing demands letting go of the vengeful anger and soul-withering bitterness that have kept a chance at happiness beyond her reach.

Rounding out the colorful ensemble are Cicely Tyson as Helen's churchgoing mother; Perry, yet again, as her loyal cousin, Brian; and Tiffany Evans as Brian's junkie wife and Helen's childhood best friend.

Though the movie deals specifically with experiences of an African-American family, its themes of recovery, revenge and redemption are universal.

Given Catholic teaching on marriage and divorce, some viewers may object to the film's resolution. Still, with its rousing gospel score, it is hard to find fault with the movie's overall celebration of faith as a source of strength in times of personal pain (a view which sustained a struggling Perry when he found himself homeless early in his writing career).

And while the film seems to suggest that Helen and Orlando do consummate their relationship, an earlier scene finds Helen confiding to her diary -- and the viewers -- that though they wanted to make love they already shared something far deeper than sex: intimacy.

Elise gives a strong performance, one that in many ways echoes her role in last year's "Woman Thou Art Loosed," which, coincidentally, was adapted for the screen by Perry from the book by Bishop T.D. Jakes, head of a nondenominational church. Both movies take faith seriously and deal with the healing power of forgiveness, reminding us that mercy is the source of true justice, one which frees both victim and offender.

The film contains some violence, including domestic abuse, mature thematic elements, an implied sexual encounter, brief drug content, and crude sexual language and humor. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Dickie Roberts: Former Child Star
synopsis: Surprisingly entertaining comedy about a washed-up former child celeb (David Spade) who, in order to prepare for a role which could reignite his career, hires a suburban family to experience what it is like to grow up normal. Directed by Sam Weisman, the film's otherwise positive, family-values message about the prizing of love over fame is muddied by several unnecessarily lewd scenes. Recurring crude, sexually related humor, a sensual encounter, as well as some crass language and drug references
full_review:
A washed-up, one-time child celeb mounts an improbable comeback and learns the true meaning of success in the unexpectedly entertaining comedy, "Dickie Roberts: Former Child Star" (Paramount).

Directed by Sam Weisman, the film imparts a positive message about the importance of home and family, while lightheartedly lampooning Hollywood's cult of celebrity. Unfortunately, the otherwise agreeable narrative is shellacked throughout by crude, sex-related humor that disqualifies it as wholly recommendable family fare.

Funnyman David Spade stars as Dickie Roberts, a former prepubescent phenom whose hit sitcom "The Glitter Gang" had made him a TV sensation back in the 1970s. Now a 35-year-old has-been, his career prospects swing between anonymity, working as a valet-parking attendant at a posh Tinseltown watering hole, and indignity, competing in cheesy celebrity boxing matches against fellow where-is-he-now wonder Emmanuel Lewis.

Convinced his star will rise again, Dickie auditions for a plum role in a major Hollywood movie to be directed by Rob Reiner -- one which, if he lands it, could be the career coup needed to jump-start his flat-lining future. But his hopes are dashed when Reiner explains that the part demands an understanding of "growing up normal" -- a slice of life the spotlight never afforded Dickie. Undeterred, Dickie rents a suburban family, complete with parents and siblings, to find out what he missed out on.

The inanity of the premise proves that first impressions can be deceiving. The movie starts off as a kamikaze-comedy piloted by yet another "Saturday Night Live" alum looking to reinvent himself on the big screen -- doomed to go down in the flames of forced, crass humor and canned shtick -- plummeting Spade's cachet to Dickie Roberts' lows. But what unfolds, in spite of the film's lewd concessions, is a surprisingly tender story. And while Spade's nasal naughtiness takes some getting used to, he imbues a rather one-note role with an appealing blend of impish charm and vulnerability, providing viewers a sympathetic rooting interest and making the film's at times heavy-handed family-values epiphanies easy to applaud.

Buttressing Spade's adolescent antics is the film's ringing endorsement of the precedence of authentic love over the superficiality of fleeting fame. Regrettably, Weisman shows little faith in the power of his story's message or in Spade's talent, acquiescing to lowest-common-denominator interests by peppering the film with superfluous sex- and drug-related humor in an effort to elicit some cheap chuckles, including a raunchy theme involving Dickie's self-absorbed girlfriend (Alyssa Milano).

On a lighter note, "Dickie Roberts" takes some clever jabs at the movie industry and at America's fascination with celebrity, especially with those fizzled stars whose trajectories have fallen off the astronomical charts. The narrative is bookended by two sequences that capture this almost pathological obsession with lives burned by the spotlight: a faux expose documenting Dickie's early life and a riotous "We Are the World"-type closing-credit musical send-off, performed by a virtual Who's Who of prime-time dysfunction.

Yet the scene which offers viewers raised on TV dinners the best flashback bang for their buck involves Dickie playing poker with fellow "formers" Leif Garrett, Danny Bonaduce, Corey Feldman, Dustin Diamond (Screech from "Saved by the Bell") and Barry Williams (aka Greg Brady). Williams, out of poker chips, ups the ante with the infamous football that broke Marcia's nose.
Marcia, Marcia, Marcia. It's always about Marcia.

Due to recurring crude, sexually related humor, a sensual encounter, as well as some crass language and drug references, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Did You Hear About the Morgans?
synopsis: Pleasant, if largely predictable, romantic comedy in which a recently separated New York couple (Hugh Grant and Sarah Jessica Parker) accidentally witness the contract killing of an arms dealer and, as part of the government's protection program, are abruptly relocated to rural Wyoming where, sheltered and shielded by a no-nonsense federal marshal (Sam Elliott) and his gun-toting wife (Mary Steenburgen), they gradually discover the joys of down-home living as they reassess their relationship. Writer-director Marc Lawrence's fish-out-of-water tale is an unabashed celebration of marriage and family life and, though it features extensive discussion of the negative effects of infidelity, is mostly free of objectionable material, making it probably acceptable for older teens. Adultery and infertility themes, off-screen marital lovemaking, a few mildly sexual jokes, at least one crude and one crass term
full_review:
Not for the first time on screen, blue-state sophisticates discover the joys of red-state down-home living in the pleasant, if largely predictable, romantic comedy "Did You Hear About the Morgans?" (Columbia/Relativity). In this case though, their enforced retreat to the wilds of the High Plains also gives dyed-in-the-wool New Yorkers Paul (Hugh Grant) and Meryl (Sarah Jessica Parker) Morgan the chance to reassess their recently strained union.

Hotshot real estate agent Meryl has shown high-powered lawyer Paul the door for being unfaithful to her during a West Coast business trip. Paul deeply regrets his one-time-only mistake. But his efforts to reunite go nowhere until the separated, though not yet divorced, pair is thrown back together when they accidentally witness the contract killing of an arms dealer who was one of Meryl's clients.

With their lives in danger -- the murderer (Michael Kelly) got a look at them, too, and Meryl's face is on ads all over town -- the couple has no choice but to enter the witness protection program which abruptly relocates them to the one-gas-station town of Ray, Wyo. Once there, they're sheltered, and shielded, by no-nonsense local sheriff and federal marshal Clay Wheeler (Sam Elliott) and his gun-toting wife, Emma (Mary Steenburgen).

As Paul and Meryl find out what a starry sky looks like outside a planetarium and learn just how much fun the annual rodeo dance can be, they have an opportunity to reconnect and overcome Meryl's recent but deep-seated mistrust. Particularly effective is a scene in which they recall the nontraditional wedding vows they exchanged; hers drawn from a Shakespearean sonnet, his self-written, and only slightly marred by one of the script's few resorts to vaguely sexual humor.

While, as part of her urban persona, Meryl identifies herself as an agnostic, there's little conviction behind the declaration, and it's further undercut when, in the scene referenced above, Paul acknowledges his belief in, and prayer to, the God she doubts.

Though writer-director Marc Lawrence's fish-out-of-water tale necessarily features extensive discussion of the negative effects of infidelity, and also includes considerable talk about the spouses' efforts to conceive, these topics are dealt with in a restrained way, and genuinely objectionable material is mostly absent. Off-color language, for instance, is pretty well restricted to a single use of the S-word and a British slang exclamation drawn from Paul when he fires a rifle for the first time.

As a result, this unabashed celebration of marital love and family life -- the straightforward values underlying the comedy are embodied by Clay and Emma's long-standing mutual dedication, which Paul and Meryl eventually seek to emulate -- is probably acceptable for older teens, despite the elements listed below.

The film contains adultery and infertility themes, off-screen marital lovemaking, a few mildly sexual jokes and at least one crude and one crass term. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Die Another Day
synopsis: Stripped of his official agent 007 status, Bond (Pierce Brosnan) teams with a strong, smart American agent (Halle Berry) in Iceland to uncover the identity of a traitor and thwart a pair of villains (Toby Stephens and Rick Yune) from provoking a nuclear confrontation. While the characters seem more superhuman than human, director Lee Tamahori orchestrates lightning-paced, nonstop action and intrigue with visually impressive imagery. Several brief sexual encounters, much stylized violence and mayhem and an instance of profanity
full_review:
The 20th official James Bond movie, "Die Another Day" (MGM), breaks new ground in that 007's cover is blown and he is tortured and left to rot in a North Korean prison for more than a year -- all before the opening credits roll.

With New Zealand director Lee Tamahori at the helm, the action and intrigue unreel at a furious pace, with death-defying stunts so preposterous one can only laugh and go with the flow. It's unquestionably mindless escapist entertainment, but entertain it does as the story zips from Korea to Hong Kong, London, Havana, Iceland and back to where it started.

And this time Bond (Pierce Brosnan) is not quite agent 007. Released in a prisoner exchange, he is virtually dismissed when he reports back to his London superior, M (Judi Dench, marvelous as ever), as he may have revealed secrets when drugged by his torturers.

Infuriated, Bond sets out on his own to identify who betrayed him and soon teams with an American agent who is as strong, sexy and smart as he is. Jinx (Halle Berry) comes slinking out of the sea (as did early Bond girl Ursula Andress in "Dr. No") in Havana and they are soon entangled in more ways than one.

The villains include Zao (Rick Yune), whose scarred visage is studded with diamonds, courtesy of Bond exploding a diamond-filled attache case in his face, and Graves (Toby Stephens), a faux philanthropist whose new sun-like invention is the world's newest superweapon. Bond learns Graves' assistant Miranda (Rosamund Pike) is actually an British operative before the action moves to Iceland, where Graves is introducing his invention at a stunning palace carved entirely of ice.

Bond and Jinx are soon separately in mortal danger, and while the traitor is unmasked the agents' survival is unlikely as the primo bad guy escapes with the invention, returning to Korea ready to provoke a nuclear response should his megalomaniac demands be shunned.

The movie is simply a series of spectacular set-pieces done in visual terms that amount to luscious eye candy. The characterizations on the other hand are ludicrous; no one seems to be remotely human. The five leads all possess superhuman strength, speed and stamina. The violence is largely stylized, but in such quantity it barely fits in the PG-13 rating, not to mention the obligatory brief bedroom scenes with superstud Bond and his willing women -- all part of the fantasy that continues to draw such a loyal audience.

It is of concern that all the mayhem and explosions are made to look exciting but, since it appears much more fantastic than realistic, it isn't as objectionable as gritty, in-your-face violence.

The cast is up to the job with Brosnan and Berry playing well off one another, but the sprinklings of double entendres are so obvious and lame they are an embarrassment. The icy chases are pretty impressive, if patently absurd, and one gasps when Jinx dives backward into the sea, but at other times the shadows of "Mission Impossible" and "The Matrix" loom large as the Bond franchise tries to stay hip and with-it so many decades after its inception.

With its stunning visuals and sky-high action quotient, James is certain to live on to die another day.

Due to several brief sexual encounters, much stylized violence and mayhem and an instance of profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Diggers
synopsis: Mostly downbeat comedy-drama about the life and loves of Long Island clam diggers (Paul Rudd, Ken Marino, Josh Hamilton and Ron Eldard) played out against the encroachment of a big fishing corporation wreaking havoc on their traditional way of life. full_review:
"Diggers" (Magnolia) is a mostly downbeat comedy-drama set in the mid-1970s, about the life and loves of Long Island clam diggers Hunt (Paul Rudd), Frankie (Ken Marino), Cons (Josh Hamilton) and Jack (Ron Eldard).

The funeral of Hunt's father, who dies alone on his boat near the film's start, is the catalyst for the younger man's reassessment of life.

As for his friends, there's the boorish Frankie, whose early scene yelling at his wife and kids while he sits on the toilet, is extremely off-putting, though Marino (who wrote the script, and comes from a generations of clam diggers) makes sure we know that despite his bark Frankie is really a loving husband and father.

Cons both deals and uses drugs. Ladies' man Jack is having an affair with Hunt's divorcee sister, Gina (Maura Tierney), which infuriates overprotective Hunt. The latter is having an affair with spoiled Manhattanite Zoey (Lauren Ambrose).

All of this plays out against the encroachment of a big fishing corporation wreaking havoc on their traditional way of life. The diggers find waters they have mined for years now off-limits to them. In one of the film's most effective scenes, Frankie decides to approach the corporation for a job and is dismissed as a nonentity.

Katherine Diekmann directs this story of the inevitability of change capably, and there are good performances all around.

Though not dull, the occasionally sordid plot is only mildly involving (more concerned with character than story development). The high quotient of expletives, however true to this particular working-class milieu, is a further detriment. Frankie has the foulest mouth of the buddies, but in addition to his basic decency he also proves to be admirably pro-life, as we observe when his beleaguered wife, Julie (Sarah Paulson), pregnant with what will be their sixth child, suggests she have an abortion and Frankie won't hear of it.

The film contains pervasive rough and crude language and profanity, drug and contraception references, rear male nudity, sexual encounters without overt nudity and sexual references, premarital situations, brief pornography images, domestic violence and gratuitous bathroom scenes. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

full_review:
An American teenager is transformed from a fox-trotting bookworm to a hot-tamale samba sensation in just a few easy dance lessons in "Dirty Dancing: Havana Nights" (Artisan).

More a re-imagining than a remake, director Guy Ferland's film hits all the narrative beats of the "inspired-by" original, "Dirty Dancing" (1987). But despite its setting being spiced up from a Borscht-belt Catskills resort in 1963 to the political hothouse of a Havana luxury hotel on the eve of the Cuban revolution, the movie lacks the flavor of the original. Like its predecessor, it does, however, still have plenty of sweaty, gyrating bodies -- and Patrick Swayze (in a small role as a dance instructor).

Romola Garai stars as Katey Miller, a Pollyanna dragged to Cuba by her father's new job for Chrysler. Katey is brainy, a point driven home by repeated references to her attending Radcliffe come the fall. She is also repressed -- conveyed via cliche by her wearing a wool cardigan sweater around the hotel's pool while her silver-spoon peers sunbathe in bikinis.

But her Ivy League ambitions and puritanical prissiness evaporate like the smoke from a Cuban cigar as soon as she meets Javier (Diego Luna), a busboy with bedroom eyes and all the right moves. As sole provider for his family, Diego quietly suffers the daily indignities of carting drinks and towels to the spoiled scions of the very American fat cats his Fidelista brother (Rene Lavan) is trying to oust from the country.

But when a spilled drink and a chivalrous walk home get Javier fired, Katey, feeling responsible, signs them up for a New Year's Eve dance contest with a grand prize of $5,000. Of course, when planning such an event, one should always double-check to make sure there are no Marxist revolutions scheduled for the same night.

John Slattery and Sela Ward play Katey's parents, themselves no strangers to cutting the rug, and, as in the original, also voice objections to their daughter fraternizing -- let alone dirty dancing -- with the hired help.

Despite a picturesque surf-and-sunset backdrop (with Puerto Rico convincingly passing for Batista-era Cuba), Ferland saddles the clash-of-cultures love affair with a political subplot. But rather than add depth to the characters and story, the glossy, faux weightiness only magnifies the superficiality of the script.
Katey's parents (the film's most visible authority figures) are generally cast in a sympathetic light, but the eroticism of the movie's choppily edited, bump-and-grind choreography imparts a misleading message that seems to equate personal fulfillment with sensual liberation.

It shouldn't be hard to find something better to do with your Havana nights.

Due to an implied sexual encounter and brief violence, as well as some mild crass expressions and a racial slur, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Dirty Pretty Things
synopsis: Soulful tale set in a small London hotel where a Nigerian overnight desk clerk (Chiwetel Ejiofor) discovers the manager (Sergei Lopez) is exploiting other illegal immigrants in a passports-for-kidneys black-market operation that threatens to engulf his virginal friend, a desperate Turkish immigrant (Audrey Tautou). Director Stephen Frears skillfully blends suspense with a twist of black comedy in a sleek, very human story of impoverished aliens forced to take desperate measures. Theme of sexual exploitation, abortion reference, surgical gore, fleeting drug abuse, frequent rough language and minimal profanity. A-III � adults (R). 2003 Full Review A Nigerian immigrant working as the night clerk in a London hotel stumbles upon a black market trade in body organs in the melancholy "Dirty Pretty Things" (Miramax). Director Stephen Frears makes visible in this movie the illegal immigrants in minimum-wage jobs that society ignores or takes for granted. And Steven Knight's well-crafted script builds suspense alongside character development. An international cast of actors also lends credibility to this tale of the displaced and dispossessed. A physician before having to flee his native land, illegal immigrant Okwe (Chiwetel Ejiofor) drives a cab by day and is a hotel desk clerk by night. He catches a few hours' shut-eye by renting the couch of hotel maid Senay (Audrey Tautou), a virginal Turk seeking asylum, who can be deported if the immigration bureaucrats discover she is working. One night at the small hotel, Okwe gets a complaint about a clogged toilet and to his horror finds the culprit is a human heart. The Spanish manager, Sneaky (Sergei Lopez), threatens to expose Okwe if he calls the police. The manager has been orchestrating a highly profitable kidneys-for-passports black market operation and when he finds out Okwe is a doctor tries to force him to no avail to perform the risky surgeries. Meanwhile, to elude suspicious immigration officers, Senay has quit the hotel for a sweatshop where the piggish supervisor blackmails her into granting sexual favors. Okwe's Chinese friend (Benedict Wong), a hospital morgue attendant, gives her shelter in the morbid surroundings since her apartment is being watched by the authorities, but she decides she must accept Sneaky's offer of a passport for her kidney. Okwe steps in with an alternative which would seem to give Sneaky just what he wanted: a skilled surgeon and a healthy, willing patient. But sneaky is an adjective better applied to the resourceful Nigerian. Okwe's mysterious background and the possibility of romance with Senay add another element to this soulful story whose only problematic area is when a friendly hotel prostitute (Sophie Okonedo) advises Senay about the abortion pill. Strong performances certainly add to the sleek allure of this strange blend of film noir with a little twist of black comedy. But it is just as much a rather heartbreaking look at abused aliens with little recourse but disturbingly desperate measures. Because of its theme of sexual exploitation, abortion reference, surgical gore, fleeting drug abuse, frequent rough language and minimal profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting

title: District 9
synopsis: Exceedingly violent yet powerful science fiction parable in which, two decades after the arrival in South Africa of an unwelcome race of human-sized but insect-shaped aliens, a bureaucrat (Sharlto Copley) for a multinational corporation charged with relocating them from the titular ghetto to a concentration camp finds his condescending attitude transformed when a chemical accident turns him into a fugitive from the system he previously served. full_review:
"District 9" (TriStar) is an exceedingly violent yet powerful science fiction parable about the dangers of prejudice and societal indifference.

Set in an alternate version of contemporary South Africa two decades after the arrival in Johannesburg of an unwelcome race of human-size but insect-shaped aliens, director and co-writer (with Terri Tatchell) Neill Blomkamp's unflinchingly harsh feature debut has specific applications to the country of his birth -- he now lives in Canada -- but far broader implications about human nature in general.

As we learn from a series of mock-documentary broadcasts and interviews, the extraterrestrials, stranded on earth by a mechanical problem with their spacecraft, quickly became a source of social tension since -- besides being repulsive by human standards -- the "prawns," as they come to be called derisively, are perceived as unintelligent and feckless.

So they've been forcibly confined in the titular ghetto where makeshift shanties and lawless streets recall the townships of the apartheid era.

Bowing to public pressure to isolate the visitors even further, the government charges a conglomerate called Multi-National United with the task of relocating them to a vast concentration camp. Thanks to family connections, Wikus van der Merwe (Sharlto Copley), a timid, irksome MNU bureaucrat, is placed at the head of this operation. The only likable thing about Wikus is his idealistic love for his wife, Tania (Vanessa Haywood).

Backed by MNU's paramilitary forces, Wikus begins to carry out the technically legal evictions with a dismal combination of condescension and ruthlessness. But an accident with an unidentified chemical he finds in one of the shacks suddenly turns him into a fugitive from the system he previously served.

While on the run, Wikus, whose experiences as an outcast gradually transform his thinking, allies himself with an alien who has been given the human name Christopher Johnson (voice of Jason Cope).

Besides segregation and colonialism -- the assignment of virtually interchangeable names to the aliens conjures up what it must have been like for native people to receive unwanted names in their conquerors' language -- the drama can also be seen as a critique of the more recent problem of South African xenophobia toward migrant workers from other parts of the continent.

Scenes of the eventual showdown between some of the aliens and their human oppressors are so graphically bloody that they would normally warrant an "O" classification, especially in conjunction with the constant use of the F-word throughout the dialogue.

But for all its grittiness, this tale of physical and moral metamorphosis -- propelled by Copley's intense performance -- offers an incisive study of the need for universal solidarity and a portrait of marital love that at least some adult viewers may find valuable.

The film contains considerable gory violence, including brief torture, pervasive rough and some crude language, and a few sexual references. title: Disturbia
synopsis: Reasonably suspenseful thriller in the tradition of Hichcock's "Rear Window" about a teen (Shia LaBeouf) -- under house arrest after an emotional outburst stemming from his dad's death -- who begins to spy on the neighbors, eventually suspecting one (David Morse) of being a serial killer. Director D.J. Caruso ("Taking Lives") handles his serial-killer theme with relative restraint, with the emphasis squarely on suspense. Some violence including two murders, an image of a corpse and some discreet shots of other dead bodies, a disturbing car accident, some crude and crass language and profanity, skimpy costuming, underage drinking, suggestive dancing, brief suggestions of infidelity and underage viewing of pornography
full_review:
"Disturbia" (Paramount) is a reasonably suspenseful thriller in the tradition of Hitchcock's classic "Rear Window" with Shia LaBeouf as teenager Kale, the Jimmy Stewart-like protagonist.

In the film's opening, a gut-wrenching car accident kills Kale's adoring father. A year later, the young man's ongoing anguish results in him lashing out verbally at his mother (Carrie-Anne Moss) and punching an insensitive teacher.

Kale is summarily put under court-ordered house arrest for the summer. During this home incarceration, he begins to spy on his neighbors. Despite the modern technology available to him, Kale relies mostly on binoculars, and through his eyes we see several comedic but obviously objectionable images such as a married man carrying on with his maid and young kids watching cable porn. When the alluring Ashley (Sarah Roemer) -- with a penchant for wearing bikinis and other skimpy attire -- moves next door, Kale finds a new focal point.

Eventually, Kale starts to suspect next-door neighbor Mr. Turner (David Morse) might be a serial killer. Kale recruits Ashley and best friend Ronnie (Aaron Yoo) for some Hardy Boys-style sleuthing.

LaBeouf, who is in nearly every scene, carries the movie, though Roemer and Yoo have good moments.

Though its serial-killer theme may push the envelope for its intended teenage audience, director D.J. Caruso ("Taking Lives") can be credited with handling the violence -- restricted mostly to the last 10 minutes of the film -- in a relatively restrained manner, and putting the emphasis squarely on suspense rather than gore.

The film contains some violence including two murders, an image of a corpse and some discreet shots of other dead bodies, a disturbing car accident, some crude and crass language and profanity, skimpy costuming, underage drinking, suggestive dancing, and brief suggestions of infidelity and underage viewing of pornography. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Divided We Fall
synopsis: Heartfelt drama set toward the end of World War II in a small, German-occupied Czech town about a married couple (Boleslav Polivka and Anna Siskova) who reluctantly hide an escaped Jew (Csongor Kassai) in their storage closet. Director Jan Hrebejk's film beautifully explores the moral dilemma of the characters ensnared in situations both horrifying and comical with gentle humor and a finely tuned narrative. Subtitles. Some violence, an implied sexual encounter and sporadic profanity. 2001

title: Divine Secrets of the Ya-Ya Sisterhood
synopsis: Passable adaptation of Rebecca Wells same-titled novel in which a young playwright (Sandra Bullock) living in New York City implies in a magazine interview that her Southern mother (Ellen Burstyn) was not a good parent, causing a terrible rift between the two women that can only be repaired with the intervention of the mother(s dearest and oldest friends (Shirley Knight, Fionnula Flanagan and Maggie Smith). Although the high melodrama is softened by a talented cast and snappy one-liners, writer-director Callie Khouri(s tribute to the fruits of female friendship among an eccentric group of Louisiana women is encumbered by confusing flashbacks from two different time periods. A live-in relationship, a scene of child abuse, mature thematic elements and intermittent profanity and crass language with an instance of rough language. A- III - adults. (PG-13) 2002 Full Review In “Divine Secrets of the Ya-Ya Sisterhood” (Warner Bros.), writer-director Callie Khouri adapts Rebecca Wells popular novel with mixed results. Calling to mind other films such as “Beaches,” “Fried Green Tomatoes,” and “Steel Magnolias,” which also paid tribute to the fruits of female friendship and, like the latter, rocky mother-daughter relationships, “Ya-Ya” centers around an estranged Southern mother and playwright daughter and an eccentric circle of aging Southern belles who try to salvage the mother-daughter relationship. In the way it presents women’s relationships, particularly Southern women, the film sporadically makes an emotional connection with the audience. And the talented cast and snappy dialogue soften the high melodrama of the talky film. But more often than not, it may leave viewers dissatisfied with its frugal character development which often crosses the line into caricature. And unfortunately, “Ya-Ya” is encumbered by confusing flashbacks from two time periods and the use of three different sets of cast members to play the women during different stages in their lives. Yet it’s likely to strike a chord with many in its target audience –- women -– while possibly pulling in a few male viewers along for the ride as it showcases the considerable aptitude these grand dames have for portraying the colorful but shallow characters. In a magazine interview, successful New York Cityplaywright Sidda Lee Walker (Sandra Bullock) takes a few swipes at her Louisianamother’s parenting skills, unintentionally setting off a bitter feud with her bigger-than-life mother, Vivi (Ellen Burstyn). Scurrying to the rescue are Vivi’s long-time pals, widow Necie (Shirley Knight) who holds the moral compass of the group, Caro (Maggie Smith), who throws back drinks as often as she reaches for her oxygen mask, and Teensy (Fionnula Flanagan), a wealthy Alcoholics Anonymous member who drives a canary-yellow convertible Rolls-Royce. Now the elderly members of the secret childhood society, the Ya-Ya Sisterhood (of which Vivi was the ringleader), the trio trot off to the Big Apple and stage an “intervention,” Ya-Yastyle. They kidnap Sidda and take her back to Louisiana to reveal to Sidda all the things she never knew about her mother -- which turns out to be a lot -- and possibly to help Sidda understand her fear of commitment that has kept her from marrying her Celtic beau Connor (Angus MacFadyen) of seven years. The women share with Sidda all their “divine secrets” -- as carefully recorded in an old, frilly scrapbook -- about their lives, loves and losses. The film rolls out these memories in a serious of flashbacks with Ashley Judd conveying the inner demons that the young Vivisuffered. However, the film never probes deeper than the surface to examine Vivi’s emotions and frustrations or how her actions impacted Sidda, the oldest of four children who bore the brunt of Vivi’s tantrums. And by the time the film reaches its dramatic climax, revealing the truth behind Vivi’s erratic behavior and then the reconciliation between mother and daughter, it is a letdown. Nonetheless, “Divine Secrets of the Ya-Ya Sisterhood” does have a few gems to offer. The foremost is the cast, but the most surprising is the film’s spiritual side. Pained by the guilt over her sins, Vivi confesses to her local priest regularly, and faith seems to have been a constant in her life regardless of the turmoil surrounding her. In her own extravagant way, Viviprays to the Blessed Virgin asking her to intercede for her and take her prayer to God and Jesus. And although the spiritual aspects are somewhat downplayed, they do exist and are presented in a confident manner in keeping with the character. Fans of the book as well as those who never picked up the novel may find that, although screenwriter Khouri tried to cram in as much as possible, so much more is missing, particularly in the background and stories of the characters. However, for those who enjoy down-home, lively female flicks, “Divine Secrets of the Ya-Ya Sisterhood” may just be fine summer entertainment. Due to a live-in relationship, a scene of child abuse, mature thematic elements and intermittent profanity and crass language with an instance of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops

synopsis: > Dick Van Dyke and Debbie Reynolds have to decide whether to call it a day after 17 years of marriage and one of separation in their divorce-riddled California community. Well paced and occasionally very funny, it's a good try that largely succeeds. A-III (br) 1967 Full Review -->

synopsis: Involving thriller in which a vacationing accountant (Edmond O'Brien) discovers he has been given a lethal dose of a toxic poison, then backtracks trying to find his killer before he dies. title: Dodgeball: A True Underdog Story
synopsis: Awful laugher about a bunch of scrappy misfits (led by Vince Vaughn) who form a dodgeball team to compete in a high-stakes tournament in Las Vegas in order to save their rundown neighborhood gym from being taken over by a state-of-the-art competitor (owned by Ben Stiller). As directed by Rawson Marshall Thurber, "Dodgeball" follows a tried-and-true David-vs.-Goliath formula, but its love-yourself-for-who-you-are message is weighed down by its puerile brand of crass comedy. Recurring crude and sexual language and humor, an instance of rough language and profanity and same-sex kissing
full_review:
With a running time just north of 90 minutes, "Dodgeball: A True Underdog Story" (20th Century Fox) is about an hour and a half too long.

Full of forced, crass humor, this doggedly dreadful movie tries to capitalize on viewers' childhood memories of gym-class trauma, resulting in an experience about as enjoyable as getting drilled in the kisser with a rubber ball hurled by some snotty seventh-grade sadist.

Vince Vaughn stars as Peter LaFleur, a rakish underachiever and proprietor of a fleabag gym called Average Joe's. The rundown joint serves as a watering hole for a motley bunch of social rejects, including a self-styled pirate (Alan Tudyk) and a scrawny nerd (Justin Long) whose most common experience with a gym locker is getting stuffed into one.

To make a dumb story short, LaFleur's nonexistent bookkeeping and kindhearted habit of letting his friends slide on paying membership dues leaves him $50,000 in arrears.

Licking his faux tan chops at the prospect of bulldozing Average Joe's and turning it into a parking lot is White Goodman (Ben Stiller), LaFleur's cross-street rival, a narcissistic fitness freak and owner of the state-of-the-art Globo Gym where the sales pitch is, "We're better than you and you know it."

With their beloved gym facing closure, the scrappy misfits come up with the idea of forming a dodgeball team with their hopes set on winning a high-stakes tournament in Las Vegas with a cash prize of $50,000.

Predictably, the lovable losers prevail against all odds and make it to the final round. But in order to go the distance they must face Globo Gym's Purple Cobras -- a team of steroid-enhanced all-stars captained by Goodman -- in a winner-takes-all showdown.

Christine Taylor plays Kate Veatch, an attorney sent by the bank to facilitate the foreclosing of Average Joe's, but who winds up being their team's secret weapon. Rip Torn plays the crotchety, wheelchair-bound Patches O'Houlihan, a legendary dodgeball icon who pilots LaFleur's sad-sack squad from geekdom to greatness and helps them connect with their inner champion.

O'Houlihan teaches them that the key to success in the sport can be distilled down to the five-point mantra, "Dodge, duck, dip, dive and dodge" -- driving home the importance of each by firing wrenches at them, "If you can dodge a wrench, you can dodge a ball."

Moviegoers would be well advised to add "dash" to that list -- as in away from any theater playing this clunker.

As directed by Rawson Marshall Thurber, "Dodgeball" follows the well-worn David-vs.-Goliath formula of such comedies as "The Bad News Bears," but its love-yourself-for-who-you-are message is weighed down by the film's preponderance of puerility including jokes about lesbianism, penile pumps, S&M leatherwear and, of course, running sight gags of people getting smashed in the face -- or considerably lower -- with spherical projectiles. A few chuckles are provided by a peppering of campy cameos including David Hasselhoff and William Shatner.

As viewers are reminded throughout the film, Average Joe's team motto is "aim low" -- a slogan which could just as easily be applied to the comedic aspirations of this movie.

Due to recurring crude and sexual language and humor, an instance of rough language and profanity and same-sex kissing, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Dogma
full_review:
- 1999

When fallen angels seek a plenary indulgence to regain heaven, the nonsensical premise leads to tiresomely witless consequences in the sophomoric religious satire, ``Dogma'' (Lions Gate).

The flimsy scenario involves the rededication of a church in New Jersey by a local cardinal (George Carlin) who attaches a plenary indulgence to those who visit the church. If the expelled angels (Matt Damon and Ben Affleck) gain the indulgence and re-enter heaven, it would prove the fallibility of God and cause the annihilation of the universe.

What's at stake here is pure twaddle, of course, based on a false understanding of an indulgence as effecting the forgiveness of sins. But then, writer-director Kevin Smith doesn't bother with a coherent plot or trying to make sense out of what is essentially nonsense. Instead, Smith fools around with updating biblical characters (Chris Rock as a 13th Apostle) and jabbing at Christian stereotypes (Linda Fiorentino as an abortion clinic worker who is the ``last descendant'' of Joseph and the Virgin Mary).

The result is at best a mindless mix of irreverence and absurdity that has more to do with hostility than humor. A disclaimer at the movie's start winks at the viewer about this being ``a work of comedic fantasy, not to be taken seriously.'' What really should not be taken seriously is Smith's commercialized ballyhoo as a talented filmmaker whose low-budget works have been relatively profitable.  

In an age of dumb-and-dumber screen comedy and the marketing bonanza of ``The Blair Witch Project,'' it's possible that the overlong, imaginatively impoverished ``Dogma'' may find some success. But if it does, its promotion will largely come from the attention given it by those protesting its excesses.

Because of anti-religious japes, some intense violence, sexual references, substance abuse, assorted vulgarities, profanity and recurring rough language, the U.S. Catholic Conference classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Dogville
synopsis: Dismal drama in which a young woman (Nicole Kidman) is protected from gangsters by impoverished villagers (including Paul Bettany, Ben Gazzara and Lauren Bacall) in exchange for her servitude in their tiny Depression-era town nestled in the Rockies. But despite hard-won acceptance, the young woman is brutally betrayed and ultimately exacts her own appalling reprisals. Although artistically noteworthy, director Lars von Trier's thoroughly misanthropic, anti-American piece makes transparent sociopolitical statements on immigration and the economics of poverty while focusing solely on the depravity of humans as it is weighted down by an oppressive, morally bankrupt tone. Nihilistic view of society, several scenes of rape and forced prostitution, brief nudity and some brutal violence

title: Dominion: The Prequel to the Exoricst
synopsis: Subdued yet somewhat involved prequel to the 1973 horror classic set in 1949 British East Africa where lapsed priest Father Merrin (Stellan Skarsgard), wrestling with a crisis of faith wrought by wartime memories of Nazi atrocities, rediscovers his belief to help a possessed native boy after an ancient evil is unleashed by the excavation of a Byzantine church. Sparse on horror gimmicks, director Paul Schrader's more cerebral movie is a marked improvement over Renny Harlin's 2004 gorier "alternate" version of the same story, yet, while thoughtfully exploring the nature of evil, faith, doubt, guilt and forgiveness, the ultimately redemptive, if at times dry, film is hampered by laggard pacing, shaky theology and narrative gaps -- not to mention some cheesy computer-generated effects. Some strong violence, including a graphic suicide, and several grisly murders and executions, demonic violence, a disturbing childbirth scene, a bloody medical procedure and a few racial slurs
full_review:
Here's something proponents of auteur theory -- that the primary creator of a film is the director -- will be chewing on for a while. Take roughly the same story, the same lead actor, the same setting, and let two directors armed with different visions and different scripts go off and make a movie.

This isn't some film-school experiment. It actually happened -- well, sort of. Several years back, the Morgan Creek production company decided to make a prequel to William Friedkin's 1973 horror classic, "The Exorcist."

Originally, Morgan Creek hired Paul Schrader to direct, but company executives felt Schrader's film wasn't scary enough (no spinning heads). So they axed Schrader, shelved the film, hired director Renny Harlin, recast some secondary roles and started from scratch. Some $80 million later, they released the refilmed movie as "Exorcist: The Beginning" in 2004. It bombed.

Schrader's subdued yet somewhat involved version is now being released -- as "Dominion: The Prequel to the Exorcist" (Warner Bros.).

The basic plot outline remains the same in both films. Set in 1949 British East Africa, lapsed priest Father Lankester Merrin (played in both by Stellan Skarsgard) wrestles with a crisis of faith wrought by wartime memories of Nazi atrocities in his native Holland, before reluctantly assuming the role of exorcist to help a possessed local boy. In both tellings, the problems start after an ancient evil is unleashed by the excavation of a Byzantine church buried in pristine condition.

Violence also erupts between the local tribesman and a regiment of British soldiers dispatched to guard the archeological dig, giving new meaning to "the devil made me do it."

In "Dominion," Clara Bellar plays village doctor and concentration camp survivor Rachel Lesno (a similar role made intentionally more sexy and played by Izabella Scorupco in "Beginning") and the idealistic young missionary, Father Francis, is played by Gabriel Mann as opposed to James D'Arcy.

Where the two films really part ways is how their respective directors handle the climactic exorcism sequences (during which Merrin rediscovers his lost faith). Harlin went for a traditional horror-film showdown, pitting Merrin against his unholy adversary in a mano-a-Mephistopheles free-for-all.

Schrader, raised a strict Dutch Calvinist, opts for a more introspective approach, having Merrin locked in a theological debate about guilt and forgiveness with Satan (androgynously played by Billy Crawford). And while Merrin is shown to be conflicted (though ultimately redeemed), the priesthood is portrayed with respect.

More a thinking-man's horror movie, "Dominion" is a marked improvement over Harlin's gorier "alternate" version, but that's not saying much.

"Dominion" thoughtfully explores the nature of evil, as well as themes of faith and doubt. In one scene Father Francis says, "Faith is not there to conquer evil, but to help (people) survive it."

However, the at times dry film is hampered by laggard pacing, shaky theology and narrative gaps -- not to mention some cheesy computer-generated effects.

The film contains some strong violence, including a graphic suicide, and several grisly murders and executions, demonic violence, a disturbing childbirth scene, a bloody medical procedure and a few racial slurs. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Domino
synopsis: Trashy, repellent action-comedy film inspired by British actor Laurence Harvey's daughter Domino's (Keira Knightley) improbable career as a model turned bounty hunter, as she and her team members (Mickey Rourke and Edgar Ramirez) get involved in a double-dealing plot to recover a large amount of cash and catch the culprits, while being filmed by a reality-TV show producer (Christopher Walken). Director Tony Scott's nonstop camera moves, quick cutting and pretentious lighting effects make for a disjointed, confusing, ugly and hardly funny mess, left unredeemed by some fleeting use of religious imagery and a "good deed" ending. Pervasive violence and bloodshed, over-the-top profanity, rough language, some sexuality, partial nudity, suggestive movements and drug use
full_review:
British actor Laurence Harvey, the charismatic star of "Room at the Top" and "The Manchurian Candidate," died when his daughter, Domino, was only a young girl. He almost certainly never imagined the job path she would choose for herself.

"Domino" (New Line) is the trashy, repellent action-comedy inspired by her improbable life as a model turned bounty hunter. The real Domino died in June at age 34.

In this fictionalized account, Domino (played by Keira Knightley) and her teammates, Ed (Mickey Rourke) and Choco (Edgar Ramirez), get involved in a double-dealing plot to recover a large amount of stolen cash and catch the culprits.

All the while, they're being filmed by a reality-TV producer (Christopher Walken), a la the setup of "Natural Born Killers."

Director Tony Scott's nonstop camera moves, quick cutting and pretentious lighting effects make for a disjointed, confusing, ugly and hardly funny mess.

Lucy Liu, Mena Suvari, Jacqueline Bisset, Delroy Lindo, Mo'Nique and Dabney Coleman are among the film's other performers who have chosen more elevating projects before. "Beverly Hills 90210" stars Ian Ziering and Brian Austin Green appear as themselves, as the series was an influence on the young Domino.

The relentless barrage of gutter language and violence is unredeemed by some fleeting use of religious imagery and a "good deed" ending that fails to erase the garbage that has come before.

The film contains pervasive violence and bloodshed, over-the-top profanity, rough language, some sexuality, partial nudity, suggestive movements and drug use. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Don't Come Knocking
synopsis: Unsatisfying story of hard-living actor (Sam Shepard) who, post-meltdown, goes AWOL and abandons his location Western movie set, returns home to his mother (Eva Marie Saint) in Nevada, and learns he has a grown son (Gabriel Mann) by a waitress (Jessica Lange) with whom he was involved years ago, while a private eye (Tim Roth) hired by the film studio attempts to find him. Director Wim Wenders, working again from a Shepard script after their "Paris, Texas" teaming, adds his artful cinematic vision to Shepard's familiar themes of the myth versus reality of the American West, the pitfalls of fame, the human capacity for violence, broken families, loneliness and loss, but there's a stilted quality to the story and the performances never quite ring true. Profanity, rough and crude language, some domestic violence, adult thematic material, brief drug references, a crass gesture, dispersal of cremated remains, brief nudity
full_review:
It just goes to show that a first-rate playwright, a renowned director and a Grade A cast are not necessarily a recipe for success.

"Don't Come Knocking" (Sony Classics) is a mostly unsatisfying film from writer-star Sam Shepard and auteur Wim Wenders, teaming once again, after their 1984 "Paris, Texas," which itself received decidedly mixed reviews.

Their new collaboration tells the story of hard-living actor Howard Spence (Shepard) who, post-meltdown, goes AWOL from his location Western movie set, much to the consternation of the Hollywood studio that, in turn, hires a private eye (Tim Roth) to find him.

After giving his spurs and horse to an old geezer in return for the man's plaid shirt and vest, Howard returns home to his mother (Eva Marie Saint) in Nevada, where he hopes for a respite from a career marred by booze, drugs, women, and scandal, as we note when he flips through his mother's scrapbook filled with tabloid clippings of his tumultuous life.

Mom drops the bombshell that Howard has a grown son in Butte, Mont. Howard travels there and encounters waitress Doreen (Jessica Lange), with whom he was involved years ago.

In the bar where she works, Doreen points to Earl (Gabriel Mann), the scruffy on-stage singer as the putative son. Howard later stealthily trails Earl -- who has a strung-out girlfriend, Amber (Fairuza Balk), in tow -- and when Earl threatens him, Howard blurts out that he's his father.

Earl goes ballistic, portending a rocky road for any tender reconciliation.

Meanwhile, a doe-eyed young woman, carrying her mother's ashes in an urn, seems to have more than a passing interest in both Howard and Earl, for reasons you'll guess before they're actually revealed.

Wenders is an accomplished filmmaker, of course, and he adds his artful cinematic vision to the familiar Shepard territory. There is, for instance, a striking sequence where Howard, after a fractious confrontation with Earl, sits in the road on an abandoned sofa, and as the hours pass, he takes stock of his life. It's a magical moment, in purely filmic terms.

Shepard's themes of myth versus reality of the American West, the pitfalls of fame, the human capacity for violence, broken families, loneliness and loss have frankly been better handled in his stage work.

Overall, there's a stilted, artificial quality to the story, and most of the performances never quite ring true, apart from Saint's welcome maternal turn.

This disjointed, slow-moving film will be best be appreciated by Shepard and Wenders' most ardent fans.

title: Don't Move
synopsis: Heavy-breathing potboiler about a doctor (Sergio Castellitto) who's just learned that his daughter's been in a near-fatal motorcycle accident, and reminisces about a time 16 years earlier when his car broke down and he raped the young impoverished woman who let him use her phone (Penelope Cruz in an admirably intense performance), leading to an obsessively passionate and kinky relationship, even after his bourgeois wife (Claudia Gerini), who intuits the adulterous affair, learns she's pregnant. Castellitto directed this alternately sentimental and repellant adaptation of wife Margaret Mazzantini's best seller, though its high-caliber acting and artsy trappings can't erase the considerable sordidness of the plot even with its tacked-on "redemptive" ending, and a soul-searching protagonist who remains self-pityingly unsympathetic. In Italian. Subtitles. Rough and crude language, brutal sexual encounters, abortion, partial nudity, graphic operating room gore, and gratuitous scenes of bodily functions
full_review:
"Don't Move" (Northern Arts) was a hit when it was released in Italy as "Non Ti Muovere" in early 2004, which must say something about the European penchant for soggy, angst-filled romance.

The film is a heavy-breathing potboiler about a doctor, Timoteo (Sergio Castellitto), who has just learned that his daughter's been in a near-fatal motorcycle accident.

As he sits in shock outside the operating room, he reminisces about a time 16 years earlier when his car broke down and he raped Italia, the young impoverished woman who let him use her phone. (This is Penelope Cruz in an admirably intense, no-holds-barred performance.) Back home, he's wracked with guilt, and later goes back to see Italia again. Does she reject him? Not a bit. Starved for love herself, and -- we later learn -- abused as a child by her father, she enters into an obsessively passionate and kinky relationship with him. (The sex scenes are brief but graphic, though there's little nudity.)

Timoteo's bourgeois wife, Elsa (Claudia Gerini), seems to intuit the adulterous affair but remains silent. Just as Timoteo is about to confess all to Elsa, the latter informs him she's pregnant.

Castellitto himself directed this alternately sentimental and repellant adaptation of wife Margaret Mazzantini's best seller. The reasonably high-caliber acting and artsy trappings can't erase the considerable sordidness of the plot even with its tacked-on "redemptive" ending. (Midway through the film, Timoteo informs Italia he doesn't believe God exists. Later, he changes his mind. Big deal.) For all his soul-searching, he remains self-pityingly unsympathetic.

Our advice: Don't go.

In Italian. Subtitles.

title: Don't Tempt Me
synopsis: Curious satire in which a nightclub singer (Victoria Abril) from heaven and a waitress (Penelope Cruz) from hell are dispatched to Earth by their respective bosses (Fanny Ardant and Gael Garcia Bernal) to battle for the soul of a boxer (Demian Bichir) who is suffering from brain damage. Director Agustin Diaz Yanes creatively portrays heaven as 1930s Paris and hell as a backstabbing corporation, but the film cannot maintain its quirky tone while muddling through the sometimes thought-provoking but often banal ideas about God and life after death. Subtitles. An implied sexual encounter and several sexual references, some harsh violence, much rough language and some profanity
full_review:
Heaven and hell battle for the soul of a washed-up boxer in the curious Spanish satire "Don't Tempt Me" (First Look).
The film from director Agustin Diaz Yanes had the potential to generate some interesting discussions on the mysteries of life after death while entertaining audiences with its wit. But the few thought-provoking ideas the film manages to put forth are drowned by the muddled and often banal ones, and it comes up short on the comedy side as well.

However, this is not to say that the film doesn't have some merit. Diaz Yanes creatively portrays heaven in delicious sepia tones as a 1930s nightclub in Paris. Hell is depicted as a backstabbing corporation where the management is -- not surprisingly -- only interested in climbing the corporate ladder without regard to who falls off the rungs.

The superb cast is likely to please fans of foreign films both for their appearance and their fine performances. French treasure Fanny Ardant is Marina D'Angelo, the sophisticated and charming director of operations for heaven. Her counterpart down under is Jack Davenport (Gael Garcia Bernal), chief executive of hell, a playboy with slick clothing and a stretch limo. Along with being the nightclub's star chanteuse, Lola Nevado (Victoria Abril) is also one of heaven's key angel operatives. Penelope Cruz stars as Carmen Ramos, a feisty waitress working in the 22nd circle of hell whose spunk lands her the job as Lola's foil.

The gist of the story is this: Souls are the commodity for which heaven and hell fiercely compete. Heaven is on the verge of bankruptcy when it gets a request from a mother to save her strong-willed son, Manny (Demian Bichir), a boxer who has had one too many blows to the head and is suffering from brain damage. But hell wants him, too. So Lola appears as Manny's wife, back to reunite with him, and Carmen shows up as his long-lost cousin, all grown up and needing a place to crash.

The film throws in a twist in Cruz's character, who was a male gangster here on Earth and has received the punishment of being turned into a woman who must wait on piggish men who harass her and treat her like dirt. This explains Carmen's attraction to women.

In its most simplistic form, "Don't Tempt Me" can be seen as presenting humans as merely pawns over which heaven and hell battle, like some Greek gods playing a game. It also resorts to having angel Lola do something "bad" in order to save Manny's soul. However, the film does get across the notion that even one soul is worth the effort, especially from heaven's point of view.
Yet the film contradicts itself several times, until it all becomes a confused mess that fails to convey any coherent message, maintain its initial quirky tone or engage the audience. And that's the basic problem with the film: It simply doesn't come together.

Subtitles.

Because of an implied sexual encounter and several sexual references, some harsh violence, much rough language and some profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Doogal
synopsis: Unobjectionable but bland computer animated story of dog and his unlikely friends -- a rabbit, a snail, a cow and a train -- who set out on an adventurous journey to find three diamonds that will release the pooch's best friend from an icy imprisonment and prevent a villainous wizard from freezing the sun. Macy) -- and there's a commendable message about "friendship being the best weapon," but toddlers -- and even their indulgent parents -- may find this a tired retread of many other superior films. full_review:
A slew of big-name voice talent fails to elevate the latest animated film from the makers of "Hoodwinked."

"Doogal" (Weinstein), based on a British stop-action animated TV series called "The Magic Roundabout," is an unobjectionable but utterly bland computer-animated story about a dog named Doogal (Daniel Tay) and his unlikely friends -- a rabbit (Jimmy Fallon), a snail (William H. Macy), a cow (Whoopi Goldberg) and a train (Chevy Chase). They set out on an adventurous journey to find three magic diamonds that will release the pooch's best friend and owner, Florence (Kylie Minogue), from an icy imprisonment in a carousel (don't ask!), and prevent a villainous wizard, Zeebad (Jon Stewart), from freezing the sun. He hops about on a spring and has co-opted an inept assistant, toy soldier Sam (Bill Hader), in his nefarious mission.

The team of heroes is guided by a good wizard (also on a spring) named Zebedee (Ian McKellen). There's a moose, too, voiced by Kevin Smith.

The tale, uninspired though most of it is, is narrated most charmingly by Judi Dench.

Co-directors Jean Duval, Frank Passingham, and Dave Borthwick's film is British in origin, has been re-voiced with many big-name stars.

There's a commendable message about "friendship being the best weapon," and given the dearth of kid-friendly films, parents should find little offensive here. But no matter how indulgent, adults and even their toddlers may sense a tired retread of many other superior films like "Wizard of Oz" and "Polar Express."

A handful of snappy lines nothwithstanding, "Doogal" is closer to Beatrix Potter meets "Teletubbies."

full_review:
According to the blood-soaked futuristic adventure tale "Doomsday" (Universal), all the inhabitants of pandemic-ravaged Scotland in the year 2035 will be either cannibalistic punk rockers or medieval-style castle dwellers. Who'd have guessed?

This diverse population is discovered by tough policewoman Eden Sinclair (Rhona Mitra). At the suggestion of her high-ranking colleague Bill Nelson (Bob Hoskins), she's been ordered by the British prime minister (Alexander Siddig) and his scheming security chief (David O'Hara) to lead a team of soldiers north to bring back an immune survivor who might help stem a fresh outbreak.

Once past the high-tech version of Hadrian's Wall that now separates the two kingdoms -- Scotland is entirely quarantined -- the task force does battle, successively, with Sol (Craig Conway), the crazed tribal leader of the punks and Kane (Malcom McDowell), the ruler of the medieval wannabes. The ironically named Eden somehow manages to be taken prisoner by both, but that's just to set up the chase scenes.

Writer-director Neil Marshall's thoroughly benighted film wallows in barbarism.

title: Dot the I
synopsis: Convoluted, kinky story set in London about a temperamental flamenco dancer (Natalia Verbeke) who, recovering from an abusive relationship, agrees to marry a gentlemanly Brit (James D'Arcy), but at her bachelorette party encounters a video-camera-wielding Brazilian actor (Gael Garcia Bernal in his first English-speaking role), setting the scene for a romantic triangle. Writer-director Matthew Parkhill's story of seamy love is not quite what it seems to be, as there are some neat Hitchcockian twists along the way, but the plot is improbable in the extreme, and the execution -- despite some clever touches -- feels semiamateurish. Much rough and crude language, sexual situations, partial rear nudity, suicide with associated gore, murder without retribution
full_review:
Here's a tale that's definitely not what it starts out to be. For the first hour of "Dot the I" (Summit Entertainment), you'd swear this was to be your typical romantic triangle story, though a downright seamy one at that.

The setting is London, and what you have is a temperamental flamenco dancer named (what else?) Carmen (Natalia Verbeke) who, recovering from an abusive relationship in her native Spain, agrees to marry Barnaby (James D'Arcy), a gentlemanly Brit who's a bit dull but at least kind to her.

At her bachelorette party, she is encouraged to follow a certain French tradition of kissing the man of her choice as a symbolic gesture of farewell to the single life. She chooses the good-looking, out-of-work Brazilian actor Kit (Gael Garcia Bernal), who's been sitting a few yards away, boldly shooting her with his video camera.

The kiss -- much to the amazement of the waiters and other patrons -- is long and lingering, and clearly she is smitten. Confused by her emotions, Carmen flees the restaurant.

Kit eventually tracks her down and after several initial rebuffs, Carmen succumbs to his charms. But still scarred from her previous experience, and doubly skittish because of a sense that she's being mysteriously stalked, she proceeds with the marriage to Barnaby.

From this point onward, the plot veers into something closer to Hitchcock territory, so we'll say no more.

Neat though some of the twists are, writer-director Matthew Parkhill's tale is fairly convoluted. The plot is improbable in the extreme, and the execution -- despite some clever touches -- feels semiamateurish, and not just because of the many interspersed scenes shot on hand-held digital video.

The volatile Carmen character is not terribly likable; she's angry much of the time and thinks nothing of flouting the law, as when she pulls a scam at a hotel to get a free meal. And Verbeke's heavily accented dialogue makes for stilted line readings.

Similarly, it takes a while to adjust to the sound of Bernal -- so prevalent on movie screens in both "The Motorcycle Diaries" and "Bad Education" -- speaking English for the first time. There is some awkward delivery, and some of his Latino charisma is diminished in this rather ordinary role. But he's more than adequate.

Tom Hardy and Charlie Cox are appropriately hateful as Kit's disreputable young cronies.

Though the overall milieu is quite unpleasant, Parkhill does score some points for casting light on the underlying voyeurism of reality television.

Wholesome Doris Day's "Perhaps, Perhaps, Perhaps" hit is used to good effect over the opening credits, but "Pillow Talk" this latest kinky release most definitely is not!
