title: Downfall
synopsis: Vividly authentic recreation of the last days of Adolf Hitler (Bruno Ganz) trapped in his Berlin-based underground hideout with other officials of the Third Reich and their families, as the Russian army closes in for certain victory at the end of World War II in 1945, all seen through the eyes of Traudl Junge (Alexandra Maria Lara), his young personal secretary, who stayed with him through his suicide and that of his mistress, Eva Braun (Juliane Kohler), and managed to escape through enemy lines. Oliver Hirshbiegel's German-language film has impeccable production values, superb performances, and generates a good deal of suspense even though the outcome is known. Some crude language, multiple suicides and wartime violence, some with attendant gore, brief but brutal scenes of amputation, partial nudity, a brief sexual situation, heavy smoking and alcohol use
full_review:
History's most infamous dictator, Adolf Hitler, has been fodder for many a Hollywood and British production over the years, but "Downfall" (Newmarket) is reportedly the first German theatrical film to deal with Hitler since the 1956 G.W. Pabst film, "Der Letste Akt" ("The Last Act"), which told the story of the Fuhrer's final days from the limited viewpoint of an ordinary soldier.

Oliver Hirshbiegel's film, an Academy Award nominee in the Foreign Film category, is a vividly authentic recreation of that same 1945 period during which Hitler (Bruno Ganz) was trapped in his Berlin-based underground hideout as the Russian army closed in for certain victory at the end of World War II.

The bunker was no small shack, but a complex of rooms where life, including elegantly served meals, and military strategizing was conducted in remarkably business-as-usual fashion.

Other famous names from the Third Reich share the claustrophobic bunker space, too -- Heinrich Himmler (Ulrich Noethen), Hermann Fegelein (Thomas Kretschmann), Joseph Goebbels (Ulrich Matthes), Albert Speer (Heino Ferch) -- some, like Goebbels, with their families.

As Hitler increasingly loses his reason, he comes to believe they will somehow be liberated, and he and his staff pore over maps looking in vain for salvation. When he finally realizes they are fighting a losing battle, he lashes out at what he perceives as his cowardly commanders, calling them "scum." He expresses the hope that the city be destroyed before the Russians take over.

He demands total obedience, even though the end is clearly near. When he hears that his mistress Eva Braun's brother-in-law, Fegelein, has left the bunker, he insists that he be found and shot. Eva (Juliane Kohler) pleads for his life, but ultimately goes along with her consort's wishes. The man is dragged out of a nearby brothel -- there are some brief shots of decadent cavorting -- and summarily executed.

Rest assured, this is no glorification of Hitler. At one point, we see him reveling in the fact that he's "cleared the land of Jewish poison."

There are parallel stories, one involving a boy, Peter, who is part of the Hitler Youth movement, and despite protestations from his father, perseveres as a street fighter.

And there's the dedicated Professor Schenck (Christian Berkel), who joins professor Werner Haase (Matthias Habich) in ministering to the sick and horribly wounded. (Be warned: There are several fleeting, but gruesome, scenes of limbs being sawed off.) The bombing and fighting scenes are quite intense, but the film doesn't wallow in its violence; what violence there is certainly reinforces the horrific nature of war, particularly on innocent civilians.

As the Russian troops move ever closer, Hitler and the others plan how best to commit suicide, placing "honor" above all else. He and Eva (whom he marries in the bunker, after dictating his testament) will take poison and shoot themselves at the same time. Hitler asks Otto Gunsche (Gotz Otto) to be sure to burn their bodies so they won't be put on display by the victors.

All this is seen through the eyes of Traudl Junge (Alexandra Maria Lara), his young personal secretary. Indeed, the film was based partly on her book "Until the Final Hour: Hitler's Last Secretary" (written with Melissa Muller). The other source was "Inside Hitler's Bunker: The Last Days of the Third Reich" by Joachim Fest.

Traudl stayed with him through his suicide, eventually managing to escape through enemy lines. The real Traudl -- who died in 2002 and was the subject of the documentary "Blind Spot: Hitler's Secretary" -- appears in a postscript at the end of the film, admitting that her youth was no excuse for ignorance of Hitler's heinous acts.

The German-language film has impeccable production values, and you have a real "you are there" feeling.

The performances are first rate. Ganz, who carefully studied Hitler's voice, impersonates him flawlessly: one minute, an almost kindly middle-aged man, the next a raving, paranoid and delusional maniac. (Traudl can't understand how Hitler can be so caring and then so brutal, and Ganz conveys this mercurial temperament.) Kohler seems to be walking the line between sanity and hysteria as Eva's party-girl persona morphs into grim realization of her fate.

Corinna Harfouch as Magda Goebbels is quite chilling in her hysteria and then her steely resolve to kill her children to protect them from the horrors to come. In one of the film's most devastating scenes, she has each of them drink a sleeping potion, and then creeps in later to put cyanide capsules in their mouths one by one. Afterward, her husband takes her outside, shooting her and then himself. And all because she can't imagine living without National Socialism!

Lara projects a sweet sincerity in her dedication to the man she feels it's her honor to serve, without perhaps understanding the enormity of his crimes, and a growing disbelief of her situation.

The film generates a good deal of suspense even though the historical outcome is known. There's also a real fascination in having this story told in a German production. As with the World War I submarine drama, "Das Boot," it's instructive to observe the war from the other side's perspective.

Subtitles.

title: Down in the Valley
synopsis: Offbeat but quite interesting story of easygoing South Dakota ranch hand (an impressive Edward Norton) who romances the much-younger, rebellious teenage daughter (Evan Rachel Wood) of a San Fernando Valley police officer (David Morse), and befriends her painfully shy younger brother (Rory Culkin), against the father's wishes. Writer-director David Jacobson's initial "young lovers" romance shifts tone dramatically midway with a shocking twist, and becomes a suspenseful drama that pays homage to elements from the classic Westerns of John Ford and Howard Hawks. Considerable profanity, rough language and crude expressions, a couple of shootings, gun use by a minor, intense domestic discord, premarital sex and nongraphic sexual encounters, and drug use
full_review:
The titular "valley" is not the iconic Western terrain you might imagine, but none other than Los Angeles' San Fernando Valley, and the Old West allusion is strictly intentional.

For "Down in the Valley" (THINKFilm) is an offbeat but quite interesting story about an easygoing South Dakota ranch hand named Harlan (an impressive Edward Norton), who romances October (Evan Rachel Wood) -- "Tobe" for short -- the rebellious (and much younger) teenage daughter of single father Wade, a correctional officer (David Morse). He also befriends her shy and emotionally fragile younger brother, Lonnie (Rory Culkin), who is clingingly attached to his big sister.

It's love at first sight for Tobe and Harlan when she and her friends stop for gas en route to the beach, and attendant Harlan fills their tank. On Tobe's invitation, he quits his job on the spot and joins the girls' outing.

Harlan's Western charm wins over Tobe, and they commence a physical relationship. Their bond deepens when she sees how thoughtful the gentle cowpoke is with Lonnie. Though he's probably twice her age, Harlan seems as innocent as she does, perhaps more so.

When Tobe takes Harlan out on the town for a night of barhopping, it is she who gives him recreational drugs, making you fear that she might be corrupting the unworldly man.

But wait a minute. Back at his lodgings, we see Harlan role-playing a prototypical gunslinger in front of his mirror. What's this all about? Is Harlan really the level-headed guy he appears to be? Something seems off-kilter.

The viewer is kept wondering about this character dichotomy, while Wade -- who demonstrates an increasing aversion to Harlan -- comes across as the bad guy, forbidding Harlan to date his daughter or see his son. Tobe, we have seen, has a grudge against her dad's occasional relationships with women, and there are several father-daughter spats that are quite ugly, with the expletives flying fast and furiously.

It's not spoiling anything to say that writer-director David Jacobson's initial "young lovers" romance shifts tone dramatically midway with a shocking twist, and ultimately becomes a suspenseful drama that pays homage to elements from the classic Westerns of John Ford and Howard Hawks.

The performances are solid across the board, with Norton (who co-produced) especially charismatic in a tricky role, and there's a good turn by Bruce Dern as an old codger whose horse Harlan "borrows" to impress Tobe.

The deconstruction of the mythic cowboy seems Jacobson's main thrust, with Lonnie's adulation of Harlan bringing to mind images of "Shane," to name one example. Though the film doesn't entirely avoid the feel of contrivance in its plotting, on the whole the film is more successful than not.

There are some violent episodes, but they are dispatched quickly with little gore, and though there are a couple of sexual encounters between Harlan and Tobe they're handled discreetly without nudity. The language used by these characters is quite strong, though, and may be a turnoff to many viewers.

title: Down With Love
synopsis: Retro-stylish romantic comedy about a sassy author (Renee Zellweger) of a best-selling who-needs-men manual charmed into falling in love by a playboy ace journalist (Ewan McGregor), as part of his underhanded scheme to debunk her man-hating manifesto and expose her as a fraud. Borrowing heavily from '60s-era Doris Day-Rock Hudson collaborations and chock full of whip-smart double entendres, director Peyton Reed offers a ringside view of a jazzy battle of the sexes, but the film's questionable view of gender roles and suggestion that promiscuity is liberating is a bit off-putting. Implied sexual situations, racy double entendres and sexually suggestive humor, as well as a misguided attitude toward sexual intimacy
full_review:
The sassy author of a who-needs-men best seller falls hard for a chauvinistic, playboy journalist in the stylishly entertaining "Down With Love" (Fox).

Director Peyton Reed swipes a page from the '60s-era Doris Day-Rock Hudson romantic comedies in this Technicolor battle of the sexes. Yet while the film employs a groovy retro-lounge aesthetic of pillbox hats and velvet-toned Sinatra tunes, its thematic undercurrents are charged with contemporary, hot-button issues concerning sexual autonomy and gender politics.

"Down With Love" is set in the New York City of the halcyon 1960s -- the mythic Gotham of Hollywood, replete with paper moons, painted backdrops and rain that falls on cue. Into this fabled metropolis sashays Barbara Novak (Renee Zellweger), a small-town girl with an obligatory suitcase full of dreams whose book, the eponymous "Down With Love" -- a self-help, women's lib manifesto -- makes her an overnight celebrity.

Assigned by Know -- "the magazine for men in the know" -- to cover Novak's meteoric rise is Catch Block (Ewan McGregor), a lady-killing lounge lizard who lands Pulitzer Prizes as routinely as he does stewardesses. The "ladies-man, man's-man, man-about-town" ace journalist vows to expose Novak as a marriage-crazed fraud by charming her into falling in love with him, thus debunking her testosterone-wary tract.

To accomplish this, Catch goes undercover, posing as a demure Southern astronaut, Maj. Zip Martin. Despite her sworn-off-men policy, Novak's three-step program of female empowerment offers little resistance to Zip's aw-shucks advances. The rest of the film is a screwball bossa nova of deception as Catch begins to reel in his prey. Along the way they fall in love, throwing a wrench in Catch's ruse and making his conquest a Pyrrhic victory on more than one level.

"Down With Love" evokes a heightened glamour right from the jazzy opening credits. The New York presented is all artifice -- a romanticized set-piece crafted to reinforce the film's enchanted moonstruck milieu.

McGregor is on the money as the martini-toting cad -- the perfect blend of Rat Pack cool and James Bond savoir faire. And Zellweger, whose on-screen chemistry with McGregor clicks from the start, imbues Novak with a balance of resiliency and girlish vulnerability. David Hyde Pierce brings his patented brand of understated comedy to the role of Peter McMannus, Catch's confidence-challenged best friend and editor, who is lovesick for Novak's feisty editor, Vikki (Sarah Paulson).

Playing on audiences' fascination with early-'60s fashion and design, Reed employs devices like split screens and period music to create what appears on the surface to be an old-fashioned romantic comedy while reinventing the genre with gender reversals more in tune with "modern" sensibilities. True to its source -- Day-Hudson collaborations such as "Pillow Talk" -- the film eschews overt sexual situations, conveying the characters' carnal obsessions through whip-smart wordplay, double entendres and cleverly suggestive image juxtaposition.

However, while there's still much to be said about the misogynistic treatment of women common in a male-dominated society, the film endorses a fatuous philosophy of liberation, dressed up in modish catch phrases and vintage couture and passed off as harmless humor. Novak's book -- a pre-feminist do-it-yourself manual to sexual libertinism -- purports that love is a game you can master by adopting men's no-strings, sex-a-la-carte attitude, freeing women from the shackles of commitment and marriage and fostering equality in the workplace. And though much of the premise revolves around Catch trying to disprove such cynical claims, the message viewers are left with falls far short of love conquers all.

Though in love with Catch, Novak must sublimate her true feelings for the greater cause: the empowerment of women to indulge in the same sort of promiscuity that infuriates her about men. Rather than working to elevate both sexes to the pedestal of mutual dignity, Novak is content to offer her libidinous fans carte blanche to join men in the gutter.

Unfortunately, the love espoused by this film is not the meet-you-on-the-top-of-the-Empire-State-Building-with-tissues variety, but a watered-down hybrid with an attached prenuptial list of conditions. And while the happy ending seems to debunk assertions that the human heart is a game-board to be mastered by skill, it does allow for some "liberated" ground rules to be set -- as the McMannus and Vikki characters cooingly inform each other during the end-credit scrawl, "I love you, but I'm not giving up my career" -- a line of dialogue seven words too long.

Due to implied sexual situations, racy double entendres and sexually suggestive humor, as well as a misguided attitude toward sexual intimacy, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: D-War: Dragon Wars
synopsis: Hilariously silly but never dull throwback to the old Godzilla movies, with a Los Angeles reporter (Jason Behr) protecting a young woman (Amanda Brooks) whose life-force is sought by a good giant serpent and a bad giant serpent. full_review:
Full Review

Aimed at undiscriminating young teen audiences and older genre fans looking for goofy fun and lively monster scenes, the oddly named "D-War: Dragon Wars" (Freestyle) harkens back to those old Godzilla movies. This cheesy Korean movie, shot in Los Angeles with American stars and a modest budget, is actually better than the U.S. "Godzilla" of 1998.

While "D-War" is no less silly and poorly written than that film, it's never dull; you either are laughing at it or are drawn into well-choreographed battle scenes between the U.S. military and, variously, a giant serpent, dinosaur-sized armadillo-type creatures with built-in rocket-launchers, small flying dragons, and a mystical mean guy in a black-leather trench coat who occasionally morphs into a sort of medieval Darth Vader.

When something resembling a giant lizard's scale is unearthed in Los Angeles, young cable-news reporter Ethan Kendricks (Jason Behr) begins having flashbacks to his boyhood. An antiques dealer, Jack (Robert Forster), revealed that the two of them were the reincarnations of an old Korean sensei and his apprentice.

In another flashback, this time to feudal Korea, we learn that the good giant serpent Imoogi and the bad giant serpent Buraki are vying for a life force called the Yuh Yi Joo, which will allow one of them to ascend to dragonhood.

Once you get through this clumsy back story then you can settle in for the guilty enjoyment of writer-director Hyung-rae Shim's exceedingly juvenile film.

In a matinee crowd with children 10 years old and younger, the action-violence of bloodless battle scenes, downed Apache helicopters and countless explosions seemed not to faze the young audience. Near the climax, downtown Los Angeles becomes a battlefield with F-22 fighter jets and Abrams battle tanks fighting dragons, a giant serpent and mystical warriors in a satisfyingly extended knock-down, drag-out fight.

The film contains a couple of instances of crude language and some crass language, one background-dialog instance of mild sexual innuendo, much bloodless medieval and modern-day warfare, numerous explosions, crashed and crushed vehicles with unseen occupants, a leap from a cliff into the sea, and a woman who is chomped by a giant serpent and tossed away. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Dreamcatcher
synopsis: Grisly horror flick in which four boyhood friends (Thomas Jane, Jason Lee, Damian Lewis and Timothy Olyphant) who became telepathically connected after performing a heroic act in their youth, battle an invading alien force that takes over people's bodies. As directed by Lawrence Kasdan, what initially seems like a well-crafted film collapses under the weight of ridiculous characterizations and an unwieldy story line that forgoes suspense and tension for gory special effects, eliciting ennui instead of terror. Much grotesque violence and recurring rough language and profanity with some coarse sexual references
full_review:
Four boyhood friends use their supernatural gifts to battle an invading alien force in the grisly horror thriller "Dreamcatcher" (Warner Bros.).

Adapted from the novel by Stephen King, the "Dreamcatcher" story is a retread of familiar themes in the fright master's work: children bonded together by some incident who then reunite as adults to fight an evil force afoot in the world. This time around, the narrative includes a sci-fi aspect in the form of invading aliens who take over people's bodies. As directed by Lawrence Kasdan, the film is initially intriguing, fooling the audience into thinking that it will be an unnerving trip through the snowy woods where it is set. But the film becomes unwieldy, forgoing the initial suspense and tension for slimy special effects that produce yawns (and sometimes laughter) instead of screams.

As kids living in a small town in Maine, Jonesy (Damian Lewis), Henry (Thomas Jane), Beaver (Jason Lee) and Pete (Timothy Olyphant), saved a handicapped boy named Duddits from school bullies. As a result, the boys were somehow endowed with the powers of telepathy and precognition. Twenty years later, the men reunite for their annual visit to a hunting cabin. But when a lost hunter appears with a suspicious red splotch on his face, suffering from hypothermia and some pretty intense gastro-intestinal problems, their cozy retreat turns sinister.

The film turns a corner here into sci-fi territory. The hunter's upset stomach is actually an alien in the form of a giant, slimy, razor-toothed worm that slithers out of the hunter's body in what can only be described as the worst possible bowel movement a human can experience. Gross for sure, but some tongue-in-cheek humor would have greased the wheels of this vehicle. Instead, the film takes itself very seriously, and the audience can't keep a straight -- or frightened -- face as two of the foursome are quickly killed off by the slithering serpentine.

There are pieces of the film that hold together nicely. The vicious alien has taken over Jonesy's body (and for some strange reason adopted a Monty Python-ish British accent), but can't seem to completely take over his mind. Jonesy's mind is represented as an actual warehouse where he files his memories under titles such as "sporting humiliations." The idea of the multistory warehouse crammed with boxes and papers and a fancy spiral staircase in the center is effective in conveying the thoughts and ideas that clutter up Jonesy's mind.

Yet as a whole, the film collapses under the weight of ridiculous characterizations and a story line that tries to cram in too much yet accomplishes little, despite its inflated length.

Morgan Freeman stars as a tough alien hunter who commands a top-secret military task force whose purpose is to eradicate the alien invaders and contain the red, spotty virus it spreads. But the miscast Freeman spouts such ridiculous lines that his hard-edged commander is more caricature than character. And Freeman looks as bored with playing this character as the viewer is seeing him do it.

The subplot of his commander going over the edge -- willing even to take human lives to contain the alien disease -- while his second-in-command (Tom Sizemore) attempts to stop him, feels like scenes from a different movie spliced in as an excuse to blow up a helicopter.

The connection to all these bizarre happenings is Duddits -- who is played as an adult by Donnie Wahlberg with a shaved head and heavy makeup to make Duddits look extremely ill. But by the time he enters the movie, it's late in the game and the viewer has already tuned out.

"Dreamcatcher" is accompanied by an 11-minute animated short entitled "The Animatrix, Final Flight of the Osiris." Fusing computer-generated animation and Japanese anime, "The Animatrix" is a collection of nine original short films conceived by the Wachowski brothers, the creators of the "Matrix" trilogy. Visually impressive but void of a coherent or interesting plot, "Final Flight" is an episode from the collection.

In the end, "Dreamcatcher's" initial potential disappears as the film's structural problems take over like the unsightly crusty alien virus that spreads from human to human.

Because of much grotesque violence and recurring rough language and profanity with some coarse sexual references, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Dreamer: Inspired by a True Story
synopsis: Warm and winning family film set in rural Kentucky about a dispirited racehorse trainer (Kurt Russell), his young daughter (Dakota Fanning) and estranged father (Kris Kristofferson), who nurse an injured Seabiscuit-like thoroughbred back to form and in the process mend their own broken relationships. Written and directed by John Gatins, the movie is a handsome and unapologetically sentimental old-fashioned crowd-pleaser, with tender performances by Fanning and Russell and heartfelt themes of family, the healing power of love and the importance of holding on to one's dreams. A few mildly rude expressions and a racetrack accident that may disturb sensitive young children
full_review:
Hollywood loves a good horse story. Just think of "National Velvet," "Black Beauty" or "The Black Stallion." In recent years, the starting gate has become crowded with movies like "Seabiscuit," "Hidalgo" and -- if the definition is malleable enough to include zebras with identity issues -- "Racing Stripes."

The newest to trot into theaters is also one of the better family films of the year. Written and directed by John Gatins, the awkwardly titled "Dreamer: Inspired by a True Story" (DreamWorks) is a warm and winning crowd-pleaser that, much like its pony protagonist, is all heart.

Loosely based on a real-life racehorse's against-the-odds comeback, the fable is about a chocolate-colored prize filly called Sonador (Spanish for "Dreamer") who suffers a seemingly career-ending injury when she breaks her leg during a race.

Sonador's slimy owner, Palmer (David Morse), orders the injured animal put down, but her dispirited, nearly bankrupt trainer Ben Crane (Kurt Russell) -- a second-generation horse whisperer who had to sell most of his family's Kentucky farm to stave off foreclosure -- refuses. The ensuing argument costs Crane his job, but he negotiates taking Sonador as severance pay.

Together with his young daughter, Cale (a precocious Dakota Fanning), estranged father Pop (Kris Kristofferson), a wisecracking stable hand (Luis Guzman) and a saddle-shy jockey (Freddy Rodriguez), Crane nurses Sonador back into shape, eventually entering her in the prestigious Breeders' Cup race against Palmer's Man O'War-like steed. And though there isn't much guessing as to the film's finish line, the touching story keeps you involved.

As in "Seabiscuit," here the crippled horse serves as a metaphor for the characters' own brokenness. As Sonador's leg mends, a parallel emotional healing transforms Crane's fractured relationship with Cale and Pop.

Crane starts out a damaged soul, but in rescuing Sonador it is actually Crane who gets a second chance. "You saved her life," Cale tells her father. "She's just returning the favor."

Fanning proves an impressive actress behind her saucer eyes and Russell is likewise solid, resulting in some genuinely tender father-daughter moments. Elisabeth Shue makes the most of her underwritten role as Crane's supportive wife.

Fred Murphy's handsome cinematography captures the region's bluegrass beauty and gives the film an elegant polish (shots of the early morning mist-covered fields are lovely) and John Debney's lilting score is appropriately uplifting. Though emotionally satisfying, the final race could have been more exciting.

Familiar plot notwithstanding, with its wholesome charm, unapologetic sentimentality and themes of family love and holding on to your dreams, "Dreamer" is a sure bet to win your heart.

The film contains a few mildly rude expressions and a racetrack accident that may disturb sensitive young children. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-I -- general patronage. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

title: Dreamgirls
synopsis: Entertaining screen version of 1981 Broadway hit charting the rise of a Motown-like 1960s girl group (Beyonce Knowles, Anika Noni Rose and Sharon Leal), and the heavyset lead singer (Jennifer Hudson) they push out of the group when she doesn't match their new svelte image, as well as an R&B singer (Eddie Murphy), and the ruthless manager (Jamie Foxx) who guides all their careers. Director Bill Condon has skillfully refashioned the show for the screen turning most of the sung recitatives into spoken dialogue, and there are especially good performances from Murphy and newcomer Hudson. Despite some flagged material, the overarching themes of loyalty, doing the "right thing," dedication to family and friends, and overcoming adversity are key. Romantic complications including adultery, a child born out of wedlock, crude language, some innuendo, mild profanity, drug use and some onstage vulgarity
full_review:
It took a quarter-century, but the 1981 Broadway hit musical has made a successful transition to the screen.

The fast-moving, generally entertaining screen version of "Dreamgirls" (Paramount) charts the rise of a Motown-like 1960s girl group consisting of Deena (Beyonce Knowles), Lorrell (Anika Noni Rose), and powerhouse lead singer Effie (Jennifer Hudson).

Ruthless manager Curtis (Jamie Foxx) takes them under his wing at a Detroit talent competition where they stop the show, and persuades them to do high-profile backup to R&B singer Jimmy "Thunder" Early (Eddie Murphy).

Before long, the Dreamettes trio breaks out on their own, and despite a romantic involvement with Effie, Curtis pushes Effie out of the group when her mercurial temperament becomes problematic, and he determines she doesn't match the group's new svelte image.

Thereafter, the film chronicles the separate fortunes of the Dreams, as they're now known, with Deena now the glamorous lead, singer Michelle (Sharon Leal) filling the empty slot, while Effie -- after a troubled reclusive period -- achieves success as a solo act, and Jimmy (who, though married, is having a long-term affair with Lorrell) works to break out of the crooner style Curtis has imposed.

Writer/director Bill Condon -- who wrote the screenplay for "Chicago" -- has, as with that property, skillfully refashioned the show for the screen, turning most of the sung recitatives into spoken dialogue. And taking a page from the way "Chicago" was done, he has used a lot of quick cuts here to make sure attention never lags.

The parallels to the real-life Supremes (whom the Dreams are meant to resemble) are emphasized with clips of TV host Ed Sullivan, who often featured that group, and album-cover art that hearkens back to Diana Ross' heyday.

The cast is uniformly excellent, but there are especially good performances from Murphy and newcomer Hudson, who delivers the show's best-known number, "And I Am Telling You I'm Not Going," a blazing outcry of defiance when she's given the heave-ho. Danny Glover as Marty, Jimmy's first manager, and Keith Robinson as C.C., Effie's brother and a songwriter also under Curtis' thumb, are fine, too.

The show's tunes by composer Henry Krieger and lyricist Tom Eyen have been augmented by four new ones by Krieger.

Despite some of the flagged material below, the overarching themes of loyalty, doing the "right thing," dedication to family and friends, and overcoming adversity are key.

The film contains romantic complications including adultery, a child born out of wedlock, crude language, some innuendo, mild profanity, drug use and some onstage vulgarity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Drillbit Taylor
synopsis: Droll portrait of the unlikely friendship between a homeless veteran (Owen Wilson) and the three high school misfits (Nate Hartley, Troy Gentile and David Dorfman) who hire him as a bodyguard to protect them from a malevolent bully (Alex Frost) and his thuggish sidekick (Josh Peck). Director Steven Brill's film, produced by the prolific Judd Apatow, emphasizes its titular character's evolution from con man to caring mentor, and his young clients' search for courage and solidarity, but dialogue rife with vulgar terms and a problematic central love story make it appropriate fare only for the mature. Brief rear nudity, implied premarital sex, frequent crude and pervasive crass language, six uses of profanity, and drug and pornography references
full_review:
Drillbit Taylor

Three high school students take extreme measures to defeat a pair of bullies in the droll comedy "Drillbit Taylor" (Paramount). Though this latest production by the prolific Judd Apatow has some endearing qualities, other elements make it appropriate fare only for the mature.

On the first day of their freshman year, scrawny Wade (Nate Hartley) and tubby Ryan (Troy Gentile) want nothing more than to appear cool. But when the two friends witness Filkins (Alex Frost), a malevolent upperclassman, and Ronnie (Josh Peck), his thuggish sidekick, stuffing undersized fellow newcomer Emmit (David Dorfman) into his own locker, Wade summons the courage to interfere.

The result is a relentless campaign of demeaning pranks waged against all three.
Rather than spend the entire school year on the run from their persecutors, the boys concoct a scheme to hire an adult bodyguard. The only applicant willing to settle for the measly salary they've scraped together is the fast-talking Taylor (Owen Wilson), a homeless veteran who dazzles them with wildly exaggerated accounts of his military experiences.

Infiltrating the school in the guise of "Dr. Illbit," a substitute teacher, Taylor is soon dividing his time between protecting his new friends and romancing his alluring colleague, Lisa (Leslie Mann). Though he confidently claims that anyone holding a coffee mug can pass for a member of the faculty, it only takes a coincidence for Taylor to be unmasked, leaving the boys more vulnerable than ever.

Director Steven Brill's film emphasizes its titular character's evolution from con man to caring mentor, and his young clients' search for courage and solidarity. But the dialogue is rife with vulgar terms, while the handling of the central love story, in which physical intimacy precedes all but the most basic social interaction, is highly problematic.

For these reasons, "Drillbit Taylor" cannot be recommended for the young viewers who are, presumably, its target audience. The film contains brief rear nudity, implied premarital sex, frequent crude and pervasive crass language, six uses of profanity, and drug and pornography references. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Dr. Seuss! The Cat in the Hat
synopsis: Overwrought live-action version of Theodore Geisel's classic rhyming kid's tale about a brother (Spenser Breslin) and sister (Dakota Fanning) whose home is turned upside down by a mischievous talking cat (Mike Myers) in a red-and-white striped stovepipe hat while their mother (Kelly Preston) is at work. While true to the spirit of the book, director Bo Welch has added story lines to flesh out the story to feature length, resulting in a bloated, visually assaulting film weighed down by tedious special-effects sequences and Myers' hyper-frenetic performance.�Minimal mildly crude humor and innuendo
full_review:
A brother and sister learn that nothing cures boredom quite like a 6-foot feline with a red-and-white striped
stovepipe hat and a penchant for mischief in the whimsical but off-target family comedy "Dr. Seuss' The Cat in the Hat" (Universal).

In 1957, Theodore Geisel -- aka Dr. Seuss -- strung together 220 rhyming words and created an instant children's classic. Forty-six years later, the same, regrettably, cannot be said of director Bo Welch, whose bloated adaptation is such a visually assaulting jumble that not even the cat's three-handled, moss-covered family credenza can clean up the on-screen mess.

The basic story has remained intact. Two kids, Conrad and Sally (Spenser Breslin and Dakota Fanning), are left home alone on a rainy afternoon while their mom, Joan (Kelly Preston), is at work. The children are given strict orders to behave themselves and keep the house tidy.

An added story line about a party Joan is hosting later that evening for her neat-freak boss, Mr. Humberfloob (Sean Hayes), ups the ante for making sure that the rooms stay shipshape. Welch also felt compelled to include a narcoleptic baby sitter, Mrs. Kwan (Amy Hill), whose presence in the film, apart from some lame sight gags, serves no purpose. Perhaps in a moment of politically correct insanity, Welch feared that parents might take offense to leaving two young children unattended.

Soon after their mother's departure, the eponymous cat (played in full body fur by Mike Myers) appears with a chapeau
full of fun. Within minutes the cat hangs a snoozing Mrs. Kwan in the coat closet and cajoles the children into breaking all of their mother's ordinances. Against the better judgment of the family's goldfish (also voiced by Sean Hayes), the children follow the cat's lead in turning the house upside-down.

The situation gets out of control when the cat opens a magic crate containing Thing 1 and Thing 2 (Danielle Chuchran and Brittany Oakes), a pair of androgynous gremlins with a knack for wreaking a whirlwind of havoc. In a concocted plot twist, the box also serves as a gateway to an alternative dimension. When the crate's special padlock is lost, it begins to transform the house into a surreal Seuss-scape.

Attempting to give the film a more updated feel, Welch has made Joan a single parent and saddled her with a freeloading boyfriend (Alec Baldwin), who feigns nurturing concern for the kids in order to ingratiate himself with her.

Those disappointed by Ron Howard's big-screen version of "Dr. Seuss's How the Grinch Stole Christmas" shouldn't expect much better results this time. Both films make the mistake of trying to stretch a few dozen verses into a feature-length film.

And while Howard's movie was unnecessarily content-heavy -- delving too deeply into the psychological origins of the Grinch's grinchiness -- Welch's film remains totally content-free, padding its threadbare narrative with protracted special-effects sequences which prove tedious rather than hilarious.

Welch seems to totally forget why people love Dr. Seuss in the first place -- his magical wordplay. He even commits the gravest Seussian sacrilege by having the cat admit he is no good with rhymes. And though the film's ingenious production design faithfully captures the bubblegum color palette and off-kilter look of Seuss' world, once Geisel's text is jettisoned,what is left is a guy in a cat suit doing a lame stand-up routine -- all of which is about as funny as coughing up hairballs.

As with Jim Carey's scene-chewing romp through Whoville, Mike Myers hogs the spotlight, bombarding viewers with his hyper-frenetic antics and rapid-fire zingers -- many retreads from his previous performances. For some reason Myers plays the part with a Noo Yawk nasal tone -- sounding more like the "Katz in the Hat."

For fans of Dr. Seuss' work, the film's high point comes early -- as in before the film -- during a pre-credit sequence in which the movie studio logos are cleverly animated in the style of the books and Chuck Jones' classic cartoon specials. Despite such a promising start, it's all downhill from there.

Anyone interested in introducing their children to this wonderful tale would be advised to rent the far superior 1971 half-hour TV version -- none of this film's forgettable tunes can touch the inspired genius of "Calculatus Eliminatus." Better yet, read them the book. In fact, a verse found on Page Two reads like a Seussian review of this movie:

"So all we could do was to sit, sit, sit, sit.

"And we did not like it, not one little bit."

Due to cartoon violence, minimal mildly crude language and innuendo, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

title: Drumline

full_review:
A talented but cocky drummer jeopardizes his college scholarship when he wants to be the star of the school band in "Drumline" (20th Century Fox).

Although Dad didn't stick around, Devon (Nick Cannon) grew up in Harlem, kept out of trouble and graduated from high school with a music scholarship to a predominately black university in Atlanta.

A hip-hop drummer with amazing technique, Devon was recruited by the band's director, Dr. Lee (Orlando Jones), and arrives on campus unprepared for the strict discipline that qualifying for the band demands. He bristles when criticized by the drum section leader, Sean (Leonard Roberts), a senior who recognizes his talent but despises his cocky attitude.

Dr. Lee is under pressure by the university president (Afem Omilami) to scrap classical selections in favor of the kind of current music their rival school uses to win in the yearly band competition. When Devon moves in on Sean's solo drum number at one of the football games, the president is impressed with his jazzy playing, but Dr. Lee and Sean realize the freshman needs to be taken down a peg or two and learn the concept of teamwork.

The story is formulaic, but the setting of a college marching band is fresh and the music and dance production numbers keep the interest level up in spite of the predictability factor.

When Devon is pulled from the band, the rival band director (J. Anthony Brown) offers him a cushy spot -- for a price that tests the young man's sense of ethics. And Devon is not the only one who has to learn some hard lessons; Dr. Lee pushes Sean to question if he is hard on Devon for the right reasons, or out of jealousy over the freshman's superior talent.

Zoe Saldana plays Devon's student love interest, Laila, in a supportive relationship that helps both of them mature without suggesting an ongoing steamy affair. There are wisecracks about virginity and comparing playing an instrument to sex but this and the occasional crude word are passing moments in director Charles Stone III's otherwise wholesome, even high-minded, film.

Although the movie feels a little long, its themes of not lying, developing integrity and working toward personal growth are real pluses. And the sturdy appeal of an underdog band taking on the rival-band-that-can't-be-beat at the conclusion sends it into feel-good territory.

Without much fanfare but a sense of humor, toe-tapping numbers and energetic camerawork, "Drumline" has been finding fans at the box office.

Due to a few sexual references and crass expressions, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Due Date
synopsis: Sour road comedy pairing a disaster-prone aspiring actor (Zach Galifianakis) on his way to Hollywood and an uptight architect (Robert Downey Jr.) rushing home to Los Angeles for the birth of his first child. full_review:
In director John Hughes' 1987 hit "Planes, Trains and Automobiles," two comic geniuses, Steve Martin and John Candy, played unlikely companions thrown together on a mishap-plagued journey home for Thanksgiving.

Tinged with tenderness, the proceedings eventually saw the two become friends after Martin's character discovered the endearing qualities lurking beneath Candy's bumbling ways.

Though it traces a similar arc, and invites comparison with Hughes' film, the sour comedy "Due Date" (Warner Bros.) is marked by a profoundly different tone: hard-edged, mean-spirited and, at times, violent.

Perhaps not surprisingly -- given that director and co-writer (with Alan R. Cohen and Alan Freedland) Todd Phillips is best known for helming last year's morally anarchic but widely popular "The Hangover" -- this frequently unpleasant odyssey also detours into comic portrayals of marijuana smoking and aberrant sexual behavior.

Phillips' odd-couple buddy flick follows the misadventures of disaster-prone aspiring actor Ethan Tremblay (Zach Galifianakis), who's on his way to Hollywood in search of sitcom stardom, and uptight architect Peter Highman (Robert Downey Jr.), who's rushing home to Los Angeles for the birth of his first child.

After Ethan gets them involved in a misunderstanding that sees them both kicked off their flight from Atlanta and placed on the no-fly list, Peter -- having lost ID, cash and credit cards in the incident -- is left with no option but to drive to the West Coast in the company of his newfound nemesis.

Ethan, a somewhat effeminate man-boy, his hair permed in curls, his soft shoes from ballet manufacturer Capezio, displays a breezy disregard for all forms of common sense so grating that Peter's mounting fury with him seems entirely justifiable. All the more so when Ethan's supposedly amusing eccentricities turn out to include a taste for pot and a habit of lulling himself to sleep via self-gratification.

As the scene queasily showcasing the latter vice makes clear, Ethan's daily indulgence in it is in no way curbed by the proximity of his traveling companion a few feet away.

The script uses the recent death of Ethan's father to try to offset the nuisance factor and win sympathy. But its hesitant forays into gentleness are consistently thwarted by nasty interludes like a rumble with a stick-wielding, wheelchair-bound Iraq War veteran and an exchange in which Peter reveals a painful childhood secret, only to have Ethan laugh in his face.

The film contains drug trafficking and use, masturbation, about a half-dozen instances of profanity, pervasive rough and much crude language as well as some sexual jokes and references. The Catholic News Service classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Duma
synopsis: First-rate coming-of-age adventure set in Africa about a headstrong young boy (Alexander Michaletos) who embarks on a journey of self-discovery when he resolves to trek across hundreds of miles of treacherous terrain in order return his pet cheetah -- which he raised since it was an orphaned cub -- to its rightful home in the wild. Beautifully crafted by director Carroll Ballard, the boy-and-his-cheetah buddy movie combines exceptional nature photography -- including some amazing shots of African wildlife -- with a warm and winning story about the bonds of family and friendship, resulting in a film that is sweetly charming without being overly sentimental. Some scenes of peril, and brief wildlife violence which may be frightening to some young children
full_review:
In Swahili, "zuri" means "beautiful," which makes it the perfect word to describe "Duma" (Warner Bros.), a first-rate coming-of-age story about a boy and his cheetah.

Set against the eye-filling backdrop of southern Africa, the tender tale revolves around a headstrong young Afrikaner named Xan (Alexander Michaletos), who, while driving home with his father (Campbell Scott), happens upon an orphaned cheetah cub, which they name Duma -- the Swahili word for cheetah. They take the animal home to their rural Kenyan ranch. As is common in these types of human-animal buddy films, Xan and Duma quickly develop an unbreakable bond of friendship.

But Xan's happiness is tempered by the unavoidable realization that one day the call of the wild will force a parting of ways.

That day comes sooner than expected, when Xan's father suddenly falls ill and dies, and his mother (an underused Hope Davis) is forced to sell the farm and relocate to the city.

Even Xan realizes that cheetahs do not make ideal apartment pets. So rather than ship Duma off to captivity in a zoo, Xan resolves to return the fleet-footed feline back to his rightful home in the wild, which lies hundreds of miles away, across lion-prowled veldts, crocodile-infested rivers and dense, insect-infested jungles. Worse still, even if they reach their destination safely, Xan worries that Duma has become too domesticated to survive on his own.

With Duma riding shotgun in the sidecar, Xan takes off in his father's motorcycle and into the unknown. Together the two friends battle treacherous terrain, scorching heat, wild animals and inner fears, as Xan's odyssey becomes a journey of self-discovery. Along the way they are aided by Rip (Eamonn Walker), a mysterious drifter whose motives are unclear.

Having grown up in real life on a farm where he raised cheetahs, South African newcomer Michaletos is perfect in the lead role and brings just the right combination of boyish naivete and mature circumspection to the character, making Xan's transformation from rash youth to manhood believable. But the real scene-stealer is Michaletos' sleek and spotted co-star.

Directed by Carroll Ballard, "Duma" combines exceptional nature photography -- including some amazing shots of African wildlife -- with a warm and winning story, resulting in a film that is sweetly charming without being overly sentimental. Ballard is no stranger to adventures involving the pairing of children with animals, having directed films such as "Fly Away Home" and "The Black Stallion."

Loosely based on the fact-based children's book "How It Was With Dooms" by Xan and Carol Cawthra Hopcraft, "Duma" is one of those rare intelligent, well-made films that all but the youngest children can enjoy, one that doesn't need sex or violence -- or, for that matter, flashy special effects -- but is content to tell that most endangered of species: a good story. It should be noted, though, that some images, including the opening scene where Duma's mother is killed by a menacing pride of lions, may be upsetting for some young viewers.

Underneath a plot inspired by "Born Free," the movie deals with difficult issues involving loss, separation, transition and death in a way that is accessible to young viewers. It also imparts a simple but profound message about the permanence of authentic love. As Xan learns, "Love doesn't stop when time passes."

In one scene, Rip tells Xan how, according to local folklore, cheetahs got the distinct black markings cascading down their snouts. He says they were formed by the tears of the first cheetah, who cried after losing her cubs. No doubt, by the movie's bittersweet emotional ending, there may be a few damp human cheeks as well.

The film contains some scenes of peril, and brief wildlife violence which may be frightening to some young children. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

full_review:
Rarely does a movie's title also serve as an apt review of the film itself, but such is the case with "Dumb and Dumberer: When Harry Met Lloyd" (New Line).

Directed by Troy Miller and full of flat jokes and vulgar humor, this mindless prequel to the equally inane 1994 "Dumb and Dumber" fails on every level and even invents some brand new levels on which to fail.

Making a dumb plot short, the new film explores the "formative years" of the title halfwits played by Jim Carrey and Jeff Daniels in the original. This time around, we go without the only two things that made the earlier film barely funny -- namely, Carrey and Daniels. In fact, much of what passes as humor in this bone-brainer has about the same comedic effect of a whoopee cushion in a school for the deaf.

While on route to his first day of high school, the mop-headed Harry (Derek Richardson) turns a corner and collides with the bowl cut, chip-toothed Lloyd (Eric Christian Olsen, a ringer for a young Carrey). The two immediately bond, realizing theirs is a match made in idiot heaven. Lloyd, whose delusional savoir faire has made him a legend in his own mind, takes the socially inept Harry -- the product of home-schooling mom (Mimi Rogers) -- under his wing, teaching him the ropes of surviving in the "big show" and educating him on how to be "cool." Lesson No. 1 ends with the two simpletons being strung up a flag pole by the school bully.

Corrupt principal Mr. Collins (Eugene Levy) and his gal pal Ms. Heller (Cheri Oteri) quickly peg the dimwits as the perfect patsies for a scam they concocted to abscond with thousands in grant money if the school can claim a "special needs" class. Harry and Lloyd are put in charge of rounding up more losers for the class, paving the way for much of the film's silly sophomoric antics. During the recruitment they run into Jessica (Rachel Nichols), the beautiful ace investigative reporter for the school newspaper who senses something fishy. She wants to blow the lid off Collins' plot but needs Harry and Lloyd's cooperation, leading the dunces to confuse journalistic interest for romantic attraction.

The only thing this clunker succeeds at is making the original stinker look almost Shakespearean by comparison. The film relies on crude humor to conceal its overall lack of anything resembling comic wit, resorting to gross sight gags to elicit cheap, forced laughs. This pandering to the lowest common denominator is nowhere better illustrated than in one scene in which Harry mistakes a melted chocolate bar in his back pocket for his own excrement. Audiences must also endure a crass adolescent-male-fantasy sequence in which bikini-clad Nichols and Rogers catfight in a pool over Lloyd's affections and end up lip-locked.

The film's tagline -- "The Evolution of Dumb" -- is indication enough that this is one link worth missing.

Due to some profanity, much crude bathroom humor, an instance of same-sex kissing, exaggerated violence played for laughs and recurring sexual innuendo, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

full_review:
����������� A young New York couple's dream apartment turns into a domestic nightmare when they find out that it comes equipped with a high-maintenance, elderly tenant in the dark screwball comedy "Duplex" (Miramax).

Though frequently funny, the film, directed by Danny DeVito (who lends his voice to narration but does not appear in the movie) subscribes to a problematic brand of pitch-black humor that tickles viewers' funny bones with a feather of murderous cruelty.

For Alex (Ben Stiller), an aspiring novelist, and Nancy (Drew Barrymore), a hotshot magazine layout designer, the future couldn't be brighter. The only piece missing from their American dream puzzle is a home of their own. This speed bump on the yellow brick road to yuppie nirvana is remedied when their shady real-estate agent (Harvey Fierstein) finds them a storybook -- and affordable, to boot -- townhouse in Brooklyn. However, in addition to its four working fireplaces, the too-good-to-be-true offer comes with one huge, nonnegotiable glitch -- Mrs. Connelly (Eileen Essel), a wizened Irish widow quickly approaching the century mark, who lives in the rent-controlled apartment on the duplex's upper floor.

But Alex and Nancy's brownstone bliss is short-lived, as the seemingly frail pint-sized Mrs. Connelly quickly becomes a gargantuan thorn in their otherwise rosy future, souring what appeared to be a sweet steal-of-a-deal.

What starts off as a trickle of good-neighborly errands soon swells into an avalanche of around-the-clock interruptions, as the grating Gaelic granny lassoes her young landlords into full-time indentured servitude, running them ragged as they attend to her every need. Unable to deliver his manuscript on schedule because of the constant disruptions, Alex is dropped by his publisher for breach of contract. Adding to their woes, Nancy is also axed from her well-paying job.

Hard pressed to find a way out of the contractual cul-de-sac, Alex and Nancy's thoughts turn homicidal, with eviction giving way to murder as the solution of choice.

Stiller and Barrymore are pitch-perfect as the desperate young couple, leavening the film's grisly thematic undercurrents with a sympathetic likability and a good-natured willingness to suffer the brunt of the film's at-times crude sight gags and slapstick silliness in order to elicit yuks, playing honey-glazed wholesomeness and calculated cold-heartedness with equal vigor. Essel also proves brilliantly bipolar, imbuing Mrs. Connelly with an amusing blend of geriatric brittleness and crusty belligerence.

Disturbingly, much of the comedy is fueled by an ugly humor that makes light of acts which, removed from their zany, over-the-top context, are nothing to laugh at. And though the screwball premise makes for some genuinely funny moments, it is difficult -- or at least uncomfortable -- for Christians to find levity in a joke whose punch line involves murder.

Due to a black-comedy murder plot, an implied sexual encounter, recurring vulgar humor and sporadic crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

full_review:
In "Dysfunktional Family" (Miramax), director George Gallo weaves live concert footage with video interviews, creating a raw and raucous portrait of comedian Eddie Griffin. Unfortunately, Griffin's unremitting foul-mouthed rants and lewd tirades detract from his comic wit.

Following in the tradition of Eddie Murphy's "Raw" and "Richard Pryor -- Live in Concert," the film, shot during a recent performance near Griffin's home town of Kansas City, Mo., assaults viewers with an unrelenting barrage of vulgarities in a verbal shock-and-awe campaign. Regrettably, this highly offensive bombardment precludes viewers from considering the occasional astute observation Griffin makes about contemporary American society.

Throughout "Dysfunktional Family," viewers are introduced to various relatives who played a part in molding Griffin and whose support helped him use comedy as a means to escape the dead-end poverty and racism of his youth. Griffin credits his mother, whose legendary tough-love tactics are lampooned throughout, as the stabilizing influence which steered him clear of delinquency and set him on a path to success. He also acknowledges the roles his two colorful uncles played in filling the void left in the absence of his biological father (whom he never met until he was 16 years old).

Griffin's inflammatory shtick seems to be fueled by an ability to find humor in even the most tragic circumstances, including his uncle's battle with addiction, his own anger at being abandoned by his father, and even the dark events of Sept. 11, 2001.

The crass material is uniformly profane and distasteful. The routine caricatures racial groups (including, in all fairness, African-Americans). Organized religion fares no better, with Griffin taking particular delight in unabashedly mocking the Catholic Mass. Viewers must also suffer through crude, misogynistic diatribes intimately detailing his sexual appetites. He defends his seemingly constant use of one particular racial epithet referring to African-Americans by stating that, "The more you say it, the less power it has" to offend.

If any positives can be gleaned, the film does, beneath its abrasive veneer, speak of the importance of family and the positive impact families can have on the lives of their members.

At one point Griffin observes that if God created him to be funny, and if he is created in God's image, then humor and joy in turn must be an integral part of God and his plan for humanity -- which is theologically sound, but one wonders what God would think of his vulgar standup routine?

Due to incessant rough language and profanities, fleeting nudity, sexually explicit references, racial epithets and a pejorative view of religion, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: The Dancer Upstairs
synopsis: Low-key thriller set in an unnamed Latin American country where a police detective (Javier Bardem), undeterred by the political corruption around him, relentlessly tries to capture the leader of a terrorist organization causing widespread chaos, while at the same time drawn to his daughter's elusive ballet teacher (Laura Morante). (R) 2003 Full Review A methodical police detective pursues the leader of a terrorist organization threatening to bring down a Latin American country in the low-key thriller, "The Dancer Upstairs" (Fox Searchlight). Actor John Malkovich makes an effectively understated debut as a director with this timely tale of corruption and terrorism, which is based on the early 1990s pursuit of the leader of Peru's revolutionary Shining Path movement. Javier Bardem portrays Rejas, a corporate lawyer so turned off by corruption he becomes a policeman hoping to make a difference. Rejas is put in charge of a small group of dedicated cops after ritualistic animal killings around the country escalate to bombings and murders. All they have to go on is the name the terrorist leader is using: Ezequiel. At home Rejas stifles his boredom with his vain and air-headed wife (Alexandra Lencastre). In taking his young daughter to ballet classes, he finds himself unwillingly drawn to her teacher, Yolanda (Laura Morante). He avoids revealing to her that he is with the police or on the trail of the country's most wanted man. When military and government leaders are assassinated, martial law is declared and the hunt taken from his supervision. With political corruption all around him, Rejas continues digging for the whereabouts of the concealed guerrilla leader, appalled at how even young schoolgirls have been enlisted as suicide bombers. His concern becomes even more personal when the ballet school where Yolanda lives and his daughter attends classes is thought to be exactly where Ezequiel is hiding. Based on Nicholas Shakespeare's novel and screenplay, the film manages the feat of being a methodical police procedural that is quietly riveting. Much of this can be credited to Bardem's perfectly pitched performance as his frustrated cop stoically endures personal and career setbacks while never losing track of his need to capture the terrorist. Morante as well gives a silky performance as the dancer who finds Rejas intriguing but is holding secrets of her own. Their relationship does not typically head for the bedroom, but to a series of choices that defines their destinies. What lifts the film above the typical thriller action-film genre is the nuanced narrative that exposes the violence on both sides, not only of the revolutionaries but by government and military officials wielding power with scant regard for the citizenry. Rejas' struggle with marital fidelity and determination to remain uncorruptable also give the drama a thoughtful and welcome moral sensibility. Although sluggishly paced, Malkovich uses on-location sites in Spain, Portugal and Ecuador effectively, with carefully composed shots and angles creating an ominous atmosphere of constant danger. The bloodbath scene where young schoolgirls set off bombs is as ugly as the work of callous real-life terrorists. And the bittersweet ending suggests that this is a war that will never be neatly won and confined to reports in history books. Smart and serious, "The Dancer Upstairs" has at times a mournful tone that makes one want to offer up a prayer for all the world's victims of terrorism. Due to some intense violence with gore, flash of nudity and fleeting sexual reference, intermittent rough language and occasional profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting
