There are no outbursts of anger, but instead a dogged determination to do God's will as he has interpreted it, which is far more frightening. Yet the underlying flaw with Paxton's character (and some of the other characters as well) is that little background or motivation is revealed. Audiences are left to wonder whether this man was a Christian at all, much less one fervent about his "faith."

However, as director, Paxton builds up considerable tension as the film continues a murder-thriller path. The violence is disturbing, especially since the camera focuses on the faces of the children as Dad's ax comes down to slay another demon. The pressure mounts as the friction between young Fenton and his father escalates, leading to some pretty gruesome twists.

McConaughey offers a subtle performance, often giving his character more depth than is actually written for him. The young actors playing the Meiks brothers acquit themselves well, especially O'Leary since the bulk of the action lies on his small shoulders. Both as an actor and director, Paxton's execution is on target, keeping the flashback-flashfoward story on course.

The story of a disturbed father and a family poisoned by the evil it supposedly rejects terrifies because it takes a good thing like faith and doing God's will, and warps it beyond recognition.

Because of intermittent violence including suicide and some rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Framed
synopsis: Wronged man (Joe Don Baker) comes out of prison to wreck a quite literal bloody vengeance upon his oppressors. Directed by Phil Karlson, it is a vicious movie that goes all out in its depiction of brutal violence, especially against women

title: Frances
synopsis: Impassioned film biography of Frances Farmer, the 1930's Hollywood starlet who bucked the system, got involved with alcohol, drugs and strange men and whose mother had her placed in a mental institution where she was abused, raped and received a lobotomy. Jessica Lange's fine performance makes this sincere, non-exploitative but rather plodding and episodic movie worth seeing. Director Graeme Clifford's depiction of Frances' suffering and fate is so unremittingly cruel, that the movie will be too harsh for many viewers

title: Francesco
synopsis: Overwrought Italian production portrays St. Francis of Assisi (Mickey Rourke) as a spiritual agitator challenging the accepted values of his 13th-century contemporaries by embracing a life of utter poverty and simplicity. Director Liliana Cavani builds an elaborate picture of the period's social injustices but fails to evoke any convincing sense of religious conviction from Rourke's embarrassingly vacuous performance. English-language version. Occasional scenes of violence, desperate poverty and brief nudity

title: Francis
synopsis: One-joke comedy directed by Arthur Lubin in which the talking mule of the title (voice of Chill Wills) helps a bumbling second lieutenant (Donald O'Connor) become a hero in World War II Burma. The picture succeeded well enough to spawn a series of six sequels. Comic violence

title: Francis Goes to the Races
synopsis: Formula series entry directed by Arthur Lubin in which the talking mule of the title (voice of Chill Wills) helps a bumbling young man (Donald O'Connor) save a woolly Kentucky horse breeder (Cecil Kellaway) and his pretty granddaughter (Piper Laurie) from losing a fixed race. Crooked gamblers

title: Francis Goes to West Point
synopsis: Formula comedy series entry directed by Arthur Lubin in which the talking mule of the title (voice of Chill Wills) keeps a bumbling cadet (Donald O'Connor) from being kicked out of the Academy by helping him win the big football match against Navy

title: Francis Joins the WACS
synopsis: Formula service comedy directed by Arthur Lubin in which an Army lieutenant (Donald O'Connor) gets into predictable mix-ups after he is mistakenly posted to a WAC base, with the talking mule of the title adding to the comic confusion. Tame gender jokes

title: Francis of Assisi
synopsis: Uneven dramatization of the life of the 13th-century saint (Bradford Dillman) who founds a religious community based on absolute poverty, seeks its approval by the Pope (Finlay Currie), encourages longtime friend Clare (Dolores Hart) to head a similar women's order, then journeys to the Holy Land, preaches to the Sultan (Pedro Armendariz) and returns to find his order spreading but changing. Directed by Michael Curtiz, the production is well-mounted and well-intended but the script is a muddle of historical fact and dramatic fiction, with results that barely scratch the surface of Franciscan spirituality

title: Frank Capra's American Dream
synopsis: Feature documentary about the Italian-American director of "It's a Wonderful Life" (1947) and many other movies celebrating the democratic character of American society and the human dignity of ordinary people. Written and directed by Kenneth Bowser, with actor Ron Howard serving as host and narrator, the result presents a complex picture of Capra (1897-1991) as both social populist and cultural elitist, as seen through interviews of his friends and colleagues as well as choice excerpts from a variety of his movies. A few scenes depicting violence and sexual innuendo

title: Frankenhooker
synopsis: Clunky horror farce about a New Jersey "bio-electro technician" (James Lorinz) who saves his girlfriend's head after she is chewed up by a power mower and attaches it to various body parts selected from a bevy of Manhattan prostitutes. Directed by Frank Honenlotter, it's soft-core trash whose few droll moments are buried in low-budget gore. Repellent violence, sex scenes with nudity and drug abuse

title: Frankenstein
synopsis: Stylish horror classic from Mary Shelley's novel about the obsessed Dr. Frankenstein (Colin Clive) who robs graves to complete his composite creation (Boris Karloff) which is brought to life during an electrical storm, then breaks free to the consternation of the local village. The tampering-with-nature fable succeeds largely because of Karloff's sympathetic portrayal of the monster as tormented victim and director James Whale's treatment of the ghoulish proceedings as something more than mere horror fare. Stylized violence and recurring menace

title: Frankenstein and the Monster from Hell
synopsis: Peter Cushing again assumes the role of the mad doctor who, with his assistant (Shane Briant) assembles a creature from assorted parts they collect at the insane asylum in which they are residents. Directed by Terence Fisher, the gore is both sickening and sick

title: Frankenstein Conquers the World
synopsis: Dubbed Japanese import directed by Inoshiro Honda begins with a Nazi submarine delivering the monster's still-living heart to Hiroshima from whose A-bombed ashes emerges a giant-sized Frankenstein but his awful make-up fails to frighten an earnest American scientist (Nick Adams) who sticks around for the finale involving another bargain-basement monster. Flimsy menace and scale-model violence

title: Frankenstein Created Woman
synopsis: Monster mishmash in which the mad doctor (Peter Cushing) restores life to a drowned woman (Susan Denberg) by transferring the soul of his guillotined assistant (Robert Morris) into her body, uith gory results. Directed by Terence Fisher, the British production has a good cast but the tangled plot mixes a nonsensical premise with bad melodrama. Stylized violence and sexual situations

title: Frankenstein Meets the Wolf Man
synopsis: Uneven series entry in which the late Lawrence Talbot (Lon Chaney, Jr.) is revived when grave robbers open his tomb during the full moon, then journeys to the ruins of Frankenstein's castle seeking release from his life as a werewolf, but finds instead the baron's frozen Monster (Bela Lugosi) and a watery grave. Directed by Roy William Neill, the result has some spooky scenes, much eerie atmosphere and a good cast (Maria Ouspenskaya, Ilona Massey, Patric Knowles and others), though Lugosi's role is miniscule and the last part of the picture is tiresomely predictable. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Frankenstein Must Be Destroyed
synopsis: Mediocre British installment in the Frankenstein saga with the mad doctor (Peter Cushing) fanatically intent on perfecting his experiments in brain transplants. Directed by Terence Fisher, the macabre setting and atmosphere are good but the gore, with heads being lopped off and blood splattering freely, is less effective than the earlier convention of suggesting such shock effects

title: Frankenstein's Daughter
synopsis: Bargain-basement horror from director Richard Cunha offers a pedestrian tale of Frankenstein's grandson (John Ashley) working in Southern California where he creates a female monster with a teenager's brain. Sexual situations and hokey menace

title: Frankenstein Unbound
synopsis: ( see "Roger Corman's Frankenstein Unbound" )

title: Frankie and Johnny
synopsis: Elvis Presley vehicle with plenty of rock-'n'-roll music, fist-swinging action and cutsie-poo romance. Allegedly based on the famous folk ballad, Presley plays a two-timing but ultimately redemptive riverboat gambler with Donna Douglas as his tired-but-true love, Frankie. Directed by Frederick de Cordova, it's light-weight fun

title: Frankie and Johnny
synopsis: Moderately engaging love story about a fed-up-with-men waitress (Michelle Pfeiffer) in a Manhattan diner who doesn't want a relationship with the new cook (Al Pacino), an ex-con who wants to offer her love, marriage and a family. With Pacino in fine form here, producer-director Garry Marshall tackles themes of hope, renewal and family ties despite the confines of an overly talky romance. Brief shots of lovemaking, numerous sexual references and some rough language

title: Frankie Starlight
synopsis: Quirky drama set in Ireland where a lonely adult dwarf (Corban Walker) recalls the story of how his French World War II refugee mother (Anne Parillaud) raised him with the help of an Irish family whose oldest daughter finds unexpected romance with him years later. Director Michael Lindsay-Hogg's bittersweet tale of offbeat romances over two generations is full of charm and pathos, yet comes up short in defining the central character of the mother. Brief violence including suicides, a bedroom scene and occasional rough language

title: Frantic
synopsis: Well-crafted suspense thriller about an American couple (Harrison Ford and Betty Buckley) who on a visit to Paris get caught up in a dangerous game of international intrigue. Director Roman Polanski provides the chills and thrills with appropriately sinister camerawork and a strong performance by Ford, but several bizarre scenes involving drugs and a grotesque corpse are not for the squeamish. Restrained violence, drug use, brief nudity and some street language

title: Fraternity Row
synopsis: Shallow and sentimental look at fraternity life in the mid-1950s in a story about an idealistic young man who becomes a pledge at a prestigious college fraternity and runs afoul of a sadistic bully. Director Thomas J. Tobin takes an uncritical view of the frat system on American campuses. Some sexual references

title: Fraternity Vacation
synopsis: Frat nerds place a wager on who will seduce Britt Ekland first. Directed by James Frawley, this "Animal House" clone offers nothing but the usual nudity and gross, vulgar humor

title: Fraulein Doktor
synopsis: World War I German spy (Suzy Kendall) engineers the sinking of Lord Kitchener's ship, steals a poison gas formula from a French scientist (Capucine) and supervises the theft of the master battle plan from Allied headquarters in Belgium. Alberto Lattuada directs the movie in an almost documentary style that encourages a suspension of disbelief. Though uneven and deliberately devoid of emotional involvement, its events are often grimly absorbing and hard to dismiss

title: Freaks
synopsis: Tod Browning, a director specializing in the field of horror and the grotesque, centered this story around a group of circus freaks who take in a normal woman in need of refuge but who betrays them. Browning endows the movie with an unusual sympathetic quality in not exploiting the deformities and monstrous appearance of his characters. The result is a unique film of the horror genre, a real classic of its kind, that is not easily forgotten by even the most sophisticated cinema-addict

title: Freaky Friday
synopsis: Breezy fantasy comedy about a straight-laced, widowed psychiatrist (Jamie Lee Curtis) and her rebellious teen-age daughter (Lindsay Lohan) who both wake up days before the mother is to be remarried only to find out that they have mysteriously swapped bodies thanks to magical fortune cookies. Well-crafted by director Mark S. Waters and buttressed by believable performances, this third retelling of Mary Rodgers' popular children's book navigates a minefield of cliches, while imparting a positive message about family values and generational respect. Complicated thematic elements and some mildly crude language
full_review:
A feuding mother and daughter get to view the generation gap from the flip side in the appealing fantasy-comedy "Freaky Friday" (Disney).

While the body-swapping premise has been well mined, including two previous film adaptations of the popular children's book by Mary Rodgers on which the movie is based -- the 1977 version starred a then-12 year old Jodie Foster -- director Mark S. Waters succeeds in giving this thematic chestnut enough of a contemporary spin to make it refreshingly entertaining.

As in any fable, the set-up is relatively simple: a mother, in this case straight-laced psychiatrist Tess Coleman (Jamie Lee Curtis), and her antithetical, rock 'n' roll daughter Anna (Lindsay Lohan) wake up one morning to find themselves each trapped in the other's body. They quickly trace the mystical mischief back to a pair of magical fortune cookies given to them during a heated argument at a Chinatown eatery.

Much of their preceding and ensuing bickering revolves around typical generational grievances -- each thinking the other's life is a relative cakewalk -- fueled by pricklier contentions.

Tess, a widow about to remarry, doesn't understand why Anna won't warm up to her doting fiance, Ryan (Mark Harmon), while Anna questions her mom's support of her high-decibel musical aspirations, especially when her garage band's performance at a local heavy metal showcase would necessitate Anna skipping out on Tess' rehearsal dinner. With the wedding less than 48 hours away, both mother and daughter desperately try to figure a way out of their cosmic conundrum and reverse the spell.

Obviously, the body-switch device offers a fertile arena for comedy. Tess, now wearing the body-pierced shell of a 15-year-old, gets a taste of high school again in all its sweet-and-sour splendor, including vindictive teachers, catty cheerleaders and that all-time academic bugbear -- pi. Not that it is all bad. She also gets to binge on fast food without counting calories and place some maternal speed bumps in the path of Jake (Chad Michael Murray), the edgy biker-boy Anna is pining over.

Conversely, Anna, trapped in her mom's menopausal skin, must contend with Tess' neurotic patients -- a load lightened by a visit to a hip boutique, where she gives her mom's body a complete hair and wardrobe overhaul. She also turns an appearance on a TV talk show, on which Tess was supposed to plug her new book, into a giant mosh pit.

Despite its farcical premise, the movie imparts a valuable message about the importance of family and understanding between the generations, evenhandedly exposing the prejudices while celebrating the differences of each. By viewing the world through each other's eyes, both Tess and Anna earn a deeper appreciation of and respect for one another -- a lesson in tolerance that transcends generation gap issues, equally applicable to political and even religious conflicts.

Also commendable is the story's insistence that the fortune cookie's spell can only be broken by an act of selfless love, a Brothers Grimm-like device that complements the film's contemporary fairy tale tone.

The movie's conceit hinges on the actresses' ability to make the body-swap believable. Full of goofy energy, Curtis seems in her element letting loose as the adult-sized adolescent. Lohan is equally convincing as the dowdy shrink immured in the perils of puberty.

Unlike much of summer fluff fare, "Freaky Friday" neither insults viewers' intelligence nor offends their sensibilities. It is charming and sweet without being overly sentimental, leaving viewers less likely to gag on its cliche moments.

The film also touches on peoples' growing inability to communicate, despite ever-evolving modes of communication. Through much of the film Tess is unable to break through Anna's defenses and really connect with her. The spotlight of irony is cast on this communication problem when Tess is shown filling her pocketbook with an assortment of cell phones, pagers and Palm Pilots -- the accoutrements of modern society, a world of individuals increasingly isolated by their interconnectedness.

Due to complicated thematic elements and some mildly crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

title: Freaky Friday
synopsis: Mother and teenage daughter (Barbara Harris and Jodie Foster) vehemently wish to trade places for a single day, only to have the wish granted to their mutual discomfiture. Gary Nelson directs a typical Disney slapstick comedy bolstered by good performances in the leads

title: Freckles
synopsis: Earnest but tedious tale directed by Andrew V. McLaglen follows the adventures of a one-armed Chicago youth (Martin West) as he gets a job with a small Western logging company, then saves it from an enterprising gang of timber thieves. Well-intentioned but painfully slow and uninvolving

title: Freckles Comes Home
synopsis: Formula homespun adventure in which the title character (Johnny Downs) returns from college, then saves his small Indiana town from a swindler (Bradley Page), getting help along the way from his high school girlfriend (Gale Storm) and a bumbling sheriff (Irving Bacon). Some stylized violence

title: Fred Claus
synopsis: Generally funny yet bittersweet tale of a sad-sack Chicago repo man (Vince Vaughn) who travels to the North Pole to help his younger, more popular brother, St. Nicholas (Paul Giamatti), at Christmas, while a devious efficiency expert (Kevin Spacey) threatens to shut down the elves' toy factory. Underneath the laughs, Dan Fogelman's script is a surprisingly resonant take on sibling rivalry, with lots of heart-tugging sentiment, and solid messages about family, self-esteem, forgiveness and ultimately redemption. Under David Dobkin's deft direction, there's sharp work by the leads and the classy supporting cast (Miranda Richardson, Rachel Weisz, Kathy Bates and John Michael Higgins). Mild innuendo, an implied premarital living arrangement, a suggestive costume, and some crass humor and expressions
full_review:
The holiday season gets off to a surprisingly delightful start with "Fred Claus" (Warner Bros.), a generally funny yet bittersweet tale about Santa Claus, aka St. Nicholas (Paul Giamatti), and his older, neglected brother, Fred (Vince Vaughn).

Ever since childhood (portrayed in a fairy-tale setting), Fred, a quiet, good-natured boy, had been in Nick's more showily gregarious, always smiling, shadow. With all of this, baby Nick became the apple of their mother's (Kathy Bates) eye. Once Nicholas became a saint, so the story's conceit goes, neither he nor his family would ever age.

Cut to present-day Chicago where Fred works as a repo man, as we observe him hauling away a pampered little girl's prized plasma TV. Things are tough financially for Fred, who is also out of sorts with meter-maid girlfriend Wanda (Rachel Weisz), who is frustrated by Fred's commitment-phobic ways.

Fred turns to Nick for monetary help, and the latter offers him a job getting out the children's toys for Christmas, so Fred is whisked to the North Pole (good special effects) by sleigh-driving elf Willie (John Michael Higgins). Once at the toy factory, he shakes things up in his affable blue-collar manner, including countermanding DJ Donnie's (Ludacris) one-song repertoire of "Here Comes Santa Claus" which Fred finds wearying.

Childhood rivalries underscore the brothers' day-to-day relationship, and are not helped by the unspoken disapproval that Mrs. Claus (Miranda Richardson) has for her brother-in-law.

Nick's biggest concern, however, is the presence of cold-hearted efficiency expert Clyde Northcutt (Kevin Spacey), who, it is patently obvious, plans to close down Santa's entire operation if Nick chalks up three infractions.

You just know Fred will eventually save the day, along with helping pint-sized Willie woo his statuesque lady love Charlene (Elizabeth Banks) and supply a troubled street kid (Bobb'e J. Thompson) with a good many life lessons in the process.

Underneath the laughs, Dan Fogelman's script proves a surprisingly resonant take on sibling rivalry, with plenty of heart-tugging sentiment. The laughs are there, including a hilarious bit where Fred attends a Siblings Anonymous meeting, with some surprising cameos (which we shan't spoil) among its frustrated members.

Vaughn and Giamatti give finely shaded, appealing performances, and Spacey has great fun with his dastardly villain role.

Though secular in thrust, the film is careful to avoid irreverence, and a well-timed underscoring of "Silent Night" at a crucial moment provides added resonance. Despite the emphasis on making all the toys, it is ultimately the act of giving -- and the importance of family at that time of year -- that is given most prominence.

Besides those themes, there are solid messages about self-esteem and the importance of forgiveness. David Dobkin's deft direction keeps the film well paced, though the film seems to end twice before coming to its actual conclusion.

There's nothing overtly objectionable for any age group (apart from the items below, the most egregious of which is the talk of Fred and Wanda "living together"), but the story is probably too sophisticated for very young viewers.

Time will tell whether the film earns classic status. But for now, despite its flaws, it's a warmhearted winner.

The film contains mild innuendo, an implied premarital living arrangement, a suggestive costume, and some crass humor and expressions. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested. Some material may not be suitable for children.

title: Freddy's Dead: The Final Nightmare
synopsis: Hideous Freddy Krueger (Robert Englund) continues to lure teenagers into suicidal nightmares until he is vanquished by his revenge-inspired daughter (Lisa Zane). Director Rachel Talalay spends more time on dream imagery and special effects than actual murders but the movie is still designed to invite laughter at adolescents being tortured and viciously slaughtered. Deadly violence depicted as entertaining and recurring rough language

title: Freddy vs. Jason
synopsis: Dreadful slasher flick pitting "Nightmare on Elm Street's" Freddy Krueger (Robert Englund) against Jason (Ken Kirzinger), the hockey-masked killing machine of "Friday the 13th." Buckets of blood flow in this mindless exercise in gory excess, directed by Ronny Yu, which alarmingly exploits carnage as entertainment. Pervasive graphic violence, teen sexual encounters with nudity, recurring drug abuse, as well as much rough language and profanity
full_review:
Just when you thought it had dredged the dregs of the summer movie barrel, Hollywood serves up a double helping of gore in the abysmally dreadful slasherfest "Freddy vs. Jason" (New Line).

Hoping to make a killing at the box office by cross-pollinating two of the most successful horror franchises, director Ronny Yu delivers, in a flick boasting Freddy and Jason, the biggest "hack job."

At the risk of dignifying this execrable exercise in bloody excess, the plot -- or what passes as one -- goes something like this: Freddy Krueger (Robert Englund), the sadistic sandman of "A Nightmare on Elm Street" infamy, is trapped in hell.

After seven increasingly ridiculous films, the parents of Springwood have wised up and taken pharmaceutical measures to prevent the town's teen-age residents from dreaming, effectively denying Freddy entree into their nocturnal noggins and systemically erasing the collective memory of his heinous crimes.

Having been rendered impotent, Freddy is left with little to do with his satanic sabbatical but plot revenge, which, in one of the film's many ludicrous conceits, involves enlisting the service of Jason Voorhees (Ken Kirzinger), the hockey-masked killing machine of "Friday the 13th" renown. Freddy, disguised as Jason's domineering mother, convinces him to take his own brand of misanthropic mischief to Elm Street in order to raise some hell -- literally -- thus paving the way for the dream demon's return.

The remainder of the derivative drivel -- which steals unapologetically from the "Big Book of Slasher Cliches" -- is nothing more than a formulaic series of graphic slayings, as Freddy and Jason go on a killing spree, engaging in a grisly game of one-upmanship, mowing down Springwood's preternaturally good-looking, oversexed teen populace.

Of course, Jason has too much fun to just bow out quietly once he has raised the townspeople's fear factor sufficiently enough to trigger nightmares -- releasing Freddy from his purgatorial imprisonment and leading to an all-out, no-holds-barred showdown between the two homicidal heavyweights.

The film's pairing of screen villains is not new to the horror genre, which has boasted twin bills ranging from the entertainingly atmospheric "Frankenstein Meets the Wolf Man" (1943) to such late-night fodder as "Dracula vs. Frankenstein" (1971) and "King Kong vs. Godzilla" (1962). But unlike these midnight movies, "Freddy vs. Jason" is something much darker than studio execs hoping to capitalize on offering two maniacs for the price of one.

The film is driven by a repulsive impulse to treat graphic violence as entertainment. Classic horror movies portrayed their respective fiends as misunderstood outcasts. More often than not it was they who were destroyed by cruel intolerance, thus gaining viewers' sympathy. But in films such as this one, serial killers are treated like rock stars, cheered on by enthusiastic fans every time they rack up another notch on their machete, earning bonus points if the method of slaughter employed is exceptionally gruesome.

Part and parcel with this coarsening is the film's promotion of substance abuse and casual sex -- both staples of the slasher milieu. However in a genre that prides itself on its lowest-common-denominator mentality, "Freddy vs. Jason" lowers the bar by including a scene in which a local slacker violates a drunken girl passed out in a cornfield.

The film also endorses a disheartening suspicion of and antagonism toward authority figures, especially parents, a thematic bedrock of horror flicks dating back to the 1950s.

The film ends with a wink -- literally -- strongly hinting that, like their implacable protagonists, these franchises just won't die; that's bad news except for those who own stock in the company that manufactures fake blood. Several of Freddy's victims plead to be awakened from their nightmares -- an unlikely request from anyone lucky enough to doze off during this bad dream.

Due to pervasive graphic violence, teen sexual encounters with nudity, recurring drug abuse, as well as much rough language and profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Freebie and the Bean
synopsis: Two freewheeling San Francisco cops careen dangerously around the city to protect a mobster they plan to arrest when the time is ripe for a promotion. In director Richard Rush's failed comedy, Bean (Alan Arkin) and Freebie (James Caan) are gun-crazy psychopaths who enjoy indulging their penchant for foul language, ethnic slurs, kinky sex and beating up hapless individuals whenever they get a chance

title: Freedomland
synopsis: Overheated and grim melodrama about an emotionally fragile woman (Julianne Moore) who says she was carjacked near a predominantly black housing project, with her assailant taking off in the car with her son in the back seat, and the police detective (Samuel L. Jackson) who attempts to uncover the truth while keeping racial tensions at bay. Joe Roth's film, based on Richard Price's bestseller, is finely acted by its two leads and by Edie Falco as the head of a missing-children advocacy group, but despite a worthy premise, a redemptive ending, and a central character imbued with a strong faith the movie is undermined by plot contrivances. Much profanity and rough language, racial epithets, riot violence, some blood, drug references, an intense emotional breakdown, an unwed mother, adultery, domestic and child abuse, a fall from a window
full_review:
In 1936, Luise Rainer won her first of two Academy Awards for her solitary emoting over the phone in "The Great Ziegfeld." If Oscars voters still reward such histrionics (and why not?), both Julianne Moore and Edie Falco can dust off their mantles right now, for each gets to deliver a knockout monologue.

Otherwise, though, "Freedomland" (Columbia) is an overheated, not to mention grim, melodrama that doesn't quite work.

The time is 1999, the place a predominantly African-American housing project in fictional Dempsy, N.J. Police detective Lorenzo Council (Samuel L. Jackson) has his hands full, keeping the peace between the project's residents and the white police force in the neighboring blue-collar town of Gannon.

When the film begins, a dazed working-class woman from Gannon, Brenda Martin (Moore in her grittiest performance yet), who has a job in an after-school program in the project, wanders into a hospital with bloodied hands. She claims she was driving near the project and was forced to get out of her car at gunpoint, thrown down to the ground, and the assailant drove off in her car with her 4-year-old boy in the back seat.

The veteran Lorenzo is assigned to protect her and get to the bottom of the abduction, though he is convinced Brenda -- who once had a drug problem -- is concealing the full truth. Despite his reservations about her, he treats her kindly, and at several points articulates a strong belief in God's will. "Let go, let God," "God always finds a way to give you another shot," and "God's grace is retroactive" are not maxims you hear in most mainstream films.

We learn later that Lorenzo's equanimity has come from having had some demons of his own, including a jailed son.

Matters are not helped by Brenda's hot-blooded Gannon police detective brother, Danny (Ron Eldard), with a bluntly provocative manner, prompting Lorenzo to work all the harder keeping racial tensions at bay.

Karen Collucci (a brunette Falco looking quite unlike her Carmela Soprano character), who heads a missing-children activist group -- her own child went missing years before -- offers the group's services to Lorenzo, who reluctantly accepts. The team then sets out to a long-abandoned youth center called Freedomland, located in a wooded area, where children had once been abused, hoping the terrible ghosts of the past may trigger some revelation from Brenda.

Eventually, the story of the child's disappearance will be revealed, but only after tensions between the two neighborhoods boil over into violence.

Director Joe Roth's film, based on Richard Price's bestseller, is finely acted by its two leads. As the asthmatic middle-aged detective, Jackson gives an effortlessly powerful performance, and Moore, whose real fireworks come near the end of the film, is convincingly fragile throughout. Falco also credibly limns a woman hurt by the past.

But despite such worthy themes as the futility of racial hatred and the cruelty of child abuse, a redemptive ending, and a central character imbued with a strong faith, Price's screenplay is undermined by plot contrivances and a heightened sense of hysteria that seems phony. The film has nowhere near the emotional payoff of the similarly themed "Crash."

In addition to Lorenzo's strong spirituality, there's a brief but reverent portrayal of a priest by actor Philip Bosco.

The street language used throughout, though dramatically justified given the milieu, will offend many viewers, but violence is kept to a minimum.

The film contains much profanity and rough language, racial epithets, riot violence, some blood, drug references, an intense emotional breakdown, an unwed mother, adultery, domestic and child abuse, and a fall from a window. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Freedom on My Mind
synopsis: Compelling documentary recalls the civil rights struggle in the early 1960s to register black voters in the segregated State of Mississippi. Produced and directed by Connie Field and Marilyn Mulford, the tautly edited archival footage, intercut with frank commentary by those who were actively involved in the movement, provides a chilling portrait of institutionalized racism as well as heartening testimony to the power of committed individuals to effect change. Scenes of racial violence

title: Freedom to Love
synopsis: Presented in the form of a serious examination of sexual freedom, interspersed with some shallow commentary, the movie is merely a poor excuse to present scenes of graphic sex and nudity

title: Freedom Writers
synopsis: Classroom drama about the efforts of an idealistic, novice high school English teacher (Hilary Swank) to transform a racially divided class of troubled teens into model students by inspiring them to believe in themselves and break the cycle of gang violence in which they feel trapped. As a way of empowering them, she has them record their personal stories, experiences and feelings in journals, which they eventually get published. Director Richard LaGravenese overcomes a predictable and, at times, message-heavy script with emotionally powerful performances by the young ensemble and redemptive themes of self-worth, the efficacy of education and empathy to overcome intolerance, and the ability of one person to make a difference. Some graphic violence, including shootings, beatings and brief but disturbing images of domestic abuse, a divorce subplot, one instance of the f-word, recurring crude language and a few racial slurs, limiting its appropriateness to older adolescents and up
full_review:
January is traditionally used by Hollywood studios to quietly dump their clunkers while moviegoers are still too bleary-eyed from holiday reveling to notice. So it comes as a pleasant surprise that the first week of the new year brings "Freedom Writers" (Paramount), an unexpectedly good classroom drama in the tradition of "Dangerous Minds" and "Stand and Deliver."

Based on true events, the gritty but ultimately uplifting story centers on the efforts of an idealistic, novice high school English teacher, Erin Gruwell (Hilary Swank), to transform a racially divided class of troubled teens into model students by inspiring them to believe in themselves and break the cycle of gang violence in which they feel trapped.

As a way of empowering them, she has the students record their personal stories, experiences and feelings in journals, which they will eventually get published under the collective title "Freedom Writers," inspired by the civil rights-era Freedom Riders. She also has them read "The Diary of Anne Frank," sensing they will identify with the Jewish teen's tragic tale.

Her unconventional teaching methods and unswerving faith in her students draw resentment from the other faculty members, including department head Margaret Campbell (Imelda Staunton), while her all-consuming dedication takes its toll on her marriage to husband Scott (Patrick Dempsey).

Director Richard LaGravenese overcomes a predictable and, at times, message-heavy script with emotionally powerful performances by the young ensemble and redemptive themes of self-worth, the efficacy of education and empathy to overcome intolerance, and the ability of one person to make a difference.

The film contains some graphic street violence, including shootings, beatings and brief but disturbing images of domestic abuse, a divorce subplot, one instance of the f-word, recurring crude language and a few racial slurs, limiting its appropriateness to older adolescents and up. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Freejack
synopsis: Ultraviolent, futuristic tale of a race car driver (Emilio Estevez) pursued by a ruthless killer (Mick Jagger) intent on selling the racer's body to a dying magnate (Anthony Hopkins). Director Geoff Murphy just marks time with his cast between the bloody shootouts that are the movie's only apparent reason for having been made. Excessive violence, implied live-in relationship and occasional rough language

title: Free Willy
synopsis: After befriending a killer whale trapped in a cramped marine park, a rebellious 12-year-old (Jason James Richter) persuades his foster parents (Michael Madsen and Jayne Atkinson) and two park workers (Lori Petty and August Schellenberg) to help free the giant animal before it is killed for the insurance money. Director Simon Wincer's beguiling relationship story affirms family values, though it must be noted the adults cavalierly break the law in saving the whale. Fleeting violence

title: Free Willy 2: The Adventure Home
synopsis: In this spirited sequel, the now 14-year-old youth (Jason James Richter) joins forces with his 8-year-old half-brother (Francis Capra) to rescue the trapped killer whale he had befriended two years earlier and, in turn, the whale saves him from a perilous situation. Director Dwight Little combines exceptional nature photography with an incident-filled narrative and uplifting values for a pleasing family film. Young children may be frightened by scenes of other youngsters in jeopardy

title: Free Willy 3: The Rescue
synopsis: Tired sequel in which the lad (Jason James Richter) who befriended the title whale attempts to protect him and his pregnant mate from being harpooned by a deadly whaler pursuing them on the high seas. Although the wildlife photography is still stunning, director Sam Pillsbury generates little suspense in the narrative and the boy-with-whale footage has become overly familiar. Brief barroom brawl and some rationalization of misdeeds

title: Free Woman, A
synopsis: German drama of a woman (Margarethe von Trotta) struggling for self-identity and fulfillment following her divorce and bitter court battle for custody of her little boy. Directed by Volker Schlondorff, it seethes with a restrained anger that leads to occasionally brutal characterizations of male stereotypes but avoids the pitfalls of exploiting women in the process

title: Freeze-Die-Come to Life
synopsis: The foolhardy pranks of a young Russian boy (Pavel Nazarov) living nearby Stalin's World War II labor camps put him and his friend (Dinara Drukarova) in peril from both state authorities and a gang of cutthroat thieves. Director Vitaly Kanevski's grimly autobiographical account depicts life reduced to the level of self-preservation where children find little warmth and are quickly hardened. Subtitles. Several instances of violence, nudity and minimal rough language

title: French Connection II
synopsis: Gene Hackman repeats his role as fanatical detective Popeye Doyle in a sequel set in France and directed by John Frankenheimer. Not nearly as successful as its predecessor, the movie is marred by its ambivalent attitude towards Doyle's ruthless methods, some strong violence and rough language

title: French Connection, The
synopsis: Tough, unorthodox New York detective Popeye Doyle (Gene Hackman) and his partner (Roy Scheider) track down a massive heroin cache in this tense, exciting, very violent look at the darker side of law enforcement. Director William Friedkin makes excellent use of New York City locations in giving his fast-paced story the grimy look of reality and the acting of the leads is first-rate. The violent action and language are in the context of a sobering, perhaps shocking, portrayal of the kill-or-be-killed undercover world of cops and dope dealers

title: French Conspiracy, The
synopsis: Dramatic re-creation of the events in a political scandal that rocked the French government in the late 1960s when Ben Barka, a Moroccan revolutionary exile, was kidnapped in France with the apparent complicity and cooperation of some French officials. Directed by Yves Boisset, the result is not an espionage thriller, but rather a careful exposition of the intelligence community that operates beneath the surface of modern governments. Stars Gian-Maria Volonte, Michael Piccoli, and Jean-Louis Trintignant

title: French Cousins, The
synopsis: ( see: "From Ear to Ear" )

title: French Detective, The
synopsis: Gallic version of an American police thriller features a tough cop (Lino Ventura) and his young assistant (Patrick Dewaere) who encounter a dishonest political machine while investigating a murder. Director Pierre Granier-Deferre spends too much time on philosophical exchanges between his policemen by Hollywood standards but its abuse of citizen's rights are familiar enough to American moviegoers. There is enough violence and moral ambiguity to make it adult fare

title: French Kiss
synopsis: Dizzy romantic comedy in which an uptight housewife-to-be (Meg Ryan) jets to Paris to save her callow fiance (Timothy Hutton) from a French siren, getting help along the way from a scheming French thief (Kevin Kline) whose crass outlook on life naturally masks a sensitive soul. Director Lawrence Kasdan's attempts to be bright and witty come over as merely slick and superficial, further handicapped by an unamusing series of altercations between scorned woman and Gallic opportunist. Some sexual situations and innuendo, occasional coarse expressions and several instances of rough language

title: French Lessons
synopsis: Producer David Puttnam's somewhat anachronistic romance details the first sexual experience of a British exchange student in Paris. Jane Snowden gives a sensitive portrayal of the youth experimenting in adult responsibilites but the dialogue is so awful and the script so woefully inadequate that the movie never achieves any credibility

title: French Lieutenant's Woman, The
synopsis: Scripwriter Harold Pinter's adaptation of the John Fowles' novel uses a movie-within-a-movie gimmick so that the story of a wealthy gentleman's pursuit of a mysterious governess in the Victorian Age also becomes a tale of two performers carrying on an adulterous affair in the present. Meryl Streep and Jeremy Irons play the dual roles of the lovers. Director Karel Reisz' result is interesting, but too pretentious and humorless for its own good. Rather graphic bedroom scene

title: French Line, The
synopsis: Leaden musical romance in which a Texas oil millionairess (Jane Russell) ducks fortune hunters on an ocean liner to Europe by hiring a woman to pose as her, then falls for a Frenchman (Gilbert Roland) who turns out to be more interested in her stand-in until voyage's end. Directed by Lloyd Bacon, the slow-paced proceedings grow tiresome with predictable comic complications and clunky musical numbers. Sexual situations and innuendo

title: Frenchman's Creek
synopsis: Romantic potboiler from Daphne du Maurier's novel in which a nobleman's wife (Joan Fontaine) flees 1668 London to escape her husband's lecherous friend (Basil Rathbone), arrives at the family's long-vacant manor on the coast of Cornwall and falls for the French pirate (Arturo de Cordova) using it as his base. Director Mitchell Leisen gets some gusto in the period action scenes but the romantic proceedings are woodenly acted and emotionally contrived. Stylized violence, implied marital infidelity and a tacked-on moral ending

title: French Postcards
synopsis: Lighthearted but aimless movie about a trio of American students in Paris (Miles Chapin, Blanche Baker and David Marshall Grant) and their various amorous misadventures. Director Willard Huyck's episodic, listless and anti-intellectual effort seeks unearned viewer sympathy for feckless youths whose acting ability seems more suited to amateur night at the fraternity house. The movie's implicit endorsement of sexual promiscuity makes it unacceptable entertainment

title: French Provincial
synopsis: Interesting French melodrama about a seamstress (Jeanne Moreau) who marries into a bourgeois family in the South of France and becomes the one who holds it together from the early 1930s to the 1970s. Director Andre Techine integrates the episodic family chronicle within the larger frame of the changes taking place within France during that period

title: French Way, The
synopsis: ( see: "Love at the Top" )

title: Frenzy
synopsis: Alfred Hitchcock's masterful suspense thriller focuses on a deranged strangler preying on women in contemporary London. The central character is an innocent man (Jon Finch) whose careless way of living implicates him as the serial murderer who dispatches his victims by means of a characteristic necktie, with accompanying perverse violence. The suspense is built on whether the wrong man will be punished for the crimes, something which is not resolved until the very last moment. Though of the same caliber as Hitchcock's best works, it lamentably resorts to some very explicit violence and brief nudity

title: Frequency
synopsis: Because of some harsh violence, a few disturbing images and fleeting crass language,

title: Fresh
synopsis: Disturbing story of a 12-year-old drug courier (Sean Nelson) who aims to take his addicted sister (N'Bushe Wright) out of their Brooklyn 'hood by pitting rival drug lords against each other, then offering to testify against them in exchange for admission to the Witness Protection program. Writer-director Boaz Yakin spares viewers no end of vicious, foul-mouthed characters in a harrowing narrative about the limited options an African-American youth has for survival in a poisonous environment of deadly violence. Some stylized violence, brief nudity and incessant rough language with frequent racial and sexual slurs

title: Fresh Horses
synopsis: A college senior (Andrew McCarthy) drops his wealthy fiancee for a rural girl (Molly Ringwald) too young, uneducated and married to give him anything but grief. In this moodpiece about obsession, director David Anspaugh provides little understanding of the characters and ignores intriguing plotlines. Off-camera illicit sex, brief violence and minimal rough language

title: Freshman Orientation
synopsis: Confusion, if not hilarity, ensues when a college freshman (Sam Huntington) poses as gay in order to befriend a sorority pledge (Kaitlin Doubleday) and win her away from her frat-brother-ex-boyfriend (Bryce Johnson); along the way, he's instructed in gay culture by a local bartender (John Goodman), nearly exposed by an ex-girlfriend (Marla Sokoloff), and gains the unsought affection of his roommate (Mike Erwin). Writer-director Ryan Shiraki's comic venture, a tale of sexual anarchy, suffers from a heavy-handed script and is more glum than amusing. Extensive sexual activity, rear and upper female nudity, brief pornographic imagery, a suicide and pervasive rough, crude and crass language
full_review:
Full Review

A tale of sexual anarchy on campus, "Freshman Orientation" (Regent) is intended to be a comedy. Yet a heavy-handed script -- together with the sad spectacle of a group of young people entrapped by their own desires -- renders writer-director Ryan Shiraki's film more glum than amusing.

College freshman Clay Adams (Sam Huntington) arrives at his new school determined to succeed with women. He soon sets his sights on Amanda (Kaitlin Doubleday), an aloof sorority pledge.

When Amanda is instructed to make a gay man fall in love with her as part of her initiation, Clay recognizes this as an opportunity to get to know her, and so pretends to be homosexual. He receives lessons in gay culture from Rodney (John Goodman), the owner of a local gay bar.

As Clay and Amanda become friends, complications multiply. Clay must contend with the hostile suspicions of Marjorie (Marla Sokoloff), an ex-girlfriend who has become a lesbian, and may blow his cover. Simultaneously, he must also stave off a reconciliation between Amanda and her ex, a fraternity brother named Tazwell (Bryce Johnson).

Amanda herself, meanwhile, is feeling confusion over her attraction to Clay, and guilt about the trick she's playing on him. Even worse off is Clay's roommate, Matt (Mike Erwin), who really is gay and has fallen for him.

When Clay becomes the victim of a supposed gay-bashing, protests erupt and chaos threatens to engulf the entire campus.

Although the film warns against stereotypes, it ends up reinforcing many of them. It also takes for granted that all sexual urges should be acted on, more or less without restraint.

Shiraki's hormonally driven screenplay is anything but humorous. And the seemingly ironic, though valid moral of the story -- that Clay and Amanda can build a strong personal rapport precisely because they are not having sex -- gets lost in the shuffle.

The film contains extensive sexual activity, rear and upper female nudity, brief pornographic imagery, a suicide and pervasive rough, crude and crass language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Freshman, The
synopsis: Shortly after arriving in New York City, a college freshman (Matthew Broderick) is bewildered to find himself involved with a Godfather-like businessman (Marlon Brando), his marriage-minded daughter, a giant lizard, federal agents and the threat of jail. Writer-director Andrew Bergman serves up an amiable comedy more distinguished by an amusing cast than the story's less-than-riveting dialogue and perfunctory pacing. Minimal rough language

title: Freud
synopsis: Earnest, plodding drama recounts the turning point for Dr. Sigmund Freud (Montgomery Clift) as a neurologist in 1885 Vienna where his treatment of a troubled patient (Susannah York) leads to his theory of childhood sexual repression, a concept rejected by his closest colleague (Larry Parks) and scorned by his peers. Director John Huston's dramatization of psychiatry's beginnings may be simplistic, especially the dream sequences, but demonstrates the limitations of the physical sciences in treating emotional disorders. Though handled with sensitivity, the subject matter may be distasteful for some viewers

title: Frida
synopsis: Visually stunning but morally troubling biography of Mexican surrealist artist Frida Kahlo (Salma Hayek) centers on not only how she painted her painful life experiences but on her enduring love for her husband, famed muralist Diego Rivera (Alfred Molina), whose flagrant promiscuity prompted her to engage in meaningless affairs with both sexes during their 25-year marriage. Directed with theatrical flair by Julie Taymor, the bold sexual content belies a theme of harmful infidelity and the couple's hard-won unconditional love despite considering themselves as artists unconcerned with traditional morality. Heterosexual and homosexual encounters with nudity, sporadic rough language and fleeting violence
full_review:
Salma Hayek gives a feisty performance in the title role of "Frida" (Miramax), a glossy dramatization about Mexican folk artist Frida Kahlo, who lived a short but passionate life of politics, sex and art.

A 1925 bus crash left the rebellious 18-year-old horribly injured after a metal rod pierced her hip, exited her groin, and portions of her skeleton were shattered. Though Frida is bedridden in a body cast, her parents encouraged her artistic talent, designing an easel and mirror positioned above her so she could paint -- with herself as a model. Frida had begun a lifetime of pouring her physical and then emotional pain into her vivid, surrealistic art in which she was often the subject of the canvas.

The movie, however, focuses just as much on her volatile relationship with famed muralist Diego Rivera (Alfred Molina in fine form), the mentor she married in 1929 despite her Catholic mother's protest (after reminding her mother that she herself chose to marry a Jewish man). Her mother objected to the 21-year age difference, Diego's atheism and his scandalous reputation.

Diego had inspired Frida's artistic ambitions, shared her left-wing politics and divorced his wife (Valeria Golino) to marry her. He also made it clear she would have his loyalty but not his fidelity, as he had no intention of reining in his womanizing ways. Intellectually, Frida accepts this nonsense about loyalty but soon jealousy and rage well up and she begins having casual affairs with both men and women. In spite of being devastated by her husband's promiscuity, she chooses to inflict the same hurt on the man she loves the most.

As directed by Julie Taymor, the film celebrates Frida's life's struggle without judging her promiscuity or bisexuality. This is troubling, yet what clearly emerges is how harmful marital infidelity was to both Frida and Diego. This is most apparent when Frida discovers Diego and her own beloved sister (Mia Maestro) are sleeping together, rupturing their close sibling relationship and bringing more pain to all three. However, through all the recriminations and separations (including a divorce and remarriage to each other) the two came to realize theirs was an enduring connection that ultimately led to unconditional love. In showing the unhappy consequences of adultery, the movie offers a cautionary note and suggests that the old chestnut that artists are not bound by traditional morality doesn't mean they won't suffer as a result.

Taymor, who brought "The Lion King" to Broadway, uses creative filmmaking techniques to incorporate Kahlo's paintings into the narrative, using animation and even puppetry in an impressive command of cinematic language. She directs with a flair for theatricality and spectacle in vivid colors that reflect Kahlo's preferred palette. The paintings shown convey Kahlo's very personal, primitive and socially conscious view of the world.

The movie is dense with incident: the startlingly filmed bus accident and her recovery; the couple's time in New York City where Diego is incensed when his patron, Nelson Rockefeller (Edward Norton), has the figure of Lenin removed from his mural; Frida's miscarriage; her affair with Leon Trotsky (an unconvincing Geoffrey Rush); and eventual devotion between Frida and Diego after her leg is amputated. In a touching moment at this point, Diego, though protesting he doesn't believe in God, nonetheless thanks him for having Frida in his life.

Hayek, herself a Mexican, is luminous in the role, an apt choice to play a fiery Latina. As a co-producer of the film which took years to get to the screen, it was a labor of love and a tribute to the artists of her homeland. One gets a better sense of Frida than of Diego, whose character comes across primarily as a hedonist with his own art left in the background.

Never less than visually involving, "Frida" is an audacious portrait of two flawed individuals, artists whose lives were ruled by often reckless passion.

Due to heterosexual and homosexual encounters with nudity, sporadic rough language and fleeting violence, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Friday
synopsis: An unemployed black youth (Ice Cube) and his pothead pal (Chris Tucker) spend the day in their South Central neighborhood of Los Angeles swapping wisecracks while observing the antics of their neighbors, ogling females, eluding a drug dealer and tangling with the local bully. Directed by Gary Gray, the low-budget production strings together a series of crude comedy sketches about ghetto life, most of which viewers will find appalling rather than amusing, though at least it doesn't glamorize guns and drugs. Sexual innuendo, bathroom humor, stylized violence, pot smoking and incessant rough language

title: Friday After Next
synopsis: Witless sequel set on Christmas Eve as two foul-mouthed cousins (Ice Cube and Mike Epps) are robbed, get fired as security guards and throw a party after which they catch the masked Santa who ripped them off. Director Marcus Raboy's crudely shrill comedy presents a negative, cliche-ridden portrait of African-Americans that is more deplorable than amusing. Positive depiction of recreational drug use, constant rough language, intermittent profanity, some violence, sexual situations with gross references, frequent racial epithets, stereotyping and toilet humor
full_review:
Three times is definitely not the charm when it comes to "Friday After Next," New Line's sequel to the Ice Cube vehicles -- 1995's "Friday" and 2000's "Next Friday."

As haphazardly directed by Marcus Raboy, and again written and produced by Ice Cube, the indulgent depiction of recreational drug use is not funny given the reality of how many lives have been disastrously affected by substance abuse. Nor are the racial epithets and the stereotyping of African-Americans an enjoyable element of this crude comedy.

The film takes place in Los Angeles on Christmas Eve, as cousins and roommates Craig (Ice Cube) and Day-Day (Mike Epps) awake to find a masked Santa absconding with their presents and the rent money. The clueless cousins head off to their new jobs as strip-mall security guards but are more interested in smoking joints in the alley, and their older-but-no-wiser uncle (Don "D.C." Curry) joins right in. The cops who checked out the robbery complaint are also seen smoking dope in their police car.

Meanwhile back at home the pair's landlady (BeBe Drake) breaks into their apartment and steals some of their weed for herself while her pumped-up ex-con son (Terry Crews) looks forward to assaulting the twosome if they don't fork over the rent money.

The foul-mouthed cousins get fired by the end of the day and throw a party where the ex-con attempts to attack a puny pimp (Katt Williams) but finds himself on the receiving end of an extended scene of genital torture. The stream of toilet humor, punctuated by the ever-present four-letter words, is another abrasive element of the picture.

It all adds up to a pretty miserable excuse for a movie in which, according to the press notes, "Craig and Day-Day learn about the true meaning of the holiday season." They must have edited that scene out.

Due to a positive depiction of recreational drug use, constant rough language, intermittent profanity, some violence, sexual situations with gross references, frequent racial epithets, stereotyping and toilet humor, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Friday Foster
synopsis: Director Arthur Marks wastes some talented performers (Yaphet Kotto, Godfrey Cambridge, Eartha Kitt and Pam Grier) in a black exploitation number adapted from a comic strip but without whatever depth and subtlety the original may have had. Excessive sex and violence

title: Friday Night Lights
synopsis: Hard-hitting drama about a season in the life of a small-town high school football team (coached by Billy Bob Thornton) as it struggles to make it to the Texas state championship. Based on the nonfiction best seller by H.G. Bissinger and directed by Peter Berg, the film is an engrossing, at times unsettling, portrait of the lives and fragile dreams of young athletes which exposes the unhealthy pressure-cooker environment where teenagers are asked to shoulder the expectations of an entire community. Much football violence, some underage drinking, two sexual situations, one with partial nudity, an abusive father-son relationship and some crude language
full_review:
"Friday Night Lights" (Universal) is a hard-hitting drama about a season in the life of a small-town high school football team battling to make it to the Texas state championship.

Based on the nonfiction best seller by H.G. Bissinger, "Friday Night Lights" is not just a "sports movie" -- though virtually every frame of the film involves football -- but an engrossing, at times unsettling, portrait of the lives and fragile dreams of young athletes and their families in economically depressed communities across America.

The film chronicles the real-life 1988 magic carpet ride of the Permian Panthers, a team out of Odessa, a dusty, football-obsessed town in the west Texas flatlands.

Director Peter Berg quickly establishes Odessa's boom-to-bust fortunes through tableaus of silent oil rigs and boarded-up storefronts, all shot in desaturated tones for added bleak effect.

Contrasting the barren landscape are the bright lights of Ratliff Stadium, site of a weekly autumn ritual where rabid locals can forget about their dead-end existences by living vicariously through the gridiron glories of their home-town heroes: among them, taciturn quarterback Mike Winchell (Lucas Black), cocky all-star running back Boobie Miles (Derek Luke) and fumble-prone tailback Don Billingsley (Garrett Hedlund) who suffers abuse from his drunken and bitter ex-jock father (played convincingly by country singer Tim McGraw).

Feeling the most heat is Gary Gaines (Billy Bob Thornton), the team's second-year coach who knows that his head will be the first to roll if the team fails to "win state."

The season starts off on a high note with a lopsided win. It proves a Pyrrhic victory when, on the last play of the game, the hotshot Miles suffers a serious knee injury, sucking the wind out of the team's sails. But as one would expect in this type of Cinderella sports story, the players find the heart to rise to the occasion in their quest for the Texas state championship. To win the Lone Star laurels they will have to beat a physically superior squad from Dallas in a David vs. Goliath showdown.

While not without its crowd-pleasing moments, "Friday Night Lights" differs from most feel-good sports movies in that it exposes the unpleasant side of high-stakes amateur athletics: an unhealthy pressure cooker where teens are asked to shoulder the expectations of entire communities and where coaches are paid more than teachers.

Football fans will find much to cheer about during the film's intense game sequences, which, though at times disorienting, are bone-jarringly realistic. Conversely, those who view football as ritualized violence may find themselves cringing through much of the movie. And while it is sometimes difficult to tell who's who under all the equipment, the frenetic camerawork keeps the audience so close to the action that helmets should be required for viewing (which would help muffle the ear-splitting soundtrack).

Unlike the book which delves deeply into the players' lives -- with detours into oil politics and race relations -- the film, while touching on those issues, keeps its narrative focus on the playing field. However, given the limited number of scenes where the actors are not in shoulder pads, the characters are surprisingly fleshed-out and several scenes are quite poignant.

Though some viewers may feel the film contains unfair stereotypes, others will applaud its emphasis on teamwork and personal excellence over winning. Opinions will also vary concerning a halftime scene where both teams pray the "Our Father" in their respective locker rooms as a prelude to another round of skull bashing.

While lacking the sociological scope of Bissinger's book, as a movie these "Friday Night Lights" shine brightly.

Due to much football violence, some underage drinking, two sexual situations, one with partial nudity, an abusive father-son relationship and some crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Friday the 13th
synopsis: Homocidal maniac menaces teenagers at a summer camp. Crude, mindless exploitation cheapie directed by Sean S. Cunningham with much blood and violence and graphic sex scenes

title: Friday the 13th, Part II
synopsis: Disgusting horror sequel with the homicidal maniac once more stalking slow-witted camp counselors who have sex on their minds rather than self-preservation. Wholly uninspired direction and script are by Steve Miner and Ron Kurz, with the usual unhealthy mix of nudity and graphic violence

title: Friday the 13th, Part III
synopsis: The 3-D version directed by Steve Miner is no better than its predecessors in the blood and gore department

title: Friday the 13th, Part V -- A New Beginning
synopsis: Directed by Danny Steinmann, this time out Freddie the maniac stalks a home for disturbed children. Violent, gory horror flick whose only goal is to shock

title: Friday the 13th Part VIII -- Jason Takes Manhattan
synopsis: Sick horror show in which bionic corpse Jason (Kane Hodder) dismembers recent grads of Crystal Lake High on a tour ship bound for Manhattan and pursues the survivors into the subways and alleys of the Big Apple. Writer-director Rob Hedden zeroes in on every gory detail in a movie that also offers profanity, recreational teen cocaine use and fleeting nudity in a brief teen sexual encounter

title: Friday the 13th, Part VI: Jason Lives
synopsis: The demonic killer is brought back from the dead via a lightning bolt to torment, terrorize and molest the decendants of his killers. This excessively violent sequel, written and directed by Tom McLoughlin, consists of little more than a succession of bloody slaughter scenes with a little explicit sex between minors thrown in for good measure

title: Friday the 13th -- The Final Chapter
synopsis: Freddie the ghoulish maniac is on the loose again as director Joseph Zito fills the screen with the usual gore and violence mixed with crude language and much nudity

title: Frieda
synopsis: Just before World War II's end, a British airman (David Farrar) arrives home with a German bride (Mai Zetterling) whom he wed after she helped him escape a P.O.W. camp, but anti-German feelings of the locals drive her to attempt suicide. Directed by Basil Dearden, the well-crafted but slow-paced melodrama examines the theme of collective guilt fron a variety of angles, some uncomfortably close to Nazi racial doctrine. Stylized violence and anti-German sentiments

title: Fried Green Tomatoes
synopsis: The youthful reminiscences of a nursing home resident (Jessica Tandy) about an unsolved, half-century-old murder mystery involving two spunky Alabama women (Mary Stuart Masterson and Mary-Louise Parker) inspire her newfound friend, a frustrated Southern housewife (Kathy Bates), to put her own house in order. An initially sluggish script hampers director Jon Avnet's beautifully acted movie but can't submerge its warm-hearted tribute to friendship, female solidarity and respect for people of color. Very brief violence and a few sexual references

title: Friendly Persuasion
synopsis: Winning adaptation of Jessamyn West's novel about a Quaker household (Gary Cooper, Dorothy McGuire and Tony Perkins) at the time of the Civil War. Director William Wyler's lyric treatment of family life and human relationships heightens the conflict between the hard realities of the war and the pacifist convictions of the Quaker faith. Still a warm and cheering experience for family viewers

title: Friend of the Deceased, A
synopsis: Glumly comic tale set in Kiev, Ukraine, where an unemployed translator (Alexandre Lazarev) hires a hit man to kill him, then changes his mind but has no way to cancel the contract except by hiring another hit man to kill the first one. Director Vyacheslav Krishtofovich creates grim social satire out of the economic instablity in post-communist Ukraine, which is seen as having left ordinary people adrift without a moral compass. Subtitles. Brief violence, fleeting nudity and sexual situati ons

title: Friend of the Family
synopsis: Weak French comedy directed by Robert Thomas about a toy inventor (Pierre Dux) and his wife (Danielle Darrieux) whose serenity is upset by a rival manufacturer (Jean Gabin) and his interest in their teenage daughter (Sylvie Vartan)

title: Friends
synopsis: Soapy, sappy sudser about two unhappy teens (Sean Bury and Anicee Alvina) running away from cruel homes who meet in the Paris Zoo and flee to a seaside refuge where instead of being friends they become lovers and parents in the pseudo-lyrical style of director Lewis Gilbert. The explicitness of their barely post-pubescent sexual awakening is not only offensive but a saddening exploitation of minors in the name of box-office romance

title: Friends & Lovers
synopsis: Inept sex farce in which a group of old pals away for a ski weekend all find new sexual partners except for the preening stud (Stephen Baldwin) in their midst. Writer-director George Haas' lame ensemble comedy is utterly contrived, badly staged and filled with bogus sentiments. A few fairly graphic sexual encounters, full frontal nudity, positive treatment of the gay lifestyle, and recurring profanity and rough language

title: Friends of Eddie Coyle, The
synopsis: Solid adaptation of a George V. Higgins' novel about a tired, smalltime Boston crook (Robert Mitchum), who wants to retire on one last job but gets caught in the middle of con men, cops and criminals, and tries desperately to find an out. Directed by Peter Yates, the story is given a fine, naturalistic treatment, tough and complex, but tight. The powerful effect of the conclusion is achieved through the movie's careful accumulation of detail, though some may be unwilling to wait for the final turn of events because of the harsh and uncompromising depiction of criminal life

title: Frighteners, The
synopsis: Tawdry horror comedy in which a minor scam artist (Michael J. Fox) is suspected of being behind a rash of mysterious heart-attacks killing townspeople, though he is actually trying to stop the malevolent ghost causing the killing spree. Director Peter Jackson's overwrought special-effects fantasy lurches badly from a comic depiction of goofy characters into the darker territory of a mass murderer returned from the grave to claim more victims. Stylized violence with some gore, fleeting sexual innuendo and recurring profanity

title: Fright Night
synopsis: This horror movie attempts to evoke chills in a quite ordinary setting when a high school youth (William Ragsdale) becomes convinced that his new neighbor (Chris Sarandon) is a vampire. A major problem with writer-director Tom Holland's approach is its uncertain tone in veering between straight horror and a spoof of horror movies. The conclusion is dominated by gory pull-out-all-the-stops special effects. Benign view of extramarital sex

title: Fringe Dwellers, The
synopsis: Insightful portrait of a young Australian aborigine girl's coming of age while struggling to break the cycle of poverty and oppression that crushes youthful ambition and enthusiasm. The contrived plot supplies an abrupt solution to a complex series of social and moral problems, but the overall perspective of director Bruce Beresford's movie provides an uplifting vision of community values and strong family ties

title: Frisco Kid, The
synopsis: A rabbi (Gene Wilder), sent cross-country on horseback during the Gold Rush to head a congregation in San Francisco, endures many misadventures that are potentially hilarious but prove only mildly funny under Robert Aldrich's direction. Harrison Ford as the badman who brings him cross-country unscathed, makes the long journey as enjoyable as the material allows. Contains some hard-edged violence and profanity

title: Fritz the Cat
synopsis: Foul-mouthed comic book feline has been brought to the screen in an animated feature that lacks not only a clever script but a sense of humor. Under director Ralph Bakshi's slapdash direction, all attempts at satire regularly succumb to sexual sordidness, putting Fritz and his friends in the same category as the humans who toil in porno pictures

title: Frogmen, The
synopsis: Standard World War II tale directed by Lloyd Bacon in which the new commander (Richard Widmark) of an underwater demolition team (Dana Andrews, Jeffrey Hunter, Robert Wagner and others) alienates his men during the invasion of a South Pacific island, then wins them over in a raid on a Japanese submarine pen. Wartime violence

title: Frogs
synopsis: Harmless looking frogs and toads send an army of snakes, leeches, snapping turtles and alligators to invade the home of Ray Milland on his swampy tropical island. Instead of playing the silly horror fantasy for laughs, director George McGowen tries for gasps in scene upon grisly scene with a transparent ecology message about nature taking its revenge

title: From Beyond the Grave
synopsis: British horror movie composed of four tales linked together by the device of a sinister antique shop and its affable proprietor (Peter Cushing). Director Kevin Connor can't improve upon the weak script, but he gets some fine performances (Ian Bannen, Donald Pleasance and Margaret Leighton as an eccentric medium right out of Noel Coward). The blood flows a little too freely in one of the stories but, other than that, it's a relatively mild little chiller

title: From Dusk to Dawn
synopsis: Repelling tale of fleeing gangster brothers (George Clooney and Quentin Tarantino) holding a minister's family hostage across the Mexican border in a sleazy strip joint where the performers turn out to be blood-thirsty vampires. Director Robert Rodriquez assaults viewers' sensibilities with a stream of gross visuals, mixing hardcore action and gory horror intended as sick, hip humor. Graphic violence, lurid sexual references, considerable nudity and incessant rough language

title: From Ear to Ear
synopsis: Tawdry French import offers a psycho-sexual thriller about two bisexual women who taunt a deeply disturbed wife into a drug-induced orgy that ends in murder. Director Louis Soulanes uses velvety amber photography to induce a mood of ennui and shrill music to suggest suspense, but its graphic sensationalism puts it in the sex exploitation category

title: From Hell
synopsis: Barbarous thriller set in 1888 London in which a police inspector (Johnny Depp) suspects a royal conspiracy as he tracks methodical serial killer Jack the Ripper who is murdering and mutilating prostitutes. Substituting gruesome visuals for suspenseful drama, directors Allen and Albert Hughes's conventional film is revolting in its imagery, with one-note characters, sloppy narrative and lackluster performances. Savage violence with excessively gory images, a few sexual encounters, frontal nudity, intermittent opium use, brief same-sex kissing and some rough language with fleeting profanity. (

title: From Hell It Came
synopsis: Ludicrous horror fantasy directed by Dan Milner is set on a Pacific island whose superstitious natives are saved by U.S. doctors (Tod Andrews and Tina Carver) from a murderous tree monster that walks on two legs. A yawner with some stylized violence and supernatural hokum

title: From Here to Eternity
synopsis: Somber picture of life on an Army base in 1941 Hawaii centers on a company whose bugler (Montgomery Clift) is punished for refusing as a matter of conscience to join the unit's boxing team, with only a hapless private (Frank Sinatra) supporting his obstinacy. Directed by Fred Zinnemann from the James Jones novel, the story also involves an affair between the company's top sergeant (Burt Lancaster) and his commander's unhappy wife (Deborah Kerr) as well as the bugler's romance with a club hostess (Donna Reed), all of which gains tragic dimension from the Japanese sneak attack on Pearl Harbor at movie's end. Sexual situations and stylized violence, including a fatal beating and a knife fight

title: From Justin to Kelly
synopsis: Pointless musical romantic comedy in which reality TV's "American Idol" winner Kelly Clarkson and her frizzy-haired runner-up, Justin Guarini, play star-crossed lovers among the thong-and-tequila spring break crowd in sunny Florida. With forgettable songs and cardboard performances, director Robert Iscove's uninspired ode to 1960s' beach-party flicks hits a flat note on every level, giving the campy charm of those bygone films a cruder MTV-like makeover. Sexually suggestive situations and frat-house humor, some mild language, as well as a glamorized attitude toward alcohol
full_review:
Some films seem like good ideas at the time, but the years prove unkind; other films are the cinematic equivalent of road kill off the bat. "From Justin to Kelly" (Fox), the pointless musical romantic comedy staring reality.TV's "American Idol" sweetheart Kelly Clarkson and frizzy.haired Justin Guarini, her fellow 15.minutes.of.famer, has skid marks all over it.

Despite leads who hitched their twin wagons to a star by singing on key, director Robert Iscove's lame ode to 1960s' beach party flicks hits a flat note on every level. Gone is the campy charm of teenybopper antecedents like "Where the Boys Are" and "Bikini Beach," replaced with a crass MTV.style thong.and.tequila fest, serving no other purpose than as a shameless cross.marketing vehicle to promote the show that spawned its two prodigiously.piped pop protagonists.

Make no mistake, while toning down the Dionysian debauchery of whipped.cream bikini contests and "margarita madness" parties to "PG" speed, the surf.and.song stinker promotes a casual carnality preoccupied with babes and booze.

To make a dumb story short, Clarkson and Guarini play star.crossed lovers on spring break in Fort Lauderdale, Fla. Clarkson .. as the Annette Funicello goody.two.shoes type .. is looking for sun and fun in the sand, carpooling it to Florida with fellow Lone Star lovelies Alexa (Katherine Bailess), the party girl, and brainy Kaya (Anika Noni Rose).

Guarini is the sensitive cog of a troika of beach party promoters, with their sights set on scoring more often than Michael Jordan. Accordingly, his "Pennsylvania Posse" consists of cardboard stereotypes, including ladies' man Brandon (Greg Siff) and computer geek Eddie (Brian Dietzen).
