synopsis: Sentimental tale of a widower (Frank Sinatra) and his loving young son (Eddie Hodges) who knows his dad's an impractical dreamer about to lose his Miami hotel unless he gets a loan from his unsympathetic brother (Edward G. Robinson) whose wife (Thelma Ritter) wants to raise the boy in New York. Director Frank Capra takes some sharp swings at measuring success in dollar signs, but overplays the emotional tangle of family relationships in a story ending with unconvincingly high hopes the boy's irresponsible father will change his ways. Comic insults and sexual innuendo

title: Holes
synopsis: An innocent youngster (Shia LaBeouf) is sent to a desert reform camp where the teens are forced to dig hundreds of holes, but with the help of a runaway pal (Khleo Thomas), he outsmarts the snarly camp owner (Sigourney Weaver) and mean overseer (Jon Voight). Based on Louis Sachar's adventure-packed novel, the film uses flashbacks to detail a century-old family curse. Director Andrew Davis offers abundant plotting and nifty visuals, offset by some undernourished characterizations. Brief violence and a crass expression
full_review:
A pair of stolen sneakers which have fallen from the sky puts a teen-age boy in reform camp where his century-old family curse finally comes full circle in "Holes" (Disney).

Unlucky Stanley Yelnats (played by Shia LaBeouf, his last name is his first name spelled backward, or is it the other way around?) is sentenced to 18 months in a camp for troubled youth when he is assumed to have stolen a basketball star's prized sneaks.

The reform camp is in the middle of the desert, 100 miles from the nearest water, so no need for guards and fences. Owned by the seldom-seen warden (Sigourney Weaver), the cruel overseer (Jon Voight in villainous moustache and pompadour do) makes the boys dig deep holes all day, every day, without explanation. And the downtrodden youngsters are none too welcoming to Stanley, whose disastrous family history is played out in flashbacks that are livelier than the contemporary story.

It seems Stanley's ancestor in the old country inadvertently crossed a Gypsy fortune teller (Eartha Kitt) who put a multigenerational curse on him as he headed off to seek his fortune in America's Old West. Sure enough, misfortune came his way when outlaw Kissin' Kate Barlow (Patricia Arquette) crossed his path and relieved him of his treasure chest. We also learn Kate was once a sweet schoolmarm whose affection for a kindly black man (Dule Hill) had dire consequences leading to her change of career.

Meanwhile, the hole-digging intensifies as Stanley befriends pint-size Zero (Khleo Thomas), who risks death by running off, eventually followed by Stanley, and together they unravel the mystery of the holes and their shared ancestral past.

Director Andrew Davis has a great deal of story to tell, based on the popular juvenile novel of the same name by Louis Sachar. It may be more exciting to read than to see, though, as the film loses energy whenever it returns from the Old West segments to the hole diggers. But humorous scenes return to Stanley's struggling family, where his inventor dad (Henry Winkler) is determined to find the formula for smell-less shoes.

Nonetheless, several characters are one-dimensional. Voight hams it up a bit much, but Weaver is comically effective as the steely proprietress of the camp -- so tough she paints her fingernails with snake venom. LaBeouf and Thomas are appealing in their roles but the movie is an odd mixture of nice with nasty, considering it's aimed at children. The feel-good ending is a crowd-pleaser that so ties up every story strand it's hard to overlook the movie's far-fetched coincidences.

But with its themes of friendship and family values, coupled with pleasing visuals, older children may just dig "Holes."

Because of brief violence and a crass expression, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

title: Holiday
synopsis: Sophisticated romantic comedy in which an honest go-getter (Cary Grant) becomes engaged to a millionaire's glamorous but materialistic daughter (Doris Nolan) only to discover he's really in love with her more intelligent and winningly down-to-earth sister (Katharine Hepburn). George Cukor directs the Philip Barry play in high style and the fine cast (including Lew Ayres, Edward Everett Horton and Ruth Donnelly) easily ridicule the emptiness of upper-class pomposity in favor of the more substantive values of ordinary people. Entertaining, meaningful fare for all but the very young

title: Holiday Affair
synopsis: Undemanding sentimental romance in which a war widow (Janet Leigh) with a young son is torn between a steady but dull lawyer (Wendell Corey) and a hard-working but dreamy salesman (Robert Mitchum). Directed by Don Hartman, the warmth of the Christmas season setting and likeable performances by the principals make the sentimental proceedings hard to resist

title: Holiday Inn
synopsis: Easy-going musical romance in which two veteran song-and-dance men (Bing Crosby and Fred Astaire) fall for the same woman (Marjorie Reynolds) while performing together in a rural inn open only on holidays. Directed by Mark Sandrich, the slim plot mainly provide an amiable context for Astaire's eye-fetching dance numbers and Crosby's crooning some pleasant Irving Berlin songs, including "White Christmas" for the first time. Romantic complications

title: Hollow Man
synopsis: Uneven sci-fi thriller about a rogue scientist (Kevin Bacon) at a secret military lab who tests his formula for invisibility on himself and is unable to reverse the procedure. Despite amazing visual effects and an intriguing premise, director Paul Verhoeven's film lurches forward trading suspense for explosions and other obvious gimmicks while only shallowly exploring the psychological ramifications of a man without societal constraints. Much gory violence, a few implied sexual encounters, some nudity and incessant rough language and profanity. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Hollow Reed
synopsis: Searing drama in which a divorced homosexual (Martin Donovan) sues for full custody of his 9-year-old son on the grounds the child is being physically abused by the live-in boyfriend (Jason Flemyng) of his ex-wife (Joely Richardson). Director Angela Pope movingly explores the characters' human passions and frailties in an insightful tale of prejudice, betrayal and self-deception. Brief homosexual activity with rear nudity, some violence including child beating, intermittent profanity and instances of rough language

title: Hollow Triumph
synopsis: Clumsily contrived crime thriller directed by Steve Sekely in which a fugitive ex-con (Paul Henreid) murders a psychiatrist who's his dead ringer except for a facial scar which he mistakenly reverses on his own face, then takes the victim's place unaware of the doctor's serious personal problems. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Hollywood Babylon
synopsis: Director Van Guylder's movie uses a few photos and brief footage of famous silent movie personalities, then dresses up actors of no ability to resemble them and stages re-enactments of their reputed escapades. Wallowing in explicit sex sequences, it is solely of prurient interest

title: Hollywood Blue
synopsis: Crude compliation of hard-core pornographic footage interspersed with sidewalk interviews of people giving their opinion of the social value of such movies. Sheer exploitation

title: Hollywood Ending
synopsis: Disappointing comedy about a has-been director (Woody Allen) who is given another chance by his ex-wife (T�a Leoni) to direct a major film, only to go psychosomatically blind, a fact that must be hidden from the studio head (Treat Williams) as well as the cast and crew. Despite several one-line zingers and a promising start, writer-director Allen's film drags as its outrageous conceit becomes increasingly unbelievable and much of the humor falls flat. A few sexual references and brief drug content
full_review:
A has-been director is given another chance, only to allow his hypochondriacal tendencies to get in his way in the disappointing comedy "Hollywood Ending" (DreamWorks).

Writer-director Woody Allen's latest film starts off promisingly, and even ends on a pretty funny joke made at the expense of French movie audiences. But the central conceit of the film -- that an aging auteur goes psychosomatically blind and must keep it a secret from everyone involved in the film he's directing -- wears thin all too soon. It turns the bulk of the movie into a flat, overlong jumble dotted with occasionally humorous moments. And several of the inside industry jokes Allen makes may go over the heads of an average audience unfamiliar with intricacies or lingo of studio filmmaking.

To a certain extent, the film is autobiographical as Allen stars as Val Waxman, a 60ish director who saw his prime a decade ago. But unlike Allen, Val hasn't been able to direct a feature film in years. In fact, when he is first seen, Val is directing a deodorant commercial in snowy Canada, which he promptly quits to return to his ditzy and much younger girlfriend Lori (Debra Messing) in Manhattan. An aspiring actress, Lori is just waiting for Val -- whose neurotic and hypochondriac tendencies have earned him a bad reputation -- to land a picture so he can cast her in it. (Although audiences are familiar with Allen's penchant for casting himself in May-December romances in his films, this conceit becomes increasingly difficult to believe, especially when the grayer, wrinkled Allen is hooking up with women 30 years his junior.)

Just as Allen thinks he's hit bottom, his ex-wife Ellie (Tea Leoni), an executive with Galaxie Pictures recommends him as the perfect choice to direct the studio's upcoming $60 million period drama "The City That Never Sleeps." Although it takes some persuading her boss and fianc� Hal (Treat Williams) and Ed (George Hamilton), a studio hanger-on who walks around with a golf putty and whose job description is unclear, Val is offered the job.

What happens next is the nightmare of an visual artist: Val goes blind. His analyst explains that it is a psychosomatic response to pressure and heavy responsibility. But his agent, Al Hack (Mark Rydell) insists the show must go on. This leads to all kinds of subterfuge to keep the cast, crew and Hal -- who actually stole Ellie away from Val -- in the dark. Although this may have been a funny concept on paper, or even in a smaller dose, the film beats out every obvious joke, most of which are uninspired as Allen bumps into furniture, talks to walls and attempts to answer questions in the vaguest manner possible. Although a clever line or two does provide a good laugh, some of the ad-libbed dialogue seems forced. And the film could have also used a more disciplined editing hand as the film goes on too long.

Dire-hard fans of the Woodman may enjoy his recognizable comedic style and wit, but there's not much of it to make the film anything more than mildly amusing.

Due to a few sexual references and brief drug content, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.(
2002
)

title: Hollywood Homicide
synopsis: Jumbled pastiche of an buddy-cop action movie in which two moonlighting Los Angeles detectives (Harrison Ford and Josh Hartnett) juggle solving a quadruple murder in the hip-hop world while pursuing real estate deals and acting opportunities. Co-writer-director Ron Shelton glosses over character development and coherent story line in a mad rush to highlight lame comic dialogue, drawn-out chases and extended shoot-'em-ups. Intermittent violence, implied casual affairs, a few racial epithets, frequent profanity and an instance of rough language
full_review:
Hollywood gets a bad reputation for churning out mindless cinematic junk, of which "Hollywood Homicide" (Columbia) is the latest example.

Name stars like Harrison Ford and Josh Hartnett will draw audiences initially, but director Ron Shelton is unable to meld this odd-couple, police procedural, action buddy comedy into satisfying movie entertainment.

It's supposed to be hilarious that Los Angeles police detectives Joe Gavilan (Ford) and K.C. Calden (Hartnett) pay as much attention to their moonlighting -- real estate for Joe, showbiz for K.C. -- as to catching killers. Unfortunately, the lame comedic situations and cliched dialogue seriously limit smiles and nearly preclude laughter.

Nor does character development fare any better. We learn K.C.'s cop father was mysteriously killed on the job, but when the killer is ultimately revealed the scene holds no emotional resonance. Likewise, we hear from a third party that Joe's had three wives and two children but from what we see of Joe they don't seem to exist.

Grizzled vet Joe and would-be actor K.C. are assigned to solve the quadruple murder of an up-and-coming rap group in a hip-hop club. But they are hard-pressed to follow up leads as Joe is desperate to broker a real estate deal for the commission payout, and K.C. is preoccupied giving yoga classes and planning a showcase of his acting talents. Yet they somehow find time for casual sex -- K.C. with a few of his yoga students, all of whom seem to be stunning twentysomethings, and Joe with an on-air radio psychic (Lena Olin).

Meanwhile, Joe's longtime enemy (Bruce Greenwood), now in Internal Affairs, is out to nail Joe however he can. And it seems all too dramatically convenient that Joe belatedly discovers his new lover is either his enemy's wife or girlfriend. The detectives' pursuit of sole eyewitness K-Ro (Karupt) and prime suspect, music mogul Sartain (Isaiah Washington), is often sidetracked as the cops juggle their off-duty hours between dames and deals.

The script, co-written by Shelton with former cop Robert Souza, wanders all over the lot to pump up the action and keep the pace moving. However, the effect is to confuse with extraneous characters and concerns that just fritter away by the conclusion. Here and there a cutely amusing moment surfaces, but more often the narrative is weighed down by drawn-out foot pursuits, car chases and shootouts that have been similarly filmed umpteen times before.

The sight of Ford sliding down an escalator banister isn't particularly funny, but then neither is this muddled movie.

Due to intermittent violence, implied casual affairs, a few racial epithets, frequent profanity and an instance of rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Hollywood Horror House
synopsis: Miriam Hopkins plays an aging, former movie star whose reveries are interrupted by a psychopathic visitor (John David Garfield) to her remote Beverly Hills estate. Thoroughly B-grade film with sex and violence directed against women

title: Hollywood Knights
synopsis: Writer-director Floyd Mutrux's vulgar attempt at slapstick comedy recounts the misadventures of a cretinous Beverly Hills car club on Halloween night. Its crudity and graphic sexuality are seriously offensive

title: Hollywood or Bust
synopsis: Anemic comedy about the misfortunes of an unlucky gambler (Dean Martin) while driving from New York to L.A. with an idiotic movie fan (Jerry Lewis), his Great Dane and a shapely singer (Pat Crowley). Director Frank Tashlin fails to get many smiles from the witless clowning of Lewis while Martin's supposed romantic charm has even less appeal than the unmemorable songs. Tiresome sexual innuendo

title: Hollywood Shuffle
synopsis: Writer-producer-director Robert Townsend provides satirical comment on black stereotyping in the movie business in a story contrasting the career aspirations of the central character (also Townsend) with his sense of dignity. The low-budget feature is fairly successful as a social satire of unconscious racial discrimination. Profanity in the context of a streetwise environment

title: Holocaust 2000
synopsis: ( see: "The Chosen" )

title: Holy Man
synopsis: Tepid tale of a failing home shopping network that is turned around when two employees (Jeff Goldblum and Kelly Preston) invite a wandering holy man (Eddie Murphy) onto the shows and his non-materialistic message sells products anyway. Directed by Stephen Herek, the feel-good comedy-drama promotes love, harmony and self-esteem in simplistic terms that lack the spark of conflict. Some sexual references and minimal profanity

title: Holy Outlaw, The
synopsis: Documentary about Daniel Berrigan, Jesuit priest, poet and pacifist, examines the man's personal witness against human indifference and the horror of war. Filmmakers Don Lenzer and Lee Lockwood rely mainly on interviews with Father Berrigan, members of his family, close friends and his religious superior, during a four-month period when the FBI was seeking to arrest him

title: Holy Smoke
synopsis: Sordid drama about a young Australian woman (Kate Winslet) entangled in an Indian cult who uses her sexual prowess to turn the tables on the American (Harvey Keitel) hired by her family to de-program her. As directed by Jane Campion, the battle of wills between the main characters quickly degenerates into an exploitative sexual tug of war, making the film seem more about manipulative lovers than a sincere effort to release a mind from the clutches of a cult. Several graphic sex scenes, full frontal nudity, homosexual situations, some violence, and intermittent foul language

title: Homage
synopsis: Plodding account of the murder of a TV actress (Sheryl Lee) by a troubled young man (Frank Whaley) as recounted by the victim's mother (Blythe Danner), his lawyer (Bruce Davison) and a prison guard (Danny Nucci). Directed by Ross Kagan Marks from Mark Medoff's play, the disjointed narrative unfolds in flashbacks providing little insight on media fame, unbalanced fans, tabloid reporting or mother-daughter relationships. Stylized violence, sexual situations including masturbation, profanity and crude language

title: Homage to Chagall: The Colours of Love
synopsis: Documentary on the occasion of Marc Chagall's 90th birthday pays tribute both to the beauty of his art and the humanity of the artist. With a script based upon Chagall's own writing and featuring hundreds of his paintings, murals and stained-glass windows, director Harry Rasky searches for the vision that inspired their creation, a quest helped immensely by a remarkable interview with Chagall himself

title: Hombre
synopsis: White man living as an Apache (Paul Newman) is on an ambushed stagecoach with people he neither likes nor trusts and who neither like nor trust him but, in the course of a struggle for survival, he wins their admiration. Directed by Martin Ritt, the picture's story of injustice is brutal in spots but it serves a purpose in this above average Western

title: Home Alone
synopsis: A large family takes off for Christmas in Paris accidentally leaving behind their timid 8-year-old (Macaulay Culkin) who becomes very resourceful in defending the house against a persistent pair of bungling burglars (Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern). The laughter ebbs and wanes in director Chris Columbus' contrived comedy, but the pace is peppy and the family message heartwarming. Minor violence and robbery played for laughs

title: Home Alone 2: Lost in New York
synopsis: Formula sequel places the resourceful 10-year-old (Macaulay Culkin) on his own in the big city, this time determined to prevent the same bone-brained bandits (Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern) from ripping off a toy store on Christmas Eve. Writer-producer John Hughes and director Chris Columbus repeat their popular comic paces in a similar lively adventure similarly hampered by exaggerated comic violence and cloying sentiment. Much slapstick violence and some menace to a child

title: Home Alone 3
synopsis: Unimaginative comedy sequel in which an 8-year-old boy (Alex D. Linz) quarantined with chicken pox booby traps his home against four crooks determined to retrieve a stolen computer chip from inside his toy truck. Writer-producer John Hughes and director Raja Gosnell repeat the basic premise of the original with few variations, resulting in little more than redundant comic mayhem. Much slapstick violence

title: Home and the World, The
synopsis: Indian director Satyajit Ray's screen version of Nobel laureate Rabindranath Tagore's novel set in 1907 Bengal centers on a triangle involving a wealthy and idealistic landowner, his willful and naive wife, and his best friend, a charismatic revolutionary who has feet of clay. Though static and talky, it provides a fascinating glimpse into a bygone era and aspects of human nature that are universal

title: Homebodies
synopsis: Handful of oldsters living in a creaking Cincinnati tenement doomed to be torn down rebel against the wrecker's ball, first by sabotaging the encroaching construction sites, then by taking more direct guerrilla actions that culminate in murder. Thanks to a sprightly set of aging character actors (Paula Trueman, Frances Fuller, Peter Brocco), it is a gripping and macabre little slice of black comedy. Director Larry Yust's ending is as grisly as it is illogical, yet its theme that the lives of old people, like those quaint Victorian houses, are all too often wasted in the face of "progress" remains to haunt the viewer

title: Home for the Holidays
synopsis: Uneven comedy about a stressed-out single mom (Holly Hunter) who flies home to spend Thanksgiving with her dysfunctional family, including meddling mother (Anne Bancroft), dotty aunt (Geraldine Chaplin) and gay brother (Robert Downey, Jr.). Directed by Jodie Foster, the formula sitcom of a family reunion beset by emotional clashes displays a mean-spirited tone in its treatment of family relationships as something to be endured rather than enjoyed. Assorted sexual references, fleeting violence and frequent profanity

title: Home Fries
synopsis: Comic misfire about two dimwitted brothers who accidentally kill their philandering stepfather whose pregnant girlfriend (Drew Barrymore) falls for one brother (Luke Wilson) while the other (Jake Busey) tries to kill her to please their crazy mom. Director Dean Parisot's drawn-out tale of dysfunctional characters is a mindless, mirthless, but not painless experience. Brief menace and violence, some sexual innuendo and occasional profanity

title: Homegrown
synopsis: Dreary tale of three dopeheads (Hank Azaria, Billy Bob Thornton and Ryan Phillippe) who unwittingly promise to sell their murdered boss' marijuana crop to both a dealer and to the mob. Director Stephen Gyllenhaal's lurching mix of supposed comedy, drama and suspense is an abysmal failure which treats drug sales as a highly profitable lark. Stylized violence, sexual encounters, brief nudity, benign attitude toward substance abuse and other criminal activity as well as much rough language and profanity

title: Home in Oklahoma
synopsis: Small-town newspaper editor Roy Rogers and St. Louis reporter Dale Evans team up to solve a murder and save a young boy from being done out of his inheritance by greedy relations in a modern-day Western directed by William Witney. Simple formula fare with a minimum of stylized violence

title: Home Movies
synopsis: Failed attempt at a screwball comedy about a high school student (Keith Gordon) who tries to become something more than "an extra in my own life" by turning it into a film about himself with the help of an instructor (Kirk Douglas). Director Brian De Palma's embarrassingly bad movie achieves the level of an almost unwatchable student film exercise. Sexual nature of some of the gags is adult fare

title: Home of Our Own, A
synopsis: Leaving Los Angeles for rural Idaho in 1962, a penniless mother (Kathy Bates) of six tries to make a home for her family out of a crumbling shack with the reluctant help of her 15-year-old (Edward Furlong) and the generosity of the landowner (Soon-Tek Oh). Tony Bill directs a gritty, often downbeat story of a loving but dictatorial matriarch who scorns charity as well as religion, but vividly instills the work ethic in her children so the family can stay together under their own roof. Fleeting violence and sexual innuendo, occasional profanity and the mother's antagonistic attitude toward organized religion

title: Home of the Brave
synopsis: World War II story of a black soldier (James Edwards) being treated by an Army psychiatrist (Jeff Corey) for paralysis resulting from his experiences on a five-man reconnaissance mission to a Japanese-held island where he's taunted by a racist corporal (Steve Brodie) and sees the death of a boyhood friend (Lloyd Bridges). Directed by Mark Robson from Arthur Laurents' play, its realistic treatment of racial prejudice holds up better than the psychiatrist's finding the soldier disabled by his guilt over feeling glad it was his friend who died and not him. Wartime violence and racial epithets

title: Home of the Brave
synopsis: In a concert performance, composer-director Laurie Anderson offers a musical diversion for the cultivated few who appreciate Far Eastern-inspired pointilist melody, Dadist minimalism and the poetry of alienation. Musically and visually dull, the concert does not demonstrate the potential of its all-digital sound track

title: Home on the Range
synopsis: Family-friendly animated adventure about a trio of cows (voiced by Roseanne Barr, Jennifer Tilly and Judi Dench) who decide to capture a notorious desperado for the reward money to save their beloved dairy farm from the auction block. Writers-directors Will Finn and John Sanford turn the traditional western on its horns in telling a rip-roaring cowboy yarn about teamwork and camaraderie, resulting in a barnyard full of fun for moo-viegoers. Some brief mild rude humor and innuendo, as well as some cartoon violence
full_review:
A trio of cranky cows must band together to save their beloved dairy farm from being put on the block in the rip-roaring animated family feature "Home on the Range" (Disney). Writers-directors Will Finn and John Sanford turn the traditional western on its horns in telling a rootin'-tootin' cowboy yarn from the other end of the branding iron, resulting in a barnyard full of fun for moo-viegoers of all ages.

The story centers on Maggie (voiced by Roseanne Barr), a brassy prize cow sold into the cozy confines of the appropriately named "Patch of Heaven" dairy farm, owned by a kindly old homesteader named Pearl. The new-cow-on-the-block's rowdy manner causes the farm's prim and proper British heifer, Mrs. Caloway (voiced by Judi Dench), to practically choke on her cud. But, while Maggie's arrival ruffles some feathers -- literally -- and gets the goat of a cantankerous old goat named Jeb (voiced by Joe Flaherty), the stir is overshadowed by a visit from Sheriff Brown (voiced by Richard Riehle), who regretfully informs Pearl that "Patch of Heaven" is set to be auctioned in three days unless she ponies up $750 in arrears.

With no way of paying, Pearl resigns herself to selling off her farm. But Maggie is one cow who doesn't kowtow. She proposes to her barnyard buddies that they try to raise the money themselves. Accompanied by a reluctant Mrs. Caloway and a ditzy cow named Grace (voiced by Jennifer Tilly), Maggie sets out to capture Alameda Slim (voiced by Randy Quaid), a notorious cattle rustler with a $750 bounty on his head.

It is later revealed that Slim, disguised as a wealthy land baron, is using the money he makes off the stolen livestock to buy up all the foreclosed farms. With the desperado's sights set on "Patch of Heaven," the bickering bovines must put aside their personal beefs and work together to prevent an udder cow-tastrophe.

Helping steer them in the right direction is Lucky Jack (voiced by Charles Haid), a jackrabbit of all trades, and Buck (voiced by Cuba Gooding Jr.), a hyperheroic horse.

While Pixar partisans continue to pen obituaries for traditional animation, "Home on the Range" proves that there is still a place for hand-drawn films. With visuals clearly inspired by classic Western iconography, the movie boasts luscious big-sky backdrops exploding with vibrant mesa hues.

Unfortunately, eight-time Academy Award-winning songwriter Alan Menken's tumbleweed score falls short of his previous Disney collaborations, such as "The Little Mermaid" and "Aladdin." However, the film does contain several whistle-worthy songs, including the title rawhide romp "(You Ain't) Home on the Range" and "Yodle-Adle-Eedle-Idle-Oo," a psychedelic hoedown reminiscent of "Pink Elephants on Parade" from "Dumbo."

Laced with enough comic wit to keep older cowpokes from sleeping in the saddle, the film, while lacking the character development and mythic scope of "The Lion King," imparts a positive message about teamwork and camaraderie. For pure fun, there's hardly a discouraging word to be heard about this "Home on the Range."
Due to some brief mild rude humor and innuendo, as well as some cartoon violence, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

title: Home on the Range
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Robert Springsteen in which a singing cowboy (Monte Hale) helps save a wildlife preserve from being closed by irate ranchers whose cattle are being killed by a marauding bear they mistakenly believe comes from the preserve. Stylized violence

title: Homer
synopsis: Midwest farm boy (Don Scardino) likes to swill cheap wine, spark his girl (Tisa Farrow), smoke a little pot and bug his dad by refusing to get a haircut and staging a one-man anti-war demonstration outside the local VFW Hall. Before mercifully ending the picture by running away, Scardino manages to sing or listen to enough songs to fill a soundtrack album, which seems about all that director John Trent has on his mind

title: Homer and Eddie
synopsis: Loveable brain-damaged man (James Belushi) and homicidal maniac with a brain tumor (Whoopi Goldberg) team up in a search for long-lost parents and $87 in stolen cash. Director Andrei Konchalovsky builds no empathy for Goldberg's repulsive role and, despite Belushi's endearing performance, the result is little more than a parade of brain-damaged freaks. Much profanity and some grisly, pointless violence

title: Homesteaders, The
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Lewis Collins in which a couple of Oregon sodbusters (Wild Bill Elliot and Robert Lowry) obtain the dynamite needed to clear their land from a distant Army post, then trek it back despite ex-Army misfits, hostile Indians and a gang of outlaws. Frontier violence

title: Hometown Story, The
synopsis: Capitalist tract from writer-director Arthur Pierson in which a defeated state legislator (Jeffrey Lynn) returns as editor of the town paper (staffed notably by Alan Hale, Jr., and Marilyn Monroe), then then goes after the local manufacturer (Donald Crisp) he blames for his defeat until the industrialist uses his plane to save the life of a third-grader. Stylized violence and mild sexual innuendo

title: Homeward Bound II: Lost in San Francisco
synopsis: Frisky sequel to the popular 1993 family film has a scrappy bulldog (voice of Michael J. Fox), sassy Himalayan cat (voice of Sally Field) and trusty golden retriever (voice of Ralph Waite) separated from their human family at the San Francisco airport and forced to deal with an urban gang of stray dogs and other misadventures as they wend their way home. Director David R. Ellis' shaggy dogs story incorporates a mushy puppy love subplot to bolster the already familiar plot of talking pets persevering to reunite with their worried owners

title: Homeward Bound: The Incredible Journey
synopsis: Left temporarily with a friend, an aging golden retriever (voice of Don Ameche), a sassy cat (voice of Sally Field) and a frisky bulldog puppy (voice of Michael J. Fox) embark on a perilous journey across the wilds of the Sierra Mountains to get home to the family they so desperately miss. In this remake of a 1963 Disney feature, director Duwayne Dunham's lethargic pacing weakens the appeal of a mostly charming live-action animal adventure that stresses perseverance and the importance of family and friendship

title: Homicidal
synopsis: Hokey thriller about a very strange lady (Jean Arless) who kills a justice of the peace, then returns to her duties caring for an aged invalid (Eugenie Leontovitch) in the home of a man about to inherit a fortune. Directed by William Castle, the menace is laboriously contrived to sustain a story which makes little sense until a twist ending involving a dual performance. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Homicide
synopsis: Powerful drama centering on an inner-city cop (Joe Mantegna) who belatedly identifies with his Jewish heritage when investigating a murder with possible anti-Semitic overtones. Writer-director David Mamet's riveting action thriller resonates with added layers of depth as the cop faces a moral dilemma that threatens to destroy all that he has steadfastly believed in. Intermittent brutal violence and much rough language

title: Hondo
synopsis: Lean Western about a hard-riding, straight-shooting cowboy (John Wayne) who gives up his independent ways to stand by a woman (Geraldine Page) whose husband has abandoned her and their young son during an Apache uprising. Directed by John Farrow, the obligatory action scenes of fistfights, cavalry patrols and Indian battles are less interesting than Wayne's strong title performance as the mythic Western hero who respects women, children and the Indian way of life. Frontier violence. The U.S. Catholic Conference

title: Hondo
