When Constance pays a visit pleading with Jacques to take her back, he panics and hastily packs his bags, heading off with Laura to a beachside resort in Brittany. Though Jacques is wary of having his heart broken again, the warm sun slowly thaws his reservations about their age difference. As they wander through the countryside, giddy as newlyweds, Jacques begins to believe that the romance can work. But love, like brie, if left out in the sun, runs the risk of melting. Jacques soon discovers what at first appeared to merely be a gap was, in actuality, a generation chasm.

Both Bacri and Dequenne inhabit their roles comfortably and manage to steer clear of typical generation-gap banter -- with the one exception being a somewhat contrived scene where Jacques escapes Laura's blaring techno music by retreating into his bedroom and putting on a Hayden violin concerto and some jazz.

The film tenderly addresses the basic human need for love and companionship. While some might interpret Jacques' actions as a textbook midlife crisis -- a desperate attempt to bolster his aging ego by flaunting his trophy nymphet, thus reasserting his wounded sexual prowess -- the filmmaker seems much more concerned with exploring the vagaries of the human heart, charting its ebbs and flows between passion and pain. Bacri invests Jacques with a haggard vulnerability and humanity that convey the inner void left by his wife's departure, an emptiness he tries to fill by striking up chance conversations with women at sidewalk cafes and ultimately by risking romance with Laura. By comparison, Laura is a child, incapable of any real commitment -- in her immaturity, she repeatedly and misguidedly equates casual sex for love.

Like the works of Camus or Sartre, the film is tinged with the scent of existential angst. By his choice of final images -- Jacques sitting on the sand, book-ended by two women and surrounded by throngs of happy beachgoers, but weighed down by his crushing solitude -- the filmmaker seems to suggest that ultimately we are all alone. This pessimism, coupled with the film's muddying of the distinction between authentic love and carnal desire, is regrettable and may prove off-putting to Catholic viewers.

Subtitles.

Due to sexual encounters with nudity, minimal rough language and some profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Housekeeping
synopsis: Interesting seriocomic probe into small-town family life in the 1950s tells the story of two girls who, after their mother's suicide, are raised by their aunt (Christine Lahti), a woman of somewhat strange and erratic behavior. Scottish director Bill Forsyth's look at growing up in an unconventional American household that's frowned upon by conformist neighbors, is quite often amusing and frequently very touching. Unresolved tensions between individual and social values

title: House of Cards
synopsis: Handsome, footloose American tutor (George Peppard) is up against fanatical Algerian ex-patriots. Good wins over evil despite conventional mystery-melodrama trimmings from director John Guillermin who uses the commonplace as a source of horror. Attractively lush Parisian milieu, some spurts of violence and gratuitous, though silly attempts at sexual titillation

title: House of Cards
synopsis: Traumatized by her father's sudden death, a six-year-old (Asha Menina) withdraws into a silent dreamworld from which her mother (Kathleen Turner) tries to extricate her using her own intuitive approach which clashed with the more traditional methods of a skeptical child psychiatrist (Tommy Lee Jones). Writer-director Michael Lessac mixes elements of mystery and near-mysticism in a visually lovely movie that compares medical science unfavorably with a loving mother's desperate attempts to save her child from becoming autistic. A child's emotional trauma and a few scenes of a youngster in mortal danger

title: House of D
synopsis: Contrived but touching coming-of-age story of 12-year-old Tom (Anton Yelchin) living in 1970s' Greenwich Village with his manic, pill-popping widowed mother (Tea Leoni), his friendship with a mentally challenged delivery man (Robin Williams), his first crush on a pretty schoolmate, and his unusual friendship with an unseen inmate (Erykah Badu) at the Women's House of Detention. Actor David Duchovny's directorial debut (from his own script) has a low-budget feel, but the story -- even with its shamelessly sentimental ending -- is compelling. The messages about the importance of being honest and finding your roots are admirable, if a bit platitudinous, and the performances are excellent, especially from young Yelchin, but also Duchovny as the adult Tom and Frank Langella as the clerical school principal. Tobacco and drug use, some profanity and crude language and expressions, sexual content and innuendo, suicide attempt, and a problematic euthanasia plot twist
full_review:
David Duchovny -- best known for his role on the hit series "The X-Files" -- shows another facet of his talent, as the triple-threat writer, director and star of "House of D" (Lions Gate), a contrived but affecting coming-of-age story.

"House of D" begins in present-day Paris, with expatriate Tom Warshaw (Duchovny) in the midst of a marital crisis with his lovely French wife (Magali Amadei). It's the occasion of their son's 13th birthday, which Tom has missed. His wife's censure prompts Tom to open up about his past, of which he's never spoken.

From that point, the film flashes back to Tom's childhood as a 12-year-old boy (Anton Yelchin) living in 1970s Greenwich Village in New York with his manic, pill-popping, chain-smoking widowed mother (Tea Leoni). It's clear that the bond between mother and son is extraordinarily strong despite her eccentricities. His attachment to her is such that he considers his safest place nestled under her bed with a reading light. Mrs. Warshaw thinks nothing of barging into the bathroom to use the toilet or talk to him when he's taking a shower, much to his embarrassment. (There's nothing kinky here, just a mother who knows no boundaries.)

Tom monitors her intake of pills very carefully, and worries that she might take too many.

His best friend is a mentally challenged adult, Pappass (Robin Williams), the school custodian with whom he shares delivery duties for a local restaurant.

And he's sweet on a pretty schoolmate Melissa (Zelda Williams, Robin's daughter), but has no experience wooing girls at his young age. It happens that he has made friends with an unseen former prostitute whom he calls Lady (Erykah Badu). She speaks to him from her high window at the Women's House of Detention, at that time located in the heart of Greenwich Village. Lady gives him pointers on how to woo Melissa, and even teaches him how to dance for the upcoming school event.

Observing Tom's growing attraction to Melissa, Pappass feels he's losing his buddy, and breaks a store window to steal a bicycle the two of them had been saving up to buy. When Tom takes the rap for his friend's transgression, and gets suspended from school for it, his skittish mother -- fearing the boy's future is ruined -- takes an overdose of sleeping pills. At this point, reader, what follows is a plot spoiler, so don't read on if such things bother you.

Mrs. Warshaw is rushed to the hospital where she remains in a comatose state. Shortly after, Tom comes home to discover unpleasant relatives have moved in and plan to be his caretakers. Learning his mother's vegetative condition is permanent, he rushes to the hospital, quickly unplugs her from the machines that sustain her, and poignantly curls up beneath her bed as at home. The hospital staff rushes in within seconds but apparently are not able to revive her.

Afterward, Tom runs away from home, never to return.

As we know, ending life before its "natural" end is morally wrong. Given the context of this particular story and the character's young age, viewers may take an understanding view of his misguided compassion without justifying it. The action is shown to have serious emotional consequences that haunt him well into adulthood, thus providing the impetus for this character to come back home and make peace with his past, including a healing "reunion" with his mother at her grave. Still, it seems a moral misstep.

Also problematic is the scene where the young Tom is seen snuggling -- fully clothed -- with Melissa on top of a bed, and at one point they go to the restaurant's meat locker to be alone together, but only to hold each other and kiss chastely.

There's also some lame humor involving Tom's French teacher, whose unwitting sexual pronunciation of certain words have the mischievous students in hysterics.

The film has a low-budget feel, and at times seems underlit and visually murky. A glossier presentation, especially given the shamelessly sentimental Hollywood ending, might have been more appropriate, but the 1970s' milieu seems accurately portrayed.

Despite flaws, "House of D" imparts overall admirable messages about the importance of honesty, friendship, filial devotion and the finding of your roots, even if served up in platitudinous doses. ("A boy has to go away before he can come back" is the general tenor.) The mercy killing is another matter, however.

The performances are excellent, especially from young Yelchin but also Duchovny and Frank Langella as the Rev. Duncan, Tom's school principal. Leoni gives a somewhat -- but only slightly -- toned-down version of her manic role in "Spanglish." At first, it's difficult to accept Williams as the simple-minded but wise man-child he plays here, but it's to his credit that we finally accept his impersonation as much as we do.

This film contains tobacco and drug use, some profanity and crude language and expressions, sexual content and innuendo, a suicide attempt, and a problematic euthanasia plot twist. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: House of Dark Shadows
synopsis: Movie version of a daytime television series about a family of vampires features Jonathan Frid re-creating his role of Barnabas, the 175-year-old owner of the spooky Collinwood estate, with Joan Bennett and Grayson Hall as residents. Directed by Dan Curtis, the melodrama often slips into a mire of gushing blood and gore amidst all the vampire lore required by die-hard horror fans. Others are likely to be repulsed

title: House of Dracula
synopsis: Murky monster tale of an idealistic doctor (Onslow Stevens) who cures the Wolfman (Lon Chaney, Jr.) after killing the prowling Dracula (John Carradine), then discovers he's been contaminated by the vampire's blood and becomes one himself until reviving the Frankenstein monster (Glenn Strange) for a fiery finale. Directed by Erle C. Kenton, the feverish plot is as unconvincing as the monsters, though the spooky visuals and eerie atmosphere offer some scary moments. Stylized violence, menacing situations and hokey moralizing

title: House of Exorcism
synopsis: Playing the role of a suave butler in a sinister mansion is Telly Savalas, who seems to be making it up as he goes along, in a standard Italian Gothic horror filled with gore and nudity, and innocent of the least trace of taste or wit

title: House of Fear, The
synopsis: Intriguing entry in the mystery series brings Sherlock Holmes (Basil Rathbone) and Dr. Watson (Nigel Bruce) to an isolated residence on the Scottish coast where the members of a club of wealthy retirees are being murdered and their bodies mutilated. Directed by Roy William Neill, the murder plot keeps one guessing as suspects are killed off one by one in a house the locals believe haunted. Much menace. no rating

title: House of Flying Daggers
synopsis: Visually dazzling martial arts love story set in ancient China about a lawman (Takeshi Kaneshiro) who finds himself entangled in a web of desire and deception when his superior (Andy Lau) assigns him to infiltrate a gang of anti-imperial insurgents by escorting a beautiful blind courtesan (Ziyi Zhang) with ties to the group to the rebels' secret forest stronghold. Part action adventure, part triangular romance, director Zhang Yimou's melodramatic sword saga of passion, betrayal and the conflict between love and duty is full of eye-popping fight sequences, but its story sometimes gets drowned out by the artistic swirl of silk and steel. Subtitles. Much stylized action violence and associated gore, attempted rape and a sexual encounter
full_review:
A lawman assigned to thwart a growing rebellion finds himself ensnared in a tangled web of desire, deception and betrayal in the sweeping and visually sumptuous martial arts love story "House of Flying Daggers" (Sony Pictures Classics).

Part sword spectacle, part triangular romance, director Zhang Yimou's kung fu saga echoes the cinematic bravura of Ang Lee's "Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon," as well as Yimou's own Oscar-nominated "Hero" and explores universal themes of passion, jealousy, vengeance and the timeless conflict between love and duty.

"House of Flying Daggers" takes place in ninth-century China, as the sun sets on the once flourishing Tang Dynasty. The flagging government is threatened by shadowy insurgent armies -- including the titular blade-flinging fraternity -- formed to protest imperial court corruption and challenge the emperor's waning power. With the anti-government forces gaining momentum, two high-ranking members of the imperial constabulary -- Jin (Takeshi Kaneshiro) and his captain, Leo (Andy Lau), devise a plot to squelch the rebels' efforts by capturing their elusive leader.

Acting on information that a beautiful blind courtesan, Mei (Ziyi Zhang), has ties to the guerrilla group, Jin, posing as a moneyed playboy, is dispatched to the brothel where Mei dances. After an electrifying set piece based on a traditional dance called "The Echo Game," Mei is arrested and imprisoned by Leo. Jin fakes a jailbreak and offers to escort Mei (who can also wield a mean sword) back to the Robin Hood-like rebels' secret base, feigning sympathy for their cause. Jin, assuming the name Wind, surreptitiously marks their trail, making it easy for Leo -- and a small contingent of imperial troops -- to track their movements.

Even a sightless strumpet can see what will happen next. Jin and Mei fall in love, setting up the tale's conflict-of-interests conundrum. Plot twists abound. Trusts are broken, loyalties questioned, hidden motives disclosed, true identities revealed and hearts are pierced by flying daggers (literally and figuratively).

With the porcelain beauty of a china doll, Zhang is breathtaking to watch, whether exchanging demure glances with Kaneshiro or kicking Tang "tuchis." Kaneshiro strikes the perfect balance between roguish charm and chivalric virtue. Together they generate quite a bit of heavy panting, including an impassioned love scene in a field of tall grass.

Unfortunately, the story sometimes gets drowned out by the swirl of steel and silk. However, the characters and their dilemmas d'amour are interesting enough to keep viewers engaged in the story during breaks in the eye-popping action.

And while "House of Flying Daggers" lacks the emotional intimacy of Yimou's more quietly poetic dramas like "Raise the Red Lantern" and the epic scope of "Hero" (not to mention the latter's almost symphonic use of color), the gravity-defying fight sequences -- elegantly choreographed by Tony Ching Siu-Tung -- are nothing short of spectacular.

The film's centerpiece is a dazzling blade ballet which takes place in and above a mist-shrouded bamboo grove between the star-crossed lovers and the emperor's death squad (enhanced, as are all the battles, by some computer generated effects). Viewers sensitive to violence should be aware that, though artfully done, the clashes contain shots of the thrown knives slicing the throats of their intended targets.

The film's melodramatic tone crescendos to operatic heights during the picture's climactic duel in the snow (all that's missing is the "O Fortuna" chorus from Carl Orff's "Carmina Burana").

Still, if you are tired of cookie-cutter action movies and are looking for something that is artistic as well as exciting, "House of Flying Daggers" hits the mark.

Subtitles.

Because of much stylized action violence and associated gore, attempted rape and a sexual encounter, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: House of Fools
synopsis: Sentimental anti-war tale set in a besieged mental hospital where the residents are left to fend for themselves when Chechen soldiers occupy it and Russian troops attack. Director Andrei Konchalovsky shows much compassion for his fragile characters as well as a measure of whimsy in suggesting they are more sane than those who wage war. Subtitles. Wartime violence, brief nudity and some rough language
full_review:
It's hard to tell the sane from the insane when the residents of a mental hospital are caught in the crossfire of Chechen and Russian soldiers in "House of Fools" (Paramount Classics).

Set in 1996, the fact-based film from Russian director Andrei Konchalovsky is set in an asylum on the Chechen border that the staff hastily abandons as opposing soldiers close in.

The lovely young Janna (Yuliya Vysotskaya), who plays the accordion to calm her fellow patients, imagines that pop musician Bryan Adams is her fiance. But when the Chechen troops occupy the asylum, one of them flirts with Janna and she takes his kidding proposal of marriage seriously, though regretting that she will break Adams' heart. (The singer appears in her hallucinations and his hit, "Have You Ever Really Loved a Woman?" wafts throughout the film).

Nonetheless, the patients bond to wish her well as she dons her prettiest white dress and hat and goes to Ahmed's (Sultan Islamov) quarters, where his commanding officer admonishes him and suggests he should marry her as offered.

Meanwhile the patients, who range from simply confused to violent, must cope with their normally structured lives being completely upended by the frightening presence of war literally at their doorstep when Russian soldiers arrive and the inevitable battles erupt.

Konchalovsky orchestrates a poignant story about the search for love in the midst of war that is beautifully acted by Vysotskaya, who brings real heart to the sometimes jarring mix of violence, dark humor and occasional touches of whimsy.

The suggestion that these holy fools are wiser than the sane soldiers that surround them is not an original insight by any means, but one can still be moved by the director's humanism and compassion for his fragile characters. The blending of professional actors with actual mentally and physically disabled patients, however, is not done smoothly.

Some may find the film's sentimentality to be a serious flaw, although its anti-war sentiment remains clear and its visuals are always handsomely accomplished.

Subtitles.

Due to wartime violence, brief nudity and some rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: House of Frankenstein
synopsis: Sprawling horror fantasy in which a mad doctor (Boris Karloff) and his hunchbacked assistant (J. Carrol Naish) escape prison, have a brief encounter with Dracula (John Carradine) on the way to Frankenstein's ruined estate, then free his Monster (Glenn Strange) and the Wolf Man (Lon Chaney, Jr.) from an ice-bound cave until their antics are ended by the local villagers. Directed by Erle C. Kenton, this disjointed parade of familiar screen monsters tries to find some fresh angles on old formulas but the result offers little in the way of originality. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: House of Games
synopsis: Eminent psychiatrist (Lindsay Crouse) becomes involved with a con artist (Joe Mantegna) and some of his shady games of deception with disastrous results for both. Writer-director David Mamet succeeds fairly well in conning the viewer with a plot in which nothing is quite what it seems. Some brutal violence, rough language and a restrained bedroom scene

title: House of Missing Girls, The
synopsis: French movie with Anna Gael as a salesgirl who freely exhibits her own contours in a sordid adventure which has her fleeing a band of abusive slavers and finding refuge with a hermit-like musician. Jean-Francois Davy directs the English-dubbed exploitation import

title: House of Sand and Fog
synopsis: Grim drama about an exiled Iranian colonel (Ben Kingsley) who buys a foreclosed house in California at an auction, but the previous owner, a recovering addict (Jennifer Connelly), refuses to give it up and enlists the help of a married cop (Ron Eldard) who has become her lover to coerce the colonel into selling the house back to her. Despite its flaws, debut director Vadim Perelman's tragic tale about the consequences of actions, both thoughtless and well-meaning, reveals the frailty of the human condition, but the film's crushing sadness is draining, as is the bleak ending. An extramarital affair, some sexual encounters with shadowy nudity, brief but intense violence and intermittent rough language
full_review:
An unopened letter becomes the catalyst for tragedy in the grim drama "House of Sand and Fog" (Dreamworks).

Dreamworks is hoping against hope that "House" will elevate its depressed box office to end a bad year on a good note. But unfortunately for the company, this is not the type of movie that is likely to have mass appeal. Debut director Vadim Perelman's tragic tale reveals with searing emotion the consequences actions -- both good and bad -- can have on frail human beings. It is moving and poignant, with a brilliant performance by Ben Kingsley. While the film's crushing sadness overwhelms the viewer, leaving one drained, the film's flaws cannot be dismissed.

Massoud Amir Behrani (Kingsley) is an immigrant and former colonel in the shah of Iran's air force who has been struggling for years to maintain the facade of prosperity. He lives with his wife, Nadi (Shohreh Aghdashloo), and teenage son, Esmail (Jonathan Ahdout), in a lavish apartment in a tony California neighborhood they can barely afford. Behrani cleans highways by day and sits behind the counter of a tiny gas station market by night, yet everyone believes he has a high-powered job with Boeing.

But now he has finally found an opportunity to advance: a Northern California bungalow by the sea put on the auction block at a fraction of its real worth. He snaps up the property with the hopes of reselling it at a big profit. This is not profiteering, but a means to survive and restore his family to the comfort they once enjoyed.

The house Behrani acquires is the one Kathy Nicolo (Jennifer Connelly) had been left by her father. Kathy, a recovering addict whose husband split eight months ago, was evicted from the house when she failed to pay business taxes. The whole affair, however, turns out to be a computer glitch, as Kathy never owed the $500 the county claimed. But Kathy also never bothered to open her mail and missed all the warnings.

Completely at loose ends, sleeping in her car and washing up in public restrooms, Kathy is helped by the kindness of a stranger: Deputy Sheriff Lester Burdon (Ron Eldard). Married (but unhappily, of course) with two children, Lester's kind gestures ignite passion and he and Kathy begin an affair, whereby he abruptly ends his marriage.

The rest of the film unfolds with the characters involved in an intricate string of missteps, accusations and poor judgments. The film succeeds in keeping the viewers off-balance by not allowing them to choose sides. Behrani now owns title to the house free and clear. His reasons for acquiring it are justifiable. But Kathy has been wronged by the county, so her feelings of outrage are understandable, despite her own part in losing the house. The film also deftly builds tension as tempers rise and desperation's cold grip takes hold, pushing the characters toward reckless and devastating deeds.

However, throughout the film, nagging inconsistencies pop up. Kathy and Lester's relationship moves fast, and while the speed is not unbelievable, the lack of spark between these two actors makes it hard to be convinced that they have "found" each other, as Lester puts it. Contrarily, the last third of the film slows considerably, until it suddenly puts things in motion toward its bleak ending.

Kingsley is fascinating to watch. He literally disappears into his character, a difficult thing to accomplish considering his distinctive looks. Precisely buttoning his crisp white shirt, he can only be one person: someone who, through no misdeed of his own, has fallen from his lofty footing and now must toil to regain it in a foreign country while watching spoiled Americans take their advantages for granted.

Unfortunately, praise cannot be lavished on Connelly. Tears flow easily from her intense eyes. But crying and looking bleary-eyed are not the same as conveying true heart-ripping emotion. She plays Kathy (who is casually wooed into drinking by Lester after three years of sobriety) as distant and wounded, but fails to make a connection with her lover and the audience.

Eldard is the real weak link. His performance is unconvincing, a problem that may be due in part to his underwritten character. He's also an unlikable bully who seems to have been just waiting for the chance to abandon his family.

"House of Sand and Fog" is the story of the American dream gone wrong. It doesn't condescend to celebrate the dire choices its characters take. Instead, it shows the horrific consequences both action and inaction can sometimes create.

Because of some sexual encounters with shadowy nudity, an extramarital affair, brief but intense violence and intermittent rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: House of Strangers
synopsis: Brooding tale of a domineering Italian-American banker (Edward G. Robinson) whose harsh treatment of his four sons has earned their enmity, but when three of them conspire against him, he seeks revenge through the fourth (Richard Conte). Directed by Joseph L. Mankiewicz, the twisty plot holds dramatic interest while its vivid portrayal of Italian-American family life contrasts the values of an older generation with those of a younger one. Stylized violence and intense family conflicts

title: House of the Dead
synopsis: Relentlessly ridiculous gorefest about a group of party-seeking college coeds trapped on an island infested with flesh-eating zombies and, luckily for them, stockpiled with lots of ammo. It is based on a popular video game. Director Ewe Boll ignores plot altogether in favor of protracted, ultraviolent scenes, as tedious as they are gratuitous. Excessive graphic carnage, extended topless nudity, lewd humor, pervasive rough and crude language
full_review:
When combining a former music video director and a script based on an ultraviolent video game involving flesh-eating zombies, the question that should immediately form in one's mind is not "Will the resulting movie be bad?" but rather "Just how bad will it be?" In the case of "House of the Dead" (Artisan), the answer is painfully, inexplicably, run-screaming-back-to-the-ticket-booth-and-demand-your-money-back bad.

"House of the Dead" -- which pretty much describes the funereal hush of the empty theaters this film would, in a just world, play to -- is a relentlessly ridiculous gorefest about a group of party-seeking college coeds trapped on an island infested with blood-sucking ghouls and stockpiled with lots of ammo. Directed by Ewe Boll, the film is so laughable that, if not for its incessant violence, peppered with gratuitous nudity, it could more accurately be marketed as a comedy.

Lured to the aptly named Isla del Muerte by an invitation to a rave party, the preternaturally good-looking zombie-fodder hitch a ride aboard the boat of a German gunrunner named Captain Kirk (Jurgen Prochnow). Kirk's stooge sidekick is played -- with equally embarrassing results -- by serial hack Clint Howard, who braves his humiliation dressed up like the Gorton's fisherman. Once on the mysterious island, however, they find out that whoever booked the place forgot to inquire about the flesh-eating undead locals who have a habit of crashing keg parties.

After the oversexed troupe hook up with some stray revelers holed up in the island's creepy cemetery and a Rambo-esque female Coast Guard officer (Ellie Cornell), the film nosedives from garden-variety schlock to a progressively sadistic bloodbath, intercut with violent video-game images. The lavishly grotesque action leads nowhere, stumbling aimlessly toward a ludicrous climax with the island's zombie impresario -- a 17th-century Spanish priest-turned-necromancer.

The film opens with the sole survivor pondering, "It all started when I came here for a rave, and it ended with the rotting smell of death." Needless to say, the stink he is referring to is coming from the projection booth.

The decorative, mostly no-name cast is so wooden that theatres should provide tweezers so viewers can remove splinters after each showing. Of course, such rigor mortis is to be expected when the dialogue and characterizations are less fleshed-out than the partially decomposed islanders.

In the film's closing hopeful-dawn-after-a-night-of-bloody-mayhem scene, a helicopter swoops down from the sky. The dazed survivor asks the pilot who he is, to which the pilot responds, "I'm here to rescue you." Unfortunately for anyone caught watching this turkey, he's about two hours too late.

Due to excessive graphic carnage, extended topless nudity, lewd humor, pervasive rough and crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: House of the Seven Gables, The
synopsis: Stale version of Nathaniel Hawthorne's novel set in 1840's Massachusetts where a greedy lawyer (George Sanders) causes the imprisonment of his innocent brother (Vincent Price) in order to find a legendary fortune hidden in the ill-gotten family home of the title. Director Joe May gets some moody atmosphere from the curse haunting the family since the 17th-century witchraft trials, but succeeds best with the perseverance of the love between imprisoned brother and aging fiancee (Margaret Lindsay). Tough sledding for children

title: House of the Spirits, The
synopsis: Impressive adaptation of Chilean author Isabel Allende's multi-generational novel about a wealthy South American family whose cruel, reactionary patriarch (Jeremy Irons) tries to control the lives of his spinster sister (Glenn Close), clairvoyant wife (Meryl Streep) and fiery, defiant daughter (Winona Ryder) who's involved with a peasant rebel leader (Antonio Banderas). Director Bille August's portrait of an impassioned family caught up in a half century of political upheaval starting in the 1920s is flawed by the the narrative's somnambulistic pacing and Iron's stilted performance, but does succeed in showing the power of love and forgiveness in coping with adversity. Intermittent political violence and some sexual encounters with brief nudity

title: House of Usher
synopsis: Melancholic dramatization of the Edgar Allan Poe story in which a man (Mark Damon) arrives at the Usher estate to find his catalyptic fiancee (Myrna Fahey) buried alive by her troubled brother (Vincent Price). Director Roger Corman gets properly edgy performances in the story of a waning family living in a crumbling mansion which is destroyed in a great fire. Some stylized violence and much moody menace

title: House of Wax
synopsis: Repulsive horror film about a group of college students (including Chad Michael Murray and Paris Hilton) who, while on a road trip, find themselves stranded in a backwater town, where they fall prey to a pair of homicidal twins (both played by Brian Van Holt) intent on turning their unsuspecting victims into wax figures that are a little too lifelike for comfort. With its formulaic plot and vapid performances, director Jaume Collet-Serra's bloody re-imagining of the 1953 Vincent Price classic quickly melts into a stomach-churning mess of slasher cliches and sadism, which packages human debasement as popcorn fare. Gratuitous gruesome violence and gore, torture images, some sexual situations and humor, including a striptease and suggested oral sex, a scene of smoking and drinking, as well as recurring rough and crude language
full_review:
There is at least 20 seconds of quality moviemaking in the otherwise repellent screamfest "House of Wax" (Warner Bros.). Unfortunately for the film's first-time director, Jaume Collet-Serra, those fleeting frames belong to a clip from Robert Aldrich's 1962 "Whatever Happened to Baby Jane?"

Billed as a "re-imagining" of the 1953 horror classic starring Vincent Price, this uninspired exercise in stomach-churning gore involves a group of college students (including Chad Michael Murray and Paris Hilton) who, while on a road trip to a big football game, find themselves stranded in a backwater quasi-ghost town somewhere between Gainesville, Fla., and Baton Rouge, La.

The creepy town's only attraction is the eponymous museum, made completely of wax, whose deranged curators -- a pair of homicidal twins (both played by Brian Van Holt) -- are intent on turning their unsuspecting victims into wax figures that are a little too lifelike for comfort. One of the twins was horribly disfigured when they were surgically separated at birth, resulting in a serious case of sibling rivalry (thus the "Baby Jane" reference).

Good-looking actors. Maniacs with knives. Vats of boiling hot wax. You fill in the blanks.

The plot is formulaic and as for the performances let's just say that better line-readings could be delivered by Madame Tussaud's waxen mannequins. Not that it matters much since "House of Wax" quickly melts into a bloody mess of slasher cliches and sadism, which, like last year's "Texas Chainsaw" remake, packages human debasement as popcorn fare, including an eye-averting scene of brutality involving a baseball bat and another where Hilton is harpooned through the forehead with a jagged metal rod.

The film's tagline is "Prey. Slay. Display" -- to which should be added "Stay Away!"

The film has gratuitous gruesome violence and gore, torture images, some sexual situations and humor, including a striptease and suggested oral sex, a scene of smoking and drinking, as well as recurring rough and crude language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: House of Wax
synopsis: After being horribly deformed when arson destroys his wax museum, a crazed sculptor (Vincent Price) takes to killing people, coating the bodies in wax and placing them on exhibit in his new waxworks until an intended victim (Phyllis Kirk) spots her missing friend (Carolyn Jones) displayed as Joan of Arc. Though the visuals are relatively tame and Price plays the monstrous villain for sympathy, director Andre de Toth provides a few scary moments and much sinister atmosphere in the waxworks, relieved by some diverting, if extraneous 3-D effects, notably a barker with paddle-balls. More menace than violence

title: House of Whipcord
synopsis: British sex exploitation movie about a woman (Penny Irving) who is kidnapped and held prisoner by some demented types who torment and degrade. Director Pete Walker's flimsy story is only an excuse for an unhealthy fantasy of sex and violence

title: House of Women
synopsis: Uneven melodrama directed by Walter Doniger is set in a women's prison where inmates are allowed to live with their children until the age of three, but the attempt of a new warden (Andrew Duggan) to change the policy sets off a prison-wide riot when he separates an inmate (Shirley Knight) from her child. Stylized violence, menacing situations and an implied sexual affair

title: House of Yes, The
synopsis: Darkly comic tale in which an unstable young woman (Parker Posey) who becomes unhinged when her brother (Josh Hamilton) who was once her lover returns from college with a fiancee (Tori Spelling). Director Mark Waters' talky story shows its stageplay origins while depicting a thoroughly dysfunctional family, but instead of being madly amusing its humor is often tasteless. Fleeting violence, implied sexual encounters, flippant treatment of incest, occasional profanity and rough language

title: House on Carroll Street, The
synopsis: Romantic thriller set in 1951 New York features a gutsy, blacklisted photo editor (Kelly McGillis) who uncovers a politically sanctioned conspiracy aimed at hiding Nazi war criminals in the U.S. Hitchcockian influence poorly realized by director Peter Yates in a stylish-looking but far-fetched movie about political hypocrisy, scripted by once blacklisted screenwriter Walter Bernstein. Brief nudity and some graphic violence

title: House on Chelouche Street, The
synopsis: Israeli movie about a widow (Gila Almagor) in 1946 Tel Aviv who decides to remarry to give her family some security, but her adolescent son (Ophir Shalitan) resents her choice, has a brief affair with an older woman (Michal Bat-Adam) and learns something about adult responsibilities. Written and directed by Moshe Mizrahi, it proves an engaging and interesting portrayal of human problems and makeshift solutions in a time of great turmoil

title: House on Haunted Hill
synopsis: At the suggestion of his wife (Carol Ohmart), a sardonic millionaire (Vincent Price) holds a party in an isolated mansion with a history of grisly murders, promising to reward any of his guests (including Richard Long, Alan Marshall and Elisha Cook, Jr.) who spend the night. Director William Castle has some fun in the low-budget fright department, ranging from spooky effects to bizarre deaths, but the tangled plot is full of holes. Menacing atmosphere and a few scares

title: House on Haunted Hill
synopsis: Formula horror film in which a murderous married couple (Geoffrey Rush and Famke Janssen) and five strangers are locked overnight in a former insane asylum whose spirits rise, intent on killing all within its walls by dawn. Director William Malone's uninspired remake of the 1958 original offers more gore than goosebumps and some nasty characters to boot. Sporadic violence, brief nudity, frequent profanity and recurring rough language

title: House on Skull Mountain, The
synopsis: Weak horror vehicle directed by Ron Honthaner begins with the death of a wealthy black woman whose heirs, one of whom is white (Victor French), gather in her remote mansion for the reading of the will, only to be beset by deadly voodoo spells. Muddled hokum with some eerie atmosphere, a few chills and occasional sexual inferences

title: House Party
synopsis: Grounded by his well-meaning dad (Robin Harris), a black, middle-class teenager (Christopher Reid) is determined to attend a pal's house party. Black director Reginald Hudlin plays up the comic obstacles that get in the way, including a gang of toughs and some buffoonish white cops. Though this growing-pains comedy has a clear anti-drug and alcohol message, it also implies that the kids are sexually active. Nonstop rough language with much sexually explicit dialogue and black rap, some bathroom humor and incidental cartoon violence

title: House Party 2
synopsis: Vulgar sequel follows a black youth (Christopher Reid) to college where he discovers his tuition check has been stolen, prompting his playboy buddy (Christopher Martin) to throw a steamy pajama party on campus to raise the needed cash. Producers-directors Doug McHenry and George Jackson inject lots of bouncy energy into the rapping and dancing but the racial and sexual stereotyping defeat the movie's attempt at comedy. Much rough language and sexual innuendo, racial stereotyping, implied sexual encounters, a flash of nudity and brief violence

title: House Party 3
synopsis: Vulgar sequel in which a black youth (Christopher Martin) sets up a raunchy bachelor party for a friend (Christopher Reid) after they take money from a music promoter for a singing act they can't deliver. Director Eric Mesa throws together a rap music situation comedy whose marginal humor is sexist, mean-spirited and features a trio of very young boys who are casual lawbreakers. Implied promiscuity, partial nudity, many racial slurs and sexist insults, comic violence and much rough language

title: Housesitter
synopsis: Kooky pathological liar (Goldie Hawn) pretends she's married to an architect (Steve Martin) who hopes to make his ex-girlfriend (Dana Delany) jealous. Director Frank Oz's misguided comedy features perky performances but falls flat with phony motivations and contrived sitcom humor. An implied bedroom encounter and much sexual innuendo

title: House That Dripped Blood, The
synopsis: Four tired tales of the preternatural are linked by the weak device of a haunted house that supposedly influences the behavior of its inhabitants. British director Peter Duffell fails to develop the least sense of dread and the only surprise is that the screenplay is by veteran horror writer Robert Bloch

title: House That Screamed, The
synopsis: Lilli Palmer plays the turn-of-the-century proprietress of a French finishing school for wealthy girls and, while her 15-year-old son (John Moulder-Brown) persues the girls, they persue the local deliveryman. The promiscuous pursuits at the school are finally relieved by several bloody murders but, by then, director Narciso Ibanez Serrador's attempts at horror are lost in a sophomoric sex teaser

title: Housewife
synopsis: ( see: "Bone" )

title: How About You
synopsis: Gentle and uplifting holiday drama about a free-spirited young Irishwoman (Hayley Atwell) who takes a job at the retirement home run by her sister (Orla Brady) and changes the lives of its four most cantankerous inhabitants: an ex-screen actress (Vanessa Redgrave), a former judge (Joss Ackland), and two quarrelling sisters (Imelda Staunton and Brenda Fricker). A formidable cast lends panache to a somewhat predictable plot in director Anthony Byrne's adaptation of a short story by Maeve Binchy, though there's a benign view of drugs and some coarse language among the generally positive messages about the dignity and enduring potential of the elderly. Drug use, mature themes, some rough and crude language, and a couple of uses of profanity

title: Howards End
synopsis: Exquisitely done drama based on E.M. Forster's novel about an aristocratic widower (Anthony Hopkins) in turn-of-the-century England who cheats a young woman (Emma Thompson) out of property left her by his wife (Vanessa Redgrave) but then falls in love with her, much to the dismay of her egalitarian younger sister (Helena Bonham Carter). Enhanced by the ensemble cast's splendid performances, the sensitive collaboration of director James Ivory, producer Ismail Merchant and screenwriter Ruth Prawer Jhabvala does justice to Forster's ironic and witty story of class distinctions and their sometimes tragic outcomes. Discreet sexual innuendo and fleeting violence

title: Howards of Virginia, The
synopsis: Long-winded saga of a colonial rustic (Cary Grant) helped by neighbor Tom Jefferson (Richard Carlson) to wed the sister (Martha Scott) of an aristocratic planter (Cedric Hardwicke) and then build his own plantation in the Shenandoah wilderness before joining Washington's ragged army at Valley Forge. Directed by Frank Lloyd, the historical dramatization is painfully artificial, with the script's patriotic intentions too obvious to be effective. Domestic misunderstandings and wartime hardships

title: Howard the Duck
synopsis: This caustic, cynical and malevolent fantasy-adventure features a fully costumed duck from outer space trying to find his way home after having been accidentally transported to a hostile Earth. Director Willard Huyck fills the screen with too much vulgarity, violent destruction and sadistic humor to make the movie of interest to any sensitive earthling

title: How Green Was My Valley
synopsis: Nostalgic chronicle of family ties based on the Richard Llewellyn novel about a Welsh coal-mining village at the turn of the century trying to maintain its traditional way of life despite changing industrial times and the power of the mine owners. Director John Ford's episodic picture of a community in transition is depicted largely through an emotionally rich, often sunny but sometimes tragic portrait of the close-knit Morgan family and its proud father (Donald Crisp) who rejects his five sons when they join the union, the mediating mother (Sara Allgood) who reconciles them, the daughter (Mauree O'Hara) who marries unhappily when rebuffed by the village's new minister (Walter Pidgeon) and the youngest of the Morgans (Roddy McDowall) recalling the family's past as a grown man leaving his beloved but now-depressed valley. Muted treatment of romantic complications and some stylized violence including the sadistic caning of a youth and a harrowing mine disaster

title: How High
synopsis: Depraved comedy about two African-American guys (Method Man and Redman) who become incredibly smart after smoking a certain type of marijuana and are admitted into Harvard, but when their supply is stolen, they are left to get by on their deficient wits alone. Vicious stereotypical characterizations, perverse mocking of American founding fathers, and a meandering plot with nary a laugh, make director Jesse Dylan's vulgar film pure garbage. Constant drug use, several sexual situations and dialogue, some violence, brief nudity, sporadic gross-out humor and pervasive rough language with some profanity

title: How I Got into College
synopsis: Mediocre high school senior (Corey Parker) aims to be accepted by the same top college that his secret heartthrob (Lara Flynn Boyle), the smartest and most popular girl in his class, hopes to attend. Directed by Savage Steve Holland, it's an innocuous, pleasant teen comedy about the very real anxieties suffered by college hopefuls and their parents. Mild rough language and sexual innuendoes

title: How I Won the War
synopsis: Unusual British anti-war movie ridicules the military concept of war as a noble game and debunks the cliches and slogans of belligerents. Michael Crawford stars as an inexperienced lieutenant assigned to build an advanced cricket field in World War II North Africa, with John Lennon as the compliant everyman of the unit which deserts at the Rhine. Directed with comic ingenuity by Richard Lester, its pacifist view of war may be controversial but it is neither anti-religious nor anti-patriotic, and it merits attention and reflection. Stylized violence

title: Howling, The
synopsis: Trashy but flashy horror movie written by John Sayles and directed by Joe Dante in which a television newswoman (Dee Wallace) finds herself in dire straits when her companions at a psychiatric retreat turn out to be a pack of werewolves. The special effects by Rob Bottin are remarkable, but not enough to justify what is essentially a sex-and-violence exploitation movie

title: Howl's Moving Castle
synopsis: Marvelous, hugely imaginative Japanese animated feature based on a popular novel by Diana Wynne Jones about a young girl (voiced by Emily Mortimer) transformed into an old lady (Jean Simmons) by a witch's curse (Lauren Bacall) who becomes the housekeeper to a handsome, but reclusive, wizard (Christian Bale) and his apprentice (Josh Hutcherson) and fire demon (Billy Crystal). Hayao Miyazaki's utterly absorbing film works so well on many levels that it can be equally appreciated by children and adults, and imparts beautiful messages about taking a moral stand, respect for the elderly, forgiveness and the senselessness of war. Subtitles in Japanese version. Battle scenes, some frightening images for very young children
full_review:
When's the last time you saw an American animated film with a feisty old woman as its heroine? Well, master Japanese director Hayao Miyazaki has no qualms about featuring such a character for he has brilliantly adapted Diana Wynne Jones' popular novel, "Howl's Moving Castle" (Disney). (Jones, by the way, was a student of C.S. Lewis and J.R.R. Tolkien.)

The hugely imaginative film concerns Sophie, an 18-year-old girl who works in a hat shop (voice of Emily Mortimer), and is transformed into a 90-year-old lady (Jean Simmons) by the curse of the Witch of the Waste (Lauren Bacall).

The setting is a sort of early 20th-century European vista, with Jules Verne-like cars and airships peppering the colorful, indeterminate European landscape.

One of most extraordinary aspects of the story is the grace and equanimity with which Sophie accepts her lot, the first indication that the film will celebrate the sagacity that comes with the state of old age.

She becomes a housekeeper to handsome, but cloistered, wizard Howl (Christian Bale), who lives in a dilapidated castle that moves around the town's periphery on mechanical legs. It looks somewhat like a metallic turkey with appendages, striking fear into the town's inhabitants. Sophie had earlier been rescued from the unwelcome advances of a couple of soldiers by Howl (not knowing his identity).

Howl doesn't recognize the old crone -- at least, not at first -- when she moves in with him and his young apprentice, Markl (Josh Hutcherson), and Calcifer, his fire demon (voiced as comic relief by Billy Crystal), who serves as sort of a generator for the peripatetic domicile.

The king of the land is engaged in a senseless war, and part of the reason for Howl's self-imposed seclusion is his desire to avoid a conflict he can't believe in. Howl expresses regret for his cowardice in not facing up to the king, and the fact that he's always running, and assuming a series of aliases.

Howl is basically a noble character, but not without an element of vanity and selfishness. (It was for the latter reason that he never finished his wizardly apprenticeship, we learn later.) When Howl loses the formula for his lustrous blonde hair, he bemoans that life is not worth living if he can't be beautiful (a sentiment he will wisely reject by the film's conclusion).

But Howl has taken in Sophie out of kindness, not through any romantic designs on her younger self, though as the film progresses it's clear there's a loving bond between the two.

Now an imperious dowager, the Witch is the primary "villain." But such is the goodhearted nature of the story that when old Sophie goes to the king to plead Howl's case for peace (one of the most remarkable sequences) she magnanimously talks the aging and corpulent Witch into climbing the long stairs to the palace. (The Witch has herself received a royal invitation.)

Later, Sophie and Howl will actually give the old Witch shelter at the castle, not for a minute treating her badly because she was responsible for their misfortune.

The camaraderie among Sophie, Howl, Markl, Calcifer and the turnip-head scarecrow (who doesn't speak, but instead hops behind Sophie on his peg leg, helping her like a sort of guardian angel) is an understated validation of fellowship.

Toward the end, the "action" elements increase, and Howl sprouts actual wings and takes to flight over the battle raging below. The film momentarily looks like a superhero adventure. But the episode is relatively brief, and germane to the story.

Miyazaki's utterly absorbing film -- which tops his last masterwork, "Spirited Away" -- works so well on many levels that it can be equally appreciated by children and adults. It imparts clear and admirable messages about abhorring a senseless war, taking a moral stand when you must, having tolerance and respect for the aged, forgiving your adversaries and appreciating life's beauty.

The amazingly detailed artwork is a joy to behold. And, best of all, it's not at all formulaic. Joe Hisaishi's affecting score is a far cry from the pop-influenced scoring prevalent in the genre, though there's a pop-sounding ballad (in Japanese) toward the end.

If you can imagine a surreal combination of "Beauty and the Beast" and "The Wizard of Oz," with the old biddies from the adult French animated feature "The Triplets of Belleville" thrown in for good measure, you'll have an idea of what's in store here.

This English-language version is completely satisfying, and the big-name voices are all superb. How nice to have Jean Simmons in a leading role again, even if we don't actually see her! And also outstanding is Blythe Danner as Madame Suliman, the royal sorceress, in love with Howl. Disney is also releasing the film in the original Japanese with subtitles, which we're sure has its own pleasures.

The film contains battle scenes and some frightening images for very young children. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

title: How She Move
synopsis: Buoyant musical film chronicling the struggles of a young Caribbean immigrant (Rutina Wesley) who, in the wake of her sister's death and the financial ruin of her parents (Conrad Coates and Melanie Nicholls-King), seeks comfort in "stepping," a traditional style of African-American dance and, despite the opposition of a former friend (Tre Armstrong), joins an all-male crew led by a charismatic step veteran (Dwain Murphy) to compete for prize money she hopes to use for tuition. While sequences of tightly choreographed stomping provide the entertainment high points of director Ian Iqbal Rashid's movie, the drama is also effective and the emphasis on education welcome. The film is possibly acceptable for older teens. Two uses of the f-word (one only mouthed), much crude and crass language, one use of profanity, one obscene gesture, drug references and suggestive dancing
full_review:
How She Move

The traditional style of African-American dance known as "stepping" gets a big screen showcase in the musical drama "How She Move" (Paramount Vantage). While buoyantly entertaining, the film gently conveys some positive moral messages along the way.

Raya Green (Rutina Wesley) is the daughter of David (Conrad Coates) and Faye (Melanie Nicholls-King), upwardly mobile Caribbean immigrants living in Canada. By the time their elder daughter, Pam, succumbs to drug abuse, however, Raya's parents have lost their life savings trying to rescue her from that addiction.

As a result, Raya has to leave her exclusive boarding school and return to the gritty Toronto neighborhood where she was raised. There she encounters a former friend turned suspicious rival, Michelle (Tre Armstrong), as well as charismatic local step veteran Bishop (Dwain Murphy), who renews her interest in the craze.

Determined to win a stepping contest with its prize of $50,000 -- money she hopes to use for private-school tuition -- Raya auditions and becomes the only female member of Bishop's "crew," the Jane Street Junta. As with any other nonacademic activity, however, Raya must conceal her interest in dancing from her wary mom.

Despite the bond she's begun to form with her teammates and a growing romantic attachment to Bishop, Raya eventually finds herself tempted by her ambition to quit the Junta in favor of a rival crew. At home, meanwhile, Faye's depression over her other daughter's death causes her to lash out at the easygoing David, straining their marriage to the breaking point.

While sequences of tightly choreographed stomping provide the high points of director Ian Iqbal Rashid's movie, the dramatic elements are equally effective. Nicholls-King is especially powerful in projecting her fears for the welfare of her surviving daughter. The script emphasizes the value of education, hard work and perseverance as well as the respectful, primarily friendship-based central romance.

These positive elements, together with a clear admonition about the devastating effects of drug use, are partially offset by some vulgar language, which -- though arguably appropriate to the setting -- precludes recommendation for younger viewers who might otherwise benefit from the movie's rewarding themes. It is possibly acceptable for older teens.

The film contains two uses of the f-word (one only mouthed), much crude and crass language, one use of profanity, one obscene gesture, drug references, and suggestive dancing. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: How Stella Got Her Groove Back
synopsis: Glossy romance from Terry McMillan's novel about a 40-year-old, career-driven single mom (Angela Bassett) who ultimately finds happiness with a man (Taye Diggs) half her age while vacationing in Jamaica. Director Kevin Rodney Sullivan delivers an idealized, comic romantic fantasy in which a one-night stand matures into a committed relationship. Benign treatment of pre-marital sex, fleeting nudity and some rough language

title: How Sweet It Is!
synopsis: James Garner and Debbie Reynolds star in a comedy-melodrama about a crazy, mixed-up American family sight-seeing in Europe. Basically a happy couple, in the midst of complications caused by their son and his girlfriend, they find themselves on the brink of extra-curricular flirtations. Forgettable froth directed by Jerry Paris

title: How Tasty Was My Little Frenchman
synopsis: Brazilian movie set in the early colonial times when a Frenchman is taken captive by a cannibal tribe and is held for execution at an upcoming festival. The final horror (and key to the title) in this black comedy is the cheerful smile of the young girl who has been his native wife as she prepares to eat her alloted portion of his dead body. Director Nelson Pereira Dos Santos does not romanticize nor sentimentalize the savages or the Europeans, but neither does his movie miss the joy of life that exists in every culture. Scenes of nudity in this semi-ethnographic movie are without any sense of sexual exploitation

title: How the West Was Won
synopsis: Sprawling Cinerama epic tracing the way West from the mountain men (James Stewart and Henry Fonda) to the settlers coming by river boat (Karl Malden and Agnes Moorehead), wagon train (Debbie Reynolds and Gregory Peck) and railroad (Richard Widmark and George Peppard), with a Civil War stopover at Shiloh (John Wayne and Henry Morgan). Mostly directed by Henry Hathaway, with John Ford directing the Civil War sequences and George Marshall the railroad segment, the result is picturesque entertainment, stereotyped history and bloated melodrama, chiefly of interest as a compendium of Western screen conventions. Some tense but stylized violence

title: How to Beat the High Cost of Living
synopsis: Three housewives (Susan Saint James, Jane Curtin and Jessica Lange) conspire to replenish their depleted finances by stealing the money displayed in a huge plastic ball in a shopping center promotion. Director Robert Scheerer's comedy has some tart humor, but is pretty mediocre going and sometimes mean-spirited to boot. Adult humor and situations

title: How to Commit Marriage
synopsis: When the daughter of real estate agent (Bob Hope) and his wife of 19 years (Jane Wyman) learns that her parents are about to be divorced, she goes off to live out of wedlock with the son of a cynical agent for rock groups (Jackie Gleason). How everyone, including Gleason and his girlfriend Tina Louise, is eventually legally united or reunited might have been the basis for some good satire but director Norman Panama treats both his characters and the institution of marriage in a consistently grotesque and sleazy fashion. Though there are a few scattered laughs, this is not a funny picture

title: How To Deal
synopsis: Lame coming-of-age clunker about a cynical teen-ager (Mandy Moore) who renounces romance only to fall in love with a close friend (Trent Ford). With gag-inducing dialogue and vanilla performances, director Claire Kilner's vacuous ode to adolescent angst and puppy love is for the dogs. An implied sexual encounter, brief sensuality, drug abuse, as well as an instance of rough language and some profanity
full_review:
A cynical teen-ager renounces romance only to find herself falling for her close friend in the coming-of-age clunker "How to Deal" (New Line).

Full of lame dialogue and vanilla performances, this vacuous ode to adolescent angst, directed by Clare Kilner, rates on the fun scale just slightly above taking your cousin to the senior prom.
Pop star Mandy Moore plays Halley Martin, a stubbornly independent 17-year-old who has vowed never to fall in love -- a logical stance, taking into account the festering emotional wounds inflicted on her family by cupid's arrows. Her parents, Lydia (Allison Janney) and Len (Peter Gallagher), have recently finalized a bitter divorce. Len, a popular local DJ and platinum-card member of the midlife-crisis club, has just announced over the airwaves that he will be eloping with the radio station's much younger traffic reporter. If that weren't enough to sour Halley on storybook endings, watching her soon-to-be married sister, Ashley (Mary Catherine Garrison), and future brother-in-law plan their wedding is about as blissful as a cockfight.

Adding still more fuel to the fire, Halley's best friend, Scarlett (Alexandra Holden), has defected to the other side, cooing giddily over Steve (Dylan Baker), a sensitive jock, who responds with appropriate lovesick, cavity-caliber goofiness. Yet when Steve dies tragically during a high school soccer game, Halley is pushed further toward a radical emotional teetotalism.

The only chinks in her otherwise impervious amour armor are her feelings for Steve's buddy, Macon Forrester (Trent Ford), a rebel without a comb who gleans life lessons from "Star Wars." Times were when such an aptitude for science fiction would earn one the appellation of "geek" and get you stuffed in a locker, but Macon's Jedi charm works its magic on Halley, though she struggles to keep the relationship strictly platonic. Of course, Macon wants something more than friendship. As Halley's life unravels, Macon begins to challenge her fears of commitment, opening the melodramatic floodgates to predictable epiphanies about vulnerability and the inherent risks involved in love.

Moore is the most recent failed example of Hollywood's fascination with cross-pollinating stars of the music industry onto the big screen. Though attractive enough, so much of her performance is spent skulking and pouting that it is difficult to invest any emotion in her dilemma. When she isn't brooding she is spouting gag-inducing bromides like, "If love beats you up, let's beat it up right back."

The same holds true for Ford, who misguidedly mistakes his sotto-voce raspiness and I'm-too-cool-to-brush-the-hair-away-from-my-face grunge-gravitas for character depth.

The basic theme, that the human heart must risk being broken in order to love, is in itself truthful, but told in such an unappealing manner even wisdom sounds stale. The film's lack of narrative flow could be attributed to the fact that the script is a crude composite of two novels by Sarah Dessen, "Someone Like You" and "That Summer."

Regrettably, at times the film equates sex with love. However, to her credit, Kilner does show that sexual intimacy can have life-changing repercussions; Scarlett gets pregnant during sex with Steve and after his death must raise the child as a single mother. At least the narrative provides a positive portrayal of a teen-age girl willing to accept the responsibility of parenthood, rather than aborting her unborn baby.

Unfortunately, this puppy love story is for the dogs.

Due to an implied sexual encounter, brief sensuality, drug abuse, as well as an instance of rough language and some profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: How to Eat Fried Worms
synopsis: Loose adaptation of Thomas Rockwell's children's book about a weak-stomached boy (Luke Benward) who, desperate to fit in as the new kid at school and silence a bully's (Adam Hicks) taunts, agrees to eat 10 worms within the span of a Saturday afternoon. With a yuck factor that may disturb some parents, director Bob Dolman's film sends a misguided message about peer pressure that undermines charming performances and themes of friendship, honesty and standing up for oneself. Scattered mildly crude language and humor, some bullying and gross-out images and a scene of breaking into a shop
full_review:
Over the past few years, Walden Media has built a winning reputation of quality in producing faithful film adaptations of celebrated children's books such as "Holes," "Because of Winn-Dixie" and "The Chronicles of Narnia," but misses the mark with "How to Eat Fried Worms" (New Line), a coming-of-age comedy with a message as unappetizing as its title.

Loosely based on the beloved tale by Thomas Rockwell -- son of painter Norman Rockwell -- the film, as in Walden's last effort "Hoot," centers on a new kid's uphill battle to fit in. Things get off to a bad start when weak-stomached Billy (Luke Benward), runs afoul of school bully Joe (Adam Hicks), who fills Billy's lunch thermos with earthworms. To save face, Billy, brags that worms are his favorite snack. Calling his bluff, Joe challenges Billy to eat 10 within the span of one Saturday afternoon.

Apart from the worms, director Bob Dolman alters the story considerably. In Rockwell's version, Billy's dilemma is not the result of bullying but a boyish dare among friends. Billy agrees to the unpalatable diet for $50 so he can buy a bicycle.

The plot-tinkering is of less concern than the new message. Standing up to bullies is well and good, but, troublingly, the movie seems to suggest that the best way to deal with peer pressure is to give in to it. Billy wants to be accepted so badly he'll do anything -- even eat worms -- to be considered "cool." (Not the best advice for kids who have to deal with more serious temptations.) In "standing up" for himself, Billy capitulates to Joe's humiliating demands.

Though light-heartedly dramatized, the film's "ick"-factor -- several scenes play like a kid's version of "Fear Factor" -- may disturb some parents, as the boys devise increasingly nauseating recipes, subjecting the squirmers to microwaves and rolling pins with a cruel glee (a humorous disclaimer assures us no worms were harmed) and take sadistic pleasure in Billy's gastrointestinal torture, however consensual.

These elements are offset by charming performances and family-friendly themes of friendship, honesty and facing one's fears.

At one point, a frustrated Billy tries to explain to outcast ally Erika (Hallie Kate Eisenberg) -- the most level-headed of the bunch -- why he can't renege on the bet. Many viewers may share her disapproving incomprehension. They may also be tempted to skip lunch.

The film contains scattered mildly crude language and humor, some bullying and gross-out images and a scene of breaking into a shop. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested. Some material may not be suitable for children.

title: How to Frame a Figg
synopsis: Dimwitted City Hall clerk (Don Knotts) accidentally uncovers some shady dealings by the boys in the back room who promote him to a high-pay, no-sweat job, but eventually he figures out why and then blows the whistle on the corrupt officials. The comedy's humor revolves around the inane personality of Knotts, as well as around the farfetched situations he bumbles into and out of. Alan Rafkin directs the appropriately juvenile script as if it were an extended TV sitcom. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: How to Frame a Figg
synopsis: Dimwitted City Hall clerk (Don Knotts) accidentally uncovers some shady dealings by the boys in the back room who promote him to a high-pay, no-sweat job, but eventually he figures out why and then blows the whistle on the corrupt officials. The comedy's humor revolves around the inane personality of Knotts, as well as around the farfetched situations he bumbles into and out of. Alan Rafkin directs the appropriately juvenile script as if it were an extended TV sitcom

title: How to Get Ahead in Advertising
synopsis: Biting British satire of the advertising business centers on an ad-man burnout (Richard E. Grant) who grows a talking boil on his neck with which he carries on a running debate over the evils of the ad game. Although writer-director Bruce Robinson's work is thought-provoking and technically sound, the satire deteriorates into a manic mad show starring a ghoulish boil. Much profanity, sexually vulgar language and an intense, though humorous, depiction of madness

title: How To Kill Your Neighbor's Dog
synopsis: Flat comedy about a chain-smoking L.A. playwright (Kenneth Branagh) who's had a recent string of flops but finds comfort and inspiration from an 8-year-old neighbor (Suzi Hofrichter) with a disability. Writer-director Michael Kalesniko's mildly entertaining film has some witty dialogue, but the sluggish pace and the soft writing outweigh these. An implied sexual encounter, recurring rough language and a few cutting remarks mocking Christianity

title: How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days
synopsis: Drawn-out romantic comedy in which an ad exec (Matthew McConaughey) boasts he can make a magazine columnist (Kate Hudson) fall for him in 10 days, unaware that for her next advice column she intends to make him dump her in the same time frame. Donald Petrie directs a contrived and unconvincing battle-of-the-sexes comedy that lacks sparkling dialogue. Sexual references, fleeting violence, some rude slang expressions and occasional profanity
full_review:
A guy takes a bet he can make a particular woman quickly fall in love with him, unaware she's targeted him as the subject of a magazine article, "How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days" (Paramount).

If the set-up sounds strained, just imagine almost two hours of watching it unfold, in full-throttle cutesy mode.

Kate Hudson's Andie is a beauty magazine columnist, wanting to write serious political stories. But her boss (Bebe Neuwirth) likes the idea of an article on all the wrong things to do that would drive a man away -- and Andie's got the assignment.

Ad exec Barry (Matthew McConaughey) wants to head the campaign for a diamond client but his boss (a bland Robert Klein) is dubious. To convince him, Barry boasts he can make any woman fall in love with him. The two women also competing for the diamond account know of Andie's assignment, so tell him Andie's the one he must woo and win.

Easily smitten by the vivacious blonde, he's puzzled after a few days when she starts filling his bathroom shelves with her cosmetics, adding stuffed animals to his decor and showing up at his office with awful shirts she insists he wear immediately. But when she barges in on his poker night with his buddies and makes him blow his nose on her command, he tells her off -- only to apologize and make up later, to her dismay. Can he put up with her possessiveness by day 10?

Yes, Kate Hudson can be adorable, but the script has her flirting and batting her eyelashes with such abandon that she wears you out. Proceeding day-by-day to the climactic 10th day, director Donald Petrie's movie makes one wish the time frame was half as long; it might have made the drawn-out movie flow twice as well.

McConaughey starts looking uncomfortable in the role once Andie shows her spoiled brat and clingy side that severely tests his resolve. He's hard pressed to be convincing from then on and the lack of sparkling dialogue in a romantic comedy is especially noticeable. The crucial scene at the diamond client's party, where each learns the other's real intentions, rings false, only to lead into the expected resolution.

Surprisingly, the movie is not really about getting them into bed, although eventually that is implied after she spends a weekend with his down-to-earth family on Staten Island.

With its pert New York City settings and an attractive-looking cast, it may please the undemanding, but it's no loss to a guy or gal to lose this flick.

Due to sexual references, fleeting violence, some rude slang expressions and occasional profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops' Office for Film and Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13

title: How to Make a Monster
synopsis: Pedestrian thriller directed by Herbert L. Strock in which a veteran movie make-up artist (Robert H. Harris) takes revenge on the studio executives who fired him by using hypnotized actors dressed in monster make-up to kill them. Stylized violence and hokey menace

title: How to Make an American Quilt
synopsis: Unsure over her recent engagement, a graduate student (Winona Ryder) spends the summer with her grandmother (Ellen Burstyn) and six quilting-bee cronies who influence the young woman's decision with tales of their own troubled romantic relationships over the years. Director Jocelyn Moorhouse salutes sisterly solidarity in a sentimental, pokey-paced tale of age bringing emotional maturity. Fleeting bedroom scenes, sexual references and an instance of recreational drug use

title: How to Make Love to a Negro Without Getting Tired
synopsis: Offensively titled French-Canadian production takes a lightweight look at racial and sexual stereotypes in Montreal where a black Haitian immigrant (Isaach de Bankole) engages in writing a novel while enjoying the sexual favors of several white women. Directed by Jacques Benoit, the result is blatantly exploitative in its positive portrayal of casual sex and promiscuity. Several simulated sex scenes, petty thievery shown as fun and some rough language

title: How to Marry a Millionaire
synopsis: Lightweight comedy in which three Manhattan models (Lauren Bacall, Marilyn Monroe and Betty Grable) hope to snare rich husbands by renting a luxury apartment, but love proves stronger than greed when each marries a guy with little income (Rory Calhoun, David Wayne and Cameron Mitchell who's actually a multimillionaire). Directed by Jean Negulesco, the one-note comic premise provides some good-natured humor but the real fun comes from the cast's droll ensemble playing. Romantic complications and mild sexual innuendo

title: How to Murder Your Wife
synopsis: Feeble comedy in which a happily unwed cartoonist (Jack Lemmon) wakes from a drunken spree married to an Italian beauty contestant (Virna Lisi) but, many contrivances later, his initial antipathy turns into love until faced with murder charges when she disappears. Director Richard Quine tries to keep the dim-witted situation light and breezy but its tongue-in-cheek praise of bachelorhood grows increasingly tiresome, culminating in a leadenly satiric courtroom sequence denouncing marriage. Sexual innuendo and comic treatment of sexist views

title: How to Save a Marriage...and Ruin Your Life
synopsis: Eli Wallach and Anne Jackson play an adulterous couple under investigation by bachelor Dean Martin who mistakenly identitifies Stella Stevens as Wallach's compliant girlfriend in a divorce action. Fielder Cook directs a not-so-funny marriage-go-round comedy that goes cheerfully around in circles leading nowhere

title: How to Seduce a Woman
synopsis: Witless one-joke sex comedy with Angus Duncan is ineptly directed by Charles Martin

title: How to Steal a Million
synopsis: Wacky romantic comedy set in Paris where the daughter (Audrey Hepburn) of an art forger (Hugh Griffith) enlists a willing accomplice (Peter O'Toole) in a complicated scheme to steal her dad's bogus masterpiece from a museum exhibit before it can be revealed as a fraud. Director William Wyler handles the droll proceedings with sophisticated elegance, but the comic results may be too slow-paced for some tastes

title: How to Stuff a Wild Bikini
synopsis: Sun-baked youth comedy in which a naval reservist (Frankie Avalon) on duty in the Pacific gets a local witch doctor (Buster Keaton) to keep tabs on his California girlfriend (Annette Funicello) through a pelican and a bikini-clad lovely (Beverly Adams) which results in fending off a suitor (Dwayne Hickman). Directed by William Asher, the zany plot strands and throwaway humor are more tiresome than amusing, especially the overdone motorcycle race at the conclusion. Slapstick violence, sexual situations and much sexual innuendo

title: How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying
synopsis: Robert Morse and Rudy Vallee whoop it up at the World Wide Wicket Company in a zestful adaptation of the Broadway musical about an ex-window-washer's schemes to reach the top of a big corporation in the shortest possible time. Director David Swift's sharp, witty spoof retains most of the original's running gags and Frank Loesser's music

title: Huckleberry Finn
synopsis: Creaky version of Mark Twain's adventure story directed by Norman Taurog follows Huck (Jackie Coogan) on his Mississippi River adventures with escaped slave, Jim, including their encounter with the Lost Dauphin (Eugene Pallette). Dated as a movie production but still some fun

title: Huckleberry Finn
synopsis: Still one of the best screen adaptations of the Twain classic with Mickey Rooney properly scrappy in the title role and Rex Ingram strong and dignified as his companion, the freedom-seeking Jim, with Walter Connolly and William Frawley as the confidence men they meet along the river. Director Richard Thorpe captures much of the youthful wonderment and the spirit of adventure that makes the original such enjoyable reading. Fine family fare

title: Huckleberry Finn
synopsis: Sugary musical version of the Twain classic, with script and lyrics written by the Sherman Brothers, features Jeff East in the title role and Paul Winfield as Jim. Directed by J. Lee Thompson, it contains a clutter of supremely forgettable musical numbers, entirely misses the book's point and adds up only to a minor children's matinee entry

title: Hud
synopsis: Powerful drama pits a hard-working Texas rancher (Melvyn Douglas) against his cynical no-good son (Paul Newman) who, while scheming to take the ranch from his aging father, amuses himself by making a play for the old man's housekeeper (Patricia Neal) and trying to corrupt his young nephew (Brandon de Wilde).
