Nongraphic sexual activity, torture, a graphic medical procedure, sci-fi violence, occasional crude language, a brief profanity, sexual humor and innuendo
full_review:
"Iron Man" (Paramount/Marvel) is a sleekly effective science-fiction tale set against a backdrop of contemporary events and driven by its main character's moral development.

By the second half of the film, that character, billionaire weapons manufacturer Tony Stark (Robert Downey Jr.) is downing a health shake, after earlier telling a bartender, "Get me a Scotch, I'm starving!"

The cause of this radical reform, not to mention the former playboy's decision to concentrate on one woman -- his loyal girl Friday, Pepper Potts (Gwyneth Paltrow) -- can be chalked up to being held hostage in an Afghan cave by ambitious warlord Raza (Faran Tahir).

There, Raza demanded that he build a replica of his most advanced product. With the help of fellow captive and scientist Yinsen (Shaun Toub), Stark instead constructed an impregnable, gravity-defying suit of armor and escaped.

Once home, Stark announces that his company will no longer make armaments -- much to the consternation of his junior partner, Obadiah Stane (Jeff Bridges), and his military liaison, "Rhodey" (Terrence Howard). He then secludes himself in his lab to concentrate on producing an improved version of his improvised outfit, which he will use for altruistic purposes later on.

Executive producer-director Jon Favreau's screen adaptation of this popular Marvel comic-book series features impressive special effects, enjoyably flippant dialogue and a relentlessly energetic performance from Downey. Though Stark's initially dissolute lifestyle is treated humorously, his gradual realization of its underlying emptiness and his subsequent interaction with Potts -- which is respectfully restrained -- are well handled.

The film contains nongraphic sexual activity, torture, a graphic medical procedure, sci-fi violence, occasional crude language, a brief profanity, sexual humor and innuendo. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Iron Man
synopsis: Uneven boxing melodrama directed by Joseph Pevney in which a coal miner (Jeff Chandler) is turned into a prizefighter by his gambler brother (Stephen McNally), then develops a taste for the ring despite its physical toll, the boos of the crowd and the threat of losing his wife (Evelyn Keyes). Brutal boxing scenes and domestic misunderstandings

title: Iron Mask, The
synopsis: Silent version of the Dumas tale in which the aging D'Artagnon (Douglas Fairbanks) and the Three Musketeers set out to rescue young Louis XIV (William Bakewell) after he's kidnapped by a powerful noble (Ulrich Haupt), then locked in an iron mask while his evil twin (also Bakewell) takes his place on the throne. Directed by Allan Dwan, the 17th-century costume spectacle is lavishly mounted but the story's melodramatic action fairly creaks, even in the 1940 sound version narrated by Douglas Fairbanks, Jr. Stylized violence and muted sexual innuendo

title: Iron Maze
synopsis: Unsavory tale of the attempted murder of a Japanese businessman (Hiroaki Murakami) as recounted to the Pennslyvania police in contradictory versions by the victim, his U.S. bride (Bridget Fonda) and her volatile lover (Jeff Fahey). Director Hiroaki Yoshida's clumsy melodrama sheds little light on the nature of truth or the clash of cultures and is further marred by choppy exposition and underdeveloped characters. Repeated staging of a violent confrontation, restrained lovemaking and recurring rough language

title: Iron Mistress, The
synopsis: Muddled tale of frontiersman Jim Bowie (Alan Ladd) who leaves the Louisiana bayous for New Orleans in 1825, makes a fortune in land speculation but, played false by a local belle (Virginia Mayo), pulls up stakes for Texas where he marries a senorita (Phyllis Kirk). Directed by Gordon Douglas, the unconvincing period romance is paced by occasional duels and fights with Bowie's specially designed knife which he ditches in the Mississippi at movie's end. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Iron Monkey
synopsis: Snazzy martial arts adventure set in a 19th century Chinese village where a corrupt politician forces a traveling physician (Donnie Yen) to capture a masked bandit (Rongguang Yu), who repeatedly robs the rich to give to the poor, by holding the physician's young son in jail. Directed by Yuen Wo Ping, the action is fantastic with several amazing stunts, while the film is sprinkled with humor and slapstick which lend a light-hearted air to the proceedings. Subtitles. Intermittent martial arts violence, fleeting sexual references and a few instances of crass language

title: Iron Petticoat, The
synopsis: Failed Cold War comedy directed by Ralph Thomas in which a straight-laced Soviet aviator (Katherine Hepburn) on official business in London falls for the wacky charms of a U.S. Air Force officer (Bob Hope) who convinces her of the superiority of the capitalist system in this pale take-off on "Ninotcha." Much unamusing sexual innuendo

title: Iron Sheriff, The
synopsis: Muddled Western in which a dour sheriff (Sterling Hayden) gives evidence convicting his son (Darryl Hickman) of murdering a stage driver in a robbery, then sets out to prove the lad's innocence. Directed by Sidney Salkow, the contrived proceedings and cliched characters have only intermittent interest. Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Iron & Silk
synopsis: A 22-year-old American (Mark Salzman) arrives in China in 1982 to teach English and absorb the culture, but spends much of his time training under the skeptical eye of a famed kung fu master (Pan Qingfu). Producer-director Shirley Sun's fact-based account of the youth's two years in China alternates martial arts sequences with an earnest, low-keyed glimpse of Chinese society which hints at the government crackdown to come at decade's end. Restrained kung fu segments

title: Ironweed
synopsis: Story set in 1936 Albany, N.Y., about a hobo (Jack Nicholson) who visits the wife (Carroll Baker) and family he had deserted 22 years before after having drunkenly caused the death of his infant son. Scripted by William Kennedy from his own novel and directed by Hector Babenco, the result is less the story of a few days in the life of a Depression-era bum than it is a challenging meditation on the quality of lost souls. Some adults will be repelled by its depiction of the brutalizing conditions in which derelicts live as well as several needlessly explicit sex scenes

title: Iron Will
synopsis: Old-fashioned underdog tale in which a South Dakota youth (Mackenzie Astin) in 1917 attempts to save the family farm and earn college tuition by competing for the $10,000 prize in a gruelling, 522-mile dogsled race from Winnipeg to St. Paul, Minnesota in the dead of winter. Director Charles Haid's outdoors adventure is rousingly rendered despite downright corny dialogue and several cardboard villains. Some menace and brief violence

title: Irreconcilable Differences
synopsis: Pre-teen girl (Drew Barrymore) sues to be free of her parents (Ryan O'Neal and Shelley Long) who have been driven to distraction by life in the Hollywood fast lane. Some parents may be chagrined over the legal and emotional precedent of the child rights issue, but director Charles Shyer can't choose whether this is light comedy or fairly serious drama. Very brief nudity in a comic context

title: Isabel
synopsis: French Canadian story of a young woman (Genevieve Bujold) who returns to a stifling back country environment upon the death of her mother and finds herself unable to escape from her strange family whose history is tied to the land. Written, produced and directed by Paul Amond, it has plenty of lushly beautiful country scenes but its moody, sinister interiors with their turgid, murky implications of incest do not add up to a satisfying experience

title: Isadora
synopsis: ( see: "The Loves of Isadora" )

title: I Saw What You Did
synopsis: Modest thriller in which two teen girls amuse themselves by making random phone calls using the title sentence to get a rise out of those who answer, until dialing a man (John Ireland) who just killed his wife and now seeks to silence the caller. Directed by William Castle, the proceedings begin as a sophomoric prank which turns dangerously serious, with increasingly tense scenes and a violent climax. Stylized violence and menacing situations involving young people

title: I See a Dark Stranger
synopsis: ( see: "The Adventuress" )

title: I Shot Andy Warhol
synopsis: Dramatizing a minor but highly publicized part of the turbulent 1960s is this picture of Valerie Solanas (Lili Taylor), a radical feminist who lived on the fringes of New York's trendy counterculture but whose paranoid perceptions of its rejection boiled over in 1968 when she seriously wounded pop artist Warhol (Jared Harris). Directed by Mary Harron, the result is a vivid re-creation of one of the more bizarre fragments of the period's cultural ferment, but the treatment lacks a larger frame of reference and is uncritical of the anti-social ideas and behavior so amply portrayed. Stylized violence, sexual situations, brief nudity, casual drug usage and frequent rough language

title: Ishtar
synopsis: Warren Beatty and Dustin Hoffman play failed songwriters who find themselves pawns in a dangerously ironic game of international intrigue in director Elaine May's failed buddy comedy set in the Moroccan desert. Essentially a story about the saving grace of comradeship, the exotic romantic adventure has some rough language, brief slapstick violence and a momentary flash of nudity

title: Island at the Top of the World, The
synopsis: Disney version of a Ian Cameron novel about an American archaeologist (David Hartman) and a British adventurer (Donald Sinden) who journey to the Arctic where they discover a tropical island atop a polar ice cap inhabited by the descendents of the Vikings. Directed by Robert Stevenson, it is burdened by a ragged screenplay, some lackluster special effects and many atrocious performances. Harmless family fun, but it could have been so much better

title: Island Escape
synopsis: ( see: "No Man Is an Island" )

title: Island of Dr. Moreau, The
synopsis: Second screen version of H.G. Wells' novel about a scientist's obsession to turn animals into human beings starts out promisingly enough with a shipwrecked engineer (Michael York) finding himself on a remote Pacific island presided over by a kind but somewhat sinister doctor (Burt Lancaster). Once Moreau's secret is out, however, director Don Taylor's movie degenerates into rather clumsy and ineffective melodrama with considerable violence and bloodshed. The 1933 version with Charles Laughton is the one to see

title: Island of Dr. Moreau, The
synopsis: Murky updating of H.G. Wells' 1896 horror tale of an airplane crash survivor (David Thewlis) held prisoner on a remote island where the experiments of a mad scientist (Marlon Brando) in turning animals into humans have resulted in grotesque mutants who come to rebel against their demented creator. Directed by John Frankenheimer, the menacing visuals aren't enough to involve the viewer in the fate of the picture's ill-defined characters. Intermittent violence and mindless mayhem

title: Island of Lost Souls
synopsis: Horror classic from H.G. Wells' story of a shipwrecked sailor (Richard Arlen) turning up on an uncharted South Sea island where a mad doctor (Charles Laughton) is hard at work trying to turn wild beasts into humans. Director Erle C. Kenton makes the grisly situation effectively menacing, though the misshapen refugees from the House of Pain are treated with some sympathy. Very stylized violence but the thematic implications of animal vivisection are not for children

title: Island of Lost Women
synopsis: Clunky adventure directed by Frank W. Tuttle with a radio newscaster (Jeff Richards) landing his disabled aircraft on an uncharted Pacific island inhabited by a scientist (Alan Napier) raising three daughters there because he's certain the civilized world will destroy itself in nuclear warfare. Of interest only as an example of the period's fears of nuclear annihilation

title: Island of Terror
synopsis: Halting horror tale directed by Terence Fisher in which London pathologists (Peter Cushing and Edward Judd) are summoned to an island off the east coast of Ireland to deal with a rapidly multiplying organism that turns people and animals into jelly by devouring their bones. Stylized violence with some guresome visuals and hokey menace

title: Island of the Blue Dolphins
synopsis: Engrossing adaptation of Scott O'Dell's children's story about the 19th-century adventures of a young Indian girl (Celia Kaye) who learns to fend for herself when stranded on a remote island off the coast of California. Produced by Robert B. Radnitz and directed by James B. Clark, the movie captures the wondrous beauty of nature and its sense of ecology provides a delightful lesson for youngsters

title: Island of the Burning Damned
synopsis: Standard British science fiction programmer with Christopher Lee and Peter Cushing combating extraterrestrial beings who invade a country inn. Director Terence Fisher engenders as musch suspense as possible with invaders who resemble nothing so much as bubbling, crawling neon pancakes

title: Island of the Burning Doomed
synopsis: ( see: "Island of the Burning Damned" )

title: Island of the Lost
synopsis: No-frills adventure directed by John Florea in which an explorer (Richard Greene) sails into the South Seas with his family and an anthropology student (Mark Hulswit), but a typhoon sinks their ship leaving them marooned on an uncharted island with cut-rate prehistoric dangers. More menace than violence

title: Islands in the Stream
synopsis: George C. Scott stars as an expatriate American living in the Bahamas who is jolted out of his self-pitying sense of failure as a man and as an artist by the demands of World War II. Franklin Schaffner has directed this adaptation of the posthumous Ernest Hemingway novel with considerable success in focusing upon the interior world of the central character, the prototypical Hemingway hero acting with style under pressure

title: Island, The
synopsis: Clumsy, brutish thriller about a writer (Michael Caine) and his young son who inadvertently come across the descendents of 16th-century pirates still plying their bloodthirsty trade in the shelter of the Bermuda Triangle. Director Michael Ritchie's fantasy veers wildly between the cruel, ridiculous and downright nasty. Excessive violence, some nudity and profantiy

title: Isle of the Dead
synopsis: Science faces the supernatural during the 1912 Balkan War when a stern Greek general (Boris Karloff) quarantines an island beset by plague and gripped by fears of a vampire. Producer Val Lewton and director Mark Robson team to fashion a quite effective tale of psychological dread filled with dark, moody photography and talk of the living dead. Mostly spooky effects but some stylized violence

title: Isn't She Great
synopsis: Campy but disappointing biography about tawdry novel author Jacqueline Susann (Bette Midler) whose steadfast manager-husband (Nathan Lane) and gaudy wardrobe helped propel her to the fame she desperately sought. Director Andrew Bergman transforms a New Yorker Magazine article about Susann into a comedy-drama that touches on her ambition and personal tragedies but is content to present just a glossy treatment of her life. Numerous crude sexual references, some homosexual innuendo, depictions of fairly explicit book covers, and recurring rough language

title: I Spy
synopsis: Noisy, charmless action-comedy in which a government spy (Owen Wilson) is forced to team with a cocky boxing champ (Eddie Murphy) in Budapest to recover a stolen U.S. superaircraft about to fall into enemy hands. As directed by Betty Thomas, motormouth Murphy and wimpy Wilson exemplify the tired odd-couple buddy formula movie routinely punctuated by a blur of crazed chases and stale shootouts. Frequent stylized violence, a sexually suggestive scene, some crude expressions and an instance of profanity
full_review:
The 1960s TV series never looked so good until the movie version of "I Spy" (Columbia) came out. The movie is all sound and fury, signifying nothing less than Hollywood's bankruptcy of creativity.

When a U.S. superweapon, a reconnaissance aircraft that can morph into invisibility, falls into the villainous hands of boxing fan Gundars (a glowering Malcolm McDowell), special agent Alex Scott (Owen Wilson) is assigned to recover it in Budapest and fly it home. He's jazzed to be working with a would-be girlfriend, agent Rachel (Famke Janssen), but bummed to be teamed with ultracocky boxing champ Kelly Robinson (Eddie Murphy) in order to get near Gundars.

Predictably, Scott and Robinson are like oil and water.

The duo's bickering and the mayhem that follows, with its crazed chases and stale shootouts, are what pass for comedy. But, as directed by Betty Thomas, motormouth Murphy and wimpy Wilson only exemplify how tired the odd-couple buddy formula has become. Robinson, who always refers to himself in the third person -- even partner Scott finds that irritating -- wisecracks at super speed but his talky exchanges with Scott simply aren't very funny.

And so we have them racing and chasing around Budapest in a car, truck, hot-air balloon -- even a funicular -- with bullets flying but viewers' patience vanishing. The choreographed fisticuffs also take on a nasty edge when the crotch area is a prime target. However, it's all such a fantasy the stylized violence never seems realistic; it's just a relief when it's all over. By comparison, the TV series with Robert Culp and Bill Cosby, on which this jumble is based, looks like a model of wit and sophistication.

The best thing about this charmless movie is seeing the streets and monuments of Budapest, which looks appealingly old-world European.

"I Spy" may be a blockbuster and the first of a franchise, but let's hope not.

Due to frequent stylized violence, a sexually suggestive scene, some crude expressions and an instance of profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Istanbul
synopsis: Director Joseph Pevney's lackluster remake of "Singapore" (1947) follows the return of an American pilot (Errol Flynn) to Turkey after World War II to retrieve some hidden diamonds, then discovers that the woman (Cornell Borchers) he had once loved but thought dead is an amnesiac married to another. Some stylized violence and hokey romantic complications

title: I Stand Condemned
synopsis: British World War I tale set in Russia where a wounded officer (Laurence Olivier) falls for his nurse (Penelope Dudley Ward) but when her wealthy fiance (Henry Baur) traps him in a gambling debt, he seeks a loan from a friendly dowager (Athene Seyler) who turns out to be a spy. Directed by Anthony Asquith, the melodramatic proceedings gain some interest from Baur's performance as an earthy war profiteer who alone can save the officer from execution as a traitor. Romantic complications

title: I Still Know What You Did Last Summer
synopsis: Pointless horror sequel in which a quartet of college students vacationing at a remote Caribbean island hotel find the staff murdered and face a similar fate from a relentless, hook-handed killer. Any thrills are bogus and the plot predictable in director Danny Cannon's mindless parade of gory slaughters and mutilated corpses. Excessive violence, sexual innuendo, recurring profanity and much rough language

title: It!
synopsis: Hokey horror with Rabbi Loew's medieval Golem turning up in a British museum where loony assistant curator Roddy McDowall brings it to life but can't control it. Writer-producer-director Herbert J. Leder updates the Golem legend with snatches of other horror movies, including "Psycho," but with little sense of suspense and less credibility. Stylized violence and sexual situations

title: Italian Connection, The
synopsis: German-Italian B-grade gangster movie about a Milan pimp (Mario Adorf) who has been set up by the mob as scapegoat for a missing shipment of heroin sought by two American hit men (Henry Silva and Woody Strode) and the result is endless mayhem and violence. Director Fernando Di Leo punctuates the physical action with lots of sex and nudity

title: Italian for Beginners
synopsis: Character-driven Danish ensemble piece about six lonely Danes, including a recently widowed pastor (Anders W. Berthelsen), a shy hotel clerk (Peter Gantzler) and a belligerent restaurant manager (Lars Kaalund), whose ordinary lives are infused with passion when they take an Italian language class. Distracting camera work aside, director Lone Scherfig's mellow comedy has a faint spiritual bent as the characters grow in understanding of themselves and their relationships, but the implication of an assisted suicide is troubling. Subtitles. A sexual encounter, serious end-of-life questions and brief rough language with an instance of profanity. The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops

title: Italian Job, The
synopsis: Tongue-in-cheek spoof of heist thrillers follows the hijacking of $4 million in gold as it is being transferred from the Turin airport to bank by staging the world's most spectacular traffic jam. Michael Caine organizes the job for mastermind Noel Coward who operates from an English prison. Before director Peter Collinson brings it all to a close with a maniacal, hair-raising auto chase, there's some good visual satire and a lot of busy acting to make up for the loose ends in the plot

title: Italiano Brave Gente
synopsis: The plight of Italian soldiers fighting on the Russian front during World War II is portrayed in the fate of four individuals, with Peter Falk and Arthur Kennedy as part of an impressive international cast. Director Giuseppe De Santis' large-scale epic mangages to retain some feeling for the human pain of war. Fairly intense battle scenes

title: It Came from Beneath the Sea
synopsis: Fair sci-fi thriller in which a nuclear sub commander (Kenneth Tobey) has a mid-Pacific run-in with a gigantic radioactive octopus, then teams with a marine biologist (Faith Domergue) to keep the monster from destroying San Francisco. Director Robert Gordon handles the formula story rather blandly, except for some feminist asides and Ray Harryhusen's effective special effects as the animated monster savages the Golden Gate Bridge and menaces the Frisco waterfront. Some stylized violence, menace and mild romance

title: It Came from Outer Space
synopsis: Chilling science fiction from Ray Bradbury's story about an amateur astronomer (Richard Carlson) who sights a UFO landing in the Arizona desert, then discovers that the area's inhabitants, including his girlfriend (Barbara Rush), are being taken over by aliens. Director Jack Arnold uses the isolated desert setting to heighten the sense of menace in the strange proceedings, though the aliens' intentions ultimately prove more benign than threatening. Imaginative family fare with an upbeat ending

title: It Conquered the World
synopsis: Hokey sci-fi tale directed by Roger Corman in which an alien creature from Venus takes control of an isolated rural community with the help of a disgruntled scientist (Lee Van Cleef), until his wife (Beverly Garland) and a fellow scientist (Peter Graves) intervene. Fantasy violence and menace

title: It Could Happen to You
synopsis: After promising, in place of a tip, to split any lottery winnings with a waitress (Bridget Fonda), a New York City cop (Nicolas Cage) wins $4 million and gives her half, infuriating his money-hungry wife (Rosie Perez). Director Andrew Bergman's Capraesque romantic comedy makes good use of the Big Apple setting in this crowd-pleasing tale of blue-collar decency triumphing over deceit and greed. Fleeting violence and an implied affair

title: It Grows on Trees
synopsis: Comic fantasy of a small-town housewife (Irene Dunne) whose worries about family finances are solved after planting two odd trees in the backyard, one of which proceeds to grow $5 bills while the other sprouts $10s. Directed by Arthur Lubin, the "dream-come-true" premise developes some playful complications but the proceedings turn more serious than the lightweight situation can bear

title: It Happened Here
synopsis: Imagining what life might have been like if Hitler had succeeded in invading Great Britain is shown in the story of a nurse who is drawn into collaboration with the puppet regime under the German Occupation. Directed by Kevin Brownlow and Andrew Mollo, it is an interesting inquiry into the nature of Nazi totalitarianism, with some scenes of brutality that, though not vivid, are extremely realistic and not for children

title: It Happened One Night
synopsis: Delightful romantic comedy in which a just-fired reporter (Clark Gable) sees a scoop in helping a runaway heiress (Claudette Colbert) escape her father (Walter Connolly), detectives and the press by roughing it from Miami to New York via buses, roadside tourist cabins and even on foot. Director Frank Capra's screwball Depression roadshow has the charm of matching opposites in Gable's hardboiled working man and Colbert's spoiled rich girl whose unsentimental journey ends with the falling "Walls of Jericho," a running gag which finally brings them together. Memorable romantic classic with plenty of fun as well as social and personal values

title: It Happened to Jane
synopsis: Enjoyable comedy in which a widow (Doris Day) with two children and a lobster business gets her lawyer friend (Jack Lemmon) to sue the railroad for ruining one of her shipments, but the company's mean-spirited representative (Ernie Kovacs) escalates the case into a national media circus. Directed by Richard Quine, it's a predictable underdog story of small-town widow and lawyer persevering until they win the case and each other, with plenty of comic confusions along the way

title: It Happens Every Spring
synopsis: Lightweight but very enjoyable comedy about a chemistry professor (Ray Milland) who concocts a wood-repellent formula that makes baseballs immune to contact with bats. Directed by Lloyd Bacon, the comic premise turns the prof into an instant big-league star whose pitches defy top-hitting batters and confound his veteran catcher (Paul Douglas). Family fun, even for those who don't like baseball

title: It Happens Every Thursday
synopsis: Dated but pleasantly sentimental comedy in which a city couple (Loretta Young and John Forsythe) buy a failing small-town newspaper, then try various schemes to make it a success. Director Joseph Pevney uses the veteran supporting cast (Frank McHugh, Edgar Buchanan, Jane Darwell and others) to keep the couple's problems from getting too serious in a picture affirming the homespun virtues of honesty, loyalty and hard work. Mild sexual innunedo

title: I, the Jury
synopsis: Gross remake of the 1953 Mickey Spillane private eye melodrama features Armand Assante as the sullen Mike Hammer out to avenge a dead friend by smashing a rogue CIA operation which uses a sex clinic as a front. Director Richard T. Heffron relies on a repulsive mix of sex and violence

title: I Think I Love My Wife
synopsis: Director and co-writer Chris Rock plays a suburban husband tempted to stray in a comedy based on the 1972 French classic "Chloe in the Afternoon." This dubious remake offers little entertainment value, a torrent of four-letter words drowning out a few good jokes, and fails to offer any original insights into marital fidelity, boding ill for Rock's career behind the camera. Pervasive rough and sexually explicit language and an instance of profanity, sexual situations and humor, one image of pornography containing rear female nudity, brief violence
full_review:
Comedian Chris Rock juggles duties as director, co-writer and star in "I Think I Love My Wife" (Fox), a dubious remake of the 1972 French classic "Chloe in the Afternoon," the last of director Eric Rohmer's "Six Moral Tales."

Rock falls short both behind and in front of the camera where he plays Richard Cooper, a suburban husband struggling to remain faithful to his wife. His film skimps not only on any special insights into marital fidelity but also on pure entertainment value.

Richard lives outside Manhattan where he works as an investment banker. He's got the proverbial itch after seven years of marriage to schoolteacher Brenda (Gina Torres), who shoulders most of the burden of caring for their two young children. In voice-over, he confesses to being primed for adultery because of his wandering eye and a lack of intimacy with Brenda. Couples therapy isn't helping. When an old acquaintance, Nikki (Kerry Washington), shows up at his office wearing a red dress, he's put to the test.

Richard's predicament plays out in repetitive fashion, with few obvious points overlooked. Twice he attends an auto show -- first with Nikki to admire a Porsche and then with Brenda to scout out minivans. Racial issues are raised occasionally though not in relation to the central theme. The women are one-dimensional. Attractive, intelligent Brenda is prone to nagging and Nikki's needy seductress is a gold digger. Every character is objectified and no one is very likable.

Directing oneself is a formidable challenge and Richard's listlessness is the only evidence that Rock tried to tone down his usual persona. The movie's funniest moment comes when Richard revs up the energy level to pick a fight with Brenda over the dinner menu.

A handful of decent topical jokes get lost under a torrent of four-letter words and sex-related gags.

When Richard finally gets himself into a seriously compromising situation, a modicum of suspense is generated about whether he'll do the right thing. Unfortunately, it's not worth sitting through "I Think I Love My Wife" to find out -- even though, ultimately (slight spoiler here), there's a morally sound outcome.

The film contains pervasive rough and sexually explicit language and an instance of profanity, sexual situations and humor, one image of pornography containing rear female nudity, and a brief violent scuffle. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: It Lives Again
synopsis: Cheap and shoddy horror movie about an epidemic of monstrous infants who kill with superhuman force. Director Larry Cohen's blood-and-gore thriller is excessive not only in its concept but also its graphic visuals

title: It Lives by Night
synopsis: When a honeymooning couple (Steward Moss and Marianne McAndrew) run into a bat while frolicking in a Western cave and the husband is bitten, he goes around by night killing people, including the local tourist trade. Directed by Jerry Jameson, it is an innocuous bottom-drawer horror movie but a love scene and some grisly gore make it inappropriate fare for the youngsters

title: It Only Happens to Others
synopsis: Written and directed by Nadine Trintignant, this is a very personal movie about the loss of a child (the Trintignant's lost their child when Jean-Louis was filming "Z"). With Marcello Mastroianni and Catherine Deneuve playing the grieving parents, the result is a movie that seems to mourn over the loss of a sweet, precious toy rather than for a human life. The director seems to have kept her own feelings private while distracting viewers with both the luminous personalities of her players and the glossy plastic backgrounds against which they emote

title: It Runs in the Family
synopsis: Pleasantly affecting serio-comedy about three dysfunctional generations of fathers and sons exploring the foibles and follies of life, love and parenting. Directed by Fred Schepisi, the on-screen chemistry of Tinseltown father-son combo Kirk and Michael Douglas facilitates the theme of reconciliation and family unity to emerge with emotional honesty despite the at times schmaltzy sentimentality of the narrative. Recurring drug abuse and sexual situations, as well as minimal vulgarities and an instance of rough language
full_review:
Three generations of fathers and sons explore the foibles and follies of life and love in the pleasantly affecting serio-comedy, "It Runs in the Family" (MGM).

Directed by Fred Schepisi, the on-screen chemistry of Tinseltown father-son combo Kirk and Michael Douglas facilitates the theme of reconciliation to emerge with emotional honesty despite the at times schmaltzy sentimentality of the narrative.

The dramedy charts the ebb and flow of the Gromberg family, whose members' professional prosperity is in inverse proportion to their ability to communicate with each other.

Heading the dysfunctional clan is Mitchell Gromberg (Kirk Douglas), the hoary patriarch and retired founding partner of a prestigious New York law firm. Having recently suffered a stroke -- a narrative element resonating with the elder Douglas -- he has begun to ponder his own mortality.

His workaholic son, Alex (Michael Douglas), a highly successful corporate attorney with a penchant for social activism, finds himself knee-deep in his own existential crisis -- though of the midlife, rather than end-of-life, variety.

To his dismay, he realizes that when it comes to parenting, the rotten apple has not fallen far from the tree. While both men were more-than-adequate providers, neither bothered to read the rest of the job description. In addition to being a lousy father, Alex isn't scoring too high in the husband department either, having cheated on his wife (Bernadette Peters) with a fellow soup-kitchen volunteer.

The most recent links in the dysfunctional chain are Alex's two sons -- Asher (Cameron Douglas), a philandering, rudderless rebel, and Eli (Rory Culkin), a precocious 11-year-old, the most levelheaded of the lot. The performance of Cameron, Michael's real-life son, marks the first production to boast three generations in the same film; also included in the family affair is Kirk's former wife, Diana Douglas, who plays his on-screen spouse, Evelyn.

When Evelyn unexpectedly dies, the facade of civility collapses -- a devastating blow to the family's tenuous tethers. Much more than Mitchell's emotional rock, Evelyn served as a peacemaker between the warring kin. Her passing and Mitchell's subsequent mourning play as some of the most tender, emotionally honest scenes in the film -- serving as poignant reminders to savor times shared with loved ones.

When Mitchell calls a truce and offers conciliatory gestures, Alex is at a loss, his father-son musculature having atrophied through years of disuse. This spirit of detente, however, filters into Alex's relationship with his own sons -- especially the wayward Asher, whose nose-diving grades and campus drug dealing are setting him on the fast track to disaster.

Predictably, the Gromberg men close ranks, make amends and gain a deeper appreciation for each other. This, of course, is not accomplished without much intergenerational sarcasm and the obligatory teary-eyed reconciliation. However, the film's theme of forgiveness, as well as the pro-family message it espouses, make these saccharine moments easy pills to swallow -- even to applaud.

Early in the film, the Grombergs celebrate a raucous Passover Seder meal. While some may find the incessant squabbling and irreverent banter of the scene off-putting, it is refreshing to see a family -- however dysfunctional -- gather together to pray. This is laudable, taking into account Hollywood's aversion to include traditional religious practices for any purpose other than mockery. Typically, families like the Grombergs -- hip, educated and progressive -- are portrayed as religiously neutral, if not openly critical and hostile.

Due to recurring drug abuse and sexual situations, as well as minimal vulgarities and an instance of rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: It's a Great Life
synopsis: Formula family comedy in the "Blondie" series starts with Dagwood (Arthur Lake) sent by Mr. Dithers (Jonathan Hale) to buy a house but winds up with a horse instead, then is invited to ride in a fox hunt held by a wealthy eccentric (Hugh Herbert) Dithers needs for a business deal. Directed by Frank Strayer, it's a typical example of the series, except that Daisy, the Bumstead's dog, gets to say a few words at movie's end

title: It's Alive
synopsis: Thoroughly nauseating movie in which a newborn baby turns out to be a bloodthirsty monster who kills some 20 people before the police stop it. Director Larry Cohen is most interested in using gore and graphic brutality for shock value alone

title: It's All True
synopsis: Account of the South American documentary begun by Orson Welles after completing production on "The Magnificent Ambersons" which was edited in his absence by RKO's new studio boss who also pulled the plug on the unfinished project and with it, Welles' Hollywood career. Directed by Richard Wilson, Myron Meisel and Bill Krohn, the documentary offers comments by Welles and others on these events as well as assembles recently discovered footage of what had been filmed into three incomplete segments about a rural Mexican youth, the Rio Carnival and a political protest by four Brazilian fishermen. Menacing situations and a child's discovery of a drowned fisherman

title: It's a Mad Mad Mad Mad World
synopsis: Overlong, overdone comedy spectacular about a random assortment of ordinary citizens who become greedy competitors in a madcap race to recover a fortune hidden by a bank robber (Jimmy Durante). Producer-director Stanley Kramer misuses practically every Hollywood comedian of the period (from Buster Keaton and Jack Benny to Jonathan Winters and Carl Reiner, not to mention actors such as Spencer Tracy and Peter Falk) in a ponderous attempt to wring laughs from car crashes and other forms of slapstick carnage. The main value of this misguided effort is its all-star gallery of comics who manage to keep the heavy-handed vehicle at least fitfully funny

title: It's a Wonderful Life
synopsis: Seasonal favorite about the joys and trials of a good man (James Stewart) who, facing financial ruin on the eve of Christmas, contemplates suicide until his guardian angel (Henry Travers) shows him how meaningful his life has been to those around him. Director Frank Capra's unabashedly sentimental picture of mainstream American life is bolstered by a superb cast (including Lionel Barrymore as a conniving banker) and a wealth of good feelings about such commonplace virtues as hard work and helping one's neighbor. Young children may find the story's dark moments unsettling

title: It's in the Bag
synopsis: Radio comedian Fred Allen stars as a flea circus owner who inherits a fortune from a distant relative, then learns the proceeds were hidden in one of five chairs sold at auction and sets out to find the buyers, one of whom is radio rival Jack Benny. Directed by Richard Wallace, the halting plot serves mainly as a peg for an uneven assortment of comic skits, notably a wartime excursion to an over-crowded movie theater. Stylized violence and mild sexual innuendo

title: It's Love Again
synopsis: British musical comedy in which an aspiring performer (Jessie Matthews) decides to break into show business by pretending to be the mystery lady all London is talking about but no one has seen because she exists only in the columns of the society writer (Robert Young) who dreamed her up. Director Victor Saville treats the resulting mix-ups and misunderstandings with amusing tongue-in-cheek earnestness while singer-dancer-comedienne Matthews pours on the charm. Romantic complications and sexual inferences

title: It's Love I'm After
synopsis: Wacky romantic comedy in which an egotistical stage actor (Leslie Howard) agrees to disillusion a young fan (Olivia de Havilland), then finds himself succumbing to her charms until his leading lady and sometime fiancee (Bette Davis) shows up and the fireworks begin. Directed by Archie Mayo, the result is creaky and entirely predictable but still fun because of the droll antics of a superb cast. Of little interest for youngsters

title: It's My Party
synopsis: Facing imminent blindness and possible dementia from AIDS, a prosperous architect (Eric Roberts) throws a two-day farewell party for family and friends, reconciling with his estranged lover (Gregory Harrison) just before taking a lethal dose of sleeping pills. Written and directed by Randal Kleiser, the script's attempts at gallows humor only intensify the maudlin tone of a movie affirming a man's decision to end his own life. Rationalization of suicide, homosexual references, fleeting full nudity and occasional profanity as well as rough language

title: It's My Turn
synopsis: Jill Clayburgh plays an intelligent independent woman who meets an out-going man (Michael Douglas) and knows enough to dump the man she has been living with (Charles Grodin). Director Claudia Weill's attempt at a Tracy-Hepburn romantic comedy lacks the essential chemistry between the principals and its delineation of sexual as well as feminist themes requires a mature perspective. Some rough language

title: It's Only Money
synopsis: Labored slapstick comedy with Jerry Lewis as a klutzy TV repairman unwittingly escaping murder attempts by a crooked lawyer (Zachary Scott) and his henchman (Jack Weston) after the fortune he doesn't know he's inherited. Directed by Frank Tashlin, the thin plot relies mainly on one's tolerance for Lewis' clowning and wacky sight gags. Comic menace and fleeting sexual innuendo

title: It's Only Money
synopsis: ( see: "Double Dynamite" )

title: It's Showtime
synopsis: Compilation of excerpts from Hollywood movies whose stars were four-footed, furry, winged or other varieties of the animal kingdom. The clips have charming appeal in their lively and nostalgic remembrance of a time when movies were perhaps less sophisticated, but definitely more fun. Good family viewing

title: It Started with Eve
synopsis: When a dying millionaire (Charles Laughton) insists on meeting his son's fiancee, the dizzy lad (Robert Cummings) brings home a hat-check girl (Deanna Durbin) and the confusion contributes to the old man's recovery. Directed by Henry Koster, Laughton steals the picture in a sly performance that goes from death bed to dance floor, imparting much needed charm to an otherwise artificial romantic comedy

title: It's the Rage
synopsis: Unsatisfying drama about a man (Jeff Daniels) who "accidentally'' shoots his business partner, triggering a series of confrontations among a group of friends and strangers that is heightened by the presence of guns. More effective as a social statement about gun control than as a movie, director James D. Stern's message film contains overwrought performances and its non-stop dialogue that makes its stageplay origins obvious. Several scenes of gun violence, a few implied sexual encounters and constant rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: It's Your Thing
synopsis: Produced by brothers Ronald, Rudolph and O'Kelly Isley who also topline the marquee and perform the title number, the movie records a June evening in 1969 when New York's Yankee Stadium shook with the Gospel singers and pop groups who strut and stomp inexhaustibly. Jackie "Moms" Mabley steals the show with a heartfelt interpretation of "Abraham, Martin and John." Some revealing costumes as well as suggestive lyrics and movements

title: It Takes Two
synopsis: Innocuous comedy in which two look-alike 9-year-olds (Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen) contrive to match up one's billionaire widowed father (Steve Guttenberg) with the other's would-be adoptive mother (Kirstie Alley). Director Andy Tennant's insipid remake of 1961's "The Parent Trap" is dully drawn-out and drably predictable. Mild cursing

title: It! The Terror from Beyond Space
synopsis: When the sole survivor (Marshall Thompson) of a 1973 space shot to Mars is rescued by a back-up ship, no one believes his story of a Martian monster killing the others until it's corroborated on the return voyage by a murderous stowaway (Ray Corrigan). Director Edward L. Cahn's low-budget sci-fi thriller has a tin-can spacecraft and novice acting, but the concept of an alien killer hunting human prey on a four-month journey through space holds enough interest without the gruesome graphics featured in its 1979 re-make, "Alien." Stylized violence and much menace

title: Ivanhoe
synopsis: The age of chivalry comes to life in this version of Sir Walter Scott's novel about 12th-century England where Saxon knight Ivanhoe (Robert Taylor) battles a host of Norman nobles, wins the hand of his lady fair (Joan Fontaine) and rescues a Jewish merchant (Felix Aymler) and his comely daughter (Elizabeth Taylor). Director Richard Thorpe's good cast does well in a story chock-full of romance, ideals, villainy and medieval derring-do, including tournaments, the storming of a castle and the ransom of good King Richard. Stylized violence

title: Ivanhoe Donaldson
synopsis: Feature documentary about the work of Donaldson, field secretary of a civil rights organization, as he helps conduct voter registration drives, freedom marches and rallies in the South during 1963. Its footage showing the sincere commitment of those involved and their reliance on non-violence in the face of provocation makes it a valuable part of the record of the times

title: I've Lived Before
synopsis: Pulp tale directed by Richard Bartlett in which an airline pilot (Jock Mahoney) has vivid recollections of a previous life as a U.S. Army aviator who died when shot down in a dogfight over 1918 France. Murky treatment of reincarnation theme

title: I've Loved You So Long
synopsis: Moving drama about a broken woman (Kristin Scott Thomas) who has been released from prison after many years for having inexplicably murdered her 6-year-old child. She is taken in by her younger sister (Elsa Zylberstein) and wary brother-in-law (Serge Hazanavicius), where gradually, embraced by the loving atmosphere of the household, including two adopted Vietnamese nieces and a stroke-victim grandfather, she has a rebirth, coming to terms with her past and slowly learning to reconnect with the outside world. Novelist-turned-director Philippe Claudel's compassionate story demonstrates profound respect for human dignity, anchored by Thomas' extraordinary performance, beautifully matched by that of Zylberstein, as the pair re-establish a sisterly bond thought lost. In French. Subtitles. An implied nonmarital encounter, suicide, a couple of crude expressions
full_review:
Currently earning rapturous reviews on Broadway for her mercurial performance in Anton Chekhov's "The Seagull," Kristin Scott Thomas shows a vastly different aspect of her talent in a moving film from France, the English actress's adopted country.

In "I've Loved You So Long" (Sony Classics), she plays Juliette, a chain-smoking broken woman released from prison after 15 years for having inexplicably murdered her 6-year-old child.

Her younger sister, Lea (Elsa Zylberstein), now a professor of literature, has insisted Juliette move in with her and husband Luc (Serge Hazanavicius), though he's wary of allowing Juliette under the same roof as their two young daughters, both adopted Vietnamese girls. Also in the household is Luc's stroke-victim father (Jean-Claude Arnaud), who can no longer speak yet seems to understand her ingrained detachment.

The taciturn Juliette must still report regularly to a parole officer (Frederic Pierrot) and, in a droll role reversal, he uses her as a soundboard for his troubles. Before long, she is allowed a job as a medical secretary, with the proviso that she not mention that she had been a doctor before her prison term.

Gradually, embraced by Lea and Luc's friends and the loving atmosphere of the household -- most especially by the children who come to love her -- Juliette has a sort of rebirth, coming to terms with her past and slowly learning to reconnect with the outside world.

The film is anchored by Thomas' extraordinary performance, her careworn face speaking volumes in the film's many close-ups, and her inner transformation wonderfully natural and credible.

Though her central character dominates the film, she's beautifully matched by Zylberstein, as the pair re-establishes a sisterly bond thought lost. Lea's seeming equanimity masks inner turmoil as we finally see when Lea lashes out at her students who discourse so knowingly on Dostoevsky and his characters' redemption, when, in fact, they know nothing of life.

Novelist-turned-director Philippe Claudel's compassionate story demonstrates profound respect for human dignity. As the characters come to know Juliette as a person, their preconceptions recede, and genuine understanding takes their place.

In French. Subtitles.

The film contains an implied nonmarital encounter, suicide, a couple of crude expressions. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.

title: Ivory Hunter
synopsis: With the moral support of wife (Dinah Sheridan) and young son, a British game warden (Anthony Steel) perseveres in establishing East Africa's first wildlife preserve, despite pestilence, bureaucrats, native resistance and greedy poachers. Writer-director Harry Watt's earnest drama features colorful action in the bush as well as an inspiring story with humane values. Entertaining family fare

title: Ivy
synopsis: Uneven thriller set in early 1900's England where a coldly ambitious woman (Joan Fontaine) poisons her penniless husband (Richard Ney) and pins the deed on her doctor-lover (Patric Knowles) in order to be free to marry a millionarie (Herbert Marshall). Directed by Sam Wood, the story turns on the persistence of a police inspector (Cedric Hardwicke) out to see justice done, but interest wanes long before that is achieved by an empty elevator shaft. Conscienceless criminal acts

title: I Wake Up Screaming
synopsis: Twisty, atmospheric thriller directed by H. Bruce Humberstone in which the sister (Betty Grable) of a murdered model (Carole Landis) falls for the leading suspect (Victor Mature), then helps him elude being framed by a vindictive cop (Laird Cregar) while searching for the real killer. Restrained violence, moody menace and some sexual innunedo

title: I Walk Alone
synopsis: Halting crime yarn in which a Prohibition bootlegger (Burt Lancaster) exits prison after 14 years to find his slick ex-partner (Kirk Douglas) has cheated him out of his share in a swanky nightclub, then winds up being framed for the murder of his best friend (Wendall Corey). Directed by Byron Haskin, the confrontations between the former partners become increasingly explosive but the meandering narrative loses focus in a romantic subplot involving the club's pianist (Lizabeth Scott). Stylized violence including a brutal beating, romantic complications and some sexual innuendo

title: I Walked with a Zombie
synopsis: Effective horror tale set on a Haitian plantation whose American owner (Tom Conway) employs a nurse (Frances Dee) to care for his strangely afflicted wife (Edith Barrett) who has had some dealings with a local voodoo cult. Produced by Val Lewton and directed by Curt Siodmak, the plot offers little more than the eerie situation's ominous atmosphere and scary visuals suggesting more than they show. Threatening situations and romantic complications

title: I Walk the Line
synopsis: Taking its title from a bittersweet Johnny Cash country-western song, the movie concerns a redneck Tennessee sheriff (miscast Gregory Peck) and his romance with a moonshiner's daughter (Tuesday Weld). Director John Frankenheimer reduces the story to a series of heavy, melodramatic surface strokes without any social or moral complexity, resulting in a movie without any substance

title: I Wanna Hold Your Hand
synopsis: Three New Jersey high school girls enact an elaborate scheme to get to see their heroes, the Beatles, on the day the singing group is to appear on the Ed Sullivan Show in 1964. Director Robert Zemecki's farcical style, rough language and a tasteless scene with a prostitute make it a decidedly adult comedy

title: I Want to Live!
synopsis: Compelling fact-based drama about a small-time crook and occasional prostitute (Susan Hayward) who in 1955 is convicted of a vicious murder on questionable evidence and, after many lengthy appeals, is executed in a California gas chamber. Directed by Robert Wise, the movie does not minimize the woman's criminal past but, by suggesting she was railroaded on the murder charge, its harrowing portrayal of her execution becomes a powerful indictment of capital punishment as well as earned Hayward's Oscar for her tough yet sympathetic performance as a victim of injustice. Adult themes and detailed depiction of an execution

title: I Want What I Want
synopsis: Anne Heywood playing both the before and after role in the story of a transsexual struggles sincerely, if not quite convincingly. Directed by John Dexter, the result is wanting in such basics as dramatic interest and clarity, as well as depth in treating the psychological, medical and moral dimensions

title: I Want You
synopsis: Contrived melodrama of the turmoil within a small-town family (headed by Dana Andrews and Dorothy McGuire) when one of its eligible males (Farley Granger) is drafted during the Korean War. Directed by Mark Robson, the soggy proceedings may be of some sociological interest but the characters are cardboard patriots more concerned about safeguarding democracy here and abroad than about the drama of their personal lifes. Dated political rhetoric and civic moralizing

title: I Was a Communist for the F.B.I.
synopsis: Patriotic melodrama based on the experiences of Matt Cvetic (Frank Lovejoy), a Pittsburg steel worker who joined the Communist Party in order to inform the Feds of its activities. Directed by Gordon Douglas, the picture emphasizes the dangers Cvetic faced working as an undercover agent for 9 years, with a subplot involving a Party member (Dorothy Hart) who risks her life to break with her Communist associates. Stylized violence

title: I Was a Male War Bride
synopsis: Uneven romantic comedy in which a suave French officer (Cary Grant) and his sharp WAC aide (Ann Sheridan) bicker on and off the job in Occupied Germany, then decide to wed, but getting "an alien spouse of female military personnel" into the U.S. turns into a comic nightmare. Directed by Howard Hawks, the romantic mix-ups in Germany have some bright moments, but the frustrated Frenchman's problems with U.S. military and immigration officials is tiresomely contrived, despite Grant's comic attempts at female impersonation. Romantic complications and sexual situations

title: I Was a Teenage Frankenstein
synopsis: Ludicrous horror tale directed by Herbert L. Strock in which a mad doctor (Whit Bissell) constructs a creature (Gary Conway) out of teen body parts, then faces the wrath of his creation. Jokey violence, some of it quite nasty, and sexual innuendo

title: I Was a Teenage Werewolf
synopsis: Horror clunker from director Gene Fowler, Jr., in which the experimental treatment used by a doctor (Whit Bissell) on an emotionally disturbed high school senior (Michael Landon) turns the troubled youth into a werewolf with disastrous results for both. Stylized mayhem, hokey menace and some sexual innuendo

title: I Went Down
synopsis: Irish crime story in which a good-hearted parolee (Peter McDonald) is forced by a mob boss (Tony Doyle) to team with a blundering ex-con (Brendan Gleeson) in hunting down the gangster's double-crossing partner (Peter Caffrey). Director Paddy Breathnach contrives to inject ditzy humor into an increasingly dark tale of revenge with unsatisfying results. Some nasty violence, a sexual encounter with nudity, occasional profanity and much rough language

title: I Will, I Will...For Now
synopsis: Limp sex farce about sexually-based marital problems stars Elliott Gould and Diane Keaton. Directed by Norman Panama, the movie's tasteless humor is structured as a parody of a sex manual with vulgar jokes and negative female stereotypes

title: The Ice Harvest
synopsis: Rancid black comedy taking place all in one night about a crooked Kansas lawyer (John Cusack) and his sleazy accomplice (Billy Bob Thornton) who embezzle $2 million from a local mob boss (Randy Quaid), but whose plans to skip town are stymied by a Christmas Eve ice storm and a series of double-crosses. Despite some pungent performances, director Harold Ramis' adaptation of Scott Phillip's mordant novel is a misanthropic mix of barbed cynicism and sordid nastiness. Recurring bloody violence, several scenes in a strip club involving partial nudity, brief pornographic images, drunken recklessness, pervasive nihilism, vulgar and irreverent humor, excessive rough and crude language, as well as some profanity
full_review:
What is it with Billy Bob Thornton and Christmas movies?

In 2003, he starred in the raunchy "Bad Santa." Now he's back serving up sour eggnog in "The Ice Harvest" (Focus), a rancid black comedy in which he plays a sleazy character that makes his petulant shopping-mall Kris Kringle almost jolly by comparison.

Based on Scott Phillip's mordant novel, with its action taking place all in one night, the movie pivots on a crooked Wichita lawyer (John Cusack) and his accomplice (Thornton) who embezzle $2 million from a local crime boss (Randy Quaid), but whose plans to skip town are stymied by a Christmas Eve ice storm and a series of double-crosses.

In the seedy company of assorted mob leg-breakers (Mike Starr), strip-club femme fatales (Connie Nielsen) and foul-mouthed barflies (Oliver Platt), the ever-affable Cusack comes off as the default "good guy." Then again, the bar is set pretty low.

Despite some pungent performances, director Harold Ramis deserves nothing but coal in his stocking for this misanthropic mix of barbed cynicism and sordid nastiness.

The movie opens with Cusack surveying a cold and uninviting Kansas vista, an apropos visual metaphor for the morally empty harvest to follow.

The film contains recurring bloody violence, several scenes in a strip club involving partial nudity, brief pornographic images, drunken recklessness, pervasive nihilism, vulgar and irreverent humor, excessive rough and crude language, as well as some profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: The Importance of Being Earnest
synopsis: Bland adaptation of Oscar Wilde's witty play about two English gents (Rupert Everett and Colin Firth) each pretending to be named Earnest to their flighty fiancees (Reese Witherspoon and Frances O'Connor). Sluggishly directed by Oliver Parker, the male leads prove charmless and Wilde's satire of frivolous upper class mores is reduced to a toothless drawing-room comedy. Romantic complications and a flash of rear nudity
full_review:
Alas, the importance of being honest requires advising that "The Importance of Being Earnest," a new adaptation from Miramax, is far off the mark. Oscar Wilde's bitingly witty satire of upper-class romantic silliness is reduced to a bland drawing room comedy.

Directed and adapted by Oliver Parker, he just didn't get zesty performances from either Rupert Everett or Colin Firth, who play two English gents each pretending to be named Earnest to their frivolous fiancees (Reese Witherspoon and Frances O'Conner, who fare better in bringing their characters to life).

Everett is charmless as selfish dandy Algernon and Firth's wealthy Jack is downright dull. This robs the story of heart as well as fun as each gets caught up in lies faking their first name to sweethearts who can only entertain marrying a man named Earnest.

Unfortunately, the entertaining does not extend to the audience very much. Some of Wilde's better lines have been cut from this version and the comic timing is affected. While the original play is sprightly, this film is sluggish.

Yet it starts out promisingly as Algernon plays a jazzy tune on the piano and asks his butler (a veddy British Edward Fox) what he thought of his composition. "I didn't think it was polite to listen, sir" the servant crisply replies.

Judi Dench brings some needed acidity to her role as O'Connor's imperious mother, who is not about to accept her daughter's engagement to the mysteriously orphaned Jack. And there are humorous moments in the subplot's tentative romance between spinster teacher Anna Massey and repressed rector Tom Wilkinson, but again, while Massey is goofily endearing, Wilkinson (so fine in "In the Bedroom") flounces about without making any real comedic impression.

There are visual compensations, however. The English countryside estate, lavish interior sets and richly layered Edwardian costumes provide appealing distraction until one remembers previous productions of this evergreen title that provoked continual chuckles of appreciation. In this adaptation, Parker tinkers with its timeframe; sometimes it feels more like the Roaring Twenties, yet there's a scene set in a tattoo parlor that looks really odd.

Perhaps Parker really is a "women's director." because the female actors leave their male counterparts in the dust, and Witherspoon, the movie's sole American, carries off an English accent pretty well.

Due to romantic complications and a flash of rear nudity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

title: The Incredible Hulk
synopsis: Intense live-action adventure about a fugitive scientist (Edward Norton) searching for a cure to the gamma poisoning that transforms him, when provoked, into a rampaging behemoth, with the help of his girlfriend and former colleague (Liv Tyler) and despite the efforts of her Army general father (William Hurt) and a British officer (Tim Roth) to capture him and exploit his powers. In between breathless chases and effective battle scenes, this latest adaptation of the popular comic, directed by Louis Leterrier, touches on serious moral issues about the use of force and the manipulation of human biology, though it squanders the initial innocence of its main characters' romance. Nongraphic premarital sexual activity, partial rear nudity, stylized violence, painful medical scenes, brief scatological humor, and occasional crude and crass language; it's possibly acceptable for older teens
full_review:
It's not easy being green; just ask "The Incredible Hulk" (Universal/Marvel).

Poisoned by gamma radiation in an Army-sponsored experiment, mild-mannered scientist Dr. Bruce Banner (Edward Norton) finds himself transformed, whenever sufficiently provoked, into the titular chartreuse-tinted, rage-tormented behemoth. Fleeing the scene of his alter ego's first murderous rampage, Banner washes up in the slums of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, where he toils as a day laborer in a bottling plant as he searches for a cure.

Pursuing him relentlessly is the mastermind of the fateful project, Gen. Thaddeus Ross (William Hurt), who's intent on exploiting the Hulk's destructive powers. Ross has an unsavory ally in Emil Blonsky (Tim Roth), a visiting British officer whose presence on this side of the water is never adequately explained, but whose obsession with becoming an invincible warrior keeps him focused on the search for the not-so-jolly giant.

The one person the Hulk will never attack is Banner's girlfriend and former colleague, Betty (Liv Tyler), who also happens to be the general's daughter. The sole survivor of his debut onslaught, she tries to get on with life, acquiring a new boyfriend, but still pines for the vanished Banner.

When an accident in Banner's factory leads to a case of gamma sickness back in the States, it provides the general with the clue he needs to trace his quarry. With Blonsky taking the lead, a crack force of commandos descends on the fugitive. But they shortly find themselves battling his hyped-up Hyde instead.

The inspiration for a 1978-82 live-action television series with the late Bill Bixby and Lou Ferrigno and a 1982-85 cartoon TV series, as well as director Ang Lee's 2003 film called simply "The Hulk," writer Stan Lee and artist Jack Kirby's popular comic-book hero first appeared in May 1962.

In between breathless chases and effective battle scenes, this latest intense adaptation, directed by Louis Leterrier, touches on serious moral issues about the use of force and the manipulation of human biology, both of which have considerable real-life resonance. But the initially innocent portrayal of the main characters' romance is squandered in a later scene which, though not explicit, tacitly endorses premarital relations, thus precluding endorsement for younger viewers.

The film contains nongraphic premarital sexual activity, partial rear nudity, stylized violence, painful medical scenes, brief scatological humor, and occasional crude and crass language; it's possibly acceptable for older teens. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: The Incredibles
synopsis: Amusing animated adventure about a family of superheroes -- headed by strongman Mr. Incredible (voiced by Craig T. Nelson) and his stretchable wife (voiced by Holly Hunter) -- living a "normal" suburban life as part of a witness protection program, when they are forced out of early retirement to save the world from an evil genius. Much edgier than past Pixar films, director Brad Bird's comic-book confection blurs the line between kids' and adult entertainment, which despite amazing visuals and a sharp-witted script falls slightly short of its title. Some action violence, including gunplay, a foiled suicide attempt and mature thematic elements
full_review:
A close-knit clan of superheroes learns that the most fantastic power of all is the love shared by a family in "The Incredibles" (Disney), an animated adventure which, though rip-roaringly entertaining at times, falls short of its title -- but only slightly.

Directed by Brad Bird, the movie marks the first foray into PG territory by computer-animation powerhouse Pixar, whose recent run of megahits includes "Toy Story," "Monsters Inc." and "Finding Nemo." Yet while decidedly edgier than those films, "The Incredibles" still packs enough of a Pixar punch to easily leap over its box-office competition in a single bound.

The story centers on Herculean paterfamilias Bob Parr aka Mr. Incredible (he-manly voiced by Craig T. Nelson), a masked crime-fighter who, along with his stretchable spouse, Helen aka Elastigirl (voiced by Holly Hunter), hangs up his cape after a slew of lawsuits force him into early retirement. One ungrateful beneficiary of his heroics complains that by foiling his suicide attempt Mr. Incredible didn't save his life, but rather ruined his death.

To escape further legal action, Bob and Helen agree to enter a comic-book version of the witness protection program and relocate to the suburbs with their three children: super-speedster son Dash (voiced by Spencer Fox), introverted teenage daughter Violet (voiced by Sarah Vowell), who can turn invisible and surround herself with an impenetrable force field, and toddler Jack Jack, who has hasn't yet exhibited any superpowers.

Bob takes a 9-to-5 job as an insurance salesman. The rest of the family also goes out of its way to appear "normal" (Dash is forbidden to exploit his fleet-footedness to win his track meets).
Helen enjoys being "ordinary," but Bob misses the rush of his former career. He reminisces about his glory days with fellow retiree Lucius Best aka Frozone (voiced by Samuel L. Jackson), but now all they have to fight is boredom and bulging waistlines.

Bob gets to scratch his itch for action when, unbeknownst to Helen, a secret assignment lures him to a remote island and back into the superhero saddle. First, however, he has to whip his flabby body back into world-saving shape.

Squeezed into his Mr. Incredible tights, Bob squares off against the killer robots of new nemesis Syndrome (Jason Lee), an evil genius who wants to rid the world of superheroes, so he can steal the limelight for himself.

Before all is said and done, Helen and the kids join in on the action, leading up to the film's "Spy Kids"-inspired climax.
Visually, "The Incredibles" is a hyper-frenetic tour de force, though it doesn't quite match the bar set by "Finding Nemo."
But that's not to say that this film isn't amazing. Cutting-edge advances in animation technology have made the human characters' expressions and movements much more fluid and lifelike, but there are still some wrinkles to iron out.

Bird lends his own voice to the show-stealing character of Edna Mode, a pint-sized costume clothier, who assures the Parrs that their new super-duds, in addition to being virtually indestructible, are also machine washable and "breathe like Egyptian cotton."

Storywise, "The Incredibles" lacks the heart -- not to mention the cuddly, easily merchandised finned and fuzzy protagonists -- of past Pixar productions. Still, the script, also by Bird, is extremely clever and supplies enough eye candy for the kiddies and multilayered dialogue and sharp wit for grownups along for the ride.

In fact, in an effort to appeal to older audience members, the film further blurs the line between kids' and adult entertainment, flirting with more mature themes like midlife anxiety and suspicions of marital infidelity. Even darker post-Sept. 11 fears creep into the dialogue. In one scene Syndrome alludes to selling weapons to countries desperate to pay through the nose "to get respect," while in another Helen warns the kids that the baddies "will kill you, if they get the chance."

Of course much of this may go over the heads of young viewers, who will probably be more concerned about when the preordained action figures and video game will hit toy-store shelves.

Ultimately, the movie's message reminds viewers that you don't need a mask and cape to be "super," urging them to strive for greatness and resist the temptation to settle into complacency. As Bob laments, "They keep coming back with new ways to celebrate mediocrity." Luckily, this film is not one of them.

Due to some action violence, including gunplay, a foiled suicide attempt and mature thematic elements, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

title: The Interpreter
synopsis: Glossy, reasonably suspenseful tale about a Secret Service agent (Sean Penn) who investigates the claim that an African-born interpreter at the United Nations (Nicole Kidman) has overheard a plot against an African dignitary accused of genocide, and though the agent begins to suspect the interpreter may, in fact, be part of the plot, he finds himself falling in love with her. Director Sydney Pollack's international political thriller is much too complex -- not to mention improbable -- for its own good, and even with intelligent performances and sharp U.N. location shooting, this is several notches below "The Man Who Knew Too Much" and other similarly themed films. Some profanity and crude language, several instances of brief but strong violence, thematic suicide material, a scantily clad lap dancer, and a glimpse of massacred bodies
full_review:
If you can imagine "The Man Who Knew Too Much," "North by Northwest" and "The Manchurian Candidate" rolled into one, you'll have a fair idea of what awaits you in "The Interpreter" (Universal), though the film is several notches below those distinguished forebears.

Still, this is a crisply filmed, reasonably suspenseful tale about a Secret Service agent named Tobin Keller (Sean Penn) -- working in tandem with Agent Dot Woods (Catherine Keener) -- who investigates the claim that Silvia Broome (Nicole Kidman), an African-born interpreter employed at the United Nations, has overheard a plot against Prime Minister Zuwanie (Earl Cameron) of the fictitious country of Matobo, where genocide is rampant.

After a routine evacuation drill, Silvia returns to her translating booth, where she hears the nefarious plan -- in Matobo's language of Ku, a rare African dialect that only a handful of nonnatives could translate. She is observed in the lighted booth, making her a target for the conspirators, who spend much of the film trying to kill her.

Agent Tobin is brought in to protect the putative victim, and is highly suspicious of Silvia, since her African ties may, he reasons, give her motive for Zuwanie to be killed. If so, she asks him, why would she have reported it?

Tobin learns that Silvia's parents and sister were killed, when she was 12, under Zuwanie's regime, and she is frantic to find her missing brother, arranges secret meetings with fellow countryman Philippe (Yvan Attal), a photographer, and appears to take an intense interest in two opponents of Zuwanie: Xola (Curtiss I' Cook) and Kuman-Kuman (George Harris).

Silvia's innocence becomes more plausible to Tobin as the story progresses, particularly when it appears that her life really is in danger.

One of the most riveting sequences involves a bomber aboard a crowded bus in Brooklyn, which channels the fearful specter of terrorism on American shores.

Eventually, wouldn't you know, Tobin finds himself falling in love with Silvia, though he is just recovering from the death of his wife in a car accident two weeks before.

Director Sydney Pollack's political thriller is too complex -- not to mention improbable -- for its own good, but the film is made with his usual craftsmanship. Pollack himself plays the small role of the Secret Service chief.

The cast is first-rate. Kidman is becoming the next-generation Meryl Streep with a different look -- and accent -- in each new film. Here, she's reinvented herself with a measured African cadence and a flaxen blonde, pale visage. Penn is solid as always giving a compelling performance.

The sharp U.N. locations are another plus (it's the first time a film crew has been allowed access to the inner areas of the complex).

Though the pacing is not consistently edge-of-your-seat variety, you won't be bored. And if the film's loopholes have you scratching your head, "The Interpreter" is nonetheless entertaining -- for this day and age -- with relatively discreet violence, and no sexual content at all to speak of. There are praiseworthy messages about the superiority of words to guns in solving international problems, as exemplified by the diplomatic Silvia and the hands-on-the-trigger Tobin, the healing power of forgiveness, and the implicit condemnation of genocidal regimes.

The film contains some profanity and crude language, several instances of brief but strong violence, thematic suicide material, a scantily clad lap dancer, and a glimpse of massacred bodies. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: The Invasion
synopsis: Effective, frequently exciting remake of the 1950s science fiction classic "Invasion of the Body Snatchers," centers on a Washington-based psychiatrist (a tense Nicole Kidman) who, aided by her doctor boyfriend (Daniel Craig), must rescue her young son (Jackson Bond) from her ex-husband (Jeremy Northam), whose body -- like that of much of the populace -- has been taken over by alien forces. Director Oliver Hirschbiegel generates considerable suspense, and the pace rarely flags, despite some continuity flaws and a rather muddled political agenda that fails to better the "red scare" McCarthy subtext of the original. A few instances of crude words and profanity, intense action violence with some blood, killings, a vicious attack by a dog on a child, and brief female disrobing but no nudity
full_review:
"The Invasion" (Warner Bros.) is an effective, frequently exciting second big-screen remake of the classic 1950s science fiction study of paranoia, "Invasion of the Body Snatchers."

Nicole Kidman plays Carol Bennell, a Washington-based psychiatrist, who begins to sense danger when her frightened patient, Wendy Lenk (Veronica Cartwright), confides that her husband is somehow "not her husband."

Carol eventually learns that alien forces are infiltrating the human population, gradually turning them into emotionless automatons (though anxious news reports speak only of a mysterious virus). Carol's ex-husband, Tucker (Jeremy Northam), the father of her young son, Oliver (Jackson Bond), is one of the first to be infected with the extraterrestrial slime. Once such victims succumb to sleep, their DNA is "reprogrammed."

When Carol's worried calls to Tucker about their son (who's with his father under visitation terms) go repeatedly unanswered, she drives to his house to reclaim the boy. Once there, she is menaced by Tucker and other shadowy figures.

She escapes, but only after Tucker spews the slime on her. Thereafter, if she falls asleep, she'll wake up in the same zombielike state as the others.

Walking through the streets of Washington, she must camouflage herself by remaining poker-faced, even when she observes horrific sights like a man falling from a rooftop.

After an exciting chase through the District of Columbia's subway system, she reaches her doctor boyfriend, Ben Driscoll (Daniel Craig), and his research colleague, Dr. Stephen Galeano (Jeffrey Wright), who has, in record time, learned all there is to know about the DNA business.

Carol is soon on her own again trying to find the boy, who's now lodged with Tucker's already transformed mother (Joanna Merlin) in Baltimore. Carol pretends to be one of "them" but is able to flee with Oliver (who is still human, though pretending not to be, as a childhood illness has immunized him). From this point, the film becomes one heart-pounding chase after another.

Kidman maintains an unbroken air of anxiety and strong maternal devotion. Craig has relatively little to do but provide emotional support for Kidman, while Northam is suitably creepy.

Director Oliver Hirschbiegel generates considerable suspense, and the pace rarely flags, despite some continuity flaws and a rather muddled political agenda that fails to better the "red scare" McCarthy subtext of the original.
