Much menace, including a terrified child

title: Last Wagon, The
synopsis: Muddled clash-of-cultures Western set in 1873 Arizona where a man (Richard Widmark) raised by Comanches and wanted for murder risks his life to save the few survivors of a wagon train massacred by Apaches. Directed by Delmer Daves, the well-intentioned story flounders in bad dialogue about big issues -- revenge, lynching, racial prejudice -- and less than credible action scenes. Frontier violence and themes of unlikely interest to children

title: Last Waltz, The
synopsis: This is a cinematic record of the last concert given by a rock group called The Band. Supplemented by interview footage and some numbers shot in a studio, director Martin Scorsese has put it all together extremely well, but its primary appeal is to rock fans. Some coarse language and an amoral attitude on the part of some of the performers

title: Last Wave, The
synopsis: Staid Australian lawyer (Richard Chamberlain) defends four aborigines accused of murder but a mysterious tribal seer divines that the lawyer is the precursor of some cycle-ending event of cataclysmic proportions. Director Peter Weir evokes a strangely eerie sense of the aborigine's transcendental link with nature in stark contrast to the sterile mechanistic environment of the city in which the trial takes place. Increasingly heavy atmosphere of the occult and foreboding of human disaster

title: Las Vegas Hillbillys
synopsis: Ferlin Husky comes out of the hills and gains success in Las Vegas in a mindless story directed by Arthur C. Pierce

title: Las Vegas Story, The
synopsis: Flimsy melodrama set in the title's gambling capital to which a fraudulent financier (Vincent Price) brings his wife (Jane Russell) whose ex-flame (Victor Mature), now a police detective, rescues her from a killer. Directed by Robert Stevenson, the romantic triangle flounders in mutual animosities until murder leads to kidnapping and a helicopter chase for a big but empty finish. Some nasty violence, romantic complications and a sexual situation

title: L'Atalante
synopsis: Lyrically romantic French classic tells of a barge captain (Jean Daste) who brings his country bride (Dita Parlo) to live aboard his boat but when they reach Paris, she goes off to see the sights and gets left behind until the crusty old mate (Michel Simon) reunites the unhappy couple. Director Jean Vigo's simple tale of love and its complications is marked by strange yet lovely surreal passages, Simon's masterfully eccentric performance and Boris Kaufman's poetic photography of life along the river. Several references to prostitution and a scene of erotic yearning

title: Latcho Drom
synopsis: Dramatically unstructured presentation of gypsies performing their music, song and dance as filmed in such diverse locales as Romania, Spain and India. In stringing together this sampling of musical performances, director Tony Gatlif provides a broad sense of gypsy musical traditions from joyous celebrations of life to lamentations of their persecution through the ages, but gives little insight into their history and culture. Subtitles. Fleeting nudity

title: Late Autumn
synopsis: Fine Japanese drama made in 1961 about a young woman who rejects marriage because she does not wish to leave her widowed mother alone but the mother tricks her into getting engaged. Director Yasujiro Ozu lightens the mood with some gentle humor, especially pointed at insufferable male smugness in a society in which women are dependent upon men

title: Late for Dinner
synopsis: Silly fantasy about a young family man (Brian Wimmer) frozen with his mildly retarded brother-in-law (Peter Berg) in 1962 and thawing 29 years later to return to his now middle-aged wife (Marcia Gay Harden) and grown daughter (Colleen Flynn). Producer-director W.D. Richter's inept attempt at heartfelt drama, comedy and fantasy overplays the story's sappy sentiment. Momentary violence

title: Late Great Planet Earth, The
synopsis: Screen version of a book proving the imminent destruction of earth using prophecies from the Old and New Testament is a mishmash of interviews with experts of greater and lesser authority, portentous narration and stock newsreel footage, with a touch of pseudo-biblical drama thrown in. Its distorted idea of the nature and purpose of biblical prophecy makes it unsuited to young and impressionable viewers

title: Late Liz, The
synopsis: Anne Baxter plays a hard-drinking woman who sifts through multiple marriages and attempted suicide before salvation hits her through the guidance of a local clergyman. Directed by Dick Ross, its rather bogus sentimentality and adult situations make it adult fare

title: Late Show, The
synopsis: Art Carney as the aging private eye (who spends most of his time watching old movies on television) feels compelled to solve the murder of his old partner (Howard Duff) who shows up on his doorstep with a fatal bullet wound. Lily Tomlin teams up in the sleuthing and the result is an above average crime entertainment directed by Robert Benton. Occasional violence and crude language

title: Late Spring
synopsis: Japanese story of a dutiful daughter who refuses to leave her widowed father until he finally is forced to trick her into marriage. Director Yasujiro Ozu's 1949 movie is a lyric study of the abiding strength of family life and relationships, warmly told and universal in its values

title: La Tia Tula
synopsis: Delicate Spanish tale of a beautiful woman (Aurora Bautista) who rejects the love of her late sister's husband, then comes to regret her proud aloofness too late. Director Miguel Picazo treats the woman's fears of marriage in the context of her cultural and religous upbringing, investing the character with a tragic human dimension that earns respect and leaves a sense of loss. Subtitles. Sexual situations, including an attempted rape

title: Latitude Zero
synopsis: Japanese science fiction movie with Joseph Cotton and Cesar Romero pitted against each other as the classic counterparts of good and evil. Directed by Inoshiro Honda, an underwater city in the Jules Verne vein, grotesque monsters, and some excellent miniature work make it a must for sci-fi fans. A couple of grisly scenes are inappropriate for small children

title: L'Auberge Espagnole
synopsis: Patchwork comedy about a French exchange student (Romain Duris) who travels to Spain and learns about life and love, while sharing an apartment with seven European students. While the Benetton-poster faces and kinetic style chosen by director Cedric Klapisch are fresh, the film's acceptance of casual sex and promotion of personal moral autonomy is more than a bit off-putting. Subtitles. Adulterous sexual encounters with nudity, lesbian kissing, recurring substance abuse, and much rough language and profanities
full_review:
"L'Auberge Espagnole" (Fox Searchlight) is a patchwork comedy about eight exchange students -- each from a different European country -- exploring the shifting tectonics of modern multicultural relationships while sharing an apartment in sunny Spain.

Though the Benetton-poster faces and kinetic style chosen by director Cedric Klapisch are fresh, the film's message -- embrace a bohemian libertinism or suffer the suffocating consequences -- is anything but novel.

Using the vibrant allure of Barcelona as a backdrop, the film follows the fate of Xavier (Romain Duris), a 25-year-old economics grad student from Paris who comes to Spain as part of an inter-European exchange program named Erasmus, after the globe-trotting Renaissance scholar. Xavier, who wants to be a writer, is heartsick about leaving behind his French-tart girlfriend, Martine (Audrey Tautou), to study abroad for a year -- a move prompted by his practical father which will lead to a job offer dealing with the burgeoning Iberian market.

Xavier arrives, unable to speak the language -- a stranger to himself in a city full of strangers. Searching for a place to stay, he falls in with a couple of fellow Frenchies, who also recently arrived from Paris: Jean Michel (Xavier De Guillebon), a bombastic neurologist, and his sultry -- albeit repressed -- wife, Anne-Sophie (Judith Godreche), whom he leaves in Xavier's charge.

Xavier scours the city for something more permanent, stumbling across a notice advertising a crammed flat shared by a veritable NATO alliance of seven similarly aged students whose personalities are as varied as their nationalities and sexual proclivities.

The polyglot lodging becomes a "L'Auberge Espagnole" -- translated literally, meaning "Spanish Inn" but in French slang also connotes a place where cultures mix -- setting the stage for predictable bonding-by-booze scenarios.

Along the way, Xavier finds himself entangled in a "menage a trois" of deception involving Martine, Anne-Sophie and one of his roommates, Isabelle (Cecile De France), a libidinous lesbian from whom Xavier receives a tutorial in international relations.

The filmmaker uses attractive young faces to peddle unattractive old ideas. Much of the film's objectionable content stems from a dangerous philosophical attitude posited by the filmmaker: "It seemed that as I made the movie, I learned with Xavier that following the most unconscious desires and mixed up impulses is a good way to grow up and experience life with freedom. In the end, it became a movie, not only about youth and travel and diversity, but about finding that freedom."

Within the context of this quote, freedom -- in the sense of moral autonomy -- justifies all the characters' actions. Once unfettered freedom becomes the film's prime directive, anything is permissible; carte blanche is granted to indulge in "the most unconscious desires and mixed-up impulses" -- even if that includes adultery. A la carte sex is de rigueur; why not? As one character states, "It's just sex."

However, Klapisch does frown on one form of free expression. Midway through the film, Wendy (Keilly Reilly), the Brit of the bunch, gets a visit from her blowhard brother, William (Kevin Bishop), whose politically incorrect babbling offends some of the roommates' ethnic sensitivities. For much of the remainder, William is treated as a pariah -- true to the hypocrisy of relativism, his tongue is not afforded the same liberties as their genitals. Of course, William is redeemed in the end when he lies to Wendy's boyfriend who shows up unexpectedly from England, in order to cover up for her while she's in bed with another guy.

Against the youthful cast's vitality, the film pits members of the older generation, composed primarily of stuffy cogs in the corporate machine, such as Xavier's father, or curmudgeons, like the landlord -- who is so out of touch with their "Real World" lifestyle that he actually complains that the flat is a pigsty and that a niche once used for a statue of the Madonna is now occupied by a robot action figure. Xavier's mom does get a bit of a free pass but, hey, she's an ex-hippie.

Regrettably, inside this Euro-pudding is little more than Euro-trash.

Subtitles.

Due to its acceptance of casual sex, adulterous sexual encounters with nudity, lesbian kissing, recurring substance abuse, and much rough language and profanities, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Laughing Policeman, The
synopsis: Detective thriller about a brutal mass murder on a San Francisco bus that veteran detective Walter Matthau pursues because his partner is one of those killed and the clues point to a previous unsolved murder case. There's the basis for a good yarn here, but director Stuart Rosenberg puts too much emphasis on violence, crude language and an exploration of the city's tawdry side

title: Laughter in Paradise
synopsis: Clever British comedy in which the relatives of late prankster Hugh Griffith inherit his estate under certain conditions, namely that pulp fiction writer Alastair Sim spend a month in jail, meek bank clerk George Cole rob his own bank, self-centered spinster Fay Compton spend a month as a domestic servant and shiftless playboy Guy Middleton marry. Director Mario Zampi gets chortles from the predicaments of all four, especially Sim and Cole, but bogs down in showing how each is changed for the better in trying to fulfill the will's stipulations. Mild sexual innuendo

title: Laughter in the Dark
synopsis: British drama about a man of some intelligence and breeding being destroyed by his infatuation for an unscrupulous schemer. The performance of Nicol Williamson, as the titled art dealer victimized by a dreadfu1 cinema usherette (Anna Karina) is skillful, and Tony Richardson's direction evidences serious intentions, but the cumulative effect is merely ludicrous with more than a little nudity and explicit depiction of sex

title: Laura
synopsis: Sparse mystery embroidered with moody romance from Vera Caspary's novel about a police detective (Dana Andrews) investigating the reported murder of the beautiful title character (Gene Tierney) whose rise in the New York social set was aided by an influential radio commentator (Clifton Webb at his waspish best). Things, of course, are not what they seem as director Otto Preminger probes the dark side of high society life while focusing on the dour detective's growing fascination with the glamorous Laura and the vitriolic journalist's feelings for his former protege. More for romantics than mystery fans, there are some scenes of menace, stylized violence and implied sexual encounters

title: Laurel and Hardy's Laughing Twenties
synopsis: Affectionate look back at the great comedy team of Stan Laurel and Oliver Hardy in a collection of excerpts from their silent two-reelers. The narrative is helpful and the sight gags irresistable

title: Laurel Canyon
synopsis: Repellent drama about an uptight Harvard med school grad (Christian Bale) who takes his straitlaced fiancee (Kate Beckinsale) home to Los Angeles, where his hip, hedonistic mom (Frances McDormand) initiates her into the epicurean joys of sex, drugs and rock 'n' roll. Despite competent performances, writer-director Lisa Cholodenko's suggestion that self-indulgence and promiscuity are liberating is more than a bit off-putting. Sporadic sexual content, fleeting nudity, several instances of same-sex kissing, recurring recreational drug abuse, intermittent rough language and profanities
full_review:
"Laurel Canyon" (Sony Classics) is a repellent drama about an uptight Harvard med-school grad who takes his straitlaced fiancee home to Los Angeles, where his hip, hedonistic mom initiates her into the epicurean joys of sex, drugs and rock 'n' roll.

Despite competent performances by Frances McDormand, Christian Bale and Alessandro Nivola, the film, by writer-director Lisa Cholodenko, espouses that most dubious of chestnuts -- that self-fulfillment hinges on jettisoning social convention and embracing libertinism.

Sam (Bale) is a young, handsome, though somewhat dull first-year resident, recently engaged to the beautiful and brainy Alex (Kate Beckinsale). They are a picture-postcard of idyllic, upwardly mobile, emotionally repressed, J. Crew love.

Having accepted a staff position at a Los Angeles psychiatric facility, Sam jets off with Alex to California, with stern admonitions from her conservative kin against becoming Scientologists -- or, worse, vegetarians. Against his better judgment, Sam agrees to move in temporarily with his mom until they find something more permanent.

Upon arrival, they are welcomed by Jane (McDormand), Sam's pot-smoking, free-loving mother, a famous record producer with a proclivity for shacking up with her musical proteges, regardless of gender. Her newest platinum-digging bauble is Ian (Nivola), a libidinous Brit rocker with a velvet voice and a predatory glance which immediately zeroes in on Alex. Sam still harbors a deep-seated resentment toward his mother for his unconventional upbringing, and remains wary of her attempts at hospitality.

Jane's sybaritic oasis on Laurel Canyon, a twisting stretch of real estate populated by arty types, represents to Alex everything missing in her cloistered life, namely an uninhibited licentiousness. At one point she sighs, "My dad is a puritan who reads Proust and wears tweed." One assumes dear old Dad's tweed seemed less square to her when he footed the bill for Harvard.

Predictably, she begins to abandon her studies and surrenders to the intoxicating, bohemian allure of Jane's entreaties. Alex soon finds herself frolicking in a pool with the reptilian Ian and locking lips with her sexually equal-opportunistic future mother-in-law. Meanwhile, Sam's fidelity is tested by the tempting advances of a ravishing co-worker, Sara (Natasha McElhone). Prompted by a pang of conscience, Jane pulls the plug on Ian and Alex's jam session, but not before Sam discovers their twisted secret tryst.

The moral vacuity that unfolds in the film could be pardoned if the characters actually learned from their mistakes, but after lamenting her indiscretions Alex actually thanks Ian for helping to "open her up." Sam on the other hand, still smitten with Sara, admits that he must sacrifice his true feelings for her in order to make it work with Alex. In the end no one is happy; happiness is not an option, just sublimation.

In one of the few emotionally honest scenes, Jane shares a cathartic poolside moment with Sam, where she expresses sincere regret over being such a failure as a mother. Her lifestyle has left her haggard and wracked with guilt, but there is no indication that her remorse will prod her to change her promiscuous ways.

Much of the narrative is mired by a discursive plot that meanders like Laurel Canyon Road itself, full of emotional cul-de-sacs which remain unresolved.

Yet far more disconcerting is the pervasive self-gratification, disguised as self-assertion, promoted throughout the film. The movie would have audiences believe that Alex will find the yellow brick road to personal fulfillment if she'd just relax, smoke a joint and exchange bodily fluids with her soon-to-be mother-in-law. This view -- liberation via libertinism -- has grown a bit long in the tooth. Its proponents have been singing the same tune since film critics wore bowler hats. Thankfully, this disagreeable film does little to bolster the attractiveness of their argument.

Due to sporadic sexual content, fleeting nudity, several instances of same-sex kissing, recurring recreational drug abuse, intermittent rough language and profanities, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Lavender Hill Mob, The
synopsis: British comedy classic in which a timid bank employee (Alec Guinness) concocts a scheme to hijack a shipment of gold bullion with the aid of professional crooks (Sidney James and Alfie Bass), then melt it down in the foundry of an accomodating sculptor (Stanley Holloway) and recast it as Eifel Tower souvenirs for export to Paris. Scripted by T.E.B. Clarke and directed by Charles Crichton, the tongue-in-cheek depiction of a perfect crime has one hilarious flaw after another, culminating in a wild police chase through London and a neat twist ending in South America. Comic crime caper and mild menace

title: La Vie De Chateau
synopsis: Set in Normandy just before D-Day, the story is about a wealthy orchard farmer (Philippe Noiret), his lively wife (Catherine Deneuve), a lovelorn leader of the Resistance (Henri Garein) and a detachment of German soldiers quartered there. Some haphazard heroics take place on the beautiful old estate before it finally becomes the landing point for Allied paratroopers

title: La Vie En Rose
synopsis: Superb panoramic biography of great French singer Edith Piaf, covering her life from birth to death, and hitting all the high points, including her impoverished childhood, miraculous restoration of her sight (which she credited to St. Therese of Lisieux), her early years as a street singer, her molding as an artist, theatrical triumphs in Paris and New York, tragic affair with championship boxer Marcel Cerdan, her sicknesses, and premature death. Writer-director Olivier Dahan jumps back and forth in time to different stages in her life, and superbly recreates the various times and places in Piaf's life, while Marion Cotillard, lip-synching to Piaf's recordings, gives an incredible performance as she morphs from foul-mouthed hoyden to vibrant star to frail wraith. Subtitles. Upper female nudity, brothel scenes, adultery, a lesbian kiss, sexual references, nongraphic encounter, some crude language and expressions, a violent though nongraphic car accident, child out of wedlock, substance abuse
full_review:
"La Vie En Rose" (Picturehouse) is not the first attempt to dramatize the life of great French singer Edith Piaf (1915-1963), but it would seem to be the best.

This is a superb panoramic biography that covers the volatile performer's fascinating life from birth to death, hitting all the high points in between, and she is played to perfection by Marion Cotillard. Writer-director Olivier Dahan leaps back and forth in time to different stages in her life, but the narrative is clear and spellbinding.

Raised by her grandmother in, of all places, a brothel (some fleeting background upper nudity here), where the women adored her, and grieved for the child's sudden blindness, later giving thanks for the miraculous restoration of her sight (which Piaf credited ever after to St. Therese of Lisieux, to whom her guardians prayed).

Piaf's departure from the brothel when her street performer father (Jean-Paul Rouve) decides to raise her is wrenching, exemplified here by the maternal Titine's (Emmanuelle Seigner) hysteria at the impending separation from the child for whom she has come to care.

While apprenticing with her father, young Piaf wows the crowds with her powerful voice, eventually becoming a street singer in tandem with her pal Momome (Sylvie Testud).

She works under the protection of the mob, a sordid situation that ultimately leads to the murder of her mentor, nightclub owner Louis Leplee (Gerard Depardieu), seriously tainting her reputation, and almost ruining her budding career.

She survives, is molded as an artist by other professionals who take her under their wing, goes on to theatrical triumphs in Paris and New York, where she has a tragic affair with married championship boxer Marcel Cerdan (Jean-Pierre Martins), who is eventually killed in a plane crash while en route to see her. All of these events are beautifully re-created.

Cotillard, whose merely pleasant turn as Russell Crowe's love interest in last year's tepid comedy, "A Good Life," hardly presaged her stunning work here. Though lip-synching to Piaf's inimitable recordings, she gives an incredible performance morphing from foul-mouthed hoyden to vibrant star to frail wraith. Along with "La Vie En Rose," her other world-famous songs -- "Milord," "Hymn to Love," and "Non, Je Ne Regrette Rien" -- are all given good measure here.

The film shows Piaf to be highly mercurial: expansive and warm-hearted one moment, self-centered and tyrannical the next. Piaf's deep religious faith -- praying to St. Therese and Jesus before every performance -- is underscored, as are the far-from-saintly other aspects of her life, including the drug use and numerous affairs like the relationship with Cerdan. Earlier, there's a particularly unpleasant episode is the young Piaf's expletive-laden rejection of the mother who had abandoned her.

"I overdid it," says the ailing lady near the end of her life, with stunning economy. Despite this and other character flaws, Piaf's story powerfully demonstrates the resilience of the human spirit, and is a worthy tribute to one of the 20th century's great artists.

Subtitles.

The film contains upper female nudity, brothel scenes, adultery, a lesbian kiss, sexual references, a nongraphic encounter, some crude language and expressions, a violent though nongraphic car accident, child out of wedlock and substance abuse. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: La Visita
synopsis: Middle-aged spinster (Sandro Milo) uses the personal columns to arrange a meeting with a seemingly eligible suitor (Francois Perier). The day they spend together is both amusing and touching as they come to discover the truth about their personalities. Director Antonio Pietrangeli's seriocomic tale is minor but deftly played

title: Law Abiding Citizen
synopsis: Brutish, blood-soaked and ultimately nonsensical revenge fantasy in which, following the murder of his wife and young daughter, an inventor who specializes in killing terrorists (Gerard Butler), goes on an elaborately staged rampage, eventually making deals with a prosecutor (Jamie Foxx) in his search for "justice." Director F. Gary Gray and screenwriter Kurt Wimmer begin with an homage to the hyper-violent "Death Wish" films and concoct an implausible ending reminiscent of an old “Scooby-Doo” cartoon. A rape, explicit torture, gun and knife violence, explosions, rear male nudity, pervasive rough and crass language
full_review:
"Vengeance is mine" has been a popular film theme through the years, almost always leaving out the crucial last three words of that quotation from Saint Paul's letter to the Romans: "says the Lord."

So in "Law Abiding Citizen," when Gerard Butler's Clyde Shelton announces, while on a murderous rampage, "It's gonna be biblical," it's just one of many nonsensical bleats in this brutish fantasy about one man's search for "justice." Director F. Gary Gray and screenwriter Kurt Wimmer begin with an homage to the old hyper-violent "Death Wish" films and, after 90 minutes of gushing body parts, concoct an implausible ending that looks like it was borrowed from an old “Scooby-Doo” cartoon.

Shelton's rage begins when his wife and young daughter are murdered by two thugs in a home invasion. Justice in a Philadelphia court means a deal with the prosecution -- one gets the death penalty but another gets just five years in prison.

That's not good enough for Shelton, of course, but he's no ordinary revenge-seeker with a gun. He's a specialist in the dark art of killing terrorists, and takes out his anger not only on the criminals, but also on everyone in the court system, using all manner of devious technology -- even from a prison cell.

Shelton makes a series of implausible "deals" with prosecutor Nick Rice (Jamie Foxx) to prevent more killings, but the strangely impassive Rice never gets there in time as Shelton gets ever more inventive.

The film contains a rape, explicit torture, gun and knife violence, explosions, rear male nudity and pervasive crass and rough language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Law and Disorder
synopsis: A taxi driver (Carrol O'Connor) and a hairdresser (Ernest Borgnine) form a number of their New York neighbors into an auxiliary police force to put a stop to an invasion of muggers, thieves and exhibitionists. Directed by Ivan Passer, there is some sharp satire on contemporary urban crime and middle-class frustrations. Some intense violence, very rough language and a number of embarrassing sexual references

title: Law and Jake Wade, The
synopsis: Contrived Western in which an outlaw (Richard Widmark) seeks revenge on a one-time partner (Robert Taylor) who ran out on him with the loot from a bank robbery, then settled down as sheriff of a small town. Directed by John Sturges, the clumsy narrative has the lawman and his fiance (Paricia Owens) taken captive and forced to lead the outlaw's gang to the missing loot on a journey ending in a ghost town during a Comanche uprising. Stylized violence and much menace

title: Law and Order
synopsis: Routine Western directed by Nathan Juran in which a retired sheriff (Ronald Reagan) refuses to help a town rid itself of a brutal gang (headed by Preston Foster), but changes his mind after they kill his brother (Alex Nicol). Frontier violence, some of it quite nasty

title: Lawless Breed, The
synopsis: Routine Western directed by Raoul Walsh presents a sympathetic account of the life of famed Texas badman John Wesley Hardin (Rock Hudson), a preacher's son who claimed he killed only in self-defense but was sentenced to a long prison term for his crimes, after which he became a peaceable family man. Shootouts and justice questions

title: Lawless Eighties, The
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Joe Kane in which a lay preacher (John Smith) is helped by a reformed gunslinger (Buster Crabbe) in averting a Sioux uprising by unmasking a crooked Indian agent (Ted de Corsia)

title: Lawless Heart
synopsis: Offbeat comic drama set in an English seaside town chronicles the romantic mishaps of a restless married man (Bill Nighy), a gay man (Nick Hollander) whose partner has just drowned, and the deceased's childhood pal (Douglas Henshall) who returns for the funeral after an absence of eight years. Although writer-directors Neil Hunter and Tom Hunsinger treat their sexual flings rather cavalierly, each man eventually learns something from bittersweet experience. Briefly graphic sexual encounters, fleeting full nudity, intermittent rough language and an instance of profanity
full_review:
A man's funeral sets off a chain of events that changes relationships in a small English seaside town in "Lawless Heart" (First Look).

The offbeat, comic drama is somewhat of a thrice-told tale. Events are repeated from the separate perspectives of the dead man's brother-in-law, Dan (Bill Nighy), the deceased's gay lover, Nick (Tom Hollander), and childhood pal Tim (Douglas Henshall), who returns for the funeral after eight years abroad.

At the funeral reception, listless husband Dan gets into a seductive conversation with a Frenchwoman (Clementine Celarie) and starts considering having an affair. While he stands her up at the last minute, he gives a lift to an intoxicated young woman who has hasty sex with him, making him ashamed of his infidelity.

Dan's wife, Judy (Ellie Haddington), is preoccupied trying to decide whether to give all of her late brother's money to his partner, Nick, even though she and Dan are financially strapped.

Restaurant owner Nick, meanwhile, is devastated by his lover's accidental drowning. He allows traveler Tim to stay in his house but is appalled by the wild party Tim throws to impress local girl Leah (Josephine Butler). Worse, at the party a drunken Charli (Sukie Smith) collapses on Nick's bed and she stays the night uninvited, demanding tea, toast and taxi money in the morning before she leaves. Oddly enough, Nick finds her intriguing and eventually seduces her, throwing him into sexual-orientation confusion.

The final third picks up as self-centered Tim decides to settle down with Leah and plans to propose in Nick's restaurant, where Dan and Judy have come to celebrate Judy's birthday. Charli is serving as a waitress for Nick and the Frenchwoman arrives to deliver flowers so everyone is conveniently assembled for possible romantic fireworks. As Dan and his wife come to terms about Nick inheriting or not, Tim for once looks beyond his own needs to encourage someone else's romantic reunion.

The movie exhibits a good sense of place and community which make the relationships seem less contrived. A dry sense of humor also makes the characters' shortcomings seem less egregious; eventually most of them learn some sort of lesson from their romantic mishaps. The very brief sexual scenes are unnecessarily explicit, but in the course of the narrative serve to underline how such casual sex is an empty, even humiliating experience.

Due to briefly graphic sexual encounters, fleeting full nudity, intermittent rough language and an instance of profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Lawless Range
synopsis: Western programmer directed by R.N. Bradbury follows the exploits of a singing cowboy (John Wayne) as he saves a group of ranchers from being driven off by a band of crooks who have learned there's a rich vein of gold under their land. Stylized violence

title: Lawless Street, A
synopsis: Cliched Western in which a veteran marshal (Randolph Scott) outguns all his foes and wins back the wife (Angela Lansbury) who had left him years before because she distained bloodshed. Director Joseph H. Lewis is more interested in shootouts and barroom brawls than in trying to make some sense out of a silly plotline. Much violence and implied adultery

title: Lawman
synopsis: Straight-shooting marshal Burt Lancaster attempts to round up seven murder suspects in a town where long-time sheriff Robert Ryan has learned to compromise with local cattle baron Lee J. Cobb. The situation results in bloodshed with justice depending upon the fastest, surest gun. Director Michael Winner seems to have pretentions about examining what or who is the law but the conclusion solves nothing. Stylized violence and blooshed

title: Lawn Dogs
synopsis: Disturbing tale in which a 10-year-old girl (Mischa Barton) stubbornly seeks out the friendship of a dirt-poor 21-year-old laborer (Sam Rockwell) but their innocent relationship is misunderstood by vicious adults, with tragic results. Director John Duigan's delivers a darkly manipulative drama of class prejudices which stacks the deck by pitting an entire community against a brash but well-meaning youth. Sexual situations, some full nudity, scattered violence and intermittent profanity as well as rough language

title: Lawnmower Man, The
synopsis: Failed sci-fi movie about a driven doctor (Pierce Brosnan) whose experiments turn a retarded man (Jeff Fahey) into a killer with psychic powers. Directed by Brett Leonard, it's little more than a computer-graphics variation on the mad scientist theme with thoroughly unappealing characters and images. Recurring violence, including a sadistic cleric, brief sexual encounters with momentary nudity and some rough language

title: Law of the Lawless, The
synopsis: When a former gunman-turned-judge (Dale Robertson) arrives in town to try the son (John Agar) of an old friend (Barton MacLane) for murder, he faces a gunman (Bruce Cabot) hired to kill him. Director William F. Claxton can't do much with the contrived script but a game cast of veterans (Yvonne De Carlo, William Bendix, Richard Arlen, Kent Taylor and Lon Chaney, Jr.) do their best to make it seem interesting. While the movie's anti-gun message is laudable, its use of violence makes it unlikely fare for children

title: Law of the North
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Harry Fraser with Bill Cody as a cowboy framed on a murder charge by a crook who turns out to have been responsible for the death of the cowboy's sister years earlier. Frontier violence

title: Law of the Pampas
synopsis: Western programmer in which Hopalong Cassidy (William Boyd) delivers some prize cattle to a South American ranch, then saves its owner from a murderous in-law (Sidney Blackmer), with a bit of help from a comic gaucho (Sidney Toler). Stylized violence

title: Lawrence of Arabia
synopsis: Set within the frame of a grand adventure is this interesting study of British hero-author T.E. Lawrence (Peter O'Toole), whose World War I exploits in leading the Arabs against the Turks made his literary works popular in the 1920s. Director David Lean focuses on the diverse aspects of the man with an ambiguity suitable to the mystery still surrounding this mythic figure. Bloody wartime battles and implications of a homosexual incident

title: Laws of Attraction
synopsis: Underwhelming romantic comedy in which two rival divorce lawyers (Pierce Brosnan and Julianne Moore) wake up married after a drunken evening and must continue as opposing attorneys on a bitter court case while carrying on a spousal charade. Director Peter Howitt's attractive cast and sumptuous production design can only compensate so much for the paucity of witty dialogue and obvious plot contrivances. Implied sexual encounters following inebriation, impersonation of a cleric, a few crude expressions and an instance of profanity
full_review:
Can two bickering divorce attorneys find marital bliss after they wake up wedded? "Laws of Attraction" (New Line) poses this question in a visually appealing but underwhelming romantic comedy. It's got a good message about commitment but it lags on laughs.

Audrey (Julianne Moore) is a high-powered New York City attorney unfettered by romantic relationships, much to the regret of her Botox-happy, ex-model mom (a frisky Frances Fisher) who is content to pass as Audrey's sister.

Fiercely competitive in the courtroom, Audrey meets her match when disheveled Daniel (Pierce Brosnan) returns to the Big Apple. He's a by-the-seat-of-his-pants type guy who always gets juicy divorce settlements for his clients.

In court he and Audrey are steely rivals. But Daniel, a romantic at heart, finds her fascinating and over dinner and far too many drinks his charm melts her defenses. To bed they go -- and to court the next morning. When he uses a down 'n' dirty tactic to win, all hope for a relationship seems doomed.

Enter a splitsville couple: rock star Thorne (Michael Sheen) and his funky designer wife, Serena (Parker Posey). Daniel represents her while Audrey has the philandering husband. And both spouses want sole possession of only one thing: their castle in Ireland.

Before you can spell "leprechaun," each attorney has winged it to the Emerald Isle to gather favorable testimony from the castle staff. Once again, Audrey and Daniel imbibe a little too much of the local brew and wake up together dressed in wedding rings and with murky memories of a priest marrying them the night before.

He's pleased; she's not. Upon returning to New York, where their marriage has already hit the gossip columns, they decide they'd better keep up a marital front while cohabiting platonically.

On the plus side, the movie is undeniable eye candy, with a gorgeous-to-look-at cast. Brosnan plays it low-key dashing, and Moore is at the height of her beauty, shedding crystalline tears reminiscent of another Moore -- Demi -- in "Ghost."

Yet you are always aware that these two are acting with a capital A. They have been far better in other roles, as has the often-remarkable Posey. She is considered queen of the indie films, but in this big Hollywood film she barely registers.

Clearly, the movie is a throwback to 1940s screwball comedies, but without the wit the snappy comebacks are few and far between.

Compensating somewhat for this is a sumptuous production design, from tony apartment interiors to softly rolling Irish hillsides. Visual panache it's got in droves, but the script doesn't always make sense of the characters' actions. At least it all comes down on accepting that marriage requires commitment and work, not to be discarded at the first hint of discontent.

Seventeen individuals are listed as producers in the credits; perhaps movie-by-committee is why this ended up as escapist forgettable fare. For a similarly themed but truly fine example of screwball comedy at its best, look at Katharine Hepburn and Spencer Tracy in 1949's "Adam's Rib."

Due to implied sexual encounters following inebriation, impersonation of a cleric, a few crude expressions and an instance of profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Laws of Gravity
synopsis: Shrill drama about two hot-tempered Brooklyn thugs (Peter Greene and Adam Trese) trying to hold on to their women (Edie Falco and Arabella Field) while secretly conniving to rip off a cache of stolen guns. Writer-director Nick Gomez blunders through a meaninglessly violent story of brutish, boastful thieves, told in ear-splitting obscenities. Some graphic violence, including abuse of women, much heavy drinking and non-stop rough language

title: Law vs. Billy the Kid, The
synopsis: Ho-hum low-budget Western directed by William Castle goes through the motions in portraying William Bonney (Scott Brady) as a misunderstood cowboy trying to right wrongs with his six-shooter. Muddled motivations and stylized violence

title: Lawyer, The
synopsis: Routine crime melodrama in which a hotshot lawyer (Barry Newman) races around California in his beat-up camper trying to get his client, philandering Dr. Jack Harrison (Robert Colbert), off the hook for murdering his wife. Directed by Sidney J. Furie, it contains frequent nudity and crude dialogue

title: Layer Cake
synopsis: Technically proficient but unpleasantly seamy story of a cocaine dealer in London (Daniel Craig) who prides himself on the efficiency of his methods, only to be caught up in the machinations of honcho Jimmy Price (Kenneth Cranham) and Price's high-powered cohort, Eddie Temple (Michael Gambon), and a stolen shipment of Ecstasy pills after which everyone is scrambling. Matthew Vaughn's thriller is too complex for its own good, with its difficult-to-follow plot (to the point of "who cares?"), tricky-to-decipher accents, flashy but empty presentation, and -- though perhaps appropriate for the underworld milieu -- more expletives per minute than any film in recent memory. One brief but graphic sex scene, nudity, brutal violence with attendant gore, pervasive rough and crude language, and drug use
full_review:
Betty Crocker this "Layer Cake" (Sony Classics) most certainly isn't.

The crime film bearing that title is the technically proficient but unpleasantly seamy story of an unnamed cocaine dealer in London (Daniel Craig) who prides himself on the clean efficiency of his methods, and looks forward to living the high life after an early retirement.

But wouldn't you know, before that can happen he's caught up in the machinations of crime kingpin Jimmy Price (Kenneth Cranham) and Price's high-powered cohort, Eddie Temple (Michael Gambon), and a stolen shipment of Ecstasy pills after which everyone is scrambling.

Director Matthew Vaughn's thriller is too complex for its own good. First, there's a plot that's so difficult to follow you'll soon find yourself asking, "Who cares?" Then there are those tricky-to-decipher accents. Add to that a flashy but essentially empty presentation, and -- though perhaps appropriate for the underworld milieu -- more uses of the "F" word than in any film in recent memory. The result is unsavory, not to mention tedious, entertainment.

The film contains one brief but graphic sex scene, nudity, brutal violence with attendant gore, pervasive rough and crude language, and drug use. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Lay of the Land, The
synopsis: Pathetic seriocomic tale of husband-and-wife college professors (Sally Kellerman and Ed Begley, Jr.) trying to ease mid-life crises by having madcap affairs which only magnify their marital problems. Writer-director Larry Arrick's juvenile attempt at poignant comedy is pretentiously misconceived, atrociously acted and badly edited. Comic treatment of adultery, brief violence, some nudity, occasional profanity and intermittent rough language

title: Leadbelly
synopsis: Screen biography tracing the troubled life of neglected Huddie Ledbetter, legendary black folk singer and master of the twelve-string guitar whose work became part of the post-World War II folk renaissance. Director Gordon Parks downplays the racial themes in favor of a musical tribute while eliciting a colorfully authentic performance from Roger E. Mosley as Huddie

title: League of Their Own, A
synopsis: In a spirited, often amusing drama about the formation of a women's professional baseball league during World War II, the narrative follows the course of a season with a team whose odd assortment of players include sibling rivals (Geena Davis and Lori Petty), a backwoods slugger (Megan Cavanagh), street-wise fielders (Madonna and Rosie O'Donnell) and a washed-up rummy as manager (Tom Hanks). Directed by Penny Marshall, the story uses the baseball diamond as an arena of team solidarity and personal self-discovery rather than as an ideological soapbox, though its feminist perspective is abundantly evident. A few mild sexual references, some vulgar language and occasional tasteless humor, including a toilet joke

title: Lean on Me
synopsis: Formula feel-good bio of controversial Paterson, N.J., high school principal Joe Clark (Morgan Freeman) focuses on his mission to clean up the crime and graffiti-infested school, restore student self-pride and raise their abysmal reading scores. Fearless, funny and nasty, Freeman is a stand-out as he rejuvenates the school. Director John G. Avildsen's cartoon movie heroics may be simplistic and the screenplay may play fast and loose with the facts, but the film should speak to older urban adolescents faced with similar school blight. Much rough language, some violence and menace and a flash of nudity

title: Leap of Faith
synopsis: During a three-day revival in a backwater Kansas town, a bogus faith healer (Steve Martin) and his mercenary manager (Debra Winger) each experience minor transformations when he witnesses a possible real miracle and she is moved by the decency of the local sheriff (Liam Neeson). Director Richard Pearce's serio-comedy of religious hucksterism has few laughs and little meaning, made all the more unsatisfactory by a vague, feel-good ending. Comic depiction of religious sentiment exploited for profit and an implied sexual encounter

title: Leap Year
synopsis: Likable romantic comedy in which a controlling Boston real estate consultant (Amy Adams) follows her commitment-shy live-in boyfriend (Adam Scott) to Ireland, where he's attending a cardiologists' convention and where she hopes to take advantage of a national tradition allowing women to propose on Leap Day, but bad weather derails her plans, forcing her to rely on a laidback rural innkeeper (Matthew Goode) to get her to Dublin in time. Though the background details are closer to 1952's "The Quiet Man" than to the post-Celtic Tiger contemporary reality, the central opposites-attract relationship in director Anand Tucker's Hibernian idyll is old-fashioned in the best sense, with physical restraint allowing room for a dexterously acted, if somewhat formulaic, portrayal of deepening emotional engagement, and helping to make this -- despite the elements described below -- probably acceptable for older teens. Implied cohabitation, some mildly sexual humor, at least two uses of profanity and one of the S-word, and a few crass terms

title: Learning Tree, The
synopsis: Director Gordon Park's lifeless cinematic version of his autobiographical novel is a highly romantic, colorful recreation of a black adolescent's coming-of-age in a mixed atmosphere of gentleness and violence, honesty, hypocrisy and bigotry. The result has more a sense of a photographic essay than of a realistic portrait of the rural black experience

title: Leather Boys, The
synopsis: British story of a failed marriage with Rita Tushingham as a teenager who weds to escape her appalling home, Colin Campbell as the immature husband and Dudley Suttton as his calculating friend. The 1963 production has an episodic story that is loosely motivated, but the acting is first-rate and Sidney Furie's direction has the ring of authenticity

title: Leatherheads
synopsis: Diverting romantic comedy, set in 1925, about a veteran professional football player (George Clooney) who hires a celebrated college star (John Krasinski) to revive his team's fortunes, only to find himself in a rivalry for the affections of a sassy, sophisticated newspaper reporter (Renee Zellweger) who's out to debunk his new teammate's heroic war record. Clooney, who also directed, evokes the tangy wit of the best screwball pairings of 1930s Hollywood and, despite a few inconsistencies in the plot and some objectionable language, creates an enjoyable period piece that thrives on the rough and tumble of the pro game's unregulated infancy. Some profanity, occasional crude and crass language, mild fistfighting, light sexual banter, innuendo
full_review:
The rough-and-tumble infancy of professional football provides the backdrop for "Leatherheads" (Universal), an amiable romantic comedy set in 1925. Despite some inconsistencies in the plot and some objectionable language, the film delivers as a diverting period piece.

Jimmy "Dodge" Connolly (George Clooney), the leading player of the ramshackle Duluth Bulldogs, has been throwing the pigskin around one cow pasture after another for 20 years. So when his financially unstable team follows many others into bankruptcy, he's not only out of work, but largely unemployable.

Hearing a radio broadcaster announce that college star and celebrated war hero Carter Rutherford (John Krasinski) has attracted a crowd of 40,000 to Princeton University's football stadium, Dodge is inspired to offer him $5,000 a game to turn pro. Once CC Frazier (Jonathan Pryce), Carter's hardnosed manager, gets Dodge to double that amount, Carter leads the reassembled Bulldogs to a string of lopsided victories.

Tipped off by Mack Steiner (Max Casella), Carter's disgruntled former comrade, sassy Chicago reporter Lexie Littleton (Renee Zellweger) begins trailing the team, hoping to debunk Carter's war record. Of course the two fall for each other, even as Lexie and Dodge express their mutual attraction in an exchange of often insulting wisecracks, in the vein of the Howard Hawks comedies of yore.

The three stars are effortlessly appealing. Clooney, who also directed, attempts to evoke the tangy wit of the screwball pairings of 1930s Hollywood, though co-writers Duncan Brantley and Rick Reilly's script falls considerably short of the crackling repartee of its Golden Age forebears. And some of the plot turns are implausible. The ups and downs of the triangular relationship among the leads could use better motivation, and not all the actions seem plausible. Why, for instance, is Lexie so willing to consider blowing Carter's cover, especially when she comes to know him as a decent guy with a puppy-dog crush on her?

But, on the whole, Clooney has made an enjoyably innocent, old-fashioned love story, with an irresistible musical soundtrack, too.

The film contains some profanity, occasional crude and crass language, mild fistfighting, light sexual banter and innuendo. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults, though acceptable for older teens. Motion Picture Association of America rating, PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Leathernecks Have Landed, The
synopsis: Dated pulp adventure in movieland China where an ex-Marine (Lew Ayres) turns gun-runner, then winds up back in the Corps by saving his former buddies from a rebel attack. Director Howard Bretherton does little with the standard melodramatics, though a likeable cast (James Ellison, Isabel Jewell and Ward Bond) makes it relatively painless. Stylized violence

title: Leave Her to Heaven
synopsis: Contrived potboiler in which a beautiful fruitcake (Gene Tierney) proves a moral monster after jilting her powerful fiance (Vincent Price) for a sensitive author (Cornel Wilde), then lets his handicapped brother drown, kills her unborn child in a fall and commits suicide in a manner that makes her adopted sister (Jeanne Crain) seem the killer. Directed by John M. Stahl, the lush settings have more interest than the thin characterizations and hokey plot. Stylized violence and domestic tensions

title: Leave It to Beaver
synopsis: Formula adaptation of the popular 1957-63 TV family series follows the trouble Beaver Cleaver (Cameron Finley) gets into after his bike is stolen and he continually skips football practice. Directed by Andy Cadiff, the thin proceedings rely on a child star whose appeal isn't strong enough to carry the weak, derivative comedy. Mild sexual innuendo, brief deception by a child and minor comic violence

title: Leave It to Blondie
synopsis: Formula family comedy directed by Abby Berlin follows the misadventures of the Bumsteads after Blondie (Penny Singleton) gets Dagwood (Arthur Lake) to enter a songwriting contest

title: Leaving Las Vegas
synopsis: Sterile story of a washed-up, alcoholic Hollywood writer (Nicolas Cage) who goes to Las Vegas to drink himself to death and the hardened prostitute (Elisabeth Shue) who helps him along the way because she finds some comfort in his company. Director Mike Figgis' self-indulgent elegy for self-destructive losers evokes as much emotional depth as watching TV test patterns. Graphic sex, occasional violence including a gang rape and much rough language

title: Leaving Normal
synopsis: A runaway battered wife (Meg Tilly) and a hard-bitten cocktail waitress (Christine Lahti) hitchhike to Alaska in hopes of finally putting down roots. Director Edward Zwick's combination female buddy and road movie is too contrived to be convincing. Recurring rough language and some sexual innuendo

title: Le Beau Mariage
synopsis: French comedy of manners and morals from director Eric Rohmer proves to be an amusing yet perceptive exploration of courtship rituals and mating practices not far different from our own. Its young heroine (Beatrice Romano), fed up with the complications of her affair with a married man, decides to get married and sets out to find her own husband. The result is a comedy of situations seen from a feminine perspective

title: Le Boucher
synopsis: Excellent psychological thriller about a schoolteacher (Stephane Audran) and the butcher of the title (Jean Yanne) who live in a small French village where a series of insane murders have taken place. Written and directed by Claude Chabrol, the script is marvellously tight and disciplined and the characterizations have an unusually solid psychological foundation. There are some shocks but they are done with all the authority of the old master, Hitchcock himself

title: Le Chat
synopsis: French study of a couple (Simone Signoret and Jean Gabin) who have been married for 25 years but whose ardor has cooled and turned to rancor. Directed by Pierre Granier-Deferre, the script is one of unrelieved bleakness, yet the two principals invest their roles with a rich human dimension as two imperfect individuals who stubbornly go on, fueled by hate, but they sometimes remember love

title: Le Depart
synopsis: Belgian story of an assistant hairdresser (Jean-Pierre Leaud) who is so obsessed with the idea of entering an upcoming motor rally that he neglects his girl friend in trying to find a suitable car. Director Jerzy Skolimowski treats his self-indulgent youth with stinging humor but also with some sympathy

title: Le Divorce
synopsis: Superficial drama in which a young American woman (Kate Hudson) travels to Paris to be with her pregnant sister (Naomi Watts), who is going through a divorce, where she begins an affair with a much older man (Thierry Lhermitte). As directed by James Ivory, the disappointingly shallow and surprisingly dark story isn't involving as underdeveloped characters fail to convincingly convey subtle cultural differences, and the mostly casual tone toward marital commitment is depressing. Some subtitles. Extramarital affairs, a few implied sexual encounters, brief violence and fleeting profanity and crass language
full_review:
Moviegoers anticipating a transporting experience from the talented directing/producing team of James Ivory and Ismail Merchant are likely to be disappointed with their latest offering, the superficial drama "Le Divorce" (Fox Searchlight).

The duo is most known for their period dramas such as "The Remains of the Day" and "Howards End," although director Ivory has ventured into the modern setting a few times with mixed success. Billed as a comedy of manners, "Le Divorce" is set in present-day Paris where young California gal Isabel (Kate Hudson) arrives to visit her pregnant sister Roxeanne (Naomi Watts). Roxeanne has just been jilted by her philandering French husband Charles-Henri (Melvil Poupaud), hence the movie's title.

Based on the novel by Diane Johnson, the film endeavors to highlight the differences between Americans and the French, especially when it comes to manners, morals, affairs of the heart, money and even food. But the story is disappointingly shallow and surprisingly dark at turns, with underdeveloped characters that fail to involve the audience. As the clunky film laboriously chugs along, the viewer cares less and less about the characters.

The story's main thread is Isabel and her transformation from valley girl to sophisticate. But Hudson does not have the acting chops to convey Isabel's interior metamorphosis. The change is solely exterior: from gauzy, bohemian shirts to stylish suits and smartly tied scarves, from long flowing curls to a chic bob. She begins an affair with her brother-in-law's older uncle Edgar (Thierry Lhermitte). But their interactions
(older-man-teaching-younger-woman-the-ways-of-the-world) feel forced and artificial.

Ivory and writing partner Ruth Prawer Jhabvala adapted the novel for the screen, but did not capture the essence of the characters or the story. They could not bring together in a convincing or involving manner the plot's many strands that range from a family squabble over a famous painting of St. Ursula by Georges de La Tour to Charles-Henri's affair with a Russian woman. One gets the sense that there is so much more to each of these characters that has been simplified (and therefore made much less interesting) for the screen.

Merchant and Ivory have assembled a talented group of actors for their ensemble cast, but the material is deficient, so none of them offer more than a standard performance. Leslie Caron stars as a stereotypical French matriarch, protecting the honor of her family through guile and manipulation. Sam Waterston and Stockard Channing are Isabel and Roxeanne's more straightforward parents who fly in from Santa Barbara to be with their daughters. Bebe Neuwirth plays an American museum expert and Glenn Close is a writer who secretly had an affair with Edgar years ago. Matthew Modine, whose performance is just a couple of frames past a cameo appearance, plays an erratic jealous American husband.

Although meant as yet another way in which the French and Americans differ, viewers may be dismayed by the casual attitude the characters take toward marital commitment. The foil to this is Roxeanne, who, faced with a divorce, has seemingly undergone a change of heart when it comes to morals. She is sickened by the casualness with which her in-laws discuss "adultery and fornication" and as a result becomes the movie's moral compass.

The settings are intimate and beautiful, but, without an absorbing story, they are little more than the pretty packaging of an empty box.

Some subtitles.

Because of extramarital affairs, a few implied sexual encounters, brief violence and fleeting profanity and crass language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Leech Woman, The
synopsis: Clunky horror tale directed by Edward Dein in which a doctor (Philip Terry) finds an African potion capable of making the old young again but a human sacrifice is needed to activate it. This is no problem for the doctor's aging wife (Coleen Gray) who maintains her youth by a series of killings, beginning with her cruel husband. Nasty stylized violence, sexual situations and marital antagonisms

title: Left Behind
synopsis: > Christian action thriller based on the first book of evangelical authors Tim LaHaye and Jerry Jenkins� best-selling series, about a handful of survivors � a TV reporter (Kirk Cameron), a born-again pilot (Brad Johnson), his teenage daughter (Janaya Stephens) and a Protestant minister (Clarence Gilyard) � trying to make sense out of the mysterious, simultaneous disappearance of people worldwide, leading them to conclude that an apocalyptic prophesy is unfolding. Director Vic Sarin stretches limited resources respectably, but the fundamentalist-flavored film is handicapped by a preachy, convoluted script, riddled with clich�s and corny dialogue and a fear-based approach to faith. Some violence, an implied affair and an underlying theology that conflicts with Catholic teachings, especially in its interpretation of scripture concerning the end times. A-III (PG-13) (2000)

title: Left Behind: The Movie
synopsis: Convoluted thriller in which the mysterious disappearance of people worldwide leads a television reporter (Kirk Cameron) to conclude that a terrifying apocalyptic prophecy is unfolding. Based on a Christian novel series about the Rapture, director Vic Sarin's film presents cliche-ridden dialogue and underdeveloped characters before an inconclusive ending hints at sequels to come. Mature subject matter, some violence and an implied affair. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Left Behind: Tribulation Force
synopsis: > The second part in the series continues the efforts of reporter Buck Williams (Kirk Cameron) and his band of believers (Brad Johnson, Clarence Gilyard and Janaya Stephens) to expose a charismatic U.N. official (Gordon Currie) as the anti-Christ and forestall his plan for world domination. Based on evangelical authors Tim LaHaye and Jerry Jenkins� apocalyptic best-sellers, director Bill Corcoran�s sequel shows little improvement over the first film�s preachy, awkward writing and underdeveloped characters. Some action violence, including a flaming body, and an underlying theology that conflicts with Catholic teachings, especially in its interpretation of scripture concerning the end times. A-III (nr) 2002

title: Left Behind: World at War
synopsis: > Based on the best-selling books by evangelical Christian authors Tim LaHaye and Jerry Jenkins, this third installment finds investigative reporter Buck Williams (Kirk Cameron) trying to avert global conflict by convincing the president of the United States (Lou Gossett Jr.) that the architect of the new world �peace� (Gordon Currie) is actually planning an attack on America that will trigger Armageddon. Directed by Craig R. Baxley and following its predecessors� heavy-handed lead, the film�s beefier budget means bigger explosions, but the writing is as bad as before. Some action violence and an underlying theology that conflicts with Catholic teachings, especially in its interpretation of scripture concerning the end times. A-III (PG-13) 2005

title: Left-Handed Gun, The
synopsis: Western misfire in which Billy the Kid (Paul Newman) determines to kill the four men who ambushed his English employer but after finishing the job, his one-time friend and now sheriff Pat Garrett (John Dehner) tracks him down. Directed by Arthur Penn from Gore Vidal's TV drama, the choppy narrative keeps going off on tangents and the acting is rooted more in the New York stage than in the sagebrush, with disappointing results. Hard-edged violence and sexual innuendo

title: Left Hand of God, The
synopsis: Fanciful melodrama set in 1947 China where an American pilot (Humphrey Bogart) downed in World War II and forced to fight for the local warlord (Lee J. Cobb) finally escapes by assuming the identity of a dead Catholic missionary, then tries to save the priest's mission from the warlord's vengeance. Directed by Edward Dmytryk, the conflict between pilot and bandit has some interest but the priestly masquerade and the romantic feelings it arouses in a mission aide (Gene Tierney) are pure Hollywood hokum. Bogus clergyman and romantic complications

title: Legacy
synopsis: Middle-aged woman (Joan Hotchkis) is too busy to notice that she is on the verge of a breakdown in director Karen Arthur's attempt to turn a myriad of feminist themes into a movie. Her treatment of a woman's repressed sexuality and guilt feelings about her life might have some use for women's discussion groups but not as a popular entertainment

title: Legacy, The
synopsis: Inferior horror movie of the satanic, let's-make-a-deal sub-genre depicts the misadventures of a bright, unmarried young couple (Katharine Ross and Sam Elliot) in a Gothic English manor. Directed by Richard Marquand, the story is extremely silly and excessively gory

title: Legal Eagles
synopsis: Robert Redford tries his best to be funny, charming and resourceful as the lawyer whose political ambitions get sidetracked when two women, a lawyer (Debra Winger) and her client (Daryl Hannah), implicate him in an art fraud that turns into a murder case. Director Ivan Reitman's shallow comedy is marred by female stereotyping and casual sex

title: Legally Blonde 2: Red, White and Blonde
synopsis: Cotton-candy comedy about dizzy material girl and Harvard Law grad Elle Woods (Reese Witherspoon), heading off to Washington as an animal rights activist in order to pass legislation that will free her pampered pooch's mother from a cosmetics research lab. Director Charles Herman-Wurmfeld's predictable fish-out-of-water sequel rehashes many of the same can't-keep-a-dumb-blonde down situations, while continuing to plug the original's message of believing in oneself. Some mild sexual humor, a homosexual-themed subplot, as well as a smattering of crass language and an instance of profanity
full_review:
Having already taken the "square" out of Harvard Square, America's favorite dizzy blonde sets her sights on giving Washington a makeover in the bubblegum comedy "Legally Blonde 2: Red, White & Blonde" (MGM).

Despite an effervescent performance by Reese Witherspoon, director Charles Herman-Wurmfeld's sequel to the 2001 sleeper hit lacks the freshness of its predecessor, rehashing many of the same blonde-fish-out-of-water jokes, making what were natural highlights in the original feel bottle-bought.

Taking up the action a few shopping sprees after the first film, Bel Air material girl and recent Harvard Law School graduate Elle Woods (Witherspoon) is juggling a demanding career as a rising young lawyer at one of Boston's top firms and planning the wedding of the century to her fiancee, Emmet (Luke Wilson). Yet upon discovering that the mother of her Chihuahua, Bruiser, won't be able to attend because she is being used as a test subject for cosmetics research, she decides to become the torchbearer for animal rights. Her zealous advocacy gets her fired when it turns out that the cosmetic company in question is one of the firm's most important clients.

In true never-underestimate-a-girl-with-a French-manicure-and-Harvard-law-degree frivolity, the well-coifed Elle packs her Prada bags and heads for the one town where vacuous thinking is de rigueur: Washington. She arrives in Jackie-O style, quickly painting the town pink. Her Cambridge connections land her a plum position on the staff of Hillaryesque Congresswoman Rudd (Sally Field). Of course, the icy reception extended by her fellow staff members, led by politically savvy Grace Rossiter (Regina King), lays the groundwork for the can't-judge-a-book-by-its-cover epiphanies down the pike.
With blithe flair and an impeccable fashion sense, Elle launches her crusade to make "Bruiser's Bill" the law of the land -- a feat easier said than done, especially for a towhead whose knowledge of Lincoln is limited to his poor choice of accessories, in one scene confiding to his statue "you were brave to wear that hat." She soon learns that there are forces working to derail her efforts and gets a crash-course in the Machiavellian machinations of corrupt backroom politics. Not one to be discouraged, Elle employs the aid of a sympathetic Deep Throat-like doorman (Bob Newhart) and a support network of her Delta Nu sorority sisters, turning the tables on her saboteurs and proving that you can't keep a good blonde down.

Of course, by time the final reel of the predictable fluff unspools, Elle not only gets the doggy legislation passed, but offers the joint houses of Congress a trite tutorial in democracy.

On more than one occasion the filmmaker genuflects at the altar of Frank Capra, paying heavy-handed homage to the heartfelt patriotism of "Mr. Smith Goes to Washington" -- even going so far as to include a clip of the 1939 Americana masterpiece starring Jimmy Stewart. As the idealistic Jefferson Smith, Stewart's impassioned filibustering leaves viewers itching to jump up and recite the Pledge of Allegiance, while Witherspoon's popcorn patriotism -- including such gag-worthy pabulum as "If we lose our voice, this country is in for a bad haircut" -- could inspire a petition to revoke her First Amendment right to free speech.
The golden-maned Witherspoon's smile lights up the screen, injecting an endearing buoyancy into what is otherwise Capitol Hill Barbie silliness. She inhabits her Jimmy Choo shoes with a sassy ebullience that should win her a "Farrah" from the blonde anti-defamation league. Regrettably, in this second tour of duty Witherspoon plays up Elle's Versace-vacuousness to the point of caricature, a marked digression from where the not-so-dumb blonde's character arc had led her at the end of the first film -- namely, valedictorian of Harvard Law School.

While many of the situations feel like retreads, the overall tone of "Legally Blonde 2" matches the cotton-candy flavor of the original, continuing its positive theme of believing in yourself and refraining from labels. However, one development that is more disturbing than white shoes after Labor Day is the not-so-subtle gay subplot involving Bruiser and a right-wing politico's Rottweiler, suspiciously sugarcoated so as to be easily digested by young audience members. This of course should come as no surprise given Herman-Wurmfeld's filmography, which includes the lesbian-themed "Kissing Jessica Stein" and a reference in the press notes to his "domestic partner."

Due to some mild sexual humor, a homosexual-themed subplot, as well as a smattering of crass language and an instance of profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Legally Blonde
synopsis: Determined to dazzle the boyfriend (Matthew Davis) who dumped her for a smarter girl, a flighty sorority co-ed (Reese Witherspoon) ends up attending Harvard Law School alongside him. As directed by Robert Luketic, Witherspoon makes the predictable, frivolous film stand out even when the light-hearted ``dumb blonde'' jokes fade. Some mild sexual references with a smattering of crass language and an instance of profanity. A-II (PG-13) 2001 (MGM)

title: Legend
synopsis: Director Ridley Scott's sumptuous fairy tale contrasts exceptionally cruel evil with extraordinarily sweet innocence in a quest to redeem a frozen world from the control of the Lord of Darkness. Tom Cruise is the hero who vanquishes the devil (Tim Curry) in an astonishing visual delight but some instances of grotesque imagery, especially the Lord of Darkness may frighten very young children

title: Legend of Billy Jean, The
synopsis: Four teenagers unwittingly become outlawed folk heroes. The value system represented is so confused that the movie is inappropriate for its intended adolescent audience. Some vulgar language

title: Legend of Boggy Creek, The
synopsis: Little town in Arkansas is bothered by a hairy monster, with a dubious footprint or two as evidence of its existence. In the fictionalized speculations about the monster's attacks, an actor made up with a lot of hair is photographed from the rear and sides in shadowy condition; he is as skillful at evading pursuing dogs and townsmen as he is the camera

title: Legend of Hell House, The
synopsis: Good British horror movie in which a skeptical physicist (Clive Revill), his wife (Gayle Hunnicutt) and two mediums (Pamela Franklin and Roddy McDowell) attempt to unravel the source of the ghastly murders that occurred when a previous group of scientists attempted to penetrate the mysteries of a deserted gothic mansion on the outskirts of London. Directed by John Hough, it has plenty of atmosphere, not a little suspense but also some intense violence and a suggestion of perverse sexuality

title: Legend of Lylah Clare, The
synopsis: Sudsy, sentimental soap opera in which a young starlet (Kim Novak) is coached by a has-been movie director (Peter Finch) who exhibits untoward interest in her that leads to tragedy. Directed by Robert Aldrich, it's a clunker with sexually suggestive scenes

title: Legend of Nigger Charley, The
synopsis: Runaway slaves (Fred Williamson, D'Urville Martin and Don Pedro Colley) are pursued by a bloodthirsty slave-tracker (Keith Prentice). Directed by Martin Goldman, the mindless action movie indulges in some foul language and incidental nudity

title: Legend of the Lone Ranger, The
synopsis: Klinton Spilsbury plays the masked champion of justice who, with the aid of Tonto (Michael Horse), rescues President Grant (Jason Robards) from the clutches of a badman (Christoper Lloyd). While moderately entertaining, director William A. Fraker's Western has considerable violence and occasional rough language

title: Legend of the Lost
synopsis: Uneven adventure tale starts in Timbuktu with an Italian doctor (Rossano Brazzi) hiring a veteran guide (John Wayne) to search for a lost city in the Sahara Desert, but the quest is complicated by taking along a local cafe entertainer (Sophia Loren) seeking to reform her life. Directed by Henry Hathaway, the travails of the journey and the secret of the abandoned city are lost in the men's sputtering rivalry over their female companion, with mostly slack results. Life-threatening situations and romantic complications

title: Legend of Tom Dooley, The
synopsis: Unaware of Lee's surrender, Confederate raiders (including Michael Landon) attack a Union coach, kill some passengers and become fugitives from Northern justice. Directed by Ted Post, the narrative is clumsily pegged to a song about doomed lovers, but the action is largely unconvincing. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Legends of the Fall
synopsis: Set on the sprawling Montana spread of their rancher father (Anthony Hopkins), the fate of three close brothers (Brad Pitt, Aidan Quinn and Henry Thomas) is powerfully affected by the arrival of the youngest brother's captivating fiancee (Julia Ormond) whom all three want to marry. Directed by Edward Zwick, the melodramatic tale of family tragedy and doomed romance gains some historical sweep by tying the narrative to the young mens' service abroad in World War I, the mistreatment of Native Americans and the ongoing backdrop of radically changing times for ranchers in the vanishing Old West. Some intense battlefield violence and revenge-motivated murders, brief bedroom scene with fleeting nudity and minimal rough language

title: Legion
synopsis: Theologically skewed apocalyptic horror outing in which a despairing God unleashes hordes of demonic angels to destroy human civilization but, rebelling against the plan, the archangel Michael (Paul Bettany) battles to defend a remote roadside cafe (owned by Dennis Quaid and Charles S. Dutton) long enough for its pregnant waitress (Adrianne Palicki) to give birth to humanity's future savior. Director and co-writer Scott Stewart's feature debut intersperses relentless violence with metaphysical mush to create a long, grim slog that leaves viewers feeling as besieged as the characters (also including Lucas Black and Tyrese Gibson) trapped in the lonesome eatery. Convoluted religious themes; constant, though mostly nongraphic, violence; an out-of-wedlock pregnancy; a couple of uses of profanity; much rough language (including at least 25 uses of the F-word); and some crude and crass terms

title: Legions of the Nile
synopsis: Soapy Italian-Spanish co-production directed by Vittorio Cottafavi in which Cleopatra (Linda Cristal) is caught between court intriguers and invading Roman armies. The English-language version alternates muscle-bound heroics with ludicrous sexual situations and innuendo

title: L'Elegant Criminel
synopsis: Before he is guillotined in 1836, a notorious French murderer (Daniel Auteuil) writes his memoirs rationalizing his life of crime. Director Francis Girod's overlong, fact-based period film leaves several key characters unexplained and fails to come to grips with what motivated the killer's callous behavior. Subtitles. Occasional violence and fleeting bedroom shots

title: Le Magnifique
synopsis: Jean-Paul Belmondo stars in a failed satire of superspy adventures of the James Bond variety. Forgettable French production directed by Phillipe de Broca

title: Le Mans
synopsis: Steve McQueen combines his acting and racing skills in a convincing portrait of a driver in the famed Le Mans competition in France. Directed by Lee H. Katzin, the drama is on the track and racing fans will find much satisfaction in the authenticity of the driving and in the beauty of the machines

title: Lemon Drop Kid, The
synopsis: Frantic adaptation of a Damon Runyon story in which a small-time bookie (Bob Hope) schemes to raise the money owed a gangster by setting up bogus sidewalk Santa Clauses supposedly collecting money for an old people's home. Directed by Sidney Lanfield, the script is tailored to suit Hope's talents for sight gags and one-liners but the humor is too fitful to sustain the cumbersome plot and phony Christmastime sentimentality. Mild sexual innuendo

title: Lemon Sisters, The
synopsis: Three lifelong girlfriends (Diane Keaton, Carol Kane and Kathryn Grody), self-dubbed Atlantic City's singing "Lemon Sisters," support each other through personal and career crises. Director Joyce Chopra's comedy features endearing performances and some heartwarming moments but is so lightweight it never gets beyond being a sentimental tribute to friendship. Brief instances of rough language

title: Lemony Snicket's A Series of Unfortunate Events
synopsis: Delightfully macabre tale of three Baudelaire orphans -- one an infant -- navigating their perilous way through various guardians into whose dubious care they've been entrusted after the death of their parents in a mysterious fire: evil Count Olaf (Jim Carrey) who has an eye on their fortune; kindly but dimwitted reptile collector Uncle Monty (Billy Connolly); and hyperphobic Aunt Josephine (Meryl Streep) who lives in a house perched high on a cliff.
