Directed by Paul Henreid, the gritty proceedings feature familiar criminal types, though of more interest are the decent citizens met along the way, including a group of likeable hoboes. Criminal rackets, sexual situations and innuendo

title: Live Flesh
synopsis: Overwrought Spanish melodrama in which an unjustly convicted ex-con (Liberto Ribal) becomes involved with the wives of the two police detectives who arrested him seven years earlier. Writer-director Pedro Almodovar transforms Ruth Rendell's 1986 novel into a soapy tale of betrayals, guilt and belated forgiveness. Subtitles. Several sexual encounters, brief nudity, fleeting violence, recreational drug abuse, recurring rough language and occasional profanity

title: Live for Life
synopsis: Long rambling story about the late maturing of a French photographer (Yves Montand) and his wife (Annie Giradot) after his affair with a model (Candice Bergen). Director Claude Lelouch sustains interest in a superficial, sentimental story with beautiful photography, locales, music and talented actors

title: Live Free or Die Hard
synopsis: Action-packed Washington-based thriller as detective John McClane (Bruce Willis in good, sardonic form) teams with a computer geek (Justin Long) to outwit a dastardly hacker (Timothy Olyphant) and deadly femme fatale cohort (Maggie Q) who intend to cripple the nation with a catastrophic computer breach. The fourth installment in the durable series starts in formulaic mode, but builds in excitement, with director Len Wiseman generating some first-rate chase sequences, but repeated profanity and one outrageously vulgar line are unfortunate detriments. Some crude and vulgar words and expressions, gratuitous profanity, a couple making out in a car, innuendo, pervasive nongraphic violence including explosions and shootings, albeit with little gore
full_review:
After the dreadful "Perfect Stranger" with Halle Berry, and a series of clever cameos in other people's movies, Bruce Willis is back in good, sardonic form as New York police detective John McClane in "Live Free or Die Hard" (Fox).

The action-packed (mostly Washington-based) fourth installment finds McClane assigned to a seemingly routine assignment apprehending a computer geek, Matt Farrell (Justin Long), in New Jersey, but becomes much more interesting when high-powered gunmen attempt to annihilate Matt as he's being arrested.

It seems Matt may hold the key to major-league hacker Thomas Gabriel (Timothy Olyphant) and his girlfriend and deadly chief operative Mai (Maggie Q), who, for reasons not revealed until late in the picture, intend to cripple the nation with a catastrophic computer breach, or what's called a "fire sale."

Disenchanted with the establishment, Matt had initially helped the villains, but when the full intent of Gabriel's nefarious plan becomes clear, Matt comes to realize it's not just some amorphous "system," but real people who stand to suffer, and from that point on he's squarely in McClane's court.

Gabriel and Mai have already hijacked the TV networks' broadcast transmissions, and are showing the public scary images of imminent disaster. The FBI seems helpless, and in fact they've already been infiltrated by Gabriel's gang.

McClane and Matt must reach the computer hub before the nation's infrastructure is fatally disabled. Along the way, the pair reach out to an eccentric colleague of Matt, a techno whiz known as Warlock (Kevin Smith) who, for all his cyber skills, still lives in his mother's basement.

With all the high-powered action stuff, there's more of a human element than in most films of this genre. Early in the film, we observe McClane scolding his estranged daughter, Lucy (Mary Elizabeth Winstead), for making out in a car. She sasses him back, but you feel she's grateful for the intrusion. Later on, when she's kidnapped by Gabriel, McClane's paternal instincts come to the fore, and it's clear that teenage defiance or not daddy is still No. 1.

So, too, McClane's fatherly relationship with Matt is essentially a positive one, with each coming to look after the other. There are echoes of the fractious, then supportive, dynamic between Willis' character and Mos Def's in 2006's "16 Blocks."

Mark Bomback's screenplay gets off to a formulaic start, but before long, builds in excitement, with director Len Wiseman overseeing some really splendid action sequences. McClane and Mai fighting to the death in an elevator shaft and an airborne car that manages to bring down a helicopter are just a couple.

There's an admirable absence of the f-word, but repeated profanity (mostly an all too common taking of the Lord's name in vain) and one especially vulgar and borderline racist line of dialogue are unfortunate detriments, and push what might otherwise have been an A-III classification into the more restrictive L category.

That's a pity, because otherwise the film ranks high on the entertainment meter as an exhilarating thriller.

The film contains some crude and vulgar words and expressions, gratuitous profanity, a couple making out in a car, innuendo, pervasive nongraphic violence including explosions and shootings, albeit with little gore. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Lives of a Bengal Lancer, The
synopsis: Gary Cooper and Franchot Tone play British officers who save the colonel's son (Richard Cromwell) and the honor of the regiment by quelling a rebellion on India's Northwest Frontier. Directed by Henry Hathaway, the rousing military adventure features a tall but lively tale of comradeship and bravery with some good action sequences and not a little humor. Stylized violence includes an off-screen torture scene

title: Live Today for Tomorrow
synopsis: ( see: "An Act of Murder" )

title: Live Wires
synopsis: Formula roughhouse comedy directed by Phil Karlson in which the Bowery Boys (led by Leo Gorcey) take on a mobster (Mike Mazurki) and break up his gang. Stylized violence

title: Living Daylights, The
synopsis: Timothy Dalton plays the new, more altruistic James Bond who foils an arms and drug-dealing scheme by KGB bigwig Jeroen Krabbe and ruthless dealer Joe Don Baker. Mellow treatment of spy triller by director John Glen includes a conventional romance with agent Maryam d'Abo and violence toned down to a level more acceptable for adults and mature teens

title: Living Free
synopsis: Sequel to Joy Adamson's "Born Free" tells of her attempts to rescue a trio of Elsa's orphaned lion cubs. Many adults will find their patience in short supply as Adamson (Susan Hampshire) and her gamekeeper-husband (Nigel Davenport) pursue their silly and sentimental ends in the name of humanitarianism while the cubs damage property and endanger themselves. Children, however, will only see cute wildlife antics

title: Living in Oblivion
synopsis: Tedious farce about a low-budget movie production whose cast (Catherine Keener and James Le Gros) and crew (Steve Buscemi, Dermot Mulroney, Danielle Von Zerneck, etc.) are beset with problems on and off the set, most of which stem from their own personal shortcomings and professional pretensions. Writer-director Tom DiCillo spoofs the struggling filmmakers with obvious fondness, though the contrived situations and broad performances are more tiresome than amusing, even for film enthusiasts. Implied sexual liaisons, brief nudity, intermittent profanity and rough language

title: Living It Up
synopsis: Lackluster musical remake of the screwball comedy, "Nothing Sacred," with Jerry Lewis as the supposed victim of radium poisoning, Dean Martin as his doctor and Janet Leigh as a reporter taking them to New York to exploit their media potential. Director Norman Taurog fails to find any charm, let alone human interest, in the glossy proceedings whose humor will escape all but the team's fans. Undemanding escapist fare

title: Living Out Loud
synopsis: Sweet-natured story of a lonely, newly divorced Manhattan nurse (Holly Hunter) and her depressed doorman (Danny DeVito) who befriend each other for different reasons, then help each other get on with their lives. Writer-director Richard La Gravenese's small story has big-hearted characters whose mid-life crises ring true thanks to nicely nuanced performances. Some sexual innuendo, minor substance abuse and intermittent profanity and rough language

title: Livin' Large
synopsis: Strained comedy about a young black man (T.C. Carson) whose overnight success as a TV reporter goes to his head and results in an identity crisis. Michael Schultz directs a situation comedy whose early promise disintegrates into an extended, one-joke routine, punctuated by some wry observations about today's ratings-mad television news coverage. Fleeting sexual encounter, a very crude double entendre and some rough language

title: Lizard in a Woman's Skin
synopsis: Italian clunker about a detective (Stanley Baker) investigating a series of murders finds the clues pointing towards a psychotic woman (Florinda Bolkan). Director Lugio Fulci's treatment of the heroine's real and imagined sexual perversions and the grisly representation of several murder victims are exploitative

title: Liztomania
synopsis: Ken Russell directs an extravagant tribute to composer Franz Liszt whom he presents as a 19th-century pop star (Roger Daltrey) whose concerts are mobbed by shrieking teenage girls who tetter on the verge of hysteria whenever his fingers touch the piano keys. Though there is much here that is good, funny and on-target, the movie flounders in excesses of every variety, most frequently sexual

title: Local Hero
synopsis: Hotshot young executive (Peter Riegert), comes to buy up a remote Scottish village to turn into an oil refinery but goes native, while the natives themselves pant after the millions he came to give them. Director Bill Forsyth's delightful comedy keeps taking strange but enjoyable turns and the prevailing mood is low-keyed zany. Some mild adult humor

title: Locket, The
synopsis: Muddled psychological tale of a very troubled woman (Lorraine Day) as told to her fiance (Gene Raymond) by her former beaus (Brian Aherne and Robert Mitchum) in flashbacks within flashbacks reaching to her childhood. Directed by John Brahm, the contrived melodrama becomes tiresome long before its predictable ending. Romantic complications

title: Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels
synopsis: Smug, convoluted caper in which four young Brits in heavy debt to a loan shark snatch a fortune in drug money from murderous thugs who have just ripped off a dealer intent on killing everyone involved in the theft. Writer-director Guy Ritchie treats the constant bloody violence as a lark all in a day's work of making a fast buck. Jokey treatment of multiple murders, benign view of crime, brief nudity, intermittent profanity and much shrill rough language

title: Lock Up
synopsis: Sylvester Stallone plays another violent cartoon hero in a behind-bars drama pitting good prisoners against bad prison officials (notably warden Donald Sutherland). Directed by John Flynn, Stallone's Mr. Nice Guy is appealing, but the grisly violence that befalls him and his inmate cohorts make this especially off-limits for youthful Rocky fans. Intense, sadistic violence and some profanity

title: Lock Up Your Daughters
synopsis: Musical farce about three sex-starved sailors is a blend of two British Restoration comedies with their stock characters and scenes cluttering its ribald scenario of permissive "wenching." Christopher Plummer stars and Peter Coe directs the slapstick action and humor at the level of TV sitcom spiced with nudity and sexual jokes

title: Locusts, The
synopsis: Tawdry tale of domestic dysfunction on a 1960's Kansas ranch whose promiscuous owner (Kate Capshaw) treats her disturbed son (Jeremy Davies) like a slave until a defiant new employee (Vince Vaughn) decides to help the lad stand up to her. Writer-director John Patrick Kelly's intended tragedy is overwrought with so many lurid revelations it fails to register as a credible story with any emotional resonance. Brief but ugly violence including off-screen suicides, many perverse sexual references, implied sexual encounters, some profanity and minimal rough language

title: Lodger, The
synopsis: Suspenseful tale in 1880's London where a couple (Cedric Hardwicke and Sara Allgood) rent a room to a mysterious stranger (Laird Cregar), then come to suspect he's Jack the Ripper and turn to a Scotland Yard inspector (George Sanders) to protect their niece (Merle Oberon). Directed by John Brahm, the sinister proceedings are heightened by Cregar's creepy performance and Lucien Ballard's moody photography. Off-screen murders, menacing situations and a psychopathic character

title: Logan's Run
synopsis: Futuristic social order is a hedonistic paradise except that its citizens are automatically exterminated at age 30. Instead of submitting, Michael York and Jenny Agutter make a run for it, pursued by zealous policeman Richard Jordan. Director Michael Anderson's rather simple-minded sci-fi chase movie is made moderately entertaining by its sets, special effects and the talents of its three principals. Some incidental nudity and disappointing downbeat conclusion

title: Lola
synopsis: Charles Bronson, terribly miscast as an aging American writer living in Britain, is smitten with a 16-year-old girl (Susan George) and marries her with predictable results. Directed by Richard Donner, the story has some interest but ultimately fails on the dramatic levels of coherence and acting

title: Lola Montes
synopsis: Heavily romantic treatment of the life of the 19th-century's most famous courtesan (Martine Carol) and her romance with King Ludwig of Bavaria (Anton Walbrook). Produced in 1955, director Max Ophul's visually masterful and lavish evocation of the Age of Romanticism plays down the heroine's amorality and paints, instead, a compassionate portrait of a pathetic and tragic figure who ends as a circus attraction for the curious

title: Lolita
synopsis: Mangled, meandering adaptation of Vladimir Nabakov's controversial novel about a mild university professor (James Mason) and his passion for a 14-year-old girl (Sue Lyon). Director Stanley Kubrick uses a comic menace (Peter Sellers) to surface the professor's guilt and shame at his vague, undefined obsession but the result leads nowhere. Mature themes related to abnormal psychology

title: Lolita
synopsis: Glossy but empty version of Vladimir Nabokov's novel about a middle-aged man (Jeffrey Irons) whose sexual obsession with a 12-year-old girl (Dominique Swain) ends tragically. Director Adrian Lyne�s titlillating treatment of the pair's cross-country sexual odyssey lacks any sense of a larger human context other than that of a troubled pedophile. Gory violence, frontal nudity, explicit sexual situations, brief drug abuse, occasional profanity and an instance of rough language

title: Lollipop
synopsis: Ailing white orphan (Norman Knox) from a Catholic mission in South Africa flees from his Afrikaner grandmother to the hills where he nearly freezes to death. Director Ashley Lazarus tells a poignant tale about racial prejudices and interracial brotherhood, somewhat sentimentalizing his stereotyped characters, yet for many reasons, it is rewarding fare for young viewers

title: Lollipop Cover
synopsis: Retired prizefighter (Don Gordon) and a 9-year-old girl (Carol Selfinger) help each other come to terms with their problems. The low-budget production is directed by Everett Chambers and the fine acting of the principals helps keep the slight but uplifting story convincing

title: Lolly-Madonna XXX
synopsis: Two neighboring Tennessee mountain families (headed by Rod Steiger and Robert Ryan) engage in a modern-day Hatfield-McCoy feud over a piece of pasture land and an innocent passer-by (Season Hubley) is held captive by one clan who thinks she belongs to the other. Directed by Richard C. Sarafian, the self-indulgent movie seems only interested in graphic displays of violence, including rape and the threat of rape

title: London
synopsis: Mostly repugnant story from first-time writer-director Hunter Richards involving a dissolute twentysomething New Yorker (Chris Evans) who crashes his ex-girlfriend's (Jessica Biel) bon voyage party, but takes refuge in the bathroom to avoid facing her, all the while snorting cocaine and engaging in mostly foul-mouthed discussions with an Englishman (Jason Statham) and other guests who drift in and out. Though ostensibly a cautionary look at the excesses of today's affluent youth, with some serious talk about the meaning of life and even a marginally redemptive ending, the sordid milieu, non-stop expletives, sexuality, and drugs result in a thoroughly distasteful and surprisingly dull melange. Pervasive rough and crude language, drug use, strong sexual content and perversity, partial and rear nudity, violence
full_review:
If you're hoping for Big Ben or the formidable Tower, you're going to be disappointed.

"London" (Destination) is, in fact, the female protagonist (Jessica Biel) of this highly repugnant story from first-time writer-director Hunter Richards.

The plot, such as it is, involves dissolute twentysomething New Yorker Sid (Chris Evans) who decides to crash his ex-girlfriend London's bon voyage party when he learns she's moving to Los Angeles.

He persuades an older Englishman named Bateman (Jason Statham) who had sold him drugs earlier in the day to come with him, and Bateman reluctantly complies.

But once there, Sid takes refuge in the bathroom to avoid facing London, all the while snorting cocaine and engaging in mostly foul-mouthed discussions with Bateman and other guests (Isla Fisher, Joy Bryant, Kelli Garner) who drift in and out. In one particularly distasteful sequence, Bateman recounts his experience in a sadomasochist club with short but seamy flashbacks.

And it is hardly an exaggeration to say that use of the f-word hits an all-time high.

Eventually, Sid is persuaded to leave the safety of the bathroom, and confront the woman he had been involved with for two years.

Though ostensibly a cautionary look at the excesses of today's affluent youths, with some pseudoserious talk about the meaning of life, the sordid milieu, nonstop expletives, sexuality and drugs result in a thoroughly distasteful and surprisingly dull melange, even with a marginally redemptive ending tacked on.
"London" is said to be the first in a trilogy. Heaven help us!
The film contains pervasive rough and crude language, drug use, strong sexual content and perversity, partial and rear nudity, and violence. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Lone Gun, The
synopsis: Routine Western directed by Ray Nazzaro in which a Texas sheriff (George Montgomery) takes on a gang of rustlers (led by Neville Brand) while saving a genial gambler (Frank Faylen) from being framed for the murder of a rancher (Skip Homeier) who has a lovely sister (Dorothy Malone). Frontier violence

title: Lone Hand, The
synopsis: Routine Western in which a young boy (Jimmy Hunt) doesn't know what to do when his widowed dad (Joel McCrea) takes up with outlaws, then marries a local girl (Barbara Hale). Directed by George Sherman, the dad's criminal activities are not what they seem and all ends well after a furious shootout. Frontier violence

title: Loneliness of the Long Distance Runner, The
synopsis: British reform school inmate (Tom Courtenay) mulls over his troubled past while making practice runs in training for the big cross-country race that the institution's head (Michael Redgrave) wants him to win. Alan Sillitoe's story of a working-class youth's rebellion against authority is directed by Tony Richardson with a gritty social realism that convincingly reflects, if not explains, the boy's alienation from a hypocritical adult world. Bleak study of the making of a juvenile delinquent

title: Lonely Are the Brave
synopsis: Thoughtful contemporary Western in which a free-spirited cowboy (Kirk Douglas) tries to break a pal out of jail, then gallops off for the protective wilderness of the mountains as a police manhunt (led by Walter Matthau) closes in. Director David Miller's engrossing narrative provides a penetrating character study of a nonconformist who has to pay the penalty for his refusal to adapt to changing times. Stylized violence

title: Lonely Guy, The
synopsis: Steve Martin plays a writer of greeting-card verses, thrown out by his lover and wandering in Central Park where he meets Charles Grodin who initiates him into the Lonely Guy fraternity. Director Arthur Hiller's comedy has sparse humor, stemming mainly from the encounters between Martin and Grodin. Some mild sexual humor

title: Lonely Lady
synopsis: Screen version of Harold Robbins' novel stars Pia Zadora as a young writer who cannot find happiness as she wins fame and fortune in Hollywood. Crass, sleazy vanity production directed by Peter Sasdy has graphic sex scenes and much nudity

title: Lonely Man, The
synopsis: Mawkish Western about an aging gunfighter (Jack Palance) who tries to make amends with the grown son (Anthony Perkins) he had abandoned as a child. Directed by Henry Levin, there's a lot of clumsy talk and gunplay before the long-delayed but expected father-son reconciliation. Stylized violence

title: Lonely Passion of Judith Hearne, The
synopsis: Disappointing movie version of the 1955 Brian Moore novel about a middle-aged Dublin spinster (Maggie Smith) who mistakes a gentleman's attentions as romantically intended and suffers a nervous breakdown when she discovers the truth. Elegantly directed by Jack Clayton, the novel's religious dimension is underdeveloped and the spinster becomes a pathetic figure of sheer desperation. Some sexual scenes involving a teen-aged maid

title: Lonely Trail, The
synopsis: Routine Western directed by Joseph Kane in which a Texas rancher (John Wayne) who fought for the Union returns after the war to an unfriendly welcome from neighbors, then steps in to protect them from a corrupt carpetbagger (Cy Kendall). Stylized violence and minor racial stereotyping. norating

title: Lonely Woman Seeks Life Companion
synopsis: Somber Soviet comedy about a 43-year-old woman (Irina Kupchenko) who posts signs around her Moscow neighborhood for a mate and then is harrassed by a drunken respondent. Directed by Viacheslav Krishtofovich, this is grim stuff with a stereotypic portrait of a single woman as desperate, cranky and past consideration as a potential mate. Minimal rough language and some sexual innuendoes

title: Lone Prairie, The
synopsis: B-Western star Russell Hayden and singing sidekick Bob Wills save a rancher from losing his land to a villainous railroad speculator. Director William Berke paces the formula action with comic relief from Dub Taylor. Stylized violence

title: Lone Ranger and the Lost City of Gold, The
synopsis: Standard Western adventure with the masked rider (Clayton Moore) and his faithful Indian companion (Jay Silverheels) taking on a band of hooded raiders terrorizing an Indian community in their search for the title treasure. Directed by Lesley Selander, the routine proceedings include a strong subplot condemning racial prejudice. Stylized violence

title: Lone Ranger, The
synopsis: Disappointing movie version of the radio and TV series pits the Masked Man (Clayton Moore) and his faithful Indian companion, Tonto (Jay Silverheels), against a crooked rancher (Lyle Bettger) who's trying to provoke an Indian war so he can mine the mountain of silver he's discovered on their reservation. Directed by Stuart Heisler, the formula script with its pedestrian plot and stock villains offers little of interest. Frontier violence

title: Lone Ranger, The
synopsis: ( see: "The Legend of the Lone Ranger" )

title: Lonesome Cowboys
synopsis: Minimal Western spoof from pop artist Andy Warhol treats its homosexual characters with repellent cruelty and is little more than an adolescent peep-show exhibition of sexual acts

title: Lonesome Jim
synopsis: Depressed young man (Casey Affleck) goes back to his Indiana home to live with his overly doting mother (Mary Kay Place), distant father (Seymour Cassel) and confused brother (Kevin Corrigan), falls for a single mother (Liv Tyler) with a small son (Jack Rovello), and ultimately comes to a better understanding of himself and those around him. Director Steve Buscemi's film is sometimes slow and meandering, and its true-to-life candor won't appeal to all tastes, but the central protagonist develops as a person, and the overall message of accepting life for what it is, not what you want it to be, is a good one. Scattered instances of profanity, rough and crude language and expressions, some crass humor, rear and partial nudity, premarital relationship, sexual banter and lewd images, prostitute character, suicide theme and drug references
full_review:
Steve Buscemi, the actor who played Tony Blundetto so memorably on "The Sopranos," is also an accomplished director, as demonstrated in "Lonesome Jim" (IFC), a quirky, slyly humorous, though often languidly paced film.

The titular 27-year-old (Casey Affleck) has been living in New York hoping to make it as a writer, but working as a dog walker and Applebee's waiter. He's in "chronic despair" -- so miserable in the world, he thinks he'd almost rather not be in it -- and has come back to his eccentric homestead of rural Indiana to have a nervous breakdown.

He's greeted effusively by his loving but overly doting mother, Sally (a very endearing Mary Kay Place), who thinks nothing of barging into the bathroom while Jim is in the tub, and speaking to him in gooey terms of endearment (though there's nothing sexual in this).

There's also his father, Don (Seymour Cassel), who takes a back seat to Mom, and glum divorced brother Tim (Kevin Corrigan), who has two small girls.

Jim passively ambles through life, sleeps a lot and eventually goes to work in his parents' factory.

He falls for an attractive nurse, Anika (nice work by Liv Tyler), with whom he commences an affair, and who surprises him, when he comes to her door, with a young son, Ben (Jack Rovello), who accompanies them on their dates.

All of Jim's melancholy talk prompts Tim to run his car into a tree, but the family rallies around Tim after his "accident" while he recovers. Even Anika spends an inordinate amount of time at his bedside, sparking some jealousy on Jim's part, though his suspicions prove unfounded.

Jim is fond of his druggy biker uncle, known as Evil (Mark Boone Junior), who works for Sally and Don. Later, it turns out that Evil has been shipping drugs from the company's FedEx account, and Sally is arrested. (She's such a guilelessly good-natured person, however, that she doesn't even complain, and befriends her jail mates.)

These events -- like almost everything in the film -- are accepted with lackadaisical equanimity, but by the end everything fits.

Buscemi's film (from James C. Strouse's screenplay) is sometimes slow and meandering. Jim is such a laid-back, unmotivated character that it's difficult to summon much interest in his predicament, and the movie's true-to-life candor (a rear view of Jim urinating, for instance) won't appeal to all tastes, but the central protagonist develops as a person, and learns the importance of accepting life for what it is, not what you want it to be.

Jim takes over coaching duties from his incapacitated brother for a young girls' basketball team. Dispirited by their unbroken losing streak, he tells them "You gotta keep playing" and "The past doesn't always predict the future" -- life lessons that pretty much sum up the film's ultimate good message.

The film contains scattered instances of profanity, rough and crude language and expressions, some crass humor, rear and partial nudity, a premarital relationship, sexual banter and lewd images, a prostitute character, a suicide theme and drug references. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Lone Star
synopsis: In 1845, Andrew Jackson (Lionel Barrymore) sends a pioneer cattleman (Clark Gable) to convince Sam Houston (Maroni Olsen) that Texas must join the Union, but along the way he gets entangled with an ambitious empire-builder (Broderick Crawford) and a lovely local editor (Ava Gardner). Director Vincent Sherman and a fine cast make the far-fetched Western adventure at least credible entertainment, if dubious history. Though the action is simple and robust, murky political intrigues keep complicating matters

title: Lone Star
synopsis: Tangled tale of justice unfolds in the story of a Texas sheriff (Chris Cooper) investigating a 40-year-old murder implicating his former-sheriff father and his dad's corrupt, trigger-happy predecessor (Kris Kristofferson). Writer-director John Sayles slowly juggles the narrative strands and character relationships, eventually pulling them all together in a thoughtful story about prejudice, integrity and healing. Fleeting bedroom encounter, brief violence and occasional rough language

title: Lone Star Raiders
synopsis: Western programmer directed by George Sherman in which the Three Mesquiteers (Robert Livingston, Bob Steele and Rufe Davis) save an elderly woman from losing her horse ranch to a crooked rival by breaking in a herd of wild mustangs and selling them to the Army. Stylized violence. norating

title: Lone Wolf and His Lady, The
synopsis: Slack mystery directed by John Hoffman in which the title reformed jewel thief (Ron Randell) helps a newspaper reporter (June Vincent) cover the exhibition of the world's third largest diamond, then is suspected of stealing it in a formula entry notable only as the last in the series. Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Lone Wolf Keeps a Date, The
synopsis: Routine series entry directed by Sidney Salkow in which the title's reformed crook (Warren William) goes after a gang of kidnappers when they try to grab his client (Frances Robinson) but make off instead with his collection of rare stamps. Stylized violence

title: Lone Wolf McQuade
synopsis: Martial arts star Chuck Norris plays a modern Texas Ranger out to get a nasty arms smuggler (David Carradine) with Barbara Carrera on hand to look sultry and utter her share of the sappy dialogue. There is considerable violence, though treated by director Steve Carver in rather stylized and unrealistic fashion

title: Lone Wolf Strikes, The
synopsis: Twisty series entry directed by Sidney Salkow in which the title reformed jewel thief (Warren William) retrieves a pearl necklace from a robber (Alan Baxter) by impersonating a crooked Dutch dealer (Montagu Love), then rescues the necklace's kidnapped owner (Joan Perry). Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Lone Wolf Takes a Chance, The
synopsis: Routine series entry directed by Sidney Salkow in which the title crimebuster (Warren William) saves a kidnapped inventor (Lloyd Bridges) from a gang of counterfeiters (led by Walter Kingsford). Stylized violence

title: Long Ago, Tomorrow
synopsis: British love story of a man (Malcolm McDowell), paralyzed from a soccer injury, and a quiet, attractive polio victim (Nanette Newman) who reside in a nursing home for the disabled. Director Bryan Forbes' story of their determination to marry in spite of their limitations is cut short by her death but the movie handles a delicate subject with great sensitivity

title: Long and the Short and the Tall, The
synopsis: ( see: "Jungle Fighters" )

title: Long Dark Hall, The
synopsis: Dim British melodrama in which the murder of a showgirl is pinned on an innocent man (Rex Harrison) whose blindly loyal wife (Lilli Palmer) is stalked by the real killer (Anthony Dawson). Directed by Anthony Bushell and Reginald Beck, the turgid proceedings belabor the obvious until justice triumphs in the last five minutes. Implied extramarital affair

title: Long Day Closes, The
synopsis: Uneventful, impressionistic look at life in mid-1950's Liverpool through the eyes of an 11-year-old lad as he takes part in the daily routines of his working-class family and neighbors. Writer-director Terence Davies' autobiographical movie is warmly nostalgic in treating his Catholic childhood, loving mother and older siblings, but the period music and visually arresting images do not sustain what amounts to a slow-moving, highly personal reminiscence. Several racist references

title: Long Day's Dying, The
synopsis: British World War II drama about three soldiers (David Hemmings, Tom Bell and Tony Beckley) trying to get back to their lines with a German prisoner. Directed by Peter Collinson, the realistic brutality used in this anti-war movie to convey the horror of war will strike some as excessive

title: Long Duel, The
synopsis: British India is the setting for this stiff-upper-lip story starring Trevor Howard as a non-conformist official who wants to treat even an outlaw native chief (Yul Brynner) with man-to-man justice. British production directed by Ken Annakin is routine escapist affair

title: Longest Day, The
synopsis: The Allied invasion of Normandy on June 6, 1944, is re-created on an epic scale in this three-hour dramatization of the operational preparations, behind-the-line activities but mostly the ferocious battle itself, with particular attention to the American landings at Omaha Beach. Directed by Ken Annakin, Andrew Marton and Bernard Wicki, the result is an absorbing account of D-Day from both sides of the battlefield, with convincing portrayals of men in combat from an international cast headed by John Wayne, Robert Mitchum and Henry Fonda. Wartime violence seen in the context of a righteous cause

title: Longest Yard, The
synopsis: Burt Reynolds stars as an imprisoned ex-pro quarterback who leads a team of fellow convicts against a team made up of guards. Directed by Robert Aldrich, the movie has a careless, slapped-together look and relies heavily on violence and foul language

title: Long Goodbye, The
synopsis: Raymond Chandler's private eye, Philip Marlowe (Elliott Gould), by helping a friend out of a jam, finds himself picked up by the police and booked as an accessory to murder and left to sort through a tangle of murder, deception, robbery, suicide and double-crossing. Directed by Robert Altman, the action is handled quite well as is the tacky atmosphere, but Marlowe and his moralities are hopelessly confused. Some rough language and brief nudity

title: Long Good Friday, The
synopsis: Tough British gangster movie in which Bob Hoskins gives a remarkable performance as a London gang lord done in by his own pride. Director John Mackenzie invests his brutal underworld story with grim but intelligent realism that some will find unnerving. Some intense scenes of violence

title: Long Gray Line, The
synopsis: Sentimental, overlong but ultimately rewarding picture of Sgt. Marty Maher (Tyrone Power), an Irish immigrant who became a physical training instructor at West Point in a 50-year career which spanned two world wars and made him a beloved father figure for generations of cadets. Director John Ford pays affectionate tribute to both Maher and the Academy in a story focused on the values of home (Maureen O'Hara plays Maher's wife) and the military, with many patriotic asides and rowdy good humor. Idealized yet interesting piece of Americana

title: Longhorn, The
synopsis: Standard Western directed by Lewis Collins with a rancher from Wyoming (Wild Bill Elliot) buying a herd of cattle in Oregon, then meeting trouble with the cowpunchers he's hired for the drive back, among whom are reformed gunmen and a traitor in cahoots with a gang of rustlers. The usual frontier violence

title: Long Hot Summer, The
synopsis: Uneven adaptation of the William Faulkner story about a wealthy Southern family whose uncouth patriarch (Orson Wells) hires a reputed barnburner (Paul Newman), comes to appreciate the man's grit and ambition, then tries to get him to marry his independent-minded daughter (Joanne Woodward). Director Martin Ritt does well enough with the rural southern setting and gets good performances from the leads, but the script is flabby and the subsidiary roles seem more plot devices than characters. Minimal violence and some sexual innuendo

title: Long John Silver
synopsis: Uninspired sequel in which the roguish pirate of the title (Robert Newton) returns to Treasure Island with young Jim Hawkins amongst his shipmates but they have to fight off a variety of rivals before getting the treasure back to England where Silver faces marriage to an doughty innkeeper (Connie Gilchrist). Directed by Byron Haskin, the Australian production is watchable entertainment but the narrative's adventure is less than original and overindulges Newton's penchant for outrageous mugging. Swashbuckling violence and mild sexual innuendo

title: Long Kiss Goodnight, The
synopsis: Overly violent tale of an amnesia victim (Geena Davis) who teams with a hired investigator (Samuel L. Jackson) to discover she was an assassin employed by a secret government agency which now has her on its hit list. Director Renny Harlin's overwrought thriller is stuffed with brutality and murderous clashes but lacks character development and coherent plotting. Excessive violence, deadly menace to a child, some sexual innuendo, occasional profanity and much rough language

title: Long, Long Trailer, The
synopsis: Thin but mostly agreeable situation comedy in which newlyweds (Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz) buy a trailer for their honeymoon in the mountains of Colorado, then face one calamity after another. Directed by Vincente Minnelli, the slapstick proceedings are mostly those of man-against-machine, in a story sprinkled with domestic arguments and sweet reconciliations

title: Long Ride from Hell, A
synopsis: Steve Reeves stars in an Italian Western as a man bent on revenge for a horse theft and the death of his brother. Directed by Alex Burks, the movie makes up in blood and sadism what it lacks in wit and talent

title: Long Ride Home, The
synopsis: Vicious psychological triangle set at the end of the Civil War pitting Union officer Glenn Ford against Confederate counterpart George Hamilton with Inger Stevens in the middle. Dwarfed by the magnificence of its Grand Canyon locations, the characters lack human interest and director Phil Karlson's movie ends up somewhere between muddled comment on the brutality of war at best and distorted, misguided melodrama at worst

title: Long Riders, The
synopsis: Slow-paced, somber Western starring the Carradine, Keach and Quaid brothers re-enacting the James and Younger gangs' disastrous raid on the bank in Northfield, Minnesota. Though it has its moments, director Walter Hill's effort is a little too pretentious to be really entertaining or enlightening. Some graphic violence and a realistic bordello scene

title: The Longshots
synopsis: Fact-based sports drama in which an unemployed former high school football star (Ice Cube) living in a depressed factory town is hired by his hardworking sister-in-law (Tasha Smith) to mind his shy, bookish niece (Keke Palmer) and, discovering that the girl shares his gift for the game, becomes her trainer and gets her a tryout with a local, previously all-boys team. Director Fred Durst's upbeat, mostly unobjectionable film is a celebration of each individual's power to bring about both personal and civic renewal. Brief sexual humor, a couple of profanities, a few crass words and mild oaths
full_review:
The fictional Midwestern city that provides the setting for the fact-based sports drama "The Longshots" (Dimension/MGM) is beset by a number of all-too-familiar problems. Its factory is closed, its main street is decaying and even the once-mighty local football team, the Minden Browns -- part of the nationwide Pop Warner youth league -- has suffered two decades of decline.

A typical victim of these depressed conditions is Curtis Plummer (Ice Cube, also a producer). Once a high school gridiron star, he's now unemployed and unkempt and spends his days drinking beer while nurturing his dream of relocating to Miami. First as a favor, but in the end as a part-time job, his hardworking sister-in-law, Claire (Tasha Smith), asks him to mind Jasmine (Keke Palmer), his shy, bookish niece.

 

An outsider at school, Jasmine has never recovered from the fact her irresponsible father, Roy (Malcolm Goodwin), deserted her and she still wears his watch as a symbol of her hope to reconnect. She's unwilling to be watched by a baby sitter, especially an uncle for whom she has scant respect, and the two bicker constantly.

By chance, though, Curtis discovers that Jasmine has an excellent throwing arm. After giving her some rudimentary training, he sets out to convince the Browns' coach (Matt Craven) that awarding Jasmine the quarterback spot on his previously all-boys team will reverse their sliding fortunes.

As the heavily tattooed lead singer of the often-controversial band Limp Bizkit, director Fred Durst may seem an unlikely heir of Hollywood's most famous American dreamer, Frank Capra (1897-1991). Yet his upbeat, mostly unobjectionable film, which also features Garrett Morris as a dynamic preacher and community leader, is a Capraesque celebration of each individual's power to bring about both personal and civic renewal.

The film contains brief sexual humor, a couple of profanities, a few crass words and mild oaths. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested. Some material may not be suitable for children.

title: Longtime Companion
synopsis: Moving but somewhat idealized portrait of how the AIDS epidemic affected the lives of three homosexual couples in New York City from 1981 to 1989. Directed by Norman Rene, the movie captures the human dimension of the illness without sensationalism or sentimentality, using understated performances to reveal the everyday heroism of "longtime companions" caring for their terminally ill loved ones. Frank depiction of homosexual life, including male kissing and embraces, casual drug use and sporadic rough language

title: Long Voyage Home, The
synopsis: Compelling dramatization of four one-act plays by Eugene O'Neill about merchant seamen (Thomas Mitchell, Barry Fitzgerald, Ward Bond and John Wayne, among them) sailing on a British tramp freighter from a Caribbean port of call to the U.S. where they take on a cargo of munitions and head through the war zone for London. Director John Ford fashions an emotionally involving picture of life at sea, focusing on the camaraderie of the crew as they face the voyage's dangers from nature and human folly as well as the temptations ashore at journey's end. Some menace and sexual references

title: Long Walk Home, The
synopsis: The 1955 bus boycott by blacks in Montgomery, Alabama, forces a wealthy white socialite (Sissy Spacek) to see her long-suffering black maid (Whoppi Goldberg) as a person and not just a personal convenience. Directed by Richard Pearce, the leads give shining performances but its attempt to contrast a black and a white family is flawed by one dimensional characterizations. Numerous racial epithets and brief violence

title: Look at Me
synopsis: Finely acted French film about Etienne (Jean-Pierre Bacri), a self-centered, celebrated writer and publisher; his unhappy overweight daughter, Lolita (Marilou Berry), an aspiring classical singer attracted more to the ex-boyfriend who cares little for her than the new one who does; and Sylvia (Agnes Jaoui), the girl's singing teacher, who takes a special interest in the girl mostly to help her writer-husband Pierre (Laurent Grevill) cultivate a friendship with Etienne to advance his career. Writer-director Jaoui's perceptive film -- co-written with co-star Bacri -- says much about youthful angst, fathers and daughters, celebrities and the sycophants who surround them, all in a marvelously real way. Subtitles. A few instances of rough and crude language
full_review:
Somehow Europeans have the knack of making keenly observant movies about the complexities of ordinary life beyond the ken of most Hollywood filmmakers.

Such a film is the affecting, character-driven "Look at Me" (Sony Classics) from France which centers on Lolita (Marilou Berry), the unhappy, overweight, 20-year-old daughter of Etienne Cassard (Jean-Pierre Bacri), an egocentric, celebrated writer. Lolita feels very much the ugly duckling, particularly in light of her father's pretty young girlfriend, Karine (Virginie Desarnauts).

Lolita has aspirations of becoming a classical singer, and her chief joys in life are her lessons and the amateur chorale of which she's a member. Otherwise, she lumbers placidly through life and seems to accept her wallflower lot. Much to her frustration, her father takes virtually no interest in his daughter's vocalizing, but is otherwise reasonably caring if utterly self-absorbed.

Lolita has a boyfriend of sorts, but we sense (correctly, as it happens) that her adoring feelings for him are not reciprocated. When Sebastien (Keine Bouhiza), a young stranger she selflessly covers with her coat when she sees him passed out on the sidewalk outside a club, asks to meet her to thank her for her compassion (and return the coat), she infuriatingly treats him with only tolerant civility, even though it's plain to see he's an exceptionally nice fellow.

Lolita's singing teacher, Sylvia (director and co-writer Agnes Jaoui), has reluctantly agreed to tutor her amateur group. Later, she decides to renege on her promise, but changes her tune when she learns the identity of Lolita's father, whose writing she admires. She also believes that getting to know Etienne through his daughter will help her novelist husband, Pierre (Laurent Grevill), currently in a serious creative funk, advance his career.

Jaoui's perceptive film -- co-written with Bacri -- says much about youthful angst, fathers and daughters, celebrities and the sycophants who surround them, all in a marvelously real way. The brilliant opening sequence in a taxicab, contrasting how Lolita lets a surly driver walk all over her, while Etienne, when he later gets in the car, puts the driver soundly in his place, is the kind of inconsequential episode that gives us immediate insight into the characters.

The acting is superb all around. Berry is just perfect: lumpish but kind, occasionally unsympathetic, and transformed when she "sings." (Her singing was dubbed by Alexandra Rubner.) Bacri is utterly plausible as the autocratic literary lion. The versatile Jaoui telegraphs a genuine caring quality but not without a degree of self-interest. Grevill, Bouhiza and Desarnauts all satisfyingly inhabit their characters, while Gregoire Oestermann and Michele Moretti are especially good as Etienne's lackey and Pierre's agent, respectively.

If the feel-good ending is rather conventional, the film rarely makes a false move.

Like that other Gallic hit, "Les Choristes," music -- here, ranging from the chorale's Baroque tunes to Mozart's "Cosi Fan Tutte" -- is used quite effectively throughout, providing texture to Lolita's character and serving as lovely underscoring for its own sake.

The film, with subtitles, contains a few instances of rough and crude language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Looker
synopsis: Beverly Hills plastic surgeon (Albert Finney) uncovers a plot by a conglomerate (headed by James Coburn) to hypnotize television viewers into buying products advertised in commercials. The scheme involves the murder of several actresses who are turned into computerized images. Writer-director Michael Crichton's confused story substitutes superficiality for social satire and flashiness for mystery. Some violence and brief nudity

title: Looking for Comedy in the Muslim World
synopsis: Amiable but low-key comedy about comedian Albert Brooks sent to India on a government peace mission to determine what makes Muslims laugh, causing a contretemps with Pakistan in the process. Brooks' brand of laid-back and understated humor and the exoticism of the Delhi settings make for pleasant viewing, along with his gently satiric spin on the present-day politics and conflict often arising over inconsequential misunderstandings. A few instances of profane, rough and crude words make this best for older adolescents and up
full_review:
By the sound of it, you might think comedian Albert Brooks is treading on politically incorrect ice with his latest movie.

But not to worry. "Looking for Comedy in the Muslim World" (Warner Independent) -- which he both wrote and directed -- is an amiable but low-key satire with a good message about America's cultural myopia and the importance of humor as a pacifier after the events of Sept. 11, 2001. And it's set in India and (briefly) Pakistan, rather than the more volatile Middle East.

Brooks plays himself at the time of a career lull. He hopes to land the James Stewart part in a revival of "Harvey," but in a funny early scene crusty director Penny Marshall (as herself) disabuses him of that notion and sends him packing.

He's in the doldrums until he receives a missive from Washington asking him to a meeting about a government mission. His eBay-addicted wife (Amy Ryan) encourages him to go. There, he learns from former U.S. Sen. (and sometime actor) Fred Dalton Thompson that he has the chance to travel abroad and learn what makes Muslims laugh.
There's no pay, beyond expenses, but hints of a Medal of Freedom in Brooks' future sweeten the proposition.

With the aid of two government handlers, Stuart (John Carroll Lynch) and Mark (Jon Tenney), he makes the long journey to Delhi, India, by coach. Agent Mark finds him a dilapidated office, and after interviewing a number of singularly unpromising candidates he hires a secretary named Maya (Sheetal Sheth), an eager young lady anxious to help.

Hanging gloomily over Brooks' head is the 500-page report he must submit at the end.
Random street polling yields few results, but eventually Brooks hatches a scheme to give a comedy improv concert to which he'll invite English-speaking Muslims. Brooks does an amusing act, but fails to elicit more than polite applause.

Red tape prevents his planned trip to Pakistan, but the agents contrive a brief illegal border crossing to that country with comic consequences.

As Brooks sincerely goes about his assigned task, he nearly causes an international incident with Pakistan.

Brooks' brand of laid-back and understated humor and the exoticism of the Delhi settings make for pleasant viewing, along with his gently satiric spin on the present-day politics and tensions often arising over inconsequential misunderstandings.

There's no racial caricaturing to speak of, notwithstanding some Pakistani comedians set up at first to look like terrorists, and present-day Indian culture is not stereotyped.
Brooks' character encounters some mildly patronizing anti-Semitism at a couple of junctures, as when he visits the office of Al-Jazeera, where officials enthusiastically pitch him the idea of starring in a sitcom with the unpromising title of "That Darn Jew." (Brooks politely declines.)

Brooks' premise is a worthy one, and who's to say the punch line might not be mightier than the sword?

The film contains a few instances of profane, rough and crude words making this best for older adolescents and up. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Looking for Mr. Goodbar
synopsis: Director Richard Brooks' harrowing account of some of the consequences of the sexual revolution stars Diane Keaton as a wildly self-destructive young single on the prowl for love and commitment. Drama tries to evoke the moral confusion that pervades the lives of young people caught up in the liberated lifestyles of the 1970s but says little about the options open to them. Details of the singles drug and sex scene including a graphic rape and murder hammer home the obvious

title: Looking for Richard
synopsis: Playful documentary exploring the historical background, Elizabethan language and dramatic stagecraft of Shakespeare's "Richard III" as undertaken by actor Al Pacino and his cohorts in preparing for an American version of the play. Also directed by Pacino, the result is an amusing hodge-podge of fact and whimsy, sometimes serious but often frivolous and at times self-indulgent, especially Pacino's hammy run-throughs in the title role. Dramatized violence, sexual references and occasional rough language

title: Looking Glass War, The
synopsis: Failed screen version of John Le Carre's story of a Polish national (Christopher Jones) who jumps ship in Britain and is promised asylum by a group of British intelligence agents (led by Ralph Richardson) who cynically plan to use him for their own espionage ploys. Directed by Frank R. Pierson, the adaptation misses the interest and suspense of the original by bogging down in unmotivated and barely credible incidents, including his affair with a German woman (Pia Degermark)

title: Looking Up
synopsis: Documentary directed by Linda Yellen offers a fragmented chronicle of the lives of three generations of a Jewish family seeking upward mobility and success in America. Although used to establish character, there are instances of vulgar language that may offend some viewers

title: Lookin' to Get Out
synopsis: Two luckless gamblers (Jon Voight and Burt Young) in debt to gangsters flee New York for Las Vegas where they stake a down-on-his-luck gambling whiz (Burt Remsen) to one last try at the jackpot. Director Hal Ashby's movie written by Voight is a total disaster, utterly lacking in charm, with unremitting vulgar language, some brief nudity and a benign view of the easy sex to be had in a resort

title: Look Out, Mr. Moto
synopsis: ( see: "Mr. Moto Takes a Chance" )

title: Look Who's Laughing
synopsis: Radio comedian Edgar Bergen and puppet Charlie McCarthy team with radio's most popular comic couple, Fibber McGee and Molly (Jim and Marion Jordan), in director Allan Dwan's feeble effort to wring smiles from a convoluted plot about building an airplane factory in Wistful Vista rather than in a rival town. Limited fun, especially for youngsters

title: Look Who's Talking
synopsis: Lame comedy about an unmarried career woman (Kirstie Alley) whose married lover (George Segal) leaves her pregnant and searching for the perfect father (John Travolta) for her baby son who "talks" (voice of Bruce Willis) to the audience as he evolves from energized sperm and embryo through birth and toddler stages. Writer-director Amy Heckerling manages through the baby's sarcastic comments to vulgarize the process of conception, trivialize childbirth and make a three-ring fantasy out of single parenthood. Much vulgar sexual humor, some rough language and a cavalier attitude toward adultery

title: Look Who's Talking Now
synopsis: Witless sequel in which two family dogs (voices of Danny DeVito and Diane Keaton) trade insults while the husband (John Travolta) fends off a lecherous boss (Lysette Anthony) determined to keep him away from worried wife (Kirstie Alley) and children over Christmas. Director Tom Ropelewski's comedy clunker tacks a talking-dogs gimmick onto a contrived marital crisis of insipid sitcom proportions. Some sexual innuendo, crude remarks and an intense dogfight

title: Look Who's Talking Too
synopsis: Silly sequel in which busy toddler Mikey (voice of Bruce Willis) confronts toilet training, a new baby sister (voice of Roseanne Barr) and his mom (Kirstie Alley) being on the outs with his new dad (John Travolta). Since virtually nothing happens in the movie, director Amy Heckerling is reduced to stringing together a lot of adorable baby shots until the grown-ups get their act together. Minor fantasy violence, sexual references and much bathroom humor

title: Looney Looney Looney Bugs Bunny Movie, The
synopsis: Compilation of vintage Warner Brothers cartoon shorts with some new material. The art work and the style of the animation are light years removed from the crude fare offered a new generation watching Saturday morning television

title: Looney Tunes: Back in Action
synopsis: Screwball adventure in which Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck help a Hollywood stuntman (Brendan Fraser) and studio executive (Jenna Elfman) recover a mysterious gem before it falls into the evil clutches of a madman (Steve Martin) bent on turning all human life into monkeys. With more falling anvils than plot twists, director Joe Dante combines live action and traditional animation to craft an entertaining comedy, and though its Acme brand of roughhousing may give some parents pause, it faithfully echoes the clever wit and wacky tenor of the original Looney Tunes, making it suitable for all but the youngest children. Cartoon violence, minimal mildly crude language and innuendo
full_review:
Finally, a film that understands that all audiences really want is to watch a rascally rabbit and a game bird with an inferiority complex save the world from an evil genius bent on turning every man, woman and child on earth into rhesus monkeys.

Throw in clever dialogue, live-action co-stars willing to be upstaged by frenetic farm fauna, and a riotous romp -- literally -- through modern art and you'll send viewers home smiling, which is precisely what director Joe Dante does in "Looney Tunes: Back in Action" (Warner Bros.).

Based on the characters created in the 1930s and '40s by the Warner Brothers animation team of Tex Avery and Chuck Jones and voiced by the late Mel Blanc, the screwball adventure blends live action with traditional cartoon animation along the lines of "Who Framed Roger Rabbit" (1988) and "Space Jam" (1996).

"Back in Action" opens with a disgruntled Daffy Duck, frustrated over playing second fiddle to his cotton-tailed confrere, demanding that studio suits give him star, er, billing in their upcoming feature. Instead, he is given his waddling papers by the studio's new all-business vice president of comedy, Kate Houghton (Jenna Elfman). Charged with escorting the toona-non-grata from the premises is D.J. Drake (Brendan Fraser), a hunky security guard and stuntman. Drake's father, Damian (Timothy Dalton), is the studio's top draw, staring in its series of James Bond knockoffs.

After his expulsion nearly destroys the Warner back lot and gets his escort fired, Daffy follows his webbed feet to Drake's doorstep. To his surprise, Drake discovers that his dad is in fact a real international man of mystery and is being held by the nutty chairman of Acme Industries (Steve Martin, doing his best Dr. Evil impersonation), who is trying to find out the whereabouts of a mysterious gem known as the Blue Monkey Diamond. Once found, the chairman plans to use the precious stone as part of his plan for world domination, which among other things will send the cost of banana stocks skyrocketing.

Drake and Daffy take off to save the day, joined soon after by Bugs and Houghton. The foursome quickly becomes entangled in a wacky web of globetrotting adventure which takes them from Las Vegas to Paris to the deepest jungles of the Dark Continent. Of course, travel time is reduced considerably when one can simply lift up the corner of the backdrop and step into a different scene.

To be honest, even back in their heyday, plot was never high in the cosmic pecking order of the Looney Tunes universe, occupying a level of importance somewhere between the laws of physics and political correctness, both of which are pleasantly flouted throughout the film. Porky Pig still stutters and Elmer Fudd, even in our post-Columbine environment, gets to keep his hunting rifle.

The human cast members seem to take extreme pleasure in the uninhibited zaniness their roles afford them. However it is Bugs and Daffy -- the best pairing this side of Crosby and Hope -- who steal the show, turning mayhem into an art form. Hollywood's three-dimensional talent pool could learn a lot about comedic timing from watching these two old pros, who have more in common with vaudeville than the video game-inspired pabulum of contemporary cartoons.

While young viewers will enjoy the zany onscreen antics, adults along for the ride will be equally entertained by the witty innuendo-laced dialogue -- most of which will be lost on tykes too busy watching Daffy remove his own beak -- and hidden humor (such as the corporate nameplates at Acme identifying board members as "V.P. of Bad Ideas" and "V.P. of Rhetorical Questions").

And though some parents may object to the considerable roughhouse violence -- anvils and incineration are still the methods of choice among toons -- the film faithfully echoes the tenor of the earlier-era cartoons, making it suitable for all but the youngest children.

As in the original cartoons -- which introduced classical music to generations of children without their knowing it -- "Back in Action" takes the opportunity to educate in between exploding carrots and mallet melees. As Bugs observes, "I think when you go to the movies you should learn something."

Adhering to that advice, "Back in Action" contains a toon-torial in modern art. The inspired sequence involves Elmer Fudd chasing Bugs and Daffy through various paintings in the Louvre's galleries -- with the animation reflecting the style of each -- including Edvard Munch's "The Scream," Seurat's pointillist "A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte" and Dali's surreal masterpiece "The Persistence of Memory."

Due to cartoon violence, minimal mildly crude language and innuendo, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

title: Loose Cannons
synopsis: Witless action comedy about two screwball cops (Gene Hackman and Dan Aykroyd) whose investigation of a bizarre murder case leads to a sleazy porno king (Dom DeLuise) linked to foreign agents seeking a lost reel of Nazi pornography. Director Bob Clark's sophomoric exercise in minimalist comedy strings together a series of dumb gags, weak spoofs, sex jokes and special effects mayhem. Much demeaning sexual humor, senseless violence and some very offensive language

title: Loot
synopsis: British black comedy by Joe Orton in which a mortician-bank robber (Hywel Bennett), his adoring pal (Roy Holder), the pal's freshly widowed father (Milo O'Shea), the dead wife's piously amoral nurse (Lee Remick) and a batty Scotland Yard inspector (Richard Attenborough) get mixed together in a tacky Brighton hotel with a fresh but rapidly stiffening corpse. Directed by Silvio Narizzano, the result is flat, chewy but indigestible

title: Lord Jim
synopsis: Disappointing screen version of Joseph Conrad's novel about courage and cowardice as seen in the Far Eastern adventures of a British sailor (Peter O'Toole), a flawed hero driven to redeem himself in his own eyes. Directed by Richard Brooks, the theme is lost in a superficial and disjointed pageant, though handsomely photographed and containing many effective individual scenes. Some scenes of violence

title: Lord Love a Duck
synopsis: Uneven black comedy starring Roddy McDowall and Tuesday Weld in a story of high school youths in Southern California which offers some biting commentary on the meaningless lives of an affluent segment of American society. While there are some good laughs at the expense of ready targets, George Axelrod's direction relies on adult treatment and dialogue, including a plot complication involving hypnosis to regulate the love lives of students

title: Lord of Illusions
synopsis: Thin but gruesome horror movie in which a private detective (Scott Bakula) tracks some bizarre murders to a fanatic cult whose diabolical leader (Daniel Von Bargen) returns from the grave on a mission to destroy the world. Writer-director Clive Barker punches up the slow-moving fantasy with periodic bloodbaths and rabid occult ravings but the picture flounders in a slack plot, one-dimensional characters and unimaginative special effects. Excessive graphic violence, implied sexual encounters, partial nudity and intermittent profanity and rough language

title: Lord of the Flies
synopsis: Pointless remake of William Golding's 1954 novel about a contingent of schoolboys who deteriorate quickly into savages while marooned on an uninhabited tropical island. With too much emphasis on the island's lush wildlife and not enough on the characters, director Harry Hook's use of novice performers, Americanisms and popular culture asides detracts from the story's parable of good vs. evil. Much profanity and some grisly, conscienceless violence between the adolescents

title: Lord of the Rings, The
synopsis: Ralph Bakshi's animated film version of the J.R.R. Tolkien epic of Middle Earth deals with the darker side of the trilogy. Since the monsters, and not the Hobbits, make a stronger impression, parents may want to think twice about their smaller children seeing this often frightening film

title: Lord of the Rings:
synopsis: Lavish final chapter of J.R.R. Tolkien's epic fantasy trilogy set in the mythic realm of Middle-earth. The third film brings to completion the quest of a humble hobbit (Elijah Wood) to destroy the Ring of Power coveted by the dark lord Sauron, while his comrades (including Ian McKellen and Viggo Mortensen) stave off the annihilation of mankind by leading a last-stand resistance against an army of Sauron's evil minions. Seamlessly blending grand-scale special-effects sequences with dramatically nuanced performances, director Peter Jackson scores a crowning achievement, as visually spectacular as it is emotionally satisfying. And though the good-versus-evil, sword-and-sorcery saga touches on transcendent themes such as mortality, free will and divine providence, the crowded narrative affords little time for clarifying exposition, which may leave those unfamiliar with the books or the two earlier movies overwhelmed. Extended battlefield violence and a few frightening scenes
full_review:
C.S. Lewis once remarked that after someone has read "The Lord of the Rings," they are "never quite the same." The same can be said of anyone viewing director Peter Jackson's lavishly shot film version of J.R.R Tolkien's epic fantasy trilogy set in the mythic realm of Middle-earth.

After 19 Oscar nominations and nearly seven hours of pure movie magic, the king returns in the much-anticipated "The Return of the King," the third and final chapter in the Tolkien triptych. And though the three films' collective price tag of $300 million is downright Hobbit-sized compared to their projected worldwide gross ($1.8 billion and climbing), Jackson has much more riding on the third installment than just money. The real validation will come from the legions of devoted Tolkien enthusiasts for whom "The Lord of the Rings" represents more than good storytelling; for them it is, as Lewis asserted, a life-changing experience.

And while his first two efforts, "The Fellowship of the Ring" (2001) and "The Two Towers" (2002), have won him both critical and fan praise, anything short of an expectation-exceeding closing act would mean that Jackson and his filmic fellowship have failed in their quest to translate Tolkien's Homeric opus to the big screen.

Middle-earthers, fear not. "The Return of the King" not only eclipses its predecessors in scope but weaves their disparate narrative threads into a cohesive and emotionally satisfying conclusion, resulting in a work both grander in scale and deeper in human drama than the two previous films (a hat trick never scored by even such hallowed Hollywood trifectas as the "Godfather" and "Star Wars" trilogies -- not to mention the overhyped, cyber-mess "Matrix" sequels).

In "The Return of the King," the stage is set for the climactic confrontation between the forces of good and evil, bringing to completion the quest of humble hobbit Frodo Baggins (Elijah Wood) as he journeys with his stalwart friend, Sam (Sean Astin), to Mount Doom in order to destroy the One Ring, a talisman of seductive power coveted by the dark lord Sauron which he would wield to subjugate all of Middle-earth. Along the way, their loyalties are tested by the Ring's poisonous influence -- as well as by the presence of their Iago-like guide, Gollum (voiced by Andy Serkis), a pathetic, mercurial creature whose will has been irrevocably perverted by the baneful band.

Meanwhile, their comrades in arms, led by the wise wizard Gandalf (Ian McKellen) and the noble though reluctant warrior-king Aragorn (Viggo Mortensen), try to buy them time by leading a last-stand resistance against Sauron's hordes, who are hell-bent -- as well as hell-sent -- on the genocidal annihilation of mankind. Like the Halflings, they must also contend with obstacles within their own camp in the person of Denethor (John Noble), a Learish royal steward whose filial favoritism lends some Shakespearean shading to the picture.

Like the two earlier installments, "The Return of the King" is rich in Christian symbolism and touches on transcendent themes such as mortality, free will and divine providence -- though, as in the books, much of the religiosity is implicit rather than explicit. An intensely devout Catholic, Tolkien drew from a variety of inspirations, including Judeo-Christian scriptures, classical and Celtic mythology and Norse sagas to craft a timeless, elemental story that gives voice to the wider spiritual realty behind ordinary life.

And while it can be seen as a cautionary tale about the corrupting consequences of absolute power, it is at its heart a tale about hope. Echoing Christ's passion, Frodo and Sam's Via Dolorosa reminds us that, through self-sacrifice, "good" will ultimately triumph over "evil." Despite Tolkien's documented disdain for allegory, obvious parallels can be made between Frodo's climb up Mount Doom and Christ's ascent of Calvary. Both bear the burden of evil. Both "suffering servants" are helped along the way -- Christ by Simon of Cyrene, Frodo by Sam.

Though much more than mere escapist fare, the film's centerpiece is the epic Battle of Pelennor Field, a massive Armageddon-like showdown seamlessly blending jaw-dropping special effects with armies of live-action extras. And while some parents may find the protracted carnage, scored to rousing Wagnerian strains, off-putting, the movie, like its source material, does not glorify war but rather defends the idea that there are things worth fighting for.

Tolkien purists may be disappointed that -- even with a running time north of three hours -- Peter Jackson was forced to delete some keys scenes from the novel, but they are sure to find their way onto the inevitable "special edition" DVD.

Jackson refuses to be hamstrung by a too-scrupulous translation of the book in trying to strike the perfect balance between integrity to the source text and the pacing demands of a feature film, a feat which, apart from a hazy romantic subplot involving Aragorn and his Elfin betrothed Arwen (Liv Tyler) and a series of false endings, he achieves with royal success.

However, even with much streamlining, the crowded narrative allows little time for clarifying exposition, which may leave those viewers unfamiliar with the books or those who didn't see the first two movies feeling lost and overwhelmed by the myriad of characters and events which unfold at an at times dizzying pace. As in the first two films, "The Return of the King," filmed entirely in Jackson's native New Zealand, boasts breathtaking vistas that provide a mythic canvas for the action unfurled on screen.

Come February, Academy voters may give "Cold Mountain" the cold shoulder and send Tom Cruise home packing with only a samurai sword in his hand, while Peter Jackson shows Russell Crowe who is truly "Master and Commander" by being crowned Lord of the Oscars. Long live the King!

While not too intense for older teens, because of extended battlefield violence and a few frightening scenes (one involving a gigantic spider), the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Lord of War
synopsis: Thought-provoking, if at times contrived, morality play about an opportunistic and morally bankrupt Ukrainian emigre (Nicolas Cage) who rises from small-time gunrunner to international arms dealer, while living a double life as a respectable family man, all the while staying one step ahead of his rivals, his ruthless clients and the law, that is, until his own conscience catches up with him. By turns action drama and black comedy (neither completely successful), the film's serious social commentary and anti-violence themes are saddled with message-heavy melodrama and standard action cliches that bog down the otherwise effective narrative. Strong images of violence, sexual situations with partial nudity, recurring drug content, some racial stereotyping, and pervasive rough and crude language
full_review:
In "Lord of War" (Lions Gate), director Andrew Niccol takes aim at the international arms trade by showing how the hands with the most blood on them are often not the ones pulling the trigger.

By turns morality play, character study, action drama and black comedy (no genre completely successful), the movie starts off with a bang -- literally -- but misses the target.

Nicolas Cage stars as Yuri Orlov, a Ukrainian emigre whose family posed as Jews to escape Soviet oppression and settled in the Brighton Beach section of Brooklyn, N.Y., where they opened a kosher restaurant.

Yuri's unfulfilled life changes suddenly when -- witnessing an attempted Russian mob hit -- he decides to become an illegal arms dealer, setting his sights on where the real money is: wars (rather than small-time street sales).

The amoral Yuri doesn't see the black-and-white dichotomy of right and wrong. From his free market perspective, it's simple supply and demand, no questions asked, no sides taken and no judgments passed.

He recruits his younger brother, Vitali (Jared Leto), whose conflicted conscience contributes to his descent into cocaine addiction.

Through a combination of moxie and salesmanship, Yuri quickly climbs the gunrunning ranks. Before long, he is supplying weapons to some of the world's most ruthless dictators. (How Yuri exactly makes the leap from peddling firearms out of a motel room to hobnobbing with warlords is left a bit sketchy.)

Following the collapse of the Soviet Union, his uncle, Dmitri (Eugene Lazarev), a Ukrainian army general, helps Yuri turn the former satellite's enormous stockpile of military hardware -- gathering dust since the Cold War thawed -- into a lucrative one-stop shop for assorted terrorists and Third World butchers.

Among his regular customers is war-torn Liberia's sadistic self-declared president Andre Baptiste Sr. (Eamonn Walker).

In between globe-trotting trips to deadly war zones, he maintains a facade of respectability, having married his trophy wife, Ava (Bridget Moynahan), who remains blissfully, though implausibly, ignorant of her husband's shadowy dealings.

While Yuri can easily stay one step ahead of the law (Ethan Hawke's pursuing Interpol agent) and his rivals (Ian Holm's old-school arms dealer), he can't escape his own conscience.

Histrionics in check, Cage manages to make his despicable character more sympathetic than he deserves to be.

Yuri's equivocations about "the legality" of an act, as opposed to its morality, resonate beyond arms dealing per se to wider debates over social justice, human rights and life issues.

The satiric film's serious social commentary and anti-violence themes are saddled at times with message-heavy melodrama (intent to humanize Yuri) and standard action cliches that bog down the otherwise sharp narrative.

The movie's most powerful visual is an opening credit sequence that traces a bullet's journey from a factory to an African war zone and ultimately to its tragic final target: the forehead of a child soldier. With economy and brutal clarity, the image argues the film's point far more effectively than the remaining two hours.

"Lord of War" raises provocative questions about the effect of illegal arms sales on the wider problem of global violence. It also spotlights the complicity of developed nations -- specifically, the United States -- in the proliferation of weapons in Third World hotspots, which was lamented by the U.S. bishops' 1995 pastoral reflection, "Sowing Weapons of
War." In it the bishops wrote, "As a nation we should seek to market our ideals, not our weapons."

The film contains strong images of violence, sexual situations with partial nudity, recurring drug content, some racial stereotyping, and pervasive rough and crude language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Lords of Discipline, The
synopsis: David Keith stars as a decent young cadet at a Southern military academy who tries to stop the hazing of a black freshman by a brutal clique trying to force him to quit the academy. Director Franc Roddam uses some fairly graphic violence and very rough language in depicting the ravages of prejudice and abuse of power

title: Lords of Dogtown
synopsis: Fictionalized drama detailing the genesis of the 1970s' skateboarding counterculture in Southern California, focusing on three teenage friends -- timid Stacy Peralta (John Robinson), cocky Tony Alva (Victor Rasuk) and self-destructive Jay Adams (Emile Hirsch) -- who, through a combination of street moxie and surfer mentality, revolutionized the sport and were catapulted to rock-star celebrity. Despite fine performances from Hirsch and Rasuk and kinetic skateboarding sequences, the vapid film, directed by Catherine Hardwicke and based on Peralta's own 2003 documentary, "Dogtown & Z-Boys," never rises above a conventional study of adolescent rebelliousness, with its more interesting elements -- the characters' broken home life, the corrosive allure of fame and money -- receiving shallow treatment. Sexual situations involving minors, some violence, underage drinking and drug use, reckless and delinquent behavior, as well as recurring crude language and gestures
full_review:
