Now, back to her "regular" job, she attempts to go undercover to thwart a gang of bank robbers, but her celebrity status wreaks havoc when a pesky fan recognizes her at a crucial moment.

Realizing her cover has been blown more or less permanently, her boss (Ernie Hudson) decides to make her the prominent "face" of the FBI, sending her out on the talk-show circuit with an effete stylist (Diedrich Bader) in tow. Though she's a down-to-earth person, and her heart's not in the new assignment, the idea of a total glamour makeover has some appeal as her boyfriend (from the first film) has just dumped her.

On the road with reluctant partner Sam Fuller (Regina King), an agent with serious anger management issues, assigned to protect her, Gracie learns the alarming news that her pal, Miss United States (Heather Burns), and master of ceremonies Stan (William Shatner) have been kidnapped in Las Vegas, which provides the impetus for her to sidestep her new role and go back into action to discover the whereabouts of her buddies.

Vegas junior agent Jeff Foreman (Enrique Murciano), designated to keep them out of trouble, eventually becomes their ally, while his supervisor Collins (Treat Williams) jealously attempts to block Gracie's efforts to apprehend the kidnappers and steal his thunder.

This is lightweight stuff, but director John Pasquin succeeds in mixing the laughs and the action effectively.

Bullock and King make appealing sparring partners, and register genuine humanity underneath the slapstick. Bullock's an adept comedienne, and King makes a strong impression, as she did in last year's "Ray."

At one point, the ladies get into drag at a Vegas female impersonator show, and pretend to be guys pretending to be girls; King gets to strut her stuff as Tina Turner. (They're on the trail of a Dolly Parton impersonator who holds the key to the kidnappers' whereabouts.)

The film imparts an admirable message about friendship and remaining true to yourself throughout, and there are even several poignant moments.

The film contains some crass expressions, mild profanity, comedic action violence, gender cross-dressing and sexual innuendo. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Miss Firecracker
synopsis: Lifetime outcast (Holly Hunter), living in the shadow of her beautiful older cousin (Mary Steenburgen), tries to win her town's annual Fourth of July beauty pageant. Adapted by Beth Henley from her play and directed by Thomas Schlamme, the result reveals an eye and ear for life lived off the beaten track in the Deep South and its characters never lack dignity no matter how wacky or how unrealistic their hopes and dreams. Some sexual innuendo and minimal fisticuffs

title: Miss Grant Takes Richmond
synopsis: Dippy comedy in which a gambler (William Holden) hires a secretarial school novice (Lucille Ball) as part of a cover operation, then is undone by her zeal to make good. Directed by Lloyd Bacon, the funny business with Ball's dumb but honest secretary is ably abetted by a solid supporting cast but the contrived situation becomes tiresome. Comic treatment of illegal activities

title: Missile to the Moon
synopsis: Low-budget sci-fi clunker from director Richard Cunha about scientists taking two escaped convicts on a space shot to the moon where they discover a dying city of women in an underground cave. Unconvincing menace and sexual innuendo

title: Missing
synopsis: Director Costa-Gavras in his first American movie presents a taut and powerful drama based upon an actual event, that of an American father's search for his son, a 31-year-old writer living with his wife in a Latin American country, who has disappeared in the midst of the brutal repression following a right-wing coup. Jack Lemmon and Sissy Spacek are outstanding as the concerned father and his daughter-in-law, with John Shea giving capable support as the missing man. Significant and absorbing work on a topical and important theme of human rights. General atmosphere of menace, a depiction of the aftermath of bloodshed and occasional profanity

title: Missing in Action
synopsis: Chuck Norris stars in a hokey, derivative movie directed by Joseph Vito about a commando operation mounted to rescue Americans still held prisoner in Vietnam. Gene Hackman did it better in "Uncommon Valor." Graphic wartime violence, rough language and Asian sterotyping

title: Missing in Action 2: The Beginning
synopsis: In a sequel with even more violence than its violent predecessor, this time around the blank-faced hero (Chuck Norris) is a prisoner of war in Vietnam a few years prior to the original. Directed by Lance Hool, this run-of-the-mill war movie overdoses on graphic depictions of brutality and sadism

title: Missing Women
synopsis: Crime programmer directed by Philip Ford in which a woman victim (Penny Edwards) of car robbers talks her way into the gang, then busts it. Stylized violence and life-threatening situations

title: Missionary, The
synopsis: Writer-producer Michael Palin (of the Monty Python troupe) also stars as the Rev. Charles Fortescue, a missionary sent to the slums of London by his bishop (Denholm Elliot) to open up a home for fallen women, and with Lady Ames (Maggie Smith) as his patron, he has great success. Unfortunately, there is a rather snide quality to the comedy's religious and social criticism and there is one incredibly crude exchange between Mr. Fortescue and a tough prostitute. Some obscene language

title: Mission: Impossible
synopsis: Framed as a traitor, a top U.S. spy (Tom Cruise) must evade capture by the CIA, identify the real culprit and prevent a list of American spies from falling into enemy hands. Based on the vintage TV series, director Brian De Palma's sleek action thriller has an impossibly complicated plot but its exciting action scenes, special effects and swift pacing make it high-style escapist entertainment. Some stylized violence and occasional profanity

title: Mission: Impossible 2
synopsis: Because of recurring stylized violence, implied affairs and minimal crass language,

title: Mission, The
synopsis: In the 1750s, the large and prosperous Jesuit Indian missions of South America were divided between Spain and Portugal. In retelling these events, Robert Bolt's screenplay focuses not on the religious but on the socio-political dimension of the colonia1 era and its injustices. The epic production is visually splendid, but Roland Joffe's direction is erratic and bogs down in contrasting a non-violent priest (Jermey Irons) and one (Robert De Niro) who leads the Indians against a colonial army. Although flawed, the work recalls a past that provides a context for current Latin American struggles. Violence and ethnographic nudity

title: Mission to Mars
synopsis: Sleek space fantasy set in 2020 when four NASA astronauts (led by Tim Robbins and Gary Sinise) head for Mars to rescue the sole survivor (Don Cheadle) of the first manned landing after a catastrophic but unexplained event on the barren red planet. Director Brian De Palma crafts an intriguing, visually alluring if quite fanciful tale of aliens and their connection to human life on Earth. Brief sci-fi violence and mild profanity

title: Mississippi
synopsis: Affable period melodrama with comedy supplied by W.C. Fields as a showboat captain and some Rodgers-and-Hart songs crooned by pistol-packing Bing Crosby who plays the Singing Killer. Director Edward Sutherland succeeds far better with Fields' comedy routines than Crosby's romantic problems with two sisters (Joan Bennett and Gail Patrick). Some comic violence

title: Mississippi Burning
synopsis: Fictionalized version of the 1964 murder of three young civil rights activists in Mississippi focuses on the conflict between two FBI agents (Gene Hackman and Willem Dafoe) over how to handle the investigation. Director Alan Parker powerfully re-creates the brutal racist climate of the times but the questionable vigilante tactics used to crack the case may confuse those unfamiliar with the real events. Unrelenting atmosphere of violence and racist rhetoric, together with much profanity

title: Mississippi Gambler
synopsis: Stale tale of a poor but honest Southerner (Tyrone Power) who, with the financial backing of a frontier adventurer (John McIntire), makes his fortune as a river boat gambler and wins the heart of a New Orleans belle (Piper Laurie). Directed by Rudolph Mate, the colorful atmosphere of the pre-Civil War setting proves of more interest than does the lackluster scenario. An assortment of dishonest characters, romantic entanglements and a duel of "honor."

title: Mississippi Masala
synopsis: Upbeat interracial love story involving a young woman (Sarita Choudhury) with family roots in India and an enterprising African American (Denzel Washington) whose romance is opposed by the families and friends of both. Only a sluggish pace detracts from director Mira Nair's warm-hearted exploration of racial taboos and family values. Very brief bedroom scene with a flash of nudity, momentary violence and minimal rough language

title: Mississippi Mermaid
synopsis: Disappointing French melodrama about the mail-order bride (Catherine Deneuve) of a rich planter in the tropics (Jean-Paul Belmondo) who proves to be an imposter when she cleans out his bank account and disappears -- but not for very long. A minor effort from director Francois Truffaut, it pays tribute to the old Hollywood action adventures while at the same time satirizing them with an incredibly absurd plot made worse by being badly dubbed into English. For Truffaut fans only. Brief nudity

title: Miss Mary
synopsis: British governess (Julie Christie) recalls the years she spent in Buenos Aires caring for the children of a wealthy family. The real interest of this Argentinian production, directed by Maria Luisa Bemberg, is its depiction of the politically confused and socially demoralized climate prior to the Peron dictatorship. Mature themes including several sexual encounters

title: Missouri Breaks, The
synopsis: Jack Nicholson heads a band of rustlers and Marlon Brando is the ruthless killer hired to hunt them down. Director Arthur Penn's failed Western is full of loose ends and fey dialogue, an embarrassing muddlement that lumbers to a brutal conclusion for want of anything better to do. Excessive violence

title: Miss Potter
synopsis: Charming, beautifully crafted story of "Peter Rabbit" author Beatrix Potter (Renee Zellweger) and her bittersweet romance with the awkward young publisher of her books (Ewan McGregor), under the disapproving eyes of her class-conscious parents (Barbara Flynn and Bill Paterson) in turn-of-the-century England. The script, music, production design and cinematography, and sensitive performances from all (including Emily Watson), under Chris Noonan's canny direction combine to make the kind of quality film that's all too rare
full_review:
Renee Zellweger and Ewan McGregor, who last lent their joint talents to "Down With Love," that breezy homage to the Doris Day-Rock Hudson comedies of the early 1960s, demonstrate their great versatility in an utterly different sort of film.

"Miss Potter" (MGM/Weinstein) is a charming, beautifully crafted story of "Peter Rabbit" author (and painter) Beatrix Potter (Zellweger), and her romance with Norman Warne (McGregor), the awkward young publisher of her books, under the disapproving eyes of her class-conscious parents (Barbara Flynn and Bill Paterson) in turn-of-the-century England.

We see how, after multiple rejections, Frederick Warne & Co. finally agrees to print "The Tale of Peter Rabbit," but only as a means to give their greener younger brother some minor busywork as his first foray into the family business. Beatrix's parents -- particularly her domineering, snobbish mother -- only seem dimly aware of their daughter's determination to legitimize her lifelong interest in stories and art. (In her quiet, but emphatic way, Beatrix would not let herself be stifled by the conventions of the day.)

But, as it happens, the slim volume turns out to be a great success, and Beatrix and Norman make a winning partnership. Though Beatrix and Norman's spinster sister, Millie (Emily Watson), quickly bond, as they have both resolved never to marry, a deep, growing love develops between Beatrix and Norman, leading to a most touchingly played proposal. The formality of the age -- they address each other as "Miss Potter" and "Mr. Warne" -- and the necessity for Beatrix to have an omnipresent chaperone is amusingly conveyed.

Beatrix's parents oppose the union as they view Norman as a mere tradesman, and Norman's elder brothers know nothing of the match either, but the couple are determined to make a life together.

We won't spoil what happens next, but we should say that the narrative takes a darker turn before coming to a sanguine, if bittersweet, conclusion. (We learn, incidentally, that in later years Beatrix would become a dedicated farmer and notable conservationist, leaving thousands of acres to the National Trust when she died in 1943.)

Richard Maltby Jr.'s well-crafted script, Martin Childs' evocative production design and Andrew Dunn's ravishing cinematography are all first-rate.

There's also a delightful use of animation. Beatrix's characters are so real to her that she sometimes sees them moving on the page. Though this is basically an adult story, as there are no objectionable elements, the film is perfectly acceptable for younger viewers.

Under Chris Noonan's canny direction, this is the kind of quality film that's all too rare these days.

title: Mister Buddwing
synopsis: Forgettable melodrama about an amnesia victim (James Garner) whose career ambitions and marital woes are shown in flashbacks and dreams as his memory returns. Directed by Delbert Mann, the story is needlessly confusing in the use of three actresses in the role of his wife and the result doesn't add up to much. Mature sexual themes including abortion

title: Mister Corey
synopsis: Muddled saga of a street-wise Chicago youth (Tony Curtis) who becomes a busboy at a country club where he's fired for trying to woo a socialite (Martha Hyer), then joins a professional gambler (Charles Bickford) in opening a Chicago casino which goes bust after he's caught in an affair with the now-married socialite. Dreary star vehicle written and directed by Blake Edwards, the glossy proceedings are emtionally bogus and dramatically flat. Stylized violence and a benign view of deceitful behavior, including marital infidelity

title: Mister Johnson
synopsis: In 1923 British West Africa, a native clerk (Maynard Eziashi) who fancies himself a true English gentleman, wrecks his cherished relationship with his British boss (Pierce Brosnan) by his carefree thieving ways. Bruce Beresford directs a charmingly realized period piece full of wry observation of British colonialism but the effect is marred by some cardboard characters and ponderous pacing. Minimal stylized violence and some racial epithets

title: Mister Roberts
synopsis: The conflicts between the bored crew and mean-spirited captain (James Cagney) of a cargo ship in the South Pacific during the waning months of World War II are tempered by the executive officer of the title (Henry Fonda) who jeopardizes his long-sought transfer to combat duty in order to get the crew a long-overdue shore leave. Directed by John Ford and Mervyn LeRoy, the result largely overcomes its stage origins, thanks to vigorous staging of the shipboard antics as well as memorable lead performances abetted by William Powell as the ship's sage doctor and Jack Lemmon as its callow laundry-and-morale officer. Broad sexual innuendo

title: Mister Rock and Roll
synopsis: Static pop musical directed by Charles Dubin in which radio disk jockey Alan Freed recounts the rise of rock and roll music, introduces performances by a number of its stars and wins over a hostile magazine editor (Jay Barney). Sexual innuendo

title: Mister V
synopsis: ( see: "Pimpernel Smith" )

title: Mistress
synopsis: Flat satire of the movie business centers around the compromises made by a failed producer-director team (Martin Landau and Robert Wuhl) when three backers (Robert De Niro, Danny Aiello and Eli Wallach) of their proposed movie insist their girlfriends be given starring roles. Director Barry Primus' sluggish mix of comedy and drama is damaged by stale characterizations and lead actor Wuhl's dull performance. Much sexual innuendo and some rough language

title: Misty
synopsis: Nicely told tale of children (David Ladd and Pam Smith) who devote themselves to training a wild pony captured on Chincoteague, an island off the coast of Virginia. Produced by Robert B. Radnitz and directed by James B. Clark, the youngsters are appealing, the history of the island's wild horses is interesting and the result is superior family entertainment

title: Misunderstood
synopsis: Gene Hackman plays a widower who is slow to come to terms with his loss and make a new life for himself and his two young sons (Henry Thomas and Huckleberry Fox). Director Jerry Schatzberg's picture is pleasant enough, with competent acting and exotic settings (Tunisia), but there are no dramatic sparks to speak of until a contrived tearjerker of an ending. Some vulgar language

title: Mitchell
synopsis: Los Angeles police detective (Joe Dan Baker) pursues two suave lawyers (Martin Balsam and John Saxon) mixed up in the heroin trade by using unorthodox methods that look suspiciously like police brutality. Directed by Andrew V. McLaglen, it's a fairly silly, slapped-together affair whose thin plot is nothing more than an excuse to string together a series of routine chases. Most, but not all, of the rough stuff is kept off-camera, substituting instead some sexual exploition scenes

title: Mixed Company
synopsis: Joseph Bologna and Barbara Harris star in a sentimental comedy drama about a couple who decide to augment their family, which already includes three children, with three more, each from a different race. Melville Shavelson directs a good-natured movie that carefully avoids any realistic situations of racial tension. Mildly entertaining, sometimes funny and touching, it seems like something made for television except for its strong language

title: Mixed Nuts
synopsis: Threadbare comedy takes place on Christmas Eve at a phone-in suicide prevention center where a trio of eccentrics (Steve Martin, Rita Wilson and Madeline Kahn) take lots of kooky calls while being visited by a stream of oddballs (including Juliette Lewis, Anthony LaPaglia and Liev Schreiber) seeking holiday cheer. Writer-director Nora Ephron's contrived attempt at screwball comedy frequently looks like amateur night due to a leaden script which wastes the comic talents of all involved. Accidental violence played for laughs, intermittent sexual innuendo and a fleeting glimpse of nudity

title: M'Liss
synopsis: Sentimental Western tale from the Bret Harte story in which the spunky girl of the title (Anne Shirley) is saved from the orphanage after the death of her alcoholic widowed father (Guy Kibbee) by the support of his saloon friends and her schoolteacher (John Beal) whose concern for her turns to love. Directed by George Nicholls, Jr., the colorful characters and the 1880's setting help compensate for a wispy story of a frontier community taking care of its own

title: Mo' Better Blues
synopsis: Self-absorbed jazz trumpeter (Denzel Washington) remains loyal to his inept manager (Spike Lee) while studiously avoiding commitment to either of his impatient lovers (Joie Lee and Cynda Williams) until his manager's gambling ways change all of their lives. Lee also produced, wrote and directed this tale of interwoven relationships which features Washington's finely-shaded performance as a character who gradually comes to terms with his egotism. Much casual use of rough language, fairly explicit treatment of sexual relationships and a graphic scene of gut-wrenching violence

title: Mobsters
synopsis: Glossy Prohibition-era gangster movie follows the bloody rise to power of young thugs Lucky Luciano, Meyer Lansky, Bugsy Siegel and Frank Costello (Christian Slater, Patrick Dempsey, Richard Grieco and Costas Mandylor) by murdering the two reigning dons (Anthony Quinn and Michael Gambon). Director Michael Karbelnikoff glamorizes the killers all through this humdrum rehash of far better gangster movies of yesteryear. Excessive violence, uncritical portrayal of murderers, much rough language, a restrained bedroom scene and occasional nudity

title: Mob, The
synopsis: Standard crime thriller in which a tough cop (Broderick Crawford) goes undercover as a longshoreman in order to get the goods on a waterfront mob (Ernest Borgnine, Neville Brand and others). Directed by Robert Parrish, there's some fanciful action along the way, with colorful characters (notably, Richard Kiley) but few surprises. Menace and stylized violence

title: Moby Dick
synopsis: Early talkie loosely drawn from the Melville novel has Captain Ahab (John Barrymore) lose leg and fiancee (Joan Bennett), then dedicate himself to killing the white whale responsible for his misfortunes, after which he returns to find his love has not forgotten him. Directed by Lloyd Bacon, the romantic subplot detracts from the epic sea yarn of man vs. blind beast, though what survives of Melville is credibly visualized with enough raw energy and rugged action to make it memorable. Stylized violence, the dangers of life at sea and romantic complications

title: Moby Dick
synopsis: Uneven adaptation of the Herman Melville classic follows the vengeful course of Captain Ahab (miscast Gregory Peck) in quest of the Great White Whale. Co-scripted by Ray Bradbury and director John Huston, it captures well the details of 19th-century whaling life but the voyage of the Pequod at the center of the story is curiously slack and largely uninvolving. Stylized violence

title: Moby Dick
synopsis: Faithful adaptation of Herman Melville's epic novel about the hunt for the great white whale of the title follows the doomed voyage of a 19th-century Nantucket whaler under Captain Ahab (Patrick Stewart) whose quest for personal revenge against the dumb sea beast results in disaster. Directed by Franc Roddam, the British-Australian TV co-production succeeds best as a sea spectacle with convincing action sequences, but the drama is less effective because of erratic characterizations and heavily accented dialogue. Scenes depicting the bloody business of whaling and the brutish character of some employed in it

title: Model Shop, The
synopsis: French romantic drama about a brief encounter between an alienated Los Angeles dropout (Gary Lockwood) and an attractive model (Anouk Aimee) who takes him to bed, tells him her life story and he gives her money for her fare back to France. Though beautifully produced and mildly appealing, the movie lacks the charm and novelty of director Jacques Demy's earlier works and their unabashed romantic exuberance

title: Modern Problems
synopsis: Chevy Chase plays an air traffic controller possessed of extrasensory powers which are put to no good use in a dreary, slipshod comedy that intersperses long boring stretches with only a few patches of fitful humor. Directed and co-written by Ken Shapiro, it has some vulgarity and incidental sexual byplay

title: Modern Romance
synopsis: Obsessive and insecure film editor (Albert Brooks) has an on-again, off-again relationship with his girlfriend (Kathryn Harrold) but he can't break this recurring cycle of misery. Also written and directed by Brooks, it is a sometimes very funny movie, but suffers from a lack of structure and too much Brooks. Still, two hilarious sequences in the cutting room might make some viewers willing to forgive the movie's frequent slow stretches. Some brief semi-nudity, occasional rough language and a muddled view of sexual morality

title: Moderns, The
synopsis: Set in Paris in 1926, this romantic drama follows the travails of some American expatriates, chief among them a struggling painter (Keith Carradine), his estranged wife (Linda Fiorentino), her nouveau riche companion (John Lone) and a frustrated society columnist (Wallace Shawn). Director Alan Rudolph re-creates a wonderful sense of the period and the artistic millieu that flourished then. Some nudity, brief violence and implications of sexual hedonism

title: Modern Times
synopsis: Charlie Chaplin's insightful fable of man versus machine centers in the artificiality of industrialized society and the anxieties caused by the Depression as Charlie dances his way through the hazards of an assembly line job. A model of silent comedic technique and refined slapstick humor, the movie marks the last appearance of the Little Tramp character as Charlie takes his final walk down the long empty road, this time in the company of Paulette Goddard who adds an element of freshness to the plot's old-fashioned romance

title: Modesty Blaise
synopsis: Monica Vitti, Terence Stamp and Dirk Bogarde in a plot about a shipment of diamonds that is merely an excuse for a series of impossible adventures and characters that parody the cliches of popular culture. The opulent sets, costumes and gadgets are stylishly photographed and the dialogue and situations are outrageously exaggerated. Director Joseph Losey obviously enjoyed spoofing areas of the dark world that he has treated seriously so often before

title: Mod Squad, The
synopsis: Inept crime picture based on a 30-year-old TV series about three young criminals (Claire Danes, Omar Epps and Giovanni Ribisi) given a second chance to work undercover for the police, then find themselves battling corrupt cops linked to a drug gang. Directed by Scott Silver, the plot is as stale as the picture's premise, but making matters even worse are surly cardboard characters in formula proceedings that prove dramatically inane and emotionally inert. Hokey violence, sexual situations, recurring rough language and occasional profanity

title: Mogambo
synopsis: Lightweight romantic adventure in which a veteran African hunter (Clark Gable) takes a client on a safari in the jungles of Kenya, then falls for his wife (Grace Kelly) until a stranded American entertainer (Ava Gardner) brings him to his senses. Director John Ford finds more romance in the exotic African settings than in the unconvincing Gable-Kelly relationship, though the humorous treatment keeps it from cloying. Romantic triangle and sexual innuendo

title: Mohammad, Messenger of God
synopsis: Dramatic re-creation of the years from 610 A.D., when Mohammad was driven from Mecca for claiming to have received a new religion from the Angel Gabriel, to 630 when the victory of Islam was assured. The best feature of this religious epic directed by Moustapha Akkad is its sincerity in recounting the birth of Islam and some of the essential tenets of the Moslem religion. An international cast includes Anthony Quinn, Irene Papas and Michael Ansara. Some scenes of restrained violence

title: Mohawk
synopsis: Colonial adventure set in the Mohawk Valley where a frontier artist (Scott Brady) falls for the daughter (Rita Gam) of an Iroquois chief (Ted de Corsia), while a crazed settler (John Hoyt) tries to stir an Indian war. Directed by Kurt Neumann, the story is more interested in the painter's romantic inclinations than the growing tension between settlers and Indians, with many of the action scenes using footage from 1939's "Drums Along the Mohawk." Frontier violence and romantic complications

title: Mojave Firebrand
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Spencer Bennet in which a lawman (Wild Bill Elliott) busts up a protection racket extorting money from mine owners after a big Arizona silver strike. Frontier violence

title: Mole People, The
synopsis: Adventure clunker introduced by USC English prof Frank C. Baxter tells of archaelolgists (John Agar and Hugh Beaumont) who discover an ancient Sumerian ruin on an Asian mountaintop, then are taken captive by its builders' descendents driven by earthquakes to live in an underground city. Directed by Virgil Vogel, the ludicrous proceedings include some unconvincing menace from the burrowing creatures of the title who have been enslaved by the Sumerians. Menacing situations

title: Moliere
synopsis: Engaging tale that speculates about what might have happened when actor and aspiring author Jean-Baptiste Poquelin (Romain Duris), who would become the playwright Moliere, disappeared from Paris in his youth, showing him enlisted by a wealthy businessman (Fabrice Luchini) to help him seduce a potential mistress, though the playwright ends up falling in love with the man's wife (Laura Morante). His farcical and ultimately morally redeeming adventures end up giving him the inspiration for his greatest plays in which comedy and moral purpose meet, allowing director and co-writer Laurent Tirard's film to give an amusing twist to the theme of art imitating life. Some crude and sexual language, some liturgical and doctrinal irreverence, as well as mild sexual scenes of a somewhat romanticized adulterous relationship
full_review:
A playful and speculative exploration of a critical time in the life of France's great playwright and genius of comic satire, "Moliere" (Sony Classics) opens with 22-year-old actor and aspiring author Jean-Baptiste Poquelin (Romain Duris) thrown in debtor's jail, his theater troupe left languishing.

This entertaining and imaginative historical fiction fills in the blanks of what happens in the next several months, when Jean-Baptiste (who would change his name to Moliere, to avoid embarrassing his well-born family by his frowned-upon profession) mysteriously disappeared from Paris, only to return a transformed man and artist.

In the script's conceit, he is bailed out by a wealthy businessman, Monsieur Jourdain (Fabrice Luchini), who enlists Jean-Baptiste to teach him how to write a play -- and act in it, too.

Young Moliere is sworn to secrecy about the arrangement and is brought into the Jourdain household in the guise of a priest, charged with tutoring the family's youngest child in faith and morals. Moliere appropriates some church language for mildly comic purposes, and at one point improvises his version of the Our Father.

The ruse is meant to keep Madame Jourdain (Laura Morante) in the dark, because with his own play, Jourdain seeks to impress, and ultimately seduce, the Marquise Celimene (Ludivine Sagnier), who hosts an aristocratic salon where cruel wit reigns supreme. In his machinations, Jourdain is both aided and taken for a fool by the impoverished nobleman Dorante (Edouard Baer), who himself is scheming to marry off his son to Jourdain's daughter and thus attach himself to the family fortune.

Jourdain gives Moliere the name of Tartuffe, which is the first hint of another of the film's conceits. "Tartuffe" ("The Imposter") is, of course, the name of one of the playwright's celebrated later works.

His comic and ultimately morally redeeming adventures in the Jourdain household will give Moliere the raw material and inspiration for his greatest artistic creations in which comedy does justice to the complexities of the human soul. Director and co-writer (with Gregoire Vigneron) Laurent Tirard's film thus gives an amusing twist to the theme of art imitating life.

Sure enough, the sumptuous costume drama, accompanied by a beautiful score, starts off as a farce, making a delightful spectacle of the pretentiousness and hypocrisy of Dorante and Jourdain, whose acting lessons provide some of the film's comic highlights. Both duly get their comeuppance.

And Moliere ends up winning the heart of Madame Jourdain after she stumbles upon some pages of his passionate romantic writing discarded in her husband's study. But complications ensue.

The film contains some crude and sexual language, some liturgical and doctrinal irreverence, as well as mild sexual scenes of a somewhat romanticized adulterous relationship. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Moll Flanders
synopsis: Uplifting costume drama based on the heroine (Robin Wright) of Daniel DeFoe's 1722 novel who triumphs over illegitimacy, poverty, prostitution and the loss of her husband and baby in her struggle to carve a place for herself in a scornful, class-conscious world. Writer-director Pen Densham embroiders the original story with additional melodramatics, but never loses sight of the characters' humanity as they choose love and hope over despair. Fleeting bedroom scenes with nudity, brief violence and minimal profanity

title: Molly
synopsis: When Molly Goldberg (Gertrude Berg) plays matchmaker, it threatens a business deal made by her husband Jake (Philip Loeb). Walter Hart directs the TV cast of "The Goldbergs," which began as a daytime radio serial about the domestic ups-and-downs of a loving Jewish family in the Bronx. Though its production values are rudimentary, its picture of family life still has charm

title: Molly
synopsis: Leaden tale in which a medical experiment restores the faculties of a mentally retarded woman (Elisabeth Shue) whose brother (Aaron Eckhart) is overjoyed at her progress toward intellectual and emotional maturity until nature triumphs over science in a bittersweet ending. Director John Duigan turns this uncredited adaptation of 1968's "Charly" into a soppy, self-conscious star vehicle that falls flat because it lacks a credible, sympathetic lead performance. Discussions of sexual matters including incest, rear nudity, emotional outbursts and some coarse language

title: Molly Maguires, The
synopsis: Fact-based, hard-hitting drama set in the Pennsylvania coal mining fields during the 1880s when the mine owners hire an undercover agent (Richard Harris) to ferret out the leaders (Sean Connery and Anthony Zerbe) of a secret band of miners known as the Molly Maguires who resort to terrorist tactics to force better pay and working conditions. Director Martin Ritt has made a thoughtful movie about the futility of using violence to redress injustices. More menace than bloodshed

title: Mom and Dad Save the World
synopsis: Silly sci-fi comedy about a far-distant planet's dictator (Jon Lovitz) who magnetically draws a suburban California couple (Teri Garr and Jeffrey Jones) to his kingdom planning to force the wife to marry him. A witless script and Greg Beeman's heavy-handed direction produce a contrived, artifical spoof that quickly fizzles. A few off-color references

title: Moment by Moment
synopsis: Middle-aged Beverly Hills housewife (Lily Tomlin) succumbs to the charms of a young drifter (John Travolta). Devoid of dramatic action, save for scenes of love-making punctuated by little spats of no consequence, writer-director Jane Wagner's movie has hardly a glimmer of wit, intelligence or credibility. Graphic and glossy depiction of adultery

title: Mommie Dearest
synopsis: Faye Dunaway plays Joan Crawford in this unpleasant screen version of the harsh biography written by her adopted daughter, Christina. Director Frank Perry alternates heavy doses of sensation and sentimentality without really getting at anything that might make its subject credible. Only occasionally does the episodic and overlong movie rise above the level of verge-of-hysteria soap opera. Some brief but graphic violence, rough language and vulgarity

title: Mo' Money
synopsis: A con artist (Damon Wayans) disappoints his younger brother (Marlon Wayans) by taking a straight job at a credit card company to impress a girl (Stacey Dash), then gets involved in a bigtime scam ripping off the firm. Director Peter Macdonald's sluggish and predictable comedy pulverizes the work ethic while it exalts stealing as the only cool way to beat the system. Grand theft glamorized, some exploitative violence, sexist attitudes with implied encounters, recurring rough language and racial stereotyping

title: Mona Lisa
synopsis: Love-starved small-time tough (Bob Hoskins in a memorable performance) falls in love with the prostitute (Cathy Tyson) he chaffeurs around town, only to be victimized by his own blind trust and devotion. This British production's depiction of underworld violence, deception and betrayal leads nowhere. Brutal violence, brief nudity and some profanity

title: Mona Lisa Smile
synopsis: Problematic drama set in 1953 about a free-spirited Berkeley grad (Julia Roberts) who lands a position teaching art history at a conservative all-girls New England college where she locks horns with the rigid faculty over her unorthodox methods, while empowering her students (including Kirsten Dunst and Julia Stiles) to free themselves from the future yoke of domesticity. Directed by Mike Newell, the film eschews character for caricature, advancing a misguided strain of feminism which, rather than fostering a deeper respect for women's dignity, promotes a view of marriage and motherhood as slave-state stumbling blocks to self-fulfillment. An antagonistic attitude toward traditional morality, an implied sexual encounter, as well as minimal crude language and profanity
full_review:
Domesticity gets a black eye in director Mike Newell's relentlessly grating melodrama, "Mona Lisa Smile" (Columbia), about a free-spirited academic who emboldens her female students to cast off the yoke of traditional gender roles. Ideologically lopsided, the film trots out the same hoary canards against marriage and maternity as roadblocks to success and self-realization and presents a skewed picture of nuptial life that borders on parody.

At the center of this paean to girl power is Katherine Watson (Julia Roberts), a bohemian proto-feminist from Berkeley who lands a post teaching art history at a conservative Massachusetts women's college in 1953. The propaganda-as-plot narrative follows a standard, free-thinking-fish-out-of-water formula.

First there is resistance, if not outright hostility, to Katherine's unorthodox teaching methods from the stodgy board of trustees and silver-spoon students. Of course, the girls' New England frigidity is soon thawed by the warmth of their new instructor's so-called liberating idealism. By the end of the film, the chintz curtains are cast aside by the winds of change and Katherine moves on to spread her be-all-you-can-be gospel, inspiring other women to shed the shackles of domesticity and enter the promised land flowing with careers and contraceptives.

Among the prim minds ripe for molding are Joan (Julia Stiles), an academic all-star torn between law school and her Ivy League boyfriend; Giselle (Maggie Gyllenhaall), the libidinous varsity vixen; and Betty (Kirsten Dunst), the snooty socialite who starts out critical of Katherine but winds up a believer. Along the way, Katherine locks horns with the college's by-the-syllabus president (Marian Seldes), befriends the spinster elocution and poise teacher (played by the ever chameleon-like Marcia Gay Harden), champions a martyred lesbian faculty member fired for distributing birth-control devices on campus, and falls for the lothario Italian professor (Dominic West). The fine talents assembled never really inhabit their roles, resulting in performances less about creating characters than serving as voices for the filmmaker's point of view.

The film's oversold thesis advances a toxic strain of feminism, which, rather than encouraging a deeper respect for the dignity of women, extols sexual liberation as an inalienable right, while painting marriage and motherhood as slave-state stumbling blocks on the yellow brick road to personal fulfillment. Married women are by and large caricatured as hypocritical gorgons like Betty's mother (Donna Mitchell) or prissy Stepford debutantes chomping at the bit to trade in their brains for a washer-dryer combo.

And while women, admittedly, have rarely enjoyed parity with men in our male-dominated society, the film's grievances against educational and social inequalities are poorly served by such heavy-handed stereotyping -- a cheap proselytizing tactic more suitable for the soapbox than the screen. In truth, the ideological girdle imposed on her students is much more constrictive than the corsets from which Katherine strives to liberate them.

Unlike Robin Williams' similar turn as motivating mentor in "Dead Poets Society," Roberts' efforts are not undertaken to inspire or expand young minds but only to tailor them according to her own narrow measurements. And while homemaking is paid lip service in the form of a Stiles tongue-lashing, the filmmaker's sympathies tip the ideological scale overwhelmingly in favor of those opposed to it as a valid life choice.

Apparently, Newell fails to see the irony in Katherine's demand that her linguistic lover stop his personal "tutorials" with his cooing students, after spending much of the film thumbing her nose at convention. Why should her personal moral dictates carry any more weight than those imposed by society? Like they say, people want morality to be subjective until they get their wallet -- or man -- stolen.

Nor does the film ever address what exactly Watson's -- and one assumes Newell's -- progressive philosophy is progressing toward -- a question commonly skirted by cultural relativists. You can only progress toward a fixed point. Once that point -- in this case, objective moral standards -- is deemed malleable, talk of "progress" is as futile and nonsensical as chasing the horizon.

Throughout the movie, art is used as an occasion to discuss deeper questions concerning conformity and self-determination. It borrows a pithy pearl from G.K. Chesterton: "Like morality, art consists of drawing the line somewhere." Unfortunately, this film asserts that art's purpose lies in erasing those lines. In the closing voiceover, the newly "liberated" Betty laments Katherine's departure but takes comfort in the knowledge that her teacher will "seek new walls to break down." There is one danger about knocking down walls: Without them, what will prevent society's roof from caving in?

Despite its breezy title, this "Mona Lisa" offers little to smile about.

Due to an antagonistic attitude toward traditional morality and an implied sexual encounter, as well as minimal crude language and profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Monday in the Sun
synopsis: Complex character study of five dock workers (including Javier Bardem) who, after being laid off, cling to each other's friendship as they try desperately to hold onto their dignity while lo oking for employment. Director Fernando Leon de Aranoa's moving tale explores the complicated relationship among men, work and identity with a commendable script, genuine dialogue and believable relationships. Subtitles. An implied sexual encounter and much rough language. The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops
full_review:
Five laid-off dock workers struggle to maintain their dignity while looking for employment in the complex character study "Mondays in the Sun" (Lions Gate).

Spanish director Fernando Leon de Aranoa has beautifully captured the essence of the delicate connection between the male ego and worthy employment. As these men cling to each other's friendship for support and affirmation of their own value, it is clear how much their identity is wrapped up in their ability to find a job. Leon also makes a statement about the futility of the Spanish government employment offices, which instead of helping the unemployed only add to their embarrassment and desperation.

The Spanish film has its own comfortable tempo which reflects the pace of the men's lives. Santa (Javier Bardem, many pounds heavier and sporting a grizzled beard), insecure Jose (Luis Tosar), sweaty-palmed Lino (Jose Angel Egid), Russian Sergei (Serge Riaboukine) and the aging Amador (Celso Bugallo) sit around their pal Rico's (Joaquin Climent) bar, drinking more than they can pay for, philosophizing or just plain shooting the breeze. All have been booted from their jobs on the shipyard in Vigo in northern Spain. And although Rico has moved on, the rest are sad sacks trying to make the ends of a very short string meet.

Santa spends his day picking up women, such as Angela (Laura Dominquez), a cheese girl in the local supermarket, and taking baby-sitting jobs from Rico's 15-year-old daughter, Nata (Aida Folch). In a telling scene, Santa is reading the story of the fun-loving grasshopper and the dutiful ant to his charge when he explodes, unable to contain himself, fuming over the self-righteousness of the ant and the plight of the poor, unfortunate souls who are born grasshoppers. His tragicomic reaction to the story is the key to unlocking the narrative's core.

The story moves along revealing how each character's personality has been affected by his job loss. Jose has become jealous of his beautiful wife, Ana (Nieve de Medina), who douses herself in perfume when she comes back from her job at a tuna-packing plant. He's afraid that his joblessness makes him less of a man in her eyes. Lino worries about his advancing age, furtively dyeing his gray hair and stealing his teen-age son's clothes in order to compete with younger men in job interviews. And Amador has become increasingly distant and enraged since his wife left to supposedly visit her sickly mother. His days are spent nursing his wounds with alcohol.

Santa is the center of the story, and he also holds the gang together. Although they may find him abrasive and bitter, the men still gravitate toward him as a means of strength and direction. It is through him that the audience most fully experiences the emotions of a proud man forced to face his limitations.

"Mondays in the Sun" is an affecting slice-of-life film that offers a sensitive perspective on the macho world.

Subtitles.

Because of an implied sexual encounter and much rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.

title: Money from Home
synopsis: Witless comedy directed by George Marshall in which a crooning sharpster (Dean Martin) tries to square a gambling debt by fixing a horse race through the substitution of his dim-witted cousin (Jerry Lewis) for the English jockey (Richard Haydn) imported to ride the favorite in a gruelling steeplechase. Bungling underworld types and comic treatment of inebriation

title: Money Jungle, The
synopsis: Routine detective melodrama about a private eye (John Ericson) who is hired to solve the mysterious murders of four geologists working aboard an off-shore oil rig. Intriguing but predictable plot competently directed by Francis D. Lyon. Violence

title: Money Madness
synopsis: Lame crime tale directed by Peter Stewart in which a waitress (Frances Rafferty) marries a pleasant-seeming stranger who turns out to be a trigger-happy bank robber (Hugh Beaumont), with predictable results. Stylized violence and much menace

title: Money Man
synopsis: Documentary follows self-proclaimed artist J.S.G. Boggs as he painstakingly creates counterfeit currency which he then tries to get people to accept at face value, not as legal tender, but as a works of art. Writer-director Philip Haas looks at this dubious art form mainly through the perspective of Boggs, striking more of a whimsical note than a balanced look at whether he is in fact an artist or a con artist. Some morally ambiguous situations

title: Money, Money, Money
synopsis: Amusing but overlong French comedy about a rag-tag band of con artists, petty thieves, bank robbers and other paunchy, middle-aged underworld types (among them, Lino Ventura, Jacques Brel and Charles Denner) adapt to changing times by turning to kidnapping political figures and extorting high ramsoms from embarrassed governments. Directed by Claude Lelouch, the source of the comedy is how the inept misfits complement each other's foolishness and become so rich and successful that they themselves are kidnapped. The Gallic humor, including a Tahitian vacation among semi-clad native beauties, may escape some viewers

title: Money Pit, The
synopsis: A young engaged couple (Tom Hanks and Shelley Long) buy a mansion and suffer humorous consequences when trying to fix it up. The strained comedy resorts to heavy doses of slapstick and the deteriorating condition of the house comes to mirror their increasingly exasperated relationship. Some sexually suggestive scenes are handled within the context of their successful efforts to build trust and strengthen commitment

title: Money Talks
synopsis: Using the same formula as his popular "Candid Camera" TV show, director Allen Funt presents a series of trite sketches and allegedly spontaneous routines designed to show how ordinary people react to situations involving money. Among the offerings, one can watch men pluck, with varying degrees of hesitancy, a dollar bill taped to the backside of a sweet young thing, or listen to Funt interview his pretty three-year-old daughter, who openly exhibits a preference for being rich. At least she's candid about it

title: Money Talks
synopsis: Mirthlessly violent comedy in which a street hustler (Chris Tucker) and a TV reporter (Charlie Sheen) are chased by the police while a gang of French diamond smugglers shoots up Los Angeles. Directed by Brett Ratner, the contrived proceedings creep along with lame but loud comedy routines and even louder gunfire, demolition derby car chases and assorted pyrotechnics. Excessive violence, sexual innuendo and rough language

title: Money Train
synopsis: Jokey buddy movie in which the lifelong friendship of two New York City transit cops is complicated by their competing for the same woman (Jennifer Lopez), then is further tested when one (Woody Harrelson) decides to pay off his gambling debts by hijacking a subway car loaded with cash, while the other (Wesley Snipes) tries to keep his partner from being caught. Director Joseph Ruben presents a violent, morally bankrupt action movie in which thieves take on the stature of heroes worthy of admiration. Uncritical depiction of crime, considerable graphic violence, a bedroom scene and constant rough language

title: Money, Women and Guns
synopsis: Routine Western directed by Richard H. Bartlett in which a detective (Jock Mahoney) is hired to locate the heirs of a bushwacked miner, then determine if one of them is the murderer. Frontier violence

title: Mongolian Tale, A
synopsis: Wistful story of the Mongolian Steppes where a caring old woman raises an unrelated boy and girl, but their plan to marry ends when the boy is sent to school in the city, then the two meet a dozen years later and reflect on the unexpected paths their lives took. Chinese director Xie Fei's poetic tale of love and loss is simple yet moving in its lyrical exploration of universal themes. Subtitles. Mild sexual innuendo, brief violence and minimal rough language

title: Mon Homme
synopsis: Strained comical account of a happy streetwalker (Anouk Grinberg) who falls for a vagrant (Gerard Lanvin) and makes him her pimp, unaware he's cheating on her with a manicurist (Valeria Bruni Tedeschi) he is greedily pushing into prostitution. Writer-director Bertrand Blier's sexist comedy views women as mindless playthings willing to be debased and abused in their desperation to hold onto a man. Subtitles. Benign view of promiscuity, several sexual encounters tinged with violence, full nudity, some rough language and an instance of profanity

title: Monique
synopsis: British exploitation movie about a French :2Oau pair'' girl (Sibylla Kay) hired to care for a young couple's boisterous children and instead seduces first the husband, then the wife and finally the trio wind up in bed together. Low-budget production directed by John Brown, it contains nudity in a sexual context

title: Monitors, The
synopsis: Failed satire about a police force of the future which relies on thought control to bring peace and order in a society beset by violence, brutality and rapaciousness. Directed by Jack Shea, a talented cast headed by Guy Stockwell, Susan Oliver and Keenan Wynn try desperately but fail to find anything humorous in a plot both tedious and inane

title: Monkeybone
synopsis: Strange comic fantasy in which a cartoonist (Brendan Fraser) in a comatose state plunges into the spooky dream world of his comic book creation and must escape back to reality before Death (Whoopi Goldberg) claims him. As directed by Henry Selick, the live action-stop motion animation film is filled with entertaining characters and kooky creations but the muddled narrative is impenetrable. Some sexual references, fleeting rear nudity, an instance of profanity and brief crass language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Monkey Business
synopsis: The four Marx Brothers (Groucho, Chico, Harpo and Zeppo) cause all manner of havoc as stowaways aboard an ocean liner and even more among some gangsters ashore. Directed by Norman Z. McLeod, the manic absurdity of the wacky sight gags and verbal mayhem keep the nonsensical situation from growing tiresome. Slapstick comedy and zany dialogue, including absurd double entendres

title: Monkey Business
synopsis: Halting comedy about an absent-minded chemist (Cary Grant) working on a youth-producing drug in a research lab where a chimpanzee concocts an effective youth formula of his own which is unwittingly tested out on the chemist and his wife (Ginger Rogers). Director Howard Hawks has a top comedy cast but the silly reversions to childhood are too thin to generate enough laughs to be very memorable. Suspicions of infidelity and other sexual innuendo

title: Monkey Hustle, The
synopsis: Black exploitation comedy about some supposedly loveable con artists who rally an inner-city neighborhood threatened by highway construction. Director Arthur Marks gets some good acting (Yaphet Kotto, Rosalind Cash, Kirk Calloway and Randy Brooks) but not much else. Some rough language and a frank treatment of sexual matters

title: Monkeys Go Home
synopsis: Disney comedy in which ex-GI Dean Jones inherits an olive farm in France, retrains four Space Program astro-chimps to help out when a shortage of local olive pickers develops and outwits a conniving real estate man with the aid of a refreshing lass (Yvette Mimieux) and the village priest (Maurice Chevalier). Andrew V. McLaglen directs a slap-dash plot with monkey-shines galore that will appeal more to youngsters than their parents

title: Monkey Shines: An Experiment in Fear
synopsis: Director George Romero's attempt to upgrade his exploitation image flops with this tasteless effort that sees a lab-tortured monkey turn killer after being trained to serve the needs of a paraplegic (Jason Beghe). Graphic injection scenes, grisly murders and mayhem, much menace and an explicit kinky sex scene

title: Monkey Trouble
synopsis: When a lonely little girl (Thora Birch) finds a runaway monkey, she hides it from her parents (Mimi Rogers and Christopher McDonald), unaware that it has been trained in pickpocketing and housebreaking by an organ-grinding gypsy (Harvey Keitel) hot on its trail. Franco Amurri directs a sweet, lively family comedy in which a youngster develops a sense of responsibility in caring for her hidden charge and reforming its behavior. Some bathroom humor and mild menace

title: Monolith Monsters, The
synopsis: Mild sci-fi thriller set in the Southwest where local folks (notably Lola Albright, Grant Williams and Les Tremayne) confront a meteorite's trail of fist-sized black rocks which turn people to stone and grow to the size of skyscrapers when touched by water -- and rain is in the forecast. Directed by John Sherwood, the initial situation is intriguing, then is stretched out in pedestrian fashion until the pace picks up again in a salty ending. Menacing situations

title: Monsieur Hire
synopsis: Intriguing psychological puzzler about a pathetic loner (Michel Blanc) who spends his nights spying on a young woman (Sandrine Bonnaire) in an apartment across the way, but when he meets and falls in love with her, the results are tragic. Directed by Patrice Leconte, the French production subtly unfolds a strange, obsessive love story that starts with a murder investigation and ends plumbing the depths of a desperate soul. Subtitles. Mature themes in a highly charged erotic atmosphere

title: Monsieur Ibrahim
synopsis: Tender tale set in Paris in the early 1960s about a motherless young Jewish boy (Pierre Boulanger) abandoned by his father, who finds an unlikely surrogate in a kindhearted, elderly Muslim grocer (Omar Sharif). Buttressed by nuanced performances from both ends of the life spectrum, director Francois Dupeyron's beautifully crafted film is a poignant, though minor, fairy tale about love, loss, friendship and tolerance. Subtitles. A few sexual encounters involving the teen protagonist and a prostitute, as well as sporadic crude expressions
full_review:
A young Jewish boy abandoned by his father finds an unlikely surrogate in an elderly Muslim grocer in the tender coming-of-age drama "Monsieur Ibrahim" (Sony Classics).

Buttressed by nuanced performances from both ends of the life spectrum, director Francois Dupeyron's intimate film is a poignant, though minor, fairy tale about love, loss, friendship and tolerance.

Set in Paris in the early 1960s, the story centers on Momo (Pierre Boulanger), a solitary 16-year-old living in a working-class neighborhood with his dyspeptic father (Gilbert Melki). Years earlier his mother and older brother (who may or not really exist) flew the coop, leaving Momo to his own devices while his father is at work. Like most boys his age, he spends his days blaring American rock 'n' roll music on the radio and fantasizing about girls. Full of adolescent insecurity, he can't work up the nerve to talk to the pretty red-haired beauty downstairs. Instead, without any parental figure to turn to for guidance or direction, Momo relieves his pubescent pangs by visiting a sympathetic prostitute.

Omar Sharif plays the eponymous Ibrahim, a paternal greengrocer who befriends the wayward youth. Having lost his wife long ago, Ibrahim, a member of the mystical branch of Islam known as Sufism, shares in Momo's inner isolation. Turning a blind eye to the boy's shoplifting, the Quran-quoting storekeeper tells Momo, "If you steal, I prefer you do it in my shop." They begin an intergenerational friendship, discussing life, love and movies, while filling each other's emotional emptiness.

When Momo's father follows his wife's lead out the door, Ibrahim is only too willing to adopt the boy as his own son. Their inner journey of self-discovery becomes an outer odyssey, as they travel to Turkey, Ibrahim's ancestral homeland, and toward the film's bittersweet climax.

Sharif brings a stately wintriness to the titular role, leavened by a soulful placidity that comes with the wisdom and detachment of age. Boulanger, conversely, is all energy, harnessing it one moment into the elation of puppy love, and exploding the next in a burst of adolescent rage. When Momo discovers that his father has deserted him, Boulanger's youthful elan is channeled into a shot of him crushing a felt hat, which is at once both violent and heartbreaking.

Some viewers will undoubtedly find the scenes involving Momo's deflowering by a prostitute troubling, to say the least, especially given the boy's age. Such valid concerns may be compounded by the devoutly religious Ibrahim's wink-wink nod of approval. However, without justifying such actions, Momo's love-starved attempts at affection should be judged in the context of his overwhelming loneliness.

His bordello encounters are less about sex than they are about a hunger for human tenderness and a thirst for interpersonal contact. The scent of innocence that perfumes these scenes is nowhere more evident than when Momo offers his threadbare teddy bear -- an archetypal symbol of childhood -- to one of the trollops in return for her kindness.

Without ever resorting to mawkish sentimentality, the film imparts a positive message about tolerance and mutual respect between people of different ages, cultures and faith traditions, denouncing as a "disease" any way of thinking that fosters divisiveness and bigotry. Ibrahim's pearls of wisdom are offered freely and, though filtered through his Islamic sensibilities, never come across as attempts to proselytize his secular Jewish charge. In fact, Ibrahim goes to great lengths to impress upon Momo his deep reverence for Judaism, as well as Christianity, taking the boy to Greek Orthodox and Roman Catholic churches as well as taking him to see whirling dervishes perform a Sufi ritual dance. While some may view this syncretism with suspicion, others may see it as a celebration of man's collective quest for God.

In one of the film's more touching moments, Ibrahim offers Momo some fatherly advice: "What you give is yours forever; what you keep is lost forever" -- a profound insight which should resonate deeply with Christians. At its core "Monsieur Ibrahim" is a story about hope and beauty. Quoting his holy book, the sage-like Ibrahim says, "You can find beauty wherever you look." Pope John Paul II echoes this when he writes, "The world will be saved by beauty." If so, perhaps this small film will play a modest part in that salvific process. Given the long, bloody history of Jewish-Muslim relations, let us pray that the spirit of harmony and shared humanity which permeates this movie is more than just a poet's -- or filmmaker's -- dream.

Subtitles.

Due to a few sexual encounters involving the teen protagonist and a prostitute, as well as sporadic crude expressions, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Monsieur Verdoux
synopsis: Written, produced and directed by Charles Chaplin, the fact-based black comedy stars Chaplin in the title role as a French Bluebeard (Chaplin) who marries wealthy women, then murders them for their money. Though his first serious role disappointed audiences of its day, Chaplin as a performer was never better in the subtlety of gesture and expression. There is much sharp wit in the script along with some great slapstick, notably from Martha Raye who proves impervious to all murderous strategems. Its criticism of society's hypocrisy, however, is often strained and its attempts to punctuate serious themes with humor is uneven

title: Monsieur Vincent
synopsis: Lucid, moving account of St. Vincent de Paul's work among the poor and the oppressed in 17th-century France, from his first labors in a plague-ravaged village and his appeals to the conscience of the aristocracy to the founding of an order devoted to charitable works and his death in 1660. Director Maurice Cloche portrays the poverty of the times and the cruelty of the regime in starkly convincing fashion, providing a solid historical framework within which Pierre Fresnay's performance in the title role shines with a warm compassion and spiritual intensity which most viewers will find irresistably compelling. Subtitles. High on the list of great religious movies

title: Monsignor
synopsis: Christopher Reeve plays an American priest with a graduate degree in finance who rises in the church hierarchy when he gets the Vatican involved with the Mafia but who pauses on the ladder of success to have an affair with a Carmelite postulant (Genevieve Bujold). Directed by Frank Perry, its melodramatic account of an ambitious cleric is so simple-mindedly wrong-headed that it would be howlingly funny if it were not so grossly insulting to clergymen and institutional religion. Some gratuitous nudity

title: Monsoon Wedding
synopsis: Exuberant ensemble comedy set in present-day India follows several subplots which spin out from the central story of the days leading up to an arranged marriage ceremony in the Punjabi culture. Modernity and tradition jostle to find common ground in director Mira Nair's intoxicating and vibrant film which positively depicts a close-knit, loving family, some of whom finally let loose long-suppressed secrets. Subtitles. An implied sexual encounter, an extramarital affair, some sexual references and sporadic rough and crass language

title: Monster
synopsis: Fictionalized drama about real-life serial murderer Aileen Wuornos (Charlize Theron), executed in Florida in 2002 for the death of six men, and her dysfunctional love affair with a young lesbian (Christina Ricci). In sympathetically portraying Wuornos, first-time writer-director Patty Jenkins walks a fine line between telling a fact-based story and justifying her horrific acts by painting her as a victim, but this unexceptional film is really about Theron's exceptional performance, which captures both Wuornos' inner turmoil and outer mannerisms, packing 30 pounds onto her frame for the role. A few lesbian sexual encounters with partial nudity, recurring violence including a rape, stereotyping of conservative Christians, as well as pervasive rough and crude language
full_review:
"Monster" (Newmarket) -- a fictionalized, though fact-based, drama which chronicles the notorious 1989-90 killing spree of serial murderer Aileen Wuornos -- is a good example of an exceptional performance wrapped in an unexceptional film.

In examining the woman labeled the "Damsel of Death," first-time writer-director Patty Jenkins walks a fine line, teetering precariously between humanizing Wuornos and justifying her heinous crimes to the point of painting her as a victim.

Leggy South African-born Charlize Theron plays Wuornos, a roadside prostitute turned killer, arrested and executed by the state of Florida for the murder of six men -- only the second female to be put to death in the state's history. The film opens with a slapdash montage of dusty memories during which Theron's voiceover recounts Wuornos' bleak past. The painful soliloquy ends on a shot of Wuornos, a study in desolation, huddled against the rain under an interstate off-ramp cradling a gun in her hands as she contemplates suicide.

Deciding against it, she wanders into the first dry place she finds, which turns out to be a gay bar. Ordering a drink she is approached by a companionship-starved young woman who introduces herself as Selby Wall (a composite character played by Christina Ricci), a native Midwesterner sent to live with conservative Christian relatives in Florida by her parents to "cure her homosexuality." Though Wuornos initially declares her heterosexuality, the two women soon become lovers.

Wall is mesmerized by the older woman's tough-talking bravura -- which quickly proves a smokescreen for the outcast's totally depleted sense of confidence and self-esteem. Likewise, Wuornos finds the youthful attention (which she confuses as love) intoxicating, clinging to the minor like a life preserver, afraid to let go lest she succumb to the undertow of utter despair and alienation. The two begin living together in fleabag motels, with Wuornos -- after a failed, pathetic attempt to enter the workforce -- resorting again to selling herself as a means of support.

A brutal rape at the hands of a sadistic john -- whom Wuornos shoots in self-defense -- serves as a psychological trip cord, unleashing a volcano of pent-up rage simmering below her surface. The floodgates of fury burst, setting in motion a murderous 13-month rampage which plays itself out against her ongoing dysfunctional relationship with Wall, culminating in Wuornos' arrest in January 1991.

While the film refrains from sensationalizing her crimes, it fails to shed any meaningful light on their underlying motivations. Beyond the hurried opening sequence, little screen time is afforded to her formative years, when she was abandoned by her parents, raped before she was a teen and pregnant before she was old enough to drive. Though no argument, no matter how heart-wrenching, can be used to condone or excuse her ghastly deeds, a fuller picture of her tragic past would have fostered deeper understanding from viewers, if not sympathy. As a result, Wuornos comes across less as a wounded animal lashing out desperately and indiscriminately at a cruel world than as a misogynistic avenging angel.

The narrative also suffers from a conspicuous absence of any scenes involving the families of the victims -- some of whom were merely good Samaritans unlucky enough to have offered a ride to the wrong hitchhiker. This conscious decision to focus solely on Wuornos denies viewers a fair, balanced telling of the events and raises questions pertaining to the filmmaker's intent. By the midway point, the film begins to lose steam, floundering between a gritty character study and a lesbian soap opera -- saved only by Theron's gutsy performance.

In a nip-tuck industry ruled by glamour, Theron showed chutzpah by packing 30 pounds onto her frame for the role. And though her portrayal is not without moments of apish mimicking, Theron's eerie metamorphosis is utterly convincing -- a disappearing act owing as much to acting ability as to prosthetics.

As a whole, "Monster" attempts to find humanity even among ugliness and depravity and reminds us that -- in the words of Florida bishops petitioning a stay of execution for Wuornos -- "Aileen Wuornos may not be free of guilt, but her life remains sacred in the eyes of God."

Due to a few lesbian sexual encounters with partial nudity, recurring violence including a rape, stereotyping of conservative Christians, as well as pervasive rough and crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Monster House
synopsis: Macabre computer-animated fairy tale about a trio of suburban kids (voiced by Mitchel Musso, Sam Lerner and Spencer Locke) who set out to investigate the haunted happenings of an eerie old house that comes to life to terrorize their neighborhood. The film is full of wildly imaginative visuals; director Gil Kenan taps into childhood fears, crafting a smart and scary thrill ride that, though darker in tone than most children's fare and therefore inappropriate for very young tykes, is more fun than fright. Some frightening images and sequences, minor crude and suggestive humor and innuendo, theft, and mildly crude language. A -II -- adults and adolescents. (PG) 2006 Full Review The computer animated "Monster House" (Columbia) -- a macabre fairy tale from the creative minds of executive producers Robert Zemeckis and Steven Spielberg -- owes more to the darkly delightful children's fantasies of Roald Dahl and R.L. Stine than the cheery pixilated confections of Pixar. No adorable clownfish or toy cowboys here! Instead, employing the motion-capture animation technique used by Zemeckis to haunting effect in "The Polar Express," director Gil Kenan taps into childhood fears, crafting a smart and scary thrill ride in which peril lurks beneath creaky porch steps, sinister shadows slink into bedrooms to terrorize dreams, and that skeletal tree branch is really out to get you! But, for the most part, he pulls it off in a way that is more fun than fright. Just the kind of film Sully and Mike, the oddball duo of "Monsters, Inc." would catch at the Monstropolis multiplex in between shifts at the scream factory. The Halloween-themed yarn centers on a trio of suburban kids -- DJ (voiced by Mitchel Musso), best friend Chowder (Sam Lerner) and precocious puppy-love interest Jenny (Spencer Locke) -- who investigate the strange happenings involving an eerie old house on DJ's block. Long presumed haunted, the ramshackle residence is a black hole into which any object that gets too close -- toys, pets, even people -- disappears. When DJ ventures onto its lawn to retrieve Chowder's basketball, his trespassing sets off the house's maniacally misanthropic owner, Mr. Nebbercracker (Steve Buscemi), who is felled by a heart attack during his fit of fury. Soon thereafter, the house comes to life ... literally. Its angry expressions provided by actress Kathleen Turner, the house's gables twist into a shingled scowl as its fanged front door grimaces hungrily at the prospect of trick-or-treaters. With no one believing them, the young sleuths take it upon themselves to save the neighborhood from the anthropomorphic abode. While lacking the surreal artistry of Tim Burton's "Corpse Bride," the spooky visuals are wildly imaginative, including a bravura sequence of the possessed edifice -- astride giant tree-trunk legs -- lumbering after the children. The film's menacing tone and ghost-story conceit are darker than most children's fare and may give younger tykes nightmares. (Then again, have you read the Brothers Grimm lately?) And while nothing is outright objectionable, there are a few elements that the film could have done without, mostly involving the behavior of the baby sitter's (Maggie Gyllenhaal) punk boyfriend (Jason Lee). But it's not all about giving the kiddies goose bumps. "Monster House" also has a touch of pathos as we learn the reason behind Nebbercracker's petulance which is fueled by misunderstanding rather than malevolence. Like all good fairy tales the film is, at its heart, a love story, one in which a boy's first kiss and an old man's parting caress are the most daunting challenges of all
