Tony Richardson's bold and sweeping direction, the beautifully muted color photography, and the bittersweet ballads about the now folk hero sung by Waylon Jennings (and composed by Shel Silverstein) are more than enough to recommend it. Some fairly graphic violence

title: Needful Things
synopsis: Disguised as a sympathetic antiques shopowner, the devil (Max von Sydow) goes about slyly manipulating the good people of a New England town to go on an ugly killing spree until the Sheriff (Ed Harris) calls them to their senses and the devil smugly goes on his merry way. Fraser C. Heston directs this adaptation of a Stephen King novel, a boring and meanspirited horror-comedy whose glib message is that evil will always triumph in the end. Recurring nasty violence, mindless mayhem and frequent rough language

title: Negotiator, The
synopsis: Convoluted thriller in which a Chicago police negotiator (Samuel L. Jackson) accused of stealing department pension funds tries to clear himself by taking hostage the detective (J.T. Walsh) heading the investigation, then persuades a negotiator (Kevin Spacey) from outside the precinct to help him prove his innocence. Directed by F. Gary Gray, the overly contrived proceedings are filled with hokey action, vague motivations and stereotyped characters who lose interest long before the formula ending. Considerable violence with some gore, life-threatening situations, recurring rough language and occasional profanity

title: Neighbors
synopsis: Director John G. Avildsen's screen version of Thomas Berger's black comedy about a staid suburbanite (John Belushi) who is driven crazy by a looney neighbor (Dan Aykroyd) is a muddled, dismal failure devoid of both laughs and insight. Senseless scene of seduction, much sexual innuendo and unusually crude language

title: Neil Simon's The Odd Couple II
synopsis: Genial comedy sequel in which fastidious Felix (Jack Lemmon) and cantankerous Oscar (Walter Matthau) are reunited after 30 years when they acrimoniously travel together to a family wedding, but keep getting arrested along the way. Directed by Howard Deutsch from Neil Simon's screenplay, the veteran actors' practiced ease at delivering zesty one-liners is the main attraction. Mild sexual innuendo, occasional profanity and a few instances of rough language

title: Nell
synopsis: A woman (Jodie Foster) living completely on her own in a remote wilderness area of North Carolina and speaking what seems only gibberish is terrified when discovered by a caring physician (Liam Neeson) who, with the help of a research-minded psychologist (Natasha Richardson), tries to communicate with her and prepare her for the likelihood of court-ordered institutionalization. Directed by Michael Apted, the beautifully photographed, sensitively acted story deals with the simple wisdom of innocence, though sluggish pacing and logical inconsistencies diminish the narrative's fable-like qualities. Shadowy skinny-dipping, a flash of nudity, brief sexual references, minimal profanity and an instance of rough language

title: Nelly & Monsieur Arnaud
synopsis: A shy Parisienne (Emanuelle Beart) is torn between committing to an overeager editor (Jean-Hugues Anglade) she is dating or acknowledging her growing feelings for her boss, an adoring author (Michel Serrault) 40 years her senior. Director Claude Sautet's melancholy romantic triangle delicately explores the emotional landscape of fragile relationships among young, middle-aged and elderly characters. Subtitles. An implied sexual affair

title: Nelson Affair, The
synopsis: Boudoir history of Admiral Lord Nelson's (Peter Finch) scandalous behavior with his beloved and presumably bewitching mistress Lady Emma Hamilton (Glenda Jackson in an eccentric performance). Scripted by Terence Rattigan and directed by James Cellan Jones, it is a literate if somewhat bland treatment of the stormy love affair

title: Nelson Touch, The
synopsis: ( see: "Corvette K-225" )

title: Neptune Factor, The
synopsis: Ben Gazzara heads the rescue submarine racing to recover the men trapped in an undersea research lab by a volcanic eruption in the North Atlantic. Canadian production directed by Daniel Petrie, the routine underwater adventure relies heavily on the special sub's scientific gadgetry and the exotic deep sea creatures which will engage the interest of younger viewers but adults may prefer staying on dry land

title: Nest of Vipers
synopsis: Italian production about a callow piano student (Christian Borromeo) who has an affair with the mother (Senta Berger) of a fellow student and then abandons her for a beautiful young heiress (Ornella Muti). Director Tonino Cervi's story of jealousy and revenge is mired in graphically depicting the affairs as well as others including incest, lesbianism and homosexuality

title: Net, The
synopsis: On the run from a hired killer (Jeremy Northam), a computer expert (Sandra Bullock) has to fend for herself in keeping criminals from getting a computer disc crucial to the security systems of the entire federal government. Director Irwin Winkler's sleek techno-thriller combines standard chase fare with the woman-in-peril formula for a mildly suspenseful, but unexceptional melodrama. Brief spurts of violence, an implied sexual encounter and an instance of rough language

title: Network
synopsis: When a TV anchorman (Peter Finch) has a breakdown and rants and raves on camera, his ratings soar and an ambitious network executive (Faye Dunaway) centers a new program concept around him over the protests of a more humane executive (William Holden). Written by Paddy Chayefsky and directed by Sidney Lumet, the heavy-handed satire on the evils of television and its effects on the public misses as often as is on target. Needless subplot involves an adulterous affair with an explicit scene of lovemaking

title: Nevada City
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Joseph Kane in which a singing cowboy (Roy Rogers) and his sidekick (George "Gabby" Hayes) save a stagecoach line as well as its railroad rival from being put of business by poet-bandit Black Bart and his gang. Frontier violence

title: Nevadan, The
synopsis: Cat-and-mouse Western in which an escaped gold robber (Forrest Tucker) gets some help from a mysterious stranger (Randolph Scott) in recovering his stolen loot despite a gang of hijackers (led by cracked George Macready). Director Gordon Douglas gets the tale of delayed justice off to an intriguing start, then bogs down in some muted romance (Dorothy Malone) before the rousing finish in an abandoned gold mine. Stylized violence

title: Nevada Smith
synopsis: Well-made Western about a youth (Steve McQueen) who, after his mother and father are tortured to death by three outlaws looking for gold, tracks them down, killing them one by one. Directed by Henry Hathaway, the revenge story is told in very violent fashion and there are some sexual references

title: Never a Dull Moment
synopsis: After marrying a rodeo cowboy (Fred MacMurray), a New York songwriter (Irene Dunne) tries to adjust to life on a small western ranch with the widower's two young daughters, boisterous local ranchers and an ornery neighbor (William Demarest) who controls the water rights. Director George Marshall's cheerful but entirely artificial comedy has some good moments but not enough to justify the title. Domestic misunderstandings

title: Never a Dull Moment
synopsis: Well-paced gangster spoof in which a TV actor (Dick Van Dyke) is mistaken for a killer by a colorful mob of would-be art thieves (led by Edward G. Robinson), then plays along by resorting to tough guy mannerisms while looking for a chance to escape. Directed by Jerry Paris, the Disney production is a likeable bit of light entertainment that will go down as easily with parents as with their children. Comic menace

title: Never Back Down
synopsis: Pointless celebration of violent machismo in which a high school student (Sean Faris) moves to Florida with his widowed mother (Leslie Hope) and tennis champ brother (Wyatt Smith) where he turns to a fight coach (Djimon Hounsou) to train him in the technique of mixed martial arts after being beaten unconscious by the obnoxious boyfriend (Cam Gigandet) of the girl for whom he's fallen (Amber Heard). Director Jeff Wadlow's film, despite some high sounding phrases in the script, glamorizes brutal physical combat. Bloody fighting, a brief scene of same-sex kissing, underage drinking, frequent crude and crass language
full_review:
"Never Back Down" (Summit Entertainment), which showcases the no-holds-barred fighting technique known as mixed martial arts, amounts to little more than a pointless celebration of violent machismo.

When his recently widowed mother, Margot (Leslie Hope), moves the family from Iowa to Florida so that her younger son, Charlie (Wyatt Smith), can attend a prestigious tennis academy, older brother Jake (Sean Faris) has difficulty adjusting to his new high school.
But the short-fused football player becomes a hero after an amateur video of an on-field fight he won back in Iowa begins to circulate.

Jake attends a decadent party (featuring beer-chugging games and two girls in a hot tub kissing each other) at the invitation of classmate Baja (Amber Heard), with whom he's smitten. There he's trapped into fighting with Baja's smirking, obnoxious boyfriend, Ryan McCarthy (Cam Gigandet), who beats him into unconsciousness. But Jake's enthusiastic new pal Max (Evan Peters), out to help him get revenge, introduces him to fight coach Jean (Djimon Hounsou).

Jean agrees to train Jake, but warns him that any student who uses his skills to fight outside the gym can never return. As Ryan persists in making trouble for him, the newly adept Jake must choose between settling the score and obeying the rules.

Director Jeff Wadlow's film, as scripted by Chris Hauty, contains several high-sounding phrases of the "fight now so you won't have to fight in the future" variety, and even invokes imagery from Homer's "Iliad" to assure us of its peaceable intentions. None of this can disguise the fact that "Never Back Down" glamorizes brutal physical combat.

Characters in the film cheer as arms are distended and ribs cracked in what amounts to a nonlethal form of gladiator games. Those committed to humane, Judeo-Christian values will likely prefer to turn elsewhere for entertainment.

The film contains bloody fighting, a brief scene of same-sex kissing, underage drinking and frequent crude and crass language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13

title: Never Been Kissed
synopsis: Drippy romantic comedy in which a 25-year old rookie reporter (Drew Barrymore) goes undercover as a high school senior to write about teen life and ends up reliving her adolescent insecurities before winning the heart of her English teacher (Michael Vartan). Barrymore's clunky performance further sinks director Raja Gosnell's contrived coming-of-age tale. Implied affairs, sex references, a sex-education scene involving condoms and occasional profanity

title: Never Cry Wolf
synopsis: Government naturalist (Charles Martin Smith), sent to the Canadian Arctic to determine if wolves are responsible for decimating the once abundant caribou herds, learns instead a lesson in survival and self-knowledge. Director Carrol Ballard's fact-based Disney drama allows the viewer to feel the wonder and excitement of the wilderness with insightful humor and stunning visuals. Some scenes of Smith eating mice and going naked in barren Arctic landsacpe

title: NeverEnding Story II: The Next Chapter, The
synopsis: A young boy (Jonathan Brandis) enters a fairy tale storybook to help the characters save their planet from an evil sorceress (Clarissa Burt). Though director George Miller's fantasy-adventure sequel is visually captivating, its bland storyline holds little interest for adults and its monsters might scare pre-schoolers. Some menacing characters and fantasy violence

title: NeverEnding Story, The
synopsis: While hiding out from class bullies, a schoolboy reads a storybook that propels him into its fantasy world where his imagination runs wild and his courage is tested. German director Wolfgang Peterson delivers a work filled with murky metaphysical references, vividly grotesque creatures and a concluding literary-inspired act of retribution that adults may appreciate more than younger viewers, although there is more than enough fairy tale ambiance to hold their interest

title: Never Give an Inch
synopsis: ( see: "Sometimes a Great Notion" )

title: Never Let Me Go
synopsis: Fanciful Cold War clunker in which an American reporter (Clark Gable) is expelled from the U.S.S.R. but returns to smuggle his Russian ballerina bride (Gene Tierney) to freedom in a sailboat piloted by a British seaman (Bernard Miles). Director Delmer Daves takes a pedestrian look at Soviet intransigence in a dated romantic adventure of possible interest to social historians. Ideological stereotypes and dangerous doings

title: Never Love a Stranger
synopsis: Turgid crime picture from the Harold Robbins novel in which a Catholic orphan (John Drew Barrymore) becomes a gangster during the Depression, then helps his Jewish boyhood pal (Steve McQueen) who's now a district attorney smash the mob. Directed by Robert Stevens, the unconvincing Manhattan melodrama is strictly formula fare, except for the religious angle whose potential is unfortunately left undeveloped. Stylized violence and sexual situations

title: Never Say Die
synopsis: Frenetic comedy set in a Swiss spa where an American millionaire (Bob Hope), mistakenly told he has only 30 days to live, jilts a gun-toting socialite (Gale Sondergaard) to wed an oil man's daughter (Martha Raye) who's unhappily betrothed to a penniless count (Alan Mowbray), intending to leave her a wealthy widow able to marry the man she loves -- a Texas bus driver (Andy Devine). Directed by Elliott Nugent and co-authored by Preston Sturges, the good cast provides occasional splashes of humor but the wacky characters and zany situations grow increasingly tiresome. Romantic complications galore and some sexual innuendo

title: Never Say Goodbye
synopsis: Soapy romance about a doctor (Rock Hudson) with the American occupation forces in postwar Vienna who marries an Austrian pianist (Cornell Borchers), but when she disappears in the Soviet zone, he returns to the U.S. with their two-year-old daughter until years later his wife suddenly turns up. Director Jerry Hopper's remake of "This Love of Ours" offers some glossy Viennese locales but is even more sentimental and contrived than the original

title: Never Say Never Again
synopsis: Aging agent 007 (Sean Connery), shunted aside by a new chief, is called back to retrieve two nuclear warheads stolen by a charming and sinister villain (Klaus Maria Brandauer). Director Irvin Kershner's version of the Bond mystique goes overboard in treating violence as spectacle and promiscuity as hyperactive heroism

title: Never So Few
synopsis: Hokey, overlong World War II tale in which an American officer (Frank Sinatra) makes questionable command decisions while leading a guerrilla unit in Japanese-held Burma, then is courtmartialed for killing a maverick Chinese warlord. Directed by John Sturges, the ponderous narrative glamorizes the self-righteous officer's exploits in the field and on leave in Calcutta wooing an undercover agent (Gina Lollobrigida) before the movie's simplistic resolution. Wartime violence, sexual situations and muddled treatment of moral issues

title: Never Steal Anything Small
synopsis: Musical comedy misfire about a petty New York hood (James Cagney) who takes over a longshoresman's local, then hijacks a shipment of Swiss watches to finance his election as union head. Director Charles Lederer can't quite make Cagney's cynical character likeable, especially his underhanded attempts to woo a sweet innocent (Shirley Jones) by breaking up her marriage. Romantic complications and comic treatment of union corruption

title: Never Talk to Strangers
synopsis: Failed thriller about a criminal psychologist (Rebecca De Mornay) assigned to assess the sanity of an accused serial killer (Harry Dean Stanton) while spending her nights with a new heartthrob (Antonio Banderas) whom she comes to suspect is trying to kill her. Director Peter Hall plods through a kinky but predictable plot whose twist ending will surprise few viewers. Some gory violence, graphic sex scenes and occasional profanity and rough language

title: Never to Love
synopsis: ( see: 1940's "A Bill of Divorcement" )

title: Never Too Late
synopsis: Uneven adaptation of the Broadway comedy about a couple who late in life have another child and the complications this causes in their lives. Under Bud Yorkin's direction, Paul Ford is practically the whole show as he tries in his hard-hearted but soft-headed way to cope with the situation

title: Never Wave at a WAC
synopsis: Lame comedy in which a daffy socialite (Rosalind Russell) joins the Women's Army Corps to get on the staff of her officer boyfriend in Paris, but can't make it through basic training because of interference from her still-caring ex-husband (Paul Douglas). Directed by Norman Z. McLeod, the comedy is almost as flat as the romance, though trainee Marie Wilson adds a certain zest and some may find it of interest as a vintage recruiting poster for "girls" seeking a military career. Battling ex-spouses and sexual innuendo

title: New Adventures of Pippi Longstocking, The
synopsis: Cheesy, cloying English-language adaptation of the Astrid Lindgren children's books sees high-spirited Pippi (Tami Erin) housed briefly in an orphanage after being washed overboard from her father's (John Schuck) ship. Peppy music, bad acting and unimaginative direction by Ken Annakin

title: New Adventures of Tarzan, The
synopsis: Feature version of a 12-episode serial directed by Edward Kull in which Tarzan (Herman Brix aka Bruce Bennett) goes to Guatemala to find a missing friend while helping an expedition search for a lost Mayan city. Vicious battles with ferocious natives

title: New Angels, The
synopsis: Quasi-documentary with 9 vignettes showing the life of Italian young people attempts to make a serious social statement but its emphasis on the erotic details of sexual situations undermines the theme of director Ugo Gregorettti's effort

title: New Best Friend
synopsis: Dreadful drama set on a Southern college campus where the local sheriff (Taye Diggs) investigates whether a shy, bookish student (Mia Kirshner) lying in the hospital accidentally overdosed on drugs or was the victim of attempted murder by her popular new friend (Meredith Monroe). Muddled when it isn't predictable, director Zoe Clarke-Williams' awful film is embarrassing with caricatured characters and an amateurish narrative that plods along interminably. Several gratuitous sexual situations including same-sex kissing, some nudity, sporadic drug use and intermittent rough language with brief profanity
full_review:
New Best Friend" (TriStar) may have clinched the race for worst picture of 2002, reaching theaters nearly three years after filming wrapped.

Predictable when it isn't muddled, the film is an embarrassment to all associated with it. The dreadful drama is set on a Southern college campus where the local sheriff, Artie Bonner (Taye Diggs) investigates whether a shy, bookish student, Alicia (Mia Kirshner), lying near death in the hospital, accidentally overdosed on pure cocaine or was the victim of attempted murder.

Not one true note is rung in this awful mess of a movie. Initially plain and ridiculously frumpy, Alicia is immediately transformed into a gorgeous, kittenish co-ed by her newfound "friends." These friends are the popular girls on campus: poor-little-rich-girl Hadley (Meredith Monroe), bulimic Julianne (Rachel True) and sex-obsessed Sydney (Dominique Swain). Alicia and Hadley are paired to work together on a class sociology project, which is the impetus for their friendship and the reason Alicia is brought into the fold.

The pseudo-thriller has Diggs, outfitted in an array of colorful short-sleeved shirts, poking around campus in what must be one of the most ineffectual investigations in movie history. Sheriff Artie walks into Alicia's room and basically pilfers evidence hoping to catch a break. Maybe his stupid behavior is supposed to be excused because, as explained the Sheriff's voice-over narration at the opening of the film, nothing ever happens in the sleepy Carolina town. So how is he supposed to know how to act in a criminal investigation? Poor Diggs, he walks around looking as lost as the script is.

Several unintentional laughs may be the only thing that keeps the audience interested or awake. "New Best Friend" is so awful that watching the film begins to feel like a surreal experience. Could I really be watching such a terrible film? Or am I trapped in some masochistic nightmare? The amateurish narrative plods along interminably. The caricatured characters spout nonsensical dialogue. And the whole movie is layered with gratuitous sex scenes including one involving two women filmed with out of focus, psychedelic camera angles. And director Zoe Clarke-Williams uses every silly camera trick -- slow motion viewing as Alicia's crush Trevor (Scott Bairstow) walks by -- in an attempt to distract viewers from the dim-witted script.

Finally, the clueless Sheriff pieces it all together, in an ending unworthy of even a "Scooby-Do" episode, and solves the mystery. Moviegoers, you have been well warned!

Due to several gratuitous sexual situations including same-sex kissing, some nudity, sporadic drug use and intermittent rough language with brief profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: New Centurions, The
synopsis: Screen version of Joseph Wambaugh's novel about a veteran police sergeant (George C. Scott) who schools a rookie cop (Stacy Keach) in handling Los Angeles street crime. Director Richard Fleischer's diffuse and episodic melodrama reduces characters and social issues to simple good-guy, bad-guy dramatics. Some bleary-eyed nightclub philosophizing comparing the collapse of law and order in Rome to present society (presumably symbolized by a topless dancer in the background) is the key to the movie's easy sympathies for the police taking the law into their own hands. Violent action and atmosphere

title: New Frontier, The
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Carl L. Pierson is set after the 1889 Oklahoma land rush when a respected trail guide (John Wayne) is made sheriff of a wild boom town which he proceeds to clean up with the help of a good badman (Alan Bridge). Frontier violence

title: New Girl in Town
synopsis: Sympathetic account of the rise of a young woman (Monica Gayle) to stardom in the world of country western music. Under the direction of Gus Trikonis, however, the heroine spends a great deal of time taking off her clothes on camera, making doubtful the movie's sincerity of purpose

title: New in Town
synopsis: Quirky, low-key but ultimately endearing romantic comedy about an ambitious Miami-based executive (Renee Zellweger) sent to downsize a food manufacturing plant in New Ulm, Minn., who learns to adjust her values from the eccentric locals and a good-looking union rep (Harry Connick Jr.). Danish director Jonas Elmer helms an engaging cast, which also includes J.K. Simmons, Siobhan Fallon Hogan and Frances Conroy, in this refreshing departure from the usual Hollywood gloss; though more amiable than outright funny, the script nicely stresses the fundamental decency of this overtly Christian community. A few crude and crass words and a single profanity

title: New Jack City
synopsis: Ruthless gang leader (Wesley Snipes) muscles in on Harlem's drug traffic while two honest cops (Ice T and Judd Nelson) fight the system to bring him to justice. Director and co-star Mario Van Peebles makes an anti-drug statement by exploiting the seamiest aspects of drug addiction in the ghetto. Excessive violence, sexual exploitation, some nudity and incessant rough language

title: New Kind of Love, A
synopsis: Slickly artificial romantic comedy from writer-director Melville Shavelson brings a lovelorn fashion designer (Joanne Woodard) together with a womanizing newsman (Paul Newman) in Paris where she gets his interest by pretending to be a prostitute among other lame contrivances. Game cast in a phony plot whose comic sexual innuendoes and situations are largely unamusing and, at times, tasteless

title: New Land, The
synopsis: Sequel to "The Emigrants" continues its story of a Swedish family (Max von Sydow and Liv Ullmann) after they and a small band of farmers arrive in the Minnesota wilderness of the 1850s and set to work establishing homesteads, cultivating the land, raising their families and acclimatizing themselves to life in the New Land. Superbly directed by Jan Troell, the historical re-creation is an extraordinary achievement in conveying a sense of the pioneer spirit out of which our nation grew

title: New Leaf, A
synopsis: A slick, money-grubbing cad (Walter Matthau) courts and marries a wealthy spinster (Elaine May) whose passion is botany. She comes to love him dearly but undeservedly as he tries various schemes to kill her until an increasing glimmer of affection rises in his own heart. Witty and fast-paced comedy, also written and directed by May, is frequently hilarious and often biting in its moral satire

title: New Life, A
synopsis: Workaholic Wall Street broker (Alan Alda) and wife (Ann-Margret) split up after 26 years of marriage and nervously enter into the singles' scene and commitment to difficult new relationships. Writer-director Alda takes full advantage of the serio-comic elements found in the somewhat predictable plot that benefits from fine acting and characterizations. Some rough language and discreet nudity in several sexual situations

title: New Life Style, The
synopsis: Trashy German production about a conservative travel agent (Horst Tappet) who attends a business convention at the seashore and is soon having a whirl with a comely blonde (Renata Van Holt). Around them, swinging couples frolic freely and interchangeably according to their perverse preferences. Presented by Peter Savage, this burlesque is badly dubbed into English, further marring a bad experience

title: Newman's Law
synopsis: George Peppard plays an incorruptible Los Angeles cop who, on the verge of arresting a drug ring, is framed on a drug charge, causing him to go off on his own to clear his record and knock off the villains to boot. Directed by Richard Heffron, the routine crime plot moves swiftly to its predictable bloody climax whose justification -- taking the law into one's own hands -- would be troubling if it were not here so unbelieveable. Some violence and rough language

title: New Moon
synopsis: One of the sillier Nelson Eddy-Jeanette MacDonald costume musicals is set during the French Revolution when a nobleman-turned-pirate (Eddy) captures a ship bearing an aristocrat's daughter (MacDonald) who spurns his love until marooned on an uninhabited island. Directed by Robert Z. Leonard, the turns of plot are outlandish but the romance is sappily endearing, backed by Sigmund Romberg-Oscar Hammerstein songs including "Stout-Hearted Men" and "Lover, Come Back to Me." Some romantic mush with unlikely appeal for youngsters

title: Newsfront
synopsis: Australian production about the lives and careers of a veteran newsreel cameraman (Bill Hunter) and his assistant (Chris Haywood) from 1948 to 1956 when the nightly television news made the weekly newsreel redundant. Writer-director Philip Noyce pays more attention to the craft of the newsreel and its content during the era of its glory than to the private lives of its characters which receive rather soap opera treatment in marital problems and love affairs. Interesting re-creation but shallow human dimension

title: Newsies
synopsis: Run-of-the-mill musical about New York City newsboys (including Christian Bale and David Moscow) going on strike in 1899 to protest higher newspaper prices decreed by publisher Joseph Pulitzer (Robert Duvall). Though it offers some skillful choreography and a sprightly musical score, director Kenny Ortega develops little dramatic interest in the characters or their predicaments. Brief violence

title: Newton Boys, The
synopsis: Fact-based story of four fun-loving brothers (Matthew McConaughey, Ethan Hawke, Vincent D'Onofrio and Skeet Ulrich) who quit their hardscrabble Texas farm in 1919 to make a living robbing banks until they get greedy and pull a $3 million mail train robbery in 1924 Chicago. Directed by Richard Linklater, the result has interest in its credible re-creation of the period but fails to earn any sympathy, let alone admiration, for the boys and their criminal exploits that the movie tries so hard to arouse. Some gory violence, sexual innuendo, comic treatment of crime and occasional profanity

title: New York Minute
synopsis: Cotton-candy comedy about twin sisters (Ashley and Mary-Kate Olsen) with polar opposite personalities -- one studious, the other a slacker -- who are sidelined on their way to an important scholarship competition and rock concert, respectively, and wind up being pursued around Manhattan by a bungling gangster (Andy Richter) and an overzealous truant officer (Eugene Levy). The frothy but forgettable fluff, directed by Dennie Gordon, keeps its screwball silliness sanitary while promoting a family-value message, that, compared to harder-edged teen fare, most parents would take in a New York minute. Some slight sibling issues and mild sensuality
full_review:
Twin sisters with polar-opposite personalities take a bite out of the Big Apple in the cotton-candy comedy "New York Minute" (Warner Bros.).

Dubbed "the most powerful young women in Hollywood," Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen have literally grown up in the public eye, cutting their teeth, almost literally, on the hit TV series "Full House," where they shared the role of Michelle Tanner, starting when they were 9 months old. They played Michelle until 1995.
So now that they're approaching age 18, what do they do in between running a billion dollar retail-and-entertainment empire? They produce a movie to star in where they each get to play their own part -- with sweet but slight results.

The dimpled duplicates play Jane (Ashley) and Roxy (Mary-Kate) Duncan, mismatched twins who live on Long Island with their somewhat aloof dad, whose medical practice has required him to miss many of the important events in his daughters' lives. Further friction is caused by Jane, a superorganized over-achiever, assuming a maternal mantle since the death of their mother, a move resented by her rebellious slacker sis.

Borrowing a plot device or two from "Ferris Bueller's Day Off," the whole movie takes place in the space of one day. Buttoned-up Jane has to deliver a speech at Columbia University in New York City as part of a prestigious competition with a scholarship to Oxford hanging in the balance.

Meanwhile, the academically challenged Roxy is planning to skip school and try to slip her band's demo tape to recording execs at a music-video shoot in midtown. Begrudgingly, the sparring siblings hop the same Gotham-bound train.

But things change in a New York minute when Jane loses her day planner which has her speech in it. After a series of clumsily contrived mishaps the girls somehow get entangled in a shady, black market DVD piracy scheme operating out of Chinatown.

They are pursued by a faux-Fu Manchu gangster (Andy Richter), who is after a computer chip that his straphanging associate had planted in Jane's bag.

Also hot on their trail is Max Lomax (Eugene Levy), an overzealous truancy officer who sees Roxy as his ticket into the crime-fighting big leagues and who tracks his punk rock prey through the city with Ahab-like tenacity.

Before all is said and done, Jane and Roxy not only work on mending their relationship, but cross romantic paths with a cute bike messenger (Jared Padalecki) and a hunky senator's son (Riley Smith).

While "New York Minute" resembles many of their earlier straight-to-video endeavors, the Olsen twins are surprisingly appealing.

The fact that they are actually sisters helps make both their bonding and bickering more believable and goes a long way to pick up their performances when their acting ability falters.

Those unfamiliar with their off-screen retail juggernaut may be surprised to see how they have blossomed into attractive young women since their "Full House" days.

However, being still on the cusp of adulthood, they retain more than a scent of apple-cheeked innocence -- which they try to erase by shaking their newly bloomed booties in mini-skirts during a frenetic concert scene and traipsing through Time Square in bath towels.

Richter is nothing short of embarrassing and his stereotyping of Asian mannerisms may offend some viewers. Levy steals the show as the bungling bloodhound.

Director Dennie Gordon's decision to shoot on location in Manhattan (with Toronto standing in for some shots) lends the film energy and, if nothing else, a modicum of authenticity. Keen-eyed New Yorkers will have fun picking out the usual logistical inaccuracies.

Overall, the frothy but forgettable movie imparts a positive, family-friendly message. And while no one will mistake its screwball silliness for great -- or even good -- filmmaking, compared to the harder-edged fare being force-fed to young viewers, most parents would take this kind of fresh-scrubbed fluff in a New York minute.

Due to some slight sibling issues and mild sensuality, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

title: New York, New York
synopsis: Nostalgic musical romance about a 1940s showbiz couple (Liza Minnelli and Robert De Niro) who seek stardom and pay the price in an adulterous affair, drugs and alcohol abuse before achieving success. Directed by Martin Scorsese, the big budget musical is technically impressive but dramatically off key in its depiction of the trials and tribulations of marriage

title: New York Stories
synopsis: Inspired trilogy of dramatic vignettes filmed in and about New York City offers director Martin Scorsese's sobering look at the end of a May-December love affair; director Francis Coppola's whimsical tale about a 12-year-old girl living in a ritzy hotel; and the show's highlight, director Woody Allen's hilarious piece in which a nagging Jewish mom gets the best of her neurotic adult son. Some sexual banter and suggestions of illicit liaisons

title: The Next Three Days
synopsis: Implausible, ethically dubious thriller about a Pittsburgh college professor (Russell Crowe) who decides to spring his wife (Elizabeth Banks) from a prison where she's serving time for murder. Writer-director Paul Haggis embeds faulty moral logic inside his far-fetched premise. Together with certain plot contrivances, its endorsement of seriously flawed behavior -- a laudable belief in his spouse cannot excuse some of the choices Crowe's character makes -- renders this otherwise well-made movie difficult to enjoy. One instance of rough language, a smattering of profanity and crass terms, some gunplay and other nongraphic violence, an off-screen suicide attempt, drug dealing, brief sexual banter
full_review:
Much of moviegoing's appeal stems from the chance to experience the improbable vicariously. But there are limits to the suspension of disbelief when it comes to dramatic thrillers that aspire to realism. In "The Next Three Days" (Lionsgate), we're asked to accept that a literature professor at a Pittsburgh-area community college would try to break his wife out of prison.

Moreover, writer-director Paul Haggis ("Crash") embeds faulty moral logic inside this far-fetched premise. Along with certain contrivances intended to smooth over the bumpy plot, this renders the otherwise well-made "The Next Three Days" difficult to enjoy. The main problem arises not from excesses involving language, sexuality or violence, but from the endorsement of seriously wayward behavior.

Based on the 2008 French thriller "Pour Elle" ("Anything for Her"), the picture stars Russell Crowe as John Brennan, adoring spouse of Lara (Elizabeth Banks) and devoted father of toddler Luke (Ty Simpkins). Without much preliminary ado, Lara is arrested for the murder of her boss, with whom she had argued earlier in the day.

Fast-forward three years and she's incarcerated at the Allegheny County Jail in downtown Pittsburgh. Luke is naturally despondent, but John, convinced of Lara's innocence, clings to his faith in the legal system. When her last appeal is denied, however, he decides to spring her from jail.

After interviewing knowledgeable ex-con Damon Pennington (Liam Neeson) and then conducting extensive research on the Internet, John hatches his high-risk plan. Often leaving Luke with his parents (Brian Dennehy and Helen Carey), John engages in reconnaissance, obtains false papers and puts the family home on the market to help raise the necessary funds.

Increasingly desperate, he even robs drug dealers, a choice which goes murderously awry.

The issue of Lara's culpability isn't settled until the very end when the full details of the crime are revealed in flashback. A discussion of Cervantes' "Don Quixote" during one of John's classes, meanwhile, provides thematic background. He interprets the novel as celebrating the triumph of irrationality over reason, concluding, "Insanity is better than despair."

John's own scheme, part fantasy, part obsession, is motivated by a laudable fidelity toward his wife that -- regrettably and unjustifiably -- comes to override all other considerations.

Even as this ambitious love story-wrapped-in-a-thriller culminates in an exciting chase, it's difficult to feel more than superficial sympathy for the Brennans. Indeed, viewers may find themselves rooting for the police.

Lara's guilt or innocence is ultimately irrelevant given John's willingness to violate so many laws, endanger so many lives (including his own and those of several meth merchants the script treats as expendable), neglect his son and selfishly allow the interests of his family to trump everything else.

Despite his technical proficiency and the fine performances he elicits, Haggis fails to paper over the glaring ethical gaps. Arguably, he makes this tale of controlled madness in the face of injustice as plausible as anyone could, though at the cost of being transparently manipulative and immorally maudlin. The takeaway: Not everybody who tilts at windmills deserves praise.

The film contains one instance of rough language, a smattering of profanity and crass terms, some gunplay and other nongraphic violence, an off-screen suicide attempt, drug dealing and brief sexual banter. The Catholic News Service classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Next Best Thing, The
synopsis: Touching but flawed drama about a single woman (Madonna), unlucky in love, who accidentally becomes pregnant with her gay best friend's (Rupert Everett) child after a boozy one night stand. Director John Schlesinger starts out with a clumsy, contrived beginning then abruptly changes tone mid-stream, but the film offers an earnest portrayal of a loving if unconventional family. Sexual situations, implied homosexual encounter, tolerant view of the homosexual lifestyle, fleeting nudity, and an instance of rough language

title: Next Day Air
synopsis: Brisk, low-budget brew of violence, street language and stoner comedy mixing dimwitted criminals with a Mexican drug lord as a pot-smoking overnight-delivery driver (Donald Faison from TV's "Scrubs") accidentally takes a package containing 10 kilos of cocaine to the wrong apartment, which just happens to contain misfit criminals (Mike Epps and Wood Harris) who plan to sell the drugs and start new lives. Director Benny Boom keeps these one-dimensional characters and the stale, predictable plot clattering along for just 84 minutes, but the only surprising twist is who survives the close-range brutality at the finish. Nonstop crude and profane language, drug use, brief upper female nudity, knife violence, the occasional fistfight, a slow-motion gun battle, racial stereotypes and an utter lack of redemptive behavior by any character

title: Next Friday
synopsis: Unfunny sequel to the juvenile 1995 "Friday" in which the central character (Ice Cube) moves to his uncle's (Don "DC" Curry) home in the Los Angeles suburbs trying to escape a bully (Tommy "Tiny" Lister, Jr.), only to find trouble with his uncle's Chicano neighbors. Director Steve Carr turns the characters into caricatures as the cast squeezes out nothing but cheap laughs from the thin material. Sexual situations, intermittent violence, recurring recreational drug use, bathroom humor and much rough language

title: Next Karate Kid, The
synopsis: By teaching her mental as well as physical discipline, a wise karate master (Pat Morita) helps to channel the anger of a recently orphaned high school girl (Hilary Swank) who is being harassed by school bullies. Director Christopher Cain downplays martial arts bouts in favor of stressing the young woman's learning to cope with adversity in a values-centered if fanciful youth film. Brief violence

title: Next Man, The
synopsis: Spoiled rich girl (Cornelia Sharpe) works as an assassin for a terrorist group, seducing and liquidating her victims in exotic corners of the world, but meets her match in a visionary Arab diplomat (Sean Connery). Director Richard C. Sarafian's mediocre, high gloss thriller offers little besides mindless violence, some gratuitous nudity and a brutal ending

title: Next of Kin
synopsis: Savvy Chicago cop (Patrick Swayze) is torn between the law and his family's backwoods code of justice when his older brother (Liam Neeson) comes to town to avenge the murder of their younger brother (Bill Paxton) by the mob. Director John Irvin attempts to contrast the feuding ethics of hillbilly and mobster clans, but the movie's numerous plot gaps, ethnic caricatures and deterioration into vigilantism weaken the effort. Much profanity and some scenes of grisly violence

title: Next!
synopsis: ( see: "The Next Victim" )

title: Next Stop, Greenwich Village
synopsis: Jewish youth (Lenny Baker) leaves his blue-collar Brooklyn neighborhood in 1953 to seek fame as an actor in Greenwich Village. His growth both on the stage and as a person is chronicled by director Paul Mazursky in a series of incidents that are often quite amusing and sometimes extremely touching. Though soft and sentimental in its portrayal of the young man and overly nostalgic about the era, the movie is positive in its assertions of values and sense of ethnic roots. One notable exception is its acceptance of abortion

title: Next Stop, Wonderland
synopsis: Off-beat comedy about romance in the 1990s follows a bright Boston nurse (Hope Davis) seeking a serious relationship via a personal ad column and a serious-minded plumber (Alan Gelfant) studying to become a marine biologist, whose paths frequently cross until accidentally meeting as kindred spirits just before movie's end. Directed by Brad Anderson, the parallel development of the two stories overplays the nurse's wry interviews with the sorry collection of men answering her ad while underplaying the plumber's problems with a loan shark, but the result pokes fun at current sexual mores and plunks for a more old-fashioned notion of romance. Ambiguous view of unmarried sexual relationships, much rough language and occasional profanity

title: Next Summer
synopsis: In a story about three generations and how each defines the nature of loving relationships, this French production features an impressive cast, including Claudia Cardinale, Jean-Louis Trintignant, Philippe Noiret and Fanny Ardant. Directed with charm and humor by Nadine Tintignant, each member of this family saga is shown grappling with the many facets of love, sex and marriage from the perspective of strengthening or weakening family ties. Adult theme

title: Next Time We Love
synopsis: Episodic tearjerker in which a struggling young couple grow apart when wife (Margaret Sullavan) finds success on Broadway and husband (James Stewart) makes good as a foreign correspondent, while their best friend (Ray Milland) waits in the wings burning a torch for the wife. Director Edward H. Griffith relies upon a talented cast to sustain a highly artifical plot that's resolved by terminal illness. Contrived marital woes and misunderstandings

title: Next Victim, The
synopsis: Italian-Spanish co-production about a succession of young ladies who lose their lives to a savage razor-wielder whose real object is to terrorize one particularly fickle young lady (Edwige Fenech). Directed by Sergio Martino, the badly-dubbed terror mystery has an obvious twist ending, predictable suspense and abundant nudity

title: Next Voice You Hear, The
synopsis: The lives of an average American worker (James Whitmore), his pregnant wife (Nancy Davis) and their young son are transformed when they hear God speaking to the world on the radio. Directed by William Wellman, the intriguing and well-intentioned concept falls flat because of the banality of the radio message directing people to perform "miracles" of "peace and loving kindness" and the clumsy day-by-day portrayal of how the father gradually changes over the course of a week. It's not silly but it's not very credible

title: Niagara
synopsis: Dark thriller set in the honeymoon haven of Niagara Falls where a wife (Marilyn Monroe) plots with her boyfriend to kill her disturbed husband (Joseph Cotten), then fears for her life when the plan backfires. Director Henry Hathaway uses the waterfall locales to provide a spectacular background for the action's suspense, though the harrowing results are far from satisfying. Nasty violence, menacing situations and sexual innuendo

title: Niagara Niagara
synopsis: Tortured tale of runaway teen lovers (Robin Tunney and Henry Thomas) turns into tragedy when the girl runs out of her Tourette's Syndrome medication and substitutes liquor and pills in a vain attempt to take the edge off her wild outbursts. Directed by Bob Gosse, the formula road movie evokes some sympathy for the afflicted teen in what is otherwise a tired story of outcasts on the run. Brief sexual encounters, much substance abuse, frequent profanity and continuous rough language

title: Nice Girl Like Me, A
synopsis: Boring British melodrama about an unwed mother (Barbara Ferris) who conceives one child in Paris, another in Venice and acquires a third infant when it is dumped in her arms by a desperate Italian mother. Directed by Desmond Davis, there is a lot of lush photography of European cities and pastoral landscapes but the story lacks any social or moral perspective that might have given it some significance

title: Nicholas and Alexandra
synopsis: British epic offers the spectacle of glittering palaces, splendid pageantry and larger-than-life characters in ornate costumes but misses the historical context making understandable why this couple were the last of the Romanovs to rule Russia. Directed by Franklin J. Schaffner, the focus is on the domestic lives of the Tsar (Michael Jayston) and Tsarina (Janet Suzman), with occasional fragmentary scenes indicating the revolutionary events that were to sweep away the entire epoch. Grand-scale romance set against a turbulent but fuzzy background, with only Rasputin's rampant sexuality to give children pause, though all will wince at his brutal murder

title: Nicholas Nickleby
synopsis: Genial adaptation of the 1839 Charles Dickens classic in which penniless Nicholas (Charlie Hunnam) sets out to reunite with and provide for his mother, sister and crippled friend (Jamie Bell) despite the machinations of his malevolent uncle (Christopher Plummer). A masterful Plummer steals the show in writer-director Douglas McGrath's compressed tale of a young man's hard-won triumph over adversity. Brief violence
full_review:
The comforting tale of a young man's triumph over adversity in 19th-century England is handsomely realized in writer-director Douglas McGrath's adaptation of the Charles Dickens classic, "Nicholas Nickleby" (MGM).

Pared down from the immense 1839 novel and the nine-hour Royal Shakespeare Company stage production, the movie still charms with its almost-too-good-to-be-true title hero (Charlie Hunnam) at the mercy of a cold and calculating uncle (Christopher Plummer).

A gentle opening, encapsulating how Nicholas and then Kate (Romola Garal) were born and tenderly raised by loving parents gives way to their father's death and their penniless arrival with their mother (Stella Gonet) at the doorstep of Uncle Ralph. He quickly dispatches Kate to work with a dressmaker and delivers 19-year-old Nicholas into the evil hands of grasping Wackford Squeers (Jim Broadbent) to work as a teacher in Squeers' distant, prison-like academy. There Nicholas befriends crippled adolescent Smike (Jamie Bell), whom sadistic Squeers and his equally rotten spouse (Juliet Stevenson) have held as a slave ever since his tuition payments ceased seven years earlier.

Appalled at the vicious treatment the Squeerses dole out to one and all, Nicholas escapes with Smike, determined to reunite with his family and somehow provide for them all. Along the way, he is pleasantly waylaid by traveling performers (led by Nathan Lane) and cajoled into starring as Romeo before he and Smike arrive in London and learn of his uncle's callous mistreatment of Kate.

Although he finds work and meets the lovely Madeline (Anne Hathaway), once again his uncle intervenes, deliberately setting in motion an arranged marriage for Madeline to the craven Sir Mulberry Hawk (Edward Fox). Even as Smike's health fails, the uncle's disgruntled servant (Tom Courtenay) aligns with Nicholas to bring a halt to his employer's lifetime of greed-fueled misdeeds.

Consummate storyteller Dickens' concern for the human condition and especially the poor shines through in this heart-warming adaptation. Of necessity, filmmaker McGrath has compressed the tale and eliminated characters, but those who remain bring their roles to vivid life. Alternately thundering then whispering, the crafty Plummer steals the show and invests his comeuppance with sudden unexpected gravitas. But nearly as riveting are Courtenay as his insolent, alcoholic servant, Broadbent as the steely, one-eyed monster and Stevenson as his witch of a wife.

At the other end of the emotional scale, Lane and Alan Cumming as the performer with a yen to dance the Highland Fling provide much-needed whimsy during Nicholas' arduous journey to manhood. Hunnam in the title role delivers considerable eye appeal, but doesn't yet have the acting chops of the other featured performers. Nor is his romance with underused love interest Hathaway sufficiently fleshed out.

The accomplished production design conveys the horrors of the ghastly boarding school and is most effective at showing how Uncle Ralph's rich but bleak home, with its collection of stuffed animals, is a house empty of life or love.

With its attention to the mistreatment of children and themes of family, friendship and perseverance, "Nicholas Nickleby" is rewarding, high-minded fare.

Because of brief violence, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

title: Nicholas Nickleby
synopsis: Memorable adaptation of the Charles Dickens novel in which a young man (Derek Bond) in 1830 England saves a youth (Aubrey Woods) from a brutal boys school while struggling to protect his mother and sister from his miserly, conniving uncle (Cedric Hardwicke). Director Alberto Cavalcanti embroiders the desperate proceedings with zestful visuals of the period setting and its quirky assortment of characters. Some frightening ordeals for young viewers

title: Nicholas, the Boy Who Became Santa
synopsis: Animated children's story about the saintly bishop in 4th-century Asia Minor whose legendary gift-giving grew into a Christmas tradition out of which developed the secular holiday myth of Santa Claus. Directed by Fernando Uribe and Steven Hahn, the half-hour video follows Nicholas as the young lad learns the joy of giving to others, grows in charity to become bishop, suffers under the pagan Romans and is imprisoned, returning to his flock years later as a white-bearded, rotund and irrepressibly jovial old man, just in time to distribute Christmas gifts. Best for preschoolers

title: Nick and Jane
synopsis: Lame romantic comedy in which a New York businesswoman (Dana Wheeler-Nicholson) tries to make her womanizing boyfriend (John Dossett) jealous by paying a sensitive cabbie (James McCaffrey) to masquerade as her lover, with unsurprising results. Writer-director Richard Mauro strings out a weak plot with a collection of odd-ball characters, such as the cabbie's rapper roommate (Gedde Watanabe) and transvestite neighbor (Clinton Leupp), but the result is an urban fantasy that delivers a few giggles but lacks any romantic charm. Sexual situations, gay stereotypes and occasional rough language

title: Nickelodeon
synopsis: Mildly humorous slapstick drama about the pioneer days of silent films stars Ryan O'Neal as young lawyer turned writer-director and Burt Reynolds as his star. Director Peter Bogdanovich's story has some amusing moments but is rather thin in dramatic developments, leaving the main focus on movie memorabilia

title: Nickel Ride, The
synopsis: Aging, small-time operator (Jason Miller) gets into a tight spot trying to put together a deal for the crime syndicate and tries to avoid his inevitable fate. Though the narrative is somewhat muddled, director Richard Mulligan's treatment of the central issue of the man's survival is taut and powerfully done, with nicely nuanced characterizations and atmosphere of menace. Element of human compassion elevates it above standard crime movie

title: Nick of Time
synopsis: Nasty little thriller about the desperate plight of a mild accountant (Johnny Depp) whose 6-year-old daughter will be killed unless he assassinates California's Governor (Marsha Mason) in the next 90 minutes. Directed by John Badham, the suspense wears thin as the harebrained proceedings are dragged out until the time limit expires in bloody mayhem intended as a feel-good ending. Some hard-edged violence, much menace and intermittent rough language

title: Night and the City
synopsis: A second-rate lawyer (Robert De Niro) invites disaster by borrowing money from the jealous husband (Cliff Gorman) of his girlfriend (Jessica Lange) to put on a boxing tournament in a venue controlled by a crooked promoter (Alan King). Writer-director Irwin Winkler's profane, edgy movie captures the hustling spirit of New York City lowlifes while leaving their intersecting relationships too vague to be dramatically satisfying. An adulterous relationship, brief violence, some sexual innuendo and much rough language, including racial slurs

title: Night at the Bijou, A
synopsis: ( see: "The Three Stooges Follies" )

title: Night at the Museum
synopsis: Lightweight but diverting comedy-fantasy about a perennial loser (Ben Stiller) who takes a job as night watchman at New York's Museum of Natural History only to learn that the dinosaur bones, stuffed animals, mummies and diorama characters (played by Robin Williams, Owen Wilson, Steve Coogan and others) all come to life after closing time, leading him on a whirlwind adventure of slapstick and mayhem, and eventually allowing him to earn back the respect of his young son. Director Shawn Levy's film could be much funnier, but the effects are terrific, Stiller is appealing, and old-timers like Mickey Rooney, Dick Van Dyke, Bill Cobbs and Stiller's mom, Anne Meara, add to the fun of this entertaining family film. There is the standard, but always worthy, message about proving yourself. Light slapstick violence
full_review:
Night at the Museum" (Fox) is a lightweight but diverting comedy-fantasy about Larry Daley (Ben Stiller), an impractical dreamer and perennial loser who takes a job as night watchman at New York's Museum of Natural History only to learn to his amazement that the dinosaur bones, stuffed animals, mummies and diorama characters all come to life after closing time.

The statue of Theodore Roosevelt (Robin Williams), a cowboy (Owen Wilson), a Roman soldier (Steve Coogan), an Indian maiden (Mizuo Peck) and others join the pachyderms, lions and a mischievous monkey named Dexter in leading Larry on a whirlwind adventure of slapstick and mayhem. Larry must keep order, as the disapproving (and dimwitted) museum president, Dr. McPhee (Ricky Gervais), will notice if anything is amiss.

At first, Larry is overwhelmed by the sheer anarchy of the creatures' nocturnal activities, but eventually he's able to restore order and earns back the respect of his young son, Nick (Jake Cherry), as well as win the appreciation of the pretty museum docent, Rebecca (Carla Gugino), whom he befriends.

Director Shawn Levy's film -- and Robert Ben Garant and Thomas Lennon's script -- could be much funnier. A loony confrontation where Larry pep-talks Attila the Hun (Patrick Gallagher) about the love he apparently lacked as a child briefly demonstrates how witty the entire film might have been. Nonetheless, the effects are pretty terrific, Stiller is appealing, and old-timers such as Dick Van Dyke, Mickey Rooney and Bill Cobbs as the feisty daytime guards, and Stiller's mom, Anne Meara, as an employment counselor, add to the fun of this entertaining family film. Oh, and there's the standard, but always worthy, message about proving yourself against impossible odds.

The film is being shown in Imax theaters as well as on conventional screens, and looks splendid when it's as big as the tyrannosaurus rex who gets the astonished Larry to play "fetch."

The film contains light slapstick violence. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-I -- general patronage. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested. Some material may not be suitable for children.

title: Night at the Museum: Battle of the Smithsonian
synopsis: Enjoyable sequel, again directed by Shawn Levy, has the ex-Museum of Natural History night guard (Ben Stiller) traveling to Washington to rescue his formerly inanimate friends -- the museum's display figures (Owen Wilson, Robin Williams, Steve Coogan) -- from being archived in the Smithsonian. With the help of Amelia Earhart (Amy Adams) and General Custer (Bill Hader), they must ward off Egyptian pharaoh Kahmunrah (funny Hank Azaria), Ivan the Terrible (Christopher Guest), Napoleon Bonaparte (Alain Chabat) and Al Capone (Jon Bernthal). Kids will love the gags (the humor stays clean) and excellent special effects, and adults will appreciate the wit of some of the D.C. museum's most iconic paintings and sculptures springing to life
full_review:
There are times when sequels, contrary to tradition, really can top the original. And "Night at the Museum: Battle of the Smithsonian" (Fox) is one such happy exception.

This enjoyable romp, again directed by Shawn Levy, takes the ex-Museum of Natural History night guard Larry (Ben Stiller) on a completely new adventure in the nation's capital.

Now a successful inventor of infomercial devices, Larry returns to the museum. His humorless ex-boss, Dr. McPhee (Ricky Gervais), informs him that the exhibition figures, which magically came to life in the first movie, are now considered out of date as the museum is about to be modernized, and have been shipped to the Smithsonian Institution in Washington for storage.

Determined to restore his friends to their rightful place in Gotham, Larry journeys south and slips into the Smithsonian's warehouse, after appropriating a guard's ID -- an amusing exchange with unbilled Jonah Hill.

While trying to free his buddies -- cowboy Jedediah (Owen Wilson), Teddy Roosevelt (Robin Williams) and the Roman general Octavius (Steve Coogan) -- from their packing crates, he inadvertently brings back to life Egyptian leader Kahmunrah (a very funny, lisping Hank Azaria). The pharaoh hopes to resurrect his ancient army and take over the world, but he needs the giant gold keypad that Larry has in hand to unleash those troops.

It then becomes a face-off between Larry and his friends, now including a reanimated aviatrix Amelia Earhart (Amy Adams) and General Custer (Bill Hader) -- the latter hoping for a comeback after his defeat at the Little Big Horn -- and the power-hungry Kahmunrah, who's formed a posse with historical baddies Ivan the Terrible (Christopher Guest), Napoleon Bonaparte (Alain Chabat) and Al Capone (Jon Bernthal).

Along the way, the iconic paintings and statues of the Smithsonian, like Rodin's "The Thinker" and one of Degas' dancers, come to life. In one clever sequence, Larry and Earhart jump into the frame of "The Kiss," Alfred Eisenstaedt's black-and-white V-J Day photo. The giant figure of Abraham Lincoln from the memorial, Albert Einstein, and the Tuskegee Airmen all get into the action which also plays out at the Air and Space Museum and the Smithsonian Castle.

There's the suggestion of a sweet, platonic romance between Larry and Earhart, though obviously, nothing can come of it, as she will return to her state as a wax statue at sunrise.

The actors from the original film have their characters down pat and make a welcome return, while the newbies are all pluses, including Chabat as a height-obsessed, hopelessly romantic Napoleon, and most especially Adams, proving again what a deft comic talent she is. Transcending caricature, she makes a spunky, likable Katharine Hepburn sort of heroine, her dialogue peppered with delightful 1930s slang, as when she spurs Larry to show some "moxie."

It's refreshing to see so many mainstream stars in a family-friendly film where the humor never becomes smutty. Thomas Lennon and Robert Ben Garant have written the screenplay as they did the first, an adaptation of Milan Trenc's children's book.

Kids will love the gags and clever special effects. Teeny Octavius confronted by what, to him, is a gargantuan squirrel is one choice sequence. Adults will appreciate the wit of those iconic paintings and sculptures springing to amazing life.

And besides providing a painless incentive to kids to learn more about history and art, the film imparts good lessons about teamwork, the overriding moral espoused by Larry near the end of the film: "The key to happiness is doing what you love with people you love."

Warmly recommended for family viewing. The film also will be screened in Imax Experience technology.

The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-I -- general patronage. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested. Some material may not be suitable for children.

title: Night at the Roxbury, A
synopsis: Witless comedy about two nerdy brothers (Will Ferrell and Chris Kattan) who haunt local nightclubs until they stumble onto romance and success in spite of themselves. Directed by John Fortenberry, the brainless proceedings feature gratingly irksome characters whose dumb antics are thuddingly dull. Implied affairs, a discreet sexual encounter, crude expressions and a few instances of profanity

title: Nightbreed
synopsis: A young man (Craig Sheffer) and his girlfirend (Anne Bobby) race to save a legendary city of dead souls from invading human nut cases, including a psycho psychoanalyst (David Cronenberg), a fascist cop (Charles Haid) and a spineless priest (Malcolm Smith). Writer-director Clive Barker's muddled horror movie features a haphazard collection of gruesome freaks, nightmare imagery and make-up wizardry. Excessive images of grisly human slaughter, some profanity and nudity

title: Night Caller
synopsis: Unsavory French production about a police inspector (Jean-Paul Belmondo) whose methods in trying to catch some bank robbers and a deranged serial murderer are both brutal and lack any sense of legal niceties. Director Henri Verneuil's disjointed crime thriller lacks any elements of tension or suspense. Violence, rough language and elements of sexual perversion

title: Night Call Nurses
synopsis: Sex comedy about nurses (Patricia T. Byrne, Alana Collins and Mittie Lawrence) who temper the needling they receive from psychotic doctors and patients by indulging in gratuitous sex relations with them. Directed by Jonathan Kaplan, it's exploitation drivel

title: Nightcomers, The
synopsis: Based on the Victorian characters in Henry James' supernatural story, "The Turn of the Screw," the movie ends where the original began and imagines the dark events transpiring between the groundskeeper (Marlon Brando) and his mistress (Stephanie Beacham) that leave two very troubled children for the new governess who arrives at the beginning of the James story. Director Michael Winner dramatizes literally the perverse tendencies and violent events (bizarre sado-masochistic games) which only lurked beneath the surface of the original James story. Climatic gore, nudity in a sexual context and a theme of evil in innocence

title: Night Crossing
synopsis: Disney fact-based drama about two families (John Hurt, Jane Alexander, Beau Bridges and Glynnis O'Connor) who make their way to freedom from East Germany by way of a hot air balloon. While there are some moments of suspense and entertainment, director Delbert Mann doesn't deal adequately with the foreign setting, culture and people. Nevertheless, it provides the family audience with a harrowing reminder of the price of freedom

title: Night Digger, The
synopsis: British psychological thriller about an aging spinster (Patricia Neal), long dominated by a tyrannical adoptive mother, who falls in love with a psychotic killer twenty years her junior (Nicholas Clay). Good acting gives credibility to a rather preposterous situation, allowing director Alistair Reid the intriguing opportunity to probe into the darker corners of the human mind and soul. The result is a mixed bag, caught somewhere between a taut chiller and a human interest story. Some flashbacks indicating the killer's twisted sexuality and several grisly murders with oppressive sexual overtones

title: Night Evelyn Came Out of the Grave, The
synopsis: Italian production about an Englishman (Anthony Steffen) who is haunted by the ghost of his unfaithful wife and lapses into periods of insanity during which he becomes a sadistic libertine. Directed by Emilio P. Miraglia, the murder mystery is secondary to the sexual aspects which feature nudity

title: Night Eyes
synopsis: Security guard (Andrew Stevens) falls for the rich divorcee (Tanya Roberts) he's guarding and winds being made the patsy in a murder case. Ineptly directed by Jag Mundrha, the story is made out of cardboard with characters to match. Graphic sex scenes with some nudity, occasional violence and rough language

title: Nightfall
synopsis: Tough crime thriller of an innocent man (Aldo Ray) pursued by a cop (James Gregory) who wants him for murder and a bankrobber (Brian Keith) who wants the loot he's lost. Director Jacques Tourneur makes it all the more intriguing by doling out the story with flashbacks as needed and the cast makes it seem convincing enough. Stylized violence

title: Night Falls on Manhattan
synopsis: Brooding drama in which an idealistic District Attorney (Andy Garcia) learns that falsified evidence resulted in his winning a conviction against a murderous drug dealer, and that his beloved father (Ian Holm) may have been one of the dirty cops involved. Writer-director Sidney Lumet probes the moral complexities of a flawed justice system and conflicting loyalties in an uneven but thoughtful tale of innocence corrupted. Brief violence, implied pre-marital affair, recurring profanity and much rough language

title: Night Flier, The
synopsis: ( see: "Stephen King's The Night Flier" )

title: Night Flight from Moscow
synopsis: Convoluted espionage story about a glowering Russian spy (Yul Brynner) who defects to the West and the CIA official (Henry Fonda) whose task is to determine whether the defector is an honest turncoat or a double agent. French production directed by Henri Verneuil has interesting details about counter-intelligence methods but the slow pace of the international yarn makes it a yawner. Some violence

title: Night Full of Rain, A
synopsis: The unhappy marriage of a rich American (Candice Bergen) and an Italian Communist journalist (Giancarlo Giannini) forms the basis for director Lina Wertmuller's story of their violent meeting and courtship told in flashbacks. Some nudity, sexual by-play and crudities

title: Night Game
synopsis: Tedious serial-killer thriller unfolds in a colorful Gulf Coast setting with a burned-out cop (Roy Scheider), his ill-suited fiancee (Karen Young) and an implausible scenario about a maniac who kills young blonds whenever the Houston Astros' star pitcher wins a game. Director Peter Masterson strikes out on this one. Some profanity, menace and grisly shots of mutilated corpses

title: Night Games
synopsis: Ludicrous and inept melodrama about a wife (Cindy Pickett), traumatized by a girlhood assault, who is cured of her frigidity by having sex with a stranger dressed in feathers. Listlessly directed by Roger Vadim, the acting is embarrassingly bad. Nudity and graphic sexuality abound

title: Night Has a Thousand Eyes
synopsis: Unusual mystery from Cornell Woolrich's story about a man (Edward G. Robinson) whose unwanted gift of seeing into the future proves a curse until he puts it to use trying to save an heiress (Gail Russell) from being murdered. Director John Farrow works up some eerie atmosphere for a plot mixing the paranormal into a murder mystery with quite diverting results. Stylized violence and theme of clairvoyance

title: Night Has Eyes, The
synopsis: Romantic British chiller in which school teachers (Joyce Howard and Tucker McGuire) trace a missing friend to the Yorkshire moors where they stumble upon a spooky mansion inhabited by a strange composer (James Mason) and two servants (Wilfrid Lawson and Mary Clare). Written and directed by Leslie Arliss, the plot's suspense doesn't measure up to the eerie atmosphere of the fog-shrouded setting and Mason's wild-eyed portrayal of a shattered veteran of the Spanish Civil War. Menacing situations

title: Nighthawks
synopsis: Intense thriller with Sylvester Stallone playing a New York City policeman assigned to an anti-terrorist unit whose mettle is tested by a clever and utterly ruthless German terrorist (Rutger Hauer). Director Bruce Malmuth fails to invest any human dimension to all the violence and counter-violence that transpires, using the situation merely as the basis for exciting melodrama. Brutal violence and rough language

title: Night in Casablanca, A
synopsis: Tame Marx Brothers comedy has Groucho managing the hotel where Sig Ruman and other fugitive Nazis have stashed stolen loot but, when they try to escape with it, Chico and Harpo ground their plane. Directed by Archie L. Mayo, the script is awfully thin and the old zany flair of the Brothers' antics is barely visible. Comic violence and mild sexual innuendo

title: Night in Heaven, A
synopsis: Married school teacher (Lesley Ann Warren) has an affar with a student (Christopher Atkins) who works as a male exotic dancer. Directed by John Avildsen, the crude effort emphasizes nudity and graphic sex while disparaging marital fidelity

title: Nightjohn
synopsis: A young girl slave (Allison Jones) on a cotton plantation in the 1830s faces the wrath of her cruel master (Beau Bridges) after secretly being taught to read by the title character (Carl Lumbly) who's determined to bring the power of literacy to his oppressed people. Directed by Charles Burnett, the television production gets strong performances from a largely African-American cast in a drama portraying the painful injustices of slavery and one man's attempt to transcend its inhumanity. Some intense scenes of physical and spiritual violence

title: Nightmare
synopsis: Gripping thriller set in New Orleans where a jazz band clarinetist (Kevin McCarthy) awakens from a nightmare convinced he's killed a man, then gets his cop brother-in-law (Edward G. Robinson) to investigate and the trail leads to a hypnotist. Director Maxwell Shane's remake of "Fear in the Night" is generally better acted and certainly better crafted than the first time around, with more memorable results. Stylized violence, threatening situations and sexual innuendo

title: The Nightmare Before Christmas
synopsis: (3-D) Rerelease in 3-D of the minor fantasy of the macabre with puppet animation telling the tale of Halloweentown's skeleton king replacing the kidnapped Santa Claus to spread Christmas fear with scary toys until stopped by a missile, then returning home to free Santa in time to make his accustomed rounds. Producer Tim Burton's story centers on the dark world of hobgoblins and monsters suddenly intruding on the bright expectations of St. Nick's annual visit, but the narrative proves tiresome in padding out the thin concept, despite all its stylish puppetry and ghoulish humor. Considerable menace and threatening atmosphere

title: Nightmare Before Christmas, The
synopsis: Minor fantasy of the macabre with puppet animation telling the tale of Halloweentown's skeleton king replacing the kidnapped Santa Claus to spread Christmas fear with scary toys until stopped by a missile, then returning home to free Santa in time to make his accustomed rounds. Producer Tim Burton's story centers in the dark world of hobgoblins and monsters suddenly intruding on the bright expectations of St. Nick's annual visit but the narrative proves tiresome in padding out the thin concept, despite all its stylish puppetry and ghoulish humor. Considerable menace and threatening atmosphere

title: Nightmare Castle
synopsis: Dubbed Italian horror movie directed by Allen Grunewald in which a mad doctor (Paul Miller) experimenting on rejuvenation by blood transfusions kills his unfaithful wife (Barbara Steele), then tries to put her sister (Steele again) in an insane asylum until undone by ghosts and an honorable physician (Lawrence Clift). Some gory visuals, menacing atmosphere and sexual innuendo

title: Nightmare in Wax
synopsis: Old-fashioned horror movie about a psychotic wax museum curator (Cameron Mitchell) who seeks vengeance on some old associates for having humiliated and disfigured him. Director Bud Townsend bridges the gaps in the story line with a little morbid humor, some mild horror and playful settings

title: Nightmare on Elm Street 3: Dream Warriors, A
synopsis: A group of youngsters are terrorized in their dreams by a restless, evil phantom who returns to avenge his fiery death at the hands of their parents. Director Chuck Russell's worn-out plot relies on gory special effects and sadistic violence with no other purpose but to shock

title: Nightmare on Elm Street 4: The Dream Master, A
synopsis: Another inept sequel about a child murderer (Robert Englund) who takes revenge for his death by invading the dreams of his teenage victims. Directed by Renny Harlin, the plot is an unhealthy brew of gruesome, gory visuals with some nudity and rough language

title: Nightmare on Elm Street 5: The Dream Child, A
synopsis: Freddy Krueger (Robert Englund) is back, stalking teenage Alice (Lisa Wilcox) through the dreams of her unborn, illegitimate child. Directed by Stephen Hopkins, there are gruesome flashbacks recalling Freddy's conception and birth as the son of a nun raped by psychos in an insane asylum as well as Freddy's usual sadistic teen-stalking

title: Nightmare on Elm Street, A
synopsis: Freddie, a long-dead child murderer, haunts the dreams of some high students who also die from them. Directed by Wes Craven, the horror movie relies on graphic gore, sexual references and images of uncaring parents for the purpose of eliciting shock and irreverent humor

title: Nightmare On Elm Street, Part 2: Freddy's Revenge, A
synopsis: Foiled in the original, the slashing monster returns in this sequel, directed by Jack Sholder, to again take possession of a teenager so that he can do some further cutting up. More blood and gore mixed with sexual titillation aimed at teenagers

title: 'Night, Mother
synopsis: Static adaptation of Marsha Norman's bleak play in which an elderly woman (Anne Bancroft) spends an evening trying to talk her middle-aged daughter (Sissy Spacek) out of her decision to commit suicide. Directed by Tom Moore, the result is basically a photographed play in which the dialogue exchanges between the two wax and wane in emotional intensity, though some will find the situation rather muddled and less than convincing. Shifting arguments for and against suicide

title: Night Moves
synopsis: Gene Hackman plays a Los Angeles private eye who traces a 16-year-old runaway to Florida living with her stepfather and his mistress who are both involved in a smuggling operation. Director Arthur Penn's muddled, badly acted detective melodrama features some brutal murders and resorts to sexual exploitation, especially of the girl, to keep things moving

title: Night Must Fall
synopsis: Chilling suspense picture from the Emlyn Williams play in which a drifter (Robert Montgomery) charms a wealthy old lady (May Whitty) into giving him a job, until her secretary (Rosalind Russell) comes to suspect he is the one being sought by the police for a series of murders in the area. Directed by Richard Thorpe, the suspense mounts quite effectively in a taut story made convincing by Montgomery's compelling performance as a psycopathic killer. More menace than violence

title: Night Nurse
synopsis: Gritty crime melodrama in which the nurse (Barbara Stanwyck) assigned to home care for a sickly woman seeks help from another nurse (Joan Blondell), an honest doctor (Charles Winninger) and a friendly bootlegger (Ben Lyon) when she suspects something fishy is going on in a household dominated by a menacing chauffeur (Clark Gable). Director William A. Wellman keeps the proceedings light and breezy until the quick but nasty conclusion. Stylized violence, sexual innuendo and illicit substance abuse

title: Night of Bloody Horror
synopsis: Gross horror movie about a mother who mummifies dead members of the family and her manic-depressive son suspected of three sensational murders. Producer-director Joy N. Houck Jr., while suggesting these may have been cases of accidental fratricide and paternal suicide, concentrates on explicit lovemaking, ax-wielding, and quarts of blood-letting

title: Night of Counting the Years, The
