synopsis: Adaptation of Barry Unsworth's novel set on an Aegean island in 1908 where a Turkish spy (Ben Kingsley) comes under the spell of a fast-talking but secretive British archaeologist (Charles Dance). Director James Dearden slowly unfolds his plot of a man who has dealt so long in deceit that he ultimately cannot trust those who would save his life. Fleeting nudity and a bloody climax

title: Passage, The
synopsis: World War II story about a fiendish Nazi (Malcolm McDowell) who pursues an escaping scientist (James Mason) and his family across the Pyrenees where they get help from a stalwart Basque guide (Anthony Quinn). Mediocre British production directed by J. Lee Thompson, it is filled to excess with sadistic violence and brutality

title: Passage to India, A
synopsis: Screen version of the E.M. Forster classic about the inability of two diverse cultures to have any but perilous contact in the British-ruled India of the 1920s as seen in a story centering around a question of rape. Though painstakingly crafted by director David Lean and superbly acted by an outstanding cast (Judy Davis, Victor Banerjee, Dame Peggy Ashcroft, James Fox and Alec Guinness), the movie fails to dramatize convincingly the mysticism at the heart of its theme. Flawed but culturally rich entertainment

title: Passage West
synopsis: Tedious tale in which escaped convicts from a Utah prison hijack a wagon train of Christian homesteaders bound for California, but by trail's end the pioneer preacher (Dennis O'Keefe) has transformed the convict's leader (John Payne). Writer-director Lewis R. Foster stages a potentially interesting situation in unconvincing fashion with a gold-strike ending that's pure hokum. Stylized violence and minor romantic complications

title: Passed Away
synopsis: Ensemble comedy concerns the reunion of a bickering Irish-American family (Pamela Reed, Bob Hoskins, William Petersen and Frances McDormand) upon the sudden death of their father (Jack Warden). Writer-director Charlie Peters turns in a fitfully funny movie whose one-dimensional characters are entirely predictable. Frequent sexual innuendo and an instance of rough language

title: Passenger 57
synopsis: Standard action yarn pits a ruthless British terrorist (Bruce Payne) against an airline security expert (Wesley Snipes) onboard a hijacked L-1011 as the lives of 200 passengers hang in the balance. Director Kevin Hooks delivers a fast-moving, somewhat muddled plot in which violence is an inevitable but not unduly glamorized ingredient. Much menace with frequent violence and some rough language

title: Passengers
synopsis: Low-key, somewhat muddled thriller in which an uptight therapist (Anne Hathaway) counsels the few survivors of a major plane crash, investigating why their memories of the accident conflict with the airline's account. As some of them start to disappear, one, an extroverted passenger (Patrick Wilson), initiates a romance. Despite appealing performances from its leads and a welcome subplot about family reconciliation and the enduring influence of loved ones, director Rodrigo Garcia's drama mostly fails to engage. Nongraphic premarital sexual activity, brief partial rear nudity, occasional crude and crass language, some innuendo and disturbing accident scenes; acceptable for older teens

title: Passenger, The
synopsis: Polish production about two women who meet by accident on an ocean liner, triggering memories of their days in a concentration camp together: one a Nazi officer, the other a prisoner. Both stories are related subjectively in flashback and their differing perspectives become both fascinating and disturbing. Although director Andrej Munk died before the movie's completion, what he did accomplish are brilliant fragments in a compelling exploration of human motivation and justification

title: Passenger, The
synopsis: Empty Italian drama in which a TV journalist (Jack Nicholson), exasperated by an assignment in North Africa and acting on impulse, switches passport photos with a European who dies of a heart attack and finds that he has assumed the identity of an international gun runner. Director Michelangelo Antonioni has made a visually stunning work, yet its plot contrivances are more irritating than mysterious and its delving into the interior of its characters is without interest

title: Passing Glory
synopsis: Fact-based story of a black priest (Andre Braugher) in 1965 New Orleans who perseveres in his efforts to arrange a match between his all-black high school's basketball team and the top city team from an all-white school. Directed by Steve James, the TV dramatization effectively depicts the era's racial tensions and the priest's frustration over the injustices of segregation, with the drama of its sports story scoring a moral victory for racial equality. Stylized violence, considerable menace and some coarse language

title: Passion
synopsis: When the Mexican authorities refuse to arrest the gang who murdered his family in Old California, a 19th-century ranchero (Cornel Wilde) sets out on his own to bring them to justice, with a little help from the sister (Yvonne De Carlo) of his dead bride. Directed by Allan Dwan, the formula plot and stereotyped characters are enlivened by some good action sequences and the colorful Hispanic settings. Stylized violence and a common law marriage

title: Passionada
synopsis: Sweet romance set in a New England Portuguese-American fishing community where a former card shark (Jason Isaacs) lies about his past to the devout widow (Sofia Milos) he has fallen for even as her daughter (Emmy Rossum) insists he teach her card counting in exchange for encouraging her mom to date him. Director Dan Ireland blends humor and torch songs into a modestly charming tale of second chances and love's healing powers. An implied affair. A-III � adults. (PG-13) 2003 Full Review A former card cheat tries to win the heart of a devout widow with a little help from her enterprising daughter in the modestly charming romance, "Passionada " (Goldwyn). The setting is the largely Catholic, Portuguese-American fishing community in New Bedford, Mass., where beautiful Celia (Sofia Milos), her precocious teen daughter Vicky (Emmy Rossum) and her wary mother-in-law (Lupe Ontiveros) all live under the same roof. Since her fisherman husband's accidental death seven years earlier, Celia has closed her heart to romance, sewing in a factory by day yet singing impassioned love songs in her native Portuguese at a local dinner club. One night, Brit Charlie (Jason Isaacs) catches her act and is completely smitten by the sensuous chanteuse. She is frosty to his pickup lines afterward, but he is persistent. Enlisting the advice of her daughter by reluctantly agreeing to teach Vicky card-counting tricks, Charlie lies to Celia that he is a wealthy ex-pat interested in opening a fishing concern -- and gradually wears down her resistance. But their love affair seems doomed since it is based on lies unless Charlie transforms himself and wins Celia's forgiveness. Director Dan Ireland brings out the humanity of the script's characters in ways that make one overlook the movie's foregone conclusion. Celia has mourned her husband for many years but now needs to open her heart to love and get on with her life. When she discovers Vicky has been gone overnight -- unaware that Vicky has been trying out her newfound gambling skills at an all-night casino -- she rages at her daughter, who is hurt that her mother has wrongly assumed she lost her virginity. Providing soothing words of wisdom is the grandmother, who serves as a bridge of reconciliation. Charlie, washed up as a card cheat, doesn't seem to realize he is at a crossroads, but finding love enables him to reform in a rather pat happy ending that brings everyone full circle -- and presumes that Vicky has ditched her gambling ways as well. One gets a sense of the Catholic community of the setting, at Mass, the Blessed Sacrament Festival and pierside blessings, especially the Portuguese immigrants whose livelihoods remain tethered to the sea. The fiery renditions of plaintive fado music (by Portugal's Misia) add an uncommon touch as well to a formula romantic plot. Leisurely paced and essentially sweet-natured, "Passionada" blends humorous touches with torch songs for a family-centered romantic comedy with its heart in the right place. Because of an implied affair, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting

Because of an implied affair, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Passion Fish
synopsis: A former TV soap opera star (Mary McDonnell), embittered by an accident that left her a paraplegic, is cared for by a no-nonsense nurse (Alfre Woodard) who is secretly battling her own demons. Writer-director John Sayles' intimate portrait of the anguished, interior struggles of two women is unsentimental and affecting when not bogged down by its sleepy pace. An implied sexual encounter and intermittent rough language

title: Passion of Anna, The
synopsis: Swedish production about a human cipher (Max von Sydow), living hermit-like on a small island, who becomes friendly with a cynical architect (Erland Josephson), his wife (Bibi Andersson), and their close friend, Anna (Liv Ullmann). Eventually he and Anna share their loneliness and then part even more hopeless than when they first met. Director Ingmar Bergman's bleak vision of people unable to find salvation from existential despair questions the meaning of life. A suicide and brief shots of mutilated animals combined with the moral ambiguity of the brief affair make this adult fare

title: Passion of Joan of Arc, The
synopsis: Silent screen masterpiece portraying the heresy trial, confession, recantation and execution of the Maid of Orleans (Maria Falconetti) in a performance of such emotional power that it still stands as the most convincing portrayal of spirituality on celluloid. Directed by Carl Dreyer, the work is essentially the interior epic of a soul, consisting largely of close-ups of Joan's face and those of her interrogators accomplished in a fashion which is never static as the camera explores the inner struggle between human frailities and spiritual strength. Some duplicitous churchmen, medicinal bloodletting and a restrained torture scene

title: Passover Plot, The
synopsis: Dramatization of a book by biblical archaeologist Hugh J. Schonfield presents Jesus as a good and pious man who believed himself to be the Messiah but his plan to fake his death by Roman crucifixion failed, leaving his disciples to invent the story of his resurrection. Directed by Michael Campos, the movie is deeply flawed in narrative construction, acting and production values but many Christians will find its muddled attempt to demythologize the Gospels repugnant

title: Passport to Pimlico
synopsis: Upon learning that a medieval document found in a World War II bomb crater makes London's Pimlico district a part of Burgundy, the residents (led by Stanley Holloway, Margaret Rutherford and Hermione Baddeley) promptly form their own governent, declare an end to post-war rationing and enter into negotiations with the British Foreign Office. Scripted by T.E.B. Clarke and directed by Henry Cornelius, the scenario takes matters to hilarious extremes as Whitehall diplomacy is outwitted by the spunky tactics of beleagured Pimlico in a delightful comedy of ordinary folk showing up the weaknesses of officialdom

title: Pastime
synopsis: Old-fashioned sports story set in the mid-1950s when an over-the-hill minor league baseball pitcher (William Russ) befriens an insecure black rookie (Glenn Plummer) ignored by his teammates. Directed by Robin B. Armstrong, the heartwarming if simplistic story of black and white heroes and villains is soft on dramatic tension but strong on sentiment and values. Brief fisticuffs and a veiled sexual reference

title: Pat and Mike
synopsis: Offbeat romantic comedy teams veteran sports promoter Mike (Spencer Tracy) with top amateur athlete Pat (Katharine Hepburn) who's aces in any competition except when her beau (William Ching) is watching. Directed by George Cukor, it's Hepburn's picture with Tracy cheering her on as she goes through her winning paces, including a scene in which Pat saves Mike from two thugs. Feminist twist on the battle of the sexes

title: Patch Adams
synopsis: Fact-based comedy-drama about an idealistic medical student (Robin Williams) whose belief in the healing power of humor leads him to risk dismissal from medical school by opening a non-traditional clinic. Director Tom Shadyac's unsubtle treatment of the unabashedly sentimental story is held together mainly by Williams' ingratiating performance and his character's appealing concept of holistic medicine. An offscreen violent tragedy, fleeting nudity and a few coarse words as well as double entendres

title: Patch of Blue, A
synopsis: A blind girl (Elizabeth Hartman), living in a dismal tenement, falls in love with the gentle black neighbor (Sidney Poitier) who befriends her, despite the shrill opposition of her mother (Shelley Winters). Director Guy Green takes an honest look at racial relations, avoids most of the obvious cliches and scores some points for human values. Mature theme

title: Paternity
synopsis: Callous egomaniac (Burt Reynolds) decides he wants a son and interviews prospective surrogate mothers. Beverly D'Angelo, a musician working as a waitress, gets the job and foolishly falls in love with the boor. Directed by David Steinberg, the ill-conceived romantic plot results in a slack and listless comedy of sexual politics with a false female stereotype and some rough language

title: Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid
synopsis: The story of Garret (James Coburn), in the hire of ruthless cattlemen, tracking down his old saddle mate Billy (Kris Kristofferson) is intended to show the slow passing of the Western frontier in the 1880s. The end result is a ponderous and depressing study of men whose time has past. It's a familiar theme for director Sam Peckinpah who, once again, cannot resist graphic depictions of blood-spattered killings and various characters' rough use of women

title: Pathfinder
synopsis: Relentlessly violent tale about a shipwrecked Viking lad taken in and raised by a Native American tribe, until 15 years later when now as an adult he (Karl Urban) sets out, virtually single-handedly, to exact revenge on returning Vikings who have slaughtered his adopted tribe and are bent on killing every other tribe in their path so as to lay claim to the land. Director Marcus Nispel's video gamelike movie eschews character development as well as narrative logic in a drawn-out series of brutal beheadings, impalements and eviscerations that overwhelm the intriguing premise of the legendary Norsemen arriving on American shores many centuries before Columbus. Excessive violence and gore
full_review:
Legend has it that half a millennium before Christopher Columbus arrived on our shores, the Vikings did. Of course, for thousands of years beforehand, Native Americans had already called this country home.

In a series of increasingly violent encounters, "Pathfinder" (Fox) attempts to capture the clash between the brutally marauding Norsemen and their prey: tribes of East Coast Wampanoag Indians.

The film starts out promisingly as a Native American woman discovers a Viking shipwreck whose sole survivor is a young blond boy taken in by the initially wary tribe and raised to manhood.

Fifteen years later, Ghost (Karl Urban), as he's now called, is still troubled by sketchy memories of his Viking kinfolk on killing sprees and bears ragged scars on his back for having refused to partake in their gleeful bloodshed.

But this insight is the extent of character development in what amounts to a violent video gamelike movie, courtesy of director Marcus Nispal.

Once the young man returns from a hunting trip to find the Vikings have come back and slaughtered his entire tribe, the movie descends into a straightforward revenge flick. He warns the other tribes, with their inferior bows and arrows, to flee. This includes Pathfinder (Russell Means), a revered shaman, and his daughter Starfire (Moon Bloodgood), who loves the young man and secretly follows him to confront the Vikings.

The Norsemen, indistinguishable from one another in their fearful horned helmets and facial armor, are uniformly and viciously evil. The Native Americans by contrast are all courageously righteous. It remains for Ghost to face down and butcher scores of better-armed warriors. Hardly credible.

Yet credit must be given for the impressive, wintry visuals which capture a nation of, as yet, spectacularly unspoiled natural beauty and a stunning avalanche scene which figures into the plot.

However, the legendary -- if not historical -- aspects of the story are overwhelmed by the unrelenting scenes of gory decapitations, impalings and eviscerations that fuel this shallow salute to murderous revenge.

The film contains excessive violence and gore. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Pathfinder, The
synopsis: James Fenimore Cooper's title character (George Montgomery) offers to guide a French force in the American wilderness of 1754 in order to betray them to the English. Director Sidney Solkow's low-budget effort turns the frontier into the usual stereotyped entertainment, however with notably unconvincing action scenes. Stylized violence

title: Paths of Glory
synopsis: The terrible slaughter of World War I is re-created in this fact-based story of a French colonel (Kirk Douglas) who tries to save his men from being court-martialed for cowardice in a failed attack that should never have been ordered. Director Stanley Kubrick's anti-war classic contrasts the horrors of trench warfare at the front with the indifference and incompetence of the generals (Adolphe Menjou and George Macready) safely quartered in the rear. Graphic battlefield violence and a harrowing execution by firing squad

title: Patrick
synopsis: Tacky little thriller from Australia about a young man (Robert Thompson) who, while being kept alive on a support system, develops a "seventh sense" that enables him to perform all sorts of disgusting stunts when he becomes attached to a pretty nurse (Susan Penhaligon). Directed by Richard Franklin, it is a painful experience in every respect, with violence and a graphic depiction of some alleged medical techniques

title: Patriot Games
synopsis: Suspenseful thriller from Tom Clancy's novel about an ex-CIA agent (Harrison Ford) who returns to the fold to protect his wife and child (Anne Archer and Thora Birch) from a revenge-crazed IRA terrorist (Sean Bean). Director Phillip Noyce rivets attention on the family's vulnerability but doesn't shield viewers from brutal terrorist executions and violent shootouts. Much violence, a brief bedroom scene and minimal rough language

title: Patsy, The
synopsis: After a famous comedian dies in an accident, his staff (John Carradine, Peter Lorre, Everett Sloane, Keenan Wynn and Ina Balin) decide to turn a hotel bellboy (Jerry Lewis) into his successor. Also written and directed by Lewis, the slack plot and klutzy slapstick action can only appeal to fans of the star's goonish brand of comedy. Mild slapstick violence

title: Patterns
synopsis: Thoughtful drama in which a callous corporation head (Everett Sloane) tries to force an aging executive (Ed Begley) to retire by bringing in a younger man (Van Heflin), but the newcomer has his own ideas about what's best for the company. Adapted by Rod Serling from his teleplay and directed by Fielder Cook, the result is a credible picture of conflict in the executive suite as corporate greed and bottom-line policies are challenged by a more human style of business management. Unlikely fare for children

title: Patterns of Power
synopsis: ( see: "Patterns" )

title: Patti Rocks
synopsis: Boring, pretentious and ultimately repellent movie in which a married clod (Chris Mulkey) cajoles a friend (John Jenkins) into joining him in trying to persuade his pregnant, out-of-town girlfriend to have an abortion. Director David Burton Morris takes an interminable car ride with two foul-mouthed sexists that finally ends with a romp in the girlfriend's bed. Unremittingly rough language and simulated sex

title: Patton
synopsis: George C. Scott's complex portrayal of World War II General George S. Patton conveys a paradoxical, multifaceted character whose love of the fray and intense will to win was grounded in a deep-seated hatred of war itself. Director Franklin Schaffner's powerful dramatization is neither a glorification of war nor an anti-war tract but pays homage to a career officer who, unfortunately, could only achieve his destiny in wartime. Violence and profanity within a realistic context

title: Patty Hearst
synopsis: The 1974 kidnapping of heiress Patty Hearst (Natasha Richardson) from her Berkeley campus apartment by the Symbionese Liberation Army is told from her point of view in an intense docudrama directed by Paul Schrader. Richardson's mesmerizing performance conveys the brutality and brainwashing Hearst had to endure. Much conscienceless violence, a continuing sense of menace and wall-to-wall profanity

title: Paul
synopsis: Aggressively, though illogically, anti-religious satire from director Greg Mottola in which two sci-fi-loving British visitors to the United States (Simon Pegg and Nick Frost) help the alien of the title (voice of Seth Rogen) escape government custody. The trio then embark on a road trip to the spot where his fellow extraterrestrials can rescue him. They're joined, along the way, by a fundamentalist Christian (Kristen Wiig) whose entire worldview is instantly shattered by the spaceman's very existence, freeing her to swear, smoke dope and fornicate at will, since there is no God and therefore no sin. In penning the script for this otherwise routine buddy comedy, Pegg and Frost prove themselves as unfamiliar with Judeo-Christian beliefs as they are contemptuous of them, since they assume that scriptural faith would be fatally undermined by the presence of intelligent life on other planets. Explicit rejection of Christian faith and morals, endorsement of homosexual acts, nonmarital sexual activity and petty theft, benign view of drug use, occasional gory violence, a few uses of profanity, pervasive rough and crude language

title: Paula
synopsis: Soggy tearjerker in which the barren wife (Loretta Young) of a college professor (Kent Smith) accidentally runs down a young orphan (Thomas Rettig) leaving him unable to speak but, with the help of her doctor (Alexander Knox), she adopts the mute boy and teaches him to speak again. Directed by Rudolph Mate, the melodramatic contrivances keep getting in the way of Young's showy display of surface emotion. Delicate treatment of infertility and a youth's protracted trauma

title: Paul and Michelle
synopsis: Noxious sequel to "Friends" returns to the perils of Paul (Sean Bury) who finds Michelle (Anicee Alvina) living with their young daughter and an understanding American (Keir Dullea). They fly off to Paris to resume their lives in a morass of sickly-sweet dialogue, carefully photographed nudity, Michelle's abortion of the American's baby and Paul's fat allowance being cut off by Daddy and they separate yet again. Directed by Lewis Gilbert, it is sheer exploitation without pretense of moral perspective

title: Paul Blart: Mall Cop
synopsis: Largely good-natured slapstick comedy relies on the physicality of Kevin James, who, in addition to co-writing the script, portrays the titular plus-size security guard defending a New Jersey mall from a pack of acrobatic thieves on the busiest shopping day of the year. Because the loveably hapless hero embodies numerous qualities infrequently championed on-screen nowadays -- including chivalry, diligence and honesty -- any moderately untoward moments in director Steve Carr's effort are eclipsed by a positive message concerning respect for those not usually deemed successful or attractive, particularly those who don't fit the ideal body mold in our looks-conscious society. Frequent violence of a slapstick nature, some suggestive humor, several instances of crude and crass language, and one sequence involving alcohol use
full_review:
Chivalry is not dead. At least not inside New Jersey's West Orange Pavilion Mall.

The lovably hapless hero of the largely good-natured slapstick comedy "Paul Blart: Mall Cop" (Columbia) embodies many other qualities infrequently championed on-screen nowadays. They include honesty, diligence and respect. And because he exhibits genuine concern for those, like himself, who don't fit the ideal body mold in our looks-conscious society, the pratfall-stuffed "Blart" overcomes a few moderately untoward moments, mostly attributable to sexual innuendo, and affirms a positive message.

Kevin James' flair for physical humor and appetite for self-deprecation carry the project. In addition to co-writing the screenplay, he stars as the titular plus-size security guard who valiantly defends his workplace from a pack of acrobatic thieves on the busiest shopping day of the year.

Having sworn a private oath to protect everyone who steps foot inside this suburban retail mecca, Paul takes his job much more seriously than shoppers take him, or than his colleagues take their duties. He patrols on a Segway, acting officiously yet with everyone's safety uppermost in mind.

His chief flaw is hypoglycemia, which is really just an excuse for using food to self-medicate -- or, as he puts it, "fill the cracks of the heart." Paul's body shows the effects of his habit of ingesting sugar whenever he's tense; and he's constantly battling the assumption he's a loser because he's heavy.

Depressed after failing the physical fitness portion of the state police exam for the eighth time, Paul is consoled at the outset by his mother (Shirley Knight) and a slab of pie smeared with peanut butter. We learn that his wife was an illegal alien who married him to secure citizenship and then took off, leaving him to raise their daughter, Maya (Raini Rodriguez). She and her grandmother want Paul to be happy and urge him to find a girlfriend. They even register him on an Internet dating site.

But he has a crush on Amy (Jayma Mays), a new employee who sells hair extensions at one of the mall's kiosks, "Unbeweaveable." Paul's fumbling attempts to court her are sunk during a night out with other mall workers when he gets embarrassingly inebriated.

His chance to prove his worthiness comes a few days later, on Black Friday, the busiest shopping day of the year. A gang with extreme-sports skills -- portrayed by actual skateboarders, bikers and athletes from the X-Games -- overruns the mall and takes hostages. Their quarry is $30 million worth of credit-card information.

Although "Paul Blart: Mall Cop" never stops making fun of its protagonist and, by implication, all those of ample girth, it's not especially mean or vulgar. Director Steve Carr's effort is not riotously funny or a sterling piece of craftsmanship either, but its faults can be overlooked given this salubrious lesson: Accept who you are, while always trying to improve yourself. A good tagline for the movie would be a request Paul makes of Amy midway through, "Don't write me off."

The film contains frequent violence of a slapstick nature, some suggestive humor, several instances of crude and crass language, and one sequence involving alcohol use. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested. Some material may not be suitable for children.

title: Paulie
synopsis: Frail comedy follows the mischievous misadventures of a wisecracking parrot (voice of Jay Mohr) who criss-crosses the country in search of the little girl who first owned him. Director John Roberts surrounds the talkative bird with good-hearted people (including Gena Rowlands and Tony Shalhoub) and one cardboard villain (Bruce Davison) in a sweet, colorful story of modest appeal. A rude expression and a muttered instance of profanity

title: Pauline at the Beach
synopsis: French comedy about six oddly assorted lovers and would-be-lovers who pursue and flee one another at a seaside resort in Brittany in late summer while talking endlessly about the nature of love. As with director Eric Rohmer's better movies, it is never dull, never less than diverting, but is satisfied with clever surfaces rather than underlying meaning. Extremely mature subject matter

title: Pavilion of Women
synopsis: Lushly photographed melodrama adapted from the Pearl S. Buck novel set in 1938 China where a middle-aged wife (Luo Yan) gifts her brutish husband with an innocent concubine whom her son (John Cho) comes to love, even as the wife and an American missionary (Willem Dafoe) struggle with mutual feelings of love. Director Yim Ho contrasts East-West cultures against the backdrop of imminent Japanese invasion in a romanticized depiction of broken vows leading to heroic redemption. Brief wartime violence and numerous but discreetly handled sexual situations. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Pawnbroker, The
synopsis: Holocaust survivor (Rod Steiger) runs a pawnshop in Harlem where his past experiences of oppression are intermingled with the present realities facing the oppressed inhabitants of a black ghetto. Directed by Sidney Lumet, the movie proves a powerful, effective parable on human solidarity and the painful consequences of injutice. Mature theme and treatment

title: Pawnee
synopsis: Western tale of a white youth who's raised as the son of a Pawnee chief (George Montgomery), then has an identity crisis when a wagon train of settlers is attacked by some of his fellow braves. Directed by George Waggner, the situation of a man caught between two worlds offers interesting possibilites but the personal conflict is secondary to the plot's superficial action. Frontier violence

title: Payback
synopsis: Violent action movie in which a thief (Mel Gibson), cheated of his share of a heist and left for dead, survives to return for the money, murdering one and all who get in the way of his revenge mission. Director Brian Hegeland depicts sadistic violence in a jokey fashion that suggests the killer is a supercool hero for ending up with the booty, a blonde and a batch of bodies underfoot. Numerous brutal beatings and killings, sado-maschistic sexual situations, drug abuse, intermittent profanity and much rough language

title: Paycheck
synopsis: Forgettable sci-fi action thriller about a high-tech wizard (Ben Affleck) who, after working on a top-secret project for a shadowy corporation (run by Aaron Eckhart), has the past three years of his memory erased, only to find himself in the cross hairs of federal agents and corporate assassins, with just an envelope full of everyday items as clues to piecing together the puzzle of his past, which he deciphers with the help of a beautiful scientist (Uma Thurman) to whom he learns he is engaged. Despite an intriguing premise based on a story by cyber-pulp icon Philip K. Dick which explores the consequences of technology unfettered by morality, the film, directed by John Woo, never kicks into gear thanks primarily to its miscast lead, lackluster action sequences and preposterous plot twists which test viewers' suspension of disbelief to the breaking point. Don't waste your paycheck. Recurring action violence and brief crude language
full_review:
It is apropos that the best word to describe "Paycheck" (Paramount), John Woo's new sci-fi action thriller about a high-tech genius with a memory lapse problem, is "forgettable." Despite an intriguing premise based on a story by cyber-pulp icon Philip K. Dick, the film never kicks into gear thanks to its miscast lead, uncharacteristically rote direction by Woo, and preposterous plot twists which test the suspension of disbelief generally accorded the genre.

Ben Affleck stars as hired tinker Michael Jennings, an engineering wizard who specializes in pirating cutting-edge technology before it hits the market and selling it -- usually in an upgraded form -- to competing corporations. After each hush-hush job he has his brain scanned and any memories associated with the project systematically erased to prevent him from divulging company secrets.

Though well paid for his services, Jennings agrees to the ever-fateful "one last job," offered by a reptilian corporate honcho named Rethrick (Aaron Eckhart), which will set him up comfortably for life to the tune of $92 million. The only catch is that this job involves Orwellian technology so supersecret that it will cost Jennings three years of his life, and consequently three years worth of memories.

Upon successfully completing his mission, Jennings comes out of the memory deletion process only to learn that in addition to forfeiting his eight-digit paycheck -- for reasons he can't remember, of course -- he is now a target in the cross hairs of federal agents (who accuse him of stealing experimental government technology) as well as a squad of Rethrick's assassins.

Without any recollections of the intervening three years, Jennings, who for some unexplained reason is also proficient in hand-to-hand combat skills, must piece together his past using only an envelope of innocuous items (including a paper clip and a transit card) which he had the foresight to mail to himself, and which serve as a bread-crumb trail through the narrative's labyrinthine maze of plot twists. Assisting him in putting the jigsaw puzzle together is a beautiful biologist (Uma Thurman) at Rethrick's think tank, to whom Jennings discovers he is engaged to be married.

Much of the allure of Dick's futuristic flights of fancy is his ability to ground his stories in the real and the identifiable. Many of the more successful screen re-imaginings of Dick's works -- such as "Minority Report" (2002), "Total Recall" (1990) and "Blade Runner" (1982) -- involve ordinary characters entangled in extraordinary circumstances, and usually tackle big, philosophical questions like "What is it to be human?" and "What is free will?" Yet, while "Paycheck" follows suit, exploring the Promethean consequences of technology unfettered by ethics, the moral dimensions are not integrated into the narrative as well as in the aforementioned Dick-inspired films.

As witnessed in "Sum of All Fears" (2002) and "Daredevil" (2003), Affleck proves once again that, while possessing a likable charm, he is unconvincing as the heroic lead -- though after his "Gigli" debacle (a memory all would gladly have erased) his credibility as a romantic lead is equally dubious. Thurman matches Affleck's mediocrity splendidly. In addition to Eckhart, the talents of Paul Giamatti, Colm Feore and Michael C. Hall are wasted on cameos and plot-placeholder roles.

Woo, who can usually get by with a shaky narrative by dazzling viewers with his superstylized action sequences, seems to have directed this one on autopilot, with its tedious parade of the uninspired shootouts and chases lacking any trace of his signature visual flair. The film does offer some brief clever moments involving the brainy Jennings using his noggin to thwart his pursuers, but they are few and far between and ultimately subsumed by the filmmaker's predisposition to pyrotechnics.

By the end credits, viewers may be lining up to have the previous two hours erased from their memory. Word to the wise -- don't waste your paycheck.

Due to recurring action violence and brief crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Payday
synopsis: Gritty study of second-rate Country-Western singer (Rip Torn) whose career has peaked without his even knowing it, and whose life is about to go right over the edge in a series of one-night stands, cheap motel rooms, good bourbon, popped uppers and downers and a ragged assortment of groupies and hangers-on. Director Daryl Duke's picture of the tormented, self-destructive anti-hero on a lonesome road with nothing at the end has the tragic sense of reality. Some rough language and brief nudity

title: Pay It Forward
synopsis: Poignant drama about an 11-year-old boy (Haley Joel Osment) whose classroom assignment to change the world blossoms into an altruistic movement with far reaching results including bringing together his alcoholic mother (Helen Hunt) and his facially disfigured teacher (Kevin Spacey). As directed by Mimi Leder, the film's exemplary message and admirable performances are undermined by an overly sentimental script. Some sexual situations, brief violence, some profanity and crass language

title: Payment in Blood
synopsis: Dreary Italian Western set right after the Civil War when disbanded military freebooters (led by Guy Madison) terrorized the Southwest. Director E.G. Rowland's badly-staged violence and even worse acting is a tiresome bore

title: PCU
synopsis: Witless, brain-dead comedy about a politically correct university whose shrewish president (Jessica Walter) overlooks protesting radical groups while seeking to expel a party-minded pack of students (led by Jeremy Piven) plotting her downfall. Instead of topical satire, director Hart Bochner has little to offer but a feeble collection of sophomoric students and their lame shenanigans. Fleeting violence, some sexual references, brief recreational drug use and an instance of rough language

title: Peace Killers, The
synopsis: Brutal motorcycle gang makes war on a commune of peaceful pot-smokers when one of the gang's women trades in her backseat on a cycle for a snug little sleeping bag at the commune. Directed by Douglas Schwartz, the resulting reprisals would make grown men blanch at scenes of utter brutality, torture, gang rape, and general mayhem

title: Peacemaker, The
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Ted Post in which a gunslinger-turned-parson (James Mitchell) relies on the Bible rather than bullets to avert a land war between ranchers and homesteaders by unmasking the railroad agent (Herbert Patterson) behind the conflict. Frontier violence

title: Peacemaker, The
synopsis: Frantic thriller teams an aggressive military intelligence agent (George Clooney) with a nuclear physicist (Nicole Kidman) in tracking stolen nukes across continents until they come face-to-face with a madman intent on setting off a doomsday bomb in midtown Manhattan. Director Mimi Leder packs the rushed narrative with car chases and shoot-em-ups, resulting in an emotionally sterile story of bogus thrills. Frequent violence, intermittent rough language and a few instances of profanity

title: Peach Thief
synopsis: Disappointing Bulgarian import tells a World War I story about a frustrated young wife (Nevena Kokanova) who has a foredoomed affair with a Serbian prisoner-of-war (Rade Markovich). The meager and predictable story lacks individuality and human resonance

title: Pearl Harbor
synopsis: Hollow drama set against the 1941 Japanese surprise attack on Pearl Harbor in which two pilots (Ben Affleck, Josh Hartnett) fall in love with the same woman (Kate Beckinsale). Flashy pyrotechnics are the centerpiece of director Michael Bay's prolonged action extravaganza whose cardboard characters, corny dialogue and contrived narrative only superficially captures the human tragedy of warfare. An intense, sustained war sequence, an implied sexual encounter, occasional profanity and intermittent crass language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Pearl of Death, The
synopsis: Updated version of Conan Doyle's "The Six Napoleons" with Sherlock Holmes (Basil Rathbone) and Dr. Watson (Nigel Bruce) out to retrieve the fabled Borgia Pearl from a master criminal (Miles Mander) and devious accomplice (Evelyn Ankers). Directed by Roy William Neill, the mystery has some dandy twists, not least a monstrous killer (Rondo Hatton) who breaks the backs of his victims' as well as their china bric-a-brac. Fairly intense for young children

title: Pearl of the South Pacific
synopsis: Turgid tale directed by Allan Dwan follows a greedy trio (Virginia Mayo, Dennis Morgan and David Farrar) to a remote island in search of black pearls but the natives kill one of them and convert the other two to their happy way of life. Stylized violence, romantic complications and idealized island paradise

title: Pebble and the Penguin, The
synopsis: Amiable animated tale in which a stuttering, lovestruck penguin (voice of Martin Short) seeks, with the grudging aid of a resourceful pal (voice of James Belushi), to return to his true love (voice of Annie Golden) after being tossed into the churning sea by a romantic rival (voice of Tim Curry). The Don Bluth production is a peppy, colorful treat for pre-schoolers though adults may not be as engaged by the thin story and routine music numbers by Barry Manilow

title: Pecker
synopsis: Generally sweet-natured satire about a Baltimore amateur photographer (Edward Furlong) whose sudden discovery by the New York art world brings intrusive, unwanted limelight to his working-class family and girlfriend (Christina Ricci) and prompts him to turn his back on fame and fortune. Writer-director John Waters' skimpy tale tosses innocent characters into raunchy settings with carefree abandon calculated to amuse more than offend, but the comic returns are slight. A discreet sexual encounter, striptease scene with fleeting nudity, indulgent treatment of shoplifting, comically intended use of a religious statue, occasional rough language and minimal profanity

title: Peck's Bad Boy
synopsis: Sentimental tale directed by Edward F. Cline in which a "regular" young lad (Jackie Cooper) runs away from home after his nasty aunt (Dorothy Peterson) comes for an extended visit and her mean son reveals the boy was adopted as a baby by his beloved widower dad (Thomas Meighan). Dated treatment but still of interest for young viewers

title: Pedestrian, The
synopsis: Demanding German drama about an aging industrialist (Gustav Rudolf Sellner) who is tortured by guilt and the fear that his secret crime as a Nazi officer responsible for an atrocity is about to be made public because of the digging and sifting into the incident by a German news magazine. Director Maximilian Schell questions what might be called a moral statute of limitations in his complex probing of personal and collective guilt. Strong subject not for casual moviegoers

title: Pee Wee's Big Adventure
synopsis: Comic personality Pee Wee Herman's search for his stolen bike takes him on a madcap chase from the Alamo in Texas to Hollywood. Directed by Tim Burton, the humor is puerile with occasional slapstick violence

title: Peggy Sue Got Married
synopsis: A middle-aged mom (Kathleen Turner), about to be divorced from her unfaithful husband (Nicolas Cage), relives her past when she faints at a class reunion and discovers that the person she was and has become are one and the same. Director Francis Ford Coppola carefully controls the sentimental romanticism inherent in this story showing the continuum of values through the course of an individual's life. Brief scene of lovemaking and some coarse language

title: Pelican Brief, The
synopsis: With her life in grave danger after figuring out who was behind the assassination of two Supreme Court justices, a New Orleans law student (Julia Roberts) turns to a investigative reporter (Denzel Washington) to get her incriminating brief in print. Abetted by exceptional performances from a fine supporting cast, director Alan J. Pakula's spiky thriller maintains suspense despite a convoluted plot. Some restrained violence and an instance of rough language

title: Pelle the Conqueror
synopsis: Unsentimental Danish production follows a turn-of-the-century elderly widower (Max von Sydow) and his young son (Pelle Hvenegaard) from their arrival on Danish shores in search of a better life to their many hardships as stablehands on a farm. Directed by Bille August, this is long and grim, but imbued with a strong feel for the landscape and low level of humanity on the farm as well as the life-sustaining love of a father for his young son. Subtitles. Brief, graphic images implying the results of incest, infanticide and castration, some violence and vulgar language

title: Pendulum
synopsis: George Peppard, Jean Seberg and Richard Kiley star in a fast-paced crime thriller about a dedicated cop (Peppard) who within the space of a few weeks finds himself on both sides of the issues surrounding civil rights of accused criminals. With strong performances and fine location photography of the nation's capital, director George Schaefer's work poses some tough questions about law enforcement and the justice system, providing enough material for viewers to draw their own conclusions

title: Penelope
synopsis: Likable romantic fairy tale about an otherwise beautiful London heiress (Christina Ricci) who, as the result of an ancestral curse, was born with a pig's snout and who, with the help of her domineering mother (Catherine O'Hara) and diffident father (Richard E. Grant) must avoid exposure by a tabloid reporter (Peter Dinklage) while searching for the man whose love can lift the spell, the two main candidates being an upper-class twit (Simon Woods) and a warm-hearted musician (James McAvoy) with a gambling problem. Director Mark Palansky's film establishes its unlikely premise quite successfully and offers some valuable observations about skin-deep beauty and self-acceptance, but the plot lags in places and the groundwork for a convincing central relationship is never really completed. Occasional crass language and innuendo, and suicide and adultery references
full_review:
Penelope

Despite a few structural deficiencies, "Penelope" (Summit Entertainment) is overall a likeable romantic fairy tale that offers some valuable moral observations.

As the result of an ancestral curse, Penelope Wilhern (charmingly spunky Christina Ricci), an otherwise beautiful London heiress, was born with a pig's snout. Unable to find a cure, her domineering mother, Jessica (Catherine O'Hara), and diffident father, Franklin (Richard E. Grant), instead faked her early death to protect her from the paparazzi, and then raised her in comfortable isolation.

Since coming of age, Penelope, at Jessica's insistence, has been striving for the one remaining solution. According to the hex's terms, if she can get someone "of her own kind" to love her, the spell will be lifted.

The outcome, however, has been all too predictable. A succession of eligible, aristocratic young men have trooped to the Wilhern townhouse, taken a gander and fled. Restrained before they can escape the grounds, they are bribed into signing a nondisclosure agreement.

When upper-class twit Edward Vanderman Jr. (Simon Woods) gets away without signing, he goes to the nearest police station to report what he has seen. Mocked as a lunatic, he finds only one person willing to believe his story: a shady tabloid reporter named Lemon (Peter Dinklage) who once tried to photograph Penelope as a baby.

Edward and Lemon join forces and enlist the help of well-born but down-at-the-heels compulsive gambler Max Campion (James McAvoy), paying him to pose as a suitor in order to get a clandestine snapshot proving Edward's tale. Instead, of course, he gradually falls in love with Penelope, who converses with him through a one-way mirror and is equally smitten.

When Penelope finally reveals herself, Max's reaction is not what she had been hoping for, and the disappointment drives her to leave home, her lower face covered in a scarf. Welcomed at a pub Max had once praised, she is befriended by tough, talkative messenger Annie (Reese Witherspoon, co-producer of the film). As these two explore the city on Annie's Vespa, Penelope's parents are in hot pursuit. So too is Lemon.

Director Mark Palansky's film establishes its fanciful premise quite successfully and becomes an adept satire of contemporary society's obsession with skin-deep beauty as well as the eccentric nature of modern celebrity. The script also emphasizes the need for loving self-acceptance.

But the movie's plot lags in places and the necessary groundwork for a convincing central relationship between the two appealing leads is never really completed. "Penelope" is not quite the truffle it might have been.

The film contains occasional crass language and innuendo, and fleeting suicide and adultery references. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested. Some material may not be suitable for children.

title: Penguin Pool Murder, The
synopsis: The first in a comic mystery series teaming schoolmarm Hildegarde Withers (Edna May Oliver) with New York City police inspector Oscar Piper (James Gleason) in solving the murder of a stock broker found floating in the municipal aquarium's penguin tank. Directed by George Archainbaud, the case has some interesting suspects (Mae Clark, Robert Armstrong and Donald Cook) but the fun comes from the comic banter between the sharp teacher and tough cop who decide to wed in an ending forgotten in subsequent sequels. Stylized violence and implied love triangle

title: Penitentiary
synopsis: A young black (Leon Issac Kennedy), wrongly convicted and set to prison, takes up boxing and battles his way to vindication. The mediocre melodrama, written and directed by Jamaa Fanaka, provides an excessively graphic depiction of the corruption, brutality and homosexuality pervading prison life

title: Penitentiary II
synopsis: Young convict (Leon Isaac Kennedy) gains freedom and respectability by his boxing skills. Director Jamaa Fanaka's sequel, however, falls far short of the barely competent standards of the original. Repulsive, brutal mess with excessive violence

title: Penitentiary III
synopsis: A boxer (Leon Isaac Kennedy) fights his way out of a prison dominated by a wealthy degenerate inmate (Tony Geary) but can't overcome the nightmarish plot absurdities and writer-director Jamaa Fanaka's near farcical excesses of violence and brutality

title: Pennies from Heaven
synopsis: Comedian Steve Martin plays a straight role in this almost unqualified disaster. As an unsuccessful peddler of sheet music in the Depression era, Martin is beastly to women and takes refuge from harsh reality by imagining lavish Busby Berkley-style production numbers. Neither director Herbert Ross nor writer Dennis Potter seem to have any idea how to adapt the story and concept for a feature movie. Besides the amorality of the hero, the plot contains scenes dealing with prostitution and abortion

title: Penn of Pennsylvania
synopsis: ( see: "Courageous Mr. Penn" )

title: Penn & Teller Get Killed
synopsis: Pointless black comedy enmeshes the comic magicians Penn and Teller in a web of self-inspired practical jokes that become more and more macabre until they backfire and snuff them out. Directed by Arthur Penn, the school-boy gags involve lots of fake blood and grisly pranks. Cavalier attitude toward death and suicide, much profanity and some sexual innuendo

title: Penny Serenade
synopsis: Sentimental tale of a childless couple (Irene Dunne and Cary Grant) who adopt a baby girl, love her as their own, then are devastated by her sudden death six years later, leaving them tortured by grief and on the verge of divorce. Director George Stevens keeps the tragic story of adoptive parents from turning into a tearjerker by making their romance brightly believable and well-paced well with gentle humor, genuine emotions and some honest tears, all of which is put across by a fine cast. Domestic tensions

title: Penthouse, The
synopsis: Failed adaptation of a play by C. Scott Forbes in which two psycopaths keep a man (Terence Morgan) and his mistress (Suzy Kendall) prisoner in their penthouse apartment, the woman in the bedroom and the man tied to a chair. Director Peter Collinson's attempt to make a statement about hypocrisy and disillusionment fails because of its contrived and melodramatic treatment and becomes little more than a tiresome exercise in sadism

title: People Against O'Hara, The
synopsis: Aging lawyer who's a recovering alcoholic (Spencer Tracy) agrees to defend a neighborhood youth (James Arness) accused of murder but when the trial goes badly, he puts his career on the line by bribing a witness. Director John Sturges' slack courtroom drama is less interesting than Tracy's arresting portrayal of a faltering veteran doing his best for a client he knows is innocent. Legal complications involving a lawyer's unethical conduct

title: People I Know
synopsis: Disappointing thriller about a washed-up New York celebrity publicist (Al Pacino), unwittingly entangled in a deadly web of murder and deceit among Gotham's movers and shakers. Director Dan Algrant's noirish foray into the shadowy world of glamour and politics borrows generously from earlier conspiracy yarns, but flounders as a result of a disjointed, hackneyed narrative and an at-times-hammy lead performance. Minimal violence, recurring drug abuse, rough language and vulgarities as well as brief sexual images and fleeting nudity
full_review:
"People I Know" (Miramax) is a disappointing thriller about a washed-up celebrity publicist (Al Pacino) who finds himself a pawn in a dangerous game involving a murdered starlet -- a crime implicating members of New York's mover and shaker elite. Director Dan Algrant's noirish foray into Gotham's shadowy netherworld of glamour and politics is mired by a hackneyed, disjointed narrative and a lead performance that at times flirts close to hammy.

Eli Wurman (Pacino) is running on fumes. An old-school press agent, his once-impressive stable of celebrity clients has all flown the coop, leaving him hanging out to dry. He has watched the media parade he helped create pass him by through his cadaverous, sleep-deprived eyes, dulled by booze and designer pharmaceuticals. He survives on the graces of his last paying client, Cary Launer (Ryan O'Neal), a world-famous movie star with political aspirations.

At one point Wurman states that he has no soul, yet it is evident early on that he is the only character with any sense of moral conscience -- visually reinforced by the framed photos plastering his walls documenting his proclivity for social activism.

The trouble begins when Launer solicits a "favor" from Wurman, which loosely translated means cleaning up a mess -- more often than not, involving some dame. This particular mess requires posting bail for a pill-popping prima donna, Jilli Hopper (Tea Leoni). The fading flack, loath to bite the hand that feeds him, agrees to help Launer out of the jam, with one stipulation -- in return, Launer must make an appearance at a civil rights benefit Wurman is organizing -- a vestige from his freedom-marching glory days.

The floozy is sprung without a hitch. But afterward she demands they make a stop at a surreal floating opium den to retrieve her "toy" -- a scene straight out of Kubrick's "Eyes Wide Shut." Back at her hotel suite things get ugly. In a deadly turn of events Jilli is murdered, while, unbeknownst to her assassin, a semi-conscious Wurman watches, passed out in her bathroom. The crime is made to look like an overdose.

It doesn't take Sherlock Holmes to figure out Jilli's killer was after her toy -- a Gameboy-like gizmo Wurman had inadvertently slipped into his own pocket. Later, viewers learn that it contains scandalous digital photos that could prove damaging in an upcoming election -- though exactly who they incriminate remains a mystery, unresolved by the film's end.

This peccadillo is excused as the film's "McGuffin" -- a term coined by Alfred Hitchcock to indicate the object sought by the characters which serves as a device to set the action in motion.

Left with only hazy, narcotized recollections of the previous evening and Jilli's enigmatic toy, Wurman unwittingly becomes entangled in a labyrinth of cover-ups and conspiracies orchestrated by unseen powers -- only now he is in their cross hairs.

Ignoring his deteriorating health, Wurman plunges head-on with his benefit, pleading and cajoling celebrities and politicians -- "people I know" -- to show up at the event. They include an incendiary Harlem minister (Bill Nunn) and a civic-minded billionaire (Richard Schiff) with more than a few skeletons in his closet. Wurman begins to unravel, unable to trust anyone -- unsure if the next morning's newspaper will carry his obituary.

Wedged messily into all this is a subplot involving Wurman's widowed sister-in-law (Kim Basinger), a southern belle wheedling him to return to the bucolic simplicity of Dixieland.

Sound a tad confusing? Don't fret; it is.

The mood of the film has a hand-me-down quality, borrowing generously from earlier political thrillers like Alan J. Pakula's "The Parallax View"; a poster of the 1974 suspense yarn is featured prominently in Wurman's office. And while the mystique of cabals and conspiracies usually proves entertaining, the suspicion and political paranoia which fuel much of the overstuffed plot won't produce the same resonance that Pakula's film did in the post-Watergate climate -- those days, too, have passed Wurman by.

Many of the film's obligatory twists, including extraneous characters making veiled threats, seem to purposely obscure the cliche-laden narrative rather than piloting it to a coherent denouement.

Pacino's gravelly performance, which entails staggering through most of the film looking like an unmade bed and sounding like Rhett Butler on valium, feels like a retread from his more recent oeuvre. As a consummate professional, however, the understated gravitas he brings to the role makes many of the movie's defects less glaring.

Due to minimal violence, recurring drug abuse, rough language and vulgarities, as well as brief sexual images and fleeting nudity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III - adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: People Next Door, The
synopsis: J.P. Miller's adaptation of his award-winning television play about a middle-class teenager (Deborah Winters) who grooves with the boys and trips on LSD to escape the reality of her hypocritical parents (Eli Wallach and Julie Harris). Drearily moralizing, one-dimensional melodrama contrasts parents who drink and hide their sexual indiscretions with youngsters who smoke dope and flaunt theirs. Director David Greene's treatment fosters false stereotypes, uses unnecessary nudity and fails to deal adequately with the serious problem of drug abuse in suburbia

title: People of the Wind
synopsis: British documentary follows the annual trek of a nomadic tribe in southern Iran which each spring must bring their sheep and cattle from winter quarters to fresh grazing lands on a journey through perilous mountain terrain. Directed by Anthony Howarth, it is the record of a fiercely independent people who accept such dangers as the price of remaining free from the influences of the outside world

title: People That Time Forgot, The
synopsis: Rescue attempt on a prehistoric island brings viewers back to the same ice-bound fastness teeming with prehistoric monsters and cavemen depicted in "The Land That Time Forgot." Directed by Kevin Connor, the British production is lackluster, with tepid acting from Patrick Wayne and Doug McClure, but its silly special effects may amuse youngsters

title: People Under the Stairs, The
synopsis: Revolting horror comedy in which a ghetto kid (Brandon Adams) gets trapped in a creaky mansion populated by a cannibalistic couple (Everett McGill and Wendy Robie), their abused daughter (A.J. Langer) and a cellar full of rampaging ghouls. Writer-director Wes Craven wallows in gore and sick humor about child abuse in a drawn-out, badly-acted terror tale. Excessive violence, some racial slurs and sexual references and occasional rough language

title: People vs. Larry Flynt, The
synopsis: Romanticized account of the rise of self-described pornographer Larry Flint (Woody Harrelson) from strip-club owner to multimillionaire smut publisher whose lawyer (Edward Norton) wins a Supreme Court decision upholding the media's prerogative to ridicule public figures as a constitutional right of free speech. Director Milos Forman turns Flynt into a poster boy for the First Amendment while depicting all those opposed to flesh-peddling as narrow-minded prudes. Sexual encounters and references, recurring nudity, substance abuse, brief violence, much rough language and occasional profanity

title: Pepe
synopsis: Tedious sentimental hokum starring Mexican comic Cantinflas as the hick groom of a stud stallion bought by a has-been Hollywood director (Dan Dailey) who restarts his career when Pepe comes up with a fresh new star (Shirley Jones) and enough money to produce a movie after spending a night gambling in Las Vegas. Directed by George Sidney, the leaden script is cluttered with several dozen Hollywood star cameos, mediocre songs and uninspired dance numbers, but most disappointing is Cantinflas whose role as a rustic simpleton draws few smiles

title: Pepi, Luci, Bom
synopsis: Vicious black comedy centers on the gleefully sadomasochistic activities of three women (Carmen Maura, Eva Siva and Olvido Gara). Written and directed by Pedro Almodovar, this 1980 Spanish production celebrates the abuse of women and treats rape as a joke. Subtitles. Scenes of rape and other violence, sexual encounters with nudity, recreational drug use and occasional rough language

title: Peppermint Soda
synopsis: French production about two sisters in 1963, one of whom is 15 and trying to cope with love, politics and anti-Semitism while her 13-year-old sister wants to follow her example but is not quite ready. Directed by Diane Kurys, the beautifully-made movie is about people in the midst of life, but many viewers may find the pace too leisurely for enjoyment

title: Perceval
synopsis: Stylized French production based on the medieval romance about the knight (Fabrice Luchini) who joins King Arthur's court, fails to claim the Holy Grail when he has the chance, and is punished for his ignorance. Directed by Erich Rohmer, the visuals beautifully evoke the world of the Middle Ages and its code of chivalry as well as the conflict in Christendom between the spiritual and temporal. Period violennce

title: Percy
synopsis: Witless British sex farce about a young man (Hywel Bennett) with a genital transplant that fascinates both the medical world and several young ladies who discover his new acquistion. Directed by Ralph Thomas, its snickering tone is even more offensive than such scenes as a nurse doing a striptease to test his convalescence

title: Perez Family, The
synopsis: A Cuban refugee (Alfred Molina) in the 1980 Mariel boatlift to Miami seeks to rejoin the wife (Anjelica Huston) and daughter (Trini Alvarado) he's not seen in 20 years, but instead is processed through immigration as the husband of a part-time prostitute (Marisa Tomei) intent on creating a bogus family in order to stay in the States. Director Mira Nair plays the initial confusions mainly for laughs, then bogs down in soggy contrivances as romance blossoms between the two refugees as well as between Molina's wife and a Miami policeman (Chazz Palminteri). Sexual situations, flashes of nudity, crude gestures and occasional rough language

title: Perfect
synopsis: Rolling Stone reporter (John Travolta) becomes involved with an aerobics instructor (Jamie Lee Curtis) while researching a story on health clubs. Director Jim Bridges' muddled and pretentious movie offers a favorable view of promiscuity and includes a thoroughly distasteful sequence with a male stripper

title: Perfect Candidate, A
synopsis: Behind-the-scenes account of the 1994 Virginia senatorial campaign between Republican challenger Oliver North, the former Marine officer best known for his part in the Iran/contra scandal, and incumbent Democratic Sen. Charles Robb. Produced and directed by R.J. Cutler and David Van Taylor, the documentary has no narration and viewers are on their own in forming judgments about the candidates, their political views and campaign strategies which turn the race into a classic of negative campaigning. Mean-spirited character assassination and few instances of rough language

title: Perfect Couple, A
synopsis: Middle-aged, brow-beaten son of a wealthy, conservative Greek family (Paul Dooley) uses a computer dating service which matches him with an aspiring rock singer (Marta Heflin). They surmount all difficulties, proving that director Robert Altman has a heart and the title is not ironically meant. The film does have some cheerful moments, and the acting is quite good, but the whole thing is so inconsequential that it often seems in danger of evaporating

title: Perfect Friday
synopsis: British caper movie tries to liven up the muddled plot revolving around bank teller Stanley Baker's clever bank robbery with an incoherently staccato narrative, false plot twists and shots of accomplice Ursula Andress undressed. Director Peter Hall's sense of timing and humor is as badly off the mark as the movie's sense of moral perspective

title: Perfect Furlough, The
synopsis: Predictable farce directed by Blake Edwards in which a conniving Army corporal (Tony Curtis) wins a vacation in Paris with a movie star (Linda Cristal), then tries to outwit the military psychologist (Janet Leigh) assigned to keep him out of trouble. Much sexual innuendo

title: The Perfect Game
synopsis: Rousing, faith-infused sports drama, based on real events, recounting the unlikely odyssey of a ragtag boys baseball team from Monterrey, Mexico, who, under the spiritual guidance of a devout but down-to-earth priest (Cheech Marin) and the leadership of a hard-driving coach (Clifton Collins Jr.) travel to the U.S. to compete in the 1957 Little League championship tournament, achieving a string of unexpected victories against far more advantaged teams. As directed by William Dear, W. William Winokur's script unambiguously presents the young players' Catholicism as the inspiration not only for their winning streak, but for their persistent refusal to allow either their impoverished circumstances or the disdainful prejudice they frequently encounter north of the border to deprive them of their dream, though a brief scene of Marin's otherwise estimable character celebrating a Tridentine Mass presents an image of worship so sloppy and repetitive as to approach unintentional parody. Racial tensions, ethnic slurs and a few mildly earthy insults
full_review:
As the universal church's Year for Priests nears its conclusion June 19, and as the overwhelming majority of dedicated Catholic clergy around the world once again find themselves smeared -- in some quarters at least -- for the grievously sinful misdeeds of a few, who would have guessed that an entirely warmhearted and positive embodiment of the priesthood would be portrayed onscreen by comedy veteran Cheech Marin?

Marin -- a long way from his persona as a doped-up dope in the Cheech and Chong string of stoner comedies -- plays Padre Esteban, the spiritual guide of a ragtag boys' baseball team from northern Mexico whose unlikely bid for sports immortality is recounted in the faith-infused, fact-based drama "The Perfect Game" (IndustryWorks).

 

Set in 1957, this is the story of an enthusiastic but initially unskilled group of youngsters, led by their future star pitcher, Angel Macias (Jake T. Austin), who enlist the reluctant help of local factory worker and ex-major leaguer Cesar Fez (Clifton Collins Jr.) to form the Monterrey Industrials, their downtrodden city's first Little League team.

Improving rapidly under coach Cesar's hard-driving regime, the lads cross the border and embark on a series of David-versus-Goliath-like victories over their far more advantaged opponents in the Little League championship tournament.

As directed by William Dear, W. William Winokur's script unambiguously presents the young players' Catholicism as the inspiration for their winning streak. Thus Marin's devout but down-to-earth padre leads the team in prayer before each game, and uses the story of Blessed Juan Diego to encourage them to accomplish great things.

 

Their beliefs also prompt the boys' persistent refusal to allow either their impoverished circumstances or the disdainful prejudice they frequently encounter during their time in the U.S. to deprive them of their dream. In a touching scene that reinforces the film's message about racial and ethnic equality, they courageously defy the rules of a segregated diner by joining, and befriending, a solitary black Little Leaguer who has been forced to eat at a table by himself, shunned by his own white teammates.

A brief scene of the otherwise estimable Padre Esteban celebrating a Tridentine Mass makes it clear that no one involved in the production had even a rudimentary knowledge of the Catholic liturgy of the time, and the result is an image of worship so sloppy and repetitive as to approach unintentional parody.

But this is a relatively small flaw in what is, overall, a rousing tribute to the power of religious faith and the values of persistence and human solidarity.

The film contains racial tensions, ethnic slurs and a few mildly earthy insults. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested. Some material may not be suitable for children.

title: A Perfect Getaway
synopsis: Newlyweds (Steve Zahn and Milla Jovovich) on a hiking honeymoon in a remote area of Hawaii fear that an unwed couple they've befriended (Timothy Olyphant and Kiele Sanchez) may be serial killers on the lam. After a reasonably intriguing central twist, though one that fails to jibe entirely with what has gone before, director David Twohy's thriller becomes overwrought and excessively violent. Considerable action violence, some of it gory, cohabitation, drug use, rear and partial nudity, a half-dozen uses of profanity, and much rough and crude language
full_review:
The natural splendors of a remote area of Hawaii provide the backdrop for director David Twohy's not-so-splendid thriller "A Perfect Getaway" (Rogue). After a reasonably intriguing central plot twist -- though one that fails to jibe entirely with what has gone before -- the shifty drama degenerates, becoming overwrought in tone and excessively violent in content.

As they head for the beautiful, but isolated Kalalau Valley on the island of Kauai, hiking honeymooners Cliff (Steve Zahn) and Cydney (Milla Jovovich) learn that the couple wanted in a series of recent, well-publicized murders may have fled to the region. So when Kale (Chris Hemsworth) and Cleo (Marley Shelton), a pair of creepy hitchhikers they had refused to pick up earlier, suspiciously and threateningly resurface, the newlyweds are unnerved.

Pressing on, they cross paths with friendly, talkative Iraq War veteran Nick (Timothy Olyphant), whose company they initially find reassuring. But his trail leads to girlfriend Gina (Kiele Sanchez), and it's not long before his tall tales of combat prowess and her dexterity with a butcher knife -- exhibited to gruesome effect on a goat Nick has felled with a bow and arrow -- have Cliff and Cydney worrying again.

Zahn's skillful impersonation of twitchy, nerdy Cliff, a Hollywood screenwriter easily overshadowed and intimidated by Nick's real-life exploits, heightens the atmosphere of uncertainty. But objectionable elements include not only the climactic bloodletting, but a prolonged skinny-dipping scene and a murky tide of four-letter words.

The film contains considerable action violence, some of it gory, cohabitation, drug use, rear and partial nudity, a half-dozen uses of profanity, and much rough and crude language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Perfectly Normal
synopsis: A young loner (Michael Riley) jettisons his plans to build a house when a flamboyant stranger (Robbie Coltrane) persuades him to spend his inheritance on a restaurant where the two would sing Italian operas to the clientele. Director Yves Simoneau's offbeat, fitfully funny comedy endearingly portrays eccentric characters who happily change each other for the better. Restrained love scene with brief nudity and some rough language

title: Perfect Murder, A
synopsis: Glossy thriller in which a heartless husband (Michael Douglas) plots to have his rich trophy wife (Gwyneth Paltrow) killed by her ex-con lover (Viggo Mortensen), but all goes murderously awry. Directed by Andrew Davis, this remake of Hitchcock's 1954 "Dial M for Murder" retains the twisty plot but by adding adultery and more violence to the mix, the result is dramatically unconvincing. Fleeting sexual encounter, brief but intense violence and some rough language as well as profanity

title: Perfect Specimen, The
synopsis: Predictable romantic comedy directed by Michael Curtiz in which a rich young man (Errol Flynn) is shielded from the world by his stern grandmother (May Robson) until he runs off with a free-spirited young woman (Joan Blondell) and proves he's perfectly capable of managing on his own. Romantic complications

title: Perfect Stranger
synopsis: Trashy, utterly nonsensical thriller about an investigative reporter (Halle Berry) who, with the help of a sleazy computer-savvy colleague (Giovanni Ribisi), sets out to expose the big-shot advertising executive (Bruce Willis) who may have murdered her childhood friend after an adulterous affair. The ill-conceived script -- peppered with so many gratuitous uses of the f-word it's almost risible -- strains credulity at every turn, and most of the seamy sexual elements have little dramatic justification, though we'll credit director James Foley with bringing some visual flair. Nonstop rough and crude language and some profanity, heavy sexual content including a graphic premarital encounter without nudity, brief pornographic images, adultery, child abuse, some violent encounters including a bloody stabbing and a bludgeoning, and a gruesome morgue image
full_review:
Chalk up another woeful career choice for Halle Berry, whose proven talent does not apparently extend to knowing when to say "no."

Her latest vehicle, "Perfect Stranger" (Revolution), is a patently trashy, utterly nonsensical thriller.

She plays Rowena Price, a fictitious New York newspaper's investigative reporter who, in the film's opening scene, threatens a slimy congressman who has a weakness for male interns. Her hard-won story never runs, thanks to the politician's connections, putting a damper on her barroom celebration with Miles (Giovanni Ribisi), her sleazy computer-savvy colleague.

Shortly after this disappointment, promiscuous childhood girlfriend Grace (Nicki Aycox) reaches out to Ro about exposing big-shot ad executive Harrison Hill (Bruce Willis in a nothing part) with whom she had been having an adulterous affair but who has now dumped her.

When Grace is found murdered a couple of weeks later, Ro impersonates a temp to infiltrate Hill's ad agency and prove him the killer. With Miles' help, she also impersonates one of Hill's chat-room flirtations to trap the powerful executive further with some provocative online text-messaging.

The ill-conceived script (by Todd Kornarnicki), which substitutes puerile vulgarity for intelligence, has this star reporter uttering so many gratuitous uses of the f-word that it becomes almost risible.

And never mind that events strain credulity at every turn, and most of the seamy sexual elements have little dramatic justification. James Foley, at least, directs with some visual flair.

The film contains nonstop rough and crude language and some profanity, heavy sexual content including a graphic premarital encounter without nudity, brief pornographic images, adultery, child abuse, some violent encounters including a bloody stabbing and a bludgeoning, and a gruesome morgue image. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Perfect Strangers
synopsis: Romantic potboiler directed by Bretaigne Windust in which a married man (Dennis Morgan) falls for an estranged wife (Ginger Rogers) while both are serving on a jury in the case of a man charged with murdering his wife in order to marry his secretary. Muddled treatment of divorce

title: Perfect Weapon, The
synopsis: Seeking the gangland slayer (James Hong) of his mentor (Mako), a kenpo karate expert (Jeff Speakman) is tricked into thinking the killer's archrival is the guilty party. Director Mark DiSalle's standard action yarn is a yawn that could pass for an episode of a TV private eye series, simply stretched out to accomodate more karate bouts. Interrmittent martial arts violence and an isolated instance of rough language and drug use

title: Perfect World, A
synopsis: Hard-edged adult thriller about an escaped convict (Kevin Costner) taking a 7-year-old hostage (T.J. Lowther) on a blood-splattered ride as he tries to elude the pursuit of a veteran Texas Ranger (Clint Eastwood) and a young criminologist (Laura Dern). Also directed by Eastwood, the story's tension revolves around the menacing situations in which the young boy is placed as he witnesses deadly violence and then participates in it. Intense menace to a child, graphic violence, sexual references and coarse language

title: Performance
synopsis: A hood (James Fox), on the run from the mob, takes refuge with a temporarily retired pop singer (Mick Jagger) awaiting the return of his inspiration in the company of several fans (Anita Pallenberg and Michele Breton). Bizarre British drama directed by Don Cammell and Nicholas Roeg is a pseudo-sophisticate's vision of evil with the kind of slick gimmickry that promises revelations but never rises above its shallow fascination with the perversities it supposedly explores. It's a morass of unrelieved violence, drug use, sex and grotesque immoralities

title: Perfume: The Story of a Murderer
synopsis: Deeply disturbing but hypnotic story set in 18th-century France about an orphan (Ben Wishaw) -- impoverished and abused but gifted with an extraordinary sense of smell -- who apprentices to a perfumer (Dustin Hoffman), after which -- incapable of normal love -- he becomes a serial killer in his quest to capture the scents of his young female victims, ultimately targeting the virginal daughter (Rachel Hurd-Wood) of a wealthy merchant (Alan Rickman) desperate to protect her.
