synopsis: Kirk Douglas plays a politically ambitious U.S. marshal in late 19th-century Texas who battles outlaws by means of his own well-trained, fantically loyal posse but runs into trouble when he brings in a popular train robber (Bruce Dern). Also directed by Douglas, the simplistic morality tale is heavy-handed in its use of violence and offensive in a needless bit of sexual exploitation

title: Posse
synopsis: Returning from fighting in the Spanish-American War in 1898 Cuba, a small band of African-American soldiers (headed by Mario Van Peebles) and a white comrade (Stephen Baldwin) head West to settle a score with the sheriff (Richard Jordan) who murdered their leader's peace-loving father. Also directed by Van Peebles, the movie certainly doesn't skimp on shootouts and portrays vigilante justice uncritically, but it also reminds viewers of the not insignificant presence of African-American settlers in the development of the West and of the particular hardships they encountered. Much stylized violence, a bedroom scene, brief nudity and some rough language

title: Posse from Hell
synopsis: Cliched Western directed by Herbert Coleman follows a small posse of misfits led by a bitter deputy (Audie Murphy) as they hunt down four killers who escaped from prison, held up a bank and fled with a woman hostage (Zohra Lampert). Frontier violence and veiled references to rape

title: Possessed
synopsis: Fed up with her job in a paper box factory, an ambitious woman (Joan Crawford) tries her luck in Manhattan, falls for a swank lawyer (Clark Gable) and becomes his mistress, then walks out to keep their affair from ruining his chance to be governor. Director Clarence Brown paces the sudsy melodrama about a kept woman's yearnings for marriage with some daffy period humor, a sprinkling of self-serving hypocrites and memorable visuals beginning with what the woman sees in the windows of a passing luxury train and ending in a gigantic political meeting. Implicit sexual affair, much innuendo and a contrived moral ending

title: Possessed
synopsis: Murky melodrama in which a troubled woman (Joan Crawford) is rejected by her lover (Van Heflin), then marries a wealthy widower (Raymond Massey) in hopes of winning him back, only to go bonkers when he turns to another. Directed by Curtis Bernhardt, the convoluted story is told in flashbacks as the woman is treated by a psychiatrist, but the main interest is Crawford's vintage performance in a split-personality role. Heavy-handed treatment of an emotionally unstable person, romantic complications and some stylized violence

title: Possession
synopsis: Romantic period piece about two literature scholars (Gwyneth Paltrow and Aaron Eckhart) who end up falling for each other as they investigate a Victorian-era poet's (Jeremy Northam) secret extramarital affair with a lesser-known poet (Jennifer Ehle). Floating back and forth between the present-day England and the Victorian age, director Neil LaBute's film has gorgeous countryside vistas and a dreamy, flirty quality, but despite the emphasis on love, the inclusion of an out-of-wedlock child and a lesbian relationship may nonetheless be off-putting. An extramarital affair, a sexual encounter, a lesbian relationship, a suicide and fleeting crass language and profanity
full_review:
The romantic period-piece "Possession" (Focus) is a decided departure from director Neil LaBute's other disturbing films. However, this dreamy film with gorgeous countryside vistas and dripping romantic notions has some unpleasant elements, such as a mild lesbian relationship and an out-of-wedlock child, which may sour the otherwise fanciful story line for moviegoers. These aspects, while mostly peripheral, are included to heighten the sense of longing in a story about love, passion and mystery. Even so, their inclusion may be off-putting.

The film takes place in present-day England and follows a pair of literature scholars, cold Brit academic Maud (Gwyneth Paltrow) and cocky American researcher Roland (Aaron Eckhart, a LaBute regular), as they track the historical path of a famous (fictitious) Victorian-era poet, Randolph Henry Ash (Jeremy Northam), who had a secret extramarital affair with the love of his life, lesser-known poet Christabel LaMotte (Jennifer Ehle).

Floating back and forth between the present and the past, "Possession" is much closer to a Merchant-Ivory production, with its majestic imagery and gushy love story, than LaBute's previous films, such as the sordid "Your Friends and Neighbors" and the disturbing "In the Company of Men." LaBute co-wrote the adapted screenplay from A.S. Byatt's 1990 novel of the same title, which won the Booker Prize for Fiction. The script admirably condenses the comprehensive novel, layering in intrigue and obstacles to love. But it isn't able to avoid narrative lags, eventually resulting in a reasonably entertaining but not completely absorbing or dramatically compelling film.

As Maud and Roland further investigate the previously unknown relationship between the two poets, their only link with the past is a cache of love letters that appear to be from Ash to LaMotte. Ash is known to have been a legendarily faithful husband, while LaMotte was living with her lesbian companion, Blanche (Lena Headey). The discovery that the two had an affair would be the literary find of the century, which is partly what spurs Maud and Roland on.

As the two scholars read the gushing love letters aloud to each other and retrace the couple's secret love journey, romance and passion creep into their modern hearts and they are off in an obvious direction. But their courtship is filled with the usual hang-ups and complications of modern-day romances (namely fear of commitment) while Ash's and LaMotte's forbidden passion is colored by the rosy notion that true love is a risk worth taking. Yet it is Ash's and LaMotte's willingness to gamble all for their love that provides Maud and Roland with the encouragement they need to proceed.

Paltrow, with her flaxen hair tightly pulled back in a bun and once again assuming a mild British accent, offers a standard beautiful-woman-afraid-to-be-hurt-by-love performance. She is attractive and appealing, but nothing more. Eckhart is a little too intense in his portrayal, although the character is pretty one-dimensional. Both Northam and Ehle throw themselves into the roles, resulting in pleasing, but not outstanding performances.

"Possession" is mostly a sweetly enchanting story that washes over the viewer. Humorous touches cut the romance that oozes out of most scenes, keeping the sugary love affair between both couples in check. The film harks back to the days when the written word could stir more passion than the fieriest kiss.

Due to an extramarital affair, a sexual encounter, a lesbian relationship, a suicide and fleeting crass language and profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned that some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

(
2002
)

title: Possession of Joel Delaney, The
synopsis: Strained horror movie with some pretensions to social commentary tells the story of an affluent New York divorcee (Shirley MacLaine) and her brother (Michael Hordern), seemingly possessed by the malevolent soul of a dead Puerto Rican youth who had brutally murdered several women. The social dimension shows the cultural gulf between the Park Avenue rich and those living in Spanish Harlem. Director Waris Hussein resorts to shock tactics considerably lessening the intensity of his film's serious subject matter by punctuating action with beheaded nude bodies and a climax that is as berserk as poor Joel

title: Postcards from the Edge
synopsis: Dramatic comedy about a young actress (Meryl Streep) forced to confront longstanding conflicts with her hard-drinking moviestar mom (Shirley MacLaine) in whose care she is released following drug rehabilitation. Written by actress Carrie Fisher and directed by Mike Nichols, the stylishly mounted look at mother-daughter relationships features splendid performances by the two leads representing the old and the new Hollywood. Comic treatment of drug and alcohol abuse, intermittent rough language and several references to promiscuous relationships

title: Post Grad
synopsis: After failing to secure her dream job, a recent college graduate (Alexis Bledel) is forced to return home to her eccentric parents (Jane Lynch and Michael Keaton) and feisty grandmother (Carol Burnett) whose antics distract her from her employment search and from her efforts to choose between her longtime boyfriend (Zach Gilford) and a Brazilian-born ladies' man (Rodrigo Santoro). A talented cast is becalmed, in veteran animation director Vicky Jenson's live-action debut, by a listless script which, though it boosts family solidarity, also features a passionate encounter between characters who have barely met and repeatedly refers to the importance of condom use. Brief nongraphic, nonmarital sexual activity, occasional sexual references, a half-dozen uses of profanity, at least one use of the F-word, and some crude and crass language

title: Postman Always Rings Twice, The
synopsis: Gritty crime tale from James M. Cain's novel in which a tough drifter (John Garfield) takes a job in a roadside diner, falls for the unhappy wife (Lana Turner) of its good-natured owner (Cecil Kellaway) whom they determine to murder, then face the law and retribution. Directed by Tay Garnett, the sexual attraction motivating the horrendous crime is effectively depicted without any explicit visuals, but the murder's aftermath grows increasingly contrived and emotionally hollow. Stylized violence, including cold-blooded murder, an adulterous relationship and much sexual innuendo

title: Postman Always Rings Twice, The
synopsis: Failed adaptation of James M. Cain's bleak, Depression-era tale of passion and retribution as an adulterous couple (Jessica Lange and Jack Nicholson) conspire to kill the woman's husband. Directed by Bob Rafelson, the slow-moving, uninvolving picture devotes most of its energy to conveying the sadomasochistic relationship between the two principals, neither of whom give very convincing performances. Excessively graphic display of sex

title: Postman, The
synopsis: Set in a lawless post-apocalyptic society where isolated towns are at the mercy of a murderous army of thieves (led by Will Patton), a wandering loner (Kevin Costner) assumes the uniform and role of a dead U.S. postman which has the unexpected effect of motivating the people to resist their oppressors and fight to restore democracy. Also directed by Costner, the movie's narrative is far-fetched but emotionally involving, appealing to sentimental notions of patriotism while overly idealizing the title character. Recurring violence, a sexual encounter with nudity, fleeting substance abuse, some profanity and an instance of rough language

title: Postman, The
synopsis: see Il Postino (The Postman) ( Il Postino )

title: Pot o' Gold
synopsis: Sentimental tale in which a bankrupt music store owner (James Stewart) is taken in by some unemployed musicians (led by Horace Heidt), then manages to get them on a radio show sponsored by his mean but very rich uncle (Charles Winninger). Director George Marshall gives pedestrian treatment to the artificial plot and its formula characters with results that are even less convincing than Stewart's singing and harmonica-playing

title: Pound
synopsis: Absurdist social satire in which the actors assume the roles of dogs waiting in the city pound to be destroyed. These sad, lonely, unfulfilled social outcasts are potential elements for a meaningful exploration of one or another aspect of the human condition. Unfortunately, director Robert Downey's improvisational approach lacks any insight and the content consists of little else but gross crudities played simply for irreverent and tasteless humor in a style that is more asinine than canine

title: Powder
synopsis: Thin tale of an orphaned albino teenager (Sean Patrick Flanery) whose supernormal powers make him a bizarre misfit in the normal world, though they inspire respectful awe in an educator (Mary Steenburgen), a science teacher (Jeff Goldblum) and the local sheriff (Lance Henriksen). Writer-director Victor Salva works hard at visualizing a character with powers beyond human ken but never develops the situation far beyond people's fear of what they don't understand. Some violent special effects, menacing situations, a flash of bare buttocks and occasional profanity

title: Power
synopsis: Richard Gere stars as a public relations expert and power broker in this glamourized depiction of the media process which creates and manipulates the image of politicians. The drama asserts that television is the major influence in mo1ding pub1ic opinion. The narrative is spotted with a profanity unnecessary for characterization

title: Power of One, The
synopsis: Touching drama about a white orphan's experiences growing up English in South Africa at the time the German-speaking Afrikaners were gaining enough political power to make apartheid the law of the land in 1948. Under John G. Avildsen's less-than-subtle direction, the action scenes of boxing bouts and racial bloodshed threaten to overshadow the inspirational story of the young boy developing courage and a keen sense of social justice. Frequent bloody violence and racial slurs

title: The Powerpuff Girls Movie
synopsis: Tedious animated feature in which a scientist creates three perfect little girls with superhero powers who help save their town from an evil monkey intent on destroying it. The brainless story in director Craig McCracken’s film, which is based on the cartoon series, is devoid of any wit, feebly offering a message on tolerance and acceptance while burning up much time on monotonous, inane action sequences. Some cartoon violence and menace with a few bad-mannered expressions
full_review:
"The Powerpuff Girls Movie" (Warner Bros.) is a tedious animated feature in which drawn-out action sequences are wrapped around a dim-witted story. But that doesn't necessarily mean that fans of the cartoon series might still not be eager to see it in the theaters.

Preceded by a forgettable short entitled "Chicken Scratch," director Craig McCraken's "The Powerpuff Girls Movie" is just the latest in a flurry of movies unleashed for the younger audience this summer, with more to come. This is a definite jump from last year when only a handful of children's flicks were out such as "Shrek." But "Powerpuff Girls" is a disappointment.

As the young viewers of the TV 'toon know, the three little girls of the title were created by Professor Utonium (voiced by Tom Kane), a scientist fed up with the crime and thuggery in Townsville. He simply wanted children of his own to whom he could teach right from wrong. Combining sugar, spice and everything nice - and an inadvertent splash of "chemical X" - Professor created Blossom (voiced by Catherine Cavadini), the bright leader of the group, Bubbles (voiced by Tara Strong), who's all cuteness and giggles, and Buttercup (voiced by E.G. Daily), the strong-willed tough cookie. But by mistake, Professor also turned his pet monkey into the evil Mojo Jojo (voiced by Roger L. Jackson), a simian with a superiority complex who speaks with a vague Asian accent and wants to rule Townsville.

Among the monotonous action sequences (there's an overlong scene where the trio, using their super powers, plays tag all around town, accidentally destroying property) is buried a feeble lesson about tolerance and acceptance. The town initially rejects the girls as freaks (a word used all too often in the film, as is "stupid") until they rescue the citizens from Mojo Jojo's fiendish clutches. Then the lasses become everyone's heroes and vow to fight crime and wickedness each day, at least until bedtime.

From the characters to the town to Professor Utonium's home, the animation has a colorful retro look. The girls' have bulbous heads and large saucer eyes that blink purposefully as they walk on rounded toes. The professor looks something like Rock Hudson with the swaggering voice of a game show host. But while the animation is inventive, the convoluted story borrows freely from live-action films such as "Planet of the Apes," "Batman" and "King Kong." The film lacks wit and droll dialogue, instead just punching the clock and hoping to catch a free ride from the success and built-in audience of the television series.

Although the cartoon violence of the movie may be equal to that of the series, it still seems likely to frighten the very young, while older children may not be disturbed by it.

Because of some cartoon violence and menace with a few bad-mannered expressions, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
(
2002
)

title: Power, The
synopsis: As his colleagues die mysteriously, scientist George Hamilton has to discover which of those involved in his pain-resistance experiment is a superintelligent being. The thriller has an interesting premise, but suspense drains off through credibility gaps in the plot and Byron Haskin's slack direction. Benign attitude toward premarital sex

title: Powwow Highway
synopsis: A philosophical conflict emerges on a journey from Montana to New Mexico between two Native Americans, one of whom (A. Martinez) dismisses Cheyenne tradition and culture as irrelevant in pulling the tribe up from Third World poverty, while the other (Gary Farmer) cherishes Cheyenne legends and longs to become a spiritual warrior. Though director Jonathan Wacks injects little suspense into his low-key road picture, it highlights the personal and political struggles being waged within the Native American community to regain and sustain their fast-disappearing culture. Some profanity, violence and a flash of nudity

title: Practical Magic
synopsis: Fantasy, horror and sappy romance collide when sister witches (Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman) kill one's abusive boyfriend in self-defense, who then returns from the dead to bedevil their lives. Director Griffin Dunne's jumbled proceedings make no narrative sense, tossing together contrived comedy, pretty faces and picturesque settings with less than magical results. Some brief violence, an implied affair, substance abuse, crude expressions and minimal profanity

title: Practice Makes Perfect
synopsis: Jean Rochefort plays a famous pianist, a conceited self-centered woman chaser, who gets a mild comeuppance when he tries to abandon his second wife (Nicole Garcia) and their three children by running off with the granddaughter (Catherine Le Prince) of an old flame (Danielle Darrieux). French sex farce directed by Philippe de Broca, it's all very light, very sentimental and passably droll for adults who enjoy such fare

title: Prancer
synopsis: Sweet-natured Christmas story about a spirited 8-year-old farm girl (Rebecca Harrell) who cares for an injured reindeer believing it is one of Santa's team. While this "E.T." clone may have its fill of cranky adults and earnest moments, John Hancock's direction has a feel for rural community life that will please older viewers while younger ones will love the reindeer and the praise lavished on the spunky heroine for revitalizing the town's Christmas spirit

title: Prayer for the Dying, A
synopsis: A political assassin (Mickey Rourke) seeks redemption while fleeing killers from the IRA to which he belonged, a mobster (Alan Bates) who wants his services and the police. A priest (Bob Hoskins) helps and comforts him in director Mike Hodges' heavy-handed drama saved by Rourke's skin-tight portrayal. Some violence and profanity cut with black humor

title: Preacher's Wife, The
synopsis: Charming remake of the 1948 fantasy, "The Bishop's Wife," in which an angel (Denzel Washington) is sent to help the discouraged Baptist minister (Courtney B. Vance) of a struggling inner-city church and his neglected wife (Whitney Houston) rediscover romance in their marriage. Director Penny Marshall's slow-paced, sentimental story about the values of faith and hope is enlivened by an engaging cast and vibrant gospel songs. Romantic complications

title: Predator
synopsis: Elite commando rescue team, on a mission into the Latin American tropics, becomes the prey of a superhuman predator who fights it out to the death with Arnold Sshwarzenegger. Director John McTiernan builds suspense in his nightmarish depiction of the hunt but the landscape is strewn with skinned, bloodied victims. Profuse profanity and gruesome stylized violence

title: Predator 2
synopsis: Sci-fi horror tale set in 1997 Los Angeles where a hotheaded cop (Danny Glover) ignores the hands-off orders of a top federal agent (Gary Busey) and vows to personally exterminate the powerful alien killer (Kevin Peter Hall) who has slaughtered his colleagues. In spite of clever lighting and special effects, director Stephen Hopkins cuts straight to the jugular with no pretense at character build-up in a grisly bloodfest devoid of human dimension. Excessive, graphic violence, full frontal nudity and continuous rough language

title: Predators
synopsis: Dreary sci-fi sequel in which a random collection of human warriors and criminals (most prominently Adrien Brody, Alice Braga and Topher Grace) find themselves unwillingly and mysteriously parachuted into a jungle by the invisibility-cloaked aliens of the title who then hunt them for sport. Despite a half-hearted last-reel lesson about the need to maintain civilized values, director Nimrod Antal's addition to the thriller franchise that began with 1987's "Predator" is mostly a survey of nasty ways to die, while Alex Litvak's script is chockablock with obscenities. Frequent graphic violence, some of it gruesome, a few uses of profanity, pervasive rough and crude language
full_review:
Toward the end of "Predators" (Fox), a character camouflages himself by covering his torso with mud. That's an apt symbol for this dreary sci-fi sequel which, despite a halfhearted last-reel lesson about the need to maintain civilized values, is mostly a bespattered survey of nasty ways to die.

As for Alex Litvak's script, it's chockablock with obscenities throughout, and even the second-to-last word of dialogue is an unprintable one.

Director Nimrod Antal's addition to the thriller franchise that began with 1987's "Predator" pits a random collection of human warriors and criminals against the invisibility-cloaked aliens of the title, who are out to hunt hominids for sport. The extraterrestrials' chosen hunting ground is a steamy jungle into which each of the earthlings has been unwillingly, and mysteriously, parachuted.

Along with their eventual leader, experienced mercenary Royce (Adrien Brody), this unsavory gang includes -- but is not limited to -- Israeli Defense Forces sniper Isabelle (Alice Braga), serial killer Stans (Walton Goggins), drug-gang enforcer Cuchillo (Danny Trejo) and Russian Special Forces operative Nikolai (Oleg Taktarov). (Given the premise, you can tell Nikolai has been up to no good in Chechnya even before he mentions it.)

A seemingly incongruous addition to their company is respectable and mild-mannered physician Edwin (Topher Grace).

As this motley crew dodges deadly booby traps, alien warthogs and the daggerlike appendages their pursuers are capable of sprouting at all the wrong moments, they cross paths with Noland (Laurence Fishburne), a slightly addled veteran of the aliens' cat-and-mouse ordeal.

But this encounter turns out to be just a detour in their bloody quest for survival, which sees the group gradually whittled down by impalings, eviscerations and other unpleasant spectacles.

The film contains frequent graphic violence, some of it gruesome, a few uses of profanity and pervasive rough and crude language. The Catholic News Service classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Prefontaine
synopsis: Fact-based story of distance runner Steve Prefontaine (Jared Leto) who set track records at the University of Oregon, competed unsuccessfully in the 1972 Munich Olympics, then became an activist for the rights of amateur athletes until his death in a 1975 auto accident. Directed by Steve James, the dramatization of the athlete's obsession to become a track star gains credibility from the use of newsreel footage and re-creations, but the story is thin on the human dimension of the characters and offers little for those uninterested in athletic competitions. Some stylized violence and a few instances of rough language and profanity

title: Prehistoric Women
synopsis: Clunky adventure fantasy follows a British hunter (Michael Latimer) into a time warp where he is taken prisoner by a Stone Age clan of women whose totem is a white rhinoceros. British writer-director Michael Carreras turns the pulp situation primarily into a showcase for an assortment of scantily clad starlets (led by Martine Beswick and Edina Ronay). Stylized violence and much sexual innuendo

title: Prelude to a Kiss
synopsis: When they kiss at her wedding, a bride (Meg Ryan) and an elderly stranger (Sydney Walker) magically switch personalities, leaving the groom (Alec Baldwin) to figure out how to get the woman he loves out of the old man's body. Director Norman Rene's featherweight fantasy barely sustains a contrived romantic comedy about the transcending power of love. An implied premarital relationship

title: Premonition
synopsis: Effective time-warp thriller about wife (Sandra Bullock) who learns her husband (Julian McMahon) has died in a car accident, only to wake up and discover he's still alive and the dreadful event will happen a few days later. Serious suspension of disbelief is required on the viewer's part, but director Mennan Yapo directs with skill, Bullock is riveting as she gradually pieces together the mystifying events around her, and there's even that rare occurrence -- a fairly positive priest character -- all in all making this unobjectionable for older teens and up, despite the flagged elements below. A few instances of profanity and expletives, a horrific car collision and a couple of minor accidents involving blood, mild innuendo, suggestion of adultery
full_review:
If movie exhibitors still programmed double features, Sandra Bullock's latest vehicle would make a dandy companion to her last big film, "The Lake House." In each, her character was caught in a perplexing time warp, though "The Lake House" was primarily a romance.

"Premonition" (MGM/Hyde Park/TriStar) is an effective, fairly tense, thriller about a dutiful wife (Bullock) who learns that her husband, Jim (Julian McMahon from TV's "Nip/Tuck"), has died in a car accident while on a business trip. (Bullock's silent processing of the sorrowful news when a police officer comes to her door is beautifully conveyed.)

The stunned Linda goes through the myriad stages of grief as she breaks the news to her daughters, calls on her mother and friends for emotional support, and tries to grapple with the unbelievable.

But lo and behold, she wakes up in the morning to the surprise of her life. Jim's suitcase and other items are in their usual places, and there he is, drinking his coffee at the kitchen counter as if nothing has happened. The events of the day before were apparently just a dream, Linda's quizzical gaze suggests. But were they? Not to give too much away, because each revelation -- improbable though most of them are -- is carefully revealed, but Linda does figure out fairly early on that the dreadful event will happen a few days hence.

This is the kind of film where red herrings abound, and just about everyone around poor Linda looks conspiratorial. And that includes Jim, who (for reasons that eventually become clear) seems enigmatically detached; her mother (Kate Nelligan) and her best friend (Nia Long); and even her two little girls, one of whom cuts herself running through a glass door, emerging like a little she-devil!

Serious suspension of disbelief is required on the viewer's part. Why does Linda coolly seek out an extremely creepy doctor (Peter Stormare) when she has already experienced him (in the future) fiendishly strapping her down and administering an injection? Why does she look so panicked when a page in a phone book is ripped out when all she has to do is dial "411" instead?

But plot holes aside, it must be said that director Mennan Yapo directs with great skill, Bullock is riveting as she gradually pieces together the mystifying events around her, and there's even that rare occurrence: a fairly positive priest character to whom Linda turns when all else fails.

Oddly, it's the priest who's a treasure trove of historical trivia about past instances of crystal ball-gazing, and when he gets down to the more priestly advice, it's the most hackneyed of platitudes, but nonetheless, he's a nice cinematic anomaly.

The flagged elements below which necessitate the adult classification notwithstanding, the film is probably unobjectionable for mature teens, as sexual elements are nil and violence is minimal.

The film contains a few instances of profanity and expletives, a horrific car collision and a couple of minor accidents involving blood, mild innuendo, and suggestion of adultery.

The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Premonition, The
synopsis: Unconvincing thriller concerns a parapsychologist's attempt to find a missing child through the foster mother's psychic contact with the child's dead mother. Though it has some eerie moments and suggests some gory horrors, one doesn't have to be clairvoyant to perceive how badly director Robert Allen Schnitzer has missed the mark

title: President's Analyst, The
synopsis: James Coburn plays shrink to the Commander-in-Chief who develops a case of the jitters when the revelations that relieve the President's tensions also happen to be state secrets. But he also discovers that he is being pursued by agents and double-agents who alternately want him to keep the lid on or blow it off. Director Theodore J. Flicker's comedy has some adult humor

title: President's Lady, The
synopsis: Tangled historical romance in which rising Tennessee politician Andrew Jackson (Charlton Heston) weds a divorced woman (Susan Hayward) before learning the divorce had not been finalized, then reweds her when it is, and goes on to be elected President despite being branded an adulterer by his political opponents. Directed by Henry Levin from the Irving Stone novel, the slick Hollywood production turns history into bad melodrama and the actors into cardboard characters. Frontier violence and romanticized marital mix-ups

title: Presidio, The
synopsis: An army officer (Sean Connery) based at the Presidio and a San Francisco police inspector (Mark Harmon) who once served under him jointly investigate a murder on the base but their past conflicts and the cop's brewing relationship with the officer's sexy daughter (Meg Ryan) complicate matters. Director-cinematographer Peter Hyams handles the car pile-ups better than he does the actors and their relationships. Several intense chase sequences culminating in brutal death and destruction, much profanity and a fairly explicit sexual encounter

title: Presumed Innocent
synopsis: A prosecuting attorney (Harrison Ford) becomes the prime suspect in his own investigation of a sensational murder case in which the victim (Greta Scacchi) was a colleague as well as his ex-lover. Director Alan J. Pakula's darkly absorbing courtroom drama weaves an intricate plot around adultery and criminal complicity while presenting a disturbing picture of the manipulation of the criminal justice system by those who administer it. Ambiguous treatment of the justice theme, some scenes of an adulterous relationship and occasional rough language

title: Pretty Baby
synopsis: The story of a 12-year-old girl (Brooke Shields), born and raised in a house of prostitution, who eventually marries historical figure E.J. Bellocq (Keith Carridine), a photographer who first came to photograph her mother (Susan Sarandon). Director Louis Malle's listless, dubiously nostalgic tour of a bordello relies on extravagant nudity and the flagrant exploitation of a 12-year-old girl

title: Pretty Boy Floyd
synopsis: Clunky low-budget gangster picture directed by Herbert J. Leder follows the Prohibition-era rise and fall of the title New York criminal (John Ericson). Much stylized violence, some of it quite nasty

title: Pretty in Pink
synopsis: Self-sufficient, self-assured teenager (Molly Ringwald) goes to the junior prom alone when let down by the boy who was to take her. Director John Hughes provides a positive portrayal of a teenager who maintains a wholesome sense of her own identity despite the peer pressures and scorn of some of her classmates. Sexual innuendo and harsh language

title: Prettykill
synopsis: When the life of a New York call girl (Season Hubley) is threatened by the schizophrenic Southern charmer (Suzanne Snyder) she has taken under her wing, she seeks help from her long-time boyfriend, a police detective (David Birney). Director George Kaczender's failed thriller plays more like a distorted caricature of a romance. Unwholesome mix of sex and violence, with some nudity

title: Pretty Maids All in a Row
synopsis: Failed sex farce stars Rock Hudson as a high school guidance counselor who cures the coeds' hang-ups by couch therapy, and solves sophomore John David Carson's perpetual erection by introducing him to teacher-sexpot Angie Dickinson. As some of the pretty coeds wind up as corpses, super-sleuth Telly Savalas questions the student counselor's methods. Directed by Roger Vadim, there is little comedy or mystery in a work whose sole purpose seems to be to exploit sex

title: Pretty Persuasion
synopsis: Dark-edged satire about a maliciously manipulative 15-year-old (Evan Rachel Wood) who recruits two classmates (Elisabeth Harnois and Adi Schnall) in accusing one of their high school teachers (Ron Livingston) of sexual misconduct, entangling all involved in a web of deceit that has tragic consequences. Despite an impressive performance by his Lolitaish lead, director Marcos Siega's cynical, mean-spirited and unjustifiably raunchy revenge tale has pretensions of social commentary but lacks any sympathetic characters and seems content to shock rather than offer any real insights on the issues explored. Recurring sexual situations, including suggested sodomy and oral sex between minors, and, in one case, between a teenage girl and an adult woman; masturbation; a suicide; brief drug content; same-sex kissing; excessive explicit sexual language; and some profanity, ethnic slurs and lewd humor
full_review:
"Pretty Persuasion" (Samuel Goldwyn) is anything but pretty. In fact director Marcos Siega's cynical, mean-spirited and unjustifiably raunchy revenge tale makes other dark-edged teen satires like "Heathers," "Election" and "Mean Girls" look positively cheery by comparison and makes their respective bobby-socked bad girls out to be candy stripers.

The film centers on aspiring actress Kimberly Joyce (Evan Rachel Wood), a narcissistic and maliciously manipulative 15-year-old attending an exclusive private school in Beverly Hills. With the face of an angel, the tongue of a viper and the heart of Lady Macbeth, Kimberly uses her seductive charm to get what she wants.

As they say, the poisoned apple didn't fall far from tree. Her father, Hank (James Woods), is a racist slob who goes off on obscenity-laced anti-Semitic rants at the dinner table, snorts cocaine and masturbates while engaging in phone sex. (The sleazy shot of Woods fondling himself in a ratty bathrobe is perhaps the film's nadir of bad taste.)

Kimberly seems to take special relish in mercilessly tongue-lashing her stepmother (Jamie King) with depraved accusations. (Her estranged biological mother barely acknowledges her existence.)

For reasons only later revealed, she recruits two classmates -- best-friend Brittany (Elisabeth Harnois) and strictly-raised Middle Eastern transplant Randa (Adi Schnall) -- in accusing one of their high-school teachers, Percy Anderson (Ron Livingston), of sexual misconduct, entangling all involved in her grand Machiavellian web of deceit that has tragic consequences.

Despite an absence of nudity, there are numerous extremely provocative and exploitative scenes, including several of teens engaging in oral sex -- in one instance involving Kimberly and an adult lesbian TV reporter (Jane Krakowski) -- anal sex and masturbation, as well as those of Percy lustfully ogling female students.

The film also has a gratuitous amount of sordid language, much of which is either spoken by (or, equally troubling, directed at) Kimberly.

Despite a mesmerizing performance by its Lolitaish lead, "Pretty Persuasion" lacks any sympathetic characters, except Randa, and its alleged "humor" is just too distasteful to be funny.

And while having pretensions of social commentary -- on such issues as the media, racism, cultural assimilation, domestic dysfunction, adolescent angst and obsession with celebrity -- the movie seems content to shock rather than enlighten (or for that matter entertain), offering no real insights on the themes explored.

The film contains recurring sexual situations, including suggested sodomy and oral sex between minors, and, in one case, between a teenage girl and an adult woman; masturbation; a suicide; brief drug content; same-sex kissing; excessive explicit sexual language; and some profanity, ethnic slurs and lewd humor. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.

title: Pretty Poison
synopsis: Psychological terror movie about a mad youth running murderously amok is of only routine interest but director Noel Black has gotten subtle and chilling characterizations from Anthony Perkins as a crazed killer and Tuesday Weld as the perverse teenage nymph who inspires him

title: Pretty Woman
synopsis: Entertaining romantic confection about a smarmy corporate raider (Richard Gere) and a feisty street walker (Julia Roberts) who fall in love against their better judgment and are transformed into good, wholesome people. The contemporary fairy tale, a meld of Pygmalion and Cinderella, shines due to its likeable characterizations and sentimental touches injected by director Garry Marshall. Strictly adult comedy fare with a romanticized view of prostitution, several suggestive sexual encounters and some rough language laced with sexual innuendo

title: A Previous Engagement
synopsis: A Seattle librarian (Juliet Stevenson), on holiday in Malta with her dull, inattentive husband (Daniel Stern), plans to rendezvous with her suave French lover (Tcheky Karyo) from 25 years earlier. Even allowing for its often farcical structure, writer-director Joan Carr-Wiggin's story, which strives for a light, whimsical tone, never seems remotely grounded in reality as the best comedies should be, the generally capable cast is undermined by dialogue that rarely rings true, and the narrative is marred by a shallow moral tone. Adultery, rough language, crude expressions, the acceptability of premarital sex and divorce, and brief drug use
full_review:
In "A Previous Engagement" (Buccaneer), Seattle librarian Julia (Juliet Stevenson) suggests a holiday in Malta with her dull, inattentive husband, Jack (Daniel Stern), an insurance man who seems to care more for his jigsaw puzzles than for her.

Julia's real motive for vacationing there is to rendezvous with the suave French lover Alex (Tcheky Karyo), with whom she had an affair 25 years earlier.

Julia's a bundle of uncertainty, though, and matters are complicated by the unexpected arrival of her two daughters (Claire Brosseau and Elizabeth Whitmere), one with a new boyfriend (Simon Woods) in tow, and the revelation that Alex, who edits a literary journal, has been having an affair with his young assistant, Samantha (Kate Miles).

Julia's reluctance to consummate the reunion with Alex leads to his barging in on a family gathering unannounced as an "old friend" of Julia's. Jack soon connects the dots, and promptly falls under the spell of redheaded divorcee Grace (Valerie Mahaffey). "If two consenting adults who aren't involved with someone else feel that little spark, then why not?" she reasons, emblematic of the script's overall tenor.

Even allowing for its often farcical structure, writer-director Joan Carr-Wiggin's story, which strives for a light, whimsical tone, never seems remotely grounded in reality as the best comedies should be.

The generally capable cast is undermined by stilted dialogue and situations that rarely ring true. Stevenson uses every actorly trick to make her annoyingly vacillating character plausible.

Above all, the narrative is marred by a shallow moral tone that glamorizes adultery even as it dutifully shows Julia and Jack wrestling with their consciences.

The film contains adultery, rough language, crude expressions, the acceptability of premarital sex and divorce, and brief drug use. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.

title: Prey for Rock and Roll
synopsis: Raw drama about the trials and tribulations of an aging rock musician and lead singer (Gina Gershon) of a Los Angeles-based all-girl band who is still looking to break into the big time. Melodramatic plot machinations and cliched views about aging in the young world of rock 'n' roll keep director Alex Steyermark's film stalled despite strong performances, while a casual presentation and acceptance of both the lesbian and bisexual lifestyles are off-putting. Some sexual encounters including a same-sex scene, brief violence, intermittent drug abuse and recurring rough language
full_review:
Director Alex Steyermark's raw drama "Prey for Rock and Roll" (MAC) asks how old is too old before you should hang up your electric guitar, but the answer is less than satisfying.

Gina Gershon stars as Jacki, the lead singer-guitarist of an all-girl punk rock band in Los Angeles which includes bassist Tracy (Drea De Matteo), lead guitarist Faith (Lori Petty) and drummer Sally (Shelly Cole). The band is still struggling, playing dive gigs and working for pennies. So for Jacki, clad in leather pants and dark eyeliner, celebrating her 40th birthday means asking herself, "At what point do I become a joke?"

The story is based on Cheri Lovedog's autobiographical rock musical about her days in the female quartet named Clamdandy. Gershon's strong performance carries the film for a while, but she cannot go the distance with the poorly written script.

A major problem with the script, written by Lovedog and Robin Whitehouse, is that it has no real story to tell. Instead, the film toils along with melodramatic plot machinations and cliched views about aging in the young world of music. The compelling question of whether or not to hold on to the rock 'n' roll dream of fame and fortune, despite the onset of middle age, hangs in the air. The screen meanwhile is filled with obvious ploys, such as a rape-revenge scenario and the death of a character, to keep viewers interested in what is otherwise a droning tale.

However, even putting this cinematic flaw aside, "Prey for Rock and Roll" has a larger obstacle to overcome as far as Catholic audiences are concerned. The film's casual acceptance of both the lesbian and bisexual lifestyles cannot be ignored.

Jacki hasn't decided which "team" she will play for. A fairly graphic sexual scene shows Jacki and her girlfriend in compromising positions. But later on she falls for Animal (Marc Blucas), the brother of one of her band mates -- and an ex-con recently released from prison. And troubled trust-fund baby Tracy has a clear substance abuse problem that leads her to perform certain sexual acts in exchange for drugs.

"Prey for Rock and Roll" rarely allows the audience to sympathize with the characters because it never goes beyond the surface.

Due to some sexual encounters including a same-sex scene, brief violence, intermittent drug abuse and recurring rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Price Above Rubies, A
synopsis: Uneven tale in which the wife (Renee Zellweger) of a Torah scholar becomes discontented with her life in an Hasidic community in Brooklyn, then is seduced by her brother-in-law and his offer of a job in his Manhattan jewelry store where she embarks upon a new life. Writer-director Boaz Yakin treats the woman's conflicts with Orthodox Jewish traditions seriously but the story of her painful path to liberation is overly contrived and often taxes credibility. Explicit sexual situations, fleeting nudity and instances of profanity and rough language

title: Price of Fear, The
synopsis: Twisty crime tale about a canine-racetrack owner (Lex Barker) on the run from racketeers while falling for a woman (Merle Oberon) who has set him up to take the blame for her hit-and-run accident. Director Abner Biberman wrings easy menace from contrived situations but the characters are flat and motivations unconvincing. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Price of Glory
synopsis: Hackneyed drama about a has-been Mexican-American boxer (Jimmy Smits) who pushes his three gifted sons to achieve the championship boxing status he could not, but results prove dire. As directed by Carlos Avila, the film's performances are weak and the clich�d plot offers no new insights into the wearied story of a bitter father living vicariously through his sons. Some violence, brief drug use and fleeting rough language

title: Prick Up Your Ears
synopsis: Harshly realistic depiction of the doomed love affair between British playwright Joe Orton (Gary Oldman) and colaborator Kenneth Halliwell (Alfred Molina). Uncompromising direction by Stephen Frears dwells too vividly on the details of sordid homosexual encounters and a concluding bloody murder and suicide scene. Vanessa Redgrave co-stars in the British production which has brief male nudity and vulgar language

title: Pride
synopsis: Inspirational true-life tale, circa 1971, about a coach (Terrence Howard) who forms a swim team at a dilapidated Philadelphia community house, demonstrating to the African-American youths that, despite the poverty and crime around them, they can compete with privileged teens both in the pool and in the world. The emotion-tugging efficiency of director Sunu Gonera, a veteran of Coca-Cola and Nike commercials, serves this period piece well, briskly hitting all its marks about hope, teamwork, believing in oneself and overcoming adversity. A small amount of crude and crass language (including two instances of the n-word), a couple of scuffles and some vague threats of violence
full_review:
Once you get past the generic title, "Pride" (Lionsgate) proves an engagingly inspirational, true-life tale of an inner-city swim team in 1971 Philadelphia. And while it treads familiar sports-movie ground it doesn't just tread water, but briskly hits all its marks about hope, teamwork, believing in oneself and overcoming adversity.

Jim Ellis (Terrence Howard) is a coach who is hired to shut down a dilapidated Philadelphia community house. The only other employee, janitor Elston (Bernie Mac), resents the interloper, and warily warns Ellis that if the "college boy" is going to scrub out the unused pool and try to fill it from a hose, then he had best be prepared to pay the water bill. But the cool of the pool turns out to be just the thing for the local teenage boys on a blistering summer's day after their basketball hoops are removed by the city.

Through example, quiet perseverance and a raising of the boys' (and eventually one girl's) expectations of themselves, Ellis eventually, with Elston's help, turns the teens into a team and makes the community house a source of local pride, showing African-American youths, despite all the surrounding poverty and crime, that they can compete with privileged suburban teens both in the pool and, eventually, in the world.

The emotion-tugging efficiency applied by Zimbabwe-born director Sunu Gonera, a veteran of Coca-Cola and Nike commercials, serves this period piece well. Howard further demonstrates the versatility that has let him range from the emasculated filmmaker of "Crash" to the scary characters of "Hustle & Flow" and "Idlewild." Mac, despite a valiant effort, fails to make his character more than an unfortunate stereotype.

The film contains a relatively small amount of crude and crass language (including two instances of the n-word), a couple of scuffles and some vague threats of violence. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested. Some material may not be suitable for children.

title: Pride and Glory
synopsis: Powerful but often brutal drama of a family of New York police officers (Edward Norton, Colin Farrell, Noah Emmerich and Jon Voight, all solid) torn apart by a major corruption scandal. Though director and co-writer Gavin O'Connor's absorbing drama starts out noisily frenetic as a drug bust goes fatally awry, the family elements eventually come to the fore, taking on the dimensions of genuine tragedy, with that age-old conflict between right and wrong in vivid play. Strong violence with bloodshed, pervasive rough language and profanity, some crude sexual expressions, drug use and suicide

title: Pride & Prejudice
synopsis: Fine new version of Jane Austen's evergreen classic concerning the five unmarried Bennet girls whose mother (Brenda Blethyn) is strenuously determined to marry them off in 18th-century England, and the crossed-signals romance between Elizabeth (Keira Knightley) and the wealthy Darcy (Matthew Macfadyen) whose apparent dislike for each other -- because of his arrogance and her judgmental attitude -- masks a profound attraction. Director Joe Wright makes the settings more realistically rough-hewn than usual, but even so the film is visually stunning and its top-flight supporting players - Donald Sutherland, Judi Dench, Penelope Wilton and Tom Hollander among them -- make this highly recommendable for all ages
full_review:
Not counting various television versions such as the memorable 1995 BBC Colin Firth-Jennifer Ehle miniseries (shown stateside on A&E), and some big-screen adaptations that took considerable license -- such as last year's Indian-flavored update, "Bride & Prejudice" -- Jane Austen's most famous work was, incredibly, filmed only once before: MGM's 1940 classic with Greer Garson and Laurence Olivier.

The MGM and BBC renderings were fine indeed, but the latest "Pride & Prejudice" (Focus) is yet another splendid dramatization.

As everyone knows, the story concerns the five unmarried Bennet girls and the strenuous efforts of their mother, Mrs. Bennet, perennially unkempt and frazzled as played by the wonderful Brenda Blethyn, to marry them off in 18th-century England.

Things are looking promising for eldest daughter Jane (Rosamund Pike), in love with the upper-crust Bingley (Simon Woods) who has come to town with his wealthy friend, Mr. Darcy (Matthew Macfadyen), in tow.

Darcy encounters second-eldest daughter Elizabeth (Keira Knightley) at a ball, and the
first meeting has Darcy disdainfully refusing to dance with Lizzie, as she's called.

Thereafter, it's crossed signals all the way between Lizzie and Darcy, whose dislike for each other -- because of his arrogance and her judgmental attitude -- masks a growing and profound attraction.

Her bad opinion of him is reinforced when she learns he had a hand in derailing Bingley's courtship of Jane, and his apparently cruel treatment of the soldier Wickham (Rupert Friend), once Darcy's childhood friend, but who now claims Darcy did him ill.

Knightley could not be more different from her recent turn as actor Laurence Harvey's punkish, heavily mascaraed, bounty-hunting daughter in "Domino." Here, she's the picture of a fresh-faced Regency-era young lady, deftly capturing Lizzie's spiritedness and charm.

Macfadyen is appropriately aloof and sullen, and is immensely sympathetic when he first expresses his love for Lizzie -- and, like Darcy, grows more appealing as the story progresses.

Director Joe Wright uses settings more realistically rough-hewn than usual; the Bennet household, for example, is a lived-in mess, and there are several shots of livestock that give you a visceral sense of the environment, but the film is nonetheless visually stunning.

Roman Osin's camera is always on the move, sometimes distractingly so, but is unafraid to linger on the beautiful vistas of the English countryside.

The supporting players are all top-flight: Donald Sutherland as the long-suffering father who quietly supports Lizzie, Judi Dench as the unpleasantly imperious Lady Catherine de Bourg, Penelope Wilton as the Bennets' kind aunt, and the diminutive Tom Hollander offering a gem of a comic characterization as Mr. Collins, a dull and fawning clergyman who, briefly, sets his sights on Lizzie.

Apart from a subplot involving a rakish character who elopes with one of the daughters with dishonorable intent, there is nothing to preclude recommendation for all ages. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-I -- general patronage. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

title: Pride of St. Louis, The
synopsis: The life and times of baseball pitcher Jerome "Dizzy" Dean (Dan Dailey) whose Arkansas twang and garbled syntax make him a beloved sports announcer after his glory years on the mound for the Cardinals during the 1930s. Directed by Harmon Jones, Daily gives a likeable performance as the clowning ballplayer whose biggest fan is his wife (Joanne Dru), while the pitching career of his brother "Daffy" (Richard Crenna) becomes one of his major concerns

title: Pride of the Bowery
synopsis: Routine East Side Kids comedy in which Danny (Bobby Jordan) gets the gang to join the Civilian Conservation Corps to make $22 a month while they help Muggs (Leo Gorcey) train for a boxing match. Directed by Joseph H. Lewis, the thin plot has Muggs blamed for another's theft, the boxing scenes are ridiculous but the footage filmed at a CCC camp has historical interest. Loud and brassy slapstick

title: Pride of the Marines
synopsis: Fact-based story of Marine Al Schmid (John Garfield) whose injuries in the battle for Guadalcanal result in blindness which he fears will make him a burden to the hometown girl (Eleanor Parker) waiting to marry him, but she knows better. Directed by Delmer Daves, the situation developes along the lines of a conventional tearjerker but the personable cast helps make the uncertainties of the characters humanly compelling. Wartime violence and its anguishing consequences

title: Pride of the West
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Lesley Selander in which Hopalong Cassidy (William Boyd) interrupts his ranch chores to help a couple of friends (George Hayes and Russell Hayden) nab a landgrabbing realtor (James Craig) in cahoots with a crooked banker (Kenneth Harlan). Frontier violence

title: Pride of the Yankees, The
synopsis: Fine drama of New York Yankee first baseman Lou Gehrig (Gary Cooper) who never missed a game in 14 years of outstanding play until forced to retire in 1939 by an incurable disease which has since borne his name. Directed by Sam Wood, the result has interest beyond the story of a baseball hero because it captures the universal qualities of character and spirit underlying the career of a man who gave his unfailing best for team, fans and family. Memorable movie even for those who don't like baseball

title: Priest
synopsis: Flawed British drama probes the conflict between religious ideals and human frailties in a story set in a working-class Catholic parish where a young curate tries to live a life of celibacy, yet initiates several homosexual encounters, partly out of torment at his helplessness in stopping a case of incest revealed in confession. Director Antonia Bird provides a credible picture of a lonely priest in a busy parish, though its emphasis on his struggles with his own sexuality strangely lacks any notion of sin and the ambiguous ending in an emotionally powerful scene of reconciliation leaves matters unresolved. Serious treatment of a very troubling subject, depictions of homosexual acts and occasional crude language

title: Priest and the Girl, The
synopsis: The story told by this 1966 Brazilian drama is of a young priest, overwhelmed by the poverty and injustice of the backward community to which he has been sent, blindly runs away in the company of a sensual young girl who looks to him for protection from her brutal guardian. Director Joaquim Pedro de Andrade's slow moving study of spiritual aridity is less concerned with his two central characters than in the barren lives of the people who inhabit a desolate part of the world

title: Priest's Wife, The
synopsis: Careless Italian romp stars Sophia Loren as a suicidal pop singer and Marcello Matroianni as the priest who becomes the object of her attentions. What begins as a rather lighthearted spoof of the issue of priestly celibacy, ends up as a humorless and bitter indictment of church law. While the viewer is mercifully spared the visual aspects of the pair's sexual relationship, director Dino Risi's irreverent and occasionally tasteless humor is more an insult to one's intelligence than to one's religious convictions

title: Primal Fear
synopsis: Clunky thriller from William Diehl's novel in which a hotshot Chicago lawyer (Richard Gere) defends a youth (Edward Norton) charged with killing a Catholic prelate who had sexually abused him, but the trial's result is a cynical mockery of justice. Directed by Gregory Hoblit, the manipulative proceedings posture a great deal about truth and justice, but the result is only an empty exercise in cheap thrills. Graphic scenes of sex and of violence as well as a cynical exploitation of a religious figure

title: Primary Colors
synopsis: Political satire involving a charismatic Southern Governor (John Travolta) whose campaign for his party's presidential nomination is threatened by allegations of extramarital affairs. Directed by Mike Nichols from Elaine May's script, the candidate's character is given superficial treatment, though some keen observations are made along the way on the political process and ethical compromises. Fleeting violence including a suicide, various implied affairs, recurring profanity and much rough language

title: Prime
synopsis: Amusing, if morally problematic, New York-based story of a 37-year-old divorcee (Uma Thurman) who falls in love with a 23-year-old Jewish aspiring artist (Bryan Greenberg). Neither aware that he is the son of her psychiatrist (Meryl Streep) -- who is determined her son will marry within his faith, but finds herself with the ethical dilemma of helping her client or protecting her son. Ben Younger's directorial debut is well-acted, and has moments of charm, but is far too casual about the premarital affair, though the affair is at least grounded by real love and affection, and the ending is admirably realistic. Scattered profanity, crude language and expressions, frank sexual talk, several nonexplicit sex scenes, strongly permissive view of premarital sex, and infidelity
full_review:
The older woman-younger man liaison has been done countless times before. Think Dumas' "Camille" and its operatic spinoff, "La Traviata." Or Colette's "Cheri."

And here it is again in "Prime" (Universal), a generally amusing, if at times morally problematic Manhattan-based story about a 37-year-old divorcee named Rafi (Uma Thurman). She has just split with her husband after nine years. Much to her surprise, and against the advice of her friends (including the obligatory gay confidants), she falls in love with a hunky 23-year-old Jewish man, David (Bryan Greenberg), an aspiring artist who lives with his grandparents.

Unbeknownst to both of them, David is the son of Rafi's psychiatrist, Lisa, played by Meryl Streep in another impressive character portrayal: brown wig, glasses and a New York Jewish cadence.

She is determined her son will marry within his faith, and as she hears Rafi's increasingly more detailed descriptions of her burgeoning love life, she puts two and two together and figures out it's her son her patient is seeing. (In the course of treating Rafi, there's some extremely in-your-face talk about her sexual activities.)

Before she intuited the truth, however, she had been encouraging the union. ("It might even do you some good," she counsels, emblematic of an overly indulgent view of premarital sex that permeates the film.)

Lisa then finds herself with the ethical dilemma of helping her client, against her better judgment, or protecting her son. Ben Younger's directorial debut (he also wrote the script) is well-acted, and has moments of humor, sometimes bordering on the farcical, and charm. Besides Streep's bravura turn, Thurman gives an appealing, sympathetic portrayal, and Greenberg is fine as David, etching a basically decent character, and making his maturation believable.

With Dave such a mature-looking 23, and Rafi such a youthful 37, the age differential is less problematic than everyone's casualness about the affair. The sexual component of the relationship is illustrated by several nonexplicit lovemaking scenes.

On the plus side, the affair at least very quickly morphs into one with real love and affection (with Rafi and David deeply committed to the relationship) -- she helps him with his painting career -- and the bittersweet ending is admirably realistic, with Rafi ultimately doing "the right thing."

Dramatically at least, Streep's tolerance of an affair she's clearly not happy about is a nice touch. Another film would have stereotypically made her the inflexible obstacle to the romance.

The film contains scattered profanity, crude language and expressions, frank sexual talk, several nonexplicit sex scenes, strongly permissive view of premarital sex and infidelity.
The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Prime Cut
synopsis: Tough slice of crime melodrama about a hired killer (Lee Marvin) sent to extol tribute from a double-crossing Kansas City gangster (Gene Hackman) who sells beef and women. As directed by Michael Ritchie, the fast-paced action becomes a senseless nightmare of white slavery, drugs and meatpacking treated with blood, gore, nudity and foul language

title: Prime of Miss Jean Brodie, The
synopsis: Poignant screen version of Muriel Spark's novel about a bright, demanding teacher (Maggie Smith) who doesn't fit the mold of a conservative girls' academy in 1930's Edinburgh where she teaches her devoted, unquestioning "gurrls" until one of them (Pamela Franklin) betrays her confidence by posing in the nude for the art teacher. Director Ronald Neame handles the moral ambiguities of the situation with great sensitivity, leaving viewers to consider an inspiring teacher's powerful influence on the young, for both good and bad

title: Primer
synopsis: Writer-director Shane Carruth's low-budget sci-fi mindbender about a pair of young brainiacs (Carruth and David Sullivan), who -- while working out of their garage, trying to come up with the next "big" thing -- discover that the gizmo they invented can be used as a time machine, which they exploit to their advantage, leading to unforeseen consequences. Despite an intriguing conceit and edgy, no-frills look, the film is weighed down by its indecipherable plot and cryptic techno-babble dialogue which will leave many viewers scratching their heads. Some crude language
full_review:
In writer-director Shane Carruth's low-budget sci-fi mindbender "Primer" (ThinkFilm), a pair of young brainiacs (Carruth and David Sullivan), working out of their garage to come up with the next "big" thing, discover that the gizmo they invented can be used as a time machine, which they exploit to their advantage, leading to unforeseen consequences.

Despite an intriguing conceit and edgy, no-frills look, the film is weighed down by its indecipherable plot and cryptic techno-babble dialogue which will leave many viewers scratching their heads.

Due to some crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Primeval
synopsis: Bloody action thriller about an American television news crew (Dominic Purcell, Brooke Langton and Orlando Jones) dispatched to a civil-war ravaged African nation to report on a giant crocodile terrorizing the locals and to bring the beast back alive with the help of a seasoned hunter (Jurgen Prochnow) and an Australian reptile expert (Gideon Emery). Allegedly inspired by true events, director Michael Katleman�s mostly suspense-free �Jaws� rip-off is undone by schlocky effects and a script that tries to wedge social-conscience commentary into its B-movie plot. Much gory violence, grisly images, recurring rough and crude language and some sexual humor
full_review:
In the bloody action thriller "Primeval" (Hollywood Pictures), an American television news crew (Dominic Purcell, Brooke Langton and Orlando Jones) is dispatched to a civil-war ravaged African nation to report on a giant crocodile terrorizing the locals and to bring the beast back alive with the help of a seasoned hunter (Jurgen Prochnow) and an Australian reptile expert (Gideon Emery).

Allegedly inspired by true events, director Michael Katleman's mostly suspense-free "Jaws" rip-off is undone by schlocky effects and a script that tries to wedge social-conscience commentary into a B-movie plot.

The film contains much gory violence, grisly images, recurring rough and crude language and some sexual humor. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Primrose Path
synopsis: Erratic sudser in which a genial go-getter (Joel McCrea) weds a young woman (Ginger Rogers), then stalks off after learning her father (Miles Mander) is an alcoholic and her mother (Marjorie Rambeau) lives off other men. Directed by Gregory LaCava, the contrived plot starts with some sunny humor, then turns increasingly maudlin until an unearned happy ending. Veiled treatment of prostitution and sexual innuendo

title: Prince and the Pauper, The
synopsis: Durable version of the Mark Twain classic in which an English prince (Bobby Mauch) switches places with a lookalike urchin (Billy Mauch) for a lark that could prove fatal unless a would-be usurper (Claude Rains) is undone by a mettlesome commoner (Errol Flynn). Director William Keighley's melodramatic style only slows the pace of the boys' misadventures after swapping the dangers of the Tudor court for the squalor of the London slums and vice versa. For all the aristocratic villainy and stylized violence, the period adventure is grand fun for family viewers

title: Prince and the Showgirl, The
synopsis: Fluffy romantic comedy from Terence Rattigan's play about the urbane regent (Laurence Olivier) of a Balkan kingdom who arrives in London for the 1911 coronation of George V and falls for a dizzy American chorus girl (Marilyn Monroe). Also directed by Olivier, the contrast between the cynical prince and the not-so-innocent starlet is obvious but fun, with some witty jabs at stuffy English characters (notably Richard Wattis) and daffy asides by the Balkan Queen Mother (Sybil Thorndike who steals every scene she's in). Sexual situations and innuendo

title: Prince of Darkness
synopsis: Failed horror movie in which a priest (Donald Pleasence) discovers a secret vault in a Los Angeles church containing a cosmic force that if let loose will become the Son of Darkness. Directed self-indulgently by John Carpenter, the boring and pretentious movie talks itself to death but sprinkles in enough blood-and-gore scenes and vomiting zombies to bludgeon moral sensibilities

title: Prince of Egypt, The
synopsis: The biblical story of Moses (voice of Val Kilmer) is retold in a beautifully crafted animated feature that focuses on the oppression of the Israelites in Egypt and God's selection of Moses to lead them to the Promised Land, though younger children may find it an overwhelming experience with some harrowing scenes. Directed by Brenda Chapman, Steve Hickner and Simon Wells, the result is an impressive animated spectacle re-creating its biblical-era story in compelling fashion, marred only by the artificiality of Stephen Schwartz's songs. Some emotionally intense scenes

title: Prince of Foxes
synopsis: Tale of intrigue and adventure in 1500 Italy where an ambitious courtier (Tyrone Power) tries to save the lands of an aged noble (Felix Aylmer) and his lady (Wanda Hendrix) from conquest by the notorious Cesare Borgia (Orson Welles). Director Henry King's elegant costume melodrama has some interesting twists as well as spectacular location photography of fortified castles and other period settings. Stylized violence, duplicity and romantic complications

title: Prince of the City
synopsis: Treat Williams plays a New York City detective who, tormented by guilt, comes forward to cooperate with federal authorities investigating police corruption. Director Sidney Lumet succeeds in portraying the human complexity in this flawed but gripping drama that has some of the inexorable force of Greek tragedy. Williams is particularly fine among a strong cast giving many excellent performances. Though the violence is extremely restrained, a somber and difficult theme with much rough language

title: Prince of Tides, The
synopsis: Hoping to help his suicidal sister, an estranged husband (Nick Nolte) relates their troubled family history to her psychiatrist (Barbra Streisand) and the two become romantically involved, profoundly affecting each other and both of their families. Also produced and directed by Streisand, the emotionally complex drama muddies the question of infidelity but is rich in themes of interpersonal communication and familial forgiveness. Momentary but violent rape scene, discreet bedroom scenes, adulterous and homosexual references and some rough language

title: Princes in Exile
synopsis: A 17-year-old boy (Zachary Ansley) finds romance and a new attitude at a summer camp for youngsters struggling with cancer. Humor and hope come shining through this moving film from Canadian director Giles Walker who keeps excess sentimentality at bay with honest performances from its young cast. Disturbifng subject matter which may be frightening to small children and mild sexual references

title: The Princess and the Frog
synopsis: Enchanting animated musical, set in 1920s New Orleans, in which a voodoo sorcerer (voice of Keith David) casts a spell that complicates the lives of a visiting prince (voice of Bruno Campos), the headstrong heiress he hopes to marry (voice of Jennifer Cody) and her industrious working-class best friend (voice of Anika Noni Rose). As directed and co-written by John Musker and Ron Clements, the lavish hand-drawn romance, which also features delightful voice work by Michael-Leon Wooley as a jazz-loving alligator and Jim Cummings as a Cajun firefly, emphasizes the value of love over material wealth and provides quality entertainment for all ages, though images of fire-breathing masks and evil sprites may scare some tots

title: Princess and the Pirate, The
synopsis: Madcap comedy in which a ham actor (Bob Hope) helps a runaway princess (Virginia Mayo) escape capture by a notorious pirate known as the Hook (Victor McLaglen), then both wind up in a pirate haven whose governor (Walter Slezak) takes them prisoner, only to be later recaptured by the Hook. Director David Butler keeps the slapstick proceedings merrily afloat with Hope's comic blunderings, zany asides and hilarious impersonation of the Hook, though Walter Brennan as a toothless tattooer almost steals the picture. Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Princess Bride, The
synopsis: Affectionate, lighthearted parody of medieval romance as a young beauty (Robin Wright) is saved from a forced marriage to a nasty prince (Chris Sarandon) by a farm boy turned pirate (Cary Elwes). Directed by Rob Reiner from William Goldman's script, the comic proceedings are marked with verbal wit and some silly turns by Mandy Patinkin, Wallace Shawn and Billy Crystal. Some comic book violence

title: Princess Caraboo
synopsis: Delightful fact-based tale set in early 19th-century England where an exotically dressed young woman (Phoebe Cates) speaking no English is found on the wayside and is embraced by the upper classes who believe she is a shipwrecked Javanese princess, until a lovestruck reporter (Stephen Rea) uncovers her true background. Director Michael Austin turns in a deft comedy that skewers the pretention of the British uppercrust and features masterful comic performances by John Lithgow and Kevin Kline in smaller roles. Mild sexual innuendo

title: Princess Comes Across, The
synopsis: Fitful comedy combining murder and romance aboard an ocean liner whose passengers include a girl from Brooklyn (Carole Lombard) trying to get to Hollywood by masquerading as a princess from Sweden, a band leader (Fred MacMurray) aware of the ruse but sweet on its perpetrator, top detectives from around the world and an escaped killer. Director William K. Howard can't quite make it all work but Lombard has a lot of fun spoofing Garbo and Alison Skipworth shines as her brassy lady-in-waiting. Mild romance and some menace

title: Princess Mononoke
synopsis: Japanese cartoon feature spins a mythic tale of ancient woodland spirits warring with human intruders while a young warrior (voice of Billy Crudup) tries to make peace between them with the help of the title princess (voice of Claire Danes) who was raised by wolves serving the god of the forest. Writer-director Hayao Miyazaki has created a beautifully animated tale of ancient Japan which mingles a mythic past with its feudal culture, though even those who enjoy its mythic imagination may find the proceedings growing tiresomely overlong. Animated violence with gory visuals and some vulgar language

title: Princess of Thieves
synopsis: Unremarkable adventure set in 12th century England about the 18-year-old daughter (Keira Knightley) of Robin Hood and Maid Marion, who must simultaneously save her captured father and safely escort Prince Philip (Stephen Moyer), the heir to the throne, back from France. Lackluster costuming, a predictable plot and pedestrian acting are the marks director Peter Hewitt has left on this continuing story of Robin Hood

title: Princess, The
synopsis: ( see: "A Time in the Sun" )

title: Princess Yang Kwei Fei
synopsis: One of the most beautiful color movies ever made, this 1955 Japanese production retells a Chinese legend about a graceful princess who dies for her emperor and whose love lives on after death. Directed by Kenji Mizoguchi, the narrative is slow and measured but the interest lies less in its traditional story than in the beauty and grace of its presentation done with an artistry that is genuine and universal

title: Prince Who Was a Thief, The
synopsis: Arabian Nights baloney about a prince (Tony Curtis) who was stolen as a baby and raised by a thief (Everett Sloane), but then discovers his true identity because of a pretty pickpocket (Piper Laurie) and fights to take his rightful place on the throne. Directed by Rudolph Mate from a story by Theodore Dreiser, the action varies from the silly to the ludicrous, with performances to match, though the ridiculous proceedings may be enjoyed by those seeking escapist fun. Some sexual innunedo

title: Principal, The
synopsis: Rowdy, inept teacher (James Belushi) becomes a dedicated administrator who takes it upon himself to tame the drug dealing felons who rule an inner-city high school. Director Christopher Cain milks an improbable plot for violence and brutality failing to provide a balanced forum for the real and pressing issues of crime in the schools

title: Prisoner of Second Avenue, The
synopsis: Uneven screen verison of Neil Simon's Broadway comedy about a middle-aged New Yorker (Jack Lemmon) who loses his job, gets mugged while his apartment is robbed and endures all sorts of other urban traumas with the help of his sensible, down-to-earth wife (Anne Bancroft). Direector Melvin Frank pumps up all the life possible in a script hinged on situations that are not very amusing and wisecracks that are only occasionally witty. Intermittent profanity

title: Prisoner of Shark Island, The
synopsis: Sentenced to life imprisonment for setting the broken leg of Lincoln's assassin, Dr. Samuel Mudd (Warner Baxter) is sent to an island fortress off the Florida coast where he earns a pardon after risking his life to save others during a yellow fever epidemic. Director John Ford's fact-based story of a doctor who became an innocent victim of his times achieves considerable impact from its credible evocation of the period and its human context. Miscarriage of justice and brutal mistreatment

title: Prisoner of the Mountains
synopsis: Two Russian soldiers (Oleg Menshikov and Sergei Bodrov, Jr.) held hostage by Chechan villagers come to know one another and their Muslim captors as their fate hangs in the balance. Directed by Sergei Bodrov from a Tolstoy short story, the quietly powerful tale of shared humanity and the insanity of war is starkly beautiful as well as emotionally engrossing. Subtitles. Brief violence and nudity as well as occasional rough language

title: Prisoner of Zenda
synopsis: Peter Sellers plays the dual role of the foppish King Rudolph of Ruritania and the stout-hearted Englishman who takes his place to foil a plot against the throne. Under Richard Quine's direction, the action and pageantry in gorgeous settings are treated realistically rather than as fantasy so that the result falls between two stools, being neither funny, nor romantic enough

title: Prisoner of Zenda, The
