The film contains nearly constant blood, gore and mutilation, cannibalism, brief frontal and upper female nudity, drug use, and much crude and some crass language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Restless Natives
synopsis: Lighthearted comedy features exquisite scenic backgrounds of the Scottish highlands in an implausible story about two youths (Joe Mullaney and Vincent Friell) who devise an outlandish scam to extort money from tourists in the hope of gaining financial security before they hit the ripe old age of 20. Their only potential problem is a vacationing CIA agent (Ned Beatty). Director Michael Hoffman concentrates on the relationship between the two friends rather than the flimsy plot and its twist ending

title: Restless Years, The
synopsis: Inane teenage sudser directed by Helmut Kautner centers on a withdrawn adolescent (Sandra Dee) whose overly protective mother (Teresa Wright) tries to shield her from making the same mistake she had made at her age, while a new classmate (John Saxon) befriends the girl and defies a bunch of small-town hypocrites. Muted sexual innuendoes and references to illegitimacy

title: Restoration
synopsis: Elaborate but uneven costume drama in which a frivolous physician (Robert Downey Jr.) in the 17th-century court of King Charles II (Sam Neill) reluctantly finds his humanity by treating London's poor after being tossed out of court on a royal whim. Director Michael Hoffman switches gears rather awkwardly in going from bedroom farce to a more substantial drama of personal transformation. Fleeting bedroom scenes with nudity and frequent references to sexual court intrigues

title: Resurrecting the Champ
synopsis: Compelling film, based on true events, about the evolving friendship between a young sportswriter (Josh Hartnett) and a homeless former boxing champ (Samuel L. Jackson) which forces the writer to take a fresh look at himself and to reevaluate his basic relationships, including those with his wife (Kathryn Morris) and son (Dakota Goyo), and the troubling memory of his deceased father. Director Rod Lurie's deeply moving -- as well as moral -- film features morally complex characters who experience redemption, an excellent script, and outstanding performances, though the boxing sequences may prove disturbing to those with a low tolerance for the sport. Occasional vulgarity and profanity, boxing violence including one sequence with blood, skimpy costuming and suggestive movements, public urination and images of a disturbing body scar
full_review:
In director Rod Lurie's compelling film "Resurrecting the Champ" (Yari Film Group), the evolving friendship between young sportswriter Erik Kernan (Josh Hartnett) and a homeless former boxer who calls himself "Champ" (Samuel L. Jackson) leads to a series of unexpected revelations.

In the course of the film, based on true events, Erik is forced to take a fresh look at himself and to re-evaluate his basic relationships, including those with his wife, Joyce (Kathryn Morris), his son, Teddy (Dakota Goyo), and the troubling memory of his deceased father. He is haunted by the professional renown and personal shortcomings of his late father, a famous boxing announcer.

Erik and Champ first encounter each other when the younger man plays the role of good Samaritan, rescuing Champ from a group of teenage bullies who are mocking and beating him. Erik only really becomes interested in his new acquaintance, however, when he learns of the homeless man's past glory. Here at last, it seems, is the "big story" Erik has been waiting for, the one that will demonstrate to his editor, Metz (Alan Alda), that he can deliver the goods. But he plans to do so by giving the story to another editor at the paper.

Such a breakthrough is important to him personally as well. Although separated from his wife (a "hard news" reporter with a reputation superior to his), Erik is determined to win her back and to be reunited with his son.

When his article about Champ is published, he indeed becomes the man of the hour, celebrated by his newspaper, wooed by others and pursued by television casting agent Andrea Flak (Teri Hatcher). When unexpected circumstances undermine his plan, Erik must make a series of difficult choices that will define who he is far more profoundly than his brief career as a celebrity.

This is a deeply moving -- and moral -- film. With the possible exception of Joyce, who serves as her husband's unswerving moral compass, all the other central characters are morally complex, and all the more interesting for it. But, for all their shortcomings, none of them proves to be beyond redemption.

An excellent script is matched by three outstanding performances. Jackson's Champ is irrepressibly optimistic, but also shrewd and careful of his dignity. Hartnett, as Erik, pays attention to the details, including his character's initial reluctance to have any physical contact with Champ. And Peter Coyote, as seedy boxing manager Epstein, turns a cameo into a showstopper.

Director Rod Lurie shows particular flair for the boxing sequences, utilizing lurid colors and speed in sharp contrast to Martin Scorsese's "Raging Bull" with its celebrated black-and-white, slow-motion techniques, although they may prove disturbing to those with a low tolerance for the sport.

The film contains occasional vulgarity and profanity, boxing violence including one sequence with blood, skimpy costuming and suggestive movements, public urination and images of a disturbing body scar. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults (though it's probably acceptable for most older teens). The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Resurrection
synopsis: Engrossing but flawed drama about a woman (Ellen Burstyn) who discovers that she has the power to heal people after barely surviving a tragic accident in which she loses her husband. The screenplay by Lewis John Carlino sets up a fascinating situation, but neither Carlino nor director Daniel Petrie is able to work it out in satisfactory fashion. The spiritual side of faith healing is dealt with in very unimaginative fashion showing the afterlife, for example, as being, quite literally, the light at the end of the tunnel. Theme and language require a mature perspective

title: Resurrection
synopsis: Brain-dead gore fest directed by Russell Mulcahy in which a Chicago cop (Christopher Lambert) goes after a serial killer collecting body parts from his victims to be reassembled at Easter as a symbol of the Second Coming. Graphic violence, frontal nudity, degrading use of Christian beliefs, profanity and rough language

title: Return from Witch Mountain
synopsis: The further adventures of the two castaway space children from :2OEscape to Witch Mountain'' with Tony falling into the villainous hands of Christopher Lee and Bette Davis who are intent on using the boy's powers for personal gain. Tia, with the aid of the lovable kind of street gang that exists nowhere outside of Disney films, rescues him in the nick of time. The sequel, directed by John Hough, is a movie that younger children will enjoy

title: Return of a Man Called Horse, The
synopsis: Sequel finds bored English nobleman (Richard Harris) back in South Dakota when his adopted Indian tribe needs a leader. After another gruesome purification ceremony consisting of mind-altering drugs and of having bones inserted into his chest, he leads his tribe to victory over their enemies. Director Irvin Kershner delivers a serious film, entertaining and beautifully photographed but, its emphasis on violence makes this decidedly mature fare

title: Return of Count Yorga, The
synopsis: Though this time the gentlemanly ghoul (Robert Quarry) falls in love (his one weakness), most of his time is spent, however, preying upon a neighboring orphanage. The sequel is properly amusing and frightening, with director Bob Kelljan sprinkling the proceedings with enough blood, however, to warrant caution for young or squeamish viewers

title: Return of Dracula, The
synopsis: Offbeat horror tale in which the legendary vampire (Francis Lederer) flees pursuers in post-World War II Eastern Europe by emigrating to California where he's taken in by the unsuspecting relatives of the man he killed for his identity papers. Directed by Paul Landres, the hokey proceedings generate little suspense though the genial small-town setting provides some eerie moments and Lederer's modern-day Dracula exudes sinister intensity. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Return of Frank James, The
synopsis: Dandy sequel to "Jesse James," largely with the same cast and settings, follows Frank as he sets out to avenge his brother's death by killing the cowardly Ford brothers (John Carradine and Charles Tannen), then gets sidetracked by a Denver reporter (Gene Tierney) from whom he learns his black farm hand (Robert Whitman) is to be hung as his accomplice unless he returns. Director Fitz Lang gets a fine performance from Fonda as the reformed outlaw who wrestles with his conscience over revenging a past wrong or saving an innocent life, then puts his life at risk in the taut trial sequence in the dramatic finale. Brief stylized violence, some muddled motives and several period racial expressions

title: Return of Jack Slade, The
synopsis: Uneven Western directed by Harold Schuster in which the title outlaw's son (John Ericson) tries to atone for his father's crimes by joining the notorious Hole in the Wall gang in 1886 Wyoming, then luring them into an ambush set up by Pinkerton agents. Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Return of Jafar, The
synopsis: Peppy animated sequel to "Aladdin" in which the evil wizard of the title (voice of Jonathan Freeman) escapes from the magic lamp and attempts to seize power by forcing reformed parrot Iago (voice of Gilbert Gottfried) to betray Aladdin (voice of Scott Weinger) and the princess (voice of Linda Larkin). Directed by Tad Stones, Toby Shelton and Alan Zaslove, the result lacks the original's superior animation and the inspired humor of Robin Williams but delivers zippy pacing to the story's misadventures along with some mildly enjoyable musical numbers

title: Return of Martin Guerre, The
synopsis: Engrossing, fact-based French production about a 16th-century peasant who abandons his wife and disappears from his native village to reappear some eight years later, much improved in every way. Accepted by his wife and most of the villagers, a squabble over property a few years later provokes the accusation that he's an imposter, and a trial with tragic results ensues. Written by Jean-Claude Carriere and directed by Daniel Vigne, the movie is partly a mystery but most of all a love story that most adults will find intriguing entertainment. Brief nudity and sexual references

title: Return of Maxwell Smart, The
synopsis: TV's secret agent Maxwell Smart (Don Adams) is assigned to thwart a villain (Vittorio Gassman) who has developed a bomb capable of destroying all the clothing in the world. Director Clive Donner's woefully inept and dull comedy relies on sexual innuendo

title: Return of Mr. Moto, The
synopsis: Muddled mystery in which the Japanese detective (miscast Henry Silva) helps Scotland Yard unmask an international conspiracy to control Mideast oil production. Directed by Ernest Morris, the low-budget picture goes nowhere with its dull formula plot and lackluster cast. Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Return of Sabata
synopsis: Frank Kramer (alias Gianfranco Parolini) directs this third installment in the spaghetti Western series spoofing spaghetti Westerns. This time the sooty-suited hero with the twitching nostrils (Lee Van Cleef) matches wits and weapons with the Irish boss of a cardboard Texas town whose citizens are being taxed to the tune of a million dollars. Sabata comes to the rescue and sneers at the audience as he rides away from his bordello beauty and a cast full of sloppily-dubbed characters

title: Return of Swamp Thing, The
synopsis: Forgettable sequel in which the crime-busting human plant (Dick Durock), a former scientist who keeps the bayou safe for kids and damsels in distress, falls for the stepdaughter (Heather Locklear) of a gene-tampering scientist (Louis Jourdan). Directed by Jim Wynorski, the cheesy sets and sleepwalking actors negate the good stuff which includes clever make-up and the heroic antics of the asparagus stalk with a heart of gold. Some sexual innuendo, rough language and much comic-book violence

title: Return of the Badmen
synopsis: Pioneering Oklahoma settler (Randolph Scott) takes on the worst of the Old West's outlaws, the nastiest of which is the Sundance Kid (Robert Ryan). There's some comic relief (Gabby Hayes) and the hero gets the girl (Jacqueline White) in the last reel, but otherwise director Ray Enright's shoot-'em-up is strictly routine action fare. Frontier violence

title: Return of the Fly
synopsis: Thin sequel in which the son (Brett Halsey) of the Montreal scientist whose molecular structure got mixed with that of a housefly continues his father's experiments, with similar botched results until his uncle (Vincent Price) intervenes. Directed by Edward L. Bernds, the hokey plot and mediocre special effects hold little interest. Some stylized violence and occasional menace

title: Return of the Gunfighter
synopsis: Retired gunslinger (Robert Taylor) sets out to find the murderers of a Mexican couple who were his friends, taking along their daughter (Ana Martin) to identify them as well as a wounded cowboy (Chad Everett) he meets along the way. Director James Neilson's formula Western has some good action sequences, a respect for the Mexican settlers of the Southwest and a strong performance from Taylor. Frontier violence

title: Return of the Jedi
synopsis: In the third installment of the Star Wars trilogy, Luke Skywalker (Mark Hamill) has a revealing confrontation with Darth Vader, Princess Leia (Carrie Fisher) and Han Solo (Harrison Ford) finally get somewhere with their romance, Billy Dee Williams saves the day with his air support and R2D2 and C3PO steal some major scenes. Directed by Richard Marquand, it's fun for action fans but the violence and tension from some of the nasty characters (Jabba the Hutt is not only scary, but disgusting) may be too intense for the younger crowd

title: Return of the Living Dead
synopsis: Written and directed by Dan O'Bannon, this is yet another tedious variation on the horror movie theme of the dead coming to life and devouring the living. Nudity, violence and bloodly gore

title: Return of the Musketeers, The
synopsis: Flabby seriocomic sequel directed by Richard Lester picks up the story 20 years later with D'Artagnan (Michael York) and his aging comrades (Oliver Reed, Frank Finlay and Richard Chamberlain) trying to stop Cromwell's execution of Charles II, thwart the court intrigues of Cardinal Mazarin (Philippe Noiret) and escape the vengeance of Lady de Winter's daughter (Kim Cattral). Aimless mix of mock heroism and cardboard villainy with stylized violence, sexual situations and religious hypocrites

title: Return of the Pink Panther, The
synopsis: The Pink Panther, the sacred jewel of the Middle East kingdom of Lugash, has been stolen again and only Inspector Clouseau (Peter Sellers) can get retrieve it. Directed by Blake Edwards, the comedy is relatively innocent and, thanks to Sellers, has more then a few funny moments. Some slapstick violence

title: Return of the Secaucus Seven, The
synopsis: Nothing much happens except a weekend of talking during a reunion of seven friends who, as college students on a 1960's protest march, once spent a night together in jail in Secaucus, N.J. Written and directed by John Sayles on a shoestring budget, the movie won't satisfy everyone, but the dialogue is bright and some of the insights are clever. The frankness of the language, especially about sex, would rule out younger viewers

title: Return of the Seven
synopsis: Director Burt Kennedy's shallow, violent sequel to John Sturges' 1960 "The Magnificent Seven," lacks original's flair and high-powered sense of adventure. Yul Brynner, Robert Fuller and Jordan Christopher are three of the deadly septet, leading a small parade back to a little Mexican town where one of their companions is being held prisoner

title: Return of the Soldier, The
synopsis: Wealthy middle-aged man (Alan Bates) returns from World War I with a case of selective amnesia. Forgotten are the years with his spoiled, ill-tempered wife (Julie Christie); remembered instead is his first love, a working-class woman (Glenda Jackson) now grown quite dowdy and, like himself, married. Well-acted English production directed by Alan Bridges from the Rebecca West novel, but the period piece is very slight and its neat resolution is unsatisfying

title: Return of the Streetfighter, The
synopsis: Japanese karate action film the villain being the American heading the Mafia branch in the Far East. Minimal production values and excessive violence

title: Return of the Tall Blond Man with the One Black Shoe, The
synopsis: French production in which Pierre Richard again stars as the concert violinist mistaken for a superspy and unaware that he is the object of assassination attempts. This time the action takes place in Rio de Janiero with the lovely Mireille Darc on hand as decoration but director Yves Robert's comic touch is not nearly as deft as it was in the original. Restrained violence

title: Return of the Vampire, The
synopsis: Minor horror tale about a vampire (Bela Lugosi) who was buried with a spike through his heart in 1918 London, then is unearthed by a bomb in the 1941 Blitz and seeks revenge on the daughter (Nina Foch) of the doctor who did him in. Directed by Lew Landers, there are a few eerie scenes in an otherwise pedestrian story with a muddled subplot about a wolfman under the vampire's spell and weak comic relief from the bemused Scotland Yard chief (Miles Mander). Stylized violence and hokey menace

title: Return to Macon County
synopsis: Two young men (Nick Nolte and Don Johnson) bound for California in a souped-up car pick up a chunky girl who constantly smiles when she is not pointing a large pistol at people and sometimes even when she is. Director Richard Compton's thin, aimless youth movie dips into sexual exploitation for want of anything better to do

title: Return to Me
synopsis: Surprisingly delightful romantic comedy in which a widower (David Duchovny) falls in love with a donor recipient (Minnie Driver) who, unbeknownst to him, has received his late wife's heart. As directed by Bonnie Hunt, the lighthearted film offers an appealing look at romance and second chances with honest, funny dialogue and good performances, although a somewhat predictable, rambling plot diminishes its charm. Fleeting profanity and crass language

title: Return to Never Land
synopsis: Mildly amusing animated sequel to the 1953 classic "Peter Pan" begins in World War II London when Wendy's daughter (voiced by Harriet Owen) is whisked off by Captain Hook (voiced by Corey Burton) to Never Never Land where she rediscovers her sense of imagination and adventure before Peter Pan (voiced by Blayne Weaver) helps her fly home. Directed by Robin Budd, the film has the usual quality animation, but its flat songs and skimpy story render it unmemorable. A few mildly menacing scenes

title: Return to Oz
synopsis: Grim, joyless sequel to the grand Judy Garland original that attempts to make up for its lack of warmth and imagination by substituting an abundance of special effects. The scariness of some of the latter are inappropriate for pre-teenagers

title: Return to Paradise
synopsis: Flawed tale of an American (Joaquin Phoenix) facing execution in Malaysia on a drug conviction unless his lawyer (Anne Heche) can convince his buddies (Vince Vaughn and David Conrad) to return and serve three years in prison for their part in buying the drugs. Director Joseph Ruben allows a premise meant to explore difficult moral choices to gradually descend into overwrought melodrama. Brief violence and recreational drug abuse, an implied affair, recurring profanity and much rough language

title: Return to Peyton Place
synopsis: Imitation sudser with a lifeless script ineptly directed by Jose Ferrer has the illegitimate daughter (Carol Lynley) of an adulteress (Eleanor Parker) write a best-selling novel about the peccadilloes of the folks in her home town. Sexual references

title: Return to Snowy River
synopsis: Enterprising horse rancher (Tom Burlinson) in 19th-century Australia must overcome an aristocratic blackguard (Nicholas Eadie) to wed the daughter (Sigrid Thornton) of an American settler (Brian Dennehy). Director Geoff Burrowes' sequel to "The Man from Snowy River" is filled with picturesque scenery and spirited horses but the human narrative is thin and the action sluggish. Stylized violence, including some fierce hand-to-hand combat, and romantic situations

title: Return to the Blue Lagoon
synopsis: Insipid fantasy in which once again a boy and girl (Brian Krause and Milla Jovovich) come of age while stranded on an uninhabited South Pacific island. Producer-director William A. Graham handles the adolescents' emerging sexuality with a self-performed wedding ceremony and a lamely predictable storyline that languidly repeats the 1980 original. Brief scenes of violence and a few shots of partial nudity

title: Reuben, Reuben
synopsis: Alcoholic, womanizing Scottish poet (Tom Conti) sponges his way through the New England campus circuit in director Robert Ellis Miller's uneven social satire which details the slow disintegration of a creative soul. The script is very literate and Conti's performance is exquiste but his several sexual conquests compound the movie's already muddled moral perspective

title: Revenge
synopsis: Intriguing but ultimately muddled tale of a newly retired Navy pilot (Kevin Costner) who is implausibly lured into an affair with the wife (Madeleine Stowe) of his best friend, a ruthless Mexican powerbroker (Anthony Quinn). Directed by Tony Scott, the exotic Mexican locale takes precedence over character development in this story of male friendship, betrayal and retribution. Some brutally graphic violence, several scenes involving adultery and a rape and incidental rough language

title: Revenge of Frankenstein, The
synopsis: Uneven horror sequel opens in 1860 as Baron Frankenstein (Peter Cushing) escapes the guillotine to reimerge as Dr. Stein in a distant town where he constructs a new creature with the brain of a deformed assistant (Michael Gwynn) but the result turns into a cannibalistic killer. Directed by Terence Fisher, the elaborate variations on the original are ambitious but prove too cumbersome to sustain interest. Stylized violence and some grisly visuals

title: Revenge of the Creature
synopsis: Thin sequel to "The Creature from the Black Lagoon" has the captured Gill Man taken from the Amazon to a Florida theme park where he's angered by a scientist (John Agar), then breaks loose, terrifies crowds of visitors and escapes with a park official (Lori Nelson). Directed by Jack Arnold, the hokey proceedings finally work up some mild tension as the prehistoric creature is hunted down but without evoking the sympathy generated by the original

title: Revenge of the Dead
synopsis: ( see: "Night of the Ghouls" )

title: Revenge of the Musketeers
synopsis: French swashbuckler in which the graying d'Artagnon (Philippe Noiret) is persuaded by his spunky daughter (Sophie Marceau) to come out of retirement and join his three Musketeer comrades in foiling a conspiracy against the young Louis XIV. Directed by Bertrand Tavernier, the 1994 production wrings a lot of tongue-in-cheek action from a breezy plot revolving around the aging heroes, a villainous aristocrat (Claude Rich) and the devious Cardinal Mazarin (Luigi Proietti). Subtitles. Period violence, sexual situations, brief nudity and ribald humor

title: Revenge of the Nerds
synopsis: Misfit college freshmen (Robert Carradine and Anthony Edwards) form a fraternity to protect themselves and fight the persecution of college jocks. The underdog heroes' attitude toward women is as reprehensible as that of their tormentors. Director Jeff Kanew's farce is full of vulgarities, much nudity and the romantic treatment of what is in effect rape

title: Revenge of the Nerds II: Nerds in Paradise
synopsis: Director Joe Roth's silly sequel has the goofy Tri Lambdas seeking to retrieve their integrity at a fraternity conference in Fort Lauderdale. Though its theme is not to judge others on surface values, it reinforces false stereotypes of women, bad habits and vulgarity via peekaboo nudity, slapstick humor and crude sight gags

title: Revenge of the Ninja
synopsis: Japanese warrior (Sho Kosugi) comes to the United States where he makes short order of an illegal drug operation and battles old enemies. Directed by Sam Firstenberg, the action is mostly of the martial arts variety but a number of weapons are used in achieving an extremely bloody victory. Excessive violence and gore

title: Revenge of the Pink Panther
synopsis: Peter Sellers romps again as the bumbling Inspector Clouseau who gains glory, inadvertently as usual, by breaking up an international drug ring headed by Robert Webber, thanks to some timely help from Webber's mistress, Dyan Cannon. Directed by Blake Edwards, the plot is cluttered and noticeably less scintillating than its predecessors. Some sexual innuendo

title: Revengers, The
synopsis: William Holden stars as a rancher who, after his family is slaughtered by renegade Indians, dedicates his life to avenging them and, with the help of a second-string wild bunch (including Ernest Borgnine and Woody Strode), he kills just about everyone who crosses his path until gentled by an Irish spinster (Susan Hayward). Directed by Daniel Mann, this violent and bloody Western has a totally unmotivated ending

title: Reversal of Fortune
synopsis: Fact-based re-creation of the successful appeal by a Harvard law professor (Ron Silver) of the conviction of Claus von Bulow (Jeremy Irons) for the attempted murder of his socialite wife (Glenn Close). Director Barbet Schroeder's wickedly witty film offers several possible scenarios for the victim's two comas and details how the case was won legally without resolving the question of von Bulow's innocence. Adulterous relationships and occasional rough language

title: Revolution
synopsis: Jack O'Connell's documentary presents a one-sided view of the hippie counterculture with an emphasis upon sex and nudity

title: Revolution
synopsis: Director Hugh Hudson's epic treatment of the American Revolution is grand spectacle but lacks a credible human dimension. What it offers, instead, are underdeveloped characters (notably Al Pacino in the central role) and episodic plot contrivances. Violent battle scenes

title: Revolutionary Road
synopsis: Impeccably filmed and acted adaptation of Richard Yates' greatly lauded 1961 novel about an unhappy suburban Connecticut couple (Leonardo DiCaprio and Kate Winslet) torn between middle-class inertia and fulfilling their youthful aspirations by uprooting to Paris. Director Sam Mendes takes a strikingly stylized approach to the repressed 1950s milieu, and the story speaks powerfully to the restrictive conformity of that era, but the thematic material -- including adultery and abortion -- and sporadically strong language may not be to every taste. Extreme domestic discord, rough language and profanity, adultery, brief upper female nudity, abortion references, two nongraphic sexual encounters and heavy smoking
full_review:
"Revolutionary Road" (Paramount Vantage) is an impeccably filmed and acted adaptation of Richard Yates' extravagantly praised novel -- a searing indictment of conformity that had defied several attempts at filming in the decades since it was published in 1961.

This ironically named story -- the ideals of the American Revolution now a "desperate clinging to safety and security" as Yates described them in an interview shortly before his death in 1992 -- charts the marriage of unhappy suburban Connecticut couple Frank and April Wheeler (Leonardo DiCaprio and Kate Winslet), who live on the titular street.

In the film's opening moments, we observe their romantic first meeting, but then flash forward to their married days where aspiring actress April's less than rapturous opening night in community theater unleashes harsh recriminations on the way home.

April's implacable bitterness drives Frank -- a New York commuter for the faceless Knox firm -- to the bed of mousy secretary Maureen (Zoe Kazan), an encounter he almost immediately regrets, especially after he returns home to find a newly invigorated April eager to uproot and move to Paris, where she says he can pursue his youthful aspirations and find out "who he is."

Frank, increasingly depressed by the numbing routine of his job, agrees. The decision causes almost seismic shock waves for their best friends, the Campbells (David Harbour and Kathryn Hahn), and Frank's office mates. They express surprise, then feigned pleasure at the Wheelers' decision, but are actually devastated by the news: simultaneously bereft and envious.

Also deeply affected is real estate agent Helen Givings (Kathy Bates), who had sold the young couple their house and looked to them as bright lights in a sea of mediocrity. She asks the pair to meet with her mentally ill grown son, John (Michael Shannon), a mathematician, as she feels just being in their presence will have a beneficial effect. During the meeting, the hulking John nails the couple's hang-ups with penetrating candor.

But just when everything seems on track for their planned adventure, Frank finds unexpected success at Knox, and April suddenly learns she is pregnant. In desperation, April suggests, to Frank's horror, that she might abort the pregnancy. (The film, by the way, never presents this in a positive light -- quite the contrary, as events take their course.)

Director Sam Mendes takes much the same strikingly stylized approach to the repressed 1950s milieu as he did for the contemporary suburban landscape of 1999's "American Beauty."

DiCaprio and Winslet -- reunited for the first time since "Titanic" -- have certainly developed, and their performances are superb. Ditto for the supporting players.

Beneath all the marital strife, Justin Haythe's script takes pains to show how the story is really about the deep-seated yearning for unrealized dreams balanced against the fragility of human nature. And, as noted, the story speaks powerfully to the restrictive conformity of that era, but this bitter tale -- including the adultery and abortion story lines, and sporadically strong dialogue -- may not be to every taste.

The film contains extreme domestic discord, rough language and profanity, adultery, brief upper female nudity, abortion references, two nongraphic sexual encounters and heavy smoking. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Revolutionary, The
synopsis: College student (Jon Voight) moves from a radical student movement, to a socialist worker's organization, to a short-lived stint in the army and, finally, to an anarchists' bomb plot. The result is less the story of a young man's political radicalization than it is the meanderings of a social misfit. Paul Williams' low-keyed direction tends to level rather than highlight plot development and leaves too many significant questions unanswered

title: Reward, The
synopsis: On the arid, sun-drenched plains of Mexico, a small band of bounty hunters are destroyed by their greed and moral decay. Director Serge Bourguignon's story of death in the desert makes its point about life by turning the desperate journey of the last survivor (Max Von Sydow) to reach a lake into the quest for a moral oasis

title: Rhapsody in August
synopsis: Three generations of a Japanese family in Nagasaki react quite differently to a surprise visit by an U.S. relative (Richard Gere) who has come to remember the family patriarch who was killed in the American bombing of the city 45 years earlier. Writer-director Akira Kurosawa presents a poignant look at the futility of war through the eyes of the elderly who remember, the middle-aged who prefer to forget, and children who are curious about their past. Subtitles. References to the horror of mass death and destruction caused by the A-bomb

title: Rhapsody in Blue
synopsis: Long but mostly engaging tribute to composer George Gershwin (1898-1937) from his early success with Broadway show tunes to his more serious works, including the title concert piece, with Robert Alda playing the composer as a driven musical genius whose ambition leaves no room for love (Joan Leslie and Alexis Smith). Directed by Irving Rapper, the Hollywood version of Gershwin's life is well-crafted melodrama, and the plentiful musical portions are first-rate. Romantic complications

title: Rhinestone
synopsis: Embarrassingly bad romantic match-up in which Dolly Parton tries to make a country-western singer out of tough New York cabby Sylvester Stallone. Director Bob Clark's unfunny musical comedy exploits Parton's physical attributes and musical abilities but merely makes Stallone look silly. Vulgar dialogue and benign view of casual sex

title: Rhubarb
synopsis: Lightweight comedy in which the scrappy cat of the title inherits a millionaire's estate, including a major-league baseball club, with the will's acerbic executor (Ray Milland) fending off nasty interlopers as the team heads for the pennant and his fiancee (Jan Sterling) develops an allergy to cats. Director Arthur Lubin turns the daffy premise into a slow-moving vehicle for mostly minor amusements. Some mean-spirited skullduggery

title: Rhyme & Reason
synopsis: Documentary celebrating almost 20 years of rap music and the hip-hop subculture as commented on by some 70 performers from Ice-T to Dr. Dre and the late Tupac Shakur. Directed by Peter Spirer, the result is basically self-promotional, providing an uncritical view of rap as a form of social protest using verbal violence and sexually explicit lyrics to express the oppression of ghetto life, an explanation which will not satisfy those who reject rap as socially irresponsible. Recurring violent rhetoric and sexual expletives

title: Rhythm on the River
synopsis: Tuneful nostalgia from director Victor Schertzinger in the slight tale of an established songwriter (Basil Rathbone) who buys his compositions from unknowns, two of whom (Bing Crosby and Mary Martin) fall for each other while trying to establish independent songwriting careers. Creaky but cheery musical with a quite charming romance

title: Rich and Famous
synopsis: Screen version of the John Van Druten play about two very different women (Candice Bergen and Jacqueline Bisset), both writers, who preserve a friendship for more than two decades despite the strains caused by emulation and jealousy. Directed by George Cukor, the glossy soap opera pays more attention to its glamorous locations than to the human dimension of its story. The sole redeeming feature is good acting by the principals. General air of vapid amorality and two graphic sexual sequences

title: Rich and Strange
synopsis: Whimsical tale in which a London couple use an inheritance to take a cruise to the Far East where the wife (Joan Barry) is charmed by a genial plantation owner (Percy Marmont) while the husband (Henry Kendall) is fleeced by a phony princess (Betty Amman), then they get shipwrecked on the return voyage and arrive home with a new appreciation of ordinary life. Director Alfred Hitchcock treats the proceedings with tongue firmly in cheek, adding a few bizarre touches and some grisly humor along the way with still enjoyable results. Stylized violence, implied infidelity and some rude language

title: Richard
synopsis: Political spoof with little satirical bite blending newsreel footage with staged segments in order to trace Richard Nixon's journey from whipping cookie batter of an evening in Whittier, Calif. to fireside reminiscenes at the White House. Directed by Lorees Yerby and Harry Hurwitz, the resulting lampoon, more than anything else, provides proof that this is a free country

title: Richard III
synopsis: Wildly imaginative updating of Shakespeare's play to 1930's Britain where civil war brings a new monarch to the throne coveted by his duplicitous brother, the Duke of Glouster (Ian McKellan), who sets out to gain it through murder. Directed by Richard Loncraine, the result places Shakespeare's Elizabethan language and medieval subject in a 20th-century context of fascist movements and absolute dictatorships that give fresh significance to the play's portrait of an autocratic villain. Stylized violence and sexual references

title: Richard Pryor Live on Sunset Strip
synopsis: Stand-up comic performance, with the usual obscenities and scatological references, though Pryor is in a mellower, more humane mood than in his previous performance movie. Under Joe Layton's direction, Pryor's humor and his perception of human nature are usually on target and often extremely funny, but his sexually oriented jokes and vulgar language may offend those unfamiliar with his style

title: Richest Girl in the World, The
synopsis: Eccentric romantic comedy in which an heiress (Miriam Hopkins) changes places with her private secretary (Fay Wray) in order to test the real intentions of a would-be suitor (Joel McCrea). Director William A. Seiter keeps the implausible situations light and mostly fun, with a fine cast making all the duplicity seem almost credible. Sexual situations

title: Richest Man in the World: Andrew Carnegie, The
synopsis: An "American Experience" biography of the Scottish-born 19th century industrialist who went from rags to riches in America by ruthless business practices, but who gave much of his wealth away believing, "A man who dies rich dies disgraced." Filmmaker Austin Hoyt explores the darker side of Carnegie's complex persona without dismissing his tremendous economic achievements and unparalleled philanthropy. A few profanities

title: Richie Rich
synopsis: Uninspired comedy about a lonely but plucky 12-year-old (Macaulay Culkin) who conspires to outwit a nasty businessman (John Larroquette) out to steal his inheritance when the boy's parents (Edward Herrmann and Christine Ebersole) are presumed dead after their private jet blows up. Director Donald Petrie's formula comedy has few surprises and only minor amusements for easily satisfied viewers. Some mock comic violence, occasional double entendres and a crude expression

title: Rich in Love
synopsis: A Southern teenager (Kathryn Erbe) puzzles over life and love after her mother (Jill Clayburgh) deserts her father (Albert Finney) without explanation and her pregnant sister (Suzy Amis) moves back home, unsure whether she wants to stay married to her new husband (Kyle MacLachlan). Director Bruce Beresford unveils richly textured characters caught between the pain of change and the mundane joys of family living. Implied extra-marital relationships

title: Rich Kids
synopsis: Uneven melodrama about the effect of divorce on two adolescents (Trini Alvarado and Jeremy Levy) whose wealthy and adulterous parents (John Lithgow and Kathryn Walker) seem unconcerned about their offspring. The two teenagers spend a weekend together in an exotically appointed bachelor apartment. The situation leads to an angry, recriminatory adult confrontation, involving spouses current and former, lovers, friends, and one or two relatively innocent bystanders Directed by Robert Young, the movie raises but doesn't probe too deeply into questions of parental responsibility and glosses over the sexual implications of the young people's weekend together

title: Rich Man's Wife, The
synopsis: Preposterous thriller in which an unfaithful wife (Halle Berry) fears being implicated in the murder of her philandering husband (Christopher McDonald) by a homicidal maniac (Peter Greene) who wants a share of the widow's inheritance. Writer-director Amy Holden Jones drags out a tawdry tale of the devious deeds of unsympathetic characters in a clumsy, slow-moving plot taxing credibility and viewers' patience. Some strong scenes of violence, threatening situations, marital infidelity and occasional rough language

title: Ricochet
synopsis: Hard-edged revenge drama pits a hero cop-turned-prosecutor (Denzel Washington) against an escaped psychopath (John Lithgow) who frames him for murder and involvement in kiddie porn. Solid action scenes and chilling performances are outweighed by director Russell Mulcahy's emphasis on killings and sexual violence. Excessive violence, the repeated use of a graphic rape scene and much rough language

title: Riddle of the Sands, The
synopsis: British melodrama about two chaps from Oxford who accidentally uncover German preparations for an invasion of England in 1901. Michael York and Simon MacCorkindale are fine as the stuffy pair who prove their mettle once the going gets tough, but they can't save a languid movie that lacks even a good villain. Director Tony Maylam succeeds best with the period atmosphere but its intrigue and derring-do are only mildly diverting

title: Ride a Crooked Trail
synopsis: Routine Western directed by Jesse Hibbs in which an outlaw (Audie Murphy) turns honest after a small-town judge (Walter Matthau) mistakes him for a famed lawman and appoints him marshal, whereupon he tracks down a bank robber (Henry Silva) and weds a former accomplice (Gia Scala). Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Ride a Wild Pony
synopsis: Colorful Disney adventure, set in the Australian Outback before World War I, in which a poor lad attempts to recover his pony after it has come into the possession of a spoiled cripple, the little daughter of the town's wealthiest family. It is up to the horse, in the satisfying conclusion, to decide for one child or the other. Better than average children's movie directed by Don Chaffey with some good touches of reality and a solid theme of human selflessness

title: Ride Beyond Vengeance
synopsis: After a long absence, a buffalo hunter (Chuck Connors) returns home with a sizable sum of money and then revenges on the three who steal it from him. Directed by Bernard McEveety, it is a tough, almost cynical story of human greed and brutality. Much violence

title: Ride Clear of Diablo
synopsis: Standard Western directed by Jesse Hibbs with a straight-shooting cowboy (Audie Murphy) trailing the rustlers who murdered his father and brother but, along the way, he becomes a sheriff's deputy and arrests the area's worst badman (Dan Duryea) whom he wrongly accuses of the crime. Stylized violence and muddled serio-comic plot

title: Ride Him, Cowboy
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Fred Allen in which a cowboy (John Wayne) saves a fine horse from being mistakenly destroyed as a vicious animal, and then the horse saves the cowboy from being killed by outlaws. Stylized violence

title: Ride Lonesome
synopsis: Strong Western in which a bounty hunter (Randolph Scott) tracks down a killer (James Best), then uses him as bait to bring his outlaw brother (Lee Van Cleef) to justice for a grisly crime committed years before. Director Budd Boetticher notches the suspense by having the bounty hunter joined on the trail by an abandoned wife (Karen Steele) and a couple of cowboys (Pernell Roberts and James Coburn) with their own designs on the killer. Stylized violence and considerable menace

title: Rider from Tucson
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Lesley Selander in which Arizona rodeo riders (Tim Holt and Richard Martin) help a Colorado friend save his gold mine from claimjumpers. Frontier violence and a woman held hostage

title: Rider on the Rain
synopsis: Intriguing French mystery thriller about a newlywed (Marlene Jobert) who kills her attacker and then is afraid to tell husband, friends, or the police. After she has disposed of the body, a stranger (Charles Bronson) begins to badger her about it and a neatly matched duel of wits ensues. Director Rene Clement has hit the mark with this suspenseful melodrama, with plenty of moody atmosphere and engaging characterizations. The tribulations of the heroine are not for the youngsters

title: Riders of Destiny
synopsis: Low-budget Western directed by Robert N. Bradbury in which undercover government agent Singing Sandy (John Wayne) foils a gang plotting to drive local ranchers off the range by depriving them of water. Tame action fare

title: Riders of the Northwest Mounted
synopsis: Low-budget adventure picture follows a Canadian Mountie (Russell Hayden) on the trail of a gang of fur robbers. Directed by William Berke, the formula story has some picturesque scenery, the singing of Bob Wills and his Texas Playboys and comic relief by Dub Taylor. Stylized violence

title: Riders of the Rio Grande
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Howard Bretherton with the Three Mesquiteers (Bob Steele, Tom Tyler and Jimmie Dodd) on the run from the law after being mistaken for gunslingers, but this doesn't keep them from saving a town's leading citizen (Edward Van Sloan) from ruin. Frontier violence

title: Ride the High Country
synopsis: Hired by a bank to escort a gold shipment from a mining camp in the Sierra Mountains, a retired lawman (Joel McCrea) takes along an old friend (Randolph Scott) who has his own plans for the ore. Director Sam Peckinpah's off-beat Western mixes in a farmer's daughter (Mariette Hartley), a novice gunfighter (Ronald Starr) and a brawling brood of brothers, but the focus is on the two veteran cowboys and their differing notions of duty and honor. Some stylized violence, sexual references and ribald humor

title: Ride the Pink Horse
synopsis: Atmospheric crime story set in a New Mexico town during a fiesta when a war profiteer (Fred Clark) double-crosses and almost kills a cynical Army vet (Robert Montgomery) who's saved by a Indian girl (Wanda Hendrix), a Mexican merry-go-round operator (Thomas Gomez) and a wry FBI agent (Art Smith). Also directed by Montgomery, the plot is full of holes but the colorful characters make the situation of more than usual interest. Stylized violence

title: Ride the Wild Surf
synopsis: Innocuous tale of college-age beach buddies (Fabian, Tab Hunter and Peter Brown) finding high waves and low-voltage romance (Shelley Fabares, Barbara Hunt and Barbara Eden, respectively) on a New Year's vacation in Hawaii. Directed by Don Taylor, the picturesque locales and surfboard action make up for the generally inept dramatic proceedings. Innocent but shallow escapist fare that children are likely to find simply tedious

title: Ride to Hangman's Tree, The
synopsis: Formula Western directed by Alan Rafkin in which a robber (James Farentino) of Wells Fargo gold shipments is forced to split the loot with an ex-partner (Jack Lord), though the result is far less interesting than "Black Bart," the 1948 movie upon which it is based. Stylized violence and some heavy sexual innuendo

title: Ride, Vaquero
synopsis: A Mexican bandit leader (Anthony Quinn) grows testy when his life-long friend and top gun (Robert Taylor) sides with a Texas rancher (Howard Keel) and his wife (Ava Gardner) against his former comrades. Director John Farrow's quirky little melodrama has its interesting moments, among them the local priest (Kurt Kasznar) taking a hand in the action and Taylor's stinging rejection of Gardner's advances. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Ride With the Devil
synopsis: Somber Civil War drama centers on two Missouri lads (Tobey Maguire and Skeet Ulrich) and a former slave (Jeffrey Wright) fighting unofficially as pro-Southern Bushwackers on the Kansas-Missouri border while they reflect on the bloody conflict and how it has torn their families apart. As directed by Ang Lee, the historical backdrop holds more interest than the plot's flatly dramatized personal stories. Recurring battlefield violence, implied sexual situations and a breast-feeding scene

title: Ridicule
synopsis: Lush costume drama set at the court of Versailles in 1783 as an altruistic country engineer (Charles Berling) discovers he must first bed the king's cunning mistress (Fanny Ardent) and develop the art of witty sarcasm before he can win the king's ear. Directed by Patrice Leconte, the satirical period piece focuses on the rampant decadence and superficiality of court life that culminated a few years later in the French Revolution. Subtitles. Brief violence including a suicide, fleeting bedroom scenes and gratuitous frontal male nudity

title: Riding High
synopsis: Happy-go-lucky racehorse owner (Bing Crosby) stakes his future on a horse he's raised from a colt and, with the help of its trainer (Clarence Muse) and a rooster mascot, wins the big race and the daughter (Colleen Gray) of an ulcer-ridden tycoon (Charles Bickford). Despite period updating and some songs, director Frank Capra's remake of his 1934 "Broadway Bill" oversentimentalizes the slim plot, though a talented veteran cast (Oliver Hardy, Margaret Hamilton, James Gleason, Raymond Walburn, William Demarest, Gene Lockhart and Douglass Dumbrille) provides some amusement. Romantic complications leading to divorce

title: Riding in Cars With Boys
synopsis: Uneven drama in which a pregnant 15-year-old (Drew Barrymore) with dreams of college and career reluctantly marries her substance-abusing boyfriend (Steve Zahn) and later finds the demands of single parenting frustrate her ambition. Told as her 20-year-old son looks back on their rocky relationship, director Penny Marshall's fact-based film succeeds as a cautionary tale and in presenting realistic characters with warts and flaws, but the film's sentimental streak culminates in a cloying conclusion. Fleeting violence, adolescent affairs, recreational drug use and an instance of rough language and profanity

title: Riding Shotgun
synopsis: Western misfire directed by Andre de Toth in which a town suspects a stagecoach guard (Randolph Scott) is in cahoots with a notorious outlaw gang, but he escapes being lynched in time to save them from the outlaws. Stylized violence

title: Riff-Raff
synopsis: Gritty look at what Britain's double-diget unemployment statistics mean in the life of one out-of work laborer (Robert Carlyle) who takes a low-paying job on a non-union construction project, becomes a squatter in a vacant apartment complex and falls for an untalented, unrealistic would-be singer (Emer McCourt). Using a largely non-professional cast whose accents require subtitles, director ken loach gets a good measure of blue-collar reality in a variation on the old story of greedy employers, exploited workers and the struggle for economic justice. Its treatment of justice themes includes a devastating accident, a premarital relationship, drug use, crude humor and much rough language

title: Right On!
synopsis: Documentary of performances by a talented but angry rock group, The Original Last Poets (Gylan Kain, David Nelson, and Felipe Luciano), whose songs echo the pain and frustration of ghetto life and insist on racial pride as the means for redeeming the future. By filming the group in New York slums framed by the Manhattan skyline, director Herbert Danska finds the visual equivalent to their music. Some violent and vulgar lyrics, but motivated by a sense of hope rather than hopelessness

title: Right Stuff, The
synopsis: Screen version of Tom Wolfe's book about the original seven astronauts is an extraordinary tribute to the pioneers of the U.S. space program, notably Chuck Yeager (Sam Shepard), Alan Shepard (Scott Glenn) and John Glenn (Ed Harris). Director Philip Kaufman captures the gallant endeavor in a style that's at once respectful yet exuberant, lavishly entertaining and very inspiring. Unfortunately, a scene involving masturbation, intended as a bit of comic relief during a sequence of laboratory tests, is mature fare

title: Rikky and Pete
synopsis: Australian road picture pairing a brother-sister team (Stephen Kearney and Nina Landis) who leave their wealthy family in Melbourne to start a new life in a mining town in the Australian Outback. Director Nadia Tass gets some offhand humor in scenes featuring Pete's Rube Goldberg inventions but the focus is on Rikky who is the stronger of the two and protective of her spacey brother. Brief nudity and much rough language

title: Rikyu
synopsis: A 16th-century Japanese warlord (Tsutomu Yamazaki) and his tea master (Rentaro Mikuni) perfect the art of the tea ceremony while clashing over the warlord's burgeoning political ambitions. Exquisite delicacy and simplicity mark director Hiroshi Teshigahara's homage to Japanese culture with powerful performances from the two opposed characters. Subtitles. Suicide within a cultural perspective

title: Ringmaster
synopsis: Tawdry tale of two sets of dim characters who bring their tangled sexual problems to the TV talk show hosted by master of insincerities Jerry Springer, with the results predictably featuring scenes of sex and violence on and off the show. Directed by Neil Abramson, this low-budget promo for the TV talk show is a tedious exercise in sexual exploitation and human manipulation. Numerous sexual encounters, some nudity, physical and verbal violence, much rough language and occasional profanity

title: Ring of Bright Water
synopsis: London clerk (Bill Travers) leaves his computerized job to move to a small cottage in the Scottish highlands with an otter. Unpretentious British story directed by Jack Couffer proves intelligent, entertaining family fare

title: Ring of Fire
synopsis: Combination crime and disaster thriller starts with a police officer (David Janssen) being taken hostage by marauding teenagers (Frank Gorshin and Joyce Taylor) who are captured in the Oregon wilderness where one of their cigarettes causes a forest fire which threatens to engulf a nearby town. Writer-director Andrew L. Stone's busy scenario shifts abruptly from the nasty teen menaces to the low-budget conflagration ending with Janssen at the throttle of a trainload of panicked townspeople in the fiery climax. Much menace, some stylized violence and occasional sexual innuendo

title: Rings Around the World
synopsis: Compilation movie showing famous circus acts from various countries produced and directed by Gilbert Cates and narrated by Don Ameche

title: Ring, The
synopsis: Small but effective picture of a Mexican-American youth (Lalo Rios) who sets out to help his family by becoming a prizefighter but, despite the efforts of a veteran trainer (Gerald Mohr), gets beaten to a pulp and quits the ring to look elsewhere for succeess. Directed by Kurt Neumann, the movie presents a positive view of Latinos while showing the seamy side of the fight game. Violent boxing scenes

title: Rio
synopsis: Buoyant animated adventure with music about a Brazilian-born macaw (voice of Jesse Eisenberg) raised as a cosseted pet in Minnesota. Informed by an eccentric Rio-based scientist (voice of Rodrigo Santoro) that her feathery friend is the last male of his species, his devoted owner (voice of Leslie Mann) reluctantly brings him back to his native land so that he can mate with his sole remaining female counterpart (voice of Anne Hathaway). But the potential lovebirds get caught up in the illegal avian trade. Lessons about environmental stewardship and love-inspired loyalty are decked out in kaleidoscopic colors and delivered in an overwhelmingly child-friendly tone in director Carlos Saldanha's 3-D flight of fancy. A few nursery-level bathroom references, a fleeting double entendre

title: Rio Bravo
synopsis: Long-winded but pungent Western in which a seasoned sheriff (John Wayne) tries to keep a killer (Claude Aikens) from being busted out of jail by his brother's army of gunslingers with only a drunken deputy (Dean Martin), an elderly cripple (Walter Brennan), a callow cowboy (Ricky Nelson) and a saloon hostess (Angie Dickinson) to back him up. Director Howard Hawks savors the desperate situation and its collection of odd-ball characters as the tension builds to the long-delayed slambang conclusion. Assorted stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Rio Conchos
synopsis: Ponderous Western in which an Army officer (Stuart Whitman) heads into Mexico with a black sergeant (Jim Brown), a hardened Apache killer (Richard Boone) and a convicted murderer (Tony Franciosa) seeking to recover 2,000 stolen repeating rifles before they wind up in the hands of Apache hostiles. Directed by Gordon Douglas, there's plenty of rugged action but it's all as wildly improbable as the plans of the mad Confederate colonel (Edmond O'Brien) who stole the rifles to arm the Apaches for an invasion of 1867 Texas. Nasty frontier violence, brutality and sexual situations

title: Rio Grande
synopsis: Veteran cavalry officer (John Wayne) commanding a frontier outpost has his hands full when his estranged wife (Maureen O'Hara) arrives with their West Point son (Claude Jarman, Jr.) but the untested youth proves his mettle on a raid across the Mexican border to rescue children captured by the Apaches. Director John Ford plays the commander's domestic problems for laughs but turns grimly serious in the climactic border raid. Stylized violence

title: Rio Grande Patrol
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Lesley Selander in which a border patrol officer (Tim Holt) takes on a gang trying to smuggle a shipment of machine guns to Mexican rebels. Stylized violence

title: Rio Lobo
synopsis: Stylish Western with John Wayne as a Civil War veteran pursuing two traitors for hijacking an army payroll, and not perturbed in the least by a small army of hired gunslingers nor a final thunderous shootout with an entire town taking part. Under Howard Hawks' deft direction, there is plenty of rough horseplay and tongue-in-cheek references to Wayne's overweight condition and old age in general. Violence, both physical and psychological, and some adult sexual references

title: Riot
synopsis: Set within the grime and frustration of prison life is a realistic drama in which an inmate (James Brown), unwittingly caught up in fast-moving events, assumes leadership of a full scale revolt by the entire prison. Director Buzz Kulik's movie is by no means casual entertainment but it is very knowing about prison life and injustices. Several violent, bloody sequences bolster the dramatic action and the dialogue is a bit rough

title: Riot in Juvenile Prison
synopsis: Tough juvenile delinquent Scott Marlowe is no match for crusading penal reformer Jerome Thor in director Edward L. Cahn's dreary low-budget clunker. Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Ripper, The
synopsis: Flat-footed melodrama in which a Scotland Yard inspector (Patrick Bergin) romances a poor working girl (Gabrielle Anwar), then uses her as bait to nab a serial killer of prostitutes in the East End slums of 1888 London. Directed by Janet Myers, the TV movie is a tired variation on the familiar story of Jack the Ripper, who is here identified as a member of the royal family, but the unimaginative plot gets lost in detailing the Victorian snobbery which keeps the inspector from solving the lurid case. Some brief graphic violence and occasional profanity

title: Rise and Fall of Legs Diamond, The
synopsis: Formula gangster movie directed by Budd Boetticher follows the ruthless methods by which its title character (Ray Danton) comes to rule the mobs of Prohibition-era New York, then is cut down by a syndicate organizing crime on a national basis in the 1930s. Stylized violence, some of it quite nasty, and sexual situations

title: Rise of Catherine the Great, The
synopsis: ( see: "Catherine the Great" )

title: Rise of Louis XIV, The
synopsis: French historical dramatization meticulously traces the gradual assumption of power by the Sun King, from the time he assumed the crown to his undercutting the noblity by enticing them to spend their lives in the frivolous splendors of the court at Versailles. Directed by Roberto Rossellini, the re-creation of the period is beautifully exquisite and painstakingly detailed but those uninterested in history may find the pace interminably slow

title: Rising Sun
synopsis: Investigating a sex murder in a Japanese-owned building, two Los Angeles police detectives (Sean Connery and Wesley Snipes) run up against a complex cover-up involving a politically sensitive sale of an American company to Japanese businessmen who must avoid scandal at all costs. Director Philip Kaufman's coldly stylish and wholly cynical thriller from Michael Crichton's novel exploits sexual violence against women in a story presenting a disturbing view of Japanese commerce on our shores. Repeated replay of a taped graphic sex killing, some nasty violence, recurring nudity and much rough language

title: Risky Business
synopsis: Enterprising young prostitute (Rebecca De Mornay) persuades a high school senior (Tom Cruise), while his affluent parents are away on vacation, to turn his plush Chicago home into a bordello for his classmates. Written and directed by Paul Brickman, it is much slicker than similar exploitation movies aimed at teenagers but it is appallingly crass in its celebration of promiscuity. Nudity and graphic sexuality as well as a benign view of deceit, manipulation and sexual indulgence

title: Rita, Sue and Bob Too
synopsis: British sex farce posing as ribald social satire about two lower-class teenagers sexually exploited by a married man who in turn ruin his already failing marriage and then exploit him. Director Alan Clarke displays a callous hand in his graphic depiction of sex with minors, including nudity and profanity

title: Ritz, The
synopsis: Screen version of a mediocre Broadway comedy about an Italian-American businessman from Cleveland (Jack Weston) hiding out from a murderous brother-in-law (Jerry Stiller) in a homosexual bathhouse where he is pursued by an off-key Puerto Rican singer (Rita Moreno) who thinks he is a Hollywood producer. Directed by Richard Lester, it's an ugly, disagreeable attempt at farce. Ethnic stereotyping and some foul language

title: Rivals
synopsis: Clunker about an Oedipal 10-year-old brat (Scott Jacoby) who is so fatally jealous of his widowed mother (Joan Hackett) and her childish second husband (Robert Klein) that he makes a humiliating mess of trying to have sex with his dumb but nubile babysitter. Director Krishna Shah is hopelessly adrift in dealing with the esoteric lifestyles of Americans with too much money. Repugnant trash

title: River Lady
synopsis: Muddled romantic adventure directed by George Sherman in which the owner (Yvonne De Carlo) of a gambling riverboat uses a slick agent (Dan Duryea) to create a logging syndicate until stopped by her former logger beau (Rod Cameron) who forms a combine of independent loggers. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: River Niger, The
synopsis: Powerful drama about a black American's struggle to forge his own identity out of a tragic history of blacks as the eternally Displaced Persons of our nation. Though director Krishna Shah fails to overcome the stage origins of the work, this does lessen the value of its hopeful message about the choices facing our society, its moving portrait of closely-knit family life and the strong performances of James Earl Jones, Cicely Tyson and Glynn Turman. Mature themes

title: River of No Return
synopsis: Slack Western in which a backcountry farmer (Robert Mitchum) saves his son (Tommy Rettig) and a saloon singer (Marilyn Monroe) from rampaging Indians by rafting downstream to safety in a town where he confronts the crooked gambler (Rory Calhoun) who had run out on them. Directed by Otto Preminger, the rugged raft scenes work up considerable tension but the rest of the picture is a letdown over the contrived relationships of cardboard characters. Frontier violence, romantic complications and sexual innuendo

title: Riverrun
synopsis: When a sea-going father (John McLiam) visits the sheep farm where his daughter (Louise Ober) and her young man (Mark Jenkins) live, he is at first amused by their attempt to get back to nature and escape the dehumanization of city life, but when he learns that she is pregnant and not formally married, he is determined to take her away. Written and directed by John Korty, the contrivances of romantic melodrama are evident but the generational theme of value systems is handled sensitively and treated with honesty

title: River Runs Through It, A
synopsis: Meditative reflections on the experiences of a youth (Craig Sheffer) growing up in rural Montana in the first part of the century, chiefly comprising his relationship with his rebellious younger brother (Brad Pitt), minister father (Tom Skerritt) and the great outdoors. Directed by Robert Redford, the tone of the episodic narrative is earnest, the pace leisurely and the result largely dependent upon how one relates to the poetry of nature. Some scenes of inebriation and discreet sexual references, several shots of rear nudity, teens in a life-threatening situation and occasional profanity

title: River's Edge
synopsis: The callous sex killing of a young high school girl is viewed by her apathetic peers as an occasion for protective support of her psychopathic boy friend who becomes the equally innocent victim of an adult psychotic (Dennis Hopper). Director Tim Hunter's picture of several troubled youths downplays emotional and spiritual issues in favor of surface sensationalism, including permissive teen sex, nudity and profanity

title: River, The
synopsis: Ernest but dull effort to dramatize the plight of the American farmer tells the story of a farm family (Mel Gibson and Sissy Spacek) who must battle nature, bill collectors and public indifference in their struggle to hold on to their land and livelihood. The characters simply do not come alive in an unfocused script directed by Mark Rydell. Some violent encounters and a restrained bedroom scene

title: River Wild, The
synopsis: Taut outdoors thriller in which a former river guide (Meryl Streep) on a white-water rafting vacation with her unathletic husband (David Strathairn) and young son (Joseph Mazzello) is forced to take two fugitives (Kevin Bacon and John C. Riley) down a deadly stretch of river, knowing the two will kill her and her family even if they survive the trip down the rapids. Director Curtis Hanson underplays the characterizations but maintains edgy suspense as the woman becomes increasingly resourceful in her efforts to save her loved ones. Frequent menace and brief shots of brutal violence

title: Road House
synopsis: Bleak sudser about a singer (Ida Lupino) who comes between best friends when her boss, the road house owner (Richard Widmark), pursues her while she prefers the arms of his manager (Cornel Wilde). Directed by Jean Negulesco, the contrived story is less interesting than the flawed characters, one of whom is driven bonkers by the unbalanced triangle. Stylized violence, some intense menace and sexual innuendo

title: Road House
synopsis: College-educated bouncer (Patrick Swayze) cleans up a nasty nightclub in Missouri only to incur the wrath of the town's sleazy kingpin (Ben Gazzara). In director Rowdy Herrington's modern-day Western, women are the resident playthings and men the resident idiots. Interminable fisticuffs, graphic sexual encounters, nudity and endorsement of vigilantism

title: Roadhouse Murder, The
synopsis: Sappy melodrama directed by J. Walter Ruben in which a cub reporter (Eric Linden) stumbles on a double murder, plants evidence of his own guilt so he can write front-page stories about being hunted by the police, then is captured, tried and convicted after the real murderer (Bruce Cabot) steals the evidence that would clear him. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Roadie
synopsis: Failed spoof of rock music's subculture follows the misadventures of a country bumpkin (rock singer Meatloaf) who is convinced by a whacky groupie to become a "roadie" or general roustabout and handyman for a traveling rock group. Director Alan Rudolph offers few good sight gags and plenty of bad ones, with lots of ear-numbing music. Some jokes about sex and drugs

title: Road Movie
synopsis: Wildly exaggerated melodrama about two truck drivers (Robert Drivas and Barry Bostwick) whose friendship is shattered when they pick up a fuel-stop prostitute (Regina Baff) in a story that ends with the destruction of the truck and the death of one of them. Directed by Joseph Strick, whatever intentions the movie had as social commentary on the dangers of the road is undone by the movie's meanness of characters and their rough language

title: Road Show
synopsis: Comic misfire directed by Hal Roach in which an eccentric millionaire (John Hubbard) escapes a mental asylum with the help of an inmate (Adolphe Menjou), then is hidden by the soft-hearted owner (Carole Landis) of a failing carnival, with predictable results. Romantic complications, slapstick violence and a comic black stereotype (Willie Best)

title: Roadside Prophets
synopsis: Shapeless road movie follows a loner (John Doe) as he motorcycles through the Nevada desert meeting assorted oddballs and outcasts along the way, including a would-be friend (Adam Horovitz) who stubbornly trails him. Writer-director Abbe Wool needles the establishment with minimal wit and drab counterculture twaddle. Implied sexual encounter, fleeting violence and nudity, occasional substance abuse and recurring rough language

title: Road to Bali
synopsis: Fitful comedy in which a hapless pair of entertainers (Bing Crosby and Bob Hope) try diving for sunken treasure in the South Seas, then vie for the affections of an island princess (Dorothy Lamour) while saving her from court intrigues, cannibals and an erupting volcano. Directed by Hal Walker, the 6th "Road" picture sputters along on a haphazard mix of silly situations, daffy one-liners and cameos by Jane Russell, Humphrey Bogart and Martin and Lewis. Menacing situations and mild sexual innuendo

title: Road to Denver, The
synopsis: Routine Western directed by Joe Kane in which a Texas cowboy (John Payne) becomes a partner in a Colorado stage line, then is confronted by his trigger-happy younger brother (Skip Homeier) who's working for the competition (Lee J. Cobb). Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Road to El Dorado, The
synopsis: Disappointing animated adventure about two Spanish con men (voices of Kenneth Branagh and Kevin Kline) who find El Dorado, the legendary city of gold, but run into trouble when the natives mistake them for gods. As directed by Eric Bergeron and Don Paul, the film has a strong cast of voices and vibrant coloring, but the story sometimes limps and the flat, formulaic music is forgettable. Mild animated violence that may scare younger children and fleeting crass language

title: Road to Glory, The
synopsis: Creaky World War I tale about a battle-fatigued French captain (Warner Baxter) who leads his company, among whom is his aged father (Lionel Barrymore), in a 1916 offensive which costs him his eyesight, then learns his Red Cross girlfriend (June Lang) loves a lieutenant (Fredric March) and returns to the front where his father guides him on a suicide mission. Director Howard Hawks struggles with the credibility of the plot's contrived melodramatics but excels in vivid scenes of trench warfare and the gallows humor of combat soldiers. Battlefield violence and muted sexual innuendo

title: Road to Hong Kong, The
synopsis: In the 7th and final "Road"' picture, Bing Crosby and Bob Hope play con artists kidnapped in the Orient by an agent (Joan Collins) of a would-be world dictator (Robert Morley) and they wind up on a one-way rocket trip to the moon. Directed by Norman Panama, the low-budget British production doesn't give the veteran duo much to work with, though occasionally the old boys put some new life in the stale proceedings. Stylized violence and a few mild double entendres

title: Road to Morocco
synopsis: Wacky comic romp in which castaways Bing Crosby and Bob Hope land in a desert kingdom, vie to wed its princess (Dorothy Lamour) and wind up captives of a rebel Arab chieftain (Anthony Quinn). Directed by David Butler, the third Road comedy continues the pair's genial buffoonery as small-time hustlers trying to woo Lamour amidst throwaway gags, one-liners, talking camels and occasional songs. Some mild sexual innuendo

title: Road to Perdition
synopsis: Gripping drama set in Depression-era Chicago in which a hit man (Tom Hanks) working for the leader of the Irish mob (Paul Newman) embarks on a journey to protect his 12-year-old son and avenge the death of the rest of his family. Examining complicated father-son relationships, director Sam Mendes’ evocative moral tale presents a calculated visual tapestry of intrigue and multi-layered characters which smoothly weaves in themes of betrayal, redemption, filial love and family responsibility.� Some brutal scenes of violence with sporadic rough language and profanity
full_review:
In director Sam Mendes’ gripping drama “Road to Perdition” (DreamWorks), a cold-blooded hit man’s livelihood and past catch up with him, challenging the love he has for his family.

����������� Mendes once again looks at dysfunctional families as he did in his nihilistic directorial debut “American Beauty.” But in his sophomore effort, he digs deeper to unearth themes of filial love and family responsibility as well as betrayal and revenge.

����������� Tom Hanks throws off his good-guy persona to anchor the film with a convincing performance as Michael Sullivan, a hit man working for John Rooney (Paul Newman), the gangster patriarch of the Irish mob in a small Illinois town in 1931. Newman proves he can still physically and verbally dominate the screen. He makes wickedness look almost dignified with his white hair, impeccably tailored suits and senatorial demeanor.

����������� As the title implies, Sullivan is on the road to utter destruction. Both Sullivan and Rooney are forced to choose between their criminal careers and family life. Sullivan must protect his 12-year-old son from Rooney after the boy witnesses a murderous scene while Rooney shelters his oldest son Connor (Daniel Craig), a hot-headed, bitter young man jealous of his father’s affection for Sullivan.

����������� The situation is complicated by the relationship between the two fathers. After Sullivan’s parents died, Rooney became his adoptive father, nurturing and protecting him and bringing him into the family business, where he holds a respected place of honor. Sullivan and Rooney each recognizes the wages of their own sins. While one is determined for his son’s sake that the violence must end, the other father perpetuates even more terrible violence to physically, not morally, save his son.

����������� The divisive morality tale is layered with regrets, bad decisions and a good dose of gruesome violence. But also weaved in with the theme of betrayal is redemption, filial love and family responsibility.

����������� Sullivan is a man who only takes a good look at his life when it is already too late. He is a man who does not take his Catholic faith to work with him, yet insists on saying grace before meals and carrying rosary beads in his gun pocket.

����������� This split life he leads -– devoted family man and deadly assassin -- comes crashing down on him with one shockingly violent act, which embarks him on a journey of revenge with his eldest son Michael Jr. (Tyler Hoechlin). It is in this journey of self-discovery for both father and son that unconditional love is seen flowing both ways.

����������� “Perdition” is an intriguing character study and an involving yarn. Its intense emotion and beauty is matched by Mendes’ evocative visual tapestry. Moody lighting, inspired camera angles and rain-drenched atmospheric sets and locations drop the viewer smack in the middle of Depression-era Chicago where the name Capone is said with reverence.

����������� Mendes does not let the audience off easy when it comes to the violence. The camera is unflinching in capturing its ugly brutality, never glamorizing the crimes. And yet there is a certain strange beauty in seeing Hanks walk determinedly though puddles with a machine gun in his hands. And the bloodshed has horrific consequences which are shown in the same resolute manner.

����������� Jude Law plays a perverted hired hit man with a penchant for memorializing his victims in a truly macabre fashion. From his dried, cracked lips and scummy teeth to his long dirty nails, Law is perfectly repulsive as he tests Sullivan’s talent as a killer and fugitive. Hoechlin is a true surprise, acting as the story’s observer and occasional narrator. Moments when his performance could have slipped into the sappy, Hoechlinis restrained and natural.

����������� The straightforward revenge story is deceptively complicated. Based on the graphic novel written by Max Allan Collins and illustrated by Richard Piers Rayner, “Road to Perdition” briefly lightens up in the latter half, providing a respite from the darkness with some unconventional bank robberies. But the laughs are only a momentary distraction from the heart of the story. As Mendes examines moral decisions with generational repercussions, the actors’ nuanced performances stand out in a sea of popcorn summer movies.

����������� “Road to Perdition” may be on the road to the Oscars.

����������� Due to some brutal scenes of violence with sporadic rough language and profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R- restricted.

__________________

����������� Navarro is on the staff of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops' Office for Film and Broadcasting.

title: Road to Rio
synopsis: After accidentally torching a carnival, a hapless pair of musicians (Bing Crosby and Bob Hope) stow away on a Brazilian-bound ocean liner where they befriend an heiress (Dorothy Lamour) hypnotized by her wicked aunt (Gale Sondergaard). Directed by Norman Z. McLeod, the fifth "Road" comedy continues the series' tradition of zany plots strewn with wisecracks, sight gags and musical interludes, this time including the Andrew Sisters and the three manic Wiere Brothers. Silly but fun

title: Road to Salina
synopsis: Dreadfully pretentious European production set in the middle of a baked salt flat where Lana Turner runs a gas station-cafe and mistakes Robert Walker for her runaway son. Her daughter (Mimsy Farmer) goes along with the situation by engaging in a sexual relationship that had originally sent the son packing. Directed by Georges Lautner, the muddled incest theme is conveyed with many arty scenes of graphic lovemaking

title: Road to Singapore
