Directed by Norton Virgien and John Eng, and promoting a positive family-values message, this delightful cross-pollinating romp should prove satisfying for young fans of both shows, while written smartly enough to keep parental snoring to a minimum.

Despite the larger format, the film retains much of series' small-screen charm, keeping the focus on the zany tykes, including bossy Angelica (voiced by Cheryl Chase), timid Chuckie (voiced by Nancy Cartwright) and Tommy (voiced by E.G. Daily), an adventurous toddler with "a diaper full of dreams." Bruce Willis lends his gravel-toned pipes to Spike, their faithful dog, transforming the milquetoast mutt into a pooch with pizzazz.

As expected, the Rugrats find themselves in quite a pickle when Tommy's dad -- appropriately named Stu Pickles (voiced by Jack Riley) -- books the gang aboard a rickety vessel called the S.S. Nancy. Faced with walking the plank, Stu explains that their originally planned cruise aboard an ocean liner would have offered far too many distractions from the vacation's intended purpose: to spend quality time together.

Barely out of port, they hit the mother of all storms and find themselves marooned on a deserted, "dogforsaken" island. However, the Swiss family Pickles soon discover that they are not alone. Further up the beach, the famous nature-documentarian family, the Thornberrys, has set up camp.

The Thornberry clan, including intrepid explorer Sir Nigel (voiced by Tim Curry), his angst-ridden teen-age daughter Debbie (voiced by Danielle Harris) and wild boy Donnie (voiced by Flea), are currently tracking down a rare and elusive white leopard (voiced by Chrissie Hynde of the Pretenders).

In true "Rugrats" fashion, the mischievous mites and their "Wild" playmates get themselves lost and in hot water in the island's treacherous jungle interior. Back on the beach, the grown-ups are worried sick and ripe for epiphanies about the importance of family and parenting mea culpas.

But in order for the castaways to find their way back home, they must learn to work together -- and quick, before the prowling leopard makes these TV favorites into TV dinners.

While obviously targeted at younger audiences, the film moves along at a good pace and packs enough of a satirical punch to allow parents to leave the No-Doz pills at home. And whereas fans of the highly successful TV shows will have fun watching their favorite little rascals on the big screen, older viewers along for the ride should get a kick out of the many cinematic references peppered throughout. Besides the obvious allusion to "Gilligan's Island," the film subtly spoofs "Titanic," "Cast Away," "The Perfect Storm," "The Poseidon Adventure" and "Planet of the Apes," not to mention paying clever homage to a famous "I Love Lucy" skit. And while the animation is not in the same sandbox as Disney, the quirky, less polished artwork lends itself well to the characters' edgy, oddball personalities.

As an extra, albeit gimmicky, bonus, "Rugrats Go Wild" features interactive "odorama" cards, which are passed out to young audience members. When a number flashes on the screen during the movie, viewers can scratch the corresponding patch on the card and sniff smells ranging from strawberries to stinky feet.

In addition to imparting a strong message about the importance of families spending time together, the film also promotes a healthy respect for nature.

The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-I -- general patronage. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- general audiences.

title: Rugrats in Paris
synopsis: Sweet animated sequel in which the whole gang travels to Paris where little Chuckie Finster (voice of Christine Cavanaugh) tries to find his widowed father a new wife and himself a new mommy. Based on the characters from the Nickelodeon series, the bright, lively animation and simple story peppered with clever quips in directors Stig Bergqvist and Paul Demeyer's film create an engaging film delightful for children and parents alike. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Rugrats Movie, The
synopsis: Animated tale based on the children's TV series in which five frisky toddlers get lost in a scary forest while trying to return the crybaby infant brother of one of them to the baby hospital. Directors Norton Virgien and Igor Kovalyov have the tykes survive assorted dangers and misadventures as they discover the meaning of friendship and helping the helpless

title: Rulers of the Sea
synopsis: Dated but watchable story of how a sea captain (Douglas Fairbanks, Jr.) and a machinist (Will Fyffe) join forces in making the first steamship crossing of the Atlantic in 1838. Director Frank Lloyd shows how the hazards and uncertainties of voyages under sail caused merchants to back the development of a steam-driven vessel, though the characters involved in its achievement are sentimentalized in standard Hollywood fashion

title: Rules of Engagement
synopsis: After a Marine rescue mission at a foreign embassy leaves civilians dead, the decorated colonel-in-charge (Samuel L. Jackson) faces court martial for murder and persuades his retired Marine buddy (Tommy Lee Jones) to defend him. Director William Friedkin's feel-good film blends action with fiery courtroom exchanges in exploring the harsh reality of life-and-death decision-making under fire. Some gory military violence, intermittent profanity and frequent rough language

title: Ruling Class, The
synopsis: Screen version of Peter Barnes' play satirizing the British upper classes in a story about the demented Earl of Gurney (Peter O'Toole in a madcap virtuoso performance) who, once he is cured of believing he is God, assumes the identity of Jack the Ripper. Directed by Peter Medak, the looney black comedy even has some hilarious song and dance numbers but the nonsense goes on much too long and becomes repetitive. Some may take the casebook condition of claiming to be the Deity as irreverent but religion is not at all under attack here

title: Rumble Fish
synopsis: Failed screen version of a C.E. Hinton novel with Matt Dillon giving an overwrought Brando imitation as a teen-ager trying to live up to the bad reputation of his brother (Mickey Rourke) and drunken father (Dennis Hopper). Director Francis Ford Coppola's confusing portrait of a youth struggling to regain self-esteem is marred by gang-war violence, some nudity and brief but graphic sex

title: Rumble in the Bronx
synopsis: Inane action flick about a Chinese martial-arts expert (Jackie Chan) who runs into a dangerous biker gang while visiting New York, and ends up persuading them to help him foil a big diamond robbery. Directed by Stanley Tong, the lame script is an uneasy blend of Chan's slapstick-brand of martial arts with more realistic bone-crunching confrontations. Recurring violence, fleeting nudity and several instances of rough language

title: Rumor Has It
synopsis: Good cast wasted in mostly distasteful story of woman (Jennifer Aniston) who believes the 1967 film "The Graduate" was modeled on her family, and tracks down the man (Kevin Costner) once involved with both her late mother and her grandmother (Shirley MacLaine), and then falls for him herself. Director Rob Reiner gets decent performances from his actors, including Mark Ruffalo and Richard Jenkins, and the basic premise is mildly amusing, but the sentimental pro-family ending fails to eradicate the squishy morality throughout. Vaguely incestuous theme, permissive view of premarital sex, sexual situations, some profanity, crude language and expressions, drug references, condom reference and partial nudity
full_review:
What if the 1967 film "The Graduate" had been based on reality? And older-woman seductress Mrs. Robinson and preppy young Benjamin Braddock's affair were to have repercussions years later?

Such is the promising, but ultimately disappointing, premise of "Rumor Has It..." (Warner Bros.), which boasts a good cast but a fairly unsavory story.

Sarah Huttinger (Jennifer Aniston) is a journalist, eking out a living as an obituary writer for The New York Times. She's engaged to marry boyfriend Jeff (Mark Ruffalo), but has doubts about her commitment. When the film opens, they're flying home for her sister's (Mena Suvari) wedding in Pasadena, Calif. (On the plane, they try to make love in the restroom with disastrous results, the first of the film's several unfunny gags.)

On her home turf, Sarah feels an odd disconnect from her family. When she learns from her grandmother, Katharine (Shirley MacLaine), that her late mother once had an affair just before marrying Sarah's father (Richard Jenkins), Sarah resolves to track the man down.

The titular "rumor" -- which motivates Sarah in her quest of self-discovery -- is that "The Graduate" (first a book in 1963, by the way) was in fact inspired by her own family, and that Katharine was the "Mrs. Robinson" of the story, which would have made Sarah's mother Benjamin's love interest. If the rumor is true, this man could be Sarah's father.

Sarah finds her mother's lover, Beau (Kevin Costner), now a famous Internet billionaire, lecturing in San Francisco, and confronts him with her suspicions that she may be his daughter.

He accepts her charges with dramatically unbelievable equanimity, and he convinces her that this could not be so -- because he's been sterile for years because of "blunt testicular trauma" sustained during a football game. He charms her off her feet, and before you know it, she's waking up in bed beside him.

Misunderstandings and conflicted emotions follow, including the titillating (to Sarah) possibility that she has indeed just slept with her own father. Though, of course, all is set right by the end, the setup leaves a distinctly bad taste.

Aniston is adequate in the lead role, but her repeatedly wrong assumptions and actions, at least as written, make her character more tiresome than appealing. Costner and Ruffalo are fine as the two men in her life. MacLaine's feisty and still glamorous grandmother role is less juicy than her recent grandmother turn in "In Her Shoes," while Jenkins and Suvari do good work as the father and younger sister.

Director Rob Reiner handles this material capably, and there's even a sentimental pro-family ending, but it fails to eradicate much of the squishy morality throughout.

The film contains a vaguely incestuous theme, a permissive view of premarital sex, sexual situations, some profanity, crude language and expressions, drug references, a condom reference and partial nudity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Run
synopsis: A resourceful law student (Patrick Dempsey) flees for his life, pursued by the mob and corrupt cops, after being innocently involved in the death of the son of a gang leader (Ken Pogue). Director Geoff Burrowes delivers a fast track of action and suspense abetted by Dempsey's winning performance and the movie's gallows humor. Considerable violence in a realistic, non-gratuitous context and minimal rough language

title: Run After Me -- Until I Catch You
synopsis: Soggy French farce about the owner of a canine beauty parlor (Annie Girardot) and her romance with a tax collector (Jean-Pierre Marielle). Director Robert Pouret makes a feeble attempt to show that middle-aged people can be as romantic, foolish and funny as any other age group. Adult situations

title: Runaround, The
synopsis: Hired to find a millionaire's eloping daughter, a private detective (Rod Cameron) has his hands full trying to bring the protesting woman (Ella Raines) back home while eluding his former boss (Broderick Crawford) who wants the reward for himself. Directed by Charles Lamont, the crosscountry romance is secondary to the comic flimflam between the rival detectives, with a trick ending appropriate to the title. Stylized violence and mild romance

title: Runaway
synopsis: Silly science fiction vehicle for Tom Selleck who plays a futuristic cop on the runaway squad, a branch of the police force assigned to corralling robots that have run amok. Directed by Michael Crichton, its unintentionally funny high-tech mayhem provides passable entertainment for action fans. Some violence and brief nudity

title: Runaway Bride
synopsis: Breezy romantic comedy in which cynical big-city reporter Richard Gere, writing an expose on smalltown bride-to-be Julia Roberts who has left several previous suitors at the altar, finds himself wanting to risk being the fifth groom whose bride may be a no-show. Director Garry Marshall gets a luminous performance from Roberts in a feel-good tale, which, though predictable, brims with warmth and charm. Very discreet sexual references and minimal profanity

title: Runaway Jury
synopsis: Middling courtroom drama based on the John Grisham novel in which a juror (John Cusack) and his girlfriend (Rachel Weisz) conspire with both sides (as played by Gene Hackman and Dustin Hoffman), offering to buy the verdict in a lawsuit against a gun manufacturer. Despite director Gary Fleder's fast-paced visuals, the thin characterizations aren't emotionally involving nor is the all-too-pat and morally flawed resolution credible. A cynical view of the legal system, some violence and minimal rough language and profanity
full_review:
A juror and his girlfriend conspire to buy a verdict for the highest bidder in the workmanlike courtroom drama "Runaway Jury" (20th Century Fox).

Based on the 1996 John Grisham novel, the lawsuit in the movie was switched from the tobacco industry to the gun industry after Big Tobacco began to lose cases. But, as often happens in a book with many characters (the opposing legal teams, their clients, jury consultants, judge, jury and alternates) the film must pare down the characterizations to quick thumbnail sketches. And the film suffers as a result, especially in comparison to the novel. Although director Gary Fleder sets a fast pace and has a great cast at his disposal, these characters simply aren't emotionally involving enough to make us care deeply.

Gene Hackman plays Rankin Fitch, a ruthless jury consultant for the gun industry who promises the rich CEOs paying him that with their lawyer (Bruce Davison) obeying his instructions to accept or reject a given juror, they will bring in the not-guilty verdict so crucial to prevent a slew of class-action suits that could bankrupt the gun industry. Fitch has a huge staff -- both high-tech types researching each potential juror and lowlifes to intimidate or blackmail them for the "right" verdict.

The wild card in the equation, however, is juror Nick Easter (John Cusack), whose background cannot be traced by Fitch's minions before the trial begins. Bringing the suit against the gun manufacturer whose firearm a disgruntled employee used to murder 11 employees is a widow represented by crusading New Orleans attorney Wendall Rohr (Dustin Hoffman).

In short order, Fitch and Rohr are each contacted by Nick's girlfriend, Marlee (Rachel Weisz), who proposes that for millions Nick can swing the jury to the desired outcome for whoever takes her up on the offer. Idealistic Rohr is appalled; Fitch wants to gets the goods on her pronto, but is persuaded to listen to her when she proves Nick is able to manipulate the jurors to do unheard-of things such as bursting forth with a pledge of allegiance in the courtroom. As Rohr finds his key witnesses suddenly compromised, he too considers the despicable offer.

But are Nick and Marlee as mercenary as they seem, and are they in actual danger from Fitch's thugs?

Despite the director's snazzy camera moves, action elements and zippy pacing, the sense of urgency isn't there, so the suspense isn't sizzling. While never boring, the film plays like a competent police procedural as the pieces in the puzzle eventually fit together. Yet the ending is far too easily accomplished to be very credible, with its morally ambiguous characters shown in a more favorable light than deserved.

Ironically, there are scenes in a church, with a cabbie whose rosary is prominently positioned and in a store featuring candles to honor different saints, but the supposed moral victory dished out is hollow.

Due to a cynical view of the legal system, some violence and minimal rough language and profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Runaway Train
synopsis: Alaskan train, whose steely-black locomotive is hurtling out of control, carries two escaped convicts (Jon Voight and Eric Roberts) along with a napping railroad worker (Rebecca DeMornay). Directed by Andrei Konchalovsky and based on a screenplay by Akira Kurosawa, something has been lost in the translation. Senseless plot, excessive violence and coarse language

title: Run Before the Wind
synopsis: New York art director (Jean Yves) races a sailboat from San Francisco to Tokyo in a semi-documentary that captures the breathtaking ocean vistas and challenging duties of the 6000-mile contest. Written, produced and directed by Brud Talbot, the movie becomes exploitation fare by punctuating the voyage with a series of sexually graphic daydreams

title: Run Fatboy Run
synopsis: Quirky romantic comedy in which a likeable British twit (Simon Pegg), despite being out of shape, must complete a marathon in order to regain the respect of his ex-fiancee (Thandie Newton), thwart her obnoxious boyfriend (Hank Azaria), vindicate the confidence shown by his trusting landlord (Harish Patel) and safeguard a friend who has rashly bet on him (Dylan Moran). Despite some errant, occasionally outrageous humor and a familiar story arc, actor David Schwimmer's directorial debut has enough sparkle and eccentricity to make it past the finish line. Two scenes of rear nudity, implied premarital sex, one use of the f-word, some crude and crass language, one profanity, obscene gestures, sexual and scatological humor, a violent fight and a transsexual character
full_review:
A likable British twit tries to prove he's in it for the long haul in the quirky romantic comedy "Run Fatboy Run" (Picturehouse).

Five years after leaving his pregnant fiancee, Libby (Thandie Newton), standing at the altar, slovenly London security guard Dennis (Simon Pegg, who also co-wrote the script) bitterly regrets this characteristic act of cowardice. But his chances of undoing the damage look slim, since Libby -- now a successful bakery owner -- is dating wealthy, athletic American businessman Whit (Hank Azaria).

Provoked by Whit's macho boasting about a forthcoming marathon, Dennis rashly declares that he, too, will enter and complete the race. This leaves the untrained layabout, who sports a gut the size and shape of a small potato sack, only three weeks to prepare.

The pressure mounts as Dennis learns that his best friend, Gordon (Dylan Moran), has made underground bets on the outcome that he can't afford to lose. Also counting on the novice's stamina are his trusting son, Jake (Matthew Fenton), and his enthusiastic Indian landlord, and self-identified biggest fan, Mr. Ghoshdashtidar (Harish Patel).

Despite some errant, occasionally outrageous humor and a familiar story arc, actor David Schwimmer's directorial debut has enough sparkle and eccentricity to make it past the finish line.

As Dennis struggles to redeem himself, the script highlights his need for maturity and commitment and identifies self-sacrificing discipline with true masculinity. These values contrast with the film's casual acceptance of contemporary sexual mores.

The film contains two scenes of rear nudity, implied premarital sex, one use of the f-word, some crude and crass language, one profanity, obscene gestures, sexual and scatological humor, a violent fight and a transsexual character. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Run for Cover
synopsis: Disappointing Western in which an ex-con (James Cagney) becomes the sheriff of a small town, earns the love of a good woman (Viveca Lindfors), then is betrayed by the crippled youth (John Derek) he's dedicated himself to helping. Directed by Nicholas Ray, the contrived action and thin characterizations give little conviction to the scenario's theme of misplaced loyalties and corrupted innocence. Frontier violence with murky themes

title: Run for the Sun
synopsis: Exotic chase thriller about an author-adventurer (Richard Widmark) and a journalist (Jane Greer) whose plane crashes in a Mexican jungle where they are rescued by fugitive Nazis (Trevor Howard and Peter Van Eyck) from whom they try to escape. Director Roy Boulting spends too much time setting up the premise, but once the couple flee into the jungle, the proceedings become quite harrowing. Stylized violence and much tension

title: Run for Your Wife
synopsis: Weak comedy about an Italian's search for an American bride highlights promiscuous sex

title: Run Lola Run
synopsis: German production provides three alternate versions of what transpires during the 20 minutes it takes Lola (Franka Potente) to race across Berlin on foot while getting the money needed to save her lover (Moritz Bleibtreu) from a drug dealer's bullet. Writer-director Tom Tykwer has used all kinds of cinematic devices from split screens to flash forwards, but what holds it together is the energy of the performers and the pace of the action, with the race against the clock central to its appeal. Subtitles. Stylized violence, drug dealing, sexual innuendo and occasional rough language

title: Runner Stumbles, The
synopsis: Fact-based story of a gifted but morose pastor (Dick Van Dyke) of a small-town parish in the 1920s who is accused of murdering a young nun (Kathleen Quinlan) to whom he had shown special attention. Director Stanley Kramer delicately tries to avoid the sensational but its superficial treatment of the Catholic context, sketchy characterizations and a bizarre climax add up to a disappointing muddle. Because it deals with the emotional involvement of a priest and nun under extremely melodramatic circumstances, it is mature viewing fare that some may find distasteful

title: Running
synopsis: Aging marathon runner (Michael Douglas), who has a reputation for choking up in the clutch both in running and in life, resolves to vindicate himself and win back his estranged wife (Susan Anspach) by making it to the Olympics. Directed by Steven Hillard Stern, the grimly determined athlete featured in the foreground proves less compelling than the pageantry of Montreal's Olympics in the background. Some foul language

title: Running Man, The
synopsis: Halting suspense story in which an English pilot (Laurence Harvey) fakes his death, then rejoins his wife (Lee Remick) in Spain after she collects the insurance money, but they fear arrest when the insurance agent (Alan Bates) who investigated the claim turns up. Director Carol Reed makes good use of colorful Spanish locations to pace a cat-and-mouse tale that never measures up to its potential. Menacing situations and an implied sexual encounter

title: Running Man, The
synopsis: Mindless action thriller set in 2017 America which is now a police state whose enemies are chased to their death by armed pursuers on a live TV game show (hosted by Richard Dawson) until one of the pursued (Arnold Schwarzenegger) kills the hunters (Jesse Ventura and others), then leads the underground opposition to victory. Directed by Paul Michael Glaser, the muddled proceedings based on this clumsy premise make little sense beyond the bloodlust of the action. Excessive violence, occasional profanity and some rough language

title: Running on Empty
synopsis: After injuring a janitor in college bombing as a protest against the Vietnam War, a couple (Judd Hirsch and Christine Lahti) have been on the run from the FBI for 15 years, but problems arise when their 17-year-old son (River Phoenix) wants to go to college and lead a normal life under his own identity. Director Sidney Lumet presents a universal family crisis within the context of an unusual family whose children have been forced to carry the burden of their parents' crime of conscience. Rough language and an implied teenage sexual liaison

title: Running Scared
synopsis: Excessively brutal crime drama about a low-level member of New Jersey Mafia crew (Paul Walker) whose ill-fated decision not to dispose of an incriminating gun has disastrous consequences when his son's best friend (Cameron Bright) steals it, touching off a frantic search for the weapon and setting in motion a cycle of escalating violence involving Italian mobsters, Russian gangsters, a corrupt cop (Chazz Palminteri) and pedophile predators. Beyond its visual slickness, writer-director Wayne Kramer's after-hours tour of Jersey's sleazy underbelly is an obscenity-soaked, one-note symphony of bloody mayhem that assaults viewers unrelentingly from its gratuitously grisly opening gunfight to its equally over-the-top climax. Pervasive strong and graphic violence, including gory shootings and beatings, scenes of child and spousal abuse, suggested pedophilia, a vulgar simulation of oral sex involving shadowy, partial, frontal female nudity and brief rear male nudity, full-frontal female strip-club nudity, drug content and nonstop rough and crude language, as well as profanity
full_review:
Long, loud, loathsome and ultimately ludicrous, "Running Scared" (New Line) plays like an overcaffeinated film student's idea of a Quentin Tarantino fever dream.

Written and directed by Wayne Kramer, the excessively brutal crime drama centers on Joey Gazelle (Paul Walker), a low-level member of a New Jersey Mafia crew, whose ill-fated decision not to dispose of a handgun used in a drug deal (during which several crooked cops were killed) has disastrous consequences when his son's best friend Oleg (Cameron Bright) steals it, sending Joey on a frantic search for the incriminating weapon.

Taking place during 18 mostly nocturnal -- and extremely bloody -- hours, Joey's hunt leads him deeper down a vice-infested rabbit hole, setting in motion a cycle of escalating violence involving Italian mobsters, Russian gangsters, a corrupt police detective (Chazz Palminteri) and pedophiles.

Cribbing from Tarantino, Sam Peckinpah, John Woo and Michael Mann, Kramer combines gritty heightened realism with self-conscious camerawork and kinetic editing to wearying effect.

But beyond its admitted visual slickness, this sleazy after-hours tour of the Garden State's underbelly is a one-note symphony of gratuitous mayhem that assaults viewers unrelentingly from its grisly opening gunfight to its over-the-top climax.

The film contains pervasive strong and graphic violence, including gory shootings and beatings, scenes of child and spousal abuse, suggested pedophilia, a vulgar simulation of oral sex involving shadowy, partial, frontal female nudity and brief rear male nudity, full-frontal female strip-club nudity, drug content and nonstop rough and crude language, as well as profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Running Scared
synopsis: Director Peter Hyams' rough-edged action comedy about veteran Chicago undercover cops (Billy Crystal and Gregory Hines) making their last drug bust before early retirement to the good life in Key West is waylaid by violence, harsh language, brief nudity and ethnic stereotyping

title: Running with Scissors
synopsis: Author Augusten Burroughs' best-selling memoirs about his wildly unconventional adolescence during which his mentally fragile mother (Annette Bening), estranged from her husband (Alec Baldwin), sent the boy (Joseph Cross) to be raised by her quack psychiatrist (Brian Cox) and his extremely dysfunctional family (Jill Clayburgh, Gwyneth Paltrow, Evan Rachel Wood, Joseph Fiennes). Director Ryan Murphy's episodic adaptation -- which may puzzle those unfamiliar with the book -- handles the provocative material with sensitivity, toning down the racier elements. Though some of the situations are, in themselves, morally objectionable (making the film unpalatable for many), the overall tone and resolution have a distinctly moral center. Pervasive rough language and profanity, a couple of discreetly handled same-sex relationships including a disturbing age-inappropriate one, other sexual themes and innuendo, scatological humor, drug use, domestic violence, an irreverent remark, discussion of suicide
full_review:
"Running With Scissors" (TriStar), adapted from author Augusten Burroughs' best-selling memoirs about his wildly unconventional adolescence in the 1970s, shows how his bipolar mother, Deirdre (Annette Bening), estranged from her ex-alcoholic husband, Norman (Alec Baldwin), gives up their son (Joseph Cross) for adoption.

A narcissist to the core, Deirdre -- with delusions of being a great poet whose oeuvre will be published imminently -- sends Augusten to be raised by her quack psychiatrist Dr.

Finch (Brian Cox) and his extremely eccentric family in a dilapidated house where a Christmas tree stays up for years, the family nibbles on dog food, and mountains of unwashed dishes clutter the kitchen. There's catatonic wife Agnes (Jill Clayburgh), daughters Hope (Gwyneth Paltrow), given to pointing to random pages in the Bible for guidance, and Natalie (Evan Rachel Wood), a nonconformist who longs to go to college and becomes Augusten's confidante, and 35-year-old Neil (Joseph Fiennes), a seriously unbalanced adopted son.

Director Ryan Murphy (who also wrote the screenplay) faithfully recreates the book's main episodes, though those unfamiliar with the original may find the narrative disconcertingly choppy and more than a bit puzzling. Still, he handles the provocative material with sensitivity, toning down the racier elements, the most troubling of which is 14-year-old Augusten's sexual relationship with Neil (mostly implied), and later, Deirdre's dalliance with a couple of women.

These, among other, situations are, in themselves, highly objectionable. However, the overall tone and ultimate resolution have a distinctly moral center, imparting clear messages about family, forgiveness and the need for boundaries in one's personal life. This last point is driven home with exquisite poignancy when, after living so long with no restrictions on his behavior whatsoever, Augusten cries out for moral structure.
The cast avoids caricature, though there is much mordant humor throughout at their expense. Bening has the showiest role and etches Deirdre's wild mood swings most skillfully, while Clayburgh is especially moving when she overcomes her lethargy and gives Augusten the maternal care she realizes he so desperately needs.

Amid an overall panorama of dysfunction and unconventionality, there are many surprisingly touching moments. Still, many Catholic viewers may find all the aforementioned problematic elements off-putting, if in fact they choose to spend time with the peculiar Finch brood at all.

The film contains pervasive rough language and profanity, a couple of discreetly handled same-sex relationships including a disturbing age-inappropriate one, other sexual themes and innuendo, scatological humor, drug use, domestic violence, an irreverent remark, and discussion of suicide. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Run of the Arrow
synopsis: After the Civil War, an unreconstructed rebel (Rod Steiger) moves West, joins a Sioux tribe (whose chief is Charles Bronson) and tries to avert a war with Army troops (led by Ralph Meeker). Written, produced and directed by Samuel Fuller, the ambitious scenario is largely unrealized on the screen, partly because of its disjointed treatment of themes including regional rivalries, Native American tribalism and the foibles of ordinary people. Much stylized violence, some of it quite bloody

title: Run of the Country, The
synopsis: Dark coming-of-age story in which an 18-year-old Irish lad (Matt Keeslar) quarrels with his policeman father (Albert Finney), moves in with a rural roughneck (Anthony Brophy) and gets a girl (Victoria Smurfit) pregnant before finally taking some tentative steps towards maturity. Directed by Peter Yates, the adolescent's eccentric misadventures mix comedy with tragedy, but the depiction of growing up on the border with the North is too fragmented to add up to a convincing whole. Some violence, strong sexual situations, brief nudity, occasional profanity and rough language

title: Run Silent, Run Deep
synopsis: Involving World War II tale aboard a U.S. submarine whose new skipper (Clark Gable) alienates his executive officer (Burt Lancaster) by passing up targets to go after the Japanese destroyer that sank his former sub. Director Robert Wise uses the claustrophobic conditions of submarine duty to heighten the growing tension between the two officers until their differences are resolved in a climactic sea battle. Wartime violence

title: Run the Wild River
synopsis: Shooting the rapids in huge rubber pontoons is a rugged way to find adventure, the challenge here taking the form of a river in southern Mexico that had never been run before. The thrills are real enough, with boats bouncing off rocks and swirling in the foaming waters, but too much footage is devoted to travelogue excursions into the surrounding countryside to pad out a documentary short into a full-length feature

title: Run Wild, Run Free
synopsis: British story in which a mute country child (Mark Lester) is befriended by a retired Army officer (John Mills) who teaches him to train a falcon and tame a wild colt, with predictable but quite satisfying results. Directed by Richard C. Sarafian, the story has appeal for adults as well as children both for its human qualities and the delights of nature

title: Rush
synopsis: Two romantically involved cops in a narcotics unit (Jennifer Jason Leigh and Jason Patric) use drugs to protect their cover as junkies, then struggle with addiction and their superiors' illegal demands to frame a suspect (Gregg Allman). Novice director Lili Fini Zanuck presents a gritty, harrowing look at the drug netherworld and the moral ambiguities of the war against drugs. Graphic shots of drug abuse, occasional violence including a suicide, brief bedroom scenes with a flash of nudity and frequent rough language

title: Rush Hour
synopsis: Mindless action tale of a cocky Los Angeles police detective (Chris Tucker) forced to team with a Chinese cop (Jackie Chan) when the Chinese Consul's young daughter is kidnapped by Asia's top crime lord. Director Brett Ratner depicts the deadly menace and brutal violence as exciting and the kind of jokey fun that has no consequences. Recurring violence, nasty menace to a child, a few racial slurs and intermittent profanity

title: Rush Hour 2
synopsis: Flat action sequel in which a smart-mouthed Los Angeles cop (Chris Tucker) and straight-laced Hong Kong detective (Jackie Chan) team up again to find a dangerous Chinese gang producing and shipping millions of counterfeit U.S. $100 bills. A few creatively choreographed action sequences cannot compensate for the forced narrative, witless comedy and no-consequences violence in director Brett Ratner's film. Recurring action violence, some sexually suggestive scenes, fleeting rear nudity and intermittent profanity and crass language

title: Rush Hour 3
synopsis: The third installment of the action comedy franchise puts the dour Jackie Chan and frantic, wisecracking Chris Tucker in Paris on the trail of a secret crime syndicate called the Triads. Director Brett Ratner and screenwriter Jeff Nathanson, who both made "Rush Hour 2," keep the car chases taut and lovingly choreograph the swordplay, gunplay and martial arts, but the rapport between the two leads is forced, and the best of the comedy seems borrowed from the "Naked Gun" spoofs. Nearly bloodless violence, crude and crass language, skimpy female costuming, implied female nudity, implied sexual activity and mild sexual banter
full_review:
The Eiffel Tower at night has never looked more spectacular in a motion picture. But until "Rush Hour 3" (New Line) gets there, the dour Chief Inspector Lee (Jackie Chan) and frantic, wisecracking detective James Carter (Chris Tucker) suffer comedic death by a thousand cuts from Parisian cliches staler than a 4-year-old box of "Freedom Fries."

Director Brett Ratner and screenwriter Jeff Nathanson, who both made "Rush Hour 2," keep the car chases taut and lovingly choreograph the swordplay, gunplay and martial arts. But six years after the second installment, the rapport between the two leads is forced, Chan seems tired, and the best of the comedy, when not resorting to a slapstick twirl with a giant in a kung fu studio, looks borrowed from the "Naked Gun" spoofs.

In this installment, Lee and Carter, who reunite in Los Angeles, fight a secret crime syndicate called the Triads. From the first film, Nathanson brings back Chinese ambassador Han (Tzi Ma) and his daughter, now 20, Soo Yung (Jingchu Zhang). Han is shot as he attempts to uncover the Triads before the World Criminal Court, Lee finds out the assassin is Kenji (Hiroyuki Sanada), his "brother" from their orphanage, Soo Yung is abducted, and the key evidence of the syndicate's existence turns out to be in Paris.

There, Lee and Carter encounter (quelle surprise!) scruffy French taxi driver George (Yvan Attal), who secretly longs to be an international spy ("The guns! The shooting! Now I know what it is to be an American!") and becomes their eager compatriot.

There's a sadistic police chief (Roman Polanski, in a surprising cameo), an obligatory dip into the Parisian sewers, and evidence hidden with sultry nightclub singer Genevieve (Noemie Lenoir) and Varden Reynard (Max von Sydow), the elegant head of the World Criminal Court, who may not be on the side of justice.

The potpourri of culture clashes also includes the unbilled Judith Ivey as Sister Agnes, a nun who calmly translates -- and paraphrases -- the rants of a Triad bad guy Carter raucously interrogates, without losing either her dignity or her deft comic timing.

The Eiffel Tower becomes a versatile jungle gym for the final showdown. And Carter's shrill, scattershot quips and occasional breaks into song propel the film as if Tucker knows his career depends on it. But when he launches into "Everybody Was Kung Fu Fighting" after dispatching a roomful of villains, it's clear this franchise has lurched to a close.

At a brisk 86 minutes, the film contains nearly bloodless violence, crude and crass language, skimpy female costuming, implied female nudity, implied sexual activity, mild sexual banter and innuendo. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Rushmore
synopsis: Offbeat comedy about a hyperactive 15-year-old (Jason Schwartzman) whose crush on a widowed schoolteacher (Olivia Williams) leads him to extremes in trying to stop his closest friend, a married millionaire (Bill Murray), from romancing her. Directed by Wes Anderson, the bittersweet tale of teenage angst is helped by performances which aptly blend humor with pathos as the youth learns about rejection and forgiveness. Brief violence, an implied affair, a few crass sexual references and a flash of nude pin-ups, a scene of underage drinking, occasional rough language and minimal profanity

title: Russia House, The
synopsis: A Russian woman (Michelle Pfeiffer) sends a politically sensitive manuscript written by her former lover (Klaus Maria Brandauer) to a British publisher (Sean Connery) who falls for her while checking out the document's authenticity for Allied intelligence agencies. Director Fred Schepisi's version of the John le Carre novel lacks a sense of urgency and the romance is flat, leaving only Connery's performance and scenic Russian locations to hold interest. Mild sexual innuendo and occasional rough language

title: Russian Adventure
synopsis: Picturesque Russian travelogue showing scenes of cities and countryside, the Bolshoi Ballet and the Moscow State Circus, but anyone hoping to learn more about what life in the Soviet Union is like will be disappointed

title: Russian Roulette
synopsis: Mediocre Canadian melodrama about the attempted assassination of a Soviet leader visiting Vancouver in which a Mountie (George Segal) becomes the unwitting tool of both Russian and Canadian counter-intelligence. Directed by Lou Lombardo, the plot is too convoluted for its own good but it's diverting, especially the lovely location photography. Some violence

title: Russians Are Coming, The Russians Are Coming, The
synopsis: Inspired farce built around the accidental grounding of a Russian submarine off the coast of Cape Cod. Producer-director Norman Jewison ably handles a fine cast including Alan Arkin, Carl Reiner, Eva Marie Saint, Jonathan Winters and Paul Ford. The movie's satire can be appreciated at several levels and will be enjoyed by the whole family
