Along with the dilemmas created by an overtaxed military, director Kimberly Peirce's earnest film also examines the difficult adjustment that awaits many returning veterans. Shriver, for instance, clings to the life he knows, fearful of what a civilian future will bring, while Tommy Burgess (Joseph Gordon-Levitt), another of King's comrades, quickly descends into alcoholism.

For those adults who can withstand a barrage of soldierly swearing and wrenching scenes of Middle East mayhem, "Stop-Loss" registers as a compelling, subtly acted piece of cinema.

The film contains graphic battle scenes with gore, pervasive rough and crude language, some crass language and profanity, sexual humor, two obscene gestures and a suicide theme. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Stop! Or My Mom Will Shoot
synopsis: Witless comedy has a meddling mom (Estelle Getty) endlessly fussing over her police sergeant son (Sylvester Stallone) and his neglected girlfriend (JoBeth Williams) while becoming his unwanted partner in a homicide investigation. Genial performances can't rescue director Roger Spottiswoode's one-joke sitcom from its flaccid predictability. Occasional violence and mild profanity

title: Stop the World -- I Want to Get Off
synopsis: British musical about an average man (Tony Tanner) who marries his employer's daughter, has a couple of kids and a few affairs, winds up with a title and the realization that he has never loved anyone but himself. Director Philip Saville photographs the stage production rather than turning it into a movie

title: Stork Club, The
synopsis: Frivolous musical comedy in which a hat-check girl (Betty Hutton) saves an elderly millionaire (Barry Fitzgerald) from drowning, then is rewarded by him annonymously rewards her with expensive gifts which cause misunderstandings when her Marine boyfriend (Don DeFore) returns from the Pacific. Directed by Hal Walker, Fitzgerald and lawyer Robert Benchley have a lot of fun with a thin premise that only makes Hutton and company look uncomfortably slow-witted. Romantic complications

title: Storm in a Teacup
synopsis: When an old woman (Sara Allgood) in a Scottish town refuses to buy a license for her pet dog, the mayor (Cecil Parker) orders it impounded, then faces a national crusade to save the dog instigated by an English reporter (Rex Harrison) who, in the process, wins the heart of the mayor's daughter (Vivien Leigh). Directed by Victor Saville and Ian Dalrymple, the droll British comedy has plenty of fun with the situation as well as class differences, political ambitions and English-Scottish tensions, but some of the dialogue is a bit thick for American ears. Incidental comic treatment of marital infidelity

title: Storm of the Century
synopsis: ( see: "Stephen King's Storm of the Century" )

title: Storm Over Lisbon
synopsis: Convoluted World War II thriller set in neutral Portugal where a Lisbon nightclub owner (Erich von Stroheim) sells military secrets to the highest bidder until he grabs an American (Richard Arlen) with information sought by Japanese agents, but the man escapes with the help of a refugee Czech dancer (Vera Ralston) and gets through to the authorities. Directed by George Sherman, the desperate proceedings are far from credible, though von Stroheim's steely portrayal of a man with no illusions is still worth seeing. Stylized violence, romantic complications and sexual innuendo

title: Storm Over Wyoming
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Lesley Selander in which a cowboy (Tim Holt) stops a range war between a cattle ranchers and sheepherders. Stylized violence

title: Storm Rider, The
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Edward Bernds in which a gunslinger (Scott Brady) sides with the small ranchers who are being forced off their land by a would-be cattle baron. Frontier violence and romantic complications

title: Stormy Monday
synopsis: Intriguing thriller set in Newcastle, England, tracks the shady tactics used by a crooked American entrepreneur (Tommy Lee Jones) to control the city's waterfront nightclub district. His principal stumbling blocks include a hardboiled jazz club owner (Sting), a reformed party girl (Melanie Griffith) and her young Irish boyfriend (Sean Bean). Written, directed and scored by Mike Figgis, the fine acting, gorgeous cinematography and incredible jazz-blues score make this a haunting film. Some brief scenes of violence and a few scenes with fleeting nudity

title: Stormy Weather
synopsis: All-black musical centers on a dancer (Bill Robinson) as he recalls 25 years in show business, starting with his entertaining fellow soldiers in World War I and ending with his performing for World War II troops and reunion with the love of his life (Lena Horne). Director Andrew Stone's loosely constructed, disappointedly thin narrative serves mainly to provide the backdrop for a lively revue of performances by the considerable black talent of the day, including Fats Waller, Cab Calloway, the Nicholas Brothers and Katherine Dunham's dance troupe. This record of the period's segregated artists is offset by its use of black stereotypes

title: Story of Adele H., The
synopsis: French romance of a 19th-century woman (Isabelle Adjani), the daughter of Victor Hugo, who exhausted her health in pursuing a worthless cad around the world, was brought back to France and lived under constant care for another 40 years, keeping a journal devoted to her obsessive passion. Director Francois Truffaut's adaptation of the journal is done with a fine blend of detachment, compassion and respect for a woman who wasted her life in one sense and yet, in another, through the journal, turned it into a creative act

title: Story of a Love Affair
synopsis: Italian melodrama about a woman (Lucia Bose) who joins her former lover in causing the death of her jealous industrialist husband with tragic consequences. Made in 1950 by director Michelangelo Antonnioni, the chief interest in the work is its focus on the social disparity between the luxury-loving wife and her jobless husband making the conclusion inevitable

title: Story of a Teenager, The
synopsis: A high school football star tries to make a home for his kid brother but their alcoholic father tragically interferes. The film is well-intended as a look at the pressures of adolescence, but its script is simply too melodramatic and its treatment woefully inadequate to the task. Some intense violence

title: Story of a Woman
synopsis: Romantic tripe about a Swedish pianist studying in Rome (Bibi Andersson) who has an affair but when she discovers her lover (James Farentino) is already married, returns to Stockholm and marries an American (Robert Stack). Years later back in Rome, she must choose between her husband and child and her passion for her former lover. Directed by Leonardo Bercovici, this dull, boring effort has an excessively graphic bedroom scene

title: Story of Boys and Girls, The
synopsis: At a sumptuous feast in 1936 Italy celebrating the engagement of a young couple (Lucrezia Lante Della Rovere and Davide Bechini) from different social classes, the intrigues and secret frustrations of the two families surface. By giving equal weight to more than 30 characters, writer-director Pupi Avati turns the sprawling narrative into an unfocused collection of slice-of-life vignettes. Subtitles. Numerous sexual references

title: Story of Christiane F.
synopsis: German drama about a 13-year-old girl (Natja Brunkhorst) who drifts into drug addiction because of the squalid environment in which she lives. Director Ulrich Edel's coldly clinical yet lurid account of the hell of drug abuse lacks a moral perspective adequate to the horrific events it matter-of-factly chronicles. Innumerable scenes of needles being thrust into arms and its depiction of sexual activity make this extremely mature fare

title: Story of F, The
synopsis: Compilation of excerpts from mostly faded stag movies whose fuzzy photography of mechanically-performed sex acts will leave viewers disgusted by the commercial shoddiness of Jim Babb's movie and its anti-censorship narration

title: Story of Gilbert and Sullivan, The
synopsis: British dramatization begins in 1875 with composer Arthur Sullivan (Maurice Evans) teaming with librettist William Gilbert (Robert Morley) to write comic operas for producer Rubert D'Oyly Carte (Peter Finch) but their happy collaboration ends some 15 years later over Sullivan's yearning to write more serious music. Directed by Sidney Gilliat, the Victorian settings are quite charming and the characters are certainly interesting but what's most appealing are the many excerpts of their works as performed by the D'Oyly Carte Company (notably Martyn Green)

title: Story of Qiu Ju, The
synopsis: A pregnant peasant wife (Gong Li) adamantly seeks justice at increasingly distant and higher levels of Red Chinese bureaucracy when her village chief (Lei Lao Sheng) remains unrepentant after having angrily kicked her husband (Lui Peiqi) in the groin. Building tragic irony with exquisite simplicity, director Zhang Yimou captures the humanity and uncompromising spirit of a powerless woman pursuing justice despite the lethargy of officialdom and the scorn of her village. An instance of rough language

title: Story of Ruth, The
synopsis: Plodding biblical tale in which the title Moabite priestess (Elana Eden) falls for an Israelite artisan (Tom Tryon) who's killed on their escape to Judah, but she follows her mother-in-law (Peggy Wood) to Bethlehem where she's scorned as an outsider until married by a respected local (Stuart Whitman). Directed by Henry Koster, the dramatization is less than convincing and, despite some colorful incidents, fails to hold interest. Period violence

title: Story of Sin
synopsis: Walerian Borowczyk's screen version of Stefan Zeromski's novel about a hopeless love affair beautifully evokes its turn-of-the-century era but wallows in passionate despair and focuses on the erotic elements of the story

title: Story of Us, The
synopsis: Drama in which Bruce Willis and Michelle Pfeiffer portray unhappy parents who are hesitating about whether to divorce as they recall the highs and lows of their 15-year marriage. Despite an ultimately positive message, the movie is heavy-handed and as directed by Rob Reiner characters are reduced to unappealing spouses constantly lurching between fury and mushy hysteria. Much shrill marital discord with profanity and rough language, a few sexual references and fleeting rear nudity

title: Story of Vernon and Irene Castle, The
synopsis: Nostalgic musical biography of a vaudevillian (Fred Astaire) and his bride (Ginger Rogers) who in 1911 team as ballroom dancers and become international favorites before Vernon's tragic death as an aviator in World War I. Director H.C. Potter's warm portrait of a loving couple is paced by elegant dance numbers, period songs and occasional comic relief (Edna May Oliver, Walter Brennan and Lew Fields). Old-fashioned family fare

title: Story of Women
synopsis: Grim French production about a poor, uneducated but coldly ambitious woman (Isabelle Huppert) who is executed for performing abortions during the German Occupation of World War II. Director Claude Chabrol uses the wartime setting to distance the subject from the controversy of today, treating the narrative in a somber, unemotional fashion that forces the viewer to confront the moral and social dimensions of abortion without the comfort of any easy answers. Subtitles. Challenging, at times unsettling, fare that requires discernment

title: Story on Page One, The
synopsis: Trite courtroom drama of a lawyer (Tony Franciosa) defending a woman (Rita Hayworth) accused of plotting with her lover (Gig Young) to kill her husband. Written and directed by Clifford Odets, it's the old story of an abused wife seeking a sympathetic shoulder, but the trial scenes are flat and unconvincing, especially the defense lawyer's swaggering examination of the lover's manipulative mother (Mildred Dinnock). Tawdry situations

title: Storytelling
synopsis: Repulsive two-part drama, the first part of which deals with a college student (Selma Blair) who sexually submits to her African-American writing teacher (Robert Wisdom) out of a sense of political correctness; in the second part, a slacker documentarian (Paul Giamatti) makes a clueless New Jersey teenager and his dysfunctional family the subject of his exploitative new piece. Equally misanthropic and misogynistic, director Todd Solondz's bleak look at the societal pressures of fitting in is loaded with selfish, nasty characters and is aimed at discomfiting and belittling an audience with traditional values. Several explicit sexual situations with frontal nudity, some drug use and pervasive rough language

title: Storyville
synopsis: A third-generation New Orleans politician (James Spader) running for Congress is unwittingly drawn into a murder investigation while his uncle (Jason Robards) discourages him from prying further into a lingering family scandal about parish mineral rights that ended in his father's suicide. Director Mark Frost's potboiler is fairly engrossing melodrama though it is awash in Southern and political stereotypes. Some violence, an adulterous encounter, occasional nudity and intermittent rough language

title: Stowaway
synopsis: After her missionary parents die in war-torn China, a little girl (Shirley Temple) makes her way to Shanghai, winds up by accident on a U.S.-bound ocean liner and helps a rich idler (Robert Young) and an earnest maiden (Alice Faye) find true love after they wed to adopt the child who otherwise will be deported. Directed by William A. Seiter, the hokey vehicle relies entirely on the child star's appeal as a spunky orphan who is fluent in Chinese, sings like a seasoned professional and knows more proverbs than Charlie Chan. Convoluted romantic complications

title: Straight Story, The
synopsis: When an ailing 73-year-old Iowan (Richard Farnsworth) learns his estranged brother (Harry Dean Stanton) in Wisconsin has had a serious stroke, he set off driving a lawnmower along the highway to make peace with him before it's too late. Directed by David Lynch, the result is a compelling character study of an elderly man whom Farnsworth's convincing performance makes as real as the photography of a part of the country where neighborliness is considered a virtue

title: Straight Talk
synopsis: Reluctantly posing as a professional psychotherapist, a big-hearted Southerner (Dolly Parton) becomes Chicago's leading radio talk-show personality, unaware that her reporter boyfriend (James Woods) is writing an expose about her. Directed by Barnet Kellman, the character's wholesome, downhome philosophy is smothered in a vanity production featuring a music track composed and sung by its star. Implied sexual relationships

title: Straight Time
synopsis: Dustin Hoffman plays an ex-con who, when pressured by a cynical parole officer (Emmet Walsh), gives up on going straight and re-enters the criminal underworld. Directed by Ulu Grosbard, there is not enough in the script to involve the viewer with the characters, and while the fine acting and austere texture of the movie earn respect, one cannot really care about what happens to anybody in the story. The violence and rough language are part of the context but the gratuitous nudity is not

title: Straight to Hell
synopsis: Madcap spoof of a spaghetti Western, this farcical celebrity showcase from director Alex Cox mixes madness and mayhem with touches of sexual seduction and teasing to evoke a sense of the Theater of the Absurd. Cameo cast including Joe Strummer, Elvis Costello and Courtney Love are all bandits trying to survive in a zany town. Some violence and sexual sight gags are not for youngsters

title: Strait-Jacket
synopsis: Cheap horror show in which an axe-murderer (Joan Crawford) is released after 20 years in an asylum to live with her daughter (Diane Baker) but soon after she arrives, there are some more axe victims. Written by Robert Bloch and directed by William Castle, the result is highly manipulative in creating an eerie atmosphere and sense of dread that is undercut by a contrived, unsatisfying resolution. Much menace and some special effects violence

title: Stranded: I've Come From a Plane That Crashed on the Mountains
synopsis: Unsettling but ultimately moving documentary recounting the ordeal of 16 Uruguayan rugby players who survived a 1972 air crash in the Andes Mountains, their harrowing 10-week struggle against the elements and their resort to cannibalism as the only alternative to starvation. Director Gonzalo Arijon uses interviews with the survivors, archival footage and re-enactments to evoke the group's desperate heroism and profound spirit of unity and to explore the moral and religious implications of their experience. In Spanish. Subtitles. Mature themes, one use of the F-word and a few crass expressions. A -II -- adults and adolescents. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America. 2008 Stranded: I've Come From a Plane That Crashed on the Mountains
full_review:
On Oct. 13, 1972, a plane carrying a team of rugby players from a Catholic school in Montevideo, Uruguay, to a match in Chile crashed in a remote section of the Andes Mountains.

More than 10 weeks later, two of the 16 remaining survivors, having hiked 44 miles over peaks 13,000 feet high, finally made contact with their first outsider, a Chilean shepherd, and were soon guiding a squad of helicopters to rescue their friends.

Among the accounts of what these students, all from privileged backgrounds, endured in the interval are Piers Paul Read's 1974 book, "Alive: The Story of the Andes Survivors," and its 1993 screen adaptation by director Frank Marshall, called simply "Alive."

In "Stranded: I've Come From a Plane That Crashed on the Mountains" (Zeitgeist), documentarian Gonzalo Arijon, a childhood friend of several of the athletes, provides first-hand descriptions of their ordeal. Using interviews with the now middle-age men, some of them filmed on a recent visit to the crash site, as well as archival footage and silent, haunting reenactments, he evokes their desperate heroism and their profound, indispensable spirit of unity.

The film also explores the religious implications of their experience as one survivor describes a crisis of faith that was resolved by joining his companions in the recitation of the rosary, while another speaks of his feelings of closeness to -- and total dependence on -- God.

As news coverage of their return reveals, a disturbing question quickly arose amid the euphoria: How had the young men held out for so long with no available food source? The unsettling answer was that, faced with seemingly certain starvation, they had resorted to cannibalism.

While this disclosure, exploited by the press, stirred considerable controversy, the survivors are unanimous in defending the morality of their decision. Their moving gratitude for the gift of continued life and the readiness more than one expressed to have his own body sustain the others after death bring to mind the self-giving of Christ in the Eucharist.

And, in fact, drawing on an analogy offered at the time by the charismatic student they regarded as their leader who died before being rescued, several compare the orderly yet harrowing procedure they followed to receiving holy Communion. While not explicitly accepting this analysis, then-Coadjutor Archbishop Carlos Parteli Keller and then-Auxiliary Bishop Andres Maria Rubio Garcia of Montevideo, Uruguay, both endorsed the extreme measure as morally justified.

In Spanish. Subtitles.

The film contains mature themes, one use of the F-word and a few crass expressions. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.

title: Strange Adventure, A
synopsis: Formula crime caper directed by William Witney in which a teen hot-rodder (Ben Cooper) is tricked by a bad woman (Marla English) into driving the getaway car for a pair of gun-happy robbers, then captures them with the help of a good woman (Joan Evans). Some nasty violence, much menace and recurring sexual innuendo

title: Strange Affair of Uncle Harry, The
synopsis: Creaky melodrama about a man (George Sanders) who lives with his two sisters but when one of them (Geraldine Fitzgerald)) breaks up his engagement to a co-worker (Ella Raines), he decides to poison her. Directed by Robert Siodmak, the slow-paced story generates little interest until the tale's twist ending. Threatening situations and mild sexual innuendo

title: Strange Affair, The
synopsis: Failed British crime melodrama about corruption in the London police department in connection with a pornography ring. Directed by David Greene, the slow and contrived plot makes sensationalistic use of violence and nudity

title: Strange Bedfellows
synopsis: Thin but frantic romantic comedy in which a London-based oil executive (Rock Hudson) reconciles with his flighty estranged wife (Gina Lollobrigida) in order to get a promotion in his staid company, then she insists on playing Lady Godiva in a left-wing protest at the American Embassy. Directed by Melvin Frank, the sour comedy falls flat on all counts except for the scenes with Terry-Thomas as an undertaker. Sexual situations and innuendo

title: Strange Behavior
synopsis: Offbeat horror movie about the revenge of a mad scientist, set in the kind of small Midwestern town inextricably bound up with this genre. What makes it unusual is that the town was re-created rather well in New Zealand by director Michael Laughlin who got a few American actors (Michael Murphy and Louise Fletcher) to journey there. Unfortunately, the story piles on the gruesome details of violent deaths to a needlessly excessive degree

title: Strange Brew
synopsis: The comic duo of Doug and Bob McKenzie (Dave Thomas and Rick Moranis who also directed) lampoon Canada mercilessly as a land of rubes and rustics in an intentionally incoherent plot about a brewery run by arch-villain Max von Sydow with Paul Dooley as his cowardly lackey. Chiefly serving as a vehicle for the McKenzie pair of spaced-out zanies, whose substance addiction happens to be beer, the comedy is a random collection of stale sight gags and boisterous stupidities that grow increasingly tiresome. Course language and a visual sexual reference

title: Strange Days
synopsis: Dreary thriller set in violence-racked Los Angeles on the eve of the year 2000 when a sleazy hawker (Ralph Fiennes) of illegal virtual reality software finds himself and his ex-girlfriend (Juliette Lewis) stalked by a psychotic serial killer. Directed by Kathryn Bigelow, the senseless plot relies on shock effects for interest rather than characters with some dimension of humanity or a story with some semblance of credibility. Repellant violence, simulated sex acts, nudity, racial epithets, profanity and rough language

title: Strange Deception
synopsis: ( see: "The Accused" )

title: Strange Incident
synopsis: ( see: "The Ox-Bow Incident" )

title: Strange Invaders
synopsis: Some less-than-cuddly E.T.'s descend upon Centreville, Ill., one night in the 1950s and stay on in human form for a quarter of a century wearing the same style clothes as when they first arrived, something quickly noted by a professor (Pal LeMat) who arrives there looking for his missing wife. The silly plot is somewhat engaging but director Michael Laughlin's handling of it is plodding and uninspired. Some messy special effects when the aliens strip off their human exteriors to reveal their true life forms

title: Strange Lady in Town
synopsis: Western misfire in which a redhaired lady doctor (Greer Garson) arrives in 1880 Sante Fe, is befriended by the tomboy daughter (Lois Smith) of the town's resident doctor (Dana Andrews) whom she alienates by treating his patients, then is ostracized because of her Army renegade brother (Cameron Mitchell). Directed by Mervyn LeRoy, the plot complications keep getting in the way of a budding romance between the rival doctors, though the tiresome results still have interest because of the story's feminist angle. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Strangeland
synopsis: ( see: "Dee Snider's Strangeland" )

title: Strange Love of Martha Ivers, The
synopsis: Darkly contrived tale in which a troubled heiress (Barbara Stanwyck) and her weakling husband (Kirk Douglas) fear a childhood friend (Van Heflin) who disappeared on the night the woman murdered her wealthy aunt (Judith Anderson), then suddenly turns up in town with a girlfriend (Lizabeth Scott). Though the story is full of cheese, director Lewis Milestone maintains interest in the characters, especially Stanwyck's twisted, tortured lady of the title and Heflin's tough, breezy gambler who knows all the angles. Stylized violence, including a double suicide, and abundant romantic complications

title: Stranger Among Us, A
synopsis: Investigating the murder of a diamond cutter in New York City's Hasidic community, a cynical detective (Melanie Griffin) is drawn to the sect's spirituality -- and its leading Hasidic scholar (Eric Thal). Director Sidney Lumet enriches a standard murder mystery-romance with a sensitive and uplifting look at a little-known religious group. Brief scenes of violence and mild sexual references

title: Stranger and the Gunfighter, The
synopsis: Italian production directed by Anthony Dawson about a gunslinger (Lee Van Cleef) and a kung-fu master (Lo Lieh) who team up to find a lost fortune, clues to which are tatooed on four former mistresses of the deceased owner. Intended as a comic mixture of sex and violence, the result is offensive

title: Stranger at My Door
synopsis: Uneven Western in which a preacher (Macdonald Carey) hopes to reform a hunted outlaw (Skip Homeier) by giving him a job in building a new church, heedless of the potential danger for his wife (Patricia Medina) and young son. Directed by William Witney, the tension between preacher and outlaw works well enough, though the other characters serve mainly as plot contrivances and the picture's reliance on several "miracles" in the last reel are less than convincing. Stylized violence, much menace and some sexual innuendo

title: Stranger in My Arms, A
synopsis: Turgid sudser directed by Helmut Kautner in which a Korean War pilot (Jeff Chandler) visits the wealthy family of a fallen comrade, learns why he was suicidal after meeting the dead man's manipulative mother (Mary Astor), then falls in love with his sweetly naive widow (June Allyson). Wartime violence, including an off-screen suicide, and romantic complications

title: Stranger in the House
synopsis: ( see: "Black Christmas" )

title: Stranger in Town, A
synopsis: Sadistic Italian Western directed by Vance Lewis in which a stranger in Mexico (Tony Anthony) makes a deal with a bandit gang to help steal a shipment of gold but when they take it all, he follows and picks them off one by one, until he has all the loot. Cynical treatment employs brutal, sadistic violence

title: Stranger Is Watching, A
synopsis: Rapist-murderer (Rip Torn) kidnaps a young girl (Shawn Von Schreiber) and a television newswoman (Kate Mulgrew) and holds them prisoner beneath New York's Grand Central Station. Director Sean Cunningham's dull, plodding thriller is derived from a novel by Mary Higgins Clark. Because of violence, rough language and the sordid nature of the story, it is not for young viewers

title: Stranger on the Third Floor
synopsis: Stylish low-budget thriller in which a reporter (John McGuire) testifies against a man (Elisha Cook, Jr.) in a murder trial, then discovers that a sinister drifter (Peter Lorre) is really the killer but finding him puts his fiancee (Margaret Tallichet) in jeopardy. Director Boris Ingster relies on dark, moody visuals to create an eerie atmosphere, with Lorre especially effective as the deranged, misunderstood menace. Threatening situations

title: Stranger Returns, The
synopsis: Standard Italian Western directed by Vance Lewis in which a lone stranger (Tony Anthony) sees bandits rob a stagecoach and kill all its passengers, then follows them and exterminates the lot. Much cruelty and violence

title: The Strangers
synopsis: Reasonably taut thriller in which a quarrelling unmarried couple (Liv Tyler and Scott Speedman) are menaced by a trio of masked intruders (Gemma Ward, Kip Weeks and Laura Margolis) at his parents' isolated summer home. Before its grisly climax, writer-director Bryan Bertino's feature debut mostly eschews bloodletting in favor of old-fashioned chills, but the script leaves many questions unanswered and its brief foray into religion and morality falls flat. Some bloody violence, nongraphic premarital sexual activity, some rough and occasional crude language, and two uses of profanity
full_review:
That 4 a.m. knock on the door isn't the Avon lady; it's "The Strangers" (Universal/Rogue).

When Kristen (Liv Tyler) and her preppy beau, James (Scott Speedman), return from a friend's wedding at which Kristen declined her boyfriend's proposal, they're set to spend the night at his parents' isolated summer home alternately moping and working through their problems. But they're interrupted by that untimely rapping and a shadowy visitor asking randomly, "Is Tamara here?"

This mysterious apparition turns out to be the prelude to hours of terror as the couple is relentlessly menaced by a trio of masked intruders (Gemma Ward, Kip Weeks and Laura Margolis). Their car is trashed, their cell phones are disabled and eventually, of course, the electricity is cut.

Before its grisly climax, writer-director Bryan Bertino's reasonably taut feature debut mostly eschews bloodletting in favor of old-fashioned chills. But the script leaves many questions unanswered (Tamara, as they say, never comes), and its brief foray into religion and morality -- via the criminals' encounter with a pair of young Mormon missionaries -- falls flat.

The film contains some bloody violence, nongraphic premarital sexual activity, some rough and occasional crude language, and two uses of profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Strangers in Good Company
synopsis: On a day's outing in the Quebec countryside, a group of elderly women find themselves stranded when their bus breaks down and they have to spend the night in an abandoned farmhouse. By placing non-actors in this bare-bones situation, Canadian director Cynthia Scott comes up with a convincing portrait of seven old women -- among them, a nun, a lesbian and a Mohawk Indian matriarch -- who pass the time while waiting to be rescued by exchanging reminiscences of their past lives and sharing common concerns about their present circumstances. Simple yet compelling evocation of the mixed blessings of old age, though young children may find some of it confusing

title: Strangers on a Train
synopsis: Uneasy thriller about the aftermath of a chance conversation between a tennis player (Farley Granger) and a rich psychopath (Robert Walker) who proposes that each kill the person the other wishes were dead. Despite the script's ragged plotting, director Alfred Hitchcock makes the concept of "crossover" murders chillingly plausible, fueled by Walker's edgy performance, Farley's inept innocence and a frightening finale in an amusement park. Faithless wife, stylized violence and mounting menace

title: Stranger's Return, The
synopsis: Dated rural melodrama in which a woman (Miriam Hopkins) deserted by her husband returns to the family farm, convinces her 85-year-old grandfather (Lionel Barrymore) she has farming in her blood, though she antagonizes her other relatives and is pursued by a married neighbor (Franchot Tone). Directed by King Vidor, the rustic setting is a lot more interesting than the slow-paced plot and the interplay between stock characters. Romantic complications

title: Strangers When We Meet
synopsis: Glossy soap opera (from director Richard Quine) about unhappy wife and mother Maggie (the beautiful Kim Novak), who, unaccountably ignored by her husband, falls under the spell of architect neighbor Larry (Kirk Douglas), also unhappily married. After some initial hesitation on her part, she succumbs. The architect's wife (played sympathetically by Barbara Rush) eventually learns the truth. Legendary comic Ernie Kovacs as a playboy writer, and Walter Matthau in an early role as Larry's sleazy friend who tries to make a move on Larry's wife, provide additional interest. The adulterous affair is made to seem rather glamorous, despite characters doing "the right thing" by the end. No overt sex, but adult material. A-III (nr)

title: Strangers With Candy
synopsis: Vulgar farce based on the Comedy Central television series about a 47-year-old misfit (Amy Sedaris) recently released from prison who tries to reform her life by going back to high school, where she competes in a science fair with some nerdy students against a team of popular kids. With wit at a premium amid the coarseness, the pressing question is how director Paul Dinello's puerile school satire attracted a cast that includes Matthew Broderick, Sarah Jessica Parker, Allison Janney, Philip Seymour Hoffman and Ian Holm. Pervasive crude and sexual humor and sight gags, including inappropriate sexual situations involving an adult and teens, brief partial female nudity, an obscene drawing, drug content involving minors, a running homosexual gag, recurring crude language and profanity
full_review:
A prequel to the Comedy Central cable television series of the same name, the vulgar farce "Strangers With Candy" (THINKFilm) revolves around a 47-year-old misfit, Jerri Blank (Amy Sedaris), recently released from prison, who to reform her life goes back to high school where she competes in a science fair with some nerdy students against a team of popular kids. By undertaking the project, she hopes to coax her dad (Dan Hedaya) out of his "self-induced coma," for which her former ways were partly to blame.

Stephen Colbert, so sharp in Comedy Central's "The Colbert Report," plays the school's gay Christian science teacher, Chuck Noblet -- he teaches creationism and his periodic table of elements is shaped like a cross -- who is having an affair with a male colleague.

With wit at a premium amid the coarseness, the pressing question is how director Paul Dinello's puerile school satire attracted a cast that includes Matthew Broderick as a rival science teacher, Sarah Jessica Parker as a guidance counselor, Allison Janney and Philip Seymour Hoffman as school board officials, and Ian Holm as the Blanks' family doctor.

Early on, Holm's character tells Jerri that for her father's condition to improve she must recreate a time "when life was good and precious and worth being conscious for." In other words, before the opening credits.

The film contains pervasive crude and sexual humor and sight gags, including inappropriate sexual situations involving an adult and teens, brief partial female nudity, an obscene drawing, drug content involving minors, a running homosexual gag, recurring crude language and profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Stranger Than Fiction
synopsis: Quirky dramatic comedy about a lonely and neurotic IRS auditor (Will Ferrell) who wakes to find his life being narrated by a seemingly omniscient voice only he can hear, which turns out to belong to a famous reclusive author (Emma Thompson) working on a new novel in which he is the protagonist and that predicts what will happen to him, including his death. By turns sentimental, funny and, in the end, modestly profound, director Marc Forster's existential farce touches on issues of fate and free will, while imparting a wonderful message that the little moments -- the smiles, hugs and small acts of kindness -- we often relegate to footnote status in the narrative of our daily living are what give life its meaning. An implied sexual encounter, brief locker-room rear nudity, a jarring traffic accident and one use of the f-word, as well as a couple of crude expressions and an instance of profanity
full_review:
Pondering God's infinite knowledge, the psalmist writes in Psalm 139, "Your eyes foresaw my actions; in your book all are written," a verse that seems particularly apropos when watching the delightfully quirky dramatic comedy "Stranger Than Fiction" (Columbia), in which Will Ferrell falls subject to a less lofty omniscience.

In what is one of the more original and entertaining films of the year, Ferrell is Harold Crick, a lonely and neurotically obsessive IRS auditor who wakes one morning to find his life being narrated by a seemingly omniscient voice only he can hear.

When psychiatrists respond with incredulity, Harold, confident he's not crazy, seeks the help of a professor of literary theory, Jules Hilbert (Dustin Hoffman), reasoning who better to ask about narration?

It turns out that the ever-present voice belongs to a famous reclusive author, Kay Eiffel (Emma Thompson) who's holed up, working on her long-awaited new novel in which the protagonist is, coincidentally, also named Harold Crick. With Harold's life mirrored in her manuscript (or is it the other way around?), everything that happens to the fictional Harold, down to the smallest detail, happens to the real one.

This doesn't bode well for Harold as Jules informs him that the main characters in Kay's books always die in the end. Luckily, Kay is mired in writer's block and can't figure out how to kill off her imaginary Harold, leaving the question open as to how the story will ultimately play out. Comedy or tragedy?

Imbuing Harold with man-child innocence, Ferrell impresses, reining in his usual mania for a more muted and melancholy performance, reminiscent of Jim Carrey's toned-down turn in "Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind." In fact, Zach Helm's intelligent screenplay has a very Charlie Kaufmanesque feel. (There is some inconsistency about whether Kay is just commenting on Harold's life or exerts control over it.)

Solid support is provided by Maggie Gyllenhaal as Ana, an opinionated baker who is audited by Harold and who provides some sweet romance, eventually drawing him out of his introversion, and Queen Latifah as Penny, an "author's assistant" hired by Kay's impatient publisher to light a fire under the scribe.

As is unfortunately the case with most movies today, Harold and Ana wind up sleeping together, but apart from that one discreet bedroom scene (they're lying under the covers -- no nudity, just snuggling) and a few four-letter words, there's nothing really objectionable in the film.

By turns sentimental, funny and, in the end, modestly profound, director Marc Forster's existential farce touches on issues of fate and free will (you could even call it a Calvinistic comedy) and imparts a wonderful message that the little moments -- the smiles, hugs and small acts of kindness -- we often relegate to footnote status in the narrative of our daily living are what give life its meaning.

The film contains an implied sexual encounter, brief locker-room rear nudity, a jarring traffic accident and one use of the f-word, as well as a couple of crude expressions and an instance of profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Stranger, The
synopsis: Atmospheric thriller set in a small Connecticut town where a government agent (Edward G. Robinson) tries to persuade the bride (Loretta Young) of a prep-school teacher (Orson Welles) that her husband is an escaped Nazi war criminal. Also directed by Welles, the sunny small-town setting heightens the cat-and-mouse tension of the ensuing manhunt which concludes in the clockworks high aloft a church steeple. Some menace and stylized violence

title: Stranger, The
synopsis: Italian-French adaptation of the Albert Camus novel about the senseless murder of an Arab tough by a Frenchman (Marcello Mastroianni) and his subsequent trial and conviction of the crime. Directed by Luchino Visconti, it is a painstaking and often beautiful translation of the Nobel Prize Winner's object lesson in existential absurdity

title: Stranger Wore a Gun, The
synopsis: Muddled Western directed by Andre de Toth has an ex-Confederate spy (Randolph Scott) join, then smash a gang of Arizona stagecoach robbers (led by George Macready) after engineering a deadly shootout with a rival gang (led by Alfonso Bedoya). Stylized violence

title: Strange Shadows in an Empty Room
synopsis: Director Martin Herbert's frantic exercise in mindless violence about a detective trying to find the murderer of his sister. The Italian production was filmed in Montreal with second-string American leads, and there is not another nice thing to say about it. Nudity, brutality and sheer nastiness

title: Strange Triangle
synopsis: Contrived story of murder told in flashback by a bank examiner (Preston Foster) who fell for an attractive nuisance (Signe Hasso) with larceny in her heart and a bank director (John Shepperd) under her thumb. Directed by Ray McCarey, the results are hardly worth the effort. Off-screen shooting and mild romantic situations

title: Strange Vengeance of Rosalie, The
synopsis: Botched contemporary horror story about a traveling salesman (Ken Howard) who is tricked by a young girl (Bonnie Bedelia) into visiting her dead grandfather's hovel in a deserted Western wasteland and then breaks his leg to keep him there. Director Jack Starrett dissipates the terror of the situation with a subplot about a menacing motorcycle hood (Anthony Zerbe) who harasses the girl both for her grandfather's hidden gold and her body

title: Strange Wilderness
synopsis: Pointless road movie about the slacker host of a failing wildlife TV program (Steve Zahn) who sets out with an equally clueless technical crew (Allen Covert, Jonah Hill, Ashley Scott, Justin Long and Kevin Heffernan) to save his show by tracking down and taping Bigfoot. Co-writer and director Fred Wolf's film attempts to draw humor from subjects like a bloody shark attack, alcoholism and bipolar disorder, perhaps not surprisingly, fails. Brief but graphic sexual activity, deformed full frontal male nudity, upper and rear female nudity, drug use, pervasive rough and crude language, including nearly 70 uses of the f-word, some crass and profane language, and sexual humor and imagery
full_review:
A road movie that goes nowhere, "Strange Wilderness" (Paramount) is as vulgar as it is pointless.

Having inherited a popular wildlife TV program from his father, pot-dazed slacker Peter Gaulke (Steve Zahn) has rapidly caused the show's ratings to plummet. Even in its new 3 a.m. time slot, "Strange Wilderness" seems headed for cancellation.

When his dad's old buddy offers Peter a map that will locate the legendary Bigfoot, Peter figures that capturing the beast on tape will build his audience numbers. This hoped-for coup, however, will require him to travel to the South American jungle and compete against a better organized and better financed competitor, Sky Pierson (Harry Hamlin).

The technical crew Peter assembles turns out to be every bit as clueless as he is. In addition to long-standing sidekick Fred (Allen Covert) and truculent intern Cooker (Jonah Hill), his colleagues include confirmed stoner Junior (Justin Long) and a beer-swilling car mechanic turned animal handler named Whitaker (Kevin Heffernan). Amid this motley crew, travel adviser Cheryl (Ashley Scott) promises good sense as well as prospective romance.

Meeting the team nearer their destination will be their gruff but well-intentioned guide, Dick (Blake Clark). Will these misfits beat Pierson to Bigfoot's cave? Can even Sasquatch footage save Peter's show?

Co-writer and director Fred Wolf's feeble attempts to find humor in a bloody shark attack, Whitaker's alcoholism and another character's dependence on Lithium merely register as puerile. As the movie reaches a crescendo of obscenity during a climactic scene in a crowded restaurant, a little girl asks plaintively, "Why are they using so many bad words?"

Well might we all ask the same.

The film contains brief but graphic sexual activity, full frontal male nudity, upper and rear female nudity, drug use, much comic violence, pervasive rough and crude language, including nearly seventy uses of the f-word, some crass and profane language, sexual humor and imagery. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Strange Woman, The
synopsis: Muddled melodrama begins in 1824 Maine where a poor but ambitious woman (Hedy Lamarr) marries a rich but elderly merchant (Gene Lockhart), tries to entice his son (Louis Hayward) to kill him, then marries an enterprising logger (George Sanders) who soon gets wise. Directed by Edgar G. Ulmer, the period picture of a woman driven by contradictory impulses is rarely anything more than tedious. Romantic complications

title: Strapless
synopsis: Fortyish American doctor (Blair Brown), living in England and supporting her fun-loving younger sister, lets down her emotional barriers and marries a mysterious stranger who then disappears. Writer-director David Hare has concocted a moodily intriguing film whose gentle pace allows the viewer to take an intimate look at a repressed woman's mid-life crisis and how it affects those whom she loves. Several instances of rough language, momentary flashes of nudity and a glimpse of a casual sexual encounter

title: Strategic Air Command
synopsis: Cold war story about the frustrations of a major league baseball player (James Stewart) and his wife (June Allyson) after he's recalled to active service with the peacetime bomber command kept in readiness to strike an attacking enemy. Directed by Anthony Mann, the transparent melodrama follows the veteran B-29 pilot's reluctant retraining to fly the B-36, then his enthusiasm for the B-47 jet bomber and conversion to the vital importance of the bomber group's mission

title: Stratton Story, The
synopsis: Fact-based dramatization of baseball's Monty Stratton (James Stewart), a Texas farm youth who becomes a star pitcher for the Chicago White Sox until losing a leg in a hunting accident, then tries for a comeback pitching with an artificial leg. Directed by Sam Wood, Stewart gives a fine performance on and off the field, with solid assists from wife June Allyson, mother Agnes Moorehead and pitching scout Frank Morgan. Convincing depiction of a successful athlete overcoming the despair of a devastating disability

title: Strawberry and Chocolate
synopsis: Sluggish comedy-drama set in Cuba where a homosexual artist (Jorge Perugorria) befriends a straightlaced student (Vladimir Cruz) unaware the youth is being pressured to report him as a likely political subversive. Directed by Tomas Gutierrez Alea and Juan Carlos Tabio, the Cuban production overcomes dramatic weaknesses and drab visuals in portraying the contradictions of institutionalized homophobia. Subtitles. Fleeting nudity in a heterosexual bedroom scene and in beefcake photos, arguments about homosexuality and occassional rough language

title: Strawberry Roan, The
synopsis: When a rancher's son (Dick Jones) is injured by a wild stallion, the foreman (Gene Autry) is ordered to destroy the horse but, instead, secretly tames it for the boy to ride, certain this will effect his recovery. Directed by John English, the sentimental story benefits from the colorful Arizona scenery and exciting sequences featuring Autry's horse, Champion, in the roan's role. Still pleases youngsters and horse-lovers

title: Strawberry Statement, The
synopsis: Phony screen version of James Kunen's novel purports to be about the radicalizing of a college student (Bruce Davison) who, drawn into participating in a campus sit-in by a pretty revolutionary (Kim Darby), winds up being gassed and bludgeoned when the police and national guard brutalize the protestors. Stuart Hagmann's gimmicky direction calls more attention to itself than to the social and political issues which the movie supposedly is addressing. Further clouding matters is the movie's emphasis on sex and the heavy-handed stylized violence of the riot sequence

title: Straw Dogs
synopsis: Introverted American mathematician (Dustin Hoffman) takes his sabbatical in the small English village where his wife (Susan George) grew up, and in her boredom, she begins to flirt with her former admirers, leading ultimately to a brutalizing double rape. The movie ends in a bloodbath precipitated by the husband's refusal to let a mob invade his home to lynch an injured man who has taken refuge there. Director Sam Peckinpah benefits from some uncommonly good acting but the characters are contrived stereotypes who would be more at home in a Western movie than the English countryside. As with the rape scene, the attack on the house is particularly brutal and vicious, wallowing in an excess of violence that the plot supposedly condemns

title: Streamers
synopsis: Screen version of David Rabe's play about barracks tension exploding into violence during the early days of the Vietnam War creates sympathy for its characters (Matthew Modine, Michael Wright and Mitchell Lichtenstein), though the presentation itself remains too stagebound. Directed by Robert Altman, the essential problem with the movie, as with the play, is the attempt to load melodrama with heavy philosophical significance. Admirable intentions but disappointing results. Some violence and rough language

title: Streetcar Named Desire, A
synopsis: Screen version of Tennessee Williams' play about the tensions that develop when an emotionally unstable widow (Vivien Leigh) arrives in New Orleans and moves in with her younger sister (Kim Hunter) whose coarse husband (Marlon Brando) resents his sister-in-law's aristocratic pretentions, learns of her shady past and destroys her chance to marry his friend (Karl Malden). Director Elia Kazan probes the loneliness as well as the volatile passions that nearly consume the drama's all-too-human characters. Mature themes with much sexual innuendo

title: Street Fighter
synopsis: Tedious comic-book adventure in which a beefy colonel (Jean-Claude Van Damme) leads an international expeditionary force against the Southeast Asian stronghold of a military megalomaniac (Raul Julia). Inspired by a video game, writer-director Steven E. de Souza has come up with a laborious assortment of make-believe violence that is as pointless and uninvolving as the stick characters perpetrating it. Mindless, though bloodless, violence and occasional coarse language

title: Street Fighter, The
synopsis: Japanese martial arts movie revolving around a missing oil heiress and a repulsive thug (Sonny Chiba) who undertakes her rescue. Superior special effects but excessively violent

title: Street Kings
synopsis: Bleak, gritty police drama about a corrupt LAPD detective (Keanu Reeves), one of several evidence-planters led by a scheming captain (Forest Whitaker), who joins with an action-hungry rookie (Chris Evans) to investigate the death of his ex-partner (Terry Crews), who was informing on him to an internal affairs officer (Hugh Laurie), and for whose murder he fears being blamed. Lead screenwriter James Ellroy's adaptation of his own novel, directed by David Ayer, has a convoluted plot and conflicted morals, at times seeming to justify its hero's brutal shortcuts, at others offering him as a candidate for redemption. Gory murders, torture and beatings, brief rear nudity, relentless rough and crude and some crass language, seven uses of profanity, and rape and prostitution references
full_review:
A corrupt Los Angeles police detective investigates his ex-partner's death in the bleak and gritty police drama "Street Kings" (Fox Searchlight/Regency).

As one of several evidence-planting rogue cops, Ludlow (Keanu Reeves) has always been protected by the group's ringleader, Capt. Wander (Forest Whitaker). But when reformed colleague Washington (Terry Crews) informs on Ludlow to Internal Affairs officer Capt. Biggs (Hugh Laurie), Ludlow is determined to intimidate his former friend into silence.

Ignoring Wander's injunction to stay away from Washington, hotheaded Ludlow trails him to a convenience store. On his way in, he notices two heavily armed gang members pull into the parking lot. Realizing they're out to rob the store, he tries to warn Washington that he's in mortal danger, but it's too late.

As Ludlow takes cover, Washington is cut down by a barrage of bullets, at least one of which comes from Ludlow's gun. (Whether Ludlow was aiming at Washington or past him at the robbers is never made clear.)

Once the resulting investigation, led by rookie detective Diskant (Chris Evans), gets under way, it becomes apparent that the only way for Ludlow to avoid being implicated is for the killers to go free. Unsatisfied with this outcome, Ludlow gradually convinces the action-hungry Diskant to help him track the perpetrators down and murder them in retribution.

The two embark on a twisted trail of evidence with torture-driven interrogations, shallow graves and bloody gunfights along the way.

Lead screenwriter James Ellroy's adaptation of his own novel, directed by David Ayer, has a convoluted plot and conflicted morals, at times seeming to justify its hero's brutal shortcuts, at others offering him as a candidate for redemption.

The film contains gory murders, torture and beatings, brief rear nudity, relentless rough and crude and some crass language, seven uses of profanity, and rape and prostitution references. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Street People
synopsis: Aimless, shamelessly derivative gangster movie directed by Maurizio Lucidi in which Roger Moore and Stacy Keach take on a cast of dubbed-in Italian heavies. Some nudity but most offensive is its mindless brutality

title: Street Scene
synopsis: Dated but still interesting social drama in which residents of a Manhattan tenement seeking relief from a heat wave sit on the front stoop exchanging gossip and banter, then in the quiet of the next morning one of the tenants (David Landau) shoots his wife and a married bill collector he suspects is her lover, with tragic consequences for their unmarried daughter (Sylvia Sidney). Directed by King Vidor from Elmer Rice's Pulitzer Prize-winning play, the result mixes static dialogue scenes with eloquent visuals of an ethnically mixed neighborhood and the Depression-era problems of its inhabitants. Stylized violence and sexual innunedo

title: Street Smart
synopsis: Magazine reporter (Christopher Reeve) writes a fictitious account of a pimp's daily activities, passes it off as fact and becomes embroiled in a dilemma when his article is subpoened as evidence in the murder trial of a real pimp (Morgan Freeman). Director Jerry Schatzberg's few insights on the subject are lost in a plot featuring mindless revenge, instances of brutality, acceptance of fornication, brief nudity and rough language

title: Streets of Fire
synopsis: Listless, boring rock 'n' roll story about a brooding outsider of a hero (Michael Pare) who rescues a rock star (Diane Lane) from a gang of bikers with the help of a straight-shooting female sidekick (Amy Madigan). Written and directed by Walter Hill, it turns out to be another tedious, stylized celebration of the macho mystique. Violence and a homosexual dance sequence

title: Streets of Ghost Town
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Ray Nazarro in which a couple of cowboys (Charles Starrett and Smiley Burnette) encounter some spooky moments while searching for a fortune in loot hidden in a ghost town, then are saved by the Durango Kid (also Starrett) when an outlaw band shows up. Frontier violence

title: Streets of Gold
synopsis: A Jewish emigre (Klaus Maria Brandauer) from the Soviet Union where he had once been an Olympic contender gets some measure of satisfaction from teaching two Brooklyn street kids the art of boxing so they can compete with a visiting Soviet boxing team. In a well-intentioned but predictable plot following the underdog formula, the movie weakly affirms believing in oneself and one's talents. Profanity and violence in and out of the ring by the principals provide no positive role models for youngsters

title: Streets of Loredo
synopsis: Standard Western directed by Leslie Fenton features a friendly trio of bandits, two of whom (William Holden and William Bendix) escape a posse by joining the Texas Rangers, then find they like the work until ordered to arrest their former partner (Macdonald Carey), now a famous outlaw. Frontier violence and romantic complications

title: Streetwalkin'
synopsis: A prostitute tries to escape from her pimp in this sordid little movie exploiting sex and violence while having pretensions as social commentary

title: Street with No Name, The
synopsis: In a story described as "from the files of the FBI," a G-man (Mark Stevens) goes undercover to worm his way into a gang run by a murderous psychopath (Richard Widmark) who tries to kill him after learning his real identity from a corrupt police official. Director William Keighley's semi-documentary approach uses some actual FBI facilities and personnel, but this doesn't add any greater credibility to the formula crime story or the actors' melodramatics. Stylized violence and threatening situations

title: Strictly Ballroom
synopsis: Old-fashioned success story of an Australian youth (Paul Mercurio) with his own ideas about dance steps teaming with an ugly duckling novice (Tara Morice) to compete for the championship in a traditional ballroom dancing contest. Directed by Baz Luhrmann, the outcome of all this is as obvious as the eventual romance between the two principals is inevitable but the movie's pleasure comes along the way in watching the energy and determination of the young dancers and their innocence in confronting unsympathetic parents and manipulative contest organizers. Mild sexual references, domestic difficulties and several instances of profanity

title: Strictly Business
synopsis: Predictable romantic comedy about young African Americans in which a mailroom clerk (Tommy Davidson) helps an executive (Joseph C. Phillips) win over the clerk's gorgeous friend (Halle Berry) in exchange for a spot in the management training program. Only the lively music in director Kevin Hooks' uninspired movie relieves the flatness of the uniformly one-dimensional characters. A few discreet bedroom scenes, occasional sexual references, racial slurs and momentary violence

title: Strike It Rich
synopsis: British adaptation of the Graham Greene novella, "Loser Takes All," this fairy-tale bonbon charts the romantic ups and downs of a divorced London accountant (Robert Lindsay) and a demure younger woman (Molly Ringwald) he meets on a bus. Writer-director James Scott nicely re-creates the look of a 1950's comedy of manners as the couple marry in Monte Carlo while he tries to parlay a "perfect system" at the roulette table into millions. Slight but refreshingly refined exploration of values and the role of chance in romance. Minimal sexual innuendo

title: Strike Me Pink
synopsis: Weak comedy about an amusement park's meek manager (Eddie Cantor) and his problems fending off a gangster (Brian Donlevy) and his crooked slot machines. Directed by Norman Taurog, Cantor's goofy routines fail to score any big laughs in this lackluster vehicle. Some stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Strike Up the Band
synopsis: Bouncy teen musical in which a high school band leader (Mickey Rooney), set on winning a network radio competition of new bands, gets the gang (including Judy Garland) to put on a show raising the fare to New York to perform for contest judge Paul Whiteman. Director Busby Berkeley paces the story's youthful enthusiasm and high hopes with refreshing musical numbers and an idealized view of small-town life and values. Pleasant fun from an optimistic past

title: Striking Distance
synopsis: Former homicide detective (Bruce Willis), demoted to the Pittsburgh police river patrol alongside a duplicitous female partner (Sarah Jessica Parker), continues to pursue the serial killer he believes murdered his father (John Mahoney), much to the chagrin of his uncle (Dennis Farina), the homicide chief. Director Rowdy Herrington steadily builds suspense in this whodunit, then throws in every cliche in the book in an overwrought climax of absurdly melodramatic proportions. Recurring violence, a fleeting bedroom scene and much rough language

title: Stripes
synopsis: After bungling their way though basic military training, Bill Murray and his troop of losers create havoc in Czechoslovakia. Director Ivan Reitman's mediocre hit-or-miss comedy has only scattered laughs and an occasional serious bit at odds with the rest. Extravagant use of nudity, sexual promiscuity and rough language

title: Stripper
synopsis: Pseudo-documentary on a strip tease competition is an exploitation movie about women who are paid to display their bodies to voyeurs

title: Striptease
synopsis: Lame sex comedy about the infatuation of a brainless, oversexed congressman (Burt Reynolds) with a dancer (Demi Moore) in a sleazy strip joint. Directed by Andrew Bergman, the listless jumble of one-note characters and situations is wedged in between numerous striptease routines. Women depicted as sex objects, frequent nudity, off-screen murders, substance abuse, profanity and rough language

title: Striptease Lady
synopsis: ( see: "Lady of Burlesque" )

title: Stroker Ace
synopsis: Race car driver (Burt Reynolds) wants to break his contract representing a fried chicken franchiser (Ned Beatty) and to seduce a principled young woman (Loni Anderson). Director Hal Needham's action comedy has plenty of racing sequences, including several crashes, and humor with a minimum of subtlety. Occasional strong language and one relatively mild bedroom scene but, all in all, it's fairly good escapist entertainment for mature viewers

title: Strongest Man in the World, The
synopsis: Two college students (Kurt Russell and Joe Flynn) accidentally concoct a formula that gives people unlimited strength. Plodding, poorly-scripted Disney comedy directed by Vincent McEveety

title: Strong Man, The
synopsis: Classic silent comedy with vacant-faced Harry Langdon as a Belgian veteran in America searching for the woman who had been his World War I pen-pal. Directed by Frank Capra, Langdon's childish innocent survives much comic adversity until he reaches a town run by bootleggers, brings down the house as the stand-in for a vaudeville strongman act and achieves his romantic quest, thereby proving love is blind. Slapstick violence, criminal menace and mild sexual innuendo

title: Stroszek
synopsis: Slight German tale of three Berliners (a street musician, a hapless prostitute and their landlord) who go off to join the landlord's son in Wisconsin but their hope in the American dream proves to be an empty one. Writer-director Werner Herzog seems to just let things happen and the result is often little more than a home movie with artisic pretensions. Mature themes

title: Stuart Little
synopsis: Fetching live-action fantasy in which a talking white mouse (voice of Michael J. Fox) is happily adopted as the son of a human family (led by matriarch Geena Davis) only to be targeted as a meal by mean neighborhood alleycats. As loosely adapted from E.B. White's 1945 classic by director Rob Minkoff, the cheery tale has ample visual appeal although purists may find the neatly happy ending a cop-out to the author's more probing tale of self-discovery. Scenes of menace and a few cuss words

title: Stuart Little 2
synopsis: Cute sequel in which Stuart (voiced by Michael J. Fox), the talking white mouse adopted by the Little family (Geena Davis, Jonathan Lipnicki and Hugh Laurie), is befriended by a tiny bird (voiced by Melanie Griffith) forced into thievery by a vicious falcon (voiced by James Woods). Director Rob Minkoffrepeats the charming visuals in a new live-action/animated adventure that underlines the value of honesty, bravery, friendship and forgiveness.� A crass expression and a few menacing scenes may be too intense for very young children
full_review:
His adventurous spirit intact, the plucky white mouse adopted by the Little family is back in the nearly-as-charming "Stuart Little 2" (Columbia).

Nestled across the street from Manhattan's Central Park, the contented Little household now has a baby girl, and Mom and Dad (Geena Davis and Hugh Laurie) couldn't be happier. Except for one thing -- pint-size Stuart (voiced by Michael J. Fox) is game to do everything a normal boy like his brother George (Jonathan Lipnicki) does, but Mom is terrified Stuart could be hurt.

Minor misadventures on the soccer field and in a toy plane further convince Mom that George should keep Stuart in his sights at all times. But with George sometimes off playing with his pal, Will, Stuart's a little lonely -- or a lonely Little.

Swooping into Stuart's life one day is Margalo (voiced by Melanie Griffith), a tiny golden bird apparently fleeing the vicious Falcon (voiced by James Woods). Stuart, instantly smitten, takes her in while her wing heals and all the Littles welcome her with open arms, even that fraidy-cat furball, Snowbell (voiced by Nathan Lane).

Never having had a loving family of her own, and unaccustomed to such caring kindness, Margalo feels terrible since she's actually in cahoots with Falcon. When he threatens to devour Stuart if she doesn't steal from the Littles, she sadly complies and flies the coop.

Sure that Margalo has been snatched, Stuart enlists Snowbell and sets out to rescue her from Falcon.

Meanwhile, George tells a little white lie to the big Littles lest they worry about their little white mouse who has gone missing. And soon the fur is flying when Falcon, Snowbell, alley cat Monty, our hero Stuart and his maiden-in-distress all collide over a dazzling diamond ring.

Director Rob Minkoff is back to helm in the new adventure based on the characters from E.B. White's classic 1945 children's story. The colorful sequel retains the endearing qualities of the original, although the story's freshness and originality suffer a bit. Bits of sly humor (mostly from Lane's snippy Snowbell) liven the familiar situation and two birds add a new element. Less successful are the extremely obvious music track selections.

What's not obvious is how seamlessly the humans blend with (five) Persian cats playing Snowbell, and the animated creatures -- whose fine detailing is amazing. The picture-postcard visuals of the Littles' townhouse and the romanticized New York City they live in are also handsomely realized.

Davis and Laurie are appealing as the idealized parents who carefully teach their children such life lessons as seeing the silver lining in a cloud, and not lying. The movie also treats themes of friendship, optimism, bravery and forgiveness in an upbeat, kid-friendly manner that should entertain children.

However, scenes of the vicious Falcon, his razor-sharp talons set to pounce, and the extended scene of a cab careening through Central Park with pedestrians in imminent danger make the movie a bit too intense for very young children, and the cabbie mutters "hell' in passing.

But for the over-7 to over-70 set, the spunky Stuart again proves to be a mighty mouse and a tiny treat.

Due to a few menacing scenes and brief naughty language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

(
2002
)

title: Stuart Saves His Family
synopsis: Mild-mannered comedy in which the struggling host (Al Franken) of a self-help talk show is continually faced with crisis situations involving his own highly dysfunctional family of alcoholics, depressives and overeaters. Directed by Harold Ramis and based on Franken's "Saturday Night Live" TV character, the movie gently mocks New Age psychobabble and ends up being sweetly touching as various family members come to grips with their addictions. Mild sexual innuendo, fleeting violence, substance abuse, occasional profanity and an instance of rough language

title: Stuck On You
synopsis: Surprisingly tender screwball comedy about a pair of small-town conjoined twins (Matt Damon and Greg Kinnear) who leave their insular home in Massachusetts for the bright lights of Hollywood so that one of the brothers can pursue his dream of being an actor. Conjoined in their creativity, sibling directors Peter and Bobby Farrelly rein in their frat-house impulses toward crass scatological jokes, grafting positive messages about filial fealty and self-esteem onto the film's sometimes tasteless Siamese slapstick silliness. Recurring sexually crude humor and language, an off-screen sexual encounter and brief alcohol abuse
full_review:
A pair of small-town conjoined twins go Hollywood in the surprisingly tender screwball comedy "Stuck On You" (20th Century Fox).

Conjoined in their creativity, sibling directors Peter and Bobby Farrelly rein in the crass scatological humor exhibited in "Dumb and Dumber" (1994) and "There's Something About Mary" (1998), grafting positive messages about filial fealty and self-esteem onto the film's Siamese slapstick silliness.

Matt Damon and Greg Kinnear play joined-at-the-side brothers, Bob and Walt Tenor, two New England bumpkins who own a burger joint in Martha's Vineyard, where their Kali-limbed hash-slinging and athletic prowess have made them local legends. What hockey team wouldn't want a four-armed goalie?

The fact that Kinnear is noticeably older than Damon is cleverly explained by the fact that Bob (Damon) was born with the lion's share of their collective liver. But blood proves thicker than bile, and together they have learned to use their disability to their advantage.

However, their unconditional support for each other is tested when limelight-longing Walt, drawn by the siren song of Hollywood, decides to pursue his dream of acting, and convinces his socially inept brother to tag along for the ride -- as if he had a choice.

Once in Tinseltown they befriend a ditsy starlet-wannabe (Eva Mendes) who hooks Walt up with an agent (Seymour Cassel), a geriatric huckster whose circa-1970s couture and negotiation skills are stuck in a polyester time warp, and whose idea of a prime gig is getting Walt a part in a porn movie.

Through a seeming stroke of luck, Walter lands a plum role on a prime-time TV series opposite Cher (playing herself). Unbeknownst to Walter, his hiring is part of Cher's plan to sabotage the show's chance of success so she can get out of her contract. Ripping a page out of "The Producers," the show becomes a huge hit, setting Walt on a most unlikely fast lane to fame and fortune. But Walt's newfound celebrity only confirms for Bob that his own small-town sensibilities are weighing his brother down -- literally. The two Tenors make a decision to be surgically separated -- only to discover that their true bond was of the heart, not the hip.

Needless to say, for the film's quirky conceit to work the story must draw viewers beyond the visual eccentricity of its protagonists, or else it remains a sporadically funny but tedious series of punch lines to a one-joke sight gag. In addition to believing that Damon and Kinnear are brothers, it is essential that their characters are likable and worthy of emotional investment. The Farrellys accomplish this by keeping the tenor -- or Tenors -- positive, portraying Bob and Walt not as societal losers but as perennial winners. In fact, they come across as the most "normal" characters in the film.

And while their physical handicap obviously fuels much of the humor, the Farrellys refrain from sharpening lighthearted lampooning into mean-spiritedness or exploitation. The sole exception is an unnecessary scene which wrings cheap laughs out of showing the obstacle their impairment poses to sexual intimacy.

The film's normalizing of people with disabilities extends to those in supporting roles, who, though frequently fair game in Farrelly fare, are never targeted as the brunt of cruel jokes. In fact, the Farrellys frequently populate their cinematic landscapes with real-life physically or mentally challenged people as a means of softening the stigma associated with being perceived as "handicapped" (their next project has the support of the Special Olympics).

And while viewers may justifiably find the Farrellys' brand of humor tasteless at times, "Stuck on You" ultimately imparts a life-affirming message about family and friendship, which, as in the Farrellys' "Shallow Hal" (2001), invites viewers to look past surface superficialities and see each person -- no matter how strange -- as a unique gift and worthy of love. In the end, it reminds us that, as Christians and members of the human family, we are all interconnected at the heart and called to share our lives, if not livers.

Due to recurring sexually crude humor and language, an off-screen sexual encounter and brief alcohol abuse, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Stuck on You
synopsis: A palimony suit serves as the peg on which to hang a series of vulgar, unfunny skits in this low-budget comedy directed by Michael Herz and Samuel Weil. Much nudity

title: Student Nurses, The
synopsis: Exploitation movie about a group of aging apprentice nurses and their sexual exploits: one has a torrid affair with a resident doctor, another gets pregnant and has an amateur abortion and one has sex with a dying teenager. Directed by Stephanie Rothman, its treatment of the sexual goings on is relatively anemic both visually and morally

title: Stud, The
synopsis: Directed by Quentin Masters and written by Jackie Collins, this embarrassingly sordid British production stars Joan Collins in a story detailing the rise and fall of a working-class youth (Oliver Tobias) whose only salable asset is his body

title: Study in Scarlet, A
synopsis: Sherlock Holmes (Reginald Owen) and Dr. Watson (Warburton Gamble) solve a series of murders involving a fortune in gems stolen from China. Directed by Edwin L. Marin, Owen makes a worthy Holmes and, though the mystery isn't Conan Doyle, it's intriguing enough to hold interest. Creaky stylized violence and Oriental stereotypes

title: Stunt Man, The
synopsis: Fugitive from the police (Steve Railsback) is hidden by a manic movie director (Peter O'Toole) on condition that he do some dangerous stunts but he makes a mistake by falling for its star (Barbara Hershey). Directed by Richard Rush, the movie-within-a-movie plot starts well but soon becomes repetitious and drags considerably thereafter. Graphic depiction of sex with extensive nudity

title: Stupids, The
synopsis: Lame-brained comedy in which a moronic family of four (headed by Tom Arnold) inadvertently foils a plot to sell illegal arms but remains none the wiser. Directed by John Landis, the movie has some amusing visuals but the thin, slapstick story is simply dumb without being especially funny. Comic violence

title: St. Valentine's Day Massacre, The
synopsis: Bloody re-creation of one of the more lurid episodes in American gangland history when Chicago's Al Capone (Jason Robards) wiped out some of his competitors. Directed by Roger Corman, the acting is overdone but, then, so too is the violence

title: Subject Was Roses, The
synopsis: Fine drama about a Bronx Irish family's domestic crisis succeeds far beyond the limitations of its basically one-set story. Starring Patricia Neal and Jack Albertson as the parents, and Martin Sheen as their serviceman son, the movie probes the love and hate that alternately bind the three together and tear them apart. Adapted from Frank Gilroy's Broadway drama, the movie contains intimate touches of family life, its joys and its frustrations, and is masterful in its revelation of human nature, jealousy and love. Mature themes

title: Submarine Command
synopsis: After World War II, a career officer (William Holden) troubled by feelings of guilt over his commander's death buries himself in a Navy desk job and shamefully neglects his wife (Nancy Olson) until given a chance to prove his courage as a sub commander in the Korean War. Directed by John Farrow, the on-shore melodramatics of the moody officer grow increasingly tiresome, though the underwater action sequences still have interest. Wartime violence and domestic tensions

title: Submarine X-1
synopsis: British World War II story directed by William Graham about the training of submarines crews for an experimental mini-sub under a harsh and disliked commander (James Caan). The underwater sequences with the miniature submarines will be enjoyed by youngsters and the only violence is the sinking of a German battleship

title: Substance of Fire, The
synopsis: Brooding drama about an aging Jewish publisher (Ron Rifkin) whose concentration on Holocaust-themed books is bankrupting his company despite practical advice from his three concerned children (Tony Goldwyn, Sarah Jessica Parker and Timothy Hutton). Director Daniel Sullivan explores themes of guilt, independence and failed familial relationships in a sluggish, talky film that fails to transcend its stage play roots. Some sexual innuendo, intermittent rough language and minimal profanity

title: Substitute, The
synopsis: Formula action thriller in which a between-jobs military mercenary (Tom Berenger) tames an unruly Florida high school class, then breaks up a gang of drug smugglers using the school as their base of operations. Directed by Robert Mandel, the cliched characters go through the motions required by a tired scenario of vigilante justice. Excessive violence and menace, a scene with nude dancers and considerable rough language

title: Suburban Commando
synopsis: Mindless sci-fi fantasy has an intergalactic warrior (Hulk Hogan) crash-landing on Earth where a downtrodden architect (Christopher Lloyd) helps him right wrongs and outsmart a pair of pursuing interplanetary bounty hunters. Burt Kennedy directs a silly movie pitting a superhero against klutzy villains in a slapstick comedy of no distinction. Much comic violence

title: Suburbans, The
