Directed by Peter Yates, the center of the movie is the character played extremely well by Cher who conveys the strength, intelligence, dedication and appeal of the role. Some graphic violence and a lot of moody tension and menace

title: Suspect, The
synopsis: Chilling suspense tale set in 1902 London where a middle-aged husband (Charles Laughton) stages a fatal "accident" for his shrewish wife (Rosalind Ivan) in order to wed another woman (Ella Raines), then has to kill a blackmailer (Henry Daniell) to keep him from going to the Scotland Yard detective (Stanley C. Ridges) investigating the case. Director Robert Siodmak uses shadowy gaslit interiors to reflect the inner turmoil of an ordinary man who turns to murder, then is undone by its consequences. Off-screen murders, marital discord and an abusive alcoholic

title: Suspect Zero
synopsis: Relentlessly dreary thriller set in New Mexico about a demon-haunted FBI agent (Aaron Eckhart) on the trail of a government-trained telepath (Ben Kingsley) who may or may not be responsible for the gruesome string of homicides he is investigating. Following a generic cat-and-mouse formula, the stylish film is weighed down by a muddled script, but director E. Elias Merhige exercises relative restraint in his depiction of its lurid subject matter. Some violence, recurring grisly crime scene images of mutilated bodies, a graphic rape with frontal nudity, as well as recurring rough and crude language
full_review:
A censured FBI agent must stalk an elusive killer who preys on the guilty rather than the innocent in the relentlessly dreary and generic thriller, "Suspect Zero" (Paramount).

Muddled and morose, the movie takes its title from a theory which hypothesizes the existence of a serial killer who fits no profile and follows no consistent modus operandi, making him nearly impossible to hunt.

Set in New Mexico, the film stars Aaron Eckhart as Thomas Mackelway, a headache-plagued G-man investigating a string of grisly homicides in which the victims have had their eyelids flayed and the film's ubiquitous signature symbol carved into their flesh. Six months earlier, while working for the FBI's Dallas office, Mackelway, flouting extradition laws, had engineered an unorthodox arrest which resulted in him being demoted to a bush-league branch in Albuquerque and the serial killer he collared getting off scot-free.

Consummate professional Ben Kingsley plays Benjamin O'Ryan, a creepy government-trained telepath who may or may not be responsible for the gruesome, but seemingly random, crimes.
"Suspect Zero" follows a predictable cat-and-mouse formula as Mackelway's obsession with exorcising his personal demons leads him into the very heart -- and mind -- of darkness, culminating in a, yawn, shocking revelation.

Though earnest in intent and stylishly crafted, the film's to-catch-a-killer-you-have-to-think-like-one premise is, by now, getting quite old.

Director E. Elias Merhige (whose directorial debut with "Shadow of the Vampire" was much more interesting) tries unsuccessfully to inject some intrigue by incorporating the concept of "remote viewing," the extrasensory ability to visualize what someone else is seeing and thinking -- though you don't have to be a clairvoyant to see how this one is going to end up.

The convoluted script is freighted with predictable red herrings and retread Serial Killer 101 atmospherics.

As with the cinematically superior "Silence of the Lambs" (1991) and "Seven" (1995), "Suspect Zero" is just the most recent example of packaging depravity as entertainment. Though in fairness -- apart from an unnecessarily brutal rape -- Merhige exhibits restraint in filming the lurid crimes and does not make O'Ryan into the kind of postmodern antihero that Jonathan Demme did with Hannibal Lecter.

And while Merhige has said he was initially drawn to the project because he wanted to grapple with the question of evil by exploring the dark side of human nature, the film offers little in the way of illumination. Without shedding any light, the gloomy movie simply uses human venality as an opportunity to sell popcorn.

Due to some violence, recurring grisly crime-scene images of mutilated bodies, a graphic rape with frontal nudity, as well as recurring rough and crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Suspicion
synopsis: Suspense tale in which a shy Englishwoman (Joan Fontaine) is swept off her feet by a dashing charmer (Cary Grant) then, learning after their marriage of his large debts, comes to fear that he is planning to murder her for the insurance. Director Alfred Hitchcock starts with a sunny love story that grows increasingly sinister as the wife's suspicions deepen until the letdown of a slapdash ending. Mounting tension and menace

title: Suspiria
synopsis: Tasteless Italian horror movie directed by Dario Argento about an innocent ballet student who finds herself in an dance academy run by a coven of witches. Excessive blood and gore

title: Svengali
synopsis: Creaky romantic fantasy from George du Maurier's "Trilby" in which an artist's model (Marian Marsh) in 19th-century Paris falls under the hypnotic spell of the strange title music teacher (John Barrymore) who makes her a celebrated concert singer but is unable to win her love without coercing it. Directed by Archie Mayo, the melodramatic proceedings are of less interest than Barrymore's eye-popping characterization of the sinister hypnotist and the vivid period backgrounds. Menacing situations, sexual innuendo and a flash of nudity

title: Swamp Thing
synopsis: Lightweight monster movie in which a botanist on a secret government project is accidentally turned into a superhuman vegetable (Dick Durock), then grows fond of a government agent (Adrienne Barbeau) who keeps getting in his way while battling gunmen sent by a crazed scientist (Louis Jourdan) to find his research records. Writer-director Wes Craven has some fun with the green crime-busting monster but wastes too much time on clumsily staged rough stuff and the tongue-in-cheek villain. Stylized violence, sexual innuendo and coarse language

title: Swamp Water
synopsis: Backwoods tale of a Georgia youth (Dana Andrews) who discovers an escaped killer (Walter Brennan) hiding in the Okefenokee Swamp but agrees to be his silent partner in trapping animals and selling their pelts, then falls for the fugitive's daughter (Anne Baxter) and sets out to prove her father was wrongly convicted by finding the real killer. Directed by Jean Renoir, the slow-paced story has interest in its depiction of the genial country setting and its folksy rural characters, though the dramatic action finally heats up as the facts about the past miscarriage of justice come to light and lead to a showdown between the guilty and the innocent in the treacherous backwaters of the great swamp. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Swan Princess: Escape from Castle Mountain, The
synopsis: Animated sequel to the 1994 orginal continues the story of the fairy tale prince and princess (voices of Douglas Sills and Michelle Nicastro) who here are threatened by a villainous wizard after a magic ball containing evil powers which is hidden in their castle. Directed by Richard Rich, there is nothing very imaginative about the story, the cartooning or the songs, though it's fantasy elements will keep young children entertained

title: Swan Princess, The
synopsis: Animated children's tale of a beautiful princess (voice of Michele Nicastro) changed into a swan by an evil sorcerer (voice of Jack Palance) while a valiant prince (voice of Howard McGillin) attempts to find her and break the spell. Directed by Richard Rich, the lovely graphics are animated in the style of Disney's "Beauty and the Beast," with the heavily romantic story paced by some lighthearted humor supplied by a frog-puffin-turtle trio assisting in the rescue of the bewitched princess

title: Swappers, The
synopsis: Pseudo-documentary about affluent middle-class marrieds in Britain who trade mates in sexual games supposedly to heal marital problems or at least provide a thrilling diversion from them. Patent sex exploitation

title: Swarm, The
synopsis: Air Force General Richard Widmark and scientist Michael Caine try to stop the progress of billions of perturbed killer bees and save the lives of the usual collection of aged and aging actors who assemble for such disaster movies. Since Widmark and Caine spend most of the movie trying to outshout each other, the bees, not surprisingly, almost prevail. Director Irwin Allen's effort would be silly if it were not so inane

title: Swashbuckler
synopsis: Witless pirate movie directed by James Goldstone that, in a mistaken attempt to combine tongue-in-cheek action with straight melodrama, is so achingly bad that a competent cast (Robert Shaw, James Earl Jones, Peter Boyle) can do nothing to make it bearable. Some brief nudity

title: S.W.A.T.
synopsis: Loud and lackluster police actioner about an elite Los Angeles anti-crime unit (including Colin Farrell and Samuel L. Jackson) assigned to guard an international drug kingpin en route to a federal penitentiary. Based on the popular 1970s TV series, the film, directed by Clark Johnson, is an adolescent boys' playground, which, while drawing a distinction between "good" and "bad" guys, treats violence as entertainment, eliciting its thrills through tedious shoot 'em ups and mind-numbing crash-and-smash sequences. Much violence, some profanity and crude sexual language
full_review:
An elite Los Angeles law enforcement unit must bring a notorious international criminal to justice in the loud and lackluster "S.W.A.T." (Columbia). In reality, the only person who should be brought up on charges is Clark Johnson, for impersonating a film director in what amounts to essentially a mindless B-movie guns-'n'-ammo fest with an A-movie price tag. Based on the popular 1970s TV series of the same name, "S.W.A.T." is an acronym which stands for "Special Weapons And Tactics" -- or, in this film's case, "Sloppily Written Action Twaddle." The story centers on Jim Street (Colin Farrell), a former team member relegated to desk duty following a controversial hostage standoff during which he and his partner, Brian Gamble (Jeremy Renner), disobeyed direct orders, an act which consequently resulted in loose-cannon Gamble getting tossed off the force altogether.

Street gets a chance at redemption when veteran commander Dan "Hondo" Harrelson (Samuel L. Jackson) arrives on the scene and is assigned to recruit five battle-tested cops in order to form a new S.W.A.T. division. Hondo sets his scope on Street, identifying with his brand of maverick moxie. Filling out the ranks are "Deke" (James Todd Smith, aka LL Cool J), Boxer (Brian Van Holt), McCabe (Josh Charles) and, in a lame attempt to give the team a feminist twist, laconic Latina Chris Sanchez (Michelle Rodriguez).

About 40 wasted minutes into the film, Johnson should have put out an all-points-bulletin for a missing plot. Mercifully, after several protracted training sequences, a sketchy story begins to emerge involving a French crime boss, Alex Montel (Olivier Martinez), who, after being nabbed for a moving violation, audaciously offers a kingpin's ransom to anyone who can spring him from police custody before he is handed over to the Feds. In a rare exhibition of racial harmony, Bloods and Crips join forces together with Asian and Hispanic gang-bangers in order to free Montel and collect the $100 million bounty. Downtown L.A. erupts into a war-zone as Hondo's crew is called in to escort the foie-gras felon to the pen.

Regrettably, the film is little more than a testosterone-driven symphony of crescendos and pauses, wringing dry the audience's already depleted adrenal glands. In fact, the final 40 minutes of the film is barely distinguishable from countless other tedious shoot 'em ups and mind-numbing crash-and-smash sequences churned out and force fed to moviegoers throughout the summer.

To its credit, the film refrains from excessive gore and clearly delineates between "good guys" and "bad guys," but any such moral distinctions are Pyrrhic victories given the flick's misguided overall treatment of violence as entertainment.

The movie's tagline, "Even cops dial 911," suggests that during certain crises even police need help. Perhaps it would have paid dividends if the screenwriter had at some point picked up the phone and dialed "emergency" as well, given his apparent shabby grasp of character and narrative development. The cardboard team members are uniformly two-dimensional, distinguished only by their skin tone and facial hair -- thank goodness that their names are printed on their flak vests, or, in Gamble's case, tattooed on his forearm.

Midway through, Montel shouts, "I'll give a hundred million dollars to anyone who can get me out of here." Viewers subjected to this clunker may contemplate making a similar deal. This movie doesn't need S.W.A.T.; it is fodder for the bomb-squad.

Due to much violence, some profanity and some crude sexual language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Sweden, Heaven and Hell
synopsis: Italian psuedo-documentary filmmaker Luigi Scattini journeys to Sweden to show all manner of excesses, sexual and otherwise, most of which are staged to sanctimonious moralization of the narrator. Sheer exploitation

title: Swedish Fly Girls
synopsis: ( see: "Christa" )

title: Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street
synopsis: Bloody but artful screen version of Stephen Sondheim's Broadway musical (and now a staple of opera houses) recounting the Victorian legend of the crazed barber (an intense Johnny Depp, singing surprisingly well) determined to exact revenge on the lecherous judge (Alan Rickman) who robbed him of his wife and daughter years before. He sets up his business over the shop of a shady baker (Helena Bonham Carter), who minces his victims into her pies. The songs notwithstanding, this is familiar territory for director Tim Burton, who has an affinity for the Grand Guignol aspects of the story, and creates an atmosphere of great tension, but the streams of blood, however stylized, and basic premise will be a turnoff for many. Brief but grisly bloodlettings and grinding of flesh, implied cannibalism, a couple of uses of the s-word, brief irreverence in lyrics and underage drinking
full_review:
Most assuredly not for the fainthearted, but otherwise "Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street" (DreamWorks/Paramount) proves a finely made adaptation of composer-lyricist Stephen Sondheim's 1979 Broadway musical.

It far surpasses the two previous cinematic incarnations of his work: "A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum" and the woefully bad "A Little Night Music."

The musical was based on a 1973 play by Christopher Bond that retold the Victorian-era legend of the crazed barber Benjamin Barker (an intense Johnny Depp, singing surprisingly well) determined to exact revenge on the lecherous Judge Turpin (Alan Rickman), who robbed him of his wife, Lucy (Laura Michelle Kelly), and baby daughter Joanna years before.

Now returned from his 15-year imprisonment in Australia, with a young sailor named Anthony (Jamie Campbell Bower) at his side, he finds out that Turpin and his henchman, Beadle Bamford (Timothy Spall), are still very much in power, and the now-grown Joanna (Jayne Wisner) is the judge's ward and intended bride.

Changing his name to Sweeney Todd, he sets up his business over the shop of a shady baker, Mrs. Lovett (Helena Bonham Carter), who has always loved Barker/Todd.

Anthony, meanwhile, has spied Joanna sitting, a virtual prisoner, in the window of Turpin's house, and he promptly falls in love. But Turpin observes Anthony, has him thrashed and orders him never to return.

Later, Turpin shows up at Todd's emporium for a shave -- and Todd, razor drawn, almost has his chance for revenge -- but young Anthony bursts in with news of his planned elopement with Joanna.

When a rival barber, the Italian mountebank Adolfo Pirelli (Sacha Baron Cohen), reveals he knows Todd's true identity and threatens blackmail, Todd cuts the man's throat, giving Mrs. Lovett the idea of baking him -- and Todd's other victims to come -- into her pies.

John Logan's screenplay manages to be remarkably faithful to the show, cutting mainly the chorus numbers that might seem artificial. Sondheim's songs are well performed. This is familiar territory for director Tim Burton, who has an affinity for Grand Guignol, and creates an atmosphere of almost unbearable tension.

The cast is outstanding. In addition to Depp's passionate portrayal of the titular madman, Bonham Carter offers a unique characterization, much different from the role's original, Angela Lansbury.

In virtually all stage productions of "Sweeney Todd," even in opera houses, the bloodletting is merely suggested. Here the blood is shown (and how!). These stylized but grisly scenes, however brief, and the basic premise will be a turnoff for many.

Vengeance, of course, is far from a Christian virtue, but everyone gets their just desserts in the end. (And we don't mean Mrs. Lovett's pies.)

The film contains brief but grisly bloodlettings and grinding of flesh, implied cannibalism, a couple of uses of the s-word, brief irreverence in lyrics and underage drinking. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Sweepings
synopsis: After the 1871 Chicago Fire, a merchant (Lionel Barrymore) spends his life building a great department store in the Loop, then is sorely disappointed when his spoiled children (William Gargan, Gloria Stuart, George Meeker and Eric Linden) show no interest in taking over the family enterprise. Directed by John Cromwell, the episodic family saga contrasts the hard-working father with his profligate offspring as well as his own shabby treatment of the loyal assistant (Gregory Ratoff) who helped make the store a success. Stylized violence, drunken excesses and sexual situations

title: Sweet and Lowdown
synopsis: Modest comedy-drama about a brilliant but utterly egotistical Depression-era jazz guitarist (Sean Penn) who callously dumps his adoring mute girlfriend (Samantha Morton) only to marry a sophisticate (Uma Thurman) who betrays him with a common gangster. Writer-director Woody Allen highlights an extensive jazz soundtrack as he amusingly mocks the artist who feels he is above pedestrian morality. A live-in relationship, brief recreational drug abuse and some profanity

title: Sweet Body of Deborah
synopsis: Shoddy Italian-French import about a young man (Jean Sorel) who concocts a scheme to murder his new wife (Carroll Baker) for her insurance money but she double-crosses him. Directed by Romolo Guerrieri, the inept melodrama offers generous portions of sex and nudity

title: Sweet Charity
synopsis: Overblown screen version of Broadway musical about a dance-hall hostess (Shirley MacLaine) who gets the romantic runaround from a series of guys who try to break her heart of gold. But her spirit is buoyant and there is true love around the corner (John McMartin). Directed by Bob Fosse, it tries so hard it gets tiresome

title: Sweet Dreams
synopsis: Moving and entertaining biography of country-western singer Patsy C1ine (Jessica Lange) whose career was cut short in a 1963 p1ane crash. Director Kare1 Reisz concentrates on characterization rather than showbiz glitter and there is some fine acting, but the movie's episodic structure undercuts its dramatic impact. Some vulgar language and vividly displayed passion, loving as well as violent, mark the relationship between the heroine and her husband

title: Sweet Hearts Dance
synopsis: Fairly innocuous slice of romantic Americana set in small-town Vermont tracks the temporary midlife breakdown of a 15-year marriage (Don Johnson and Susan Sarandon) and the efforts of their kids and friends to get them back together. Nice performances, but director Robert Greenwald provides a stronger portrait of male bonding than marriage. Locker-room language, implied infidelity as well as premarital sex and brief flashes of nudity

title: Sweet Hereafter, The
synopsis: When a rural Canadian town is devastated by a tragic schoolbus accident, a big-city lawyer (Ian Holm) arrives to represent those whose children were killed or injured, but his pursuit of the facts in the case comes to divide the community until the testimony of a teen (Sarah Polly) injured in the accident destroys the basis of the lawyer's suit. Writer-director Atom Egoyan parallels the lawyer's own sense of loss over his drug-addicted daughter with the bereavement of the town's residents and their tangled relationships with their children and each other as the community struggles to bring closure to their grief. Stylized violence, sexual situations, brief nudity and occasional rough language

title: Sweet Home Alabama
synopsis: High-spirited tale in which a small-town Southern girl (Reese Witherspoon) hides the truth about her previous marriage and humble Southern roots in hopes of marrying an up-and-coming politician whose mother is the mayor of New York City. Directed in breezy fairy-tale manner by Andy Tennant, the movie suggests following your heart and being true to yourself, but plays fast and loose with the main character's attitude toward the sanctity of marriage. Some alcohol abuse, mild profanity and homosexual references. A-III � adults. (PG-13) 2002 Full Review In "Sweet Home Alabama" (Touchstone) a transplanted Southern girl seeks a secretive, quickie divorce back home so she can marry a sophisticated New Yorker. Everything seems perfect for Melanie (Reese Witherspoon), who also happens to be a budding young fashion designer with a new line of clothing being sold at New York's most exclusive department stores. She seems to be on top of the world, except for one tiny secret she is concealing from her fiance, Andrew (Patrick Dempsey), and his mother, the mayor of New York (Candice Bergen): She is already married. Directed by Andrew Tennant, the film finds Melanie going back home after seven years away to get her husband (Josh Lucas) to sign divorce papers. At first Melanie acts as though she is going through a bit of culture shock as she revisits her home town of Pigeon Hole, Ala., with her old friends accusing her of being stuck up. It doesn't take her long to cozy up to the bar, play a friendly game of pool and hear the tune of the title song at a town fair to get back the twang of her Southern drawl. Though handled in a breezy fairy-tale manner, the film tackles mother-daughter relationships as Melanie's mother, Pearl (Mary Kay Place), feels responsible for her daughter leaving her husband, family and friends behind for the glamour of New York, a world away from the insular mentality of small-town Alabama. Although Pearl seems loving toward her husband (Fred Ward), she's disappointed with their simple life and so encouraged her daughter to go after the things she only dreamed of but never had. In addition to not owning up to her fiance about her previous marriage, Melanie has also glamorized her Southern heritage as more "Gone With the Wind" than folksy and just a step away from trailer-park class. At first Andrew wants to drop Melanie like a hot potato when he learns the truth, but he soon realizes that his status-conscious mother will get her way in breaking them apart. Andrew then professes that he cannot reject her because her parents are poor. While the movie eventually has its heart in the right place, "Sweet Home Alabama" plays fast and loose with Melanie's commitment to her marriage vows. In the interests of light-hearted comedic elements, her indiscretions get blown over as if they are harmless little white lies when in reality they are serious, even reckless. The film begins showing Josh as a redneck whom she must bribe and antagonize into divorcing her. There is also the implication that Josh has not done anything with his life as she flashes her giant diamond in his face, comparing him to the successful Andrew. Sadly, the film never completely concedes that happiness is achieved through true love and commitment, as too much value is placed on economic and social success as the driving force that brings the main characters together. Nonetheless, a typically Hollywood-happy ending materializes to take the sting out of the film's glossing over of its moral questions. Due to some alcohol abuse, mild profanity and homosexual references, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops
full_review:
In "Sweet Home Alabama" (Touchstone) a transplanted Southern girl seeks a secretive, quickie divorce back home so she can marry a sophisticated New Yorker.

Everything seems perfect for Melanie (Reese Witherspoon), who also happens to be a budding young fashion designer with a new line of clothing being sold at New York's most exclusive department stores. She seems to be on top of the world, except for one tiny secret she is concealing from her fiance, Andrew (Patrick Dempsey), and his mother, the mayor of New York (Candice Bergen): She is already married.

Directed by Andrew Tennant, the film finds Melanie going back home after seven years away to get her husband (Josh Lucas) to sign divorce papers. At first Melanie acts as though she is going through a bit of culture shock as she revisits her home town of Pigeon Hole, Ala., with her old friends accusing her of being stuck up. It doesn't take her long to cozy up to the bar, play a friendly game of pool and hear the tune of the title song at a town fair to get back the twang of her Southern drawl.

Though handled in a breezy fairy-tale manner, the film tackles mother-daughter relationships as Melanie's mother, Pearl (Mary Kay Place), feels responsible for her daughter leaving her husband, family and friends behind for the glamour of New York, a world away from the insular mentality of small-town Alabama. Although Pearl seems loving toward her husband (Fred Ward), she's disappointed with their simple life and so encouraged her daughter to go after the things she only dreamed of but never had.

In addition to not owning up to her fiance about her previous marriage, Melanie has also glamorized her Southern heritage as more "Gone With the Wind" than folksy and just a step away from trailer-park class. At first Andrew wants to drop Melanie like a hot potato when he learns the truth, but he soon realizes that his status-conscious mother will get her way in breaking them apart. Andrew then professes that he cannot reject her because her parents are poor.

While the movie eventually has its heart in the right place, "Sweet Home Alabama" plays fast and loose with Melanie's commitment to her marriage vows. In the interests of light-hearted comedic elements, her indiscretions get blown over as if they are harmless little white lies when in reality they are serious, even reckless.

The film begins showing Josh as a redneck whom she must bribe and antagonize into divorcing her. There is also the implication that Josh has not done anything with his life as she flashes her giant diamond in his face, comparing him to the successful Andrew. Sadly, the film never completely concedes that happiness is achieved through true love and commitment, as too much value is placed on economic and social success as the driving force that brings the main characters together. Nonetheless, a typically Hollywood-happy ending materializes to take the sting out of the film's glossing over of its moral questions.

Due to some alcohol abuse, mild profanity and homosexual references, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Sweetie
synopsis: Surreal, off-kilter Australian drama about two bizarre sisters -- one thin, sour and inhibited (Karen Colston), the other schizophrenic, plump and insatiable for food, sex and attention (Genevieve Lemon). Directed by Jane Campion, it's an uncomfortable, unconventional study of adult female sibling rivalry and the long-standing ties that bind and choke off all that is good and healthy in a family. Scenes of graphic sexuality and psychological breakdown may be disturbing to some, yet the work's unusual artistic and family vision warrants serious attention. Nudity and rough language

title: Sweet Jesus, Preacher Man
synopsis: Low-budget black exploitation movie about a criminal (Roger E. Mosley) who poses as the new pastor of a small congregation (after incinerating the real clergyman) in order to double-cross a white racketeer. Director Henning Schellerup has a flair for confusing characters and situations in dimly lit scenes. Excessive violence, some explicit sex and rough language

title: Sweet Liberty
synopsis: The lighthearted vehicle written and directed by Alan Alda is a disappointingly shallow view of the sexual and professional frustrations of an amiable historian (A1da) whose book is being made into a movie. The comic touches don't override the movie's celebration of permissive casual sex with several partners as an acceptable route to mutual trust and devotion

title: Sweet Light in a Dark Room
synopsis: Czechoslovakian drama set in Nazi-occupied Prague where a student makes an attempt to help a Jewish girl hide from the deportations. Director Jiri Weiss maintains a grim wartime atmosphere and his two young principals (Dana Smutna and Ivan Mistrik) are credible in a life-and-death situation

title: Sweet Lorraine
synopsis: Young woman (Trini Alvarado) rediscovers family ties and a sense of belonging while working for her grandmother (Maureen Stapleton) during a summer at a resort hotel. Director Steve Gomer mixes nostaglia with delicate romance in a family story marred only by some harsh language in a kitchen scene

title: Sweet Nothing
synopsis: Grim chronicle of the descent of a Wall Street office worker (Michael Imperioli) into a desperate crack addict and dealer who loses his wife (Mira Sorvino), children and nearly his life to his addiction. Directed by Gary Winick, the fact-based drama contrasts the addict's rationalization of his drug habit with the reality of its self-destructive effects. Brief violence, fleeting video porn footage, frequent drug abuse and much rough language

title: Sweet November
synopsis: Strained romantic remake in which a free-spirited young woman (Charlize Theron) takes in a different man every month, her latest being Keanu Reeves, who falls in love with her but soon discovers the sad secret behind her brief romances. As directed by Pat O'Connor, the drama's slack story line is barely engaging and, though treated offhandedly, the film's subtext of promiscuity is unsettling. A few sexual encounters with fleeting nudity, brief profanity and some crass language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Sweet November
synopsis: Sappy romance about a woman (Sandy Dennis) who is in the habit of changing male roommates each month and November happens to be Anthony Newley's turn. The reason for living life in joyous monthly installments is because the woman is dying of the standard Hollywood non-disfiguring but incurable disease. Directed by Robert Ellis Miller, there is some gentle humor at work in the script but the basic theme of the movie is unacceptable, even though given mild treatment

title: Sweet Revenge
synopsis: Stockard Channing plays a tough teenage car thief and Sam Waterson is the good-natured lawyer who constantly comes to her rescue only to be rewarded with contempt for his efforts. Director Jerry Schatzberg attempts to carry off a kind of conversion of his heroine at the end of this run-of-the-mill comedy melodrama but its morality (she sets fire to a valuable car bought with stolen money) is highly ambiguous

title: Sweet Ride, The
synopsis: Trashy tangled tale having to do with the wasted lives and energies of a pack of Malibu beach bums (such as Tony Franciosa and Michael Sarrazin) and their assorted girlfriends (most notably, Jacqueline Bisset). Directed by Harvey Hart, its sexual misadventures are not redeemed by one character's sudden moral awakening

title: Sweet Saviour
synopsis: Exploitation movie featuring Troy Donahue in a sick and revolting movie based transparently on the Charles Manson-Sharon Tate murder sensation. Written, produced and directed by Bob Roberts, it's a tawdry attempt to cash in on a notorious tragedy

title: Sweet Sixteen
synopsis: Bleak drama about a resourceful, working-class Scottish teen (Martin Compston) who becomes entangled with a vicious drug dealer in order to raise enough money to buy a home for him and his recovering-addict mother (Michelle Coulter). Director Ken Loach elicits a nuanced performance out of his adolescent lead to create an engaging portrait of a boy on the cusp of adulthood, struggling to make sense out of life's sometimes harsh realities. Subtitles. Much rough language, as well as profanities, recurring drug abuse and some instances of violence
full_review:
"Sweet Sixteen" (Lions Gate) is a poignant tale of a Scottish teen driven to extreme measures to better his own life and the lives of his loved ones. True to his life's work as chronicler and poet of Britain's working classes, director Ken Loach elicits nuanced performances out of his adolescent leads to create an engaging portrait of a boy on the cusp of adulthood, struggling to make sense out of life's sometimes harsh realities.

The story focuses on Liam (Martin Compston), a resourceful lad just shy of his 16th birthday. His jailbird mother, Jean (Michelle Coulter), is doing time on drug-related charges but is due to be released soon. Liam, when not hustling a buck or getting into trouble with his loose-cannon mate, Pinball (William Ruane), dreams of starting life anew with his mum, safe from the reaches of his mean-spirited grandfather (Tommy McKee) and Jean's low-life boyfriend, Stan (Gary McCormack), a sadistic petty drug dealer who routinely strong-arms Liam into helping him ply his trade -- noncompliance resulting in savage beatings.

After some particularly brutal tough love, Liam moves in with his sister, Chantelle (Annmarie Fulton), an overworked single mom barely older than Liam juggling homemaking duties and correspondence courses in the hope of bettering her lot. Though she is sincerely worried about her brother's welfare, her no-nonsense sensibilities and less-than-confident prognosis of their mother's rehabilitation inject an unwelcome dose of reality into Liam's idyllic optimism.

Undeterred, Liam -- audacious as he is desperate -- takes matters into his own hands, literally, by stealing a stash of drugs from Stan and selling them at a profit. When his entrepreneurial moxie catches the eye of a local crime boss (Martin McCardie), Liam finds himself in way over his head. And though the lucrative business arrangement sets him on the yellow brick road to a better life with his mom, it comes at grave cost: his soul.

Though much of what unfolds on the screen is fueled by violence -- both physical and emotional -- the film is an elegiac exploration of the powerful bond between parents and their children. While neither justifying nor glamorizing heinous crimes perpetrated by the young protagonist, Liam's actions are presented as a misguided attempt to create, by any means necessary, that which will give his life meaning and completeness: a family. Liam's rage is a primal scream, an existential self-defense against the despair threatening to destroy his hope of a better life.

And though he destroys lives in the process, viewers should not overlook Liam's wounded humanity. The final haunting image reveals his brokenness -- a boy longing for his mother, willing to forgive her faults, but unable to control the forces keeping them apart. As the filmmaker observes, "Fragility and often a wild courage, even if misplaced, can sit easily side by side."

Chantelle stands in as a positive counterpoint to Liam's recklessness. She does not use society as a convenient scapegoat; she demands accountability for the ill-advised choices Liam and Jean have made. For her, virtue is a matter of hard work and does not suffer behaviorist fools gladly.

This modest film, which may prove daunting to viewers in the early goings due to the actors' heavy Scottish brogues -- necessitating subtitles throughout -- flowers beautifully and offers moments of genuine pathos without airbrushed sentimentality or a pat resolution.

Subtitles.

Due to much rough language, as well as profanities, recurring drug abuse and some instances of violence, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Sweet Sugar
synopsis: Exploitative women's prison-escape movie with Ella Edwards and Phyllis Davis as the black and white ring leaders. Directed by Michel Levesque in Costa Rica, the bargain basement proceedings are soured with the usual violence, lewd characters, nudity and dirty dialogue

title: Sweet Sweetback's Baadasssss Song
synopsis: Melvin Van Peeples wrote, produced, directed and stars as Sweetback, a name derived from his sexual prowess, who brutally murders two brutal cops and becomes a fugitive from The Man. The result is a largely incoherent chase movie, utterly defeated by flashy camera effects, overly graphic sex and violence, extraordinarily rough language and degrading stereotypes, black and white

title: Swept Away
synopsis: Sporadically funny romantic comedy in which an American magnate's haughty wife (Madonna), stranded on a deserted island with an Italian fisherman (Adriano Giannini), falls in love with him after he gives her a taste of her own medicine. As directed by Guy Ritchie, Madonna is convincing when arrogant but drippy when lovestruck by the appealingly earthy Giannini in this remake of Lina Wertmuller's 1974 satire, which pits the fisherman's simple values against her greedy materialism. Implied sexual encounters, fleeting nudity, brief violence, much rough language and minimal profanity

title: Swept Away
synopsis: Italian satire about a spoiled rich woman (Mariangela Melato) marooned on a deserted island with proletarian brute (Giancarlo Giannini). Directed by Lina Wertmuller, the battle of the sexes between classes gets swept away in some extensive depictions of lovemaking

title: Swept from the Sea
synopsis: Engrossing drama from Joseph Conrad's story in which a Ukrainian immigrant (Vincent Perez) bound for America in the 1890's is shipwrecked on the rugged English coast of Cornwall where he courts a lonely servant girl (Rachel Weisz) and they wed to live in blissful isolation from their hostile neighbors until tragedy strikes. Directed by Beeban Kidron, the British production succeeds as a lyric love story of two strangers clinging to each other in an alien land, told with feeling for its characters and lushly photographed landscapes, with enough period detail to satisfy even those who ordinarily disdain movie romantics. Some stylized violence, a restrained sexual encounter, an illegitmate birth and occasional profanity

title: Swimfan
synopsis: A high school senior swimming star (Jesse Bradford) regrets cheating on his sweetheart (Shiri Appleby) with a seductive new classmate (Erika Christensen) who stalks him, exacting a violent revenge when he refuses to continue the relationship. Director John Polson conjures up a tamer teen version of "Fatal Attraction" that is essentially predictable and forgettable. A discreet sexual encounter, brief violence, implied affairs and an instance of profanity
full_review:
A high school senior's worst nightmare materializes in the form a seductress-turned-stalker in the derivative suspense drama, "Swimfan" (20th Century Fox).

Thanks in part to supportive girlfriend Amy (Shiri Appleby), Ben has overcome a drug problem and become the high school's swimming star, with a shot at an athletic scholarship. The two seniors are planning a future together, possibly moving in together when they get to college.

Sultry new classmate Madison (Erika Christensen), however, corners Ben at a vulnerable moment alone in the pool one night. He is too ashamed to tell Amy he has cheated on her and soon finds Madison insistently insinuating herself into his life. When he resists her, Madison turns vengeful.

The poorly developed script gives us no notions why the petulant Madison turns psycho but soon her sly manipulations get him thrown off the swimming team, fired from his after-school job -- and suspected of murder. Next Madison sets her sights on rival Amy.

Director John Polson's teen thriller falls apart in the unbelievable final act but is none too involving beforehand, either. The story comes across as a cautionary tale, a tamer teen version of 1987's "Fatal Attraction" without the fiery performances of Glenn Close and Michael Douglas. Here, Christensen and Bradford are subdued versions of the illicit couple whose one-night stand will have fatal consequences. The swimming scenes are sleekly photographed but the movie simply coasts along building little momentum.

Kate Burton is wasted as Ben's mom and Dan Hedaya is given little to do but scowl as Ben's skeptical swim coach. Viewers are likely to find Ben's character exasperating for getting involved with someone so obviously bad-news from the get-go. Nor is Madison's ability to outwit two armed cops very credible.

The movie's sense of morality clearly suggests infidelity can have dire consequences and therefore is to be avoided. For the Catholic audience, however, the suggestion of teen-age abstinence would have been welcome.

Due to a discreet sexual encounter, brief violence, implied affairs and an instance of profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Swimmer, The
synopsis: Adaptation of the John Cheever story about a middle-aged suburbanite (Burt Lancaster) who swims home through the pools of his affluent neigbors, a journey recalling his wasted life. Directed by Frank Perry, the swim is a long one and the recollections, especially of past affairs, lead to only a banal conclusion

title: Swimming Pool, The
synopsis: Static French plot revolves around a triangle (Romy Schnedier, Alain Delon and Maurice Ronet) with nubile Jane Birkin coolly observing and finally taking part in their sexual games. Placed in a glamorous resort setting, the inner sterility of these social parasites is conveyed with deadening dullness. Moral issues drown in waves of ennui

title: Swimming to Cambodia
synopsis: Moderately interesting monologue written and delivered by actor Spalding Gray who sits at a desk talking about his personal reflections on life and his profession, mostly centered on what he experienced in Thailand during the filming of "The Killing Fields" (1984). Director Jonathan Demme makes a straightforward record of Gray's stage performance, punctuated by fades, a few film clips and a modest variety of camera positions. Some graphic descriptions of Khmer Rouge atrocities in Cambodia, a few sexual references including a brief account of prostitution in Bangkok and some rough language

title: Swimming Upstream
synopsis: Alternately inspiring and sordid true story of Australian swimming champion Tony Fingleton, who grew up with a brutish, alcoholic father (Geoffrey Rush), and a loving, supportive mother (Judy Davis). Russell Mulcahy's film, with a script by Fingleton himself (based on a book written with his sister, Diane), features superb performances by Rush and Davis, but the former's character is so unpleasantly -- if realistically -- drawn that the steady pattern of drunken violence, unaccountable malice toward his son, and abuse toward the wife seriously compromise the uplifting aspects of the story. Many scenes of domestic violence, heavy drinking, a smattering of rough and crude language, a suicide attempt and some sexual references
full_review:
Bravura performances by Geoffrey Rush and Judy Davis, and a story of professional triumph over domestic adversity, don't entirely compensate for the sordidness of this true-life story of Australian swimming champion Tony Fingleton in "Swimming Upstream" (MGM).

Directed by Russell Mulcahy from a script by Fingleton, the film charts Tony's progress from young boy to world-class swimmer under the resolutely disapproving eye of a father who doesn't love him.

The film -- based on a book by Fingleton, co-written with his sister, Diane -- begins in the 1950s, and young Tony is living with his siblings, including the brutish Harold Jr. and kindly John, and their parents, the alcoholic wharf laborer Harold (Geoffrey Rush) and the long-suffering and loving Dora (Judy Davis). The father clearly favors the macho, bullying Harold Jr., whom he sees as epitomizing what a man should be. Harold Jr. torments Tony relentlessly, even slamming down a piano lid on Tony's hands while he's playing.

Dora is supportive of Tony, whose artistic leanings (besides playing the piano, he reads Shakespeare) are despised by the father who sees them as marks of effeminacy. (In a later scene, Harold will snatch "Hamlet" from Tony's hands and disdainfully toss it in the swimming pool.)

Dora urges Tony to be "strong in the head" to protect himself from his father's continual belittling. She also reinforces the fact that only he has the internal capacity to make something of his life, rather than relying on his father or even her.

One day Harold accompanies Tony and John to the local pool, where unbeknownst to him, they have become amazingly proficient.

Harold watches with calculating wonderment, and from that point on, shifts his sights to training John and Tony, pushing them almost beyond endurance, as he watches from the sidelines with a keen eye. John is clearly his favorite, though, and Harold repeatedly shows lack of interest in any of Tony's triumphs.

Years pass, and the two boys are good enough to enter competitions. John scores an early victory, but eventually, much to the father's disdain, it is Tony who moves out in front.

The father leans on John to persevere, and under his father's urging, secretly enters a race against his brother, but eventually Tony comes out on top again, causing a rift between the two brothers, once so close.

Harold frequently becomes seriously violent, striking anyone in his way, including Dora. The children urge her to escape the never-ending pattern of abuse, but Dora can't bring herself to break free and even attempts to take her own life.

As Tony goes from triumph to triumph, it's clear he's desperately seeking his father's love, but Harold, infuriatingly, refuses or is incapable of giving it.

The father's malice is puzzling. He calls his son a "poufter," but does he really think the boy is gay? Though we learn he had a horrific childhood -- his mother having sexual encounters with strangers who, it is implied, also abused him -- Harold's unaccountable resentment (or, at best, indifference) to Tony, particularly after the latter's success, is as puzzling as it is ultimately tiresome for the viewer.

By the end, we're supposed to feel some pity for the father, but he still emerges as pretty despicable, in spite of Rush's nuanced portrayal.

You root for Tony to get away from his intolerable home life, but his ultimate decision to go to Harvard seems more a case of running away from a miserable situation than a wholly positive achievement. Yet Tony's understanding and ultimate rapprochement with his father and bullying brother, and Dora's loving devotion to Tony and empathy for her husband deliver the right message.

Rush adds another indelible portrait to his gallery of screen performances. And it's good to have Davis back on her native Aussie ground, after her triumphs as Judy Garland and Nancy Reagan on American television. Her distinctly unfeminist devotion to her husband and compassion for his son bear the authentic ring of truth for a housewife of that era.

Jesse Spencer (who portrays Tony), Tim Draxl (John) and David Hoflin (Harold Jr.) are good as the brothers, and well-matched by Mitchell Dellevergin, Thomas Davidson and Kain O'Keefe as their younger selves.

Mulcahy directs this slice-of-life drama with a sure hand, and uses a split screen sportslike technique for the swimming scenes and fanciful water imagery, which adds visual variety.

Overall, this schizophrenic film is more of a "Daddy Dearest" downer than the "Chariots of Fire" type of tale that it might have been, but Rush and Davis are reason enough to see it.

The film contains many scenes of domestic violence, heavy drinking, a smattering of rough and crude language, a suicide attempt and some sexual references. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Swimming with Sharks
synopsis: Dark comedy about the Hollywood food chain as a nasty studio executive (Kevin Spacey) is taken hostage and brutalized by his crazed assistant (Frank Whaley) who's driven to murder when his writer-girlfriend (Michelle Forbes) shows up. Writer-director George Huang uses flashbacks to show the assistant's gradual demoralization by his manic boss, but goes overboard in depicting the man's revenge and ironic aftermath. Some vicious violence, sexual situations and rough language as well as profanity

title: Swindle, The
synopsis: Lightweight Gallic Suspense story of two con artists at a Swiss resort to fleece a dentist's convention, but when the younger one (Isabelle Huppert) latches onto a gold courier, her cautious partner (Michel Serrault) plays along on a scam that leads to a Caribbean resort and a gang of deadly professionals. Writer-director Claude Chabrol's twisty plot puts his petty thieves out of their league and in fear of their lives in a scam of big-time operators, though the larger question is whether the two are trying to con one another. Subtitles. Stylized violence, criminal activities and occasional rough language

title: Swing Vote
synopsis: Smartly made if unabashedly formulaic comedy about a beer-chugging, slovenly single father (Kevin Costner) whose civically minded child (Madeline Carroll) surreptitiously tries to vote on his behalf, leading to an anomaly where his vote will determine the U.S. presidential race between the incumbent Republican (Kelsey Grammer) and his Democratic rival (Dennis Hopper). Costner and Carroll have good chemistry, though his character's predictable reformation takes annoyingly long, but the important messages of director and co-writer Joshua Michael Stern's film -- the importance of every vote and the integrity of the political process -- are entertainingly conveyed, and the script wisely takes a nonpartisan position. Much crude language, profanity and crass expressions; heavy drinking; brief irreverence; and some domestic discord
full_review:
If you had any doubts about whether a visit to your local poll on Election Day really counts, the smartly made, consciousness-raising comedy "Swing Vote" (Touchstone) may help eradicate them.

 

Unabashedly formulaic but generally entertaining, the story concerns Bud Johnson (Kevin Costner), a beer-chugging, slovenly single father whose civically minded 12-year-old child, Molly (Madeline Carroll), runs their chaotic New Mexico trailer home.

Completely apathetic, Bud has zero interest in the upcoming presidential election -- with incumbent Republican Andrew Boone (Kelsey Grammer) facing off against Democratic rival Donald Greenleaf (Dennis Hopper) -- but Molly has taken it on herself to register him to vote.

 

On the appointed day, she's begged him to meet her at the voting place, but he lingers at his local watering hole, and ironically passes out after slamming into a "Vote Today" sign. The disappointed girl surreptitiously forges her dad's name in the register and attempts to vote on his behalf, with the volunteer attendant fast asleep, but a cleaning lady knocks off the power just as Molly's about to vote.

Bud and Molly are soon visited by some top state politicos who inform them that Bud's recast vote in 10 days' time will affect the state's five electoral votes, and therefore decide the next U.S. president.

They recommend Bud keep his identity secret, but it's not long before a resourceful local TV reporter, Kate Madison (Paula Patton), discovers the truth.

Both candidates and their respective campaign managers, Democrat Art Crumb (Nathan Lane) and Republican Martin Fox (Stanley Tucci), go to extravagant lengths to woo Bud, the former throwing a big bash at which Bud can resurrect his Willie Nelson knockoff band, and the latter offering a grand tour of Air Force One.

Comic complications ensue, with each candidate trying to take the stance of whatever ill-informed remark the clueless Bud happens to make. Throwing their own positions to the wind, Greenleaf and Boone take flip-flopping stands on everything from abortion to gay marriage to illegal immigration, as demonstrated by some satiric TV spots. The script plays it neutral on these topics, targeting the candidates themselves who are shamelessly willing to go to any lengths to win the popular vote.

Costner's terrific, and he and Carroll have good chemistry, though Bud's predictable reformation takes annoyingly long to happen. The script (co-written by Jason Richman and director Joshua Michael Stern) has Costner play the apathetic slob for virtually the entire film, and that includes multiple uses of the s-word and quite a bit of profanity.

Molly continually berates him for this, even telling him "You gotta stop using Jesus as a cuss word all the time."

Were it not for this gratuitously crass language, Bud's constant drinking and a sordid domestic incident near the end, the film could be warmly recommended to all ages

But those caveats aside, the overriding messages -- the importance of every vote and the integrity of the political process -- are painlessly delivered, with the script wisely taking a nonpartisan position.

The film contains much crude language, profanity and crass expressions; heavy drinking; brief irreverence; and some domestic discord. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Swingers
synopsis: Lame look at the egocentric lives of several young men (Jon Favreau, Vince Vaughn and Ron Livingston) whose search for work in Hollywood seems limited to partygoing and bar-hopping looking for showbiz contacts and available women. Director Doug Liman tries to give a comic tone to the aimless proceedings but the material is too thin to be amusing and the characters are too wrapped up in themselves to be interesting. Sexual situations, heavy drinking and much rough language with some profanity

title: Swinger, The
synopsis: Good girl (Ann-Margaret) poses as a bad girl in order to sell some of her stories to a sex magazine. Directed by George Sidney, it is a silly exercise in titillation

title: Swing High, Swing Low
synopsis: Uneven romantic melodrama in which a fun-loving trumpet player (Fred MacMurray) weds a wise-cracking singer (Carole Lombard) while both are stranded in Panama City, then gets a gig in New York, becomes a big hit and forgets his wife until he hits the skids. Director Mitchell Leisen can't save the sentimental story from turning into a tearjerker, despite high-spirited characters and some very funny situations. Romantic complications

title: Swingin' Pussycats, The
synopsis: German sex comedy about three sexually agile sisters who scamper insatiably about their spacious estate to romp with any visitor, nobleman or commoner. Directed by Alexis Neve, it's totally unamusing exploitation fare

title: Swingin' Stewardesses, The
synopsis: Director Michael Thomas turns a standard European travelogue into soft-core pornography in a badly dubbed, ridiculously inept, thoroughly tedious exploitation movie

title: Swing Kids
synopsis: The friendship of two music-loving adolescents (Robert Sean Leonard and Christian Bale) in 1939 Hamburg is savagely torn apart when they reluctantly join the Hitler Youth and one buys into the racist Nazi philosophy. Despite its good intentions, director Thomas Carter's manipulative drama is a thoroughly artificial-looking Hollywood version of anti-Semitism in pre-war Germany. Some stylized violence, racial and ethnic slurs and an instance of rough language

title: Swing Shift
synopsis: Young housewife (Goldie Hawn) takes a job in an aircraft factory after her husband (Ed Harris) enlists in the Navy at the start of World War II. Making friends with an independent young woman (Christine Lahti), she eventually falls into an affiar with a personable young man exempt from service (Kurt Russell). Directed by Jonathan Demme, the flawed but superbly acted and often quite moving movie recaptures the hopes and fears, the aspirations and idealism of a now vanished era. Though sympathetic in its depiction of adulterous conduct, it clearly shows that adultery is harmful. Occasional rough language

title: Swing Time
synopsis: Down-on-his-luck hoofer (Fred Astaire) rides the rails to New York City, teams with a comely dance instructor (Ginger Rogers) and they score as the town's top dancing duo in such numbers as "Waltz in Swing Time" and Astaire's solo showstopper, "Bojangles of Harlem." Director George Stevens keeps the pair's romantic misunderstandings light and lively, gets strong comic relief from Victor Moore and Helen Broderick and effortlessly stages such songs as "A Fine Romance" and "The Way You Look Tonight." Elegant entertainment for all but the very young

title: Swiss Family Robinson
synopsis: Good Disney version of the classic adventure about a shipwrecked family (headed by John Mills and Dorothy McGuire) living in a tree house on a deserted island learning to survive offers an engrossing picture of family devotion and solidarity. Nicely directed by Ken Annakin, much of the fun for children will come from the delightful and inventive conveniences the family builds and their relationships with the island's wildlife including an elepant, turtle and ostrich

title: Swiss Miss
synopsis: As American boobs selling mouse traps in Switzerland, Stan Laurel and Oliver Hardy provoke some smiles in a bland story about the misunderstandings between a Viennese composer (Walter Woolf King) and his leading singer (Della Lind). Directed by John G. Blystone, the comedy involves Stan and Ollie with an irascible cook, a faithful St. Bernard, a bubbly pipe organ and a perplexed gorilla on a Alpine footbridge

title: Switch
synopsis: Murdered by a trio of his enraged ex-lovers, an incorrigible male chauvinist (Perry King) is returned to earth as a female (Ellen Barkin) to mend his ways or it's hell for him. Writer-director Blake Edwards' one-joke comedy does not sustain the humor beyond obvious, vulgar situations and its contrived, last-minute pro-life message is thoroughly unconvincing. Blatant sexist attitudes, barroom brawls played for laughs, recurring rough language, frequent sexual innuendo, some recreational substance abuse and brief nudity

title: Switchback
synopsis: Grim thriller in which a relentless FBI agent (Dennis Quaid) tracks a cunning serial killer (Danny Glover) who has kidnapped the agent's child while on a cross-country killing spree. Glover's chilling portrayal of an unpredictable psychopath helps compensate for the far-fetched plotting in writer-director Jeb Stuart's somewhat gory tale. Intermittent violence, nude pin-up photos and occasional profanity

title: Switching Channels
synopsis: Failed adaptation of "The Front Page," updated to a 1980's TV newsroom, tracks the love-hate relationship between a star newswoman (Kathleen Turner) and her ex-husband boss (Burt Reynolds), with a foppish lover (Christopher Reeve) in the wings. Weak chemistry between lead actors and clumsy direction by Ted Kotcheff. Some rough language

title: Swoon
synopsis: Bizarre, arty dramatization of the 1924 Leopold-and-Loeb murder case stars Craig Chester and Daniel Schlachet as college students convicted of the thrill-killing of a young Chicago boy. Looking like an extended music video, writer-director Tom Kalin's low-budget movie is more concerned with playing up the homophobic and anti-Semitic prejudices of the 1920s than in offering a balanced or insightful examination of the crime and its consequences. A few discreet homosexual bedroom shots, two off-camera murders and minimal rough language

title: Sword in the Desert
synopsis: Small but effective melodrama in which a U.S. sea captain (Dana Andrews) smuggles a group of refugees into 1947 Palestine, then gets caught up in the Jewish underground's struggle against the British forces controlling the country. Directed by George Sherman, the picture contrasts the idealism of the underground fighters (Jeff Chandler, Stephen McNally, Marta Toren and Liam Redmond) with the captain's initial cynicism which by story's end has been transformed in the good will of Christmas Eve on the road to Bethlehem. Stylized violence

title: Sword in the Stone, The
synopsis: Disney cartoon version of the Arthurian legend of a young squire who, with the help of a wizard, becomes the king of England by pulling a sword from a boulder. Directed by Wolfgang Reitherman and featuring the voices of Sebastian Cabot, Karl Swenson and Rickie Sorenson, the movie is pleasant viewing for children but offers little for older members of the family

title: Sydney White
synopsis: Quirky campus comedy in which an irrepressible tomboy (Amanda Bynes) leaves her home and widowed father (John Schneider) for college, pledges her late mother's sorority with the support of a fellow initiate (Crystal Hunt) and despite the hostility of its snooty president (Sara Paxton), but ultimately finds her true role as housemother and guiding spirit of "the Vortex," a ramshackle dorm occupied by seven of her school's most marginalized students -- including an endearing panallergic student (Jack Carpenter) and a socially inept genius (Jeremy Howard) -- and as the girlfriend of a surprisingly generous fraternity brother (Matt Long). The clever re-imagining of a venerable fairy tale (the title is a hint), director Joe Nussbaum's film is for the most part an appealingly innocent romance that also possesses a commendable set of moral values. Some crass language, some innuendo, implied nudity, alcohol use, brief gay references and a transvestite poet. Such elements may make the film unsuitable for younger teens
full_review:
"We're all dorks!" That's the reassuring message of "Sydney White" (Universal), a quirky campus comedy about an irrepressible tomboy who becomes the guiding spirit of a group of outcasts at her college.

As raised by her widowed plumber father (John Schneider), Sydney White (Amanda Bynes) is a young lady with a good deal of self-confidence and no airs. Yet she leaves home for college hoping to join the prestigious sorority to which her late mother once belonged.

Sydney soon gains the support of another sorority pledge, Dinky (Crystal Hunt), and of Tyler (Matt Long), a fraternity brother who's quickly smitten with her. Tyler's ex-girlfriend, the snooty sorority president, Rachel (Sara Paxton), on the other hand, is far from impressed. She eventually manages to sabotage Sydney's application for membership, and sends her into social exile.

With nowhere on campus to live, Sydney turns to the residents of "the Vortex," a ramshackle dorm populated by seven of the school's most marginalized students. These collegiate underdogs -- typified by the endearing, panallergic Lenny (Jack Carpenter) and the socially inept, intellectually eccentric Terrence (Jeremy Howard) -- take her in, and she rapidly becomes their housemother and champion.

Questioned about the state of their living quarters, her new friends explain to Sydney that the student council, of which Rachel is also president, is entirely controlled by, and run for the benefit of, the campus's Greek letter societies. But nothing can be done, they assure her, because no one can unseat Rachel. Even as her romance with Tyler continues, Sydney decides to find out if that's true.

The clever re-imagining of a venerable fairy tale (the title is a tip-off as to which one), director Joe Nussbaum's film is for the most part an appealingly innocent romance. It also possesses a commendable set of moral values.

These are best exemplified in a scene which comes as a surprise both to Sydney and to the audience, revealing as it does an unexpectedly generous aspect of Tyler's character. At other points in the film, Tyler also shows himself to be vulnerable, sympathetic and tolerant.

These qualities, and Sydney's positive response to them, form the basis of a relationship that is not only idyllic, but mature and enduring as well. And therein lies the promise of a genuinely happy ending.

The film contains some crass language, some innuendo, implied nudity, alcohol use, brief gay references and a transvestite poet. Such elements may make the film unsuitable for younger teens. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Sylvester
synopsis: The story of a girl and her horse. Good acting by Me1issa Gi1bert and Richard Farnsworth as a gruff but lovable trainer, but little e1se to recommend this cliched tale directed by Tim Hunter. Vulgar language, a graphic near-rape and implied premarital sex propel the narrative out of its romantic framework

title: Sylvia Scarlett
synopsis: > Hepburn masqueraded as a boy, with co-star Cary Grant as a Cockney con-artist in this film which has since developed a cult following. Directed by Cukor, the offbeat comedy also stars Edmund Gwenn as Hepburn�s father and Brian Aherne

title: Symphony for a Massacre
synopsis: Low-budget but well-executed French crime story of five thieves trying to figure out which among them is responsible for stealing their loot. Director Jacques Deray works out the serio-comic plot neatly with fine performances from Michel Auclair, Claude Dauphin and Charles Vanel. Subtitles. Stylized violence and sexual situations

title: Synanon
synopsis: Edmond O'Brien, Chuck Connors, Eartha Kitt and Richard Conte star in a movie about the work of Synanon House, a haven for the cure of drug addiction near Santa Monica, California. Directed by Richard Quine, the movie's problem lies in exploiting too many side stories to the detriment of making understandable the problems with which it deals

title: Synecdoche, New York
synopsis: Surreal, pessimistic drama in which a theater director (Philip Seymour Hoffman), deserted by his artist wife (Catherine Keener), endlessly rehearses a constantly expanding autobiographical play while battling bizarre illnesses and seeking emotional fulfillment from his second spouse (Michelle Williams) and an on-again-off-again lover (Samantha Morton). Writer Charlie Kaufman's directorial debut, an ambitious meditation on life, love, creativity and death, though impressively acted -- especially by Hoffman -- makes only sporadic references to faith and presents both artistic and personal failure as inevitable. Strong sexual content, including brief graphic sexual activity, adultery, rear and upper female nudity, frequent rough and some crude language, a few uses of profanity and a suicide

title: Syriana
synopsis: Intermittently engaging but mostly confusing political thriller which explores corruption in the international oil industry through a mosaic of interlocking stories involving: a veteran CIA operative (George Clooney); a reform-minded Arab sheik (Alexander Siddig); an energy analyst (Matt Damon) grieving the death of his son, and a Washington lawyer (Jeffrey Wright), hired to facilitate a shady merger between two Texas oil giants. Directed with unvarnished realism by Stephen Gaghan, the well-acted film touches on important moral questions about the global pursuit of wealth, but strains for narrative coherence under the weight of its convoluted multiple plots. Strong violence, including a graphic scene of torture, and some rough language and profanity
full_review:
In his "Poetics," Aristotle argued that works of drama should, ideally, have a unity of time, place and action. Translated, that means a tight, focused story is better than one that goes off in too many directions, which is precisely the problem with "Syriana" (Warner Bros.), an ambitious, intermittently involving, but mostly confusing political thriller about corruption in the international oil industry.

Written and directed by Stephen Gaghan, "Syriana" -- Washington insider speak for a hypothetical reshaping of the Middle East -- is set against the backdrop of a fictional petroleum-rich Gulf nation.

As in his Oscar-winning screenplay for "Traffic," Gaghan interweaves multiple stories to create a kaleidoscope of greed and intrigue.

The main players include: Bob Barnes (George Clooney), a veteran CIA operative whose loyalty is repaid by betrayal; Prince Nasir (Alexander Siddig), the reform-minded heir apparent of an oil-rich emir; Bryan Woodman (Matt Damon), an energy analyst who becomes entangled in Nasir's dealings through personal tragedy; Bennett Holiday (Jeffrey Wright), a Washington lawyer hired to facilitate a shady merger between two Texas oil giants; and Wasim (Mazhar Munir), a young Pakistani migrant worker recruited by a militant Muslim cleric, after he and his father are laid off from one of Nasir's refineries.

If the narrative wasn't congested enough, there's also an estranged father-son relationship between Barnes and his teenage son (Max Minghella); and Holiday and his boozing father (William C. Mitchell).

Rounding out the overcrowded cast are Christopher Plummer, Chris Cooper, Amanda Peet and William Hurt, all in underwritten roles.

When the disjointed story lines finally dovetail, the result is as unsatisfying as it is improbable.

On a positive note, the ensemble's performances are top-notch across the board -- especially Clooney, who deserves credit for continually choosing interesting roles and not coasting on his matinee-idol looks, packing on 30 pounds for the part.

The documentary-style camerawork by Robert Elswit gives "Syriana" an unvarnished realism and enhances the visceral tension of several scenes, including an intense kidnapping and interrogation sequence not for the faint of heart. The film's Middle East locations also contribute to its overall visual verisimilitude. (It is the first major Western film allowed to shoot in Dubai.)

The film's cynical tone is best illustrated in a scene in which a character lectures Holiday on how "corruption is our protection. Corruption is what keeps us safe and warm."
Making movies with mosaic narratives is nothing new. From D.W. Griffith's "Intolerance" (1915) to this year's "Crash," filmmakers have employed a patchwork approach to explore complex stories and issues from various perspectives.

Gaghan has been quoted as saying that interlocking story lines provided the different points of view that the subject matter demanded. But while touching on important moral and social justice questions involving the global pursuit of wealth, the film loses much of its emotional impact by not having a strong central protagonist with whom to empathize.

In contrast, movies like "Schindler's List" and "Hotel Rwanda" worked well because they told their stories through one character, thereby making complicated topics -- the Holocaust and the Rwandan genocide -- accessible and personal.

The film contains strong violence, including a graphic scene of torture, and some rough language and profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
