synopsis: Overblown Western in which an ex-Reb (Clark Gable) and his nasty brother (Cameron Mitchell) join a rancher (Robert Ryan) on a cattle drive from Texas to Montana during which they battle blizzards, Sioux attacks and misunderstandings over a woman (Jane Russell) rescued along the way. Directed by Raoul Walsh, the formula story bogs down in cliched action and stereotyped characters, with unsurprising results. Frontier violence and sexual situations

title: Tall Story
synopsis: Romantic fluff from the Howard Lindsay-Russel Crouse play in which a serious-minded college basketball star (Anthony Perkins) proves no match for a conniving, marriage-minded co-ed (Jane Fonda). Produced and directed by Joshua Logan, the thin proceedings generate few laughs in poking fun at college athletics, hypocritical academics and students' raging hormones. Sexual situations and innuendo

title: Tall Stranger, The
synopsis: Murky Western directed by Thomas Carr in which a Union officer (Joel McCrea) returning home after the Civil War is saved from a bushwacker (Michael Ansara) by a wagon train of settlers whom he in turn saves from being massacred in a war between a Colorado cattle baron and a ruthless band of rustlers. Shootouts, fist-fights, a woman fighting off an attacker and an endangered child

title: Tall Tale: The Unbelievable Adventures of Pecos Bill
synopsis: Largely unimaginative fantasy-adventure set the West of 1905 where a 12 year-old boy (Nick Stahl) conjures up a trio of legendary folk heroes (Patrick Swayze, Oliver Platt and Roger Aaron Brown) to save the family farm from villainous land grabbers. Director Jeremiah Chechik's scenic yarn features trite preachments about family values although the narrative often resorts to brawn and bullets to solve problems. Frequent stylized violence and fleeting sexual innuendo

title: Tall Target, The
synopsis: Engrossing thriller set in 1861 aboard a Washington-bound train as New York City detective John Kennedy (Dick Powell) tries to thwart an assassination plot to kill President-elect Lincoln. Director Anthony Mann keeps the suspense tight and the period details add interest, but the ending is a bit of a let-down. Stylized violence

title: Tall T, The
synopsis: Credible Western in which a cowboy (Randolph Scott) foils the plans of ruthless stagecoach bandits (Richard Boone, Henry Silva and Skip Homeier) to ransom a mine owner's daughter (Maureen O'Sullivan). Director Budd Boetticher establishes the murderous nature of the bandits early on, then builds the tension while waiting for the ransom until the cowboy takes on the trio in the final shootout. Stylized violence and menace

title: Tall Women, The
synopsis: Spanish Western directed by Sidney Pink about a wagon train of women facing hostile Indians on the wild frontier has excessive violence and sexual innuendo

title: Tamarind Seed, The
synopsis: Russian spy (Omar Sharif) falls in love with a secretary in the British Foreign Office (Julie Andrews) and their romance becomes hopelessly entangled in international intrigue. Directed by Blake Edwards, its fine cast and gorgeous location photography are wasted by a script that misses both as love story and as spy thriller

title: Taming of the Shrew, The
synopsis: Sparkling but noisy adaptation of the Shakespeare play with bravura performances by Elizabeth Taylor as the comely shrew and Richard Burton as the rowdy tamer. Director Franco Zeffirelli's inventive staging preserves the flavor of the orginal but never seems firmly in control of the action or the actors. Mature treatment

title: Tam Lin
synopsis: Domineering, aging millionairess (Ava Gardner), living on a sinister Scottish estate with a coven of coed decadents, keeps her current paramour (Ian McShane) in line by showing him a few grisly snapshots of what happened to past lovers whose attentions wandered. Hothouse melodrama is best summed up as a soggy misfire by novice director Roddy McDowall

title: Tammy and the Bachelor
synopsis: Sappy romantic comedy in which the innocent teenager of the title (Debbie Reynolds), raised by her grandfather (Walter Brennan) in a bayou backwater, knocks the socks off the scion (Leslie Nielsen) of a once-wealthy family. Directed by Joseph Pevney, the silly situation and insufferable homespun wisdom of the heroine were stale then and haven't gotten any fresher since. Sugary confection not for all tastes

title: Tammy and the Doctor
synopsis: The third outing of the homespun lass from the Mississippi bayous sees Tammy (Sandra Dee) as a nurse's aide spreading her country wisdom among the staff (Peter Fonda, Macdonald Carey and Margaret Lindsay) and patients (Beulah Bondi and Reginald Owen) of a Los Angeles hospital. Directed by Harry Keller, the hokey script offers bland situations and plenty of bogus sentimentality, though youngsters may be amused by the silly goings-on

title: Tammy Tell Me True
synopsis: This time around Tammy (Sandra Dee) hikes across the swamp to enroll in a nearby college where she helps a rich old lady (Beulah Bondi), saves the marriage of a dean (Virginia Grey) and snags a bemused professor (John Gavin). Director Harry Keller's sugary concoction of contrived situations mistakes the virtue of simplicity for the bane of banality. Bland family fare

title: Tampico
synopsis: Minor World War II espionage thriller in which the captain (Edward G. Robinson) of an oil tanker marries a survivor (Lynn Bari) of a torpedoed ship, then suspects she's a Nazi agent. Directed by Lothar Mendes, there's little action and the identity of the traitor is wildly implausible. Wartime violence

title: Tampopo
synopsis: Wry Japanese satire in which a young widow's unsuccessful noodle business is transformed by a burly truck driver is laced with comic asides relating food to passion, commerce and art. Director Juzo Itami's droll, earthy farce has several sexually suggestive scenes, one with partial nudity, which mars the basically innocent appeal of the story

title: Tanganyika
synopsis: Far-fetched adventure directed by Andre de Toth is set in 1903 British East Africa where an American timber contractor (Van Heflin) goes after an escaped killer (Jeff Morrow) who's behind a native revolt, but the manhunt is slowed in rescuing a wounded traveler (Howard Duff) and the survivors of a massacre (Ruth Roman and two children). Stylized violence

title: Tango Bar
synopsis: Beautifully filmed and choreographed anthology of tango dancing set in Argentina and framed by the personal and political musings of a fictional trio of cabaret performers (Raul Julia, Ruben Juarez and Valeria Lynch). Keeping the love triangle and repressive politics in the background, Puerto Rican director Marcos Zurinaga concentrates on the trio's songs and monologues about the history and evolution of the tango as well as staging some breathtaking tango numbers plus clips of tango dancing from Hollywood and foreign movies. Subtitles. Implied sexual relationships

title: Tango & Cash
synopsis: Ultraviolent supercop saga featuring an unlikely pair of Los Angeles detectives (Sylvester Stallone and Kurt Russell) who dislike each other's style but wind up working together to nail the criminal mastermind (Jack Palance) behind their being framed for murder. Directed by Andrei Konchalovsky, the result is a sophomoric exercise in rock'em-sock'em macho violence and bloodletting. Excessive violence, insulting sexual references and rough language

title: Tank
synopsis: Career Army sergeant uses a Sherman tank to rescue his unjustly arrested son from a vicious southern sheriff (G.D. Spradlin) and then heads for the state line stirring the sympathy of the nation. Audience reaction to director Marvin Chomsky's movie is likely to be much less spectacular because after the breakout, the story becomes increasingly silly and unentertaining. Some violence and rough language

title: Tank Force
synopsis: World War II clunker directed by Terence Young is set in the Libyan Desert where some captured Australian soldiers (notably Victor Mature, Leo Genn and Anthony Newley) make their escape, then are recaptured by pro-German Arab nomads, only to escape again. The wartime violence makes it unlikely children's fare

title: Tanks Are Coming, The
synopsis: Formula World War II tale directed by Lewis Seiler in which a hot-shot platoon leader (Steve Cochran) in an American tank unit battling its way through France is roundly hated by his men but, by the time they cross the Siegfried Line into Germany, they realize his harsh methods have saved their lives by making them better soldiers. Wartime violence

title: Tap
synopsis: An entertaining look at the redemption of a talented tap dancer (Gregory Hines) who took a wrong turn and must choose between a potentially low-paying, rewarding career as a dancer and a lucrative life of crime. Writer-director Nick Castle creates a respectful tribute to this American artform and is especially mindful of tap's black roots. A lusty kissing scene, brief heavily shadowed nudity within a fleeting sexual encounter and some locker room language

title: Tape
synopsis: Absorbing drama set in a seedy motel room in which a bitter slacker (Ethan Hawke) confronts an old friend (Robert Sean Leonard) about stealing and possibly having raped his high school girlfriend (Uma Thurman). Set in real time, director Richard Linklater's caustic film contemplates the nature of truth, particularly on sexual matters, but the conclusion's drawn out proceedings become a bit draining. Sporadic drug use, a brief scuffle and much rough language and profanity

title: Taps
synopsis: Highminded teenage cadets take control of a military boarding school when they learn the authorities are going to close it. George C. Scott does his usual fine job as the officer who inspires the boys to make their stand and Timothy Hutton is good as the insurgent leader. Directed by Harold Becker, the rather implausible youth-in-revolt drama fails to make its story of courage and leadership very credible. Some violence and coarse language

title: Tarantula
synopsis: Effective monster fantasy in which a scientist (Leo G. Carroll) experimenting on a growth nutrient becomes grotesquely disfigured, then dies while a spider injected with the nutrient escapes into the Arizona desert, grows bigger than a house and heads for town until stopped by the local doctor (John Agar) and some jet fighters. Director Jack Arnold gets plenty of menace from the low-budget production, though the scientific experiments at the beginning are more frightening than the rampages of the special-effects monster. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Target
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Stuart Gilmore in which a couple of cowboy straight-shooters (Tim Holt and Richard Martin) bust up a gang of railroad landgrabbers in 1893 Texas. Stylized violence

title: Target
synopsis: A middle-aged father (Gene Hackman) gains the admiration of his son (Matt Dillon) when his wife (Gayle Hunnicutt) is kidnapped on a European trip, and dull o1d Dad, who has a secret CIA past, becomes transformed into a superagent as the two attempt to find Mom. Directed by Arthur Penn but so preposterous that it skirts parody in spots, it is, nonetheless, entertaining fantasy fare, especially for fathers weary of feeling 1ike Rodney Dangerfield. A bit of rough language and some violence

title: Targets
synopsis: Modest crime thriller concerning a psychopathic killer (Tim O'Kelly) on the loose with an arsenal of weapons and a retired movie actor (Boris Karloff) who confront each other in a drive-in movie theater. Written and directed by Peter Bogdanovich, the contrast between the horror of reality and that of fantasy don't quite come off, partly because Karloff in his few scenes steals the film. Some stylized violence but no insights

title: Target Unknown
synopsis: Standard World War II tale of a 1944 B-26 bomber crew (led by Mark Stevens) whose German captors (led by Robert Douglas) use devious means to learn of an upcoming raid. Directed by George Sherman, the cat-and-mouse game between German interrogators and U.S. airmen holds interest until the Americans escape in a melodramatic attempt to use the French underground to contact their airbase and stop the raid. Wartime violence

title: Target Zero
synopsis: Contrived Korean War story in which a U.S. infantry patrol (led by Richard Conte) comes across a nurse (Peggy Castle) as well as a British tank while fighting their way back through enemy lines. Director Harmon Jones plods through an unconvincing plot whose wartime heroics aren't helped much by pretentious dialogue and an improbable romance. Battlefield violence

title: Tartu
synopsis: ( see: "The Adventures of Tartu" )

title: Tarzan
synopsis: Ferocious animated tale about an orphaned human baby raised by a jungle gorilla (voice of Glenn Close) who as an adult (voice of Tony Goldywn) encounters his first humans, including a duplicitous hunter (voice of Brian Blessed) intent on capturing his beloved ape family and spunky Jane (voice of Minnie Driver), who tempts Tarzan to return to civilization. Based on Edgar Rice Burrough's characters dating back to 1912, the animation by directors Kevin Lima and Chris Buck is accomplished and the characters appealing, but several fast-paced action scenes of predatory violence are too intense for younger children. Intensely menacing hunting scenes

title: Tarzan and His Mate
synopsis: Dandy sequel to 1932's "Tarzan, the Ape Man" concerns the return of the safari guide (Neil Hamilton) to the African escarpment hoping to bring Jane (Maureen O'Sullivan) back to civilization, though his partner (Paul Kavanagh) wants only the ivory in the elephant's graveyard and shoots Tarzan (Johnny Weissmuller) to get it. Directed by Cedric Gibbons, the jungle adventure features battles with fierce native tribes, animals ranging from friendly to murderous and the contentment of the loving couple in their primitive paradise. Stylized violence, incidental nudity, sexual innuendo and African stereotyping

title: Tarzan and the Amazons
synopsis: Thin jungle adventure directed by Kurt Neumann in which Boy (Johnny Sheffield) guides an archaeologist (Henry Stephenson) to a lost city of women warriors whose priestess (Maria Ouspenskaya) spares their lives, then greedy expedition members (Barton MacLane and J.M. Kerrigan) loot the city until Tarzan (Johnny Weissmuller) comes to the rescue. Stylized violence

title: Tarzan and the Great River
synopsis: Tarzan (Mike Henry) journeys to the upper reaches of the Amazon to put a halt to some occult goings-on by a tribe of headhunting terrorists. Directed by Robert Day, it's an exciting enough adventure, if all-too-familiar for older members of the family

title: Tarzan and the Green Goddess
synopsis: Slap-dash feature version of a serial directed by Edward Kull with Tarzan (Herman Brix aka Bruce Bennett) in the jungles of Guatemala trying to recover a sacred Mayan idol in which is hidden the formula for a super-explosive. Hokey stylized violence

title: Tarzan and the Huntress
synopsis: Formula jungle adventure directed by Kurt Neumann in which Tarzan (Johnny Weissmuller) saves Jane (Brenda Joyce) and Boy (Johnny Sheffield) from the murderous guide (Barton MacLane) of a zoological expedition that has far exceeded its agreed quota of animal specimens. Stylized violence and mild sexual innuendo

title: Tarzan and the Jungle Boy
synopsis: Newspaperwoman comes looking for a youngster lost years before in the jungle and runs into a slew of obstacles, including some unfriendly natives (led by Rafter Johnson). Tarzan (Mike Henry) flexes his muscles and puts everything right in director Robert Day's routine adventure

title: Tarzan and the Leopard Woman
synopsis: Formula jungle adventure directed by Kurt Neumann in which Tarzan (Johnny Weissmuller), Jane (Brenda Joyce) and Boy (Johnny Sheffield) are taken captive by a murderous leopard cult led by a woman (Acquanetta) fighting colonial rule, with Cheetah coming to the rescue for a Samson-like finale. Stylized violence and threatening situations

title: Tarzan and the Lost City
synopsis: Lackluster tale teams the Ape Man (Casper Van Dien) with his fiancee (Jane March) as they help a jungle tribe prevent a band of mercenaries from plundering their sacred treasures. Directed by Carl Schenkel, the tame, humorless movie has little sense of adventure but plenty of beefcake shots of the title actor. Sporadic stylized violence

title: Tarzan and the Lost Safari
synopsis: Standard jungle adventure directed by Bruce Humberstone has Tarzan (Gordon Scott) save the five occupants of a downed airplane from being turned over to a hostile tribe by a greedy hunter (Robert Beatty). Stylized violence

title: Tarzan and the Mermaids
synopsis: Exotic adventure directed by Robert Florey in which Johnny Weissmuller makes his 12th and final appearance as Tarzan, this time rescuing a woman (Linda Christian) from the high priest (George Zucco) of a bogus god worshipped by her island people until the Ape Man reveals their "god" is only a greedy mortal after their pearls. Stylized violence

title: Tarzan and the She-Devil
synopsis: Formula jungle adventure directed by Kurt Neumann with Tarzan (Lex Barker) saving Jane (Joyce MacKenzie) and a herd of elephants from nasty ivory poachers (Raymond Burr, Tom Conway and Monique Van Vooren). Stylized violence

title: Tarzan and the Slave Girl
synopsis: Hokey jungle adventure directed by Lee Sholem in which Tarzan (Lex Barker) tracks some kidnapped women to a hidden city where he frees the captives while saving Jane (Vanessa Brown) and a jungle nurse (Denise Darcel) from being entombed alive, then helps a doctor (Arthur Shields) cure the city of a deadly disease. Stylized violence and brutality

title: Tarzan and the Trappers
synopsis: Pulp adventure directed by Charles Haas and Sandy Howard in which Tarzan (Gordon Scott) captures a poacher, then thwarts a greedy group of treasure hunters seeking a lost city. Comic-book heroics with hokey violence

title: Tarzan and the Valley of Gold
synopsis: Standard jungle adventure directed by Robert Day with Tarzan (Mike Henry) getting involved with some spies

title: Tarzan Escapes
synopsis: Familiar African adventure in which Jane (Maureen O'Sullivan) is visited by London cousins who want her to return with them just long enough to collect her inheritance, but their guide (John Buckler) is more interested in capturing Tarzan and selling him as a side-show attraction. Directed by Richard Thorpe, a number of previous encounters with animals and native tribes are reused here with the new storyline woven around them with agreeable results. Stylized violence

title: Tarzan Finds a Son!
synopsis: Enjoyable adventure in which Tarzan (Johnny Weissmuller) and Jane (Maureen O'Sullivan) rescue a baby boy from a crashed airplane, then five years later have to save him (Johnnie Sheffield) from greedy relatives (Ian Hunter and Frieda Inescort) after his inheritance. Director Richard Thorpe paces the sunny scenes of happy jungle life with the harsh realities of the wild and the deceit of civilized outsiders. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Tarzan Goes to India
synopsis: Formula adventure featuring picturesque Indian locales where Tarzan (Jock Mahoney) befriends an orphaned boy, then uses the lad's elephant to lead a herd of rogue elephants through a mountain pass before they are drowned by the opening of a new dam. Directed by John Guillermin, the pedestrian plot has scant interest save for the scenery and the thundering herd of elephants. Some stylized violence

title: Tarzan's Deadly Silence
synopsis: The Ape Man (Ron Ely), despite being temporarily deafened by an explosion, saves a native tribe from the exploitation of a megalomaniac trying to set up a jungle empire. Directed by Robert L. Friend, it's the usual wilderness adventure, though fans may be disappointed that there is no Jane and no blood-curdling jungle call. Directed by Robert L. Friend

title: Tarzan's Desert Mystery
synopsis: Routine adventure in which Tarzan (Johnny Weissmuller) and Boy (Johnny Sheffield) save a woman magician (Nancy Kelly) from Nazi agents (Otto Kruger and Joe Sawyer), avert a war between desert tribes and fight off a giant spider while gathering medicinal plants requested by Jane, now an Army nurse. Directed by William Thiele, the contrived proceedings plod along rather aimlessy until the predictable ending

title: Tarzan's Fight for Life
synopsis: Formula jungle adventure directed by Bruce Humberstone with Tarzan (Gordon Scott) helping a dedicated white doctor save his bush hospital from a tribal witch doctor (James Edwards) and a renegade band of warriors (led by Woody Strode). Stylized violence

title: Tarzan's Greatest Adventure
synopsis: Routine action adventure filmed in Africa with an articulate Tarzan (Gordon Scott) tracking a band of killers (Anthony Quayle, Niall MacGinnis and Sean Connery) on their way to a hidden diamond mine. Directed by John Guillermin, the proceedings are rather sluggish until the action heats up in a fairly nasty showdown. Stylized violence and psychopathic criminals

title: Tarzan's Hidden Jungle
synopsis: Standard adventure directed by Harold Schuster with Tarzan (Gordon Scott) saving a U.N. doctor (Peter Van Eyck) and his nurse (Vera Miles) from an unfriendly tribe (headed by Rex Ingram) stirred up by murderous poachers (led by Jack Elam). Stylized violence and mild sexual innuendo

title: Tarzan's Jungle Rebellion
synopsis: Archaeologist (Sam Jaffe) searching for a lost civilization, a native looking for a sacred statue to establish his rule over the jungle and a group simply after gold come up against the lord of the jungle (Ron Ely). Director William Whitney follows the formula without much conviction

title: Tarzan's Magic Fountain
synopsis: Fanciful jungle adventure directed by Lee Sholem in which Tarzan (Lex Barker) tries to keep greedy outsiders (Albert Dekker and Charles Drake) from finding a hidden mountain city whose waters restore youth and heal the sick, though Jane (Brenda Joyce) complicates matters by trying to guide an aviatrix (Evelyn Ankers) and her husband (Alan Napier) there. Stylized violence

title: Tarzan's New York Adventure
synopsis: Enterprising series entry with Tarzan (Johnny Weissmuller), Jane (Maureen O'Sullivan) and Chita off to New York to find Boy (Johnny Sheffield) after he's abducted from the escarpment to perform in a circus. Directed by Richard Thorpe, Tarzan takes civilization in stride as he climbs down a skyscraper's exterior, dives off the Brooklyn Bridge and leads a troop of circus elephants to the rescue. Menacing situations

title: Tarzan's Peril
synopsis: Routine jungle adventure in which Tarzan (Lex Barker) rescues an African queen (Dorothy Dandridge) and her people from a warring tribe, then hunts down the villain (George Macready) who sold them rifles and has taken Jane (Virginia Huston) hostage. Directed by Byron Haskin, the movie drags between action sequences, though Barker's Tarzan is a rather personable fellow. Stylized violence

title: Tarzan's Revenge
synopsis: Routine jungle adventure with Tarzan (Glenn Morris) rescuing a woman (Eleanor Holm) on safari with her parents (George Barbier and Hedda Hopper) from an Arab prince (C. Henry Gordon) who has paid the safari guide (Joe Sawyer) to kidnap her. Directed by D. Ross Lederman, the situations are more humorous than dangerous, though there's a tense battle on a rope bridge across a chasm and by movie's end Tarzan has found a mate. Some stylized violence

title: Tarzan's Savage Fury
synopsis: Formula jungle adventure directed by Cyril Endfield in which Jane (Dorothy Hart) persuades Tarzan (Lex Barker) to guide a thief (Patric Knowles) posing as his cousin, Lord Greystoke, across the desert to the land of a fierce tribe rich in diamonds. Stylized violence

title: Tarzan's Secret Treasure
synopsis: Routine jungle adventure directed by Richard Thorpe in which Tarzan (Johnny Weissmuller) has to save Jane (Maureen O'Sullivan) and Boy (Johnny Sheffield) after they're kidnapped by a ruthless gold hunter (Tom Conway), then captured by a savage tribe. Stylized violence

title: Tarzan's Three Challenges
synopsis: Exotic adventure with Tarzan (Jock Mahoney) leaving Africa for Thailand where he saves the young boy chosen by Buddhist monks to be the country's spiritual leader from being killed by the king's wicked brother (Woody Strode). Directed by Robert Day, the Thai locales are a welcome change to the usual jungle setting, though the action remains much the same. Stylized violence

title: Tarzan the Ape Man
synopsis: Director Joseph M. Newman's flat and unengaging remake of the 1932 original features a lethargic performance by Dennis Miller in the title role and an anemic portrayal of Jane by Johanna Barnes. Stale wildlife adventure

title: Tarzan, the Ape Man
synopsis: Embarrassingly inept version of the jungle hero's adventures with Miles O'Keeffe in the title role, Bo Derek in various stages of undress and the ape in the cast the only character to emerge with any dignity from a debacle directed by John Derek

title: Tarzan the Fearless
synopsis: Feature version of a serial directed by Robert F. Hill in which a woman (Jacqueline Wells) on a safari to find her missing father is saved from Arab slavers by Tarzan (Buster Crabbe) who then rescues her father from a vengeful priest (Mischa Auer) guarding the statue of an Egyptian god whose fingers are embedded with priceless emeralds. Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Tarzan the Magnificent
synopsis: Standard action adventure directed by Robert Day in which Tarzan (Gordon Scott) captures a killer (Jock Mahoney) in the jungles of Kenya and, despite ambushes by his murderous father (John Carradine) and three brothers, takes him and some stranded travellers (notably Lionel Jeffries, Betta St. John and Alexandra Stewart) to the nearest police post. Stylized violence, some of it quite nasty

title: Tarzan Triumphs
synopsis: World War II adventure in which Tarzan (Johnny Weissmuller) and Boy (Johnny Sheffield) help a woman (Frances Gifford) free her jungle village from Nazi paratroopers after oil and jewels. Directed by William Thiele, Tarzan kills a number of paratroopers without resorting to firearms, though Boy shoots one with a pistol and Cheetah uses a machine gun to get another. Stylized violence, including Nazi brutality

title: Task Force
synopsis: On the eve of his retirement, an admiral (Gary Cooper) recalls his part in the struggle after World War I to prove to the Navy the importance of aircraft carriers, his marriage to a fellow pilot's widow (Jane Wyatt) and his role in the battles of Midway and Okinawa. Written and directed by Delmer Daves, the personal story is most interesting in the early years of carrier development, then gets lost in the World War II battle scenes. Wartime violence and patriotic sloganeering

title: Taste the Black Earth
synopsis: Polish dramatization of the 1920 uprising against the Germans occupying the coal mining region of Silesia is shown through the eyes of a young lad who refuses to let his six older brothers go to battle without him. Written and directed by Kazimierz Kutz, the movie is less an historical narrative than a patriotic ballad told with great feeling, much visual poetry and emphasis on the absurdities of civilians pitted against soldiers

title: Taste the Blood of Dracula
synopsis: Disappointing British horror movie wastes its first half on a ridiculous club dabbling in sex and satanism while the remainder is routine-to-inferior vampire lore in which Dracula (Christopher Lee) has only one big scene. Directed by Peter Sasdy, it offers only some slack suspense and almost no psychological terror

title: Tatie Danielle
synopsis: Wickedly dark comedy about a sly 82-year-old widow (Tsilla Chelton) who moves in with her nephew's family and proceeds to make their lives miserable while appearing to be frail and helpless. French production directed by Etienne Chatiliez deftly blends wit and satire while questioning preconceptions about the elderly and skewering adults who patronize them. Subtitles. Occasional sexual innuendo, brief bedroom shot of a married couple and a few vulgar expressions

title: Tattered Dress, The
synopsis: Melodramatic clunker directed by Jack Arnold in which a top New York lawyer (Jeff Chandler) is charged by a vengeful Nevada cop (Jack Carson) with bribing a juror (Gail Russell) in a local murder case, with the outcome reuniting lawyer and estranged wife (Jeanne Crain). Some stylized violence and heavy sexual innuendo

title: Tattoo
synopsis: Bruce Dern plays a man obsessed with the mystique of tattooing who kidnaps model Maud Adams and proceeds to decorate her body with the fervor of a graffiti artist embroidering his own subway car, until the contrived plot suddenly turns perverted hero into expert lover. Directed by Bob Brooks, the dreary, pretentious story lacks any credible sense of logic. Some nudity and graphic sexuality

title: Tattooed Swordswoman, The
synopsis: Japanese Yakuza (gangster) movie about an imprisoned woman's dream which after her release comes back to haunt her. Director Teyuo Ishii's effort has more of interest than the usual spectacular swordplay because it vividly incorporates elements of supernatural horror within its traditional revenge plot

title: Taxi!
synopsis: Blue-collar tale of a hot-tempered New York cabbie (James Cagney) who marries the daughter (Loretta Young) of a cabdriver killed by a rival taxi company, then goes after the goon who did it, with unconvincing results. Director Roy Del Ruth projects the taxicab war with suitable gusto, but overdoes the cabbie's cocky violence, including knocking out the winner (George Raft) of a dance competition and belting his wife on occasion. Nasty stylized violence, muted sexual innuendo and tacked on moral ending

title: Taxi
synopsis: High-octane, low-wattage buddy comedy about a bumbling New York City cop (Jimmy Fallon) who enlists the aid of a speed-demon cab driver (Queen Latifah) to help him catch a gang of beautiful but deadly female bank robbers (led by Gisele Bundchen). Directed by Tim Story, this revved-up remake of a 1998 French film has a full tank of high-speed car chases, but is running on fumes when it comes to laughs. Recurring vehicular violence, two robberies, a sexually suggestive frisk sequence, crude language and an instance of profanity
full_review:
In the high-octane, low-wattage buddy comedy "Taxi" (20th Century Fox), Jimmy Fallon plays a bumbling New York City cop who enlists the aid of a sassy cab driver (played by Queen Latifah) to catch a gang of beautiful but deadly female bank robbers.

A revved-up remake of the 1998 French film written by Luc Besson, "Taxi" has a full tank of high-speed car chases, but is running on fumes when it comes to laughs.

The framing is simple: "Saturday Night Live" alum Fallon plays dunce detective Andy Washburn, whose traffic mishaps have made him the laughing stock of his precinct and have landed him in the doghouse of his beleaguered ex-girlfriend-turned-boss, Lt. Marta Robbins (Jennifer Esposito).

As punishment for crashing a car into a bodega during a failed sting operation, Andy has his driver's license revoked and is demoted to walking a beat. While responding to an armed robbery, he jumps into the back seat of a cab driven by Belle Williams (Latifah), a street-savvy speed demon with a souped-up taxi who dreams of being a race car driver.

They arrive at the crime scene just in time to pursue a quartet of scantily clad Brazilian bombshells, whose long-legged leader (played by supermodel Gisele Bundchen) -- in addition to being a crack shot -- shows she can match Belle skid for skid. With his badge on the line, Andy convinces the hell-on-wheels hack to help him nab the crooks.

From here on, "Taxi" shifts gears into a fast and furious game of cat-and-mouse, consisting of little else than a series of pedal-to-the-metal drag races through the streets of Manhattan (with little regard for pedestrians), as tedious as they are over the top. Director Tim Story puts the brakes on the rubber-burning action just long enough for some stale comic pit stops between its odd-couple leads (neither of whom you care much about).

Though wasting her talent on this limp material, Latifah is undeniably in the driver's seat, figuratively and literally. Fallon manically mugs his way through most of the film, rehashing the same tousle-haired goofy shtick he used on "Saturday Night Live." Ann-Margret provides some minor chuckles as Andy's alcoholic mother.

All in all, this is one "Taxi" ride not worth the fare.

Due to recurring vehicular violence, two robberies, a sexually suggestive frisk sequence, crude language and an instance of profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Taxi Blues
synopsis: Set in present-day Moscow, an embittered cabdriver (Pyotr Zaichenko) reluctantly befriends a self-destructive Jewish saxophone player (Pyotr Mamonov) whose alcoholism causes continual crises. Writer-director Pavel Longuine's character study of two vastly divergent personalities touches on class conflicts, alienation and anti-Semitism in Russia's troubled society with compassion, rude humor and unaccustomed frankness. Subtitles. Brief scene of fairly graphic sexual relations, partial nudity, minimal violence and vulgar expressions

title: Taxi Driver
synopsis: Disturbing portrait of a troubled New York cabby (Robert De Niro), apparently traumatized by service in Vietnam, lost in his macho fantasies and infatuated with a political worker (Cybill Shepherd) whose rejection triggers his suppressed rage into an orgy of killings. Director Martin Scorsese's excursion into urban alienation and irrational violence lacks a distancing objectivity and its attempts to shock are excessively graphic in scenes of bloodshed

title: Taxing Woman, A
synopsis: A woman tax collector (Nobuko Miyamoto) faces her biggest case in trying to crack the sleazy operation of an adult hotel scion (Tsutomu Yamazaki) which leads to various comical interactions. Director Juzo Itami delivers a sometimes amusing but overlong satire on tax evasion which in Japan apparently is fast becoming a national pastime. Subtitles. Several graphic sexual encounters with nudity, a brief sequence involving the physical battering of a woman and some rough language

title: Taxing Woman's Return, A
synopsis: Sequel picks up the career of the feisty Japanese tax inspector (Nobuko Miyamoto) as she investigates a bogus fundamentalist religious sect helmed by a charismatic influence peddler (Rentaro Mikuni). Written and directed by Juzo Itami, the sharp satire of Japanese tax crimes shows the conflicting roles of women in modern Japan and underscores how exploitative bogus "religions" can be. Some rough language, grisly violence and adultery

title: Taza, Son of Cochise
synopsis: Formula Western directed by Douglas Sirk has the title character (Rock Hudson) struggling to fulfill the peace treaty signed by his dead Apache father (uncredited Jeff Chandler) while his younger brother (Bart Roberts) conspires to join a warring band of Apaches led by Geronimo. Frontier violence and Indian stereotypes

title: Tea and Sympathy
synopsis: Dated coming-of-age melodrama in which an effeminate college freshman (John Kerr) suffers all kinds of humiliations from manly fellow students until his housemaster's wife (Deborah Kerr) decides to act as a surrogate love partner. Directed by Vincente Minnelli from Robert Anderson's adaptation of his own play, the stagy proceedings are overlong and dramatically unconvincing. Sexual situations

title: Teachers
synopsis: Nick Nolte stars as a harassed but effective and idealistic teacher in a zoo-like high school. Directed by Arthur Hiller, the crude, disjointed effort seems just another teenage exploitation movie. Rough language, nudity and a sympathetic view of abortion

title: Teacher's Pet
synopsis: Wacky and witty animated musical about a dog (voiced by Nathan Lane) whose quest to become a real boy leads him and his master (voiced by Shaun Fleming) to the lab of a mad scientist (voiced by Kelsey Grammer) who claims he can transform animals into humans, yielding unintended and comic results. It is based on the popular TV series; director Timothy Bjorklund's canine take on the Pinocchio story offers something for everyone, peppering it throughout with zany sight gags, whip-smart zingers, classic film references and even an educational musical number, all while smuggling under the cover of laughter a message about friendship and the dangers of science overstepping its boundaries. Brief, mildly crude humor
full_review:
A canny canine learns that the grass is not necessarily greener on the other end of the leash in the wacky, whimsical and witty animated musical, "Teacher's Pet" (Disney). It is based on the popular cartoon TV series, and director Timothy Bjorklund puts on the dog in this doggedly funny film which has more than a dog's chance of doing well at the box office. But enough with the pooch puns.

Nathan Lane lends his voice to Spot, a motor-mouthed mutt who finds life on all fours strictly for the dogs. Suffering from an acute Pinocchio complex, Spot wants nothing more than to be a "real boy" -- in fact, the film opens with an amusing send-up of the 1940 Disney classic. In the absence of a blue fairy, Spot takes matters into his own paws by pinning back his floppy ears and marching off to school with his master, Leonard (voiced by Shaun Fleming), posing as his best friend, Scott -- a ruse facilitated by Spot/Scott's ability to talk with humans.

When the precocious pup gets wind of a wacko scientist, Dr. Ivan Krank (voiced by Kelsey Grammer), who announces on a "Jerry Springer"-like TV talk show that he can transform animals into humans by manipulating their DNA, Spot hightails it -- literally -- down to Florida, where, coincidentally, Leonard is spending the dog days of summer with his mom/fourth grade teacher (voiced by Debra Jo Rupp), a finalist in a National Teacher's Award competition.

But as Spot soon finds out, you should be careful what you wish for. The Dr. Moreau-like Krank turns out to be just that, as evidenced by his earlier failed attempts at species swapping which resulted in such swamp mutations as Adele, the mosquito girl (voiced by Megan Mullally), and Dennis, the gator boy (voiced by Paul Reubens). Undeterred by the possibility of a similar fate, Spot refuses to just roll over and play dead. But when a miscalculation of doggy years by Krank yields unintended results, it is up to Leonard and his other two pets -- a scaredy-cat named Mr. Jolly (David Ogden Stiers) and a cantankerous canary named Pretty Boy (Jerry Stiller) -- to get Spot out of the genetic doghouse.

This is one teacher's pet which deserves straight As. The zany film offers something for everyone. Regardless of whether they are fans of the show, kids will find their ribs tickled by the flick's kooky characters and outrageous sight gags.

But Bjorklund makes sure to throw more than a few funny bones to adults along for the ride with zingers like, "Time sure flies when you're changing species," and by peppering the lunacy with film references to "The Sound of Music," Mel Brooks' "Young Frankenstein" -- and even Jimmy Cagney's "White Heat" -- that only parents will catch. Bjorklund even bites the hand that feeds him by parodying classic Disney animated features like "101 Dalmatians," "Snow White," and even the big cheese himself, Mickey Mouse.

The animation, by renowned illustrator Gary Baseman, is at once both primitive and highly stylized, exploding with color and vibrancy. Baseman has created a world populated by toggle-nosed, linguini-limbed denizens like the egg-faced Leonard and his frog-like classmate, Ian (voiced by Rob Paulsen), both of whom look more mutant than Krank's botched experiments. The "most bizarre" award goes to Mrs. Boogin (voiced by Estelle Harris), a pasty, pink-haired crone who will have every liposuctionist in the audience salivating.

The hyperfrenetic, at times surreal, sequences involve houses which burst into song on cue, echoing the animated flights of fantasy of vintage Bob Clampett, Tex Avery and Max Fleischer. Complementing the inspired visuals are songs which range from the near-operatic, "I'm Movin' On," to the hilarious spoof of Disney sentimentality, "A Boy Needs a Dog." The film also features a jazzy version of the Doris Day standard, "Teacher's Pet."

Like early Warner Bros. "Looney Tunes," which dropped as many cultural references as Acme anvils, "Teacher's Pet" is educational as well as entertaining, offering young viewers a lesson in geography by way of the rip-roaring musical number, "A Whole Bunch of World," which compresses comments on all 50 states in under two minutes. The film also contains a rapid-fire, almost subliminal romp highlighting masterpieces of Western art.

And just in case comedy-camouflaged educational numbers aren't incentive enough, the boy-and-his dog story -- well, more precisely a boy-and-his-dog-who-wants-to-be-a-boy story -- also imparts a message about friendship and the dangers of science overstepping its boundaries, smuggled in under the cover of laughter. See Spot. See Spot run. Run to see Spot.

Though the film has brief, mildly crude humor, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-I -- general patronage. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

title: Teacher's Pet
synopsis: Agreeable comedy in which a tough New York newspaper editor (Clark Gable) enrolls in a night school journalism class after falling for its instructor (Doris Day), then faces her contempt when she discovers his deception. Directed by George Seaton, the two leads brighten the plot's mulling over the relative merits of experience and education in the newspaper profession, with Gig Young adding some amusing support as a genial psychology professor. Romantic complications, mild sexual innuendo and a lengthy segment involving inebriation and its painful aftermath

title: Teaching Mrs. Tingle
synopsis: Corrosive black comedy in which three high school seniors tie their nasty history teacher (Helen Mirren) to her bedposts, taking scandalous bedroom photos of her with the school's drunken married coach in order to prevent their being expelled for cheating. As written and directed by Kevin Williamson, the smug, emotionally manipulative tale of self-absorbed adolescents conniving to control a cruel adult is morally bankrupt in lionizing the teens' outrageously anti-social behavior. Implied justification of criminal acts, an off-screen sexual encounter, some violence, underage drinking and an instance of rough language

title: Tea for Two
synopsis: Slack, unimaginative backstage musical loosely based on "No, No, Nanette" and directed by David Butler is set in the 1920s with a frantic producer (Billy De Wolfe) after a socialite (Doris Day) to back his new show of which she becomes the star singing duets with its songwriter (Gordon MacRae). Mild sexual innuendo

title: Team America: World Police
synopsis: Intentionally outrageous adventure-comedy, with songs, by the "South Park" creators, featuring surprisingly lifelike marionettes (strings and all), about a governmental police team out to thwart global terrorists in Paris, the Mideast and Korea. A Broadway actor is drafted to help the squad take on the nefarious Korean dictator, Kim Jong II, who with the help of Chechen and Middle Eastern terrorists is planning to unleash weapons of mass destruction upon the world. Dexterous puppetry and eye-catching production design -- and yes, some humorous moments -- in Trey Parker's follow-up to "South Park: Bigger, Longer & Uncut," but puppets and humorous intent or not, the sexual content, overall vulgarity and frequent violence go way over the top. Sexual activity both straight and gay, extreme violence, including dismemberment and blood, ethnic stereotypes, crude and profane language, albeit all done by puppets
full_review:
The creators of "South Park" have turned from animation to puppetry in their latest big-screen extravaganza, which skewers everything from Broadway musicals to weapons of mass destruction. Inspired by the old British puppet animation series, "Thunderbirds," the film is an elaborate sendup of producer Jerry Bruckheimer's action films.

"Team America: World Police" (Paramount) from director Trey Parker -- in collaboration with his co-producer/creator/writing partner, Matt Stone -- concerns the exploits of an international police squad as it chases down terrorists across the world: Paris, Cairo, the Panama Canal and Korea.

The first we see of the team in action is a confrontation with Middle Eastern terrorists (the first of several wince-inducing racial stereotypes) in the famed City of Light, which by the time the shooting ends is totally decimated. Team leader Spottswoode later attends a Broadway play, "Lease" (read "Rent"), where star Gary Johnston is wowing them with a satiric song about AIDS (one of many bad-taste moments), and goes backstage afterward to speak with Gary.

After Spottswoode assures Gary that his interest in him is not sexual, but that he needs to help save the world by being a spy (in other words, to "act like a terrorist"), he brings Gary to the squad's elaborate headquarters -- housed behind the facade of Mount Rushmore -- where he introduces him to the team of Chris, the martial arts expert; Sarah, the clairvoyant; Lisa, the psychology expert; and Joe, the quarterback. Gary is told his help is needed to stop the terrorists or else devastation will be inevitable, and "all the worst parts of the Bible" will come true.

In spite of an immediate attraction to the blonde Lisa, Gary refuses the offer, until a soul-searching trip to Washington jogs his patriotism, and he decides duty to his country stands above all.

Cosmetically altered to look like a Middle Eastern terrorist, Gary and the team set out for Cairo, Egypt, where he becomes "Achmed" and narrowly escapes with his life.

Eventually he and the team take on Kim Jong Il, leader of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, who plans to destroy the world with WMD's, with the help of members of (uh-hem) F.A.G., the Film Actor's Guild, including such liberal Hollywood do-gooders as Alec Baldwin, Matt Damon, Michael Moore, Susan Sarandon, Sean Penn, Tim Robbins, Samuel L. Jackson and more. Baldwin comes in for special skewering.
The "real" people portrayed here are not immune to the puppet violence. To cite one example, the United Nations' Hans Blix is fed to a shark by Kim Jong Il, with graphically gruesome results.

There's a certain novelty in having puppets go through the motions of everything from kung fu moves to gross-out vomiting, but the sexual activity and the violence ultimately go way over the top.

The songs are not without wit, though sometimes -- as with the AIDS song -- are intentionally tasteless. A Ben Affleck putdown, "Pearl Harbor Sucked and I Miss You," and a paean to Alec Baldwin are funny in their loony way.

Everyone's fair game for spoofing in Stone and Parker's world: from the U.S. government -- sometimes accused of "policing the world," thus the "world police" concept -- to Hollywood's bleeding heart liberals. There's something to offend everyone, but the left gets it harder than the right. As indicated, bad taste abounds: even jokes about 9-11 -- the date, if not the actual events -- are included.

To give credit where it is due, the marionettes are quite amazing on a technical level (courtesy of the Chiodo brothers), but the level of sexual activity and gory violence -- albeit done in the name of humor -- makes the film impossible to endorse. They get points for the
production design which is eye-catching, witty and clever, to be sure.

Definitely not one for the kids, and probably not for most sensitive adults either.
Because of sexual activity both straight and gay, extreme violence, including dismemberment and blood, ethnic stereotypes, and crude and profane language, albeit all done by puppets, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
