Mature theme, marital discord and a few instances of profanity

title: Trust
synopsis: Mean-spirited attempt at black comedy in which a pregnant teenager considering abortion (Adrienne Shelly) brings home a volatile stranger (Martin Donovan) but her mother (Merritt Nelson) and sister (Edie Falco) react with extreme treachery. Writer-director Hal Hartley presents a vicious vision of middle-class family life with no insights but plenty of nasty role models. Casual attitude toward abortion, poisonous parental figures, minor violence and intermittent rough language

title: Trust the Man
synopsis: A good cast is wasted in this tepid and coarse domestic comedy-drama about an actress (Julianne Moore), her philandering house-husband (David Duchovny), her commitment-phobic brother (Billy Crudup), and his longtime live-in girlfriend (Maggie Gyllenhaal). Writer-director Bart Freundlich's film offers the occasional sharp observation about modern-day relationships, but the characters' infidelities and casual attitude toward sex is highly problematic, despite the morally acceptable wrap-up. Much rough language, a few instances of profanity, needlessly frank sexual talk, premarital and adulterous relationships, a casual approval of pornography, a couple of sex scenes without nudity, some gratuitous scatological elements and a same-sex kiss
full_review:
A sterling cast is wasted in the tepid and often coarse comedy-drama "Trust the Man" (Fox Searchlight) about an insecure actress, Rebecca (Julianne Moore), who has taken a break from films to star in a play at New York's Lincoln Center.

It's clear that she and her house-husband, Tom (David Duchovny), are having some marital problems, especially in the intimacy department, as they tell their marriage counselor (Garry Shandling).

Rebecca's slacker brother ,Tobey (an especially good Billy Crudup), lives with his longtime girlfriend, Elaine (Maggie Gyllenhaal), an aspiring writer. The relationship has been coasting along for seven years, but now Elaine decides she wants to get married and have a baby, and the commitment-phobic Tobey -- who's obsessed with death -- can't handle it.

Before long, Tom falls under the spell of Pamela (Dagmara Dominczyk), a predatory mother he meets when picking up his child from school. And when Tobey and Elaine come to a parting of the ways, Tobey falls under the sway of former girlfriend Faith (Eva Mendes), now married.

Writer-director Bart Freundlich's film offers the occasional sharp observation about modern-day relationships, but the characters' infidelities and casual attitude toward sex is highly problematic, despite the morally sound wrap-up, which plays out in an improbable but amusing scene on Rebecca's opening night.

Moore, Duchovny, Crudup, and Gyllenhaal are all pros, and watching them in anything has its rewards, but even from a dramatic standpoint there is something phony about the setup, and inasmuch as this is also a comedy genuine chuckles are few.

The film contains much rough language, a few instances of profanity, needlessly frank sexual talk, premarital and adulterous relationships, a casual approval of pornography, a couple of sex scenes without nudity, some gratuitous scatological elements and a same-sex kiss. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Truth about Cats & Dogs, The
synopsis: Insecure about her looks, a radio talk show host (Janeane Garofalo), persuades her gorgeous girlfriend (Uma Thurman) to impersonate her when an admiring radio fan (Ben Chaplin) asks her out. Director Michael Lehmann's contrived, mistaken identity comedy essentially stresses the value of friendship, love and inner beauty although it is marred by a gratuitous, phone-sex scene. Implied masturbation, some sexual innuendo, occasional profanity and an instance of rough language

title: Truth about Spring, The
synopsis: Despite different social backgrounds, an adolescent tom-boy (Haley Mills) and a young Harvard graduate (James MacArthur) find romance while searching the Caribbean for sunken pirate treasure. Directed by Richard Thorpe, the comedy adventure is set aboard a sailship whose captain (John Mills) and rascally crew (Lionel Jeffries, Harry Andres and Niall MacGinnis) abet the growing friendship between the charming young couple. Gentle, old-fashioned entertainment

title: Trygon Factor, The
synopsis: Muddled British mystery directed by Cyril Frankel in which a Scotland Yard inspector (Stewart Granger) traces a series of unsolved robberies to a bogus order of nuns. Violence

title: Tsar to Lenin
synopsis: Documentary on the Russian Revolution presents rare footage of the royal family, the Bolshevik leaders, the complicated events of the February and October revolutions and the subsequent terrors of the Civil War. Valuable as this footage is, the movie is relatively unsophisticated in the use it makes of it

title: Tsotsi
synopsis: Powerful, beautifully acted film about vicious South African hoodlum (Presley Chweneyagae) who shoots a woman and steals her car, not realizing her baby is in the back seat, and how his life is transformed by the experience. Though the squalid underworld milieu, and the periodic acts of violence will not be to every taste, writer-director Gavin Hood's adaptation of an Athol Fugard novel ultimately becomes into an incredibly moving experience with a truly redemptive ending sure to bring a lump to the throat of the patient viewer. Subtitles. Pervasive rough and occasional crude language, some profanity, two violent killings, a shooting, brief breastfeeding images, gambling
full_review:
"Tsotsi" (Miramax) -- South African jargon for a black urban criminal -- is the second film to open in February with the theme of a carjacking involving a baby in the back seat. But that's where the similarities end between the well-intentioned but flawed "Freedomland" and this Oscar nominee (for Best Foreign Language Film).

The Johannesburg underworld milieu is, at first, harsh and repellent. And from the early scenes where the vicious hoodlums, 19-year-old Tsotsi (Presley Chweneyagae) and his gang -- Boston (Mothusi Magano), Butcher (Zenzo Ngqobe) and Aap (Kenneth Nkosi) -- target a prosperous man on the subway, surround him on a crowded train, stab him to death and make off with his cash, you may feel the film will be too hard to take.

Matters are scarcely better when shortly afterward in a bar, Boston chides Tsotsi for his callousness and lack of decency, and Tsotsi brutally beats him.

But when we next see Tsotsi menacing a wheelchair-bound panhandler whom, we're sure, will meet some grisly fate, the man's piteous condition and indomitable spirit in the face of adversity breaks through Tsotsi's heartlessness, and he leaves the man alone.

Still unreformed, though, Tsotsi stakes out an affluent gated house, and confronts a woman returning home (Nambitha Mpumlwana), shoots her when she tries to stop him from stealing her car, and drives off. Only later does he discover there's a baby in the back seat. Against all probability, he bonds with the infant and decides to secretly care for it.

We get a glimpse into Tsotsi's past and learn that he had a rough upbringing with a violent father who kept him from his gravely ill but loving mother, forcing the young David (his real name) to flee home, and live with other homeless children in a desolate area with large industrial pipes as their only shelter. Rarely have the privations of childhood leading to crime been so persuasively dramatized.

Tsotsi can barely take care of the child in the squalid shantytown where he lives, so in desperation, he forces an attractive young widow, Miriam (Terry Pheto), to breastfeed the infant, the first step in a transformation that will lead to a redemptive ending that doesn't feel simply tacked on like so many films that wallow in violence or sex.

The film works as well as it does because of the superbly nuanced performances. Chweneyagae accomplishes the impossible in etching a hateful character whom we ultimately feel is deserving of great compassion. And he also succeeds in making his rather abrupt about face utterly believable. Pheto is outstanding, exuding, as she does, warm understanding for the thug who has invaded her home.

The dreary setting (brown tones predominate), the sordid action and the periodic acts of violence will not be to every taste, but if you stick with it, writer-director Gavin Hood's adaptation of Athol Fugard's 1980 novel ultimately becomes an incredibly moving experience and the finale -- with its haunting underscoring -- is sure to bring a lump to the throat.

"Tsotsi" has deservedly won a slew of international film awards, and has been dubbed by author-playwright Fugard as "far and away the best film that has been made" of any of his works.

Subtitles.

The film contains pervasive rough and occasional crude language, some profanity, two violent killings, a shooting, brief breastfeeding images, and gambling. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Tucker: The Man and His Dream
synopsis: Dramatized portrait of the maverick (Jeff Bridges) whose innovative automobile designs challenged the lackluster product of Detroit's car industry after World War II. Director Francis Coppola has a hard time blending the documentary and dramatic aspects of his scenario and ends up portraying his subject in mostly one-dimensional terms, with moral issues (good guys vs. bad guys) treated in similar black-and-white fashion as well. Mild rough language

title: Tuck Everlasting
synopsis: Charming fantasy about a young girl (Alexis Bledel) whose first love (Jonathan Jackson) and his welcoming family offer her a chance to remain forever young with them. Director Jay Russell crafts an uplifting tale, based on Natalie Babbitt's novel, with enough twists, turns and excitement to keep young and older audiences in suspense. Some violence, mild sexual innuendo and a fantasy interpretation of immortality. A-II Adults and Adolescents (PG) 2002 Full Review "Tuck Everlasting" (Disney) is a charming, fairy-tale fantasy about a young girl's first love and how she is tempted by him to live a life staying forever young. Set at the turn of the last century, two families inhabit the environs of Treefall: the prosperous Fosters, who helped build the town, and the nomadic Tuck family, who have come and gone over the years. The Fosters (Victor Garber and Amy Irving) reside in a grand, gated house and live a cultured life of privilege, propriety and property, which they expect their only daughter, Winnie (Alexis Bledel), to assume. The Tucks, led by spooky Angus (William Hurt) and kind Mae (Sissy Spacek), with their two sons, the zestful Jesse (Jonathan Jackson) and older, brooding Miles (Scott Bairstow), are a clan of wanderers who camp out in the wilderness forest that is part of the Foster estate. The Tucks have a family secret. A hundred years ago, as pioneers, they discovered a virtual fountain of youth in the spring waters of a tree stump on the Fosters' land. Not only do they stay young, but the waters make them impervious to death and even injury. Ostracized by an earlier generation as devil worshippers, they now keep only to themselves, but must periodically return to the Foster estate to drink the waters and thus preserve their immortality. Tracking the Tucks across the country is a mysterious Man in a Yellow Suit, played with eerie slyness by Sir Ben Kingsley. He has heard of the Tuck legend passed down through the generations and now is bound and determined to find the elusive Tucks. "One must never announce one's presence to the prey," he warns. When Winnie's parents decide she needs the discipline of a girls' boarding school, she flees into the adjoining forest where she stumbles upon young Jesse Tuck drinking water from a tree stump. Before he can show Winnie the way back home, brother Miles drags Winnie back to the Tuck homestead. At first suspicious, the Tucks soon take Winnie into their trust and open her eyes to the beauty of the natural world just beyond the gates of her house, all the while offering to return her home. Before long Winnie falls in love with Jesse and forgets that she ever wanted to leave. Meanwhile, the Fosters have the whole town out looking for Winnie and it is The Man in the Yellow Suit who becomes pivotal in Winnie's fate when he spies her on a lake with Angus. Soon she must make a crucial decision about how and with whom she wishes to live her life. Based on Natalie Babbitt's novel and directed by Jay Russell, the uplifting tale has enough twists, turns and excitement to keep both young and older audiences in suspense. The film does a fine job of storytelling with a stellar, Academy Award-winning cast and some very good newcomers. Added to that are idyllic period sets and costuming that are the Disney trademark, a musical score which evokes the carefree spirit of Celtic leprechauns, and lush cinematography that nicely captures the scenic outdoors and warm interior details. For the most part, it is a gentle tale that also visits the perennial question of how to preserve the natural world pristinely against the manmade forces of commerce and civilization. Yet one must remember the movie is a fantasy lest it present a confusing and false idea of the world to younger, impressionable minds. While it does not fully endorse a childish Peter Pan-like existence, it does depict immortality as resulting from the animistic forces of "nature" as opposed to Christian beliefs in God and his salvation that leads to eternal life after death. As a period fantasy piece, however, "Tuck" has genuine appeal and hopefully will have a long life at the box office. Due to some violence, mild sexual innuendo and its fantasy interpretation of immortality, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops
