title: Tuff Turf
synopsis: WASP golden boy finds himself at inner-city high school and makes things even tougher for himself by going after the girl friend of a gang leader. Mindless youth exploitation movie directed by Fritz Kiersch with a blaring musical score and some scenes of despicable violence

title: Tulsa
synopsis: During the 1920s, a cattleman's daughter (Susan Hayward) gambles on a wildcat oil well, strikes it rich, then almost loses all before being saved by conservation-minded friends (Robert Preston and Pedro Armendariz). Directed by Stuart Heisler, the romance is more in the building of an oil empire than in the heroine's life but the real conflict is between oil derricks and grazing cattle. Some fisticuffs and an oil field burning out of control

title: Tulsa Kid, The
synopsis: Western programmer directed by George Sherman in which the former gunfighter of the title (Don "Red" Berry) sides with a small rancher in a range war that pits him against the veteran gunfighter (Noah Beery) who had raised him as a youth. Frontier violence

title: Tumbleweed
synopsis: Standard Western directed by Nathan Juran in which a cowboy (Audie Murphy), mistakenly blamed for the Indian massacre of a wagon train, escapes a posse while trying to get proof of his innocence which is finally established by the strange horse of the title. Frontier violence

title: Tumbleweeds
synopsis: Modest, insightful drama in which a flighty, much married Southerner (Janet McTeer), having fled her latest husband with her 12-year-old daughter (Kimberly J. Brown) for San Diego, is about to repeat the pattern with a new boyfriend (Gavin O'Connor) when her daughter demands she stop running from her problems. Also directed by O'Connor, the loving mother-daughter relationship is acutely observed as is the mother's sad dependancy on males for self-worth until helped by supportive friends. A live-in relationship, frequent profanity and shrill domestic discord

title: Tune in Tomorrow...
synopsis: Comedy set in the 1950s about a flamboyant writer of radio soap operas (Peter Falk) who manipulates a romance between a novice news writer (Keanu Reeves) and his 35-year-old aunt by marriage (Barbara Hershey) as grist for his sudsy scripts. Director Jon Amiel orchestrates an offbeat but overproduced comic fantasy that is enlivened by Falk and Hershey's feisty perfomances, great period costumes and vibrant New Orleans setting. Some make-believe violence, mild sexual innuendo and minimal rough language

title: Tune, The
synopsis: Fanciful animated story in which a struggling songwriter on his way to the office to meet a deadline gets sidetracked in a surreal world of wacky characters who give him the inspiration for a hit tune. Director Bill Plympton's slyly witty tale boasts a distinctive visual style and 10 whimsical songs, but its helter-skelter procession of events seems padded to accommodate a feature-length running time. Some cartoon violence

title: Tunnelvision
synopsis: Sick satire about television programming of the future features Howard Hesseman, Betty Thomas, Chevy Chase and Larraine Newman. Directed by Neal Israel and Brad Swirnoff, it offers a series of degrading, detestable and altogether unfunny vignettes

title: Turbo: A Power Rangers Movie
synopsis: Inane action fantasy from the children's TV series has the teen rangers trying to stop a power-mad Valkyrie (Hilary Shepard Turner) and a volcano monster from wreaking havoc on the entire universe. As clumsily directed by David Winning and Shuki Levy, the lame result is a choppy mix of formula mythic characters, derivative situations and extended martial-arts battles. Special-effects violence and stylized mayhem

title: Turbulence
synopsis: Formula thriller in which a terrified flight attendant (Lauren Holly) locks herself in a jumbo jet's cockpit hoping to land the storm-tossed aircraft after a crazed serial killer (Ray Liotta) shoots the pilots. Director Robert Butler's frantic melodrama eventually becomes unintentionally funny with its overwrought damsel-in-distress cliches. Intermittent violence, recurring rough language and occasional profanity

title: Turistas
synopsis: A tropical paradise becomes a torture chamber for a group of (mostly) American tourists (including Josh Duhamel, Beau Garrett, Melissa George and Olivia Wilde) marooned in Brazil when they're tricked into hiking to a remote jungle cabin where they're held captive by a "gringo"-hating doctor (Miguel Lunardi) who wants to harvest their internal organs. Murky and only mildly suspenseful, director John Stockwell's grisly Third World revenge fantasy is an empty exercise in exploitative sex and sadism held together by a formulaic plot skimpier than the bikinis that dominate the female wardrobe. Intense and gratuitous violence, including a graphic surgical procedure with nudity, reckless drinking, drug content and references, an implied sexual encounter with partial nudity, suggestive dancing, sensual images, obscene graffiti, some sexual humor, as well as much rough and crude language and some profanity
full_review:
Translated into English, "Turistas" (Fox Atomic) means "don't waste your money."

Actually, it's the Portuguese word for "tourists," referring here to the unlucky assortment of vacationing Americans, Europeans and Australians served up for slaughter while traveling through Brazil, in director John Stockwell's thriller, which taps into current anti-Western sentiment abroad, resulting in a grisly Third World revenge fantasy.

The preternaturally good-looking bunch includes American brother-sister team Alex (Josh Duhamel) and Bea (Olivia Wilde), Bea's best friend, Amy (Beau Garrett), adventurous Aussie Pru (Melissa George), and hedonistic Brits Finn and Liam (Desmond Askew and Max Brown).

Marooned after their rickety bus crashes, the pleasure-seekers kill time at a beachfront bar, where the surf is inviting, the women beautiful and the exotic drinks spiked. Their tropical paradise starts to turn ugly when they wake to find out they were robbed.

Tricked by a local, Kiko (Agles Steib), who offers them safe haven, the foreigners are led deep into the jungle to a remote cabin where they're held captive by his uncle (Miguel Lunardi), a "gringo"-hating doctor who wants to harvest their internal organs and lectures them on global inequality as he goes about his gory business.

Murky and only mildly suspenseful -- an escape through a maze of underwater caves provides some tension -- this empty exercise in exploitative sex and sadism is held together by a formulaic plot skimpier than the bikinis that dominate the Brazilian female wardrobe.

This is one tourist trap definitely worth avoiding.

The film contains intense and gratuitous violence, including a graphic surgical procedure with nudity, reckless drinking, drug content and references, an implied sexual encounter with partial nudity, suggestive dancing, sensual images, obscene graffiti, some sexual humor, as well as much rough and crude language and some profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Turk 182
synopsis: In rescuing a little girl from a burning building , an off-duty New York fireman (Robert Urich) is badly injured. When he's refused compensation, his young brother (Timothy Hutton) embarks on a campaign for justice by embarrasing the mayor with graffiti signed "Turk 182," his injured brother's nickname and badge number. A crude, noisy movie directed by Bob Clark with pretensions to folk epic grandeur. Sexual promiscuity

title: Turner & Hooch
synopsis: Diverting man-and-beast comedy about a small-town cop (Tom Hanks) who takes in the nasty, drooling watchdog of a murder victim (John McIntire), becomes fond of the overgrown pet and the mismatched duo end up solving the murder. Scenes pairing the ugly dog with handsome Hanks are amusing and the pooch enables the cop to fall in love with the local veterinarian (Mare Winningham). Director Roger Spottiswoode mamages to make the lightweight tale entertaining and somewhat affecting. Brief but intense violence, an implied sexual encounter and minimal locker-room language

title: Turning Point, The
synopsis: Above-average crime melodrama follows a tough-minded journalist (William Holden) who can't resist helping an idealistic special prosecutor (Edmond O'Brien) break a crime syndicate boss (Ed Begley). Director William Dieterle's shady underworld characters make credible foes for the lawmen, with taut action scenes, especially a hitman (Neville Brand) seeking his target in a crowded prizefight arena. Stylized violence

title: Turning Point, The
synopsis: Shirley MacLaine and Anne Bancroft star as one-time rival ballerinas who renew their feud when MacLaine's daughter (Leslie Browne) joins Bancroft's troupe. Directed by Herbert Ross, the old-fashioned sentimental melodrama is set against the glamorous world of ballet, with plenty of grand dance sequences. Brief nudity and a benign attitude toward illicit sex

title: Turn It Up
synopsis: Sluggish musical drama about a gifted hip-hop artist (Prakazrel "Pras'' Michel) trapped in the projects who struggles to make it big without resorting to illegal means. Writer-director Robert Adetuyi's well-intended narrative never rises above its flaws, boring the viewer with wooden performances and dead end plot twists. Recurring violence, some drug abuse, an implied sexual encounter, and constant rough language with some profanity and racist slang. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Turtle Diary
synopsis: Adaptation of playwright Harold Pinter's story of an author (Glenda Jackson) and a bookseller (Ben Kingsley) who are brought together by their mutual aspiration to free three sea turtles from the London acquarium. Director John Irvin's delicate, contemplative narrative is a testament to gentle souls who set simple goals and celebrate small, private victories. Brief but intense scene of violence

title: Turtles Can Fly
synopsis: Quietly powerful drama set in Kurdistan on the eve of the U.S. invasion of Iraq, which follows the shattered lives of three orphaned children: a hustling street urchin (Soran Ebrahim) who runs a business installing satellite dishes and clearing fields of land mines, an armless boy (Hirsh Feyssal) who may be clairvoyant, and his sad-eyed sister (a haunting Avaz Latif), traumatized by an unspeakable crime which robbed her of her innocence and will to live. Putting a human face on "collateral damage," director Bahman Ghobadi elicits strong performances from his three nonprofessional leads, and the film, shot entirely in a refugee camp on the Turkish-Iraqi border, serves as a grim but compelling meditation on the obscenity of war, told through the eyes of its most vulnerable victims. Subtitles. War violence, an implied rape of a minor, a murder of a child (with extenuating circumstances), a suicide, and recurring disturbing images of maimed children
full_review:
"Turtles Can Fly" (IFC) is a quietly powerful drama, set in Kurdistan on the eve of the U.S. invasion of Iraq, which follows the shattered lives of three orphaned children: a hustling 13-year-old street urchin, Soran (Soran Ebrahim), eking a living installing satellite dishes and clearing fields of land mines; an armless boy, Henkov (Hirsh Feyssal), who may be clairvoyant; and his sad-eyed sister, Agrin (Avaz Latif), traumatized by an unspeakable crime which robbed her of her innocence and will to live. Latif's haunting expression stays with you long after the movie ends.

Putting a human face on "collateral damage," director Bahman Ghobadi elicits strong performances from his three nonprofessional leads, and the film, shot entirely in a refugee camp on the Turkish-Iraqi border, serves as a grim but compelling meditation on the obscenity of war, told through the eyes of its most vulnerable victims.

Subtitles.

War violence, an implied rape of a minor, a murder of a child (with extenuating circumstances), a suicide, and recurring disturbing images of maimed children. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.

title: The Tuxedo
synopsis: Drawn-out fantasy in which cabbie-turned-secret-agent Jackie Chan dons a tuxedo that gives him superhero powers as he teams with a novice agent (Jennifer Love Hewitt) to thwart a water mogul's plot for world domination. Director Kevin Donovan's generally innocuous action comedy is a James Bond wannabe whose continuous choreographed fight scenes may thrill Chan fans but few others. Brief deadly violence, much comic violence and some sexual innuendo
full_review:
"The Tuxedo" (DreamWorks) is a James-Bond-wannabe action comedy in which James Bond is James Tong (Jackie Chan), a mild-mannered cabbie-turned-secret-agent. Once Tong dons a specially customized tuxedo he can leap, run, kick and slug with abandon, sure to please every Chan fan -- but what about the rest of us?

These frequent fisticuffs usually include Tong's rookie agent partner (Jennifer Love Hewitt) punching and kickboxing by his side while predictably acting hostile toward him -- even though you know she won't be able to resist his puppy-dog expressions for long. But long is the operative word here. With a feeble story in the background (megalomaniac seeks global domination by controlling the world's water supply) the silly proceedings soon play like a drawn-out fantasy -- but they would have played better at half-hour sitcom length.

Aside from that, novice director Kevin Donovan turns in workmanlike visuals and orchestrates the fight scenes to be more comic than violent. Yet an early scene in which another agent is drowned initially gives the film a nasty edge, but once Chan shows up the action is mostly innocuous if not involving.

A scene in which Tong doesn't realize his own strength and accidentally KOs soul legend James Brown (playing himself) draws chuckles when Tong goes on stage as his replacement. Soon after, the airhead girlfriend (Mia Cottet) of the villain (Ritchie Coster) tries to seduce Tong but he is too busy fighting off the interchangeable goons who populate the picture as punching bags for the two hyperactive agents.

Subsequent scenes where the twosome discover the villain's underground lab are cut-rate versions of Bond movies -- with similarly cut-rate excitement.

Because of brief deadly violence, much comic violence and some sexual innuendo, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Twelfth Night
synopsis: Screen version of Shakespeare's comedy of mistaken identities in which a shipwrecked woman (Imogen Stubbs) disguises herself as a man in a foreign country whose ruler (Toby Stephens) and the countess (Helena Bonham Carter) he hopes to wed are both taken in by her male impersonation which becomes complicated by her falling in love with the ruler while the countess falls in love with her. Adapted and directed by Trevor Nunn, the droll fantasy of mixed-up lovers is highly amusing, often charming and paced by a madcap subplot, but the real enjoyment is in watching a talented cast having fun with nonsensical roles. Mild sexual innuendo

title: Twelve Chairs, The
synopsis: Uneven comedy set in the Soviet Union of 1927 when a deposed nobleman (Ron Moody) learns that the family jewels were hidden in a confiscated dining room chair but his search is complicated by a suave con artist (Frank Langella) and a greedy priest (Dom DeLuise). Written and directed by Mel Brooks, the comedy depends upon old-fashioned mugging and slapstick spiked with some modern cynicism but by the end the farce turns to bathos and disappointment

title: Twelve Chairs, The
synopsis: Soviet cinema is not known for its levity or wit and yet both are in evidence in this large-scale extravaganza in the picaresque adventures of a grasping ex-aristocrat (A. Gomiashvili) and a conniving proletarian (S. Filippov) who are forced to work together in searching for a fortune hidden in a chair seized during the Revolution. Directed by Leonid Gaidai, it is a good-humored and often hilarious picture of the flaws and strenghts that made up life in the Soviet Union of the 1920s and the ending has considerably more bite than the boisterous 1970 Mel Brooks version

title: Twelve O'Clock High
synopsis: Tense World War II story of a U.S. B-17 bomber group based in England whose commander (Gary Merrill) is relieved for fretting over casualty rates but the straightlaced officer (Gregory Peck) who succeeds him eventually cracks under the emotional strain of ordering men to risk their lives flying hazardous daylight missions. Director Henry King's character study of men in war has a strong supporting cast (notably Dean Jagger, Millard Mitchell and Hugh Marlowe), a thoughtful script and stunning wartime footage of air combat. Much psychological tension

title: Twentieth Century
synopsis: Screwball comedy in which a Broadway producer (John Barrymore) turns a model into a star (Carole Lombard), but goes bust after she deserts him for Hollywood, then tries to win her back on the train journey from Chicago to New York. Directed by Howard Hawks from a script by Ben Hecht and Charles MacArthur, the squabbles between this egocentric duo pace the madcap proceedings aboard the title train and put over by a top supporting cast (Walter Connolly, Roscoe Karns and Etienne Giradot as an escaped lunatic). Sexual situations and innuendo

Flashy but shallow fact-based psychological drama in which a gifted MIT senior (Jim Sturgess) reluctantly joins a group of other math whizzes led by a hard-edged professor (Kevin Spacey), and including the girl he'd like to date (Kate Bosworth), in a scheme to win at blackjack by counting cards in Las Vegas casinos, eventually drawing the ire of a veteran security consultant (Laurence Fishburne). Director Robert Luketic's film shows the perils of greed and hubris, but also celebrates revenge and the value of indiscriminate "life experiences." Nongraphic, nonmarital sexual activity, brief rear nudity, a same-sex kiss, some crude and crass language, and sexual humor
full_review:
An MIT geek turns Las Vegas gambler in "21" (Columbia). Based on a true story, this psychological drama, like the casino capital itself, is flashy but shallow.

Gifted, hard-working senior Ben Campbell (Jim Sturgess) has one consuming ambition: to attend Harvard Medical School. He has the grades to achieve this goal, but not the money. Nor are his academic achievements enough to win him the full scholarship he covets, since he lacks the unusual life experiences that might make him stand out.

A surprising solution is offered by hard-edged professor Micky Rosa (Kevin Spacey).
Impressed by Ben's performance in his class, he invites him to join a clandestine group of math whizzes who travel to Las Vegas each weekend to win high stakes at blackjack by the legal but frowned-upon method of counting cards.

Reluctant at first, Ben eventually gives in when Jill Taylor (Kate Bosworth), a member of the group and a girl Ben has long wanted to date, visits him at his $8-an-hour clothing store job and renews the invitation. Still, he insists he'll quit as soon as he's amassed the $300,000 that will see him through Harvard.

Inevitably, Ben becomes Micky's star pupil, impassively studying the cards as the chips pile up in front of him. But his success has not gone unnoticed by veteran casino security consultant Cole Williams (Laurence Fishburne) whose job includes putting the "beat down" on card counters until he's convinced them to leave town for good.

Director Robert Luketic's film shows the perils of greed and hubris, as dissension grows among the conspirators and Ben becomes dangerously careless. But "21" also celebrates revenge and the value of indiscriminate "life experiences."

The film contains nongraphic, nonmarital sexual activity, brief rear nudity, a same-sex kiss, some crude and crass language, and sexual humor. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Twenty-One
synopsis: Trashy comedy in which a smugly promiscuous 21-year-old swinger (Patsy Kensit) recounts her meaningless sexual adventures in London before heading to New York for more of the same. Co-writer-director Don Boyd presents only crass, self-involved characters in a tasteless and repelling movie not worthy of 21 seconds' viewing. Positive attitude toward promiscuity, several bedroom scenes with brief nudity, shots of drug mainlining and much rough language

title: Twenty Plus Two
synopsis: Convoluted crime story directed by Joseph M. Newman in which a private eye (David Janssen) links an unsolved murder case to the disappearance of a 16-year-old heiress 12 years before, which leads him to a myriad of suspicious characters (including Jeanne Crain, Dina Merrill and Brad Dexter). Stylized violence, sexual innuendo and an unwed pregnancy

title: Twice in a Lifetime
synopsis: This is a big, glossy valentine to adultery in which a 50-year old steelworker (Gene Hackman) falls in love with a barmaid (Ann-Margret) and leaves his wife (Ellen Burstyn) and children. Directed by Bud Yorkin, the movie lacks authentic characters and motivation, relying instead upon a dense sentimental smokescreen in its attempts to justify the husband's wholly selfish actions

title: Twice-Told Tales
synopsis: Vincent Price stars in Nathaniel Hawthorne stories of love beyond the grave ("Dr. Heidigger's Experiment"), a father's obsessive protectiveness ("Rappaccini's Daughter") and a Puritan family curse ("The House of the Seven Gables"). Directed by Sidney Salkow, the adaptations are largely flat and unimaginative, though the last evokes something of the eerie atmosphere intended by Hawthorne. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Twice Upon a Yesterday
synopsis: Breezy romantic fable in which the clock is magically turned back so that a cheating boyfriend (Douglas Henshall) can have a second chance with his girlfriend (Lena Headey) only to discover that she too had begun a clandestine affair. Director Maria Ripoll's bittersweet tale follows four characters who learn that love can't flourish in an atmosphere of betrayal and deceit. Brief sexual encounter, a live-in relationship, intermittent rough language and a few instances of profanity

title: Twilight
synopsis: Flawed suspense story in which a retired private eye (Paul Newman) becomes involved with the wife (Susan Sarandon) of his terminally ill friend (Gene Hackman) while trying to figure out their part in the long unsolved murder of her first husband. Director Robert Benton's twisty mystery is ably abetted by a veteran cast (including James Garner) whose skillful performances distract from a major plot contrivance. Intermittent violence, implied sexual encounters, brief nudity, some rough language and recurring profanity

title: Twilight
synopsis: Gothic romance about a self-possessed high school student (Kristen Stewart) who moves to Washington state to live with her divorced father (Billy Burke) and falls for a mysterious classmate (Robert Pattinson) who turns out to be a vampire. Though set against a lush, misty background, director Catherine Hardwicke's stylish screen version of Stephenie Meyer's best-selling 2005 novel for young adults never takes itself too seriously, as the conflicted central relationship -- restrained by the gentlemanly bloodsucker's scruples -- parodies both adolescent awkwardness and teenage yearning. Brief but intense action violence, a scene of mild sensuality, a few sexual references; acceptable for older teens

title: Twilight for the Gods
synopsis: Halting South Sea adventure from Ernest K. Gann's story of assorted troubles aboard a leaky two-masted sailing ship whose hapless captain (Rock Hudson) dallies with a mysterious passenger (Cyd Charisse), while the fretful crew (Arthur Kennedy, Wallace Ford and Charles McGraw) ponder mutiny. Director Joseph Pevney tries to build some suspense as the dangers of the voyage mount but the soggy romance and contrived plot sink the effort. Some menace and sexual situations

title: Twilight in the Sierras
synopsis: Western programmer directed by William Witney is set on a sheep ranch employing ex-cons, but when one turns up missing, his singing parole officer (Roy Rogers) finds he's been kidnapped by a gang of counterfeiters who need his talents as an engraver. Stylized violence

title: Twilight of the Golds
synopsis: Earnest drama about a Jewish family whose grown son (Brendan Fraser) is gay and whose married daughter (Jennifer Beals) ponders abortion after learning that her fetus carries a gene supposedly linked to homosexuality. Director Ross Marks insightfully explores fractured relationships as family members confront homophobic attitudes, struggle to accept or forgive one another, and embrace unconditional love. Serious treatment of an abortion decision, brief male kissing, occasional profanity and an instance of rough language

title: Twilight People
synopsis: The title refers to the gruesome results of a mad doctor (Charles Macaulay) in trying to create a new breed of humans but his experiments have yielded only a bat man, a panther woman, a wolf girl and assorted other odd hybrids. Low-budget Philippine production directed by Eddie Romero, the childish story goes from the utterly unbelievable to the ludicrous, but its violent conclusion is not for the youngsters

title: Twilight's Last Gleaming
synopsis: Burt Lancaster plays a cashiered Air Force general who seizes control of a nuclear missile launching site in an attempt to alter government policies. director Robert Aldrich, not known for his subtlety, has made an extremely clumsy, if well-intentioned movie, whose ham-handed approach to a complex moral issue, as well as its extreme, if sporadic, violence and rough language make it questionable fare at best

title: Twilight Time
synopsis: Shapeless, sentimental Yugoslavian production directed by Goran Paskaljevic centers on an old man (Karl Malden) returning from America to spend his remaining years in his mountain village where he winds up caring for two young grandchildren with the help of a friendly schoolteacher (Jodi Thelen). Dubbed in English. The slow-paced narrative offers few insights into another culture

title: Twilight Zone - The Movie
synopsis: Anthology movie, inspired by the popular 1960s television series, is made up of five separate episodes by four different directors, and only the one about an airline passenger (John Lithgow) who spots and odd-looking creature sitting on the wing, rises above mediocrity. Some frightening effects here and in three of the other four segments make it inappropriate fare for younger viewers

title: Twin Dragons
synopsis: Muddled action comedy in which twins separated at birth finally meet in Hong Kong after a concert pianist (Jackie Chan) is mistaken for his brother (also Chan), a petty crook on the run from a murderous crime ring. Directed by Tsui Hark and Ringo Lam, the dubbed 1992 production gets lost in a wild and woolly series of confrontations that are as confusing to the viewer as to each of the brothers' girlfriends, assorted gangsters and concert officials. Martial arts violence, sexual situations and some course language

title: Twin Falls Idaho
synopsis: Small but involving tale in which identical twin brothers whose torsoes are joined into one are befriended by a prostitute (Michele Hicks) who tries to help when one of the brothers (Michael Polish) gets ill but they wind up in the hospital facing an operation to separate them in hopes of saving the other (Mark Polish). Directed by Michael Polish from a script co-written with brother Mark, the picture is thin on narrative details but it succeeds in portrayal of the closeness and yet distinct individualty of Siamese twins whom viewers come to appreciate not as freaks of nature but as people with special problems. Sexual situations, drug abuse, some rough language and occasional profanity

title: Twinkle, Twinkle, Killer Kane
synopsis: ( see: "The Ninth Configuration" )

title: Twin Peaks: Fire Walk with Me
synopsis: The characters from the "Twin Peaks" TV series appear in a big-screen clunker about events leading up to the murder of promiscuous, drug-addicted teenager Laura Palmer (Sheryl Lee). Director David Lynch's sleazy, self-indulgent horror show goes nowhere slowly, spending an endless 134 minutes revealing nothing of interest beyond Ms. Lee's inability to act. Numerous perverse sexual situations, some of them violent, several bloody murders, frequent drug and alcohol abuse, recurring nudity and rough language

title: Twins
synopsis: Often hilarious tale of twin brothers separated at birth but reunited 35 years later after the big guy (Arnold Schwarzenegger) has been raised to be sound of mind and body on a South Pacific island while the little guy (Danny DeVito) grew up in an orphanage where he began his sleazy life of petty crime and womanizing. Though sluggishly directed by Ivan Reitman, the two actors manage to carry this tale of mismatched twins who learn to love and trust one another so that, in the end, goodness, family and marriage triumph over greed, gluttony and sexual promiscuity. Some violent cartoon fisticuffs and graphic rub-outs mostly played for laughs as well as some locker-room language and promiscuous behavior

title: Twins of Evil
synopsis: British horror movie about a 17th century witch-hunter (Peter Cushing) whose voluptuous twin nieces catch the eye of a depraved devil worshipper (Damien Thomas) and soon one of them is drawn into his evil sphere but Cushing is unable to tell which is the witch. Directed by John Hough, it's an exercise in pumped-up suspense with more than usual reliance on graphic gore, nudity and a spot of kinky eroticism

title: Twist and Shout
synopsis: Danish import about two teenagers experiencing the pains of growing up in the 1960s without any parental guidance to help them cope with their adolescent sexual desires and the tragic consequences that result. Nudity, sexual encounters and graphic depiction of abortion

title: Twist Around the Clock
synopsis: Formula musical directed by Oscar Rudolph in which a music agent (John Cronin) attends a country dance, discovers the Twist and promotes it into a national dance craze, with the aid of Clay Cole's band, the Marcels, Chubby Checker, Dion and Vicki Spencer. Romantic complications

title: Twisted
synopsis: Abysmally bad thriller about a newly promoted homicide detective (Ashley Judd) with a tortured past who becomes the prime suspect in a serial murder case she is investigating with her partner (Andy Garcia). Director Philip Kaufman unskillfully navigates a minefield of ridiculous cop cliches and laughable dialogue to craft one of the funniest movies in recent memory; the only problem is it's not supposed to be a comedy. Several sexual encounters with fleeting rear nudity, recurring images of crime scene gore, some brief violence, as well as frequent rough and crude language
full_review:
A female homicide detective with a tortured past becomes her own prime suspect in the abysmally bad neo-noir thriller "Twisted" (Paramount). Navigating a minefield of moth-eaten cop cliches and laugh-inducing dialogue with all the grace of an elephant with vertigo, Philip Kaufman has succeeded in inadvertently crafting one of the funniest movies in recent years; the only problem is it's not supposed to be a comedy.

Ashley Judd stars as recently promoted Jessica Shepard, a brassy boozer with a new gold shield and an off-duty appetite for trolling seedy bars looking for one-night stands of rough sex. When each guy she sleeps with winds up a victim in the string of serial murders she is investigating, all clues seem to point to her as the killer. Compounding the already contrived conceit, Jessica also suffers from inexplicable blackouts, raising self-doubts about her own innocence. Of course, by this time audience members may themselves wish that they could suddenly lose consciousness -- at least until the end of the movie.
Playing the role of red herring is Andy Garcia as Jessica's partner, Mike Delmarco, himself a magnet for suspicion. Rounding out the for-the-paycheck hamfest is Samuel L. Jackson as Police Commissioner Mills, who raised Jessica after her own father (Mills' former partner) may or may not have killed himself along with her mother.

At one point in the film, Jackson, the early front-runner for this year's Best Scene-Chewing Performance, snaps at the suggestion to pull Jessica off the case, qualifying his objection by saying, "It will ruin her career." If professional humiliation is what he's worried about, forget the case; just remove her name from the opening credits.

The film opens with a moody, mist-covered shot of San Francisco Bay -- an apt metaphor for the fog of laugh-out-loud incoherence to follow. Kaufman, whose directing credentials include such critically acclaimed films as "The Right Stuff" (1983) and "The Unbearable Lightness of Being" (1988), plunges headlong into the cheesy world of made-for-TV melodrama. "Twisted" desperately tries to be sexy but can't generate enough inertia to break free of the gravitational pull of its hackneyed script. It is pulp without pop or pizzazz. Leaving no crime cliche unturned, Kaufman even has one of the police interrogators ask a frazzled Jessica, "Where were you on the night of September the 25th?"
Watching "Twisted," it is hard to keep a "straight" face.

Due to several sexual encounters with fleeting rear nudity, recurring images of crime scene gore, some brief violence, as well as frequent rough and crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Twisted Nerve
synopsis: British psychological thriller about an unstable young man (Hywel Bennett) who gradually loses control of his faculties and becomes a homicidal maniac. Directed by Roy Boulting, the plot tries to integrate the effects of heredity and environment upon the youth but the sexual nature of the problems touched upon in the course of the movie make it adult fare

title: Twisted Obsession
synopsis: American screenwriter (Jeff Goldblum) living in Paris is lured into a web of deceit and infidelity by the teenage sister (Liza Walker) of the director (Dexter Fletcher) with whom he is working. Filmed in dark, murky fashion by director Fernando Trueba, the minimal plot serves little purpose but to exploit the innocent appeal of a young actress depicted as an experienced sexual manipulator. Exploitative use of nudity, some restrained scenes of sexual activity and occasional rough language

title: Twister
synopsis: As a series of killer tornadoes bears down on their puny van, meteorologists Helen Hunt and Bill Paxton forget their marital woes in hopes of making a scientific breakthrough -- and escaping with their lives. Director Jan De Bont's jolting special-effects thriller hits a brick wall each time the danger subsides and the script's one-dimensional characters return to the fore. Much meteorological mayhem and recurring casual profanity

title: Twist of Fate
synopsis: Tawdry melodrama directed by David Miller is set on the French Riviera where a former U.S. entertainer (Ginger Rogers) falls for a French artist (Jacques Bergerac) whom her obsessive British lover (Stanley Baker) mistakes for a third-rate thief (Herbert Lom), with dire consequences. Stylized violence, contrived menace and the sudsy heroine's implied affair with a married man

title: Twist of Sand, A
synopsis: Returning to the African coast where years before he had sunk a Nazi sub and massacred its crew, a British sea captain (Richard Johnson) and his partners (Jeremy Kemp and Honor Blackman) retrieve a fortune in diamonds but one of them wants it all. Directed by Don Chaffey, the crime caper has plenty of atmosphere but suffers from a hokey plot and an overly contrived ending. Much menace and some nasty violence

title: Twitch of the Death Nerve, The
synopsis: Sadistic Italian terror movie directed by Mario Bava starts with the strangling of a crippled countess and from their to non-stop slaughter of her husband, offspring, hirelings and neighbors. The horror is the sickening way in which the murders are perpetrated. Repugnant violence

title: Two
synopsis: Danish exploitation sequel to "I, a Woman" makes no pretense at being anything but a cold exercise in senseless promiscuity, almost mechanical in its frequent exposure of Gio Petre's body. Director Mac Ahlberg adds insult to injury by tacking on an absurdly insincere moral ending

title: Two Bits
synopsis: Spiritually uplifting Depression-era story about a 12-year-old boy (Jerry Barone) trying to earn a quarter to go to the movies, though worried his aging Italian grandfather (Al Pacino) may die that very day. Director James Foley sensitively captures the period's economic hardships and generous gestures of the neighbors as well as the child's love for his widowed mom (Mary Elizabeth Mastrantonio) and grandpa. Mild sexual innuendo and a neighborhood suicide

title: Two Brothers
synopsis: Captivating family drama set in Southeast Asia about a pair of tiger cubs, separated by fate, whose lives ultimately cross paths when they are reunited in a fighting arena and pitted against each other as forced enemies. Director Jean-Jacques Annaud earns his stripes, combining stunning wildlife photography with tenderhearted storytelling from the animals' point of view to craft a remarkable fable about family bonds and the healing power of love. Some minor violence and ongoing menace to the animals
full_review:
Some readers may recognize "Tiger, tiger burning bright" as a line from William Blake's poem "The Tiger." But for summer moviegoers it might also be the best way to summarize French director Jean-Jacques Annaud's captivating tiger tale, "Two Brothers" (Universal) -- a film burning bright with both beauty and heartfelt emotion.

In 1989, Annaud's "The Bear" struck a chord with audiences with its touching depiction of an orphaned grizzly cub left to fend for itself.

Annaud once again earns his stripes in "Two Brothers," combining stunning wildlife photography with sure-handed storytelling to craft a feel-good fable about the bonds of family and the healing power of love.

Set in the lush jungles of Southeast Asia, the film opens with two magnificent Bengal tigers frolicking like lovebirds among the exotic ruins of some ancient temple. They mate and give birth to a pair of cubs -- the pugnacious Kumal and his timid twin, Sangha.

As fate would have it, tragedy separates the two brothers soon after their birth. Kumal is sold off to a circus where, caged and abused, he comes to learn that the most savage of beasts is man. Inhumanely forced into submission by a sadistic tamer (Moussa Maaskri), Kumal is trained to growl on cue and jump through flaming hoops, declawed of his natural fighting spirit by depression and cruelty.

Initially, Sangha fares better. After being captured by a hunting party, he is adopted by the colonial governor's gentle-natured son, Raoul (Freddie Highmore), who lavishes affection on the jungle cat. But when a provoked Sangha mauls the family dog, he is shipped off, against Raoul's tear-filled protests, to the private menagerie of a local prince (Oanh Nyguen), where he is turned into a killer and made to fight for sport against other tigers.

Fully grown, the two brothers find themselves reunited in the arena during a royal festival. Pitted against each other as forced enemies, they must put their brotherly bonds to the ultimate test.

Guy Pearce plays a big-game hunter whose path becomes inextricably intertwined with those of the two tigers.

You don't have to be a fan of animal movies to recognize "Two Brothers" as a tour de force in family-friendly filmmaking. As a film, it is visually masterful, poetically poignant and extraordinarily entertaining.

Bold in his ambition to tell the story from the tigers' point of view, Annaud succeeds brilliantly in not only investing his striped stars with distinct personalities, but in making their complex inner life easy for human viewers to relate to on an emotional level. In fact, for a film where two tigers get the, er, lion's share of screen time, "Two Brothers" is suffused with remarkably rich humanity. And though this film contains considerably more dialogue than "The Bear," the most powerful moments are still those which unfold in silence.

Early on, the mother tigress cocks her head, alerted to the presence of the hunters, echoing in gesture the foreboding dread expressed by Bambi's mom's warning, "Man is in the forest" -- perhaps the most chilling line ever uttered on film. And while some sequences may be upsetting to very young children, most of the aforementioned mistreatment takes place off-screen.

The film definitely plays on viewers' emotions, but is done with such disarming grace that few but the most hardened cynics are likely to register complaint.

Though the story can be interpreted as conveying several messages, the simplest -- and, therefore, most profound -- is that love is stronger than hatred and cruelty.

Simply put, this marvelous and magical movie is -- to quote another famous tiger -- grrreat!

There is some minor violence and ongoing menace to the animals. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-I -- general patronage. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-- parental guidance suggested.versimplified conspiracy theories, resulting in a misleading, manipulative and at times self-contradicting interpretation of facts.

title: Two Can Play That Game
synopsis: Lively romantic comedy in which a sassy love expert (Vivica A. Fox) takes her own advice to keep her man (Morris Chestnut) in line but gets surprising results when her boyfriend is counseled by his buddy (Anthony Anderson) on game playing. Writer-director Mark Brown's glossy battle-of-the-sexes film is sprightly paced with some droll observations on lovers' mind games despite its superficial story line and prevalent sexual dialogue. An implied sexual encounter, many sexual references and intermittent crass expressions with a few instances of rough language

title: Two English Girls
synopsis: Director Francois Truffaut has made the perfect companion piece for his previous "Jules and Jim" with the situation this time neatly reversed as a man (Jean-Pierre Leaud) falls in love with two sisters but is unable to make a commitment to either. Some viewers will find the situation completely amoral, and often ridiculously romantic, but as a picture of life at the turn of the century, with its very formal etiquette, suppressed emotions and artifical manners, it couldn't be better. Subtitles. Sexual situations

title: Two Flags West
synopsis: Rambling tale of captured Confederate troopers (led by Joseph Cotten) released from a Union prison in 1864 to fight Indians in New Mexico, then are driven to the point of desertion by their Reb-hating commander (Jeff Chandler). Directed by Robert Wise, the script is cluttered with undeveloped plot turns and stereotyped characters, but the rugged location photography is excellent and the action scenes are well-staged, especially the climactic attack on Fort Thorn. Frontier violence

title: Two for the Money
synopsis: Uninvolving drama about a former star college quarterback (Matthew McConaughey) with a Midas touch for picking winners seduced into the high-stakes arena of sports gambling by a con-man oddsmaker (a hammy Al Pacino) who runs a top betting operation and grooms him as his protege, until he hits a cold streak. No likable characters and a lame script make director D.J. Caruso's testosterone-juiced morality play a bad bet. A sexual encounter with suggested shadowy nudity, a wince-inducing sports injury, gambling themes, a crass scene of urination and much rough and crude language and profanity
full_review:
At one point in director D.J. Caruso's uninvolving drama "Two For the Money" (Universal), Al Pacino, who plays a blustering bookie, tells a group of fellow recovering gambling addicts that the root of their problem lies in some inherent personal flaw. "We're lemons!"

So, it must be said, is this movie.

Delivering yet another master class in apoplectic acting, the gravel-voiced icon stars with Matthew McConaughey, as Brandon Lane, a former star college quarterback with a Midas touch for picking winners. After a career-ending injury, Brandon finds himself in a dead-end gig predicting scores on a Las Vegas 900-number.

His talent catches the attention of Walter Abraham (Pacino), a "Jimmy the Greek"-like oddsmaker who recruits Brandon to a big-time sports betting operation he runs in New York City, which Walter assures him is perfectly legit. (They only offer "free advice," taking a commission on the winnings.)

Part mentor, part con artist, Walter grooms Brandon as his protege, including a running tutorial on how to say the f-word. While his hunches stay hot, Brandon is the toast of the town, enjoying a high life of fast cars, beautiful women and $1,000 bottles of wine.

But their surrogate-father-son relationship cools when Brandon hits a cold streak, a turn of luck that threatens not only their friendship but their lives after they lose their clients (including a thuggish Armand Assante) millions of dollars.

As with these types of modern morality plays, Brandon is tempted by the standard seductions of money and glamour, but, though he temporarily succumbs to their allure, there is never much doubt that he will be humbled and reach the end credits with his soul intact.

McConaughey alternates between smug and shirtless-smug, and Rene Russo makes the most of her limited role as Walter's long-suffering wife, Toni. Elevating scenery-chewing to an art form, Pacino is always watchable.

McConaughey's cockiness and Pacino's histrionics aside, the real problem with the testosterone-juiced movie is that it lacks a likable character (except maybe Toni) or a strong script.

Smart money will go elsewhere.

The film contains a sexual encounter with suggested shadowy nudity, a wince-inducing sports injury, gambling themes, a crass scene of urination and much rough and crude language and profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Two for the Road
synopsis: Producer-director Stanley Donen's saga about a modern marriage on wheels that skids dangerously but doesn't quite crack up, teams Audrey Hepburn and Albert Finney as the troubled couple. By following the pair on their various jaunts through Europe, Donen provides both a fluid vehicle for narrative development as well as strikingly scenic backgrounds

title: Two for the Seesaw
synopsis: Glum drama from William Gibson's play about a morose lawyer (Robert Mitchum) who leaves Nebraska for a fresh start in New York after separating from his wife, falls for a wacky dance teacher (Shirley MacLaine) from the Bronx, then broods over whether to marry her. Director Robert Wise treats the lawyer's mid-life crisis with undeserved sympathy, dampened further by his unlikely romance with the free-spirited dancer and a sentimental ending that leaves viewers flat. Troubled personal relationships

title: Two Gentlemen Sharing
synopsis: Failed British drama about a white Londoner (Robin Phillips) and an upwardly mobile black from the West Indies (Hal Frederick) who share a London mews apartment, have their separate problems and end with one discovering his homosexuality and the other returning to Jamaica. Director Ted Kotcheff's treatment lacks any subtlety, especially in several lovemaking scenes

title: Two Girls and a Guy
synopsis: Shrill exploitation clunker in which three emotionally distraught people exhaust themselves shouting foul-mouthed recriminations at each other before two wind up having sex while the third muses on the possibilities of a threesome. Writer-director James Toback has come up with a shoddy piece of merchandise whose idea of dramatic conflict is verbal assault and sexual promiscuity without any insight into the characters or what they have gone through. Exploitative sexual themes and situations, constant rough language and occasional profanity

title: Two-Gun Lady
synopsis: Low-budget Western directed by Richard H. Bartlett in which a vaudeville trick-shot artist (Peggy Castle) teams with an undercover lawman (William Tallman) to get her father's killer. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Two If by Sea
synopsis: A dull-witted thief (Denis Leary) with a stolen Matisse hides out with his girlfriend (Sandra Bullock) for a weekend in a unoccupied seaside mansion where they pretend to know the absent owner to a suspicious neighbor who has something to hide himself. Bill Bennett directs a vacuous comedy of all-too convenient coincidences in which gutter language is a poor substitute for wit. A lame rejection of a life of crime, implied affair and much rough language and profanity

title: Two Jakes, The
synopsis: Sequel to "Chinatown" (1974) has its Los Angeles private eye (Jack Nicholson) haunted by painful memories of a previous case while trying to uncover the real reasons why his client (Harvey Keitel) killed the man having an affair with his wife (Meg Tilly). Also directed by Nicholson, the well-crafted performances and lushly atmospheric setting gets bogged down from the start with too many characters and an overly intricate plot. Sporadic violence, restrained sexual depictions and occasional rough language

title: Two-Lane Blacktop
synopsis: Introspective young man (folk-rock singer James Taylor) who lives on the road in his 1955 Chevy coupe races the owner of a Pontiac G.T.O. (Warren Oates) in a back roads tour across America. Director Monte Hellman's low-key approach does not romanticize his drifters of the road but along the way shows some of the reasons why they have opted out of the mainstream. Some realistic street language

title: Two Men and a Girl
synopsis: ( see: 1947's "Honeymoon" )

title: Two Men of Karamoja
synopsis: Documentary account of seven months of conflict and change in Uganda's Kidepo Valley National Park as the British chief warden prepares to turn the preserve over to a native warden. Directed by Natalie and Eugene Jones, the movie examines not only the park's wildlife problems but its native population whose tribal structures are changing with the times. Much of this ethonograhpic material is best suited for adults and older adolescents

title: Two Minute Warning
synopsis: Gathered in the Los Angeles Coliseum are an assortment of disaster veterans (Charlton Heston, John Cassavetes, Martin Balsam and David Jansen) and 100,000 extras when a sniper is spotted, the police move in and the arena is turned into a Roman forum of bloodshed and graphic violence. Directed by Larry Peerce the mindless fantasy plays on fears and anxieties of random senseless violence in extreme fashion

title: Two Moon Junction
synopsis: Slick soap opera about a rich Southern belle (Sherilyn Fenn) set upon marrying a rich young Yuppie (Martin Hewitt), but not before being lustfully distracted by a carnal worker (Richard Tyson). Although artfully photographed, with gorgeous plantation settings and a solid supporting cast (Louise Fletcher, Burl Ives and Kristy McNichol), writer-director Zalman King comes up with nothing more than glorified soft porn. A sequence of extreme violence, several scenes with frontal nudity and explicit sexual encounters and much locker room language

title: Two Much
synopsis: Failed comedy in which a con artist (Antonio Banderas) becomes engaged to a wealthy divorcee (Melanie Griffith), then woos her brainy sister (Daryl Hannah) by pretending to be his own brother. Directed by Fernando Trueba, the lame proceedings are listlessly contrived, leadenly performed and rely more on sexual innuendo than comic wit. Sexual situations and references with occasional coarse language

title: Two Mules for Sister Sara
synopsis: Prostitute masquerading as a nun (Shirley MacLaine) in order to help Mexican rebels is joined by cowboy loner (Clint Eastwood) in undertaking the capture of a French garrison and they fall in love. Directed by Don siegel, there are sone good action sequences but the comic irreverences (a supposed nun smoking, drinking and cursing like a trooper), like the movie, are not to be taken seriously

title: Two Ninas
synopsis: Formulaic romantic comedy in which a forlorn twenty-something writer (Ron Livingston) falls for two women with the same name. Nothing can save director Neil Turitz's derivative debut from its sleep-inducing, feeble plot that wearies with its predictable situations and endless banalities. A few sexual encounters, several sexual references and recurring profanity and rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Twonky, The
synopsis: Comic sci-fi misfire written and directed by Arch Oboler in which a college professor (Han Conried) finds his new TV set is actually a robotic machine from the future which proceeds to take charge of his life until the professor rebels. Slapstick violence and sexual innuendo

title: Two of a Kind
synopsis: John Travolta and Olivia Newton-John have the misfortune to star in a dreadful movie about God's sending a quartet of angels to earth to try and reform two nasty people. Written and directed by John Herzfield, it is for the most part innocuous, except for some profanity

title: Two of Us, The
synopsis: Excellent French story of a little Jewish boy (Alain Cohen) who is hidden from the Nazis on a remote farm in Occupied France by an elderly anti-Semite (Michael Simon). Directed by Claude Berri, the movie is a very touching, gentle sort of comedy, told simply through an accumulation of incidents rather than a tightly-knit plot. Everyone can identify with and enjoy the warm, human relationship between the old man and the young lad

title: Two or Three Things I Know About Her
synopsis: Director Jean-Luc Godard's paean to Paris (the "Her" of the title) follows the fragmentary story of a part-time prostitute (Marina Vlady) but Raoul Coutar's camera is focused on the ever-changing face of a modern city. Though the movie is heavily laced with philosophical asides and interruptions, it is often amusing, at times illuminating and always stunningly beautiful in its picture of a great city

title: Two People
synopsis: Trivial romantic claptrap about a Vietnam deserter (Peter Fonda) and a jaded divorcee (Lindsay Wagner) who meet in Marrakech, talk their way to Casablanca, make love in Parish and finally fly to New York where he is going to turn himself in. Directed by Robert Wise, the budding romance is totally unmotivated and certainly made no more credible by a ridiculously over-extended, semi-nude love scene

title: Two Rode Together
synopsis: On a mission to rescue women and children taken captive by Comanches, an idealistic cavalry officer (Richard Widmark) bickers along the way with a frontier marshal (James Stewart) who's only interested in the reward offered by the captives' families. Director John Ford uses the conflict between these familiar Western character types to take a darker, less poetic view of the tragic confrontation between the forces of civilization and the waning powers of a less developed native culture. Some stylized violence

title: Two Seconds
synopsis: Tough-minded tale in which a Manhattan construction worker (Edward G. Robinson) is tricked into marrying a taxi dancer (Vivienne Osborne), then suffers a breakdown when his riveter buddy (Preston Foster) falls to his death from a skyscraper and finally murders his wife for causing all his woes. Director Mervyn LeRoy gets a realistic performance from Robinson who starts the picture in the electric chair while the events which put him there are shown in gritty Depression-era flashbacks. Stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Two Tickets to Broadway
synopsis: Formula musical in which struggling singer Tony Martin is duped by devious agent Eddie Bracken into developing an act with would-be showgirls Janet Leigh and Ann Miller for Bob Crosby's TV show, with predictable results. Directed by James V. Kern, the result features some charmless production numbers, lackluster songs and feeble slapstick comedy. Romantic complications

title: Two Weeks in September
synopsis: Failed French romance directed by Serge Bourguignon in which a model (Brigitte Bardot), living with a man in Paris, accepts an assignment in London where she acquires a new lover and then can't decide which one she really wants. suggestive treatment of illicit sex

title: Two Weeks Notice
synopsis: Bland romantic comedy in which an altruistic activist lawyer (Sandra Bullock) gives notice to her vacuous, wealthy boss (Hugh Grant), neither of them ready to admit they are in love. Writer-director Marc Lawrence's cliched script and predictable path undermine the comic talents of the leads. Sexual situations and references and fleeting drunkenness
full_review:
Sandra Bullock and Hugh Grant's talents for light comedy are all for naught in the bland romantic comedy, "Two Weeks Notice" (Warner Bros.).

For fans of the two, the opening credits featuring actual photos of each from babyhood to adolescence may prove more appealing than the movie itself.

The paper-thin story has real estate magnate George Wade (Grant) getting activist lawyer Lucy Kelson (Bullock) to work for him on the condition he not tear down her Coney Island neighborhood's community center.

Soon he is dependent on her to make every itty-bitty decision for him while she becomes frustrated with such trivial concerns. Informing him she's out the door in two weeks, she's also put off when he instantly hires as her replacement a red-headed hottie, June (Alicia Witt), with gold-digger moves.

Lucy's jealous, George is dumb and June is obvious, a combination which doesn't make for a smart comedy with romantic sparkle.

Writer-director Marc Lawrence's flat script is the chief offender. With such banal dialogue as "you have to use your powers for good rather than evil," the cliches are all in place. Bullock is game to repeat her winsome comic klutziness and Grant is back to twittering his eyelashes for laughs, but the situations and the banter between them is ordinary, not screwball or clever. At least, Donald Trump's cameo as a fellow land developer adds unintended comedy with his wildly outdated hairstyle.

Much time is given to establishing that Lucy has been an idealistic protestor since birth; her parents raised her to be a committed lawyer and social activist. (You also know this by the drab flower-child outfits she wears until she has to wear monotonous power suits in the corporate world.)

But we have no idea why George is such a self-absorbed airhead (or why Lucy is unconsciously in love with him since his chief asset, money, means nothing to her). One glance at June and we know everything we need to know about her and what she's after. So the romantic triangle crawls along to its assured outcome without delivering much entertainment.

Because of sexual situations and references and fleeting drunkenness, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Two Years Before the Mast
synopsis: Stodgy dramatization of the account written in 1840 by Richard Henry Dana (Brian Donlevy) describing the brutal conditions and unjust treatment he witnessed as a seaman aboard a U.S. merchant ship whose crew is finally driven to mutiny against their cruel captain (Howard da Silva). Though saddled with a script focusing on the travails of the ship-owners's shanghaied son (Alan Ladd), director John Farrow manages to convey the harsh realities of a sailor's life in the age of sail. Restrained depictions of brutality in a human rights context

title: Tycoon
synopsis: Long but intriguing drama in which an American engineer (John Wayne) is hired by a South American aristocrat (Cedric Hardwicke) to build a railroad tunnel through a mountain, then makes an enemy of his powerful employer by wooing his daughter (Lorraine Day). Director Richard Wallace alternates the hard, dangerous work of construction with the cultureal differences dividing engineer and emploer, not least of which are differing notion of romance and marriage. Some stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Tyler Perry's Daddy's Little Girls
synopsis: Romantic drama about a hard-luck Atlanta mechanic and devoted single father (Idris Elba) battling to get custody of his three daughters (Sierra Aylina McClain, Lauryn Alisa McClain and China Anne McClain) from his ex-wife (Tasha Smith) and her drug-dealing boyfriend (Gary Sturgis). To help pay the bills, he chauffeurs a successful, but unlucky at love, attorney (Gabrielle Union) whose offer to help him with his legal fight leads to romance. Written and directed by Christian filmmaker Tyler Perry, the earnestly sentimental script is not without some formulaic elements, but the honest performances and strong affirmations of faith, family and community -- as well as its positive depiction of African-American fatherhood -- outshine the shortcomings. Sexual humor, including a brief crude sight gag, some violence, drug references, an implied sexual encounter, a false accusation of rape and some crude expressions
full_review:
The agreeable romantic drama "Tyler Perry's Daddy's Little Girls" (Lionsgate) is so full of earnest sentimentality and unabashed good will that only a cynic would holds its flaws against it.

Idris Elba plays Monty, a hard-luck Atlanta mechanic and devoted single father battling to get custody of his three daughters (Sierra Aylina McClain, Lauryn Alisa McClain and China Anne McClain) from his abusive ex-wife, Jennifer (Tasha Smith), who's now living with her thuggish boyfriend, Joseph (Gary Sturgis), the neighborhood drug lord.

Gabrielle Union is Julia, a successful attorney Monty chauffeurs to make some extra cash -- and who winds up representing him in his legal fight after she witnesses a heated hospital blowup between Monty and Jennifer.

As you might guess, while preparing for the court hearing, the uptight Julia -- who has sworn off men after getting burned by a past relationship -- falls for the decent, hardworking Monty, even as she worries how her snooty peers will react.

Written and directed by Christian filmmaker Tyler Perry (who plays the pistol-packing matriarch in the popular "Madea" movies), the sweet story is not without some formulaic elements, but the honest performances and strong affirmations of faith, family and community -- as well as its positive depiction of African-American fatherhood expressed by its tagline "Give life. Teach love" -- outshine the shortcomings.

The film contains sexual humor, including a brief crude sight gag, some violence, drug references, an implied sexual encounter, a false accusation of rape and some crude expressions. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Tyler Perry's Madea Family Reunion
synopsis: Wacky but warm follow-up to the 2005 dramedy "Diary of a Mad Black Woman," which finds outrageous southern matriarch Madea (played in drag by Tyler Perry) helping one niece (Rochelle Aytes) escape her abusive live-in fiance (Blair Underwood); another niece (Lisa Arrindell Anderson) find love with a gentlemanly bus driver (Boris Kodjoe); and a wayward youth (Keke Palmer) turn her life around, all the while planning a family gathering. Once again written and directed by Perry, the sequel follows the original's lead, combining off-the-wall humor and serious story lines with strongly religious overtones, resulting in an heartfelt and agreeable affirmation of faith, family and forgiveness -- highlighted by emotional speeches by Cicely Tyson and Maya Angelou about black dignity -- that's easy to applaud, despite its message-heavy sentiment and intermittent vulgarities. Domestic abuse violence, brief drug references, scattered crude sexual and scatological humor, and some crass expressions
full_review:
Though neither Martin Lawrence nor Tyler Perry make particularly attractive women, when it comes to heart, "Tyler Perry's Madea's Family Reunion" (Lions Gate) wins the "drag" race over Lawrence's recent "Big Momma's House 2."

In this wacky but warm follow-up to the 2005 dramedy "Diary of a Mad Black Woman," Christian playwright-turned-filmmaker Perry once again dons wig and housedress as outrageous Southern matriarch Madea, who here must help one niece (Rochelle Aytes) escape her abusive live-in fiance (Blair Underwood); another niece (Lisa Arrindell Anderson) find love with a gentlemanly bus driver (Boris Kodjoe); and a wayward youth (Keke Palmer) turn her life around, all the while planning a family gathering.

Written and directed as before by Perry, the sequel follows the original's lead, combining off-the-wall humor and serious story lines with strongly religious overtones. The unabashedly uncynical result is a heartfelt and agreeable affirmation of faith, family and forgiveness -- highlighted by emotional speeches by Cicely Tyson and Maya Angelou (in cameos) about black dignity -- that's easy to applaud, despite its message-heavy sentiment and intermittent vulgarities.

The film contains domestic-abuse violence, brief drug references, scattered crude sexual and scatological humor, and some crass expressions. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Tyler Perry's Why Did I get Married?
synopsis: Raucous humor alternates with a serious examination of the challenges of married life as four couples gather in the Rockies for their annual vacation and retreat: a best-selling pop psychiatrist (Janet Jackson) resists her architect spouse�s (Malik Yoba) efforts to come to grips with a recent family tragedy; a successful lawyer (Sharon Leal) is too busy for her increasingly exasperated husband (Tyler Perry); a tough talking salon owner (Tasha Smith) tyrannizes her ex-NFL player husband (Michael Jai White); finally, an emotionally abusive husband (Richard T. Jones) heaps insults on his overweight wife (Jill Scott) while reserving his affection for her supposed friend, and his mistress (Denise Boutte). The film, as written, directed and produced by Tyler Perry features some very effective comedy and, though the dramatic elements are less successful, the script as a whole presents a resounding reaffirmation of the value of committed marital love. Some crass language, two uses of profanity, frank sexual discussions, including references to a character with venereal disease, one incident of domestic violence, domestic discord and divorce,
full_review:
Raucous humor alternates with a serious examination of the challenges of married life in "Tyler Perry's Why Did I Get Married?" (Lionsgate). The film, based on a stage play of the same title, explores the relationships of four affluent African-American couples as they gather in the Rockies for their annual vacation and retreat.

Patricia (Janet Jackson) is a pop psychologist and best-selling author. Ironically, however, she resists her architect husband Gavin's (Malik Yoba) efforts to come to grips with a recent family tragedy.

Dianne (Sharon Leal), a successful lawyer, is too busy to devote any time to her increasingly exasperated husband, Terry (Tyler Perry). Meanwhile, Angela (Tasha Smith), a tough talking salon owner, tyrannizes her former NFL player husband Marcus (Michael J. White).

The victim of relentless emotional abuse, overweight Sheila (Jill Scott) is joined, not only by her vituperative husband, Mike (Richard T. Jones), but by her supposed friend - and his mistress - Trina (Denise Boutte).

Even as the couples renew old friendships, underlying conflicts endure. Once unpleasant secrets are revealed, affecting all four couples, the gathering disperses, with the spouses forced to reflect on their futures.

The film, as written, directed and produced by Tyler Perry, features some very effective comedy. Smith is especially enjoyable in the role of a tippling, not-to-be-silenced coiffeur with attitude.

The movie's dramatic elements resemble, at times, a fictionalized version of "Dr. Phil." Yet the film's resounding affirmation of enduring marital love is especially timely in this commitment-phobic era.

The film contains some crass language, two uses of profanity, frank sexual discussions, including a character with venereal disease, one incident of domestic violence, marital discord and divorce. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: An Unfinished Life
synopsis: Captivating story of embittered Wyoming rancher (Robert Redford in a career peak) -- caregiver to a ranch hand (Morgan Freeman) badly mauled by a bear -- who gives shelter to his son's widow (Jennifer Lopez) and the 11-year-old granddaughter (Becca Gardner) he never knew he had, when the woman flees her abusive boyfriend. Director Lasse Hallstrom's film, though not devoid of cliches, is sensitively acted, ravishingly photographed and vividly conveys an admirable message about forgiveness and letting go of the past. Despite profanity, rough language and irreligious remarks (courtesy of Redford's salty but basically honorable character), some brief episodes of domestic violence and implied premarital sex, the film is uplifting entertainment for adults and mature adolescents
full_review:
You might suspect something amiss with a movie that's been sitting on the shelf for two years, but if you pass up "An Unfinished Life" (Miramax) you'll be missing one of 2005's best.

This is a totally captivating tale of forgiveness and rebirth in its story of an embittered Wyoming rancher named Einar Gilkyson (Robert Redford), who takes care of ranch hand Mitch (Morgan Freeman), badly mauled by a bear.

Einar reluctantly gives shelter to his son's widow, Jean (Jennifer Lopez), who shows up unexpectedly with the 11-year-old granddaughter, Griff (Becca Gardner), he never knew he had. They are fleeing the abuse of Jean's violent boyfriend, Gary (Damian Lewis).

Written by Mark Spragg and Virginia Korus Spragg, the film features top-level acting all around, but with Redford outstanding. This is a career peak for him. He completely inhabits his ornery, grizzled man's-man character who -- after the death of his beloved son -- shuts himself down to life. His dialogue is liberally sprinkled with profanity, so you know he'll eventually soften under Griff's openhearted and liberating presence.

He's not particularly religious, insisting, for instance, that anyone who comes to his door be treated well, unless "it's some guy selling God," which he gruffly dismisses with an expletive. But in every other respect, he's an honorable man.

In addition to his ministrations to Mitch, he defends Nina (Camryn Manheim), the local diner's waitress, from the predations of three drunken louts.

Einar -- who talks to his son graveside every day -- blames Jean for his son's death (she had been driving, and lost control of the car).

Mitch -- another splendid Freeman portrayal -- spends most of his time in his shack, calling on Einar to give him morphine shots when the pain gets bad. The brotherly bond between the two men is admirable, and so profound that young Griff at one point mistakenly thinks they must be gay, much to their amusement.

Mitch's assailant plays a big part as the bear roams the town, causing great consternation. Einar wants to shoot him, but local sheriff Crane (Josh Lucas) stops him in the nick of time and sees to it that the bear is captured and put in the care of the local zoo owner.

Far from despising the bear, Mitch worries about the bear's well-being, and demands that Einar feed the now-caged bear. With Griff at his side, Einar dutifully complies. Mitch's instinct to show the bear mercy is a powerful, if obvious, metaphor.

Jean, meanwhile, officially reports her situation to Crane, in case Gary should show up again, and before long, motivated in part by Jean's intense sense of loneliness -- especially in light of Einar's unwelcoming coldness -- they commence an affair. Griff is angry about their liaison, as her mother has had a pattern of hooking up with disreputable men. But this will prove different, as Crane shows himself a decent man.

The pacing is leisurely, but the underlying threat of Gary's reappearance and the omnipresent bear wreaking more havoc add a good measure of suspense.

Director Lasse Hallstrom's film, though not devoid of cliches, vividly conveys its positive message about healing, letting go of the past and living life to the fullest despite tragedy.

Though the life of Einar's son is referred to as "unfinished," the title also reflects Einar's emotional paralysis.

Lopez -- in a smallish part -- is well-cast and believable as a guilt-ridden woman on the run, while the versatile Lewis could not be more different from the veddy British Soames, an obsessed suitor of another stripe, that he played in the recent BBC "Forsyte Saga."
Manheim is terrific as the good-hearted waitress who copes better than Einar with the loss of a child (her daughter drowned, we learn).

Lucas plays his share of bad guys, but here he's allowed to play one of the good ones.
Gardner is refreshingly down-to-earth, and even the grizzly -- Bart II in real life -- acquits himself well. (The bear, symbolizes, none too subtly, those parts of our past of which we must let go.)

Lush location scenery and painterly photography (by Oliver Stapleton) are other pluses in this evocative and beautifully redemptive slice of Western Americana.

Despite profanity, rough language and irreligious remarks (mostly courtesy of Redford's salty but basically honorable character), some brief episodes of domestic violence and implied premarital sex, the film is uplifting entertainment for adults and mature adolescents. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
