Directed by Edwin Sherin, the heavy-handed plot development contains much violence and smatterings of sex and near-nudity

title: Valentine
synopsis: Ridiculous horror flick in which four women, friends since childhood, are threatened by a nerd from their past who exacts revenge for their merciless teasing at a junior high school Valentine's Day dance. As directed by Jamie Blanks, the amateur film's cherub-masked killer produces more laughs than gasps as the clueless female characters prance around in search of true love in a preposterous plot that barely holds together. Intermittent violence with gore, a few sexual situations, brief nudity and fleeting rough language with some crass expressions. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Valentino
synopsis: British director Ken Russell's screen biography of Rudolph Valentino (Rudolf Nureyev) is a boring, overdone piece of pretentious trash having only the remotest connection with the famous movie star's life. Nudity and graphic sexuality

title: Valentino Returns
synopsis: Lackluster 1950's coming-of-age drama about the frustrations of a young adult male (Barry Tubb) searching for sex on a typical Saturday night in his pink Cadillac. First-time director Peter Hoffman's effort fizzles into small-town vignettes that lack punch. Some rough language laced with sexual vulgarities, implied promiscuity and some nudity

title: Valerie and Her Week of Wonders
synopsis: Czechoslovakian fantasy in which a 13-year-old girl's daydreaming transforms her ordinary world into one filled with strange adventures, bizarre characters and the first vague stirrings of sexual awareness. Directed by Jaromil Jires, the setting is a picturesque village at the turn of the century, affording lush imagery, striking compositions, colorful costuming and ornamental detail that lend themselves easily to a surrealistic picture of a young adolescent's imagination. Literal-minded viewers may be confused by the movie's lack of narrative guideposts but the juxtaposition of religious and Freudian symbolism invites deeper psychological probing by those so inclined

title: Valiant
synopsis: Whimsically entertaining, if a bit featherweight, computer-animated adventure set in World War II-era England about a tiny but stalwart carrier pigeon (voiced by Ewan McGregor) who is given the dangerous mission of delivering a vital communique from occupied France safely to England while being hunted by a squadron of ruthless German falcons. Despite a script that is a little light in the plumage, the visually vibrant film imparts a positive self-esteem message that "it's not the size of your wingspan, but the size of your spirit." Some scary images that may frighten the youngest viewers and a few innocuous flatulence jokes
full_review:
To paraphrase the old song, be kind to your fine feathered friends, for that pigeon may be a war hero. In fact, next time one lands outside your window, you might want to salute him rather than shoo him away.

During World War II, 54 nonhuman combatants were honored with the Dickin Medal -- England's animal version of the Purple Heart -- for distinguished military service. Of the recipients, which included dogs, horses and a cat, 32 were carrier pigeons, a statistic that inspired the telling of "Valiant" (Disney), a computer-animated adventure from the creators of "Shrek," about a tiny bird who comes up big.

Set in World War II-era England, the featherweight but whimsically entertaining tale centers on a runt named Valiant (cutely cooed by Ewan McGregor) who joins Great Britain's Royal Homing Pigeon Service despite naysayers who tell him he is too small.

The plucky pigeon makes his way to London where he is taken under the wing of artful dodger Bugsy (voiced by Ricky Gervais), a flying fleabag with a cockney accent who unwittingly enlists as well. Rounding out the recruits are monocled Lofty (voiced by Pip Torrens) and twins Toughwood (voiced by Brian Lonsdale) and Tailfeather (voiced by Dan Roberts), neither "the sharpest beak on the block."

A large portion of the paltry 75-minute film involves mildly amusing slapstick sequences of the brigade -- designated "Squad F" -- as they're whipped into flying shape by the gruff drill-pigeon Sergeant (voiced by Jim Broadbent).

Directed by Gary Chapman, the film takes flight when the misfits are deployed behind enemy lines in occupied France to relay an important communique safely back to England. Victory or defeat for the Allies rests squarely on Valiant's scrawny wings.

Flying between them and success, however, are a squadron of pigeon-eating German falcons: Panzer raptor General Von Talon (voiced by Tim Curry), who rules the skies with an iron beak, and his two lackeys Cufflingk (voiced by Rik Mayall) and Underlingk (voiced by Michael Schlingmann).

There are comical moments in the "Hogan's Heroes" vein, with Von Talon an avian Colonel Klink ("Ve have vays of making you squawk!"). There are, however, a few menacing moments that may be a bit intense for very young children.

The information that Valiant ends up delivering anchors the plot elements in history poignantly. The resolution is foreshadowed by a haunting image of the Allied fleet crossing a mist-shrouded English Channel.

Compared with recent animated films like "Shrek" and "Finding Nemo," the writing and characters in "Valiant" are a little thin in the plumage. The vibrant animation has a more classic old-fashioned look that, refreshingly, doesn't bombard you with hip pop-culture references. Adding to the movie's overall period feel is George Fenton's swing-era score.
An opening 1940s' newsreel sequence is quite funny.

Despite its flaws, "Valiant" imparts a positive self-esteem message that "it's not the size of your wingspan, but the size of your spirit."

With it getting harder to find family entertainment that doesn't sneak in age-inappropriate content, "Valiant" is one movie that won't ruffle many parents' feathers.

The film contains some scary images that may frighten the youngest viewers and a few innocuous flatulence jokes. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-I -- general patronage. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is G -- general audiences.

title: Valkyrie
synopsis: Generally well-made and engrossing World War II thriller about the true-life final plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler and take over the government by a group of disenchanted army officers (Tom Cruise, Bill Nighy, Kenneth Branagh, Eddie Izzard, Tom Wilkinson and Terence Stamp). Director Bryan Singer maintains a taut, suspenseful pace, performances are fine (including Cruise, though he seems a bit miscast in the European milieu), and objectionable elements are minimal. Some wartime violence, suicide, executions and a single use of the F-word

title: Valley Girl
synopsis: San Fernando Valley girl (Deborah Foreman) throws over her handsome but dumb Valley boyfriend in favor of a punk rocker from Hollywood (Nicolas Cage), much to the consternation of her friends. Directed by Martha Coolige, this Romeo and Juliet variation makes some gestures in the direction of satire, but essentially is another teen exploitation movie, with graphic nudity and rough language

title: Valley of Gwangi, The
synopsis: A group of riders from a Wild West show (headed by James Franciscus) go in search of a major attraction in a hidden Mexican valley where prehistoric monsters survive protected from the outside world by a band of mysterious gypsies. Directed by James O'Connolly, the far-fetched adventure depends mostly on Ray Harryhausen's special effects and one's own imagination

title: Valley of Hunted Men
synopsis: Western programmer directed by John English in which the Three Mesquiteers (Bob Steele, Tom Tyler and Jimmie Dodd) track down three escaped Nazi P.O.W.s on a crime spree in Montana while foiling Axis spies after a new rubber source discovered by a German refugee (Edward Van Sloan). Stylized violence

title: Valley of Mystery
synopsis: Airliner crash-lands in South American jungle among whose perils are a tribe of headhunters, but the pilot (Richard Egan) manages to keep the survivors alive until rescued by helicopters. Director Josef Leytes turns a routine adventure story into a slack melodrama of little interest. Stylized violence

title: Valley of the Dolls
synopsis: Trashy melodrama based on a trashy novel about decadence in the world of show business and the deleterious effects of gulping pep and sleeping pills. Directed by Mark Robson, the insight is nil, most of the acting is embarrassingly bad and it elicits only pained disbelief at its amateurishness and a few laughs where none was intended

title: Valley of the Dragons
synopsis: Minor sci-fi adventure from the Jules Verne story, "Career of the Comet," is set in 1881 when a Frenchman (Cesare Danova) and an Irishman (Sean McClory) are swept up by a comet which, on a previous pass of Earth some 100,000 years before, had picked up examples of prehistoric life. Director Edward Bernds lends little credibility to the prodceedings, but Verne's audacious premise is sufficiently diverting for those who don't mind bargain-basement cavemen and dinosaurs. Stylized violence and mild thrills

title: Valley of the Kings
synopsis: American archeologist (Robert Taylor) helps an Englishwoman (Eleanor Parker) search for evidence proving the biblical account of Joseph's sojourn in the land of the pharaohs. Director Robert Pirosh muddies matters with murderous conniving by greedy traffickers in antiquities, but the result is worth seeing for its grand vistas of famous sites in ancient Egypt. Some menace and stylized violence

title: Valley of the Sun
synopsis: Odd-ball Western in which an Army scout (James Craig) averts an Apache uprising by exposing a corrupt Indian agent (Dean Jagger) while wooing the sidewinder's girlfriend (Lucille Ball). Director George Marshall mixes in a lot of rough humor with the low-budget action and flavorsome romancing. Some positive Indian stereotyping and a bit of stylized violence

title: Valmont
synopsis: Visually lush but emotionally empty adaptation of the 18th-century novel, "Les Liaisons Dangereuses," the story centers on the sexual intrigues among a circle of French aristocrats, notably the title character (Colin Firth) and his one-time paramour (Annette Bening). Though director Milos Forman tries to humanize these upper-class libertines, he seems more interested in re-creating the rich opulence and frivolous style of a world that disappeared with the French Revolution. Restrained treatment of immoral relationships

title: Vampire Bat, The
synopsis: Creaky horror story of a German village fearing a vampire is in its midst as a mad doctor (Lionel Atwill) leaves victims drained of blood needed for his experiments. Director Frank Strayer does better with the spooky atmosphere than the sinister proceedings in a weak script notable only for a cast including Melvyn Douglas, Fay Wray and Dwight Frye. Stylized violence and menacing situations

title: Vampire Circus
synopsis: British horror movie in which a traveling troupe of gypsy vampires (Adrienne Corri and Anthony Corlan) visit a Serbian village to revive a dead count who had been killed there 15 years before. Director Robert Young tries to make up for the script's lack of wit and suspense with a fair sprinkling of incidental sex, but with little success

title: Vampire in Brooklyn
synopsis: Unamusing horror parody in which a wary New York City cop (Angela Bassett) is romantically pursued by a suave vampire (Eddie Murphy) intent on getting her to willingly join the undead. Director Wes Craven's flat mix of horror, comedy and grisly special effects is about as comatose as its title character before sunset. Some gory violence played for laughs, scene of a mock preacher convincing his flock evil is good and much rough language

title: Vampire Lovers
synopsis: Minimal British horror movie about a female vampire with lesbian inclinations who ravages the young maidens of a peaceful little hamlet. Directed by Roy Ward Baker, the movie emphasizes blood and sex at the expense of more traditional horror elements

title: Vampire's Kiss
synopsis: After picking up a vampire (Jennifer Beals) in a singles' bar, a New York Yuppie (Nicolas Cage) turns into a blood-sucking vampire by night and a manic monster terrorizing his young secretary (Maria Conchita Alonso) by day. Directed by Robert Bierman, the misogynist movie depicts men as sorry victims of women who exist only to lure men to self-destruction. Much profanity and promiscuity, laced with flashes of nudity and bloody sexual encounters

title: Vampires
synopsis: ( see: "John Carpenter's Vampires" )

title: Van Gogh
synopsis: Laborious depiction of the final days of the suicidal artist (Jacques Dutronc) living in the suburbs of 1890's Paris where he distracts himself with an alleged affair with the daughter (Alexandra London) of his benefactor (Gerard Sety). Maurice Pialat's tedious direction and Dutronc's stony performance only reveal surface details of the artist's mundane existance without adequately conveying his mental state or the scores of paintings he feverishly finished in his final days. Implied affairs and some nudity. Subtitles

title: Van Helsing
synopsis: Dreadful action adventure about a notorious monster hunter (Hugh Jackman) sent to Transylvania by a secret Vatican agency and charged with helping a local vampire slayer (Kate Beckinsale) rid the world of Count Dracula (Richard Roxburgh) and other fiendish creatures including werewolves and Frankenstein's monster (Shuler Hensley). Despite stylishly gothic atmospherics, this long, loud and ludicrous monster mash, directed by Stephen Sommers amounts to little more than overwrought special-effects sequences without any thought given to story -- let alone characters to sink your teeth into. Incessant comic-book violence, an implied sexual encounter, some innuendo and frightening images
full_review:
A legendary monster-hunter sets up stakes in Transylvania in the disjointed, distended and all-around dreadful action adventure "Van Helsing" (Universal).

One would think that a film containing Dracula, a werewolf and Frankenstein's monster would be a can't-miss. Think again. Full of headache-inducing action sequences, the clumsily structured film is more lumbering than Frankenstein's monster, mostly due to a script that lacks any bite and that has enough stale dialogue to make an audience howl with laughter -- full moon or not.

Hugh Jackman stars as Gabriel Van Helsing, a notorious bounty hunter working for a clandestine Vatican agency charged with ridding the world of fiendish creatures; of course, a much greater service would be ridding the world of awful films. Conflicted over his violent vocation, Van Helsing justifies his enigmatic employment partly as a penance for past crimes, the details of which remain shrouded even to him thanks to an inexplicable amnesia. "Some things are better left forgotten," he concludes -- starting with this movie.

After a roughhouse round of Hyde-and-seek with a digitally created Mr. Hyde (voiced by Robbie Coltrane) in the bell tower of Paris' Notre Dame Cathedral (one can only assume Quasimodo is subletting), the holy hired gun is summoned back to Rome. There he is given new marching orders: Travel to Transylvania and terminate Dracula (Richard Roxburgh) before the count kills the sole surviving scion of a royal bloodline of vampire hunters, Princess Valerious (Kate Beckinsale), who is bent on avenging her ancestors and ending an ancient curse on her family.

Accompanied by a mousy monk, Friar Carl (David Wenham), Van Helsing heads off to Transylvania where he teams up with Valerious. Of course, with all the wooden stakes and crucifixes they had to pack, little room was left in their saddlebags for a plot. The rest of the supernatural silliness involves little more than Van Helsing going against Dracula and his blood-sucking brides (Elena Anaya, Silvia Colloca and Josie Maran), who transform into bat-like demons and terrorize the local village with aerial assaults. Along the way he also tussles with werewolves, finds an unlikely ally in Frankenstein's monster (played with humanity by Shuler Hensley) and foils a diabolical plot by Dracula, serving as a reminder that even counts should never count their eggs before they're hatched. Emotionally, nothing is at, er, stake.

As directed by Stephen Sommers (who also helmed the equally overwrought "The Mummy" and "The Mummy's Return"), the long, loud and ludicrous affair unfolds as a series of dizzying, albeit visually spectacular, special-effects sequences, wrapped in appropriately dark and rainy gothic atmospherics without the slightest concern for narrative coherence -- or, for that matter, spatial relations. For a far more fun take on the Transylvanian trio, rent 1948's "Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein."

Jackman is appealing as the grim slayer. Roxburgh tries to inject some life into the undead Dracula, but the material doesn't give him much to sink his teeth into.

In a nod to political correctness, Sommers has made the clandestine Vatican bureau Van Helsing works for a syncretistic stew of interfaith employees -- including Buddhist monks and Muslim imams -- a choice that may irk some Catholics, as may a scene involving Friar Carl requesting sexual favors as reward for saving a village maiden.

One highlight involves a lavish masquerade ball shot in the de-consecrated church of St. Nicholas in Prague and choreographed by Debra Brown of the famed Cirque du Soleil.

In its heyday, Universal produced some of the most iconic horror films in Hollywood history, including the landmark "Dracula" (1931) staring Bela Lugosi, Boris Karloff's "Frankenstein" (1931) and "The Wolf Man" (1941) staring Lon Chaney Jr. The film opens with a stylish black-and-white tribute to those films in which a mob of angry villagers brandishing pitchforks and torches storm Frankenstein's castle. Universal is lucky that irate moviegoers don't do the same at cinemas.

Toward the end of the movie, Frankenstein's monster bemoans the fact that he is "accustomed to pain," but by that point so is the audience.

Due to incessant comic-book violence, an implied sexual encounter, some innuendo and frightening images, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Vanilla Sky
synopsis: Stupefying drama in which a thirty-something womanizer (Tom Cruise) is terribly disfigured when a jealous conquest (Cameron Diaz) runs her car off a bridge with him in the passenger seat after becoming enraged about his latest love interest (Penelope Cruz). Adapted from 1997 Spanish film "Open Your Eyes," director Cameron Crowe's film is initially intriguing before becoming increasingly incomprehensible as the elaborate narrative plays games with reality and illusion, cryogenics and character identities. A few sexual encounters and vulgar references, brief violence including suicide and recurring rough language with some profanity

title: Vanishing Point
synopsis: Speed demon (Barry Newman) attempts to outrun the police of four states aided by a blind disc jockey (Cleavon Little) who monitors police frequencies. Directed by Richard C. Sarafian, the plot is aimless, marked by a number of hair-raising near crack-ups and some gratuitous nudity

title: Vanishing, The
synopsis: Three years after the disappearance of his wife (Johanna Ter Steege), the husband (Gene Bervoets) is contacted by the abductor (Bernard-Pierre Donnadieu) and eventually learns her fate -- as well as meets his own. Directed by George Sluizer, the Dutch-French production is an unsettling and far-fetched psychological study in which the good guy is no match for the seemingly normal sociopath he's pitted against. Subtitles. Much menace and occasional restrained violence

title: Vanishing, The
synopsis: Flat Hollywood remake by Dutch director George Sluizer of his own eerie 1991 foreign thriller pitting a methodic maniac (Jeff Bridges) against a young man (Kiefer Sutherland) obsessed with finding his long-missing girlfriend (Sandra Bullock), even if it means losing his new love (Nancy Travis) or his own life. In bowing to alleged American preferences for action over emotional complexity, Sluizer strips the narrative of the suspense and mounting sense of dread that made the original so memorable. Brief but intense climatic violence, a live-in relationship and minimal rough language

title: Vanishing Westerner, The
synopsis: Formula Western directed by Philip Ford in which a pair of lawmen (Monte Hale and Paul Hurst) pose as wanted killers to get the goods on a slick gang of murderous robbers. Frontier violence

title: Vanishing Wilderness
synopsis: Slow-moving, incoherent parade of unrelated wildlife scenes, directed by Arthur Dubs and Heinz Seilmann, with an obnoxiously cute narration by Rex Allen. It ranks low on the scale of well-made nature documentaries

title: Vanity Fair
synopsis: Splendid adaptation of William Makepeace Thackeray's classic about heroine Becky Sharp's struggles to survive in Regency England. Reese Witherspoon makes a captivating heroine and holds her own amid a top-notch British cast. Directed by Mira Nair with a sure hand, the story has all the elements of an epic: romance, a war background (the Napoleonic Wars), villains, misunderstandings, reconciliations and more. A slight flash of partial nudity, a little violence and some sensuality
full_review:
Reese Witherspoon gives an assured performance as Becky Sharp among a stellar cast of top-flight English actors in Mira Nair's epic retelling of William Makepeace Thackeray's classic, "Vanity Fair" (Focus).

Dramatized many times on screen and television, this film is one of the most satisfying. The famous Miriam Hopkins version -- "Becky Sharp" from 1935 -- was notable for its pioneering use of the Technicolor process, and there was a notable "Masterpiece Theatre" telecast on PBS in 1972 with Susan Hampshire in the lead, among many other productions.

This production is beautiful to look at -- albeit the production design here is grittier than more genteel past productions. Director Mira Nair can be forgiven a somewhat revisionist slant as Becky is less the manipulative schemer as usually presented, but rather just a smart girl trying to survive in perilous times. Nair makes clear that Becky is operating in a world without a safety net. In that era, if you lost your money or position, it could be a very short fall to the gutter.

The story's a compelling one, which explains the piece's enduring popularity. Against a backdrop of the Napoleonic Wars, the young orphaned Becky (Witherspoon), daughter of a struggling artist, resolves to reinvent herself and make her way in the world. With confident serenity, she leaves the girl's boarding school where she's been treated like a slave, and goes to work for the upper-class but rustic Sir Pitt Crawley (Bob Hoskins), to whose household she brings clarity and order, thereby making herself indispensable. Before long, she ingratiates herself with the imperious Aunt Matilda (Eileen Atkins in a hilarious portrayal), and moves with the old woman to London.

Though Matilda loves imprudent romances in novels, she has a fit when Becky marries her nephew, Rawdon Crawley (James Purefoy), and disinherits him. (It is Atkins' indignant rising from her tub upon hearing the news that provides the film's only snippet of partial nudity.) Meanwhile, Becky's best friend, Amelia (Romola Garai), is enamored of the callous George Osborne (Jonathan Rhys-Meyers), whose imperfections Amelia refuses to see, marrying him in spite of paternal objections. She, in turn, is loved by the decent Dobbin (Rhys Ifans, superb in a completely different role than the recent "Danny Deckchair").

Eventually, Becky comes under the influence of the lecherous Marquess of Steyne (Gabriel Byrne), which threatens the impoverished but solid relationship with Crawley. Up to this point, Becky had thought she was adept at managing the false values of high society, but this time she's in over her head.
There's a whole gallery of fine performances by a stellar British cast, including Jim Broadbent as Osborne's unforgiving father, Geraldine McEwan as a busybody relation of the Crawleys determined to expose Becky as a sham, and others too numerous to mention.

But it's the captivating Witherspoon, seemingly on screen almost every minute, who rivets your attention. She has the uncanny ability to communicate what she's thinking at every turn, which makes her strategic rags to (not quite) riches story especially compelling. She also makes Becky's actions -- not always admirable -- plausible.

Nair gives the story the epic sweep it deserves, depicting a great canvas of balls, great crowd scenes with soldiers going off to war, a picturesque and grimy London, and other Regency period detail that encompassed the circus of life of that time. Some of the story is reminiscent of "Gone With the Wind," including one scene you'll recognize right away with its uncanny parallel to Margaret Mitchell's story.

Julian Fellowes, who won the Oscar for "Gosford Park," has written an intelligent screenplay in collaboration with Matthew Faulk and Mark Skeet, underscoring the theme: Who among us who achieves our desires is truly content?

If Nair pays homage to her own heritage by overemphasizing the Indian aspects of the story, there's no harm done to basic narrative. An Indian musical number -- straight out of Bollywood -- with Becky in the lead seems wildly out of place here, colorful and rather fun though it is. And the novel's ending is slightly changed, so that India figures more heavily in the plot's resolution.

Because of a slight flash of partial nudity, a little violence and some sensuality, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG--13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Vanquished, The
synopsis: Post-bellum clunker directed by Edward Ludwig has an ex-Confederate officer (John Payne) return to his Union-occupied hometown to get enough evidence to convict its corrupt administrator (Lyle Bettger) but winds up, instead, on the run from a trumped-up murder charge. Stylized violence, romantic situations and reconstruction woes

title: Vantage Point
synopsis: Propulsive thriller about an attempted assassination of the U.S. president (William Hurt) as he delivers an anti-terrorist speech in Spain, as seen from eight different perspectives including his Secret Service men (Dennis Quaid and Matthew Fox), an American tourist (Forest Whitaker), an American TV producer (Sigourney Weaver), a Spanish security officer (Eduardo Noriega), and myriad other characters on the scene during the shooting and the deadly bombings which immediately follow. Director Pete Travis demonstrates a great affinity for this kind of material, while the cast delivers committed performances. Plot improbabilities aside, the script is clever, while culminating in a heart-pounding car chase. Much action violence which, though intense, is not gruesome, frequent uses of the s-word uttered under duress, some mild profanity
full_review:
As a wise man once said, it all depends on how you look at it. The aptly named "Vantage Point" (Columbia), a propulsive thriller about an attempted assassination of a U.S. president (William Hurt), gives us the same events in the same time frame from eight disparate perspectives.

President Ashton is in Salamanca, Spain, and he's just about to deliver a speech at the conclusion of a peace summit between Western and Arab leaders when shots ring out and he's propelled backwards. Minutes later, bombs go off, causing devastation and panic in the picturesque Plaza Mayor square. (Most of the filming was actually done in Mexico.)

Among the participants and onlookers are Secret Service agents Thomas Barnes (Dennis Quaid) and Kent Taylor (Matthew Fox), the former only just recovered from taking a bullet for the president during an assassination attempt a year before; Howard Lewis (Forest Whitaker), an American tourist with a camcorder; American TV producer Rex Brooks (Sigourney Weaver), watching the events from a control room; and Enrique (Eduardo Noriega), a Spanish security officer tackled by Barnes in the melee.

Other characters whose roles become clearer as the same events play out over and over again are paramedic Veronica (Ayelet Zurer), affable local Suarez (Said Taghmaoui), who strikes up a conversation with Howard in the crowd, Anna (Alicia Jaziz Zapien), a cute little girl with an ice-cream cone who gets separated from her mother, and myriad others on the scene during the frightening events. To say more would ruin the revelations that come with each successive version of events.

Director Pete Travis demonstrates a great affinity for this kind of material, while the cast -- amid all the high-speed mayhem -- manages to deliver committed performances, all the more impressive given the high action quota. Quaid is outstanding, conveying his character's emotional turmoil, as he rises to the occasion of nailing the perpetrators. And Whitaker's Everyman tourist is effortlessly empathetic.

Though the plot is implausible in numberless ways, Barry L. Levy's script is quite clever, and repetition of the principal events, "Rashomon"-style, adds fascinating detail and never grows tiresome, while culminating in a heart-pounding car chase, one of the best ever captured on the big screen.

The script's stance on the world situation -- underlying all the heavy-duty action -- is a humane one, and the views espoused by President Ashton in his principal segment of the film have an admirably moral grounding.

The film contains much action violence which, though intense, is not gruesome, frequent uses of the s-word uttered under duress, and some mild profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults (though acceptable for older teens). The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Van, The
synopsis: Gawky youth (Stuart Getz) becomes a Don Juan when he buys a van in this shoddy low-budget sex-exploitation movie directed by Sam Grossman

title: Van, The
synopsis: To support their families, two unemployed Dublin pals (Colm Meaney and Donal O'Kelly) partner in selling fish and chips out of a truck, but the demands of running a business bring their lifelong friendship to the breaking point. Director Stephen Frears finds much good-natured humor in the mens' disorganized venture -- and the strength of their wives to remain emotionnally supportive of their well-meaning but hapless husbands. Fleeting nudity, momentary violence, some profanity and frequent rough language

title: Vanya on 42nd Street
synopsis: Playwright David Mamet's stripped-down version of "Uncle Vanya," Anton Chekhov's 1899 play about the troubled relations within a Russian family living on a poor country estate, is performed under Andre Gregory's direction in a rehearsal held in a once-grand, now-dilapidated Broadway theatre. Giving a contemporary edge to the work's themes of regret and hope, director Louis Malle shifts between the real world and the theatrical, showing the company off stage as well as on, thereby capturing the transformation of the actors into the play's characters, notably Wallace Shawn's embittered Vanya, Larry Pine's idealistic doctor and Brooke Smith as Vanya's yearning niece. Domestic tensions and romantic complications

title: Variety Girl
synopsis: Thin tale saluting the philanthropic work of the movie industry's Variety Clubs as a couple of would-be starlets (singer Mary Hatcher and comic Olga San Juan) seek a career at Paramount Pictures. Directed by George Marshall, the result is of interest chiefly for cameos by the studio's roster of stars (Bing Crosby, Bob Hope, Gary Cooper, Barbara Stanwyck and many more) as well as directors Cecil B. DeMille and Marshall

title: Variety Lights
synopsis: Delightful Italian comedy about a traveling theatrical troupe whose frustrated star (Peppino De Flippo) drops his fiancee (Giulietta Masina) when a novice actress (Carla Del Poggio) joins the troupe. Directed by Federico Fellini and Alberto Lattuada, the world of small-time show people is filled with infectious good humor, much whimsy and some pathos. Subtitles. Romantic complications

title: Varsity Blues
synopsis: Hokey formula tale in which a high school football team (led by James Van Der Beek) gets rid of its mean, dishonest coach at halftime in the championship game. Directed by Brian Robbins, the bogus proceedings are devoted largely to the teens' activities off the field, especially their drunken escapades and quest for sex. Sexual situations, nudity, alcohol abuse, intermittent rough language and occasional profanity

title: Va Savior
synopsis: Airy French romantic comedy set during the run of a pay in Paris where six self-absorbed characters flirt with new or former romantic partners before reviving their current relationships. Though overlong and casual in its treatment of love affairs, director Jacques Rivette takes a gently rueful look at ambivalent couples and the comic aspects of the mysteries of sexual attraction. Subtitles. Implied affairs and brief nudity

title: Vatel
synopsis: Flat culinary drama that revolves around Francois Vatel (Gerard Depardieu), the devoted valet of the financially troubled Prince of Conde (Julian Glover), who stages an elaborate 3-day feast to help his Prince regain the favor of King Louis XIV (Julian Sands). Director Roland Joffe's epicurean delight is just empty calories without a solid screenplay or engaging performances to accompany it. A suicide, brief violence, a few implied sexual encounters and some homosexual references. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Vault of Horror, The
synopsis: Unimaginative British horror movie offers five tales, interwoven with vampires, voodoo, murder and torture, with a cast including Daniel Massey, Terry-Thomas, Glynis Johns and Curt Jurgens. Directed by Roy Ward Baker, there is too much emphasis on mutilation and blood for younger viewers, and not enough psychological terror to chill the hearts and imaginations of horror devotees

title: Vegas Vacation
synopsis: Witless comedy with Chevy Chase and Beverly D'Angelo as the parents of two teenagers on the loose in a Las Vegas gambling resort. Directed by Stephen Kessler, the family's misadventures are mostly dull, entirely predictable and woefully unamusing. Comic sexual innuendo, the allure of gambling and mild profanity

title: VeggieTales: The Toy That Saved Christmas
synopsis: In this edition of the computer-animated series, a wicked toymaker's TV commercials for Buzz-Saw Louie dolls have all the Veggie kids clamoring for their own until one of the dolls decides there must be more to Christmas than breakable toys and escapes the factory to find out what it is. The half-hour video has plenty of humor, singable songs and imaginative animation as the doll learns that Christmas is about giving and "especially about a little baby named Jesus who was the greatest gift of all." Enjoyably worthwhile family fare

title: Veils of Bagdad, The
synopsis: Tired Arabian Nights tale directed by George Sherman in which a seeming carefree adventurer (Victor Mature) in 1560 Bagdad woos a married woman (Virginia Field) as well as a dancing girl (Mari Blanchard) in order to learn what they know about a plot against the Ottoman emperor, Suleiman. Period violence including a torture sequence, romantic complications and sexual innuendo

title: Velvet Goldmine
synopsis: Nihilistic tale boringly details the rise and demise of two decadent rockers (Jonathan Rhys Meyers and Ewan McGregor) who become lovers during the London-New York glitter rock scene of the early 1970s. Writer-director Todd Haynes' empty tale of excess and self-indulgence goes nowhere in between numerous raw musical performances. Glamorization of bisexual lifestyles, full frontal nudity, sexual situations, substance abuse, occasional profanity and recurring rough language

title: Velvet Touch, The
synopsis: Psychological drama in which a Broadway actress (Rosalind Russell) kills her manipulative producer (Leon Ames), then matches wits with the policeman (Sydney Greenstreet) investigating the murder. Director John Gage does well with a fine cast and dandy backstage settings but stumbles in dragging out a less-than-perfect crime story. An act of deadly violence, much tension and some romantic complications

title: Velvet Vampire, The
synopsis: Low-budget horror about newlyweds (Michael Blodgett and Sherry Miles) who come for a weekend in a desert hotel whose hostess (Celeste Yarnall) is desperate for new blood. Director Stephanie Rothman requires hardly a stitch of clothing for the atrocious acting of all participants in this silly exercise

title: Vengeance of Fu Manchu, The
synopsis: Master criminal Fu Manchu (Christopher Lee) sets out to murder all the world's chiefs of police and, through plastic surgery, replace them with his own men but is foiled by Scotland Yard's Nayland Smith (Douglas Wilmer). Directed by Jeremy Summers, the British production's weak story makes middling adventure entertainment. Stylized violence

title: Vengeance of She, The
synopsis: Weak British adventure fantasy based on characters created by H. Rider Haggard in which an occult power compels a young woman (Olinka Berova) to journey to a hidden city in North Africa to become the lost queen of its ruler (John Richardson). Directed Cliff Owen, the action is pedestrian and the plot mistakes silliness for imagination. Mild violence

title: Vengeance Valley
synopsis: Below-par Western in which a ranch foreman (Burt Lancaster) protects his shiftless half-brother (Robert Walker) until the nasty lad's treachery leads to a final showdown between them. Directed by Richard Thorpe, the drearily detailed plot of mistaken loyalties is relieved only by occasional scenes of cowboy life on the open range. Stylized violence and an unwed-mother subplot

title: Vengo
synopsis: Absurd drama about two feuding gypsy families living on the edge of Seville intent on extracting revenge on each other for murdered relatives. The slender plot is neither convincing nor remotely dramatic, but the passionate flamenco music that permeates writer-director Tony Gatlif's film reflects a way of life more accurately than the trite story line. Subtitles. Some violence, fleeting rear nudity and brief crass language. (

title: Venice-Venice
synopsis: Frail, talky story in which a self-consumed director (Henry Jaglom), promoting his movie at the Venice Film Festival, becomes involved with an adoring Parisian journalist (Nelly Allard) who follows him home to Venice, California to pursue their relationship. Also written and directed by Jaglom, the thin plot is given some interest by intercutting remarks from a variety of women who feel betrayed by Hollywood movies that led them to believe life would be filled with glamor and perfect romance. Benign attitude towards unmarried intimacy and some rough language

title: Venom
synopsis: Brainless and bloody voodoo-themed horror movie set in a backwater Louisiana town where a crowbar-wielding truck driver (Rick Cramer) becomes infested with evil spirits through black magic gone awry and terrorizes a group of teenagers. High on body count and cliches and low on suspense, director Jim Gillespie's bayou blunder is little else than a series of shock-value slayings strung together by a silly supernatural plot. Much graphic and gory violence, including impalings and dismemberment, occult mumbo jumbo, brief sexual suggestiveness, recurring rough and crude language and profanity
full_review:
"Venom" (Miramax) is a brainless and bloody voodoo-themed B-horror movie set in a backwater Louisiana town where a crowbar-wielding truck driver's (Rick Cramer) corpse becomes infested with evil spirits through black magic gone awry and, once reanimated, terrorizes a group of teenagers (including Agnes Bruckner and Bijou Phillips).

High on body count and cliches and low on suspense, director Jim Gillespie's bayou blunder is little else than a series of shock-value slayings strung together by a silly supernatural plot.

The film contains much graphic and gory violence, including impalings and dismemberment, occult mumbo jumbo, brief sexual suggestiveness, recurring rough and crude language and profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Venom
synopsis: Deadly snake cavorts about a household taken over by ruthless international terrorists in this mediocre and farfetched melodrama directed by Piers Haggard. A fine cast, including Klaus Kinski, Nicol Williamson, Oliver Reed, Sarah Miles and Sterling Hayden, is wasted in a mindless effort that features violence and some restrained sexual activity

title: Venus
synopsis: Mostly downbeat London-based story about an aging actor's (Peter O'Toole in top form) unhealthy obsession with the lower-class young woman (Jodie Whittaker) working as caregiver to his best friend (Leslie Phillips), a fellow thespian. Though director Roger Michell's film has a number of positive aspects and several tender moments, particularly those having to do with the actor's desire to educate and inspire the girl -- and there's a duly redemptive ending as well as accomplished performances by a fine English cast (Vanessa Redgrave, Richard Griffiths) -- the fetishistic nature of the central relationship, the high quotient of bad language, and overall grubby milieu push this into the objectionable category. Pervasive rough and crude language and profanity, alcohol and tobacco use, abortion reference, premarital sex, upper and rear female nudity, unpleasantly specific medical references and imagery, some violence
full_review:
"Venus" (Miramax) is a mostly downbeat London-based story about Maurice (Peter O'Toole), an aging actor, and his unhealthy obsession with Jessie, a lower-class young woman (Jodie Whittaker) working as caregiver to his best friend, her great-uncle Ian (Leslie Phillips), a fellow thespian who loathes the sullen and unkempt girl at first sight.

Maurice wants to educate and inspire Jessie, and he does, in fact, take her for first-time outings to the theater, museum and beach, and tries to instill a love of Shakespeare. At the same time, he presses her to let him touch her in a sensual -- if not overtly sexual -- way.

There are also several generous (on his part) shopping expeditions. At one point, he offers to buy Jessie a becoming dress, but at the checkout counter, he confesses that he doesn't have enough money to pay for it, one of several scenes where character motivation is puzzling. Near the end, for instance, Ian unaccountably accuses Maurice of "degrading" his grandniece after he seemed perfectly aware of Maurice's actions all along.

He also gets her a job as an artist's model where she must pose in the nude (with Maurice gleefully spying on her). To placate her, he takes her to the National Gallery to look at the Rokeby Venus of Velasquez, henceforth calling her by that moniker.

Jessie gradually responds to Maurice's kindnesses, as she partly tolerates his amorous attentions, but she eventually falls for a tattooed young thug with predictably nasty results.

On the plus side, writer Hanif Kureishi's screenplay -- directed by Roger Michell -- has a number of positive aspects and more than a few tender moments. And as you might expect, there are accomplished performances by a fine English cast, including Vanessa Redgrave as Valerie, Maurice's ex-wife, and Richard Griffiths as Donald, one of the men's cronies at the local cafe. There's no denying this is one of the very best of O'Toole's latter-day performances, while Whittaker, despite her character's initial off-putting appearance and unpleasant mien, convincingly blossoms as the film progresses.

Still, despite an ending involving forgiveness and redemption, the fetishistic nature of the central relationship (Maurice's interest in Jessie is as much carnal as paternal), the high quotient of bad language (would these Shakespeare-quoting old codgers really salt their conversations with the "f" word -- and worse, so liberally?), and overall grubby milieu regrettably push the film into the objectionable category.

The film contains pervasive rough and crude language and profanity, alcohol and tobacco use, abortion reference, premarital sex, upper and rear female nudity, unpleasantly specific medical references and imagery, and some violence. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Venus Beauty Institute
synopsis: Unconventional comedy-drama set in and around a Parisian beauty salon about the lives and loves of three beauticians (Nathalie Baye, Mathilde Seigner and Audrey Tautou). Director Tonie Marshall's film touchingly looks at vanity, loneliness and the passing of time in often amusing ways, but some characters' promiscuous behavior is unsettling. Subtitles. Several sexual encounters, brief violence, substance abuse, full frontal nudity and intermittent rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Venus in Furs
synopsis: European co-production about a beautiful woman who, after being raped, mutilated and murdered, returns from the dead seeking vegeance on her killers. Directed by Jess Franco, its below-standard production values complement its ludicrous sex-exploitation plot

title: Vera Drake
synopsis: Superbly written and acted period drama (circa 1950) of a lower-middle-class English housewife (Imelda Staunton) who, unbeknownst to her family, helps desperate women who have become pregnant by performing abortions, until a young woman nearly dies after Vera's ministrations, and the authorities apprehend her. Master filmmaker Mike Leigh's abortion theme will be troublesome for Catholic viewers, but his approach to the controversial subject leaves the moral judgments to the viewer. Staunton's performance is towering, and the human dynamics extraordinarily natural in the narrative of a woman who wants to help others, but who simply doesn't appreciate the consequences -- moral or physical -- of her actions. Abortion theme, and one sexual situation
full_review:
Imelda Staunton and an ensemble cast, a well-crafted screenplay and direction by Mike Leigh elevate this tale of an unsophisticated woman who, unbeknownst to her husband and children, leads a double life as she performs abortions on young women in difficult circumstances.

Leigh's "Vera Drake" (Fine Line Features) tackles the difficult abortion theme with objectivity. His heroine is a cheery, lower-middle-class housewife (Staunton) in postwar Britain, circa 1950, with a loving garage-mechanic husband, Stan (Phil Davis), and two grown children who live at home: painfully shy Ethel (Alex Kelly), being courted by the sad-sack Reg (Eddie Marsan), and tailor's apprentice Sid (Daniel Mays).

The middle-aged Vera, who works as a domestic, is guileless and simple, and thinks a cup of tea is the solution to all the world's ills.
But there's another side to her that soon becomes apparent: Besides helping sick neighbors and such, she also assists young women who are "in the family way" by performing abortions, then illegal. She sets off to various flats -- many of them quite shabby -- where, in a warm but no-nonsense manner, she administers a soapy disinfectant solution with a syringe. She then tells the girl that in a day or two she'll feel some stomach pain, should go to the bathroom to relieve herself, and "it will all be over." The audience is left to imagine the rest.
Vera takes no money for this task, but simply sees herself as assisting these young girls who feel they have no other recourse. Later, we learn that Vera's old school chum, Lily (Ruth Sheen), who procures Vera's assignments, is taking money on the side.

We also see Susan (Sally Hawkins), a more affluent young woman and the daughter of one of Vera's employers, who is raped on a first date. Leigh does make a point of showing the callowness of many of these young men who, in predatory fashion, make the move on women.

In contrast to Vera's clients, Susan goes to a regular doctor, recommended by a girlfriend. But the relatively cold demeanor of the medical profession and the psychiatrist (Allan Corduner), who needs to know if there's insanity in her family before she can be certified for an abortion, stand in stark contrast to Vera's more human manner.

Eventually, the mother of one of the young ladies recognizes Vera. The daughter later becomes gravely ill, and the mother rushes her to the hospital, where the authorities insist on knowing how the girl's miscarriage was induced. The mother is bullied into revealing Vera's name.

In the film's most unbearably suspenseful moments, Vera's family is having a cozy celebration of Ethel's engagement to the doltish Reg, as the police, headed by Detective Inspector Webster (Peter Wight), close in. When they finally knock on the door and ask to speak to Vera, the family is flabbergasted. What, they wonder, could the police possibly want with the quiet woman who leads such an exemplary life?
The police -- portrayed as kindly and understanding, but firm in their need to see justice done -- interrogate Vera at the station house.
Staunton's heart-wrenching realization of what she's done, and the impact it will have on her family, is acting of the highest order. The camera stays on her face unflinchingly, and you feel every ounce of her pain.

Vera seems utterly incapable of thinking of what she's been doing as abortion; she's simply "helping girls out," she insists through her quiet tears.

Leigh is careful not to make any of the authority figures -- even the clerk at Vera's trial (Jim Broadbent) -- villains.
Depressing as the subject matter is, the period atmosphere provides visual interest and there's always the joy of watching great acting. As this small, feisty, utterly ordinary woman, Staunton gives an indelible performance. Tremendous as she is -- and she'll be a strong contender at Oscar time -- the entire cast is simply superb.

As for the abortion theme, the procedure isn't glorified in any way. The women involved are almost all desperate, and even though Vera's methods seem relatively benign, the women's fear and sorrow at what they are doing is achingly evident.
Leigh goes to pains not to make Vera a heroine. Nor, to my mind, does the film proselytize for abortion. The director leaves conclusions to the viewer, many of whom are likely to note that there is retribution on every level -- personal and public -- for Vera's well-intentioned, if misguided, actions. While the medical "establishment" is depicted as unfeeling and hard, even a "do-gooder" like Vera can put a woman at risk.

Leigh's script has all the subtle nuances of "real" people reacting to a domestic crisis. Vera's son, Sid, tells her what she did was
"wrong" and "dirty." "Little babies," he says to her in disgust.

No matter how much you'll share Sid's critical feeling, "Vera Drake" is devastating viewing.
Interestingly, Leigh dedicates the film to his parents: a doctor and a midwife.

Because of the abortion theme and one sexual situation, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Verdict, The
synopsis: When a drunken wreck of a lawyer (Paul Newman) presses a medical malpractice suit against a Boston Catholic hospital represented by a powerful attorney (James Mason), he overcomes his personal problems by relying upon his heart instead of his mind during the extended court battle. Though director Sidney Lumet's script has a faulty perspective on church procedures, Newman's performance outweighs such defects. The sexual aspects of the story are done with the greatest restraint, but it does contain some foul language from one of its characters

title: Veronica Guerin
synopsis: Truth-based story about an Irish investigative journalist (Cate Blanchett) whose murder in 1996 for exposing high-level organized crime made her a national hero and helped turn the tide in Ireland's war on drugs. While Guerin's real-life martyrdom makes for compelling drama, the biopic, directed by Joel Schumacher, fails to offer any meaningful insights into what fueled its subject's passion, focusing almost entirely on a superficial documenting of the dangers she faced, hedging awkwardly between grittiness and gloss, and resulting in a stylistically schizophrenic -- yet ultimately engaging -- portrait of heroism. Recurring graphic violence and drug abuse, an implied sexual encounter, as well as much rough and crude language and profanity
full_review:
"Veronica Guerin" (Touchstone) tells the truth-based story of an Irish investigative journalist whose murder in 1996 for exposing high-level organized crime made her a national hero and helped turn the tide of Ireland's war on drugs.

While Guerin's real-life martyrdom makes for compelling drama, the biopic, directed by Joel Schumacher, hedges awkwardly between grittiness and gloss, resulting in a stylistically schizophrenic -- yet ultimately engaging -- portrait of heroism.

Australian actress Cate Blanchett plays slain crusader Veronica Guerin, a fearless, uncompromising reporter whose sense of moral outrage over Dublin's spiraling heroin problem -- which had reached crisis proportions by the early 1990s -- sets her on a collision course with the city's ruthless drug lords. Ostracized by many in the news establishment for her spotty professional pedigree and unconventional style -- dealing face-to-face with informants in pubs and brothels rather than conducting interviews over the phone -- what Guerin lacks in credentials she more than makes up for in moxie and a bullheaded tenacity to score the scoop.

Writing for the country's top-selling paper, The Sunday Independent, Guerin channels her journalistic zeal into blowing the lid off the hydra-like drug gangs whose turf wars had turned Dublin into a combat zone of death and violence. Confident that the pen is mightier than the sword, she embarks on a campaign to effect change by exposing the pushers' brutality, as well as the ineffectiveness of laws that allow the gangs to operate with impunity.

Bucking the system, Guerin starts down a dangerous path, tapping for information contacts on both sides of the law, including a shady underworld braggart named John Traynor (Ciaran Hinds).

Piece by piece Guerin begins to uncover a paper trail of laundered money leading to a brutal kingpin named John Gilligan (Gerard McSorley). Ignoring pleas from family and co-workers fearing for her safety, Guerin persists in pursuing the story, refusing to give in to Gilligan's intimidation tactics.

Braving threats, bullets and beatings, she is sucked deeper by her investigation into a lethal vortex that ends tragically at an intersection on the outskirts of Dublin. There she is gunned down, execution style, by a motorcyclist who pulls up alongside her car stopped at a traffic light. The film ends with a coda showing how her death galvanized the anti-drug forces in Ireland and acted as a catalyst to bolster the country's criminal laws.

While effectively documenting the dangers faced by Guerin, the film fails to plumb the emotional depths of such a complex character or shed light on why she would risk her life and the safety of her family for a news story. Apart from a smattering of perfunctory scenes of Guerin's domestic life with her husband, Graham (Barry Barnes), and their young son, no attempt is made to open a window into her soul. Her character seems bereft of inner conflict. The film keeps Guerin at arm's length, content to observe her heroism without ever really trying to understand it.

Because of the filmmaker's refusal to plunge into deeper psychological waters, Guerin, as depicted, comes across at times as reckless and her bold defiance is tinged with a scent of foolhardiness. Throughout the film her husband's concerns are met with replies extolling self-fulfillment above personal safety -- with little mention given to her maternal responsibilities. Without any insights into what makes her tick, these responses seem myopically cavalier, if not selfish -- leaving viewers with the sense that her single-minded dedication, no matter how just the cause, is driven as much by ego and obstinacy as it is by passion.

The story also is not well-served by the filmmaker employing visuals and music that seem to cue the audience to the desired emotional response. Such manipulative attempts to manufacture emotion, rather than trusting in the narrative's inherent drama, diminish the film's overall cathartic impact. While reigning in their usual blockbuster banality, Schumacher and producer Jerry Bruckheimer -- whose resumes include such social realism classics as "Batman Forever" and "Bad Boys" -- seem ill-fitted for the project, at times eschewing the grittiness the film demands for slicked-up superficiality.

No amount of Hollywood evisceration, however, can strip the story of its ability to inspire and edify. "Veronica Guerin," despite its flaws, is a powerful testimony of courage and personal sacrifice, which eloquently illustrates the Christian calling to "hunger and thirst for justice" -- even at the cost of one's life.

Due to recurring graphic violence and drug abuse, an implied sexual encounter, as well as much rough and crude language and profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Veronico Cruz
synopsis: This Argentinian film tracks the life of a shepherd boy (Gonzalo Morales) whose isolation in a remote region is lifted by a new schoolteacher (Juan Jose Camero) who ultimately brings the boy to the city to search for his political-dissident father. Director and co-writer Miguel Pereira captures well the indigenous population, the stark landscape and the encroachment of the outside world, including political turmoil from revolving military dictatorships and the Falklands War. English subtitles. Incidental rough language, some brief intense political interrogations

title: Veronique
synopsis: Warm, sensitive French movie follows a perceptive 13-year-old girl's not especially eventful summer. Director Claudine Ghuilmain fulfills her modest aims in showing the youngster's experiences and some misunderstandings in what is little more than a string of vignettes best appreciated by adult viewers

title: Vertical Limit
synopsis: Action-packed tale in which a former mountain climber (Chris O'Donnell) leads a rescue team up K2, the world's second highest peak, where his sister (Robin Tunney) and two others are trapped inside a deep crevasse with only hours to live. While director Martin Campbell's script is sometimes ludicrous, its hair-raising series of life-and-death situations prove consistently suspenseful. Much intense peril, fleeting implied drug abuse, brief sex references and minimal rough language and profanity. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Vertigo
synopsis: Fine suspense thriller from Alfred Hitchcock in the tale of a retired detective (James Stewart) called back for a private investigation of a seemingly shady lady (Kim Novak). Naturally they fall in love and land in high danger. Jimmy gulps and stammers a lot, Kim just smolders and Hitch masterfully pulls the strings

title: Very Bad Things
synopsis: Sick black comedy in which five buddies accidentally kill a prostitute during a bachelor party, then turn murderously on each other and innocent bystanders to keep from being discovered. Writer-director Peter Berg's smirky attempts at graveyard humor miss the mark as the movie steadily descends into an orgy of grisly killings. Recurring gory violence, a sexual encounter, prolonged nudity, recreational drug use as well as constant profanity and rough language

title: Very Brady Sequel, A
synopsis: The lives of the every-bouncy Brady Bunch are turned upside down when mom (Shelley Long) and dad (Gray Cole) welcome into their home a devious con man (Tim Matheson) claiming to be her presumed-dead first husband. Director Arlene Sanford makes feeble, goofy fun of the sprightly, stuck-in-the-'70s family who remain blissfully unaware they are in the nastier '90s. Numerous double entendres, fleeting comic violence and an instance of profanity

title: Very Curious Girl, A
synopsis: French social satire about the revenge a young gypsy (Bernadette Lafont) takes on the people of a small village who have exploited her and her mother. Director Claude Makovski has elicited strong and convincing performances from a cast mainly of villagers and peasants in creating a strange atmosphere of a primitive morality based on ignorance, simplicity and superstition

title: Very Happy Alexander
synopsis: Elegant French comedy about middle-age rebellion in which a brow-beaten husband (Philippe Noiret) scandalizes his neighbors by leading a life of lazy indolence after the death of his finger-snapping wife. He finds a soul-mate in a shiftless woman (Marlene Jobert) but when she snaps her fingers, he leaves her at the altar. Directed by Yves Robert, it is essentially a bucolic poem in which Noiret's warm, human performance makes convincing the urge to return to the unregimented life of Eden

title: Very Natural Thing, A
synopsis: Young man leaves the monastic life, becomes a high school teacher and takes a male lover whose promiscuity eventually results in a break-up. Director Chistopher Larkin's movie is a sincere and obviously deeply-felt effort to present the moral dilemmas of a homosexual relationship but it is painfully naive about film technique and embarrassingly romantic about its theme. Several nude scenes of male grapplings

title: V for Vendetta
synopsis: Provocative futuristic thriller based in London about a masked antihero (Hugo Weaving) who enlists the aid of a young office worker (Natalie Portman) to undermine a totalitarian government headed by an Orwellian dictator (John Hurt) and his cowering advisers (Stephen Rea, Rupert Graves, Tim Pigott-Smith). Director James McTeigue, working from a Wachowski Brothers adaptation of Alan Moore (uncredited by choice) and illustrator David Lloyd's graphic novel, has crafted a reasonably intelligent political allegory, with emphasis on character development, ideas and even a bit of romance, rather than simple mindless violence, the performances are first rate, and the film's theme of the individual's responsibility in standing up to tyranny -- while questioning the moral limits of opposition -- is worthy, and stops short of imparting a universal anti-authoritarian message. Some discreetly handled violence with bloodshed, a hanging, scattered profanity, rough and crude language and expressions, minor lesbian-themed flashback and implied gay male character, corrupt Anglican clergyman, attempted rape, sexual innuendo, drug use
full_review:
As every British, if not American, schoolboy knows, Nov. 5 commemorates the infamous day in 1605 when Guy Fawkes planned to blow up Parliament.

He failed and was executed. But the masked antihero known only as "V" in "V for Vendetta" (Warner Bros.) intends to follow through on Fawkes' intent. Such is the premise of this provocative futuristic thriller.

Fawkes' cause was repression of Catholicism, though his misguided actions only made things worse. V is an opponent of a modern Orwellian tyranny. England is under a totalitarian regime headed by Chancellor Adam Sutler (John Hurt), who barks orders from a giant monitor while his cowering advisors -- Chief Inspector Finch (Stephen Rea) and his lackey Dominic (Rupert Graves), Dascomb (Ben Miles), chief of propaganda, and Creedy (Tim Pigott-Smith), head of the secret police -- scramble to do his bidding.

Hugo Weaving is the sympathetic voice of V, who wears a sinister Guy Fawkes smiling mask throughout the entire film. Despite his violent deeds, we peg him as more "good" than "bad" early on, when he comes to the aid of British Television Network employee Evey (Natalie Portman), as she's about to be roughed up by Sutler's thugs.

Grateful to V, she accompanies him to his rooftop where, to the strains of the "1812 Overture," he blows England's famed courthouse, the Old Bailey, to smithereens.

Evey is remarkably accepting of all this, due (we later learn) to her parents paying with their lives for their dissident activities. Which is why when V is apprehended after turning up at the BTN to wreak havoc, Evey aids his escape, the act branding her as his accomplice.

But he has no compunctions about violently dispatching characters such as Lewis Prothero (Roger Allam), the BTN's "Voice of London," a mouthpiece for the corrupt government, or later, a lecherous Anglican bishop (John Standing), whom he snares using Evey -- posing as a schoolgirl -- as bait.

Stephen Fry plays Gordon Dietrich, a colleague who has private reasons for fearing the government: homosexuals are outlawed under Sutler's rule, as illustrated by a sidebar flashback about a lesbian couple who apparently met a violent end.

Director James McTeigue, working from a Wachowski Brothers adaptation of Alan Moore (uncredited by choice) and illustrator David Lloyd's graphic novel, has crafted a reasonably intelligent political allegory, the usual improbabilities aside, with emphasis on character development, ideas, and even a bit of romance, not mindless violence. The vigilante exploits are handled with relative restraint given the genre.

The faceless Weaving works wonders with voice and body language alone. Portman makes a spirited heroine. The British supporting cast is first rate, Pigott-Smith an especially flavorful villain, and Sinead Cusack superb as a coroner with a sinister past.

Though vengeance is, of course, unequivocally incompatible with Catholic teaching, the film makes clear that every one of V's victims was, at least, a perpetrator of some heinous action. V is, at heart, a high-tech Zorro or Robin Hood.

The film's political overtones are obvious. "America's war grew worse and worse," we learn by way of backstory, and Sutler's repressive measures were only "in the name of national security." But despite the subtext, this is very much a fantasy world.

At times, the film feels long and a tad repetitive with, for instance, one too many scenes of Hurt's video image. But overall, "V for Vendetta" is absorbing, and its theme of the individual's responsibility in standing up to tyranny -- while questioning the moral limits of opposition -- is worthy, and stops short of imparting a universal anti-authoritarian message.

The film contains some discreetly handled violence with bloodshed, a hanging, scattered profanity, rough and crude language and expressions, minor lesbian-themed flashback and implied gay male character, corrupt Anglican clergyman, attempted rape, sexual innuendo, fleeting background sexual photos and drug use. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Vibes
synopsis: Three spirited performers can't save this muddled mess about two psychics (Cyndi Lauper and Jeff Goldblum) lured to Ecuador by a seedy adventurer (Peter Falk) hoping to psyche out hidden Incan treasure. Director Ken Kwapis misuses many comic lines as well as his talented cast. Some sexual innuendo and minimal rough language

title: Vice Squad
synopsis: Prostitute (Season Hubley) is saved from from the clutches of a brutal pimp (Wings Hauser) by a stalwart policeman (Gary Hanson) in a loathsome, unremittingly brutal and squalid movie directed by Gary A. Sherman

title: Vicky Cristina Barcelona
synopsis: Best friends vacationing in Spain -- one nonchalantly uninhibited (Scarlett Johansson), the other respectably pragmatic (Rebecca Hall) -- accept a charming artist's (Javier Bardem) invitation for a cozy weekend in a resort town, leading to triangular complications, eventually muddied further by the arrival of the artist's volatile ex-wife (Penelope Cruz), and the formation of a temporary "menage a trois." Though this diverting romantic comedy is almost fablelike in presentation (and therefore not to be taken literally), the cast and locale engaging, overt sexual elements minimal, and the characters' actions not entirely devoid of moral weight, the premise of the film may still prove problematic. An implied sexual threesome, a casual view of nonmarital sex and two brief nongraphic encounters, an implied extramarital dalliance, a nihilistic worldview, a few crude words and profanities, and brief gun violence
full_review:
Writer-director Woody Allen continues his artistic reinvigoration in Europe. After three films in England, he has moved on to Spain with felicitous -- if with somewhat morally tangled -- results.

 

"Vicky Cristina Barcelona" (MGM/Weinstein), ostensibly a romantic comedy, concerns best friends vacationing there -- nonchalantly uninhibited Cristina (Scarlett Johansson), and respectably pragmatic Vicky (Rebecca Hall). They are staying with the latter's distant relative, Judy (Patricia Clarkson).

 

After a gallery opening at which Cristina had admired him from afar, charming artist Juan Antonio (Javier Bardem) approaches the pair at a restaurant. He boldly invites them for a cozy weekend in picturesque Oviedo, indicating with disarming candor that lovemaking will be on the agenda.

Much to Vicky's dismay, Cristina accepts, and Vicky -- already engaged to Doug (Chris Messina) -- goes along as reluctant chaperone. But after a day of sightseeing, Cristina is felled by food poisoning just at the point of succumbing to Juan Antonio. So it is Vicky who spends time with him. They have a brief fling, and Vicky is smitten.

But when Cristina recovers, and resumes her romantic courtship with Juan Antonio, Vicky -- whose certainty about her impending nuptials has been badly shaken -- nobly steps back.

 

Cristina moves in with Juan Antonio, and all seems blissful until he gets a call about his volatile ex-wife, Maria Elena (Penelope Cruz), whom he had divorced after she tried to kill him. She has now attempted suicide, and Juan Antonio informs Cristina that Maria Elena will be recuperating in the spare room.

 

Cristina is dismayed by this unwelcome guest, but after an uneasy start, the women bond, with Maria Elena even mentoring Cristina in the latter's budding photography endeavors. Before long, as Cristina casually relates to a disapproving Vicky and Doug over lunch, the relationship evolves into a "menage a trois" (off-screen), with Cristina somehow proving a calming influence on the combustible -- can't live together, can't live apart -- Spanish pair.

 

Almost fablelike in presentation, including the use of a dispassionate narrator (Christopher Evan Welch), the plot's amoral elements are considerably diluted. You never quite take the characters or their actions seriously.

Overt sexual elements are virtually nil, and the characters' actions are not entirely devoid of moral weight, but many will find the premise of the film -- a sort of contemporary homage to Truffaut's classics, "Jules and Jim" and "Two English Girls" (both featuring romantic trios and a narrator) -- problematic nonetheless.

The Barcelona locations are predictably attractive, and the leads are in good form, particularly a fiery Cruz and Hall, daughter of English director Sir Peter Hall, whose character provides the movie's conscience, and who plays "American" most convincingly.

 

It's refreshing to see Bardem playing an attractive (if unprincipled) character, after his creepy turns in "No Country for Old Men" and "Love in the Time of Cholera," though it's Juan Antonio who's the mouthpiece for Allen's by-now tiresome claim that life has no meaning.

 

If the situations presented here are provocative, Allen's dialogue -- pointedly "natural" -- never really sheds profound light on the moral issues as those Truffaut films did. Along the way, however, he does provide a few trademark insights into love and relationships and, of course, some laughs. For those who find that sufficient, and look at the brief "menage" as a fanciful fiction, the film may prove a diverting bauble, but little more.

 

The film contains an implied sexual threesome, a casual view of nonmarital sex and two brief nongraphic encounters, an implied extramarital dalliance, a nihilistic worldview, a few crude words and profanities, and brief gun violence. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Victors, The
synopsis: Uneven series of vignettes about an American infantry squad (George Peppard, George Hamilton, Vince Edwards and others) led by a tough but decent sergeant (Eli Wallach) from 1942 London to 1946 Berlin, focusing on some bittersweet romantic encounters (Jeanne Moreau, Melina Mercouri, Romy Schneider, Elke Sommer and Senta Berger) along the way. Written, produced and directed by Carl Foreman, the picture's anti-war theme dispenses with battlefield heroics, showing instead a deserter's execution, black soldiers attacked by white racists, surrendering Germans killed by a French unit and civilian victims of the conflict. Wartime violence and sexual situations

title: Victor/Victoria
synopsis: Unemployed singer (Julie Andrews) dresses up as a man in order to get a job as a female impersonator and soon is the toast of 1934 Paris. Helping her along the way is an aging homosexual (Robert Preston) and complicating her life is a Chicago nightclub owner (James Garner). Directed by Blake Edwards, the humor is fitful, more slapstick than witty, and the situation stretches itself thin long before movie's end. Benign attitude toward homosexuality, though given the farcical context, unlikely to blur the moral outlook of adults. A-IV (PG) ( 1982 )

title: Victory
synopsis: World War II story about a soccer game staged for propaganda purposes between a crack German team and a ragtag group of Allied prisoners of war (Michael Caine, Sylvester Stallone and legendary Brazilian soccer star Pele, among others) who use the match to effect an escape from the packed Paris stadium where they are playing. Effectively directed by John Huston, the result is a sports movie with some taut wartime suspense. Solid entertainment for the whole family. The U.S. Catholic Conference classification is

title: Victory
synopsis: World War II story about a soccer game staged for propaganda purposes between a crack German team and a ragtag group of Allied prisoners of war (Michael Caine, Sylvester Stallone and legendary Brazilian soccer star Pele, among others) who use the match to effect an escape from the packed Paris stadium where they are playing. Effectively directed by John Huston, the result is a sports movie with some taut wartime suspense. Solid entertainment for the whole family

title: Videodrome
synopsis: Seedy operator of a sleazy television station (James Woods) gets hooked on the unrelenting sado-masochism of a program called Videodrome which is actually a sinister plot against humanity carried out by some villains steeped, like the movie itself, in ill-digested media theories of Marshall McLuhan. Written and directed by David Cronenberg, there are some hints of satire, but no hint of intelligence or perspective, and its imagination is as dull as it is perverse. Sado-masochistic sex and exceedingly gory violence

title: Vietnam, Texas
synopsis: Trashy drama about a Catholic priest (Robert Ginty) who battles a gang of Vietnamese refugees in Houston to find the daughter he fathered as a soldier during the Vietnam War. Also directed by Ginty, the inept result is an unsatisfying mixture of ambiguous idealism and lethal mayhem. Hard-edged violence, references to prostitution and occasional rough language

title: View to a Kill, A
synopsis: In another 007 adventure for the perpetually ado1escent, James Bond (Roger Moore) is pitted against a rather pallid villain (Christopher Walken) who wants to remove all competition for his new computer chip by inducing an earthquake that will ob1iterate Silicon Valley. Director John Glen's pulp action-adventure fantasy has excessive violence and a benign view of promiscuity

title: Vigilante
synopsis: Brutal variation on the theme of the good guys getting fed up and taking the law into their own hands features Robert Forster joining forces with some vigilantes after his family is attacked by degenerate punks. Directed by William Lustig, the proceedings are cynically exploitative and incredibly violent

title: Vigilante Hideout
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Fred C. Brannon in which range detective Allan "Rocky" Lane arrives in an 1885 desert town to hunt down a cattle thief but finds instead a gang of bank robbers. Stylized violence

title: Vigil in the Night
synopsis: Worthy tale from A.J. Cronin's novel about an English nurse (Carole Lombard) whose selfless dedication to duty wins over a tough matron (Ethel Griffies), a demanding physician (Brian Aherne) and the hospital's crass chairman (Julien Mitchell), then proves a heroine battling a deadly children's epidemic. Directed by George Stevens, this homage to the nursing profession is often melodramatic, especially a subplot involving the nurse's sister (Anne Shirley), but the sentiment is sincere and the demands of nursing are depicted convincingly. Life-and-death situations and a sexual reference

title: Viking Queen, The
synopsis: Generally inept, tawdry spear-and-sandal epic set in rustic Britain during the Roman occupation where the haughty overseer (Don Murray) of a defeated but proud Viking tribe falls in love with its queen (Carita). British production directed by Don Chaffey, the tale of carnage and intrigue lavishes the budget on bloody action and skimps on the costuming to near-nudity

title: Vikings, The
synopsis: Energetic re-creation of the Norse sea raids on England during the Dark Ages pits a Viking leader (Ernest Borgnine) and his son (Kirk Douglas) against an English princess (Janet Leigh) and the escaped slave who becomes her champion (Tony Curtis). Directed by Richard Fleischer, the story is romanticized hokum but the action is full-blooded and the performances colorful. Much stylized bloodshed and carnage, as well as some sexual references

title: Village of Dreams
