Successful television talk-show host RJ Stevens (Martin Lawrence) long ago left behind the rural Georgia clan that raised him, not to mention the name by which his relatives once knew him. His current upwardly mobile lifestyle involves docilely obeying his controlling fiancee, Bianca (Joy Bryant), and cheerleading for his 10-year-old son, Jamaal (Damani Roberts), at soccer practice.

At the boy's urging, RJ agrees to return home for the first time in nine years to attend his parents' (James Earl Jones and Margaret Avery) landmark anniversary celebration. What better way, he finally concludes, to show off how far he has come and how far his siblings and cousins back in Dry Springs haven't?

From tough-guy older brother Otis (Michael Clarke Duncan), who's the local sheriff, to aggressive sister Betty (Mo'Nique) and con-man cousin Reggie (Mike Epps), they're an eccentric bunch. But one figure in particular stands out: RJ's childhood nemesis, competitive cousin Clyde (Cedric the Entertainer) who was taken in by RJ's parents after being orphaned, and is now a flashy car salesman.

To RJ's consternation, no one in the family actually takes his big-city airs seriously. To them he's the same Roscoe who would always lose out to Clyde, in love as well as sports. (Their amorous competition concerned beautiful neighbor Lucinda, played by Nicole Ari Parker, who now shows up at the festivities as Clyde's guest.)

Of course, RJ's interest in Lucinda is reawakened. So too are old resentments toward Clyde.

Writer-director Malcolm D. Lee's film promotes some positive moral values and scores some telling points about its characters' various pretensions, especially through the wry patter of Epps' Reggie. But much of the humor concerns the characters' sexual habits, from the intimate details of RJ and Bianca's cohabitation to Betty's interest in prison inmates. There's even a running gag about the unlikely relationship between Bianca's lapdog and the family bloodhound.

When it can't get a laugh, "Welcome Home Roscoe Jenkins" is all too willing to settle for a snicker.

The film contains a nongraphic but aberrant premarital sexual encounter, partial frontal female nudity, one use of the f-word, much crude and pervasive crass language, some profanity, much sexual humor, drug references, a condom reference, gambling and dogs mating. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Welcome Home
synopsis: Shot down over Cambodia in 1970, an Air Force flyer (Kris Kristofferson) is officially declared dead but 17 years later, when illness separates him from his new Cambodian family, he returns to the States to renew ties with the American family he left behind. As directed by Franklin J. Schaffner, this weepy melodrama fails to shed light on the very real problems facing Vietnam veterans and their kin. Some profanity and an adulterous sexual encounter

title: Welcome Home, Roxy Carmichael
synopsis: A small town anticipates the return of their one Hollywood celebrity, but none more eagerly than her former beau (Jeff Daniels), now a family man, and an alienated 15-year-old (Winona Ryder) who suspects Roxy may secretly be her mom. Director Jim Abrahams takes a basically frivolous story and, helped by Ryder's fine performance, develops it with charm, warmth and a small dose of insight about human relationships. References to a premarital relationship, minimal vulgar expressions and a flash of nudity

title: Welcome Home, Soldier Boys
synopsis: Four Vietnam vets (Joe Don Baker, Alan Vint, Paul Koslo and Elliott Street) pull into the sleepy hamlet of Hope, New Mexico, gang-rape a girl, kill everyone in town and then burn it to the ground. Directed by Richard Compton, the gruesome and ultimately cynical movie contributes nothing to understanding the problems of Vietnam veterans. O (R) ( 1972 )

title: Welcome Stranger
synopsis: Sentimental comedy about a likeable, good-natured doctor (Bing Crosby) arriving in Maine to fill in while a town's elderly physician (Barry Fitzgerald) takes a vacation, then has to win over the suspicious locals, a lovely schoolmarm (Joan Caulfield) and the cranky old doc himself. Director Elliott Nugent gets disappointing results from the artifical plot and setting, while the testy relationship between the two doctors grows maudlin rather than endearing. Romantic complications

title: Welcome to Collinwood
synopsis: Passable crime comedy set in a Cleveland working-class neighborhood where several petty crooks (including William H. Macy, Sam Rockwell and Michael Jeter) plot a big robbery that goes entirely awry. Written and directed by Joe and Anthony Russo, the film's clueless characters are mostly lovable losers but the jaunty tone can't fully compensate for the skimpy narrative. Brief violence, recurring profanity, minor sexual innuendo, fleeting rear nudity and much rough language
full_review:
"Welcome to Collinwood" (Warner Bros.) visits a hardscrabble Cleveland neighborhood where a bunch of disorganized petty crooks think they can pull off a perfect crime. But since these guys can barely pull a wrapper off a stick of chewing gum, all goes awry in this passable crime comedy. It's like a Coen brothers film, but never quite as clever -- although it's also written and directed by two brothers, Joe and Anthony Russo.

When a lifer tells jailbird Cosimo (Luis Guzman) of an apartment safe with $300,000 in it just waiting to be cracked, Cosimo tells his girlfriend (Patricia Clarkson) to pay someone from the 'hood to do the time for him so he can make a beeline to the booty. At first she can't find a patsy, but the lowlifes she approaches all want in on the safecracking. Soon, aged Toto (Michael Jeter), ambitious Leon (Isaiah Washington), lonely Basil (Andrew Davoli) and baby-toting Riley (William H. Macy), whose wife is in jail and needs to pay a $1,000 fine to get out, all are looking for the patsy.

They turn to boxer Pero (Sam Rockwell), who pulls a fast one on Cosimo, getting all the details they need so the rest of them can do the crime while Cosimo's still doing the time.

Enter a wheelchair-bound former safecracker (George Clooney) who wants no part of this crowd but agrees to give them lessons in safecracking for a fast five hundred.

The plan is for Pero to romance the maid (Jennifer Esposito) from the apartment next door, get the keys and break though the wall to the apartment with the safe. Unexpectedly, love enters the equation, upsetting the apple cart. Pero falls for the maid and doesn't want to get her in trouble, while Basil wants to marry Leon's sister (Gabrielle Union) who will only have an honest man.

The fraternal filmmakers set a jaunty tone and the film makes the clueless characters into lovable losers. Hardened criminals they're not, though they don't stint on constant cursing or take a lot of interest in making an honest living. The visuals, dominated by shades of orange and amber, effectively capture the Collinwood neighborhood where the dreams may be big but the paychecks sure aren't. Loosely based on the 1958 minor classic, "Big Deal on Madonna Street," the plot falls into slim-pickings territory but the quirky characters are fleshed out rather divertingly. The ensemble cast works well together, no one trying to shine above the others -- including Clooney in what is basically an extended cameo.

The lapses in logic, how Pero gets put in the pen beside Cosimo, then is set free the moment he gets the info he needs, and why the incarcerated Cosimo's girlfriend is so anxious to marry this lowlife, are simply glossed over.

The movie meanders along with its comic complications, nicely buoyed by a music track that goes from polka to other ethnic selections.

Because of brief violence, recurring profanity, minor sexual innuendo, fleeting rear nudity and much rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Welcome to L.A.
synopsis: Listless and pretentious account of the amorous adventures of a young song writer (Keith Carradine) whose charm is such that women jostle and trample one another in a mad rush to enjoy his favor. Writer-director Alan Rudolph's unsurprising message is that sex without love is unrewarding and that Los Angeles has some sort of monopoly on self-deception. Gratuitous nudity. O (R) ( 1977 )

title: Welcome to Mooseport
synopsis: Lukewarm comedy about a local handyman (Ray Romano) who, in an attempt to win back his girlfriend (Maura Tierney), decides to run against a former president (Gene Hackman) for mayor of his quaint New England town. Part triangular romance, part political satire, director Donald Petrie's flat farce pokes fun at the electoral process and media scrutiny of candidates' private lives while espousing a belief in the basic decency of Main Street America, but fails to make good on its campaign promises of comedy. Some sexual humor, instances of rear nudity and minimal crude language
full_review:
All's fair in love and politics is the theme of the lukewarm comedy "Welcome to Mooseport" (20th Century Fox). The film is part triangular romance, part political satire, and the odds of director Donald Petrie's farce winning a landslide at the box office are about as slim as Dennis Kucinich delivering a State of the Union address.

TV funnyman Ray Romano stars as Handy Harrison, an aloof fix-it man who owns a mom-and-pop hardware store in the quaint New England town of Mooseport, Maine.

Gene Hackman plays Monroe "Eagle" Cole, the wildly popular outgoing U.S. president who decides to pitch his tent in the idyllic hamlet once he leaves office. Cole arrives in town, eager to retire to a life of leisure and lucrative speaking engagements while he licks his wounds over his recent messy divorce. But no sooner has the Eagle landed than Cole is approached by the town council, asking him to run for mayor.

But his campaign trail takes an unexpected turn when Harrison tosses his hat into the ring and announces his candidacy after Cole makes a pass at the handyman's veterinarian-girlfriend (Maura Tierney), turning the quiet town of Mooseport on its antlers.

While it makes some witty observations about the electoral process and the media's scrutiny of candidates' private lives, the film fails to make good on its campaign promise of comedy. In fact what starts out as a promising premise ends up as politics as usual -- early expectations quickly deflated. And though much of the humor is laced with cynicism, "Mooseport" is fueled by a Capraesque belief in the basic goodness and decency of Main Street America.

The easygoing Romano is likable but his what-you-see-is-what-you-get talent seems better suited for the small screen. As always, Hackman is a pleasure to watch, bringing a well-honed professionalism that elevates even the most mediocre material and raises the performance levels of everyone else in the scene. The same goes for the chameleonic Marcia Gay Harden, who plays Cole's lovelorn chief of staff.

Christine Baranski injects some much-needed energy into the mix as Cole's ex-wife, whom he refers to as the "Wicked Witch of the West Wing" and who bears a coiffed resemblance to another ambitious former first lady. Occasional laughs are also provided by Rip Torn as Cole's wacky campaign manager, as well as by the commander-in-chief's overzealous Secret Service handlers.

In one scene the ex-prez's baby-faced PR director (Fred Savage) advises Cole that a sense of humor would help him in the polls, informing him, "Funny is your weakness." It is also the film's weakness. And while none of this is an impeachable offense, one may want to veto seeing "Mooseport" until it comes out on video. Besides, there is another campaign coming up that will probably provide loads more laughs.

Due to some sexual humor, instances of rear nudity, and minimal crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Welcome to Sarajevo
synopsis: Fact-based story of a world-weary British TV journalist (Stephen Dillane) who grimly reports on civilian massacres in wartorn 1992 Sarajevo, then attempts to smuggle a 10-year-old girl back with him when he returns to London. By focusing on the touching story of one child's fate, director Michael Winterbottom's semidocumentary hits home emotionally in decrying the insanity of genocide. Some violence, numerous gory corpses, fleeting nudity and occasional rough language

title: Welcome to the Club
synopsis: Generally witless comedy about a naive Quaker morale officer (Brian Foley) who attempts to integrate a postwar Hiroshima officer's club, and comes off more as a fool than as a nice guy going through some sobering disillusionment. Directed by William Shenson, the result is rather depressing and, whatever its good intentions in trying to satirize both the military and bigotry, it contains considerable offensiveness, notably foul language. O (R) ( 1971 )

title: Welcome to the Dollhouse
synopsis: Painfully funny story of a geeky 11-year-old suburban girl (Heather Matarazzo) and her efforts to become popular which are continually undermined by her mom, siblings and taunting classmates. Writer-director Todd Solondz insightfully and unsentimentally captures the seventh grader's nightmare existence which just a little kindness from those around could dramatically change for the better. Fleeting violence, some sexual references and recurring rough language

title: We Live Again
synopsis: Hollywood version of Leo Tolstoy's novel, "Resurrection," about a Russian prince (Fredric March) who learns years later that he has ruined the life of a peasant girl (Anna Sten) on his aunt's estates by leaving her pregnant, then tries to atone by joining her when she is sent to Siberia for a crime of which she is innocent. Director Rouben Mamoulian evokes both the beauty of the Russian spirit and the injustices of the czarist regime but the characters and their emotions are melodramatically thin. Muddled treatment of an idealistic theme

title: Wells Fargo
synopsis: Interesting saga of the title overland express as portrayed in the exploits of its field agent (Joel McCrea) who forges the line from New York to St. Louis in the 1840s, establishes an office in 1850 San Francisco, then constructs a series of relay stations from Missouri to California on the eve of the Civil War. Directed by Frank Lloyd, the story is paced by frontier action and colorful pioneer lore, but the agent's marriage to a Southern belle (Frances Dee) adds some dark melodramatics that cloud the last portion of the picture. Stylized violence and domestic strife

title: We Own The Night
synopsis: Powerful character-driven drama set in 1980s New York about a drug-taking nightclub manager (a splendid Joaquin Phoenix) who changes his dissolute ways when his police-officer brother (Mark Wahlberg) is shot -- and their police-chief father's (Robert Duvall) life threatened -- by the Russian mobsters who control the venue. Writer-director James Gray sustains a taut, tragedy-drenched mood, the action secondary to the human drama; performances are fine, including Eva Mendes as Phoenix's girlfriend; and the narrative has an admirable gravitas, marred from a moral standpoint only by a revenge killing that is out of step with Catholic teaching. Sporadic but strong violence, rough language, some crude expressions and profanity, vigilante killing, some grisly crime images, drug use, sexual encounter and upper female nudity

title: We're Back! A Dinosaur's Story
synopsis: Magically transported to present-day New York City, four friendly dinos are saved by a gruff street urchin and a lonely little girl when an evil circus master changes them into snarling monsters. Steven Spielberg's animated production of Hudson Talbott's children's story sacrifices much of its charm and character appeal for an overabundance of busy and noisy misadventures that may delight children a lot more than their elders

title: We're No Angels
synopsis: Minor comedy in which bumbling convicts (Humphrey Bogart, Peter Ustinov and Aldo Ray) delay their escape from Devil's Island to save a kindly but inefficient French shopkeeper and his wife (Leo(G) . Carroll and Joan Bennett) from the machinations of a crafty relative (Basil Rathbone). Director Michael Curtiz gets some laughs from the unlikely antics of the good-hearted cons but the plot's intended whimsy falls flat. Devious deeds aplenty

title: We're No Angels
synopsis: Heavy-handed comic misadventure in which two escaped convicts (Robert De Niro and Sean Penn) hide out in a monastery pretending to be priests while they figure out a way to cross the border into Canada. David Mamet's script has plenty of comic possibilities in contrasting the spiritual impoverishment of the two earth-bound clods with the faith and innocence of the unworldly community of monks, but director Neil Jordan plays the piece so broadly that the result may appear to some as an irreverent farce, questionable in taste and treatment of religion. Some sexual references, several scenes of hard-edged violence and a bemused agnostic attitude toward religion

title: We're Rich Again
synopsis: Wacky Depression comedy in which a stock market casualty (Grant Mitchell) hopes to recoup his fortune after his daughter (Joan Marsh) marries a millionaire (Reginald Denny), but when her dizzy country cousin (Marian Nixon) arrives for the wedding, chaos follows. Directed by William A. Seiter, the zany proceedings feature running gags with a polo-playing grandmother (Edna May Oliver) and a frustrated process server (Edgar Kennedy), but the thin plot belabors the obvious. Light treatment of marriage and sexual innuendo

title: Werewolf of London
synopsis: Creaky but still effective monster tale in which a botanist (Henry Hull) is bitten by a werewolf while searching for a rare flower in Tibet, then returns to London with the plant only to learn too late its bloom is an antidote to becoming a wolfman. Directed by Stuart Walker, the twisty plot has the Tibetan werewolf (Warner Oland) turn up as a respected professor who steals the blooms for himself, leaving London to be terrorized by the botanist-wolfman during the four nights of the full moon. Stylized fantasy violence and menace

title: Werewolf, The
synopsis: Pedestrian monster fantasy directed by Fred F. Sears has a poor fellow (Steven Ritch) roaming the U.S. countryside after being turned into a wolfman by a botched radiation experiment. Stylized violence and unconvincing chills

title: Wes Craven Presents Dracula 2000
synopsis: Far-fetched thriller set in the present day, in which an antiques dealer (Christopher Plummer) travels from his home in London to America to save his daughter (Justine Waddell) from his life-long nemesis, Dracula (Gerard Butler). Despite a few frightening moments, director Wes Craven's sleek update has no bite with ordinary special effects and a convoluted narrative that ends with a cockamamie explanation of Dracula's origins. Intermittent violence with some gore, a few sexual references, fleeting partial nudity and sporadic rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference

title: Wes Craven's New Nightmare
synopsis: In the 7th of the "Nightmare on Elm Street" horror series, an actress (Heather Langenkamp) and her little boy (Miko Hughes) begin having violent nightmares which trigger the return of maniac Freddy Krueger (Robert Englund) who makes repeated attempts at killing them. Writer-director Wes Craven unreels a trite series of mother-and-child-in-peril situations in a suspenseless sequel featuring smug cameo appearances by the director and his studio boss. Some horror-fantasy violence, frequent menace to a child and a few instances of rough language

title: Westbound
synopsis: Standard Western about a Union officer (Randolph Scott) put in charge of a stagecoach line carrying California gold past Confederate sympathizers (led by Andrew Duggan). Directed by Budd Boetticher, it offers the usual brand of heroics and villainy but little else. Stylized violence

title: Westerner, The
synopsis: Cowboy Gary Cooper sides with the sodbusters against the cattlemen led by Roy Bean (Walter Brennan), the hanging judge of Vinegaroon, Texas. Directed by William Wellman, the situation is familiar but flavorsome and wryly fashioned, particularly Brennan's performance as the ornery judge whose ideal is the English singer, Lily Langtry. Periodic stylized violence

title: Western Union
synopsis: A reformed outlaw (Randolph Scott) and a rich tenderfoot (Robert Young) help a Western Union engineer (Dean Jagger) fight off Indians and Confederate raiders (headed by Barton MacLane) while stringing the last link in the telegraph line connecting the East and West coasts in 1861. The heroic theme is directed by Fritz Lang, with plenty of Western action and colorful characters galore, including Slim Summerville's comically fearful cook. Frontier violence and Indian stereotypes

title: West of the Badlands
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Joseph Kane in which a New York doctor (Roy Rogers) wrongly sought by the law shows up in 1875 Idaho where he's befriended by an old codger (George "Gabby" Hayes) and a pretty saloon owner (Maude Eburn), then joins a band of outlaws (led by Joe Sawyer) in order to stop their raids on his new friends. Mild violence

title: West of the Divide
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Robert N. Bradbury features John Wayne masquerading as an outlaw in order to get the man who killed his father 12 years before, during the course of which he saves a rancher's daughter (Virginia Faire Brown) and finds his longlost kid brother

title: West Point Story, The
synopsis: Strained musical romance in which a down-on-his-luck Broadway director (James Cagney) is required to live as a cadet while staging the military academy's annual revue (headed by Gordon MacRae), with some help from his devoted assistant (Virginia Mayo) and a friendly movie star (Doris Day). Directed by Roy Del Ruth, the dim plot's contrived romances are strictly formula fare, with only the academy setting and Cagney's energetic song-and-dance numbers to hold interest. Comic violence, romantic complications and much duplicity

title: West Side Story
synopsis: Rousing Broadway musical, with choreography by Jerome Robbins and music by Leonard Bernstein, is a contemporary, inner-city adaptation of the classic Romeo and Juliet theme, with Richard Beymer and Natalie Wood playing the star-crossed lovers set apart ethnically and by their opposing street gang backgrounds. Directed by Robert Wise, the picture captures the grit of life in the city's lower depths, with glimmers of hope and elements of tragedy in a delicate balance, carried along by song and the dance numbers that pulsate with energy and verve. Some of the social issues, relationships and street language, however, require a mature perspective

title: Westward Ho
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Robert Bradbury is set in 1866 when a California cowboy (John Wayne) organizes the Singing Riders, a vigilante band dedicated to ridding the West of outlaws, in particular, the gang who 16 years before had killed his parents and taken his baby brother. Frontier violence with vigilantes aiding outnumbered lawmen

title: Westward the Women
synopsis: Distaff Western chronicles the adventures of 140 women (Denise Darcel, Marilyn Erskine, Hope Emerson, et. al.) recruited in Chicago as prospective brides for California settlers, making their way cross-country in a wagon train led by a tough but increasingly bemused wagonmaster (Robert Taylor). Directed by William A. Wellman, there are plenty of dangers and some losses along the trail but the trek's sentimental ending is never in doubt. Stylized frontier violence and mild sexual references

title: Westworld
synopsis: James Brolin and Richard Benjamin vacation in a futuristic resort where, during the fun and games, a Western gunslinger robot (Yul Brynner) malfunctions, turns on the vacationers and starts to stalk them. Unfortunately, after about ten minutes, writer-director Michael Crichton has explored all the subtleties of the one-idea situation. Some ludicrous nonsense about "willing" female robots

title: Wetherby
synopsis: Vanessa Redgrave plays a schoolteacher in a small town who becomes the indirect victim of an act of violence that seems to be wholly unprovoked. But was it? This superbly acted but somewhat thin and contrived murder mystery, written and directed by playwright David Hare, explores the question of suicide in a careful, literate and sometimes compelling fashion. Good entertainment for mature viewers, although there is some violence and a few fairly restrained bedroom scenes

title: We Were Soldiers
synopsis: Powerful Vietnam War drama about the first battle between American troops, led by fatherly Lt. Col. Harold G. Moore (Mel Gibson), and the Viet Cong enemy. Despite slim characterizations and a few cliches, writer-director Randall Wallace's harrowing true story depicts war with raw, graphic imagery that underscores the wrenching loss of human life as it touches briefly upon the formidable struggle to reconcile Christianity and warfare. Constant war violence with many bloody, chilling images and some rough language with profanity

title: We Will All Meet in Paradise
synopsis: Thin French comedy about the life and times of four overaged, overindulged, middle-class Dead End Kids (Jean Rochfort, Claude Brasseur, Guy Bedos and Victor Lanoux) as they go through a round of sophomoric escapades. Directed by Yves Robert, the result is a tepid comedy of manners whose sole merit is the considerable charm of the performers. Adultery figures in the plot

title: Whale Rider
synopsis: Evocative coming-of-age tale set among contemporary New Zealand Maoris where a 12-year-old girl (Keisha Castle-Hughes) secretly trains to become the warrior-like tribal leader against the fierce objections of her tradition-bound grandfather, the aging chief (Rawiri Paratene). Writer-director Niki Caro sensitively weds the ancient culture's rites to hardscrabble times, in the process dramatically exploring the role of community, change, and father figures in the formation of youngsters. Brief sexual and drug-related reference
full_review:
Determined to win her grandfather's love and respect, a 12-year-old Maori girl defies his edict that she not learn warrior skills in the evocative tale "Whale Rider" (Newmarket).

The very contemporary retelling of the Maori legend is written and directed by Niki Caro, based on the 1986 best seller by Witi Ihimaera, New Zealand's first published Maori novelist.

Local legend holds that the sea god Paikea arrived in their North Island village of Whangara on the back of a whale. Aging tribal chief Koro (Rawiri Paratene) is distraught when his son's wife dies bearing twins, with the male infant dying as well. Resenting Koro's insensitivity to his baby daughter, the grief-stricken father (Cliff Curtis) gives her the male-only name of Paikea and leaves New Zealand.

Called Pai, the child (Keisha Castle-Hughes) is aware her grandfather wishes her brother had lived instead, but her grandmother (Vicky Haughton) provides the affection her grandfather feels but does not show.

With no male heir available to lead, Koro begins training local boys in the gestures and fighting stances the new leader must possess. Pai surreptitiously practices and excels in the necessary skills, exhibiting a natural leadership lacking in the unmotivated boys around her.

When Pai's father returns for a visit, an ugly flare-up again distances him from his own father and he offers to take Pai back to Germany with him. She is sorely tempted but decides her destiny is to prove herself to her grandfather as the person he is seeking to succeed him.

Despite Koro's refusal to acknowledge her talents, she speaks in beautiful tribute to him at a school ceremony where she has won two top prizes. Apologizing for upsetting his tradition-bound ways, she can hardly get the words out as he has not shown up to hear how much she loves and honors him. Instead, on the way, Koro is sidetracked by a crisis of beached whales that will test the resolve of the entire village -- and trigger a significant change of heart.

Castle-Hughes makes a radiant debut as the loving child whose youth belies her emotional and spiritual maturity. Indeed, her willingness to sacrifice herself for her people is Christ-like, and her ability to forgive her grandfather's many slights deeply touching. Caro orchestrates a remarkable exploration of an ancient culture confronting change during hardscrabble times while pulling together as a community to maintain their sacred ties to nature. Although Pai is specifically battling the tribe's rigid patriarchy and accepted gender bias, the narrative embraces universal themes and evokes intense emotions.

Each in their own way, Paratene and Haughton, as the very differing grandparents, bring a strong presence to their roles and were undoubtedly helpful to 11-year-old Castle-Hughes.
The all-Maori cast and the on-location shooting in the village of Whangara, on New Zealand's east coast, only adds to the cinematic experience. Viewers are sure to notice the exquisitely carved interiors of the tribe's meeting house, but it is the interiors of the spirit of this indigenous people that is so impressively celebrated in "Whale Rider."

Because of a brief sexual and drug-related reference, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Whales of August, The
synopsis: Two aged sisters (Bette Davis and Lillian Gish), sharing a cottage on an island off the coast of Maine, rely upon each other since one is blind but wealthy and the other is poor but kind. Director Lindsay Anderson's picture of old age and sibling rivalries is finely told through mood and characterization, and though sentimental, it is full of heart and small truths. Some incidental profanity

title: What Happens in Vegas
synopsis: An inebriated couple -- a commodities trader (Cameron Diaz), dumped by her longtime boyfriend, and a womanizing slacker (Ashton Kutcher), fired from his closet-building job -- get married in Las Vegas, much to their later regret, and must live with the consequences when they return to New York and a judge orders them to try to make the marriage work for six months, if they are to decide who keeps the $3 million jackpot they won at the slots. Director Tom Vaughan's romantic comedy is lame, tasteless and unfunny, despite a premise that could work in better hands, while the warm-if-predictable ending fails to erase the sophomoric ineptitude of what has come before it. Pervasive vulgar humor, implied premarital cohabitation, scatological elements, some skimpy costuming, much crude language and brief profanity
full_review:
In case you were wondering about that title, "What Happens in Vegas" (Fox), what transpires in a nutshell is this: The protagonists marry each other while thoroughly intoxicated, and later win a ton of dough.

The not-so-happy-the-next-morning couple are commodities trader Joy (Cameron Diaz), who had just been dumped by her longtime boyfriend, Mason (Jason Sudeikis), and Jack (Ashton Kutcher), a womanizing slacker fired by his own father (Treat Williams) from his closet-building job.

To drown their respective sorrows, the two (at first, strangers to each other) New Yorkers take off for the fabled Sin City -- in tandem with their respective best pals -- Tipper (Lake Bell) and Steve (Rob Corddry), the latter also Jack's lawyer. They meet when they accidentally wind up in the same room, sparking the first of several tiresome slapstick sequences.

The mix-up gets them upgraded to penthouse suites, and a slew of vouchers. The couples team up, get (as noted) wildly inebriated, and Joy awakens the next morning with a ring on her finger, much to her and Jack's embarrassment and regret.

Later in the casino, they amicably agree to split, but just as they're walking away from each other, Jack plays Joy's quarter in a slot machine, and they hit the jackpot.

When they return home, a judge (Dennis Miller) orders them to try to make the marriage work for six months before ruling on who keeps the $3 million winnings.

Director Tom Vaughan's romantic comedy, from a humor-deficient script by Dana Fox, is lame and tasteless, even though sex scenes as such are nil. Even so, the Judd Apatow brand of gross-out comedy is, by comparison, a paragon of delicacy and wit.

For the most part, Diaz comes off better than Kutcher -- his character is unrelievedly annoying as written -- though they both recover something of their dignity in the movie's more serene final scenes. Corddry's one-note misanthrope is a loathsome bore. Queen Latifah offers a few moments of welcome serenity as the savvy court-appointed marriage counselor.

In more adept hands, the basic premise could have been a charmer, however predictable, but even when the film eventually shifts gears for its warm and fuzzy homestretch, a flashback coda jolts us back to the sophomoric ineptitude of all that has come before it.

The film contains pervasive vulgar humor, implied premarital cohabitation, scatological elements, some skimpy costuming, much crude language and brief profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: What a Girl Wants
synopsis: Contemporary fairytale about a spirited American teen-ager (Amanda Bynes) who travels to London in search of the father she has never known only to find out that she is the daughter of a blueblood politician (Colin Firth) running for Parliament. Directed by Dennie Gordon, this delightful modern Cinderella story celebrates the bonds between parents and children and the possibility of second chances that love affords. Instances of mildly offensive language and scattered sexual innuendoes
full_review:
"What A Girl Wants" (Warner Bros.) is a contemporary fairy tale about a precocious American teen-ager (Amanda Bynes) who travels to London in search of the father she has never known.

Inspired by the 1958 film "The Reluctant Debutante" and directed by Dennie Gordon, this delightful modern Cinderella story celebrates the bonds between parents and children and the possibility of second chances which love affords.

Daphne Reynolds (Bynes) feels incomplete. She has style, charm and a bright future. She lives in New York's Chinatown with her doting, bohemian mom, Libby (Kelly Preston), a wedding singer who has raised her daughter in an atmosphere of spirited independence. Daphne, however, longs to meet the father she has only heard about in her mother's bedtime stories -- a dashing Englishman Libby had shared a whirlwind romance with 17 years ago while traveling through the Moroccan desert.

Working weddings with her mom has afforded Daphne a front-row view of countless brides dressed in storybook gowns dancing "that special dance" with their dads -- an all-too-painful reminder of the lost relationship which will deny her from ever sharing in that joyous ritual.

Armed only with her unabashed joie de vivre and a photo of the debonair Brit, Daphne impetuously hops across the pond to seek the one missing piece of the puzzle that will make her life and her family complete.

Once in London, Daphne befriends a young punk musician, Oliver (Ian Wallace), who, as Cupid would have it, immediately falls for her charm. Together they track down her father, who just happens to be a high-profile Tory politician, Lord Henry Dashwood (Colin Firth), who is currently embroiled in a hotly contested campaign for election in Parliament.

Needless to say, her arrival triggers a series of events, which put Dashwood's political plans as well as his personal life in a tailspin. At times both comic and touching, Daphne slowly has a liberating effect on Dashwood's self-imposed highbrow stodginess. The aristocrat, however, must ultimately choose between acknowledging the brash Yank as his daughter, thereby jeopardizing his political ambitions, or walking away from his one chance at true happiness. As Lady Jocelyn (Eileen Atkins), the Dashwood matriarch and resident fairy godmother, ruefully observes, "For 600 years this family has been sacrificing parts of its body for England. You are going to have sacrifice your heart."

Further complicating the situation are the machinations of Dashwood's conniving fiancee, Glynnis (Anna Chancellor), and Glynnis' Machiavellian father, Alastair Payne (Jonathan Pryce), both of whom contemptuously view Daphne as gauche. Years earlier, the elitist Payne had likewise deemed Libby unsuitable and plotted the lovers' eventual break-up.

No fairy tale would be complete without a jealous stepsister (Christina Cole) and a broom closet in which Daphne is locked on the night of the royal ball.

Bynes, the popular star of Nickelodeon's "The Amanda Show," brings comedic timing and a youthful grace to the role of Daphne, with saucer-like eyes which reflect the vulnerability of a girl on the cusp of becoming a woman. Firth's Dashwood conveys with restraint and subtlety the stiff-upper-lip pathos of a man torn between happiness and duty. His measured Prince Charming balances Bynes' zestful Cinderella.

While the film has instances of mildly offensive language and scattered sexual innuendoes, its strong moral message reinforces the important role a parent plays in a child's life and the sometimes-courageous sacrifices demanded of a parent's love. As such, some parents may feel the film is fine for their pre-teens as well.

True to its storybook inspiration, the movie reaffirms the timeless message that if you remain true to yourself and embrace the uniqueness of every person, dreams can come true. To our cynical society, such optimism may seem dubious. Perhaps we need more fairytales, especially in light of current events which seem to preclude hopes of "happily ever afters."

The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

title: What a Way to Die
synopsis: ( see: "Beyond Control" )

title: What a Way to Go!
synopsis: Deadly one-joke comedy told in flashbacks as psychiatrist Bob Cummings listens to widow Shirley MacLaine explain how the untimely demise of husbands Dick Van Dyke, Paul Newman, Robert Mitchum and Gene Kelly left her enormously wealthy, but all she wants is penniless janitor Dean Martin. Directed by J. Lee Thompson, the lumbering production glitters with period costuming and decor but the witless plot and humor are painfully heavy-handed. Much sexual innuendo

title: What Dreams May Come
synopsis: Gooey afterlife fantasy in which a doctor (Robin Williams) killed in a car crash is reunited with his deceased children in the hereafter, then chooses to seek out his artist wife (Annabella Sciorra) in hell following her suicide. While director Vincent Ward's painterly visuals are exquisite, the incoherent treatment of afterlife reunions renders the movie largely unappealing. A suicide, theme of reincarnation and minimal profanity and rough language

title: Whatever
synopsis: Downbeat coming-of-age story of two high school seniors (Liza Weil and Chad Morgan) from dysfunctional families who sneak out to drug parties and try casual sex, but end up going in very different directions. Writer-director Susan Skoog captures the adolescent angst of rudderless girls lacking parental guidance, but the unsentimental narrative is flawed by one girl's sudden transformation. Brief violence, teen promiscuity, much substance abuse, frequent rough language, fleeting nudity and occasional profanity

title: Whatever Happened to Aunt Alice
synopsis: Suspense thriller with Geraldine Page as a widow, left without any observable means of income, who combines murder and gardening as profitable pastimes in bilking a series of housekeepers out of their life savings. Routine chiller directed by Lee H. Katzin. A-II (PG) (1969)

title: Whatever It Takes
synopsis: Forgettable romantic teen comedy in which a socially awkward boy and a popular high school jock hatch a plan to woo their respective dream girls, producing unexpected results. As directed by David Raynr, the "Cyrano de Bergerac" imitator lacks any original spark with its predictable plot and strained comedic efforts. Several sexual references, adolescent drinking and some rough language

title: Whatever Works
synopsis: A pessimistic New York grouch (Larry David) finds his life transformed when he reluctantly shelters a homeless but irrepressibly cheerful young Southerner (Evan Rachel Wood), and they fall for each other. Though undeniably clever at times, writer-director Woody Allen's comedy of manners mocks evangelical Christians through the waif's parents (Patricia Clarkson and Ed Begley Jr.) and heavy-handedly rams home the message that, in a meaningless universe, any path to temporary fulfillment, particularly that of unbridled sexuality, ought to be pursued. Adultery, implied group sex and homosexual activity, images of full nudity, a suicide theme, some sexual humor, at least one crude and one crass word, and about a dozen uses of profanity

title: What Every Woman Knows
synopsis: Droll adaptation of the James M. Barrie play about a bright but practical Scotswoman (Helen Hayes) who helps get her dashing but dim intended (Brian Aherne) elected to Parliament, then as his wife furthers his career while extricating him from a foolish infatuation with an English beauty (Madge Evans). Directed by Gregory La Cava, the proverbial tale of the woman behind any successful man is treated with disarming humor and convincing performances. Romantic complications and implied infidelity

title: What Happened Was...
synopsis: Unsettling two-person drama about a middle-aged paralegal (Tom Noonan) and a thirtyish secretary (Karen Sillas) in the same firm whose awkward first date begins with dinner in her Manhattan studio and ends up revealing both as very troubled adults, quite unlike the workaday personalities they project. Also written and directed by Noonan, the dramatic situation is intriguing as a reflection of the loneliness of urban life and the individual's need to have some sense of belonging. Concerns regarding emotional intimacy, some sex and drug references and occasional rough language

title: What Just Happened
synopsis: Perceptive, sporadically funny comedy as a beleaguered producer (Robert De Niro) tries to salvage his latest film starring Sean Penn (as himself), and convince star Bruce Willis (also as himself) to shave a bushy beard before filming another, and reconcile with his separated wife (Robin Wright Penn). Much of the humor of director Barry Levinson's satire strives for a trenchant insider look at Hollywood, though not all the jokes land, but there are good performances by John Turturro, Stanley Tucci, Catherine Keener and others, while De Niro manages to convey a sympathetic portrait of a man in the throes of midlife crisis. Much rough language and some profanity, crude expressions, brief violent images with gore, an implied nonmarital sexual encounter and a drug reference
full_review:
In the long tradition of movies that aim to give an insider look at Hollywood -- "A Star is Born" and "The Bad and the Beautiful" among them -- comes the perceptive, if only sporadically funny, comedy "What Just Happened" (Magnolia).

Based on Art Linson's memoir, the fictionalized screenplay (by Linson) centers on beleaguered producer Sam (Robert De Niro), who deftly manages to juggle a host of professional and personal headaches.

First, he needs to salvage his latest film, the violently artsy "Fiercely" starring Sean Penn (as himself). The film has bombed in a preview screening, and studio chief Lou (Catherine Keener) is demanding edits before the film is unveiled at the Cannes Film Festival. (Michael Wincott is a hoot as the druggie British director who must re-cut the film so a dog doesn't perish in the final frames.)

On another front, Sam must convince star Bruce Willis to shave a bushy beard before filming begins on his next movie. If the beard doesn't go, the studio will drop out. Willis sends up his image outrageously, particularly in an explosive F-word-laden tantrum sparked by the beard request.

After that, Sam leans heavily on Willis' nebbishy agent Dick (John Turturro) -- who lives in quivering fear of his own clients -- to convince Willis to shave.

All the while, Sam is hoping to reconcile with wife Kelly (Robin Wright Penn), and he resists the efforts of their divorce counselor to keep them apart. He's further disturbed when he learns Kelly might be having a fling with his screenwriter buddy, Scott (Stanley Tucci). And he's mortified to discover that his teenage daughter, Zoe (Kristen Stewart), may not be the sheltered girl he imagined.

Much of the trenchant humor in director Barry Levinson's satire works, though not all the jokes land. But there's pleasure in watching the performances, while De Niro -- in one of his best recent roles -- manages to convey a sympathetic portrait of an overextended power player in the throes of midlife crisis.

The film contains much rough language and some profanity, crude expressions, brief violent images with gore, an implied nonmarital sexual encounter and a drug reference. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: What Lies Beneath
synopsis: Plodding ghost story in which a wife (Michelle Pfeiffer) feels haunted by a menacing spirit who turns out to have been involved with her geneticist husband (Harrison Ford). Director Robert Zemeckis attempts to generate Hitchcock-like suspense but falls far short with glaring plot holes and an abundance of thriller cliches. Some violence, sexual situations with implied adultery, occasional profanity and an instance of rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference

title: What Lola Wants
synopsis: ( see: "Damn Yankees" )

title: What Price Glory
synopsis: Stagey remake of the 1926 original with Captain James Cagney and Sergeant Dan Dailey as brawling Marines in World War I France where they battle over a barmaid (Corinne Calvet) before going back into the line. Director John Ford lets the romance slide in favor of manly horseplay and military heroics, with disappointing results. Wartime violence and romantic tomfoolery

title: What's Cooking
synopsis: Warmhearted comedy that follows the Thanksgiving dinners of four Los Angeles families (including Alfre Woodard, Maury Chaykin, Joan Chen and Kyra Sedgwick) as they cope with situations ranging from parental dismay over a daughter's gay lifestyle to teenage violence to infidelity. Highlighting the ethnically diverse aspects of Angelino families, director Gurinder Chadha's film contrasts dynamic families -- African-American, Latino, Jewish and Asian -- while connecting them through turkey and love in an often humorous and touching manner. Brief menace, a lesbian relationship, fleeting rear nudity and intermittent crass language with an instance of rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference

title: What's Eating Gilbert Grape
synopsis: A compassionate stranger (Juliette Lewis) helps a frustrated young man (Johnny Depp) deal with the burden of heading a dysfunctional household consisting of his mom (Darlene Cates), who's a 500-pound recluse, and his mentally disabled younger brother (Leonardo DiCaprio) who is often a danger to himself. Though the narrative sometimes ambles and rambles, director Lasse Hallstrom's offbeat, often downbeat drama features finely honed performances and a poignant script that never insults the emotional, mental or physical frailties of its characters. An implied affair and brief violence

title: What's Good for the Goose
synopsis: Failed British movie in which a glum bank manager (Norman Wisdom) is introduced to the psychedelic world of free love, loud music and general aimlessness by an uninhibited hitchhiker (Sally Geeson) who is always ready to disrobe and jump into bed. Directed by Menahem Golan, the movie's attempt to pass this off as social comment fails to overcome the exploitative elements that predominate. O (R) ( 1970 )

title: What's Love Got to Do with It
synopsis: Musical biography of rock singer Tina Turner (played by Angela Bassett) focusing on her rise to fame and troubled marriage to abusive husband Ike (Laurence Fishburne) until she left him and established a solo career. Director Brian Gibson serves up a spirited but ultimately superficial look at the entertainer, offsetting the ugly hysterics of a violent relationship with glossy musical set-pieces. A discreet bedroom scene, some intense domestic violence, occasional recreational drug use and recurring rough language

title: What's So Bad About Feeling Good
synopsis: Colorful tropical bird infects the rude, scowling citizens of New York City with a mysterious happiness virus and within hours everyone is smiling and polite to one another, including George Peppard and Mary Tyler Moore playing reformed hippies. But when New Yorkers also quit gambling, smoking and drinking, the government develops an antidote to protect their tax revenues. Produced and directed by George Seaton, it's an amusing little satire on urban life that some may find infectious. Romantic complications

title: What's the Worst That Can Happen
synopsis: Failed comedy about a billionaire tycoon (Danny DeVito) who snatches the lucky ring off a thief (Martin Lawrence) he catches robbing his house and triggers a battle of wills between the two men over the good-luck charm. Sluggish and dull-witted, director Sam Weisman's flimsy narrative is mostly a snore with a few cheap laughs. An implied sexual encounter, brief comically intended violence, sporadic profanity, some crass words and fleeting rough language. The U.S. Catholic Conference

title: What the Bleep Do We Know
synopsis: Part documentary, part narrative film which uses a loose story line about an unfulfilled wedding photographer (Marlee Matlin) as a launching pad for discussions of quantum physics, the intersection of science and spirituality, and the underlying nature of reality. Directed by William Arntz, Betsy Chasse and Mark Vicente, the docudrama incorporates amusing animated segments and interviews with academics to explore its difficult subject matter in a lively and engaging manner. However, while the film raises some interesting questions, its arguments often become muddled by New Age mysticism which promotes private spirituality over traditional organized religion. Mild sexual content and a few crude expressions
full_review:
Part documentary, part narrative, "What the Bleep Do We Know?" (Lord of the Wind Films) is an unwieldy metaphysical mishmash which wraps a loose story line about an unfulfilled wedding photographer (Marlee Matlin) around discussions of quantum physics, the intersection of science and spirituality, mind-body consciousness and the underlying nature of reality.

Directed by William Arntz, Betsy Chasse and Mark Vicente, the thought-provoking film takes a lively and novel approach to its mind-bending subject matter, incorporating slightly cheesy special effects, amusing animated segments and talking-head interviews with academics (including a woman who claims to get esoteric knowledge by channeling the spirit of a 35,000-year-old warrior) into the bare-bones story.

The movie's overriding thesis is that there is no objective "real world" out there, independent of our subjective experiences, only "waves of possibilities," the crux of its argument being that we each, in effect, create our own reality.

On a positive note, "What the Bleep" invites viewers into a deeper appreciation of the mystery and interconnectedness of the created universe.

However, the film derails into a muddled morass of pseudoscientific hokum, Gnostic mysticism and New-Age mumbo jumbo. And while the overall film remains open-minded to transcendent experiences, it is, at times, critical of traditional organized religion, pushing instead a less dogmatic brand of personal spirituality.

Because of mild sexual content and a few crude expressions, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.

title: What Women Want
synopsis: Leaden mix of fantasy and romantic comedy in which a womanizing advertising executive (Mel Gibson) who can read the minds of all the females around him steals the ideas of his new boss (Helen Hunt) to get her job even though they are becoming romantically involved. As directed by Nancy Meyers, the one-joke premise soon wears out its welcome in contrived and pathetically predictable situations. A sexual encounter, fleeting recreational drug use and sexist remarks. The U.S. Catholic Conference

title: Wheeler Dealers, The
synopsis: Romantic comedy about a cunning Texas high-roller (James Garner) who falls for a Wall Street broker (Lee Remick), then is indicted for helping her sell stock in a product that went out with high-button shoes. Director Arthur Hiller's comic treatment of stock market hijinks is no longer as wacky as it once seemed, though the characters still please. Romantic situations

title: Wheel of Fortune
synopsis: ( see: "A Man Betrayed" )

title: When in Rome
synopsis: Perky romantic comedy about a work-obsessed New York museum curator (Kristen Bell) who travels to Rome for her sister's (Alexis Dziena) wedding and falls for the best man (Josh Duhamel), but their path to bliss takes a detour when she defies local custom by removing several coins from the "Fountain of Love," causing the quartet of eccentric strangers who deposited the change (Danny DeVito, Will Arnett, Jon Heder and Dax Shepard) to become hopelessly infatuated with her. While the youthful, slightly pixilated priest (Keir O'Donnell) who performs the nuptials comes in for some gentle ribbing, director Mark Steven Johnson's pleasantly diverting, blithely illogical ensemble piece is mostly worry-free with only a fleeting scene of newlywed friskiness barring endorsement for teens. Brief nongraphic marital lovemaking with implied nudity, mildly irreverent portrayal of a clergyman and a few crass expressions
full_review:
While the familiar proverb that supplies its title ultimately derives from the advice of one church father (St. Ambrose of Milan) quoted in the writings of another (St. Augustine of Hippo), the perky romantic comedy "When in Rome" (Touchstone) draws on the Eternal City's religious heritage only incidentally.

The graceful 17th-century church of St. Mary Magdalene -- known colloquially as La Maddalena -- does, however, provide the setting for the marriage ceremony at which its two main characters first meet and begin to fall in love.

Beth (Kristen Bell) is a work-obsessed curator at New York's Guggenheim Museum who has reluctantly taken 48 hours of personal time to serve as her sister Joan's (Alexis Dziena) maid of honor. The gent catching Beth's eye is best man Nick (Josh Duhamel), once Italian groom Umberto's (Luca Calvani) college roommate, and now a Gotham sportswriter.

Despite Beth's unhappy track record in previous relationships, the pair quickly bond during the lavish -- though, thanks to awkward Beth and accident-prone Nick, also comically disaster-plagued -- reception. But just as Beth's hopes begin to rise, she witnesses an incident that convinces her that Nick is a frivolous cad.

Wading despondently through the waters of the nearby "Fountain of Love," Beth shows her renewed cynicism by removing several of the coins that passers-by customarily toss into the basin for good luck in matters of the heart. According to the film's fanciful mythology, this ill-advised gesture immediately causes the quartet of eccentric strangers who deposited the change to become hopelessly infatuated with her.

So, once back in the Big Apple, Beth finds herself being relentlessly pursued and incongruously wooed by sausage magnate Al (Danny DeVito), street magician Lance (John Heder), aspiring artist Antonio (Will Arnett) and Gale (Dax Shepard), a would-be model enthralled by his own physique. (The fact that all four just happen to be New Yorkers like Beth is only one of many improbabilities in David Diamond and David Weissman's blithely illogical script.)

Though Nick eventually regains Beth's trust, successfully explaining away his apparent misbehavior, another obstacle arises when Beth suspects a poker chip she also retrieved from the fountain is his, meaning that he is merely under a spell and not freely -- and therefore truly -- in love.

Father Dino (Keir O'Donnell), the youthful, slightly pixilated priest who performs Joan and Umberto's nuptials, and who reappears in a couple of last-reel scenes, comes in for some gentle ribbing. But he's essentially an appealing character, and the closest the humor comes to anything remotely troublesome is the sight of him break dancing in his chasuble over the closing credits.

Otherwise, director Mark Steven Johnson's pleasantly diverting ensemble piece is mostly worry-free, with only a fleeting scene of newlywed friskiness that sees Joan in the kitchen wearing only an apron and Umberto, embracing her from behind, wearing apparently nothing at all, to bar endorsement for teens.

The film contains brief nongraphic marital lovemaking with implied nudity, mildly irreverent portrayal of a clergyman and a few crass expressions. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: When a Man Loves a Woman
synopsis: After an airline pilot (Andy Garcia) discovers that his wife (Meg Ryan) has become a secret alcoholic, they get professional help but each must learn to change destructive behavior patterns in order to save their marriage and nurture their two small daughters. Despite its sometimes soggy treatment, director Luis Mandoki's inspirational drama is credible in its depiction of the tragic consequences of alcoholism on a family and its wrenching struggle for recovery. Scenes of drunkenness with fleeting nudity and minor violence as well as intermittent rough language

title: When a Stranger Calls
synopsis: Mediocre remake of the marginal 1978 psychological thriller about a high-school student (Camilla Belle) who, while baby-sitting at a secluded lakefront home, is terrorized by the phone threats of an unseen homicidal stalker, only to discover that the calls are coming from inside the house. Director Simon West forgoes plot and plausibility in favor of easy jolts, but does manage to create an unnerving atmosphere of isolation and suspense through suggestion, while keeping the violence relatively tame. Some violence, including a hand skewered by a fire poker, scenes of menace and child peril, implied murders, brief images of dead bodies and scattered crude language
full_review:
"When a Stranger Calls" (Screen Gems) is not bad as far as B-movie psychological thrillers go. There's lots of sweaty-palm-inducing shadow play and things going bump on a dark and stormy night. But, in the end, that's all there is.

Camilla Belle stars in this mediocre remake of the marginal 1978 horror film. As with Carol Kane in the original, she plays a high school student who, while baby-sitting at a secluded lakefront home, is terrorized by the phone threats of an unseen stalker ("Have you checked the children?"), only to later discover that the calls are coming from inside the house.

Director Simon West forgoes plot and plausibility in building an atmosphere of isolation and suspense, which, though unnerving, ultimately grows tedious.

And while he accomplishes his set task for the most part through suggestion and massaging viewers' paranoia, the final 20 minutes unravel into action mode.

There is some intense tussling between the plucky heroine and homicidal maniac, but West keeps the body count low and the violence relatively tame.

If you're in the mood for some easy jolts, you could do worse, but if you're looking for sophisticated cerebral chills "When a Stranger Calls," don't answer the phone.

The film contains some violence, including a hand skewered by a fire poker, scenes of menace and child peril, implied murders, brief images of dead bodies and scattered crude language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: When a Stranger Calls
synopsis: Homicidal maniac (Tony Beckley) stalks a babysitter (Carol Kane) in this plodding, mediocre thriller directed by Fred Walton. Some intense violence and the impending threat of violence are adult fare

title: When Dinosaurs Ruled the Earth
synopsis: British production directed by Val Guest is a few cuts above the average prehistoric monster movie which, aside from some Hollywood bikinis on the cavewomen, has some authentic-looking overgrown reptiles, birds, and dinosaurs. It's an enjoyable movie for the youngsters, not too scary and colorful enough to hold short attention spans

title: When Eight Bells Toll
synopsis: British adaptation of an Alistair MacLean novel about a Bond-type government agent (Anthony Hopkins) and his gentle partner (Corin Redgrave) who are dispatched to the Western Highland lochs to find out what lies behind the disappearance of several gold-carrying ships. Directed by Etienne Perier, the plot employs masterful twists and cross currents, but though handled with restraint, it is adult fare both in story and treatment

title: When Father Was Away on Business
synopsis: Yugoslavian production set in the time of Tito's break with the Soviet Union, has a plot following a philandering husband who is denounced by his mistress as a politica1 deviant and ends up in a labor camp. This warm human comedy by director Emir Kusturica ends in the resolution of personal problems and politica1 differences during a madcap wedding feast of family forgiveness. Some coarse language and partial nudity are treated with restraint

title: When Harry Met Sally...
synopsis: Story of the unlikely ways people connect with suitable marriage partners focuses on the comic and touching travails of one couple (Billy Crystal and Meg Ryan) over a dozen years as they wander in and out of each other's lives. Director Rob Reiner's comedy about love, commitment, sex and friendship intercuts distracting testimonials from elderly couples about how they met. Though there is much graphic talk about sex and love in Yuppieland and an indiscreet spoof of female orgasm, the movie demonstrates that true love and commitment are still here to stay. Implied sexual promiscuity

title: When Night Is Falling
synopsis: A solemn young woman (Pascale Bussieres) on the verge of marriage to a Protestant theology professor (Henry Czerny) chooses instead to join a traveling circus to be with her lesbian lover (Rachel Crawford). Writer-director Patricia Rozema's romanticized lesbian love story heavy-handedly presents the young teacher's crisis in faith, marriage and career as no match for the exotic creature who awakens latent homosexual desires. Positive portrayal of homosexuality, extended sex scenes with nudity and occasional rough language. O (nr) ( 1995 )

title: When Strangers Marry
synopsis: Twisty crime tale in which a bride (Kim Hunter) gets some help from a former beau (Robert Mitchum) when she comes to suspect her secretive husband (Dean Jagger) is a murderer. Directed by William Castle, the plot is overly contrived but the characters invite sympathy and most viewers will be unsurprised by the trick ending. Menacing situations and romantic complications

title: When the Cat's Away
synopsis: Serio-comic tale of a lonely Parisienne (Garance Clavel) who gets lots of help searching for her lost cat, particularly from older women, but others prove more interested in romance than locating the missing feline until the picture's sweetly hopeful ending. Writer-director Cedric Klapisch's wistful story of a single woman whose search for a pet turns into a quest for the right man to share her life is treated earnestly, yet with humor in an odd series of unsuitable encounters before a real prospect finally turns up. Subtitles. Several restrained sex scenes, sexual references, coarse expressions and occasional rough language

title: When the Daltons Rode
synopsis: Forced off their land by a crooked developer (George Bancroft), the Dalton Brothers (Broderick Crawford, Brian Donlevy and Stewart Irwin) become feared outlaws, though a steadfast friend (Randolph Scott) tries to clear their name. Directed by George Marshall, the old story is played for all its worth until the final demise of the Dalton Gang in a Kansas City shoot-out. Stylized violence

title: When the Legends Die
synopsis: Above average Western in which a sharp rodeo hustler (Richard Widmark) takes in an 18-year-old Ute Indian (Frederic Forrest) and teaches him the tricks of the trade but the youth does not see the value in taking money from suckers and returns to the reservation, sadder but wiser. Produced and directed by Stuart Millar, the fine character study of the two principals is chiefly what is of interest here, and not its commonplace message. Implied sexual affair

title: When the West Was Young
synopsis: Western programmer from a Zane Gray story about a bushwacked surveyor (Randolph Scott) who helps a horse rancher (J. Farrell McDonald) and his ward (Sally Blaine) fight off an outlaw gang. Director Henry Hathaway embellishes the simple action tale with colorful details and an appealing romantic subplot. Frontier violence

title: When the Whales Came
synopsis: Some 70 years after an 1844 legend about a curse befalling England's Scilly Isles for slaughtering a pack of beached whales, a deaf hermit (Paul Scofield) manages to successfully warn neighboring islanders to lay off some newly beached whales. In a tedious adaptation of Michael Morpurgo's children's book, director Clive Rees lets a lovely story with the gentle hermit, two island children and an ecological theme get bogged down in boring extraneous action and predictable period caricatures. Occasional menace involving parental abuse and minimal rough language

title: When Time Ran Out
synopsis: Paul Newman, Jacqueline Bisset, Burgess Meredith, Ernest Borgnine and other unfortunates are trapped on a Pacific island when the local volcano lets go. Directed by James Goldstone, the disaster epic is so dreadful that it could put an end to the disaster epic once and for all, though it probably won't

title: When Trumpets Fade
synopsis: World War II tale of an embittered private (Ron Eldard) who becomes a hero in spite of himself when his infantry unit is mauled by the German Wehrmacht during the 1944-45 Battle of the Hurtgen Forest along the Belgian-German border. Directed by John Irvin, the television production re-creates the inhuman carnage of the battlefield with special-effects realism but its anti-war story never gets beyond the usual movie stereotypes of men in war, especially the heroic anti-hero at its center. Gory battlefield violence, coarse humor, numerous sexual expletives and occasional profanity

title: When Worlds Collide
synopsis: With Earth doomed to destruction by an onrushing star, scientists build a rocket ship to serve as a new Noah's ark hoping to continue the human race on a new planet. Director Rudolph Mate's doomsday scenario is about as convincing as the wooden romance between Barbara Rush and Richard Derr, though the special effects by producer George Pal help build some interest in the desperate situation. Apocalyptic fantasy which may trouble young children

title: Where in the World Is Osama bin Laden?
synopsis: Genial but not particularly insightful documentary in which average citizen Morgan Spurlock's ostensible search for the titular terrorist takes him to North Africa and the Middle East, where he mingles with the mostly friendly locals and ponders the origins of Islamic extremism. Spurlock, who also directed, rehashes the familiar shortcomings of American policy in the area, and makes a vague plea for a more humane world, but suggests no specific reforms. Two gory scenes, three uses of the f-word, and occasional crude and crass language
full_review:
The genial but not particularly insightful documentary "Where in the World Is Osama bin Laden?" (Weinstein) chronicles average citizen Morgan Spurlock's ostensible search for the titular terrorist. Although Spurlock, who also directed, doesn't get his man -- no spoiler that! -- he does get the chance to ponder the origins of Islamic extremism.

Learning that his wife is pregnant, Spurlock (who directed and starred in 2004's "Super Size Me") experiences the paternal urge to protect his imminent offspring from the threats of the modern world. Of all of these -- many illustrated in a cartoon sequence that includes a predator that may or may not be a clergyman -- he settles on the brand of terrorism that produced the 9/11 attacks as the most pressing.

Deciding, quixotically, that he can succeed where the U.S. military and the CIA have failed, Spurlock prepares to travel to some of the world's least welcoming hot spots in search of al-Qaida's No. 1. He receives all the necessary inoculations, then learns how to protect himself from car bombs, hand grenades and the rigors of being kidnapped.

His subsequent globetrotting, to Jordan, Egypt, Morocco, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Israel and the Palestinian territories, allows him to mingle with the mostly friendly locals, many of whom decry the current U.S. administration, but only a few of whom are openly hostile to the American people.

In a series of hotel-room reflections, Spurlock meditates on these encounters, finding them an eye-opening revelation since they dispel the myth, which he assumes his viewers share, that all Muslims are violent fanatics.

Resuming his wanderings, Spurlock broods on the familiar shortcomings of American policy in the area: support for repressive regimes, foreign aid that never reaches the people, etc. He makes a vague plea for a more humane world, but suggests no specific reforms.

The film contains two gory scenes, three uses of the f-word and occasional crude and crass language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Where Angels Fear to Tread
synopsis: Satiric comedy filters through tragedy in E.M. Forster's turn-of-the-century story of a wealthy English widow (Helen Mirren) who impulsively marries a penniless young Italian (Giovanni Guidelli) against the wishes of her in-laws. As directed by Charles Sturridge, the cultural clash between fiery Italian and straightlaced Britons affords several well-observed character studies. Brief violence

title: Where Angels Go...Trouble Follows!
synopsis: Weak sequel to "The Trouble with Angels" in which a liberal young nun (Stella Stevens) tries to update the convent boarding school under a traditionalist Mother Superior (Rosalind Russell) by leading a busload of nuns and students to a peace rally. Directed by James Neilson, the old pros in the cast (Binnie Barnes, Mary Wickes, Van Johnson, Robert Taylor and others) overcome the painfully contrived story and turn it into light, unsophisticated entertainment

title: Where Danger Lives
synopsis: Dark, muddled tale of a doctor (Robert Mitchum) on the run from the police with the wife (Faith Domergue) of the man (Claude Rains) he believes he killed. Directed by John Farrow, the tension is artificial in a situation that has little interest. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: Where Eagles Dare
synopsis: A spy-counter-spy melodrama set in the Bavarian Alps during World War II pits Richard Burton, Clint Eastwood and Mary Ure against what must be half the German army ensconced in a castle literally inaccessible except by cable car. Brian Hutton directs the Alistair MacLean script which consists of an interminable, totally implausible series of killings, escapes and pyrotechnic displays

title: Where God Left His Shoes
synopsis: Somber but touching inner-city drama in which a down-on-his-luck professional boxer (John Leguizamo) and his 9-year-old stepson (David Castro) spend Christmas Eve crisscrossing New York in search of a job that will qualify him to move his family -- including his wife (Leonor Varela) and daughter (Samantha Rose) -- out of a homeless shelter and into a housing project. A brief but inappropriate sexual discussion aside, writer-director Salvatore Stabile's deeply felt but unsentimental portrait of life on the economic margins, with its social humiliations and bureaucratic stonewalling, quietly asserts the power of human dignity, marital fidelity and family solidarity in the face of challenging circumstances. Some instances of petty crime, one use of the F-word, some crude language, brief sexual references and a physical abuse theme
full_review:
[Please note: In addition to its limited theatrical release, the film is also available through Video on Demand on many cable television systems.]

"Where God Left His Shoes" (IFC) is a deeply felt but unsentimental portrait of life on the economic margins that features an understated script and restrained but touching performances from a small cast led by John Leguizamo.

He plays down-on-his-luck professional boxer Frank Diaz. Two months after being evicted from their apartment, Frank and his family -- wife Angela (Leonor Varela), their daughter Christina (Samantha Rose) and Angela's son Justin (David Castro) -- have a shot at moving out of their cramped homeless shelter and into a housing project.

Frank's been working at a construction job "off the books," but in order to qualify must prove he has a legitimate and steady salary. With a deadline of 6 p.m. on Christmas Eve, he and 9-year-old Justin crisscross New York in an urgent quest for employment, their search made all the more poignant by the festive mood of the city around them.

Justin's own father had physically abused both him and his mother. At once savvy and vulnerable, he disparages Frank freely, but longs for his affection nonetheless. Despite being driven to some low-level crimes such as turnstile-jumping and shoplifting, Frank is fundamentally decent and does his best to mentor the boy, warning him against the corrosive effects of fear.

A brief but questionable sexual discussion between these two aside, writer-director Salvatore Stabile's study of inner-city frustration -- aggravated by social humiliation and bureaucratic stonewalling -- quietly asserts the power of human dignity, marital fidelity and family solidarity in the face of even the most challenging circumstances.

Leguizamo is perfectly assured throughout, and his role in this somber tale offers him the chance to display a subtlety and gift for emotional shading largely absent from his portrayal of an up-and-coming lawyer in the Christmas-themed comedy "Nothing Like the Holidays."

The film contains some instances of petty crime, one use of the F-word, some crude language, brief sexual references and a physical abuse theme. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.

title: Where It's At
synopsis: Las Vegas casino owner (David Janssen) teaches his disinterested son (Robert Drivas) the tricks of exploiting the tourist trade but the lad beats his father at his own game, gains control of the casino and then hands it back, realizing it is his father's whole life but will never be his. Director Garson Kanin tries to gloss over a most implausible script by resorting to some sexual diversions. O (R) ( 1969 )

title: Where Love Has Gone
synopsis: Trashy sudser from Harold Robbins' novel about an artist (Susan Hayward) who divorces her war-hero husband (Michael Connors) after he's driven to drink by her domineering mom (Bette Davis), then takes a series of lovers until their 15-year-old daughter (Joey Heatherton) murders one of them. Directed by Edward Dmytryk, the soapy proceedings are dressed up in a glossy production whose shallow characters waste the talents of the cast. Stylized violence including a suicide and much sexual innuendo

title: Where the Boys Are '84
synopsis: Four women college students (Lisa Hartman, Lorna Luft, Wendy Schaal and Lynn-Holly Johnson) go to Fort Lauderdale for the spring break and carry on like amateur hookers, but viewers are supposed to believe its very wholesome and therapeutic. Director Hy Averback's updating of a silly 1960 movie contains nudity, sexually oriented humor and an appalling moral outlook. O (R) ( 1984 )

title: Where the Buffalo Roam
synopsis: Bill Murray portrays famed underground journalist Hunter S. Thompson, who seems to have derived much of his inspiration from drugs and alcohol. Director Art Linson tries to blend serious social concern with outrageous comedy but is only intermittently successful. Rough language and use of drugs

title: Where the Heart Is
synopsis: Because of some flippant attitudes towards sex and pregnancy, a few sexual encounters, brief subplot involving pedophilia, fleeting rough language and some profanity,

title: Where the Heart Is
synopsis: Pointless, humorless farce about a wealthy demolitions expert (Dabney Coleman) who attempts to teach his three grown but spoiled offspring a lesson in self-sufficiency by leaving them stranded in an abandoned Brooklyn tenement. Director John Boorman shows little sensitivity to family responsibilities and is offensively crass in dealing with minority issues and the reality of homelessness. Some nudity in the context of artwork, rough language and sexual innuendoes

title: Where the Lilies Bloom
synopsis: Four sturdy Appalachian children keep the death of their widowed father a secret so the state won't take them away to an orphan's home and provide for themselves out of the profits of "wildcrafting" (collecting and preparing certain herbs and wild flowers prized for their medicinal qualities). The Robert B. Radnitz production directed by William A. Graham tells its story of youngsters learning to care for themselves in the adult world with warm humor and genuine sensitivity for the conditions of life for the rural poor. A rare and satisfying entertainment for the entire family

title: Where The Money Is
