synopsis: Gene Wilder directs and also stars as a philandering advertising manager who pursues a beautiful model (Kelly Le Brock) while keeping his wife (Judith Ivy) in the dark. It is an ill-conceived and clumsily-executed attempt to recast a French farce about adultery ("Pardon Mon Affaire") in an American mold. Nudity and a benign attitude toward illicit sex. O (PG-13) ( 1984 )

title: Woman Next Door, The
synopsis: Weak French romantic melodrama about a happily married couple who move next door to another happily married couple but, as it happens, the wife who has just moved in (Fanny Ardant) and the husband next door (Gerald Depardieu) had had a stormy love affair seven years before and soon the two are off and running again. Director Francois Truffaut handles this material with his usual adroitness, but to little purpose in a story that proves banal and unmoving, with some questionable amorous sequences

title: Woman Obsessed
synopsis: Turgid sudser from the Canadian northwest where a farmer's widow (Susan Hayward) marries her brawny, inarticulate hired man (Stephen Boyd) but comes to regret it. Directed by Henry Hathaway, the picturesque locales of the setting are a lot easier to watch than the cliched story of a woman's soured romance. Domestic misunderstandings and natural catastrophes

title: Woman of Dolwyn
synopsis: ( see: "The Last Days of Dolwyn" )

title: Woman of Straw
synopsis: Intriguing British mystery in which the cunning nephew (Sean Connery) of an aged, irascible millionaire (Ralph Richardson) convinces a beguiling nurse (Gina Lollobrigida) to marry the old man in order to get a share of his wealth. Director Basil Dearden sets up the mercenary situation convincingly, then bogs down in some improbable plot twists for a disappointing ending, though Richardson's rougish performance is worth catching. Some grisly situations, amoral characters and sexual innuendo

title: Woman of the Ganges
synopsis: French writer Marguerite Duras' story of a man at a resort during its winter off-season where he meets, or perhaps imagines that he meets, the woman of the title whom he had loved in India long ago. Also directed by Duras, the highly verbal movie takes place not on the screen, but in the mind of the beholder willing to plumb its blend of time, memory and illusion

title: Woman of the Town, The
synopsis: Intelligent Western opens in 1919 with Bat Masterson (Albert Dekker) working as a reporter for a New York paper, then flashes back 50 years to Dodge City where he takes the job of marshal, comes to admire a high-minded dance-hall belle (Claire Trevor) and stops her dangerous ex-suitor (Barry Sullivan), with tragic results. Directed by George Archainbaud, the melodrama follows the sterling lawman as he learns the futility of violence from the "painted angel" of the title, despite shootouts along the way. Frontier violence and romantic complications

title: Woman of the Year
synopsis: Robust romantic comedy in which a good-natured sportswriter (Spencer Tracy) romances a high-powered political commentator (Katharine Hepburn), then has his hands full trying to get her to fit into his schedule after they wed. Director George Stevens paces the opposites-attract premise with some hilarious funny business but what succeeds best are the performances of the two principals who prove entirely likeable in this wry battle-of-the-sexes comedy. Veiled sexual references and innuendo

title: Woman on Top
synopsis: Escapist comedy about a sizzling chef (Penelope Cruz), who leaves her native Brazil and stifling macho husband (Murilo Ben�cio) for San Francisco, where she lands a television cooking show that is an instant hit. Whimsical visual effects and exotic locations notwithstanding, director Fina Torres' dull film capitalizes on the aesthetic pleasures but lags behind in engaging narrative content. Includes mysticism, a few sexual encounters with nudity, minor homosexual innuendo and brief crass language with fleeting profanity. The U.S. Catholic Conference

title: Woman Rebels, A
synopsis: Creaky melodrama set in Victorian England where a young lady (Katharine Hepburn) falls for a scoundrel (Van Heflin), raises her illegitimate child as her niece while working for a woman's magazine, then uses it as a vehicle to crusade for women's rights. Directed by Mark Sandrich, the contrived storyline may not be very convincing today but the picture still holds interest as an early attempt to deal sympathetically with the theme of women's equality. Veiled sexual references

title: Woman's Decision, A
synopsis: Sensitive, extremely well-acted Polish triangle story whose heroine (Maya Komorowska) is married to a wonderful husband (Piotr Franczewski), has an affectionate son and a modern apartment in Warsaw but finds herself wanting to give it all up for the company of a footloose man (Marek Piwowski). Directed by Krzystof Zanussi, it is a perceptive study of the interior struggle each of the characters undergoes during the course of the narrative

title: Woman's Secret, A
synopsis: Transparent sudser in which a radio singer (Gloria Graham) is shot and her dour manager (Maureen O'Hara) arrested for the deed while their mutual friend, a debonair songwriter (Melvyn Douglas), seeks the truth along with a cop (Jay C. Flippen) whose wife (Mary Philips) knows a romantic triangle when she sees one. Despite the capable cast, director Nicholas Ray makes matters seem even duller than they actually are in numerous flashbacks slowly explaining the obvious. Brief violence and romantic complications

title: Woman's Tale, A
synopsis: Somber drama about an elderly, cancer-ridden woman (Sheila Florance) who, with her devoted young nurse (Gosia Dobrowolska) at her side, grittily determines to extract all the enjoyment she can from her final days. Though director Paul Cox elicits moving performances from both women, the life-affirming theme is delivered with belabored heavy-handedness. Uncritical attitude toward the nurse's extramarital affair and brief nudity

title: Woman's Vengeance, A
synopsis: When a rich Englishwoman is poisoned, her unfaithful husband (Charles Boyer) is convicted and sentenced to death, though a physician (Cedric Hardwicke) suspects the wife's best friend (Jessica Tandy) is guilty. Directed by Zoltan Korda, the murky plot gains interest from solid performances by the cast and moody period photography. Romantic complications

title: Woman, Thou Art Loosed
synopsis: Soul-inspiring drama about a young woman (Kimberly Elise) who, with the help of a compassionate evangelical minister (T.D. Jakes), struggles to come to terms with her troubled past and find redemption, while awaiting execution for murder. Based on the best-selling novel by Jakes, the hope-filled film deals with difficult subjects -- including sexual abuse, addiction and murder -- though in a way which challenges viewers of faith to take seriously the Christian imperatives of love and reconciliation. Several instances of violence, including the implied rape of a young girl, a sexual encounter with blurred nudity, recurring drug content and some crude language
full_review:
"Woman Thou Art Loosed" (Magnolia Pictures) is a potent and soul-inspiring drama about the healing power of forgiveness.

Based on the best-selling novel and stage play of the same name by evangelical author and pastor T.D. Jakes, the quality film deals with difficult subjects -- including sexual molestation and murder -- though in a way which challenges viewers of faith to take seriously the Christian imperatives of love and reconciliation.

Kimberly Elise stars as Michelle Jordan, a young woman raped as a child by her mom's live-in boyfriend Reggie (Clifton Powell). Loretta Devine plays Cassie, Michelle's mother whose fear of "losing her man" and being alone blinds her to the evils perpetrated on her daughter.

The film is bookended by a scene of a revival meeting with Jakes (playing himself) preaching to a packed house. Michelle enters -- distraught -- and approaches the altar. In a sudden fit of rage, she pulls a gun from her handbag and fires off several rounds, killing someone in the crowd. The victim's identity is initially withheld, though it becomes less of a mystery as the story unfolds.

Jakes visits Michelle on death row as she awaits execution. They talk and he coaxes Michelle to open up to him about the painful events which set her downward spiral in motion.

The film see-saws between past and present, as Michelle recounts her tragic tale of childhood abuse and neglect, which she says robbed her of not only her innocence but her hope. In short order, the film proceeds to show how these early violations plunged Michelle headlong into a self-destructive abyss of drug addiction, prostitution and prison, before arriving back where the movie began.

Elise delivers an emotionally penetrating performance, but, sadly, one which will probably be overlooked for Oscar consideration because of the film's limited release. Jakes, who also financed the project, has a presence to match his sizable frame, and exudes a sincerity which is both charismatic and consoling, cultivated no doubt through years of real-life pastoral experience.

Echoing the moral conscience of "Dead Man Walking" and informed by the Christian understanding of each individual's sacred value, the picture attempts to neither justify the characters' wrongdoings, nor minimize their humanity by painting them as irredeemable villains.

Instead, it portrays them as flawed, but still worthy of our compassion and understanding, or at the very least -- as in Reggie's case -- forgiveness. To help in this effort, the film contains soul-searching interludes where each character gets to address the audience directly. Moreover, the film clearly advocates accountability, emphasizing that a vital step on the road to recovery and repentance involves taking responsibility for one's actions.

Lifting its title from the verse in the Gospel of Luke where Christ cures a crippled woman, the grace-filled film speaks to the brokenness in each of us, and manages to maintain a tenor that is both unflinchingly raw and edifyingly hopeful, avoiding, for the most part, any slushy sentimentality.

As directed by Michael Schultz, "Woman Thou Art Loosed" sees sin for what it is: ugly, destructive and spiritually suffocating. But it does not offer pie-in-the-sky piety as an easy antidote to the human condition. Instead the movie agrees with C.S. Lewis that "hell is locked from the inside."

Ultimately, the movie suggests that the key to freeing ourselves from our self-imposed imprisonment is to let go of our anger and accept the gift of God's "harsh and dangerous love," to borrow a phrase from Dorothy Day, which demands that we extend forgiveness to even those least deserving of it.

Due to several instances of violence, including the implied rape of a young girl, a sexual encounter with blurred nudity, recurring drug content and some crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Woman Times Seven
synopsis: Italian potpourri of comedy, farce and pathos is directed by Vittorio De Sica with Shirley MacLaine as the heroine of each episode. It is needlessly marred by one tasteless and provocative sequence. O (br) ( 1967 )

title: Woman Under the Influence, A
synopsis: The woman of the title (Gena Rowlands) is a mother of three small children in the middle of a nervous breakdown while her husband (Peter Falk), a rough, callous but loving man, is totally unable to cope with the situation. Directed by John Cassavetes in his characteristic improvisational style, the result is full of the small realities and individual details that make up ordinary human experience but it is short on the sort of heightened drama one expects from a conventional movie narrative

title: Women
synopsis: Sensitive Hungarian character study of an unlikely and slowly developing friendship between the wife of a successful engineer (Marina Vlady) and a factory worker (Lili Monori) whose husband is an alcoholic. The melodramatic plot and its soap opera problems simply provide the background against which director Marta Meszaros explores the human needs that draw these two women together despite their differences in character, education and social position. Mature themes

title: Women in Cages
synopsis: Philippine exploitation movie directed by Gerry De Leon about a group of women prisoners who use their sadistic lesbian matron as a hostage to escape into the jungle where they fall prey to bounty hunters and flesh-peddlers. Heavy-duty debasement. O (R) ( 1971 )

title: Women in Cellblock 7
synopsis: Inanely plotted, badly acted and atrociously dubbed Italian exploitation movie about a woman who goes to prison to get evidence to save her father. Abundant nudity. O (R) ( 1977 )

title: Women in Love
synopsis: British adaptation of the D.H. Lawrence novel about the gradual involvement of two couples, one (Alan Bates and Glenda Jackson) having a rather healthy though incomplete relationship while the other (Oliver Reed and Jennie Linden) tragically ends in suicide. Directed by Ken Russell, the acting is first-rate, the photography almost too beautiful and the treatment of the convoluted relationships remains on the superficial level of the physical. Lengthy naked wrestling match between the men is more symbolic than erotic. O (R) ( 1970 )

title: Women in Revolt
synopsis: Three women from different social levels (female impersonators Candy Darling, Holly Woodlawn and Jackie Curtis) get caught up in the Women's Liberation Movement. Typical of the poor film quality and sexual explicitness of Andy Warhol's efforts in the past, it makes men, women and sex look ridiculous, ugly and perverted. O (nr) ( 1972 )

title: Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown
synopsis: After an actress (Carmen Maura) is deserted by her live-in lover (Fernando Guillen), she attempts to face down the coward before he leaves town with another woman. Written and directed by Pedro Almodovar, this Spanish farce explores without exploitation the comic vicissitudes of male-female relationships. Subtitles. Some rough language and a benign attitude toward sex and pregnancy outside of marriage

title: Women's Prison
synopsis: Tawdry programmer directed by Lewis Seiler in which the warden (Ida Lupino) of the women's division in a prison also housing male inmates is a sadist who is finally put in a straightjacket by the prison doctor (Howard Duff) after her brutality causes a riot. Much stylized violence and sexual innuendo

title: Women, The
synopsis: Lavish screen version of Clare Boothe's satiric play in which a New York socialite (Norma Shearer) whose husband has fallen for a calculating gold digger (Joan Crawford) goes to Reno for a divorce, then returns home to pick up the pieces. Directed by George Cukor, the all-female cast (Rosalind Russell, Paulette Goddard, Mary Boland and many others) provides a comic compendium of feminine stereotypes and caustic comments on the battle of the sexes, much of which is unflattering to women but it is the unseen males who get the worst of it. Comic treatment of sex and marriage

title: Wonder Boys
synopsis: Fitfully amusing comedy about a grouchy, pot-smoking English professor (Michael Douglas) who, daunted by the success of his first novel, is laboring to finish his second and in the process unwittingly takes an odd but gifted writing student (Tobey Maguire) under his shaky wing. Skillful performances and the picturesque campus setting enhance director Curtis Hanson's character-driven movie but they aren't enough to sustain interest in the sluggish and insubstantial narrative. Recurring recreational drug abuse, implied homosexual encounter, an extra-marital affair and some rough language

title: Wonderful Country, The
synopsis: Convoluted Western directed by Robert Parrish centers on an American (Robert Mitchum) who's made a career as a gunslinger in 1880's Mexico, but the love of a good woman (Julie London) and the assassination of his boss (Pedro Armendariz) lead him back to the States to join the Texas Rangers. Stylized violence and sexual references

title: Wonderful Crook, The
synopsis: Off-beat French comedy about a good-natured, but inept young man (Gerald Depardieu) who, in order to pay the employee's wages of his family's furniture business, undertakes a series of holdups and falls in love with one of his victims (Marlene Jobert). Neither his wife (Dominique Labourier) nor his employees suspect his double life until the police arrive to arrest him. Directed by Claude Goretta, the movie details in a warmly humorous manner the complications that can arise from a simplistic notion of "doing good." Brief nudity and vulgar language

title: Wonderful, Horrible Life of Leni Riefenstahl, The
synopsis: Absorbing account of how German movie director Riefenstahl came to make "The Triumph of the Will" (1934), the powerful Nazi propaganda film which made her unemployable after World War II, though she never joined the Nazi Party nor was ever accused of being anti-Semitic. Written and directed by Ray Mueller, the subtitled German production also interviews the 90-year-old Riefenstahl about her subsequent career as a photographer, yet keeps returning to the question of how an artist, no matter how disinterested in politics, could have been so blind to the evils of a repressive regime. The subject of a movie-maker's social responsibility has importance for more than film students

title: Wonderful World of the Brothers Grimm, The
synopsis: Lavish but plodding Cinerama production interweaving the story of the 19th-century German brothers (Laurence Harvey and Karl Boehm) with dramatizations of three of the many folk tales they popularized despite personal adversities. Co-directed by George Pal and Henry Levin, the Rhineland locales and period settings are better realized than either the biographical material or the special effects used in the fairy tales. Intermittently diverting for youngsters, though a long sit for their elders

title: Wonderland
synopsis: Fact-based story of porn-movie king John Holmes' involvement in a grisly quadruple homicide which took place in the Laurel Canyon neighborhood of Los Angeles in 1981. Full of graphically disturbing violence, director James Cox sets out to explore a morally bleak landscape so devoid of redeemable features that it is nearly impossible for viewers to invest any emotional interest, let alone sympathy, in the film's mostly repellent characters. Excessive graphic violence, sexual encounters with partial nudity, recurring drug abuse, much rough and crude language, as well as profanity
full_review:
"Wonderland" (Lions Gate) tells the fact-based story of porn-star John Holmes' involvement in a grisly quadruple homicide, which took place in the Laurel Canyon neighborhood of Los Angeles in 1981. Full of graphically disturbing violence, director James Cox sets out to explore a morally barren landscape so devoid of redeemable features that it is nearly impossible for viewers to invest any emotional interest, let alone sympathy, in the film's mostly repellent characters.

Told in "Roshomon" fashion, the visually self-conscious film weaves together multiple points of view of the events leading up to the brutal slayings. In each, Holmes (played by Val Kilmer), whose implication in the crime elevated it from run-of-the-mill tragedy to a three-ring tabloid circus, remains the central figure.

When the action takes up, Holmes' smutty star has already fallen. Still clinging to his slimy sex-industry laurels, Holmes, a washed-up junkie desperate for cash and cocaine, is forced to slither from one party to the next in order to score his next hit. Riding shotgun on his spiraling-out-of-control tour of dopeville's seedy motels and drug dens is Dawn Schiller (Kate Bosworth), Holmes' underage, strung-out girlfriend, who, along with his estranged ex-wife (Lisa Kudrow), form the narrative's dysfunctional love triangle.

Amid the bottom feeders, Holmes befriends Ron Launius (Josh Lucas), a loose-cannon dealer, and his "business partner," David Lind (Dylan McDermott), a tattooed biker and stone-cold killer. While partying at Ron's haunt, high -- literally and figuratively -- above the eponymous Wonderland Avenue, Holmes ill-advisedly suggests that they rob the sybaritic pleasure palace of his friend, Eddie Nash (Eric Bogosian), a notorious L.A. club owner with a fearsome reputation for viciousness.

With Holmes working from the inside, the robbery goes smoothly, netting the Wonderland gang $250,000 in drugs and loot. Shortly afterward, Nash retaliates, ordering the gruesome Wonderland massacre in which Ron, an accomplice and two of the crews' girlfriends are bludgeoned to death with lead pipes; another victim (Christina Applegate) survives the bloodbath, but suffers brain damage. Lind, fearing for his life, turns himself in to the authorities and spills the beans about the robbery. He also rats out Holmes, who may have played both sides against the middle in order to save his own skin.

Much of Kilmer's performance, which roller-coasters between cocaine-rush highs and lows, seems to be a retread from his last foray into self-destructive hedonism as rock star Jim Morrison in Oliver Stone's 1991 "The Doors." Like Stone's pretentious opus, "Wonderland" fails to achieve the sense of cultural importance it desperately seeks.

Why should anyone really care about Holmes, who comes across as nothing more than a pathetic, self-indulgent loser? As a character, he lacks any traits worthy of empathy or warranting interest. Perhaps the screens of text which bookend the film offer the clearest, self-incriminating argument against the lifestyle depicted. The first boasts that Holmes made more than 1,000 pornographic movies and slept with more than 14,000 women. The film closes with a coda stating that in 1988, at age 44, John Holmes died of AIDS.

While steering clear of adulation, the film does attempt to paint Holmes as a tragic figure worthy of compassion if not sympathy -- which is more than is allowed the film's only "religious" character. In a cameo role, Carrie Fisher plays a Christian woman who reaches out to Dawn in an attempt to rescue her from her dead-end existence. Dawn repays the woman's kindness by snorting cocaine and having sex with Holmes in her bathroom amid devotional pictures of the Blessed Virgin. Upon discovering them, the woman throws them out of her house ranting stereotypical holy-roller chastisements worthy of Dana Carvey's Church Lady.

What is most disturbing about the film is not that it chooses to explore such morally bleak territory, but that in doing so it fails to shed any redemptive light on the darkness. Cox seems content to limit his depressing palette to just two colors -- black and pitch black. In opting for a canvas so bereft of humanity -- let alone hope -- the story is stripped of its cautionary merits. This of course should be of little concern to the filmmaker, who seems more intent on exploiting the sleazy tabloid angles of sex and murder than on actually offering any insights into the tragic events or lives depicted.

Anything but wonderful, "Wonderland" isn't worth the visit.

Due to excessive graphic violence, sexual encounters with partial nudity, recurring drug abuse, and much rough and crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Wonder Man
synopsis: Sappy Danny Kaye vehicle in which he doubles as a murdered nightclub comic whose spirit inhabits the body of his scholarly twin brother, thereby confounding police, gangsters and the brothers' girlfriends (Virginia Mayo and Vera-Ellen). Directed by Bruce Humberstone, there are a couple of good song-and-dance numbers and some funny routines but the phantom-brother gimmick wears thin. Minimal stylized violence

title: Wonders of Aladdin, The
synopsis: Embarrassingly inept comic adventure with Donald O'Connor as an over-aged Aladdin and Vittorio de Sica as a cut-rate genie all mixed up in the old story of a magic lamp. Directed by Mario Bava and Henry Levin, this dubbed Italian misfire suffers from an impoverished script and threadbare fantasy effects. Much sexual innuendo and comic violence, including a sadistic torture scene

title: Won Ton Ton, the Dog Who Saved Hollywood
synopsis: Director Michael Winner's wretchedly thrown-together slapstick comedy about a wonder dog of the old silent movie era is made all the more tasteless by seeing performers one once admired in a series of painfully inane cameos. It is definitely not for young viewers. O (PG) ( 1976 )

title: Woo
synopsis: Dopey comedy crudely chronicles a madcap blind date between a cautious law student (Tommy Davidson) and an impetuous beauty (Jada Pinkett Smith) who attracts trouble wherever they go. Director Daisy Von Scherler Mayer's lame battle-of-the-sexes comedy is a tiresome collection of witless pranks and dumb jokes. Brief violence, much sexist humor, racial slurs, sexual innuendo, fleeting nudity, occasional profanity and frequent rough language

title: Wooden Man's Bride, The
synopsis: In 1920's China, a woman (Wang Lan) whose groom is accidentally killed on their wedding day is forced by her mother-in-law (Wang Yumei) to live as a married woman with a wooden statue of her dead spouse until the kindly servant (Chang Shih) she comes to love resorts to desperate means to free her. Director Huang Jianxin's visually haunting melodrama explores a harsh feudal society in which the honor-bound but inwardly seething characters eventually rebel against the old lady in order to marry. Subtitles. Some gory violence, fleeting nudity and an instance of rough language

title: Wooden Soldiers
synopsis: ( see: "March of the Wooden Soldiers" )

title: Woodstock
synopsis: Documentary about the landmark musical event that brought together a half million young people to hear a parade of such talented performers as Richie Havens, Joan Baez, Country Joe and the Fish, The Who, Sha-na-na, Arlo Guthrie, Crosby Stills and Nash, Joe Cocker and so on. Directed by Michael Wadleigh, it is dazzling in image and sound but as a record of this particular music festival, it concentrates on the positive themes of love and peace, giving scant attention to the drugs and commercialism that for many marred the event. Brief nudity and some rough language and lyrics

title: Wood, The
synopsis: Drawn-out but warm-hearted tale of three African-American buddies, one of whom (Taye Diggs) vacillates about taking his vows hours before his wedding while another (Omar Epps) recalls in flashback their awkward teenage fumblings with the opposite sex. Essentially a coming-of-age tale, director Rick Famuyiwa presents overly familiar macho posturings to limited comic effect before the three are prepared to accept marital commitment. Sexual situations, brief violence, fleeting rear nudity, minimal profanity and much rough language

title: Working Girl
synopsis: A 30-year-old secretary (Melanie Griffith) with the training and dreams to make it big as a Wall Street stockbroker is held back by sexist male boses and a treacherous female boss (Sigourney Weaver) but when she transforms herself into a polished professional, her appealing vulnerability attracts the right boss (Philip Bosco) and suitor (Harrison Ford). Directed by Mike Nichols, the upbeat story balances its women-in-the-workplace concerns with a delightful Cinderella story that will entertain and enlighten even diehard anti-feminists. Much rough language laced with sexual innuendo and some frontal nudity within brief graphic sexual situations

title: Work Is a Four Letter Word
synopsis: British comedy about a man (David Warner) who grows mushrooms that have a narcotic effect. Directed by Peter Hall, its premise is better than the results

title: World According to Garp, The
synopsis: Uneven screen version of John Irving's novel about a fragile writer (Robin Williams) overwhelmed by catastrophes, bizarre events and his indomitable mother (Glenn Close). Under George Roy Hill's direction, Williams by going all out to turn the character into a lovable schnook makes his problems seem even crueler and more arbitrary than they might have been. Some nudity and graphic sexual references

title: World Apart, A
synopsis: Fact-based drama set in 1963 South Africa concerns an anti-apartheid white journalist (Barbara Hershey) and her inability to give her three young daughters the same love and devotion she channels into the political arena. British director Chris Menges skirts over the political and social issues to focus on the mother-daughter conflict. Some emotional and physical political violence, an off-camera suicide attempt and the suffering caused one of the daughters because of her parents' political activities

title: World for Ransom
synopsis: Low-budget espionage caper directed by Robert Aldrich is set in Singapore where an American undercover agent (Dan Duryea) rescues a nuclear physicist (Arthur Shields) from a kidnap gang (led by Gene Lockhart). Stylized violence, menacing situations and sexual innuendo

title: World in His Arms, The
synopsis: Romantic adventure with a Yankee sea captain (Gregory Peck) who's grown so rich poaching seals in Russian-owned Alaska that he decides to buy it from the Czar, but along the way falls for a Russian countess (Ann Blyth), battles a Portuguese freebooter (Anthony Quinn) and is captured by a Russian gunboat. Director Raoul Walsh submerges the 19th-century romance in high-seas derring-do and imperial despotism with the action sputtering to a bogus ending. Stylized violence and romantic complications

title: World Is Not Enough, The
synopsis: Typical breathless Bond fare in which 007 (Pierce Brosnan), sent to protect a murder target (Sophie Marceau), finds she has joined forces with a sinister psychopath (Robert Carlyle) in a plot to seize control of the world's oil supply. As directed by Michael Apted, the fast and furious action eventually wears itself out in an overlong, overly elaborate by-the-numbers plot. Much stylized violence and a few discreet bedroom scenes

title: World of Buckminster Fuller, The
synopsis: Educational documentary directed by Robert Snyder provides a coherent outline of Fuller's basic concepts as well as a personal portrait of a humanist who put his scientific knowlege to the task of considering the present under the aspects of the future rather than from the conventional wisdom of the past

title: World of Hans Christian Andersen, The
synopsis: Feature-length cartoon about the childhood of young Hans and where he got some of the ideas for his highly imaginative fairy tales. The animation is colorful and creative, though stylistically comparable to Saturday morning TV shows. It provides a wonderful world of fantasy to absorb the small fry at a matinee

title: World of Henry Orient, The
synopsis: Peter Sellers stars in a wacky comedy about a fair-to-middling concert pianist whose pursuit of extra-curricular love (Paula Prentiss) is foiled by the unwitting but persistent efforts of two teenage girls who just may be his only fans in all the world. Directed by George Roy Hill, the acting is very good, the comedy nicely paced and the romantic element only in the background

title: World of Susie Wong, The
synopsis: Exotic but unappetizing tale of the rough life and times of a Hong Kong lady of the night, toned down from Paul Osborn's play in the Hollywood version starring Nancy Kwan as Susie and William Holden as her American love interest. Directed by Richard Quine, its plush production of a sentimental romance may have some interest for hardy adults, but not for youngsters or those with reservations about a drama which unfolds, for the most part, in a seamy brothel. O (br) ( 1961 )

title: World's Greatest Athlete, The
synopsis: Frustrated coach (John Amos) vacationing in Africa discovers a Tarzan-like jungle youth (Jan-Michael Vincent) and brings him to his sunny California campus where he starts making a shambles of the record books. Directed by Robert Scheerer, it is the Disney studio's special-effects men who save the day for sports as well as for parents who with their children will have to take the yawns along with the laughs in this matinee special

title: World's Greatest Lover, The
synopsis: Failed comedy written and directed by Gene Wilder who also stars as a hapless oaf who goes to Hollywood in the 1920s hoping to win a studio-sponsored world's greatest lover contest. The direction is inept, the writing shows no vestige of wit or originality and Wilder's performance is loud, vulgar and supremely unfunny. Boring but its low level of humor is not for young viewers

title: World Trade Center
synopsis: Two police officers (Nicolas Cage and Michael Pena) wait to be found after being crushed in the rubble of the World Trade Center terror attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, while their frantic wives (Maggie Gyllenhaal and Maria Bello) wonder if they've survived, and intrepid good Samaritans (Michael Shannon and Stephen Dorff among them) search the rubble for signs of life. Some may be disappointed that director Oliver Stone eschews an epic approach by focusing on this relatively small, true-life story which nonetheless paints an inspiring picture of bravery, fortitude and sacrifice in the face of enormous adversity. Some intense scenes of peril and suffering, a few profane and crude words uttered under extreme circumstances, injured victims, some bleeding and a brief but disturbing image of the towers with a long shot of a falling body may preclude viewing by younger adolescents
full_review:
On Sept. 11, 2001, it seemed inconceivable -- particularly to those living in New York City -- that Hollywood would dare make a film out of such tragedy, or at least not for many years to come. But now, a mere five years later, comes the second such major release of the year.

It was with relief that we noted how well "United 93" (about the hijacked flight brought down by brave passengers over Pennsylvania) avoided exploitation with its dry, documentary-style approach, and a no-name cast.

"World Trade Center" (Paramount) does not feel exploitative either, but with its ad campaign showing the twin towers looming large over its two protagonists, and director Oliver Stone's reputation for epic stories, some may be disappointed by the narrow focus here.

For at heart, this is a true-life rescue narrative, resembling, in its essentials, many we've seen before. The events depicted might just as easily be happening in, say, a Pennsylvania coal mine.

The film starts with Sgt. John McLoughlin (Nicolas Cage) of New York's Port Authority Police Department rousing himself at 3:30 a.m. for his commute to the city. We also see his colleague, Officer Will Jimeno (Michael Pena) and others coming to the city on what is presumed just another ordinary day.

When the World Trade Center is attacked, they are among the numberless police and fire personnel that rushed to the scene. John, Will and a few other brave police volunteers prepare to enter the building for rescue work, but seemingly within minutes, they are trapped under the rubble beneath the concourse of two of the towers, unable to see the other, but at least able to communicate. A third colleague, Dominick Pezzulo (Jay Hernandez), only survives a short while, at one point contemplating suicide, gun in hand, but shoots in the air instead.

The film, from this point, shuttles back and forth between close-ups of the men's faces, in their darkened prison, trying to stay awake, as they know to succumb to sleep would be fatal, while we see their suburban wives, Allison (Maggie Gyllenhaal) and Donna (Maria Bello), frantic with worry, and later, intrepid good Samaritans -- most especially ex-Marine Dave Karnes (Michael Shannon), who searches for survivors with religious fervor, and a handful of Emergency Service Unit officers and paramedics (Stephen Dorff, Stoney Westmoreland and Frank Whaley) -- join the rescue effort. Toward the end, Karnes expresses a desire for revenge, one of the only statements in the film that could be construed as political.

Cage gives a totally committed performance and manages to subjugate his movie-star persona, while Pena is equally impressive. Gyllenhaal and Bello are a tad less successful. On the whole, though, everyone does a conscientious job playing "ordinary," even at the expense of some drama.

There are some spiritual elements of note. In his delirium, Will sees several shadowy visions of Jesus throughout the ordeal, and at one point they poignantly recite the Lord's Prayer.

To his credit, Stone avoids sensationalism. There's really just one shot of the building after it's been hit, with a big gaping hole in its side. Visually, the film is, by its very nature, more than a little static.

Nonetheless, Stone and screenwriter Andrea Berloff have given us an inspiring picture of bravery, fortitude and sacrifice in the face of enormous adversity, and whatever the film's shortcomings, that's undeniably a story worth the telling.

This film contains some intense scenes of peril and suffering, a few profane and crude words uttered under extreme circumstances, injured victims, some bleeding and a brief but disturbing image of the towers with a long shot of a falling body, which may preclude viewing by younger adolescents. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: World Without End
synopsis: Fanciful sci-fi adventure as the first manned space flight speeds out of control through time, returning to Earth in the year 2508 A.D. to find the survivors of a nuclear holocaust living underground, while human mutants rule the planet's radioactive surface. Writer-director Edward Bernds focuses on the efforts of the spaceship's crew (notably Hugh Marlowe and Rod Taylor) to get the survivors to quit their unhealthy subterranean city and retake the now radiation-free surface from the mutants. Fantasy violence

title: World Without Sun
synopsis: Documentary made by oceanaut Jacques-Yves Cousteau details the human conquest of underwater space. It is an opportunity to see and experience an incredibly beautiful part of creation, till now hidden from human eyes

title: Worth Winning
synopsis: Adolescent male fantasy about a shallow Philadelphia TV weatherman (Mark Harmon) who bets a friend (Mark Blum) that he can propose marriage to three women (chosen by the friend) in three months and be accepted by each. The heel gets his comeuppance, but director Will Mackenzie treats him more sympathetically than the three female guinea pigs (Maria Holvoe, Madeleine Stowe and Lesley Ann Warren) in a sexist exercise demeaning to women. Sexual promiscuity including adultery and some profanity laced with sexual vulgarities. O (PG-13) ( 1989 )

title: Woyzeck
synopsis: Stark German adaptation of Georg Buchner's 19-century play about a much-abused soldier (Klaus Kinski) in a small garrison town who goes mad and brutally murders the woman (Eva Mattes) he has been too poor to marry. Directed by Werner Herzog, the story of a man's alienation and descent into irrationality is powerfully acted and its dark mood unrelieved

title: Wraith, The
synopsis: A brutally murdered teenager (Charlie Sheen) returns as an avenging angel to race to their deaths the depraved auto gang that had killed him. A deadly supernatural demolition derby filmed on the picturesque highways of Arizona sells violence, vengeance and a few sexual inferences with foul language to a youth market already overburdened with negative role models

title: Wrath of God, The
synopsis: Hard-drinking, gun-toting renegade priest (Robert Mitchum) joins forces with two other fugitive misfits to erase a fanatical madman-rancher in Central America during the revolutionary 1920s. Directed by Ralph Nelson, the result is downright painful in some sections, embarrassing and simply ludicrous in others. Some heavy violence

title: Wrecking Crew, The
synopsis: The only funny aspect of this limp spy spoof is watching Dean Martin lumber through it as super-agent Matt Helm entrusted to guard a gold shipment from Denmark to London, giving rise to jokes about Danish pastries (one of whom is Elke Sommer). Directed by Phil Karlson, the level of crude sexual humor is beneath adolescent interest. O (PG) ( 1968 )

title: Wreck of the Mary Deare, The
synopsis: What starts as a dandy mystery goes sour after a salvager (Charlton Heston) boards a floundering, storm-tossed freighter and discovers it abandoned by all but the captain (Gary Cooper) who insists he is still in command of the vessel. From there on, matters pale considerably as director Michael Anderson plods through the captain's trial by a maritime court, with entirely predictable results. Some stylized violence

title: The Wrestler
synopsis: Seamy but powerful character portrait of an aging professional wrestler (a superb Mickey Rourke) whose marginal career is threatened by a heart attack, as he initiates a tentative romance with a stripper (Marisa Tomei) and makes fumbling efforts to reconnect with his estranged daughter (Evan Rachel Wood). Director Darren Aronofsky's study of loneliness, set in a landscape of trailer parks and strip malls, is unsparing in its portrayal of the titular sport, the sadistic impulses of its fans, and the demeaning sexuality of the strip club where the protagonist unwinds, but the drama's artistic intent and achievement are clear, as are the fundamentally decent aspirations of the troubled man at its core. Strong sexual content, including graphic nonmarital sexual activity, some nudity, brutal wrestling scenes, drug abuse, pervasive rough and much crude language, and some uses of profanity
full_review:
"The Wrestler" (Fox Searchlight) is a seamy but powerful character portrait set in a landscape of trailer parks and strip malls. A superb Mickey Rourke plays aging professional grappler Randy "the Ram" Robinson. With his quarter-hour of fame two decades behind him, Randy continues to climb into the ring and torture his body until he's felled by a heart attack.

Isolated from the fans, who provided his only emotional support, Randy initiates a tentative romance with Cassidy (Marisa Tomei), a dancer at a local strip club who's seen better days herself. He also makes fumbling efforts to reconnect with his estranged daughter, Stephanie (Evan Rachel Wood).

Director Darren Aronofsky's study of loneliness is unsparing in its portrayal of the titular sport and of the sadistic impulses of those who flock to it. Cassidy quotes verses from Isaiah that refer to the "suffering servant" whose wounds heal others, and compares Randy's ordeals to the torments endured by Jesus (as she saw them played out in Mel Gibson's "The Passion of the Christ").

But there's no tone of irreverence in her comparison.

Despite a high level of violence (sometimes bloody) -- Randy's opponents use props such as barbed wire and a staple gun -- and despite the frank and demeaning sexuality of Cassidy's environment, this drama's artistic intent and achievement are clear.

So too are the fundamentally decent aspirations of the troubled man at its core. Randy's climactic silent prayer, accompanied by tears and ending in the sign of the cross, sees Rourke convey genuine, if desperate, faith with the same assured heft he brings to every moment of this memorable comeback role.

The film contains strong sexual content, including graphic nonmarital sexual activity, some nudity, brutal wrestling scenes, drug abuse, pervasive rough and much crude language, and some profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Wrestling Ernest Hemingway
synopsis: Slow-moving, sentimental portrait of the unlikely friendship that developes between two lonely old men -- a foul-mouthed, lecherous former sea captain (Richard Harris) and an introverted retired barber from Cuba (Robert Duvall). Directed by Randa Haines, it's an actor's feast with Harris chewing up whatever scenery he can find while Duvall concentrates on being slow and deliberate in everything, including his Hispanic accent, though Sandra Bullock's performance as a friendly waitress is brightly refreshing. Some lengthy discussions of love and sex, flashes of rear nudity and occasional rough language

title: Wristcutters: A Love Story
synopsis: Gritty, downbeat drama set in a purgatorial afterlife for suicides, three of whom -- a young slacker (Patrick Fugit) in search of the girlfriend (Leslie Bibb) for whose sake he killed himself, a young woman (Shannyn Sossamon) who insists she is there by mistake, and a Russian musician (Shea Whigham) whose entire family took their own lives -- become friends on a road trip during which they encounter the leader of a commune (Tom Waits) and a self-proclaimed messiah (Will Arnett). Writer-director Goran Dukic's film is engaging for the first 15 minutes or so, after which, despite its welcome stance against suicide, it becomes random, visually uncomfortable and ultimately stupefying. Brief upper female nudity, much rough and crude language, some crass language, four uses of profanity, graphic wounds, blood and a suicide theme
full_review:
�Wristcutters: A Love Story" (Autonomous) is a gritty, downbeat drama set in a purgatorial afterlife reserved for suicides. Despite an interesting premise -- and a welcome moral stance -- the film soon becomes random and visually uncomfortable. Ultimately, it becomes stupefying.

As payback for his girlfriend, Desiree (Leslie Bibb), dumping him, a young slacker named Zia (Patrick Fugit) slits his wrists. He discovers, however, that the punishment for suicide is confinement in a grungy, tedious underworld not much different from the one he abandoned. He finds he still needs to work at a menial job, and must share his new quarters with an annoying roommate. Learning that Desiree has also killed herself, Zia sets off to find her. He is joined by Eugene (Shea Whigham), a failed Russian rock musician whose entire family took their own lives.

Hitchhiking along the way is Mikal (Shannyn Sossamon), a young woman who insists that, having died of an unintentional overdose, she is there by mistake. She is in search of the "people in charge" who can remedy this error.

Driving at night with damaged headlights, the three new friends almost run over Kneller (Tom Waits), the leader of a nearby commune. While waiting for someone to repair their car, they also encounter a self-proclaimed messiah (Will Arnett) who is preparing to sacrifice himself in order to transport his followers to a better place. (We learn it's possible to take one's life in this world, too, though the next one may be even worse.)

The result of his proposed altruism is left ambiguous. So too is the extent of the intended analogy with Christianity.

Writer-director Goran Dukic's film, based on a novella by Israeli writer Etgar Keret, is engaging for the first 15 minutes or so, and its resolute rejection of suicide is heartening. But the plot meanders, and the relentlessly ugly environment through which the characters travel becomes increasingly off-putting.

This desolate, littered landscape, rendered still harsher by Vanja Cernjul's cinematography, is as punishing for viewers as for Zia and company. By the time the film reaches its admittedly clever final scene, you may be too depressed -- or exhausted -- to care.

The film contains brief upper female nudity, much rough and crude and some crass language, four uses of profanity, graphic wounds, blood and a suicide theme. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.

title: Written on the Wind
synopsis: Soapy sudser about the troubled life and death of a weak-willed Texas oil tycoon (Robert Stack), the strong wife (Lauren Bacall) who tries to reform him and his best friend (Rock Hudson) who secretly loves her while disdaining the love offered him by the oil man's dissolute sister (Dorothy Malone). Director Douglas Sirk's trashy exercise in sentimental melodrama is slickly contrived and mindlessly boring. Much alcohol abuse, some stylized violence and veiled sexual references

title: Wrong Arm of the Law, The
synopsis: Comic caper in which the London underworld (headed by Peter Sellers and Bernard Cribbens) join forces with the police (notably Lionel Jeffries) to nab an Australian gang masquerading as city policemen. Directed by Cliff Owen, the droll proceedings feature a cast of top British comedians who prove a lot funnier than the often cumbersome plot. Stylized violence, sexual innuendo and a comic view of criminal activities

title: Wrong Box, The
synopsis: British black comedy revolves around the bumbling attempts of someone to kill off members of a family in order to obtain a large inheritance. Directed by Bryan Forbes, the script is not very sharp but the acting of John Mills, Ralph Richardson, Michael Caine and Peter Sellers is first rate. The most hilarious performance, a classic of its kind, belongs to Wilfred Lawson as the old family retainer

title: Wrongfully Accused
synopsis: Uneven comedy in which a gullible violinist (Leslie Nielsen) becomes a fugitive from justice while hunting down the terrorists who got him framed for murder. Writer-director Pat Proft uses Nielsen's deadpan delivery to spoof up "The Fugitive" and other movies with goofy sight gags, comical props and silly situations that are fitfully funny. Slapstick violence, sexual situations and minimal profanity

title: Wrong Guys, The
synopsis: Often entertaining story about a wilderness reunion of a pack of onetime Cub Scouts who are threatened by their old neighborhood bullies and an escaped con who wields a mighty range of weaponry. Directed Danny Bilson is aided by a cast of young, stand-up comics (Louie Anderson, Richard Lewis, Richard Belzer, Franklyn Ajay and Tim Thomerson) who have their own particular comic shticks. Mild profanity

title: Wrong Is Right
synopsis: Failed black comedy in which Sean Connery plays a television news commentator who finds himself in the middle of a struggle between an American President (George Grizzard), his political rival (Leslie Nielsen), Arab terrorists and assorted villains to gain possession of two suitcases containing nuclear bombs. Writer-director Richard Brooks tries to satirize amorality in high places but the humor is flat and the story terribly jumbled. Graphic violence

title: Wrong Move, The
synopsis: Tedious, empty German drama in which a moody would-be writer (Rudiger Vogler), who doesn't like people and has no interest in politics, takes a rambling journey through West Germany. Written by Peter Hanke and directed by Wim Wenders, the random incidents and various characters met along the way occasion little interest for the young man and less for the viewer. Mature themes

title: Wrong Turn
synopsis: Schlocky slasher flick about a foursome of oversexed twentysomethings (including Desmond Harrington, Eliza Dushku and Jeremy Sisto) lost in the West Virginia wilderness and hunted by a trio of flesh.hungry, homicidal hillbillies. Buckets of blood flow in this clunky formulaic gorefest directed by Rob Schmidt, who leaves no cliche unturned and succeeds in killing off viewers' interest as quickly as he kills his cardboard cast members. Much graphic violence, recurring rough language, an implied sexual encounter, lewd humor and drug abuse
full_review:
A group of oversexed twentysomething slackers find themselves on the road trip from hell, as they flee a trio of flesh.hungry, homicidal hillbillies in the schlocky gorefest "Wrong Turn" (Fox).

Buckets of blood flow in this formulaic clunker directed by Rob Schmidt, who succeeds in killing off viewers' interest as readily as he kills off his cardboard cast. In truth, it is Schmidt, not the axe.wielding berserkers, who is guilty of the real hack job here.

The plot -- if that is not too dignified a term .. is pure slasher 101. First you need a chiseled lead like Chris Flynn (Desmond Harrington), a young medical student on his way to an important interview in Raleigh. Then an obstacle, a jackknifed truck jamming traffic on the highway fits the bill nicely. This initiates a bad decision: leaving the safety of the highway to take a back.road detour cutting through a stretch of remote West Virginia wilderness. Flynn is soon lost and stops to ask for directions at a gas station where the toothless proprietor offers him the compulsory y'all-be-careful-now warning.

Next the recipe calls for victims since every slasherphile knows it is only etiquette that the star stays alive to see the end credits. This proves easy enough, since Flynn's car coincidentally crashes into a van full of marooned campers .. young, attractive campers at that .. whose tires were blown by barbed.wire snare strung like a trip.cord across the dirt road. They instantly bond and agree to split into the two requisite slasher groups. The first, also known as the "leads," go to fetch help, leaving behind the second less fortunate group, recognized as the "expendables." Meanwhile the cinematic sacrificial lambs do what expendables are paid to do, namely, die horrible deaths at the hands of the film's redneck cretins.

Meanwhile, Flynn and his new best friends, who include Clay (Jeremy Sisto), his fiancee, Carly (Emmanuelle Chriqui), and her conveniently unattached friend, Jesse (Eliza Dushku), stumble across a ramshackle cabin and decide to investigate; all professional slasher thespians seem prone to inexplicably poor judgment. Undeterred by the neo.Hannibal Lecter decor, replete with a refrigerator full of human body parts, they linger long enough for the maniac moonshiners to return home with the grizzly remains of their friends in tow. Through an opening.credit montage of news clippings viewers learn that the psychos du jour are a brood of cannibalistic backwater goobers, grotesquely disfigured by inbreeding.

The remainder of the film is a tedious cat.and.mouse game between the hunters and the hunted, made laughable by tired references to "Deliverance." It is never a question of whether someone will get killed, but only who will get done in first and by what ghoulish means: arrow through the eye, garroted by barbed wire, or the always popular axe to the head?

The film quickly plummets from the repulsive to the utterly ridiculous, setting up a predictable can't.keep.a.good.inbred.maniac.down finale, with several false endings sure to send popcorn flying. The whole messy affair is punctuated by a big boom and an obligatory end.credit capper which leaves the door open for an even bloodier sequel.

True to the genre's two.note repertoire of shock and disgust, the filmmaker seems gleefully content with assaulting audiences with a sickening barrage of gross images and gratuitously graphic violence. To its credit, except for some lewd humor and an implied, sexual encounter, the film is not as sexually exploitive as other past slasher flicks. In fact, the only thing bare is the film's script, as in threadbare.

A warning for parents or any viewer actually considering plunking down cash for this mindless dreck: The only wrong turn you can make is into the theater.

Due to excessive graphic violence, recurring rough language, an implied sexual encounter, lewd humor and drug abuse, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O .. morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R .. restricted.

title: WUSA
synopsis: Confused political melodrama about the right-wing owner (Pat Hingle) of a New Orleans radio station, its liberal disc jockey (Paul Newman), his waitress girl friend (Joanne Woodward) and a manic social worker (Tony Perkins). Director Stuart Rosenberg toys with ill-formed notions of political polarization and reduces them to cliches in a nearly incoherent plot

title: Wuthering Heights
synopsis: Classic romantic melodrama from the Emily Bronte novel about the doomed love between Cathy (Merle Oberon), a Yorkshire doctor's daughter, and Heathcliff (Laurence Olivier), the downtrodden orphan who grows up with her, then runs away to make his fortune only to return to find Cathy wed to another (David Niven) and his riches meaningless without her. Directed by William Wyler, the well-crafted melodrama succeeds in evoking the fierce passion of Heathcliff's tormented yearnings for his lost love which allow him no peace until their spirits are united after death. Physical and mental cruelties, romantic obsessions and a spite marriage

title: Wuthering Heights
synopsis: Good British version of the Emily Bronte romantic classic of tragic love on the moors stars Anna Calder-Marshall as Cathy and Timothy Dalton as Heathcliff. Director Robert Fuest has made a conscious effort to enable young viewers to identify with the doomed pair but in doing so, he has softened the rough edges of the characters and the malevolent nature of their relationship. Good cast and fine creation of mood and period

title: W.W. and the Dixie Dancekings
synopsis: Burt Reynolds plays a professional con man who takes in hand a hapless group of country musicians. Director John(G) . Avildsen's comedy is often hilarious and is marked by fine acting. One scene at a drive-in is adult fare

title: WXIII: Patlabor the Movie 3
synopsis: Third in an animated Japanese movie series in which two police detectives investigating suspicious deaths on the waterfront discover the perpetrator is a bioengineered monster lurking in Tokyo Bay. Director Takayama Fumihiko's animation is well done but the jumbled narrative is a mishmash of sci-fi Japanese monster movie and plodding police procedural. Some fantasy violence, a suicide and several instances of rough language. Subtitles
full_review:
The animated "WXIII: Patlabor The Movie 3" (Pioneer) is a confusing story, although less so for those familiar with the prolific Japanese video, comic book and TV and movie series.

For the uninitiated, it helps to have thick press notes with a glossary that gives name to the ravenous, biological monster-machine, WXIII, that two police detectives eventually discover is the cause of mysterious deaths around the Tokyo waterfront. "Labors" are industrial giant robots operated by humans, while Patlabor refers to the Tokyo Police Department's own patrol robots dealing with Labor-related crimes.

Director Takayama Fumihiko's animation is sometimes exceptional in its use of perspective and the characters' facial expressions can be quite evocative. Particular attention has been paid to the sound effects as well.

Yet the movie becomes a mishmash of sci-fi Japanese monster movie, murky conspiracy thriller and plodding police procedural. It's a long haul to the climax despite the unexpected thread of tragedy developed in the last half-hour.

Called in to investigate a series of deadly accidents around Tokyo Bay, laconic Senior Detective Kusumi (voice of Katsuhiko Watabiki) prefers old-fashioned personal questioning of witnesses while his younger partner, Hata (voice of Hiroaki Hirata), is a whiz on computer tracking of individuals and corporations that may be involved. Suspicion falls on a biomedical laboratory, and Hata is disturbed to find his new girlfriend, Saeko (voice of Atsuko Tanaka), is a genetic research scientist there.

In a frighteningly filmed close encounter, the two cops discover the waterfront killer is a huge biological organism-weapon whose origins trace right back to Saeko's lab.

Dropped into the mix is suspicion of an American military conspiracy, and the sole character to speak English lets loose a totally gratuitous stream of rough language. After Hata learns why Saeko was intimately involved in the secret creation of WXIII, the monster is lured from the depths of Tokyo Bay (shades of Godzilla?) to face down the police department's sturdy Patlabors.

The director deserves credit for developing the human relationships among Hata, his partner and his girlfriend rather than just focusing on robots and the humongous monster machine in their midst. But the blend of romance, action, mystery and sci-fi is jumbled and the pacing listless. In the end the film seems as awkward as its title.

Subtitles.

Because of some fantasy violence, a suicide and several instances of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

title: Wyatt Earp
synopsis: Violent, over-long, revenge-themed Western in which reluctant lawmen Wyatt Earp (Kevin Costner) and two of his brothers (Linden Ashby and Michael Madsen) dole out six-shooter justice in lawless towns of the Old West, until, joined by buddy Doc Holliday (Dennis Quaid), they track down and willfully execute the Clanton-McLaury gang who dared defy them. Though visually impressive, director Lawrence Kasdan's shallow treatment of the characters centers in the depiction of Earp as a remorsely cold-blooded figure who is ultimately elevated to heroically triumphant stature. Much gory violence, justification of murders, discreet bedroom scene, fleeting nude photo and an instance of rough language. O (PG-13) ( 1994 )

title: Wyoming
synopsis: Routine Western directed by Joe Kane in which a pioneer ranching family (William Elliott and Vera Ralston) build a large spread after the Civil War, then get involved in a range war when homesteaders start moving into the area. Frontier violence

title: Wyoming Kid, The
synopsis: ( see: "Cheyenne" )

title: Wyoming Mail
synopsis: Routine Western directed by Reginald LeBorg in which an undercover government agent (Stephen McNally) passes himself off as an escaped convict in order to join a gang of mail train robbers (notably Ed Begley, Howard da Silva, James Arness and Richard Jaeckel), then bring them to justice. Stylized violence

title: Wyoming Outlaw
synopsis: Western programmer directed by George Sherman in which the Three Mesquiteers (John Wayne, Ray Corrigan and Raymond Hatton) help a starving Dust Bowl family by getting the goods on a corrupt political ring selling county jobs and pocketing relief funds. Stylized violence

title: Wyoming Renegades
synopsis: Murky tale of an ex-outlaw (Phil Carey) who tries to go straight but has to shoot it out with Butch Cassidy's Wild Bunch before his reformation is accepted by his neighbors. Directed by Fred F. Sears, it's a tired exercise in overly familiar territory. Stylized violence

title: Wyoming Roundup
synopsis: Western programmer directed by Thomas Carr in which a straight-shooting cowboy (Whip Wilson) stops off in a cattle town, replaces its late sheriff and averts a range war. Frontier violence

title: Wyoming Wildcat
synopsis: Western programmer directed by George Sherman in which a cowboy (Don "Red" Barry) returns from the Spanish-American War to find his rancher father heading an outlaw gang, then is suspected of complicity until his dad painfully squares matters. Frontier violence and a good badman

title: X-15
synopsis: Routine service melodrama directed by Richard D. Donner in which an Air Force pilot (Charles Bronson) breaks a speed record, then joins the program testing the experimental craft of the title which is being developed for manned space flights. Tense moments for test pilots and their families

title: X2: X-Men United
synopsis: Entertaining sci-fi actioner about outcast humans whose mutated genetics endow them with superpowers with which they battle evil counterparts bent on world domination. Directed by Bryan Singer and based on the enormously successful Marvel Comics series, the sequel, while continuing the original's positive message of tolerance, relies too heavily on imaginative special effects and action sequences at the expense of character and narrative development. Recurring comic book-style violence and some crass language
full_review:
Taking up pretty much where "X-Men" left off, director Bryan Singer's highly entertaining sequel "X2: X-Men United" (Fox) continues the ongoing struggle between good and bad mutants, as they vie for their place in the sun, while asking the burning question, "Can't we all just get along?"

For the uninitiated, the X-Men, adapted from the enormously successful Marvel Comics series, are a band of humans whose mutated genetics give them extraordinary powers which they use to battle their evil counterparts. Being mutants, however, makes the X-Men -- and the thousands like them walking anonymously among mere humdrum homo sapiens -- targets of suspicion and derision by the rest of humanity, which cannot accept their differences. This theme is driven home in the opening shot, as a somber voice intoned over an image of Earth observes that tolerance has never been one of mankind's strongest attributes.

Under the tutelage of the wheelchair-bound, cue ball-headed Professor Charles Xavier (Patrick Stewart) -- the "X" in the X-Men and the world's most powerful telepath -- the X-Men have learned to control and direct their respective abilities for the greater good of man- and mutantkind, seeking peaceful coexistence.

Their ranks include: Logan, a.k.a. Wolverine (Hugh Jackman), an indestructible, cigar-chomping, fighting machine with regenerative healing powers, a bad-attitude, and retractable metal claws to boot; Cyclops (James Marsden), a preppy mutant with eyes that shoot laser beams; Storm (Halle Berry), who possesses the power to control the weather; and Jean Grey (Famke Jansen), both telekinetic and telepathic.

At the outset -- in the second-most-outlandish scenario ever to take place in the Oval Office -- Nightcrawler (Alan Cummings), a blue-skinned, fork-tailed mutant who can vanish and dematerialize at will, mops the floor with the small army of Secret Service agents protecting the president. The assassination is foiled, but an ominous message is left behind, "Free Mutants Now."

The attempt on the president's life fans the flames of the ongoing Red Scare-like debate over how to best handle the "mutant problem," a story line carried over from the first film. The attack strengthens the position of anti-mutant hawks, prompting the president to authorize Gen. William Stryker (Brian Cox), an ex-military scientist, and rabidly anti-mutant, to handle the situation as he deems fit. Viewers later learn that Stryker has a personal ax to grind with Xavier, who was unable to "cure" Stryker's own son -- a mutant himself. To Stryker, the only good mutant is a dead mutant; coexistence is not an option.

Armed with presidential marching orders, Stryker, along with a crack unit of commandos, storms Xavier's mutant school, capturing many of the campus' "gifted" students. After making mincemeat out of Stryker's special-ops, Wolverine escapes with several teen mutants.

Meanwhile, Storm and Jean Grey are dispatched by Dr. X to lasso Nightcrawler, the enigmatic assassin from the opening sequence, whom they find holed up in a Boston church. Far from being a cold-blooded killer, Nightcrawler turns out to be a good-hearted and devoutly religious German mutant who suffered indignities as a sideshow attraction because of his freakish looks -- and who has no recollection of the attack on the prez.

As if matters weren't complicated enough, Magneto's (Ian McKellen) alluring but ne'er-do-good stooge, Mystique (Rebecca Romijn-Stamos), a shape-shifting metamorph, springs him from the maximum-security prison in which he was incarcerated at the end of the first film. This plot twist sets the stage for the physical and philosophical battlefield pitting the mutant-hating Stryker against the human-hating Magneto, each hell-bent on the other's annihilation -- with the balance of power in the hands, claws and forked tails of Xavier and his merry X-Men.

As in the original, Singer takes advantage of the motley crew's persona-non-grata status to explore the theme of intolerance and its underlying cause: fear of the "different." The X-Men's commitment to protecting others -- even those who consider them deviants and actively seek their destruction -- echoes Christ's mandate to "love your enemies, and do good to those who persecute you." One of the heroes even pays the ultimate price, illustrating the Christian ideal of laying down one's life for one's friends.

The film is replete with religious imagery and allusions. Nightcrawler prays the rosary throughout the film, talks openly about angels and counsels other characters about the necessity of faith -- even reciting the Our Father during an exceptionally harrowing sequence. His piety -- which easily could have been dispensed with -- comes across as genuine and is treated with a reverence rare in Hollywood fare.

The characters, though by and large true to the source material, are underdeveloped. Even McKellen and Stewart, actors of considerable caliber, come across as caricatures, lacking the depth exhibited in the original film. Magneto, despite all his deliciously evil quips, has been reduced to a cardboard villain lacking only a mustache to twirl. In the first film, viewers benefited from seeing Magneto's childhood in a Nazi death camp, sent there because he was deemed different -- an injustice he will not let happen a second time. In the final assessment, Magneto is not all that different from Xavier; he is just reacting to humanity's lack of humanity -- albeit misguidedly.

Part of the problem lies in the fact that so much of the screen time is dedicated to bravura action sequences rather than character and narrative development. Also, this film, unlike its predecessor, suffers from lack of background, making it difficult for viewers new to the franchise to keep score.

While "X2" treats itself seriously, it still does allow a few mordantly amusing moments. Though the film leans heavily on violent action sequences, they are couched in an unrealistic, comic-book style so as not to be taken seriously -- though, understandably, their consequence-free, video-game nature may leave a bad taste in some parents' mouths.

Due to recurring comic book-style violence and some crass language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: Xala
synopsis: Black African satire, filmed in Senegal, about a prosperous businessman who takes a third wife but, unable to consummate the marriage, is convinced someone has cursed him with a spell of impotence and spends all his money seeking the help of witch doctors. Director Ousmane Sembene's metaphor of impotence is vividly applied to the neo-colonialist values of the African middle class that is the movie's main target

title: Xanadu
synopsis: Olivia Newton-John sings her way through her role as a materialized Greek muse who inspires a middle-aged musician (Gene Kelly) and a young artist (Michael Beck) to become partners in a nightclub. Directed by Robert Greenwald, the movie offers little but special effects, optical devices and a few vulgar dance numbers in what is essentially an illustrated sound-track album

title: The X-Files: I Want to Believe
synopsis: Second big-screen version of the long-running TV series in which two former FBI agents, one now a full-time doctor (Gillian Anderson) and the other a fugitive (David Duchovny), are recruited by a current bureau official (Amanda Peet) to work with a purportedly psychic disgraced priest (Billy Connolly) to solve a kidnapping. Director and co-writer Chris Carter's rather ordinary film touches on issues of faith, forgiveness and medical ethics, but treats them only superficially as it pursues an unlikely, somewhat ghoulish plotline. Action violence, surgical gore including severed limbs and body parts, implied nonmarital relationship, sexual references, occasional crude and crass language and a profanity
full_review:
"The X-Files: I Want to Believe" (Fox), which reaches theaters six years after the last episode of the television series aired, proves a grim investigative drama with an unlikely and somewhat ghoulish plotline.

Ex-FBI agents Dana Scully (Gillian Anderson), and Fox Mulder (David Duchovny), long the bureau's go-to pair for all things paranormal, have left alien-hunting behind, she by choice, he by necessity. Scully is now a full-time doctor, while Mulder is a fugitive from charges trumped up by his superiors to discredit him.

 

When current bureau official Dakota Whitney (Amanda Peet) asks the two to assist in a kidnapping investigation, it's understood that, if he surfaces, the case against Mulder will be dropped. But the request comes at a bad time for Scully.

She's been caring for Christian (Marco Niccoli), a courageous young boy dying of a rare disease, and her concern for him has become as much personal as professional. Despite this, she not only agrees to help, but travels to Mulder's remote hideout and convinces him to do the same.

The hunt is being guided by -- of all people -- a Catholic priest, Father Joseph Crissman (Billy Connolly), both a convicted pedophile and a purported psychic. Appalled by Father Joe's crimes, Scully insists he's a fake, but Mulder is more open-minded, recognizing that the seedy clergyman may have a chance for redemption.

Scully, meanwhile, clashes with another man of the cloth. Respectable but hidebound hospital director Father Ybarra (Adam Godley) is determined to ship her terminal patient off to a hospice, rather than allow Scully to attempt an experimental course of treatment.

 

Director Chris Carter, co-writing with TV collaborator Frank Spotnitz, has created a rather ordinary second film derived from their popular 1993-2002 small-screen series. The central conflict between Duchovny's charismatic idealism and Anderson's show-me cynicism is weakened by a slow, derivative story.

The script raises issues of medical ethics, faith and forgiveness. Is Scully right to insist on every possible remedy for the dying child? Does her persistence in keeping him alive merely demonstrate a lack of faith? Is forgiveness possible even for a Father Joseph? But, these themes are treated only superficially.

 

Inconsistencies abound. For example, how does Scully so easily shuttle back and forth between the operating table and the various crime scenes?

The film contains action violence, surgical gore including severed limbs and body parts, an implied nonmarital relationship, sexual references, occasional crude and crass language and a profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

title: X Files, The
synopsis: Meandering story based on the title TV series in which two stubborn FBI agents (Gillian Anderson and David Duchovny) stumble upon a global conspiracy involving frozen aliens, a mutating virus and the possible colonization of Earth by extraterrestrials. Directed by Rob Bowman, the result is little more than a two-hour series episode with the usual murky visuals of menacing aliens amidst elaborate theories of government and corporate conspiracies which are never resolved. Brief violence, menacing situations, occasional profanity and an instance of rough language

title: Xiu Xiu: The Sent-Down Girl
synopsis: In the waning days of China's Cultural Revolution a young girl (Lu Lu) sent by the government to learn horse herding techniques on the remote western plains alongside a stoic herder (Lopsang) eventually allows local officials to use her sexually in hopes of getting permission to return home. Director Joan Chen's bleakly poetic melodrama captures the desperate loss of innocence and ensuing tragedy as symbolic of so many lives disrupted or destroyed in that era. Subtitles. Brief violence including suicidal behavior, some sexual encounters with nudity and an instance of rough language
